Resident Evil 2 Remake is honestly one of the best survival horror games I have ever played. The Raccoon City police station is absolutely top tier, the atmosphere is intense, you always feel like something is coming and ammo is never enough.

I only have around 17.2 hours played, plus some extra time in offline mode, so the real playtime is probably higher, it just doesn’t always track properly... I also watched a lot of YouTube guides because some puzzles and routes were really confusing for me and I would have been stuck without them.

Mr. X is both the best and the most annoying thing in the game. On one hand it creates insane tension when you hear his footsteps and you don’t know where he is, but sometimes it just gets frustrating when he keeps chasing you while you just want to solve something in peace.

Leon and Claire campaigns are both good, but Claire felt a bit weaker in terms of weapons. Boss fights are mostly fine, but some of them are kind of “meh” and more about surviving than actually being epic.

Overall though, I really love this game. The atmosphere, graphics and remake style all fit perfectly. It can just be a bit too stressful at times and I would probably shorten a few sections.

Overall a very strong experience, just not without frustration and a bit of rage here and there

Everything just feels right is a hard thing to say about a remake without it sounding like faint praise, but it's the most accurate thing I can offer. The movement, the pacing, the way encounters are designed to make you think rather than just react. The gunplay has weight to it, and the resource management keeps you honest in a way that stops feeling punishing and starts feeling like part of the language of the game.

The puzzles are where it surprised me most. They're intuitive and well designed, and they do something a lot of games forget to do, which is actually make you slow down. never felt like filler, always felt like a natural part of the rhythm. The atmosphere is doing serious work throughout. The sound design in particular is kind of insane; every creak and distant noise had me second-guessing myself in ways that felt earned rather than cheap. and the music has that rare quality of knowing exactly when to step back and leave you alone with the silence, which is honestly harder to get right than the dramatic cues.

Leon is easy to root for, and Ada is a perfect foil. The story is simple on paper, but it works because the characters carry it and the tension between them stays interesting without overcomplicating itself. I still have Claire's side to get through, so this isn't a complete picture yet. But even just this half, I had a genuinely great time. It feels modern without losing what made the original special, and honestly, I think it surpasses it. "Modern masterpiece" is a phrase I don't throw around lightly, but it applies here.

Resident Evil 2 Remake does an good job of combining nostalgia with modernized gameplay. It takes the core of the original into mind, while reimagining it in a way that feels fresh and engaging.

Mechanically, the game modernizes the original formula while still retaining a familiar structure. Movement, combat, and exploration feel smoother and more responsive, but the design still reflects the tension and pacing that defined the original.

It makes a good balance between nostalgia and modern gameplay, making it accessible and enjoyable for both longtime fans and newcomers.

My first playthrough, as Claire Redfield, took about 9 hours. A second run is significantly shorter  and while I didn’t finish Leon’s campaign, it doesn’t differ dramatically from the first playthrough, though there are enough small changes to keep things interesting. The game also includes additional challenges to complete, which adds replay value.

Overall, if you can pick it up on sale for around €20, it offers solid value for the experience.

RE2 Remake is a super cool display of a classic turned into something new whilst staying true to itself. A fantastic way to experience this part of Resident Evil series and with that is a great test demo for the new (at the time) RE Engine which is certainly one of the best engines as it is specifically designed for this type of game. Anyways, RE2R was quite fun and addicting to play overall, the more flush and modern control scheme is much more widely applicable to gamers in general but keeps some snappy feeling to the guns and movement throughout the game. The RPD is probably going to be one of the coolest locations in the entire series, especially experiencing it for the first time as Leon really makes it interesting as your first day on the job. The story itself was really cool, much like the first game too, it actually made me end up liking Claire’s campaign a lot more after being able to tie it all together and get the true ending. It really felt like a story concluded rather than just surviving the nightmare, which isn’t just what resident evil is in general of course, but remained the standout moment in the game that emphasized those feelings. Exploration and reading the files was neat adding to my knowledge from the first game and seeing the S.T.A.R.S office is a treat.
The sewers are not my favourite for sure, the game sorta slows done a bit and feels a little crappy at times, certainly a cool area on your first play through but it does get a bit diminishing, G2 specifically feels like a boss of chance at times. The Lab does make up for it though and remains a cool area throughout and overall I think RE2 is tremendously solid and fun to play through all achievements but even more so if you just play once for the story. Hardcore mode brought that RE1 feel to the game that I definitely prefer, it makes it still feel like Resident Evil in the new playstyle which does resemble many other horror games to an extent. The extra gamemodes were really cool to play too, I didnt think that Resident Evil would have something like this so it was cool to see, especially the fourth survivor mode basically felt like a small test of your ability to make quick decision making and avoid large amounts of enemies with the small amount of items you have. Overall I find that this remake is a great follow up to the first entry of the game the gameplay and story remains great overall and whilst I do think this game isn’t as good as the RE1 Remake, it absolutely stands its ground as a fantastic experience.

Final point is the map, it kinda feels like a soulslike game sometimes with how much you're progressing through difficult pathways just to discover a shortcut and find yourself circling back to an earlier point. I've never had the courage to play any horror games in the past, but I've always heard of the main franchises and how popular they are (Resident Evil, Silent Hill and Dead Space) and how beloved they seem to be, so I've been curious about them for some time now.
So I started my journey... with RE3 Remake, which while the game is good I felt it was too short and there was a common criticism from the OG fanbase regarding cut content.
It wasn't until I played RE2 that I realized why some people didn't like RE3 and I can see why.
RE2 is an amazing game that fully immerses you into a zombie apocalypse, taking the role of either Leon Kennedy or Claire Redfield trying to solve the mystery of the event while escaping out of there.
This games biggest strength it's in the atmosphere and sense of dread that fills you with every decision. Your resources are low so you want to save them as long as you can, to achieve that you start to take riskier decisions and some of them will punish you for that, your health gets lower so you use a health item and then you see... something horrible that you've never seen before; a new monster with a grotesque design that makes you panic, "you don't have health items any more" , "what kind of resource do I use against it?", "are there more of them?" this questions start to run in your head and by then you get jumped by a zombie you walked past and now everything falls apart, you'll also need to take the decision of getting rid of some of your inventory to carry the key items right now or return to a box, risking getting injured and save them to then come back for the key item again.
However it's not always bleak, the game rewards you for your sacrifices and for exploring the levels they've made for you. There are secrets and shortcuts that you can unlock that progress the story as well as reward you with upgrades and resources to keep going, not only that there are a few places inside the game that are considered safe heavens. so you can take a break and breath. Although all of that usually comes with a cost, if there's a new weapon rewarded to you, if you get more inventory space it's because something worse is going to appear soon, and whenever you think the game has offered everything to you, the game will have something more to terrorize you with... once you hear the loud footsteps, you'll never want to hear them again.
Overall, an amazing game that pumps your adrenaline, soaks you in fear and will give you an experience that only this type of games can deliver. Not to mention even 7 years later, this game still looks and sounds amazing (it even has widescreen support).

Resident evil 2 (2019) is a survival horror game, the remake of a PS1 game. And while the graphics and shooting parts got a huge upgrade, the puzzles, map layout, inventory management and, sigh, the story remained similar to a PS1 era game – i.e. pretty outdated.

The graphics of the game are good enough. A lot of posters might appear pixelated in the vanilla game, but I used a HD texture mod, which sidestepped the problem for me. What surprised me was how well it handled high framerates. Even at 120 fps, my video card stayed silent.

For the voice acting I chose Japanese. The voice acting was surprisingly bland. Japanese voice acting is stellar most of the times, but not in this game. Side characters, like the wounded cop in the police station does a much better voice acting than Leon or Ada, the protagonists on the path I played through, who just sounded disinterested. It was as if they were on a boring excursion, and not in a situation of life or death peril. As far as I can tell, the game doesn’t have music, just ambient sound effects – good enough for a survival horror game.

I played the game in assisted mode, and mostly with a controller. The controller aiming was heavily assisted, to the point that I could hardly target the arms of zombies on the ground, since it tended to snap to the head instead. Strangely, during certain boss fights it was reluctant to snap to the weak points of the boss. In those instances I had to use mouse aiming, to shoot on the obvious weak points, that the controller snap seemed to just ignore. It is strange, as for normal enemies it was quite happy to snap to the weak points.

Dealing with the zombies is straightforward, but some boss encounters have gimmicky solutions. You can progress only once you figured out the gimmick the game requires, and carry that out. Shooting your full load of ammo can’t solve these situations. Also there will be some cases of a special kind of encounter, where the only solution is to run away from that particular monster. In fact you don’t have to “kill” the zombies either, once they are on the ground you can reasonably expect to run past them (at least in the assisted, i.e. easy mode).

The maps received a color coding – blue rooms are for fully explored, red rooms still contain collectibles, or important interactions I guess. The discovered collectibles also get depicted on the maps. I assume the latter was a quality of life change in the remake. Speaking of quality of life changes, if you select an item that can be combined with something, the compatible items are highlighted in your inventory – but not in the storage boxes (or they were just out of screen in the list). Since your inventory is very small, it can require quite some item shuffle to try items with various items stored in the storage box.

The inventory was quite restrictive, to the point that I didn’t even bother with the Magnum and its ammo, just stashed it into the shared storage. The shared storage is indeed a shared one, magically sharing the items stored even between different locations. Some items are red herrings. In the assisted mode I had no use whatsoever for the toxicity reducing / temporary immunity items, though those might have a role in a normal playthrough. The items that have no further need will receive a little red checkmark in the lower bottom. Those can be safely deleted – or just stashed away in the shared storage, which seemed infinite, for my needs anyway.

The game has a few points in the story where it autosaves. A circle will appear in a corner when this happens. The only user save is at the typewriters. In assisted mode you can freely save at them, other difficulties might require collectibles to enable saving. With the limited storage those ribbons would be annoying, even if stacking to a single slot. Thankfully the mechanics requiring them was missing entirely during my assisted mode playtrough.

The game had a strange bug – it always stayed on the primary monitor detected on the first run. Even in windowed mode it refused to be transferred to my secondary monitor. I had to look up a solution on the internet – there is a workaround, but it is surely a strange bug. A pity, since otherwise the graphics settings are quite detailed and intuitive. The game kept insisting on asking to use HDR, even if I just don’t like that (my OLED monitor would have fake HDR anyway, it certainly lacks the high luminosity). Despite answering repeatedly with no to it, it just offered the question the next time again. Eventually I allowed it, didn’t like that, and switched off. After that it stopped bothering me with it.

Resident evil 2 has quite a few mods, but I used only one, the HD texture pack. For a vanilla game I had to overwrite the 0 byte sized .pak re_chunk_000.pak.patch_003.pak with the 2.8Gb mod file. The poster textures appeared similar to what was suggested on the mod screenshot, so I guess it worked.

The game has 2 story modes, one for Leon and one for Claire. Unfortunately, as I found out both stories share 90% of the story events. Leon has Ada as a side character, while Claire will have someone else. Some characters will be / act different, and perhaps some boss fights will be different. All in all, it will still be the same experience mostly, with supposedly exactly the same puzzles. I completed the Leon storyline, and started the Claire one too, but soon abandoned it in the police station, as it was mostly the same sequence of events as for Leon.

In the end I enjoyed both Resident evil revelations and Resident evil 5 more than this game. Not sure why the high appraise for this particular title. Still, I recommend it, as it is not a horrible game, but those previous two were more enjoyable for me, yet they are less loved by the general public. I already bought Resident evil 3, and eventually I intend to play other titles in the series too.

RE2 offers an amazing mix of horror and action, great world building and a cast of badass characters. All of this, and more, backed by a superb soundtrack.

There is a little learning curve that might deter inexperienced players - not to say that the game is difficult per se, rather that it's quite unique and might take time to get used to for some people. However, it's totally worth to do. Gameplay is smooth and all core mechanics blend together very well. The two main ways of playing RE2 are either to explore every location and gather as many items and lore-bits as possible, or to challenge yourself with finding a perfect route to avoid enemies and gather only story essential items in a 'speedrun-esque' playthrough - both of which are super satisfying and I say that as a person that is not really into speedrunning. Though I recommend doing the former as a 2nd playthrough!

Resident Evil 2 is also an excellent game to 100% in terms of achievements. The amount of content is vast, with 2 separate campaign scenarios per main character as well as quick side stories that explore some of the supporting cast. Even though both scenarios share the same principle and action still takes place in the same locations, they feel unique and fresh and I found myself replaying them one after another without getting bored. This is mostly due to great level design - the game features a lot of backtracking (especially if you mismanage your equipment), but thanks to the layout of the areas, it doesn't feel annoying to do so, I would even say that it's quite enjoyable. Environmental storytelling is brilliant which makes all the areas feel like major events did actually happen prior to our heroes' arrival and we can use our imagination to fill the gaps.

I would also want to put the spotlight on the soundtrack - especially on the tracks for Ghost Survivors gamemode. While I think that the main story has some great tracks, the music for side scenarios really takes the cake - themes for the 4th Survivor, Runaway, No Time to Mourn and Forgotten Soldier modes are extremely good and I find myself listening to them quite often. These side stories greatly enhance the experience and make all the events that take place in Raccoon City feel much more impactful.

Our main characters - Leon and Claire (and Ada/Sherry), are fantastic and both are super fun to play as, and to listen to their thoughts and interactions as we progress further and further down the horror.

If you are interested in the RE universe, but have not really decided whether to play the games, then all I can say is that it's totally worth it. I had a great time perfecting Resident Evil 2 and consider it a must-play for anyone that is into horror/action, or just anyone who is into generally good games.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is Capcom at their best: modernizing a survival horror legend without losing what made the original iconic. Playing through both Leon and Claire’s campaigns really highlights how well the game is structured — it’s essentially two perspectives of the same nightmare, and it never feels repetitive in a bad way.

The standout element, without question, is Mr. X. The way he stalks the Raccoon City Police Department completely changes the pacing of the game. He’s not just a scripted scare — he’s a constant pressure system. You’re never fully relaxed, even in “safe” areas, and that tension is what elevates the whole experience.

Visually, the game is still impressive today. The lighting, grime, and detail in environments like the RPD make everything feel grounded and oppressive in a believable way. Capcom really nailed that “apocalyptic realism” aesthetic.

Sound design deserves just as much credit. The footsteps, distant thuds of Mr. X, and ambient creaks do a lot of heavy lifting in building fear. Sometimes what you don’t see is more stressful than what you do.

Gameplay-wise, it keeps the classic Resident Evil formula — limited resources, backtracking, puzzle-solving — but refines it into something smoother and more modern. It’s accessible, but still punishing enough to keep survival meaningful.

If there’s any critique, it’s that once you understand the structure, replay runs can feel a bit more predictable. But honestly, that’s also part of its charm — it becomes less about fear and more about mastery on repeat playthroughs.

This game gives me the feeling of “revisit like a kid again” vibes every time I decide to play it. That’s usually the sign of something truly well-made: it doesn’t just scare, it stays fun to come back to no matter what.

Overall this is easily one of Capcom’s best remakes and one of the strongest modern survival horror games. It respects the original while standing confidently on its own.

I finally pulled the trigger and played Resident Evil 2 Remake after letting it sit on my backlog for years. Verdict? I’m glad I did — it was a blast!
In preparation for Resident Evil 9, I decided to dive back into the remakes, starting with this one because Leon’s my guy. The game looks fantastic, the graphics hold up beautifully, the puzzles are solid, and that ever-looming danger of your new trench-coat-wearing “friend” Mr. X had me genuinely spooked. Nothing says “welcome to Raccoon City” like a 9-foot tall bald guy in a fancy coat chasing you through the police station like he’s late for a very angry meeting.
That said… I might just be turning into a cranky old man. I adored the original Resident Evil 2 back in the day. It lived rent-free in my top 5 favorite games for years — I played it constantly. The remake is really good, but it didn’t quite recapture that same magic for me.
Leon’s campaign was excellent. Seeing Ada again was a treat, and they did her justice. His playthrough felt fun and satisfying. Claire’s side, on the other hand… not so much. They animated her with these massive Ariel-from-The Little Mermaid eyes and a super rounded, almost childish face. She looked less like a tough college student and sister of a legendary S.T.A.R.S. member, and more like she should be asking for a hug instead of dodging zombies. Leon also got the better weapons, which made his story way more enjoyable to blast through. Sorry Claire — you got the emotional support shotgun while Leon was out here dual-wielding everything.
Still, I’m happy I finally knocked this one out (with a rocket launcher, naturally). It was a solid ride, and now I’m motivated to tackle a few more Resident Evil games on my road to Resident Evil 9.Final score: 8/10. I’ll leave the other two points safely stored in the item box… right next to the green herbs and that one frustrating puzzle I had to look up.

Positives
This is a remake thus it is no surprise that the graphics are indeed great, the voice line are good and the gameplay when it come to framework work great even with my less than ideal pc.

The game development is both linear in the sense that it's pretty hard to get lost progression wise but at the same time open enough for you to come back and freely explore anything that you might have missed in areas like the police station and the sewers.
When it come to mobs and difficulty it's honestly phenomenal. Never once did I feel that a death of mine wasn't well earned whether it was me not playing attention to healing and ammo or just being in a rush and not realizing that a Licker was in the hallway it always boils down to me not playing good enough, this is the case even in the Hardcore mode.
Some other thing that were in my opinion a positive but I can't really can't be bother to talk too much about them are
-The bosses

-The extras and generally the sear amount of stuff that you can do such as the s plus unlocks which I won't be spoiling here.

Negatives
Now come the time of judgement, as a new player I went ahead and did my fair share of investigation to both the original RE2 as will as the series as a whole and for some of the old player what I will be telling next come as no surprise whatsoever.
The second run makes absolutely no sense, like at all.
This was originally a huge part of the original game and here it honestly becomes this rushed abomination that greatly annoys me.
It wasn't so bad before I learned what could have been some much more, with choices from the First Run actually making a significant difference on the second run.
This isn't all, actually the second run is supposed to be taking place at the same time as the first run thus this is the reason that you actually see the characters meet at curtain point in the gamer, armed with this knowledge the more you think about it the worst it gets, with the final boss of the male protagonist dying at some point in the female protagonist POV.

Pros:

Graphics: Brand‑new, pretty, modern RE Engine look... at least there’s that.

Gameplay: Defence mechanics, reworked aiming, and a “new‑gen” RE feel if you like that style.

“New” stuff, if you’re into supplemental fluff.

Cons:

(RE 2 Remake Story spoilers)

[spoiler]Original Story>Remake Story

Claire’s character and rewriting:

In the remake, Claire’s dialogue had to have that forced “empowerment”, her “I can handle myself” line right after Marvin saves her life, unlike Leon, makes her sound like an ungrateful, “empowered” b*tch instead of a strong, grateful survivor.

In the original, she was already capable and rough‑around‑the‑edges, but these Capcom remakes keep adding snappy “feminist” lines that clash with the tone and feel more like a script quota than real character.

Chief Iron's death originally, was just brutally chopped in half... no fake sympathy, no moral‑gray “poor guy,” just a deserved, grotesque end. 

The remake turns his death into a cheap emotional beat for Claire, where she acts weirdly soft and compassionate toward Irons, like he’s some tragic victim, even though he warned her with a shot, threatened to kill her twice, and kidnapped Sherry for ransom. Classic suicidal empathy to feel sorry for the criminals.

Ben’s Tragedy and William’s Tone:

The original’s grounded horror is sacrificed for location-breaking twists. 

In the original, William Birkin was a terrifying, lab-bound monster whose presence felt earned and logical. 

In the remake, he becomes a "sewer-ninja" who teleports across the city to the orphanage with zero explanation... purely to serve Claire’s arc and trigger the Irons cutscene.

This ruins Ben’s quiet, tragic death in the RPD. Instead of a vulnerable moment for Leon and Ada, Ben is unceremoniously killed by Mr. X for cheap spectacle. Meanwhile, the "tragic parasite" beat is stripped from Ben and handed to Irons. 

For a monster of Birkin's size to emerge from the depths of the underground and spawn in an orphanage across town... without noise or signs of entry... shatters the immersion.

Ultimately, the remake bends the narrative logic around Claire’s emotional arc and "tragic victim" tropes, completely abandoning the location-based horror and the weight of Ben's original role.

Ada’s rewritten personality:

Ada’s character gets completely twisted in the remake, especially compared to the original.

Original Ada showed why spies also have their limits, which actually felt human, hearing William’s roar, rushing into the cell, staring at Ben’s mutilated body, touching her chest, and whispering “Oh my God, what was that?” in a soft, shocked way.

Remake Ada turned into a cold, snug, insolent, insufferable b*tch and emotionally detached, constantly throwing out that “I know better than you” energy instead of showing vulnerability like in the original.

In the original, she actually lost hope when injured, and Leon gave her reassurance and bandages, showing both her vulnerability and his gallantry.

The remake deletes that “damsel in distress” Ada scene because modern writers apparently can’t tolerate a woman being carried or helped by a man, so instead they make her snap at him: “Don’t push your luck, rookie,” as if Leon is some opportunistic “soy‑boy” and she’s too strong to ever need help.[/spoiler]

(RE 4 Remake Spoilers)

[spoiler]Later, Capcom adds the “damsel‑carry” back in the RE4 Remake by giving Ashley a bridal‑style carry when Leon rescues her, as if to say, “Okay fans, we heard you... here’s your ‘carry’ moment.”

They literally swapped the cables: remove the organic, emotional Ada‑carry in RE2 Classic, then re‑plug it into Ashley in RE4 Remake as a shallow, aesthetic‑driven fan‑service move. It’s the same “let’s rewire the story for social‑justice optics first, actual tone and continuity later” energy.

The “wall gimmick” pattern like RE4 Remake

The same cheap tricks show up again in RE4 Remake, only with different characters:

The remake keeps using the same lazy trick: shove an enemy through a wall to ruin Leon’s moment and then hand the real spotlight to a female character.

In RE4 Remake, Leon sees two chainsaws sawing through the wall, where 99% of people would backoff away from the blades... instead, he goes towards them to do a pointless risky wall backflip, as if that would make up for his iconic heroic laser‑room wall backflip and acrobatics... which was stripped from him and given to Ada in Separate Ways like a trophy.

It’s the same “wall‑behind‑the‑wall, spectacle‑over‑logic” mindset used in RE 2 Remake where Mr X breaks through the wall to kill Ben, ruining the cutscene in favour of Claire: they don’t care about the original’s pacing or character arcs, they care about modern, cinematic “cool” moments and female‑centric beats.[/spoiler]

(Back to RE 2 Remake Spoilers)

[spoiler]Leon’s rewritten personality neutered:

Leon’s arc and personality are the biggest victims of this rewrite:

He’s turned into a polite, hesitant, emotionally flat agent who never really asserts himself or acts like the tough, no‑nonsense rookie he was in the original.

He never calls out Ada for being reckless and stupid the way he did in the original, which kills both his backbone and the tension between them.

At the same time, every female character gets a “this is my moment” beat tacked on, even when it clashes with logic or tone.

Leon gets pushed into a soft‑spoken, passive “puppy soy‑cuck” role, always reacting to women instead of driving the story.

Tone and new “canon” lore:

The original balanced horror, camp, and character; 

The remake tries to be “darker,” “progressive,” and “cinematic,” but it just feels like a shallow, trophy‑chasing remake trying to look modern instead of respecting the legacy.

Now Capcom is using RE 9 Requiem and other new media to treat this RE2 remake as “official” canon via flashbacks, and it’s clear they’ll soon do the same for the RE4 Remake.

They’re cementing all these forced changes, stupid wall‑setpieces, and woke‑scripted lines as the new Resident Evil lore, which means future projects will keep reshaping Leon’s arc, Claire’s original rough‑around‑the‑edges toughness, Ada’s mysterious and vulnerable yet not‑b*tchy vibe, and the whole series’ tone, instead of preserving the original’s real horror experience and character integrity.

If you only care about graphics and “new” gameplay, testing new mods, this might be fine.

If you're a true fan of the original lore, and care about Leon’s arc, Claire’s original grit, Ada’s mysterious yet human presence, and a real horror experience... not just the freshness of something new that you read once, use, and throw away like a hookup vibe... than this remake will leave you with disillusionment.

As someone who has decided to get into the Resident Evil series following the release of the latest installation to the franchise - Resident Evil Requiem, I can definitely say that RE2 remake is the best starting point.
Now, to take a couple of things into account, I am particularly biased about some of the game aspects in this franchise. This review is aimed and probably will be best received by people who are used to more modern games and modern game engines and are looking into getting into the RE franchise as a whole, but are unsure if they would like it.
Of course, if you do not mind outdated tank controls, fixed camera angles and do want to experience this franchise to it's entirety, I do recommend playing the games that come in release order BEFORE Resident Evil 2. But if you are someone who I mentioned above, I'd strongly advise against it.

''So, should I get into the RE franchise? What's it about? What is RE2 about?''
- Capcom's Resident Evil (Biohazard) is the grandfather of the survival horror game genre. It's a masterclass in puzzle-solving, intense action, inventory tetris, locations and areas that are literally designed by ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Jigsaw himself. The themes and background are about global biological threats, weapons and outbreaks, usually all tied to only a few antagonist characters or one representative of many. 
- The Resident Evil 2 remake's narrative is centered around a viral outbreak in Raccoon City in September 1998. The game shifts and blends the stories and experiences of two different protagonists who are trapped in the city and must work their way out.
In order to get the full story, you must play trough both their tales. It does not fully matter in which order you choose to play them in. (Although it was first believed to be Claire's route first in the original game, the remake changed that. So there is no playable route that aligns with the series established lore. The true canon is a selective combination of events pulled from all four scenarios. The later games cherry pick plot points to validate as canon events.)

With that out of the way, let's talk about the gameplay.
The gameplay aspects of the Resident Evil Franchise consists of survival horror, strict inventory & resource management, exploration and backtracking, intricate puzzle-solving and a combat system revolving around environmental awareness and ....very stubborn demanding precision.
In Resident Evil 2 you are dropped into locked-down areas and environments where you must solve puzzles to escape while managing your resources and avoiding or confronting different monsters. 
Progress is extremely gated and almost always requires backtracking, as you might find a key item and realize it goes into a specific room, while receiving another that you need to open a locker 5 rooms away.
The monsters in this game are extreme bullet sponges and take a lot of firepower to put down and with the very limited ammunition and resources, you are forced to make intense inventory management and strategic decisions, all while remembering the environment and figuring out what goes where.

My personal remarks on this game would have to be the puzzle-solving and pacing. While Leon's route (B especially) is paced pretty well, the same I cannot say for Claire or Leon's A route. And it all comes down to the
backtracking. I am not lying when I tell you that they had Jigsaw design this police station and every other area.
The only way the game tells you where to use many of the key items you obtain is by map indicators, so please pay attention to the environment. While I do enjoy backtracking in other Resident Evil games, the backtracking in RE2 absolutely slaughters the pacing for me. 

To put simply and overall, Resident Evil 2R is an impressive game, remake and starting point for modern gamers used to modern graphics, engines and gameplay who want to get into the Resident Evil franchise.
As someone who's admired Capcom for their less known titles like Ace Attorney and Street fighter, I can't believe I didn't get into this franchise sooner.

After years pass I hardly come back to this game because of how this game feels-- which is rushed because of the missing zapping and horrible connections to the A/B scenarios. Not only that but also nerfing Claire's beauty too and the voice acting does not at all feel bad on purpose ever since the other remakes have the same issues.

Overall, the game is pretty nice.
I played it after RE4, so initially I was expecting a completely different experience, but I got surprised (positively) by the completely different atmosphere. The initial sections of the Police Station are incredible, and later on, after you become more confident, the game still manages to keep the tension high.
The puzzles are not hard, but the feeling of slowly making everything work to reach the end, is really nice.
The Sewers and the Umbrella Laboratory are solid as well, as areas they are not as developed as the Police Station, but the overall level design still keeps the memorable and enjoyable.

Now let's move to the issues, and I have to start from the elephant in the room, Mister X.
I've played a lot of games in which you have to run from an invincible entity, and while this gimmick allows the game to keep the player under pressure, in the case of Mr X this pressure easily transforms into annoyance, killing the whole mood of the latter parts of the Station.
The second big issue, is how the A/B scenario was managed. I did Leon A/Claire B, and while initially the game seemed to give Claire a new area to explore and new puzzles, I quickly realized how underwhelming reality was; they have just recycled most of the map, giving the player some crumbs to keep him entertained till the "true final" part. Needless to say, it didn't work out amazingly, at least for me, and it felt like a lazy way to make the player sink a few more hours into the game.
The last one is not an incredible issue, but it's still quite annoying, and it's the inventory management. It's not terrible, but sometimes it feels like you're gambling on what you're gonna need in the next area.

A nice game, the atmosphere is amazing, and it feels really different from any other game I've played before.
It doesn't have that many issues, but those that are present are way too big to just ignore them.

This was my very first Resident Evil game and I am very glad I chose to start with RE2R. I bought it during a Steam sale as a bundle with RE3R (another great game).

My first playthrough was on the standard difficulty, which I think is the ideal way to start if you're new to Resident Evil but experienced with other 3rd-person action/exploration games and their mechanics. I actually had to restart my first attempt around the 1 hour mark because I soft-locked myself from progressing further by using up all my ammo killing every single zombie I came across. This is one of those games where "just run" is sometimes the answer.

The game was challenging throughout, though not unfairly. Mr. X dogging me for a good portion of the game as Leon kept the pressure up and made me seriously consider my plan every time I stepped out of a safe room.

I've never been great at puzzles, but the ones in this game where there more as minigames than something you'd have to settle in for 20min to solve. They never stumped me for a long time.

The boss fights are fun and don't overstay their welcomes, though I think RE3R has it beat as far as spectacle in that realm.

The inventory system is deliberately limiting, and finding another hip pouch genuinely feels like a small victory; now you don't have to choose between carrying items to defend yourself and carrying the keys you need to progress. It really forces you to make tough choices about what to take with you and what to leave in the safe rooms. You end up finding a balance between carrying weapons and ammo, heals, and key items, but not until very late in the game did I ever feel like I was carrying enough of all three at a given time.

The bonus content is fun too. 3 missions (and a 4th, very hard one if you complete the A- and B-side campaigns for both Leon and Claire) that offer some bite-sized alternate looks at Raccoon City's demise.

Overall, this probably shares the top spot with RE4R as my favorite Resident Evil game so far. I've played this, RE3R, RE4R, RE6, and RE9. The replay value for RE2R is huge with the 4 possible playthrough options, all of them offering something unique to their runs but familiar enough that your mechanical gameplay experience in one will carry over almost 1:1 to another.

I highly recommend RE2R to anyone who is even slightly interested in playing a Resident Evil game. I would pay full price for it if I had to, but Capcom runs so many sales throughout the year that it's best to just wait a few weeks and pick it up at a discount.

[h1]Resident Evil 2 (Remake) Review[/h1]
[h2]~19.5 Hours | Multiple Playthroughs[/h2]

After putting in about 19 and a half hours and playing through both scenarios, I can confidently say this is how I wish these games were always made.

Coming off Resident Evil 0 and Resident Evil 1, this remake was a massive breath of fresh air. I’m mainly playing through these games for the story, and this one actually kept that motivation alive. No awkward fixed camera angles, no clunky controls, no painfully cheesy delivery—just a clean, modern experience that still respects the original.

[h2]What It Does Right[/h2]

[list]
[*]Inventory system is actually fun to manage instead of frustrating
[*]Graphics are insanely good
[*]Voice acting and storytelling are strong across the board
[*]The Tyrant (Mr. X) is genuinely terrifying
[*]Multiple playthrough structure adds real value
[/list]

The Tyrant deserves special mention. Hearing him stomping through the halls, knowing he’s actively hunting you, with the music ramping up when he’s close—it’s easily the most tension I’ve felt so far in these games. You can’t just dump ammo into him either. Best you can do is slow him down and keep moving. That pressure carries the game hard.

The game itself is pretty easy overall. Puzzles are straightforward, sometimes a little too straightforward. I kind of wish they kept more of that old-school puzzle complexity intact because nothing here really stumped me.

[h2]A/B Scenario System[/h2]

One of the coolest things this game does is how it handles replayability.

I recommend starting with Claire. Her story feels more impactful upfront.

After finishing, the game pushes you into a second run from the other character’s perspective (Leon), and it fills in the gaps. You’ll constantly be thinking during your first run:
[i]“Where the hell is the other character right now?”[/i]

Then the second run answers that. Same overall story, but from a different point of view with a different entry path. That’s something more games should do.

[h2]Where It Falls Short[/h2]

[list]
[*]Second run is a little too similar to the first
[*]Some contradictions between A and B scenarios
[*]Characters sometimes feel absent instead of interconnected
[*]Minor story beats feel underexplained (Claire’s brother situation)
[*]Weapon variety could be better
[/list]

The biggest issue is the A/B scenario execution. It’s a great idea, but it doesn’t fully commit. Both characters end up doing a lot of the same things, finding the same items, and even fighting the same bosses in ways that don’t always line up cleanly. It breaks immersion a bit when you notice it.

Also, the B scenario ending feels a bit abrupt, and the Tyrant kind of just shows up without much introduction. Not a dealbreaker, just noticeable.

[h2]Overall[/h2]

Honestly, the fact that I have to sit here and think hard about negatives says everything.

[b]This is easily the best Resident Evil experience I’ve had so far.[/b]

It’s fun, it’s clean, it’s tense when it needs to be, and it respects your time way more than the older titles. Yeah, it could’ve pushed the A/B system further, but what’s here is still really solid.

[b]Verdict: Recommended[/b]

If you’re playing these games for the story or just want a great survival horror experience, this is 100% worth your time.

Resident Evil is at its best when you're put into a big environment with a bunch of puzzles and locked areas that you slowly gain access to, and the RPD might be the best setting in any RE game.

Somehow, the Resident Evil franchise is one I had never touched before this. I had always heard about it, but never felt compelled to try it myself. Thanks to the last Steam sale, I finally picked up the remakes, with Resident Evil 2 as my first entry into the series. And wow, it was impressive.

There is a lot I can, and will, complain about, but it has been a long time since I played a game that I could comfortably sink hours into without wanting to stop. I just kept playing, and time flew by as I explored the RPD.

Performance is fantastic, especially considering how good the game looks. The usual TAA blur is there, but the art direction more than makes up for it. The lighting, textures, and environments all come together really well to create a great atmosphere.

The gameplay is generally strong too. The playable area is relatively small, but you quickly learn your way around, which becomes essential due to the lack of objective markers. The lack of hand-holding in general is something I really appreciate. The puzzles are complex without being frustrating, and they provide a nice break from the constant tension.

Movement is smooth, but I did find myself wishing for a faster sprint, or even a basic dodge. Trying to run past zombies, which you often have to do, can look a bit ridiculous when your character refuses to move faster than a light jog. Enemies are also serious bullet sponges. I understand why that is necessary for the game’s balance, but it can still feel a bit silly. Sometimes enemies survive five or more headshots, especially when playing as Claire, and they do not always stay down even when they fall. I am not sure how you would fix that without changing the game entirely, but it did take some getting used to.

The characters are strong overall. Leon’s voice acting is a bit bland, but the rest of the cast is excellent. Even the side characters feel meaningful and help build the world. I actually preferred my B playthrough, as it skips some of the slower early sections. Claire in particular is great, and using the grenade launcher never really got old.

That said, the overall canon feels a bit strange. Doors that Leon unlocked in my first playthrough were locked again for Claire, and both characters somehow fight the same bosses without ever really crossing paths. Items also seem to exist for both characters at once. It is a bit messy. Still, Claire does feel noticeably different to play as. Her weapons are less powerful, enemies are harder to stagger, and it pushed me to adjust my playstyle, which I appreciated.

I was not a fan of Mr. X. He is not particularly scary or intimidating, especially once you realise there are plenty of rooms he simply cannot enter for no clear reason. He ends up being more annoying than anything else, constantly interrupting exploration and forcing you to retreat to a safe room and wait for him to wander off. That is not especially fun. I am also fairly sure many of his appearances are scripted, as he often seems to show up at the exact moment you complete an objective.

Even with all of these criticisms, I can comfortably say this is one of the best games I have played in the last year. An easy 9 out of 10, and good enough that I have already picked up the rest of the series to play through.

It's a linear story/puzzle game set in a horror universe. Overall this game is not really scary, but it does give you that 'on edge' feeling most of the time. This is mainly achieved by making resources sparse. You do not have enough bullets to consistently kill every zombie, because not all of them stay dead, meaning every encounter is a choice to risk running around them, or killing the zombies and play it safe.

At the time of review I played through the game at a slow pace, clearing pretty much every room until it became blue on the map. This is not needed, but the optional puzzles are simple enough that it makes me want to figure all of them out.

Overall: 8/10
Story: 8/10 - The overall story was okay, the pacing also massively picked up after leaving the police station. Nothing wild going on, but enough to keep me invested and pushing on at all times. I'm a sucker for the zombie scenery, especially during the initial outbreak where people are still learning about them, this is what bumps the story up to an 8/10 for me.
Graphics: 9/10 - The graphics are phenomenal, really helping along the immersion. The bullets creating wounds where you shoot the zombies adds a lot to the experience. The characters outfits evolving as they grow more badass sneakily allows you to grow more attached to them.
Voice acting: 7/10 - The voice acting was good, but not phenomenal. Some emotional scenes were harder to connect to because of the average voice acting (talking about the Leon story line, from what I have seen so far, the voice acress for claire is better)
Music: 7/10 - The music is great for enhancing the tone of the game, but no real memorable soundtracks occur.

Edit after playing the game through with claire:
I was afraid the game would be too similar playing it through with a second character, it was not. Plenty of the puzzles are changed and some are replaced entirely. The weapons are also different enough that the traversal of the map also feels a bit different.

Resident Evil 2 is the kind of game that makes you question every bullet you fire and every door you open. From the moment you step into Raccoon City, it’s just pure tension—limited ammo, tight corridors, and the constant feeling that something *very bad* is about to happen.

The police station is easily one of the best settings in gaming. It’s basically a giant puzzle box filled with zombies, secrets, and poor life choices. Backtracking never feels boring because there’s always that lingering dread of what might be waiting around the corner now.

And then there’s Mr. X…
Nothing quite prepares you for casually solving a puzzle and suddenly hearing **THUD… THUD… THUD** getting closer. The man doesn’t run—he doesn’t need to. He *knows* you’re panicking.

Leon and Claire both bring great moments, but Leon especially delivers that perfect mix of rookie cop energy and accidental action hero:

* “Jesus Christ!”
* “That explains the horrible things I’ve seen.”

Combat is slower and more deliberate than RE4, and that’s what makes it so good. Every shot matters. Every mistake costs you. And somehow, that’s what keeps you coming back.

Only downside? You will absolutely waste ammo shooting zombies that refuse to stay down.

Overall: 10/10. Stressful, atmospheric, and insanely satisfying. Come for the zombies, stay because you’re too scared to quit.

anyways, nitty gritty time; gameplay--how was it?

related statement; i have OCD. this may not seem relevant, but it is very, VERY relevant to me when speaking about any resident evil game, or even just survival horror games in general. when you give me 50 bullets, and my pistol holds 10, i'm not going to keep the 50. i'm going to reload my pistol once, then stow away the other 40 in case i end up needing them later down the line. this kind of schizo behavior has put me in situations that i would otherwise never have ended up in had i been playing any other game. in short; my desire to preserve resources until they're absolutely needed essentially overrides my natural survival instinct and god-given precognition abilities to a point where i'm actively betraying myself by means of kleptomaniacal urges

speaking of this, RE2 has an amazing mechanic that i'd like to take a moment to appreciate; the map. you see, when you find a map, rooms you haven't entered are greyed out, but once you enter a room for the first time, it turns red on your map. HOWEVER! if you search the entire room and find everything in it, the room will turn blue on the map to indicate a "completed search," which (again) means that you've found everything there was to find in that room. safe to say, i did not leave a single section of the game before collecting every possible item. i'll admit that these tendencies are most likely linked to my existential dread of somehow softlocking myself into a position where i have no ammo. to this same extent, RE2 likes to remind you at very frequent points that ammo is a finite resource throughout the game, and if you go all trigger happy, you WILL screw yourself over. even so, that's not to say RE2 is a hard game. ok well, actually, i lied. it is pretty hard, but the autosaves are very generous to ensure you don't get set back too far from a single mistake. not to mention, the hints that you're given across the game as to where to go and what to do are... ok, they're subtle at best, and painfully obvious in reality, so don't worry if you're bad at puzzles, they basically solve themselves if you pay attention to the environment and actually use your eyes to read... y'know, to read text? dialogue? does anyone even remember how to do that? i give up, i'm done with the gameplay section of this review

RIGHT THEN! STORY!

for lack of a better word, the story of RE2 is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ insane, but if you've played any resident evil game before, you'll find this to be such a common occurrence, so much so that you're desensitized to it. something i'd also like to add is that if you want to experience the entire story of the game, you'll have to play it twice. i wasn't sure where to fit this detail in during the gameplay section of this review, so i'll shoehorn it in here. if you play as one character, you play as the other for your next run. note, do not make the same mistake i did and start an entirely different playthrough, just save at the end of your first run and reload it to play as the counterpart character's B/alternate run. despite taking place in almost all the same locations, the 2nd run of this game is vastly different from the first, so if you don't play this game's 2nd run and think you've beaten it, YOU'RE WRONG! go back and play the game twice to experience the actual story

This is one of those games that make me feel stupid for not playing it sooner. Before playing this, I had essentially never played Resident Evil before. Any of them. Because of this game, I'm now obsessed. 

First of all, I just have to praise the attention to detail that this game has. Its absolutely gorgeous of course, but more than that it just feels like it was made with such love and care. I have to say that the Raccoon City Police Department is one of the best examples of level design that I have ever experienced. The game has puzzles aplenty, and good ones too, but the best puzzle is traversing the building. Plotting your route with care, having to take into account your resources and what obstacles you might find is just brilliant. The Metroidvania style of exploration where you gradually unlock new ways to explore is really well done. Finding one item, leads you to another and then suddenly you have a whole new area to explore. It makes for a really engaging core gameplay loop. 

Adding to this experience, is the brilliantly designed Mr X, or 'Tyrant' if we're being technical. From the moment you meet him, he's absolutely terrifying. Every encounter feels like cardio. The genius of his gameplay though is what he's like when he's not right behind you. I spent many minutes of my playthrough stood very still in what I felt like was a safe spot, just listening to his footsteps and trying to figure out if I could safely sneak away. Those footsteps too, are so scary in the simplest way. I recently found myself a little unnerved hearing a family member's footsteps coming up my stairs in real life, all because of this game. Just excellent. Mr X's presence really enhances the traversal puzzle I mentioned earlier too. Moving from one safe room to another takes strategy, and the journey is tense. Do you try to run and risk alerting him? Do you go slow but risk him getting closer? Do you shoot zombies in the way? Its brilliant. 

There's so much replayability to this game too. First of all, doing a second run as the other character feels so different. Weapons are completely different, enemies are different, story moments are different. Its basically like a whole new game. Then there are a bunch of fun bonus missions. I decided to save these for another time, but honestly it they really add to the value of the game. 

I could go on and on but just to mention a few other positives. Firstly, the character design and voice acting is so on point. Its really well done, and after playing the next game I definitely noticed that extra level of polish here. The sound design is incredible too. It sort of has to be, but it is. It takes the atmosphere to the next level, and it really adds to the experience. 

I'm excited to play more of the Resident Evil series after this, and while I know there are plenty of great games to come, I just know that from now on this game is going to be especially memorable to me.

Resident Evil 2 is a perfect remake that shows how horror games should be remade.

The atmosphere of Raccoon City is truly flawless. Every corridor is narrow, every sound is unsettling, and you constantly play with the feeling of "what's going to happen next?". The game takes the classic zombie theme to new heights with modern graphics and excellent sound design.

The separate stories of Leon and Claire significantly increase the desire to replay the game. While the puzzles retain the old Resident Evil spirit, the balance between action and suspense is perfectly adjusted.

Mr. X is a separate story… His entrance into the room completely changes the game's tempo and truly creates a sense of panic. The feeling that he's constantly following you is one of the game's strongest aspects.

As minor criticisms, inventory management can sometimes be challenging, and some sections are overly tense, so they might not appeal to everyone. But that's the point of the game anyway.

In short:

One of the best in its genre in terms of horror, atmosphere, and remake quality.

[h1] I have a love-hate relationship with this game. [/h1]

The game is amazing. Atmosphere of this game is amazing. On the first playthrough I was ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ my pants when I was slowly walking through the RPD station. The first few hours were great and I have nothing wrong to say about. The way how zombies behave, the way how they react to shots. What else can I say? Very enjoyable experience.

What really bothers me? There are several mechanics that are not communicated to the player in any way. This breaks the flow and unfortunately can break the fun. On my first playthrough I found out about one mechanic only after half of the game and I found out about this through my friend (without him I would still wonder why the enemies are bullet sponges). 

Another thing, which makes the game annoying? Well... first one is Mr. X. In general, Mr. X is not that bad. That's a very good concept after all. Stalker enemy can really increase the pressure on the gameplay and increase your adrenaline levels (which is great!). What really irritate me that there's too much of him. Not in a way that he appears frequently throughout the game. The issue is when there is a first fragment with him, he's too much of a burden. It's really annoying that you have really no time and space to breathe. It's not the issue of him. It's the issue of intensity. After some time it just becomes more of a hassle rather than fun. 

And most probably the worst thing in the game. [b]Birkin[/b]. Oh my god, I hate his fragments with all my heart. The fights are badly designed and not fun at all! I can't even count how many times I was close to throwing my keyboard out the window. They screwed this up so bad in one fragment that the only thing you have to do is to stand for a minute or two in one place and wait until the boss will allow you to go to the next fight section (on a side note, this fight is the worst of all. Frustrating as ♥♥♥♥). In general Birkin was the reason why I almost gave up on the game. 

In the end, I dealt with him and I finished the game. I'm planning to finish it once again as the game gives you the "2nd run" playthrough. So yeah... just to summarise it all. The game is great except for some parts that can make you want to bang your head against the wall. I recommend to play this game if you're willing to go through those fragments... or you're a masochist who actually enjoys pain... especially the mental kind... like I do.

Overall, the combat is very satisfying. Blowing off zombies heads with shotguns is pretty damn fun. I do think the handgun was a bit underpowered though, especially compared to the one-shot power of the shotgun - The handgun could take 15 bullets to kill a zombie or 1 depending on your crit luck and that felt pretty weird, especially with the limited ammo in the game. Boss gimmicks are generally decent but nothing amazing - just okay.

[h1] Horror [/h1]
The horror in this game is super good, especially because of [spoiler] Tyrant . When Tyrant first shows up, he's terrifying. Doesn't speak, just speed walks at you like a menace. His theme, loud footsteps, design all come together so nicely and I don't think any other creature in any game has scared me as much as he did. [/spoiler] I generally think zombies in games aren't super scary and they aren't that scary in this game either and feel cartoonish as all zombie games do in my opinion. [spoiler] Lickers [/spoiler] however are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ terrifying whether its the first or last time you see them. They have such amazing design in my opinion and are just so damn scary. The [spoiler] G-virus swamp creatures are scary at first but kind of lose their charm once you're forced to face 4 of them and realise you can just use R+B herbs to basically nullify them completely. The G-Virus overall isn't that scary imo, even the Final Birkin form was more just cool than scary. Lickers were much better in this regard. [/spoiler]. The horror is especially great at the start of the game where you have VERY limited ammo, only a handgun and you haven't fought zombies before and dont know what to do. Later in the game, zombies are no longer scary but you encounter more variants. Overall, very good scarries.

[h1] Sound [/h1]
In terms of sound design, I think the music itself is okay. Particularly [spoiler] Tyrant/Mr X's [/spoiler] theme combined with the loud footsteps really drove in the terror. Annoyingly, sometimes intense music would play even after everything was over/you had escaped the combat but that's not too bad just gives you paranoia. SFX was amazing though.

[h1] Performance [/h1]
for a pretty weak pc, I expected needing to use the lowest settings for graphics but I didn't. This game looks gorgeous and barely ever lagged. Did crash one time tho.

[h1] Other [/h1]
Puzzles are fun, never too confusing. Whenever you found secrets, you truly did feel very rewarded for it which is nice. Story is good. This was my first ever Resident Evil title and I gotta say I really enjoyed myself with this. The game utilizes every space and every item in a way that I rarely see, the characters are mostly great and enjoyable, the gunplay feels simple and yet satisfying, and I think this is a benchmark for how remakes should be approached in the industry. 

The map design is really the highlight here; every single room in every level is utilized and every single item in those rooms are utilized so it trains the player to engage with their surroundings and get to feel it rather than just run through it. The puzzles are simple enough but have real meaning, the pacing for the most part is right on, and I ended up having a great time with this. 

My biggest criticisms comes from difficulty adjustment and Mr X. I started the game on Normal mode but realized after about an hour in that the game doesn't give you nearly enough ammo to deal with basic encounters, forcing you to run past enemies to save your ammo for the bigger enemies later down the line. This sucks because it forces you to rush through levels rather than taking your time like I mentioned above. I ended up getting stuck in a part of the police station with a zombie, two lickers, and Mr. X all on me at the same time with only one pistol mag and I just gave up and restarted the game on Assisted mode. Playing the game on Assisted basically just means that the game gives you the proper amount of ammo to take your time and search through each level without having to rush past half the enemies you come across. It also helps with aim assist, but I could take or leave that. 

The biggest reason why I can't see myself doing another run is Mr X. I hate unkillable enemies in games because after about the second or third time you encounter them, it stops being scary and just becomes annoying - and this is no different. Mr X is pretty scary the first and second time you bump into him, but after that, he just becomes a nuisance. If he catches you off-guard in an enclosed space, you basically just have to backtrack to a safe room or expend a grenade to get him off your tail so you can get back to what you were doing. After his introduction, it made me want to rush through the rest of the level just so I could be rid of him, which again, takes away from the experience of playing through the game.

Really loved the gameplay, the story, and the overall design, but can't really see myself revisting this one for the reasons listed.

My introduction to the Resident Evil series and I was not disappointed. Easily one of the best story-driven games I’ve played so far. As someone who had never really played horror games before, I was worried it might be too scary, and yeah—at first? [i]TERRIFYING.[/i] But once you get into it, you realize the fear is part of what makes it so addicting. I’m so glad I stuck it out, because [b]WOW.[/b] I could not stop playing.

[h1]COMBAT + FIGHTS:[/h1]

The combat isn’t overly complex, but that’s what makes it work. Limited ammo and resource management create constant tension, forcing you to think before every encounter. As someone who isn’t a hardcore gamer, I was proud to get through all the boss fights without needing tutorials.

You also quickly learn that you are NOT that powerful —sometimes a single shot to stun and RUN is the smarter move. By the end of the game I was out here planning fights, conserving ammo, and feeling like a genius. 

Near the endgame, I LOVED the flamethrower and how it could permanently deal with the ivy zombies. Grenades and flashbangs added some really fun options for crowd control and dealing with tougher enemies (lickers). Once I got more comfortable, I found myself getting creative with how I used my resources, which made for some pretty fun moments!


[h2]ATMOSPHERE & DESIGN:[/h2]

The sound design and soundtrack are [b]UNMATCHED.[/b] This game reaches a different level of horror realism with the unique sounds each enemy makes, The ambient noise and eerie music had me on edge even when I knew I wasn’t in immediate danger. You can really feel the care that went into this aspect—it shines through in every moment.

For my first Resident Evil game, I was blown away by the enemy design. [spoiler]William Birkin’s[/spoiler] evolution throughout the game is incredible—each form gets more grotesque, but still retains traces of humanity. [spoiler]G3[/spoiler] might be one of the coolest (and grossest) bosses I’ve ever seen.

The greenhouse section nearly took me out (WHY is the music like [i]that[/i]), but the ivy zombies were easily my favorite. Their unique movement made them feel completely different from anything else in the game. The way they regenerate unless you burn them??? Horrifying. [b]OBSESSED.[/b] 


[h3]STORY:[/h3]

The story is what drew me in, and it [b]ABSOLUTELY[/b] delivered. The game does a phenomenal job of worldbuilding, showing the collapse of Raccoon City during a biohazard outbreak. The opening cutscene set the tone perfectly, and from there I was hooked.

The graphics are great, the voice acting is top notch, and the cutscenes are incredibly well done. Outside of cutscenes, Leon was a fun protagonist and lowkey funny. Man is out here cracking one-liners while I'm panicking.

I also loved the files and notes scattered throughout the game. Reading through messages from Umbrella scientists added some seriously disturbing lore around the G-virus and made the world feel so much deeper. Exploring and uncovering those details became one of my favorite parts of the experience.

[b]IN CONCLUSION,[/b]

If you’re on the fence about playing Resident Evil 2—just do it. I’ve never played anything quite like it, and it completely pulled me into the survival horror genre.

I [i]NEVER[/i] replay games. [b]Ever.[/b] 

BUT I’m already excited to jump into a second run and go for all the achievements. That alone says everything.

Resident Evil 2 Remake hooked me immediately. Coming from RE3, this was only my second game in the series, and Leon’s campaign absolutely delivered — atmosphere, pacing, tension, everything. It’s an easy 10/10.

Claire’s route, though, feels like a big disappointment. Capcom introduces two protagonists but doesn’t commit to giving them truly different experiences. Most of Claire’s path is a repeat of Leon’s: same areas, same events, even the same boss encounters. The moment I realized the garage sequence plays out almost identically, it killed my excitement.

Playing Claire started to feel like homework — something I had to push through just to unlock the final ending. And that’s the problem: the game forces you to replay nearly the same campaign to see the full story, without offering enough new content to justify it.

If Claire had a more distinct route, this could’ve been a 10/10 masterpiece. But because of the repetitive structure, I’d drop it to a 6/10 overall. The gameplay and graphics are flawless, but the Claire`s campaign design really let me down after how strong Leon’s story was.

Again, don’t get me wrong — if you find this game on sale, grab it. It’s absolutely worth playing. The reason I give it a 6/10 is because the internet hypes it as “the best Resident Evil ever,” “a masterpiece,” and so on. And yes, Leon’s story is a masterpiece. But that’s only half the game. I don’t understand how people can praise it so much when the second half is basically the same thing all over again just to reach the ending.
Moral of the story: never trust internet praise and reviews blindly.

Game’s really good. Glad to be able to get into the RE series via remakes like these. 

Great, graphics, modern intuitive controls, good gun feel also. It also runs really well on older hardware with most things to max (i7 3rd gen + 1080 GTX) Really well put together overall. Which is why the not so good things aren’t that huge an issue (with the exception of the DLC practices) but they do slightly stain an otherwise excellent game.

One note:
I misunderstood what the extra modes are all about. I thought they’d be mini stories of other survivors in the city but they’re rather challenge modes with a really tiny bit of story. The focus is on the gunplay and running through the level rather than the story. Something to keep in mind if you had a similar misunderstanding of what they are. For me at least they’re annoying. Especially the 4th survivor one. But for those that like the challenge (sometimes downright absurd challenge) it might be fun.


A couple of things that are not so good
- The timing of appearance of a certain monster in the 2nd run. It is way too soon. It just creates frustration rather than terror and slows the game down to a crawl since you can’t run without alerting it. What should have been a quicker run is now way slowed down because of this. It really feels like a way to pad out the game.

-2nd run starting pistol. You keep getting upgrades constantly for a pistol (Matilda) for which you can’t find ammo as it’s just not available in this run. I don’t understand why. Your gun will never have ammo but the upgrades keep coming in. And the other pistol (M19) for which ammo exists and you get it quite quickly once you start gets 0 upgrades in the whole run.


Some small things that could be better:

- Claire’s 1st run has items and areas that are not accessible nor will ever be. Instead of marking those spots where those unobtainable items would be used as points of interest it should have clearly not been labeled as such. It’s just weird to not have that info (or rather, to have that info about the items) when there is info for everything else that can be acquired. It makes it seem like you can get those items when you can’t.

- The police storage area code machine. The keyboard caps requirement doesn’t have enough basis in reality since you could get the signal pressed/sent without a keyboard cap, especially with the parts left intact in the game. If you’ve ever had to fix a keyboard it would be quite glaring of an issue.

- Facial animations are sometimes weird. Especially Claire’s. They don’t feel natural. There were also some desync issues in a couple of cutscenes.
- There are some technical issues with the games that are a bit annoying. I’ve seen it in other RE games also. For some reason some functions keys (not all) like the volume ones on my laptop get disabled in this game. And some other OS wide keys like print screen also are disabled. Considering the consistency of it across games it’s probably something up with the games/engine.
- SMG’s feel like pea shooters. Unfortunately, an entire class of weaponry that just is risky to use. High ammo usage, low damage, reload often. Little advantage to using them.
- If you kill a zombie from further away, they sometimes drop frames in animations. Very obvious frame drops on them alone.


One big totally unnecessary stain on the game: 

The DLC approach though is simply put, greedy and very disrespectful. Not only to they have day 1 cosmetics (most but not all of the costumes) which are split up for sale in the greediest way possible (one by one), they’re also selling what amounts to cheat codes (when these used to be free things that devs let be for players to have fun and in this case is a simple config switch) and reselling old assets that would just be a simple settings switch from a menu (old soundtrack + effects). Greed + greed + greed. 
Avoid the DLC. Only way to stop these things happening is to not buy them.

I just want to say I was never a fan of horror games simply because I am a scaredy cat, and the first horror zombie game I played was Left 4 Dead, but I played it with friends so it was less scary. Playing Resident Evil 2 was a whole different experience for me. It was far from the usual co-op and cozy games I go for, so you can imagine how stressed I was during my playthrough, how I hated the noise those zombies make, and my bad aim. You might ask then, why did you play it? Honestly, it was because of Ada Wong, but that is a story for another time. 

Before I go on too deep, I want to say I am no professional horror game critic and this is from my personal experience as a beginner to this franchise. For someone like me who never tried shooting games before, I have to say this game was pretty straightforward even for newbies like me. I had difficulties switching weapons and throwing the flash bangs and bombs, but that is not the game's fault. It was a skill issue on my part, but I got the hang of it pretty much as I kept going. The graphics and sound were beautiful and haunting. There were sections I almost chickened out and wanted to rage quit because the atmosphere was too much for me. You could say it was pretty effective. Mr. X even started appearing in my dreams for three consecutive nights. 

And those puzzles? They made me think. It cleared my pandemic brain fog. I also just want to say I hate those lickers too. I hate those ugly creatures with a passion. I think my only gripe is the inventory. As a beginner, I was saving all my herbs and sprays because I knew the big fights were coming, and as someone who loves being able to carry a good number of things, the limited bag space annoyed me. 

As for the writing, I truly enjoyed it, especially the emotional beats. During my playthrough, I tried really hard to avoid Officer Marvin Branagh. I kept my distance so I would not trigger the event where he turns. I guess I was just trying to preserve whatever humanity he had left while he was sitting in that chair. But when I had to go back to the main lobby of the RPD, I had to pass him and the event triggered. I did kill him though, instead of letting him wander around. Yeah, I have attachment issues, sue me. 

During the confrontation between Ada and Leon, I was screaming, because as a bookworm I have read scenes like this a hundred times. I knew Ada Wong lied to Leon when they met at the parking garage. She lied about being part of the FBI, but what do you expect? She is a mercenary. She did not know Leon, and she was not expecting a civilian to still be around. During the entire playthrough, Ada kept telling Leon to leave Raccoon City because it was too dangerous. But Leon stayed. Why? Because he wants to help people. He wants to find and stop whoever was responsible for everything that happened in Raccoon City. He wanted to save anyone he could save.

Did Ada use Leon's self-sacrificing heroism to her advantage? Definitely. I will not deny it. Was Leon gullible and stupid for trusting Ada? No. Absolutely not. Raccoon City was collapsing and he was a rookie cop on his first day. He had no framework for what was happening, and then suddenly a confident and competent woman shows up with an FBI badge and a believable cover story. With that context, trusting Ada was not stupid. It was the only rational response for him. Was the kiss from Ada manipulative? Oh hell yes. Leon was getting suspicious so she had to shut him up, but you can tell he still had questions. So during their confrontation, despite pointing guns at each other, neither one pulled the trigger.  And I was screaming. I want more. I know this is a horror game but I would love to learn more about Ada Wong. 

Fast forward to my fight with G3 William, who loves throwing things around like a kid having a tantrum. I hated it so much I was cursing the entire time. I tried four times before I finally got him. During my final battle with Mr. X I handled it better and only died twice, with Gethsemane by Sleep Token playing in the background.

Anyway, I feel like I talked too much. I just want to say I truly enjoyed it. This game scared me senseless but I am glad I kept playing, and once I get my PC upgraded I will get into the rest of the franchise. My game crashed five times but I persisted. I still have not done Claire's story yet, which I will get to later. This is just my initial review (to be continued...)

A great reimagining of the original game, but by no means a replacement to it. 

The updated controls, graphics and seamless traversal between areas without loading times are all very appreciated. However, Capcom's engine, despite being great for indoor environments, shows its limitations in outdoor areas. This results in an inability to replicate properly the beginning of the original RE2 in the city, which was longer and more epic. The original instilled an urgent need to get to the police station due to its (false) promise of shelter, and the contrast between the city and the RPD sections really helped with that. Meanwhile, in the remake, getting to RPD feels like a mere formality. 

There are other things that haven't been replicated properly, such as the depth of Scenarios A and B. 

However, the remake is still a great game on its own merits. Great graphics. Great optimization. Great controls. Great gameplay. Insanely high replay value. The deeper and more complex way in which the new Mr. X works and the new gore system also allow the game to distinguish itself from the original, despite what was lost. 

Truly a must have.
