The starting point for modern Resident Evil games.
I replayed it seven years after release and this is what I think:

- Gameplay still holds up, walking simulator with light puzzles
- Light shooting that is tied up into the resource managment
- Graphics are pretty much as good as they get, with good performance
- Dialogue and voice acting still corny but fun
- 8h of playtime for 100% 1st playthrough, 12h for the true ending
- No tank controls

A bit more in depth: 
Gameplay loop:
You walk around collecting consumable items like ammo and healing items, while looking for key items, sometimes literal keys. While doing so you decide whether you kill the zombies, or ignore them along the way, with the latter being able to bite you in the back later on once they swarm you, and the former may leave you ammoless for future fights. It's a blend of resource and inventory managment, with some strategy, horror and light shooting gameplay. A surprisingly good formula, the puzzles are easy enough for anyone to solve, with some clearly being way more fun like the chess one and others being simply a means to an end to get you to walk from point A to point B like the medallion ones.

The horror?
As for horror... I always played at midnight for the spookyness factor but this is definitely more game than horror and I think that's a good thing. But then again I don't get spooked easily from pixels on a screen.
The way they implemented horror wasn't by adding cheap jumpscares, instead they slowly lure you into dangerous situations and then put you under pressure to deal with it, so the worse you are under pressure, the more spooked you will get, but on the other hand if you're really good at gaming you'll probably have a laugh at some situations due to how forgiving the game actually is when you're not affected by the "pressure".

2nd Playthrough:
Once you finish the game you can replay it from the perspective of Claire and see a few different vantage points, but overall it's very similar to the first playthrough. 
I'd still recommend doing it for the true ending, especially since you can finish it quite fast IF you still remember all of the paths. Though it definitely felt like an afterthought.

Overall, the game aged like wine and will be playable even in 2030.

This is my second Resident Evil game after RE9: Requiem. I think this is one of the best games of our generation with very little flaws. 

Let's talk about the flaws, The A/B scenario system doesn't make any sense to me, the game makes it seem like both of the scenarios cannot happen in same timeline but also it does happen in the same timeline? And as a consequence the ending, the one you get after beating scenario A as one character and scenario B as another character, felt weird to me. I have heard this was a lot better in the original. And that's pretty much it for the flaws.

Everything else is perfect. I loved the RPD, the level design is just fantastic, interconnected rooms with puzzles and metroidvania elements. I am impressed with how the game mixes it up with the constant sense of dread that Mr. X brings to the table. Mr X, he is easily the best part about the game. it was a nice change of pace from RE9, having someone on my ass constantly, trying to think on your toes. You are forced to learn the layout of the station so as to avoid rooms of Lickers while Mr. X is on your tail. The gameplay loop is fun & engaging.

The weapon ammo system is also kind of ingenious, like how same gun can utilize different caliber bullets, it helps them feel fresh throughout your playthroughs. 

The story is good, characters are Charismatic, though I do think it would have been better if Leon, Claire and Sherry had lot more character interactions throughout the game.

The sound design, I think this might be one of the best examples of a game that incorporates sound design into its gameplay loop in a clever manner. I mean, with Mr. X constantly roaming the RPD you are forced to pay attention to each and every noise and ambient sound. And his theme song is soo... *chef's kiss*. Those moments when you can hear his soundtrack but you can't figure out where he is coming from were one of the most tensed I have ever been.

For anyone on the fence, if you are reading this review, I hope I have put your doubts to rest. Go for it.

Resident Evil 2 Remake: The Gold Standard of Horror

The Atmosphere: 10/10
Capcom’s use of the RE Engine is masterful. The way light flickers in the RPD hallways and the "wet" sound effects of zombies shuffling in the dark create a constant sense of dread. The audio design—especially hearing Mr. X’s heavy boots stomping a floor above you—remains some of the scariest use of sound in any modern game.

The Gameplay: 9/10
Combat: It’s satisfying but punishing. Zombies aren't just "mobs"; they are obstacles that take a surprising amount of lead to stay down. The dismemberment system (shooting off limbs to slow them down) is still a highlight.

Puzzles: As you’ve seen with the Chess Plugs and the Greenhouse Cartridge, the puzzles are classic "90s logic" but updated to feel tactile and rewarding.

Inventory Management: This is the real "boss" of the game. Choosing between a herb, a key item, or an extra stack of ammo is where the real strategy happens.

The "X" Factor (Mr. X)
The Tyrant is the game's greatest achievement. He turns a puzzle-heavy exploration game into a terrifying game of cat-and-mouse. He forces you to think on your feet and often ruins your "perfect" plan, which keeps the game from feeling too predictable.

The Cons (The Small Flaws)
The "B" Scenarios: While playing the 2nd Run is essential for the true ending, many fans feel the stories overlap a bit too much (you'll solve the same puzzles and fight almost the same bosses), which can feel slightly repetitive.

Movement: Some find the movement a bit slow/weightless, especially when you're trying to dodge a fast-moving boss.

Verdict
Score: 9.5/10

Resident Evil 2 is a rare example of a remake that surpasses the original in almost every way. It respects the source material while making it feel like a cutting-edge horror experience. Whether you're a veteran or a newcomer, it is arguably the best survival horror game of the last decade.

It's not a bad game to start the franchise with if you're new to it.

My only real issue with this game is each character's stories not overlapping properly and being largely similar. For example, you will often experience the exact same boss fights in the same areas regardless of who you play as, thus contradicting major events. Stuff like that really breaks the immersion of the story for me. I don't know why they couldn't have tried to make two unique stories that overlap in a consistent manner.

Other than that, the gameplay is solid, albeit primitive compared to more recent Resident Evil titles. Though it makes sense considering this is a remake of a really old release. There's also some extra game modes to play that mainly exist for players who are desperate for more RE2 content, as they're incredibly short, frustrating, and non-canon.

Overall, after sinking nearly 60 hours into this game to unlock all the achievements, (pretty frustrating btw), I would say it's worth a shot. Not the strongest entry in the franchise, but its streamlined gameplay makes up for the story's inconsistencies.

To me, one of the trickiest balances in game design is the split between fun and challenge. It’s fun to be challenged, but too much challenge can take a serious bite out of the fun. Stressful games like Dark Souls and Darkest Dungeon have found success by finding players that will accept them on their own unique terms, but that’s not the only way to bridge the gap. I know that now because of Resident Evil 2, a game that can be stressful, terrifying, and incredibly fun all at once. Honestly I didn’t even think it was possible to thread that needle so effectively, but RE2 has the magic touch that can push you to your breaking point and make you love every second of it.

Something has gone terribly, terribly wrong in Raccoon City. A vicious, unstoppable virus has torn through the town, leaving the residents either dead or undying. It’s a hell of a first day on the force for rookie cop Leon Kennedy, and a huge complication in Claire Redfield’s search for her brother. Their paths will cross several times in this chaos, as they search for both answers and escape. The architects of this disaster are still at large, and may be closer than either Leon or Claire would think, along with some shadowy figures who have their own interests here. But there’s a ruined city, a litany of puzzling obstacles, and countless zombies between them and their goal, and it’s going to take a little luck and whole lot of nerve to get through.

For the record, I never played the original Resident Evil 2, and I haven’t even played any versions of the first game in the series. I’m jumping into this with only some basic cultural literacy here, but RE2 is perfectly accommodating to newcomers. The plot is perfectly simple at its core: zombies everywhere, don’t die. I understand there are plenty of references to other games in the details, but you definitely don’t need to study the wiki to shoot zombies and collect crests. Indeed, the quality of the game’s cutscenes and voice acting is so incredibly high that you’ll surely find yourself engrossed in the unfolding drama regardless of your background knowledge. The presentation here does a ton to sell the experience of a zombie apocalypse, and heighten the tension or humanize situations when most effective.

The real star of the show, though, is the action. Following an intense intro that wastes exactly no time getting to the good stuff, you’ll find yourself in a vast police station that’s all kinds of falling apart. Zombies are breaking in the windows, crawling out of the vents, and laying in wait for their next meal. As Leon or Claire, you’ve only got what you can find to deal with them, which includes a very modest amount of weapons, ammunition, tools, and medicine. Your foes in this game are not the mindless hordes you might be accustomed to from other zombie titles, as they can take bullet after bullet to the head without breaking their pace. Every single undead is an existential threat to you, with the potential to take your health from full to zero if you don’t take them seriously. You won’t have the resources to dispatch every single zombie, either, so resource management is absolutely essential.

And this all goes double for the more exotic foes you’ll face as you descend deeper into the mystery! The result is a game that’s intensely stressful every single time you depart from a safe room, that can terrify you simply by putting a common enemy in an uncommon place and letting them do what they do. Your life is threatened here in a way most horror games don’t have the gumption to do, because not only can the monsters kill you, defeating the monsters badly can kill you. Being far away from your save point or stash of items with no bullets or no healing items is terrifying unlike any jump scare or chase scene, and perfectly evokes the true horror of zombie media, that of inevitable doom. That feeling only gets stronger when the game reveals more of its threats, one of which has become iconic in how it heralds your absolute downfall.

Resident Evil 2 is chock full of sequences you don’t want to go through. You’ll see things through windows or on your map that you know will be total nightmares to endure. And you’ll do it, because the experience is so rewarding. The tight over-the-shoulder controls and aiming give you all the tools you need to use every bullet effectively and dodge past foes. Weapon impacts are forceful and meaty, and if you’re any sort of gorehound then you’ll be treated to some top-tier blood and viscera as the bullets fly. Seriously, I have never seen a game that modeled bullet impacts on heads so effectively, and if it wasn’t happening to zombies I’m not sure I could handle it. But getting that lucky shot that splits an undead’s head like a watermelon is all the more gratifying for the absurd explosion of flesh that announces it.

Really, this is about as close as you can get to the perfect zombie survival game, if slow zombies, thin resources, and risky combat are what you’re looking for. And there’s tons of it to experience, too, with the A and B routes for both characters that reveal different bits of the story and offer different challenges. There are additional modes as well, and a fair number of unexpected twists and secrets along the way, all of which should last you dozens of hours to uncover. The only reason you’d punch out early from this one is to give yourself a breather, though, because it’s an absolute master class in turning stress and challenge into pure fun.

The original Resident Evil 2 is one of my favorite games of all time. One of those games where you have a defining memory of the first time you played it, and the impression it left upon you. My neighbor got it for Christmas back when it first came out, and we spent the entire day playing it. I don't think we touched another present. It may not seem this way now, but the graphical advancement from Resident Evil 2 to Resident Evil 1 was incredible. Combine this with the massive increase in scope (the outbreak from the first game has spread to an entire city), it was everything you could possibly ask for in a sequel. 

REMake 2 is everything you could possibly ask for in a Remake. Is it better than the original? Hard for me to say, as the nostalgia for the first game overrides any sense of objectivity. But it's damn good, and the perfect way to experience the game for newer gamers who just can't get past the original's fixed cameras and tank controls. 

Trying to be as unbiased as possible, there are things I like about both. The original has a bit more character, but the REmake is more polished. The Police Station is better in the original, but I enjoyed the Sewers more in the Remake. Some of the guns, like the Spark Shot, have been improved, while others don't have quite as much kick as they did in the original. Lickers are more engaging to fight than in the first game, but the standard zombies are a little too bullet-spongey -- focused headshots in particular feel like they should do a lot more damage. 

As someone who has enjoyed Resident Evil since the very first game in the series, I wish fans would just stop all the fussin' and the fightin' about which one is best, when they're both excellent. Given the state of most game remakes, I'm just happy Capcom produced something that's actually worth a comparison with the original game, and not outsourced slop.

I finally picked up the Resident Evil 2 & 3 Remake bundle during the last Steam Sale, and man, I’m glad I did. This was my first ever Resident Evil game, and after hearing for years that this is the gold standard for survival horror, I can safely say it actually lived up to the hype.

The vibe in the Raccoon City Police Department is just top-notch. It’s eerie as hell; I found myself bracing for a jumpscare every time I had to open a door or turn a corner. Unlike other zombie games, the enemies here are tanky. They do not go down fast, and since resources are so limited, the survival aspect is no joke. The game is basically one giant, intertwined puzzle. You’re constantly backtracking, managing a tiny inventory, and hunting for key items or weapon upgrades.

Then there’s Mr. X (fck this man bruh). Having that guy stomping around the hallways while you’re trying to solve puzzles is nerve-wracking.

Playing through the different perspectives of Leon and Claire was a cool touch, and the side segments with Sherry and Ada (mommy, sorry) kept the gameplay feeling fresh. It gives you a much better picture of what actually went down. Although the continuity of the A and B scenario for both is kinda iffy but ehh, its fine. 

I’ve heard the original  version actually has some deeper story mechanics and "Zapping System?" features that didn't make it into the remake, so I’ll probably check the OG out eventually. But for now, I’m hooked. I’m definitely planning to 100% some of the other games in the series next.

With this and RE7 being the start of being more "serious" with more melodramatic moments mixed into the campy B-movie zombie movie tones that the series started with, I adored playing this through as a more faithful Horror game than most of the 2010's era RE games, with massive positives being;
The atmosphere is second to none, everywhere feels oppressively hostile, overrun, and dark - and despite how dark everything feels and looks, there wasn't much problems with brightness or lighting of the game its self.
Story is in my opinion minorly improved over the original, as much as there's things I dearly miss (The helicopter crash scene in the original immediately comes to mind) I think this tells the story in a slightly more believably interesting way.
Gameplay is naturally improved between giving more control to movement, inventory management gets less stressful as the game progresses as a natural reward for fully exploring, weapons mostly feel well tuned so there isn't much problems (there is one problem I'll get to in a minute), and it strikes a good balance between resource management and giving you an abundance of what you want to clear big sequences easier.


Things I feel mixed on/or are outright negatives are pretty straightforward;
I think the characterization of characters here is worse not better or comparably similar, a great example I think is Chief Irons, without going heavy into any spoilers [spoiler]in the original they didn't immediately make him villainous, even if you could tell he's bad they went for more visual storytelling in the unnerving atmosphere around him and his dialogues just not sounding "right". Whereas here all subtlety is lost for.. Bad man is extremely evil, you hate this guy because he's bad, duh.[/spoiler]. Another example I think fits is Annette but that's harder to explain without heavy spoilers, and there's more examples even between how Leon and Claire talk/are portrayed that I think misses the mark.
OST is either interchangeable or worse than the original; some of the tracks changed for modern "eerie" sounds over the standout classic moments like the main saferoom jingle - unless you pay a nickel and dime's worth more money for DLC wink wink nudge nudge - or are just cleaner versions of the original soundtrack which I do appreciate, but I don't want to give brownie points for doing the bare minimum expectation.
The map layout/locations are worse than the original I feel; namely there's rearranged and changed order of events, and the sewers here is painfully boring, it wasn't much better in the OG but it respected that fact that it's supposed to just be a 'transition' zone so the length of it there only lasted maybe 10 minutes on a blind playthrough, whereas here it drags on painfully without speedrunning level offhand knowledge.

As I'm sure you can tell from other reviews, this is a great game. But I'd like to bring attention to something I've never seen anyone else mention: Is Mr. X annoying to deal with? Are you expected to play the entire game with him randomly blocking progress and forcing you to drop what you're doing to run?

And the answer is: no! For starters, despite the impression you might have gotten, he only shows up for the first time when you get your final objective before you leave the police station. He's NOT in the game from the beginning. There are points later in the game where he’s reintroduced, but as before, it’s normally when you’re about to leave the level. There’s also certain rooms he’ll never enter, so you don’t have to worry about getting soft-locked in a save room.

Secondly, there's no unfair BS involving his AI. He genuinely roams around, manually checking rooms, even when he’s off-screen. The game does not tell him where you are. The only way he can zero in on you (aside from if he, y’know, sees you) is via noise. If you’re stomping around when he’s close by (i.e you can hear him stomping around) then he’ll start heading your way.

He can hear gunshots from far away though, which causes him to make a beeline to where he heard them coming from. But so long as you don’t linger after killing an enemy, he should arrive to an empty room, with you having hauled ass long ago. 

Seriously, it’s all very fair. There’s even a YouTube video of a guy following him around for ages, and he only gets caught when Mr. X does a 180 at a dead-end. I only had one occasion where he got between me and where I wanted to go. But since there’s multiple paths though the station, I was able to take the long way around. 

Basically, if you’re interested in playing this game, but the idea of being constantly pursued by an unkillable enemy sounds tedious, don’t worry!

Playing Resident Evil 2 as my first entry into the franchise completely exceeded my expectations and set an incredibly high standard for the rest of series. The graphic design and level of detail are exceptional, but what impressed me most was the overall design of the game. The map layout is brilliantly constructed. Every time I returned to play, I felt a genuine sense of excitement and curiosity about where the game would take me next or what new area I would uncover. The transitions between locations felt seamless, and nothing ever felt repetitive.

The story was surprisingly engaging for a single-player game, which i feel is something that can be difficult for games to achieve these days. The characters are well-developed and each has a distinct personality, making them feel relatable and memorable.

What stood out the most, however, was the tension and atmosphere. Even after multiple sessions, the game still managed to catch me off guard with its scares. Encounters with Mr. X were intense, his presence in the police station created a constant sense of dread. No other game has made me feel that level of anxiety while being chased, even hearing his footsteps get closer and closer to me made me feel nervous. I found myself carefully planning when and how to leave safe rooms just to avoid him, which added a unique layer of strategy and fear that felt both thrilling and immersive.

The balance of the gameplay is also remarkable. Regardless of how much ammunition you have or how powerful your weapons become later in the game, you’re never truly safe. Even a basic enemy can still pose a serious threat, which forces you to stay alert at all times. The game has a way of humbling the player, and that’s part of what makes it so effective and a survival horror game. I found that the puzzles were well designed and straight forward, They never disrupted the flow of the game, which kept the overall experience engaging without forcing me to step away and look at a youtube video for a solution.

That said, where the game really shines and stands out for me personally is its approach to progression without relying on hand-holding. It doesn't overwhelm you with hints or doesn't guide you in the "right" way. Instead it relies on you to interact with the world as the player. You're urged to explore every inch of the map, take note of locked doors, blocked paths or unfamiliar items, and gradually piece together what you need to do or where you need to go to move forward. As you continue playing you naturally begin to connect the dots, discovering items, examining them, remembering locations that were inaccessible. It creates this really satisfying loop of exploration and discovery. I enjoyed how the game makes you form your own mental checklist without ever telling you to do so. You start keeping track of objectives in your head, which makes progression feel earned rather than guided. Because of this, every unlocked door or a new weapon or item unlocked feels rewarding. You’re not just following instructions you’re actively thinking, remembering, and problem-solving. It adds a layer of immersion that makes you feel genuinely involved in the experience, and it’s a big part of why the game remains so engaging from start to finish.

Overall, I would consider this game a masterpiece and is defiantly at the moment my favorite Resident evil game. I’m genuinely glad I experienced it, and it has given me a strong craving to explore the rest of the franchise.

This if my first time playing Resident Evil 2, so here are my thoughts. (And as a note, I've only played Leon's story on Hardcore difficulty.)
I am currently going through the games (mostly) in order, so going from Resident Evil 1 to 2 was a significant change of pace, but a welcomed one. I don't mind the changed camera angles and graphics as the core gameplay of resource management, facing your fears, and running away are still the same. Something I didn't touch on in my RE1 review were the characters. I likely didn't do that because they weren't anything to touch on as the first game doesn't have nearly as many character interactions as 2 does. That being said, I see why Leon is so popular, and I've only seen his first appearance so far. To get it out of the way, he's hot. And he's genuinely just a kind guy. He puts others above himself and will prioritize their safety over his. I will note however, he doesn't seem to have any flaws? He's the epitome of "boy scout" and isn't selfish, he doesn't have any ulterior motives... Nothing bad from what I can think of, and I can't tell if that's a good thing. But, because of that, I won't count it as bad.

This isn't as well put together as my first review so let me go into everything neatly. First off, I enjoyed the gameplay. Seeing RPD in it's proper setting (not through Dead by Daylight like I've seen it) was cool. The set pieces are so beautifully done, and I always looked forward to seeing more. Second, the characters were mostly well done. Claire kind of felt out of place if that makes sense? I know she has her own story going on, but it would've been cooler to really see their stories "feel" like they intertwine. But, overall the characters were nice. Marvin was cool, Ada was awesome, and everyone in-between were nice additions. Third, the Tyrant/Mr. X, (I will be calling him the Tyrant) was AWESOME. I loved hearing his footsteps get closer, and hearing doors open just a room over. Pushing around a corner only to see him looming over you was scary. His consistent appearances, though spread out, made for an unnerving time each appearance. And lastly, the story. If I'm being honest, it was alright. It felt really similar to the first game to the point where I'm pretty sure they just copied and pasted the script for RE1's ending, added the Tyrant in there, and called it a night. The ending felt lazy. But, everything else was honestly fine. Seeing Raccoon City properly after being mentioned in RE1 was cool. Seeing references to Jill and Chris is always welcomed, and the progression felt natural.

Overall, I recommend this game to anyone wanting to get into Resident Evil, as this is a good starting point if you don't want to/can't play Resident Evil 1.

The Sherry orphanage section is a standout though—being completely defenseless was a nice switch-up and actually made things tense. On the flip side, Ada’s section felt undercooked. It’s short and mostly just “hack this, move on.”

The RPD is easily the best area in the game—packed with detail, great layout, and fun to explore.

The sewers? Not so much. They’re annoying, especially the chess puzzle. That said, once you’ve done both runs, you can breeze through it. Same goes for the lab—it’s a bit underwhelming, not many puzzles, mostly bosses. Fine for a first run, but nothing amazing on replay.

I know I’m sounding harsh, but overall this is still an amazing game and I’m glad it exists.

My only real issue is the A/B scenarios. I just wish they were more different and actually lined up properly. They don’t really make sense happening at the same time—for example, certain boss events completely contradict each other depending on the run. If you’re expected to play both for the “true” ending, they should feel more connected.

Even just more interaction between Leon and Claire—like radio communication—would’ve made a big difference.

Return to form for Survival Horror: All that matters is getting through it. The game is designed so that you always feel like you're just barely getting through it, so be sure to lock in every bit of good progress through saving.  Brick by brick, you will conquer this game.

Don't get freaked out about not having enough resources; The game gives you what you need, and you can't get "softlocked".  Don't get discouraged by dying; The game has an auto-difficulty that increases when you're performing well, and it will rank you down on deaths and make the game a little easier the next try, particularly on Standard difficulty. Use every circular path you can to kite and evade attackers -- refer to "pillar dancing" as a term.  There are many circumstances where you might have to get past something to find the gear you need to handle them the next time you come through (if you think it's a good use of resources).

No matter how impossible the game feels, remember that there's plenty of speedruns on YouTube showing sub-hour runs, and they can teach you a lot of tricks if you watch them after feeling stuck.

While this remake is well done, It sacrifices everything that made the original Resident Evil 2 memorable

-Loss of the deep A/B scenario system
The remake simplifies the original structure: campaigns no longer feel like two complementary perspectives of the same events, but rather variations. The idea of a shared narrative where one character’s actions affect the other is mostly gone.

-Weaker coherence between scenarios
In the original, playthroughs were interconnected (items taken, different routes, cross-events). In the remake, this connection feels much looser, reducing the sense of a living world.

-Less systemic storytelling
The original let the story emerge through design (exploration, decisions, consequences). Here, the narrative feels more guided and less integrated into gameplay systems.

-Weaker sense of character coexistence
In the original, Leon and Claire felt like they truly shared the same timeline and space. In the remake, that illusion is diminished.

Closing thought
The remake improves mechanics and presentation, but sacrifices part of the original’s narrative ambition—especially its unique, system-driven approach to multiple perspectives.

This is straight-up the best damn remake ever made, full stop. Capcom didn’t just polish up the 1998 classic... they rebuilt the whole nightmare from the ground up with the RE Engine and turned Raccoon City into a living, breathing hellscape that still gives me chills months later.
The second you step into the Raccoon City Police Department, you feel it: that thick, oppressive dread. Flashlight beams cutting through blood-slicked hallways, distant moans echoing off the walls, and the constant paranoia that something’s about to crash through a window or locker. The zombies? Disgusting masterpieces. You can blow limbs clean off, watch them stagger and adapt, and every headshot feels earned because ammo is tighter than your ex’s grip on drama. Inventory management is pure brain-tetris — you’ll be dropping herbs and mags just to squeeze in one more key item, and it never stops being tense.
And then there’s Mr. X. That towering, trench-coated terminator doesn’t just chase you — he owns the building. His heavy footsteps booming closer while you’re trying to solve a puzzle? Peak horror. I’ve screamed, laughed nervously, and full-on sprinted through doors like my life depended on it (because it did). The sound design is god-tier: rain hammering the windows, creaking floors, zero hand-holding music during exploration. It’s just you, your nerves, and the dark.
Leon and Claire’s campaigns both slap hard with their own flavor — different weapons, unique encounters, and enough fresh twists to make the second run feel like a whole new descent into madness. The story’s dark, the characters are likable without being cheesy, and the gore? Chef’s kiss — grotesque but never over-the-top. Puzzles are clever, exploration rewards you constantly, and the bonus modes (looking at you, Tofu) are the cherry on this undead sundae.
If you’re new to Resident Evil or a die-hard from the tank-control days, this is the one. It respects the original’s soul while delivering modern controls, jaw-dropping visuals, and tension that’ll have you checking shadows in real life. Capcom set the bar so high with this that every other remake should be taking notes.
Overwhelmingly Recommended. Buy it, survive it, love it.
Played both campaigns + extras — 40+ hours and still going back for more.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is everything a modern reimagining of a classic survival horror should be. The story is gripping, balancing tense atmosphere with emotional character arcs that keep you invested from start to finish. Whether you’re following Leon’s rookie determination or Claire’s fierce resolve, the narrative feels both faithful to the original and fresh enough to stand on its own.

The remake of Resident Evil 2 is the first of the modern RE remakes that I have played, and I really enjoyed it! I have not played the original Resident Evil 2, but from what I've heard from those who have, this game does a pretty good job at doing it justice.

You get to choose between two characters, Leon S. Kennedy or Claire Redfield. Each character has two different scenarios to play through, an A scenario and a B scenario. The RE storyline picks and chooses moments from each for the canon, so there is no story correct way of playing them. I played through Leon A then Claire B first before doing the rest. The main difference between Leon and Claire playthroughs are the weapons available to each. Leon starts with a basic handgun (Matilda), but is able to unlock a pump action shotgun (W-870), a pistol with magnum rounds (Lightning Hawk), and a flamethrower. Claire starts with a basic 5-round revolver (SLS-60) but is able to unlock a grenade launcher (GM 79), a submachine gun (MQ11), a laser sighted pistol (JMB Hp3), and something called a spark shot which is like a very powerful taser that fries things rather then stunning them. Most of the weapons have upgrades you can find as well. I played with controller and found the aiming and shooting mechanics very satisfying. The RNG health of the enemies combined with the variety of weapons and ammo makes for a lot of variety in how you play through.

Apart from the main zombies and other enemies, the main threat to both characters for a significant part of each story is Mr. X, this game's stalker type enemy. I know he is considered a devisive character, but I think he adds a lot to the game, especially in terms of replayability. The first time I played through this game, I knew nothing about it and what to expect as I went through it. It took me a long time to get through it. But as you replay it, you start to memorize the rooms and it loses a bit of what makes its scary.  Mr. X is what keeps replays of the same scenario fresh. If you're looking to speed run the game like I did, or are even just following a guide, Mr. X will force you to improvise. He makes plans fall apart, and that is scary. You thought you were going to calmly walk past the licker? Nope, he found you, you're running! The way his AI works is really cool, with him actually looking for you going from room to room.

Overall, I think this is a great game with tons of replayability. I really enjoyed gettiing the 100% for this one!

September 30th, 1998, the day a rookie cop died. Or at least… that’s how the story goes.

Resident Evil 2 Remake was my second trip into the RE universe, right after Resident Evil 4 Remake, and it felt like stepping off a high-octane horror roller coaster into something slower, tighter, and far more suffocating. This game goes back to basics. Ammo is scarce, spaces are claustrophobic, and the stillness of the police station creates a tense atmosphere that scared the absolute c### out of me a few times.

What stood out most to me is the atmosphere. The tone is dark, and at times lonely. Raccoon City didn't slowly fall, it crashed. Through Leon Kennedy’s first day on the job, you witness the results of that collapse firsthand: streets in ruin, barricaded corridors, and bodies slumped just convincingly enough to make you think they're dead.

What really sells the game for me is how grounded everything feels. The gunplay is weighty, but never empowering. You’re forced to be deliberate, to think before you act. Every bullet has value. Every new inventory slot feels valuable. The game reinforces that classic survival horror mindset of prioritizing, adapting, and making do with what you have.

And then there’s the station! The R.P.D. is an amazing setting! It feels like a carefully designed puzzle box, looping back on itself in ways that reward attention and memory. While later areas like the sewers don’t quite reach the same heights, they don’t really need to, since the encounters and story help carry the momentum forward.

Even without nostalgia for the original, there’s a clear sense of intent behind everything. I can feel the care in how the game is built, in how it balances fear, exploration, and restraint. It knows exactly what it wants to be, and it commits.

Overall: 8.5 Residents / 10 Evils.

Resident Evil 2 is a story of two individuals stumbling across an experiment gone wrong and surviving the fallout. It blends survival (combat + resource management) with exploration (progressively unlocking a large map) in a tense environment where zombies might be around every corner. This is a shooter, but ammo is scarce and you are only a few hits away from death at all times. Sneaking past or disabling an enemy is sometimes easier than destroying it. There are two paths the story takes (A + B). Completing A with one character unlocks B with the other, which is a remix of the first path but with different start, end, item placement, and a few different events. Depending on thoroughness, each route takes roughly 10-12 hours.

I enjoyed this game primarily for its metroidvania-style exploration, but the combat was fun and engaging too. The visuals and audio are excellent, and the UI is polished and useful. There are plenty of weapons to manage, each suited for different situations. Puzzles and minigames range from straightforward to elaborate. Enemies are varied and can be quite challenging. Inventory management is crucial -- you will never have enough room to carry everything you want all at once.

It's not a perfect game, and it does have a few flaws. In the mid-game, there is a special enemy that is effectively invincible, and once it appears, your tense exploration becomes a game of cat-and-mouse, trying to avoid alerting it to your presence while bouncing from safe room to safe room. This stealth element keeps the police station from getting dull, but also really constrains when and how you can explore. [spoiler]Also later on it appears as a boss and your weapons can suddenly do damage, contradicting what you learned about it earlier.[/spoiler] The lategame map is a lot more linear and has less interesting routing. [spoiler]There is a character death fakeout that is never really explained well.[/spoiler] One of the most common items has very situational utility -- I only used one once across the two route playthroughs.

The flaws exist, but the game is strong and very enjoyable (especially if you love metroidvanias or survival shooters). Getting it on sale is best, but if you enjoy the Resident Evil series it's worthwhile at full price.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is a survival horror game about two characters named Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield, who are trying to escape Raccoon City from a zombie apocalypse. After going through the first one, I was genuinely excited for this one because I heard how much critical praise it got. I’m only playing the remake, not the original, since I don’t own that version and am sticking to this one. So I wouldn’t know of any similarities or differences between those two versions, so I’m just sticking to the remake as its own thing and how I feel about it, which I think is kind of a fantastic game. 

The look of this game is incredible. The cutscenes look just as clean as the gameplay itself. I did feel the survival horror from the first game is still in this one as well, that you have to make sure to keep the ammo you have and just ignore the zombies unless they’re in your way and you don’t have time to dodge and weave. The main location of the game, which is the Raccoon City Police Station, is a fantastic set-piece that I much prefer over the mansion in the first one. Different areas got me really curious about where I’m going, so I find it memorable that it’s gonna be stuck in my brain cells. When playing as either Leon or Claire, there are some differences in gameplay mechanics that I find interesting, whether it be different weapons, rooms, or Mr. X going after you more.

Speaking of Mr. X, he is one freaky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who comes in the most inconvenient times, which got me scared and tense up, so I keep pausing the game whenever he shows up. I generally felt like he was going after Claire more so than Leon, which was so bizarre to me. It reminded me of the time I played Resident Evil 7 when the father went after me, which gave me a flashback to that game that I also really enjoyed.

The story is relatively engaging, which got me into the lore of the Resident Evil games, and I now know more about Leon, Claire, and Ada. I’m generally surprised to hear that Claire isn’t in much of the main series of Resident Evil unless you play the side games or watch the movies, because I really like her character in this one, who’s just trying to survive and really cares about Sherry. As for Ada, this is the type of femme fatale that actually worked for me, which has been rarely showcased in films I’ve seen. She’s mysterious, where you don’t know much about her throughout the game until it’s close to the end, but there was something about her that got me really wanting to know about her, and she didn’t come across as annoying or anything like that.

If there’s anything I have issues with, it’s the sewers set-piece. I honestly find that area annoying due to the worst creatures I have to deal with that got on my nerves, who really wanted to waste a lot of ammo. So when going back to it a second time as Claire after going through it as Leon, I was not looking forward to going to the sewers again. The spark shot weapon helped a lot through it, but I wanted to move on to the next location. Other than that, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a ton of fun with fun bosses to deal with and side games that were a nice bonus to the main game, which got me looking forward to more of these types of games.

Review of Resident Evil 2 Remake

After giving it several tries, I have to admit that the game is just not for me. It offers a scary atmosphere that hits all the right places. It is everything from the lighting, the background music, and the atmospheric sounds that make you always feel on edge when you walk around a corner. The game is very simple in many ways, and with its dynamic way of adjusting the difficulty, I never felt completely lost. The story is short, but through several unlockable bonuses, two playable characters who each have two unique stories you can play, and bonus game modes, you can still get many hours of entertainment out of it. The point where I lost interest in the game was the pace.

The game can be played quickly, but being careful, saving your resources, and using what you have in the best way makes the game much easier. This does not mean that you can just run forward and kill all the zombies, but the way the game is structured keeps pushing you in a different direction. This becomes especially clear when there is an enemy early in the game that will constantly chase you, where you cannot do anything but run from it, since the enemy cannot be killed.

I can clearly see why the game is so loved, as it does not compromise on what the essence of the game is, which unfortunately will make some people fall in love with it, while I on the other hand felt that the mechanics were more of a problem than a benefit.

I will give the game 7 out of 10.

[h1][b]Resident Evil 2 (Remake 2019)[/b][/h1]
[b]Genre:[/b] Survival Horror
[b]Perspective:[/b] 3rd Person
[b]My Rating:[/b]⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

[i]The second entry of the Resident Evil canon series. In this Remake we play as either Leon S Kennedy (a rookie cop on his first day) or Claire Redfield (a college student on the search for her brother Chris Redfield, one of the main characters from the first game). As they arrive in Racoon City, they find the city in shambles as a mysterious virus has taken over and turned every resident into bloodthirsty zombies.[/i]

[h3][b]The Positives[/b][/h3]
[list][*]I am judging this game by itself as the original RE2 was sadly banned in my country and I had no means back then to get to play it so I can’t compare the two (yet). I enjoyed the story-pacing of this Remake - the bits of papers and notes scattered around helped to flesh out what happened to the city after the events of Resident Evil 1.
[*]I loved the old classic games so this Remake hit the mark for me to give it modern controls with the modern graphics and free camera but it still kept the puzzles and searching through the different areas to progress just like the RE1 HD Remaster did. Find a key there to go back to here, find a filmroll you need to develop to find an item way over there… I loved it.
[*]Leon and Claire are amazing characters and I loved their portrayal in this - they both were both caring, scared at times but still badasses fighting through to survive. Nicely fleshed out characters. …and can we talk about how innocent and naive Leon still was here? It’s so interesting to see him be a rookie, still believing he can save everyone and the world before we get to know him in RE4 being way more serious but still a goofball as he is here in RE2. Claire is also amazing, I like that she isn’t a damsel as Chris taught her well. You might argue how she can stay so calm in a literal zombie doomsday apocalypse as a college girl and just strut through it (which I agree with) but who knows, maybe Chris did tell her something after the mansion incident. I love how they fleshed out the relationship with her and Sherry - it’s heartwarming how she is so feral in bringing Sherry back to safety!
[*]Mister X might be predictable as he isn’t as freeroaming as you might think but he CAN pop up at the weirdest moments! (The game sometimes has a muffled sound bug where you can’t hear the bloke even with headphones so imagine turning around and getting smacked across the universe out of nowhere!). However, it is fun to be in a safe room or having progressed and suddenly you hear the heavy footstomps coming towards you from afar… Once you know how he works it’s still fun as you can find plenty of ways to tease him :)
[*]This game has a good amount of content and replayability value (at least to me)! I hear from others the scenarios weren’t done as well as in the original (which I can’t judge as I haven’t played it yet) but I found the A- & B-scenarios different enough to make them fun to experience. Of course different difficulty settings, costumes and the general weapon unlocks as we know from every RE-entry. But we also have a mode called “Ghost Survivors” with what-if scenarios about several characters of the main storyline who sadly did not make it out alive from Racoon City. Another mode is the scenario where we play an iconic character of the series called HUNK - a special soldier who always makes it out alive out of any situation - and there is the Tofu-Mode where you play HUNK’s scenario but as a piece of Tofu (yes, literally). You can unlock different types of Tofu, each with their own setup and loadout ranging from cheesy easy to diabolical in difficulty. The last mode to unlock is the No-Way-Out scenario and let me tell you it is hell itself. You play as the sheriff from the intro of the game in his what-if scenario - in which you have a very limited loadout and need to kill 100 enemies spawning in on you whilst all you can do is running around in the gas station shop room - the only ammo and weapons you get is from the enemy drops and if you fudge up you’re done. It requires learning the mode, planning ahead and praying to RNGesus that he will have mercy on your soul. All these modes have rewards as well to unlock: Different accessories to wear which sadly only work in the Ghost-Survivor content not in the main game. That insane mode of the sheriff I just mentioned? If you unlock a specific task in that mode, you can get yourself the cat-ears, giving you unlimited ammo for every weapon you use.
[/list]
[h3][b]The “Not So Goods”[/b][/h3]
[list][*]The controls of the game were overall very smooth but sometimes Claire/Leon would weirdly “spam to the side” before running into the direction you actually wanted to go. Also sometimes the controls felt very “floaty”.
[*]Sometimes zombies were able to grab you when you weren’t even anywhere near their range. A minor bug maybe? Annoying nevertheless, especially in high difficulties.
[/list]
[h3][b]Would I recommend it?[/b][/h3]
[i]Yes![/i] ❤️
[i]As I have said, I sadly cannot compare it to its original glory (yet) but I can say I enjoyed my time with this Remake. I have played it on Xbox as well and I have sunken quite a lot of time into it overall - I really enjoy playing it again and again. The sheriff-mode is a nightmare and I don’t know how I haven’t thrown the controller into my monitor when I suffered through it but overall I love the game and all the stuff it offers.
Now in hindsight with RE4R (the same team that made this I’ve been told?) it is such a shame how awful RE3R turned out to be. This game set a high standard up for me and RE4R an even higher one and RE3R is just stinky - I can only imagine how amazing that would’ve been if the devs of this game also made the third Remake :(

5 minutes later:

Walking slowly like I’m in a funeral procession
Checking every corner like rent is due
Pausing the game because I heard something IRL....

WHY ARE THEY ALWAYS BEHIND ME 😭

Bro came in looking like a rookie cop and left carrying my entire emotional damage.

Me playing:
“Leon, go check that hallway.”

Also me:
“WAIT NO LEON COME BACK WE DON’T NEED TO GO THERE”

Final verdict:
No regrets. Still amazing. Still terrifying. Still makes me act like I’ve never played a horror game in my life.

Resident Evil has always accidentally had the most interesting political implications with their games. Yes, America is a corptocracy where all significant innovations come from the private body, yes, there are alligators in the sewers, yes, the same people making vaccines are also developing bio-weapons. Yes, for every admirable thing Umbrella has done, from providing miracle first aid regenerative sprays from cultivated herbs from the Arklay mountains, they also more or less own the entire state government revolving around Raccoon City. 

Not only do they have the police force literally under their thumb, but the police station is basically a fortress blocking one of the many entrances and routes to the NEST. And worst yet, the same ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who designed the floor plans and traps for the Spencer Mansion, probably also developed the museum-turned-police station of the RPD.

Resident Evil is perhaps the most schizo horror series ever made, it has some of the best and most accurate, faithful milslop in games with some of the most iconic character designs in any medium. Leon has recently gained renewed fame and significance, as well as the GOAT Hunk, so why not now, than ever, to return to one of my most played horror games?

I have been a die hard fan of Biohazard/Resident Evil since its first releases on playstation. I still remember playing the Gamecube ports as well and of course, Resident Evil Zero and Resident Evil REmake. But how does RE2 hold up, arguably the most significant of the original zombie trilogy of RE games? The original RE2 is still a bonafied classic and an undefeated legend of survival horror, while it lacks the taste and high brow narrative of the best Silent Hill has to offer, Resident Evil lends itself to being actually fun to play despite its flaws. 

RE2 Remake is such a controversial idea at first, why remake an amazing game? And the answer is simple, the original tank control, fixed camera angle RE games were innovative and gorgeous and while RE1 remake is still amazing, modern gamers would love to experience a modern take on this story. Little did we know, this remake would go on to soft-reboot the Resident Evil current canon and honestly, I don't think anyone can be upset about that besides the hardcore nostalgia goggles collectors. 

I sincerely think this is one of the best games of all time, if not the absolute best in what Resident Evil can offer in certain points. However, it definitely has a retro puzzle feeling true to its origins and the challenges and difficulty is frankly, far higher than most gamers will anticipate. The game is a breeze to playthrough once you memorize what you are doing, but the first playthroughs are still nerve wracking and trying events to get through. 

Graphically, it still holds up well and the gore and body damage system is still revolutionary with almost no peers. Zombies stumble as their legs full off, their guts spill out when cut in half with shotguns, grenade shrapnel completely shreds their flesh and renders them to near skeletal remains, strips of flesh and limbs scattered along the floor. The gore has literal staying power and its shocking. The gross mutated monsters are gross, everything has such a disgusting texture to it that it really feels like you are shifting through ♥♥♥♥ in the Raccoon City sewer system. 

The third person camera adds just enough tension of keeping some things out of sight, while also being very functional and well adjusted. Being chased by Mr. X is still horrifying, but overall, there are few games that can make you feel perpetually uneasy. The grim atmosphere of Resident Evil is revoltingly a delight to the environmental senses, even when you are equipped with the infinite ammo weapons from subsequent S rank runs, the game can still put you into tight situations that really make you such your stomach in and hold your breath. Leon quips and swears as his bullets miss, Claire's gungho, cowboy attitude at times makes her seem like twice the bad ass Leon ever was and Ada... Wongs a lot. 

The puzzles can be frustrating and the amount of backtracking is nauseating, but this is the true Resident Evil experience defined for the modern age without losing its origins. I have beaten the hardest challenges this game has to offer and somehow, I still haven't gotten all the hip inventory space despite numerous S rank runs across all difficulties. Whatever. 

The music is effective, the sound effects are horrifying and memorable if not out right corny at certain points, but the visuals are stunning and the blood and gore effects have so much impressive tech behind them. Leon got slashed by a licker and the wound stayed on him for a full hour and eventually faded into a fresh scar on the flesh. The fact the models throughout the game increasingly get dirtier, bloodier and more beaten up, giving you a great sense of progression and this simple details elevates the experience a lot. 

4th Survivor, of course, is an incredible challenge that will push your patience and mechanics racing for certain times, but it is so rewarding each time you pull off a persona best. Ghost Survivors certainly... has some missions, but fun enough mechanics they are worth acing once or twice. Tofu Survivor is worth a laugh and its super funny to show someone such a challenge who is not familiar with Resident Evil's silly humour.

Maybe not as fun as it used to be on the 7th playthrough for both paths, but its hard to ever say anything truly negative about the game when it really is a master class in not just how to make a remake, but how to make a Resident Evil title.

Resident Evil 2 (2019) Remake Review

The 2019 remake of Resident Evil 2 is a masterclass in survival horror, blending modern visuals with classic tension in a way that feels both fresh and faithful. From the moment you step into the rain-soaked streets of Raccoon City, the game establishes a relentless atmosphere that rarely lets up—and much of that tension comes from its intense gameplay and ever-present threats.

One of the most memorable elements is the terrifying presence of Mr. X. Unlike traditional enemies, he isn’t confined to scripted moments; he stalks you persistently through the police station, his heavy footsteps echoing down corridors as you try to solve puzzles or conserve precious ammo. He constantly forces you to rethink your routes, often blocking your path just when you think you’re making progress. This dynamic creates a sense of dread that never fully fades, turning even familiar areas into nerve-wracking encounters.

The game also shines in its clever puzzle design. From medallion statues to intricate key systems and hidden mechanisms, the puzzles strike a satisfying balance between challenging and rewarding. They encourage exploration and careful observation without becoming frustrating, making each breakthrough feel earned. Combined with limited resources, these puzzles enhance the survival aspect, forcing players to make meaningful decisions under pressure.

Another standout feature is the second playthrough option. After completing your first run with either Leon or Claire, you unlock a “2nd Run” scenario that not only increases difficulty but also expands the story. It offers a parallel perspective, showing what the other character was experiencing during your initial playthrough. This adds depth to the narrative and provides new surprises, altered item placements, and different story beats, making it feel like more than just a simple replay.

Sherry Birkin’s storyline is another highlight. Her segment adds emotional weight to the narrative while offering a unique gameplay change of pace. Watching her struggle to survive amidst the chaos of the outbreak makes her role feel meaningful, and it’s especially rewarding to see how she ultimately escapes Raccoon City. Her story ties into the larger plot in a way that strengthens the overall experience and makes her survival feel significant, its also nice to see how a key charecter survived the outbreak and how it affected them.

After roughly 12 hours of gameplay, Resident Evil 2 Remake proves itself to be an incredibly engaging and polished experience. Every moment feels purposeful, whether you’re solving puzzles, managing inventory, or narrowly avoiding Mr. X’s relentless pursuit. It’s a game that respects your time while delivering consistent tension, strong storytelling, and excellent replay value.

In the end, Resident Evil 2 (2019) is not just a remake—it’s one of the best survival horror experiences available. Those hours you find yourself playing are packed with fear, excitement, and satisfaction, making it absolutely worth playing for both newcomers and longtime fans of the series.

This is truly a blast to play. I played in my favorite way to play games: VR. (I played the entire game from start to finish, TWICE, and with the extra modes I needed to clear, cleared).

Hardcore difficulty, crosshair removed, and a couple fun gameplay mods (RE2 true headshot mod to match the movie canon where regular zombies are one-shot to the head but the special zombies stay the same). I absolutely love the puzzles in this game, brainteasers left and right. The entire game was never a chore, as the horrors that fill the rooms as you solve puzzles are phenomenally paced. I had ants in my pants the entire time. 

The jumpscares were in total immersion while in VR, causing me to panic or get anxious in so many sections because the realistic-looking graphics amplies every haunting scenario through skyscraper's worth of ceilings. Pair poor aim skill with the vastly quick infected in this game, and you get shaky hands and a rapid heartbeat wanting to get to safety asap. Imagine seeing larger-than-life creatures [spoiler] like MR. X, or any of the bosses frankly... [/spoiler] right in front of you. My fear is somewhat taken care of by the botched planning in saving supplies throughout the game. Multiple first attempts, I ran out of ammo or weapons for bosses. I had to reset the game to master my route. That includes memorizing the paths between rooms and the safest routes from this game's stalker enemy. Gosh, that terrified me every single hour I stayed in this evil residence.

The gunplay in this game, I LOVE. The horror? ABSOLUTELY DREADFUL and fun. The story? Really awesome, but the canon was confusing to pinpoint. Eventually, I got the accurate timeline of events to my own perspective. The 2nd playthrough really drove home the actual event canon, and I loved replaying the game with different enemies. There was zero frustration replaying the game again in Hardcore, considering I remembered the puzzles, even if they were in different spots or changed slightly. The two extra modes are the most action-packed, hell-raised experiences I ever seen in gaming. I never saw that many zombies in a single file line ever. I'm certain those modes are the ultimate test in my ability to go guns blazing in a world that terrified me so much.

Now, I'm going to rewatch the Snapcube fandub of this game. My favorite RE Remake so far!

In a lot of ways the original game has been expanded upon with better puzzles, a more in-depth sewer area, much improved dialogue, and an absolutely frightening Mr. X. And even though the game has moved away from the traditional fixed camera angles, the remake overwhelmingly succeeds in creating an environment full of suspense and uncertainty.

The combat has seen a massive overhaul into a third person shooter with more involved boss fights, targetable limbs, utility items and more. The unique weapon selections between Leon and Claire gives a very unique feel in how the individually face enemy encounters. Not to say this is an action game, it's still very much a survival horror experience where you're carefully managing your resources and inventory

Sadly the game lacks the interconnected Part A/B playthroughs the original provided. Run A/B in the remake simply offers a new starting point where the items and puzzles are remixed.

Making a return are the classic Hunk and Tofu run, along with expanded cast of Tofus to choose from with their own unique inventory setup. A very fun little side mode to sink hours into.

[h1] A Stunning Remake [/h1]

I started RE2 Remake the day after finishing RE1, with high expectations, and I have to say the game almost delivers on all fronts.

The atmosphere of Raccoon City is perfect. The police station is a beautiful map, and the backtracking is much better handled compared to the first game. Mr. X is incredible : unsettling, always present, and just hearing his footsteps sends chills down your spine.

Resources are generous compared to RE1 : running out of ammo is rare, while healing items need to be used more sparingly. Enemies are varied, boss fights are challenging yet fun, and the level of detail in the environments is outstanding.

I played first with Leon and then with Claire, as intended by the game structure (though you can swap the order if you want). My first run (Leon A) was one of the best horror-action experiences I’ve ever had. However, past a certain point, with better equipment, I found that, aside from the boss fights, tension and anxiety decrease slightly.

[h3] Positive Points : [/h3]
[list]
[*][b] Atmosphere and environments :[/b] Raccoon City and the police station are meticulously detailed and perfectly balanced between exploration and action.
[*][b] Mr. X :[/b] a truly terrifying presence that induces real anxiety, without relying on cheap scares.
[*][b] Enemies and boss fights :[/b] varied, fun, and well-balanced.
[*][b] Attention to detail :[/b] objects, environments, and lore are incredibly well crafted.
[*][b] Pacing :[/b] action and exploration segments are harmoniously balanced.
[/list]

[h3] Negative Points : [/h3]
[list]
[*][b] Limited replay value :[/b] The second campaign with Claire doesn’t offer a completely new experience compared to Leon. Many paths are similar, only some cutscenes are different, and puzzles change slightly, but the overall experience remains largely the same. Personally, I was a bit disappointed because I expected something truly new, as the game itself encourages you to play the "other side of the story".
[*][b] Simple puzzles :[/b] most puzzles aren’t very challenging, the only one I got stuck on was the plant lab puzzle, simply because I misunderstood the mechanics.
[*][b] Sewers :[/b] less fun compared to the main areas, it feels more like a "transition" zone.
[*][b] Jumpscares :[/b] all jumpscares feel cheap and mechanical. Personally, I don’t mind the momentary fright itself, but I find this kind of scare one of the laziest and most ridiculous ways to try to scary the player. It gives you the feeling of, "okay, we have to scare you like this because we don’t know how else to do it". By contrast, Mr. X genuinely creates anxiety and fear through constant, well built tension.
[*][b] Forced narrative choices :[/b] some story moments feel like they exist just to push the plot forward, although I still found the story and lore very engaging.
[/list]

[h3] Conclusion [/h3]

Despite a few subjective flaws, RE 2 Remake is an excellent game, arguably one of the best video game remakes ever made. The atmosphere, tension, attention to detail, and pacing are top notch, perfectly balancing action and exploration. If you love horror games with a strong action component and want to see how a classic can be modernized without losing its essence, this is a true masterpiece. The minor flaws don’t detract from an experience I wholeheartedly recommend.

The same goes for the bestiary, which you quickly exhaust and find rather uninteresting. Not to mention the two or three boss fights (it’s actually the same enemy all three times) which are more tedious than anything else; you're forced to run circles around a bullet sponge without the ability to parry or dodge, you just bombard its weak points (which are about as subtle as a sledgehammer).

Resident Evil 2 RE is my favorite entry in the franchise so far in my journey through the series.
It's so damn good I played the original, and that game was excellent too.

I can't really put into words why I specifically love this particular title.
It really just comes down to it being such a tight, well crafted, gripping adventure into the terror of Racoon City in the midst of the T-Virus outbreak.

Everything from the beginning to the end is fabulous (even the sewers). As a somewhat new-comer to the Horror genre of games, I think this really is in my top 5 recommendations for new horror fans. The pacing is excellent and the descent into danger is handled really really well.
The atmosphere is second to none in RE2RE. Creaks and groans echo through the halls from all directions. Blood is painted violently against the walls. When you inevitably cross paths with a zombie, the gut reflex of fight or flight hits you and it really immerses you into the world. The new rendition of the soundtrack really adds to the experience of being in this terrifying situation alone.

I don't think I can really point out any flaws. The game does have a learing curve if you are new to survival horror, such as inventory management, bullet counting, choosing fights, learning to run away and bait the enemies. This did cause me to reset a couple saves back to fix my mistakes, but that isn't an issue since the more you know and the better you are at the game, the faster you blast through it.

RPD will go down (for me and many others) as arguably the best puzzle-box styled horror map of all time.
The addition of Mr X in both campaigns is such a horrific and awesome change. 
The other sections of the story are also super fun.

Both Leon and Claire's playthroughs are super fun and offer a lot of changes to make the campaigns worth it.

This is definitely my favorite survival horror game so far.

OK, before recommending this to you all, has anyone at least
played the classic versions of RE2, RE3 or even RE4...nobody?

OK then. Forget everything you learned in RE5 & RE6, but instead
take everything you've learned from RE7 & Village/RE8...and prepare yourselves.

Everything about the remake of RE2 will be similar but also play out differently,
zombies are numerous & will overwhelm you if cornered or out of ammo & heals.
Also, your knife won't do much to keep you alive, and will break after prolonged use
...instead, gather gunpower & use it to craft ammo types for whatever you're packing.

And besides the bosses you fight when playing Leon or Claire...there is one enemy
that will pursue you throughout the campaign...but mostly when you play as Leon.
This enemy is T-103 Tyrant, aka "Mr. X". Mr. X is extremely resilient & will hunt you down
no matter where you go with the exception of scripted events that allow you to catch a breather.
But point in case: no matter where you are, no matter where HE is...he will find you. How?
Here's a hint: noise, primarily from footsteps, doors slamming shut or gunfire...Mr. X can pick
up on the source of that & hone in on your last known location...so to ensure you remain off his radar,
tip-toe like you do around Lickers...with zero noise.

That aside, the game itself is very engaging, scary, but overall fun too.
Another note is like the PS1 version, the game has 2 scenarios for each character, which means
item locations & puzzles/codes are different from Scenario 1. Remember that!

Do I recommend this game? Absolutely.
Think of it as a Tutorial for RE3 remake.

So be prepared when thrown into the world of Survival Horror...Good Luck.

Like many of the other Resident Evil games, my first playthrough was through a VR mod. Resident Evil 2 in PC VR is a completely different level of survival horror. Being inside the RPD station makes everything feel tighter, darker, and way more intense. Hallways feel claustrophobic, zombies are way scarier up close, and hearing Mr. X’s footsteps in VR is pure anxiety. To me, it felt a lot more realistic and life like in VR than the previous ones I have played. However, that doesn't mean it was scarier.

The immersion makes simple things—like opening doors or checking corners—feel stressful in the best way. Gunfights are more tense and precise, and managing ammo while physically aiming adds real pressure. It perfectly balances classic survival horror with modern VR immersion.

It’s not quite as terrifying as RE7’s first-person design, but the atmosphere, puzzles, and iconic setting make it insanely fun and memorable.

The Resident Evil 2 Remake is in my opinion what a remake should be but does have its flaws, firstly nothing will compete with the original games they add so much tension and story to the game that these remakes just miss the mark on.

Firstly you will find yourself playing as either Leon or Claire, for those who are new Leon is a rookie cop heading into raccoon city for his first day on the job and claire is heading into raccoon city to find her brother Chris. both characters first meet at the gas station after Leon saves claire from a lurking zombie attempting to bite her from behind.

Now the game really starts when you reach the city streets and head for the RPD (Raccoon Police Department) you navigate a through a few zombies into a tight alleyway before ascending some stairs to see the sight of the station towering over the city being such a landmark feature of the RE series. now my first critic here is the outside section itself in the original you have a much longer outside sequence where you truly get the feeling of survival horror, the streets are swarmed and with the janky controls of the OG and the locked camera angles you get as you navigate leon/claire through the streets adds to the intensity. in the remake your outside initially for a couple of minutes max with no real problems to face. 

Once you reach the RPD Leon/Claire bolts the gated entrance shut to keep the swarms outside from entering this is where the game treats you. you approach the Doors to the RPD and push them open to be welcomed to a warm masterpiece a place of safety youve just locked out the undead and you are greeted to a stunning hall with prestigous architecture on display with a box to store items and a typewriter to save this feels like the safest place.

You spend most of your time navigating the RPD which at first will feel like a maze, shutters to open, doors that require certain keys, safes to crack, armory lockers to find pieces too even being able to access the S.T.A.R.S armory and obtain higher grade weapons the station is yours to explore. but your never alone

throughout every nook and cranny of the station are undead officers, colleagues you would have been welcomed by on your first day heading into the west office you can even see the welcome they was planning you. your main objective in the station is to escape and you do this by finding 3 medallions around the station all needing there own 3 symbol puzzle to be solved. along the way you will encounter the tyrant (trenchcoat) or more commonly known as MR X who is a officially known as T-00 he will be a lovely fella and spend his time lurking around the RPD trying to find you and detecting you from you running and shooting at other zombies. 

T-00 is a B.O.W (Bio Organic Weapon) his model is a T-103 Tyrant series which was massed produced by umbrella and was tasked to be dropped into raccoon city and retrieve a sample of the G-Virus and eliminate any remaining survivors, you can hear him a mile away with his loud ass footsteps echoing throughout the station. I personally love how he interacts through out the station, his movement speed is just slower than your jog so you always have the chance to make that split decision to get away however he can open most doors within the station. 

Im getting too carried away with this and dont want to spoil the game for anyone who hasnt already played this beauty so i wont say anymore.

overall the game is great is does miss bits from the original that would have been nice to see but have to take it for what it is, it lives up to the survival horror the pacing is good making the RPD the main place you spent most time. the atmosphere is perfect, flickering lights, dark hallways and only a trusty flashlight to light the way most of the time.

would have been amazing to be able to explore more of the streets in the beginning to really get the sense of "theres no coming back from this" as i said before the original masters this making it difficults to progress until youve learnt the controls and adjusted to the way you aim and the camera angles the game provides. 

The graphics look unreal, the most up to date version adds ray tracing and HOLYYYYYY SHIII it looks gorgeous. but use Non RT for mod compatibility (modding scene are gods btw) 

finally my personal preference in my most recent playthrough as crazy as it sounds was to turn off the BGM (background music) it really intensified the game for me, walking around RPD after clearing corridors of zombies to be alone with my own footsteps, the sound of rain hitting windows doors creaking open, showers left running you really understand the situation and you really get sucked into it more without the music. and of course MR X and his loud ass footsteps kept me alert hearing his boots smack the floor from across the RPD not knowing where he is or what angle he came from really added to the atmosphere.

Will always love the game series, unfortuantely too broke for requiem rn but i will love that just as much as all the others. TY for Reading :)

RE2 was my introduction to the Resident Evil franchise, and what an entry point it turned out to be. It has since become one of my favorite game series of all time.

The atmosphere is the foundation of everything. The Raccoon Police Department is a masterclass in environmental design, every sound, every shadow, every enemy placement working together to keep you in a constant state of dread. Resources are scarce enough that you're never truly comfortable, which makes the world feel genuinely threatening rather than just aesthetically dark. That tension is what pulls you deeper into the story, the characters, and the puzzles, none of which disappoint.

What really elevates it, though, is how it all compounds. The soundtrack builds on the atmosphere, the dual playthrough structure with Leon and Claire adds new context to everything you thought you understood, and by the end you realize the whole experience was more layered than it first appeared.

This game is a work of art. Play it.

Played this game (both runs), and all I can say is that this is a solid introduction to anyone that hasn't played a Resident Evil yet. As someone that had this as my entry point to the franchise, I was NOT prepared. Being overwhelmed with items and having no inventory space to put them into (I am a crazy hoarder in games, every bullet counts to me) made me mald so hard, but hey, if the game is good, its good.

And it IS good. 

The atmosphere alone carries Raccoon City feels genuinely miserable in the best way possible. Everywhere you go its dark, wet, and something is trying to eat you. The graphics hold up really well too, like this does not look like a game from 2019 at all.

Story-wise, Leon and Claire are both great leads and doing both campaigns to get the full picture was worth it. They're not the deepest characters ever written but you root for them, which is enough when you're running away screaming.

Also the game will teach you very quickly that resources are not your friends and that every decision matters. Coming from someone who picks up literally everything in every game this was a personal attack.

Overall if you're looking to get into Resident Evil and don't know where to start, just play this. It's scary, it looks great, the story is fun, and it will humble you. 10/10 would get traumatized again.
