I just finished Leon’s story in Resident Evil 2 Remake and since this was my first survival horror game, I think it’s fair to say it left a pretty strong impression on me.

First of all - the atmosphere is amazing. The RPD feels dark, tense, and honestly pretty scary. It’s rare for a game to actually make me nervous while playing, but this one managed to do it several times. The music and sound design do a great job building tension, and exploring the police station for the first time was genuinely memorable.

The gunplay and combat mechanics are also pretty satisfying. Weapons feel good, and deciding whether to fight zombies or just avoid them is part of the strategy.

However, the game can also be very frustrating at times.

Resources are extremely limited, which I understand is part of survival horror, but sometimes it felt a bit too restrictive. I often had to run around the huge RPD building trying to find puzzle items just to progress. Because of that, I ended up checking tutorials quite often just to figure out where something was.

The map system also didn’t help much. There are no real objectives telling you where to go next. The only hint is that rooms turn blue when fully looted and red when something is still there, which is helpful but also confusing, especially early on.

Another thing that annoyed me was the defense system. If a zombie grabs you and you don’t have a knife or grenade, you basically just take damage. It would have been nice if there was some kind of skill check mechanic where you could try to break free.

I also feel like some mechanics are a bit unnecessary - for example barricading windows. Zombies constantly breaking windows and coming inside just felt more annoying than interesting.

And then there’s Mr. X / Tyrant.

This guy follows you everywhere and never seems to get tired of it. At some point it stopped being scary and just became exhausting. Hearing his footsteps constantly while trying to solve puzzles wasn’t exactly fun.

SPOILERS BELOW

The early part of the game in the police station was honestly the hardest for me. Learning the mechanics, solving puzzles, and dealing with limited resources made it feel confusing and unnecessarily difficult.

Once the underground parking area opened and Mr. X appeared, the game became so stressful that I sometimes played it almost out of frustration rather than enjoyment.

After escaping the RPD with Ada, things started to feel a bit better. The game was still full of puzzles and maze-like corridors, but at least it felt more like a challenge rather than pure punishment.

The G-virus lab section near the end was actually my favorite part. It felt interesting and different, but unfortunately it was also pretty short and didn’t have much story around it.

The bosses are another story.William Birkin and Mr. X basically feel immortal. You defeat them, they fall into the abyss, explode, mutate… and somehow they just come back stronger every time. I’ll give Mr. X credit though - he’s incredibly persistent when it comes to hunting you down.

Final thoughts

The game has an incredible atmosphere, great sound design, and tense moments that really stand out.

But the missions and puzzle-heavy progression can sometimes feel frustrating, especially for someone new to the genre.

Since this is my first experience with survival horror, I don’t really have much to compare it to. Still, despite the annoyances, I can say I had a good time with it.

Overall rating: 7/10

[h1]One of the Greatest Remakes of All Time[/h1]
After proving they knew what they were doing with their IP in Resident Evil 7, Capcom finally got to work on the long-awaited remake of Resident Evil 2. For context, the original Resident Evil trilogy released on the PS1 and the remake of the first Resident Evil came out on the GameCube. RE2 was long overdue for a remake and thankfully Capcom didn't disappoint with this stellar piece of survival horror magic that may just be the best Resident Evil game released under the RE Engine.

RE2 follows the story of Leon Kennedy, a rookie cop on his first day of the job, and Claire Redfield, the sister of one of the original Resident Evil's protagonists Chris Redfield. The two are caught in the middle of a zombie outbreak in Raccoon City and must take refuge in the local police station. But this isn't an ordinary police station, for one, being an art museum originally leading to sprawling architecture, and it also being constructed right above the underground labs of the series antagonist Umbrella Corporation. You'll deal with zombie cops, mad scientists, and terrifying bioweapons built by Umbrella designed to hunt you down and kill you. You'll have a choice of two protagonists, Leon or Claire, and depending on which character you choose will result in different weapons, keys, and story moments for you to experience. Leon gets wrapped up in the conspiracies of the mysterious Ada Wong, Claire ends up building an older sister dynamic with a young girl named Sherry. All these subplots intersect at the Umbrella labs for an explosive and climactic finale that leaves you fully satisfied and eager to replay the game as the other character.

Resident Evil 2 has amazing visuals and sound. The RE Engine gives the game an outstanding presentation, and this is the first time the series really felt like it had achieved cinematic quality in its dialog, performances, and emotionally hard hitting moments. The remixed songs and audio effects are great, giving new weight and depth to this horror classic's iconic atmosphere.

The gameplay is a modern third person shooter horror game with an emphasis on resource management and route memorization. Zombies don't die easily and you don't have the resources to mag dump every foe you come across. In addition to guns, you have sub weapons like knives and grenades that are arguably best used when grabbed by a zombie, thus allowing you to fend them off before they land a fatal bite. The shooting feels responsive, but the erratic nature of the zombies and the random chance of scoring crits are all ways the game faithfully recreates the tension of shooting enemies with tank controls in the original. Really terrifying and challenging, but oh so satisfying when you overcome your enemies.

In terms of content and respecting the original game, RE2 remake isn't quite as phenomenal as the GameCube remake of the original Resident Evil, but it's pretty damn close. You have both campaigns for both characters, plus their B scenarios being represented in the "2nd Run" mode. After you finish the game as one character, you unlock the 2nd Run for the other character which allows you to basically play through the entire game from the perspective of either Leon or Claire whilst the other character was experiencing the bulk of the story. Depending on who you pick for this mode, again, results in different weapons and items being available. This leads to almost four total campaigns across Leon and Claire and their 2nd Runs combined. This is already a ton of content when factoring in unlockable weapons and items for replays. In addition to this, the game thankfully retains the super difficult unlockable mode called "The 4th Survivor" where you play as the faceless, gas mask wearing badass of the series, Hunk. Finishing this mode will then also unlock the hilarious easter egg from the PS1 original called "Tofu Survivor" which needs to be played to be believed.

Since this game's release, Capcom also added a bunch of free DLC in the form of what-if scenarios involving other side characters whose fates were sealed in the original story but are given a second chance here. Plus these extra modes have their own unlockables as well.. yeah. This is an AMAZING bang for your buck and still remains a challenging and fully featured horror game all these years later. If you want to experience what Resident Evil is all about, BUY THIS GAME. You won't regret it.

Resident Evil 2 is a wonderfully-done survival horror, and probably one of the most intense. Although, in my opinion, Dead Space is better (will not be accepting comments on this matter). Despite that, I believe this game exceeds its competitor in one way, and that is being more difficult overall. Whereas Dead Space could be gamed through abusing its ammo director and some overpowered weapons, you are at the whims of whatever Resident Evil gives you. No biasing towards overpowered weapons here. It is survival horror in a nearly pure sense (Outlast being absolutely pure in this case). Unless you know where every item is, you will be forced to consider how to use as little as possible for maximum gain with whatever you are given at the time.

In Dead Space, you have to be patient, calm, and know which enemies are better prioritized first as you traverse the USG Ishimura in a steady, linear fashion. There is more structure to it because you know what must be done next through clear objectives. Resident Evil 2 is more open with how it lets the player traverse its setting and solve its mysteries. Because of that, it's very reliant on letting the player organically progress through exploration normally, while relying on brute force memorization of strategies to optimize at its most difficult. This can include knowing when you have to waste bullets or just run past, knowing where and when to go to optimize time/inventory (really in S+ runs), and praying to GOD that you don't experience bad RNG. 

That is the one problem with this game, is that the RNG is HORRENDOUS in some areas. If you are doing a Hardcore S+ run, you better hope you saved before coming to one of these sections (and you only get 3 saves to acquire S+, so good luck I guess). There are many strategies that rely on hope. Hopefully that G-Adult doesn't chaingrab me while I run past, hopefully that zombie isn't at the door to lunge at me so that I don't have to waste a secondary, and HOPEFULLY I can kneecap this zombie to get past with fewer shots because Mr. X is chasing me and wants to punch the hell out of me. You better HOPE you don't lose 30 minutes of progress, if not more, to this game of chance. When you have this much that could go wrong, harder difficulties are no longer fun challenges, but just a chore.

That didn't stop me, however. I got a B for Leon on Hardcore because I didn't care. However, I learned about the infinite minigun, and I HAD TO HAVE IT. When my primal brain sees minigun, it needs it. So I got S+ with Claire, now its time to use the minigun for about 10 minutes and not touch the game for awhile.

I was first introduced to the Resident Evil series through the remake of Resident Evil on the GameCube. Growing up, I didn’t have much access to games, so while I played that and Resident Evil 4 many times, my experience with the original Resident Evil 2 was fairly limited. I knew the characters and the story, but I didn’t grow up replaying it the same way many fans did.

As an adult, I’ve gone back and played the original several times and have now spent many hours with Resident Evil 2.

Overall, this remake does a lot of things incredibly well. The modern controls, visuals, and atmosphere bring Raccoon City to life in a way the original never could. Zombies feel dangerous again, resources are limited, and being constantly hunted by Mr. X adds a layer of tension that keeps you on edge throughout the game. The way Leon is written here also feels much more natural compared to the original.

My biggest complaint is the A and B scenario system. This remake had the opportunity to make Leon and Claire’s stories feel completely unique, but the differences between them are fairly small. Outside of certain moments, like Claire visiting the orphanage or the characters reaching NEST in slightly different ways, their routes through the game are very similar.

Another thing that stands out is how the original game handled the dual scenarios. In the original Resident Evil 2, Leon and Claire kept in contact through radio and occasionally crossed paths during the story, which made it feel like both characters were experiencing the same outbreak from different angles. In the remake, they only meet at the beginning outside the RPD and then again at the very end when escaping NEST. Because they travel through many of the same locations, it would have helped the narrative if they interacted more often so their parallel journeys felt more connected.

What makes this stand out even more is that Leon and Claire barely encounter each other during the story and only reunite at the very end. Because of that, I really wish the developers had made their campaigns more distinct so it truly felt like two separate perspectives on the Raccoon City outbreak.

That said, this is still an excellent game. The gameplay, atmosphere, and replayability make it one of the strongest modern entries in the series. Despite my criticism of the scenario system, this remake is probably the most definitive way to experience Resident Evil 2 today.

Resident Evil 2 (Remake) is the perfect example of how to modernize a classic game without losing its identity. Capcom managed to recreate the survival horror formula while improving the gameplay and presentation in all the right ways.

Exploring the Raccoon Police Department is easily one of the highlights of the entire game. The building is designed like a giant puzzle box where locked doors, shortcuts, and keys slowly connect as you progress. Later areas like the Orphanage, the Sewers, the Underground Facility or the NEST laboratory help keep the pacing fresh and add even more atmosphere. The puzzles are well designed and encourage exploration instead of simply moving from one objective to another. 

You can start you first run as either Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield, each has their own campaign. Their stories are interconnected and seeing the events from two different perspectives adds a lot of replay value. This is a smart way to recycle content without forcing the player to replay the entire game from scratch. From different weapons to different bosses, there are enough changes to make each run unique.

Despite all these strengths, the game has a few flaws. There is no clear indicator when a zombie is permanently dead unless you get lucky with a critical hit and blow off their heads, which can make encounters feel inconsistent, especially on hardcore. The boss fights are also a bit underwhelming, often taking place in small arenas where you just shoot, run a few meters away to avoid getting hit, and repeat. Finally, the game lacks meaningful expansion DLCs and the additional modes that exist can feel frustrating rather than enjoyable to complete.

Overall, Resident Evil 2 (Remake) is an outstanding survival horror game worth playing and it should be the first choice of any newcomer to the series.

Some information for Resident Evil reviews. If it is a remake, it will be measured against the game which it attempts to be a remake of, as well as the standard categories of:  Story, Characters & Gameplay.

Story:
As a remake of RE2, this is quite faithful to the overall story, cutting out some parts from the original, modifying some and replacing parts too. It does however add some depth to the events and some of the characters which is welcome. Some parts of the game such as the orphanage are new additions here and also has some bearing on future titles in the series. Altogether, the game's story has a nice flow to it, simplifying some parts which were a little tedious in the original (not that its bad there, just makes more sense here). Being able to play the story from the perspective of both main protagonists with differences is present as it was in the original, although the scenario A/B system has left a little to be desired when standing against the original. This is however a remake and as such it being a carbon copy of the original maybe isn't the best path to tread. If you remember the original or want to experience the story in a modern way, you won't be disappointed here.

Characters:
I'll start by saying that the Voice Acting for both Leon ( Nick Apostolides ) and Claire ( Stephanie Panisello ) was stellar. here. They both portray their characters at this point in time well, being their first step into the nightmares brought to them by our resident B.O.Ws. As far as their characters in game, they behave mostly as you would expect from people in this scenario, especially first timers and given their positions. Claire is by all means a civillian and Leon is the Rookie cop who wants to save everyone. The behaviours and mannerisms are much more grounded here as opposed to the original which was just an implementation of their time. Games have come a long way as far as immersion and reality imitation and so this being a newer version, these aspects can be felt much more here. Marvin Branagh ( Christopher Mychael Watson ) was given a larger role here than in the original which was a very appreciated thing and again the good VA work reflects that. Chief Irons ( Sid Carton ) gives a more menacing version of the Chief in the remake with a classic villainous approach rather than the slightly strange personality he had in the original. Sherry ( Eliza Pryor ) also has a bit more screen time here and the portrayal of a frightened girl amongst terror is done well. Ada ( Jolene Andersen )is done classically here as the mysterious agent/spy type going up against Annette Birkin ( Karen Strassman ) and these characters are given a nice amount of screen time. Overall the character portrayals are done very well here and the cast was perfect for the purposes they serve in the characters.

Gameplay:
The classic survival horror gameplay style was brought beautifully to life in the RE2 remake, being faithful to the original for the most part, with a very welcome addition of inventory upgrade pouches beyond what was possible in the original. The slight reimagining of the RPD allowed for fair placement of item boxes whilst not eliminating the strategy of inventory management else facing a lot of backtracking. The game play whilst controlling all playable characters left you in the position of someone who was not experienced in this type of situation and as such can only act accordingly. The more modern 3rd person approach as opposed to the fixed camera angles & tank controls of old allowed for good innovation in jump scare moments as opposed to the camera doing that work. It also made the strategy of attempting to survive these encounters a bit easier to manage. The various additions to gameplay here such as the defensive weapons and the ability to board up windows allowed for some fresh flavour to the original RE recipe.

Reimagination of a Remake:
The additions to the remake across the categories far outweigh any cuts and along with the fact that is quite faithful to the original, this game sets the bar for all other remakes to come after it in the series. The reinvention of certain puzzles keeps them fresh and the addition/changing of some of the enemy types into more of a stalker rather than a set encounter provides a boon to the horror in 'survival horror'

Verdict:
I don't have anything bad to say about this game. I hoped for some more variation to the A/B scenarios more in line with the original but what is present is enough I believe. If you're looking for the formula that the modern remakes have been/will be measured against, look no further. If you want a game that stays faithful to the source material but innovates (albeit moderately), want no longer. Every Resident Evil fan or aspirant and survival horror enjoyers alike should play this. You do not have to play the original but rest assured if you do want to, you will get 2 unique experiences.

Rating: 10/10 — A Survival Horror Masterpiece

If you are looking for a game that perfectly balances tension, strategy, and pure terror, this is it. Resident Evil 2 isn't just a remake; it’s a masterclass in survival horror.

From the moment you step into the Raccoon City Police Department, the game grips you. The lighting and sound design are incredible—every creak of the floorboards or groan in the distance kept me on edge. The "thrill" the developers managed to pack into the gameplay loop is constant; you never truly feel safe, and that's exactly what makes it so addictive.
This isn't a "run and gun" action game. It forces you to manage your resources carefully. Every bullet counts, and every herb is precious. Deciding whether to fight a zombie or try to slip past it creates a layer of stress that makes the eventual scares hit much harder.
The game is genuinely scary. It doesn't rely solely on cheap tricks; the horror comes from the oppressive atmosphere and the feeling of being hunted. That said, the slight jumpscares are placed perfectly—they aren't constant, but they are effective enough to make you jump out of your seat when you least expect it!
Whether you’re a fan of the original 1998 classic or a complete newcomer to the series, this is a must-play. It is polished, terrifying, and worth every penny.

One of the few modern Resident Evil games that is actually worth a replay, despite its shortcomings. Enjoyable from beginning to end even today, and it managed to bring back the slow and cripple Zombie as a real treat even with modern TPS camera and controls.

The game has a lot of good things, so I think it's best to mention the few negative points about the game:

[olist]
[*] The game removed enemies from the original game, most notably the insect enemies (roaches, giant moth, and giant spiders). They also removed crows and a minor variation of the Licker. I think these enemies can work in a modern RE game (and as for now, Requiem has the spiders), so it sucks they got cut.

[*] They butchered the A and B routes. In the original, A and B routes decide which boss you would have to fight throughout the adventure (A for Birkin, B for Mr. X), alongside exploring different routes and encountering other characters. In this remake, Leon will ALWAYS fight Mr. X, and Claire will ALWAYS fight Birkin and babysit Sherry. The only difference is in the intro (whoever meets Marvin first at the station) and the end (whoever has to fight mutated Birkin). Everything else is exactly the same between routes. I think they wanted to make a canon to follow, but who knows.

[*] I had massive stutter issues with this game that required obscure fixes to solve (like increasing pagination size). This is weird because I never had this problem with a pirated copy. Maybe it's Capcom's new anti-piracy program. Look at my specs and tell me massive stutters are acceptable for a game like this.
[/olist]

With all that being said, the new additions, such as reworked enemies, the need to check inventory items to solve puzzles (something that was a minor detail in the original games), defense items like in Remake 1, no loading screens between rooms, and mixing powder to make ammo, were welcoming changes. It also comes with the extra modes from the original (Hunk and Tofu, Tofu now has more variations if you finish it over and over), plus an additional 4 puzzle scenarios. And while many people didn't like the new Ray-Tracing update, I thought it was really good, as it fixed many of the problems that Screen Space Reflections had, and it looks really nice.

Overall, I enjoyed this game even when it feels like "Resident Evil 2: The Hollywood Movie" with all the swearing and lame lines. Customer satisfaction: 9/10.

[h1]Resident Evil 2 Review[/h1]

[hr]
[h1]Overview[/h1]
Resident Evil 2 is easily one of my favorite Resident Evil games of all time. I never played the original versions growing up, but when the remake released I played it on PlayStation 4 and later again on PC where I completed all the achievements.

This remake is honestly incredible. It takes the core ideas of the original game and completely rebuilds them with modern design, visuals, and mechanics. The result is one of the most atmospheric and memorable survival horror games out there. Even after multiple playthroughs, it is still a very fun and tense experience.

[hr]
[h1]What It Is[/h1]
Resident Evil 2 is a survival horror game set during the Raccoon City outbreak. You play as either Leon S. Kennedy, a rookie police officer starting his first day, or Claire Redfield, who arrives in the city searching for her brother.

Both characters experience the outbreak from slightly different perspectives, and the game features separate story routes that intersect throughout the campaign. Each run takes you through a series of locations while solving puzzles, managing limited resources, and trying to survive the growing chaos.

[hr]
[h1]Level Design and Exploration[/h1]
The level design is one of the strongest parts of the game. The Raccoon City Police Department, or RPD, is easily the highlight. It is a large interconnected location filled with locked doors, puzzles, shortcuts, and hidden rooms.

When I first played the game I spent several hours just exploring the police station and trying to figure out how everything connects. The game does not always hold your hand, so progression often depends on reading notes, solving puzzles, and slowly learning the layout of the building.

That sense of exploration and discovery makes the early sections of the game incredibly memorable.

[hr]
[h1]Combat and Survival Mechanics[/h1]
Resident Evil 2 leans heavily into survival mechanics. Ammo is limited and you constantly have to decide whether it is worth fighting enemies or trying to avoid them.

At the start you only have basic weapons, so encounters can feel very tense. Later in the game you unlock stronger weapons, but resource management remains important. Gunpowder can be used to craft additional ammunition, which helps if you manage your inventory carefully.

Some enemies later in the game can take a lot of bullets, which can either feel frustrating or push you to think more strategically about when to fight and when to conserve ammo.

[hr]
[h1]Mr. X and the Pursuit System[/h1]
One of the most iconic parts of the remake is the Tyrant, commonly known as Mr. X. Once he appears, he begins actively hunting you through parts of the police station.

At first this mechanic is incredibly exciting. Hearing his heavy footsteps in the distance while you are trying to solve puzzles creates a lot of tension. You constantly have to decide whether to run, hide, or quickly finish what you are doing before he finds you.

However, after a while the constant interruptions can become a bit irritating. When you are trying to focus on solving puzzles or figuring out where to go next, having him repeatedly force you out of rooms can sometimes break the flow.

[hr]
[h1]Story and Characters[/h1]
The story itself is simple but very effective. Leon's campaign in particular is very fun to play. Watching him go from an inexperienced rookie to someone capable of surviving the outbreak is a great character journey.

Claire is also a strong character and her route adds some additional story moments. The way the two campaigns intersect is interesting, although the continuity between both routes does not always perfectly line up.

Still, the characters, voice acting, and presentation are all very strong and help carry the game forward.

[hr]
[h1]Later Areas and Boss Encounters[/h1]
While the early parts of the game are fantastic, the later sections are not quite as strong. The sewer area in particular can feel tedious and less interesting compared to the RPD. The puzzles there can become a bit frustrating, especially when managing inventory and dealing with enemies that take a lot of ammo to defeat.

The laboratory section near the end is more interesting than the sewers but still does not quite reach the same level as the opening police station area.

Boss fights are also somewhat repetitive. Many encounters revolve around attacking the same weak points, which can make later fights feel a bit predictable once you understand the pattern.

[hr]
[h1]What Works[/h1]
[list]
[*]One of the best survival horror atmospheres in the series
[*]The RPD police station is an amazing location to explore
[*]Strong characters and excellent voice acting
[*]Tense resource management and survival gameplay
[*]Mr. X creates some incredibly memorable moments
[/list]

[hr]
[h1]What Falls Short[/h1]
[list]
[*]Sewer section can feel tedious and less interesting
[*]Mr. X can become frustrating during puzzle solving
[*]Boss fights follow similar patterns across encounters
[*]Later areas do not match the quality of the RPD section
[/list]

[hr]
[h1]Verdict[/h1]
Thumbs up. Resident Evil 2 is an outstanding remake and one of the best survival horror games available today. The atmosphere, level design, and tension throughout the early parts of the game are incredible. Even if some later sections are weaker, the overall experience is still fantastic and absolutely worth playing.

You probably already know this is a great game. Visually astounding, great performance, and excellent attention to detail. Genuinely scary and incredibly tense with an interesting story and likable characters with fun puzzles. 

[h3] Gameplay [/h3]
- Guns feel great and punchy. Reloads are satisfying. 
- Puzzles were fun and tense maneuvering around zombies. 
- Found Mr. X to be fun for the first round and irritating on re-plays. Even with 3D audio enabled, it was difficult to tell where he was in relation to me, which led to many surprise encounters or boring, several minute long safe room camping encounters. They've seemed to figure this out much better in RE9. Audio sounds amazing everywhere else in the game. 
- Didn't know this while playing, but apparently there's adaptive difficulty that makes zombies take more hits before dropping if you have a ton of ammo. Absolutely hate this. On one hand, it makes it more difficult to soft lock yourself, but on the other, it disincentivizes good aiming and resource management. 
- Inventory management was very fun and led to a ton of tension trekking back and forth from the item boxes. 
- The lack of dodge or side-step felt weird; like it makes sense to do a 180 around when a zombie is lunging at you. It also felt weird how some of the more scripted segments didn't have the characters break into a faster jog. Look at some of Grace's 3rd person movements in Requiem. While a bit exaggerated, it's a lot more immersive to watch. 

[h3] Story [/h3]
- I felt Clair's story offered better dialogue, character development, and an overall more intriguing through line with its connection to Umbrella.
-  Leon's story was definitely entertaining, and really, it was just fun watching him. His attachment to the police station and reaction to those he came across really helped solidified his character, but I think I appreciate it more in retrospect [this was my first RE game]. I do think it's way more cheesy and some of his physical feats easily suspend disbelief with him just being a "rookie cop". 

Overall, very good. I do find this the hardest to go back to out of the modern RE games because of Mr. X and the adaptive difficult, but this is honestly subject to personal preference. The location's are iconic and very well designed.

I wish I could give a mixed review on this game. I don't hate it or anything. But I won't sing praises either. I've never played the original Resident Evil so this is coming from a fresh perspective.

The game looks great and runs amazing on old hardware. The gameplay is ok and scratches a specific itch for completionists. Running around collecting things is fun. Outside of that there's nothing amazing of note. It's a typical AAA game. The ride is fun if you turn your brain off. Unfortunately there's nothing rewarding about what you do game wise, let me explain:

The game feels like it's meant to be experienced as if you're watching a movie. This means being smart about ammo, or fighting zombies isn't rewarding, regardless of the difficulty you play at. Running around to get extra gun parts won't make you stronger. Killing zombies with the upgraded gun vs normal gun feels the same. Killing zombies feel like it's based on luck. Sometimes the zombies stay down permanently, sometimes they get back up. Ammo is provided at a confusing pace. Exploring doesn't net you more. It's as if the game just wants you to run and gun to the next cutscene.

Well the game still looks very pretty and very cinematic. Okay I can get behind that. Just turn your brain off. I've played titanfall 2, I love being put in the middle of a cinematic set piece. I follow the story, I enjoyed the game every step of the way. Until I get to the end, and the ending was just, a cliff hanger? 

This is when the game turns. The game tells me that to experience the full story, I have to play as the other character, Leon. Except when I start the game as Leon, I go through the same levels, the same puzzles, the same boss fights. And now I'm also going and talking to the characters I should not be talking to because Claire (the other character) talked to them already! Some characters die at a time inconsistent with what I remember from Claire's story? Is this an alternate world? But then why do the two characters link up and meet as if the other story was canon? Why make this confusing on a story level? I already gave it a pass on the gameplay, the least they could do is keep the story consistent so they don't throw me off??? And that's when the game went from fun, to a chore.

TLDR: Brain off and go vroom. Enjoyable first half. Don't play the second half. Buy on sale. Typical AAA game.

You already know this game is good, but if you're interested in a few tips for this game, here there are:
[spoiler]
1. One of the great strengths of this game is the map. Make good use of it. Try every door to mark it on the map if you can or cannot open it. Gather every resource until the section of the map turns blue. BEWARE: Unfortunately, the map does not seem to track documents, so even if the map turns blue it does not mean you collected all the documents. You'll need many of them to unlock padlocks and such.
2. You fill find planks to board up windows. Use them as soon as you see opportunities to use them, ideally when you see a zombie at an unbroken window. Do not hoard them! It will save you ammo and make the mid/late game easier.
3. Want to explore absolutely every spot in the map? Too bad! Leon does not get the heart key, so don't bother looking for it. (I think Claire does not get the club one)
4. Flamethrowers are pretty cool but I'd highly recommend keeping most of your ammo for the plant zombies, as this is presumably the only weapon that will perma-kill them.
5. Do not waste precious ammo on G2. Just run from it until you reach the crane/container section and make use of it to dispose of G2.
6. This game is incredibly well balanced on medium difficulty. If you're not running on fumes, chances are it's better to kill a zombie if you see it, because you'll be backtracking quite a bit. It will also make your life easier when running from Mr. X. The game will make it very obvious when it's significantly better to just run away.
7. Last but not least, you do NOT need to play the first game to enjoy this one. Sure, there are a couple of small references made to the first, but this game has it's own charm and story and I think I might have been better off going into this game blind.
[/spoiler]

Hope you enjoy it as much as I did!

Resident Evil 2 (Remake) ended up being my second favorite in the series, right behind Resident Evil 4. I had a great time with it from start to finish.

Playing through both Leon and Claire’s scenarios was one of the best parts of the game. Even though the story overlaps, the two campaigns feel different enough to keep things interesting. The weapons you get, the routes you take, and the way certain events play out give each run its own feel. It never felt like I was just replaying the same thing again. I ended up finishing both scenarios and going for the true ending, which felt like the proper way to experience the full story.

The police station is easily one of my favorite settings in the series. Exploring it slowly, unlocking shortcuts, and figuring out puzzles while managing limited ammo keeps the tension high the whole time. The game does a really good job making you think about every bullet and every room you walk into.

Mr. X is also a huge part of what makes the experience memorable. The first time you realize he’s actively stalking you through the building is honestly terrifying. Hearing his footsteps getting closer while you’re trying to solve a puzzle or move items around is stressful in the best way. It constantly keeps you on edge.

I know the original Resident Evil 2 had four scenarios that were more distinct from each other, and some people were hoping the remake would replicate that system more closely. Even with that change, I still think the two-scenario structure here works really well and delivers a great experience.

Overall, it’s a fantastic remake with great pacing, tense exploration, and two really enjoyable campaigns. Between Leon and Claire’s stories, the creepy atmosphere of the Raccoon City Police Department, and the constant pressure from enemies like Mr. X, it’s a game that’s easy to come back to and replay.

RE2 was by all means an amazing title to the franchise. To the combat, the simple but amazing story for 2 new characters, and puzzles, this game was the most enjoyable to me so far. The guns that both Leon and Claire get are both super fun to use, The high powered pistol, grenade launcher shotgun, and SMG with Claire was a lot of fun to use, maybe more than Leons flamethrower and Pump shotgun. I did think Leons story was all be it, a little cheesy, but the romance between him and Ada is sure to continue later down the series, and Leon making his main focus to not only protect the city but also help Ada destroy the G-virus was awesome. I did think Claires story won me over more, as Claire is not a police officer like Leon, Jill, or any past characters we've played as. She is just a normal citizen, at least that's what you would think until she starts moving like she is a trained officer of the law. She optionally decided to 1v1 Birkin on his 3rd stage instead of running away. And on the 4th stage she decided to square up with him all to protect Sherry, who is the main focus for Claire after figuring out that Chris is on "vacation" in Europe and her main focus then becomes saving this little girl and getting her to safety no matter what it takes. Its all so last of us coded and that's maybe why I liked Claires story more. The addition of the loot pouches was an amazing addition into the game and I wish looking back at it that RE1 had the same as it would've made it more enjoyable for me if so. One thing I felt this game needed more of was bosses and the lack of. It tries to fill the game with "stages" rather than more bosses as opposed to RE1 and RE0, as Birkin has over 5 stages if you're doing the true ending, and Mr. X has multiple chase sequences and the final boss with Leon. Not to say I did not enjoy either bosses because they were both amazing and fun but I still believe they could've added a little more. One example is the Plant 43 room, instead of making grass zombies come to life they could've made that room a full blown plant boss like RE1, but since its evolved it would come to life and attack you from all over the arena, with its heart/eye exposed at certain points for the character to shoot. I also think a cool animal boss could've been done because I really liked the animal bosses in the past games ( No I am not counting the crocodile that chases you for literally 30 seconds and dies ). To end this long review on a short note, even though the game has its issues ( as every game does ) its still my favorite of the franchise right now. It has the combat, simple but cool story that is perfect for both characters, fun and engaging puzzles, and great bosses and chase sequences. So with all that being said, my official rating for RE2 would have to be a 9/10.

Heck, even the "Quickdraw Army" (that starting pistol I was complaining about) is better against bosses at the end of the game than it is against regular zombies, which should be child's play to dispatch by that point.

When compared to other REs, this remake was clearly trying to hit the survival-horror genre harder than the other games in the series with Leon as the main protagonists. With the release of Requiem, I thought I’d finally post my final review of RE2 that had been sitting in my drafts.

At its core, the Resident Evil series has always been a “survival horror” puzzle game first, and an action game second. However, every RE game still plays a bit differently, so if you really enjoyed one, you may not enjoy another. RE2, in particular, has a lot of backtracking and is riddled with puzzles… which is honestly not my usual cup of tea. I very much preferred the gameplay style of RE4 (2005), where it was more action focused, and less puzzle oriented. On top of that, the true ending also required two playthroughs, which did not sound that great at first. However, this was how RE was originally played. When I first looked at the achievements for this game, I thought “Nah, I’d have to play the game 6x to get all this”. But after I finished my first playthrough, I actually enjoyed it so much that I am now working towards the challenge of 100%, and I actually really recommend the second playthrough.

I really respect horror games that don’t solely rely on jump scares to scare you, and RE2 is one of those that really use the atmosphere and music (or lack thereof) to keep you on your toes. If you are careful, you can mostly hear the zombies or lickers in the next room. Or, if you don’t care, you can also just run through the dark corridors, get jumped on, and get freaked out, but that’s on you. Still, there were still several jump scares as it is /still/ a horror game… be careful opening lockers, and watch out for the ceilings ;)

Story and characters are pretty basic, nothing mind blowing but also not bad. It works very well with the gameplay, and that’s all you need sometimes. (I do actually love the characters though) On standard difficulty, inventory management is not too terrible, as there are just the right amount of expansion slots and save rooms at the perfect distances. Resource management may be tricky depending on your playstyle, but ammo was still quite generous and I wouldn’t worry about it too much if you’ve explored quite thoroughly. (Just don’t kill every single zombie that you see). Mr. X may be a pain for some people, but this mf couldn’t catch me even once (ex Dead by Daylight player here - just lead him to the other side of the police station before doing anything on the side you need to be at). On hardcore difficulty, ammo does become more scarce, and you have a lot less inventory slots to deal with. I don’t have much to comment on the puzzles itself because I don’t like running around without knowing what to do (also I’m stupid) so I did cheat a bit with just having a guide telling me the general area of where I’m supposed to go.

A lot of people only play the game once through the perspective of one character, but to see the full story, I really recommend a second run of the second character. I’ve played a lot of games that require a second playthrough and they fall into one of two categories: 1) It was a slog to get through because it was too identical to the first run, or 2) enough elements of the second playthrough were changed enough to keep it interesting. RE2 is the latter thankfully. For the second run, the story still takes place in pretty much the same setting and order of main events, but there are several new areas you are able to access, with a few puzzle items now in different rooms, as well as enemies spawning in new locations to keep you on your toes. (I will never forget the horror of suddenly hearing Mr. X’s footsteps out of NOWHERE in the 2nd playthrough because they didn’t do a cutscene intro like in the first playthrough). There are also NPCs that are unique to Claire and Leon’s story, resulting in enough cutscene diversity to make it different enough from the first playthrough. You may think you know the way through the second playthrough, but you will be surprised.

If you played Leon first, you will unlock Claire (2nd run), and if you played Claire first, you will unlock Leon (2nd run). There isn’t much reason to do the first run with both characters unless you want 100% achievements as both the first/second runs are identical - it’s just the order you choose to play the character as that is different. From what I’ve read, it seems fans typically suggest to play as Claire for the first run, and Leon for the second. (I did the opposite though because I just wanted to see my babygirl Leon first)

A perfect example of a high-quality, well-optimized remake, the kind that almost never happens in modern gaming.
From the very first minutes, the game (and its game design) cleverly triggers that nostalgia for the old RE2 on PS1, but without the “graphics shock” of going back to a great classic that aged visually.
The engine is fast and well optimized: even on an old GTX 1650 Ti with only 4GB of VRAM, the game runs on medium-high settings with stable FPS and still looks beautiful.
Summary: if you want a remake that respects the original, feels modern, and doesn’t run like trash, this is it. One of those rare cases where “remake” actually means “upgrade".

Update: 
P.S. For the first couple of hours, this felt like a near-perfect remake and a great survival horror game. Then the shiny presentation wore off and the game revealed how mechanically dated and rigid it really is. Beneath the modern visuals, there is an old, stale framework of backtracking, arbitrary puzzles, and repetitive busywork, with almost no meaningful gameplay evolution, no memorable set pieces, and barely any story to keep things going. The opening promises far more than the rest of the game ever delivers.

Resident Evil 2 is my first game in this franchise. I owned it for a while, and with my friend's growing interest in the franchise and with me wanting to get into it eventually, I thought this would be the perfect time to start.

The game mostly delivers in its graphics and atmosphere.
Every time you leave the main area, you realize a tonal shift, with the sound design amplifying every single thing you hear. It isn't just the rain, but, for example, zombies that manage to break through the windows make it clear that you're not in some kind of impenetrable fortress, that every hour you waste, the ammo becomes less and the threats greater.
Another thing I loved was the charming animation. I'm not sure if this is due to budget constraints, but whenever you interact with an object, you see it moving on its own or something floating into place. There are barely any instances where you see the protagonist directly interacting with these during gameplay segments. It has tons of charm due to it feeling like something I would see in an old game, which perfectly enhances this "old but new"-feel this remake has.

Gameplay-wise, it's fine for the most part.
My favorite part wasn't the gunplay, the bosses, or the horror, but instead the puzzles and inventory management.
Most of the puzzles are rather straightforward and can be solved by simply finding the right key, a letter, or an object; however, the item management really makes it work. You can inspect all the items you collect, and sometimes while inspecting, you'll see a button prompt, meaning that you can interact with it some more. Every time these popped up, even if it was just to simply open a box, it felt sort of magical, since it makes these items feel a little more tangible.
What's also great is that you can combine some of the items. At the beginning it's rather simple. See ammo? Combine it with the ammo you already have to not waste an inventory slot. Though, the more you progress, the more you start looking for stuff to combine to be more efficient and to avoid wasting any space. Occasionally, you also find progression items to combine. Stuff like putting a battery in something should not be this fun, but it is.

Unfortunately, I can't really say the same for the combat and horror part.
Resident Evil 2's atmosphere manages to make you feel dread, but during the enemy encounters it's missing for me.
Zombies feel more like a hassle to fight. You shoot them down, then you pass them. Eventually they stand up for round 2, and every time I'm not scared, overwhelmed, or even happy to do more battling. Instead I think, "How many times do we have to teach you this lesson, old man", and either shoot them down for the final time or walk right past them. Most of the combat here isn't a whole lot of fun, as you don't feel like you're in a tight spot. The only exception is when the game combines the zombies with these mutants that only react to sound. That is the single time it really makes you weigh your options and think about the risks you might be willing to take to clear the room or save ammo for tougher moments.
Sadly, the boss fights aren't interesting either - I would even say they're worse. Pretty much every boss feels like I'm doing the exact same strategy. Walk in circles to avoid the attack, build up a little more distance, then shoot a few times, and repeat. None of the battles discourage this tactic, making every single boss feel like they're the exact same.

The least interesting part, though, is the story.
I enjoyed the worldbuilding with all the additional lore and the letters. At the end, some of the puzzle pieces connect and manage to create a proper mental picture of what happened, and even Claire's story is somewhat interesting.
Leon, on the other hand...man, I feel nothing. He's just your basic goody-two-shoes cop, who is a bit naive but means well. Ada is not really intriguing, even though her gameplay makes her seem like she could be. None of the dialogue here feels truly natural or believable, and the moment the ending credits rolled, I genuinely was confused and asked myself, "That's it?"
In addition, the story also doesn't truly benefit from the two scenarios. Claire and Leon always meet, and ideally both stories should complement each other, but instead we get two timelines. Both stories can't really happen without the other one contradicting it, so I'm more confused by how any of this is supposed to make sense or work in tandem with each other.
At the end of the day, I really couldn't care for anything character- nor story-wise, leading to a lot of the worldbuilding doing the heavy lifting.

Overall, Resident Evil 2 is alright, with some things, such as the riddles and item management, being pleasant surprises. The other issues, however, feel like they constantly contradict each other. It's trying to be a scary game, but every combat encounter is a chore. It wants me to care for the story, but both campaigns shoot each other in the foot. 7/10.

Zombie media has gone so far off into its own corner, that I was legitimately surprised that this is the second scariest Resident Evil game I've played (The first being 7). This remake takes gameplay and control inspiration from RE4, but feels much more like an actual survivor horror game. 

+ Beautifully reimagined locations
+ Controls better then any other 3rd person Resident Evil game
+ The zombies are legitimately scary, the fact burning bodies is the only way to truly count them as dead for good means you're always at least a bit tense. It adds so much to the already incredible atmosphere.
+ Use of lighting and shadows to keep things spooky
+ Tyrant is a fantastic "Unkillable Stalker" villain, with a great uncannily unsettling design and terrifyingly heavy footfalls. 
+ A fantasticly Resident Evil plot, still maintaining the old horror movie cheese, but with an updated layer of seriousness that balances terror and fun wonderfully. 

- The second run is pretty mediocre. It's still worth doing, as it's doable in a weekend, but you're just kind of following your original playthrough's footsteps with some notes. 

 That's really the only negative I could think of. This game is fantastic. I truly understand why Resident Evil 2 is such a beloved classic. I've played plenty of remakes and remasters that either change what made the original shine, or end up just shining a light on how poorly the game has aged. This remake shows how far Resident Evil has come, while putting the strengths of the original 2 on full display.

Overall Rating: Masterclass (Action Horror)

I was never an avid Resident Evil player in the past, but I knew how iconic the franchise was so I would pick up their games while on big sales incase I ever decided to give them a go. Now, I am three games deep into the Resident Evil universe and am so glad for it. I started with RE4R at the recommendation of my friend and enjoyed the survival action aspect of the game but never really felt too challenged, I knew I could always roundhouse kick my way out of a tight spot. I finished just in time for Requiem and thought it was fantastic, the contrast of survival on one hand and action on the other played off each other very well. I had RE2R left in my library so I thought it would be fitting to finally check out Leons origin story and wow what an absolute gem of a game, easily my favorite so far. The blend of survival action and survival horror was perfect. You never felt over geared but at the same time you never felt like you were in too bad of shape to press on, but some encounters would require a little brain power and perhaps some reloads. I liked the way the infected played, they are slow and lumbering but can be a problem at grappling range and you couldn't always count on your melee to counter. It was cool how you never knew how much ammo you were going to need to finish them off or if they would even actually die the first time, it made you think very methodically in most situations. The looming threat of Mr. X also added a nice stress factor knowing you were constantly being hunted. Running from safe room to safe room, looking over the map to plan your next move. The puzzles were fun as well, some more difficult than others but still very manageable. RE2R seems to give you less direction on where to find what your looking for than the other games, this adds a nice component to the survival horror element as you have to carefully comb every room or risk having to double back and waste more time and resources. Overall I would rate this game a solid 9/10. It is extremely well rounded and I would recommend to anyone who is a fan of the genre and also those who are not, as I once was but now am.

Although RE2R is very faithful when it comes to the main story, I did notice that some areas were missing / replaced or changed beyond recognition. That being said, I personally prefer the original over the Remake, as the original's atmosphere is simply unmatched, and it also tells the story in a much more engaging and believable way. Resident Evil 2 Remake had me stressed in the best way possible. From the second you step into the police station, the atmosphere just hits. It’s dark, quiet, and you always feel like something is about to go wrong.

The zombies aren’t just basic enemies either — they’re actually scary. They move slow, but they don’t stay down easily. Every bullet feels important. Sometimes I’d hesitate to shoot because I didn’t want to waste ammo. That survival tension is what makes it so good.

And then there’s that feeling when you hear footsteps getting closer and you realize you’re not alone… I was genuinely nervous exploring certain areas.

The puzzles are satisfying without being annoying, and the map design is smart. Unlocking shortcuts and slowly mastering the police station feels rewarding. It’s not just running and shooting — it’s thinking, managing resources, and staying calm under pressure.

Visually, the game looks amazing. The lighting, rain, and character details make everything feel realistic and immersive. It’s one of those games where you stop and just appreciate how polished it is.

It’s scary, intense, and incredibly well-made. Whether you’re new to the series or a long-time fan, this remake proves how a classic game should be modernized.

Honestly, it’s survival horror done right.

[b]Resident Evil 2[/b]

[i]A survival horror game where every bullet, every step, and every wrong turn matters.[/i]

[b]Core Gameplay Loop[/b]
The game revolves around exploration, puzzle solving, and carefully chosen combat. You move through interconnected areas unlocking shortcuts, collecting key items, and slowly expanding the map. Progression feels deliberate — you rarely brute force your way forward, you plan routes and manage threats.

[b]Combat & Enemy Pressure[/b]
Combat is intentionally tense rather than empowering. Weapons feel impactful but ammunition is limited, forcing you to decide whether enemies are worth engaging or simply avoiding. Zombies are slow but persistent, soaking up bullets and making encounters feel risky rather than routine.

Enemy placement plays a big role in the tension. Clearing a room doesn’t always guarantee safety later, so you’re constantly weighing short-term relief against long-term resource loss.

[b]Movement & Control Feel[/b]
Movement is smooth and responsive, which is important because positioning matters in almost every encounter. Dodging around enemies, lining up precise shots, and navigating tight corridors becomes second nature over time.

The over-the-shoulder perspective keeps visibility tight, which amplifies tension when entering new rooms or hearing something moving just out of sight.

[b]Inventory Management[/b]
Inventory space is limited, and this becomes a constant strategic puzzle. Carry too many weapons and you won’t have space for key items. Carry too many healing items and you may run out of ammo when it matters.

Item boxes provide relief, but planning what to bring with you for each run through an area is a key part of the gameplay loop.

[b]Puzzles & World Design[/b]
Puzzles are integrated naturally into the environment. Finding keys, unlocking shortcuts, and discovering hidden rooms makes the map feel like a large mechanical puzzle rather than a series of disconnected levels.

Backtracking isn’t filler — it’s part of the tension as previously explored spaces evolve with new threats.

[b]Replayability[/b]
Multiple character routes and scenario variations encourage replaying the game. Knowing the map on later playthroughs shifts the experience from survival to optimisation, which adds another layer of mechanical depth.

[b]Verdict - 10/10 [/b]
[b]Resident Evil 2[/b] excels at mechanical tension. Limited resources, tight level design, and deliberate combat create a survival experience where planning and awareness matter far more than raw firepower.

Although I have several complaints regarding the incorporation of certain modern trends which I find annoying regardless of the game they are found in, I would still recommend this remake for anyone looking for a good action horror experience. For a survival horror experience play the classic game.

I personally prefer the original 1998 survival horror classic as it is completely different experience. This remake being an action horror game does not and cannot replace the original survival horror game. One should play both if there is opportunity.

The original has a 1950s B science fiction monster movie cheese that I absolutely adore. This remake tries to be completely serious and visceral horror, at least when the characters aren't spoiling the atmosphere by commenting every few minutes. The remake also focuses much more on combat than the original.

Personal Annoyances With Modern Trends:

1. I do not like when the characters speak or physically react outside of cutscenes. I do not need the character I am playing to react to things, I can react just fine on my own. In addition, not every character needs to be a snarky, sarcastically clever, disrespectful, and/or obnoxious. The limited number of phrases combined with the frequency of the comments is distracting and in my opinion it destroys any tension the game should be building. It is no different than if someone beside me were constantly commenting, making jokes, and quips, while I play. To mitigate this and make the game tolerable to play and replay, I muted voice volume and turned off subtitles. If not for this I probably would never replay this game, it is that annoying to me. Unfortunately, muting the voices and turning off subtitles effectively renders cutscenes completely unintelligible but as I have been familiar with the story for decades at this point I typically skip them anyway.

2. Breakable knife. I detest weapon durability in games and this is possibly the dumbest use of the mechanic in my opinion. Yes, there are nearly a dozen combat knives which can be picked up throughout the game but it is a needless nuisance which distracts from simply playing and enjoying the game. This hassle can be avoided by unlocking or purchasing the infinite knife.

3. The game feels needlessly bloated and padded. I find my desire to revisit the game greatly impacted knowing that by the end I am not really having fun anymore. Even with infinite ammo weapons unlocked, it feels overly long and I would rather play and complete a run in the original game and save 4-8 hours of my life for other shorter but overall more enjoyable gaming experiences.

4. Modern video games really do take themselves too seriously, especially those aiming for "realism" whatever that means in a video game. This is a video game, I have been playing video games for nearly 40 years, I do not now nor have I ever believed what is happening on the screen is real. If a game is going to be about a virus mutating people and creatures into monsters requiring the player to confront and dispatch or escape said monsters, may I suggest that leaning into the absurdity is far more entertaining than for everything to be played straight. Maybe it is because, with only a handful of exceptions, I have not been scared by a horror game since 2004. Maybe its because developers tone down horror now because some people find it "too scary". Either way if you aren't going to go all in on the horror and allow it to be truly scary at least lean into the absurdity and make it entertaining.

5. Excessive sign posting. I will commend the developers for not splashing yellow paint everywhere but putting interaction icons on everything is just as bad. Any game that incorporates these cannot claim to contain exploration. For all the time developers spend trying to add "realism" to video games they sure do implement the most unrealistic ways of pointing the player to the next destination.

UPDATE:

I have now put nearly 80 hours into this game and in doing so I have identified several other annoyances.

6. Auto Saves and infinite saves. Knowing I can save whenever I want and even if I don't the game will autosave removes an element of fear and survival from "Survival Horror". This is proof the game is action horror not survival horror. Additionally, auto saves sign post boss battles thus giving away the surprise and removing the shock value. Yes, you can play hardcore mode, but that is its own annoyance covered below.

7. Hold / Tap button to do a thing prompts. Just let me press the button once, why must I hold and or tap its not immersive, you already destroyed that with the prompt to begin with. These are just remnants of QTEs and they should also be forgotten.

8. The second or B scenario pistols. Including scenario specific weapons is fine forcing the player to use them is not. Replacing all handgun ammo pickups with special ammo for the scenario specific weapons forcing the player to manually craft regular handgun ammo to use the normal pistols adds nothing to the game and is the very definition of arbitrary and asinine. It doesn't help that I have never cared for the ammo crafting mechanic even going back to the original RE3. Just give me normal ammo pick-ups, crafting a limited combination of ammo doesn't add anything meaningful to the game its just padding.

9. The second or B scenarios in general are just lazily implemented offering nothing new or interesting to engage the player. Other than the additional final boss, there no reason to ever play the second scenario.

10. Bullet sponge zombies. In the world of Resident Evil it has been established on multiple occasions that a single head shot can and will put a zombie down for good. So why then can I turn a zombie's head to mush in this game and they keep coming? It made some sense in the classic games because aiming at the head was not really an option so all shots from the pistol were shown as body shots except for critical hits. If the developers are going to allow the player to directly aim for the head there is no excuse for a single head shot to not bring a zombie down in game. The simplest solution to this would be to either add more zombies or reduce ammo pick-ups or both. But doing that would make this a survival horror game like the original rather than the action horror the franchise has been since RE4.

11. Boss battles feel excessive, further proof the game is action horror and not survival horror.

12. Hardcore mode, while removing auto saves and requiring ink ribbons to save really doesn't limit the player that much given there are at least a dozen ink ribbons throughout the game. Hardcore mode does exacerbate and amplify other annoyances. Zombies can absorb more bullets, even to the head. Boss battles feel even more excessive.

13. Mr. X is not scary, he is annoying. When I first played the original Mr. X was scary but on every subsequent playthrough he was just annoying. In the remake Mr. X never scared me but Capcom doubled down on him being annoying. On subsequent playthroughs one realizes he is almost completely scripted just like the original and the player can minimize the number of encounters with him if tasks are performed in a specific order. I don't think this is a bad game, but I also think it's extremely overrated and it made some mistakes that are completely unacceptable, so as always I rather take a stance that adds to the conversation instead of being a seal clapping like everybody. Here's some VERY negative aspects of this game.

- Secret adaptive difficulty that punishes players for playing well and rewards bad players for doing badly, plus inconsistent zombie HP and damage in the entire game system, this kind of randomness does NOT have a place in survival horror nor even was on RE classic survival horror era, this is made to please modern audiences that do not want to engage with the options the games gives to them to play on a smart way

- Almost all the writing and dialogue is worse than the OG RE2, in fact the entire game is an insult to the OG game's writing, unlike RE1 Remake that actually respected its source material and expanded on it, instead RE2 changes things to make them worse, better voice acting and "pretty graphics" DO NOT make a game's writing good or better

- No real A/B scenarios, they didn't even need to create 4 story lines like the OG, all they had to do was create a real seamless A and B route but they didn't even attemp to do that so even if  you ignore the OG game writing you can't even make it make sense timeline-wise on its own

- Some filler scenes part of the game that add 0 to the plot of the character, Claire's conflict with Irons being probably the worst of them all and the sewers "expanded and reworked" is also a perfect example of more being less/worse

- What excuse did Capcom have for ANYTHING related to bad writing, lore, dialogue and timeline issues? NONE, they have FOUR original RE2 scenarios, Outbreak spin-offs, multiple book and manga adaptations of RE2 to make a retold with everything fitting in a way that made sense, and they didn't even TRY

- Before you say "but nobody plays RE for the story, that is correct, however here's the problem, the OG RE2 was THE (classic) RE game with the most attention to lore, that's why it's such an issue all of these bizarre mistakes Capcom did, and making the writting WORSE isn't excusable neither

There's always a caveat with Resident Evil games that while they are quite scary and spooky, they're ultimately pretty scripted. Each room is a separate cell, monsters usually do not cross artificial boundaries. It's probably why they're so replayable; knowledge overrides fear, most tension subsumed by route planning. 

They've experimented with shattering these barriers before: Resi 1 Remake literally broke down doors, merging cells unexpectedly and Nemesis in 3 chases you across the city. But it's manageable. Even within one run, the unexpected becomes the expected. Nemesis isn't really going through each door, he's spawning in each cell as part of a scripted chase. 
There is never a constant breach of the player's space. Rarely danger in "cleared" rooms, rarely a reset of how to navigate an entire zone. Take your time. Enjoy the sights! Do the fun puzzles, reap the rewards. Because Umbrella are about to drop off a curveball seven feet tall. 

Mr.X, the fedora-wearing, stalkermaxxing freak, is the series' most electric antagonist. The police station is no longer a police station, it's a hunting ground. Your turf is assailed; this is a shared space and you need to move, move, move. 
Heavy footsteps batter the room above, doors are slammed closer... and closer...
Some safe rooms provide brief moments of solace, but you'll still hear him stomping through the very same labyrinth that your objective just so happens to be in. Good luck. 

While I respect the original Resi 2, this mechanic puts it over the original for me. It's a very different game operating on a very solid, familiar foundation. Less a B movie and more horror-thriller, charm turned down and grounded characterisation/tone/atmosphere turned up. Both are very different games and actually benefit from the other's existence. With sensibilities of the times being so far apart, who's really surprised that this is the case?

The only disappointment is the implementation of the B campaign. It's far less reactive to the A playthrough, and doesn't really line-up very well — as a result the player has to morph a weird canonical sludge together in their head for the plot beats to fully make sense. Still, it's fun to actually play through cause the gameplay loop is so sick, especially on hardcore. 
Anyone who's new to the series and is put off by 1's remake, start here. It nails everything great about the franchise and then some. Just hold onto your flash grenades: Mr. X is down bad and he's waiting right in front of your favourite objective marker.

At the top of the survival horror genre, and one of Capcom's finest.

There's not much to say about this game that's not already been said. RE2 is one of the greatest remakes in video game history as well as one of the best games in its own genre, and RE2's competition is fierce even within its own series. Everything feels deliberate from its gunplay, enemy placement, boss design, level design, and replayability. The developers of this game wanted you to play it multiple designs and refine your skill and understanding of the game. It's marvelous and a joy to experience.

Not to sound hyperbolic, but I struggle to find a fault. Perhaps the late game pacing is a problem, and the HDR implementation is poor, but that's about it. The moment to moment gameplay is a blast and exploring the interconnected map scratches that harder and harder to reach discovery itch that's becoming so rare in games. For a game that's actually quite repetitious in its level design, it never quite overstays its welcome. Backtracking through the environments feels rewarding because they constantly give you new tools to discover new items and increase your survivability. The reward system is sewn masterfully into the narrative and allows you to refine your route in consecutive playthroughs. There's few other games like it. 

I can't recommend it enough, especially for its common sale price of $10. This is a must play.

I couldn't possibly glaze this game enough, it's easily one of my favorite games of all time. It hits the perfect balance between horror games that focus almost entirely on horror and leave you nearly defenseless, and "horror" games that are essentially just shooters with a horror theme. The series would move further and further in the latter direction following the third game, but here is the sweet spot. It gives you enough ammo and resources to handle whatever it throws at you but never lets you feel truly confident, you are still nervous around every corner and genuinely scared when you hear Mr X's footsteps getting closer. 

They also hit the nail on the head with replayability. To truly get the full story, you play the game once as Leon (my king) or Claire, and then once more as the character you didn't choose for the first run. It's not just the same game twice, you get to experience a parallel, but unique perspective of the events of Racoon City. To top it off, there are some banger extra challenge missions to play if you get bored of the main game.

All in all, this is a 10/10 game sure to be loved by returning fans of the series and new players alike.

Thrilling survival horror, amazing atmosphere, great exploration, fun puzzles and of course, amazing emergent moments due to the Tyrant.

If you are a newcomer to the series, this is an amazing place to start off on, as it tells the beginning of Leons side of the RE series.

The replayability is also great because of the 2 main route runs with Leon and Claire, where both get a few unique sections exclusive to them, as well as their B routes in which they get an exclusive gun, harder puzzles and a slightly different and faster progression path.

The one complaint I would have is perhaps that you can often feel bogged down with how limited your inventory space is, so you end up wasting time running back and forth offloading things to the item box or a puzzle you need to solve, however, this is part of the gameplay loop and as you learn the ins and outs of the game, you also learn to optimise when to save, what to take, what to leave and where to go.

Overall, a must play for every Resident Evil fan, even for the RE4 remake enjoyers like myself. The slower, delibarate combat, resource management and puzzling is just awesome to experience. And of course running for your life from the Tyrant.

Resident Evil 2 (2019) isn’t just a remake; it’s a masterclass in how to modernize a classic without losing its soul. Capcom managed to capture the oppressive dread of the 1998 original while delivering a technical powerhouse that feels completely cutting-edge.

Visuals: The lighting—or lack thereof—is incredible. Your flashlight cutting through the thick, wet darkness creates a constant sense of claustrophobia.

Gore Tech: The "zombie damage" system is disturbingly detailed. Seeing limbs react realistically to every shot makes the combat feel heavy and impactful.

Inventory Tetris: You are constantly weighing the value of a herb versus a key item.

Decision Making: Do you use your last three bullets to down a zombie, or do you risk a bite to save the ammo for later? This constant risk-reward loop keeps the brain engaged even when the heart is racing.

Playing through as both Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield provides two distinct flavors of the story. While they explore the same halls, their unique weapons, supporting casts (Ada Wong and Sherry Birkin), and slightly different paths offer great replayability.

"Resident Evil 2 Remake is the gold standard for the genre. It proves that you don't need 'action-movie' theatrics to be exciting—just a dark hallway, a flickering light, and the sound of something hungry around the corner."
What an unreal game. Atmosphere is so good, balanced game design, and a really fun story. Can't recommend this enough!

The last time I played Resident Evil 1 and 2 was many years ago on the original PlayStation. Revisiting Resident Evil 2 as an adult through the remake brought a strong sense of nostalgia — but also renewed excitement for the future of the franchise.

In my opinion, this remake played a major role in keeping Resident Evil relevant.

Updating the graphics and modernising the gameplay helped bring the series into a new era without losing what made it special. The RPD station especially was a highlight. Walking through those halls again — now fully realised with modern visuals and atmosphere — felt both familiar and fresh. It respected the legacy while improving on it.

I played both Leon and Claire scenarios, and experiencing both perspectives added replay value. The end boss fight was genuinely difficult at the time, which made finally overcoming it feel earned rather than handed to you.

The standout horror element for me was Mr. X. Once he starts hunting you, the tone shifts completely. Hearing his footsteps above you, not knowing when he might burst through a door, creates constant tension. In tighter environments especially, it becomes claustrophobic and urgent.

Some zombie encounters also deserve credit. The way they grab and overwhelm you up close keeps even standard enemies threatening.

My least favourite section was the Ada segment. I’ve always viewed Ada as a badass antagonist, but her playable section didn’t fully live up to that image for me. The scanner tool and puzzle design weren’t my favourite parts of the game. That said, it’s a minor criticism in an otherwise excellent remake.

It’s difficult to directly compare Resident Evil 2, 3 and 4 to Resident Evil 7 and 8. The former represent legacy Resident Evil — rooted in nostalgia and the classic formula — while the latter define the newer era of the franchise. Both are strong in their own right.

Resident Evil 2 Remake proves that a remake can honour the past while evolving for the future. For longtime fans and newcomers alike, it’s exactly how a remake should be done.
