Great remake, just as good as the original. It's familiar enough to not lose sight of the original concept, but just different enough to offer a fresh new experience.
[hr][/hr]
Visuals and sound design are top notch. They allow you to easily immerse yourself while naturally aiding the player in a lot of decision making. Color coded environmental guides are used correctly without being distracting or intrusive.

The story is believable, but a little misleading. Unlike the box art, Leon and Claire are rarely going to be fending off hordes of zombies back to back. Staying true to the original, they don't really cross paths a whole lot. Each character offers different storylines, weapons, enemy placements and puzzles. but they only fit loosely together in sequence of events.

You'll go up against the most dynamic classic zombies to date. They're durable, restless and horrific. Some will shamble around making them a harder target. They crawl across the floor and lunge at you. Many are just sleeping until you tread too close.
You really have to think about each one as their own obstacle rather than just some enemy to kill. They respond really well to limb targeting and have mechanical purposes for each. They can be a little bs at times, but only when you're taking risks.

Classic zombies aren't the only threat and each have their own behaviors and methods for dealing with them. 
The whole game is like one interconnected puzzle. All of the resources are carefully placed to get you to think about what's important. They've improved the inventory management system across the board, but you can still opt for a tougher challenge by forgoing item boxes or item slot upgrades.

Capcom made sure to encourage players to rechallenge themselves to do it faster with less resources. There's a surprising amount of game modes and unlockables for such a short game. The only thing missing is a built-in randomizer.

The weekly challenges are more interesting than they first appear. It's satisfying to complete the game under various conditions, it really changes how you tackle each situation. Getting a little medal and your name posted on their leaderboard is just the icing on top.

Resident Evil 2 Remake - Review 

Revisited this one for the first time since its release. I remembered a good amount, but I was still surprised replaying this, to see just how much I enjoy this one. 

Pros: 
- Perfect atmosphere that keeps you constantly on edge
- Locations are excellent, the police station is so iconic and fun to explore, the sewers are stressful and the lab is a fun 3rd act (one of the stronger of the entries I’ve played, as I find the 3rd act tends to be the weakest ie, RE4, RE7, RE8) 
- Gameplay is solid, gunplay isn’t as smooth as RE4, and I feel like the zombies sometimes take way too many headshots to kill, but it adds to the stress I suppose
- The inventory system is quite small, so deciding what to keep matters most here, you don’t get to change the way items are stored direction wise like in other entries (my favourite system) but it works well in its own way 
- You have to backtrack a lot, which I personally really liked. You get lost easily, but it all adds to the feeling 
- Mr. X, while not appearing a ton, always leads to some great chase scenes 
- Excellent audio design, with Atmos, you get a great sense of direction in this, and the audio design is very atmospheric with floorboards creaking, footsteps heard above, etc… 

Cons: 
- A&B storylines could’ve used more differences and don’t entirely overlap in a way that makes sense
- The dogs have terrible AI and almost never land an actual hit an can be avoided 
- Could be a bit longer (only took me 5 hours to get through one campaign) 
- Some cut enemies and weapons from the original

Overall it’s an excellent game that brought a horror classic over to a modern style in a very successful way

For some reason, I totally skipped the original. I've played RE 1 and Nemesis as a kid (not so much though), but this one flew by me. Yet it's regarded as one of the best games in the franchise, probably the best in the original trilogy. 

As I've recently started my RE journey, finally this one came on my playlist and after all the hype and memes, I've tried to avoid spoilers at all cost. How was it? Fantastic! I love it, no wonder this is considered as an example of how to remake a game. 

The good stuff:

- The atmosphere, horror tension and build up. 
- Visuals are fantastic, RE engine is such a beast, with literally zero stutters and issues I've encountered. 
- Game in general is super responsive with opening inventory, picking and combining items, loadings are super fast (I literally load game in like 2-3 seconds) etc.
- Gameplay is super addicting, gunplay is even better (headshoting a zombie while it explodes is one of the most satisfying things in gaming I've seen).
- Boss fights are good and simple enough. 
- Mr. X is great(ish) addition as a stalker enemy. His footsteps alone are tense.
- William Birkin and his phases are ICONIC. Literally the best designed monster in franchise, and one of the best designs in general! I love me some good body horror.
- Overall pacing is great, game does not overstay it's welcome.
- You would think regular zombies are just fodder, but no. Here they are actually a threat if you underestimate them. 
- Bonus content is fun.

The mid/bad stuff:

- Mr. X. He's fantastic, for the first time. After a while, at least for me, he became such a nousance and chore to deal with. And my God, his music when he shows up is hillarious (the bass drop). 
- I don't like the adaptive difficulty. If you're "good" at the game, sometimes it can take up to 10+ bullets to kill a freakin zombie. 
- G adults and sewer section in general. HORRIBLE, F*** them, I hate them and I dread the one section in sewers (don't worry, you will know what I'm talking about).
- There are lots of complaints about the cut content, and yes after seeing it, it does indeed suck that they haven't made campaigns a little more different and unique from each other. Never played the original though, so it didn't bother me, but I get the frustration for the original fans.

That's pretty much it, I literally can't complain much about this game, because it's that great! What it sets out to do, it does it extremely well! Totally recommend it, even at full price. On discount it's a steal.

Resident Evil 2 has been a game I had in my mind for a very long time ever since I stumbled across one of my favourite streamers attempting a no-hit run of it. The game looked sick as ♥♥♥♥ but I always considered myself a bit of a coward when it comes to horror games even though I actually love them.

Earlier this year I decided to give the RE saga a fair shot because it has always been alluring, and I´m really glad I did. Starting with RE1 really made the differences between that game and this one pop out. The technical improvements between the two are astonishing and I don't think it would be fair to compare both of them on those categories. Nevertheless, I was very happy to see that the spirit of the first one was kept with RE2.

Long, cramped corridors and an unrelenting, choking environment that keeps you on your toes at all times. There is barely any downtime to breathe and take a rest, partly because of how short the game can be if you know all the puzzles and bossfights in advance, but still. It's not just Mr. X putting the fear of god in you as soon as you hear his loud ass footsteps get even louder, and the fact that there's very few times when you actually don't hear them. It's also the game forcing you to overcome your fears and face the horrors in front of you. There's no two ways around many sections: sometimes you just have to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ face that annoying licker and get way too close to it to keep moving forward.

And I think that's the essence and groundwork that RE1 laid back then. Facing the struggle and moving forward in spite of it, even when you are scared to the core and barely even walking.

The way the game achieves all this is frankly amazing. Sound design is superb, and in fact it's so good that it's hard for me to explain WHY. Just the way the screams and grunts were recorded, the way they echo through the many halls and corridors and the AMAZING spatial sound that allows you to accurately pinpoint the location of even Mr. X, makes it into a truly terrifying experience. There's something inherently scary about KNOWING where something is if you do fear that thing. Being jumpscared by a silent Mr. X might give you a heart attack, but KNOWING he (or a Licker/dog/zombie/etc...) is close and getting closer.... well, that puts a kind of constant pressure on you that makes the whole game feel incredibly oppressive and stressing in a (maybe masochistic) good way.
Still, this is one of those things that you NEED to experience in order to understand. Really, my ears were delighted throughout all the game, even if it was the reason I almost CRIED (being a bit hyperbolic here...) a couple of times.

Aside from that, enemy design, lighting, level design, etc... They are all MOSTLY good. And I say mostly because there's a negative jump in quality between the RPD and the rest of the levels. While the other levels aren't bad by any means, except maybe the Sewers (EVEN THOUGH I DID ENJOY THE BOSSFIGHT AND THE CHESS PUZZLE), the RPD is just way too good and hard to come close to. It's like the Mansion from RE1, although maybe not AS good for me. The mansion being all a giant ass puzzle was really fun and amazing for me so it's hard to top that even for the RPD, but the police station has been memorable all the way through and I hold it close to my heart :3. The puzzles, storytelling, ambience, design, interconnection... It's just REALLY good.

Leon and Claire are an absolute BANGER of a cast, and while I think Leon is the superior character (of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ course, it's LEON), Claire's B run with Sherry and Annette's storyline struck me harder emotionally than Leon and Ada's tenure. Feels like that run fleshes the game out better as a whole, while Leon's run is more focused on himself and how this forged the Leon we all know and love.

The combat is good. Nothing to write home about, honestly, especially after experiencing what RE4 brings to the table. It's simple, maybe a bit too simple and lacking for that reason, but it kinda just gets the job done. It's there, it's needed, but sometimes it feels like it should offer more (as it does in RE4).

All in all, this game is a masterpiece in horror. It's scary as hell and not in a jumpscare-y way, but rather by oppressing and stressing you out, keeping you tense all the way through, ESPECIALLY at the start.

I picked up Resident Evil 2 Remake thinking I'd be bashing in some zombie heads and then everything would be fine. What I actually got was two campaigns of pure anxiety, heart attacks every 15 minutes, and a personal vendetta against Hardcore mode.

First of all, the atmosphere? Immaculate. The Raccoon City Police Department is basically a haunted house designed by someone who hates you personally. The lighting and sound design are so good that I started side-eyeing my own hallway at home.

Leon and Claire both feel fantastic to play. Their campaigns are intense, well-paced, and just different enough to justify multiple runs. And then there’s Mr. X. This man does not walk - he power-struts. The moment you hear those heavy footsteps, it’s over. I have never been more motivated to solve a puzzle faster in my life.

Now let’s talk about Hardcore mode.
Whoever designed Hardcore mode clearly wakes up every morning and chooses violence.

Limited saves with ink ribbons? Bold.
Enemies that refuse to die? Brave.
Two lickers and Mr. X in the same hallway? Personal attack.

Going for the Hardcore achievements nearly cost me my sanity. I learned the exact number of bullets required to down a zombie. I memorized optimal routes like I was studying for a final exam. I started treating every ink ribbon like it was a rare artifact. I really started questioning my life choices.

But here’s the thing: it’s so satisfying. The tension is perfectly tuned. Every resource matters. Every encounter feels earned. And when you survive with one green herb and a dream, you feel like a tactical genius.

Visually, it’s stunning. The RE Engine makes everything look disgusting in the best possible way. Zombies are horrifyingly detailed, environments drip with atmosphere, and the whole experience feels polished to perfection.

Now let’s talk about Leon.

Sir.

This man shows up to his first day on the job and immediately handles a city-wide zombie apocalypse with better composure than I handle mild inconveniences.
10/10. Would absolutely survive Raccoon City again.
For Leon (and Ada, but mostly Leon).

RU:
Resident Evil 2 — это редкий пример того, как нужно делать ремейки. Capcom не просто подтянули текстуры, а полностью пересобрали классику 1998 года, сохранив при этом тот самый густой дух «ужаса в замкнутом пространстве». Игра построена на движке RE Engine, и выглядит она потрясающе даже спустя несколько лет после релиза.

Детализация окружения: Полицейский участок Раккун-Сити превратился из набора декораций в зловещее, дышащее место. Капли дождя на стеклах, игра света и тени в темных коридорах — всё это работает на атмосферу.

Модели персонажей: Леон и Клэр выглядят максимально реалистично. На их одежде видна грязь, кровь и намокание.

Система повреждений (Gore-система): Это, пожалуй, лучшая реализация в индустрии. От выстрелов у зомби буквально отлетают куски плоти, обнажая кости и мышцы. Это не просто «мясо» ради «мяса» — это дает четкую визуальную отдачу от стрельбы.

ENG:
Resident Evil 2 is the perfect example of how a remake should actually be done. Capcom didn't just slap on some high-res textures; they completely rebuilt the 1998 classic from the ground up, all while nailing that thick, "claustrophobic horror" vibe the original was known for.

The game runs on the RE Engine, and honestly? It still looks drop-dead gorgeous even a few years after launch.

🎨 Graphics and Atmosphere
Environmental Detail: The Raccoon City Police Department isn't just a set anymore—it feels like a living, breathing nightmare. Between the rain streaking down the windows and the way the light dances with the shadows in those pitch-black hallways, the atmosphere is just off the charts.

Character Models: Leon and Claire look incredibly lifelike. You can actually see the grime, blood, and soak-factor on their clothes as things get messy.

The Gore System: This is arguably the best implementation in the entire industry. When you blast a zombie, chunks of flesh literally fly off, exposing bone and muscle. It's not just "gore for the sake of gore"—it gives you this super satisfying visual feedback every time you pull the trigger.

You're not a superhero with unlimited ammo and confidence; you are just trying to survive, counting bullets, listening to footsteps, and debating the whether opening that door is bravery or pure stupidity. So this was my very first dive into the Resident Evil universe and let me start by saying: I am the furthest thing from horror fan. I am scared of every sound in real life, so me playing horror games is unlikely...

And yet… this game had me hooked.

What really surprised me was how perfectly it balances combat, puzzles, and horror. It’s not just you walking down a dark hallway and wait to get jump-scared(Some exceptions are made). The jump scares? Scary but manageable. They got me some times, sure.
But the Tyrant?

That man is a problem.

I played most of my run with scuffed audio, so I couldn’t properly hear him stomping around. Which means he would just… appear. I open the door and he's standing there. Resident Evil 2 Remake offers a masterfully well done survival horror experience that everyone fans of the genre should experience 

You know it, I know it. This game is absolute peak and arguably top 3 of the entire franchise.

Survival Horror Done Right -
The very core of this game is all about survival horror and it’s safe to say that they absolutely nailed this aspect. The raccoon city police department goes down as easily one of the greatest explorable areas in gaming and the detail and passion put into this area is incredible. You genuinely feel like you’re exploring an actual lived in area and uncovering all its discoverable rooms and items is nothing short of pure dopamine overload. It works as a horror set piece extremely well too, having super dark corridors and hallways and the pure silence + deadly enemies hiding behind every ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ corner waiting to inappropriately touch you gives an extreme sense of dread and tension to the player. Every second being in this area is 10/10 for me, simply one of the best horror experiences I’ve ever seen in a game. 
Also….Mr X definitely gonna give it to ya in this game if you weren’t ready. 

Story - (specifically Leon’s) 
Story is good too, rookie cop’s first day turns into a complete and utter ♥♥♥♥ show and how he slowly progresses into the goofy, badass (and possibly sexy) lovable character we all know and love

His relationship with Ada is also really charming and likable, you buy into their chemistry and the actors do a great job making them simply enjoyable to see together and how their story progresses and ends I found to be surprisingly more emotional and investing than I remember (tho I wish there was more of them together)  

Gameplay -
This game is really fun to play, you will be naturally short on ammo and heals often but it helps make exploring and finding resources always worth it and feel rewarding. Guns are all solid, shotguns in particular feels amazing since you can take a little more off the top than the pistol and the zombies actually stay ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dead. 

Yeaaaa..zombies are kinda annoying at times with just how much lead they can tank and still not go down (least on hardcore) shooting off legs is usually much more viable and easier but still leaves them alive and an active nuisance to you anytime you gotta tread past an area with them which is an element I do like and understand but sometimes can lead to frustration since you almost always have to confront enemies even if you got 2 bullets to your name. Don’t get me wrong I love the aspect of having to face enemies in tough situations, the tension is unreal but at times it can feel more frustrating than fun if that makes any sense. 

Bosses -
Bosses are mostly decent to mildly annoying at times, I find the areas of these fights to be kinda awkward fighting around and the movement doesn’t really allow you to dodge effectively if at all. The tyrant boss at the end of the game had this cheap one shot gimmick that annoyed tf outta me on hardcore since I had no ammo.

The second half of the game outside of RPD I don’t think is quite as good since the area isn’t as polished and detailed as RPD but they’re all consistently enjoyable and I liked the look of the lab towards the end and the set piece of it. The campaigns are kinda short, taking about 5-9 hours on average but the pacing is done well and doesn’t drag anything out. 

RE2r is an experience that must be played if you’re into horror, it’s so impressive just how well done this game turned out and it easily goes down as one of the best remakes we’ve ever seen. Do yourself a favor and play this game 9/10

Even as I return for what must be the nth time to the Resident Evil 2 remake, I am still left absolutely flabbergasted at how much of an amazing survival horror game it is. The Raccoon City Police Department is one of the best, most intricately designed locations I have ever had the pleasure of exploring and mastering. The gunplay feels excellent. The enemies are just difficult enough to never turn into either bullet sponges or push-overs (much of this can be attributed to the game's hidden difficulty slider that tunes enemies based on how well you're doing in your playthrough). Many of the light puzzle elements feel just right, with them breaking up the survival-horror elements with just a bit of necessary downtime and levity. The bossfights are great, and the soundtrack even more so, with it weaving through horror ambience and orchestral spectacle with pinpoint precision. And Mr. X just rules; if you know, you know.

Ultimately, the only thing that brings the entire experience down a bit for me is everything to do with the sewers. I don't particularly like either the level design (way less interconnected than other parts of the game) nor the big goop enemies (stay far away and shoot at one specific weak spot with little in the way of interesting resource management elements).

TL;DR: Fantastic game, but the part of the game that's covered with faeces brings down the experience just enough for me to not think it's a perfect game.

[h3]☣️ RE2 Remake - Masterclass in Survival Horror [/h3]
[hr][/hr]
[b]📌[u]Overview:[/u][/b]

[b]Resident Evil 2 Remake[/b] is Capcom calmly walking into a room full of modern gaming trends, ignoring every single one, and saying:
“[i]This is how you remake a classic. Don’t overthink it.[/i]”

I went in knowing the legacy but without much emotional baggage. I’d flirted with the old-school [b]RE[/b] games years ago [b]RE0, RE1, RE2, RE3, Code Veronica[/b] mostly out of curiosity, rarely commitment. Over the years my Steam library ballooned with [b]RE[/b] titles, yet I’d only actually finished [b]RE4 (2014 HD Version)[/b] and [b]RE5[/b]. Loved [b]RE4[/b]. Had dumb co-op fun with a buddy in [b]RE5[/b]. [b]RE5[/b] leaned hard into action-heavy gameplay, while [b]RE4[/b] mixed cheesy action with survival horror in a way that somehow just worked.

[b]RE0 Remastered[/b] and [b]RE6[/b]? Tried them more than once. Attention span clocked out after a couple of hours.

So I promised myself I wouldn’t buy newer [b]RE[/b] games until I cleared my [b]RE[/b] backlog. Naturally, I ignored that promise, impulse-bought everything I was missing on Steam during a recent sale 🫣, and plunged straight into [b]RE2 Remake[/b].

Best irresponsible gaming decision I’ve made in a long time.

[b]🎮 [u]Gameplay & Survival Loop:[/u][/b]

This is survival horror that doesn’t care about your comfort.

Not “[i]here’s a gun, go feel powerful.[/i]” More like “[i]here’s six bullets, one locked door, and consequences.[/i]”

Exploration is tense, resource management is borderline cruel, and every decision feels like negotiating with your future regrets. Kill a zombie now? Waste ammo. Walk past it? Enjoy meeting it again later, faster, angrier.

The RPD/Sewers/Lab are all elite-tier level designs. Compact, interconnected, and quietly malicious. You learn its layout, feel smart for five minutes, and then the game punishes that confidence immediately. Backtracking never feels like padding. Something always changes, and it’s never good news.

[b]🧩 [u]Puzzles:[/u][/b]

Actual puzzles. Imagine that.

No glowing hints. No excessive hand-holding. Just logical, environment-based puzzles that respect your intelligence and mildly mock you when you get stuck. They’re woven into the environments so naturally they feel like part of each location’s personality.

[b]🔊 [u]Sound & Music:[/u][/b]

Sound design here is doing most of the psychological damage.

Footsteps echo just long enough to make you freeze. Zombies groan from places you desperately hoped were empty. Music knows exactly when to disappear and let silence bully you. When it kicks in, it’s pure tension with zero filler.

This game proves audio alone can ruin your nerves.

[b]⚙️ [u]Visuals & Technical Polish:[/u][/b]

Still looks fantastic years later. Moody lighting without turning everything into grey sludge. Weighty animations. Zombies that look properly awful. Gore is detailed without becoming cartoonish, and damage persistence ensures enemies never feel disposable.

Technically, it’s smooth, stable, and well-optimized. 

[b]📖 [u]Story, Characters & Pacing:[/u][/b]

[b]Leon[/b] and [b]Claire[/b] both get meaningful campaigns that actually justify replaying the game. This isn’t “[i]same game, different jacket[/i].” Pacing is tight, the narrative doesn’t drag, and the game knows when to shut up and let gameplay speak.

Tone stays grounded without slipping into self-parody. Personally, I enjoyed playing as Claire more. Her run felt smoother and easier to manage overall, maybe better tools, maybe just better vibes.

[b]🔁 [u]Replayability & Modes:[/u][/b]

This is where Capcom really twists the knife.

I finished both campaigns, then went for the Second Run aiming for an S Rank as [b]Claire[/b] to see the true ending. Expected a cinematic payoff. Instead, I got one more final boss fight on train against a Stage 5-G variant, under four minutes on the clock, almost no ammo, and my last manual save sitting smugly 90 minutes back.

Completely impossible. Had to rewind, redo everything, play smarter, conserve better, and finally scrape through with an S Rank. And that’s just on Standard. Hardcore is still untouched, silently judging me from the menu.

After the true ending, I tried out all available extra modes with different survivors but didn’t make it out of any of them. At that point I was fully cooked mentally and emotionally, so I bowed out and moved on to my next [b]RE[/b] backlog victim… [b]RE7[/b], full-on horror mode engaged.

Unlockables, rankings, extra modes, and multiple viable runs give this game absurd replay value without padding.

[b]💰 [u]Value:[/u][/b]

For the amount of content, polish, replayability, and sheer quality here, this game punches way above its value and is an absolute steal on sale.

[b]⭐ [u]Final Verdict:[/u][/b]

[b]Resident Evil 2 Remake[/b] isn’t just a great remake. It’s a genre benchmark. Tight design, brutal survival mechanics, intelligent puzzles, exceptional audio, and pacing that never wastes your time.

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ - Capcom didn’t just remake a classic. They reminded everyone how survival horror is done right.

Single handedly (kinda) bringing the survival horror genre back from the dead back in 2019, Resident Evil 2 isn't a perfect 1:1 remake, however, it is probably the best way to get into the genre and one of the shining examples of why the genre is so great.

Not a shot for shot translation but a innovative reimagining of the fundementals of the 1998 original, Resident Evil 2 consistently toys with players expectations both for returning fans and brand new players alike. Puzzles, items and encounters are smartly reworked and positionally change to keep the experience fresh and the anxiety high, sucessfully recreating that original feeling that 98 induced so well. 

Gone is 98's mobility limited and postionally focused as a result of the 20 age gap, instead Capcom smartly replaces it with a much more aggressive enemy variety, which duck and move to take advantage of the player's mobility, as well as their increased resistance to damage to help shrug off bullets like they're nothing and incentivse the player to maneuver around them - spirtually akin to the original's gameplay style. In addition, Remake 2 also adds a lot of really nice quality of life additions that were previously introduced in RE 7, leading to one of the best feeling survival horror experiences period and for the time, the best we had ever felt at that time, only later out done by RE 4 Remake and Dead Space Remake.

Every iconic element is just translated so well to a 3D space. The police station dominates on this front, it's expertly translated and conveys such a huge sense of scale, with familar rooms translated to a completely new perspective but still capturing the essence of the 98 original. Arguably however, the best translation is Mr X, who now acts as a persistent stalker enemy throughout the station, causing an indescribable amount of anxiety as you have to navigate the new layout of the station, manage enemies and engage with puzzles all at the same time. It just grips you from the get go and forces your brain into a flow state under a large amount of stress.  

However, you have to acknowledge some of the flawed/rougher areas of the remake that especially stick out when you've recently played 98 original. The zapping system is completely missing unfortunately, which is a real shame considering that it was a very initavtive additon to the 98 original, adding some further planning and problem solving between the 2 runs. It's those 2 runs which remake lacks depth in the most, the A and B scenarios are very similar which ultimately effects the overall replayability and narrative cohesion of the package. There's a lot of crossover between scenario A and B which leads to plot incosistencies a few too many times for the remake's own good, with the biggest offender being that both Clair and Leon fight the same bosses in the same area which feels comparatively lazy when 98 had completely seperate encounters and boss fights. Additionally, while it's not a huge deal, they do cut a couple of enemy types, like the mutated spiders, which ultimately leads to a lesser variety of enemies.

That being said, RE 2 is without a doubt one of the best traditional suvival horror experiences to this day, not replacing its original experience, but complementing it and striding onwards to spear-head the revival of modern day survial horror for the big triple A space.

I played the originals almost 30 years ago, and sadly they have sat unfinished on a shelf or in a box in all that time. I just didn't enjoy them that much back then, but this reimagining of a genre defining game has changed all that.

Played the entire Leon A scenario for the first time, in one session. This is some good ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥, and it has solid replayability. To my surprise, the Claire B scenario was well worth it thanks to the unique interactions and boss fights versus Leon A. On top of that, the extra modes add even more content if you’re a masochist, so props for that too.

There's about a dozen different ways Resident Evil 2 could have gone wrong: The hit or miss company that Capcom is remaking one of the most classic RE games in the style of third-person action/adventure games that have bloated the industry since Resident Evil 4. This struggle to keep the original's gameplay and map design in tact on top of crafting a narrative that takes itself quite seriously, with far improved cinematography and acting performances. It's a recipe for an underwhelming experience that leaves you wondering why it exists in the first place. Resident Evil 2 Remake is a welcome exception.

I've never played the original, but the tight level design and the meticulous encounters across each room are continuously thrilling, and the game did well with not falling into the trap that the new perspective could have set for it; Combat is still incredibly suspenseful, not only for the presentation, but for the constant dread of losing essential ammo hanging over your head. To give me this feeling for both of my playthroughs shows just how much care was taken to keep players on edge. Unless you hear that save room music, you're always a corner away from a unique encounter that will test your resource management. 

It's no wonder that, with how much a normal enemy makes the player think and fear, that the many encounters with the Tyrant are as thrilling as they are. The giant stalker enemy excels in both the sound design of his boots stomping across the floor and his hollow, null expression. Backtracking is made infinitely more thrilling with his presence as he roams the hub world. Not only does the character succeed in his own right, but he is an excellent reminder of how disadvantaged the player has always been.

He is never going away, and he is never going to stop, and any situation you find yourself in going forward can go from manageable to lethal in an instant. All it takes is hearing those boots in an adjacent room, stomping closer and closer. It's just great

The survival aspect is great, but its intensity may lead to some frustrating moments, as the horror of certain scenarios is overshadowed by the annoyance of a particular zombie that is taking a firing squad to the face over minutes, but continues to stand up, or your player character uttering voice lines out of your control when standing inches away from an enemy that can only track you with hearing.

These were exceptions, but my playthrough was a few days longer due to setting the game aside because of these uncommon, but frustrating moments that just killed any immersion or momentum I had going in an area. Skill issue, perhaps.

The story of the original game has been faithfully adapted and revamped, giving the incredibly cheesy plots that the series is known for some well deserved and earned dramatic moments with the remake's take on the plot. It's nothing ground breaking, as Resident Evil has never been known for its subtlety, but the mix found between the game's more serious tone and remaining loyal to the inherent goofiness that is the franchise is commendable.

Adapted faithfully as well are the two routes, with both choices offering a different playable character, weapons unique to them, and their unique view on the events of the story. I mostly enjoyed seeing Claire's perspective after she is separated from Leon, but the canonicity of the route left me confused more often than not. There are many instances where Claire's route changes from Leon, being given more access to parts of the hub world Leon could previously not access or certain narrative moments that are altered in minor ways to accommodate Leon's presence elsewhere in Racoon City, such as the Tyrant not chasing Claire in some key moments where its clear to an observant player that he would be busy stalking Leon. But at the same time, Claire fights multiple bosses throughout her route that contradict the flow of events in Leon's story.

That's not to say this was a substantial issue, but Claire's route, my second playthrough, was far more compelling when I was seeing a whole new side of the narrative or fighting a boss that Leon never even saw a hint of in his route. These are somewhat of a rarity in Claire's route, and the time spent in her playthrough that felt like repetition was noticeable, especially around the midpoint. By the time of the true ending, I was left satisfied with Claire's route, as her final hours of playtime finished strong narratively and gameplay wise, with my favorite set-piece and solid development/conclusion for a character I feel sorely needed it during Leon's route.

Resident Evil 2 was exactly what I expected, and I thoroughly enjoyed it. It's a landmark achievement of the survival horror genre brought to an entirely new generation of players. My preference with the series will always lie in the more action-packed entries such as 4 and 5, but this classic has aged very well in a modern format. It's success is measured in many ways, but I feel one that goes understated is how easily players of the original game and this remake discuss their preferred games. 

When a legendary original game and a remake that had to grow in its shadow during the entire development cycle can coexist so easily and bring the community veterans and newcomers together over the shared love of what is a fundamentally identical, but very different game, that is a remake that has more than earned the right to exist.

[b]Gameplay: 8/10[/b]
Gameplay in Resident Evil 2 Remake feels very good, especially with the new inventory. No longer are you waiting to open your inventory to access your map or having to transition an entire screen to get as such. Now it pops up with a gray filter applied to the background with a minimalistic type look. Players are no longer [i]"limited"[/i] to fixed camera angles has we have a third-person over the shoulder camera view to play the game and it works quite well. The new crosshair gives you a very short waiting period to fully focus in on your target allowing for the potential at a higher chance of critical shots if you take the chance to wait. Throughout the game, you have the chance to find upgrades for your weapons like the OG, even new ones that weren't in the original. The gameplay of this is new, but also feels reminiscent of the OG in many different aspects. Biggest thing is no more tank controls, often described as an obstacle of the past hardware, it has been replaced by a standard movement system with the joystick.

[b]Music: 7/10[/b]
The subtle ambience throughout the entire game helps gives the game the vibe some people believe the original lacked, a disturbing, desolate, destroyed RPD after being ravaged by zombies and other creatures. However, they still follow the roots and within certain save rooms have made a new, much more subtle version of the well-loved classic RE2 save room theme. You can even bring back the original music of the game and have it applied to multiple sections,[u] although for a price[/u]. The entire game will retain the classic music, however, the sewers gets the Marshaling yard's theme throughout the entirety of the sewers section.

[b]Replayability: 6/10[/b]
The original Resident Evil 2 has a unique system known as the "Zapping System" where certain actions as one character can affect the playthrough of the other character in the next playthrough. Most well known for it's A/B scenario playthrough system. You could witness the events of RE2 OG playing as Leon and run into Claire here and there in the A scenario. Unfortunately, that system was almost entirely removed, what is left is the new "2nd run" system. It is unlocked by completing a playthrough with one character and you would do the 2nd run as the next character, simulating the system that used to be, in an inferior manner. You are given a new type of starting weapon per character during the second run, it replaces any ammo pickups with the ammo in that new weapon, and said new weapon does NOT use the same pistol ammo as the regular starting pistols. You must find gunpowder and rely on your resources more in the 2nd run than the 1st.

[b]Difficulties: 7/10[/b]
Resident Evil 2 Remake offers 3 difficulties, Assisted, Standard, and Hardcore. Differing from the two difficulties from the OG (Easy, Normal). Assisted allows for health regeneration starting from danger to going up to caution, aim assist, great deal of resources and ammo, and you start the game with the Samurai Edge (Wesker Model). Enemies have minimal health offering easy crits and quick kills, a mode for someone new to Resident Evil or someone who just wants to experience the story with little to no challenge. Standard is slightly easier than what normal mode would be on the original with enemies taking only 3 shots, or sometimes as many as 5-9 shots. You get enough resources to hold you down if you use them in necessary situations. Hardcore is where your nightmare will begin, minimal resources and ammo will be spread throughout the game, and you must pick when you use them and what you use them on carefully. Enemies will take 7-9 shots if not more to take down so you must strategize which enemies are only absolutely necessary to kill. While also providing more enemies, they take off more health than both standard and assisted, one grab bite could put you down into yellow caution from full health. Last but not least, hardcore requires you to use ink ribbons, same as the OG. Standard and Assisted have infinite saves and have autosave, hardcore will make you choose when you should save causing a great risk to lose much progress from a death.

[h2]WARNING: This next section contains SPOILERS for the story.[/h2]

[b]Story: 8/10/b]
[spoiler]The story of Resident Evil 2 is one of the best throughout the series, making it beloved among many. Featuring the one and only, Leon S. Kennedy, and starring heroine Claire Redfield. Leon, being a rookie cop for the RPD late on his first day. Claire Redfield's goal of going to Raccoon City is to seek out her brother Chris who went off the radar after the mansion incident a few months prior (RE1 events). Leon & Claire meet at a gas station on the outskirts of the city where they narrowly escape a horde only to enter their worst nightmare. As Leon, you meet Ada Wong, appearing as an FBI agent to Leon revealing her goal is to secure the G-Virus to takedown Umbrella until her true identity is exposed to him at the end of the game. As Claire, you'll stumble across the scared Sherry Birkin who is hiding from a monster that follows you throughout the game. Leon & Claire each have their own "Stalker" type enemies, Leon pursued by the T-00 commonly known as "Mr. X" a T-103 series Tyrant whose goal is to eliminate any remaining RPD survivors and retrieve the Golgotha Virus (G-Virus) sample. Claire is greeted to William Birkin, a scientist for Umbrella who was one of the developers of the G-Virus who took his own serum so Umbrella couldn't "steal his work". William Birkin continues to mutate into a more grotesque beast throughout the game going through a total of five stages. Leon and Claire are parted by an unescapable destiny and their only way out is to trudge through Raccoon City to find a way out and escape.[/spoiler]

[b]How it compares to the original[/b]
The game takes what made RE2 [i]unique[/i] such as the Zapping System and almost completely removes it. The sewers section was extended to be longer, at the expense of removing the Marshaling Yard section, even some small areas apart of the Lab have been cut as well. Claire and Leon's playthroughs are almost identical with some story changes, while the original had you fighting certain bosses in different locations and filling in the gaps of the story based on which character you played as first. In the remake, the main characters only run into each other about 2 times.

[h2]Overall: 7/10[/h2]
Resident Evil 2 Remake does a good job at retelling the story of the 1998 classic, while it suffers by taking away the things that made the original unique, it attempts to compensate for those losses. It offers an improved graphical experience that might make it easier for newer fans to be attracted to. The original games were known for their challenge, but this remake retains challenge and also makes it slightly user friendly by introducing modern concepts such as third-person over the shoulder camera, moving while shooting, autosave and infinite saves with a variety of difficulties for different situations. If I was a new player in the Resident Evil series, this is where I would begin and recommend newcomers begin as well. This game gives a fine tasting of what the Resident Evil series has to offer.

As a longtime fan of the Resident Evil series since I was about twelve—back when the zombie craze was at its peak—playing the Resident Evil 2 remake felt both nostalgic and refreshingly modern. The original RE2 has always been my favorite entry in the series, largely because of Leon, and this remake does an excellent job of honoring what made that game special while updating it for a new generation.

One of the remake’s greatest strengths is how it encourages multiple playthroughs. Each run feels rewarding, and the Raccoon City Police Department gradually transforms from a terrifying maze into a strangely familiar space that almost feels like a second home. That sense of growing mastery over the environment is incredibly satisfying and keeps you invested long after your first completion.

Combat is tight and responsive, clearly inspired by the fluidity of Resident Evil 4 while maintaining the tension of true survival horror. Every encounter feels meaningful. You’re constantly making split-second decisions: do you stand your ground and clear a path, land a quick headshot to buy just enough time to slip past, or conserve resources and run? These tense moments perfectly capture the essence of survival horror, where panic and strategy exist side by side.

The puzzles strike a strong balance between accessibility and challenge. They’re intuitive enough to avoid frustration, yet complex enough to make you pause and think for a few minutes. Solving them adds a welcome layer of pacing that breaks up the action and deepens the sense of exploration.

Story-wise, it’s classic Resident Evil. If you’ve played the series before, you know what to expect: a blend of cool action set pieces, creepy atmosphere, and a touch of signature cheesiness. The remake delivers all of this with modern presentation and polish, making the narrative engaging even for returning players.

Overall, Resident Evil 2 Remake is an outstanding reimagining of a beloved classic. I’d recommend it not only to longtime fans of the franchise but also to newcomers looking for a strong entry point into the series. It captures the spirit of Resident Evil at its best and delivers a tense, replayable survival horror experience.

[h1]Resident Evil 2 (2019) Review[/h1]

I played this reimagining at launch, but I recently returned to it on Linux to see how it holds up as we approach [i]Resident Evil Requiem[/i]. On a technical level, the RE Engine is a marvel.

However, despite the polish, I have mixed feelings. While the atmosphere and gameplay are fantastic, the decision to scrap the original's proper "zapping" system (A/B scenarios) in favor of a watered-down "2nd Run" mode hurts the narrative cohesion. It is a great game, but it doesn't quite hit the "perfect remake" status of the 2002 mansion overhaul.

[h2]The Good[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Atmosphere[/b]: The sound design inside the RPD is incredible, especially using 360-degree audio to track Mr. X
[*][b]Modern Gameplay[/b]: The over-the-shoulder combat feels fluid and the gore system adds a gruesome layer of feedback
[*][b]Performance[/b]: Runs like a dream on PC, though Linux users should switch to the DX11 branch for stability
[*][b]Mr. X[/b]: The Tyrant is no longer scripted but a constant, roaming threat that forces you to change your route
[*][b]Voice Acting[/b]: The cast does a great job grounding the horror without losing the characters' personalities
[/list]

[h2]The Bad[/h2]
[list]
[*][b]Scenario System[/b]: The 2nd Run mode feels like a remix rather than a true alternative perspective, creating plot holes
[*][b]Pacing Issues[/b]: The sewer section drags on repeat playthroughs and becomes a chore to navigate
[*][b]Mechanics[/b]: Knife durability and adaptive difficulty feel like they punish skill mastery rather than reward it
[/list]

[h2]Summary[/h2]
Resident Evil 2 (2019) is a tense, beautiful, and mechanically solid survival horror game. However, by streamlining the story and cutting the true A/B scenario interactions, it feels less complete than the original 1998 classic. It is definitely worth playing, but it sits a step below the 2002 Remake and the RE4 Remake in terms of faithfulness.

[h1]Resident Evil 2 Remake (2019)[/h1]

[h2]Graphics:[/h2]
☑️ Beautiful
☐ Good
☐ Decent
☐ Bad
☐ Don't look too long at it

The textures are flawless, and the characters and zombies with their detailed damage system for different shots/hits are truly impressive. Even the ability to examine any item in the inventory is a nice touch that improves the experience.

The location design is absolutely stunning. RCPD, the sewers, and the laboratory are so contrasting and unique that each has its own special atmosphere: a somewhat depressing and oppressive, yet still human police station; creepy, dirty, and disgusting sewers; a sterile and terrifying laboratory.

[h2]Gameplay:[/h2]
☑️ Very good
☐ Good
☐ It's just gameplay
☐ Mehh
☐ Just don't

Exploring locations is fantastic, especially with the inventory limitations and smartly placed shortcuts. The loot distribution is well-thought-out and synergizes perfectly with the inventory system: you constantly have to make careful decisions — take the item now or come back later, explore a new room now or clear inventory space first, and if I run to the storage box, will I have enough health and ammo to get back?

The feel of shooting and "body weight" is just amazing. Each weapon has its own weight and damage that you feel not only on enemies but also on the characters themselves, for example in reload times or firing rate. The body physics are masterful. Wounded main characters gasp, slow down, and cough. Zombies fall, stumble, and tumble out of windows in a way that makes their clumsiness feel believable.

The suspense-horror aspect is excellent thanks to realistic zombie behavior and various enemies. Regular zombies can lie motionless and then grab your leg a minute later (even if they took half a magazine to the head before), they can wander around or suddenly run at you. Special mention goes to the Tyrant — an absolute game design masterpiece. The idea of an unstoppable monster that just follows you everywhere creates a constant feeling of stress and tension.

But there's a HUGE downside: the terrible synergy between Leon's and Claire's story campaigns. They simply overlap each other instead of complementing. In the original RE2, the heroes' stories intertwined much better — they contacted each other more often and explored locations in parallel (decisions could affect each other). In the remake, you have to walk through the same rooms and perform almost the same actions (practically 1 to 1), with minor differences that are mostly in the story. I'm glad I lowered the difficulty for the second playthrough, otherwise such repetition would have been exhausting.

[h2]Story:[/h2]
☐ Lovely
☑️ Good
☐ Average
☐ Some lore
☐ No Story

The game is an important part of the overall RE lore, which I'm not familiar with yet. I can only say that the whole story with Umbrella Corporation is interesting enough to make you want to learn more.

Leon's story is more chill, a kind of action movie about a first day at work that turned into hell, spiced up with flirting with the hot Ada Wong.

Claire's story is more interesting plot-wise. While searching for her brother, she gets caught up in a local zombie apocalypse, where besides her own survival, she also has to save a little girl named Sherry.

Overall, both stories keep your attention, they're interesting to follow, and the characters are so charismatic that they create genuine attachment.

[h2]Audio:[/h2]
☑️ Eargasm
☐ Good
☐ Just Ok
☐ Bad

Absolutely the best sound design I've encountered in games. Shooting, walking, heavy breathing when injured, zombie growling, and of course, the SOUND OF TYRANT'S FOOTSTEPS — it's a real Eargasm.

[h2]Difficulty:[/h2]
☐ Easy
☑️ Easy to learn / Hard to master
☐ Difficult
☐ Dark Souls

On the easy difficulty level, the game honestly throws too much loot at you. Normal difficulty is perfectly balanced: resource scarcity keeps you on your toes and makes you look for efficient routes, but never leads to complete despair.

The so-called "puzzles" are mostly quite intuitive, sometimes you need to think a bit. Exploring locations is also straightforward — when you find a key, it's usually more or less clear what to do with it. The excellently made map helps with this.

What's unexpectedly challenging is the controls. They're somewhat console-sticky. The character's weight, especially when injured, is really noticeable, which often led to taking unnecessary hits. Sometimes it was frustrating, but overall this "feature" brought a lot of emotions.

This game is straight out of the past, and that is not a bad thing. It is slow, and it has its charms being over a 25 year old game. But the remake is excellent. 

What this game has is atmosphere, and the hallmarks of a GOATed survival horror.

You definitely get the jank being such an old game, and the combat can be unpolished, and tedious sometimes, but it is never unfair. The combat generally is fairly easy, and the bosses are never too tough on the standard mode.

The story is the generic trope, someone creates a secret virus, it gets out and zombies appear, well this is one of the GOATs. Also, the writing has an emotional depth of a rock, which improved greatly over some of the future RE games.

The voice acting is also serviceable, and the character polish is straight High Concept, but in the end all together you surely are going to have a lot of fun playing this game.

Generally I do not like replaying games as I am starved of time, but this game I highly recommend playing the 2nd run as it gives you a lot more of the story, and definitely the proper "True ending" to the story, which is much better than the initial ending.

Replayed on PC to prep myself for RE: Requiem. It’s still just as good as it was back in 2019, better now that I’m on PC. This is still one of the best RE games, next to both RE4's and RE7. Arguably the best one, even.

Everything about it works so well: the more horror-focus, the combat being slower and methodical, resource management, routing as you get better and better, the story being surprisingly well done for a RE game & one of the better ones, knowing when to shoot and when to run, Mr. X, etc. I could go on but this game perfectly knows what it wants to be and any fan of horror or action-horror should play it. The replayability, as it is with most RE games, is heavily addicting but even more so when chasing the S and S+ ranks. Additionally, Capcom did a great job supporting it with content updates, such as Ghost Survivors, so that was a nice touch. 

My only criticisms are (1) some poor graphics options (I.e. anti-aliasing + FSR1, Bloom, Film Noise, Lens Distortion. For me, Bloom + Film Noise + Lens Distortion would cause distracting visual artifacts like fizzling and some strange sparkling effects when raining) and (2) that the bosses are just okay. It’s better to disable some of the graphical options as with those on, cutscenes and general graphics during gameplay can really look worse and it’s bizarre. At least REFramework can help with injecting DLSS/FSR4 into the game. Additionally, raytracing in this game barely makes a visual difference and it eats performance fairly badly with extremely minor visual gain. Lastly, bosses are primarily lame at first due to their simplicity and the player movement being slow, but I did grow to like them after several playthroughs as you learn how to deal with their movesets. Still, I wouldn’t call them a positive. 

Overall, amazing game. Can’t recommend it enough. And playing as HUNK to end the game as your last gameplay section is still a top-tier experience with the music and using everything you learned from the main story. 9.5/10.

A very, VERY good remake of one my favorite survival horror game of all times. Great gameplay, memorable level design, some good expansion of the side characters like Marvin and Chief Iron, and a good reimagining of the original 1998 story though not without hiccups and flaws. The one I really hate is that they remove the unique difference between Leon and Claire A/B scenarios, replacing them with 1st and 2nd run instead that barely changes the gameplay and story.

The boss fights(besides the finale) for Leon and Claire are now all the same, for example; if you defeated the first Birkin boss fight in Leon 1st run, you will still fight him in Claire 2nd run AT THE SAME LOCATION which was just stupid.
In the OG, the boss fight for Leon A/Claire B and Claire A/Leon B are all uniquely different, if you fight Birkin in Leon A, then in Claire B you will fight Mr X instead and the same applied to Leon B/Claire A scenarios. Not only that, but you are also rewarded if you choose to fight Mr X instead of running away from his invincible ass like the remake forced you to do throughout the game. The remake also switched one of the boss from the OG to a more common monsters you find in the sewer. I'm glad they remove the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ spiders, but truth to be told I would rather very much face them instead of this new annoying ass sewer monster.

Items and weapons you choose to pickup in your 1st no longer affect the 2nd run of the story, making the replayibility a little bit pointless as they are very little difference besides minor item placements changes(and I mean VERY minor compared to the OG) with just a few unique cutscenes at the early and the end part of the ggame only.

[h2]Experience[/h2]

I first played Resident Evil 2 Remake back in 2021. I didn’t get very far - I failed to find the valve handle, got stuck at the showers, and eventually dropped the game. In hindsight, it was entirely on me: I didn’t explore properly and, worst of all, I didn’t use the map to clear rooms until they turned blue. Pure laziness.

Fast-forward about 5 years. RE2 Remake was the second-to-last Resident Evil game in my Steam library that I hadn’t finished yet, and with Resident Evil 9 / Requiem coming out next month, I decided to finally give it another chance. I also had more time to play - and since RE2 is essentially required to fully understand what happened in Raccoon City, it felt like the right moment.

This time, I played through both Leon’s story and Claire’s second run, fully completing the game and experiencing the entire RE2 Remake story and both endings.

Overall, I had a great and genuinely fun experience. The visuals still look fantastic, and the sound design is excellent.

I also came in much better prepared this time. After my painful experience with RE0 - where I wasted ammo on every enemy and reached the end with almost nothing - I learned to preserve ammo as much as possible. In RE2 Remake (and basically every RE after RE0), I avoided unnecessary fights and saved heavy ammo like shotgun shells, flame and acid rounds, and magnum ammo unless I absolutely needed them.

Another thing I finally learned was how useful grenades are. That might sound ridiculous, but in previous RE games I relied almost exclusively on guns. Using grenades properly made a huge difference here.

So far, this stands out as a nearly perfect Resident Evil game for me.

[h2]Cons[/h2]

The only part that became genuinely frustrating - especially if you’re trying to conserve healing items and ammo - was the lead-up to the G Phase 2 boss fight in both Leon’s and Claire’s runs.

In the main power room, Birkin randomly stabs through the ceiling with his claws and later breaks through the rolling metal door. These moments aren’t even the actual boss fight yet, but they can easily cost you health and resources if you’re unlucky or don’t know how they work.

I eventually got so frustrated that I looked up a speedrun strategy on how to avoid getting hit in those two situations - and once I did that, the problem was completely solved.

[h2]Bugs / Glitches[/h2]
[list]
    [*]In the main power room ceiling section, standing in a very specific corner - just outside the grid area - completely prevents Birkin from hitting you. This isn’t RNG-based; it’s 100% consistent.
    [*]When Birkin breaks through the rolling metal door, standing on the far left side causes his hitbox to be in a "void" state during the animation. You can literally run past and through him without being blocked or taking damage.

Resident Evil 2 Remake: 3/5 “Judged as a game, not a remake.”

PROS:
1. Graphically phenomenal.
2. Mood & Vibe are a lovely mix of genuine horror movie and a cheesy action flick… as it should be. 
3. Made zombies scary again!
4. Rhythm of the game is very addicting: Safe spot, new place, gets scary, then wraps back around an unlocked shortcut.
5. Map Design. 

NEUTRAL: 
1. Voice Acting varies between movie-like and horrendous depending on the character.
- Good Voice Acting: Annette Birkin, Claire, Sherry, and Irons
- Bad Voice Acting: Leon (annoyingly) and Ada (annoyingly)
2. Puzzles: (p.s. Itty bitty nitpick but none of them make ANY sense lol). The Police Department has ZERO good puzzles (other than the mini-safes). They're either item-checks or just passwords that are handed to you at random points. Ada’s hacking section is literally just a DPI-check and was incredibly annoying, even if not terribly difficult. The sewers, Sherry’s section, and the Lab actually had a lot of fun and interesting puzzles!
3. Item management is actually a pretty fun mini-game within itself. However, due to how large the maps are and how slow the player is, backtracking to drop stuff off if you’re full is boring & frustrating. 
4. Bosses in general are pretty hit or miss. 

CONS:
1. Mr. X. Conceptually an awesome idea but falls SUPER flat in execution for me. Generally, this game dissuades you from actually killing every enemy you come across (exceptions in some cases for easier navigation), and this is entirely fine. However, this game FORCES you to backtrack at times. This means you either must sprint, which alerts him, or shoot the zombie to either stun or kill it, which alerts him. Sometimes you can hear him multiple floors up and track his movements, which is awesome. Other times, you get smacked in the back of the head with zero audio. This is likely due to another complaint, he randomly teleports to you. He ignores you in some key areas, sure, but that doesn’t prevent him from cornering you and keeping you locked in certain sections of the building unless you take a hit. It’s scary for like 2 minutes, then it’s annoying for the remaining 2 hours. Far worse in Claire 2nd Run. 
2. Continuity makes no sense, there is NO way Leon and Claire could possibly be acting at the same time with how the story is presented. 
3. SO MANY attacks feel undodgeable. 
4. I like resilient zombies… but this is ridiculous. 
5. 2nd Run adds so little for the time you put in, feels trivial.

Very enjoyable game. This was my first initial introduction to the RE franchise, and I personally hold it as my second favourite of all the ones I've played, closely behind RE4 Remake.

Firstly, a couple of the slight negatives about the game, which are entirely my own opinion. The biggest issue I have with this game is just how slow it feels like the main characters are. For Claire it's a little annoying but not entirely unreasonable, seeing as she's just a civilian woman caught up in a hellish environment, however I for the LIFE of me cannot understand why Leon is so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ slow all the time. He's an extremely fit, professionally trained police officer running around in a post apocalyptic zombie infested hellscape and can't seem to manage anything more than a brisk jog for 95% of the game. Man needs to start hauling some serious ass. I just really wish the maximum running speed of the MCs wasn't akin to that of a slightly perturbed tortoise. 

Also, I personally think one of the bossfights on Leon's side involving a certain "crane with a storage crate" is one of the most tedious and downright annoying fights in any game ever. If you've played the game, you know which one I'm talking about. It's clunky, way too short whilst somehow feeling way too drawn out, and just a pain in the ass when I get to it.

Now, onto the many positives about the game. The graphics, design and atmosphere of it are incredibly done. The story is interesting on both sides and the characters are all worth becoming emotionally invested in, even some of the minor side characters (talking to you, Lt Branagh my GOAT). The combat and gunplay is, for the most part, enjoyable whilst still managing to be somewhat challenging at times. There's a good variety of weapons and upgrades for each one, and the boss fights are (mostly) fun and engaging.

Then there's Mr X, EASILY one of the best parts of this game. He's very briefly mentioned in a note you pick up near the start of the game, before having one of the most BADASS introductions I've seen. From then on, he's 7 feet of pure terrifying MENACE, whose aura is only bolstered by his intimidatingly loud footsteps that can be heard from what feels like miles away. His theme is also great too. Really spikes tension through the roof when that starts playing. 

There's plenty more great things about this game, but I'd highly recommend playing it for yourself to experience them. Amazing game, definitely a must-play title.

Honestly, what really stood out to me in this game was the atmosphere and graphics. The Raccoon City Police Department (RPD) is easily the highlight, it’s dark, detailed, and super immersive, making me feel like I was actually trapped in that nightmare. The gameplay and controls are also spot on. The over the shoulder shooting feels smooth and satisfying, striking that perfect mix of action and survival horror. And man, the Mr. X/Tyrant mechanic is unforgettable. Having him constantly stalk me added so much tension and fear, and it really cranked up the horror factor. As a remake, I’ve got to give it credit, it respects the original 1998 version while modernizing the puzzles, layout, and pacing in a way that feels fresh. The sound design deserves a shout out too, the eerie audio, especially in the RPD, made every step feel nerve wracking and added a ton to the immersion.

That said, there are definitely things that bugged me. The “B” scenarios, or Second Run, were a letdown. Compared to the original, they barely felt different from the A scenarios, with almost no unique story beats or puzzle changes. The boss battles also didn’t do much for me, they felt weak and kind of uninspired compared to other Resident Evil games. Zombies being bullet sponges was another frustration. Having to pump so many headshots into them broke the immersion and made combat feel more like run and gun than strategic survival. Enemy variety outside the RPD wasn’t great either, fighting G-adults in the sewers got repetitive fast. And finally, I wish there was more interaction between Leon and Claire. Their stories felt too disconnected, and it missed an opportunity to build stronger character relationships and make the narrative more engaging.

The atmosphere, gameplay and sound is top-tier, Mr. X roaming the map makes the game tense as you hear his big footsteps, a very good remake of a classic. I do recommend this game.

The Cost of Survival in Raccoon City – A Review of Resident Evil 2

Overall Rating: 9.75/10

Resident Evil 2 is a masterclass in survival horror, balancing relentless tension with thoughtful design and unforgettable atmosphere. Set during the collapse of Raccoon City, the game places players in a nightmare where every bullet matters and every hallway feels dangerous. Stepping into the roles of Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield, players experience the outbreak from two distinct yet intertwined perspectives, grounding the chaos in personal survival. It honors the legacy of the series while elevating it with modern presentation and refined mechanics, resulting in an experience that feels both classic and terrifyingly fresh.

Visual Design and Atmosphere: 10/10
Raccoon City is oppressive, detailed, and dripping with dread. From rain-soaked streets to dimly lit interiors, every environment feels carefully constructed to keep players uneasy. The iconic Raccoon Police Department stands as the heart of the experience—a sprawling, labyrinthine structure filled with locked doors, hidden shortcuts, and creeping dread. Lighting is exceptional, using darkness and shadow to obscure threats and build constant tension. The RPD evolves from a place of refuge into a psychological battleground that players come to know intimately.

Story and Narrative: 9.5/10
The story unfolds through discovery and pacing rather than heavy exposition. Files, notes, and environmental storytelling slowly reveal the tragic downfall of Raccoon City. Leon and Claire’s separate campaigns offer unique character moments while reinforcing the larger Umbrella conspiracy. The narrative moves hand in hand with the survival gameplay, maintaining momentum while never pulling focus away from the constant struggle to stay alive.

Gameplay and Survival Mechanics: 10/10
Every system is built around scarcity and consequence. Ammo is limited, healing items are precious, and inventory management remains a constant source of tension. Combat is deliberately restrained—zombies are resilient, encounters are risky, and avoidance is often the smartest choice. Exploration, puzzle-solving, and combat are tightly interwoven, creating a survival loop where preparation and restraint are just as important as marksmanship.

Sound Design and Music: 10/10
Audio design heightens tension at every turn. Distant groans echo through halls, footsteps signal unseen danger, and environmental sounds keep players constantly alert. The music is used sparingly but memorably—most notably the iconic save room theme, which provides brief reprieve and reinforces the game’s tension through contrast. Moments of fear are amplified while silence continues to carry much of the horror’s weight.

Replayability and Longevity: 10/10
Resident Evil 2 rewards multiple playthroughs, with Leon and Claire offering distinct perspectives that change how you approach exploration and combat. Each run presents subtle variations in enemy placement and resource availability, keeping players on edge even in familiar areas. The game’s tight balance of scarcity, danger, and strategic decision-making ensures that every return to Raccoon City feels tense, challenging, and entirely worth revisiting.

Conclusion: 9.75/10
Resident Evil 2 stands as one of the finest examples of survival horror ever created. Through masterful atmosphere, disciplined gameplay, and impeccable pacing, it delivers a constant sense of pressure where every decision matters.

Final Verdict:
Resident Evil 2 is a masterclass in modern survival horror, successfully translating a classic design philosophy into a contemporary experience without sacrificing tension or identity. By placing Leon and Claire at the center of an oppressive, interconnected RPD, the game builds fear through atmosphere, resource management, and relentless pressure. Every system reinforces survival, creating an experience that feels both respectful of its roots and confidently refined for a new generation.

The original game had to fit in the 2 megabyte memory of the Playstation 1 console, so they had a 3d world, but the "museum-turned-police-station" basically was "pre-rendered" at the studio, and then they took a screen shot of that, and then your character (and the NPCs and monsters) were actual polygon-stitched-together-into-automatas. [h1]Ah, Raccoon City.[/h1]
The game that truly pushed Resident Evil into the spotlight.

While the first game was a masterpiece in its own right and laid the foundation for everything that followed, Resident Evil 2 is where the franchise really found its identity. The way it tells its story through multiple perspectives and routes was groundbreaking at the time. You step into the shoes of either Leon, the rookie cop on his very first day, or Claire Redfield, the determined sister of Chris. Two characters, two journeys, one nightmare of a city.

The remake absolutely did wonders. Using the RE Engine, Capcom brought this familiar story to a whole new audience with a modern touch while still respecting its roots. For those who played the original on the PlayStation, this feels like a warm but unsettling homecoming. That said, it’s not a one-to-one remake. Some elements from the original are missing, but new ideas and refinements were added on top, making it feel fresh rather than copied.

One of the strengths of RE games is how they reward replayability. The more you play, the more confident you become. You learn shortcuts, optimize routes, shave off minutes in speedruns, and slowly grow bolder when tackling Hardcore difficulties. RE2 shines here. Leon and Claire already offer two distinct runs, but with the A and B scenarios, that number doubles. Four different playthroughs, each with meaningful variations, and that’s before factoring in difficulty modes.

The game stays true to survival horror. This isn’t a full-blown shooter like later entries such as RE5 or RE6. Combat feels refined, especially when targeting limbs and managing crowds, but it never lets you forget that resources are limited. Inventory management matters. Every bullet, herb, and key item forces you to think ahead. It keeps you tense, cautious, and constantly planning for what might come next.

Visually and technically, the game is an absolute feast. The RE Engine is pushed to its limits, delivering an atmosphere that screams Resident Evil. The environments drip with dread, the lighting is phenomenal, and the character models are incredibly detailed. The enemies are especially impressive and, at times, downright disturbing. William Birkin, in particular, is a grotesque work of art that perfectly embodies horror.

During my first runs, I was constantly on edge. Later on, once you learn enemy patterns, the game becomes more manageable, even on Hardcore. And then there’s Mr. X. A relentless presence that stalks you through the halls like a nightmare you can’t wake up from. Stressful at first, almost routine later, but always effective.

The bonus content deserves a mention as well. The extra missions were a nice addition, even if they stressed me out more than once. I’ll admit it, I needed a guide to fully understand them. Still, they offer interesting “what if” scenarios, spotlight minor characters, and give us an iconic, badass look at HUNK. On top of that, the unlockables, artwork, and character models are a joy to explore. The level of detail in those models alone is worth appreciating.

[h1]RESIDENT EVIL 2. REMAKE[/h1]

I liked this game. This is the second game in the Resident Evil series that I have completed. The shooting mechanics, zombies, and bosses are made with high quality, and the system of managing items — where and what to put and what to carry in the inventory — is well designed. The healing system and different types of weapons are well developed and their mechanics are good.

The story flows smoothly without any plot holes, all events are logical in the first playthrough, but the second playthrough (New Game 2), where we play as the second character during the same time period as the first one, does not fully match the story. There are separate locations for both characters, but one way or another the main events take place in the police station, and for some reason the characters do not meet there. They also solve the same puzzles and pick up the same items, the only difference is that they are located in different places and sometimes in new locations.

Despite the similarity of the two playthroughs, the game does not become boring. Different weapons and different situations make the player play differently, which prevents boredom. I completed the main game as Leon and the second playthrough as Claire on normal difficulty, and then completed the main game as Claire and the second playthrough as Leon on hardcore. I can say that it is better to play immediately on hardcore — the game becomes much more interesting.

I would also like to point out that playing as Claire is much easier, even several times easier, because of the grenade launcher. Leon’s campaign is extremely difficult, since he does not have any AOE weapons like the grenade launcher, and lickers become a real challenge for him. It is also good that in the second playthrough there is more space for the Tyrant — he appears more often and does not disappear from the police station, constantly interfering with gameplay.

The bonus modes are also good. The only difference between them is the character models and slightly different inventory, but unfortunately the goal is the same for all of them — reach the finish as fast as possible. The main differences are enemies, route, and inventory. A bit of humor was added in the form of the Tofu mode. At first it seems funny, but in reality it is the only truly difficult bonus mode, and when other Tofus unlock, completing these modes stretches over several days because of the high difficulty.

The character animations are high quality, facial expressions as well. I would also like to praise the very high-quality sound. Ambient sounds, music, and weapon handling sounds are very pleasant to listen to. The number of bugs is extremely small, and I am sure some players will not encounter even a single one.

Brian Irons, the chief of police of Raccoon City, is very well voiced and very well performed in his role — it is very high quality and pleasant to watch this character. There is a psychological and sad connection in Claire’s story with Sherry. Sherry is very well portrayed as a sad girl (you really feel sorry for her), and the scenes with her mother, especially closer to the finale, are very touching — I will not spoil.

One personal wish would be to make the Tyrant faster — he walks too slowly. The game is made very well, and even after completing the game 100%, replaying it again is not difficult.
