Resident Evil 2 Remake is more than just a successful remake to me; it’s a reminder of why survival horror can be so powerful when it’s done right. From the moment I step into Raccoon City, the game pulls me in completely. The dark hallways, distant sounds, and constant feeling that something could be waiting around the next corner create a tension that never really lets go. This game doesn’t rely on cheap jump scares — it builds true, lasting anxiety.

Playing as Leon and Claire, you genuinely feel their fear, confusion, and determination to survive. The police station feels like the heart of the experience: familiar, yet always hostile. And then there’s Mr. X — hearing his heavy footsteps echo through the halls is enough to make you freeze. Even when you think you’re safe, you never really are. The game makes you live its horror rather than simply play it.

Visually and atmospherically, the remake is outstanding. The lighting, environmental detail, and sound design all work together to immerse you completely. Limited ammo, careful inventory management, and the constant need to choose whether to fight or flee elevate the game beyond simple action and turn it into a true survival horror experience.

That said, as much as I love the game, I can’t ignore its biggest weakness — Claire’s campaign. While playing as Claire is still enjoyable and her character and story moments (especially with Sherry) are emotionally strong, the second campaign doesn’t offer enough new ideas to feel truly fresh. Too often, you’re solving the same puzzles, in the same locations, in almost the same way. After finishing Leon’s story, the sense of discovery is noticeably reduced.

The differences between Leon and Claire mostly come down to weapons and a few story elements. From a gameplay perspective, the campaigns are simply too similar. Reusing nearly identical puzzles makes the second playthrough feel more routine than it should, and while the tension and atmosphere remain strong, the element of surprise is largely gone. With a bit more creativity and risk-taking, Claire’s campaign could have felt far more distinct.

Even with these flaws, Resident Evil 2 Remake remains a phenomenal experience. It’s a remake made with clear respect, care, and love for the original. The reason these criticisms matter is simple: the game is so good that it feels like it could have been even better. And that’s not disappointment — that’s admiration.

Resident Evil 2 is one of those games all horror fans have to play at least once in their lives. The grandfathers of horror games are Resident Evil and Silent Hill, and with both making a serious comeback in recent years, plenty of new players have been able to enjoy them in their remastered (or continued) glory.

I'll be honest, this was my first time ever beating Re2 to completion (both Leon and Claire scenario + true ending).  It was fun, and it was irritating. Resident Evil does not mess around with difficulty. It will make you stare at the game over screen while gritting your teeth and sighing. It is often unforgiving, even on standard difficulty. I loved it, but also resented it. Sometimes I just wanted to progress but a lack of items or heals made me have to backtrack over an hour to grab some more supplies within RPD. Leon's route is rather easygoing, but for some reason playing as Claire for the second run is like putting toothpicks in your toenails and kicking a wall. It was worth it, though, for the true ending.

Gameplay wise it is smooth and responsive. The graphics are great, the story is fun (although a tad inconsistent between the two scenarios, but whatever) - I am mostly playing through the original trilogy to prepare for Re9 where we return to Raccoon City, so I wasn't coming in expecting a masterpiece, which is probably why I enjoyed it as much as I did. Also, as a fun little side note, despite a non-creepy appearance, Mr. X consistently jump scared me and made me squeal like a little girl. Very enjoyable XD Also, hats off to the bonus scenario "4th Survivor" where you play as Daddy Hunk. Really just a solid remake.

Overall, I rate Re2 Remake an 8/10

This was really quite good. I didn’t find it to be all that frightening (except for that heavy-footed fedora wearing neckbeard bastard), having played RE7 beforehand, but this game has such a dense atmosphere and such a compelling setting that I was immediately sucked in. 

After playing RE5 recently, I found the boss fights in here to be great in comparison, although I do think RE games have a trend of trying to insert heavy action sequences, while not all being the video game called Resident Evil 4, but that issue wasn’t as pronounced in this game as it is in others. 

This game knows what it does right, and it leans on it for 90% of the runtime. Walking through a long dark corridor, hearing the rain spilling onto the floor from a broken window, a broken window you aren’t fully certain was always in such a state. Slowly walking past a monstrosity as it crawls on the ceiling, while you hear the heavy footfalls of you-know-who, somewhere in the station. 

I think this game was informed quite a bit by RE7, which seems to be the turning point for CAPCOM getting their ♥♥♥♥ together. The puzzles, dense atmosphere, and stalker mechanics all seem very similar (although I must confess my goat Jack Baker probably falls short of Mr X despite being more terrifying.) The enemy design, gunplay, and characters (♥♥♥♥ u ethan) are far improved here. Enemy corpses are perpetually on the map, keeping you in a constant state of anxiety going through any area you have previously cleared, as you never know when what you thought was a bullet ridden zombie might grab your ankle as you walk by and take a chomp. 

The first few hours in the police station are the best parts of the game, but I don’t think the rest of it is terrible, just the quality bar is immediately set so high, it makes anything that comes after look a step down. It does the RE thing where the horror slowly dissolves into a more action focused, sci-fi thing in a secret Umbrella lab which - you’ll never guess - may or may not explode as you escape it. Still, I do think this is a game of exceptional quality which any survival horror fan will enjoy.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is an excellent remake of the original , the atmosphere is oppressive, the sound design is unsettling, and the over-the-shoulder camera makes every encounter feel tense and personal. The core impact of the horror genre is still very much present, and in many moments, it even surpasses the original in terms of immersion.


However, when compared to the original Resident Evil 2, the remake feels noticeably shorter and somewhat incomplete. Several elements from the original game are missing or simplified—such as certain enemy types, locations, and gameplay mechanics that added variety and replay value. The A/B scenario system, which was a major feature of the original, is present in name but lacks the depth and impact it once had.
Mr. X adds constant psychological pressure that keeps the fear alive throughout the experience.

Overall 7/10, good replay for those who have played the original but better experience for those who have played any other from the franchise and probably the best experience for those who havent played any.

[h1] Incredible Horror Experience [/h1]

Resident Evil 2 has everything I wanted and expected after playing through RE1 and then some. It exceeded every one of my expectations and had me glued to my computer from start to finish. It even made me excited to play through it a second time for the true ending, something few games can do. From my first steps into the police station all the tension that made the first game so good was there. Hearing zombies outside or the footsteps of someone chasing you as you try and navigate the cramped hallways will put anyone on edge. The combat felt amazing, and ammo here is truly limited. There were plenty of times, even in my second playthrough where I had a handful of bullets and this created some of the most memorable moments in the game for me. Having to choose if you fight or run, and praying that there will be some more ammo around each corner is exhilarating. I also loved the story of the game. Claire and Leon both have a different set of side characters and motives, making each of their playthroughs worth experiencing, especially since you see some slightly different areas in each one. Overall I absolutely loved my time with this game, and I highly recommending giving it a playthrough. This was my first Resident Evil game, and aside from Alan Wake which is barely scary, this was also my first survival horror game. I’m so happy I gave it a try.

I didn’t magically fall in love with horror media, because I still feel very uncomfortable being scared and I dislike jumpscares a lot. But I would be lying if I said the perfect scary atmosphere in this game didn’t improve every other mechanic significantly. Exploring such well crafted levels like the RPD with that oppressive atmosphere just improves the whole experience.

By far my favorite part was the gameplay loop, which is essentially a metroidvania if you think about it. As you explore you reach dead ends that are only unlockable with certain items, keys, or codes that you need to find, so it’s a continuous cascade of finding new paths and unlocking previously blocked ones. All the rewards feel extremely satisfying too, because having more ammo alleviates that tense nervous feeling, getting a bigger inventory is like a godsend, and more healing items leave you with more room for error. It all culminates in a super satisfying loop.

The story was corny in the best way possible. Leon is the goat and Claire is best mom, and even though the writing is goofy at times, I feel like that is part of the charm.

I can imagine this is a very hot take, but Mr. X was the part I disliked the most. Don’t get me wrong, I really love him as a concept, and for people that love horror he must be amazing. But since my favorite part was exploring, he made it a bit of a hellscape for me. This is obviously personal preference, and he is still a major and amazing component of this perfect horror survival game (and thankfully he is not present the whole game).

Must play, even if you don't like horror games!

In what quickly became my favorite Resident Evil so far - this entry is nothing short of masterful.

An incredible evolution of the original, remastered with some glorious additions and beautiful graphics, Resident Evil 2 (2019) is something to behold.

Gratifying from beginning to end this three-act adventure puts you through the stops of its tropes: tight halls, underground muck, and sterile walls.
What's interesting is how new this feels while in its evergreen soul - quite old. I see these tropes as developed and aware, but have to remind myself the tropes in this title are the foundation of said tropes. Confusing. I know.

This game does them brilliantly.

While I loved the first game, I found it's sewers overwrought, and it's ending a little too dragged out.
While it's initial mansion elements - brilliant - felt to go on a little too long.

This title cleans all of this up perfectly.

It is concise. Deliberate. And intentional. All while upping the ante.

To take place in a police department alone is subversion at its finest. There is an underlying sense of safety. Shouldn't there be? Weapons and fortress alone of such a building.

The developers and writers let you bask in this throwing their patented zombies down a hallway or two, letting them slam their viscera fists on the glass.

However, after these first couple hours, where I said "this isn't scary" - the game develops. Introducing a new enemy type, draining you of your ammunition, and debuting what is now infamous in the franchise: the stalker.

A large, unstoppable, uninterruptible force. Slowly moving towards you, intent on stopping you. Its footsteps clanking in the distance and behind walls, invading areas once deemed safe and clear.

This genius addition pushes you forward. It persists. It stalks. And it upends any safety.

This one large addition, is met with a multitude of tiny minute details that increase the terror.

The famous RE formula sees to your development as a character. The classic arc is to start you with a knife, maybe 5 rounds in a pistol, and over its course land you into an action hero. To equip you with the power to fight back and take corners without fear.

This title, basks in this line. Yes, there are moments where you possess your flamethrower and rocket launcher and deal your damage and rule the world.
But this is generally saved for few moments - mainly boss fights.

With a short runtime, this game is - for the better - unable to allow this. You are always conserving. Always considering.

Unlike other titles, your turning of corners is always a question of what resource to use. What secondary to have equipped in case grabbed. It's a constant flux of resource, keeping you on your toes until it's last breath.

And this short runtime does not diminish the game.

First off - it's always good when a game knows to end the party. Nothing is worse than a game or a movie or a book struggling to find its conclusion, dragging out as I the audience roll my eyes and check TimeToBeat, or the runtime, or the page count.

And second - this game comes with a B-Side. The other perspective, allowing you to take on the game in a re-contextualization once finished.

I played Claire A, and Leon B, as I figured Leon would know the department better and have more confidence than Claire. To me it made sense to see his through second, as I found this confidence myself.

The addition of a B-Side is brilliant. Not only do I get to re-experience the game in a whole new light, but I also get different segments and set-pieces.

And it shocks me how many people online say playing the B-Side is mainly just replaying and not much is changed but puzzles and some cut scenes. It's bonkers to see it as some re-hashing. I didn't find that at all.

The metroidvania aspects were captivating, allowing me access to different rooms, different orders of items, and even different uses for some.
And the added segments were chunks of gameplay, entirely different pieces.
And on top of that, it was a blast solving areas and puzzles with the knowledge I foggily could remember.

And as I did all of this I experienced a new fear - me being an idiot. With my confidence I found myself wasting ammo and ignoring enemies and setting my path ignorantly to what was around me - landing me in hot water repeatedly.

There was one point in my B-Run where my rushed ignorance lead me to a boss fight with nothing but the items I could scavenge in the arena.

What consequential beauty. :')

Resident Evil 2, a classic in the survival horror genre, holds a special place in my heart. Released originally in 1998 and revived in 2019 with stunning visuals and updated mechanics, this game captures the essence of fear, suspense, and adventure like few others can. There are several reasons why I adore Resident Evil 2, and I’d like to share some of those insights here.

Firstly, the atmosphere of Resident Evil 2 is nothing short of mesmerizing. The ominous sounds, dark corridors, and detailed environments create an immersive experience that pulls players into the gloomy world of Raccoon City. From the eerie silence punctuated by distant groans to the unsettling ambience of the police station, every moment in the game is designed to elicit fear and tension. The redesigned visuals in the 2019 remake intensified this atmosphere, breathing new life into the beloved classic while maintaining the dread that fans loved.

The game's storyline is another pivotal reason for my admiration. It follows two protagonists, Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield, as they navigate the horror unleashed by the T-Virus. The narrative is engaging and well-crafted, blending action and horror seamlessly while developing the characters in a meaningful way. I found myself emotionally invested in Leon and Claire's journey, cheering them on as they faced relentless enemies and uncovering the dark truth behind the outbreak.

Moreover, the gameplay mechanics are incredibly well-executed. The combination of resource management, puzzle-solving, and combat creates a perfect balance of challenge and strategy. Every decision matters, whether it's choosing when to engage enemies or managing limited ammunition. This aspect encourages players to think critically and plan their actions carefully, adding to the overall tension. The different paths available for Leon and Claire also enhance replayability, allowing me to experience the game multiple times without it feeling repetitive.

The iconic enemies and bosses, particularly the terrifying Mr. X, are another highlight of Resident Evil 2. His relentless pursuit of the player adds a unique layer of suspense, as I constantly felt the need to be on my toes. The thrill of trying to outsmart and evade him while solving puzzles creates a heart-pounding experience that is hard to replicate in other games. The variety of zombies and other creatures further diversifies the gameplay, keeping me engaged and on edge.

Lastly, the community surrounding Resident Evil 2 has enriched my experience even further. Engaging with fellow fans through forums, discussions, and social media has allowed me to share theories, tips, and nostalgic moments. This sense of camaraderie makes playing Resident Evil 2 not just a solitary experience but a shared journey with others who appreciate the game as much as I do.

In conclusion, my fondness for Resident Evil 2 is rooted in its atmospheric world, engaging story, challenging gameplay, and vibrant community. It is a timeless classic that not only defined a genre but also created lasting memories for those who dared to face the horrors within Raccoon City. Whether revisiting the original or experiencing the remake, Resident Evil 2 remains a cornerstone of my gaming passion, and I look forward to many more thrilling adventures within its terrifying embrace.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is, in my opinion, a standout entry in the Resident Evil series and an absolute must-play for fans of survival horror. At the time of writing, I have logged 33.2 hours across four playthroughs, each offering a unique perspective on Raccoon City’s terrifying outbreak.

My first run was Leon A on Standard difficulty, taking me 9 hours, 1 minute, and 34 seconds with 53 saves, earning a C rank. Shortly after, I played Claire A, finishing in 2 hours, 4 minutes, and 58 seconds with 19 saves and earning an S rank. My third playthrough was Leon B on Standard difficulty, completed in 1 hour, 18 minutes, and 18 seconds with 9 saves, earning another S rank. Finally, I challenged myself with Claire B on Hardcore difficulty, completing it in 1 hour, 5 minutes, and 34 seconds with only 2 saves, achieving an S+ rank. Screenshots of all my results are publicly available on my Steam profile for anyone curious.

This is not my first experience with RE2R. I attempted it a few years ago on PS4 but stopped shortly after encountering Mr. X. The intensity of the game after that point, combined with the fact that I have a severe anxiety disorder, made the game incredibly overwhelming at the time. However, my love for Resident Evil lore drew me back, especially with the announcement of Resident Evil 9’s February 2026 release. Determined to play the series in chronological order, I completed Resident Evil Zero and Resident Evil 1 beforehand, earning every achievement on all three games and perfecting them all on Steam.

Resident Evil 2’s 2019 Remake delivers a perfect balance of tension, atmosphere, and gameplay refinement. The over-the-shoulder camera, realistic lighting, and meticulous sound design amplify the horror, making Raccoon City feel oppressive and dangerous at every turn. The game is incredibly well-paced. Even repeated playthroughs remain engaging thanks to the different scenarios between Leon and Claire, as well as the B scenarios that expand the narrative.

The game’s design is both challenging and rewarding. Inventory management, limited resources, and the ever-present threat of zombies and Mr. X create a genuine sense of urgency. Each encounter tests your planning and reaction skills, and the multiple difficulty options allow you to scale the challenge to your preference. The final playthrough on Hardcore, with only 2 saves, was particularly exhilarating and gave me a real sense of accomplishment.

As someone who has played most of the Resident Evil games - including RE3R, RE7, and RE8 - I can confidently say that Resident Evil 2 Remake is my favorite Resident Evil game so far. Its combination of tight gameplay, immersive environments, and compelling narrative make it a benchmark for modern survival horror. That said, I am eagerly anticipating Resident Evil 9, which, based on what Capcom has shown, has the potential to surpass even this masterpiece.

If you enjoy survival horror with atmospheric tension, intricate level design, and compelling storytelling, Resident Evil 2 Remake is an absolute essential. Even for those who have tried it in the past, returning to Raccoon City is worth it, especially if you are chasing those S and S+ ranks like I did.

by far the longest 100% game completion I've done for resident evil. with that being said there's quite a few things I love and hate about RE2.

to start, the campaign in it's entirety is great as a homage to the original resident evil 2, as this was my first ever resident evil game, I came back to discover everything it has to offer and completely have 100% every bit of it. the scenario system (while quite dull..) is an interesting experience, I don't personally like the B playthroughs as it doesn't change much besides starting you off in different segments of RPD, and key item location changes (and the obvious ''true ending'') I felt like this all could've been packed into the standard game, and to just have Leon 1, and then Claire 1, with Claire being the true end to the game, but I digress; it's great to be able to choose who you want to play. 

my main big gripe as a Completionist when it comes to RE2 is that you have to do a crap ton of playthroughs just to 100% re2. to start off my first playthrough was just me experiencing the game for the first time. My second playthrough was discovering everything as well as getting some side Achievements. my third playthrough was hardcore with Leon, then my fourth was hardcore on Claire, then I got S+ hardcore with Claire, then S+ standard with Leon. then i also did two separate runs on standard for the Minimalist and the Frugalist achievements.

in total that is 8 playthroughs of RE2 but.... even with all of that being said, it was an enjoyable experience (besides the total nerve-wrack that was S+ on Claire A Hardcore for the infinite minigun...) I loved how re-playable this game is! each play though has me thinking on how fast I can go compared to my previous runs as well as learning the best routing for things like A small Carbon Footprint achievement. as well as myself using the infinite minigun for Frugalist, just absolutely shredding all zombies and the bosses! very fun, and while I don't quite like the sheer amount of playthroughs, it still remained a great experience overall :)


Now for the DLC's...... RE2 has the Ghost Survivors which is a ''what if'' scenario based off of the small side characters (like kendo the gun shop owner in Leon's playthrough) and has you escaping different segments of the game to reach an exfil point and survive. while the concept is pretty simple, overall I did NOT enjoy these small DLC's... while they are free, the four DLC's are just annoying to complete and feel like a huge barrier for anyone trying to 100% re2. sometimes i wonder if CAPCOM does this on purpose just to annoy us completionists. one of the DLC's is called ''No way out'' which has you fighting in the gas station at the very start of the game, fighting off 100 zombies and getting items throughout the game mode to try and Survive. there is a record for completing this mode while only shooting 60 handgun rounds. while it seems simple, the last two waves are an absolute pain in the ass and it was overall a horrible experience and personally took me 20+ attempts to defeat. I ended up watching guides and made my own personal guide to jot down each zombie spawn in each wave just to complete this record; which grants you infinite ammo in all of the ghost survivor game modes. using the infinite ammo doesn't update your time in each mode, but for my sake i just needed to complete each of the DLC's for the records.

there is also another DLC called ''the 4th survivor'' which pays a homage to HUNK from the original re2, which is a soldier that never seems to die. in this mode you need to escape the sewers to exfil and try to race against the little time you have before the nuke goes off from the main story. it's overall a decent DLC and fun to learn, and it's especially good for trying to learn how to dodge zombie attacks.

however..... after completing the 4th survivor game mode, you unlock a parody mode called the ''tofu survivor'', which has you play as 5 different tofu's, each with their own special niche in terms of what weaponry they use to go through the same scenario as the 4th survivor. for my sake all i needed to do was complete each scenario with each tofu and I've 100% re2! but each of their niche's they have isn't for good I'm afraid. while some tofu's are fun (looking at you Uiro-Mochi, who only has grenades throughout the entire run) most of them are just absolutely annoying to try and complete. the main one being the first tofu you play as. he only has a few heals and a metric butt load of knifes, it must've took me 5 tries to complete the run with him. same can be said with the ''Annin Tofu''. but for the sake of this review I'm keeping it short. I just don't like this extra mode and it's quite frustrating after a few tries. but it's there for those who enjoy it.


to summarize, I think resident evil 2 is a great game and I enjoyed it as my first entry into the resident evil series. while the DLC's for re2 are quite lackluster, I'm giving RE2 a 8/10!

Score: 8.5 / 10
The 2019 Resident Evil 2 Remake is a masterclass in reviving a classic, trading fixed cameras for tense over-the-shoulder action. It successfully blends the tight resource management and terrifying atmosphere of the original with modern graphical fidelity and stellar combat.

The Good: Core Mechanics and Narrative
At its heart, the gunplay is excellent. The third-person perspective feels weighty and satisfying, making every bullet count in a world where resources are perpetually scarce. You'll spend as much time carefully aiming for a headshot as you will desperately deciding whether to fight or flee, perfectly capturing the classic survival-horror loop.

Adding to this tension is the challenging and rewarding puzzle design. The game demands attention to detail, forcing you to think strategically about key placement and safe combinations. Solving a complicated lock is a satisfying moment of reprieve amidst the chaos.

Furthermore, the game's narrative holds up remarkably well. Given its 1998 origins, the interwoven stories of Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield fighting through the Raccoon City disaster are compelling and foundational to the series. The characters are well-realized, and the overall plot feels like a genuinely classic horror experience. Visually, the recent updates incorporating RTX have made this a stunning-looking game, bringing modern shine to the famously gloomy RPD halls.

Room for Improvement
While the RPD station is iconic, a key drawback is that exploration can become tedious. The constant backtracking through the same corridors and hallways, essential for progression, can sometimes feel repetitive and slow down the game's pace. This reliance on map repetition occasionally detracts from the immediate excitement.

Additionally, the persistent horror elements, namely the terrifying Tyrant (Mr. X), did not feel like a central threat for the majority of the game. For players seeking constant high-stakes terror, the game’s tension might only truly ramp up during the final boss encounters, leaving much of the preceding run feeling more action-oriented than overtly scary.

Conclusion
Resident Evil 2 Remake is a highly polished, mechanically sound, and essential survival-horror experience. It succeeds where it matters most: delivering excellent combat and challenging puzzles wrapped in a beloved, well-told narrative. While the perpetual feeling of exploration can drag and the persistent horror doesn't always hit hard until the climax, it remains a fantastic game that expertly updates a piece of gaming history.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is less of a horror game and more of a stress simulator featuring zombies, zero ammo, and a 300-pound fashion model who refuses to leave me alone.

I walked into the police station thinking, “I got this.”
Five minutes later I’m barricading windows with pieces of wood like I’m trying to survive a budget home renovation show.

The zombies?
Unfair. Absolutely unfair.
I shoot them once: nothing.
Twice: nothing.
Twenty times: they fall over for about 0.5 seconds and then immediately stand back up like “haha anyway—”.
Their jaw is literally hanging off and they’re still clocking in for work.

The police station makes NO sense.
Who designed this?
Why do the doors require chess pieces?!
Why is there a secret underground facility with more laboratory equipment than the entire nation of Norway?
Why do I need a heart-shaped key??
WHO BUILDS THIS??

And then the game decides:

“Hey, you seem calm. Time to introduce Mr. X.”

This dude enters the game by lifting a helicopter like it’s a pillow.
He stomps around the station 24/7 like a walking fridge with anger issues.
You can hear him from a mile away and he ALWAYS KNOWS WHERE YOU ARE.

I hide in a room.
He stands outside.
I move one inch.
He kicks the door like he’s collecting rent.

He doesn’t run.
He doesn’t hesitate.
He just approaches with the slow confidence of someone who’s already won.

Every encounter with him is:
	•	hear footsteps
	•	panic
	•	run
	•	scream
	•	run into zombie
	•	scream louder
	•	use all ammo
	•	realise you forgot the medallion
	•	cry

Best moments:
	•	Shot a zombie in the knees so it crawled after me like a cursed Roomba
	•	Mr. X punched me into the next dimension
	•	Dog barked IRL because I yelled “NO NO NO NO HE’S RIGHT THERE”
	•	Took damage while pausing because I panicked and missed the button
	•	Forgot how to read map under pressure and died in a hallway I’ve walked 10 times

Pros:
	•	Chaos
	•	Panic
	•	Leon’s hair stays perfect under all circumstances
	•	Claire’s grenade launcher = emotional support
	•	Mr. X teaches cardio
	•	Atmosphere so good it made me whisper “please stop” at my screen

Cons:
	•	My heart rate
	•	Zombies have PhD-level durability
	•	Mr. X needs to take a day off
	•	Inventory space is a cruel joke
	•	Probably aged 7 years while playing

Final Verdict:
Resident Evil 2 Remake is pure, beautiful chaos.
I fear every hallway.
I fear opening doors.
I fear footsteps.
I fear everything.

10/10 — amazing game, but someone please tell Mr. X to give me personal space.

[h3]Nostalgia with ray tracing: looks amazing, plays like history class[/h3]

[b]TL;DR[/b]: [i]Resident Evil 2 Remake is gorgeous, loud, dramatic, and undeniably iconic - but it’s still a lovingly restored antique. Great to look at, occasionally great to play, and constantly reminding you exactly how old it really is. [/i]

Turns out even a whole new engine can’t rescue 1998-level pacing and layout. The “legendary atmosphere” everyone keeps preaching about? Mostly jump scares and zombies screaming behind you like a bad Halloween attraction - subtle as a brick.

Half the game is a constant debate with yourself: [i]Do I shoot this one, or do I awkwardly sidestep it like an ex in a supermarket aisle? [/i] Meanwhile, you’re rationing ammo like it’s the apocalypse and Capcom taxes bullets per shot. And for reasons known only to the nostalgia committee, they rebuilt the entire PS1 floor plan brick by brick: same hallways, same broom-closet rooms, same backtracking loops that will make you question your life choices.

Sure, the new engine looks incredible. But underneath all that modern tech, it’s still pure 1998 mayhem, just running buttery-smooth now.

[b] Update after game completion [/b]

I had to finish it - I forked over full price for it, but you don't have to.

To be fair, the game does get better after you finally escape the Raccoon City Police Department. The problem? You have to grind through hours of deja vu hallways to earn that tiny slice of actual momentum. It’s like Capcom hid the fun part behind a paywall made of keycards and backtracking.

Playing as Claire: people keep calling it the “second half” of the game, but let’s be honest: it’s the same game reheated and sprinkled with “emotional journey™” seasoning. Same locations, nearly identical story beats, just packaged as “a different perspective” so you don’t notice you’re basically doing New Game+, but with more red jackets. More content? More story? Haha, no. But hey, you get to solve those puzzles again.

Never played the original, but I really had a hard time putting this one down. I love survival horror games, and I think aside from RE4R, RE2R is definitely in my top 20 horror games of all time. I'd highly recommend this game to both new and returning fans to the series.

As someone who never touched the original Resident Evil 2 before playing this amazing remake, I thoroughly enjoyed the game from beginning to end. The gameplay, voice acting, score, the ambience, and story all made sense and came together beautifully. The puzzles weren’t too hard to solve, and Mr. X genuinely felt like a real threat throughout the entire RPD station.

My favorite part of the game was the RPD station; my least favorite was the NEST area, as I felt it was too short — though the final boss fight with Birkin made up for it. Leon’s campaign was a solid 9/10. Claire’s campaign was slightly better thanks to her dynamic with Sherry. The Ghost Survivors mode also made the game even more enjoyable and replayable.

After playing the original RE2 and then replaying the remake, I realized the NEST area was indeed cut short, just as I initially thought. The zapping system was also nonexistent, which I found to be an odd change since it was one of the things I enjoyed most about the original. Nonetheless, that doesn’t make the remake bad by any means. I believe it improved on many aspects of the original, and the achievements were challenging but fun.

Overall, the game is an absolute banger — so much so that I bought it on Steam during a sale even though I already owned it on my PS4 when it first came out.

I can only confirm that it is rather well made remake that you will play through more than just once.

While they have taken modern approach to survival horror games here, RE2R maintains the classic challenge system for which are Capcom games like Resident Evil or Onimusha known for.

There were however some flops made when they've made this game. Some smaller, some larger.
For the smaller issues: I for example couldn't leave unnoticed that zombies that walk around the 2nd floor corridor near the art room once the helicopter crash into police station, still have hair even though they are fully engulfed in flames. Even after they get completely burnt into cinders, they still have hair. Nothing game-breaking but still quite noticeable detail.
Another thing I consider issue that was never fixed is that when you make blunder and die, you have to load the last save twice or quit to main menu and then continue from last save, because when you select continue or load the latest save from game over screen, game timer remains as of the time of death instead of the time when the save was taken.
I'm also quite disappointed that there is only one alternative costume per character that can be unlocked by playing the game. Rest have to be purchased as DLC from store.

As for the larger issues: I consider the 2nd run to be completely wasted potential for the story mode.
It's practically identical to the selected character's main story, rather than telling what they were doing during main story events of the other character.

Thus Clare on 2nd run often have to repeat same things that Leon did already in his main story, fight the same boss fights as Leon have fought already, and rescue Sherry from exact same location in sewers where Leon rescued Ada after fighting G-William in exact same fight.
Not to mention [spoilers ahead] that Tyrant is being killed by G-William in Claire's story after elevator ride from below the orphanage, yet Leon's 2nd run story follows the main one as if that never happened.

Long story short: 2nd run is poorly made shortened version of the main story, nowhere near it's potential, rather than side story of what the other characters were doing meanwhile.

Despite all of that, I've enjoyed the main story of the game, looking forward to the challenge modes, and I can recommend this game to others.

The best survival horror game I've played next to Parasite Eve 2 and the original Resident Evil and Resident Evil 7 Biohazard. This game is really that good. The environment you're put in makes you feel very on edge. Like at any moment you could be attacked and I feel like that adds so much to the experience of a survival game. That you can never really feel safe unless you're in the save room.

I played as Claire. The game eases you in quickly without really any tutorial needed. Good for immersion. There's very little on the UI to take away from that either. The camera angles are well done and I think they did well to copy that same terror from the original Resident Evil mansion. Hallways are narrow, dark and plenty of windows that can be broken into from outside keep you on your feet.

Pacing is good. While there is a sense of urgency to progress the story, I didn't feel rushed playing this game. I took my time to clear out each room and love that there is a color indicator to tell you when a room is cleared or still something you're missing. I only had to consult a guide once for something. This is a huge quality of life feature in the game and without it a lot of other survival horror games miss the point and have you backtracking for days figuring out what you missed.

The gunplay is satisfying. It'll take more than one headshot to kill most zombies. At times you're better off just running away and saving your ammo. It's a game of resource management and wits. There's not enough ammo here to go crazy like in CoD zombies. You have to be methodical about it but still fairly generous amount of ammo if you rather go in guns blazing.

I have to admit the story really engaged me. As with typical RE games you learn more from reading documents and letters as you progress through different areas. It's like you're a detective piecing together evidence and written testimonials to form a picture of what transpired.

Puzzles are well done. All of them were quite straight forward. The way the game is designed you can't progress without having solved the important ones so there's incentive to go through every area to find what you need to complete the next puzzle.

The game looks terrific in 4k. Great audio as well. It's like watching a movie but you're in it and you better find a way survive to see how it turns out. Would definitely replay some day with Leon

[h1] 9/10 [/h1]
I'm not a fan of horrors in fiction and I usually just avoid them by a longshot. However, even with my dislike towards this genre, the first half of this game, exploring through the police station, was one of the best and most authentic gaming experiences I've ever witnessed.

[h2] PROS: [/h2]
[b] + Visual Design [/b]
Overall astonishing graphics for even deper immersion, especially the amazing lighting.

[b] + Breathtaking Atmosphere [/b]
Perfectly set up tense atmosphere to keep you engaged and immersed. The fear is created through visual aspects and audio, not some cheap jumpscares.

[b] + Survival Aspects [/b]
Ammunition and other useful items are scarce. The player is forced to make decisions when to use ammo, because if used recklessly, it will run out very soon. Thanks to the limited amount of available resources, the exploration is recommended and therefore even more rewarding.

[b] + Audio Design [/b]
First time I've had a shiver ran down my spine upon hearing someone's footsteps.

[b] + Exploration/Puzzles [/b]
Exploration is incorporated into the main story. You have to find stuff to progress further.
There are a lot of optional rooms and other interactions waiting to be found with useful treasures.
Puzzles are decent, requiring at least slight brain usage.

[b] + Detailed Gore [/b]
The damage done on zombies is visually very detailed. Only near the end of the game, I realised I can shoot off their limbs to cripple them, potentionally saving ammunition that would have been wasted on an unnecessary kill.

[b] + Mr. X [/b]
I love him.

[h2] CONS: [/h2]
[b] - Abrupt Ending [/b]
I respect that the ending is trying to stay faithful to the original game, nevertheless it still ruined my overall experience and satisfaction from the ending. You have to complete the game multiple times to achieve the "true" ending, which is fine, but I feel like it should've been available even in the first run. The game isn't that different when played from the perspective of the other character, at least to me it's not worth a whole replay, just to get an extra scene or two at the end.

[b] - Boss Fights [/b]
The boss fights aren't as creative as they could have been.

[b] - Slight Loss of Atmosphere Towards the End [/b]
The pacing got way faster at the cost of a great horror atmosphere.

[b] - Mr. X [/b]

Resident Evil 2 RE:make is an incredible love letter to the original Resident Evil 2 from 1998. It takes a lot of inspiration from the original design and reimagines it to make for a much more modern and great experience for both new and returning audiences. While not everything this game does is "perfect", I can accept the flaws this game has as the pros heavily outweigh the cons. Which is something I cannot say the same about my ex-wife...

This game has a fair amount of replay value that doesn't feel artificial, as I have manually chose on my own accord that I want to replay THIS remake on several occasions. Leon and Claire's characters were given a bit more personality that I am honestly a fan of. This game doesn't stiff us on any extra content either we are given A & B scenarios (more on that later). We get the Fourth Survivor Hunk minigame, along the Tofu reskins, which I am surprised we got, and we got a "what-if" gamemode with the Ghost Suriviors. Which is a fair amount of content for a $60, but I probably would still settle for a cheaper price tag as the game is nearly six years old now (as of writing). But hey, it's still worth a helluva lot more than my ex-wife.

Mr. X has gotten a huge upgrade in this game, he has been transformed to a relatively consistent looming threat in both scenarios. He is no longer restricted to scripted events that would basically end as you change loading zones. The heavy footsteps you hear in the RPD is genuinely freaky, and sometimes encountering him can force you to reroute which is awesome. Chief Irons is painted to be a massive [CENSORED] and a [CENSORED] in the RE:make. Which is in my opinion better than his original appearance, because screw that guy. Ada is fun, the rest of the side characters don't deviate much from the original material so that is good.

I did mention not everything is perfect about this experience. And most of that boils down to how certain things in this RE:make versus the 1998 release. My main two gripes are the beginning voyage to the RPD, and the A&B scenario system. In the 1998 release, the player is required to outrun hoards of zombies to make it to the RPD, with a lot of content and environments to explore before even arriving to the game's main set-piece. The "voyage" in the RE:make is following a linear path that doesn't deviate and doesn't have different affecting outcomes depending on which routes you take. Which is very similar to the arguments with my ex-wife, no matter what approach I took, it would still lead to the same hellish outcomes. Even worse, the B scenario doesn't have that voyage at all, you start within the confines within the RPD. This linear routing does have some effects inside the RPD; however, it is much more tame and I will not dock it there. The second issue being that the A & B scenarios don't carry weight on each other in the RE:make. It's kind of hard to explain, but the original worked on two disks. One for the A scenario, and one for the B scenario. Some of the items you took from A scenario would directly affect the player when playing the B scenario, as they wouldn't be there. That doesn't exist here, it is a similar story where the beats all still hit, just at different points. But again, the pros of this RE:make are much greater than the cons.

All in all, Resident Evil 2 RE:make is an experience I can recommend to both new and original players. And in most situations I would probably recommend the RE:make over the original, and they can play the original afterwards if it interests them. RE2make presents fewer, but still equally fun puzzles and games within it's confines, unlike my ex-wife as she dealt in a greater amount manipulative games which are not very fun. For players that have never played Resident Evil, RE2make is a great starting point and introduction to the series, aside from RE1, RE1 Remake and mayyyyyybeee RE7.

Resident Evil 2 Remake delivers with its tense, atmospheric survival horror experience. The story is straightforward, we have a standard zombie apocalypse setup, I was engaged, and the atmosphere always succeeded at scaring me. The sounds in the game were also intimidating, Mr. X's footsteps always had me on edge, and the sudden banging of zombies on windows or doors added to those panic moments.

Mr. X is easily the most intimidating presence in the game. From the moment he appears, he just hunts you and keeps that tension alive. Regular zombies were fine, but I did dislike how many headshots it sometimes took to take one down, and even then they could stand back up. I've seen online people complaining about ammo management, but I personally never had any issues. I always felt like I had enough ammo and I was able to kill almost every zombie I saw coming my way. Shotgun shells were a bit scarce, which does make sense since it is a stronger weapon.

Gameplay was solid, though movement felt weird early on, and I did sometimes question Leon when the dude is barely jogging in intense situations, like when being chased. Puzzles were generally good, but backtracking sometimes felt tedious and slowed the game's momentum for me. After finishing Leon's story, I decided not to play as Claire just yet. I don't think I can go through with it knowing I need to solve the same puzzles and run around in the same places, but I will revisit that later.

While the game did feel a bit on the shorter side, overall, I think this game offers a great atmosphere, mix of tension, solid gameplay, and it's worth to play at least once.

Resident Evil 2 Remastered really impressed me with its incredible atmosphere and overall design. The game nails that dark, oppressive feeling that the series is known for, and wandering through the police station or the streets of Raccoon City feels both nostalgic and fresh at the same time. Visually and stylistically, it’s definitely one of the strongest entries in the franchise.

The story itself is solid — not groundbreaking, but enjoyable enough to carry the experience. Compared to Resident Evil 1 or Zero, it feels a bit more modern and structured, though it doesn’t quite hit the same classic charm for me.

One thing I wasn’t a huge fan of is the constant pressure from enemies that are always lurking behind you. There’s rarely a moment to just breathe or explore at your own pace, and that took away a bit of the enjoyment for me. Still, despite that, I absolutely loved my first playthrough.

I’m really looking forward to jumping into the second run, aiming for 100%, and continuing on through the series until I eventually reach Requiem.

Overall, Resident Evil 2 Remastered is a fantastic experience, atmospheric, intense, and well-crafted — even if it doesn’t always let you relax.

RE2 is what I would describe as a traditional survival horror as items are limited in slots having to choose to carry items that are weapons, puzzle pieces, ammo, healing, etc. in specifically those slots. This makes resources very scarce and have to rely more on strategy for how to get to locations.
RE4 gets more action oriented as storage is generally more flexible as puzzle pieces are stored entirely differently and you can have more flexibility in limited space for weapons ammo, etc. Additionally the merchant mechanic makes it feel more action paced as killing enemies is more of a must in RE4 for currency.

Thought I give it a try since it was on sale but boy was that a mistake. I have yet to find a game as nonsensical as this one. A police station with a built in escape route predicated on solving a medeival puzzle. Also Sorry Chris, you can’t get your gun until you solve this Victorian Royalty Exhibit Puzzle Box. 

The Raccoon City Police Station is, frankly, a spatial joke: a police headquarters that functions like a gothic puzzle dungeon where basic movement is impossible without jewels, crests, relief plates, and medieval mechanisms. It asks you to believe trained police officers conducted daily operations in a building where half the rooms are locked by Renaissance escape-room gimmicks. 

The environment feels like a curated obstacle course rather than a lived-in space, the threat feels constructed instead of emergent. The world feels like a themed attraction, not an actual place undergoing catastrophe.

The game’s reliance on arbitrary locks, jewels, and levers to gate progression interrupts narrative flow, constantly reminding reminding you that you're navigating a game rather than surviving in a coherent world.  Those arbitrary obstacles scream “game mechanics first, story second.” You aren’t surviving; you're solving designer-imposed riddles. Such BS can work for fast paced shooters like Doom (Green card to yellow to red), not a horror STORY, that predicates on worldbuilding, characters and motivations to create stakes and TENSION.

Leon and Claire are but thin sketches, their personalities conveyed more through posture and archetype than meaningful interaction. Supporting characters like Sherry, Ada, and Annette are motivationally inconsistent, shifting behaviors to suit cutscene tension rather than psychological continuity.

The tension built by the setting collapses under the weight of these mechanical contrivances, and no amount of moody lighting or zombie groans can mask the cognitive dissonance. RE2 struggles not because it lacks atmosphere, but because it consistently sabotages the very immersion it demands.

Basically it's a contrived rat maze that you're being pushed through, making "the plot" happen. Shut off your brain or forget about any immersion and just slog it till the end, like I did. I tried to play Claire's story after but having to endure the police station ordeal over again made me quit after an hour.

-The atmosphere in the game is there and it is maintained quite well.The tension in the game with the same Tyrant is very good - really makes you nervous.

I might be one of the few people I know that don't like this game that much.Every other list of "best Resident Evil games" will have RE2R ranked very close to the top, if not in the first place, and I totally disagree, really. RE3R rightfully receives a lot of critics for cutting a lot of content from the OG RE3: Nemesis, but I barely hear people complaining about the fact that RE2R cut almost all the differences the original game had between a playthrough A and B. 

The TLDR review is: Resident Evil 2 (1998) is better. Much better. I would recommend playing the original versions of RE2 and RE3 before (or even instead of) the remakes. You can find them on GOG for a fair price. But I understand most people nowadays may not be inclined to deal with tank controls and PS1 graphics, and, if you are one of those, just enjoy RE2R and RE3R for what they are. 

From now on, the review will have SPOILERS:

In RE2, you run through scenario A with Claire or Leon and then you go through scenario B with the other character (the canon way is Claire A, Leon B by the way). In the 1998 game this will lead you to different boss encounters during each run. 

G-Creature, for example, is always the first boss for scenario A, no matter wich character you chose, and that boss fight is not reutilized in scenario B. The same goes for the giant crocodile: it is the second boss for scenario A, but doesn't appear in scenario B. The final boss fight for scenario A is always the 4th form of Birkin (which is also exclusive to scenario A). In scenario B, the first boss will always be the 1st form of Birkin, you'll have to deal with Mr. X and the final boss is the 5th form of Birkin. All of those encounters exclusive to scenario B.

You can see they made an effort to distinguish scenario A and B. Not only the characters have exclusive weapons, but they also interact with different characters throughout the campaign and have to beat different bosses. By the other hand, in RE2R you'll deal with some bosses in your scenario A and then you'll have to beat the exact same bossfight (same arena, same everything) in scenario B. This happens for the first, second and third encounter with Birkin. It's mind-boggling, really. I cannot believe this game is praised as much as it is when it is a clear downgrade from the original in some aspects. The most outrageous change in my opinion is that Mr. X now appears in both scenarios, and that was a BIG difference in the OG where he just appears in scenario B. It really made that B run feel special.

To be honest, I don't really care that much about the story in RE games... that's not exactly why we like Capcom games, so I would be a little more inclined to ignore these incoherencies in the narrative if the gameplay was good enough, but I don't think it is. I think the atmosphere in RE2R is just fantastic through and through, but from all the over the shoulder games in the numbered series (with Revelations included) that's probably the worst the combat ever felt, no joke, I HATE the combat in this game. Guns feel very underpowered and even if the dismemberment is the best in the franchise (better than RE3R or even RE4R btw), I did not enjoy encountering zombies in this one. The RNG is through the roof, I bet you the original game from 1998 had more reliable patterns than the remake.

I remember entering the cafeteria near the reception of NEST in my first playthrough (on normal difficulty) and putting 7 bullets to the forehead of a zombie for him to finally fall, and I got so pissed I had to load the save to try it again. It took me 1 shot with the exact same weapon, and the zombie's head exploded. My average experience was much more akin to the first encounter with that zombie: a bunch of bullets and nothing happens. Maybe I'm the unluckiest guy in the world with RE2R RNG, that would explain why people love it so much while I would rather replay RE3R any day of the week than it, and it did not get better when I decided to replay the game earlier this year to get all the achievements (and I got them all, by the way). I genuinely think the combat in this game is worse than it was in the original game, so the only thing that was actually improved were the graphics.

I would still recommend, I guess... being one of the worst games in a franchise where most games are GOATed is not exactly the end of the world, but I actually think RE2R is not that bueno.

A solid remake, although it doesn't eclipse the original. Third person shooting is the biggest change, and one that is done well. Careful aiming is now a core part of combat, making it just as vital as positioning yourself and waiting for the right opportunity to attack. It is a welcome addition to the RE formula.

The police station portion is excellent, the clear highlight of the game. Everything outside of the station is mostly a linear list of sequences that are much less enjoyable, especially on repeated playthroughs.

SPOILERS AHEAD!!!

The main story beats are the same as the original, but the delivery isn't as good. It often feels rushed, the main duo barely interact with each other, and the buildup to Birkin is largely missing. He is unceremoniously dropped on the player early in the game, without any explanation whatsoever. In the original, Chief Irons, Sherry and the reporter gave a nice buildup to G before the reveal. Almost none of that is present here.

Instead, the tyrant, Mr X takes a much larger focus of the game, almost center stage at times. Considering that he was just an extra surprise in the original, this was a strange shift in the remake. (Mr X's role is something Nemesis would have benefited from in RE3R, but the less said about that remake, the better.) I don't mind Mr X, he is implemented well, I just wish it didn't come at the expense of Birkin. His character is barely present in the remake's story, he is used purely as the vehicle for G.

They've decided to increase the complexity of the sewers, but make the Laboratory smaller. Another weird design choice, since, unsurprisingly, the sewers are far less interesting than the Labs.

The second run, or B scenario isn't as expansive as it was in the OG. It is still worth doing though, to see the differences with the other main character.

Enemies are decent, the zombies in particular are handled great, as these slow moving tanks. The game gives you many tools to maneuver them with. Lickers, on the other hand, were handled with less grace. There are only a couple of ways to deal with them, it almost feels like they came from a different game, to be honest. Very gimmicky enemy.

The bosses are ok overall, the problem is, they move relatively fast, and you don't. Movement feels sluggish during boss fights, almost as if you were underwater. Good luck trying to move out of the way in time from a claw swipe enveloping half the screen.

I should close this out by saying that the audiovisual presentation is great, a real treat to experience. I recommend RE2R overall, but you should get your hands on the original Raccoon trilogy, which is available digitally nowadays, and represents the pinnacle of the series.

So i finished this game after playing RE7, RE8, RE4R and i have to say that visuals look good, sounds great, and nails the moody Raccoon City vibe. The problem is, once you get past the atmosphere, the game design starts fighting you. Zombies take half a magazine to kill, and even then, they might “wake up” later because of the game’s cold-spawn system. You’re punished for engaging zombies in a zombie game.

Exploration, one of the series’ best traits, becomes a chore. The RPD is basically a maze of same-looking corridors and offices that all blur together after a while. Most rooms exist only to host a single key item or puzzle piece, then never matter again. There’s no sense of discovery — just checklist progression. Worse, Mr. X and the respawning zombies turn exploration into stress management instead of curiosity. You’re not exploring because you want to, you’re just trying to survive long enough to grab the next key. Compare that to RE4R, where every area feels handcrafted — treasure, secrets, combat routes, new enemies — the map itself rewards you for looking around. In RE2R, it’s just find item, unlock door, repeat.

Combat is almost entirely unrewarding. Killing enemies drains scarce ammo and gives you nothing in return. Compare that with RE4 Remake’s elegant loop of fight -> loot -> upgrade — RE2 Remake just leaves you weaker after every encounter so It encourages speedrunning instead of exploration, which is bad, boring design.

Technically, it’s polished, and the atmosphere is strong. But as a game, it’s shallow. The enemy roster is tiny — zombies, lickers, sewer monsters, plant zombies —that's all XD. The campaign feels more like a museum tour of 1998 than a modern survival-horror experience.

The best start to the series, it's got Claire Redfield in it!

Pros

The Zombies are Tough: They aren't the easily killed enemies from later games. Every zombie takes lots of ammo and is a genuine threat, making you conserve your resources.

Mr. X : The Tyrant chases you everywhere. His constant, looming threat is the best part of the game and keeps the tension sky-high.

Great Controls: The modern over-the-shoulder camera and controls feel smooth and make the combat satisfying, even when you're panicking.

Cons

Mr. X Gets Annoying: After the initial scare wears off, having the Tyrant constantly chase you during necessary puzzle-solving or backtracking just becomes frustrating.

Rating: ★★★★★ (5/5)
Developer: Capcom
Release Date: January 25, 2019

A Masterclass in Remakes

The Resident Evil 2 Remake is not just a polished update of a classic—it's a full reimagining that sets a new benchmark for how to respectfully modernize a beloved title. Built from the ground up using Capcom’s RE Engine, this game takes the best elements of the original 1998 version and rebuilds them for a new generation with stunning visuals, immersive sound design, and refined gameplay mechanics.

Atmosphere & Graphics

The first thing that grabs you is the atmosphere. Raccoon City Police Department has never looked better—or more terrifying. Dynamic lighting, realistic character models, and richly detailed environments make every hallway tense and every encounter unforgettable. The game nails the oppressive, claustrophobic vibe that made the original so iconic while enhancing it with modern visual fidelity.

Gameplay & Mechanics

Gone are the tank controls of old. The remake uses a modern over-the-shoulder third-person perspective, similar to Resident Evil 4, but keeps the survival horror roots intact. Ammo is scarce, inventory management is key, and enemies—especially the dreaded Lickers and the unstoppable Mr. X—are genuinely dangerous. The combat feels tight and weighty, encouraging strategic play over mindless shooting.

Story & Characters

You play as Leon S. Kennedy, a rookie cop on his first day, and Claire Redfield, a college student searching for her brother. Both characters have separate campaigns with intertwining storylines, offering great replayability. The story is simple but effective, and the updated voice acting and character animations bring real emotional weight to the horror.

Sound Design

Every creak, moan, and distant shuffle puts you on edge. The sound design is masterfully crafted, especially when using headphones. The heavy footsteps of Mr. X are enough to make your heart race, even before you see him.

Final Verdict

The Resident Evil 2 Remake is a triumph. It honors the original while elevating it in nearly every way—making it approachable for newcomers and nostalgic for long-time fans. With excellent pacing, intense atmosphere, and strong storytelling, RE2 Remake proves that survival horror is far from dead.

If you’re a fan of horror, this is a must-play.

[h1] Great modernisation of classic survival horror [/h1] 

Resident Evil 2 is a fun, tense adaptation of classic Resident Evil gameplay to modern graphics and controls.
As either a fresh-faced, pre-RE4 Leon, who still climbs down ladders like a normal human, or as Claire Redfield (sister of The Boulder Puncher), you have to survive and escape the zombie virus outbreak of Raccoon City. Most of the game takes place in a labyrinthine police station, full of rooms to clear and puzzles to solve.

As in older survival horror games, resource management is a constant concern. You will have to make every shot count and be ready to avoid enemies if necessary. Zombies are tough and will often get back up after you gun them down, which can sometimes be a bit frustrating, but does preserve the economic focus of the genre. Skilful movement and aiming will help you only so much, planning and clever decision-making are more important to your success.

The game is tense, but not massively scary and there are few genuinely creepy moments, in part due to the somewhat limited enemy variety. The puzzles are a lot of fun and at times quite challenging and there are plenty of optional items to find if you're thorough.

One playthrough will last you between 6 and 9 hours, but there are two story modes with divergent content and stories.

While I wouldn't say that the game is an absolute masterpiece, it is still great fun and well worth playing.
I'm glad I bought it, but I'm also glad I got it deeply discounted.

Resident Evil 2 Remake — Reviewed by Albert Wesker

Ah… Resident Evil 2 Remake.
Imagine my surprise when I discovered that Capcom, in its infinite wisdom, chose to exclude me from the proceedings entirely. No sunglasses. No refined intellect. Just two rookies fumbling about with bullets and herbs. Truly... a tragedy.

Still, I decided to observe — purely for research purposes, of course.
Booting up the game, I’m greeted by Leon S. Kennedy, looking as naïve as ever. “Rookie cop survives zombie apocalypse,” they said. I call it statistical anomaly. Watching him stumble through the Raccoon City Police Department is like watching a chimpanzee discover fire — entertaining, but painful.

Then there’s Claire Redfield. Ah yes… another Redfield. Because one wasn’t enough. She storms through the chaos wielding a grenade launcher like she’s ordering coffee. At least she has initiative — I’ll give her that.

The visuals? Glorious. Every glistening organ, every droplet of blood, every shambling corpse rendered with such decadent precision. I could almost applaud the virus’ handiwork — if I didn’t already perfect it myself.*

Then comes Mr. X.
The moment he burst through that wall, I nearly spilled my tea. The man’s persistence is admirable, if not… adorably misguided. He’s the kind of brute Umbrella made when they wanted results — not intelligence. A hammer, not a scalpel.
I suppose not everyone can be me.

As for the gameplay — tight, tense, and unrelenting. Ammo management. Inventory panic. That feeling of dread creeping in when you realize you’re cornered and low on health… ah, nostalgia. It’s almost romantic.

And yet, as I watch these survivors crawl through the wreckage of Raccoon City, one thought dominates my mind:
If I were there… it would’ve been over in seven minutes.

Still, I must give credit where it’s due. Capcom managed to bottle fear, tension, and nostalgia into one exquisite virus of a remake. A true success. Almost… Umbrella-worthy.

Final assessment:
A masterful recreation of chaos.
9 out of 10.
Would be a perfect 10 if they’d had the decency to include me — but then again, perfection is something only I achieve.

[h1][b] TLDR: Tense atmosphere and a terrifying game world creates the best of what survival horror has to offer. [/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Graphics
➕Excellent survival-horror gameplay
➕Puzzles
➕Atmosphere


[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Can be overly punishing survival mechanics
➖Audio way too quiet
➖Clunky combat at times

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [8/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place primarily inside an old museum that has been repurposed to a police station. You then explore an underground sewer area that connects to a high-tech laboratory. Each area in the game world if fantastically created, not only from a traversal standpoint - which is essential as you’re evading enemies, but also from an interaction standpoint. There are tons of items essential to your survival, meticulously placed among realistic appearing clutter. Everything looks beautifully terrifying and matches my expectation perfectly of a zombie outbreak. 

There are two distinct stories you can play through - Leon and Claire. While they each take place within the same areas, they are different in the NPCs that appear and the items you use, and more importantly to the plot, both Leon and Claire have different objectives as they progress through Raccoon City. 
I found the narrative to be good, nothing mind-blowing, but good enough to where I wasn’t disappointed and wanted to continue. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [7/10] [/b] [/h1]
Like the narrative, the mechanics can be split into two different flavors - combat and puzzles. 
Combat is exactly what it sounds like, but with an emphasis on the “Survival” part of the survival horror genre. You need to constantly be aware of your resources (bullets/healing) and try your best to conserve your items as you explore the station to complete puzzles. 
The puzzles are very interesting and often a mixture of inventory management with exploration and minigames. Since inventory is very limited, you’ll constantly need to weigh the importance of carrying combat items with the needed items for puzzles. This provides a great dynamic that once again truly exemplifies excellence in survival horror. 
It’s not all perfect, though, I found the combat to be terrible at times, especially with anything melee. Any time a licker jumps on you, or a boss is all up in your face, it just feels awful to move/aim/get away while they are doing their animations. It's almost like the game feels like an engine experiment for a 3rd person perspective at times. 

The difficulty can also be excessive. I started a play through as Leon on Standard and was feeling the resource pinch a few hours in. Zombies often end up needing ~5+ rounds to the head to fully kill them, vs ~3 rounds to the legs to disable their movement. Due to ammo scarcity, the game subtlety pushes you in the direction of disabling zombies instead of killing them, which often clashes with my preferred play through of “Everything scary must die now.” As such, I restarted on the easier mode (Assisted) and found it to be better for me. 
Likewise, deaths can often happen and while you don’t lose any items or anything, you do lose time and some checkpoints can be quite far back. 

[h1] [b] Graphics (Quality/Technical) – [9/10] [/b] [/h1]
The graphics are amazing. Combined with how well built the game world is, the look and feel of each zone is just superb, and I have no complaints from a fidelity perspective. 

On the technical side, I was disappointed how you can’t choose your default display monitor. I run dual monitors, and it is incredibly annoying having the game constantly open on my secondary monitor. Furthermore, the game for no reason at all randomly resets the monitor display on startup. Sometimes it works fine, others it takes a bunch of tweaking to get it right. 
Otherwise, performance wise, the game runs perfect on my system capped at 120 FPS. 
I noticed no bugs. 
i9-13900KF | RTX 4090 | 64GB RAM | 1440p @ 240hz | Windows 11 installed on SSD 

[h1] [b] Audio – [8/10] [/b] [/h1]
Great audio. The vast majority of the time, there is no music, except when you’re being chased. The silence definitely adds to the atmosphere. 

There is voice acting and it is perfect. No complaints. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
You can finish the game in around ~7 hours for a play through, but you should really do two walkthroughs - once as Leon, another as Claire.  Most of the maps will be the same, most of the items will be in the same pickup spot, albeit different items, so there can definitely be some repetition, but I think it's different enough where I was surprised on my 2nd play through. Two walkthroughs are the only way to get the true ending as well. Anymore, and it's just for achievements or if you enjoy the game, or for time attack/rankings, as the game itself is rather linear with no real choices to make.

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [8/10] [/b] [/h1]
Resident Evil 2 (RE2) is the pinnacle of survival horror. This is a remake of what is essentially the Diablo to ARPGs, RE2 is what defined the genre and its return proves that even after 20 years, the potential is still there. 

What RE2 does right is an amazing world to explore, creative puzzles to solve, and the tense thrill of surviving under the stress of inventory management. Somehow, combining horror with survival makes for a calculatingly fun experience, more so than a frustrating one. 

The biggest thing for me to call out as a negative is the clunky combat when you are faced with any fast melee enemies. Things like lickers or especially the boss(es) that get in your face, shows the limitations of the engine and view perspective as it turns quickly into a clunky mess until you can run away. There is no dodging or rolling, so you have to quickly turn and run to avoid things like charges or leaps. 

Overall, I greatly enjoyed my time doing two playthroughs for RE2. As someone who doesn’t like horror all that much, I found myself enjoying RE2 quite a lot. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
The base price of $40 is a bit steep, but the sale price of $9 is a steal.

The reincarnation of Resident Evil 2 is now coming to being six years old and I felt it would be obsolete now that the game-play loop of Resident Evil has seen major steps forward in its sequels but this is an instant timeless classic that deserves an argument for standing on the podium for being one of the best survival horror games ever made.

(+)  The entire design docket of RE2R is survival horror and there are only a few flairs of action in the entire thing.  The whole core of the game is feeding the loop of surviving the night and it's wonderfully designed and presented perfectly.  I loved the game-play loop of managing your limited equipment and having to think adaptively as there's always danger through every door.  The fidelity in the games presentation is first-class and although I had everything locked in at max it ran beautifully at >120 fps.  The game is still stunning and I especially loved how bodies would react to punishment, especially cloth and flesh tearing dynamically to slashes or blood pouring through bullet holes.  I adored how the station unravels to the sewer system underneath and then the lab further down as you're backtracking with new tools and clues for new areas.  RE2R uses the classic puzzle-key system but even something a little out-of-place fits nicely into the stellar environmental story telling.  I was just transfixed playing this, I really couldn't get enough and I'm already thinking of running through the parallel story that I missed when doing Leon-A, Claire B.  The sound design is a staple of the RE games and I think with sound being compressed through corridors, suppressed by wooden floor boards and screaming through glass it's probably the best implementation of sound in a game I've ever heard.  You're set loose in Raccoon City without any objective markers or barks from over the radio and I loved having to mentally map out the world and link clues to rooms and getting through on cleverness and bravado.  There's a fantastic variation in enemy design and it does one of my favourite things in really thinking about enemy design as it differs from parts of the map you're in which really makes it easy to invest in the world and immerse yourself in the game.

(-)  The game is a re-imagining of the classic RE2 so the controls can feel a little fiddly and clunky but this mostly adds to the atmosphere and panic of never innately mastering it in one play-through.  It's a little nitpick but I felt parts of the performances could have been punched up, it sometimes felt that I was stepping in dogmuck moreso than seeing a corpse's brain fall through its skull from gunfire.  I didn't really feel both scenarios welded together as with a B-scenario, which is needed to see the true ending, lapped over the initial play-through with repeat puzzles and bosses. I did have one technical annoyance of it always re-setting my graphic options meaning I had to go in and change them back so I never just jumped back into my save.

Overall, this is a masterpiece and everyone knows it.  It's effortlessly re-playable and relentlessly engaging.  It worked perfectly with my X1X controller and I completed the full run-through in just under 13 hours.  I would recommend this game to everyone, either wanting to start their love affair with Resident Evil or just wanted the scare themselves stupid for Halloween.
