A thoroughly enjoyable survival horror adventure which pairs excellent pacing with solid game design that kept me on my feet and deeply immersed throughout my journey in Racoon city.  

The first thing that struck me before even getting into the gameplay was the graphics. I never thought I'd get excited watching an overweight American truck driver munching on a juicy cheeseburger, but that cutscene achieved just that. Seems silly in hindsight, I'd seen the trailer like everyone else, but I guess it never really hit me how much Resident Evil was back until I was the one with the controller in my hands playing it for myself, even if I was 6 years late!  

One of my main qualms about modern games is that everything looks the same aesthetically. It's a particularly corporate design that's hard to describe but dominates in many so called AAA games leading to everything looking plastic, bland and subsequently soulless. I'm glad to say Resident Evil 2 avoided that curse and retained it's identity. Of all the locations we go to, the police department is my favourite. I genuinely felt like I was in the famous Racoon Police Department building as I explored it, rather than an unimmersive imitation. It really felt lived in as a direct result of the clever, realistic level design and attention to detail given to every area. 

The notes left added to this greatly, revealing information about the building's history and its inhabitants, progressing slowly from mundane things such as an arrest report to more desperate, disturbing writings of those trying to survive as the situation worsened massively. All this immersive design provides the perfect platform for the rest of the game to build upon, utilizing it's gameplay mechanics and wider story to construct an experience that I found to be fantastic, well crafted and highly memorable. 

Having played the remaster of the first game and some other survival horror titles, I've learned that there is a formula for the gameplay of resident evil games. It can essentially be broken down into; explore area, solve puzzles, move onto next area, fight a couple bosses in between, complete the game. All the while you need to be on the lookout for healing items, ammunition and missable puzzles that can lead to additional bonuses, such as the magnum pistol in this game and of course the numerous infected that eat lead for breakfast, above all else the big bad Mr X!  

I cannot possibility express to you how much I love this formula! The lack of ammo requiring the need for strategic conservation and the enemies overall toughness really empathised for me how dangerous the outbreak was and how I really was just a survivor desperately trying to stay alive. It creates a level of fear I've not felt since playing the original outlast. One wrong move could be your last and every encounter is intense. There were moments where I was constantly on edge and this really hooked me more than anything else. If you were able to just blast your way through all the enemies without issue it would drastically decrease the quality of the game and take me out of it almost completely. The difficulty enhances the experience greatly, I'd go as far as to say it's mandatory for this game. 

The game also features heavy exploration. You need to explore and solve puzzles which I thought were creative and balanced difficulty wise. I'm not exactly the sharpest upstairs but even I was able to solve all the puzzles (with the exception of the infamously annoying lab dispersal cartridge liquid puzzle) with a bit of patience and contemplation. It provides a good sense of direction for the player as it gives us a good reason to look around and really pay attention to detail. Progressively unlocking areas and piecing things together was really rewarding and it was so enjoyable to see my efforts pay off as I advanced the story and grabbed myself some goodies that a less sharper eye would miss.  

There is some backtracking which I've never been a fan of in games however this is kept to a minimum and the level design compensates for this by connecting everything really well. For example working our way around the west of the station to get a key that then unlocks a previously locked door which opens directly into the main hall, which acts as a sort of hub area at the start of the game. It's a brilliant design philosophy that keeps the flow of the game in check. It's exactly why the dungeons in Skyrim were so fun, you'd explore the entire thing then there would be a creative way to let you get back to the exit quickly such as a hidden passage leading straight to the main entrance. 

The story itself is great despite its simplicity. Without spoiling anything, it provides answers to why things have gone to hell and the narrative is given some additional depth with the side character you meet, which is different depending on who you choose to play as in the campaign. I won't go into any detail as for fear of revealing to much to the new player, but what I do want you to know is that these side characters are deeply interesting and do actually add to the story in their own unique way. They're not simply just 'there', they feel included and impactful. 

You even get to play as said side characters for a brief period during the campaign too. It was a unexpected change in gameplay but a welcome one as it kept things fresh and didn't bog down the story in anyway. One second to last thing I'd like to praise is the animations. They're so life like and immersive, specially when it comes to the cutscenes which flawlessly switch back to gameplay without any abrupt screen cutting or fading to black. It's all seamless and well made. I'm assuming motion capture was used and if so it was used brilliantly. 

One last thing I'd like to mention is that this game comes with additional content beyond just the main campaign. It has a mode called ghost survivors which are challenging missions with new characters and some new scenarios where in the player needs to get from A to B as enemies get progressively harder, and unlockable in game rewards, such as costumes, that can be earned by beating the game on it's hardest difficulty, including a fourth survivors mode. So if you beat the game and want to get more out of it, give yourself a challenge and you'll be rewarded for your efforts! 

All in all, everything just sort of comes together to create an experience as memorable as it is enjoyable, and I highly recommend everyone gives this game a go. It's original version is a classic and I've no doubts as time goes on this one will be considered a classic also.

Resident Evil 2 (the remastered edition) is nothing short of a masterpiece. There’s no debate here: Capcom managed to take a beloved classic and completely reimagine it into one of the greatest survival horror experiences in gaming history. Even in 2025, with countless AAA releases flooding the market, this game still feels untouchable.

The atmosphere is relentless, the dark corridors of the Raccoon City Police Department feel alive, oppressive, and terrifying in the best way possible. The visuals remain stunning, the lighting is cinematic, and every sound design choice, from the distant creaks to the haunting growls, keeps you on edge. 

What sets Resident Evil 2 apart is how perfectly it balances modern design with old-school survival horror tension. Ammo and resources feel scarce, every encounter matters, and yet the game never feels unfair. The pacing is immaculate, the story is faithful yet refreshed, and the dual campaigns between Leon and Claire give it enormous replay value.

This isn’t just a great horror game—it’s one of the best games of our time. Six years later, it remains a benchmark for how to do a remake right, and honestly, for how AAA gaming should strive to be: focused, polished, atmospheric, and unforgettable. Resident Evil 2 earns its place as a timeless masterpiece.

I've played this game to update my surface level knowledge of the RE Universe. Prior to RE2 Remake the only RE game that I know like the back of my hand was RE4. I have played it religiously as a kid on my PS2 and that gave me the initial entry to the RE Universe. RE2 Remake was nothing like the previous RE games that I have played but it didn't make me feel like it was distant because some elements that were familiar to me were present. I haven't played all the RE games and I know each one will have similarities and significant differences when it comes to the story, game play etc. This review has been crafted, and is a reflection of my opinion that's been influenced based on what RE games are familiar to me, what I've played, and the capacity of my RE Universe knowledge.

Since RE is mostly about zombies, of course Combat is gonna be a big part of it. 
The combat system present in all the [b]remakes[/b] is streamlined and identical. But this was a breath of fresh air from RE4,RE5, and RE6 which I've previously played. 
Zombies and bosses work differently here unlike the other games where you can potentially purge everyone you see.

RE2 Remake(and to some extension the other remakes) will teach you:
-Resource, and inventory management. 
-Picking your fights
-Learning silly movements and juking zombies as if you're playing Dead by Daylight
-Pathings that you take will either be beneficial or consequential in your run.

Some will say that you can easily see these things being present in the other RE games, fair point. 
But fighting zombies in this game is not as straightforward as you thought so. You have to rely on crits, aim on certain areas, head shots won't guarantee a kill, and you have to double down on them to [u]make sure the undead is actually dead[/u]

The storytelling, shifting thru different characters and world building is insane. This game also allows you to learn more and touch up on stories of characters that would usually be written out or just finished for the plot's sake. In some sense you won't be leaving this game wondering too much about [hr]What happened to this person? Is there more that I can learn about them[/hr]

Overall this game is superb and I would rate it 10/10, it is expected that you might see this game differently because we have varying experiences and knowledge about the RE Universe so not knowing some characters or stories might confuse you and not give you the same effect. Unless you're just like me with the same circumstances.

Resident Evil 2 (2019) Review: A Masterful Reimagining That Delivers Unforgettable Tension

Resident Evil 2 (2019) is the ultimate proof that a remake can not only stay true to its roots but also surpass its predecessor in almost every way. Capcom’s reimagining of the 1998 survival horror classic brings the horrors of Raccoon City to life in breathtaking detail, delivering a visually stunning, emotionally charged, and absolutely nerve-wracking experience. This game is an instant classic, successfully blending nostalgia with innovation and giving both old fans and newcomers an unforgettable ride.

Visually Stunning: A True Showcase of What’s Possible in Modern Gaming

The first thing that strikes you about Resident Evil 2 (2019) is just how beautiful it looks. The game runs on the RE Engine, Capcom’s proprietary engine, and the result is nothing short of spectacular. From the detailed, atmospheric lighting in the dark corridors of the Raccoon City Police Station to the grotesque, terrifying zombie models, everything feels meticulously crafted. The gore and decay in the environment are believable and visceral, drawing you into a world that feels real yet horrifyingly unnatural.

The lighting and shadow effects are particularly impressive, enhancing the horror experience. The way the flashlight illuminates dark rooms, casting ominous shadows, creates an atmosphere of constant tension, keeping you on edge at all times. Every inch of the police station feels alive, from the dilapidated offices to the chilling sound of distant moans echoing through the hallways.

A Compelling, Gripping Story: Familiar Yet Fresh

At the heart of Resident Evil 2 (2019) is the compelling story that has stood the test of time. Players take on the roles of rookie cop Leon S. Kennedy and college student Claire Redfield as they try to survive a zombie apocalypse that has overtaken Raccoon City. While the plot remains largely the same as the original, the reimagined version breathes new life into the characters and their interactions, making the story feel both nostalgic and fresh.

Leon is still the naive, determined rookie, while Claire is the fierce and resourceful survivor, but their performances feel more nuanced and emotional thanks to excellent voice acting and motion capture. The game expands on their personal stories and relationships, particularly with the addition of their respective side characters—Ada Wong and Sherry Birkin—adding depth to the narrative without overshadowing the game’s horror elements. These emotional beats create a connection to the characters that makes their struggles feel all the more real.

The pacing of the story is expertly balanced, keeping the player invested from beginning to end. You’ll constantly uncover new details about the outbreak, the sinister Umbrella Corporation, and the tragic events unfolding in Raccoon City. Each new twist and turn adds to the mounting sense of dread.

Nerve-Wracking Gameplay: Every Moment Feels Like a Battle for Survival

Resident Evil 2 (2019) isn’t just a visual and narrative triumph—it’s also a masterclass in tense, nerve-wracking gameplay. The game retains the fixed camera angles of the original, but with a modern, over-the-shoulder perspective that enhances both the horror and the action. Every corner you turn could hide an ambush, and every encounter feels like a fight for survival.

The resource management and combat are what really make this remake shine. Ammo is scarce, health items are limited, and the tension never lets up. You’ll need to think carefully about how to use your resources, often deciding between taking on enemies head-on or finding an alternate route to avoid them. The puzzles, while not overly complex, fit perfectly into the game’s atmosphere, and solving them gives you a satisfying sense of progress.

But what really heightens the tension is the looming presence of the Tyrant, Mr. X. His sudden appearance in the police station is a game-changer, turning what was previously a relatively contained experience into a nerve-shredding game of cat-and-mouse. The terrifying sound of his heavy footsteps echoing through the halls, combined with the fear that you never know when he’ll appear, makes for some of the most intense moments in the game. This cat-and-mouse dynamic, especially in the latter half, gives the game an edge that keeps the stakes high throughout.

A Perfect Balance of Horror and Action

What’s remarkable about Resident Evil 2 (2019) is how it manages to balance the slow, deliberate tension of survival horror with more intense action moments. The combat is not as frantic as in later entries like Resident Evil 4 or Resident Evil 5, but it’s far more grounded. Every shot counts, every zombie encounter feels consequential, and when you face off against the grotesque mutations of the virus, you’re left with a sense of dread and awe.

The game’s difficulty levels offer a variety of challenges, ensuring that even hardcore fans of the series can find a level that keeps them on the edge of their seats. The classic ‘hardcore’ mode, in particular, will test your nerves and survival skills, with enemies that are even more aggressive and fewer resources to rely on.

Sound and Immersion: The Final Ingredient

The sound design in Resident Evil 2 (2019) is critical to the game’s atmosphere. The muffled groans and snarls of zombies, the distant sound of Mr. X stomping around, and the creaking of the building all combine to create an unnerving sense of isolation and fear. The lack of a traditional soundtrack in some sections only adds to the tension, leaving you to wonder what’s around the next corner. Every sound is purposeful, and the silence only serves to make each noise more impactful.

Final Verdict

Resident Evil 2 (2019) is a spectacular remake that sets a new standard for how classic games should be reimagined. It respects the legacy of the original while breathing new life into every corner of Raccoon City, with stunning visuals, a compelling narrative, and gameplay that will keep you up at night. The heart-pounding tension and unforgettable moments ensure that this game isn’t just a one-time experience—it’s something you’ll want to revisit over and over again.

For anyone who appreciates survival horror at its finest, Resident Evil 2 (2019) is a must-play. It’s a perfect blend of nostalgia and innovation, and it’s a game that will go down as one of the best remakes ever made.

Then I realised that it was actually better to avoid most combat where possible to save my ammo for bosses and this is where the magic truly sets in. 

Each encounter isn't an obstacle to blast though mindlessly, they become like puzzles. Can I avoid these enemies without wasting any ammo? Is it worth only taking down one enemy to allow more space for movement? What do you get if you take Resident Evil, strip it of all its charm, charisma, style, and fun and replace it with over-wrought dramatics, shakey camera, and vain attempts at "real" horror? An incredibly silly game that fails to live up to its predecessors, fails to be entertaining, fails to be scary, and marks the start of the downward spiral of the entire company. [spoiler] Ok, that was more RE7 but this was the first "abuse second-hand nostalgia" game. [/spoiler]

The characters waddle around like geriatrics in desperate need of a hip replacement. The truest terror the game evokes is in the moments the player realizes he or she needs to get to an item box to retrieve or deposit something and feeling their life ebbing away as the protagonists shuffle slowly toward the destination. 
The entire Mr X system only serves to exacerbate the arduous lack of speed by forcing the player to not "run", which is really more a light jog than anything, or make a large loop to lose him. Aside from that he is only a jump scare device. 
There is very little horror to be found outside of jump scares. The player controls too well, ALA post-Mikami RE, befitting of an action horror game. The zombies provide very little challenge and are instead very unsatisfying bullet sponges. An uppercut or haymaker would have been so, so, so very appreciated. Attempting to mix 4/5's camera and control with a fairly direct copy of 2 fails at being either.
Player cannot use the RE 4/5 control scheme for no reason. Having quick turn on B and not A is a PITA. 
The weapons are flaccid in sound and impact. Did Capcom get these animations off the asset store? It feels [i]exactly[/i] like the Killing Antidote and hundreds of asset flip TPS's. It doesn't feel like the flagship product of a major company. Where is the energy and passion?
Everyone is ugly and over acted. The RE Engine has already aged these games terribly. The truck driver's stretchy face in the intro is down right goofy looking; he strongly reminds me of L.A. Noir. Resident Evil 5, 6, and REmake will look good [b]forever[/b] because of their strong style direction and "next-gen" fidelity. [spoiler] The Revelations have awful art direction, 4 shows its age but still is aesthetically pleasing, 0 still looks great. [/spoiler] 
The overly smooth animations displace the characters from the stage. Nobody feels like they're actually there interacting in the environment or each other, like crude CGI over a real background. This is a common problem with mo-cap exacerbated by attempts for hyper-realism.
The inherent absurdity of the world clashes terribly with the attempts at serious trauma. There is a charming place between a story taking itself too seriously for the setting versus making a joke of itself and the former Evils landed there neatly. The De-makes do not - they take themselves far, far to seriously. Resident Evil has always been campy/hammy, excepting 4 which was cheesy instead, and the American FPS games which [strike]aren't really RE[/strike] are just miserable and ugly. 
The voice acting and mixing ranges from okay to bad. Wonky dialogue delivered poorly while the game insists it's dramatic and traumatic and serious is unbearable. Characters now swear regularly because clearly that makes it "mature". [spoiler] It does not. [/spoiler]

The listless vessels who exist only to consume didn't associate 3 with some beloved history and so couldn't pervert it to feel part of something greater without any actual understanding or care. How many people who were "super into this game, such a big fan, totally love Resident Evil" went and played previous titles? A single percentage at best. The core base who are actually invested are detonated for temporary attention in pure myopic globalist capitalism. Where does Capcom go from here? They've lost Itsuno, they've lost Mikami, they've burnt up the games that would entice the "wider audience". A, G-d forbid, potential RE5 Remake is such a fiasco it'd be wild to see them try. Brief Description

In this game you choose to either play through the game as Leon Kennedy, a rookie police officer on his first day, or Claire Redfield, a cool motorcyclist girl (sister of Chris Redfield) who looks like Maddie Ziegler. Zombies are afoot! Raccoon City is in shambles! Zombies!

Both stories are slightly different, and after completing one character's play through, you play an abridged version of the other's. I played a full-length Leon play through and abridged Claire one after.

Pros
-Amazing gameplay. The scaling, skill-based difficulty, plethora of weapons and grenades, and 7 million different enemy types-- this remake is super cool :) This is coming from someone who has not played the original version of RE 2 and still needs to though.
-Some say that Mr Dr X is done crazy well in the remake. I agree. He is sadly FANTASTIC and his footsteps and AI freak me OUT. He single-handedly made this game the most terrifying one I have ever played.
-The controls are modernized compared to the tank controls of the original Resident Evil games. They are done very well! Part of me does miss the old scheme though with fixed cameras. Maybe it would be cool to get a modern spin off game in the franchise with that old layout but I doubt that would happen-- that is just a girl like me dreaming.
-Did I say this game is so so so scary? It is. I don't know why. It is insane.
-The script is so funny. You are in for a treat.
-Gotta praise the character design, they're all neat. Oh my God and Kendo don't get me started. My heart. Some scenes are just amazing.

Cons
-The abridged play through after still felt a bit repetitive. Not sure exactly how exactly they could have gone about making that part a bit better. Maybe making it a bit shorter? I am not sure.

Overall, loved this game :) Corny as it is, it still is peak beyond belief. Anyone should play but grab a buddy if you're a scaredy cat!

Leon and Ada are probably the most affected, I can’t stand Leon and Ada in this game. Leon is incredibly annoying, and Ada is completely unlikeable.

Even setting aside the gameplay changes compared to the RE1 remake, cutting the A and B scenarios is a screw-up. This is more of a personal thing, but I don’t like Leon and Claire’s faces in this game. I’ve seen costume and face mods for Leon and Claire that look way better and more like the original game than the official designs in the remake (and yes, I’m also comparing them to the classic costumes in the remake).

The sewers aren’t my favorite part of the game, but they’re clearly an improvement over the sewers in the original RE2. In the original game, it was just a quick area you breezed through in 5 minutes. I don’t like the lab at all, I hate its modern-minimalist design. I’d even go so far as to call it generic, if you compare it to other lab designs that appear in modern TV shows or movies (they all look the same). The lab in the original game had more of an industrial design, like a factory (I liked that design better).

I didn’t say everything I wanted to say because this is already too long, but despite all the criticism I’ve expressed about this remake, it’s undoubtedly the best of the modern RE remakes, at least when compared to their respective original games obviously.

I finished Resident Evil 2 Remake, and it stands as one of the best remakes ever made. It modernizes the classic while staying true to its roots, delivering an unforgettable survival horror experience.

What I loved:
--Outstanding remake of the original with phenomenal graphics and art direction.
--Raccoon City feels alive and believable, with exceptional facial animations.
--Perfect gameplay balance—neither too fast nor too sluggish, keeping combat tense.
--Zombies are convincingly animated, adding unpredictability and challenge.
--Great inventory redesign with quality-of-life improvements.
--Fantastic story that respects the original while expanding key elements.
--Strong character development and memorable moments.
--Short but highly replayable thanks to multiple campaigns.

What I didn’t love:
--The game is quite short; Leon’s and Claire’s campaigns each last about 3–4 hours.
--Both campaigns share too many locations, puzzles, and encounters, making them feel repetitive.
--Would have loved more unique content given the scope of a remake.

I want to start this review by saying that I was born in 1993 so I was too young to have played the original game on release. I was (still am) sort of a child that scares easily so playing this was not on the table even though my older brother did play the original and I sometimes watched him, so I kind of have vague memories of how I felt during watching because yeah scared way to easily. 

So oh my god this game is absolutely breathtaking on every front that it set out to do. They nailed the atmosphere to a T, the horror in this game is the definition of good horror and not just jump scares, although there're some and because of that, you really cant see it coming. This game excels in building tension to the extreme.

The gameplay is really tight although it is meant for the characters to be sluggish to control, but if you get a feel for the game then you wont have this problem at all because they nailed every animation for the player character as well as every enemy of which there are a ton of them with great variety in how to take them down. And the puzzles are so smart and mind teasing that you get excited every time you find one to crack it, especially if you pay attention and explore, then you will find more often than not that the answer has been in front of you all along.

The sound design is another aspect that carries the game into new heights. I do recommend to play this game with headphones or at least crank that volume up cause you will need it to help you during the game to be able to spot enemies before they spot you. Also the enemies sounds' are so unique that you can identify which type of enemy just by their sound.

Visuals are something that speak for themselves if you've seen anything online about this game, but I would actually recommend to not see a single material or even screenshots because everything is absolutely gorgeous and it hits the first time or even the tenth time you see something in game with the amount of attention to detail and the world building. 

The story I would say is great but it's a 20 year old story, you already know what's going to happen but how it happens is still amazing to witness. There aren't many twists per se but there is one that made me actually audibly exclaim given that I haven't played the original so there's that too.

I totally recommend this game for anyone who's a fan of horror games in general and it is a must play for fans of the franchise, doubly so if you're a fan of the original. And it goes on sale constantly so there's really no reason to not check it out at the very least and I promise you, you will get hooked.

The Resident Evil 2 Remake on PC is a masterclass in reimagining a classic, striking a near-perfect balance between honoring its roots and modernizing gameplay for a new generation. Built on Capcom’s RE Engine—a graphical powerhouse that would go on to define the visual identity of the franchise—the game delivers stunningly atmospheric environments, photorealistic character models, and grotesquely detailed monsters that elevate the horror to visceral new heights. What makes this remake so impressive is its respect for the original’s storyline; rather than reinventing the wheel, it streamlines and enhances the pacing without sacrificing the emotional beats or iconic moments that made the 1998 version beloved. It captures the essence of Resident Evil 1’s survival horror foundation—tight resource management, oppressive atmosphere, and puzzle-driven exploration—while injecting just enough action to keep the narrative momentum alive. One of the most brilliant additions is the stalker enemy Mr. X, whose relentless pursuit across the Raccoon City Police Department transforms the game’s tension from ambient dread to pulse-pounding terror. The developers masterfully designed his AI to chase players dynamically, not just in scripted sequences, making every hallway and safe room feel vulnerable and heightening the suspense in a way few games have achieved. It’s a design choice that fans desperately wished had been carried over into the Resident Evil 3 Remake, which, while competent, lacked the same depth and fear factor due to its more linear structure and underutilization of Nemesis. In every way, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a triumph—faithful, terrifying, and beautifully executed—and stands as one of the finest examples of how to modernize a classic without losing its soul.

The game has a few strengths – specifically, two:

It manages to capture the atmosphere of the original (at first glance), and for that, it deserves a positive review.

The over-the-shoulder camera works relatively well here, and the game could have been a good survival horror… unfortunately, it’s not, and that leads us to the negatives.

The graphics could have been very good, but the incompetent designers at Capcom decided to take the easy route, as lazy corporate drones tend to do today. They applied a hideous blue filter, like some color filter, which ruins the atmosphere by turning the game into almost a black-and-white experience, and it also prevents players from recognizing details in the already dark environment. Yes, the original game was a colorful title set in a fully lit police station, but today's designers operate on the principle of "we want lots of money for little work," so they simply turned down the lighting to the minimum, and now you’re constantly walking through rooms and corridors in the dark – because "darkness is scary, right?" Instead of creating a truly terrifying atmosphere, the designers just "turned off the lights," and that’s supposed to solve everything without any effort on their part. The darkness and the blue filter are so poorly done in this game that you often notice your character has a glowing orb around them, which increases visibility in the immediate surroundings, making it look absolutely ridiculous.

The soundtrack, which was simply brilliant in the original game in both its quality and concept (each area has its own theme), is practically non-existent here, so apart from a few forgettable 15-second melodies, there is complete silence throughout. The exception is the escape from the laboratory, where Clair has a relatively good soundtrack and Leon has a very forgettable one.

The characters and dialogues are idiotic even for stand alone game – much like the design of many environments, they make no logical sense. But - if you’ve played the original, you’ll be horrified by how much the characters are destroyed personality-wise, and at best, they’re just sad parodies of the originals. There’s no point in mentioning how Claire looks visually or the awkward jacket in the first shot of the game where you can’t see anything, despite a deliberate zoom on her back that was supposed to fix that. (Yes, if you look closely, there’s still “Made in Heaven” on the jacket, but to make the parody worse, there is a hand-held rocked proppeled grenade instead of an aerial bomb… absurdity has no limits). Claire and Leon meet in the game only once, for a few seconds of pointless dialogue.

The A/B scenarios (here referred to as the 1st and 2nd runs) practically don’t exist. It’s just the same game played exactly the same way, only with two different characters. Spoiler: Annete shoots Birkin in the first run, then the first character has a boss fight with Birkin -> Annete dies -> then you play as the second character -> Annete "comes back from the dead" -> shoots Birkin again, who also "comes back from the dead" -> another boss fight -> Annete dies for the second time, probably for real.

The boss fights, which I don’t think belong in survival horror or should be a secondary feature (like in the original series), are boring and completely unnecessary. Generally, enemies, including the most basic zombies, can’t be killed. And I mean, they literally can’t be killed – you practically don’t need weapons in this game, because they will only frustrate you as you realize that the developers turned what could have been a decent game into total trash. A regular zombie can survive an INFINITE number of headshots from an SMG – I stood over one that was lying on the ground and emptied about 250 rounds into it, and after a few seconds, it simply got up and continued chasing me. If you’re not a teenager trying to speedrun or exploit game glitches, but you want to enjoy a true gaming experience with a bit of horror – this game isn’t for you. I get that in Japan, they only have airsoft toys and don’t know how real weapons work, but they could at least hire an advisor from a more culturally developed country where weapons are allowed. Mr. X, who appeared in the original in several places, and whom you had to deal with at the end, is still here. Again, some 10-year-old kids, who have nothing better to do, write in reviews that it’s great, but trust me, it’s not – Mr. X is invincible, a constant presence following you everywhere. Given the excessive backtracking, it becomes truly annoying and tedious. Of course, right outside the save room door, he’ll stop and walk away… very logical. You have to endure his annoying presence for most of the game, where the zombies are already immortal, so the tension that the original game provided evaporates, and you’re left with pure boredom.
Interesting enemies that added uniqueness to the environment and significantly contributed to the atmosphere, such as crows, spiders, or giant moths, are of course not in the game at all, because the developers would probably have work to do with them, so they simply cut them out.

To make the game somewhat playable, you’ll need to heavily modify it, install reshade, alternative shaders, mods with more enemies, adjustments to enemy stats so they react to weapon hits and actually dies, etc. etc. This, in itself, is a lot of work, and you’ll only figure out what mods to install after the boring and pointless first playthrough. And now we get to another highlight – Capcom’s stance on mods. According to them, mods are bad, so they take an antagonistic stance towards them and do everything in their power to make sure you can’t tweak their awful game into anything close to being playable. Even if you mod everything (without RTX, of course, since Capcom released an RTX patch that deliberately broke all previously released mods), you’ll find that the game is so inconsistent that sometimes mods work perfectly, sometimes a little, and sometimes not at all. It happened to me several times that one morning I killed a zombie with a headshot, and by the afternoon, they were able to withstand hundreds of bullets without any damage. So even if you manage to mod the game into something fun after putting in considerable effort, it just won’t work consistently.

Overall rating: 10% for recalling the original atmosphere. For everything else: 0%. As a bonus – the game was probably made because players started (probably a more fun and better) Resident Evil 2 remake on their own, so Capcom had to quickly release their own remake, even though they hadn’t planned to do so at all. Then they realized that remaking old 90s games is a money maker, because their modern crap like Resident Evil 39 (how many have been released?) no one cares about, so now they’re ripping off old games to release them in butchered and shortened forms and make some money.

So overall, 10% rating.

After playing the even worse Resident Evil 3 Rebutchered and realizing how they feel about their own customers, players, and modders, I’ll NEVER buy anything from Capcom again, even if it cost a single cent until they release an official SDK for modding RE engine games.

This is a personal review coming from someone who's never played or watched a resident evil game before. I'll focus on the more substantial pros and cons rather than worrying about the common misconceptions of what makes a game good or bad (example: minor bugs, good graphics, loyal fan-base, nostalgia).

Pros: Great atmospheric horror with likeable characters & well-paced unfolding of the story. The gameplay mechanics are solid, the way you can use or conserve different items to aid your survival & using different methods to fight off enemies. Hot take, but I think as frustrating as Mr. X could be lol, he was a great addition to creating more suspense during the second half of the game. This is also a fantastic remake.

It's cons. At times, moving from one area to another felt sluggish, and certain tasks were tedious due to limited inventory space for key items, often forcing me to run far back to a storage container. My biggest criticism is the map system. I don't think the game specified that I had to pickup all items in an area for it to marked as cleared- which often left me confused on where I was supposed to go. I suppose this contradicts most RE games but I would like if there was more exploration in store rather than the entire game set in one location.

Overall: The Leon campaign only took me about 8 hours to complete and I'd say it's worth playing at least one of the two if you've got time to spare and want a tense, creepy experience. Honestly a fun single player horror if you let yourself be immersed by it.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is one of the most striking examples of how to update classic games. Capcom did their best, and the remake turned out to be very successful. The player is greeted by detailed locations, realistic lighting, and precipitation, which perfectly emphasize the gloomy tone of the story. The dark corridors of the police station, the abandoned streets of Raccoon City, and the terrifying laboratories create a tense atmosphere, and the soundtrack makes you look back with every step.

The gameplay combines survival horror with elements of exploration, resource saving, and solving interesting and intricate puzzles. The third-person shooting system with precise aiming adds depth to the battle, and limited ammunition makes you act carefully. Each of the main characters has their own path: Leon S. Kennedy is a favorite of millions of players, a young and idealistic police officer who is entering the service for the first time, and Claire Redfield is a determined girl looking for her brother. Their campaigns complement each other, opening up different scenes and characters. Ada Wong deserves special attention - a beautiful, cunning, and mysterious woman who leaves a lot of questions.

An equally important part of the game is Mr. X (Tyrant) - a ruthless stalker and, in fact, a biological weapon created by Umbrella Corporation to eliminate witnesses and eliminate threats. His heavy footsteps, which can be heard even through walls, make you constantly look back, and his appearance causes real stress and perfectly enhances the atmosphere of hopelessness.

Among the disadvantages is the increased difficulty for beginners, as saving resources and constant danger will require patience. Some players may miss new story branches or expanded locations, and the artificial intelligence of enemies sometimes gives out strange moments. In addition, Claire's playthrough is almost identical to Leon's, which reduces the variety of replayability. 

Nevertheless, Resident Evil 2 Remake remains an example of the perfect balance between respect for the original and modern gaming standards - a game that gives you fear, excitement, and a desire to return to Raccoon City again.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is survival horror done right. It takes the classic 1998 game and turns it into a modern masterpiece while still keeping that tense and claustrophobic feeling the original was known for. From the moment you step into Raccoon City, the atmosphere is heavy. Dark hallways, flickering lights, and the constant sound of something lurking nearby make you feel on edge the entire time.

The story is simple but effective. You play as either Leon S. Kennedy, a rookie cop on his first day, or Claire Redfield, searching for her missing brother. Both campaigns are slightly different, giving you more reasons to replay. The pacing is great, with moments of calm exploration quickly turning into pure panic when a zombie crashes through a window or you hear Mr. X’s heavy footsteps getting closer.

The combat is satisfying but also stressful. Ammo is limited, which means you cannot just blast every zombie you see. Sometimes it is smarter to run than fight. The zombies themselves are terrifying. Even when you think one is down, it might grab your ankle when you walk past. And then there is Mr. X, who stalks you through the station in one of the most tense video game experiences I have had.

The remake nails the visuals. The RE Engine makes everything look incredible, from the rain soaked streets to the disgusting detail on zombie faces. The sound design is just as impressive. Every creak, growl, and thud makes you constantly check over your shoulder.

I gave it a 9 instead of a perfect score because while it is an amazing remake, some of the puzzles can slow the pacing a bit too much and a couple of backtracking moments feel repetitive. But honestly, those are small issues in an otherwise incredible package.

One thing I highly recommend is playing Leon’s campaign first and then doing Claire’s campaign second. This not only gives you the full perspective on the events in Raccoon City but also unlocks the true ending. Seeing how their stories connect and how they face the final moments together makes the whole experience feel complete. After doing both, I cannot imagine playing just one campaign and calling it done.

Now for the ratings

Story: 8
Simple but works perfectly for a survival horror game

Combat: 9
Tense, strategic, and every bullet matters

Graphics: 10
One of the best looking horror games ever made

Characters: 9
Leon, Claire, Ada, Sherry, and the creepy villains are all memorable

World and Immersion: 9
The police station and surrounding areas feel alive and terrifying

Music and Sound: 10
Perfect horror sound design and atmospheric music

Polish: 9
Runs smooth with almost no technical issues

Final thoughts

Resident Evil 2 Remake is one of the best horror games I have ever played. It respects the original while improving almost every aspect. It is tense, scary, and rewarding, and even after finishing it, I wanted to jump back in and try the other campaign. If you want a game that keeps your heart racing, this is it. And trust me, do both campaigns for the full, satisfying experience.

What can I say other than it is a great remake. Capcom did everything they could to keep the game as original though with some changes to modernize it, and keep it a little different from the original. 

If you like me love Resident Evil, this is sure to keep you entertained.

In terms of reinterpretation of the original PSX game Resident Evil 2 is very faithful, but it is not a one to one remake, instead you can view it as a reimagination. The Core Structure of the game is kept as well as the eerie atmosphere from the original, but they introduced enough changes that hardcore fans will have a complete new experience. While the main storyline remains mostly intact, certain events and locations have been adjusted, streamlined, or completely redesigned. These changes don't always improve the gameplay, but they do give the game its own identity.

One of the most noticeable changes is in the layout of key areas. The Raccoon City Police Department, for example, keeps the iconic structure of the original but has been slightly reworked to reduce unnecessary backtracking. The building feels familiar but not identical. Other locations, like the sewers and the underground laboratory, have been entirely redesigned. In these sections, the game starts to show some weaknesses. The redesigns are more linear and introduce a new enemy type that comes off more frustrating. These segments feel less polished and slightly disconnected from the otherwise carefully paced game flow.

As in the original, players can choose to play as either Claire Redfield or Leon S. Kennedy, with each character experiencing a slightly different version of the story. The differences between their campaigns aren't dramatic, but they do offer enough variation to encourage multiple playthroughs. However, the "2nd Run" mode which is supposed to present an alternate perspective on the events of the game feels underdeveloped. It mostly repeats the first scenario with only minor differences, and it gives the impression that this mode wasn't given the same attention as the rest of the game and is there because the original game had this mode as well.

A improved addition from the original is the Tyrant. Unlike in the 1998 version, where his appearances were mostly limited to scripted events in Scenario B, the remake introduces him as a persistent threat during both playthroughs. He roams the police station dynamically, forcing players to stay alert and make decisions under pressure. This mechanic adds a layer of tension that fits well with the survival horror tone, though it can become tiresome in repeated runs. Especially for those revisiting the game multiple times, his presence sometimes feels more like an obstacle and less intimidating.

On the technical side, the remake offers significant improvements. The new RE engine eliminates loading screens between rooms, allowing for a more seamless and immersive experience. This also means enemies can follow players between areas, adding an extra element of danger to transitions that were previously safe. The graphics are impressive, with detailed character animations, environmental effects, and expressive facial features that react to pain or distress. There are Animations, when the Protagonist is on low health, reflecting his or her critical state. These touches enhance the atmosphere without feeling overproduced. Inventory and menu management is kept simple and effective and is really easy to use in this game.

Combat, however, remains one of the weaker aspects. The shooting mechanics are based on the over the shoulder perspective introduced in later entries like Resident Evil 4, but the gunplay feels inconsistent. Enemies are unusually resilient, often soaking up bullets in unpredictable ways. The game doesn't reward precise aiming, and critical hits appear to trigger randomly. Boss fights follow a similar pattern: most of them are resolved by using the most powerful weapons available until the enemy drops. There's not much strategy involved, and the encounters rarely evolve in complexity beyond their visual presentation.

Still, they have modernized combat, and I think a compromise has been made here to give the series a more modern approach, because restrictive movements such as tank controls, etc. are gone and this is a good thing. But on the other hand, this also takes away some of the tension, because I have full control when shooting and don't have to worry about whether I'd rather flee from a situation. It's a change that I don't necessarily like, but at least I can understand why it didn't make it into the remake.

The game is short, bit it offers a decent amount of replay value. Several additional modes return from the original, including the "2nd Run," the "4th Survivor" mode starring Hunk, and the brutaly "Tofu Survivor" campaign this time with more tofu with different flavors. For players looking for a tougher experience, the Hardcore mode provides stricter save limitations and a more punishing resource economy, which is very similar to the original game.

Capcom didn’t just remake Resident Evil 2 — they rebuilt it from the ground up and somehow made a 1998 classic feel brand new while preserving everything fans loved.

The atmosphere is thick with tension. The Raccoon City Police Department is a character in itself — every hallway, every creaking door, every flickering light adds to the dread. You feel the weight of every bullet you spend, and the sound design is so good that you'll panic the moment you hear Mr. X’s boots echoing down the hall.

Leon and Claire’s campaigns are distinct enough to encourage replayability, and the story is perfectly paced — blending action, puzzles, and pure horror. The graphics? Gorgeous and grotesque in the best way possible. Zombies feel dangerous, not just cannon fodder.

It’s one of the best remakes ever made, and honestly, one of the best survival horror games period.

TL;DR:
✅ Incredible atmosphere
✅ Tight gameplay and controls
✅ Legitimately terrifying moments
✅ High replay value
✅ Mr. X will haunt your dreams

Whether you’re a longtime fan or totally new to Resident Evil, this game is an absolute must-play.

Resident Evil 2 Remake tells an old story with updated graphics, controls, and quality of life improvements without straying so far from the original title it seeks to recontextualize. The immersion I experienced in my first playthrough remained consistent throughout both Leon and Claire's respective stories, and the scares were of equal potency. I never felt as though there wasn't a solution to the problems presented to me. The puzzles are excellent, and even the speed running and achievement hunting presented a fun, albeit an admittedly grueling challenge to overcome.

Ultimately this game has something for everyone. For returning players, it offers nostalgia. For new players, it offer's a thrilling story with campy dialogue and body horror. This is a review after completion of both A and B runs and seeing the true ending. This is a fantastic remake, the gold standard that every remake should strive to be like. This game is a masterpiece of survival horror brought to life for a new generation of gamers. It maintains the magic of the original while bringing it up to code to stand among games released today. This game does cheat the original like RE3R (I still love RE3R anyways), it is still RE2 at heart but given new life.

The game was given far more than a face lift, it truly rebuilds the game from the ground up. One of the most major elements is game play. Gone are the fixed camera angles and clunky tank controls of the original. This time it is rebuilt as a TPS where you are in complete control of the camera!!! If you have played any of the other remakes you have an idea of what to expect from the gunplay. You will be be shooting your way through the enemies of RE2 while being mindful of your resources. This game will give you a tough time at points, especially in the RPD. Early on healing items are limited and ammo even more so. This forces you to play smart and think "is that zombie really worth killing". But I hope you can think fast because who knows what what might be after you. You will be exploring the RPD and other locations as either college student Claire Redfield or rookie cop Leon S. Kennedy. Depending who you choose your weapons and certain missions will vary, this adds noticeable difference between characters, especially if you are doing an A/B true ending run. 

The story takes place during the infamous Raccoon City incident and follows Leon and Claire along with a supporting cast of characters. After the outbreak in the city Leon and Claire find themselves trapped in the RPD and slowly unraveling the truth behind all this. The story was interesting a genuinely kept me engaged for the roughly 8 hour run time of each campaign. The highlight of the story shines with it's characters who have depth, motive, and personality. They feel like real people, not some copy and paste cardboard cutouts sold off as the MCs. It also ties into the larger RE universe very well which makes it not only an essential piece of the lore, but also serves as the first chapter to Claire and Leon's stories. 

RE2 being a horror game will always raise the question "how scary is it?", I'm here to tell you, it deserves it's place as one of the franchises scariest games. The atmosphere of the dark and stormy environments combined with the grotesque enemy design and uncertain resources always keeps you on your toes. The pressure put on you by the menacing tyrant is also no joke. If you don't like jump scares though, don't worry. The game doesn't really have many jump scares, it relies on other methods to scare you. Another thing to note is that I would like to throw up a blood/gore notice. I know that game lists blood and gore in the age rating but I would like to elaborate for those who may be sensitive. I, myself, don't have an issue, but i know that isn't true for everyone. I know that there is a general stigma around people who can't gore and games, so this rarely gets mentioned, if you don't care then skip to the next paragraph. This is probably one of the more grotesque entries in the series and uses that to unsettle/scare you. There are scenes of graphically mutilated corpses and and body horror, take this into account if you are sensitive. 

The sound design is once again amazing in the VA department, the actors have delivered and amazing performance that truly adds to the game. On the other side the music is nothing special, mostly just ambient tracks to build atmosphere, not much else to say.

Graphically it is another masterpiece that leverages the best technology on the market to deliver a truly stunning experience. It performs well and can be run on a wide range of hardware, granted you are willing to dip into the graphics quality for those extra frames. 

A short explanation of the A/B runs is that after beating your first run as Claire/Leon you will get an option to start and altered "Second Run" as the character you didn't choose first time, this leads to the true ending. IMO it is worth doing and different enough to not be boring even if played back-to-back.

My only real issue is the boss fights. Like RE3R they got repetitive fast and and kinda felt like a drag (however there aren't many). 

In conclusion/TLDR, it is a faithful remake that impresses on all fronts and performs well. It is a great game for people looking for a little scare without pissing themselves. It is a great entry for seasoned and new RE players alike which will set up some of the best characters in the franchise. I give it a 9/10.

The setting, characters and story are some of the best in the franchise. The game looks amazing, and the lighting and sound helps maintain tension, leading to some genuinely scary moments.

Loved this game—an instant classic. It strikes the perfect balance of adventure, puzzle-solving, shooting, and horror. There’s this one unforgettable moment where you’re ambushed by 10+ of them, limping around, barely surviving—only to discover the shotgun drops them in one shot. Brutal. Perfect. The sound design is incredible. Bosses are a bit average, but the set pieces they create are fantastic—Mr. X especially. X gonna give it to you indeed (not even sure that’s his right name, but if you know you know). Resident Evil 2 (2019) is a great game with improved graphics, providing an enjoyable experience. RE 2 also features an over-the-shoulder third-person perspective, unlike the rather annoying fixed camera angles of RE 0 and 1.
Looks way better than the last one, has different modes. Jump scares still get me and it's fun.

I played the original through twice before starting this, and I was really consistently impressed with what was familiar, and what felt fresh. All of the important stuff is still there, but it's been adjusted, expanded, sometimes re-interpreted. Remake doesn't feel accurate honestly, they really did go back to the drawing board on a lot of elements. You feel it most in areas like the sewers, and in characters like Annette Birkin (who really strongly benefited from a rewrite, I feel).

The presentation here is absolutely incredible, though it's a much darker and colder atmosphere than the original. The storytelling was top notch, the writing and delivery in particular just felt like a stellar reinterpretation of the original. Especially stood next to the original, it feels incomparable. They really took advantage of all the tools and technology that have become available since 1998 and the difference is incredible.

I did find the game itself somewhat frustrating at first, due in part to a hidden adaptive difficulty mechanic that doesn't just make the game easier if you're struggling, but harder if you're doing well. I also struggled with what seemed to be the intended way to play; conserve ammo to such a degree that you should take hits just to avoid using ammo. Run away, bait enemy attacks, basically avoid conflict as much as possible.

It's a matter of taste, of course, it just didn't end up being for me. You put a bunch of cool weapons in my hand, and I want to use them. 

I love that a lot of the classic weapons are here; Leon's obscure West German pistol, the M-79, the Desert Eagle etc. They're all beautifully rendered and animated, in particular I just love how characters hold long weapons while walking around, and how there's an actual sling when they're in reserve! When you damage enemies it's visceral and raw; you can blow limbs off, split heads, blow chunks out of an enemy. It's intense.

It's a shame though that most weapons feel pretty weak. Handguns are pretty bad even at taking out legs, usually requiring 3-4 shots on a stumbling target to drop them. The shotgun doesn't reliably break heads, even at point blank range. Automatics are pitiful. That's one area where I'd say the original is still better; shooting stuff in classic RE2 still feels much more satisfying. Guns just never felt powerful enough to me (magnum excluded).

Like I said though it's down to taste and expectations, you should know going in this is a horror game first and not an action game first like 4, 5 and definitely 6. It's an incredible game -- a really compelling version of the Resident Evil 2 story.

Now this is the first time I've written a review for a game and I doubt many will see it, and even tho I have yet to fully finish it I need to talk about what is undeniably the scariest game experience I probably will ever have. This comes in the form of the terminator-like behemoth, Mr. X or the Tyrant. 

Now what exactly makes this thing horrifying. To properly understand you must how it works and the background. So around a third of the way into the game you have by this point gotten used to the zombies and while the zombie dogs and Licker's are scary at first they can be counter-played quite easily once you understand their mechanics. Now enter Mr. X. At first you don't really get a good look at him as he's mostly obscured from view. However that does not make it any less unnerving when you see his giant arm burst through a stone wall and brutally murder your only way out of the police station you are trapped in. You manage to make it out and start getting back to completing puzzles and advancing the story but little do you know the real terror has only just begun. 

After putting out a helicopter on fire you begin to backtrack towards it only to see Mr. X single handedly lift the chopper up and jam it into the wall. From this point forward this terminator on steroids actively pursues you throughout the station. moving at a pace just slightly slower than the player Mr. X is a near relentless force that cannot be put down by any of your weapons and at most only stunned for a few seconds. However the the largest fear factor comes not from his massive frame closing in on you but his presence in the station. His lumbering footsteps being a constant reminder to the player to hurry up whatever task or objective they have for fear that he will suddenly appear. This is amplified by the fact that Mr. X can follow the player into just about every room besides a select few. This means that unless you can somehow lose him you must constantly be on the move which can present its own problems. due to the stations zombie and licker infestation and our limited ammo, we can only kill so many and believe me when I tell you there is nothing more terrifying than running from a 7-8 foot killing machine on legs while your escapes are blocked by hordes of the undead.

Now all this may seem bad enough but there's even more layers of horror to this. Now because of the incredible development and thought that went into this game Mr. X never despawn's and then appears again at scripted moments like many horror games do. He is quite literally always there in the station searching and hunting you, even in areas that haven't been rendered by the player Mr. X will hunt, waiting for you to enter the wrong room and walk right into his cold line of sight. He also has very acute hearing, meaning that firing a gun is basically an open invitation to be beaten into the floor. even running is risky as he can hear that too. Another aspect of his horror is how calm he is. He offers essentially 0 facial expression or even sound to clue to player in on any of his deeper thoughts, if he even has any. It also but blatantly obvious he could chase us down in seconds if he wanted to but for better or worse he chooses to be just barely slower. than you This could be interpreted multiple ways. of course there is the boring answer being he would simply be overpowered if the player truly had no advantage however I at least like to imagine there could be a deeper motive. Does he like playing with his food? Giving them a false sense of chance and hope? or is there some part of his human self left that wants us to succeed? There is no clear cut answer but the mystery of it only benefits his intrigue in the long run.

Add all of that to the fact that the map you have become pretty comfortable in for the most part is now inhabbited by this monster beyond your full understanding creates the ultimate horror game stalker that no other game I've ever played before or since has been able to capture even half the magic of what made this thing truly terrifying to experience. So to anyone reading this while considering getting the game, DO IT. It may a scarring experience you may need to take a break every 10 minutes to calm your mind but I promise that when you look back on it all with a smile and want to go through it all over again, only to emotionally scare yourself again. But that's just one the many things that is so amazing and frustrating about this damn near masterpiece of a horror game.

Item management and folding level design is emphasized in Hardcore because the limited item space and choosing which items to carry when you backtrack through the level are a staple in the RE formula and a lot of it is lost if you play it on easier difficulties. Ink Ribbons are a resource that you have to manage as well as they are limited and can discourage save scumming. ALSO, DO NOT EMPTY YOUR BULLETS ON ZOMBIES! Resident Evil 2 is a prime example of how to do a remake. Developing this game from the ground-up with the RE engine was the best choice Capcom could've made. No typical remastering, in which the resolutions and textures are reworked. The graphics are just astonishing and beautiful. The two characters, Leon Kennedy, Claire Redfield and, not-to-forget the mysterious Ada Wong, are both amazing characters you're certainly gonna enjoy to get invested into. Especially Ada, where it's not entirely clear, whose side she's really on.

RE 2 impresses with extremely atmospheric lighting effects, very detailed facial expressions and animations and the best looking zombies one has ever seen in any game before. Although only a handful of different models were used doesn't change the fact how amazing and deeply detailed they look like.

Exploring the dark hallways and sewers, learning the structure of the police station and solving complicated puzzles requiring you to memorize various steps are really fun and time-consuming simultaneously. The police station, the underground beneath and the scientific lab are all so well-designed and connected and in every corner, there might be something waiting to get explored. It's surely worth investing all your time into discovering every hidden item/message possible. Exploring also allows you to find expansions of your maps showing which rooms are still to be discovered or whether everything in the already-searched rooms has been taken.

Inventory and ammunition management is key to survive in this game. You're always in danger of running out of ammo and healing items and you can't always carry everything you need to keep progressing through this game. You need to make use of items before you can replace them without other ones and have to look whether you can combine any to make space for other stuff. 

The sound design has been developed excellently allowing the player to be fully immersed into the gameplay experience, as there is little-to-no music playing during the gameplay, which leaves room for creaking doors, thunderstorms and rain to be heard by the player, whilst already have to fight through groups of scary and bloodthirsty undead, which includes Mr. X, a Tyrant super-zombie with a blank facial expression who is almost impossible to take down and generally is better to just hide from.

When it comes to the negative, the 2nd runs are to be named. They are basically short versions of the actual campaigns of each respective protagonist. There isn't really anything different compared to the main campaigns, if I remember correctly, aside from the fact that certain items are moved to new locations, but that's already it. After I finished Leon's A run, the only option for a 2nd run was Claire's and not Leon's, but after I finished Claire's A run, I had to option to choose between either Leon's or Claire's B run. How does this make sense? Also: In Leon's B run, the cutscene early on with the truck driver was completely removed and Leon's part was shown instead. Not even in Claire's B run it was cut out, so why only during Leon's?

Capcom has done a fantastic job with remaking the legendary classic called Resident Evil 2 and turning it into a modern, thrilling and atmospheric game, which feels like it's an entirely new game with a new story. I can't recommend giving the respective 2nd runs a shot tho, as they're basically just the campaigns in a shorter, more rushed version. However, the main campaigns are more than recommendable. Your first ever playthrough of any of these campaigns is certainly one you'll never ever forget in the whole of your life.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is survival horror at its absolute finest — a masterclass in how to reimagine a classic without losing what made it legendary. From the moment you step into the Raccoon City Police Department, the tension never lets up. The atmosphere is thick with dread, the lighting and sound design are some of the best in any modern game, and every creaking door or distant growl keeps you on edge. Visually, it’s stunning — rain-soaked streets, flickering hallways, bloodied rooms, all brought to life with RE Engine detail that makes every shadow matter. The over-the-shoulder camera makes encounters feel intimate and terrifying, and the zombies? Brutal. They take bullets like sponges and still find a way to lunge at you, making every shot count. Inventory management, puzzles, and exploration are all perfectly balanced — a constant push and pull between risk and reward.

Leon and Claire both feel like fully realized characters, and their separate campaigns add genuine replay value instead of filler. And then there’s Mr. X — the relentless, trench-coated nightmare who turns every quiet hallway into a heart-pounding escape sequence. Capcom absolutely nailed the pacing, mixing horror, action, and puzzle-solving without ever dragging. Even on second or third playthroughs, the game holds up — Hardcore Mode and speedruns give it serious replay depth. Whether you're a longtime RE fan or brand new to the series, RE2 Remake is a near-perfect blend of nostalgia and innovation. This is how you do a remake.

People praise this to the moon back, but straight up I think this is just a demake. It's a polished, good-looking reimagining - but it drops the ball in a few important ways. One of the biggest letdowns is the dialogue. It’s stiff, awkward, and often totally forgettable. The original had that cheesy B-movie charm; the remake tries to be more serious and cinematic, but it ends up with bland exchanges that lack personality. Leon and Claire both come off like generic action heroes half the time, and the writing just doesn’t give them much depth. Even the emotional scenes feel flat, like they’re just going through the motions without much heart.

Another big issue is how much content got cut. Fans of the original will immediately notice that a lot of locations, scenarios, and even enemies didn’t make it into the remake. Where’s the giant spider? Or the crows? Or the moths? These weren’t just random monsters - they helped make the Raccoon City Police Department and sewers feel strange and dangerous. Their absence makes the world feel a little emptier, more sanitised. And the remake ditches the fully fleshed-out “A/B” scenario system too. Instead of two truly different playthroughs depending on who you start with, we just get minor changes and recycled content. It’s a huge missed opportunity.

Don’t get me wrong, the game looks great and plays fine, but it plays it too safe. It strips out some of the quirky personality and complexity that made the original stand out. In trying to modernise the experience, it ends up feeling hollow beneath the shiny surface.

(In a way) Visually, it’s stunning, and the atmosphere is spot on—but honestly, playing it just felt like a grind after a while.

The biggest issue for me was the constant backtracking. I get that it's part of the old-school survival horror formula, but this game takes it to another level. And then there’s the ammo. Or rather, the lack of it. I understand limited resources are part of the tension, but there’s a fine line between challenging and just flat-out annoying. Half the time I’d walk into a room with two bullets and a prayer, knowing I’d have to reload a save if anything stronger than a zombie showed up. It made me dread combat—not in a “this is intense” way, but more like “I’m not sure I even want to deal with this anymore.”

I can appreciate what Capcom was going for, and I know a lot of people love this game, but for me, the pacing and resource balancing really dragged the whole experience down. I left more frustrated than satisfied.

This game is a masterpiece, the sense of horror and tension is unmatched once you get into the police station and you are pursued by Mr. X/Tyrant. Unfortunately that is where the game peaks (and it's a really high peak, almost 10/10), because then it becomes an 3rd person action game where that initial tension diminishes, due to you acquiring better gear (this criticisism can be applied to the whole series to be honest), but it's still a very enjoyable game. I give it overall a 9/10, but with a caveat. See below.

However, if you already played the original game from 1998, you will notice that the story has been streamlined from 4 campaigns to basically 2 and a half (even though the game has 4 "different" scenarios). And by half, I mean that Leon and Claire campaigns are practically identical from start to finish, except the middle part where you play as [spoiler]Ada for Leon or Sherry for Claire for a few minutes[/spoiler] and the boss you fight at the end is different for Leon and Claire, and this also includes the "2nd Run" as this game calls it. In both campaigns, either first time or 2nd run, you solve the same puzzles with both characters, regardless of who arrived first to RPD, and you can get the true ending of RE2 Remake by playing both campaigns. 

You see, in the original game, there was Leon A, Claire A, Leon B and Claire B. The first campaign dinamically changes based on the choices you do on your first playthrough, because it is intended that both Leon and Claire are in RPD at the same time, but they arrived at different points as the game progressed. Leon A means that Leon got to RPD first, therefore on your second playthrough you are going to play as Claire B, with a different starting point and taking into consideration what Leon did on the first playthrough, then you can play Claire A and Leon B and see the differences. 

For example, there is a part in the OG game where Leon/Claire finds a locker and you can choose between getting a Machine Gun or an inventory expansion (or both if you are a masochist), then in their B scenarios, Claire/Leon (respectively) will have to choose the item you left in your first playthrough, HUGELY affecting the gameplay. Another example would be a section in RPD where you can lock via circuit some windows in a corridor so the zombies don't get in, if you do this in the A scenario, then in the B scenario the windows will already be locked for a while, but it will short-circuit and the windows will open, exposing you to more zombies. NONE of this is in the Remake, basically what it does is that the other character has to solve the same puzzles to progress but from a different route in the "2nd Run" (also some item locations and codes are different but it's very minor) which doesnt make sense storywise. Considering all this, it will make you realize the humungous amount of cut content this game has compared to the original, BUT at least this one has 4 new modes the original didn't have: Ghost Survivors, which are what-if scenarios of some characters you encounter in the game, and they are useful to learn when to shoot and when to run. So, in the end, it's understable if you feel a bit disappointed in this remake, because it is basically more a RE-imagening more than a RE-make, with it's own canon apart from the original.

I will say, I had a lot of trouble with the game and my Nvidia GPU (4090) at first. Crashes happening a few minutes into starting the game consistently. I've been interested in the story and characters since I was a kid, I remember watching my Dad play the original RE (& being understandably terrified!) and I got very excited to get into the series when it was 'my time'. Sadly, whenever I tried to play Resident Evil, and boy did I try, I seemed to bounce off the series. It never clicked for me, and I never had fun playing, so I chalked it up to it just not being my thing.

Seeing the trailer for Resident Evil Village back when it was announced perked up my interest again, and while I didn't play it at the time, I did buy the game during a steam sale. Recently, DBD reignited my interest in these characters, and during a big sale by capcom I decided to take the plunge and buy the remake trilogy (2,3,4) I like to think I'm pretty on the pulse with game releases, but I genuinely didn't know these were a thing! 

Playing 2 at first was a nightmare, self-admittedly my own fault. I was playing it wrong, going commando in every room and spraying bullets like there was no tomorrow. I got the first puzzle piece then had absolutely no ammo, and I felt frustrated, annoyed and wanted to give up. Looking online I saw some tips (shoot the knees, don't always shoot when you can juke!) and I felt like an idiot. Resident Evil wasn't the bad one in our relationship, it was me! 

I restarted again and something clicked.
