[h1]Holy smokes Scoob, we’re being chased around a police station by a white man![/h1] 
[b]The return to the 1998 R.P.D. was equally haunting as it was interesting. It brings the iconic story to modern audiences and adapts the gameplay to today’s standards – what else would you want from a remake?[/b]

Clair and Leon arrive at Raccoon City to find out that the streets had been repurposed for a set for the next George A. Romero movie. Unfortunately, they are unaware of this and start gunning down all the zombie actors.



Seriously though, we have the duo consisting of The Unluckiest Man on Earth, and miss “oh, I’m just looking for a family member”. When starting a new game, you can pick whichever you like more.

Leon’s first day on the job as a rookie cop starts with having to deal with a zombie apocalypse, during which he meets an absolute Asian baddie that [spoiler]manipulates him and breaks his heart[/spoiler], only to finish off with some buff Blade LARPer whose skin had never seen sunlight, that wants to break every bone in the Golden Retriever’s body. Meanwhile, Clair’s just kinda making friends. C:

Nah, not really, she also has it hard being beaten by an overweight sadist police chief while that white pale discord mod in a hat is also chasing her. However, when Leon [spoiler]gets cheated by Ada[/spoiler], Clair makes friends with Sherry, the little girl getting caught up in all that mess. Her campaign feels more wholesome.

[spoiler]I like both sub-plots – Leon and Ada have this romance that is never meant to be. Continued in the next games, kind of being enemies, but always helping each other out in the end. I think it was done here pretty well - when confronted with the truth Leon stood his ground even though he was in love; Ada couldn’t shoot him which showed that she had grown to genuinely like him as well. I thought the kiss was a stretch, them knowing each other for like 3 hours, but if you think it was a manipulation tactic, it makes sense.[/spoiler] Final scene really cool and dramatic. Clair’s campaign was a little bit more wholesome. She takes care of Sherry like a big sister, and it’s just nice to see among all the chaos.

For a RE game, the delivery doesn’t seem too cheesy or unrealistic, actually the game seems pretty believable. The voice acting is also pretty good, besides that one voice crack of Clair when she goes down the staircase to meet Leon. “I’ll be rIGhT thEre” my as.s.

To see the true ending you need to also beat the 2nd scenario, preferably with the other character. It’s a cool addition, but it lasts like 5 minutes which makes me wonder why even lock that behind a second playthrough? While 2nd scenarios don’t really make sense story-wise, I guess they improve replayability – Mr. X appears earlier; item and enemy placement are shuffled. Overall, it seems a bit harder.



Both campaigns take you through the exact same areas with minor differences. These involve segments and boss fights exclusive for the specific character, but besides that the areas stay the same, maybe with different item/enemy placement. Leon and Clair also have some different weapons and even key items, letting them into areas inaccessible to the other character.

The formula stays the same, you’re supposed to escape the station by solving puzzles and fighting with/evading enemies. [b]I don’t know why the escape is always through the most roundabout way involving a secret lab somehow, but that’s just how it works[/b]. During the exploration of the station and areas beneath it you’ll find a plethora of resources. Ammunition and guns, herbs that can be mixed into different healing items or buffs, key items for progressing and other stuff like boards which you can cover windows with. The higher difficulty the more important it is to use your resources wisely and manage your inventory better. Every encounter is a decision, fight only when you need to, blah blah blah.

One thing that just feels bad is the movement speed – It’s like I criticized Sebastian from The Evil Within for being a cop that can’t sprint for longer than 2 seconds, it’s similar here – Leon can’t sprint at all, he just leisurely jogs around the station. And I get it, survival horror and stuff, but if you look closely even the run animation doesn’t make sense, it looks like it’s designed for him to move faster, but he kind of runs in place like a looney toons character. It’s alright most of the time, but during some boss fights you’re supposed to kind of “dodge” to the sides, but all you can do is pray that he jogs far enough away, which is awkward. 

I liked the combat for the most part – if you don’t want to kill everything (recommended) you can stun a zombie with a headshot and run past it. If you do get grabbed, you can use one of your defensive items – knives, flashbangs or frags. It’s less effective than just using them normally but saves you from damage. It’s worth noting you can’t counterattack when grabbed from behind. You can also destroy limbs to make zombies fall, for example.

Other enemies require specific approaches – Lickers are fast and deadly, but you can sneak around them. Dogs are fast but weak. Bosses and G-Adults have these mutated eyes that are their weak points, very satisfying to pop, [b]like my grandma’s pimples[/b]. Mr. X is an intimidating presence, but you can dodge and outrun him for the most part. It’s worse [b]when he camps at your door like a bi.tch though[/b]. You can temporarily stun him with enough bullets, but it feels like a waste.

Aiming is nice once you get the hang of it. If you stand in place for a while, the reticle will focus up and you supposedly deal 50% more damage. The game doesn’t tell you that though, and if you have a lot of ammo, you’ll probably get impatient anyway and shoot normally. The rooster of weapons for both characters is not big, but it is deliberate. Besides handguns, Leon gets the shotgun, flamethrower and magnum; Clair gets the grenade launcher, a big taser rifle and an SMG. Both characters get an incendiary weapon to deal with one specific type of enemy that requires fire to stay down permanently.

The game gives bonus weapons for next playthroughs for different completion ranks – these mostly require clearing the game under specific times. Boosts replayability and rewards learning the game. Also, there is the Ender chest to store items every playthrough.

{*CUT1}



The game looks beautiful and realistic. [b]I love the dramatic rainy aesthetic. Blood dissolving in rain puddles reflecting the neon lights of the dead city; corpses burning in the streets, abandoned cars overturned like makeshift barricades, creating a lifeline for the last surviving people. Sounded poetic? Well, it’s like Westopolis from 2005 Shadow the Hedgehog, and now that I ruined your day with that reference, we can move on.[/b] Environments really cool, designed for the game, but realistic enough that you don’t notice. Unique locations and vibes. I love the character and enemy designs in the game, especially when it relates to gameplay, like the eyes being weak spots. Idle animations feel realistic as well.

The game has a really good sound design with good ambiance, which makes it really immersive. Random noises echoing throughout the station make you jump. However, Tyrant’s footsteps volume sometimes seems inaccurate, sometimes giving you the wrong idea where he is. The OST has some really cool tracks, although I get the feeling like it is much too quiet in some parts. It’s more focused on scary ambiance, but I would love to listen to more actual “save theme” music.



While I would appreciate a little more flexibility with movement, it is an amazing horror experience and an example of a good remake. The new RE games are great, but it is good that they’re bringing the original Raccoon incident to modern audiences – a good way to see how it all started.

This game punishes you for trying to engage. If you're looking for a survival action game with rewarding difficulty, this ain't it.

So it was probably a mistake to play Resident Evil 2 Remake after the RE4 Remake, because it really exposed how much better pretty much every system in RE2 could have been. I can appreciate that RE2 was a pioneer of the survival horror genre, but this remake didn't do it for me.

Inventory management is restrictive. Obviously purposefully so, but it's odd because you can store infinite items in your box and there are storage boxes everywhere. So you never have to make tough decisions about which items to keep, instead what happens is you make several trips back and forth from the same area to claim everything. It's annoying, but you do it anyway because ammo is restrictive, and so it feels necessary.

Really, there should have been a "Send to storage" feature from your inventory (RE4 feature).

Ammo and supplies are in a pretty good space where it feels as though you never have more than enough, except at the very end of the game. I like how that encourages exploring, and I liked that I almost ran out of ammo a few times. That did increase the tension and made even basic enemies feel scary.

Unfortunately the enemies themselves are the worst part of the game. I have a lot to say about them.

Basic zombies are extremely frustrating because of how inconsistent and tanky they are. Sometimes they go down in 3 shots, sometimes it takes 10. After they are down, they can wake up again at any time. Then it takes another, uncertain, number of shots to put them down again. But of course they could wake up again!

In one particularly annoying case, I counted spending over 30 rounds of handgun ammunition to finally kill one single basic zombie. It got up so many times and took so many bullets that in the end I thought it was scripted to get up again and again... forever! But no, it did eventually die. I understand that was probably a deliberate choice to build flavour and tension, but shooting a zombie in the head 30+ times and having it still not pop is frankly unfun and completely unbelievable.

Furthermore, running over a "dead" zombie that is actually alive will cause it to grab you leg and damage you in an unavoidable animation. So if you think you can simply down, and then run over the zombies, you've got to think again! You need to stand, and wait, to make sure you've actually fully cleared the room before you move on, or risk eating free damage. It's frustrating, slow, and boring.

More advanced enemies thankfully do die, and they do so in a much clearer manner. But their movements and attacks are so much tougher to deal with that it makes them frustrating in their own way. They are all faster than you and many attacks are flaily and unavoidable. I had a lot of healing items so it wasn't a problem, but it's not fun to know you are going to tank free damage from an enemy that can jump the entire hallway with an attack you have no dodge move for.

Because there is no loot reward for killing enemies like in RE4, it makes even seeing tougher enemies feel like a major annoyance. You'll have to kill them because otherwise they'll catch and kill you, but you'll get nothing for it other than the frustrating experience.

Boss enemies are the worst of the worst. None of them have interesting designs, they are all just miscellaneous flesh heaps with eyeball weak points, and most fights involve you running away from them to make as much distance between you as possible to squeeze in a couple shots. And bosses are tanky.

Are my shots doing no damage because I've missed the barely-detectable weak point? Or did it hit the weak point and it's just going to take 50 bullets? In RE4 there is very clear feedback about how your actions affected enemies, not so in RE2.

In fact in some fights, each shot does literally nothing and it turns out you weren't supposed to be shooting the boss at all, only running away to buy time to then run away more. In one absolutely egregious case, you fight a boss in a small room with no exit for a few minutes until you deal enough damage to make it fall off a ledge. A few scenes later, the same boss appears in another small room and you are forced to fight him for a few minutes... until a door opens that lets you escape. Any ammo spent in this time is completely wasted. The third time the exact same boss appears to fight you in another small room, he is inexplicably vulnerable again and you have to shoot to kill.

The only way to know whether a fight is for fighting or for running is to have played the game before to know how it's scripted. That really takes me out of the game world. It makes me feel like a passenger and like I need to ask the game, "So what do you want me to do here?" at every encounter. It's not very fun.

And the absolute worst of the worst of the worst is the final boss. He is an invulnerable character that has been chasing you for the entire game, even pursuing you in regular level segments while you try to do puzzles or clear out normal enemies. He's been colossally annoying, but he's here for the final fight and it's finally time for you to take your revenge... except he's still invincible. The entire fight is you running away from him on a small platform, tanking his flaily, hard-to-avoid attacks for three or four minutes until a deus ex machina kills him for you in one shot.

Coming off a RE4 high, I really wanted to like RE2... but I fell out of love with it by the halfway point. I simply realized that there's no satisfaction in any of the systems. Fighting enemies sucks. Exploring often uncovers more enemies to fight which sucks. Puzzle solving involves manoeuvering around invincible chasing bosses and respawning enemies and so it also sucks. Even the story is boring. Who would have guessed Umbrella was behind it all again? And this this time not with the T-Virus, but with the... G-Virus!

I know I'm playing this with the hindsight of RE4, but still I wouldn't recommend this game. It's like when they remade it they turned it into a wannabe RE4-lite. So go right to RE4 and play that instead. It's clear that it's where all the love and attention went in this remake trilogy.

Whether you're a nostalgic fan of the original, or just a fan of zombie games in general, or even just a fan of puzzles and escape rooms, Resident Evil 2 (Remake) is a blast! From the halls of the mansion-like RPD, to the chaos-ridden streets, to the grimy sewers, and the futuristic lab- each part of the game has its own distinct feel, and its own distinct obstacles and enemies to face.

The controls are pretty easy, and the enemies have somewhat predictable patterns, but I still found myself being surprised at some of the jump scares and twists that the game pulls on you when you're not alert. Overall, where this game thrives is in its atmosphere (specifically with the classic soundtrack turned on). The music is perfect and fits the mood of each area, the flickering lights, the AC noises, the shuffling of the zombies where it's unclear how close or far they are... it all adds up and makes a beautifully haunting experience.

The cutscenes and animations are very well done, and almost never break immersion (except for some of the zombie death ragdolls, though they can be kinda funny). The voice acting is really good, especially from Sherry, the little girl. Her fear is palpable and her emotional moments really got me tearing up. Claire is also a good voice actor, even though sometimes she doesn't seem that scared ig? Her determination and her quick thinking is badass, though, I wish she seemed a bit more tense given the situation.

All in all, great game, I'd give it an easy 8 or 9 out of 10, and would definitely say it's worth the money, especially on sale.

Overall, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a fantastic reimagining of a classic, and one of the best survival horror experiences you can play today. If you're a fan of the series, especially Claire or Leon, this one’s a must.

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 73:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆ (9/10 stars)

[i] Resident Evil 2 Remake [/i] is a phenomenal reimagining of the 1998 classic—one that doesn’t just slap on prettier graphics but fully rebuilds the game from the ground up. With its stunning visuals, atmospheric tension, and tight design, it stands tall as one of the best survival horror games ever made. It’s both a love letter to longtime fans and a pitch-perfect entry point for newcomers.

🧟 [b] Pros: [/b]
[list]
[*] Absolutely gorgeous and terrifying visuals. The RE Engine shines here: slick rain-soaked streets, grotesque gore, dynamic lighting—all of it creates an oppressive, immersive atmosphere. 

[*] Survival horror perfected. Every bullet counts. Every encounter feels dangerous. Inventory management is tense, and conserving resources is a constant source of anxiety. For about half the game, you'll be annoyed because there's so many items and not enough hip pouches.

[*] Mr. X. The sound of his boots stomping through the police station? Iconic. 

[*] Two playable campaigns. Leon and Claire offer different perspectives and variations on the story, giving you good replay value.

[*] Incredible sound design. Groans behind walls, distant thunder, and the dreaded stomp of Mr. X create one of the best audio horror experiences in any game.

[*] Leon and Claire are both likable protagonists. Claire’s fierce loyalty and Leon’s dorky, idealistic rookie cop energy are both incredibly endearing. 

[*] The RPD station is THE pinnacle n level design. Feels like a character in its own right. Unlocking shortcuts, discovering secrets, and backtracking never gets old.
[/list]

🎮 [b] Cons: [/b]
[list]
[*] The campaign B-scenarios could’ve been more distinct. While marketed as two interlocking campaigns, in practice they repeat a lot of content, with only a few small changes. I got bored after playing Claire's campaign and had to put the game down for a while. 

[*] Enemy placement can feel cheap. Sometimes you’ll clear a hallway only to come back and suddenly it’s full of zombies again.

[*] Puzzle variety is good but not outstanding. A few can feel arbitrary or underwhelming, mostly variations on the “find the right shaped item” theme.

Resident Evil 2 (Remake) — 9.5 h played (Leon A & Claire B cleared)  
Score: 9 / 10 (Short but Superb)

Capcom’s remake is everything I loved about the 1998 classic—tense corridors, smart puzzles, and Mr. X dread—reimagined with modern controls and photoreal gore.  It’s over quicker than I wanted, yet every minute is polished survival-horror gold.

WHY IT WORKS  
• **Faithful, not slavish** – Same police-station layout, key puzzles, and A/B character routes, but new scenarios keep veterans guessing.  
• **Modernized mechanics** – Over-the-shoulder aiming, quick-turns, and contextual knives make combat tight without losing the series’ signature tension.  
• **Atmosphere on overdrive** – RE Engine delivers dripping hallways, reactive flashlight shadows, and zombie dismemberment that’s equal parts gruesome and satisfying.  
• **Mr. X pressure-cooker** – The Tyrant stalks you in real time; hearing those footsteps down a marble corridor still spikes heart-rate.  
• **Dual campaigns** – Two protagonists, different weapons, and altered boss routes add meaningful replay value even if each run is brisk.

WHERE IT COMES UP SHORT  
• **Length** – A first play-through clocks 7–10 hours; a second scenario is faster once puzzles click.  
• **Story depth** – Beats are faithful to the original, but characterization remains 90s B-movie thin.  
• **Backtracking fatigue** – Late-game key hunts can feel like lock-and-key busywork on repeat runs.

FINAL VERDICT  
A lean, beautifully modernised survival-horror experience that respects its source while feeling entirely current.  If you crave a tightly paced, adrenaline-spiking weekend game—and don’t mind credits rolling sooner than in RE 4 or Village—Resident Evil 2 Remake is essential.

As somebody who never played the original, I would call the Resident Evil 2 remake a pretty good time overall. The story is unapologetic 90's zombie camp, the main characters simple but likeable (especially my sweet boy Leon), and the gameplay satisfying and reasonably challenging with high potential to 'solve' the game and breeze through it once you get good if you're into speed-running.

What really makes the game for me is its sound-design and hit-detection on zombies. Capcom has managed the rare feat of making a game where the enemies are major bullet-sponges but shooting them still feels good. It's almost a shame that resource management is such a major part of the game, because once you blow your first zombie's head off with a shotgun you're going to want to do it again and again. The guns all sound great, the zombies and variants appropriately growly and creepy, and the boss-fights are soundtracked with grand orchestral tracks that wouldn't feel out of place in a Souls game.

The bosses themselves, mind you, are distinctly un-soulslike, with most of them being quite easy and predictable, and others being perhaps a bit too faithful in their recreation of early Playstation gameplay jank (looking at you and your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ container, G2).

My only major complaint about the game is that it feels a bit small at times. RE2 reuses spaces constantly, something I imagine is carried over from the original which was released in a time when this sort of recycling was more accepted, but would have probably been better left behind in favor of an expanded map in the modern version of the game. It's pretty bad, and it kind of feels like you're backtracking for half the game.

The main game took me about 13 hours to beat (the story being divided into two 'scenarios', A and B) which would be a good length, but in keeping with the game's recycling issue, story aside, beating the second scenario feels a lot more like replaying the game with a different set of weapons than it does playing the second half of a game.

It feels unfair to fault a remake too heavily for faults that come about from it being faithful to the original, so with that in mind I'd rate the RE2 Remake a respectable 8/10, would shotgun a zombie again.

What an amazing game! I mean, really—what else is there to say? The RE Engine just makes everything so much better in terms of visuals and gameplay. After getting all the achievements in this game, here are my thoughts.

I have to admit, I haven’t played the original Resident Evil 2, but in my humble opinion, you don’t need to in order to enjoy this remake. The pacing, the zombies, the actual survival horror elements—like managing your resources instead of just mowing down enemies (not that you'd want to, because zombies don’t die in this game)—are all incredibly well done.

I love that they give you the option to switch between the remake and original soundtrack. Having two different character runs is also much appreciated, along with the additional game modes that add replay value.

Like any game, some trophies are a pain to get, but overall, the achievement list is pretty doable for most players.

This is actually the first Resident Evil game that got me into speedrunning, thanks to how short the game is once you know what you're doing—roughly an hour and 20 minutes. It’s easy to squeeze in multiple runs in a single day.

The only disappointing aspect is how similar the scenarios feel between Leon and Claire. A bit more differentiation would’ve made replaying both characters feel more unique.

Also—enjoy being bitten! It's almost impossible to avoid it sometimes.

In the end, this game is a must-play for any Resident Evil fan or survival horror enjoyer.

When Capcom announced a full remake of Resident Evil 2, fans were cautiously optimistic. The original, released in 1998, was a landmark in survival horror. But could it be modernized without losing its soul?

The answer is a resounding yes.

Resident Evil 2 Remake isn’t just a graphical overhaul—it’s a masterclass in how to bring a classic back to life without sacrificing its identity. Built from the ground up in the RE Engine, this version keeps the core of what made the original special—tense atmosphere, limited resources, and tight level design—while updating nearly every element for modern sensibilities.

Set in the zombie-ravaged Raccoon City, the game lets you play as either rookie cop Leon S. Kennedy or college student Claire Redfield. Each campaign follows a parallel path, filled with unique encounters, puzzles, and overlapping story beats. The dual-scenario design encourages replayability without feeling repetitive, and both characters are given far more emotional depth than in the original.

The shift to over-the-shoulder, third-person perspective is a game-changer. It adds precision to the combat while maintaining the tension of the fixed-camera classic. Zombies are tougher, hungrier, and horrifyingly unpredictable. Shooting one in the head might not drop it. In fact, it often doesn't. Every bullet matters.

Then there’s Mr. X. This trenchcoat-clad tyrant isn’t just a boss; he’s a walking panic attack. His heavy footsteps become the soundtrack to your anxiety, especially when you’re already low on health and out of ammo. He’s a brilliant addition to the pacing—keeping you moving, forcing you to make mistakes, and adding a layer of persistent dread that few games achieve.

Visually, the game is gorgeous in a grotesque way. The lighting is moody, the gore is detailed to a disturbing degree, and the police station—the game’s central labyrinth—is both a nostalgic and chilling environment. The sound design is equally meticulous. From distant groans to the echoing clank of Mr. X’s boots, every sound matters.

If there’s one drawback, it’s that the story, while serviceable, doesn’t quite match the emotional punch of the gameplay. But let’s be honest—Resident Evil has always been more about survival than Shakespearean drama.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is a near-perfect reimagining of a survival horror classic. It’s scary, smart, and beautifully brutal. Whether you’re a longtime fan or new to the series, this is one of the best horror games of the decade—and proof that some nightmares are worth reliving.

[h1]Confession of a Newbie[/h1]
[hr]                                                                                                                                                                                            [/hr]
I have never been particularly close to the Resident Evil game franchise. I watched all the movies with Milla Jovovich, but I’ve only heard something about the games somewhere, and they never really left a deep impression on me. The hype around the Resident Evil remaster passed me by because it didn’t evoke any nostalgia or positive emotions. As a result, my opinion about the game will be an honest reflection of its core without sugarcoating.
I would like to start with the positive aspects. What really surprised me was the unusual setting of the game. When I first launched RE 2, I thought it would be a game in the style of Dead Space, but how mistaken I was. Naively shooting all my bullets at useless zombies and thinking I no longer needed to conserve ammo because there were no enemies I couldn’t handle, I encountered him… Tyrant. At that moment, my gameplay turned upside down because now I was not the hunter — Mr. X became the hunter. He didn’t react to gunfire in the usual way; instead, he punished even the slightest delay with a brutal death animation. From that moment on, there’s no room for error when he appears — you can’t afford to waste time studying the map, because he’s always nearby. Even if you think you’ve hidden successfully, he mysteriously appears behind your back at the worst moment, scaring you out of your mind. Most likely, my gaming experience was influenced by the fact that I thought I’d be playing a different game — and how awesome that was!
I was definitely pleased with the nice graphics, engine physics, and storyline. But with all due respect, why is the game so short? I understand it’s just a remaster and that we have access to a second storyline, but I still wanted more. Surely those who bought the game at launch were left asking themselves: “Is that it? Was that all? What did I spend my money on?” However, I bought it at a big discount and can’t complain — for its price, it justified every euro spent. Perhaps those are all the cons. Overall, I highly recommend this game to everyone who hasn’t played it yet!

I was playing through all of the remakes for a first time experience and was hooked after RE1. RE2 in contrast is a good game, and expands on the first one quiet well. However, there are things I don't really like about it. 

For one I feel randomized pursuer type enemies actually detract from the experience. For certain scenes and scenarios they can be great and cause a player to try and succeed under pressure, however if the game doesn't support the player then the end result is failure, death, reload, and try again with continually decreasing tension each time. When pursuers are used at random then they become nothing more than a nuisance where the player stops focusing on something to get away and then has to go back to it, not difficult, just annoying. 

Secondly I take issue with the apparently varying level of strength between enemies. Namely a headshot is not an instant death to them. Many people argue that this shouldn't be the case because its never been a thing in RE to which I retort that in the first game, there is a note that says they can be permanently put down by burning them OR BY DESTROYING THE HEAD. In both games this is exemplified by critical shots that blow the head wide open, how they differ is that RE2 has shifted into a more skill based game having you manually aim shots, making it more infuriating when some enemies go down to a single bullet while others can soak up 10. It would have been much better for there to be a more limited amount of ammo or larger groupings of enemies to make the player choose whether it is better to clear an area or avoid it. 

For all my misgivings I still think RE2 is a good game and it kept up many of the puzzles and story beats that I enjoyed from the first game. It does delve much closer into realism with the setting than the slightly comical haunted house of the first game, but this has it's own strengths and weaknesses. Despite not being as good as the first game, I believe it is still worth playing and have good expectations for the rest of the series if they are even close to the quality of this one.

Review: Resident Evil 2 – A Powerful Commentary on Ceiling Fan Anxiety
★★☆☆☆

Listen, I don’t know what game everyone else played, but Resident Evil 2 is clearly about a man named Douglas Pinecone, a retired sock inspector, who finds himself trapped inside a rotating IKEA showroom during an interdimensional toothpaste shortage.

The game opens in a dimly lit forest filled with whispering eggplants. You play as Douglas, armed only with a rubber crayon and a vague sense of betrayal. Within minutes, you’re introduced to your main companion: the ghost of your childhood goldfish, Billy, who communicates exclusively through Morse code and cereal box coupons.

Now, the game claims to be “survival horror,” but the real horror comes from trying to navigate the endless quick-time events involving interpretive dance battles against haunted beanbag chairs. One of the early boss fights involves convincing a sentient toilet not to sing show tunes. I failed that one. The game remembered. It always remembers.

Billy (the fish, not the raccoon pretending to be him) repeatedly begs you not to flush the grenade. He warns you. Pleads with you. Says things like:

“Not again, Douglas. Not after what happened in the lemon dimension.”

But I didn’t listen. I thought maybe this time it would open the portal to the sandwich realm. Instead, it just summoned The Janitor. Not a janitor. The Janitor. He screamed in binary and ate my inventory screen.

The crafting system is bizarre. You combine shoelaces and regret to make a “Tactical Banjo,” which is only useful if you correctly answer trivia about obscure mid-80s Canadian soap operas. If you fail, Douglas just sits down and hums the entire Bee Movie script.

The graphics are… wet. Not in quality, just in vibe. Everything feels damp. Everything is damp. Except the mirrors. Don’t look in the mirrors. They show things. Things I haven’t told my therapist.

By the time you reach the final level (a courtroom being run by a panel of judgmental ceiling fans), Billy is screaming constantly, the toilets are multiplying, and Douglas is wearing a bathrobe made of unpaid parking tickets.

In summary, Resident Evil 2 is a bold, if confusing, meditation on loss, ceiling fan betrayal, and why you should never, under any circumstances, flush a live grenade—even if it’s whispering compliments.

Final Verdict: 2 stars. I think the game was mocking me. Billy says I’m not real. I must go now. The sink is calling.

The original RE2 was my favorite in the series for a long time. This game was almost nothing like it, but I'm going to rate this as a standalone.

Great, story, cinematics, development of the big bad, voice acting, models, music. Everything was great. The way the story and the tension builds is really good. I didn't play the DLC yet, I might later.

ONLY a few complaints I have - 1) headshots seem to do nothing, except heads explode sometimes for seemingly no reason. 2) I heard there was some sort of dynamic difficulty - I think that's completely unnecessary. There are different difficulty modes and that's what they should be for, I don't want a game to get harder because I'm learning how to play better. I could just go up a difficulty if I start to get bored. 3) Didn't realize I was actually supposed to do like Leon first run then Claire second run. That was weird due to the naming convention. So I did Leon 1st, Claire 1st, then Claire 2nd. Realized Claire 2nd seemed to be much harder as I guess I triggered the Tyrant a bit early and I kind of just lost interest after that, didn't see much point in continuing since I already beat it twice and this was much harder so putting off for now. 4) The continuity of stories 1st and 2nd seem like they are supposed to add up, they just don't. So IMO it would have been better to just have a Leon and a Claire story and not make things too complicated by making either go into the police station first - not having a 1st and 2nd for each. It would have made more sense that way (like Claire not having to find the emblems in the same places Leon found them in his 1st run in her 2nd run - how would she even know she was supposed to do that?) That just didn't hold together.

But yeah, besides those quirks, I did enjoy this entry.

By 2019, the Resident Evil franchise was in a pretty good place. After struggling with its identity for nearly a decade, Capcom's excellent survival horror game Resident Evil 7: Biohazard put the franchise back on the map in the eyes of many horror fans, winning numerous accolades and selling over 12 million copies. It's only natural, then, that after rebooting the series with an original title Capcom would return to the familiar: in this case, a remake of the similarly excellent Resident Evil 2, perhaps the pinnacle of 90s survival horror. In my eyes, the Resident Evil 2 remake doesn't even come close to replacing the original, but I don't think any sane developer should have attempted to in the first place. Instead, it acts as a late-2010s complement to it, offering a modernized interpretation of the game with a drastically different vision yet still capturing similar feelings of tension and atmosphere as the original did. Resident Evil 2 remake carves its own path while respecting the source material, becoming an instant survival horror classic.

Part of why Resident Evil 2 succeeds as well as it does is due to the game design. In this case, Capcom truly understood what made the original survival horror titles so compelling on a gameplay level. Playing on the hardcore difficulty mode proved to be a thoroughly rewarding experience that could often be highly difficult yet never once felt like it was pushing me beyond my capabilities, nor like it was asking more than it provided. While the tank controls and fixed camera angles of the original game are long gone, the game makes up for the difficulty those could provide with new challenges, such as location-based damage and the need to properly align and aim your shots. Player movement feels perfect, giving you just enough delay and weight to make the player feel vulnerable but just enough responsiveness and speed to make maneuvering around monsters a skill to master, and mastering said skill is highly satisfying. A major improvement is the difficulty, something that was sorely lacking in the original, being oddly easy for a survival horror game. Enemies are highly dangerous and even a single zombie represents a major threat, which is the main reason why RE2R remains such a tense and stressful experience. I've had many otherwise perfectly planned runs ruined when I forgot to account for a stray zombie shambling around. Mr. X has been a massive point of contention among fans, with some deriding the stress he brings, though I consider him to be a massive gameplay revelation on the same tier as the crimson heads from the remake of Resident Evil 1. He fundamentally changes how you play the game and forces you to be stealthy, as gunshots, slammed doors, or even running can alert him to your position. I didn't find him unbearably difficult, in fact, I got a hang of him fairly quickly, but I can't discount the incredible amount of stress he adds to the experience, and this kind of stress is exactly what I want in a game of this genre. The RPD is a sprawling puzzle box that, as any good RE game should, feels impenetrably labyrinthine at the beginning but eventually expands and opens up as the player learns to best plan routes and unlocks new areas. Later areas such as the underground and the laboratory aren't nearly as expansive but are certainly unnerving in their own right. I also really appreciate the addition of lickers being blind, once again forcing stealth which can become additionally tense to avoid if you have Mr. X in pursuit. RE2R is a game that demands the player keep track of every move they make and it's a level of player immersion that I highly respect and wish more games accomplished. On a mechanical level, this might be a perfect survival horror game.

Resident Evil 2 isn't perfect overall, however, and while the game's flaws struggle to feel little more than marginal, they are at least moderate hindrances that prevent it from getting a perfect score from me. There's a lot of online controversy about how the game handles the dual scenarios, with many arguing they're exactly like one another. I disagree, after playing Leon A to Claire B, I found that both campaigns are reasonably different to make them both worth playing and largely felt in line with how the originals handled it. However, I was disappointed that most of the boss fights were the same, with only one or two appearing only in one campaign as opposed to the original which had a lot more variance. William Birkin G2 is a fairly disappointing fight, relying heavily on the arena's gimmick and the maneuverability you have in that fight is probably too limited, though if you conserved your ammo he won't be too difficult even on hardcore. I also disliked the G-Adults as enemies. Their large stature already makes them difficult to avoid, especially with their propensity to grab and poison the player, but considering how they almost always appear in groups it can lead to being stunlocked. At one point I had to basically daisy chain R/G/B herb combos to get by five of them in a row. These are relatively minor and fleeting issues, but they were noticeably frustrating when they did occur.

I had to cut out a lot of this review due to Valve's text guidelines. Let me assure you this game is fantastic!

Resident Evil 2 remake doesn't replace the original game. Very few, if any, remakes do. Nor does it supersede it. Rather, the game matches many of the original game's qualities, but in different ways that feel both refreshingly modern and nostalgically classic. The near-perfect survival horror game design, anxiety-inducing horror, fine-tuned difficulty, improved storytelling, highly detailed visuals, and rock-solid atmosphere nearly make me forget about a handful of the game's somewhat annoying sections. It does certain things better than the original, and it does certain things worse, so it's really a give or take on which game I prefer. An immediate modern classic, Resident Evil 2 is the game that should be held as a benchmark for all survival horror games going forward.

Resident Evil 2 (Remake): An Exemplary Remake, Resurrecting a Horror Classic

Overall Impression:

Resident Evil 2 (Remake) is not just a re-release of the iconic 1998 game, but a complete reimagining that carefully preserves the spirit of the original while offering modern gameplay and stunning graphics. Capcom has managed to create something more than just a nostalgic trip, but a complete horror experience that can scare and captivate both newcomers and veterans of the series.

Pros:

•  Stunning Graphics and Atmosphere: The RE Engine works wonders. Raccoon City looks grim, dirty, and incredibly detailed. Lighting, sounds, and animation create an unparalleled atmosphere of horror and despair.
•  Improved Gameplay: The classic Resident Evil gameplay has received modern controls, a third-person camera, and an improved combat system. The game has become more dynamic and responsive.
•  Respectful Treatment of the Original: The developers have respectfully treated the original, preserving the main locations, characters, plot points, and puzzles.
•  Two Campaigns for Different Characters: You can play the game as Leon and Claire, each with their own unique storyline, weapons, and skills. This adds replayability.
•  Nemesis - Mr. X: Mr. X is one of the scariest and most memorable enemies in video game history. His relentless pursuit creates constant tension and forces you to look for new ways to retreat.
•  Many Secrets and Easter Eggs: The game is full of secrets, easter eggs, and references to other games in the Resident Evil series, which will delight fans.
•  Excellent Optimization: The game is well optimized and runs smoothly even on mid-range computers.

Cons:

•  Some Plot Changes: Some plot points have been changed or simplified compared to the original, which may disappoint some fans.
•  Monotony of Locations: Despite the excellent graphics, some locations, such as the sewers, may seem monotonous.

Who is this game for:

•  Fans of the Resident Evil series who want to experience a classic game in a modern interpretation.
•  Horror lovers who appreciate atmosphere, tension, and scary moments.
•  Those who are looking for a game with an interesting story, memorable characters, and complex puzzles.

Who is this game NOT for:

•  Those who don't like horror and prefer a more action-oriented approach.
•  Those who don't like games with limited resources and difficult bosses.

Do I recommend this game?

Resident Evil 2 (Remake) is one of the best remakes in video game history. It not only carefully preserves the spirit of the original, but also offers modern gameplay and stunning graphics. If you like horror and haven't played Resident Evil 2 yet, this is a great reason to catch up.

Score: 9.5/10 (For an exemplary remake, excellent graphics and atmosphere, but with a small minus for some plot changes).

Resident Evil 2 is a third-person survival horror game that is a remake of a much older game. It uses new graphics and updated controls, so it is easier to play and look at. The game takes place in a city where many people have turned into monsters. The player can choose between two different characters, and both go through the same places, but in different ways. The story starts outside the city, and after entering, both characters go through different paths.

The game has two main story modes and some extra game modes, but I have only played Leon mode, as the plot is mostly the same, with some differences in perspective and events.. There is a mode that shows stories of other people who are not part of the main game and what could happen if things were different. There are also a few mini-games where the goal is to escape from a place filled with many enemies. These extra modes are shorter and offer various types of gameplay, depending on the mission or character.

Overall, Resident Evil 2 is a strong remake with modern graphics, clear movement, and detailed sound. It keeps the main idea of the original while using better design and smooth controls. It is a good choice for anyone looking for a survival horror game with more than one way to play.

[h1] The revival of Survival Horror? [/h1]

[h2] The amazing things [/h2]

[h3] Story [/h3]

The story is split into two perspectives the perspective of Leon (Scenario A) and the perspective of Claire (Scenario B). To get the full Story and the true ending you need to complete both Scenarios, but after beating one of them you get a New Game + type mode which speeds up the game a lot for you, and gives you some new challenges. 

The story is pretty amazing and both Scenarios kept me wanting to find out more. Since these games are from the Remake Universe they obviously differ a bit from the originals but, they don't change it too much to make it feel weird.

Quick Summary:

 Leon S. Kennedy a Rookie police officer, arriving a day too late in Racoon City to begin his new job at the Racoon City Police Department, has a terrible first day at his new job, the City is overrun by Zombies and he has to get through all of this to find a way to find out what happened and then leave this place.

Claire Redfield, the sister of the S.T.A.R.S Member Chris Redfield is looking for her brother and arrives in Racoon City to find ou t about his whereabouts after not getting answers from him. As she arrives she notices the city has been overrun and quickly goes to the Racoon City Police Department in which her brother was last seen at his work.

[h3] The Gameplay [/h3] 

The gameplay feels like a modernized version of the old school survival horror genre. It combines a dreadful and scary atmosphere with managing your bullets and healing items. And successfully creates a scary remake of the old games. 
The game features freely explorable interconnected levels which often require backtracking which are very rewarding. You can always go to previously completed rooms.

The zombies feel truely scary, and keep getting back up even after pretending to be dead. Also they react to their environments, if you shoot them in the leg they fall on the floor and sometimes even get cought falling against a wall, also you can take of their limbs with higher calibre guns or with your combat knifes. You never can truely be sure a zombie won't stand up again.. until you shoot them multiple times.

Mr X. the creepiest and most amazing part of this game. Imagine being followed by an immortal snail that always is on your tails but you always outrun it... now replace that with a giant guy that is bent on killing you and isn't afraid of following you a bit faster.. So anyway after some time there will always be this unkillable muscular guy that keeps following and looking for you in the police department, only the safe rooms are safe( its in the name). 

[h3] The not so cool things [/h3]

Sadly some content from the original was cut and we didn't get two additional scenarios that existed in the original game. 
You will be disappointed if you play Resident Evil 3 Remake right after finishing this game.
Scenario A and B have some pretty big continuity errors

[h2] My honest opinion [/h2]

This game is an amazing horror game that offers a lot of replay value, and has to be finished at least 2 times for its full story and glory. The different areas are seamlessly connected and you never know if the corridor is truely safe or if theres a new threat waiting for you.
I really loved finishing this game and never felt like it was a drag or chore playing this game. 

I will give this game a 9/10 for its amazing gameplay and spooky atmospheres that truely spooked me often and it also being a good remake of the oldschool survival horror genre.

[b]Working on the backlog[/b]

Even with AAA games we tend to have a big list of games we still need to play. And some great titles such as RE 2 can easily end up on this list. I purchased this one 2 years ago but I have only managed to play it recently. Initially, I wanted to use the word "complete" but I only did one story run with Leon from start to finish which is nowhere near when it comes to the things you can this in this remake.

[b]Biohazard[/b]

The first RE was number 4 for me. But when it was initially released for PC... boy did it look ugly! Then we played number 5 with a friend at least 3 times. 6 was a chore and we hated it. I had enough of the series after that, to be honest, but with 7 I enjoyed it once again. In fact, RE 7 was the one where I have all DLCs. I was reluctant to continue with number 8 for some reason. I didn't like the direction they went with but the remakes were more interesting to me. 

[b]Comparison[/b]

I checked some videos and in addition to the technology (which is obviously an upgrade compared to the 1998 version) I understand they retained the A and B scenarios. Story-wise, you play the same campaign with Leon and Claire but you take different routes. In order to see the true ending you need to complete both. There are character-specific alterations so once you complete the story with Leon (scenario A) you can switch to Claire and pick the "2nd run" option already (scenario B). This is already an interesting concept, something that increases longevity and additional options / modes will be available after you have done the 2 scenarios. But more on them later.

[b]Controls[/b]

Oh yes, no more tank controls and this also means no more fixed camera angles. Are we feeling comfortable with controlling Leon then in his fight against hordes of zombies? Well, yes and no. I mean, close-combat became more and more interesting in later episodes. I think in number 6 you could hit and even kick. There were ways to do melee combat without wasting any bullets.

But remember those games had more sophisticated enemies! We are back to walkers here, most of the time. And you have those clickers and zombie dogs that can quickly jump at you. Headshots with the zombies are a must. You can also destroy their knees and try to get around them. The game is a pure survival horror where every battle can be deadly and conserving ammo is a must!

An interesting concept while holding different firearms is to equip so-called sub-weapons. You need to hold SPACE and after that you can throw a flashbang, a grenade or just melee with your combat knife. In case enemies capture you, you don't necessarily get hurt but you have the option to use the aforementioned tools to push away the enemies. It's fun when you stab a zombie only to remove the knife later on from the corpse. Or you put the grenade in its mouth which can  explode with a well-aimed shot.

[b]Graphical evil[/b]

The game looks fantastic! Zombie come in many forms (as in body shape and clothing). Shots hitting them can chip away pieces of their bodies (heads can be blown off, hats can fly off, limbs can be torn off). The way their body interacts with the environment is just great! That includes us: for instance, imagine that we do a headshot and the zombie in front of us immediately dies but its body falls onto us. Leon feels the weight of the dead body and pushes it away with audible disgust in his voice. 

[b]Scripted evil[/b]

Some of the dialogues are as cheesy as they get. Especially, when we team up with another person later in the story. Other than that the game has a lot of cutscenes with great voice acting and 3 main locations to go through. It's best not to rush the story as backtracking can be very rewarding when you find a special keycard or any other item that allows us to access a new location (e.g. a room, a locker) with a new weapon. Upgrade parts can be found in safes that make our weapons deadlier. Our inventory is limited: be on the lookout for hip pouches to increase its size.

[b]Longevity?[/b]

Yes, multiple playthroughs are needed for all achievements. You can do a fast run to get an S+ rank (my "casual" run granted me a C rank only) and there are achievements for completing the game on hardcore difficulty setting. So if you complete Leon's and Claire's 2nd run, too, and a hardcore walkthrough that is at least 6 playthroughs.

Then we have "The Ghost Survivors". 4 additional but short campaigns with different NPCs we met with Leon and Claire, all of whom died. These stories are a sort of "What if?" scenarios: they are all given a chance to escape and go through locations we got familiar with during the main journey. Only 3 are available at the beginning - the last is a bonus with a guy who needs to eliminate 100 zombies instead of reaching an extraction point. All these focus heavily on the action.

[b]Any annoying bits?[/b]

Of course, it's an RE game! Puzzles can be interesting but the backtracking for a new weapon or weapon upgrade can be tedious sometimes. Going back to locations previously cleared can make some new zombies spawn or those already shot will just wake up. Even with the hip pouch upgrades, inventory limit is often reached so it's best to look for the typewriter (which allows saving) as it is usually in rooms where there is also a big chest allowing us to store what we cannot take with ourselves. Try to store these items instead of discarding them which is always an option.

I found the police station the best and most interesting part of the game and I was annoyed to meet a creature later on in the story that keeps patrolling and chasing us. It is impossible to defeat this monster but we can only immobilize it for a short period of time to escape. After progressing with the story it disappears for good and we can still return to RPD to collect anything we left behind.

[b]Summary[/b]

RE 2 is a fantastic game. Is it better than the original? I don't know, I never played that one. Hardcore fans have probably already shared their view on this. If you liked recent entries (and don't mind switching back from the first person perspective), don't hesitate to play this one.

Claire’s path was just as powerful. Her protectiveness over Sherry, her fierce determination… she was never just “the other character.” She was a hero in her own right. And let’s be honest—Ada and Claire are both sexy in their own way. Ada with her mysterious charm and red dress, Claire with that tough, no-nonsense badass vibe. Queens.

The final fight with William Birkin was chaos in the best way—pure adrenaline. And Mr. X? That towering nightmare never lets you breathe.

Visually stunning, emotionally charged, and terrifying from start to finish.

Resident Evil 2 Remake: A Spine-Chilling Classic Reborn

let’s talk about Resident Evil 2 Remake—a game that takes the 1998 classic and cranks the horror dial to 11. As a fan of survival horror, I dove into this on Steam, and man, it’s a wild ride. Here’s the lowdown on what makes it awesome, what’s a bit rough, and why it’s a must-play for horror junkies.

Pros: Why It Slaps

Creepy Vibes on Point: The environments—like the eerie Raccoon City Police Station—are straight-up intimidating. Dark hallways, flickering lights, and blood-smeared walls create an atmosphere that’ll have you checking over your shoulder. It’s pure horror magic.

Tyrant’s Terrifying Stalk: Mr. X, the relentless Tyrant, is a game-changer. His heavy footsteps and knack for busting through doors add a layer of panic most horror games can’t match. He keeps you on edge, forcing you to rethink every move.

Nostalgia Done Right: Fans of the OG will geek out over familiar areas, zombie types, and iconic models, but it’s polished for 2025. It’s like revisiting your childhood home, but it’s got a killer new paint job.

Gorgeous Graphics: The RE Engine delivers jaw-dropping visuals. From glistening zombie gore to detailed environments, it’s a feast for the eyes. Every corner looks disgustingly perfect.

Sound That Scares: The audio is chef’s kiss. Creaking floors, distant groans, and Mr. X’s thudding steps amplify the fear. The sound design alone will make your heart race.

Steam Deck Friendly: It runs smooth on Steam Deck and still looks dope, though it’s not quite as crisp as on a beefy PC. Perfect for portable scares.


Cons: A Few Hiccups

Controller Clunkiness: Playing with a controller felt a bit off for me. Aiming and movement weren’t as slick as I’d hoped, especially in tense moments. Mouse and keyboard felt better.

Puzzling Puzzles: Some puzzles stumped me hard. I had to hunt down guides to find items or figure out solutions, which broke the flow a bit.

Tyrant Overstays His Welcome: Mr. X is scary as hell, but his constant stalking can get old after a while. Sometimes you just want a breather, you know?

Story’s Kinda Meh: The plot is classic Capcom—awkward, a bit cheesy, and mildly funny in that B-movie way. It’s not bad, but don’t expect a narrative masterpiece.

Final Thoughts

Resident Evil 2 Remake is a banger for horror fans or anyone who loved the original. It’s easily one of the scariest games I’ve played—and I’ve tackled all the Dead Space and F.E.A.R. titles. The atmosphere, Tyrant’s relentless pursuit, and top-notch visuals make it a heart-pounding experience that’s not for the faint of heart. Despite some controller woes and tricky puzzles, it’s a survival horror gem. If you’re down for a scare, grab it on Steam (https://store.steampowered.com/app/883710/Resident_Evil_2/) and brace yourself. I’d give it a solid 8.5/10—now go survive Raccoon City!

I don't know any other game that switches between finely crafted metroidvania survival gameplay to two toddlers in wheelchairs chasing each other up a flight of stairs quite like this mess of a game. The writing goes from unique to absolute garbage in actual seconds and so does the story, the puzzles and just about any aspect of the game. 

The basic zombies are some of the most threatening in any game I've played, yet all "specials" come across as being designed by the developers children... which are probably those same toddlers in wheelchairs I talked about earlier. One moment you are exploring a beatiful building at the edge of your seat, and the other you are suddenly in a completely different area, which is completely linear, featuring the most unfun enemies in gaming since space invaders.

The bosses... man I don't even know what to say about these walking piles of meat and sh*t. It honestly amazes me that the developers could not think of a better boss fight than the same bag of hitpoints walking towards you in a square room with nothing happening. Like every single bossfight is the exact same with, SOMETIMES, a new skin... othertimes its the actual same skin and you just have to do it again. The gameplay here consists of rolling in your little wheel chair with your little toddler while the other toddler tries to catch you in his own little wheelchair. Both of you move at a snails pace but none quite catch up, except for the fact that you are in a tiny square room, so actually you CAN't get away. The objective is to stunlock the bastard otherwise he will do an RNG attack that is either: 1. A massive multihit AOE swipe that can not be avoided if you are cornered OR 2. a pathetic jab that can not hit even if you stand still. That is the gameplay of these so called "boss fights"

Despite all this is had fun with the game for some ungodly reason. Playing on Hardcore made it tense enough that the regular gameplay sections were very engaging and something as simple as figuring out if a zombie is worth the ammo to "full kill" or not felt rewarding, and because the game loops around on it self many times, killing a zombie is rarely a mistake longterm, but saving your ammo can help you in the short term, until you get more powerful weapons. This made the game feel doable despide the limited ammo, ASSUMING YOU DON'T MISS TO MUCH!

Resident Evil 2 Remake – An Amazing Game

This is one of those Capcom games that doesn’t disappoint. The story follows Claire and Leon as they head to Raccoon City for different reasons, only to find themselves in the middle of a zombie apocalypse. Both characters are very well written, and the same goes for the supporting cast—Marvin, Ada, Kendo, and even Sherry. Capcom clearly put a lot of effort into the narrative and character development, making every interaction feel meaningful.

The game’s environments—the police station, the parking garage, the sewers, the lab—are all incredibly well-designed. Just walking around the map is a pleasure (as long as Mr. X isn’t chasing you). The first time you step into the police station, the atmosphere is so well done that it leaves you in shock. The lighting, sound design, and level layout make every corridor feel tense and immersive. Dark hallways filled with zombies, Mr. X relentlessly hunting you—it’s genuinely terrifying, even on multiple playthroughs.

Gameplay & Difficulty
The gameplay is simple and easy to understand. It strikes the perfect balance between survival horror and action. Whether you’re a beginner or an experienced gamer, you can pick it up and enjoy it. The inventory management system forces you to make strategic choices, while the limited resources keep the tension high.

Enemies on Normal mode are fairly easy to take down, but they can still surprise you if you’re careless. However, for those brave enough to play on Hardcore mode—good luck. That’s all I have to say. Limited saves, stronger enemies, and more punishing damage make it a true survival horror experience.

The puzzles in the game are also well-designed, never too easy but not frustrating either. They add to the classic Resident Evil experience without breaking the pacing of the game.

Trophies, Achievements & Replayability
As for trophies and achievements, some are easy to obtain, while others are much more challenging. But the worst one, and I think many would agree, isn’t the Mr. Raccoon collectibles—it’s the "Librarian" achievement, which requires you to read every single file in the game. And let’s not forget the challenge of completing the game on Hardcore mode with an S rank—a true test of skill and patience.

That being said, Resident Evil 2 Remake has incredible replay value. With the different campaigns (Leon A, Claire B, and vice versa), bonus modes, unlockables, and the speedrunning community, there’s always a reason to revisit the game. The New Game+ mode adds a layer of depth, allowing players to optimize their routes and challenge themselves further.

Extra Modes & Additional Content
The additional Survivor modes are interesting because they let you explore more about the side characters. They’re short but enjoyable, offering a fresh take on the gameplay formula. The Ghost Survivors DLC, while not story-heavy, provides an extra challenge with alternate "what-if" scenarios.

Also, if you’re looking for zombie variety—trust me, you’ll find plenty. From the classic slow-moving zombies to Lickers, G-mutants, and the terrifying Mr. X, the game constantly keeps you on edge. The first time encountering each enemy type is a genuinely memorable experience.

Final Verdict
If you're looking for a game to get into the Resident Evil franchise, this is one of my top recommendations. No bugs, well-written characters, a perfect atmosphere, and a fantastic balance between horror and action—it’s an absolute must-play for both fans of the series and newcomers alike.

[h1]Resident Evil 2 Remake – A Horror Classic Reborn[/h1]

Capcom’s Resident Evil 2 Remake is a stunning reimagining of the 1998 classic, bringing the best elements of modern gaming while preserving the heart-pounding tension and atmosphere that made the original so memorable. This remake isn’t just a fresh coat of paint—it’s a complete overhaul that enhances every aspect of the experience.  

[h2]Graphics & Atmosphere[/h2]  
The RE Engine delivers breathtaking visuals, from the eerie dimly lit hallways of the Raccoon City Police Department to the grotesque detail of the zombies. The lighting and shadows create an oppressive atmosphere that keeps you on edge, while the rain-drenched streets and flickering lights make every environment feel alive and immersive.  

[h2]Gameplay & Combat[/h2] 
The over-the-shoulder perspective modernizes gameplay while keeping it tense and strategic. Every shot counts, and resource management is crucial. The zombies are terrifyingly resilient—headshots don’t guarantee kills, and they lurch unpredictably, making every encounter a nerve-wracking experience. The sound design enhances the horror, with unsettling groans, distant echoes, and the ever-looming threat of Mr. X’s heavy footsteps.  

[h2]Story & Replayability[/h2] 
The dual campaigns featuring Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield offer unique perspectives and slight variations in story beats, encouraging multiple playthroughs. The characters are well-developed, with improved voice acting and writing that make them more relatable. The game also includes bonus modes, such as *The 4th Survivor*, adding even more content for dedicated players.  

[h2]Final Verdict[/h2]  
Resident Evil 2 Remake is a masterclass in how to remake a beloved classic. It respects the original while modernizing the gameplay and visuals in a way that makes it accessible to both longtime fans and newcomers. With its intense survival horror elements, stunning graphics, and engaging gameplay, this is one of the best horror games of the decade.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is a game where you're constantly torn between admiring the stunningly detailed environments and screaming in terror as a zombie tries to eat your face. It's a survival horror masterpiece that also doubles as a jump scare simulator, proving that the best way to stay in shape is by running away from mutated monstrosities.

Mr. X, the giant, trench coat-wearing stalker, is basically the Terminator, if the Terminator had a really heavy limp and an unhealthy obsession with personal space. He's not scary, he's just...inconvenient. Like a persistent telemarketer, but with a penchant for smashing through walls.

The game also excels at making you feel perpetually under-equipped. You'll spend most of your time meticulously managing your inventory, deciding what's more important: a handful of bullets or that one green herb you found in a toilet. This leads to many a tense moment where you're facing down a horde of undead with nothing but a knife and a prayer.

And let's not forget the zombies, who are impressively persistent. They'll shamble after you with the single-minded determination of a toddler chasing an ice cream truck. They're not fast, but they're incredibly stubborn, and they have a knack for showing up at the worst possible moment, like when you're trying to solve a complicated puzzle or have a quiet moment of reflection.

Ultimately, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a thrilling, terrifying, and often hilarious experience. It's a testament to the power of video games to make us feel a wide range of emotions, from heart-pounding fear to laugh-out-loud amusement. Whether you're a seasoned horror fan or a newcomer to the genre, this game is sure to leave a lasting impression...and possibly a few new grey hairs.

Having now played both RE2's and RE3's remakes, I think that though both are good, RE3 is a bit better, but also a bit shorter.
RE3 cuts out the less fun bits for me, giving a more focused (and slightly more action-focused) experience, while doing away with some elements from RE2 that were less fun.

Like knife durability.
Seriously, what kind of shoddy knife breaks entirely after being used around ten times?

But let's focus on what this game does right - the graphics are great, the controls are great, and the game's level design is really interesting in that metroidvania style of gameplay (with slightly less focus on random puzzles that the old games were prone to throw in). You make your way through the police station, finding keys and other objects that help you take new paths, unlocking new areas. The puzzles, if you can call them that, aren't especially complicated, you mostly will just know what you need at any time, so if you're looking for brain teasers, this might not be the game for you.
But if you want an action-focused metroidvania where using fairly scarce resources well is a priority, then this is a really fun one. 

My one issue, really, is the mysterious Mr. X that keeps showing up. I played Alien Isolation many years ago, and the way the creature in that game acted is in many ways similar to the constant "companion" in this game. I think my main issue is that it doesn't scare me, which makes its appearances more annyoing than anything else.
Contrasting this to equivalent sections in RE3: Nemesis, I much prefer how that game handles the continuous threat. In large part because it's more choreographed, built into the story, instead of being a game mechanic that just happens at times.

You will have to decide for yourself, though, which sounds more fun (or scary, if that's what you're after) - an enemy that can appear at any place and any time, forcing you to change your plans on the fly, or an enemy that shows up at exactly the worst possible moments because that's how the story is.

I personally enjoyed both RE2 and RE3 remakes, because though the gameplay is mostly the same, the framing through the world and scenario make them feel different enough that it's not just re-treading the same thing.

I feel like Capcom is really doing amazing work with their RE-remake series, and I look forward to more releases in the future - because I just can't appreciate the old games with their tank controls. Maybe a future RE-series remake game with more focus on puzzles could be nice? I hope to find out.

I never played the original so I don't have the hang-ups some of the OG players have. I love the game, find it infinitely re-playable and can't recommend it enough! That's not to say I don't have some pros and cons, which I will list below.

Let's start with the cons:
> Only one con really, continuity! I originally played Leon's 1st scenario and Claire's 2nd; however, the environmental elements of Leon's play-through make more sense if you play Claire's 1st scenario and Leon's 2nd. Apparently this is the way it should be anyway. Regardless which scenario you play 1st there are still glaring continuity errors between the two scenarios, I won't give spoilers but repeated puzzles are the most notable. I mean, if Claire has already been there and solved that, why does Leon have to do it again, and vice versa. If you play the RE3 Remake those continuity errors become even more prevalent. Honestly, I know it may have rubbed some of the OG players the wrong way, but I think aspects of the story in RE2 should have been switched with RE3 and vice versa. Certain locations, interactions and narratives make more sense for Jill than Leon or Claire. 

Pros:
> Despite the continuity errors the stories are engaging and so immersive. You feel the weight of the narrative through every interaction, be it with an ally or an enemy. 
> The pace is perfect, affording you the choice of speed-running or taking your time.
> The voice acting is brilliant, except maybe for Leon. Leon has some cheesy lines that I feel would be difficult to deliver genuinely for anyone; however, the delivery in the game is almost cartoonish at times, making Leon seem far more one-dimensional than he is.
> The NPCs feel fleshed out and real. You can tell there is a greater backstory to each character despite some of their appearances and dialogue being limited.
> The amount of puzzles was wonderful!

The original Resident Evil 2 is a widely beloved game, though comes just shy of being an unambiguously perfect masterpiece that everyone collectively agrees is amazing. Amongst the original trilogy of titles, they all tend to have ups and downs and favourites are a huge deal of preference. What people won't argue about though is that Resident Evil 2 [i]is[/i] good.

Naturally, adapting something that has such a significant influence on the genre and Resident Evil series as a whole being the introduction of Claire and Leon is tough, and this game has had a thousand eyes watching carefully and nitpicking every aspect from the instant they revealed they were going over the shoulder. Years later the positive reception speaks for itself, but from my years-later perspective does it live up to the original? No. It's [i]actually better[/i].

This game, the RE2make's biggest hurdle is how it chose to adapt the original. Corny as they can be, many aspects of the early RE games including their presentation is a big deal for series fans and I think trying to modernize them walks a tight rope of removing the identity or actual strong aspects like the monstrous design of the G creatures and rich atmosphere of the police station. And insults where they're due, RE2make erodes the musical identity of original in a way that's extremely frustrating and the one thing that sticks out as an obvious downgrade. Outside of that, however? The areas are richly recreated with similar floor plans and aesthetics, yet expanded with greater puzzles, detail, and even new areas that make the trek around the police station an engaging and winding trip that really engages you. Later areas are more linear and less iconic but were still highly engaging to me as the combat was slowly but surely ramped up to it's logical conclusion towards the end.

There's not a lot to talk about with RE2's story. It's very similar, but just kind of better. All the voice actors do an excellent job, many little contrivances in the way certain characters or elements were presented in the original are improved (Chief Irons' role being a massive beneficiary of this) and characters are simultaneously more grounded while aligning better with their future incarnations in the case of Ada Wong or Claire Redfield. Leon and Claire especially only suffer from their really awkward 5 minute relationship they pretend is closer than it is, but otherwise are excellent protagonists in this game who blend a level of fearful response to the horrific situation they've been placed in with a jaded persona that creeps in towards the ends of their stories that really show you how Over This ♥♥♥♥ they are by end.

RE2make's standout, however, is the mechanics. The eternal fear of adapting tank control, fixed-camera games to over the shoulder is that you risk ruining the defining enemy design and iconic encounters of the original. RE2make, however, gives deep thought to every last obstacle the player encounters and makes each of them a distinct type of terrifying to contend with. Regular zombies have adopted many of the qualities of crimsonheads, moving in highly unpredictable ways and constantly coming back to life at random moments in order to limit your navigation or go for surprise attacks, forcing you to weigh if you want to waste resources to keep them down or not. The dogs are much faster than the player and can move around the environment in unpredictable ways due to their smaller size you have to keep in mind. Lickers are brutally aggressive and demand situational awareness that makes their presence incredibly stressful. Mr. X has received a lot of complaints, and while I think he might be a bit too wasteful to fight in my opinion, he's still an insanely effective reinvention of the stalker enemy archetype that adds an unexpected variable even the most cynical survival horror veteran won't always be able to see coming.

The game also gives great reworks to many other of it's late game creatures including the G mutants, bosses, and plant-related freaks, but I'm not so inclined to comment on them especially if you're using this review to decide whether or not to buy the game. The other mechanical aspect I think it excels at is difficulty - variable enemy HP, limited inventory and some of the most deliberately sparse yet never unfair ammo distribution I've ever seen makes A and especially the B run a deeply engaging test of risk assessment and decision making many games aren't even comparable to. This game will give you grey hair at times and make you think you're softlocked into a situation you can't get out of, but there's always a way.

In the end, it's just all positive all the way down. The mechanics are genius, the world is gorgeous and well-realized, and the A and B run manage to differ in fun and significant ways that really play on the familiarity you think you'll have after your first run. Which is nice, because I honestly wouldn't have even minded playing basically the same game twice. It's a masterpiece, baby.
