Resident Evil 2 Remake - A Masterpiece of Survival Horror

Having completed Resident Evil 2 Remake on PS4 when it first released in 2019, I found myself coming back for more on Steam. Yes, I had to repurchase it, but it was absolutely worth it. This is a game that perfectly blends the nostalgia of the original with modern advancements, and the result is a survival horror experience that stands as one of the best in recent years.

Let’s start with the pacing. It’s perfectly executed. The game balances exploration, puzzle-solving, and combat in a way that keeps you engaged from start to finish. The sense of dread is palpable, but the game never feels like it’s dragging. There’s always just enough tension to keep you on edge, but never so much that it feels overwhelming. When things do kick into high gear, the action ramps up without ever feeling forced, and the game knows exactly when to slow down and let you breathe before throwing you back into the fire.

The art style is another standout. The level of detail in every environment is impressive, with the police station, sewers, and other locations all feeling incredibly immersive. The lighting and shadows create a tense atmosphere, and the character models, particularly the zombies, are disturbingly well done. The realism is striking, and the visual design enhances the sense of immersion, drawing you into the horrifying world of Raccoon City.

Staying true to the original is a key achievement of this remake. The core story and gameplay remain intact, which will appeal to fans of the original Resident Evil 2. The puzzles, enemy encounters, and character interactions are all still there, but they’ve been enhanced to provide a more polished experience. Whether you’re a returning fan or a newcomer, the game does an excellent job of keeping the spirit of the original while offering a fresh and visually stunning experience.

As for the technical side of things, the game runs smoothly on PC, with beautiful textures and lighting that make the world feel alive, even in the most horrifying moments. The controls are intuitive and responsive, and the upgrades to the inventory and map systems make navigating the game world much more user-friendly without sacrificing the challenge.

In summary, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a perfect example of how to modernize a classic without losing what made it great. Its pacing, attention to detail, and faithfulness to the original make it a must-play for fans of the franchise and newcomers alike. If you’ve played it before, it’s worth revisiting, especially on PC where the visual and performance upgrades elevate the experience.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is a masterclass in survival horror, and I have no hesitation in recommending it to anyone looking for a gripping, well-crafted game that still respects the past while looking forward to the future.

- You have no ability to dodge. There is no dodge button, the best attempt you have is running around clumsily.
- Locking the player in with invincible enemies that stalk you forever. Very frustrating, albeit scary for those who enjoy a frustrating kind of fear.

+ It's not a terrible game, but unless you are a diehard nostalgic / Resident Evil franchise fan, I actually would not recommend this game.

The Resident Evil 2 remake breathes fresh air into the Resident Evil universe, providing a modern game experience to be enjoyed by new and old Reident Evil fans alike. While some things, such as sections in the sewers and giant spiders are missing from this remake, the game does its best to stay true to the original while also changing just enough to keep it fresh for those who've played the original. It also improves the interactions with various side characters such as Marvin and Ben. 
One major gameplay improvement is Mr. X, in the original you only encountered Mr. X in the B scenario, so for anyone who wasn't expecting it, it was quite the shock te see him lift the helicopter in the hallway of the first playthrough scenario. Mr. X is also much more of a stalker enemey in this game, in the original he appeared in scripted areas, but in the remake he searches the RPD for the player and even listens for the sound of bullets while tracking them down, not to mention the music and stomping sound of his steps when he finds you are terrifying everytime.
The extra modes are also fun and challenging, and provide interesting What If esque scenarios of Raccoon City citizens such as Kendo, Sheriff Cortini, and Katherine. In addition to Ghost Survivors there is also the iconic Tofu Survior from the original RE2.

Negatives: The impact of character choice doesn't matter much at all, in the original voices made in one playthrough could make the game easier or harder in the second, but that doesn't play out in the remake at all.
There should have been more interactions between Leon and Claire, but ultimately they have like three in the game, the beginning cutscene, the gate outside the helicopter crash site, and the end of the game.

Overall the Resident Evil 2 remake is a great remake that falls short in very few aspects, but improves on many more, it is not only a great remake but a great game that is a very fitting introduction to the Resident Evil universe for new fans.

If you’re new to the Resident Evil series, imagine a zombie apocalypse set in a small town where everyone’s a bit too into the whole "flesh-eating" thing. You play as either Leon, a rookie cop with zero survival instincts, or Claire, whose brother is missing. Both are trying to survive in a now-zombified Raccoon City.

You’ll spend most of your time solving puzzles (mostly involving keys and doors – don’t worry, it’s not *that* complex) while dodging zombies and trying to remember if you left that one health pack in the other room. It’s a delicate dance of managing ammo, healing items, and your sanity, because enemies don’t stay dead and your character moves like they’re stuck in molasses. 

Now, the combat is tougher than a brick wall. Ammo is scarce, enemies are fast, and headshots are *not* your magical solution to everything. They still take multiple shots to go down – how tough are these zombies?! The horror isn’t just in the monsters; it’s in trying to survive the *horrible* amount of healing items you’ll never find when you need them.

On the flip side, the game looks stunning. It’s like Resident Evil 7’s graphics had a baby with the original RE2 and it became the most atmospheric, dread-filled baby ever. You’ll explore tight corridors, get startled by every noise, and panic when a zombie bursts through a window.

In short: It’s a nightmare, but a *beautiful* one. It’ll frustrate you, challenge you, and make you question if you can handle even one more undead encounter. If you’re a fan of survival horror, this remake will push all the right buttons – even if it sometimes feels like you’re trapped in a zombie-filled nightmare with *no* healing items.

Resident Evil 2 Remake - A Masterpiece of Survival Horror 

Having completed Resident Evil 2 Remake on PS4 when it first released in 2019, I found myself coming back for more on Steam. Yes, I had to repurchase it, but it was absolutely worth it. This is a game that perfectly blends the nostalgia of the original with modern advancements, and the result is a survival horror experience that stands as one of the best in recent years.

Let’s start with the pacing. It’s perfectly executed. The game balances exploration, puzzle-solving, and combat in a way that keeps you engaged from start to finish. The sense of dread is palpable, but the game never feels like it’s dragging. There’s always just enough tension to keep you on edge, but never so much that it feels overwhelming. When things do kick into high gear, the action ramps up without ever feeling forced, and the game knows exactly when to slow down and let you breathe before throwing you back into the fire.

The art style is another standout. The level of detail in every environment is impressive, with the police station, sewers, and other locations all feeling incredibly immersive. The lighting and shadows create a tense atmosphere, and the character models, particularly the zombies, are disturbingly well done. The realism is striking, and the visual design enhances the sense of immersion, drawing you into the horrifying world of Raccoon City.

Staying true to the original is a key achievement of this remake. The core story and gameplay remain intact, which will appeal to fans of the original Resident Evil 2. The puzzles, enemy encounters, and character interactions are all still there, but they’ve been enhanced to provide a more polished experience. Whether you’re a returning fan or a newcomer, the game does an excellent job of keeping the spirit of the original while offering a fresh and visually stunning experience.

As for the technical side of things, the game runs smoothly on PC, with beautiful textures and lighting that make the world feel alive, even in the most horrifying moments. The controls are intuitive and responsive, and the upgrades to the inventory and map systems make navigating the game world much more user-friendly without sacrificing the challenge.

In summary, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a perfect example of how to modernize a classic without losing what made it great. Its pacing, attention to detail, and faithfulness to the original make it a must-play for fans of the franchise and newcomers alike. If you’ve played it before, it’s worth revisiting, especially on PC where the visual and performance upgrades elevate the experience.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is a masterclass in survival horror, and I have no hesitation in recommending it to anyone looking for a gripping, well-crafted game that still respects the past while looking forward to the future.

It does the best it can but it fails to capture the essence of the original. There are too many reasons why that is the case, but I'll give one example: the soundtrack. Part of the original game's genius was the masterwork soundtracks that greatly contributed to the tense and unsettling atmosphere. In RE2R there is virtually no soundtrack at all save for generic and ultimately forgettable ambient tracks. This small but important detail greatly dials back the atmospherics. Silence can be a useful tool in creating tension in the player, but only if it's used sparingly and timed right. On the music end, RE2R is practically silent the entire game, so any tension created by it quickly fades and you're left with a reduced horror experience.

If you've never played the original you will probably be impressed by this game because you will have nothing to compare it to. If you're like me and have played the original through multiple times and have an understanding of what made it a great game, you will likely be disappointed with RE2R.

As someone who had never played any Resident Evil games before, I wasn’t sure what to expect going into Resident Evil 2 Remake, but I was blown away by how quickly it drew me in. This game is a fantastic introduction to the Resident Evil franchise.

The first thing that grabbed my attention was the atmosphere. The game’s visuals are absolutely stunning, Raccoon City feels dark and gritty. The lighting, the detailed environments, and the eerie sound design all come together to create an intense atmosphere where you never feel safe. From the abandoned police station to the zombie-infested streets.

The survival horror elements are incredibly well done. The game doesn’t just throw endless waves of enemies at you, ammo is limited, and every bullet feels precious. 

The game does a fantastic job of making you feel vulnerable and constantly worried about what’s lurking around the next corner. Also loved the balance between exploration, puzzle-solving, and combat. The police station itself is like a giant twisted maze. I spent a lot of time searching for keys, solving puzzles, and trying to figure out where to go next, all while trying to avoid being overwhelmed by zombies. Every room felt like a mini puzzle to figure out, and that kept the game feeling fresh and engaging.

Even though Resident Evil 2 Remake is a remake of a classic, I never felt lost as a newcomer. The story is easy to follow, and the two main characters; Leon and Claire are likeable and relatable. The voice acting and motion capture work make them feel real, and I found myself genuinely invested in their fates. Plus, the story is packed with twists, so I was always curious to see what would happen next.

One thing I didn’t expect was how emotional the game could be. While it's scary, it’s also very immersive. The characters, the situation, and the environment all drew me in emotionally. You get attached to the characters quickly, and the moments where you're trying to help or save others really hit hard.

For someone like me, who had never touched a Resident Evil game before, Resident Evil 2 Remake was the perfect entry point into the series. It blends survival horror with action and exploration perfectly, and I found myself absolutely hooked.

Graphics & Atmosphere

Using the RE Engine, Resident Evil 2 delivers photorealistic environments, detailed character models, and stunning lighting effects that enhance the horror experience. The dark, claustrophobic hallways of the Raccoon City Police Department (RPD) look more terrifying than ever, and the real-time lighting and shadows add to the tension.

Gore and zombie damage are incredibly detailed, making combat feel visceral. Watching a zombie’s flesh decay in real-time as you shoot adds an extra layer of horror.

Pros:
✔ Gorgeous visuals with realistic lighting.
✔ Atmospheric and terrifying environments.
✔ Detailed zombie damage mechanics.

Cons:
✖ Some occasional texture pop-ins.
✖ Certain areas feel slightly underutilized.


---

Gameplay & Combat

Capcom has replaced the original’s fixed-camera angles and tank controls with a modern over-the-shoulder third-person perspective, similar to Resident Evil 4. This makes combat more immersive and intense, as zombies are unpredictable, resilient, and hard to put down.

Resource management is crucial—ammo is limited, forcing players to think carefully before shooting. The puzzle-solving elements remain faithful to the original, providing a perfect balance of action and survival horror.

Pros:
✔ Smooth and responsive controls.
✔ Zombies are truly terrifying and hard to kill.
✔ Classic puzzles return, adding depth to the gameplay.

Cons:
✖ Some enemy animations can feel slightly clunky.
✖ Inventory management can be frustrating for new players.


---

Story & Replayability

Players can experience the intertwined campaigns of Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield, each offering different perspectives on the outbreak. The "2nd Run" mode changes enemy placements and puzzle solutions, encouraging replayability.

Additionally, the Mr. X (Tyrant) mechanic keeps players on edge—his relentless pursuit is one of the most terrifying aspects of the game.

Pros:
✔ Well-told, engaging horror story.
✔ Multiple campaigns with different perspectives.
✔ Mr. X adds constant tension and unpredictability.

Cons:
✖ Some cutscenes feel slightly rushed.
✖ Story differences between campaigns aren’t as deep as expected.


---

Final Verdict – Is It Worth It?

Capcom has successfully modernized a survival horror masterpiece while staying true to the original’s spirit. With stunning visuals, intense gameplay, and horrifying atmosphere, Resident Evil 2 Remake is one of the best horror games ever made.

Final Score: 9/10
✔ Incredible visuals and atmosphere
✔ Terrifying, intense gameplay
✔ High replayability with multiple campaigns
✖ Some minor pacing issues
✖ Inventory management may frustrate some players

If you’re a fan of survival horror, this is a must-play!

[b]Resident Evil 2 Remake[/b] - the perfect revival of a classic.

[b]Capcom[/b] has managed to do the incredible - [b]Resident Evil 2 Remake[/b] doesn't just retell the story of the legendary 1998 horror, but reimagines it, keeping the spirit of the original and offering modern mechanics.

[h3]Atmosphere and visuals[/h3]
The first thing that strikes you is the incredible detail of the environments. The city of Raccoon City and the police station building are rendered with loving attention to detail: dilapidated corridors, shivering lights, pools of blood and shadows hiding the unknown create a sense of anxiety and fear. On the RE Engine, the game looks amazing - especially impressive are the lighting effects and realistic zombie animation.

[h3]Gameplay and Balance[/h3]
[b]Capcom[/b] carefully reworked the game's mechanics, replacing fixed cameras with a third-person view, but retained the survival feel. Limited resources force you to think through every expenditure of ammo and health kits, and the leisurely but tense pace keeps you in constant suspense. [b]Mr. X[/b], who now stalks the player in real time, adds to the game's horror and unpredictability.

[h3]Plot and Characters[/h3]
The story of [b]Leon Kennedy[/b] and [b]Claire Redfield[/b] is presented with new details and excellent acting. The characters are livelier, their motivations are better developed than in the original, and dialog is more natural. The game's two scenarios still offer a different perspective on the events, making the playthrough more variable.

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
[b]Resident Evil 2 Remake[/b] is a reference remake that shows how to revive a classic. It combines a tense horror atmosphere, excellent graphics, elaborate gameplay and an engaging story. It's not just a game for fans of the series - it's one of the best horror games of the decade.

[h3]Total Score: 9.5 / 10[/h3]

This is an exceedingly fun game! I've never played a [i]Resident Evil[/i] title before but after this, I am sorely tempted to give at least the next Leon Kennedy entry a try!

I think my favorite part is the earnest and involved attempt to reproduce RE's *goofiness*. It's a tone that I haven't seen in any other game - and if I did, I'd just think they're riffing of [i]Resident Evil[/i]: the late '90s aesthetic, the combination of horrible photorealistic monsters & zombies, an inkling of slapstick abuse directed at its protagonists and the cheap-action-movie-script-passed-through-localization-translators quality of the dialogue. I would call it a relative of Hideo Kojima's writing style, but very distinct and stand-alone. I streamed this game for my friend and we had amazing fun laughing with what is, ostensibly, a horror game. I must stress: the tone is intentional. The developers know what they're doing here, recreating the inherent silliness of early games in a very high-fidelity context. I had a blast playing this game,really captured the horror and survival horror element,especially on my first playthrough.

Pros:
+ Having two different characters with different story perspectives adds SOME depth (as this feature is also one of the game's biggest weaknesses). Player can only reach true ending after playing the game on both characters, which is a great design choice. One simply doesn't get the full experience without playing both Claire and Leon.
+ Pretty graphics. The game allows for a neatly realistic outlook.
+ The game allows to greatly customize video and graphical settings
+ Great music. It's fitting and builds ambiance and immersion in the story and world.
+ Great attention to detail. The environments feel lived. Items are lying around as in real life. The environments feel just as you'd expect them to be after a zombie outbreak. Everywhere you go it's obvious that chaos rules now.
+ Nice blend of action and survival horror. Effective combat requires landing headshots and conserving ammo and other items. Ever since [spoiler] encountering The Tyrant [/spoiler], the game felt only more horror-leaning. The feeling of being unsafe works wonders when you traverse the environment, solve puzzles and shoot zombies. 
+ Exploration is rewarded with different items and upgrades and clues on how to obtain them.
+ Inventory management system is good. The more you solve puzzles, the more you can carry.
+ Both Claire and Leon have a decent set of guns they can use.
+ Expanding the arsenal feels rewarding. Different guns have their own uses. The game gives you an option to try grenade-firearm combos and use guns pretty freely. It seems you can deal with all enemies and bosses with all the weapons, even if they all have their own strengths. In the end, I didn't feel like any single gun was totally useless.
+ The story progresses fairly well, remaining interesting and entertaining for the whole game. Claire's objective to [spoiler] find Chris Redfield turns into survival against zombies, which later turns into an attempt to save Sherry. When you think you've saved her, you realize you're not done. You keep going on, and the story turns into an escape attempt [/spoiler]. While the story progresses, more is revealed about the world. A few new characters are also introduced fairly well. They have their own working role in the plot. As for Leon, his story [spoiler] goes from getting to the police station to survival and getting out, which turns into working with Ada, which turns into ending what started the outbreak, which turns into an escape attempt [/spoiler].
+ There's a bit running back and forth, but it's not painful. More so, it forces you put yourself in danger again and again.
+ Great voice acting. Claire and Leon react to the world around them during combat situations, for example.
+ Examining items has a function in creating immersion (although it's obviously not the main one).
+ I mostly liked the main boss design, and how it evolves throughout the story. 

Cons:
- The last chapter could've used a bit more of attention to detail (despite it's theme) - I feel like a bit more attention to detail was put in the other two chapters, especially the first.
- I'm not sure if it's just medium difficulty, but a part of me wished [spoiler] The Tyrant [/spoiler] could've also invaded your save rooms. It would've only increased the stress. Yes, it's a way to get to safety, but it also kind of turns the cat-and-mouse thing into a waiting game. It would've been even better if [spoiler] The Tyrant [/spoiler] could break open save room doors etc. and let zombies in.
- The game is a bit too short. I was hoping for a bit longer experience despite the fact that playing both Claire and Leon is obviously recommended. One more 'chapter' would've been a nice addition in my opinion.
- I wish there'd be a bit more to the boss's design - attacks, body changes etc..
- Playing the '2nd playthrough' mode is a nice idea. However, I wished there'd be more new areas and puzzles. It mostly felt like running through the game again but with some small tweaks to make it a bit faster. You have mostly same puzzles, objectives, environments and boss fights. Storywise it doesn't make any sense - on your first playthrough Leon/Claire solves certain puzzles and fights bosses, and then on the second playthrough the other character literally does almost everything same. Playing '2nd playthrough' mode felt like my first playthrough didn't matter. The 2nd playthrough should literally show the effects of Leon/Claire's actions from the other characters perspective (or even better, have you do something that impacts Leon/Claire in your first playthrough - this way you'd better see the two sides of the story).
- Characters can't run, but only jog. It's ridiculous that you can't run when trying to evade a massive zombie monster's attacks. There's not even a dodge ability. I died rather many times during bosses because of this - the mechanics were always easy, but for some reason Claire and Leon aren't fit enough to do a bit of running despite the fact that both can carry several firearms simultaneously....smh.

---
All in all, Resident Evil 2 is a really good game. It felt tedious once or twice when I ran around fetching some objects to complete puzzles, but other than that, it was a smooth, nicely flowing, enjoyable ride - so much so that I played my second playthrough almost right after the first. Immersion was great. Combat was fun and engaging. Puzzles were a tad bit too easy. Characters were interesting and had their own respective roles in the plot (even better that playing on both Claire and Leon allows you to see a different side to one of the major characters).

8/10 A great gaming experience. Does well what it sets out to do. Keeps player engaged for the whole ride. For the price of 7.5 EUR, this game was an absolute steal. However, I cannot give this game more than 8 just because it heavily encourages the player to do another playthrough on the other character, but the story on 2nd playthrough is just such a damn let down - the actions of Claire /Leon on your first playthrough should be visible, but NONE of them are. I view 2nd playthrough as a major part of the whole experience, and I was oftentimes disappointed by the puzzles, same environments and redoing everything as I did on the first run. The 2nd playthrough should feel like an EXTENSION of the first one, but sadly, it basically never does.

This is real survival horror, where it always seems like you’re just barely scraping by. Leon and Claire take extremely similar paths. Here's a quick review of my thoughts after beating "Resident Evil 2 (Remake)" on the PC.

+- Graphics are downright beautiful. Great lightning, textures, effects, and the works. The only issue I have is that there were so many times when the quality of textures would shift to all over the place. Suddenly, I’d zoom in on a puzzle and the wall would just change to a more high-res texture after a second. It looked really unnatural. Plus, there are some assets in this game that are extremely low quality. I was in the basement area and found a pipe attached to the wall that was so low-res, it looked like it was from a GameCube game. Luckily though, these distractions never hindered the gameplay, so there’s that.
+- Puzzles are a mixed bag. Not one of them were really great. There’s actually not a lot of puzzles in this game now that I think about it. So many require a ridiculous amount of backtracking to get them done. Half the time, it was worth it and I do enjoy the feeling of working the mental cogs to solve these puzzles. Though, if I could choose one major issue with the puzzles, it would be the backtracking. There’s just way too much of it in the game. And not the good backtracking like most Metroid games have. In this game, it’s just running through empty hallways and areas to get to a place on the opposite side of the map.
+- Overall scariness is pretty lackluster. I wouldn’t really qualify this as a horror game, per say. There’s no freakiness, no really scary enemies, no really scary areas, and nothing that suddenly jumped at you. The best horror game I ever played in terms of scariness was the Dead Space remake, and the RE2 remake doesn’t even touch the level of scariness that that game has.
+- The over-the-shoulder camera gets the job done most of the time. But when it comes to fighting hordes of enemies, there is a clear lack of awareness of enemy placement. Perhaps you could say this is part of the horror aspect, but it doesn’t work when you know you’re surrounded by zombies but you only get an upper torso level camera perspective of Leon or Clarie when you are fighting them off. Comes off as more annoying and frustrating than scary when I get bitten by a crawling zombie behind me that I couldn’t see because I was fighting the two in front of me.
- Story is dumb. You have no idea what is going on for the majority of it. So much of the dialogue feels padded and stupid like it’s a 6-year-old’s idea of what adults sound like. Things just happen because they happen with no real point to them. Ending just showed up with no real feeling of accomplishment because you never knew what you were trying to accomplish. Not a good story. The first RE game was simple: just get out of the mansion. The plot of RE2 changes every 2 hours: find the police station, escape the police station, find the sewers, escape the sewers, find the lab, escape the lab, THAT’S THE GAME, FOLKS!!! Just felt like there was no heart to it. It sucks because there was a real emotional, sad moment in this game, but then it’s completely brushed off to continue the trek back into the dreck. Really empty and laughably bad story.
- Enemies are literal bullet sponges. Even the most basic of zombies can take up to seven bullets to kill. Seven! And they were even all headshots! The Lickers are even worse because they take more bullets to kill, plus can practically kill you in two hits. The big sewer baddies took what felt like 50 bullets to kill, plus you can’t sneak past them. I hate all of this game’s enemies. Literally all of them. Plus, none of them were scary compared to how annoying they were to deal with. Half because of the camera and the other half because you’ve used up a good third of your ammo killing two zombies… oops, and they’re not dead yet.
- Just like the enemies, Mr. X is more annoying to deal with than scary. Plus, he makes traversal 5x worse so there’s that. Luckily, he only shows up during the last 10% of when you’re in the police station. He’s not even in the sewers or labs and only appears during the escape sequence in the basement. I don’t know why he’s even in the game at all. Doesn’t add anything to it.
- As much as I hate Mr. X and the enemies in this game, the worst offenders are the bosses. All the boss fights with G and Mr. X are like if you put a snail in a bowl with a frog (oh, and you’re the snail). Your pathetically slow moment and damage output makes fighting these guys, conservatively speaking, absolutely utterly and completely retarded. The second boss fight with G is the worst one though because of the ridiculously tiny area (more like a ledge) you are put in to face him. I hate, just hate every boss in this game.
- Speaking of retarded moments, this game has its fair share of them outside of boss battles too (as if this game couldn’t get any worse). The most predominant ones are fighting enemies or trying to get past them in small areas, getting ganged up on, and always having barely any room for items.
- You can’t change the game difficulty for a file you’re in. Oh, wait. Yes, you can. The only way to do so is to die three times in a row, then the game will be gracious enough to ask you if you want to permanently change to the lowest difficulty. Do I have to explain why this is dumb, or is everyone here smart enough to realize why this is dumb? I hope the latter.
- All the bonus story modes are just “run through zombie infested areas”, that’s it. Really, really uncreative. Don’t know why these were included or even made in the first place.
- Really dumb changes to how the original game was. The most obvious ones were the lack of the spider enemies, the alligator boss fight was changed to a running sequence (just… why?), you can’t crush zombie heads with your foot, and the knife breaks now. Housten, I think we’ve lost our minds.

At first, when this Remake came out, I was stunned. I couldn't believe it. Capcom made a remake of RE2, and it's actually good???? What????? This is the same company that produced RE6 and the two Revelations games... how did we get here???

Well, some time has passed, and I have lowered my fondness of this game. In hindsight, a lot of this game is just... meh. Like it works. It's a solid game, but as a Remake of RE2... man... there is a lot of missed opportunities and just flat-out missing content. 

Gameplay-wise, it's fine. Normal RE gameplay of get from A to B, unlock door with item, find new item, unlock another door, yada yada yada. Evade enemies in the process and pepper bosses with the weapons you find. It works for what it is. 

But, despite its graphical fidelity, the original RE2 still holds up fairly well. As a game, there's just more to it. The Zapping system with Leon and Claire having both characters play fairly distinct campaigns two times and Extreme Battle Mode in particular. 

The 2nd Scenario system in this Remake is a half-assed attempt at trying to replicate that Zapping system. I don't know. To me, do it right, or don't do it all. 

And Extreme Battle Mode is completely missing which is mind-blowing given this game's third-person-perspective. Hell, it would be a much better fit in a game like this than in the original. Instead, we got Ghost Survivors. Well, did you like Hunk's 4th Survivor mode? Well how about playing it an additional three times with characters you don't care about? Sounds fun, huh? Or how about playing as the NPC Sheriff in the beginning of the game in a pseudo-Mercenaries-style survival mode? Again, Capcom, you had Extreme Battle Mode - just use that. It was fine. 

Ugh. Just disappointing. Missed opportunities abound. 

As for changes in the story from the original, eh... most of them are okay. 
I like Claire's entrance a bit more - it makes a little more sense that she would stop at a gas station outside the city and then be greeted with the horrific reality of what Raccoon City has become instead of like in the original where she made it all the way into the city and then got her first glimpse of the apocalypse. 
Leon on the other hand... I feel his introduction is a bit nonsensical. The game has it that he "got a call to stay away," well... does Leon not live in the city where his job is? What was he doing on the outskirts? You'd think if it was his first day on the job, the police would be throwing him at all sorts of tasks. The original made a tad more sense where he was just driving in his jeep around the city already on patrol and came across a body in the street. 

So, little things like that are peppered throughout this Remake. Like Marvin's introduction for instance - way better in the original. He actually gives a better clue to the player as to what the hell is going on:
 
"About two months ago, there was this incident involving zombies" - directly referencing the events of the first game. 

Here, Marvin replies to the player asking "Does anybody know what caused this?" with "Not a clue."

Are you kidding me? The STARS team gets almost completely wiped out and Marvin doesn't know a single thing about that? It feels rushed. Like this game was kinda "speedrun-developed" if that makes sense. Like Capcom was like "Guys, let's see how fast we can churn out a competent retelling of the RE2 events." 

And the voice-acting... oh boy. I don't what's going on with Capcom and their casting department, but they are having a hard time. In this game in particular, I'd say most actors are fine, but I really REALLY R E A L L Y do not like Leon's VA. Nothing against the guy personally, but as a replacement for Paul Haddad... no. This guy just ain't Leon. They could have used Paul Mercier or Matthew Mercer, and I don't know what shenanigans is preventing them from doing so, but they would be vastly preferred. Same sort of story with their other RE games. Get Roger Craig Smith back as Chris for Christ's sake. C'mon. And what about TJ Rotolo for the Dead Rising Remaster? You honestly couldn't grab him for that? What is happening at the casting department in Capcom??? I mean hell, did you guys see that trailer of the new Onimusha game? Good Lord. Are good VAs hard to find or something? 

But back to RE2: as a Remake of RE2, I feel this game misses a lot. It feels like it was pushed out to meet a deadline more so than to be a legitimate Remake of RE2. Oh sure, most of the elements are here, but the charm isn't. If all you wanted was just Leon and Claire going through the RPD but as a third-person-shooter, you might really like this game. Personally, I wanted RE2, but all of it: every aspect of it and made better. 
I don't know. Call me crazy, but if you're gonna remake a good game, do it right. 
Y'know. Don't take away what was good and don't add bad ideas.
And maybe try playing some of your own games before attempting to remake them. I swear, with the cuts in content and changes to story, it legitimately feels like the development director either hasn't played the original game or just watched some clips of it or maybe just played a few minutes of it and watched someone else play the rest. Capcom can't quite seem to find the right balance with this if the other Remakes are any indication.

The best Resident Evil ever made!
This game had everything I wanted: intense horror moments that make you worry and feel genuinely uneasy; shootouts with zombies and bosses that never became repetitive and always caught me off guard, making me want to engage rather than avoid them.

The puzzles weren’t too difficult, but their number and placement were perfect. Each one pulled me in as I tried to figure it out. The story is captivating and never feels ridiculous—on the contrary, it’s interesting and absolutely mesmerizing.

And what can I say about the Tyrant? Every time he appeared, the sound of his heavy steps gave me chills. His pursuit through the station kept me on edge the entire time. With every encounter, I wanted more and more to finally overcome him, especially since he always managed to track me down.

The atmosphere is phenomenal: the sense of danger, the constant uncertainty about what lies ahead, the tension and intrigue—they stay with you throughout the entire playthrough. The game is also special because it sets the stage for everything that comes later in the series.

So, what can I say overall? This game is perfect for anyone who enjoyed other Resident Evil titles—here you’ll find everything the previous entries might have lacked. The story, the gameplay—everything looks and feels top-notch and is absolutely worth the money.

More than twenty five years after the original Resident Evil 2, Capcom have surpassed themselves and shown how a remake is done right. RE2 Remake is a reimagining of the original yet expands on gameplay and visuals, all the while trying to maintain the core elements and stay true to its predecessor. Players return to the haunting Raccoon City, and can control either Leon or Claire in separate, yet converging, campaigns. The T-virus has spread throughout the city and once normal people are turning to zombies or even worse creatures. Both protagonists arrive in the city on the same day and are trying to piece together what is transpiring and how the evil Umbrella Corporation fits into it all. The game is filled with action and a lot of tense moments. One of the main antagonists is Mr. X, a towering and terrifying creature who will relentlessly pursue us throughout many parts of the game. He can be slowed down but not stopped, and hearing his thunderous footsteps as he approaches truly adds a level of tension and dread. 

While the original had fixed camera angles, RE2 Remake has an over-the-shoulder view, modernizing the gameplay. The combat is engaging, and the game also focuses on survival and puzzle elements. Players need to explore their surroundings and find ammo and equipment to survive. Visually this game has been completely overhauled and improved thanks to the RE Engine. Player and zombie models are superb and highly detailed. The lighting and shadows create a quintessential survival horror atmosphere. Notable environmental highlights are the police station, sewers and lab. The voice acting is solid and compelling. Sound work such as the moans and groans of zombies as well as the aforementioned Mr. X's footsteps truly make this a harrowing experience. The game also ships with DLC that adds more content with different scenarios and challenges. 

Resident Evil 2 Remake is one of the most impressive remakes I have ever played and Capcom has provided a prime example on how to modernize and improve on a classic while not losing its main essense. The Resident Evil series pioneered the survival horror genre and if this, and future remakes, are anything to go by, it will remain one of the best.

I've already played the snot out of this game after first experiencing it a few months ago, and I will continue to do so. It is currently my favorite Resident Evil (currently in the process of playing through the series), so I figure it's about time I leave a review.

In my opinion, the older RE games perfectly embody Survival Horror. A limited number of resources and limited inventory, requiring you to think carefully about how to proceed. Narrow corridors and confined spaces, making confrontations inevitable with the otherwise non-threatening shambling corpses. A constant tension while you try to survive through both atmospheric elements (ambient music and graphic style) and gameplay ones (the aforementioned examples, plus fear of the unknown; being unable to tell what enemies might be hiding around the next corner, and the worry of an area that you previously cleared out no longer being safe). And in some cases, a constant threat hounding you that you have no hope of eliminating, and you have no choice but to avoid. These factors offer so much more to horror than any number of cheap jump-scares and other tactics can offer. Resident Evil 2 Remake may not play in the style of the old RE games, but it still manages to retain all of the above factors, and even enhances some of them.

A playthrough will typically only take you a few hours to complete (less if you're very familiar with the game), but there's still a lot to offer here. Both playable characters have significant differences in their experiences at the Raccoon City Police Department, from the weapons available to them to the different areas they explore. Further, even more changes are present in a 2nd run, offering a total of four different ways you can play through the game. There are also three different difficulties and a ranking system (largely based on time to completion) as well as incentive to play them, which altogether makes this game extremely replayable. And I'm still not finished; there are a variety of shorter scenarios (10-20 minutes each) you can play through, each offering their own challenges and rewards. To top it all off, if you still want more out of the game like I did (and still do), RE(dot)net offers weekly challenges for both the main game and one of the side modes.

I feel like I can't accurately describe exactly why I find this game to be such a fun and quality experience to the point that I've replayed it at least 20 times now. But I highly recommend playing this masterpiece. Be warned though; the greatest horror in the game is found early on. If you don't want to be scarred for life, don't look at the gas prices!

I have always been a huge fan of Resident Evil since elementary school. My excitement skyrocketed when the RE 2 Remake was released in 2019, but I didn't have a console or PC to play it. Watching YouTube videos about it felt so good, and then, after six years, my dad bought me a Lenovo LOQ for my college needs. After finishing S+ on Standard and Hardcore of both L and C, and 3 outta 4 mini-games (aka Ghost Survivors), I would like to rewrite a review for Resident Evil 2 Remake.

    The process of learning this game was not exactly a "fun" experience. It lacks too many documents for the player to read and pick up many techniques. The whole RE series is well known for its limited backpack space, scarce resource on higher difficulty, leading to the thing known as "resource management" in a "horror game", RE2 no exception. These led me to give it a "no" in the past.

    Yet, when players pay enough attention to the locations of resources in map, they will notice that these locations are engineered deliberately and delicately. If the player can plan well, in many cases, certain resource placements, e.g. a grenade or flame rounds, are here for immediate pick-up-and-consume to clean up (or stun) hostiles nearby; lickers, one of the only two non-human zombie types, have special weakness that can be exploited on Hardcore, making wiping out easily manageable. Boss fights are NOT difficult at all even on Hardcore, if but also ONLY IF one knows how to exploit the Boss weakness and punish them accordingly, which won't take much to find out if one is willing to retry a few times with various ammo types.

    Mini-games follow roughly the same logic as above; I never beat Hunk or No Way Out as I lost interest at that point, but the other three Ghost Survivors have their level structure in terms of resource placements and works fine, I can finish the three without damage if I pay attention.

    And meta-wise, it is a loyal reconstruction of the original game, rebuilding and improving the gameplay experience (unlike RE3 in which a major part of the original is discarded), and being released in 2019, a relatively newer era, it offers nice graphics and has RT implant, which doesn't make a real difference though, as RT back then was a too young technology with efficiency and realization problems, more or less still so today in 2026.

    It's fine, I guess. I will call it finished for me, and might never really visit it again (at 77h) though.

This game is great, it has some decent puzzles, and very suspenseful setting. The music and art direction are top notch. However, there are several annoyances that really REALLY get on my nerves by the second playthrough. 

The enemies are bullet sponges, and while the game does give you plenty of ammo to deal with them, it is still tedious to play. It can be a bit frustrating when after sending ten rounds of ammo into a random zombie's head, you still get grabbed and injured.

Mr X is also a pretty annoying gimmick. I am not a fan of stalker enemies in games and never have been. The first playthrough he's alright, he appears about halfway through the police station and by the time you start figuring out how to avoid him, it's almost time to move on from the police station. However he reappears sooner in the second playthrough, after having already  worn out his welcome before the first playthrough is over. The second playthrough, after you already have him figured out, he isn't difficult to avoid, just annoying, he's just there to waste your time and show up just as you're about to finish a puzzle so you can move on and force you to run around or go back to the safe room and wait for him to give up the chase. I think his gimmick would have worked better if he had been introduced in the second playthrough and not the first.

My final issue is the controls can be a little clunky and unpolished feeling, more than a few times i had Claire and Leon stick on the inside of doors, and some of the enemy attack hit boxes can make this very annoying to deal with.

All that said, the game has atmosphere in droves, and by the end of the game a lot of the complaints I have are gone anyway, as you get more powerful weapons and leave the police station. I definitely recommend this game for someone who WANTS to like resident evil, and wants an older RE game experience, but can't get into the older RE games due to old control schemes and such. It's a pretty fantastic game all annoyances aside and I definitely enjoyed my time with it.

I can’t say that Resident Evil 2 offers anything entirely new for the survival horror genre. The goal of the game is to give you a classic, time-tested story of survival in a world where every step could be your last. Zombie apocalypse, narrow corridors, limited resources, constant tension—these are all familiar elements to fans of the genre. But! And this "but" is significant, substantial, and definitely worth mentioning.

The game is executed at the highest level. This is a remake that doesn’t just retell the old story—it does so in a way that completely immerses you in the terror and chaos of Raccoon City. Realistic graphics, meticulous attention to detail, spine-chilling sound design, and an incredible atmosphere all make every moment of the game genuinely engaging.

The gameplay is perfectly balanced: simple mechanics that never feel boring and a level of difficulty that keeps you on edge. Solving puzzles, conserving ammunition, running from tyrants and zombies—every action in the game forces you to think ahead.

This is a high-quality survival horror, where every detail is crafted with love for the original and respect for the fans. It’s perfect for those looking to spend an evening in a constant state of tension and fear, challenging their nerves.

[list]

[h3]Highlights[/h3]  
[list]  
[*][b]Mr. X:[/b] The Radiant Reyna of Raccoon City. Struts around like he owns the place, pre-fires corners, and doesn’t care about your eco round.  
[*][b]Zombies:[/b] They’re like Silver players—slow, clueless, but somehow still deadly when they swarm.  
[*][b]Inventory management:[/b] Feels like choosing between a Vandal and full armor with 3 credits left. You always pick wrong.  
[*][b]Sound design:[/b] Hearing Mr. X stomping is like hearing the spike plant in Valorant—pure dread, but now the spike is coming for [i]you[/i].

[list]  
[*]No skins for your guns.

[*]And worst of all, you can’t bunny hop to safety.  
[/list]

[list]  
[*][b]Shotgun > Operator.[/b]  
[*]Every encounter feels like clutching a 1v5.  
[*]Zombies don’t flame you for your aim.  
[/list]  

[b]Verdict:[/b] If you’re okay with eco rounds every game and running from a living tank, RE2 is the perfect training for when Valve adds zombies to CS:GO.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is the pinnacle of survival horror, a brilliant reimagining of the 1998 classic that combines cutting-edge technology, an immersive narrative, and the tense gameplay that made the series famous! 
It’s not just a remake, it’s a masterclass in how to update a beloved game while staying true to its roots.
As a long-time Resident Evil fan, this version stands out as the best and my favorite release in the entire series. 
The game brings Raccoon City to life in stunning detail, with photorealistic visuals that amplify the terrifying atmosphere. 
The streets, the police station, and the sewers all feel alive, every shadow, every flicker of light adds to the horror. 
The decision to use an over-the-shoulder camera rather than the fixed angles of the original, injects a fresh intensity, drawing you into every narrow hallway and giving you a closer, more personal view of the terror around you...
The gameplay is a perfect blend of modern action and classic survival horror. 
The combat is visceral and impactful, with zombies that don’t just die easily, you have to manage your ammo and make each shot count. 
The puzzles are clever but not overly complicated, offering a satisfying sense of progression without slowing down the pace. 
The addition of modern mechanics, like quicker inventory management and smoother movement, makes it feel like a natural evolution of the series rather than a completely different experience.
The voice acting, motion capture, and character animations are top-notch, especially for Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield, who have never felt more human, with personalities and motivations that shine through. 
The voice direction and story pacing draw you deeper into their emotional journeys as they face the horrors of the outbreak.
Resident Evil 2 Remake also nails the balance between fan service and innovation. 
It stays faithful to the core story and environments, but it also introduces new elements, like expanded areas and more complex interactions with enemies, to keep even the most seasoned fans on edge. 
The upgraded A.I. of the enemies, the unpredictability of Mr. X’s pursuit, and the overall pacing make each encounter feel unique, tense, and rewarding.
For anyone who loves the Resident Evil series, this remake is a dream come true. 
It’s the perfect example of how to modernize a game while preserving the essence that made it so special in the first place.
This is the best Resident Evil game, period!

This is the contender for the best survival horror game in the modern era, with RE7 being it's only competition. These 2 games capture the essence of survival horror and narrative driven gameplay. I sat here and thought about why we enjoyed games from an earlier time period and I came to the conclusion that in modern games, any genre, the reward is items. From looter shooters to MMOs. 

But for games like this, the reward is the [b] story. [/b] I was eager to find out what happened next and why I was doing what I had to. In most games now, all you do is go from point a to point b, and get some convoluted story that you can't connect to, and kill random enemies. And speaking of kill, the combat mechanics reflect it. It's slow, you take time to line up your shots, and on top of that, if you miss with a grenade launcher you feel like restarting the game.

RE2 gives me a reason to traverse the world as well as interact with it. Should you waste ammo on a zombie or try your hardest to evade it? That choice, especially on higher difficulties is one that players have to make that makes you feel like survival is risk versus reward. With the newer RE games it's all action, [i] which isn't bad, [/i] but to me it isn't really survival horror. Kill everything in sight and be rewarded for it.

I legit came back to play this game (going to complete both stories again) and was continuing from an old save file. After realizing that when I killed an enemy he didn't drop any loot I quickly regretted saving so hastily. And it was so refreshing to know that my number of saves was limited on higher difficulties due to the ink ribbon requirements (which was replayed by no auto saves on higher difficulties, but it's just not the same).

I have always struggled with the Resident Evil Franchise, I have a love hate relationship with horror games generally, in that I love the setting and themes and aesthetics but struggle with jumpscares and the actual experience of anxiety and fear itself. Resident Evil has the added layer that all the remasters and games prior to this that I had tried had the same fixed camera angles and janky controls that they originally had. As such this has been a franchise I have always wanted to tackle but I have felt intimidated by for the reasons above and when I heard about the remakes at the time I dismissed them as being any different.

I can say that was a mistake and that this game pushes the franchise into the modern era of gaming with a great spectacle and an engaging experience, the gunplay is tight and the game looks great (as one would expect from a modern remaster). I will say now that the overall gameplay loop, the progression, the mix of puzzles and combat, the boss fights, overall I'd say they all make for a great game, which speaks to the legacy of the original game, I can understand why it's regarded so highly.

Before I go on further regarding the narrative and certain gripes I do have with the game I feel the need to explain my experience with the game. I started with the Leon Campaign, Whilst I found the plucky do-gooder cop angle somewhat grating it was something I came to accept (especially considering the original narrative was made in 1998). I really enjoyed the general progression of the game, I recall feeling so lost in the Police Station Initially and feeling unable to wrap my head around how to progress and achieve my goals. As I slowly came to understand the map and explore it piece by piece I started to feel my confidence grow, until Mr X was introduced and I went back to feeling utterly helpless and anxiously planning my routes in anticipation of his encounters completely terrified of being caught by him. By the time I made it to the sewers I had a grip on the gameplay and what to expect, however it would be kept fresh with the introduction of new enemies, the same applies to the lab with the inclusion of the boss battles.

This first playthrough was the best experience I had with the game and I could of happily left it there and would of likely had a higher impression of the game. That being said throughout the story we had been bumping into Claire and her seemingly different story and I was curious to playthrough as her to experience what I assumed to be an alternative campaign. What I found out is that rather than an alternate story this was more an alternate run of the same story a "re-imagining" if you will. Whilst certain events are different and the characters you interact with are different (Sherry and the Chief vs Ada and Annette) you're essentially playing the same game with slightly different cutscenes and different weapons.

Now Initially I didn't mind this, mastering the new weapons and discovering what was different proved enough of an initial challenge to keep me engaged. However I soon came to find issues some personal and some of the games doing, Firstly I much preferred Leon's weapon loadout to Claire's yes the launcher made lickers easy, however her revolvers are garbage and getting the laser pistol was great but it happens far too late into the story. I also found Claire's story much much more grating than Leon's but I will discuss this in detail later. lastly I came to find many of the sections I had simply seen as challenges to surmount before as frustrating or padding for the progression. That last point is not really true, however it's indicative of the issue of having the "dual" runs, any of the thrill, or suspense, or tension or really any sense of fear is completely drained upon a second playthrough. This is not to say that the game has no replay value, trying to master the games mechanics and explore anything you missed and trying to get the achievements are all engaging. However I did not start this new run with the expectation of this, I started it with the expectation of a different narrative and so pushing myself to replay the game after just finishing it for the sake of seeing what was different immediately after already finishing it did not make for a great experience. By the time I was in the sewer I was just going through the motions and doing what I could to finish the story hoping that something might surprise me, but besides an alternative final boss nothing did. I really think more could of been done by the game to explain the nature of these two runs, if I knew that it was essentially just an alternate run of the same game I wouldn't have rushed into it.

This leads me to the narrative of the game, which I can forgive to an extent given the dated nature of the game, many mainstream console games of the 90's opted for serviceable but lean stories, but there were some parts I found outright insufferable. Leon is a rookie cop on his first day at the precinct, he is naively moralistic and trusting, to a ridiculous degree but this does fit the outline of the character we have been given. We don't learn a great deal about him in depth but through his actions and his profession his actions generally make sense and form a believable story. Claire's story on the other hand is ridiculous to an extent where it grates on me personally, She comes to the city to find her brother only to find hell on earth. Now I can understand why she'd press on with Leon, she's strong independent and cares for her brother, but all she finds is a letter from Chris telling her he isn't there.... SO WHY DOES SHE CONTINUE TO GO ON??? The game solves this by shoehorning Sherry into the equation, which can serve as a motivation for her to not make sure she is put in harms way, but from here out Claire's story amounts to a suicidal mission to save a child she does not know from harm. I have more nitpicky details with certain choices but honestly I won't waste the time, I will just leave to by saying that ending with Claire was a way to really ruin my experience of the game.

I will make a small acknowledgement to the "extra modes" in the game, these are essentially time trials to traverse closed parts of the maps with more enemies than you typically see in the story. These are more akin to gameplay challenges, if you really enjoy the gameplay of the game I'd recommend them, but there is basically no additional story content here, As such they were not really my cup of tea.

To try and wrap this up and summarise my thoughts I am really glad that this game exists, It was great to finally get into the RE Franchise with updated controls and a modern over-the-shoulder camera. I really like the overarching story beats and gameplay experience, uncovering the mystery of the police station and the umbrella facility was engaging and enjoyable. If you’re into survival horror, Resident Evil 2 Remake is an absolute must-play. It’s not just a simple remaster; it’s a full-on remake that completely reimagines the 1998 classic while keeping the soul of the original intact.

What I Loved:
    •    Graphics & Atmosphere: The visuals are incredible. From the dimly lit hallways of the RPD to the disgusting, fleshy mutations of the monsters, everything feels gritty and real. The lighting and sound design alone can make you jump out of your seat.
    •    Gameplay: It’s a perfect mix of modern controls with that old-school survival horror vibe. Ammo is scarce, so every bullet counts, and the puzzles give you a real sense of accomplishment without being overwhelming.
    •    Mr. X: This guy is terrifying. The way he relentlessly stalks you throughout the police station is pure nightmare fuel. Hearing his footsteps in the distance is enough to make you panic.
    •    Story: Leon and Claire’s campaigns are engaging, and their perspectives give you a reason to replay the game. The characters feel more human this time, with great voice acting and more realistic dialogue.

What Could Be Better:
    •    The A/B scenario system isn’t as distinct as it was in the original, which might disappoint some old-school fans.
    •    If you’re new to survival horror, the difficulty might feel punishing at first.

Final Thoughts:

This remake sets the bar for how remakes should be done. It’s not just nostalgia—it’s a genuinely fantastic game that blends modern mechanics with the atmosphere of classic survival horror. Whether you’re a fan of the original or jumping in for the first time, Resident Evil 2 Remake is worth every second.

Great remake. I really liked it. I just didn't love it.

The pros :
- They absolutely nailed the atmosphere.
- The game looks gorgeous.
- The RPD is re-imagined fantastically. It feels familiar & fresh at the same time.
- The enemies & bosses are terrifying, particularly Mr. X.
- The puzzles are fun to solve.
- The combat is great. Shooting feels weighty and the guns are fun to use.
- Inventory management is way better than the original. It's basically the same as RE7.
- The sound design is great. The new OST is also fantastic.
- The re-writes of some characters from the original is a welcomed changed. I'm actually emotionally invested now.
- The performance is great across the board. Even for characters that only have a few lines.
- Plenty of extra modes to play after beating the game.

The cons :
(Most of these will be just me complaining about 2nd scenario, regardless of who you choose to play.)
- Continuation errors are plenty. Plot lines from 1st & 2nd scenarios just don't line up. This is especially annoying considering the original RE2 didn't have this problem. In fact, in the original, there are stuff that one character can do that will affect things for the other character. There's none of that in this remake. It's like both scenarios are alternate timelines of each other and yet the game never told us that.
- Uncreative way of reusing bosses. You just straight up fight the same bosses in the same places in both scenarios. So which one is canon???

At the beginning, I felt tempted to play because the graphics are amazing. Then I realized the game is very rich in horror—and it is.
The whole game is dark and has a macabre atmosphere, with blood on the floor and walls, broken windows and doors, storms, jump scares, and tight spaces.
In my first playthrough, I didn't find it too difficult to explore and complete the objectives. Basically, your map is very dynamic and shows if you’ve cleared 100% of a room or if there are still missed items. Because of this, it becomes easy to find and loot items.

In my opinion, the most difficult part of this game isn't getting lost while looking for mission items, but rather managing and saving weapon ammo. In some parts of the game, you’ll face a lot of enemies with very limited ammo. In your first playthrough, you’ll probably often find yourself running out of ammo or having very little left. On your second run, you’ll suffer because the game is sooooooooo miserable when it comes to ammo.

The character gameplay is good but not perfect. It’s very slow, and it’s hard to get past zombies without taking damage. In some scenarios, like the sewers, you’ll struggle a lot if you don’t have enough ammo. The story is pretty amazing—too bad Leon and Claire don’t interact much, unlike in the classic RE.

I understand that RE games don’t focus on combat or killing hordes of zombies. The main focus is survival, saving items and resources and using them at the right time. But, man... The fact that you need to spam bullets just to kill one zombie is frustrating. You save ammo the entire game, and then, when you have 60 bullets, you face three zombies, kill them, and suddenly you’re low on ammo again. I know this is part of the old RE experience, but if we could kill a zombie with seven headshots, fine. But two full clips? That’s just too much.

The boss fights, for me, are very good. They’re challenging, but after finishing the game two or three times, you’ll get the hang of it.

I really recommend this RE. The horror is amazing, and all the character models are incredible, whether it’s the survivors or the zombies. I’ve finished it three times, and it’s worth it.

[b]The Resident Evil 2 Remake is an extraordinary reimagining of the 1998 classic, bringing players back to Raccoon City with a perfect mix of nostalgia and modern enhancements. With updated graphics, refined gameplay mechanics, and a deep focus on storytelling, this remake is a masterclass in survival horror.[/b]

[h1]A Returning Classic[/h1]
[b]The game offers two intertwined perspectives, showcasing both Leon Kennedy's and Claire Redfield's struggles during the outbreak. Leon's journey highlights his transformation from a rookie cop to a hardened survivor, while Claire’s path focuses on her determination to protect Sherry Birkin, a child caught in the chaos. Both stories are well-developed, offering a sense of depth and emotional connection to the characters.[/b]

[h1]Engaging Multiple Perspective Gameplays[/h1]
[b]The addition of Ada Wong's segments brings a fresh layer of intrigue, as her espionage-themed gameplay contrasts perfectly with the survival horror. Similarly, the Ghost Survivors mode introduces side stories of other characters, exploring what-ifs and adding more replayability to the game.[/b]

[h1]Visuals and Atmosphere[/h1]
[b]Visually, the game is stunning, with the RE Engine delivering atmospheric lighting and grotesque enemy designs. Every encounter with zombies and the relentless Mr. X feels heart-stopping, thanks to impeccable sound design and dynamic music that heightens tension. Sometimes Mr. X comes out of nowhere and that is Scary AF.[/b]

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Faithful yet innovative retelling of a classic.
[*]Stunning visuals and terrifying atmosphere.
[*]Engaging dual-protagonist campaigns with meaningful storylines.
[*]Replayable content with Ghost Survivors mode.
[*]Intense and satisfying survival horror gameplay.
[/list]
[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Some puzzles may feel repetitive.
[*]Mr. X's relentless pursuit can be frustrating for some players.
[/list]
[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
[b]The Resident Evil 2 Remake is a love letter to fans of the original while being an excellent entry point for newcomers. It blends cinematic storytelling, gripping gameplay, and unforgettable moments, making it one of the best survival horror games in recent years. If you haven’t returned to Raccoon City yet, now is the perfect time.[/b]

Resident Evil 2 Remake – More Than Just a Game

Back in 2019, when the game first launched, I was just a kid. I didn’t have the money or means to play it myself, so like many others in my situation, I turned to YouTube. Watching gameplay videos became my version of playing. I still remember those late nights, eyes glued to the screen, completely immersed in the world of Raccoon City. That period didn’t just entertain me—it sparked something. A genuine passion and curiosity for this game and the Resident Evil universe as a whole.

Years later, I finally got my hands on a copy for Xbox One, and stepping into that world myself for the first time felt... surreal. I’ve now spent over 40 hours with the game across both Xbox and PC, and I’m not done. Resident Evil 2 is one of the very few games that actually made me want to replay it after finishing it—and not just once. I’ve tried different difficulties, aimed for S-ranks, explored every inch, solved every puzzle, and yes, I even started chasing that 100% completion like a proud completionist in the making.

What makes this game special isn’t just nostalgia—it’s how incredibly well-crafted it is. From the eerie silence in the RPD hallways to the panic when Mr. X casually decides to ruin your life (again), everything is executed with precision. The puzzles are satisfying and never too obscure, the map design is clever and encourages exploration, and the horror elements walk that perfect line between terrifying and thrilling. And let’s not forget the dual protagonists—Leon and Claire—each with their own perspective and route. It’s basically two campaigns in one game, with different story beats and unique areas to explore. That alone gives it incredible replay value.

The characters are easy to care about, the shooting mechanics are tight, and the storytelling is surprisingly emotional for a zombie-filled nightmare. Honestly, Resident Evil 2 Remake is comfort food for my gamer soul—yes, it’s terrifying comfort food, but still.

Now, years later, I proudly own the physical Collector’s Edition, RE-themed merch, a few figurines, and every mainline Resident Evil title. You could say the remake didn’t just impress me—it converted me into a full-on RE fan for life.

If you’re looking for a game that combines survival horror, tight gameplay, smart puzzles, and a story that pulls you in, this is it. Whether you’re new to the series or a longtime fan, Resident Evil 2 Remake delivers. It’s one of those rare titles that exceeds the hype and stays with you long after the credits roll.

For me, it’s easily in my top 10 best games of all time.

It's clear that this game was a labour of love from everyone involved - near perfection!

Having played through the original, I really enjoyed how the remake wasn't a 1:1 recreation, but instead remixed the level design, puzzles, and even some of the story beats. This keeps it fresh and interesting for the returning player. On the gameplay side, Capcom should be commended for preserving the original's loop of surviving horrible monstrosities and solving puzzles. With the puzzles, it feels like some of the fat has been trimmed for an even tighter, tenser experience. 

For newcomers and the modern player, the game is slightly more forgiving, with unlimited typewriter saves, checkpoints and craftable ammo (on normal difficulty). It never feels too easy, though, and I think Capcom struck a fine balance just right.

The re-imagined police station is gorgeous and the sewers feel much scarier. You actually feel like you are wading through ♥♥♥♥ - and it's great how you can see the grime build up on your character, too. Most of the original enemies return, and their re-designs are all faithful and terrifying. Seeing all the exposed vertebrae on the Licker is super nasty and cool. The new enemies are also great, especially in the last chapter of the campaign.

Special shout-out to the visuals and sound team. In addition to the designs mentioned above, I absolutely loved the lighting, gore and injury detail. The sound design is absolutely top-notch, from the guns to the zombies to the environments. Even running on wooden floors sounds great.

I must mention that the mod turns on and off when you press T, which I needed to use when I completed the library puzzle.
