Resident Evil 2 (2019) is not just a remake. It is a reawakening of what survival horror should be — a visceral, emotional journey through a world that feels alive with dread and loss. Capcom took everything that made the 1998 original a cornerstone of the genre and reimagined it with breathtaking realism and emotional depth. From the first moment you step into the Raccoon City Police Department as either Leon S. Kennedy or Claire Redfield, you’re not just playing a game; you’re entering a nightmare that is all too real, filled with grotesque creatures, overwhelming danger, and heartbreaking moments of human vulnerability. This is a game that tests not only your survival instincts but your humanity, forcing you to confront your deepest fears and your desire to protect others in the face of an apocalyptic nightmare.

At its core, Resident Evil 2 is about survival — not just surviving the monsters lurking in the shadows, but surviving the emotional toll of a city on the brink of total collapse. The atmosphere is oppressive, thick with a sense of dread that never lets up. As Leon, the rookie cop, or Claire, the determined young woman searching for her brother, you must navigate the chaos of Raccoon City after a viral outbreak has turned most of the population into flesh-eating zombies. But the terror is not just in the horde of undead; it’s in the unknown — the feeling that everything around you is falling apart, and that you’re alone in this fight.

The first thing that strikes you about Resident Evil 2 is how immersive it is. The world feels alive, even in its death. The detail in every corner, from the blood-splattered walls of the police station to the decaying remnants of a city on the brink of destruction, builds an oppressive, horrifying atmosphere. The lighting, too, is masterfully done: flickering fluorescent lights, dimly lit corridors, and the occasional flash of lightning outside the windows, all make you feel like you’re in a world on the brink of total collapse. Every hallway feels like a trap, every door could lead to safety or certain death. The claustrophobia of the environments feeds into the emotional weight of the game, constantly reminding you that you’re alone, that help is nowhere to be found, and that your survival is entirely in your hands.

But the real heart of Resident Evil 2 is in its characters. Leon and Claire are both survivors in their own right, and their stories intertwine as they navigate the horrors of Raccoon City. Leon is a rookie cop, wide-eyed and full of hope when he first arrives, but as the night progresses, he becomes a more hardened, determined character — but not without showing vulnerability. Claire, on the other hand, is searching for her missing brother, Chris, and her journey becomes a powerful narrative of family, resilience, and hope. Both characters bring their own emotional weight to the story, but it’s the humanity in their interactions that make the horror all the more gut-wrenching. You aren’t just fighting zombies; you’re trying to survive while holding onto the flickering remnants of hope, trying to protect the ones you care about while constantly being pushed to your breaking point.

The emotional toll is palpable. Every time you think you’re safe, you’re reminded that the world outside is unforgiving, and the weight of your decisions becomes crushing. The game’s narrative never forgets that, even in the middle of a zombie outbreak, the emotional journey is what keeps you invested. When you see survivors trapped by the zombies, or witness the brutality of the monsters, you can’t help but feel helplessness. But it’s not all despair — there’s a sense of hope, too. There’s a drive to keep going, not just to survive, but to make sure the nightmare doesn’t continue. You’ll want to push forward, not only for yourself, but for the people you care about, even if it means facing your darkest fears.

The pacing of the game builds this emotional tension flawlessly. The action is intense, and you’re constantly battling against the clock as you solve puzzles, search for supplies, and fight off increasingly dangerous enemies. The original game was known for its sense of isolation, and this remake nails that feeling, but it’s not without moments of pure adrenaline. When you’re in combat, every bullet counts, and each decision about whether to fight or run can make the difference between life and death. The limited resources — the precious ammo, herbs, and health sprays — force you to think carefully about every step. The tension is amplified by the feeling that you’re constantly running out of time, but there’s also an underlying fear of being overwhelmed. The moment when you hear that signature, terrifying sound — the heavy footsteps of Mr. X, the towering, relentless antagonist who pursues you throughout the game — it’s enough to send you into a panic. You’re not just fighting to survive the zombies; you’re trying to escape the crushing weight of fear, knowing that he’s always just around the corner.

The monsters in Resident Evil 2 are not just terrifying because of their grotesque designs (though, make no mistake, they are terrifying). They are personal. The zombies, the Lickers, the mutated monsters — they’re physical representations of the destruction of Raccoon City, but they also reflect something deeper about the human condition. They are the corruption of life, the loss of self, the idea that survival comes at the cost of everything that made you human. The game doesn’t just ask you to kill; it asks you to confront the emptiness that these creatures represent. Each battle is an emotional one, not just for survival, but for the remnants of humanity that you’re desperately trying to hold onto.

And then, of course, there’s Mr. X — a manifestation of relentless fear. The feeling of being hunted is at the core of his terror. When he appears, the world suddenly feels smaller, more dangerous. Every door you open could lead to him. Every corner you turn could be your last. And yet, it’s not just about the monster itself; it’s about the emotional impact he has. He’s not just an obstacle — he’s a representation of the loss of control. He’s the physical manifestation of the city’s collapse, and the fear that no matter how far you run, you’ll never be safe.

One of the most profound aspects of Resident Evil 2 is its persistence of hope in the midst of absolute horror. Despite the death, the despair, and the uncertainty, Leon and Claire continue to fight. They continue to push forward, even when it seems like everything is against them. There’s something profoundly human in their perseverance. Their emotional journeys are about more than just survival; they’re about the desire to reconnect, to save others, and to restore some semblance of hope in a world that has been ravaged. And the emotional payoff when you finally escape the horrors of Raccoon City — when you get a moment of reprieve, of peace — is earned through every sacrifice, every bullet fired, and every puzzle solved. It’s a cathartic release, but it’s not the end of the story. You know, deep down, that survival in Raccoon City comes at a cost. And that cost is something both Leon and Claire will carry with them forever.

Resident Evil 2 is more than a remake. It’s a return to horror — a game that pushes you to your emotional and psychological limits while keeping you on the edge of your seat with every tense moment. It’s a story of fear, survival, and ultimately, redemption. A test of human resilience in a world consumed by madness, it makes you realize that sometimes, the scariest monsters aren’t just the ones chasing you down the hallway. Sometimes, the real terror is what we carry inside ourselves and what we’re willing to sacrifice to stay human.

We'll start off by saying ive never played a horror game before. though i have played RE2 original, ive never come to finish it of course. this was a good chance for me to try out a horror game and this was an amazing first choice. First, lets talk about the game then we'll go into different sections
THE GAME.
the game is simply amazing to say the fact. each part was cooked to perfection, marinated with enough flavor to not let it be overwhelming but be enough for a pleasant experience. the gameplay is addicting with additions to puzzles and exploration. the gunplay is fine, its serviceable to a fact but could've been better especially with the more focus on combat in later parts. you could account the sluggish combat to be because of leon since hes an "amateur" but if you're a new police recruit, you probably had extensive combat training to not feel like a brick, especially with that twink body. james made sense in SH2 og, this mostly didn't. that fantasy wont come true until Resident Evil 4. I found it much more difficult with the significant sensitivity changes on controller, it was quite hard to grasp aiming at a sufficient level. Now that we talked about the basis of the gameplay that will continue to be mostly the same for most of the game, we'll continue with the story. 
THE STORY
the story sort of exemplifies a double narrative in the eyes of both Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield. While I haven't finished Claire's B run yet, ive finished Leon's A run yet and safe to say, i found the story to be quite cheesy at time with its B movie tier thats distracting but charming. The escalation of the story from the RPD to the sewers then to the NEST lab is also welcome, how it changes the atmosphere before you get bored of it. The focus on combat in later levels made it pretty sluggish though unfortunately, i really enjoyed the sort of puzzle format the RPD layout had, but later levels was practically shooting galleries. not bad, but now what i really expected.
LEON SECTION 
personally, i found the leon section to be quite interesting, but loses its momentum after the garage in the sewers. still its pretty damn good and quite enjoyable. my only gripe with leon and claire by extension is The Tyrant or Mr. X whichever you prefer. one of the things the game did greatly was to introduce the player to the RPD much earlier so they can get in gripes with the map and know each way, though i still think The Tyrant a useless addition. while yes, it did add onto the horror aesthetics, i thought it was more so just annoying and very unintuitive. its practically useless only adding in horror elements in places that should NOT have the horror element. its addition is a mixed one, but i somewhat welcome it. The later part of the Leon section also HEAVILY relies on combat and while it was welcome, it sort of removed what made the earlier parts much more memorable. think of it like the mansion part of RE village. everyone remembered it, not the other stuff. The short Ada section was pretty useless. the off-the-rails in and out adventure that was sort of annoying with all the hacking stuff and only used for plot development that couldve just been scrapped.
OVERALL OPINION.
Personally, i think this game so far deserves an 8/10. it wasnt exactly the masterpiece i was expecting according to steam reviews but i still found it pretty enjoyable and a really good game to play. I'd recommend this to anyone looking for a combat-centered survival horror and not for anybody looking for a puzzle with horror to solve.

Just barely reaching "recommended" for me, the Resident Evil 2 remake could at-times feel like more of a mediocre action movie than a narrative-based video game, featuring shallow dialogue, an under-explained plot, and underwhelming boss fights. However, I found the gameplay to be much better than in the RE1 remake, the visuals are an extreme upgrade, and the puzzles are much more engaging. Would recommend buying at a steep discount.

Playtime: 9.9 hours

[u]Narrative: 5.5/10[/u] - Though the general plot is attractive in its own right, too many significant plot points are veiled by disjointed clues, notes, and other methods throughout the game, despite other environmental storytelling being minimal. This results in a new player "finishing" the game without moderately understanding the plot, reserving that right for diehard fans with a lot of time on their hands or a lot of Wikipedia articles read. This is further hampered by a sense of urgency in the puzzle-solving that doesn't quite allow a new player to explore said clues. Environmental storytelling is minimized past corpses scattered across the rooms and aforementioned notes. Dialogue is classic action-movie cringe. Similarly, the plot often feels squandered by overused action tropes.

[u]Visuals: 7.5/10[/u] - The visuals are an extreme upgrade from the original RE2, featuring modern lighting effects, higher-quality textures, and even ray tracing. However, the game is optimized for TAA anti-aliasing, which makes everything extraordinarily blurry, diminishing all the aforementioned improvements (thankfully, you are able to disable TAA. However, all other AA methods do not result in satisfactory AA). Lighting glitches were common throughout, particularly reflections. Otherwise, the combination of lighting and shadow effects makes certain locations quite atmospheric, matching the theme of the game well. The police station looked fantastic.

[u]Audio: 6.5/10[/u] - A fine score, fine voice acting; audio was fine.

[u]Gameplay: 7/10[/u] - Though I haven't played the original RE2, I played the 2015 RE1 remake and rated it poorly because of how much I hated the gameplay. The gameplay in this one was a significant improvement, nixing the more punishing aspects of the game, allowing autosaves and saving without items required to do so, streamlining puzzles, and changing perspective from a static camera to a third-person camera. However, the controls could still often feel clunky, and most boss fights culminated into 'lure them this way so that I can slide past them.' Repeat 25x. Lack of explanation on "safe rooms" from one of the main bosses. It was also annoyingly easy to accidentally activate assisted difficulty mode on the death screen. Inventory management was much better than in the RE1 remake.

[u]Character Design: 4/10[/u] - Though the characters themselves and their backgrounds could be compelling, the dialogue is absolutely awful. It's like the writers watched Fast and Furious on repeat and wrote down what the characters said immediately after a car exploded, and then copied them word-for-word into the script. This game is about as superficial as it gets, with little to no emotional depth or complex themes explored. 

[u]Environment and Level Design: 8/10[/u] - This game is much more straightforward than the RE1 remake, which I appreciate. I was rarely confused and didn't have to look up a walkthrough for this one. The puzzles and associated clues were spread out well. Navigating the maps was relatively easy and moderately more linear. Rooms and settings were laid out well and environment props were plentiful, leaving no rooms feeling like empty offshoots. The boss fights wherein the player is trapped in a sort-of arena with them were disappointing from a gameplay perspective. Basically all settings looked great, from the police station to the parking garage to the sewers. Shoutout to Dead by Daylight for having me memorize the police station before I ever played.

[u]Overall Engagement: 8/10[/u]

[u]Performance: 7/10[/u] - 2k144, highest settings w/ RT, lighting glitches throughout; may be related to framerate. Also played on Steam Deck, 90 fps, medium settings, some tearing of textures. Optimized for extremely blurry TAA, and other AA methods aren't satisfactory. No game bugs encountered.

[u]Replay value: 4/10[/u] - Two character selections with slightly modified gameplay and plot. "Real" ending requires a second playthrough. Not significant replay value for me because the changes are minimal and the overall gameplay is linear.

[b]Overall:  6.5/10[/b]

Great game overall. It brings back many elements of survival horror that worked so well in the classic games. The visuals are really well done - the graphics look great, and the way lights and shadows are handled is excellent. Plus, the gore is on point. You can clearly see the impact your weapons have on enemies, with blood pouring from wounds, and with precise shots, you can completely detach limbs from zombies' bodies.

Speaking of guns, while the arsenal isn’t particularly large, every weapon serves its purpose. The game heavily encourages exploration, during which you can find upgrade parts for most of your weapons. The puzzles are absolutely on point. They’re never unfair and can be solved relatively quickly, but they require you to think, which I really appreciate.

The boss fights are okay - your usual "shoot the weak spot until it dies" kind of deal. Thankfully the designs are creative, and the fights don’t drag on too long. The best part of the game for me, personally, is Mr. X. His presence forces you to think on the fly instead of sticking to a pre-planned route. While you can fight him and temporarily disable him, it brings no real benefits. So, avoiding him and staying on the move is generally the better strategy.

Another great feature is the sound design and music. While there isn’t much music, the tracks that play are all fantastic. And the sound of Mr. X’s footsteps as he approaches will give you nightmares.

Of course, the game isn’t without flaws. The most notorious issue is the movement. Running straight is fine, but turning feels like skating on ice while being pulled by rubber bands. This makes it hard to maneuver, and even fitting through a door can sometimes be a struggle. Some enemy hitboxes are downright broken, like the G-Mutants (trust me, you’ll find out the hard way).

The biggest disappointment, or rather missed opportunity, is the 2nd scenarios. While they offer some new content, like changes to enemy and item placements and puzzle solutions, they don’t feel unique enough. It’s a shame because much more could have been done to differentiate them.

All in all, it’s a great game, and you should definitely give it a try!

Amazing game with some flaws here and there.

The level design is excellent for the most part, never had to google anything (except maybe photo-hinted treasures, the pictures are quite vague), locations are very memorable, even though I expected the opposite, because what can possibly look distinct in police station and sewers... apparently, everything.
The game design though tends to be a little rough around the edges. Especially when we talk about some particular enemy encounters and bosses. Sometimes you just don't know what to do. Like during segments with sewer monsters. Killing them with regular guns is very inefficient, so I had to spend a couple of hours on this segment trying out different things. Trying to lure them out to a wider space where I'll get the chance to run past them, but alotta times they just grabbed me no matter what. If you break free from the grab with a grenade, for some reason, it won't stun them at all, so if you try to run past them after a grenade, you will fail. But if you throw your grenade normally and not during a grab, it will indeed stun them for a brief period of time. These moments feel quite luck based and frustrating. But they wouldn't be that big of a deal if I hadn't played on Hardcore. And Hardcore really makes you fear for your life.
I like challenging games, and RE2's highest difficulty really makes you lock tf in, but one particular feature makes Hardcore infinitely harder than Standard. Ink Ribbons. The fact that you can save only using a rare consumable item is very immersive and adds alotta challenge, but sometimes this "should i save now or later" gamble can BRUTALLY backfire. There's always a chance that you might lose like 30 minutes of progress or more, and it's a pure pain when it happens. Because you constantly don't know what awaits you next. Maybe the game just decides to throw a boss or a new enemy on you, and you don't know how to deal with it yet, so you probably gonna die or waste a very unnecessary amount of resources. And considering these somewhat janky rng based encounters I mentioned earlier, it feels very unfair sometimes. I personally would've loved if they gave just a tiny bit more of ink ribbons, because you are constantly running really tight on them, even when you try to save up for later.

As someone who has never really played a Resident Evil Game, or even a horror game for that matter, I heard all about the series from friends and social media, I thought I’d start with RE2, since I wasn’t sure how I’d feel about the tank controls of the original game and I have to say I was hooked immediately. The Gas Station tutorial and intro to the Police Station do an amazing job not only setting the tone, but teaching that fighting isn’t always going to be an option. From there, we find ourselves in the police station, and this is the part that really hooked me on the game. Having this massive building to explore and puzzles to solve without any clear objectives forced me to explore and manage my resources carefully since I wasn’t sure what I’d be facing. The game does a fantastic job building that tense survival horror feeling and I was having a blast.

My favorite part was when Mr. X showed up. While it sounds crazy to like a part with a relentless, unkillable enemy, it was the peak point of both survival and horror. Hearing him walking around, not knowing if he’s on the other side of the door I'm walking through, and trying to solve puzzles with him constantly chasing me was intense and is what really hooked me on the series.

While I really enjoyed playing, it did have its weak points. The boss fights were my least favorite parts since right beforehand you’re given a bunch of ammo and it becomes an action packed fight. Some of them try to spice things up and add a unique mechanic, but most of the time it’s just running around an arena and shooting the big glowing weakness on the enemy. The final boss in both scenarios is the worst offender of this, giving both Leon and Clare a super weapon to fight them. But since this is the final boss I can see why they’d want to go out with a bang. The bonuses are also a mess. The 4th survivor tries to be a more action packed affair, but they still heavily rely on the ammo and resource conservation from the game, and feel pretty luck based to complete. The ghost survivors were also pretty boring since it’s mainly the same maps we played in the base game, but with a slight twist. 

I didn’t speak too much about the base game because it’s honestly something you should just experience for yourself. If you’re looking for a good survival horror game this one is one of the best. There’s even an assisted mode if you’re new to the genre and want to experience it in a lower stakes setting. I’d also try to avoid playing with a walkthrough or buying the infinite ammo weapons you’re first time through so you can really experience it.

Resident Evil 2: the game that lets you relive the nightmare of Raccoon City, only now with jaw-dropping graphics, and a relentless trench coat enthusiast who just wants to give you a really aggressive hug.

The story hits all the right beats - mystery, horror, and just enough cheesy dialogue to remind you this is, at heart, a Resident Evil game. You’re either Leon Kennedy, the world’s unluckiest rookie cop, or Claire Redfield, a determined college student searching for her brother. Your mission? Survive, escape, and try not to scream every time a zombie bursts through a door. With separate campaigns for Leon and Claire, along with multiple endings and bonus modes like The 4th Survivor, the game offers plenty of reasons to return. Exploring the nuances between the two characters’ paths adds depth and variety.

The remake trades in the original’s fixed camera angles for an over-the-shoulder perspective, instantly modernizing the gameplay while retaining its survival horror roots. Every encounter is a challenge; resources are scarce, and every bullet counts. Do you risk using ammo to take down a zombie, or conserve it and pray you can sneak by?
And then there’s the inventory management. You’ll quickly learn to curse the existence of puzzle pieces and key items. Want to pick up that healing herb? Too bad, you’ve got an ornate chess piece taking up precious space, and you just know it’ll be important later.

Puzzles are back, striking a balance between satisfying and head-scratching, because nothing says "end of the world" like finding out you need a crank, a spade key, and the patience of a saint to unlock one door. They add a layer of classic Resident Evil charm.

Mr. X, he’s one of the most memorable parts of the game. This towering figure relentlessly hunts you down, forcing you to stay on the move and rethink your strategies. His presence is both exhilarating and nerve-wracking, perfectly encapsulating the game’s blend of tension and terror.

Thanks to the RE Engine, Resident Evil 2 is a visual marvel. The detailed environments immerse you in the eerie atmosphere of the Raccoon City Police Department, and the lighting and shadows play with your nerves at every turn. The audio in this game is a standout feature. From the unsettling groans of zombies to the deafening silence of empty hallways, every sound is designed to keep you on edge. And Mr. X’s heavy footsteps? They’ll haunt your dreams.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is a reinvention that surpasses the original in almost every way. It delivers a perfect balance of nostalgia and innovation, offering an unforgettable experience for both fans and newcomers.

The best part of this game is undoubtedly the Tyrant, the unkillable, trenchcoat-wearing killing machine that stalks Leon and Claire throughout the game. His heavy footsteps can be heard through walls and ceilings making you always aware that he is hunting you down and he will never go away. That mechanic to me is the best part of this game. The constant fear that something that I literally cannot beat is always looking for me makes even safe rooms feel unsafe and forced me to always stay on my toes. I love this and I wish other games effectively utilized this mechanic more.

This is a very good game that is only elevated by playing it in VR where things are a lot bigger and a lot more immersive. For a horror game I think that is a must, but I imagine RE2: Remake is just as fun in flatscreen as well. If you like genuinely good and fun horror games, get this!

I don't often find myself getting scared or tensed up playing horror games, but I have to hand RE2R It's Flowers here, as I was a frightened little birdie maneuvering through that police station. My first few encounters with Tyrant were incredibly anxiety-inducing, creating an immense amount of pressure to either run to a save room or risk expending needed materials. Scripted or not, simply hearing his heavy footsteps close in as I finally feel a sense of progression never failed to supply a mixed emotional bag of dread and accomplishment. 

However, after my fair share of encounters with Mr. X, I started adapting to his mechanics and presence and thus began to love the thrill. What's more, the exceptional sound design further pushes that intense atmosphere and pressure tightening around you, creating a feeling you can't find in many horror games. What the development team created here with Its environment and sound design, making each new area, room, and hallway feel fresh and alive, is what I thrive to experience in survival horror games.

Though, as much as I adored my time with this game, I found Tyrant's footsteps more horrifying than anything present in the latter half of the game, as I can't say I'm too fond of the Sewers-Lab stretch. With the excessive amount of ammo and material handouts, I felt it took away from the survival aspect. Rationing and strategizing with what I had was easily one of my favorite parts of the game, as I found it challenging, though I suppose it's not that big of a deal and is more of a little nitpick. I enjoyed what was new, though It wasn't good enough to void my feelings of boredom. Negatives aside, I enjoyed my time and will forever recommend this to anyone wanting to broaden their horizons with a fresh survival horror experience. 1 rookie cop. First day on the job. Raccoon City. Viral outbreak. Out of control. Pharmaceutical companies. Bio-weapons. Babes. Bazookas. Explosions. Short run-on sentences said in a gruff tone of voice and manner. 

RE2 Leon S. Kennedy is the origin story era Batman of the Resident Evil universe. See his origins unfold in what is quite possibly the gold standard of the remake craze of the 8th console generation. The greatest franchise reboot since... Resident Evil 4. And likely the very thing outside of Resident Evil 7 that saved a floundering Japanese game company titan who had struggled to release a title with any kind of consistency since Resident Evil 4 OG itself for over half a decade. 

Capcom was struggling bad post Resident Evil 6. People forget that. I knew when starting this game that it was going to be good from start to finish, what I didn't expect is to enjoy it so much I completed both playthroughs right after one another. 

Resident Evil 2 Remake has Leon Kennedy and Clare Redfield who have different story lines that run parallel to each other in the timeline (kinda?) with an additional two playthroughs where they swap their "A route" playthroughs with each other. These routes have different areas that both characters are allowed to access, you will have to think how you navigate around the map since some shortcuts won't be accessible depending on the character. Leon and Claire have different weapons they discover throughout the story as well.

This game has a well-crafted immersive environment. I'm a big fan of how the map is designed and how it slowly opens up as you discover new key items to go to unlock new areas. It's almost metroidvania-like in how you unlocked shortcuts and new routes as you progress through the game. The map forces you in situations where you might need to run through a room which has a ton of enemies to unlock a shortcut or new weapon which made it feel rewarding. 

To talk about the enemies briefly without spoilers, they are all great. Your generic zombies will sway their bodies to make headshots harder to land or run directly after you to grab you. The only special enemies have clear weaknesses but can be lethal if you're careless. Finally.. HIM; if you know, he's incredible oppressive and will make you re-think your game plan.

I recommend this game because it does so many things right and it has a ton of content. The thrill of going through an area you haven't explored and finding a shortcut which takes you back to an area early on is a great feeling. Your first playthrough will also be your longest but after that your subsequent playthroughs will be shorter. There is a lot of dread but also a rewarding experience when you persevere through it.

I played Resident Evil 2 with great pleasure and want to share my impressions. I will say right away that I really liked the game, and I recommend it for purchase.

The first thing that catches your eye is, of course, the fascinating plot. It keeps you in suspense from beginning to end, making you worry about the characters and empathize with them. I would especially like to note the atmosphere of the game. It is simply amazing! Gloomy corridors, dark rooms, ominous sounds - all this creates a tense and frightening atmosphere. And the zombies, who even after death get up and pursue you, only increase the fear and make you be on your guard.

However, the game also has some drawbacks. For example, the need to run back and forth and think for a long time about what to do next can be a little tiring. This is especially noticeable when playing for the second character, when you have to go through the same thing, as was the case with Lyon.

Important Note :
Resident Evil 2 Remake is the first Resident Evil game I ever played. This game, is the one that made me fall in a love/hate relationship with the series. I have no past nostalgia, or bias for console versions, did not grow up with the game. I came into the series with no prior experience in it, squeaky clean!


RE2R is [b]easily[/b] my favourite of the series. This is after having completed EVERY Resident Evil game available on PC, up until Resident Evil 4 Remake. This includes RE 0, 1 - 7, Village, the Revelations series.
RE2R is also the one I was most anxious to play a second time.


It's a mix of things really; the location, the characters, not too long, not too short, the fluid movement, the clean UI/Inventory, the atmosphere, the sound, the graphics. It feels like a faithful remake, with all the perfect tweaks to make it feel modern.


I won't hide it, there are things in RE2R that [i]frustrated[/i] me. But, these are really just down to my own playstyle; I tend to be slow, I play lot's of walking simulator games and turn-based games. I quickly lose my temper in the "quick-paced" moments of RE2R; like some of the boss battles, or when being "hunted" - [i]albeit, slowly[/i] - by the Tyrant.

Honestly though, these are such minor gripes, and this won't affect most players. This probably wouldn't have affected me this way back when I was more of a "shooters" gamer. I'm getting old, [i]okay!?[/i].

Naturally, there are things I dislike as well, but I understand their inclusion. For example; [b]the randomness of critical hits that kill walkers[/b]. I know this is a [i]thing[/i] of the series. But, [i]why[/i] one zombie can take 10 headshots, [b]and still get up ?[/b] When the one next to him took 2, [b]and his head blew open ?[/b]

It's a way to keep the low zombie count, make ammo critical to conserve. To motivate you to simply try and ignore walkers. The game isn't a zombie shooter. So, within the confines of the game, because of how well some of the other elements are done, I'm [i]okay[/i] with this.

Naturally, there are also some graphical glitches here and there. Some reflections and post-processing issues. Nothing that will break the game, and at least, the game is very fluid most of the time.



Few frustrations aside, I really enjoyed the characters; played both, Leon [1st Run] and Claire [NG 2nd Run]. I really appreciate how they have a slightly different approach, different weapons and even different parts in the cutscenes and locations. Different endings also makes it interesting to play more than once.

The weapons are very well done. The amount of times I was just amazed at the nice crisp POP of a handgun. Some dedicated shooters don't even get the sounds this nice! This game also did gun sounds the best in the series, by far.

I'm a little bit of a gun-enthusiast, in the sense that I like the "fireworks" they provide, the sounds, how they look, and the history behind some of them. RE2R has some VERY interesting models that you wouldn't see in any other game. 

Leon's "Matilda", or [b]Heckler & Koch VP70M[/b], is quite a striking and unique firearm. It's a very interesting choice, probably my favourite firearm in the game, simply due to its real-world rarity and history.

Claire's "JMB Hp3", or [b]Browning Hi-Power Mark III[/b] is also a very interesting model to have used. The Browning Hi-Power is a very significant pistol and a very well-regarded one too. It's well-known, but not "popular".


Anyways, I'm off to play my favourites of the series a second/third time, and maybe after that I'm going back to Resident Evil HD for another run.

[h1] Absolute peak [/h1]
As a beginning of the RE Remake saga, RE2R is perfect, save some annoying details.
Incredible atmosphere, curated by amazing graphics, lighting and level design, a true survival horror experience, which creates the suspense not with the help of a handful of zombies or an invincible Nick Valentine following you around, but with the scarcity of the tools presented to you and the ineffectiveness of said tools. This is what differentiates RE2 from, say, Dead Space, since there you are able to buy ammunition on demand, making you a stacked powerhouse against enemies, while here you simply survive.

[h2] "Knock me down, and I'll keep getting back up." [/h2]
Here, a single zombie can chew seven pistol shots and two shotgun blasts to the face and still get up like nobody's business. Similarly, said zombie can get their head split open from a couple of shots. If only I knew how this works, I'd use this system, but alas. 
With each upgrade comes respite, as you start to use your ammunition more effectively. If the beginning of the game is a run around the Police Station with little to no ammo, which is wasted on the enemies, then late game is you carefully using each available tool at your disposal to bend the game to you.

[h2] A tiny rant [/h2]
My gosh the bosses are bad. Like, come on, they're so mediocre I can close my eyes and see a dozen of similar ones across all the games I've played. The fact that the bossfights are literally the *WORST* part of the game only solidifies this feeling. 
While sluggish and somewhat delayed movement of the main characters makes up a lot of the atmosphere feel a lot more unforgiving, the very same movement critically demolishes any feeling of fairness and decency when talking about bosses. Their hits are heavy, they can and will stunlock you, they are your usual "hit the weak spot" enemies, and the boss arenas are tiny, which adds to the difficulty because said bosses can corner you and just be a pain in the ass in general, so good thing that they aren't the main course.
Bossfights are trash, period.

[h2] Ending [/h2]
Despite the flaw of bosses being mediocre at best, RE2R I consider to be the best introduction to survival horror, with great attention to detail, good, but questionable balance, and entertaining plot and characters (I didn't mention them before because they can just be summed up as entertaining). 
Definitely a must-play, buy it ASAP if you wanted to at least once in your life.

Resident Evil 2 : By Triple F

The 2019 remake of "Resident Evil 2" by Capcom takes the essence of the 1998 classic and transforms it into a modern survival horror masterpiece, blending nostalgia with cutting-edge visuals and redefined mechanics. Set in the overrun Raccoon City, players follow rookie cop Leon S. Kennedy and college student Claire Redfield as they attempt to escape the zombie-infested streets and uncover the dark secrets of the Umbrella Corporation. By using Capcom’s RE Engine, "Resident Evil 2" successfully updates both graphics and gameplay while staying true to the atmospheric, tension-filled experience that made the original a hallmark of horror gaming.

The graphics in "Resident Evil 2" are among its most striking features, bringing Raccoon City and the iconic R.P.D. (Raccoon Police Department) station to life with a level of detail that enhances the horror. The RE Engine delivers photorealistic visuals, from the intricate lighting casting eerie shadows in hallways to the gruesome level of detail on zombies, whose skin decomposes with every shot. Environments are dimly lit and claustrophobic, increasing the sense of dread and vulnerability as players inch their way through dark corridors. The overall art direction builds a consistently tense and oppressive atmosphere that pulls players into the horror, making them feel as if they’re genuinely trapped in a nightmare.

"Resident Evil 2" reimagines the original tank controls and fixed camera angles, replacing them with a modern, over-the-shoulder perspective that retains the horror without sacrificing immersion. This change significantly impacts gameplay, making exploration and combat feel more fluid while still leaving players feeling vulnerable. Ammo and resources are scarce, forcing players to make strategic choices about when to fight or flee. Every shot counts, especially as enemies can soak up a surprising amount of bullets, and headshots don’t always guarantee a kill. This limitation adds to the survival horror tension, where each encounter feels risky and heightens the player's awareness of resource management.

The AI of enemies, especially zombies, is another aspect that elevates "Resident Evil 2" as a horror experience. Zombies are tenacious, breaking through doors and windows and pursuing the player relentlessly. Their unpredictable behavior means that even a single enemy encounter can lead to heart-pounding moments. Moreover, the infamous Tyrant, or "Mr. X," serves as a constant, looming threat. Once he begins stalking the halls of the R.P.D., his relentless, unstoppable nature forces players to think carefully about every move and use stealth to avoid detection. The tension builds as players hear his heavy footsteps echoing nearby, creating an omnipresent sense of danger.

The game’s narrative is delivered in two interwoven campaigns for Leon and Claire, each providing a unique perspective on the events unfolding in Raccoon City. Players gain insight into different aspects of the story and interact with different characters, such as the mysterious Ada Wong and the brave Sherry Birkin. While the campaigns overlap, each offers unique encounters and puzzles, encouraging players to experience both to get the full story. This dual-campaign structure adds replay-ability, as each run provides fresh challenges and contributes to a more complete understanding of the plot and the horrors of the Umbrella Corporation.

Capcom also revamped the game’s puzzles, a staple of the Resident Evil series, making them feel more modern while staying true to the spirit of the original. Players must find keys, solve riddles, and combine items to access new areas, which adds a cerebral element to the game’s pacing. The puzzles are cleverly designed, requiring exploration and keen observation without feeling like roadblocks. These moments offer a break from the combat and tension, but the sense of dread is ever-present, as solving a puzzle often leads to opening a new door or venturing into an unknown area filled with fresh threats.

Altogether, "Resident Evil 2" (2019) is a masterclass in survival horror, combining an unsettling atmosphere, gripping gameplay, and a faithful yet reimagined narrative that does justice to the 1998 classic. With stunning visuals, tight resource management, relentless enemies, and unforgettable scares, it sets a new standard for horror game remakes. For fans of the original and newcomers alike, "Resident Evil 2" is an essential experience that redefines what it means to survive a nightmare, delivering a terrifying journey that lingers long after the credits roll.

The guns all feel good to use, there's some decent variety with a few unlockables in typical RE fashion. You have your grenade launcher, magnum, the usuals. Claire gets a nifty zap gun that can fry enemies. The knife is treated as a sub-weapon in this remake with limited durability, flash and frag grenades are in the same camp with the former being really handy for killing or slipping by lickers.

In terms of difficulty, Standard is great for a first playthrough, resources feel just scarce enough but not annoyingly so. Ammo conservation matters. RE2 Remake is pretty damn good overall. If you're like me, going through all the REmakes for the first time, this is the first over-the-shoulder camera that allows you to aim and shoot with the mouse. Storage and save locations are plentiful and if you play on standard difficulty you'll be able to save freely without the infamous Ribbon Ink. It sports 2 characters to play, each with an A scenario and a B scenario (first and second playthrough). The general story is the same but the scenarios are different enough to pull you into a couple of playthroughs. It also has a handful of secondary missions (the easiest still being brutally difficult).

RE2 Remake is beautiful and overflowing with that RE charm. You get the same creepy, gorey, zombie filled darkness as RE1 but with modern graphics, and it's fantastic. The atmosphere is great, with the sounds and music really helping to immerse you into the unfriendly, infected world. You'll regularly find yourself spinning around, thinking you aren't alone in the dimly lit room.

It's not perfect, and unfortunately the flaws are present from the first few minutes and last until the final bosses. There is an ever present RNG factor in this game. RNG affects zombie location and damage done (and to a lesser extent ammo and healing items). You might shoot a normal zombie in the head and explode it with a single bullet, the next normal zombie's head may tank an entire magazine and still get up the next time you walk into the room. Even shots to the shoulders, elbows, hips, and knees can end up draining your ammo. Or not. It's a roll of the dice. The community will advise you to not kill every zombie, which is good advise, but you won't know which ones to kill and which to let live until you've played through at least once.

Additionally, sometimes zombies will just be silently waiting for you around a corner or on the other side of a door. This leads to some damage taken that doesn't entirely feel earned. Some zombies groan so loudly that you can hear them through walls, others are practically mute until after they bite you. Sometimes you NEED to get through a door to progress and there's a zombie on the other side rubbing their hit box against the door handle.

Lastly, your character never quite feels like they move fast enough. I found myself reacting with my camera quickly to zombie attacks, but my character always lagged behind. The faster you spin the camera, the longer you have to wait for your in game model to catch up. Even when zombies are chasing you down, your character is acting less like their life is in danger and more like they just spilled their drink on the coffee table and need to grab some paper towels.

The RNG damage, sneak attacks, and slow movement speed can become extremely frustrating at times. These elements can make you feel robbed at best and force you to reload at worst. You can still absolutely get more skilled at the game and you're rewarded for playing better, it is not 100% RNG. I was able to noticeably get better with each playthrough until I got S rank, but the looming threat of randomness is always present. In a game based around managing your ammo, healing items, and inventory space, the RNG of combat feels like a bad contrast.

Despite that, the game is still fantastic and you can have an amazing time in between bouts of bad RNG. It feels great to succeed. The blood, guts, and torn flesh look wonderful. And if you are having a hard time you can easily find other frustrated people in the comment sections around the internet, giving you some cathartic validation as they put the RNG in this game on blast.

One of if not the best horror games I have ever played. This is should be seen as the foundation for all horror games with this style in mind.

I cannot understate how amazing of an experience this was. There is an outrageous amount of detail into every little thing. I particularly loved the detail of how Leon has trigger discipline, and Claire did not (at least for her starting weapon). This is such a small thing to add into the game, but it honestly added so much for me. Seeing something so missable and knowing that someone took the time to reflect each characters training with guns through this small animation, it really felt special.

Beyond stunning visual detail and such great attention to it, the game has extremely effective horror baked into it. There is the usual limited ammo shebang, but for the first time in my experience with horror games, I felt the impacts of this. You WILL run out of ammo. You WILL have to run away from some encounters. You WILL be harshly punished for missing shots. Taking time to aim is everything, and this adds such a threat to usually slow enemies. But even that is balanced out with how slow your character is. Yes they can run, but they don't zoom by enemies, they briskly jog by them. Running is balanced in this way. It will not solve every issue, but rather a select few. I love this balance so much. You want to run, but you can't always do that, so you have to shoot. You want to shoot, but can't always do that, so you have to run. This creates such a tension I have never felt in horror games before. You do not know what solution you will have to use, and you cannot be certain that this solution will work. This keeps you scared throughout your playthrough.

At least, for the first playthrough. The second scenario flips the game on its head. Instead of slowly and carefully exploring, you know everything. You know the solutions to the puzzles, you know what works for fighting, and you know how to be fast. This is a feeling like no other in games. This second run is a nice spice on the usual run through. It becomes more focused on action instead of horror, and I love it so much. Yes, there are still moments where you do not know what to do and will be scared, but in general your skill from the first run carries you through. This harsh change from fearfully exploring to bravely running is such an amazing feeling.

Something I loved a lot was the use of the Tyrant enemy. He might be my favorite enemy in any game ever now. He was so consistently horrifying, and genuinely made me jump so many times. His never ending, merciless walk towards you is scary in a way I never knew was possible. Of course, the end of the game as a nice surprise for those who enjoy him so much, but I won't spoil it. Amazing enemy design.

The story is great too. It is honestly so simple but effective. Simple stakes, simple characters, and simple progression. There is a nice mystery to figuring out what is going on, but it is a lot more fascinating than what you would expect from this game. The voice acting sells it the most for me. Leon and Claire are wonderfully voiced, and are a joy to listen to.

That is once you get used to it. I am very used to pure vocal silence during horror games, and Leon yelling "♥♥♥♥!" at every little thing pissed me off at first. Specifically, there was a moment where you had to be silent because there was a Licker in the area (Enemy set off by noise but not sight). I was doing good, but then a zombie flopped into the room. Leon then yells "Damn it!" or something of the similar and freaks me the hell out and (I think) activated the Licker. That may have been from me running in response to the noise though. Funny experience, and very memorable, but that could be very annoying for some people.

Besides that, I have very little complaints. There is one REALLY bad boss fight that pissed me off a bunch, but it ultimately was fine once you got the hang of it. Nothing game breaking. Any hiccups the game has are way outweighed by the sheer quality of everything else. Sound design, graphical fidelity, and atmosphere stand out in particular to me. This game knows what it is doing and excels at it.

Ultimately, this is a phenomenal game that should be seen as the cornerstone of action focused third person horror. 9.5/10. Perfect horror. Perfect fear. And man, that resident was quite evil.

Resident Evil 2 Remake: A Thrilling Game of Zombies, Mystery, and Cheeks to Die For

Capcom’s Resident Evil 2 Remake isn’t just a masterful return to Raccoon City; it’s a showcase of how survival horror can thrive in modern gaming. But let’s not beat around the bush (or buns): this game also features the finest pair of protagonists whose backsides deserve their own accolades.

Plot: Zombies and Sass (and a Dash of Ass)
The game throws you into a nightmare as Leon S. Kennedy, a rookie cop with a jawline so sharp it could cut through Umbrella’s lies, and Ada Wong, a femme fatale with enough mystery to keep you guessing—and enough poise to keep you staring. Their chemistry is electric, and let’s face it: they’re both rocking jeans tighter than a Resident Evil puzzle lock.

As Leon navigates the zombie-infested Raccoon City Police Department (RPD), Ada struts into the chaos in heels that scream, “I came here to work secrets and serve looks.” Together, they unravel conspiracies, dodge zombies, and somehow make surviving the apocalypse look way too good.

Gameplay: Survive, Solve, and Admire
The remake elevates the original’s gameplay with tight, over-the-shoulder combat, atmospheric exploration, and puzzles that demand as much brainpower as admiration for the sheer chutzpah of Leon's posture. Whether blasting zombies or unlocking doors, every moment feels tactile, tense, and stylish.

And let’s not ignore the elephant in the room—or rather, the dump truck in the room. Leon’s combat roll has no business being that...dynamic. Every time you crouch, sprint, or swivel, it’s clear Capcom put just as much care into crafting his assets as they did into the RE Engine’s lighting system.

The Horror: Spine-Chillingly Beautiful
The zombie designs are grotesque and terrifying, but it’s Leon and Ada who keep stealing the show. Ada’s trench coat moment? Iconic. Leon’s distressed denim during a high-stakes boss fight? Unfairly distracting. Even Mr. X, the unstoppable, trench-coated tyrant, can’t compete with the duo’s sheer confidence and undeniable posterior power.

Deep Joke: The Leon and Ada Edition

Why don’t Leon and Ada ever get ambushed by zombies from behind?
Because even the undead can’t stop admiring the view.
Graphics and Atmosphere: Darkness Has Never Been So Well-Lit
The RE Engine brings Raccoon City to life with stunning detail, from the flickering lights of the RPD to the shiny...textures on Leon’s uniform. The way shadows play across Ada’s coat is mesmerizing—until she ditches it to reveal her dress, a piece of fashion so impractical yet captivating it deserves a DLC all its own.

Character Interactions: Flirtation Meets Frustration
Leon’s earnest heroism and Ada’s enigmatic coolness are a match made in survival horror heaven. Their banter is as sharp as their aim, and the unspoken tension between them could rival the T-virus in potency. Leon’s puppy-dog loyalty? Endearing. Ada’s smirks and side-glances? Dangerous.

Final Thoughts: The Whole Package (and Then Some)
Resident Evil 2 Remake isn’t just a near-perfect survival horror game—it’s a celebration of iconic characters, intense gameplay, and rear views that will haunt your dreams (in a good way). Leon and Ada might be running from zombies, but let’s be real: the rest of us are following closely, very closely.

Play it for the horror. Stay for the story. Admire it for the, uh, “attention to detail.” And remember: in Raccoon City, the only thing more dangerous than a zombie bite is Leon S. Kennedy in a pair of tight jeans.

Story & Setting
The story of Resident Evil 2 Remake follows two protagonists: Leon S. Kennedy, a rookie cop who finds himself trapped in Raccoon City on his first day of duty, and Claire Redfield, a college student looking for her brother, Chris. The two characters have separate campaigns that ultimately converge as they both try to survive the outbreak of the T-virus, which has turned most of the city's population into flesh-eating zombies.

The story is largely the same as the original, with some minor changes and additions to flesh out certain characters and events. What the remake does exceptionally well is creating a more cinematic narrative. The dialogue is sharper, the pacing is more fluid, and the horror elements are ramped up to create an engaging, pulse-pounding experience. The setting, Raccoon City, is a dark, decaying metropolis filled with abandoned buildings, dangerous creatures, and the lingering threat of the Umbrella Corporation’s sinister influence. The Remake presents Raccoon City with a more detailed, fully realized world that feels lived-in and hauntingly atmospheric.

The core of the story is driven by the characters’ personal stakes—Leon trying to survive his first day as a cop while uncovering the truth behind the outbreak, and Claire searching for her brother while navigating the perils of the city. The game has a great sense of urgency, and the tension between the human characters and the monstrous threats around them is palpable. The addition of cutscenes and voice acting elevates the narrative, making it feel more immersive and cinematic.

Gameplay & Mechanics
Resident Evil 2 Remake retains the survival horror formula that made the original so popular, but it modernizes it with tighter controls, updated combat, and more fluid gameplay mechanics. The core gameplay loop is still all about exploration, solving puzzles, resource management, and surviving against a relentless wave of enemies. However, the game’s shift from the fixed camera angles of the original to a third-person over-the-shoulder perspective gives the game a more modern, dynamic feel, without losing the tense, atmospheric tone that Resident Evil is known for.

One of the standout features of Resident Evil 2 Remake is its incredibly immersive, atmospheric environments. The game uses a detailed, fully realized 3D environment that heightens the tension. The abandoned Raccoon City Police Department (RPD) is your primary location early on, and it is a masterpiece of design. The RPD building is a labyrinth of locked doors, hidden rooms, and dangerous hallways, all rendered in stunning detail. The environment feels like a character in itself—creaky floors, dark corners, and flickering lights make every step feel ominous.

The combat is thrilling, tense, and satisfying. Resident Evil 2 Remake offers tight, responsive controls, making it a bit easier to control Leon and Claire compared to the original. The zombies (and other monstrous creatures) are terrifying, and it feels incredibly satisfying to shoot them in the head and watch them drop. However, bullets are scarce, and the game constantly forces you to make tough decisions on when to fight or when to run. The game offers a variety of weapons—from handguns to shotguns to the iconic flamethrower—and each has its own weight and feel. Ammo management is always a challenge, and you’re constantly balancing the need to conserve resources while surviving the undead onslaught.

The enemies in Resident Evil 2 Remake are a mix of horrifying zombies, mutated creatures, and terrifying bosses that will have you on the edge of your seat. The zombies are slow but relentless, and they can overwhelm you if you’re not careful. The game introduces a new dynamic with the terrifying Mr. X, a relentless, nearly indestructible pursuer who stalks you throughout the police station and beyond. His constant presence keeps you in a state of fear, as he never gives you a moment’s rest. This constant pressure adds an element of anxiety and urgency to the gameplay.

Exploration and puzzle-solving are integral parts of the game’s experience. The puzzles are mostly environmental, requiring you to find and combine items or solve riddles to unlock new areas or gain access to vital resources. The puzzles are simple but rewarding, and they help break up the action, giving you a chance to catch your breath (if only for a moment).

The game offers two main campaigns: Leon’s and Claire’s, with each providing a slightly different perspective on the events unfolding in Raccoon City. Both campaigns are similar in structure, but there are enough differences in terms of story, puzzles, and encounters to make each feel fresh. There’s also a New Game+ mode that encourages replayability, giving you additional reasons to dive back into the horrors of Raccoon City.

Visuals & Sound Design
Visually, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a technical marvel. The game uses the RE Engine, which allows for stunning, lifelike visuals and incredibly detailed environments. The lighting is masterfully used to create a sense of dread, casting long shadows and illuminating just enough of the environment to keep you constantly on edge. The character models are impressively detailed, with facial animations that bring the characters to life. Every grotesque zombie, every horrific boss, and every blood-streaked hallway is rendered with meticulous detail that adds to the game’s realism and horror.

The sound design is equally impressive. The game uses sound to build atmosphere and suspense, from the creaks of distant doors to the gut-wrenching moans of zombies. The game also employs subtle sound cues to alert you to threats, like the heavy footsteps of Mr. X as he relentlessly hunts you down. The music is haunting and atmospheric, and it’s perfectly tuned to match the tense moments of gameplay. The voice acting, especially for Leon and Claire, is solid and adds to the emotional investment in their journey.

Performance & Technical Aspects
Resident Evil 2 Remake runs exceptionally well on most systems. The RE Engine allows for smooth, high-quality visuals with little to no performance hiccups. The game is optimized for a variety of hardware, so even mid-tier systems should be able to run it without significant issues. Load times are fast, and the game’s fluid camera and combat system feel responsive and smooth. Even in intense moments when hordes of zombies are attacking, the frame rate remains steady, allowing for an uninterrupted experience.

There are minimal bugs or glitches, and the game’s optimization is generally excellent, making it a smooth experience from start to finish.

Final Thoughts
Resident Evil 2 Remake is a perfect blend of nostalgia and innovation. It takes everything that made the original a classic—its horror, tension, exploration, and challenging combat—and refines it with modern mechanics, visuals, and gameplay. The game’s environments are hauntingly atmospheric, its combat is thrilling and challenging, and its pacing keeps you on the edge of your seat from start to finish. Mr. X and the unpredictable nature of the game ensure that the tension never lets up, and the gripping story will keep you invested throughout the entire experience.

[h1]Resident Evil 2 - A Timeless Classic.[/h1]


[h3]Introduction[/h3]
• [b]I can confidently say it's one of the best survival horror experiences of all time. Capcom has masterfully balanced nostalgia with modern gameplay mechanics.Although i wasn't the biggest fan of [u]Resident Evil Franchise[/u] ive always enjoyed some games and i find this one specifically very important in the Franchise.[/b]

[h3]Storyline[/h3]
• [b]Playing through the gripping story of Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield multiple times never gets old. Each playthrough uncovers new moments in the plot, and the expanded storylines add depth to what was already a compelling narrative. The tension and suspense keep you hooked. The story itself felt entirely good and you really feel yourself in these characters skin whenever something happens through it.[/b]

• [strike]Minuses of the Storyline[/strike]
1. [b]Predictable Plot Twists: Feels like the storyline contains predictable plot twists and lacks the element of surprise found in other games.[/b]
2. [b]Character Development: While the main characters are well-developed, some side characters feel underdeveloped and lack depth.[/b]
3. [b]Pacing Issues: The rhythm of the story can feel at times uneven, with some sections dragging on while others rush through important plot points.[/b]

[h3]Graphics and Visuals[/h3]
• [b]The game’s visuals are truly amazing and exceptional. The detailed environments and lifelike character models make Raccoon City feel terrifyingly real (no joke). Whether it's the lighting or the gruesome detail on zombies, the graphics never cease to impress, even after some first impressions the good graphics are there and you can see the developers wanted to make a maximum Vibe out of it. While the game uses dynamic lighting effectively to create a tense atmosphere, there are moments when the lighting can be too dark, making it difficult to see important details or navigate through certain areas. Also there are rare issues with textures popping in late or not loading correctly, breaking immersion but thats very rare and per general  you will very very rare see them or never at all tbh.[/b]
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3352501052

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
• [b]The gameplay remains engaging throughout. The survival horror mechanics, like managing good resources and solving intricate puzzles, are perfectly balanced. The over-the-shoulder camera and updated controls make the game accessible while retaining the challenge. Even after countless hours, the combat and exploration don't lose their edge.[/b]
• [b]Also i'd hate myself if i didn't named actual gameplay issues that i noticed some ''Loyal'' players in fan-base avoid or ignore to say at all, but i will do it.[/b] 
1. [b]Repetitive Puzzles: Some players find the puzzles repetitive and not particularly challenging. The same mechanics tend to be reused, leading to a lack of variety.[/b]
2. [b]Inventory Management: The limited inventory space can be frustrating, especially when you're in the heat of the moment and need to select items quickly, you will deal with that all the time so be prepared for any scenario.[/b]
3. [b]AI Behavior: Enemy AI can be inconsistent. Sometimes the zombies  can feel too predictable at times, while at other times, their behavior doesn't make logical sense.[/b]

[h3]Sound Design[/h3]
• [b]The sound design is impeccable. The chilling soundtrack and realistic sound effects amplify the horror elements, making every encounter with zombies and monsters nerve-wracking. Wearing headphones truly immerses you in the game’s super realistic atmosphere.[/b]

[h3]Replayability[/h3]
• [b]I can attest to the game’s incredible replay value. Multiple endings, different character paths, and various difficulty levels ensure that each playthrough offers something new. Plus, the added challenges and modes keep things fresh. If you're into such games, i am sure you will spend alot of hours.[/b]

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
• [b]Resident Evil 2 Remake stands out as a timeless classic reborn. It’s not just a nostalgic trip for fans of the original but a good game in its own right. With its great story, stunning visuals, and intense gameplay, it's a must-play for anyone who loves survival horror. Absolutely recommend.[/b]

A brilliant revival of a survival horror masterpiece! A must-have! Overall score: 10/10

As someone who has played the original, the Resident Evil 2 remake is a fantastic homage to a survival horror classic. The balance between nostalgia and modernization is perfect. It retains the heart-pounding tension of the original, but the enhancements in graphics, sound, and gameplay mechanics make it feel fresh for both new players and veterans alike. The atmosphere of dread is constant, and Mr. X's persistent hunting is one of the best implementations of a pursuer in modern games. It's stressful and exhilarating all at once. The only downside might be for those who are less familiar with survival horror mechanics—it can feel overwhelming at times, especially with the scarcity of resources. Overall, Capcom’s Resident Evil 2 remake is a near-flawless experience that sets a high bar for future remakes. Whether you’re a fan of the series or a newcomer to the genre, this game is a must-play.

Story: 10/10

Set in the familiar, yet terrifying, Raccoon City, Resident Evil 2 follows two protagonists: Leon S. Kennedy, a rookie cop on his first day of duty, and Claire Redfield, a young woman searching for her missing brother, Chris. The story remains faithful to the original, with each protagonist having their own unique campaign. While Leon’s path revolves more around his duties as a police officer and survival, Claire’s narrative introduces a more emotional aspect, especially with her relationship with Sherry Birkin. The narrative unfolds with a mix of mystery and tension, as the characters navigate the deadly city overrun by zombies and grotesque bio-organic weapons, most notably the relentless Tyrant (Mr. X). Capcom’s updated storytelling fleshes out key moments from the original, adding more depth to the characters and their interactions.

Graphics: 10/10

Visually, the Resident Evil 2 remake is stunning. Powered by the RE Engine, the game showcases highly detailed environments and character models. The haunting atmosphere of Raccoon City's Police Department and the grimy, decaying streets are beautifully rendered with dynamic lighting and textures. Zombies look amazing, their flesh ripping apart with every gunshot, contributing to a deeply immersive horror experience. The facial animations, particularly for Leon, Claire, and other key characters, are incredibly lifelike, helping to add emotional weight to cutscenes and interactions.

Sound: 10/10

The sound design in RE2 is integral to the horror experience. From the distant moans of zombies to the ominous, heavy footsteps of Mr. X, the game uses sound to keep players on edge. The eerie music is used sparingly, but effectively, heightening moments of tension. Silence, in particular, plays a significant role in creating dread, as you never know what lurks around the corner. The voice acting is excellent, with well-delivered lines that add authenticity to the characters and story.

Gameplay: 9.5/10

Resident Evil 2 masterfully combines modern mechanics with the franchise’s traditional survival horror elements. The over-the-shoulder camera, first introduced in Resident Evil 4, makes aiming and shooting much smoother than the original tank controls. However, this doesn’t diminish the game's difficulty. Ammunition is scarce, and conserving resources becomes a key strategy, forcing players to carefully consider whether to fight or run. Exploration is essential, with puzzles and locked doors scattered throughout the environments. The inventory management system is well-executed, with limited slots requiring players to make tough decisions about what to carry. Additionally, the enemy AI is relentless—zombies are tough to put down, and Mr. X’s constant stalking adds a layer of unpredictability and terror, keeping the pressure high throughout.

Replay Value: 8.5/10

One of the strongest aspects of RE2 is its replay value. Each campaign (Leon’s and Claire’s) provides a different perspective on the story, and completing one unlocks a second scenario for the other character, offering more layers of the plot and different gameplay experiences. Additionally, Capcom has included several unlockables, such as costumes and weapons, as well as extra modes like the 4th Survivor and Tofu Survivor, which provide challenging but fun diversions from the main story.

The graphics are nothing short of phenomenal. The detail in the environments, from the dimly lit police station to the eerie sewers, creates an immersive experience that pulls you in and won’t let go. Each location is meticulously designed, encouraging exploration and rewarding players with both lore and hidden treasures.

Gameplay is fluid and intuitive, with an over-the-shoulder perspective that modernizes the controls while maintaining the series' signature tension. The enemies, especially the iconic Lickers and the relentless Mr. X, are genuinely terrifying, making every encounter feel life-or-death. The combat system balances action and strategy, encouraging players to conserve ammo and make tactical decisions.

The story remains true to the original while adding new layers of depth. The character development of Leon and Claire is compelling, making their journey through the horrors of Raccoon City even more engaging. The voice acting and motion capture bring them to life in ways that resonate emotionally with players.

Puzzles are well-designed, blending seamlessly with the gameplay without feeling forced or tedious. Each challenge feels rewarding to solve, adding to the overall sense of accomplishment as you navigate through the game’s terrifying world.

The soundtrack enhances the atmosphere perfectly, with chilling scores that heighten the sense of dread and urgency. Whether you’re creeping through the dark or facing a horde, the audio experience is masterfully crafted.

In summary, Resident Evil 2 remake is a triumph that honors its predecessor while establishing itself as a benchmark for modern survival horror. It’s a game that not only pays homage to the past but also paves the way for the future of the genre. Whether you’re a longtime fan or a newcomer, this game is a must-play experience that will leave you on the edge of your seat.

I’ve always been afraid to dive into horror games, especially zombie-filled ones like Resident Evil 2. But after taking the plunge, not only did I finish the main campaign, I also completed the Second Run—and I’m so glad I did!

My Experience:

Terror and Thrills: From the first moment you step into the Raccoon City Police Department, the tension is insane. Every hallway, every shadow had me on edge, but the atmosphere is so immersive that I couldn't stop playing.
Conquering My Fear: I was genuinely afraid to play, but the mix of horror and the thrill of survival kept me hooked. The way the game balances terror with action is masterful—enough to scare, but not enough to make me quit.
Second Run is a Must: After finishing the first campaign, I immediately jumped into the Second Run. The alternate scenarios and added difficulty made it feel fresh and challenging. It’s almost like playing a whole new game!

Why It’s 10/10:

Incredible Atmosphere: The sound design, lighting, and visuals are so well done. You never feel safe, and that’s what makes it so good.
Puzzles and Exploration: Resident Evil 2 nails the balance between combat and puzzle-solving, keeping things tense and rewarding as you progress.
Mr. X: Need I say more? The moments when he’s stalking you are pure adrenaline. His relentless pursuit was both terrifying and awesome.

Final Verdict:

For someone who avoided horror games, I found myself absolutely hooked on Resident Evil 2. The fear, the survival, the satisfaction of completing both runs—this is a perfect 10/10 for me. If you’re hesitant like I was, take the leap—you won’t regret it!

This game is fun for a first time playthrough, once as Leon and once as Claire to get the full story. It is really cool going through the good ol' police station in 3D, having the zombies be slow but very damage-spongy makes for an interesting approach to the game, and the Mr. X mechanic is quite interesting and adds a cool dynamic to the first half of the game. I am not denying that the game is pretty good, I would just state that this game is an 8 outta 10 at best, and insanely over-rated / over-hyped. The 96% this has on Steam is insanity, but not as insane as having this game be a nominee for 2019 game of the year (I guess it was a pretty rough year for gaming. Why wasn't DMC 5 a nominee? Seriously? What a joke!)

I guess if I had to state my biggest gripes in no particular order, it'd be as follows:

1) The base game is pretty simple and easy once you figure out the general mechanics, it doesn't deviate from the formula too much. Then, classic to a lot of more recent Capcom games, going to the hardest difficulty from the standard difficulty is such a chasm of difference... Like maybe have a regular "hard" difficulty and rename "hardcore" to "insane" or something. Why not? The only time I died on standard was when I had to face....

2) ...The boss fights. The boss fights in this game are all gimmick fights where you die a bunch as a beginner's trap, then you realize "oh, I'm just supposed to wait?" or "oh, I'm just supposed to use this finicky crane?" or "oh, it's just a QTE where I have to memorize the boxes I need to dodge?" They were just all kinda lame. You either knew the gimmick, or it was your first time playing. Just not very good design.

3) No replay value. In the OG PS1 game, you had Claire A / Leon B, Leon A / Claire B scenarios where the cutscenes and plot revelations would be slightly different. You'd also unlock a bunch of crazy modes, and have a Survivors mode with a bunch of different characters with different load outs, you'd have one bomb defusing mode where you have to hunt them down, it was a lot and always fun revisiting your old save file every few years. In this game you just have LEON AND CLAIRE, that's it, whoever has the second run has Mr. X in the mansion earlier. Then the DLC modes, 3 of them play the exact same, where you go through the station/sewers from a different starting point as a different character picking up items and surviving. The 4th DLC mode has you running through the station/sewers but with no item pickups. Bottom line is they all play exactly the same as the base game, but less fun and uninspired. What happened to all the cool extra modes from RE7? That was fantastic! This is just kind of lame.

4) General nitpicky stuff. Combat/aiming up-close can feel glitchy, zombie's reach can feel elastic (kinda BS, to be honest), the sound design is all over the place with some sounds being extremely muffled and others making your ears bleed. Another thing is when you die the first time to gimmicky bosses, the game over screen asks if you want to swap to the lowest difficulty which YOU CANNOT REVERSE! This option is the default selection too, which is madness! If you don't catch what happened and are mashing keys/buttons to get back into the game, and then save, congrats: your save file is Fked! Game design like that should be punishable by death. To quote AVGN: WHAT WERE THEY THINKING!?!

Anyway, it still is a good game, I'm not taking that away from Capcom and the fans, but for this game to be a 96% on Steam and be a 2019 game of the year contender makes it so people approach this game with very, VERY high expectations, which this game just flat-out does NOT live up to. It's a pretty good 8 outta 10 that if you can get on sale, makes for a nice one-time playthrough before you uninstall, move onto the next game, and then forget all about this one.
