Resident Evil 2 is a survival horror game created by Capcom, launched in 1998 for the legendary PlayStation. It garnered a lot of praise and fans, making it one of the most iconic and profitable series in gaming. I never managed to play it, even when I had my PlayStation. The game always scared the ♥♥♥♥ out of me because I was around 6 at the time and I didn't understand English yet. However, my cousins always liked the game and played while I watched (while covering my eyes in fear). The series, especially the second game, always had that strange and mysterious magnetism on me because of that. Years later, Capcom Remade the game. New graphics, new platforms, new tweaks and new approach. I will not be comparing the two versions of the game because I did not play the original. This is the review of someone that never played this series before, and it will be written from a totally fresh "outsider" perspective. 
	Resident Evil 2 Remake is a survival horror game launched by Capcom in 2019. It excels in everything that it sets out to do and should be the gold standard for modern horror games. The game is a blend of 3rd-person shooter and puzzle, with a big coat of horror over everything. Resident Evil 2 works in a "scenario" model, which means that at the beginning, you are given the option to choose between two playable characters: Claire or Leon. Your first playthrough will be with that first selected character and after that, you will have to choose the other one to witness the "true ending" and have a more complete experience of the story, characters and gameplay. The scenarios are similar, however some side characters and items do change substantially, and the two stories intertwine along the way (especially at the end). It is highly recommended to play both scenarios back-to-back because the game demands some skills from the player along the way that build into one another. The game has a godlike level design, and it expects a good grasp of it from the player. Yes, you have access to a map, but the enemy distribution and escape routes are made in such a way that you must make quick decisions to avoid attrition and waste of resources, while trying to make sense of some puzzles. This is empowering and puts the game in the hands of the player while creating new challenges that put you on the edge. This blends seamlessly with my next point: horror. The improved graphics gave texture and realism to the various situations in which our heroes find themselves, which greatly enhanced the horror factor because now things have weight and presence. 
	While the graphical quality is top tier, I cannot make this review without mentioning the most effective way that the game scares you: sound. The sound design is so well-made that you get goosebumps in almost every encounter. Not only in encounters, but the whole level oozes danger and mystery with well-timed and realistic sound effects that make it feel like something is always in the corner waiting for you. From the glass shattering to the water drops and doors slamming in the distance, everything is hellbent on making you feel uncomfortable. After all that, we still have to touch on the gameplay, and let me tell you, it does not disappoint. Your health and movement are perfectly balanced: you are not too weak and slow, but at the same time, your mistakes can be very costly, which makes you consider and think your actions. This comes into play with the resource management since you can easily run out of ammo or healing items, making the whole experience feel calculated and almost turn-based, and with the constant fear that the game instills, you are always trying to plan ahead of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that is waiting in the next room. Puzzle-wise, the game is also good, with puzzles that are often simple in a way that does not overstay their welcome but still offer a little challenge and a change of pace from the constant fear and adrenaline. The puzzles are also a good indicator of your progress: since you are always backtracking and looking for new items, they often act as obstacles that, when solved, give good rewards and development in the map and story, opening new pathways and shortcuts. 
	Overall, an amazing game worth playing and praising.

### Resident Evil 2: Short Review

**Overview**  
Released in 2019, Resident Evil 2 is a modern remake of the classic 1998 survival horror game. Developed by Capcom, it revitalizes the original with stunning graphics, improved mechanics, and a richer narrative.

**Gameplay**  
The game shifts to an over-the-shoulder camera perspective, offering a more immersive experience. Players control Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield, solving puzzles, managing limited inventory, and facing terrifying zombies. Combat is strategic, with a focus on resource management, making every encounter tense and thrilling.

**Graphics and Sound**  
Visually, the game is a standout, with detailed environments and impressive lighting effects that create a haunting atmosphere. The audio design enhances immersion, featuring unsettling soundscapes and strong voice acting.

**Narrative**  
The story remains true to the original while expanding character backstories and themes of survival and horror in the face of bioweapon catastrophe.

**Conclusion**  
Resident Evil 2 is a masterful remake that balances nostalgia with modern gaming standards. It’s a must-play for horror fans, delivering a captivating experience that honors the legacy of its predecessor.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is nothing short of a triumph in the survival horror genre. From the moment I stepped into Raccoon City, I was completely immersed in its haunting atmosphere, expertly crafted environments, and an engaging storyline that honors the original while delivering a fresh experience.

Graphics and Sound: The visuals are stunning, with meticulously detailed environments that make every corner of the Raccoon Police Department feel alive and claustrophobic. The lighting effects create an eerie ambiance that keeps you on edge, and the sound design is equally impressive. Every creak, growl, and distant gunshot pulls you deeper into the terrifying world, amplifying the tension at every turn.

Gameplay: The controls are intuitive yet challenging, providing a perfect balance of tension and excitement. The revamped mechanics enhance the classic gameplay, allowing for smoother navigation and more strategic encounters with the terrifying enemies. In preperation for RE9 I decided to play through Resident Evil 2 Remake, 3 Remake, and 4 Remake.

RE2R overall was a decent game, but it was also very flawed in some places. I started with Leon first as that felt like the more fitting run to start with as I thought he was the "main" character (I'll get to that). The Metroidvania-style exploration side of the game was easily the best part; exploring the R.P.D., unlocking areas and solzing puzzles, finding new weapons and equipment, and avoiding Mr. X was really where this game shined its brightest and really flexed the best it had to offer, and this is where I had the most fun. I've never been big into horror games but this game actually wasn't as scary as I expected, that's not to say though that I didn't get jumpscared a few times cause I absolutely did and there were plenty of moments where I felt afraid to move through a particular area/past certain enemies. The combat and gunplay also felt great, each gun felt like it had a usecase and choosing when and how to use your ammo/grenades/knives to most effectively get through an area while using as little as possible was always a fun challenge. The dismemberment system, while I didn't engage with it much, was really neat and presented you with the choice, or sometimes challenge, of either just immobilising an enemy to conseve ammo or kill them to make traversal easier.

The boss fights though are the first thing that really let this game down. Most of them are just not fun and have some sort of stupid gimmick that makes the fight really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sometimes and not enjoyable (I'm looking at YOU William fight #2). The first William fight I spammed the knife and accidentally killed him very quickly lol. The third William fight with Leon I will say though I actually really enjoyed, I felt it was well balanced and fair and I didn't have that "this is so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" feeling at all during it. That's about the only praise I have though as the bosses past this point once again sucked, and don't even get me started on Claire's boss fights! Somehow they're even worse!!

Speaking of Claire, her run for me felt ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ terrible and I did not enjoy a single moment during her run. It was just frustrating to play and I was constantly running into "this is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" moments that just left me feeling miserable and having a bad time. The worst part though, for me, wasn't the boss fights (which are BAD) or the combat (which somehow felt a lot worse) but how baffling her story is. It directly contradicts and conflicts with a good chunk of Leon's story which makes the overall story of the game really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ confusing. The way I've had to look at it is that if something happens that conflicts between the 2 stories (i.e. Claire fighting William in the lab and his wife surviving for longer than in Leon's run) then what happened in Claire's run is "canon" and Leon's isn't, and this really sucks to me. I know some stuff with Claire's run was really rushed but it really feels like 0 thought was put into the story of her run at all.

I would say that if you want to play RE2R for the gameplay play Leon's story, and if you want the story play Claire's, but to get the true/best/canon ending you HAVE to play both story's and I really hate when games do that; it's never fun.

Overall I do think that RE2R, despite my many complaints, is a decent and fun enough game to still recommend you play it if you're at all interested. I think if I were to ever replay it I'd just stick to Leon's run as that is where I had the most fun.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is everything I wanted it to be. It respects the original while fully updating it for modern gaming. From the moment I stepped foot in the rain-soaked streets of Raccoon City, I knew this wasn't just a remake—it was something more. The darkness crept in from every corner, with only my flickering flashlight to cut through the gloom. I could hear the shuffling of the undead before I saw them, my pulse quickening as I raised my gun, unsure if I had enough ammo to survive. Every bullet felt precious, every missed shot a stab of regret.

Navigating the halls of the RPD felt eerily familiar but new at the same time. The attention to detail was astounding—creaking doors, distant groans, and the oppressive silence between each terrifying encounter. When I first heard the heavy, echoing footsteps of Mr. X, my heart froze. Knowing he was out there, relentless and unstoppable, made every move a calculated risk. I would stop, hold my breath, and listen, praying that the sound of his boots would fade away. But he was always there, hunting me.

The puzzles provided a brief respite, though never long enough to feel safe. I was constantly glancing over my shoulder, the tension never letting up. And yet, amidst the fear, there was something beautiful about the world Capcom had rebuilt. It wasn't just the upgraded graphics or enhanced lighting—it was the atmosphere. Every shadow, every bloodstain told a story.

By the time I made it to the sewers, I was a nervous wreck, but there was no turning back. I was fully immersed in this nightmare, living each moment of survival as if it were my own. Resident Evil 2 Remake didn’t just revive a classic—it pulled me into the horror, and I loved every second of it.

I was the one who not following RE series and I attach for this one, At first I just bought this game for fun during the winter discount because it was cheap. but after playing it it is very good and surprising. Initially, from my perspective, I only played the classic Re 4 and didn't play the original Re 2 in the past, I was very happy with this remake. this is my review

Pros
•	The story is very simple but interesting about Raccoon City which has been infected with a virus outbreak from Umbrella Corp. We can see two sides of the story from 2 POVs, namely Leon and Claire, who of course have different paths.
•	The mechanical gameplay is also very unique, but of course with very good updates to suit this era of release. Very action-packed and satisfying with every shot
•	The graphics themselves are very beautiful even at normal settings. Starting from the light, shadows and environment, it is very well described. From the rainy weather until entering the lab, everything was pictured well
•	for the location set which is described in a very horror way, we as players are made uncomfortable in each location and it is really very dark in places where we only rely on flashlights
•	There are also many types of weapon variations, from small to large, for survival purposes, it is also easy to understand, from bullets to healing, everything is easy to get and easy to understand while making it.
•	The conversations between the characters also have emotion and soul, the voice actors and cutscenes are also very well portrayed
•	there are many and unique puzzles and hidden places that are very challenging to solve
•	Boss fights are also easy to fight and understand, even though they take a little effort to beat, they are very exciting to fight
•	Plenty of hidden items, weapons and secrets to find, with exploration rewarding attentive and careful players.
•	Varied, challenging gameplay situations that keep the experience fresh from start to end.
•	Audio horror factor hearing the zombies constantly banging their hands on windows and doors trying to break into the police station and it also helps gameplay wise when a zombie you thought was dead suddenly starts snarling back to life.

Cons
•	For big games, the playing hours may be too short, but I understand this is because it maintains the tempo and originality of the previous series
•	No dodge feature, I know it's said here that Leon and Claire are beginners but the dodge feature also needs to be included. I often die and run out of bullets because there is no this feature
•	Apart from zombies like that, we have to have a knife or throwing item which is not effective here
•	Zombies that are shot can also come back to life, which is very troublesome here and uses up a lot of bullets

Conclusion : this is the best remake game I have ever played. I'm glad they made a remake of the game because it can bring in new players like me who never played this series before. This series also made me suddenly happy with the Resident Evil series and wanted to follow this game series.

Essentially combining the two for one larger experience. You end up with about 30 hours of story, which I think is plenty. Especially since at this point in time you can get both games for about $10.

There were a couple things I disliked, but I would consider them minor. Some graphical issues. I also found it odd that RE1 took the time for your character to take each step down stairs. In 2 and 3, they just kinda float down. Something I missed from 4 (The original RE game I played, so I'm very biased) was targeting limbs on an enemy caused them to react. Shoot in the arm, they grab their arm. Shoot in the leg, they drop to a knee. While these occur earlier in the series, the remakes came out well after 4. I feel like that would have been worth their time to add to these games. It just makes the monsters feel much more real when they react to where you shoot them.

Overall though, I really liked 2+3. Combining the two resolves the length issue most people complain about. I enjoyed Mr X and Nemesis in their own ways. By and large its very pretty and ran well on my system. I was following along with the story, never skipping cut scenes. Leon is amazing (Again, 4 was my first game) but Jill and Claire might be some of my favorite protagonists you can play in video games.

From the moment you step into the Raccoon City Police Department (RPD), Resident Evil 2 grips you with its oppressive atmosphere. The game’s visual overhaul, powered by the RE Engine, brings incredible detail to the environments, making every dark hallway, bloodstained floor, and crumbling wall feel both realistic and terrifying. The use of lighting and shadows, combined with the impeccable sound design, creates an atmosphere of tension and dread that never lets up.

The over-the-shoulder camera, a departure from the original’s fixed perspectives, modernizes the gameplay while maintaining the horror. This shift provides a more immersive and fluid experience without sacrificing the claustrophobic, heart-pounding moments that Resident Evil is known for. Each encounter with zombies is nerve-wracking, as enemies are tougher and more unpredictable, requiring careful resource management and precise aiming to survive. Every shot counts, and the game constantly pushes you to make smart decisions, whether it's about conserving ammo or deciding when to engage or flee.

Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield, the game's dual protagonists, are wonderfully brought to life with updated character models, performances, and voice acting. Their individual stories, which overlap in intriguing ways, add depth to the overall narrative. Playing through both characters' campaigns offers unique perspectives on the outbreak, with different weapons, scenarios, and enemies, encouraging replayability.

One of the standout features of Resident Evil 2 is the return of the infamous Mr. X. His relentless pursuit of the player throughout the police station is one of the most terrifying aspects of the game. The constant threat of being stalked by this towering, unstoppable force adds a layer of suspense that keeps you on edge at all times. His heavy footsteps echoing through the halls as he gets closer is a masterful touch that increases the tension dramatically.

Puzzles, another hallmark of the series, have been revamped as well. They strike the perfect balance between challenging and intuitive, rewarding careful exploration and observation without feeling frustrating. The backtracking and item management that defined the original Resident Evil 2 are present here, but they’re streamlined in a way that respects modern players' expectations without losing the essence of what made the original game’s design so compelling.

The game also offers plenty of fan service for longtime players, from familiar locations to iconic enemies like the Lickers, but it does so in a way that feels fresh. The addition of unlockable modes like The 4th Survivor and Tofu Survivor provides extra challenges for hardcore fans, keeping the experience engaging long after the credits roll.

In short, Resident Evil 2 is not just a successful remake—it’s a survival horror masterpiece. Capcom has managed to recapture the magic of the original while making it accessible and exhilarating for a new generation of players. Whether you’re a veteran of the series or a newcomer, Resident Evil 2 delivers a terrifying, unforgettable experience that stands among the best in the genre.

[h1]Capcom gave clamoring fans exactly what they wanted. Each part of the experience whether it is the story, gameplay, visuals, or audio have all come together making Resident Evil 2 a great.[/h1]


[h1]A little bit about old classic:[/h1]
[b]Resident Evil 2 from 1998[/b] is an amazing game and one of the best horror games of all time. With this, I think, hardly anyone will argue. Her ideas were sometimes far ahead of their time, hitting the ceiling of the technologies of the time: two playable characters, four interconnected story campaigns, several additional....


[h1]Changes:[/h1]
Despite the sometimes photorealistic [i](RE Engine really suits the game)[/i] graphics, [i]«over-the-shoulder view»,[/i] and dozens of smaller changes, the remake doesn't forget about the lessons of the classic [i](1–3)[/i] series for a second. [i]Resident Evil 7,[/i] for all its merits, only reminded of the golden days of the franchise, but RE2-2019 is a classic, just brought up to modern standards.

I want to run [i][b]RE2 (2019)[/b][/i] as both characters, just to… Well, to be with them again. Twenty one  f🇺​​ck🇮​​🇳g years later. A man who does not know the series and has not seen the original, will spit on the history;
don’t throw tomatoes at me for these words, but the plot, to put it mildly, has never been Resident Evil strong point – and the remake does not change the situation, even though he’s trying really hard.


[h1]Ammo is a luxury![/h1]
Whoever you choose, you have to do the same thing: survive and try to get out of Raccoon City as soon as possible. And this task, as in the original, is far from being the easiest. The whole city is teeming with zombies, there is never enough space in the inventory, there is never too much ammunition.

And it is in this area that [i][b]RE2 (2019)[/b][/i] pleases the most, because the remake perfectly understands the essence of the original source and presents where it can be improved without changing the original. Indeed, at its core, [i][b]RE2 (2019)[/b], like RE2-1998,[/i] is a marathon test of stressful thinking and the player’s ability to make decisions under growing psychological pressure. It's not so much the zombies themselves that are frightening, but the possible consequences of meeting with them - the loss of exhaustible resources.


[h1]About the game:[/h1]
Capcom is great at combining cosmetics with practical ones: zombies waddle, slowly, uncertainly, unpredictably swaying from side to side. They are just hard to hit, and sometimes shots cause them to deviate, so quickly putting a couple of bullets in the head will not work. What if there are more zombies? At least two or three? This is already a huge waste of resources.

[i][b]RE2 (2019)[/b][/i] never makes you feel safe; zombies turn from simple monsters into obstacles. You have to think not only about how to get to a particular location, but also about the way to get there. What to sacrifice and what to save.

This feeling of insecurity, as sticky as a wet T-shirt, increases exponentially when [b][i]Mr. X, the «Tyrant»,[/i][/b] is added to the case. Especially when he's walking five paces behind you, that huge sense of tension haunts you. Thanks to modern technology, the big guy now chases you around and reacts quickly to the sound of gunfire, and lags behind the main character only in strictly specified plot moments. And that’s usually not for long.


[h1]Verdict:[/h1]
[i][b]Resident Evil 2 2019[/b] is the rarest example of an almost impeccable rethinking of material that has already been worked out more than once. And the industry, which still cannot decide what the difference is between a remake, re-release and remastered, now there’s someone to learn from! This is how remakes should be done. Now Capcom simply has no excuse in case the hypothetical Resident Evil 9 fails.

This remake brings an important change for the camera , the third-person perspective retains the survival horror essence and improves it by making everything more immersive.


The story can be played with two protagonists : Leon and Claire and after if you finish one playthrough the other is slightly different and for those hungry for more content there are extra stories and a lot of challenges to complete. It's impossible to finish everything in one run or two, i decided to complete the campaigns without touching the hard achievements but more of that later in the cons section.

From the moment i entered the gas station i was impressed by the graphics ..it's a great feel to be able to play at this level of quality a game released so many years ago but now with modern textures and effects.
Character models, particularly for Leon, Claire, and the various monsters, are incredibly rendered. The facial animations are detailed and expressive.


I really liked the gore elements ,you can dismember enemies and wounds can look amazing ..there is blood everywhere and the enemies look fantastic..but they're not so smart ..you can't have both i suppose!
The tension and the fear element is present and you can really feel it, i believe its mostly due to how vulnerable you feel, but don't worry once you get to know the game areas and how to avoid enemies it becomes a lot easier.


My problems with this game was the puzzles and the stupid backtracking and the inventory management where you need to run half of the map to put a item inside an item box just to have the necessary spaces to solve another puzzle. The ammo is scarce and for greater difficulty runs you need to learn everything inside out, i also didn't like how i needed to repeat the same puzzles in my second playthrough that's lazy level design if you ask me.


In conclusion Resident Evil 2 deserves all the positive feedback it received on steam, it's a great horror game and if there are people like me who haven't played it yet ,try it and have patience because it's worth every second of your time !

What makes a good game is not frame rate, or how detailed the graphics are, or how many levels it has, or how much content there is, or how big the game world is, or how good the animations are.

Great games make you feel. The feelings that I get to experience while playing a game, or the lack of feelings, is what decides whether a game is good or not.

This game makes me feel. And not in the way that you’re guessing.

You probably think I have some type of nostalgia for the original RE2. Nope. I didn’t like that game. I feel nothing for the OG RE2. In fact, I have negative feelings towards it because the main thing I experienced while playing was boredom.

You’re second guess might be that the feels I got was from the games story. Nope. This game’s story is not good. The scripted story is not good.

The gameplay stories in this game. That’s what causes me to experience such strong feelings.

This game can cause me to feel such desperation. Playing on hardcore with limited saves, or playing no-ink ribbon runs means that every single decision I make matters. 

The real story of this game, is not what Capcom wrote. It’s not the story that the voice actors read. That is not the real story. The real stories are the gameplay stories. 

The one time I literally screamed out loud “RUN!!!” because I hadn’t saved in a long time and my plan to escape the Holding Cell area went up in flames. 

That one time when I was doing a no-ink ribbon run. I made it all the way to G2 with tons of resources. I barely got hit the entire game. But then misfortune happened and all my plans on how to defeat the boss went up in flames. 

Plan A. First 30 seconds of the boss fight - Fail. 
Plan B. First minute of the boss fight - Fail. 
Makeshift Plan C. Second minute of the boss fight - Fail. 
Makeshift Plan D. Fourth minute of the boss fight - Fail. 
Fifth minute of the boss fight - Game over. 

The last 6 hours… down the drain. Or was it? The feelings I got to experience. The triumphs during the journey leading up to the fight. The desperation during the fight. The despair afterwards. 

The desperation and fear I got to experience during that time where I had no health. A zombie banging on the door behind me and a licker on the ceiling in front of me in a narrow hallway. My only path to safety.

The triumph of making it from one corner of the map to the other with Mr. X chasing after me the whole time. Thinking on my feet since the zombies can break open doors and travel between rooms. 

The despair that I got to feel when plans A through D failed on the G2 boss fight on a run that had been going perfectly. I went from feeling smug to feeling despair in a matter of 5 minutes. 

How many other games can give you the opportunity to experience feelings like this?

Resident Evil 2 Remake is a graceful modernisation of the survival horror experience that Capcom pioneered and perfected all those years ago. Coming from RER the most significant change for me was the transition to an over a shoulder perspective and a dynamic camera that the player controls. This is the first survival horror game I’ve played with this style of camera, and while I do love the way that the fixed camera in RER frames each part of the mansion uniquely in a way that is very arresting and filmic, I also can’t deny that this shift allows for far better control of your character, makes exploration far more interactive as the player has to move and centre their camera to navigate and uncover items and importantly it facilitates proper robust third person shooting, where you need to precisely aim at the bobbing heads of each zombie, introducing a whole new dimension and element of tension to gameplay as aiming is completely in your control, every miss you feel that much more severely and every shot you land is equally more satisfying. 

Although you now have complete control of the camera, Capcom have done well to maintain the frequency of jump scares that dynamically arose when zombies would lurk between camera transitions or behind corners you can’t see around, leaping out and biting you suddenly. They have achieved this by centring the character towards the left side of the screen, keeping the proximity between camera and character tight and darkening environments a fair bit when compared with the PS1 original, this obscures zombies just enough so that you always have to be paying attention to avoid being bitten. Additionally, when you do get grabbed and bitten, you feel it more viscerally than ever before as the camera is able to pan extremely close, letting you really see the carnage when zombies chomp down on Claire or Leon’s neck. This phenomenon is vital to the experience that these games offer so I’m glad to see it hasn’t been diminished here. 

An outstanding addition in Resident Evil 2 Remake is the introduction of a pursuing super enemy. Mr X is far faster and more aggressive than any other enemy, he cannot be defeated only delayed or avoided and he will not stop hunting you until you complete certain objectives that allow you to escape from him briefly. Your encounters with him are unscripted as his AI will route different paths through the police station to catch up to you as you desperately try to advance where he obstructs you. This forces you to utilise the map to avoid dead ends and create diversions through the use of shortcuts just to slow him down and lead him away from where you need to go. His appearances are used sparingly to great effect, completely up ending the usual pace of the game, creating moments of immense tension that make the player frantic and genuinely frightened. Mr X is uniquely terrifying because of his excellent character design and animation which is intensely menacing and uncanny, the way he composedly marches towards you at a constant pace that never fluctuates embodies this completely.

Other than this though the gameplay here is decidedly very classic and similar to its predecessor. There are simple puzzles that involve referring to cryptic documents, corelating any useful information to your recent discoveries, examining and combining key items you’ve found which you must then use with the corresponding interactable aspect of the environment. You must frequently manage your inventory, evaluating whether it is necessary to carry an item at any given time as having more spaces free in your inventory will hopefully allow you to collect every item you find in a new part of the station you visit without needing to do a return trip after offloading, only to risk being bitten again by zombies you left alive or those that wake up. However not bringing enough healing items or the right weaponry and enough ammo can lead to a quick death, you must make educated guesses as to what you will need between save rooms. You must also make constant decisions about what type of weaponry to use when faced with combat, or if any at all as the resource is limited. For example, it is often best to use a handgun for dispatching isolated zombies as they are slow and pose the least threat, however if they are grouped up it would be best to use a grenade as using a handgun is inefficient and can lead to you getting overwhelmed quickly and bitten by two zombies simultaneously for extra damage to your health. Vitally you must conserve the use of strong weaponry for strong foes like the lickers, or boss encounters, as likely the quicker you can defeat them, the more damage you avoid taking, expending less of you finite healing resources. But each weapon and ammo take up space in your inventory and it is impossible to carry everything at once so you must always try to make do with what you are currently carrying. Item crafting also factors into resource management, as you can combine different colour herbs to achieve different mixtures with varying effects. Oftentimes it is better to stockpile blue and green herbs to combine with red herbs you find later as these mixtures have more powerful effects and take up the same amount of inventory space, however you may need to use green herbs separately to avoid death in some instances. The same goes for gunpowder as waiting to combine the right types can create ammo for powerful weapons that is otherwise fairly scarce.

The R.P.D is an incredible setting. The infusion of the pieces of art left behind from when it was a museum is distinct, with the sculptures oftentimes hiding vital secrets. Each room you visit is extremely detailed and has its own personality, these feel like real and individual spaces thanks to the breathtakingly varied interior decoration on display, with each prop and texture being carefully curated for each. The Library and Main Hall were particular favourites of mine. The game also uses music sparingly which allows you to really take in these environments deeply, letting you bask in the ambience they evoke and feel the loneliness that comes from navigating them by yourself. The layout and interconnectedness of the Station overall is ingenious, I love the way that you are woven through it, gradually reaching new parts of the map as you find more keys, exploration is engaging as you frequently need to consult your map to know where you need to head next, the path forward is almost never a straight line. RE2R trusts the player to figure things out instead of babying them with intrusive objective markers or hints. Some of the shortcuts you unlock are truly remarkable, such as the elevator that transports you from deep underground all the way back to where you started, the Main Hall. This was magical in a way that was very reminiscent of what Dark Souls made me feel the first time I played it.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is a clear example that more triple A games should stray away from sparse and flat open worlds in favour of creating smaller, curated and interior spaces that are actually in service of exploration and not just there to waste your time with emptiness and mindless traversal in a straight line towards an objective marker for minutes at a time.

A good blend of old and new

I was skeptical of this remake since its announcement, but most of my concerns were alleviated upon release and by playing it. There is some cut content, like the Giant Spiders and the iconic RE Crows, and a few areas here and there, but luckily there isn’t too much that’s been clipped from the original in this remake. 
Graphics are great. The music is good, just not on par with the classic soundtrack, so thank goodness it’s an option to swap it for the OG. The gameplay is solid, bringing back the over-the-shoulder third person camera popularized by (the original) RE4. Some things have been swapped around, like what items are where and some locations are in different zones from the original game, but it can be viewed as a positive for those of us that are overly familiar with the OG’s layout. And then there’s Mr. X himself. His revamped gameplay design is outstanding. Him being able to show up randomly or whenever you make too much noise and begin actively searching rooms for you is some of the most tense, nerve-wracking and fun challenges I’ve had in a horror game for a long time.

Really the only complaints I have about this game are the cut content (even if it was a relatively small amount) and the replacement of some of the original voice actors that were more then willing to come back. Sometimes there are a few lines that fell flat from some of the new actors that I feel the legacy actors would have delivered better. That, and the Ghost Survivors dlc is brutally hard at times. I imagine Souls fans would love that dlc.

Overall this is a better example of a step in the right direction for Resident Evil than RE7 or RE8 were. This is closer to the original vision of RE than those games, while doing a better job of incorporating newer elements.

So it's been a little over 5 years since this game has come out. In that span of time, I remember playing this in high school on a laptop that really had no business playing a game this graphically intensive, having been given a copy by someone I was friends with at the time, opting for the Xbox One version later to play with my dad at a respectable framerate and resolution, and returning as an adult in 2024 to a new machine altogether that can finally handle the PC version. That being said, having just played the original and the 2019 remake in a row in the span of maybe... 3 days between each other, I have some different opinions than I did at launch.

The game itself is not my favorite, and even the original wasn't my favorite despite being my introduction to the series. There's goofy choices that were made that make it generally difficult to play, I'd say the sewer section was the most questionable (though it was VERY welcomed to be expanded upon since it's so short in the original), the only real issue being the [spoiler]G Adults[/spoiler] having their own dedicated room with no space whatsoever and being spammed all throughout the sewers. It doesn't necessarily make it bad, but it made for a frustrating experience, nonetheless. The other points in the game that I would say were the most frustrating was [spoiler]fighting G (Birkin) in the crane area (seriously though, if you need a spoiler 5 years after release that's based on a 26 year old game, just play it :D)[/spoiler] and of course the ever famous [spoiler]giant alligator fight[/spoiler], mainly due to there being a chase that until you figure out the pattern is really just a trial and error situation which would be fine if not for the fact that it's a one hit death if you are bit.

The good things of this version include the original music and (some) sound effects being available alongside the new music and sounds (for a price, of course, unless you pre-ordered the game). There's also the new movement which isn't stiff in this version, though still being... "awkward" and flawed, I found myself having to stop moving while trying to run through a door a few times during the game as Leon/Claire would just run in circles trying to get into the door as they keep bumping into the wall, leading to a few moments of unfair damage being taken. Of course graphics are top notch, even now, the hair effects look nice although there's a weird pixel-y effect on them even at max graphics on an RTX 3060 at 1440p, but it's nothing that gets in the way, just an odd note. In other news, the final major upgrade I think is being able to freely look around the environment; it not being a game utilizing pre-rendered backgrounds this time, it allows for the ability to get up close and personal with random details in the environments like if you want to read a can of paint for example, although this obviously comes with a heavy performance hit by comparison.

In general, I still am not the biggest fan of RE2 remake, but looking back, my opinions of it being bad originally were likely based in nostalgia for plopping in a random PS1 disc my dad let me use and experiencing something I never seen in a game before, and looking at it with a fair and open minded lens as an adult, I can say it is a worthwhile experience, even if I'd suggest trying it on sale. It comes with 4 separate campaigns, two side missions to test your abilities (4th Survivor and the Tofu Survivor respectively), and a DLC set called the "Ghost Survivors" which focuses on characters like the mayor's daughter and even Robert Kendo, the gunshop owner, who originally have a whopping screen time of 2 minutes, each.

My final ranking for the game is a rock solid 7/10, graphics gets an 8/10 (maybe even a light 9/10), controls get an 8/10, and nostalgia value gets a 10/10. Not bad Capcom! <3

Playing the RE2 Remake for a few hours reminded me why I never liked this franchise. Back, forth, back, forth, ad infinitum. I remember playing the original when I was a kid. The remake is as frustrating as the original used to be.

The graphics of the remake are certainly a bit better and the camera angle and controls are certainly, incomparably better than the original. But the gameplay? Holy macaroni! They seemed to designed the “puzzles” in the most frustrating way possible. In order to get anywhere in this game you will find yourself going through the same corridors, rooms, halls, and space over and over again. It only gets worse as you play longer, because each puzzle has puzzle pieces that you can only discover/recover by going all the way to the highest floor, then all the way to the lowest manhole, back, forth, and again and again. That, it seems, used to be the idea of solving puzzles when they made the game.

I wish the remake had streamlined the puzzles so they could be resolved in a bit more linear way (going through the same passages and room only a million times instead of several million times).

Gameplay: 3/10
Graphics: 5/10
Controls: 7/10
Mechanics: 4/10 (cannot jump, cannot run fast enough, etc.)

Should you buy the game: Depends. If this is your first game in this genre, no. There are vastly better games with great storylines, mechanics, gameplay, and all (e.g. Metro). If you know exactly how the original used to play and you don’t mind the experience, then by all means.

Re-playability: 0/10 (once you play it through, you will need more than 2 decades to recover before you might attempt to play it again).

Horror factor: 5/10 (this is actually a high mark compared to how far the genre has come already).

It has a vastly different atmosphere, and in my opinion the main and most crucial difference is not the removal of "tank controls", nor the missing "door opening cutscenes" or any of these details many detractors complain about.
The main thing that makes the difference, for me, is the music.
The original game had music throughout the entire duration, with only a handful of quiet areas (and let me tell you...the sudden realisation that you were in an area without music...created some of the best tension). This remake, meanwhile, ditches the music for 90% of the game, trading it for silence and ambience sounds.
Both versions work wonders, but i legitimately think that apart for mechanical changes, this is the part that i felt the most when it comes to changes.

OG RE2 was my first game in the series, I played it on the N64 way back in the early 2000's so I was excited when this remake was made. This game is beautiful and terrifying at the same time. Each time a door is opened or a puzzle is solved I'd find myself tensing just in case something horrific decided to pick that moment to bust through the glass or drop from the ceiling. The monster designs are excellent though I didn't really enjoy how difficult the default zombies were to kill. That said the lickers, dogs and the infamous Mr. X were incredible. Special shout out to the Ivy zombies and their distinct breathing noises which gave me uncomfortable RE4 regenerator flashbacks!

Probably my only real gripe with this game, especially having played the living daylights out of the og, is how the A and B scenarios don't really line up. In the original the character in the first run would encounter different bosses (mostly G and his varieties) while the second run character would square off manly against Mr. X. The characters would also run into each other with greater frequency and decisions made in the first run would affect the second character's run. This in turn led to four distinct scenarios (Leon A, Claire B, Claire A, Lean B) that made it worth playing the game at least four times. Here the changes are so minor and the stories less interconnected that not much changes from run to run, it's a bit disappointing especially considering how they managed to create 4 distinct yet interwoven stories back in the cartridge era but now with all our advancements in tech they ended up cutting content. 

Still, I greatly enjoyed my time with this game and if you love survival horror this game will definitely scratch that itch!

[h1]Unwritten, Unsee (A Novice No Longer)[/h1]

My first day on duty was meant to be a moment of welcome, but I step instead into a city unrecognisable, awash in chaos. The very streets of Raccoon City seem to have swallowed my expectations whole. I imagine the offices where I should have been greeted—perhaps the lights dimmed low, the laughter of colleagues mingling with playful jests, the warmth of camaraderie. I can almost see it: the welcome I once envisioned. But as I take in the reality before me, that image slips away like mist at dawn, leaving only the grey despair of what’s left behind.

The sign above the door, though misspelled with a clumsy hand, moves me in a way I cannot quite explain. It is not the inaccuracy that strikes me, but something deeper—the stark absence of what was meant to be. I recall, with surprising clarity, the words I once spoke to Claire: that we would find sanctuary within these walls. Yet now, there is no one left but Marvin, whose life hangs by a thread. In the absence of others, I am forced to become my own protector. But if I turn to others for help and find none—do I, then, take up the mantle of those fallen, carry their burden of duty? This reversal, this sudden shift of responsibility, is as unsettling as it is profound. Am I capable of guarding myself? Or is survival defined, in its purest form, by the simple act of surviving?

This shift, sudden and sharp, mirrors the feeling of donning the officer’s uniform. It’s as if the weight of it changes everything. In those moments when no one else steps forward, I am left to assume command. My desk, once a quiet sanctuary, is now piled high with paperwork, bathed in shadow. The sounds that fill the space are not the clatter of daily tasks, but the low, guttural growls of those who were once my comrades. 
They teach us how to manage every conceivable crisis, but this... This is different. 
This is something that even the most seasoned veterans could not have prepared for. I feel like a rookie—and indeed, I am—but in a city teetering on the edge of ruin, I see that the world outside is no different from the chaos that now inhabits these walls.

As I move through the corridors, trying to offer aid where I can, a question lingers in my mind: can one truly be taught to survive? Before the uniform, I was the one crying out for help. Now, clothed in it, I find that I must offer aid to myself. Can there be a manual for survival, a guide that existed even before this outbreak—something that could have prepared me? Marvin’s only answer is a gesture—a silent communication that speaks volumes.

Marvin, wounded and fading, helped me lower a metal shutter to protect us from the infected. He was there when I needed him, but does this make me a survivor? Or was it simply luck that spared me? If luck is all that defines survival, then this journey is nothing but a series of fortunate accidents—a fluke. But I have training, experience. I am no blank slate. Marvin, even in his injury, understands more than I give him credit for. He sees what I am capable of. What I am becoming. In this hellish place, I am starting to find a rhythm—a way to dance with the darkness.

Survival is no mere game of chance. It is the application of everything one has learned, everything one has absorbed. It is not simply the act of firing a weapon, but the ability to remain composed in the face of the inexplicable—to trace the threads of chaos and follow them, even as everything collapses around you. Each step I take is a refinement of what the academy taught me. Yet it is not the length of my survival that matters, but the quality of it—the sheer determination to face every new horror that emerges from the shadows.

Every step becomes an act of growth, of learning how to inhabit this nightmare. Fear often whispers in my ear, urging me to act rashly, to fire without thought, to let panic rule. But survival, I have learned, is about knowing when to pause—when to hold your breath and wait for the right moment. I must face what’s before me with purpose, with clarity. Only then can I unearth the secrets the precinct guards so fiercely. Secrets that no manual could ever prepare me for.

The lessons I am learning now, they are becoming part of me—just as natural as breathing. There is no manual that could contain the wisdom I am gaining. Survival is found in the actions I take with each new step I make. When I see Claire again, I realise this is what it means to still be alive. Not because we understand survival in some perfect, textbook sense—but because we have each made the choice to keep going, to keep learning, to keep striving. We are not novices anymore. We are shaped by our efforts, tempered by the fire of this trial. We are not walking blind, but with a quiet understanding of what we must do next.

And what of the novice? What is a novice truly? Someone new to their profession, to the game of life itself, with all its unpredictable twists and turns. With that one gesture, Marvin made it clear to me: I am no longer a novice. The strength I seek is not in others, but within myself. Just as I have discovered the hidden ‘Wellcome Leon’ signs upon my desk, I now see, in this place, the irony of learning survival. It is a lesson that was always there, hidden in the shadows, waiting to be uncovered.

In this precinct, all that remains is the echo of protection—a faint, lingering trace of what once was. Yet what I am discovering now, amid the wreckage, is not only survival, but its true form: the constant, arduous effort to remain oneself, to retain one’s virtues amidst the wreckage. This is the essence of succour—meeting Sherry and Claire, offering what little we can. And then there is Ada Wong—a mystery who stands apart from us all. She is neither a novice nor a survivor, but something else entirely. A secret, perhaps, reserved only for the uninitiated.

Though none of us are experts, we have turned this trial into something more—a chance for refinement, a recalibration of our very selves. This is how we survive—not through luck, nor by simply outlasting the days. And now, as I face Mr. X, it is as if he is the final, unspoken challenge—the last obstacle in a journey that has already begun to shape me into something I had not known I could be: a survivor.

[h2]📝 Main Pros, Cons, and Suggestions:[/h2]

🟩 Pros:

+ You are playing in enclosed areas, but you are not forced to "follow this path" or "that path". You plan and create your own route to your destination.
+ When you hear the word "Puzzle", you think of something boring, right? Resident Evil 2 changes that term with its brilliant and unique puzzles.
+ You can kind of pick your own playstyle. You can run and gun among the creatures, or take a more tactical approach.
+ You really get into the universe and the surrounding environment around you.
+ Satisfying replayability


🟥 Cons:

- The gameplay lacks some small quality of life additions. For example, while your inventory is full, you can't pick up ammo from ground. Like why? I should be able to replenish my ammunition without putting it in my inventory first.
- The game save system is not your usual system; they are only available on specific areas of the map, which you interact with manually and save. This is not a con for me, but if you are a person who dies most of the time, and if your game crashes, you will keep losing your progress and start doing the same things all over again (Depending on when did you last save your game).
- This is not really a con but if you're not an average gamer, if you have a bad aim. This game will be hardcore for you. You should try the assisted mode for that.
- Not another con but the last two boss fights on Claire's segment was kind of disappointing (easy). You just have to shoot them, while on the other bosses you need to think tactical.
- They missed the opportunity to make a unique campaign for Claire, instead of reorganizing the puzzles of Leon's segment.

🏷️ Suggestions:

~ Start your first playthrough with Leon. Preferably in "Normal" difficulty.
~ After you finish playing Leon's segment. Play as Claire in the 2nd run, in which you will see the true ending of the game (I enjoyed Claire's segment more than the Leon's segment).
~ You don't have to spend dozens of bullets on each creature, just stun them and dodge them.
~ You gotta pick all those Hip Pouches man, the inventory space is crucial in this game.
~ Don't panic. Panic is your nemesis in this game. Have fun getting bitten by the zombie who's camping just behind the door!

Really amazing in almost every aspect.
The only problem I have with this game is the fact that the boss fights are just absolutely terrible.
The first boss literally consists of running around in a circle for a few minutes, while shooting from time to time.
Additionally, whether you win or lose a boss fight is almost entirely dependant on how much ammo you bring into the fight. On my first run (on Hardcore difficulty), I even essentially soft locked myself because I did not have enough ammo to finish the first boss, and that's honestly just pretty annoying game design.

But the horror aspect of the game is absolutely amazing. It very rarely relies on cheap jump scares, but most of the time the atmosphere and enemies make it absolutely terrifying.

The gameplay is relatively straight forward most of the time: shoot zombies until they don't get up anymore. However, depending on the type of enemies you are facing and how many there are, you can choose from different approaches. For example, it is possible to stop normal zombies from walking by shooting their legs, massively slowing them down - which is really helpful when faced with multiple opponents at once. 
Some enemies also allow you to sneak past them, which is not only pretty convenient, but also absolutely terrifying, knowing that one wrong move may cause you to be spotted.

The puzzles you have to solve are mostly very simple, but still really fun and engaging.
Progressing through the individual areas as a whole feels really rewarding.
One thing I especially love is the fact that enemies do not respawn - that makes it feel like every kill really counts, and I honestly wish more games would follow that approach.

The game also consists of two major storylines, each following a different protagonist. These can be finished within a few hours (my first run took me about 4). However, after completing one of these stories for the first time, you unlock an alternate version of the other storyline, which changes a few plot points as well as some things about the areas you explore. 

All in all, it's honestly a real masterpiece and definitely part of my top 10 favourite games.

As somebody who is normally horror game averse, I had avoided playing the Resident Evil games up until I saw the RE2 + RE3 bundle available for $15, as I figured it would at least be worth a shot at that price. I'm glad I did, as Resident Evil 2 ended up being one of the best games I've played through in recent memory.

Resident Evil 2's horror is primarily based around atmosphere and surviving encounters with limited resources, and while there is the occasional jumpscare, they are used sparingly and appropriately, rather than being cheaply abused like in so many other horror titles of lesser caliber. The varied puzzles and problem solving also helps to break up the action, giving a very well-rounded experience overall.

Technically, the game is also astoundingly beautiful—both in terms of graphics and sound design—so much so that it's almost impossible for me to wrap my head around the fact that it was released over half a decade ago. I'm also unable to recall any bugs or other issues during my ~16 hours of play, so I feel comfortable calling the game polished to a mirror finish.

In fact, I had such a great experience with this game that I ended up buying the newer Resident Evil 4 remake from last year before I had even finished both routes in this one, which really says it all. I'm excited to play the other two remakes, and hope to see even more Resident Evil games of this style in the future!

Certainly! Let’s delve into the eerie world of Resident Evil 2, a game that masterfully blends nostalgia with modernized gameplay. Here’s my review:

Resident Evil 2: A Remake That Shines Bright
Introduction
I have fond memories of playing the original Resident Evil 2 in my dorm room back in 1998. The CGI cutscenes seemed incredibly realistic at the time (oh, 1998 me, you had so much to learn!). Fast forward to 2019, and Capcom has gifted us with a ground-up remake that I’ll remember for a long time.

Visual Overhaul
Gone are the pixelated characters navigating pre-rendered backgrounds. Instead, Resident Evil 2 now boasts fully 3D environments, over-the-shoulder gameplay, atmospheric lighting, and impressive facial animations. The zombies? Juicier than ever! Their lurching movements and detailed dismemberment system make for a gruesome delight.

Loyal to the Original
While some events have been rearranged or expanded upon, this remake remains mostly loyal to the dark and twisted story of the original. Set two months after the zombie outbreak of the first Resident Evil, it unfolds mostly within a spooky police station.

Atmosphere and Sound Design
The game’s atmosphere is rich, thanks to gorgeous lighting and incredible sound design. It pulls you into its detailed, creepy world, offering a huge amount of fun and challenging content. Capcom manages to stay true to the 1998 sequel while subtly nodding to the games that followed.

Conclusion
Resident Evil 2 is a gold-standard for how to do a remake. It combines nostalgia with fresh gameplay, making it an awesome experience for both old and new players. If you’re ready to face the nightmare once again, step into Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield’s shoes—you won’t be disappointed.

I've always been interested in the Resident Evil franchise, but I never knew where to start. You can start here. 

RE2make is a masterclass in survival horror with a well-written plot, terrifying map design, and some of the most baffling decisions I've seen in a videogame. I really enjoyed this game, but I do have some problems with it. I have completed the game as Claire and intend on revisiting the game to play Leon's route at some point in the future, though not the particularly near future if I'm being honest. Yet again, RE2make is great, but I'd rather just play the other games in the series than replay it right now.

Stuff it does well:
-scary
-like absolutely terrifying at times. Kind of comical at others. [spoiler]Mr. X is so well executed. He's a big guy in a black trenchcoat with a funny hat who punches you to death and he's absolutely the scariest thing in the entire game. You will fear his footsteps[/spoiler].
-decent and satisfying combat (a good 80% of the time)
-w story. It's not going to make you cry but it's more than enough for a game like this.
-Claire calling constantly asking the zombies what the f#ck is going on will never not be funny to me.

1. A very specific part of the game that should have been handled better overall. [spoiler]In the Claire route, a major boss fight near the tail end of the game is triggered after picking up an item. There is no confirmation screen to do this and taking this item locks you into fighting the boss immediately afterward. This is fine, if you die, you can reload from the last save and look for ammunition and healing to be better prepared. Unfortunately, there's a save station between this item and the boss, and you have no idea that saving over your file here will prevent you from going anywhere until you kill this boss. I feel like this could be solved by having picking up this item trigger a cutscene that throws you right into the boss arena, but it doesn't do that. I was hardlocked into fighting arguably the hardest boss in the route with five bullets, five acid rounds, and half of my health bar. I was able to win the fight, but it took about fifteen restarts. This absolutely shattered the pacing of the experience and made the final boss feel like a joke.[/spoiler]

2. The enemies are such bullet sponges that pistol bullets are practically useless. Zombies will [spoiler]simply get back up after you kill them with normal rounds[/spoiler]. Other enemies are basically immune to them, especially [spoiler]lickers[/spoiler]. There are a few situations where you'll have to [spoiler]hit an enemy weak spot[/spoiler] where the pistol is useful. Especially if you're playing at Claire, the pistol is useless [spoiler]until you get the high-power rounds, which I fairly sure you get all of ten of or something[/spoiler].

3. Ammo crafting is a chore and I kind of hate it. Like, this is such a nitpick, but I would rather just find ammo in the environment than have gunpowder clogging up my inventory. [spoiler]I missed the SMG so I just had like 5 high-grade white gunpowder in the storage box by the end of the game[/spoiler].

4. The game never tells you that [spoiler]you can backtrack. I didn't realize when I could go back to RPD so I missed the SMG not once (because I forgot to bring the badge with me to the S.T.A.R.S. office while being chased by Mr. X) but twice[/spoiler].

5. The bosses suck, at least for Claire they do. It's probably better for Leon. [spoiler]You just fight William 4 times, that's it. I'm pretty sure he's actually the only boss in the Claire route. His entire gimmick is to just shoot his eyeballs and run away because good luck dodging his attacks, except the time you have to push him into the abyss with a shipping container[/spoiler]

Other than those things, great game. Highly recommend. I haven't been giving letter grades for a while so this one's an [b]A[/b], good and worth the money, it goes on sale for 8 dollars often.

One of the most intricate and borderline flawless remakes that I have ever had the pleasure to journey through. 

Capcom has succeeded profusely in replicating their iconic 1998 original RE2 game, bringing to life a contemporary and dynamic imitation with the same overbearing sense of danger through every door and an unnerving isolating darkness that cannot be described, but only experienced through the eye of the player. 

Gameplay is high-powered and energetic at times, as well as slow-paced and unnerving at others. Players have to endure the agonising stalking of Mr. X/Tyrant, and face off with William Wesker in various boss fights throughout. Classic terrifying creatures such as the Lickers and even the Ivy make appearances during certain chapters. Playing as Leon, Claire and Ada in the main story is sensationally fun, full of wit and original. I expected nothing less.

I applaud and congratulate Capcom for giving such a dedicated and hypercritical fanbase the chance to relieve such fond childhood memories through a new version of a game that that has remained untouchable for the last 21 years.

[h1] The original was better [/h1]

This is a real remake of RE2, in the sense that they remade the game entirely. While the gameplay and graphics are very good, the game loses a lot in terms of story and locations. Think of RE2 Remake as a downgraded version of RE2 in a modern key. Here are my main complaints about this game:

1) The music and sound effects. In the original RE games (at least 1, 2, and 3) you were basically playing a horror movie. Hence, the music was playing a central role. It was always present and set the atmosphere of the game. In the Remake, it is barely noticeable.

2) There is less to explore in RE2 Remake. [spoiler] Just compare the lab in the Remake with that of the original RE2. Yes, they added the orphanage, but was that really necessary or interesting?  [\spoiler]

3) The stories do not complement each other. In RE2, part A and part B were almost totally complementary. [spolier] In the Remake, even the bosses remain mostly the same! [\spoiler]

4) Ada Wong. Just do yourself a favor and play Leon's part B in the original RE2. In the original games, she was more like a real human being, with true feelings and relatable goals. Here, she looks like a character from a spy movie with Johansson and the Rock, which unfortunately seems like the case for all the characters in modern RE games.

Overall, buy this game on discount if, like me, you are a old RE veteran and just want to waste some hours on a game that, after all, is fun. If this is your first RE2 experience, I recommend getting your hands on the original one and then, maybe, giving a try to this Remake as well.

[h1] THIS GAME SAVED MY LIFE [/h1]

First off, this game is a bit sentimental and holds a special place in my heart for a couple of personal reasons that don't really have to do with the game itself which I would like to get into first. During 2019 to 2020, I was not in the best place when it comes to my personal life and without getting into any detail, it was one of the roughest years and times that I've had, and to cope, I turned to my love for video games... and Resident Evil was one of my favourite game franchises and my favourite survival horror game series of all time, so I played the heck out of Resident Evil 2 remake and to summarize, this game actually helped me and saved my life which is crazy, but some video games can and will do that to you depending on who you are. So I don't just love this game because it's phenomenal, but because of the reasons I just stated and for that, it will always hold a special and sentimental place in my heart! Thank you Resident Evil, and thank you Capcom!

Now personal stuff out of the way, this game is an absolute masterpiece and is a prime example of what a good and faithful remake looks like. Those who played through the original PS1 version knows just how good that game was during that era, and this remake does the original, and the whole series as a whole complete justice and beyond. The story while not perfect, is still good enough, the graphics and art style are simple yet beautiful even in 2024, the gameplay is fun but challenging (in a good way), the puzzles can really get you to use your brain and get you thinking, and the horror/atmosphere itself is just incredible whether you're being chased by the dreaded Mr X himself, or you're walking through a dark hallway with endless anxiety flowing through your body as you turn and wonder what's around through each corner. This game is just absolutely incredible and I definitely recommend it to every Resident Evil and survival horror fans alike, this game does not disappoint at all and to this day, it still remains as one of my favourite video games of all time!

FINAL VERDICT: 10/10

Both visuals and sounds are doing a fantastic job immersing you in a dreadful situation your characters have found themselves in, but the level, enemy, and encounter designs are what truly keep you on your toes the whole time. The puzzles are intuitive yet sometimes pretty clever, and, together with resource management and routing, they form a solid, thoughtful gameplay loop punctuated by seamless transitions between levels and locations. These environments are emaculately well done, too, although hardly original by todays standards. The Orphanage, though, will definetly stay in my mind for some time. The later levels dragged just a bit in my experience and culminated in bossfights I would consider tedious, but that didn't hinder my enjoiment much. The plot is challenging for me to say anything about, as the Resident Evil mythos is very mature and influential, so nowadays the story may feel a tad naive, but it surely is competent, and the characters, although shallow, are appealing. Resident Evil 2: Remake was a fantastic way for me to experience a classic and is a great game overall.

Honestly, this is probably one of the best games in the whole series. Not REmakes, games.

Let me explain.

So the first 3 Resident Evil games (plus the first REmake and Code Veronica) had a fixed camera angle with tank controls. As much as it enhanced the survival horror experience, it honestly had to go in order for Capcom to make any more successful sequels.

Resident Evil 4 came out in 2005 and, while it was a huge success, it altered not only the Resident Evil series, it also affected videogames in general by making every game feel like an action movie for no reason. The next Resident Evil games, 5 and 6, went so far into this style, that there was a need for a change.

Resident Evil 7 was a breath of fresh air. With an entire different set of characters (mostly) and a basically disconnected story, it didn't have all the must-haves for a Resident Evil sequel, but it was a true survival horror experience, that put the franchise back on the map.

When it was time to REmake Resident Evil 2, Capcom wasn't 100% sure on how to make this. There was a time where the game still had a fixed camera angle and a story that deviated less from the original (will get back on that later). However, Capcom figured that the fixed angles wouldn't do well with a modern audience, but a first-person, like RE7, would also be too much of a deviation, so, the third-person camera angle became the norm for the REmakes.

There isn't anything specific to say about the gameplay, it is, of course, better than the original, which came out 21 years earlier, surprise surprise.

The music is extremely good, Collapse, which plays near the end of the game, and Final Judgement, the theme of the final boss (which I will not spoil) that shows up at the end of the Leon runs, are my personal favorites. However, some other pieces of music can't really compare to the originals like the RPD theme, the Save Room theme and the theme of the Claire boss (also won't spoil). This is a very subjective opinion, but, the music was, in general, very 50/50. (ok but WHY do I have to buy the original audio DLC for the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ "Resident Evil 2" at the start of the game? It's like the FIRST thing you hear every time you start a Resident Evil game).

The scares are ok, I guess, maybe a little cheap sometimes. Don't get me wrong, the game is horrifying the first few playthroughs, but it's the jumpscares that I feel don't really fit the game. Thankfully, there's only a handful of them in the game.

The puzzles are inoffensive, I guess, mainly because they're not really puzzles, they're more like "you can't use this, go find thing 1 and thing 2 to use this" which I guess it's fine, I got to admit that the feeling you get once you solve these "puzzles" is unlike any other.

The actors did a great job portraying the characters considering the shoes they had to fill. Although some lines were delivered better than others.

The enemies are great, wasn't a fan of the discount regenerators or the fact that the G adults are basically bullet sponges.

The extra game modes (4th Survivor and Ghost Survivors) are decent. definitely a fun little challenge when you beat the campaign.

The only thing that stops this game from being perfect is the fact that the 1st and 2nd runs don't connect and also contradict each other, where in the original they felt like one big campaign.

Some other general comments I want to make:
- Mr X being called "Tyrant" is a horrible diservice to the most threatening enemy in the game.
- Mr X showing up in both runs makes playing the 2nd run feel even less intense.
- Sherry's segment is probably the worst part of both runs.
- Meeting chief Irons' in this game doesn't give him enough time to become a proper character and is just your average evil bad guy that only gets his exposition through notes and -almost- no dialogue.

Overall, I'd say this is a solid 8.5/10. It's great, but I think they should've put more time in designing the runs.

Resident Evil 2, despite its cult following and reputation as a classic survival horror game, disappoints in its modern incarnation due to several glaring flaws that hinder the overall experience.

One of the most significant issues with the game is its outdated gameplay mechanics. While the original Resident Evil 2 was groundbreaking in its time, the remake fails to modernize its controls and gameplay systems adequately. Tank-like movement controls and cumbersome aiming mechanics feel clunky and frustrating, especially when compared to more fluid and intuitive controls found in contemporary games.

Additionally, the game suffers from pacing problems. Despite its relatively short length, Resident Evil 2 often feels padded out with tedious backtracking and fetch quests that do little to enhance the overall experience. This results in moments of boredom and frustration, detracting from the tension and atmosphere the game tries to build.

The story, while intriguing in concept, fails to fully engage players due to lackluster writing and characterization. Characters often feel one-dimensional and clichéd, with dialogue that can be cringe-worthy at times. This lack of depth makes it difficult for players to invest in the narrative, diminishing the emotional impact of key story moments.

Furthermore, the game's reliance on jump scares and cheap thrills feels lazy and uninspired. While horror games thrive on creating a sense of dread and unease, Resident Evil 2 often resorts to predictable scare tactics that fail to elicit genuine terror. Instead, it relies on shock value to compensate for its lack of genuine scares, resulting in a hollow and unsatisfying experience.

Finally, the game's lack of replay value is a major disappointment. Once you've completed both character campaigns, there's little incentive to revisit the game, as the experience remains largely the same with each playthrough. This lack of variety and depth ultimately undermines the game's longevity and diminishes its overall value.

In conclusion, while Resident Evil 2 may hold nostalgic appeal for fans of the original, its modern incarnation falls short of recapturing the magic of the original. With outdated gameplay mechanics, pacing problems, lackluster storytelling, and a reliance on cheap scares, it's hard to recommend this title to anyone other than die-hard fans of the series.

Resident Evil 2 is a fantastic remake of a beloved classic and the first RE I ever played. The atmosphere is supremely tense, the sound design is incredible and the game is impeccably balanced, interesting, fun to play and really damn scary at times.

The story is good, with both routes shedding a slightly different light on the events in Raccoon City. As the second run is slightly different per character, you can technically play through the game four times and still discover slight variations on item placement and story. Item management is key, as your inventory is severely limited, and ammo is precious, so don't shoot every zombie you see! It creates a tense atmosphere, trying to progress while conserving ammo and health. Probably nothing new for RE veterans, but given this was the first ever RE title I played, it definitely surprised me how fun even a limited inventory can be.

Each run is relatively short, with about 7 hours or less for me, and I did two runs. I am satisfied now, but there are hardcore difficulties and optional challenges for those that can't get enough of zombies jumping out at them from dark corners. Most of all, though, the game is just expertly made. The graphics are fantastic and the sound design, as mentioned, makes you jump even at your own shadow, with a haunting soundtrack in the background.

I really only have two criticisms. First, the HDR implementation of the game just straight up doesn't work most times. The only way I found to get HDR to work with my monitor was to restart my computer and immediately launch the game, otherwise it was extremely washed out. Also, disable Auto HDR, else there will be issues.

The second criticism pertains to the story, so spoiler tag ahead: [spoiler] While I love that the game has two routes, both from the perspective of Leon and Claire, and finishing one grants you the 2nd run of the opposite character, with slight differences and an expanded true ending, I was disappointed at how little difference there ended up being. Aside from both having different weapons and there being a few small areas unique to each character, 80 % of the game is still shared between both of them. You have to do many of the same things with both Leon and Claire.

That would be fine, but it creates continuity issues and weird inconsistencies. Many of the things that happen with one character shouldn't happen as another character will have already cleared out the area and should be ahead time wise, yet you have to both do the same things, with the same hazards and even some of the same bosses that should already technically be dead. The only way I found it to make sense is to just assume that one character "replaces" the other when in an area both have to go through, and the other character just catches up in that version of the story - but, as I said, there are a lot of inconsistencies here. I heard that, in the original RE2, they at least meet up a few times and talk over Walkie Talkie otherwise, which doesn't happen here and removes the opportunity for some bonding. Whatever! [/spoiler]

Either way, RE2 is a fantastic remake and an incredibly atmospheric, tense and fun survival horror. I absolutely loved this game. Capcom is really on a great streak this last decade or more, and I can't wait to explore the rest of these games.

In short, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a triumph of survival horror, a game that sets a new standard for the genre and leaves an indelible mark on anyone brave enough to step into its world. Whether you're a die-hard fan of the series or new to the horrors of Raccoon City, this is an experience you won't soon forget. Gameplay-ul este echilibrat și variat, oferind o combinație de acțiune, explorare și rezolvare a puzzle-urilor. În timp ce te lupti cu zombi și alte creaturi de coșmar, trebuie să explorezi medii detaliate și să găsești indicii și obiecte cheie pentru a avansa în poveste.
