This is a very good survival horror game. You take on the role of either Leon Kennedy, a rookie cop, or Claire Redfield, the sister of special forces agent Chris Redfield from the first Resident evil (and RE5, RE6 and Village), as they try to survive a zombie apocalypse. As of writing this review I have only played the Leon campaign and started on the Claire campaign. The atmosphere is great in this game. The dim lighting, the sounds from the zombies, the design of the zombies all fit together perfectly. 

But there are some aspects that drag this game down. While it's really cool to try to avoid zombies and survive, what I don't appreciate are the puzzles. I know that is a thing from the original game, and it does scream 90s video game, but it didn't really click with me. I appreciate a good puzzle, but the way it's done in this game sometimes just seems illogical and out of place. The police station that the majority of the game plays out in is a really cool place, but why are there so many weird puzzles? They try to explain it as the station being a refurbished museum, but when have you ever seen a museum with escape room level puzzles? It takes me out of the game a bit, because it doesn't seem fitting. Some puzzles absolutely do fit, but it usually just involves you running to a safe room, getting the stuff you already picked up for the puzzle, then running through to get to the puzzle or find the item and then run to the puzzle. Due to the way you solve most puzzles, the tension from the survival horror atmosphere diminishes in my opinion. I think puzzles where you have to use clues and solve something is better than puzzles where you just have to find the corresponding item because it's quite obvious what you need to solve it. 

What is absolutely worst in this game is the follower mechanic. Minor spoilers ahead. In the game, there is this giant of a man who appears in front of you at one point. He's invincible, can only be staggered if you're willing to waste your scarce amount of ammunition on him and he follows you. If you manage to outrun him, he will search for you everywhere. This sounds like a decent idea for a survival horror game on paper, but considering the gameplay loop of finding an item get back to a puzzle, solve the puzzle where the item and the puzzle are usually on wildly different parts of the map, this becomes less of a scary system and more of an annoyance that's just hindering your progress. It's just not that interesting.

I like the game, it has really good atmosphere and the inventory management, the story and the characters are really well done. It just has some annoying parts to it.

The game takes place not long after the first Resident Evil and you play 2 separate stories with 2 characters that inter connect with each other.
You can play either Leon's story or Claire's.

For both stories, you play 90% the same levels apart from the very start and a side story with characters they meet.

Leon is a cop starting his first day in Raccoon City working at the RPD. Unfortunately a zombie apocalypse has broken out and now he has to get to saftey and save people whilst solving the mystery of the virus.

On the other hand, Claire has come to Raccoon City looking for her brother Chris and meets Leon at a gas station on their way to Raccoon CIty and are both attacked by zombies.

However each story has 2 seperate side stories within the story. For Leon, you play as Ada Wong for a little bit and for Claire, you play as Sherry.

The horror is really well done and i actually jumped a few times at the jump scares.

Next there is the Lickers which are alot like Clickers from the Last of Us. They are blind and rely on sound to find out where you are. they are super fast and can climb walls and are very spider like.

Next there are huge monsters in the sewers that can poison you and live in the water.

Resident Evil 2 is a masterpiece. A great game that has its shortcomings but a great game nontheless. 

The gameplay and graphics shine, as they serve the main purpose of the game. To make you feel the horror of the situation, to make you feel week and vulnerable and cautious at all times. It is essentially a puzzle game. You explore the environments, you collect clues and useful items an you use them to solve the obstacles. Then you get new clues that help you progress and so on. It is a very nice loop, done right, as you never feel stuck at all.

The backtracking. It is not backtracking in its essence because you don't have to "go back". It is a small environment that you visit again and again. You're not even running in circles, because every time you visit a room, you have more clues and items to progress. It is a spiral in which you familiarize with the rooms and the items and the puzzles and use this knowledge to your advantage. Kudos to the environment and puzzle designers that created such a dense place full of character.

The puzzles aren't much of a puzzle, in a sense that you eventually stumble on the solution. A locked door? There is a key somewhere. A code? Somewhere there is a clue. A statue that is missing something? Somewhere there must be a photo of it. And that is nice because you actually feel the progress you're making, as it becomes clear what are you looking for. 

The combat compliments the game. As the movement and the exploration, the combat is slow and deliberate and thoughtful. You have a limited amount of guns and bullets so you have to make each bullet count, aim carefully and stay still for max accuracy. Those 2 seconds that you need to aim precisely are tense and the choice of waiting for a sure shot or shot early and miss is a choice that elevates the horror of the game.

There are 2 things that put me off, but not that much as to dislike the game.

A) Bland narrative. The narrative stays at the bare minimum so the payoffs and twists never work. E.g In Leon playthrough, Claire appears 3 times. There is not time to make the chemistry between them work. Ada is interesting, but in the end she feels like a promise of the character she could have been. Leon's motives are bland and so are the villains'. There aren't enough characters, enough dialogue, enough cutscenes to establish a coherent narrative, which is basically catered through the gameplay. In the end the story boils down to "Bad corporation, get the virus".

B) Timed sections and the Nemesis. This was a kind of dealbreaker for 2 reasons. First I just don't like to be rushed. Let me take my time ok. The game is scary by itself, I don't need a ticking clock to cause me anxiety. But, it also feels contradictory with the essence of the game itself. The slow, careful and deliberate movement, in which you check every corner twice goes out the window. Now you run like hell and bypass all enemies as if you were speedrunning. I know that it is "horror", but is a different kind of horror that just doesn't fit quite in.

The game has little replaybility value. Yes, there is a Claire walkthrough, but it is the same puzzles with the same answers, just in different sections of the map. Give it a try, but it adds little value in my opinion. If this game had a better narrative, a story that I might want to experience again (see Alan Wake) I'd give it another try. But no matter how good the gameplay is, it would be difficult to play it again, since I already know the solutions to the riddles. 

Still a great game and totally worth its money

Despite these shortcomings, Resident Evil 2 still offers a chilling and thrilling experience for fans of the survival horror genre, but it falls a bit short compared to the high expectations created prior to its release.

[h1]I understand the hype.[/h1]

It's funny how with certain things, you can see why they're so beloved, even when there are glaring flaws. A game of shooting zombies and solving puzzles, with a corny B-movie storyline sounds pretty dime-a-dozen. And yet RE2 Remake is considered an instant classic. 

I can see why.

The game is visually beautiful, creepy as hell, fun to play, and the voice acting is top notch. It has a nice balance between action and puzzle solving, the setting is great (particularly RPD), and Mr X is a lot of fun (those footsteps!).

On top of that, there's a surprising level of depth here. On the one hand, this is a linear, narrative-driven story that is straight forward and simple. But on the other hand, this game has a depth to it in terms of replayability and the desire to improve your speed and efficiency. There's a charm and instant familiarity to it that just makes the game fun.


The game is not without its drawbacks, though:

- The Sewers aren't nearly as good as the RPD, with level design that can border on annoying.
- The RPD feels too short. It's a great setting, and even though you come back to it later, it still feels too short compared to the Spencer Mansion in RE1. Also, as much as I liked the RPD setting, nothing beats the art design and ambiance of the Spencer Mansion.
- The Claire and Leon campaigns have too much overlap. They're maybe 25% different, with the rest being mostly the same. It's still fun to go through both, but I would have likeD it better if the writers had found a way to integrate the two campaigns so that they feel more complementary. They should have weaved together more thoughtfully rather than just being redundant with some branching.
- I would have liked to see more enemy variety. There isn't nearly as much variety as there is in RE1 or even RE3. Also, the boss fights were mediocre here.

Despite those criticisms, this is still a fantastic game that I highly recommend to anyone with even a passing interest.

The first area, the police station, is one of the best designed areas in a game. Everything about it is super suspenseful and satisfying in equal measure.  The levels are almost metroidvania-esque in design, full of shortcuts and keys to older areas. Exploration is rewarded handsomely with upgrades to your weapons, inventory slots and other boosts to your power. The zombies are threatening without being too bs, and can respawn, which means old areas are never fully safe. 
The later areas all suck, almost completely abandoning the non-linear aspects of the first area. To be honest you could comfortably stop playing after the first boss and you've experienced the best this game has to offer. I know that a lot of that is due to the constraints of this being a remake, so they had to follow a similar structure but I still think that it could be way better. Is RE2R worth it? And what about mods?
Well, I've played close to 100 hours out of this game, which means a few runs.
You got to play routes “A” and “B” with both Claire and Leon. Routes are not that different, but there is enough variation to bring the overall play time up to a good amount of hours.

Game is well done, with good graphics, sound effects, character and environmental design.
The screen is a little blurry, so I do recommend using Reshade for post processing mod.
To be honest, almost all my games are run with post processing mod, so RE2 would not be different.

I really like the character design in game.
Don’t recall much about the PS1 game version, since I’ve last played many years ago, but Claire and Leon are great, not only in their aesthetic, but also the voice over.
Many other characters follow the same line, which makes the game story more engaging.
The environment is very detailed, and can feel a little claustrophobic at times, which adds a lot to the survival horror immersion.
Lot's of gore, and creatures design do an excellent work bringging the T-Virus outbreak to life.

Mouse and keyboard is the way I play it, so controls are very responsive for aiming.
Some zombies do have erractic movement, making difficult to shot in the head, so I can’t imagine myself playing this game with a controller.

There is a good variety of weapons, however ammo is very limited, so player got to use it sparingly, at least until you finish the game and unlock weapons with infinite ammo.
I got to say the infinite ammo weapons don’t increase the game fun. It’s not designed to be a zombie shooter game, so even with infinite ammo, and being capable of blowing every zombie head out, it doesn’t feel right.

Inventory is quite small, which will make you do lots of back tracking.
It’s my understanding this is a game design characteristic for this genre, so not much to say about it.

Puzzles are nicely done, to the point that you will not need to look for a walkthrough at the internet, but still making you work for it. Something which is hard to find in today’s games.

When Capcom last updated the game, all my mods stopped working.
I’ve rolled it back to version dx11_non-rt to be able to bring back the mods.
At Nexus mods there are a few good mods for weapons and outfits. The game costumes are very nice, but which game doesn’t get better with mods? Come on, totally worth it.

Overall, RE2R is a good re-imagine of an old classic.
It doesn’t follow exactly the original game, but it is well done and fun enough to satisfy fans of the franchise.

[h1] A Modern Classic of Survival Horror [/h1]  
Resident Evil 2 is a **fantastic** remake that modernizes a beloved classic while staying true to its survival horror roots.

[h2] GOOD [/h2]  
[list]  
    [*][b] Outstanding Remake Quality [/b]  
    This is a top-tier reimagining of the original, with rebuilt environments, modern controls, and cinematic presentation that still preserve the tension and pacing of the 1998 game. It feels like how people remember the original, not how it actually was.  

    [*][b] Fresh Mechanics and Systems [/b]  
    Over-the-shoulder shooting, detailed dismemberment, and improved inventory and boarding-up systems add depth without sacrificing the core survival horror feel. These updates make exploration and combat more tactile and strategic.  

    [*][b] Rich Features and Updated Classics [/b]  
    Multiple campaigns, unlockable modes, and remixed scenarios give plenty of reasons to replay. Classic elements like item management, puzzle-solving, and key-based progression are brought back with modern polish so it doesn’t feel dated.  

    [*][b] Expanded Story Beats [/b]  
    Familiar characters and events are fleshed out with new scenes and better pacing, filling in gaps the original never fully explained. You get a clearer sense of what is happening around Raccoon City and why, without losing the mystery and dread.  
[/list]

[h2] BAD [/h2]  
[list]  
    [*][b] No Zapping System [/b]  
    The original’s A/B “zapping” mechanics are effectively gone, which is disappointing if you loved how one character’s actions influenced the other’s route. The new scenario structure is good, but it doesn’t quite replace that old-school interplay.  

    [*][b] Occasionally Frustrating Controls [/b]  
    While generally solid, movement and aiming can feel clumsy in tight spaces or under pressure, especially when you are trying to line up precise shots or kite multiple enemies. In a game this tense, small control hiccups feel extra punishing.  

    [*][b] Heavy Backtracking [/b]  
    The design leans hard on revisiting areas with new keys and items, which fits the genre but can drag for some players. If you are not into route optimization and map memorization, the loops through the station and sewers may wear you down.  

    [*][b] Bullet Sponge Zombies [/b]  
    Regular zombies can absorb a surprising number of bullets, especially on higher difficulties, which can feel excessive. It reinforces the survival aspect but sometimes crosses into annoyance when headshots don’t reliably put them down.  
[/list]

[h2] Final Thought [/h2]  
Resident Evil 2 is the kind of remake the series **deserved**—carefully built, respectful of the original, and confident enough to change what needed changing. Despite missing the old zapping system and leaning into some occasionally frustrating design choices, it stands as one of the best modern survival horror experiences. Grab it when you can or in a bundle; if you have any love for Resident Evil or horror in general, this one is absolutely worth your time.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is what happens when millions of dollars are put into a project with a limited scope. Every room has little touches, every plot point has nuanced presentation, and every enemy is a Certified Problem©. The main campaigns (Leon/Claire A) have less than 100 enemies each, but they require the player to make decisions that are informed by their inventory, their objectives, and their knowledge of enemy behavior. That decision making only becomes more tense when an unstopped pursuer can be right around the corner or the next cutscene introduces a new boss. Sure, by the end a player will probably have the game systems figured out, but that's when the second campaign unlocks that has enough changes to keep experienced players on their toes. What unlocks after that second campaign is a handful of challenge modes which crank up the difficulty substantially. None of that content comes at the cost of technical artistry, which is just outstanding. Resident Evil 2 Remake is a premiere survival horror experience that caters to anyone with a slight interest in the genre, reinforcing why the Resident Evil franchise became as popular as it is.

Few video game series ever manage to pull away from the video game masses and reach main stream appeal.. They become something more then video games and become part of pop culture, games like Super Mario Brothers, Pac-Man, Tetris, etc etc etc.. Another one of those games which have stretched far beyond their gaming origins is Resident Evil, with movies, novels, and a slew of video games mentioning the name Resident Evil will get someone's attention..


While the original game was a complete classic, with some of the earliest known examples of Jump Scares (that dog jumping through the window still gives some of us nightmares) and a completely new and original game design, play and ideas. (No lying, if you were alive when Resident Evil 1 released you were enamored by its' uniqueness gameplay) The sequel followed suit a few years later, expanding what made the original great and helping pave the way for the pop culture phenomenon that Resident evil would become one day..


The Story - Like the original game the story features two separate playable characters and stories.  You can pick between Claire Redfield, the original games male protagonist Chris Redfield's sister, or Leon Kennedy, a brand new RPD police officer. The first, second and third game seem to have some continuity errors as far as cohesive storyline goes but to sum it up, Racoon City has a viral outbreak (zombies) which has thrown everything into disarray. Leon stops at a gas station to get gas when he notices something weird going on.. He heads inside to investigate when he's attacked. Claire happens by on her way to Racoon city to search for her brother Chris. After seeing the zombies and having an issue with an exploding Semi, they start off on their horrific adventure to discover what happened in Racoon city, try to help put a stop to it, and stay alive.. 


Gameplay - If this was 1998, I'd go into detail about how the game works, but since it's 2024, if you don't' know how a third person shooter works then I don't know what to tell you.. The only unique aspects of the game are the various Puzzles you need to solve as you progress.... (or do like most of us do and hit up You tube. IGN, or other sources for all the information you'll ever need..  


One part that has to be talked about are the Ghost Stories, during the course of the game you'll run into several people with tragic backstories, if you finish the game you can unlock (I think by beating the game, I bought the unlock all pack so I don't know for sure) where you can run an alternate reality where you can alter that one person's outcome.. The stories are relatively short, the longest one was maybe 20 minutes, they are fun and challenging experiences to help add to the experience. IIRC about 5 of them exist..

TLDR: Survival horror at its finest

I played my first Resident Evil game last year (the 2002 remake of RE1) and while I enjoyed it some, I was ambivalent about continuing the series. I finally decided to give RE2 a shot and am glad I did.

The story picks up with two new characters: Leon, a rookie cop, and Claire, who's coming to Raccoon City to find her brother Chris (one of the playable characters from the first game). The pair quickly meet each other, and then met the zombie victims of Umbrella, and the story is off and running.

This RE2 remake ditched the fixed camera angle in exchange for an over-the-shoulder third-person perspective. I know some fans of the original preferred the previous camera scheme but after playing RE1 I liked this much better. Movement, picking up items, inventory management, and using weapons all feel very natural. The visual presentation is great; the detail and the gloomy, foreboding halls and rooms set the mood perfectly. So is the directional sound and (unlike the clips I have seen of the original games), here both dialogue and voice acting are fantastic. The overall story is adequate, though I don't think it's groundbreaking or will surprise many players. This remake tries to maintain the late-90s aesthetic from the original game, with such things as the tech level (the absence of everyday electronics like cell phones, and important messages being available on VCR tapes) and the price of fuel shown at the gas station in the game's opening.

Leon and Claire trod much of the same ground in their own stories, though there are some areas, weapons, and cutscenes that will only be seen in their separate playthroughs. Each story also features a short stint playing as another character--the mysterious Ada Wong for Leon, and the young girl Sherry for Claire. I enjoyed Ada's sequence well enough but Sherry's was mostly just "press shift to sprint, and stand in this spot to avoid detection."

Making choices is really the heart of RE2, and there are tough ones to be made. Inventory space, while expandable, is limited and every slot counts. Though I didn't think the puzzles were overly difficult, trying to make sure I carried things I needed to avoid backtracking through dangerous areas was always a balancing act. While some of the puzzles in the first game had a certain "fun-house" quality to them, here the puzzles felt intutitive and logical for the scenario. Not every solution and combination was immediately obvious but I think most players can solve them, given enough time and exploration. But that's the rub ...

The halls of the police department (and later areas) are swarming with zombies and other mutated beasts. Contrary to many other games featuring shambling corpses, the regular zombies in RE2 are rather durable. In my runs, some soaked up five or six headshots from the basic (starting) pistols before going down for good. Better weapons, like the shotgun, magnum pistols, and grenade launchers, can one-shot a zombie but the ammo for those tends to be more finite--so it's back to the concept of managing inventory and supplies, and really thinking about which monsters need to be killed and which can be avoided. Leaving "living" enemies behind means having to cope with them a second or third time as you pass through the areas again. Unlike other mobs, the zombies are not super fast in pursuit but when close, they can lurch forward with surprising speed and take a chunk from the player's health. This is especially common when you put a zed down, can't get beyond it immediately, and sight unseen, it rises behind you and attacks. Sooner or later, the damage will catch up to you; I died a number of times, in bloody and glorious ways. Fortunately, autosaves are a thing. Probably doesn't need to be said but I will anyway: this game is way too violent and graphic for most pre-teen children.

To stave off imminent death when grabbed, there are defensive weapons, like knives and flash grenades, that a player can equip to avoid a bite at the last moment. Many mobs can also be stunned or temporarily incapacitated with a few shots, which is usually enough for the player to slip past. Whether to dodge, stagger, or kill a mob all come down to a player's playstyle, ammo inventory, and comfort level.

Beyond zombies, there are other enemies requiring their own strategies. At times, the player will be stalked by a hulking indestructible mutant in a trench coat, who (unlike regular mobs) will pursue the player into semi-safe areas, such as the main hall of the police station. This adds to the player's stress and tension (it did mine, anyway).

Then are boss fights against some of the biggest and ugliest monsters, including three major confrontations late in the game. All are in fairly claustrophobic areas and the close proximity (along with the player's general lack of mobility) means that boss attacks are often difficult to avoid. It can be done but will probably take a few tries to learn their patterns and timing. The boss fights for me were the most difficult segments of the game. I got through by sheer perseverance but I have a feeling casual players may be more frustrated than challenged.

Beyond Leon's and Claire's playthroughs, there are several very short "what-if?" scenarios for other random survivors (which are not canon, since all of these survivors are killed or implied to be killed in the main story). I found these to be incredibly difficult compared to the regular campaigns. They're fine for a change and I gutted through all on the lowest difficulty setting, but I didn't enjoy them that much. If you do them, spend a lot of time running.

I personally didn't encounter a single error or glitch. In fact, this felt like one of the most bug-free modern games I've played. Load times are brief and the entire game felt like it ran very well. There are several purchasable DLCs available, most of which are cosmetic outfits, extra weapons, or unlocks of in-game rewards. None are necessary to play or complete the game.

RE2 is a relatively tough game to max achievements. Getting full completion requires multiple finishes, speedruns, harcore mode runs, and collectibles scattered across different character playthroughs. I reloaded several sections to get a few time-sensitive achievements. I suspect any dedicated player could manage 100% but it will take some time.

Considering that I am very hit or miss with survival horror, I thoroughly enjoyed my time in RE2, enough so that I'll not only continue on to RE3 but will also put RE2 on the finite list of games I'll pull off the shelf to replay.

Pros
- Combat, puzzles, and inventory management require thought and planning
- Outstanding ambiance, sound, and graphic presentation
- Decent replay value

Cons
- Boss battles may be too challenging for casual players
- Extra scenarios kind of "meh"

Final Score: 8.5/10

Resident Evil 2 for the PS1 is a deserved regular in the upper echelons of survival horror. By the late 2010s, a remake was long overdue. Capcom finally obliged, and boy did it do them a world of good. 2017 onwards has been a second golden age for Capcom: the once wayward developer, infamous for on-disk DLC and treating Mega Man like a bastard child, now releases hit after hit, games that are both critical and commercial juggernauts. Resident Evil 2, I feel, is what solidified this success.

A good remake is one that modernizes a classic yet preserves its spirit. Resident Evil 2 passes this test with flying colours. For someone who first played the original shortly after learning to tie his shoelaces, this game looks like what my child mind - unbothered by how pixelated and polygonal things were - imagined the PS1 version to be. Great care has been taken to breathe new life into the original's visuals; however, this game looks great even on its own terms. If you shoot a zombie, he'll lose a chunk of flesh at the exact point of impact. If its raining outside, your character will get realistically drenched. If a character smiles, you can count their individual teeth (which was at first almost uncanny to me, not being used to realistic teeth in games).

While RE2 could easily have dwelt in the past, its gameplay also looks ahead. This game blends old and new survival horror conventions: resource management, puzzle-solving and exploration are combined with hide, seek, or flat-out flight from an indestructible monster as in Amnesia: The Dark Descent. It makes for a thrilling and at times unpredictable game that kept even an RE veteran like me on his toes. The combat is solid, and in all honesty, this game feels better to play than the original. There, I said it.

The first third of this game is a masterstroke. It feels oppressive and stressful, yet so compelling, and its gameplay is so well-designed that you'll get 'organic' jumpscares. There is rarely a time where you feel completely safe. That said, this game does peak early. The police station is far more fulfilling to explore than the later sewer section and the underground lab. (Spoilers for anyone who's been under a rock for 26 years - RE2 has an underground lab). While they're still fun, a great deal of tension is removed from the game once you've gotten past the iconic locations.

First impressions last, but after 19 hours with RE2, I can see that it's not the flawless game I thought it was in the honeymoon phase. Most egregiously, unlike the original, there aren't four scenarios in this remake. To be completely honest, there aren't even two. Oh, you can choose between Leon and Claire - you have to play both, to get the real ending. But apart from about ten minutes' worth of differences, depending on your character, there is really only one scenario in this game. The original RE2's scenarios melded into each other perfectly, with the characters even meeting each other at various points. In the remake, almost the whole campaign - including puzzles, boss fights and rooms visited - is the exact same, and while it may be good enough to warrant playing twice with different characters, it's still recycling.

Not only do Leon and Sherry never interact till the end, but there are scenes regarding Annette Birkin that make it impossible for the two scenarios to be set in the same continuity - and it's up to you to decide what's canon. I'm not a fan of that, really - it means there's less content than the original. A few extra modes - including a nail-bitingly tense special mission as beloved characters Hunk and Tofu - round out the offering.

Regardless of these nitpicks, RE2 is an excellent game that's accessible to new players and familiar to series veterans. This is a triumph whose high Capcom still rides five years later. Now do Dino Crisis.

Amazing experience all around. (Disclaimer, I only played the A sides and I played on Standard only)

Firstly, amazing visuals. Lighting is important in accentuating the emotion the player should have, and I never grew tired of fact this game takes place in a single night because of it. The flashlight automatically turning on/off depending on where you are, illuminating a near perfect amount of light, as each object has a very realistic reflection that makes it worth playing on high-end hardware (something I plan to do sometime in the future).

The zombies. Their cries matching the energy of the zombie's position in the moment are perfect, and I loved how each type had its own cries similar to L4D2. Eventually, it was easy to tell how often they reused models for zombies, and normally its worth criticizing, but instead I'd rather commend how refined the normal zombie's movements are. I wish it were easy to describe in words, so take my general word for it: they're scarily accurate. The way RE2R works in damage-dealt to the zombies is both inconsistent and refined. For the power weapons like the shotgun, thumper, D-eagle, most will efficiently one-shot, but the ammo is more scarce to compensate. Down the other side of the spectrum, the normal pistol has copious amounts of ammo, but has the most amount of health scaling evident. Generally, zombies go to the ground in 3 shots to the head, but rarely out for the count. Usually between 3-10 seconds, giving enough time for the opportunity to run, shoot another zombie, or wait patiently to see it rise with a bloody head. You can waste a shot and shoot the laid down zombie, and if they react viscerally, they're not dead and need a few more shots to the head. This sounds annoying, and a waste of time, but I believe this was done intentionally to spice up each and every encounter with them. This inconsistency in killing them for good makes them manageable alone, but very threatening in groups. When shot in the head, they usually knock their head back as a reaction to the shot, though the game allows them to ignore knockback if you let them get too close. 9 times out of 10, its your fault for grabbing you because you let them get close. One shot kills are rare enough to never rely on, and never upset at happening as you see their heads burst in the direction you shot them. These mechanics are only worth highlighting, because altogether they create a truly threatening game from beginning to end. And for major zombies, each type has a weakness to exploit, never necessary, but always worth taking advantage of once learned. Boss fights are intense, and the ending fights are the highlights. Won't say more.

Mr. X is amazing, he's frightening, fast, and will ♥♥♥♥ your ♥♥♥♥ up if left unchecked. His footsteps reverberate throughout the whole police station, and its never unfair with his lack of ai puppy-guarding that plague most characters in his role for other games. One of the best moments in my first playthrough, learning how to combat him. I hope any new players aren't spoiled by his introduction until they experience it themselves.

I love the characters, they're iconic, have great voice actors, great motion capture, and their interactions are organic with a touch of 80-90's dialogue, adding a spicy flavor to otherwise solid writing. They truly found the perfect people to play Leon and Claire, among everyone else as well, but L/C are the highlights. An air of innocence with their young, inexperienced lives, their charisma is charming and a nice source of levity among a very dark setting. 

The music accompanies each situation rather well, with my favorites being the safe room tune and the final boss music. Intense, and cinematic. Not much to say, music in a game like this needs to be atmospheric to properly guide the player's emotions/state-of-being. 

Rapid-fire time: I love the game visually showing your health when it goes down; how the game is designed for you to get rid of most key items not long after acquiring, and will display when its completely done being used; the reward for back-tracking to finish clearing rooms with key items not-in-your-possession; the fact the map displays when there's no more loot to grab; displaying items on maps accurately, including some key items that can be mixed up easily, like literal keys; the section of each story where you play as another character aren't intrusive at all and not very long to boot; the fact that this game encourages multiple playthroughs, and going at a reasonable pace will result in 10 hours for a single playthrough max, this game respects your time; the copious challenges and that most unlocks are charming costumes/accessories.
 
Okay, time to talk quick tips and negatives, sadly it's not a 10/10 game. If stuck, use a guide and go by the name of the objective. Free up a few slots when entering a room/planning to move from a save point, your storage chest will be your best friend. Don't be afraid to run by zombies when low on ammo/in a tight spot, you can always come back to kill them later. Lastly, save often.

Negatives, only a few big ones. Hated the fact you have grenades and flashes, and THEY'RE ONLY MEANT FOR DEFENSE, in what world does that make sense, let alone the fact that LEON IS A TRAINED COP. Why does it work where you're encouraged to do four playthroughs, when Leon and Claire are 85 percent the same as it is, differed by weapons, some story elements and the final boss. I severely dislike how the game tries to tie the two stories together when they're almost entirely separate, L and C have great chemistry but its a shame they don't interact more. Why do you need to do all four endings to get the game's "true ending". That should be for people who do both A sides, not both A and B sides, especially when its 10 minutes of extra content and that's with dying more than once. 

DLC costumes and whatnot, for a retail $60 game when there's already in-game costumes, that's as scummy as you get. Don't bother buying them unless you're planning on doing all four playthroughs. The game has more than enough for you if that's your jam.

Personal Notes:

A fantastic series of games depicting the resident evil universe as a game adaption, the second game specifically takes you through the story of two characters with slight differences between the two but the over all story being the same. You also find both characters consistently keep meeting, this is great because you can see both the lead up and aftermath of each meeting allowing you to understand the story even better. The lore itself is very in depth although it does help a lot to understand the entire story as the knowledge just from this game doesn't help you understand how it begins and what happens after, for that you will need to play the other games. As for the graphics the game looks outstandingly beautiful with the performance being amazing for the quality. The music and sound is fantastic and I did not come across one bug throughout my play time, the use of Mr X was also very unique as he relied a lot on sound which you could use to your advantage. The game isn't too long or too short and is just about right, the difficulty is a little harder than normal games but you quickly get use to it with some difficulty coming from you needing to manage your supplies/bullets. 

Overall it is a fantastic game, a good introduction into the story and is very cheap now so well worth the cost. The performance is amazing and the sound track is very suitable. The game is part of a large story built with lore and different stories that all entangle building a deeply rich lore based world. I feel it necessary to only mention that the extra "DLC" costumes are a little pointless as the original default character costumes look amazing so these are not necessary at all and should only be seen as a method to support the developer more.

This was my absolute first ever Resident Evil game and I was glad this was my first. I can finally confidently say I understand what fans of the RE franchise are talking about and why RE is the gold standard of the horror genre. 

First, the graphics are superb. The RE engine looks amazing and runs surprisingly well on low to medium machines. I played this exclusively on the Steam Deck and with some minor tweaking (a big performance boost is to change the rendering from normal to interlaced) and ran at max settings without Ray Tracing and the fps was generally above 60fps. The character models are also extremely well done and the expressions look very impressive. They even modeled the characters after real-life people.

The gameplay is exquisite. The forced backtracking into older areas of the game is apparently a RE staple but extremely novel and fun to me. I've seen no other video game that forces you to take the time to go back to old areas of the game actually enjoy doing it without it feeling like a chore. Old areas give great rewards or new discoveries for those who take the time to go back. Locked/inaccessible doors and shortcuts unlocked further on made it seem like you are playing through the dungeon planned out by some evil mastermind. Areas and things that confound you first time around made complete sense later from a different perspective.  There is an extremely satisfying feeling of just how some things "fit" as you progress through the game. The Gameplay mechanics like MR. X were absolutely terrifying and his iconic foot stomps and surprise reveals literally sent me into panicked overdrive mode trying to outrun him and finding safe rooms every time he appeared. The fact that all of these mechanics and level designs were all original to the 1998 game from over 20 years ago is the *chef's kiss* of perfection.

If you are new to the RE franchise, I highly suggest  you start here and NOT at RE1. The remakes switch from single camera view to third-party target reticle view is so much better than the originals' tank controls. The original RE1 remake is almost unplayable when I tried it. I really had to force myself to complete it and finally got used to it enough to enjoy it. 

RE2 was so good that I completed two playthroughs as both characters and I did all of the extra missions. While most games have NEW GAME+ mode that's a bit of an afterthought that gives some underwhelming rewards, the replay value of RE2 is a cut above. Replaying the game as either Leon or Claire is a brand new experience with new areas, new weapons, different approaches, and even new characters and a different story. The replay doesn't feel tedious and actually feel more like sequels than a replay. You also need to complete both character's runs in order to get the full story and ending.

I am happy to report that this was a masterpiece in storytelling, design, and atmosphere.

[h1]Resident Evil 2 - A Masterclass in Survival Horror Immersion[/h1]

Hey there, before we get started, let me lay down the basics. If you're not big on horror games or they make you a bit nervous, hang tight. I'm here to show you why this game could be a good intro for you into the horror genre.
And if you're a pro gamer who's tackled Alien: Isolation, Outlast, or Silent Hill, listen up. I'm gonna explain why giving this game a shot is totally worth it, and what makes it stand out. So, whether you're new to horror or a seasoned player, there's something for everyone here. Let's dive in.


[h1][b]Overview[/b][/h1]


Resident Evil 2 stands out as one of those timeless classics in gaming that you'd give anything to wipe from your memory, just so you could relive that initial experience all over again. It's a masterclass in game design, meticulously crafted with an eye for detail that's hard to match.
The storyline isn't just some throwaway plot; it carries real weight, drawing you in with its intrigue and suspense. And let's not forget the characters – they're not just pixels on a screen; they're memorable personalities that stick with you long after you've put down the controller. But perhaps what truly sets Resident Evil 2 apart is its environment – it's not just a backdrop; it's a living, breathing world that immerses you completely, a rarity in an era dominated by sprawling open-world games.


[h1]Immersion[/h1]


The single most important thing which makes this game immersive is because of its environment because the game involves backing tracking which means going back to places you've been before to solve puzzles and find secrets. 

[b]Let me give you some quick examples:[/b]
[list]
[*]throughout whole game you will be limited in resources like ammo or health and killing zombie in this game doesn’t drop any supplies or items so how you are dealing with every single enemy makes a huge difference.
[*]if zombie breaks a window and you don’t fix it next time you come to the same place there will be zombies hiding or waiting for you in the same location.
[*]When you backtrack, it gets tense because you're low on supplies and run into new problems like tougher zombies and changing surroundings. You have to make decisions about which paths to take, and your choices can affect whether you survive or not.
[*]The game has tricky puzzles that need logic, observation, and sometimes mixing items. It feels good when you figure out the puzzles and uncover secrets, making the game more fun and engaging
[/list]


[h1]Attention to detail[/h1]


Shooting in zombies make them stumble and you can break their limbs saving you ammo.


Learning the layout of the map is crucial for backtracking efficiently. When you explore carefully, you'll find hidden items and shortcuts that make the journey easier. This adds a layer of strategy
to the game, where each decision on where to go next can have a significant impact on your survival.

The late 2010's really brought this franchise alive. Beginning in 2017 we got RE7, this game, RE3 remake, RE8, and RE4 remake in a 6 year timespan. Reminds me of how Capcom pumped out Street Fighter games in the mid to late 90's. I've only played 7 and this, but so far it's all been good.

	RE2R is a sort of 're-imagining' of RE2, in that it doesn't strictly follow the original and moves some things around. New rooms and pathways are present. The sewers section has been greatly expanded. And most importantly, Mister X is now present in both scenarios. Mister X was originally only available on the B-Scenario of the original. So whoever you played first, the second play through for the opposite character faced X.
	
	It's a perfect sequeway into talking about the A/B scenario system and what they did differently here. RE2 effectively had 2 maps, with slight alterations. Whoever you played first got map A, whoever came second had map B. B-Scenario had some changed bosses, rooms, and interaction with the A scenario. Closed the shutters in the police station in A scenario? Can't do it in B. Left ammo behind in A? B benefits from this. 

	The 2 slightly altered maps is still present here, but the 'zap' system (whereby a few actions affect the other scenario) is completely absent. Most importantly, the story itself stays the same whether they're first or second. Previously a few details changed depending on what scenario the character was in. If you played Claire B, Sherry isn't infected. In A, she is. Leon A and B changed how Ada left us.

	I played RE2 less than 2 years ago, and whilst I don't remember every detail I do remember how inconsequential it was replaying the game 4x in a row. While some fans may quibble with me on how shameful it is that the story stays the same no matter what, the differences weren't so large that I felt grateful replaying the game 4 times over. Even the zapping system was negligible. The A/B system was a late addition in RE2's development, so it never felt fully fleshed out to me. 

	I guess what I'm trying to say is: I don't mind the change. There's a few other things missing, such as Leon and Claire interacting more in the original than here. But I wouldn't call this butchered.

	While different, the game is as good if not better than the original. RE2 is still good fun, but the remake kept a lot of what made it fun. The focus is still on puzzles and exploration, while the ammo and weaponry is kept on a leash. We don't have pre-set camera angles, but areas have been darkened and a flashlight is necessary a lot of the time. Which leads to a few zombies and Mister X creeping up on you throughout your playthrough. The game is still able to frighten the player.

Perhaps they could've 'spruced up' the original by further differentiating the two playthroughs. You can't fault this game for it, but expanding instead of deleting the zap system would've been cool. Repetition is something in the original, so how you go about changing that without making this a new game altogether would've been tricky. But it's worth thinking about. 

Mister X is perhaps the biggest addition and 'enhancement' in terms of taking an original idea and fleshing it out further. In the original his chasing was scripted and only in select locations. Here it's throughout the RCPD, but only in the RCPD. I've heard critiques that it 'breaks the game pacing' by forcing players to move about quicker. His introduction isn't early, and his walk speed is slow so it never bothered me. It's nice taking the original idea and implementing it with enhancements of its follow-up (RE3). It's ironic that X behaves as Nemesis did, and Nemesis in RE3R behaves as X did. But that's for a separate review.

	Before wrapping this up, I have to mention how incredible the game looks. It uses the same engine as RE7, but looks better. I assume its because 7 is a PS4 era game, whilst RE2R is a PS4 and PS5 release. So the ceiling on graphical fidelity is raised. It helps that ray-tracing is implemented properly (ray-tracing looked somewhat shoddy in certain parts of 7). 

	Better than the original? 'Definitive' version, like REmake? Given that it changes some things, subtracts a few parts, and gives you a different camera angle I wouldn't say it supplants the original. But it is just as good and you can't go wrong with either version.

В своё время CAPCOM представила публике совершенную модель Survival Horror с элементами головоломок. Resident Evil 2 Remake перешла в 3D, но смогла полностью сохранить свою атмосферу и настроение, чего так боялись потерять фанаты. Quick Text Review:

-Shooting mechanics are simple and fun (If these zombies take a while to go down) trying to hit them as they surge forth and shamble in hard to predict ways
-Nice resource management (If backtracking can sidestep some of it)
-It's fun to explore the police station and find ammo, weapons, mods etc. and unlocking the safes and lockers through investigation (if nothing is particularly well hidden: Find the code and go back to this place)
-The puzzles are simple and logical but give a nice change of pace
-The Tyrant is amazing and will seemingly hunt you in an organic fashion (Which is scary) with rare moments where you can slip by undetected as though it can actually see and hear (Perhaps a parlor trick but what a trick)
-The audio design is great and delivers a quiet horror atmosphere with unnerving noises usually - was that a zombie (If most of that greatness comes from the fact that you can hear the thudding of the Tyrant's boots as it hunts you from a different room, the noise getting louder as it gets closer)
-The story is a functional survival horror tale (As the original was) where you inevitably end up in the same kind of place responsible for the outbreak, but I think new cinematics have been added that can amplify it a bit. I grew up playing Resident Evil 4, which I loved immensely. I wanted to try the Resident Evil 2 remake (and maybe 3) before I tried the Resident Evil 4 remake.

Overall I really enjoyed it. I was very scared several times (especially playing at night!) and the zombies are believable. I [i]loved[/i] dreading a [spoiler]Tyrant[/spoiler] encounter. That dude was a beast. 

The parts of the game I didn’t enjoy too much was the chunkiness of movement and how certain enemies are bullet sponges.

I understand that this is a console port, but holy smokes why does there need to be a second long delay when your character turns (Q button)? One of the most basic mechanics of a Resident evil game is doing a 180 degree turn to face your adversaries after running from them, but in this game when you perform the turn, there’s a second long delay where your character is frozen in place and cannot fire/move your cross hairs. I eventually had to stop using this mechanic because by the time I’d be ready to aim and fire the gap between me and an enemy would be too close.

Also, why do some basic zombies take like 10 head shots to kill? You’ll empty a clip in one, they’ll drop, stand back up, and repeat. There may have been two instances where they stood up twice, which is BS. The sewer monsters were the worst instance of this – I eventually stopped shooting them and attempted to snack on a purple herb and run past them because these things took about 5 full magazines to kill. 

Another annoying instance of the bullet sponging was during my second encounter with 
[spoiler]Will Berkin[/spoiler]. He appears, and my initial instinct is to shoot him down (because that’s how I beat him the first time) but nope, you aren’t supposed to do that. He’s all of a sudden invulnerable. The game wants you to run down to the lower platform and use a machine to kill him...so that ammo was wasted.

Like I said above, try to get this game on sale. I couldn’t justify paying full price for this, but I really enjoyed my first play through and am looking forward to doing another one!

Resident Evil 2 is an absolutely beautiful remake of what I assume was an equally beautiful game. The game looks absolutely gorgeous, controls flawlessly and does nothing but amaze with it's satisfying combat and winding hallways. I adore this game and everything that it allowed the following remakes to do, but I do think the RCPD is slightly lacking compared to even the original Resident Evil and it's mansion environment.

 I love the change from locked camera angles to third person, this was an incredible choice. Although the locked camera angles can create some unique scenarios and allow the developers to programs special events off screen and the like, I love the freedom gained with third-person, and there was no shortage of jump-scares or surprise attacks even with the camera under my control. Although I do wish some puzzles were more complicated than just having the correct key or finding a code on a piece of paper. Don't get me wrong it's not all that much different from the OG but something just feels missing in the puzzle regard, or that might just be the fact that moving around with locked camera angles made the whole first game feel like a puzzle just to get around, not sure.

 Regardless of nitpicking this is an incredible game with some incredible replay value and nice little bonus modes to explore some of the other characters you've met in the world and see what they got up to. If you love horror, if you love puzzles, if you love shooting, and more of all if you love corny dialogue, please play this.

Quite enjoyable and polished remake of an action/puzzle/horror game which I skipped back in the day, because of how janky it looked. Game story can be can played with either Leon or Claire, the two main characters of the story, but you don't get a full different story for each character, what you get is more like a variation of single story with some different elements. 

The somewhat clunky or intentionally restricted gameplay may put some players off. You can pretty much only walk, run, shoot and perform scripted actions, meanwhile most enemies are really mobile and some are really fast and deadly. Aiming is another thing game relies heavily on, this makes some boss battles really annoying.

I played the game blind, without any guides, and the design choice of using scarcity as game mechanic became obvious a bit too late, this mechanic was something that didn't really work that well, late game became very tedious. Inventory management and navigation/planning with a map are the core parts of the game, and these are actually pretty enjoyable. 

The game offers you the option to complete tasks in any order at first, but as it progresses, it becomes increasingly linear. The middle portion of the game — the sewers, was not my favorite since I felt like I didn't know where to go or what to do on my first run. 

Graphics look good, a lot of attention to detail was put on the characters, the environments, and even for the damage and environment effects. Even though this is a few years old game, it has beautiful modern looking shaders and lighting. Cinematic cutscenes get really old after the first run (skippable), but there is still a lot to see and find, if you are a completionist type of player.

[h1][b]Resident Evil 2 – A modern survival horror benchmark[/b][/h1]

[b]Verdict:[/b] Recommended

[b]Context:[/b]
I am a picky player who cares about tight pacing, strong atmosphere, and gameplay that feels polished minute to minute. I like survival horror that rewards smart movement, resource discipline, and learning the space instead of mindless action. With Resident Evil 2 Remake, I came in wanting a clean, modern take on a classic, and it delivered.

[b]The good:[/b]
[list]
[*]Excellent survival horror pacing that keeps tension high without feeling unfair.
[*]Strong atmosphere and level design that makes exploration feel purposeful.
[*]Combat and resource management hit that satisfying risk versus reward loop.
[*]Replay value is solid thanks to different routes, scenarios, and challenge runs.
[/list]

[b]The not so good:[/b]
[list]
[*]If you want nonstop action, the slower, deliberate survival style may feel restrictive.
[*]Some backtracking is part of the design and will not be for everyone.
[*]Expect stress and pressure, it is the point, but it can be exhausting in longer sessions.
[/list]

[b]Who should play this:[/b]
[list]
[*]Players who want modern survival horror with strong atmosphere and tight design.
[*]Fans of tense exploration, puzzle solving, and careful resource use.
[*]Anyone looking for a highly replayable horror campaign.
[/list]

[b]Who should skip or wait:[/b]
[list]
[*]Players who prefer action first and hate being limited by ammo or healing.
[*]Anyone who dislikes backtracking and methodical map clearing.
[*]People who are not in the mood for constant tension and jumpy moments.
[/list]

[b]Final thoughts:[/b]
Resident Evil 2 Remake is the kind of game that does not need a long speech, it is simply well made. It nails the core survival horror loop and stays consistently engaging from start to finish. If you are even mildly interested in the genre, it is worth playing at full price, and it is an easy buy on sale. I could see myself revisiting it any time I want a tight, satisfying horror run.

RE2 probably has the best level design for a game of its size, and it is a small game. Most of the game takes place in a police station plus the surrounding area, and the game makes use of every last drop of its setting. The station becomes a character to learn and at the same time its inhabitants aren't going to let you figure it out that easily. 

I appreciate the pacing of the game the most. It's tight and concise, a quality that seems to be lost in the numerous (great) games that have come out in recent years. RE2 is short, but it doesn't waste a single second of your time. 

No cheap jumpscares, just great thrills. Even if you're scared of being scared, the game isn't long enough for it to be a slog. If you find it too much within two hours of playtime you know what you can do.

I've always found the original RE games to be rather overrated and I know a lot of the games' fanbase would crucify me for saying that, but I ended up liking this remake a lot.

My biggest beef in the original REs was that you could never move while shooting.  You'd have to stand still while multiple zombies fly up your rear-end.  Not to mention you had to shoot them in the head about seventeen times before they'd die.  I'm glad the remake actually enables its players to more effectively succeed.

Gameplay is what you would expect.  Lots of zombie killing, things to find, puzzles to solve, etc.  You have 
a pretty useful map that helps you know where you may have missed something.  The dialogue and voice acting is pretty cheap, which is to be expected from Japanese developers, but they usually make up for it in gameplay.  I don't think the plot and storyline are much different from the original, but I can't be 100% sure on that.

So, you can play the story as one of two characters where some parts are different and others remain the same.  Then, there's a whole separate run that can be played with varying differences.  So, there's quite a bit of replay value.

In addition to the story, there are some other game modes that can be played, some of which need to be unlocked first by completing "records", or "challenges" as I would call them.  Completing these "records" can also unlock different items for use in the story.

The 4th Survivor is a survival run-through challenge with limited resources and a crapload of enemies, which is very challenging.  That's not the end of it.  Apparently, beating this unlocks "tofu" characters.  I'm not kidding, you're literally a piece of tofu throughout the whole challenge.  It's incredibly silly.  And there are five different tofu types, each with varying weapons, equipment and silly Japanese one-liners that I didn't understand.  Oh yeah, and the tofu runs have heavy metal music playing in the background, which I really liked.  Finally, the "tofu" runs are egregiously difficult to beat.

Then, there are the Ghost Survivors stories.  You start off with three of them and unlock the fourth.  They are difficult.  You have limited weapons, ammo and consumables, but lots of enemies to work through.  They will test your judgment greatly.

My greatest beef with this game was character slowness.  "Oh, no!  I'm being chased by an invincible tank of a zombie dude and he's quickly gaining on me!  Better keep jogging as casually as I can!"  Seriously, developers can do better than this.

In the end, I'm sure Resident Evil fans would really like this.  Still, people who aren't too much into the franchise, like me, would also like it.

This game nails survival horror. It brings back everything that made the first game great and nothing that made the first game bad. The remake looks incredible. The combat is very good. The rest of this review only concerns the second run (after you beat the game, you can play through it again as the other character).
I'm not usually interested in playing a game a second time immediately after beating it. I only played through RE1 once. After looking online, it seemed like many people believed doing both runs in RE2 is necessary to consider the game "beaten". There are many differences between the runs, and you have to do both to unlock the true ending so I decided to do both for this game. For the most part, I enjoyed the second run. It's mostly the same places but the enemies therein and the path you take are different. The story is also different, but it can feel awkward. At times I can see where Leon's story and Claire's story match up and it feels like they are happening together. At others it's impossible for both stories to be happening together. The true ending is fine, but nothing to write home about. All in all, I would prefer they either committed more to the second run, making it clear that it's a core part of the game and making the plot actually line up with the first run, or just not have the second run and put more content into the first. Luckily the game is good enough that playing it again is still a lot of fun.

Resident Evil 2 Remake offers a visually stunning experience that pays homage to the original game while adding modern flair. The graphics are impressive, capturing the eerie atmosphere of Raccoon City with meticulous detail. The story, centered around Leon and his evolution into a special agent, is engaging and keeps you invested in the unfolding chaos.

However, the gameplay shift introduced by Capcom raised some concerns for me. While some argue the difficulty is too easy, I found it unnecessarily challenging. Managing resources, particularly ammo, became a frustrating ordeal. This prompted me to switch to assisted mode, though it felt like a compromise that detracted from the authentic experience the game intended to deliver.

The addition of Ada's perspective and the EMF hacking mechanic added a refreshing twist to the gameplay. It didn't drastically alter the experience, but it provided a welcome change of pace, preventing staleness.

The game's backtracking mechanic is both a strength and a weakness. Navigating the intricately designed environments adds a layer of mystery and complexity, encouraging multiple playthroughs. On the flip side, the constant back-and-forth, coupled with respawning zombies, can dilute the zombie survival experience. Nevertheless, the level design is commendable, offering a sense of exploration and discovery with each return.

The non-linear nature of the game, allowing exploration and backtracking, stands in contrast to more linear Resident Evil titles. Each area's depth demands substantial time, making the overall experience dense and complicated. The two campaigns, with some overlap and new elements, enhance replay value and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the narrative.

Additionally, the inclusion of adaptive difficulty intrigued me, although I was initially unaware of its existence. The system responds to the player's performance, dynamically adjusting the challenge. While it's a clever concept, it might inadvertently punish skilled players. Had I known about it earlier, my approach to the game's difficulty settings might have been different.

Resident Evil 2 Remake boasts additional modes and content, though I haven't explored them extensively. The promise of diverse gameplay experiences adds to the overall appeal, making it likely that I'll revisit the game in the future.

In conclusion, despite some frustrations with difficulty and backtracking, Resident Evil 2 Remake offers a gripping and visually impressive experience. The adaptive difficulty system and multiple campaigns enhance replayability. I'm eager to dive into Resident Evil 3 and hopeful that Capcom continues remaking other titles in the series.

I also found the soundtrack rather bland with nothing standout that I'd play in my car on my way to work.

However the gameplay is quite tense and fun, and the graphics are amazing as all the other modern Resident Evil games. That slow paced survival gameplay was the main reason that I still did a couple of playthroughs even after 100% completion, just because how much fun it was and because of all the amazing unlockable weapons and costumes. Not to mention the very cool changes in each playthrough between the two main characters. Also level design is sublime and the interconnected map reminds me a lot of Dark Souls level design philosophy. 

It was quite a fun achievement list as well, most of them including collectibles can be done without a guide. Although the Extra modes was where the fun ended for me. That's where the game forget all about slow paced survival game design, and throws seemingly unending enemies at you. With "No way out" extra mode being the worst offender, where the game puts you in a tight space and throws 100 zombies at you to kill with somewhat limited resources! After playing it again, I am gonna wirte a new review, because I think my last one wasnt entirely fair.
For me, the game has gone up from 3,5/10 to 6/10.
I still dont think its half as good as people make it out to be, it has some significant flaws that you cant deny. But I am just gonna explain where the game does good and where it loses its points:

The story and graphics are really good. Cant say much more there. They are definitely up to standard for that time. The progression system is awesome, its designed in a clever way and pretty satisfying. The puzzles are designed pretty well and are satisfying to solve.

But the game loses me in pretty much every other aspect. The bosses are complete arse, no one can deny that. The only boss in the game, that is "okay" is the 3rd Birkin Fight, the others are so unremarkable, boring or badly designed, its not even funny. And they dont even make sense in the storyline, as both Leon and Claire often fight the same bosses in each storyline, which makes no sense. -2 points

I get that the inventory management is supposed to play a big role in the survival horror franchise, but I dont care, its still garbage. Progression items taking up inventory slots is such a cheap way of dragging out the length of the game, it pretty much just makes you run back and forth between locations to grab items that you couldnt pick up earlier because your inventory was littered with items that you NEED to proceed in the game. And those often take up ungodly amounts of space. -1 point

Enemies are bullet sponges and sometimes dont have a clear weak spot, which makes them tedious to fight. -0,5 points

And lastly, limited saves on veteran mode. Worst mechanic I have seen in a long time. How many times I saved doesnt reflect my skill in any way, but the game wants to make it look like it. -0,5

In the end, the game is merely "okay". It is much worse than RE4 Remake, in every way. If you want a really good remake, go play RE4 Remake, its ungodly good.

This is a game that does everything nearly perfectly:
     
     The difficulty is just hard enough to create tension with you and your environment, but just easy enough to where the mechanics are easily accessible and allow for a gentle skill curve. There are multiple game modes and story lines the player can follow up on that keeps the stories and their respective progression relatively fresh.
     I find it really impressive how the action, survival, and horror mechanics all click with one another, allowing for a truly unforgettable experience. Each of the two stories between Leon and Claire feel unique to each other, making it worth playing them each thoroughly.
     The controls are very intuitive and responsive, feel both smooth and snappy, which allows for a very satisfying gameplay loop that rarely gets tiring.
     My only con with the game though is that if a new resident evil player comes to play completely blind and finds themselves in a really difficult spot, and has used up a large amount of the finite resources given to them, the difficulty gradually spikes, making it quite frustrating at times. But as long as you think in terms of "what can i afford to use" rather that "whats everything i can use", you'll be perfectly good to go.
     It is very very much worth it to anyone considering getting this...

Having just completed Resident Evil 2, I'm compelled to share my exhilarating journey through the Raccoon City Police Department and the nightmarish streets beyond. As someone relatively new to the Resident Evil series, this reimagining of a classic has left an indelible mark, proving that survival horror can be both nostalgic and utterly gripping in the modern gaming landscape.

The narrative follows Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield, two distinct characters with their own perspectives on the unfolding chaos in Raccoon City. The storytelling is masterfully executed, blending suspense, horror, and occasional moments of respite to create a truly immersive experience. The intertwining campaigns added a layer of complexity to the plot, and discovering how their paths converged kept me invested from beginning to end.

The atmosphere in Resident Evil 2 is nothing short of chilling. The abandoned police station, shrouded in darkness, is a masterclass in environmental design. Every creak, distant groan, and the echo of my footsteps contributed to an atmosphere that was both tense and unnerving. The dynamic lighting and weather effects further heightened the sense of dread, creating an environment where I was never truly at ease.

Gameplay-wise, Resident Evil 2 struck a perfect balance between survival horror and action. The limited resources and scarcity of ammunition constantly forced me to make strategic decisions, and every encounter with the relentless undead felt like a life-or-death struggle. The puzzles scattered throughout the police station added a cerebral aspect to the experience, breaking up the tension with moments of critical thinking.

The revamped third-person perspective brought a fresh and modern feel to the classic formula. The controls were responsive, making combat encounters intuitive and satisfying. The redesigned zombies were a sight to behold, each one more grotesque and terrifying than the last. The addition of Mr. X, a relentless and imposing pursuer, elevated the tension to new heights, turning every step into a nerve-wracking experience.

Graphically, Resident Evil 2 is a visual marvel. The attention to detail in character models, environments, and the gruesome demise of the undead showcased the capabilities of modern gaming technology. The sound design was equally superb, with eerie music and spine-chilling sounds that perfectly complemented the horror unfolding on-screen.

In conclusion, Resident Evil 2 is a triumph in survival horror gaming. The perfect blend of atmospheric tension, strategic gameplay, and a gripping narrative make it a must-play for both fans of the series and newcomers alike. As I reflect on my time in Raccoon City, I can't help but appreciate the craftsmanship that went into creating an experience that is not only faithful to the original but also stands as a testament to the evolution of the survival horror genre. If you're looking for a game that will keep you on the edge of your seat from start to finish, Resident Evil 2 is a hauntingly beautiful nightmare that delivers on every front.

I played through the game on PS4/5 many times before the PC version. This is a great Resident Evil and a superior remake in some many ways, but also it is a terrible RE2 Remake in many other ways. It should have been homerun, but it really isn't for many that will have fond memories of the original. For a thumbs up this is about to be extremely negative. 

One of the biggest grips is there really is no real "Zapping System" form the original present here, and I feel like the game just isn't a proper remake without. Run A and B are pretty much the same with no interlocking story. Your second run fights the same bosses and many of the same story beats with Leon and Clarie never interacting past one interaction and a couple of letters. While you really had to excuse some concessions in the original, I would have hoped this would have been improved for the remake not negated. The replay value is seriously hurt by this. 

"The Story" is more fleshed out in the original and a continuation of the RE1 but too many details left out in the remake especially that RE1 happened and RE2 is the indirect outcome of RE1. 

"Controls" are infinitely better than the original but also purposely made worst for sake of survival horror. This may or may not bug you. This makes sense in some ways but in others doesn't. Other than RE4 all of the newer Resident Evils whether 1st person or 3rd person the player is somewhat purposely gimped in the controls for the sake of the survival horror. RE2 leaned far heavier in the Action than Horror, and I really would have rather have seen it control more like that. More like RE4 and less purposely made worse. 

"HDR" is a train wreak on PC in the REngine. It seems to have been this way since the Ray tracing update, which broke it in different ways in every Resident Evil game. The best way I could find to make it work more reliably is the turn it off in game and turn on Auto-HDR in Win 11 because the info is already there and just works so much better. Special K can also be used to fix HDR as well if you prefer that. Ray Tracing and HDR effects in REngine are very subtle, but it doesn't change they are a mess on PC. 
HDR is either washed out or busted and in game controls don't offer enough control over brightness to fix it. Many PC monitors don't have enough controls on the monitor itself to fix it so the only way to fix it is by using desktop controls, which usually the in game HDR has a fit if you alt tab.  

One thing I will say is that "Ultrawide" even to the extreme ends of the spectrum with "Super Ultrawide" are fantastic. This game looks glorious @ 7680x2160 (32x9 aspect & dual 4k) with a little DLSS, some settings adjustments, and a beefy enough system you can easily hit 120fps.

Overall I do like the game but some of the most important aspects of RE2 are missing in the Remake unfortunately. This along with busted settings on PC  really make it harder to recommend if you enjoyed or remember the original.

Resident Evil 2 (2019) is a remake of a game with the same name that was first released in 1998 for Playstation. The remake take a modern approach for the "outdated" mechanics and, while not all things are present from the original, improved many aspects. I will point out the difference of the OG and the remake here:
- fixed camera and tank control (the "outdated" mechanics) were replaced with third person camera (the modern approach)
- the remake is darker and more gloomy, and for my opinion it is scarier than the original
- overhauled the police station map, which is great! Not because the OG was bad, but for more freshness rather than lazy copy paste
- the story is much more consistent, the OG has kinda different timeline for each scenario, while the remake make it the same timeline with more continuity.
- some enemy, bosses, and map changes to reflect the story and gameplay changes

and now I will point out the pros and cons:
pros: 
- A Very good third person game and also a very good horror game. Even though it switched from the clunky tank controls to the more dynamic third person, it still feels clunky and hard to fight enemies. And with limited resource and inventory, it makes a very good survival horror aspect
- Very good graphics
- The story is solid
- Have many unlockables for replayability

cons:
- this game is kinda heavy. Even though you can change the graphic settings, I don't think the lower option looks good. I think it's the same for all games with RE Engine so be wary of that.
- some frustating area and with the fact that enemy behavior is random, it kinda makes the game somewhat frustating

the two campaigns are pretty similar, with a few differences in boss fights and objectives. leon's campaign was a lot more fun to me. i enjoyed his story with ada, as well as his campaign's weapons were much more fun to use. claire's campaign felt a little more boring (though, it could be because i played her campaign second and therefore already played through most events). her campaign's guns are also a lot less fun. the grenade launcher was awesome, but her numerous handguns felt incredibly weak. for me, that was unfortunate since i used the handguns a lot, excluding boss fights and in areas with a lot of zombies.

the game has all sorts of puzzles to solve and codes to discover. they provide some challenge to the game, but they also dont feel so difficult that theyre impossible to complete. ammo conservation and inventory management is also a huge aspect. of course, you can expand your inventory with hip pouches, store items in the item box, and craft more ammo with gunpowder. however, this only gets you so far, especially in the early game when youre still collecting items and having to haul around key items. near the end of the game, you generally have a larger ammo reserve so you can pump a lot of dmg into the final bosses.

speaking of the final bosses, resident evil 2 has tons of really cool bosses and monsters. i wont go into detail on them to avoid spoilers for the campaign, but i really enjoyed fighting the different enemies. i also really liked how the enemies all had weaknesses that you could discover either by trial and error or by reading the files around raccoon city. its a lot nicer to be able to shoot different weak points or utilize other weapons than hoping you land nothing but headshots on everything.

DRM is not always a bad thing, if used correctly, it protects initial sales. Then good publishers will remove it later on allowing for better experiences.
