Denuvo a very good DRM, since there’s few who know how to crack it, even then it’s tough. Denuvo itself costs ~$5,000 per month for the license, ~$60,000 a year. A game’s sales can’t keep up with the fee forever, and the DRM has to be removed/replaced to salvage income. 

Enigma is $59,920 cheaper. It costs about $400 for initial purchase, and $80 annually for upkeep. TL;DR: It's a 4/10 game. It's from the '90s so take it with a grain of salt. It's just kind of there. I don't have massive nostalgia for Resident Evil because I never played it in the '90s on PS1. The graphics are good but the story is meh and split up over multiple playthroughs. You have to play the game FOUR times to get the entire story. The boss fights are stupid. You're probably better off watching a walk-through video on Youtube and buying the newer games.

Longer version: The graphics are good. It's the first thing you'll notice about this game. However, the intro video of the trucker eating the burger is the most disgusting part of the game. I don't need to hear LOUD LIP SMACKS AND CHOMPING right in my ear in the first 30 seconds of a game.

Unfortunately, this is the kind of game that you MUST watch a walk-through in order to play it. Don't bother trying to play it without one because you will just get frustrated. You'll still get frustrated with the walk-through but slightly less so. There's very limited ammunition so you cannot kill every single zombie. You have to know who to fight and who not to. You'll also need to know exactly where everything is since you can't fight everything. Hence the walk-through.

The boss fights are a pain in the rear. There's really only two boss fights and they're back to back right at the end of the game which is weird. You'd think they'd have like a mid-point boss fight and then a finale. The boss fights are bad because there's only one specific way to accomplish them. There's no room for creativity. You have to have the timing perfect to be standing in the right spot at the right time so you don't get hit. It basically requires you to know exactly where the hit boxes are. If you get hit you might as well reload the game because your character will naturally enter a very long, drawn out animation during which you're locked out of control. However, the boss is free to move about and wind up for swing #2. This means that the boss has started swing #2 right about when you're going to gain control of your character again. Swing #2 is a freebie for the boss. You can take about 3 hits max before you're dead and when you die it's a pain in the rear. The death animations are very, very long and drawn out. So much so that you're better off ALT+F4ing to close the game quickly and then open it up again and try again.

You cannot dodge attacks; you can only slowly walk away and hope you don't get hit. Also the controls for secondary attacks are weird. Press and hold space bar, wait for animation, then left click and wait for another animation before you can attack. However, at that point the boss has moved away from where your grenade is going so it was all pointless.

And then to top it all off, if you defeat the boss, guess what you get to do it again because this game has FOUR playthroughs that you  MUST do to get the entire story. What a stupid idea. I'm fine with having it split up between two separate stories. That actually sounds kind of cool. But this is just the same story 95% the same as you already did. What a dumb idea.

With all that being said, get the game if you really want to relive that '90s video-game frustration. If you don't want that then just watch a Youtube video on the story and purchase one of the later games.

The controls are more responsive, and the updated camera system adds a modern touch without losing the classic survival horror feel. Whether you’re a veteran fan of the series or a newcomer, Resident Evil 2 Remastered is a remarkable achievement. Resident Evil 2 Remake, released in 2019, stands as a shining example of how to masterfully reimagine a classic. Capcom successfully resurrected the survival horror masterpiece, delivering a haunting and intense experience that pays homage to the original while introducing modern gaming elements.

Visually, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a triumph. The RE (Reach for the Moon) Engine showcases its capabilities, bringing the decaying Raccoon City to life with breathtaking detail. From the eerily dimly lit corridors of the police station to the grotesque designs of the undead, the game's atmosphere is nothing short of captivating. The photorealistic graphics contribute to the overall immersion, enhancing the sense of dread and tension.

The narrative remains faithful to the original, following Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield as they navigate the zombie-infested city. However, Capcom took the opportunity to deepen the story, providing more depth to characters and introducing new narrative elements. This narrative expansion not only serves as a treat for series veterans but also engages newcomers with its compelling and well-paced storytelling.

One of the standout features of Resident Evil 2 Remake is its innovative over-the-shoulder perspective, a departure from the fixed-camera angles of the original. This shift in perspective enhances the player's connection to the characters and intensifies the fear of the unknown. The tight controls and responsive aiming system make combat satisfyingly tense, emphasizing resource management and strategic decision-making.

The revamped gameplay mechanics extend beyond combat. Puzzles are cleverly designed, challenging players to think critically and rewarding them with a sense of accomplishment. The interconnected environment encourages exploration, and the ever-looming threat of the relentless Tyrant (Mr. X) adds an extra layer of tension, transforming the game into a nerve-wracking experience.

Resident Evil 2 Remake excels in the audio department, using haunting ambient sounds and a chilling soundtrack to create an atmosphere that constantly keeps players on edge. The groans of zombies, creaking floorboards, and distant echoes contribute to the overall sense of dread, making each encounter a heart-pounding experience.

The game's replay value is commendable, offering two distinct campaigns for Leon and Claire, each providing a unique perspective on the unfolding catastrophe. Additionally, the multiple difficulty settings and unlockable content provide incentives for players to return to Raccoon City and face its horrors in different ways.

In conclusion, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a masterclass in survival horror, seamlessly blending nostalgic elements with modern design to create an unforgettable experience. It successfully captures the essence of the original while introducing innovative features that elevate it to new heights. Whether you're a long-time fan of the series or a newcomer to survival horror, Resident Evil 2 Remake is an absolute must-play that sets a high standard for the genre.

Another excellent remake on Capcom's part. This is an awesome modern take on the classic 1998 Resident Evil 2. You'll explore the iconic locations such as the Raccoon City Police Department, solve puzzles and defeat bosses with the help of an Over The Shoulder Camera (like RE4) and brought alive by the RE Engine's visual prowess. 

Overall, you're getting a streamlined scenario with the classic gameplay loop of item management, resource management, exploration and puzzle solving that have all made a successful transition to the new camera angle and presentation. You can aim freely but, in exchange the enemies take a lot of hits to go down. The new RPD layout makes A LOT more sense than the original, the Sewers feel creepier with ample use of shadows and lighting, and the Lab has a totally different feel than before. It's also very replayable thanks to multiple difficulties, two characters with two scenarios each, and side content to go along with a runtime that doesn't overstay it's welcome. 

My only gripes are that there's no "Zapping" System (picking up an item as Claire during Scenario A would make it disappear for Leon in his B scenario and vice versa). And that the scenarios don't really fit together well. In this the A scenario of your choosing is what actually happens and you have to imagine what the other character is doing because the B scenario has things that literally can't happen to both. The B scenarios were an afterthought and it shows. 

Even with those flaws, this is an excellent game that's well worth playing whether you're a veteran or newcomer. The Over The Shoulder Camera and movement should feel right at home for newer players or are used to modern games making this an accessible point of entry.

I played this game after finishing the Resident Evil 3 and 4 remakes, and it might honestly be my favorite remake entry in the series so far. [b]TL;DR:[/b] buy it if you like third person horror games!

[h3]Pros[/h3]

- [b]Beautiful graphics and sound design[/b], which really breathe life into the horror aspect despite being played a third-person perspective
- A [b]decent length of play time[/b]; playing a single run is fun, but would highly recommend rounding out the story by using the "2nd run" option for the other player character at least
- [b]Reasonable difficulty curve[/b]; limited ammo can seem daunting at first, but with frequent saving (in non-hardcore mode) and some skilful inventory management, this heightens the challenge instead of feeling like a chore. 
    - You're [b]incentivized to seek out hidden items and areas[/b] to fully experience the game to get more resources, and the map tracker feature marking unexplored rooms as red is very helpful.
    - Keep an eye out for [b]helpful loading screen tips[/b] every time you die!
- Some really fun player [b]customization and mods[/b] available if you're into that!

[h3]Cons[/h3]

- For newcomers to the franchise, the layout of the RPD police station can be [b]labyrinthine and frustrating[/b]. The map addresses a lot of these concerns, though.
    - Even for non-newcomers, the amount of [b]backtracking[/b] involved can be very tedious. The player character's movements can feel a tad slow at times due to the lack of sprint, especially when being actively pursued by monsters.
    - You also [b]can't access the entire map[/b] on any single playthrough: a minor frustration, but can interfere with the OCD of having unexplored regions on the map.
- While I found the difficulty reasonable (as someone who feels they're a casual-average skill level gamer), this game pulls no punches and [b]throws you straight into action[/b] which can be daunting if you're unfamiliar (and taunts you to play the game on easy mode if you keep dying).
- Some of the [b]puzzles[/b] (2nd run chemical lab puzzle was one that comes to mind) can slow down the pace quite a bit amidst heavy action sequences.

The remake of Resident Evil 2 dropped seemingly out of nowhere for me, and people absolutely loved it, myself included, all for good reasons.
An already iconic game, with a fresh paint and modernised mechanics - a great way for old veterans to experience the game anew as well as gather completely new fans all together.

The gameplay flows like butter on a hot toast here, with a focus on the horror aspect of Resident Evil games. Yes, you have a lot of tools to utilise and help you survive, however in comparison to the next couple of games - Claire/Leon have their capabilities slightly more limited due to the lack of any sort of dodging mechanic, and the usage of knife being focused more on being your last line of defence more than anything, instead of a tool that you will actively be using in combat in later games - and that's okay.

Resident Evil 2 feels a lot more cramped, dark and claustrophobic which gives it that specific horror theme in my opinion. This doesn't mean however, that the map is small by any means.
The graphics and gore are amazing, however for some reason the protagonist just remains hugely untouched to any visual damage with a few small exceptions, which feels unnecessarily restrictive in comparison to the otherwise great gore that you can inflict on other zombies.
There's a fair amount of puzzles and backtracking here, and the map will actively reflect whether or not you have collected all the possible items in the area, which makes both looting and crafting very satisfying.
My next point here is going to be Mr. X - some love him, others hate him - he's going to be following you almost everywhere, appear in random places to ruin your plans, and you can not just kill him like that, only slow him down and outrun. Great mechanic which adds a bit of a twist to the mix and forces players to often think quickly on their feet.
Lastly, the game has some solid replay-ability thanks to the fact you can compete for a better score at the end of the campaign with some nice unlockables and outfits. Additionally, there's a few other gamemodes which you can try, they're nothing to write home about, but they're fun enough to try a couple of times, possibly try for a high score if that's your jam.

The Resident Evil 2 Remake flawlessly recaptures the dread of the PS1 original while updating it for the modern era. Step into the zombie-infested streets of Raccoon City as Leon and Claire once again - this time with gorgeous new graphics.

The familiar police station and sewers have been expanded and improved. Solve new environmental puzzles and watch out for zombified lickers crawling on the ceiling - yikes!

Combat is weighty and satisfying thanks to the over-the-shoulder camera and intuitive controls. Line up clean headshots or blow zombies away up close with the trusty shotgun - feels so good!

The Tyrant Mr. X stalking you adds thrilling tension. Nothing like hearing his ominous footsteps rapidly approaching when you're low on ammo! Escape requires thinking on your feet.

With additional modes like The 4th Survivor, the RE2 Remake retains the challenge of the PlayStation original while modernizing it masterfully. Old and new fans alike owe it to themselves to experience survival horror done right!

This is my first introduction to the Resident Evil series and I must say this was very worth the purchase that was on sale. 

Perfect balance of the horror aspect, just enough to get the adrenaline going if its your first time playing, and not too much where you'd be constantly trying to brace for some scares.
In some other horror games, I personally think that those loud, abrupt jumpscares can be a total turnoff for the faint hearted players alike, but RE2 was definitely much easier to handle, to a point where i'd be itching to continue multiple runs of the game now. Currently progressing through Claire's storyline and im also looking forward to what changes on the 2nd runs of both Leon's and Claire's side.
Puzzles are quite easy to follow along, but can be tedious going around looking for clues and then going back to the puzzle spots.

Headshots don't even kill Zombies reliably and you have to shoot or sneak past the same Zombies a lot of times. The only thing they do better is the controls and camera are like RE4 and onwards -the quick turn and melee actions.

I personally don't like this, I think it's a step backwards from what we got before and I would only recommend it to people who liked the old games.

I originally bought the game a few years ago. I played Standard difficulty and kept getting killed, eventually ran out of ammo and didn't play anymore. 

Fast-forward to this year, and I was determined to give the game another chance. I have since completed all the runs for Standard mode, finished all but the "Tofu" (if you know, you know) extra game modes, and will probably hop on and give hardcore a try. 

The game is a bit tedious in the way that you must backtrack a lot (and often you need to "rehearse" how to clear certain areas), but the original RE2 was like this as well. Once you learn a few standard operating procedures regarding how to approach the gameplay, the game is a lot easier and more enjoyable. 

It definitely is a scary experience, especially the first time around! I highly recommend a play-through, and even if you only want to do the basic stuff, it's still worth the purchase price. I'm considering buying RE4 and RE5 next. I definitely got some adrenaline pumping while playing this game and it makes me want to do some more horror genre!


*EDIT: July 2024, I have 100%ed the game. All Ghost Survivor modes complete, all Tofu runs complete, all story modes S+ in standard and hardcore. I have unlocked all records for the story and Ghost Survivor modes, which includes all concept art, character models, and infinite weapons. I'm very happy that I didn't pay to unlock everything, but limped through it all. Hardest for me were No Way Out (gunslinger record), Forgotten Soldier, and several of the Tofu runs. S+ runs were manageable due to watching YouTube guides. Now I get to play for fun, I've been putting the difficulty on hardcore mode and cherry picking the rocket launcher or submachine gun.

It is a masterpiece. When I meet someone who says: "I don't like zombie games." I ask: "Did you tried RE 1 or 2?" If not then what do they know about zombie games, since they haven't played the two best zombie games in known universe. So perhaps that is all that needs to be written to show you what I think about this game. This is how a remastered version of a legendary game should look like. You can feel the care and emotions of developers. It has been some time since I played it, so here is how I remember it even now. 

It starts with a classic selection of characters. Leon or Jill. Then a road A or B. Every option is unique, I can assure you. In option B characters switch places and go via the road the other character did, in option A. There are bigger and smaller differences. I loved it since way back in the 90's. The road B is like a bonus game. Legendary police station is here again and it’s so great. You will be going thru the burning Racoon City. Streets filled with zombies, cars fill the streets, again at one point you need to run thru city bus to get thru blockade. But as all locations in the game, it is modified compared to old. I think I haven’t seen anything that was the same as in old game. As you progress thru the story, you will learn what is happening, why, what caused it. All clicks together pretty well. It makes nice connections to RE 1. Basically they were able to deliver the same game but it looks new, locations, items, some enemies, scripts, few mechanics, all is the same but a bit modified in a way that old fan like me is happy. Even the controls are better. Camera changed, but it is not FPV, it is hybrid that allows for surprises. That does not grant you full awareness and creates a space of horror. But overall I like it more than the old camera. Music sound and voices are great. Visuals and graphics as well. Controls too. 

Some examples of what you will encounter: be assured to experience all joys and stress as advertised. You will be running from zombies trying to conserve ammo. Or you will come to that story item only to learn that you shouldn’t have picked that ammo way back. Because your inventory is limited and now full. Then run zombie slalom to the nearest storage and back again. Jumpscares here and there. Some memorization or puzzle here and there. And other joyful moments. Nemesis is coming. Run. It is good that you can outrun him. In some areas you can even lose him. You will try to kill zombies with a knife, only to learn you need to practice so much for it to work that you rather switch to other weapons. And store the knife for the rest of the game. 

As you obtain better weapons, new enemies will be introduced. New routes will be created. Like some walls destroyed. Keys obtained to open new doors. Locations are so well crafted. They are labyrinths at first and as you are progressing thru story and open new rooms, there will be shortcuts created for you to lift off the need to go long ways. So it won't bore you. There are so many fine tunes in the game. Puzzles are just exact, not too hard, not too easy.
The game is an equilibrium of all the things inside. It makes a symphony with all the instruments it was given. I always loved the modifications to your weapons. They are here again and are great. I think even now they reload your weapon. They removed a few enemies from old and given as few new ones. For me the worst were the sewer enemies. I miss that new Nemesis is not murmuring “STARS” any more. 
Oh man how I love that all side characters are here and it is again done in such a great way. You still get to control them at some points.

In the first part, you also left the Mansion, but there was no such thing as a point of no return. In the second part, you leave the first main setting relatively quickly, without this actually being made clear. In addition, you are rushed through the story. At the beginning of the game, a creature appears out of nowhere that can't be defeated yet - stupid if you shoot all your ammunition. This creature also appears again and again later on, so that you don't get too caught up in the game's setting and don't take too much time to get into the story, which is at least occasionally told via some pre-apocalyptic notes. Just how half-heartedly the story is implemented can be seen again at the end - we will probably never find out what happened to the other characters, to whom a scene was dedicated shortly before the end, but who were never mentioned again afterwards. In general, the ending was purely a chain of coincidences that somehow (apparently) led to a goal.
The battles in the game seem very tough, you rarely have the feeling that you can do anything against the opponent in larger boss fights - fortunately, coincidences such as weapons that fall into the player's hand at just the right moment for the fight in particular often help here.

I'm writing this off as a missed opportunity. I don't know if it was rushed development or a desire to preserve nostalgic details, but even while this remake successfully updates the original's graphics and stilted mechanics it declines to give other elements the same treatment. And let's not forget TWO FULL CAMPAIGNS are included - which is still a bonkers amount of content. I admittedly only completed with Leon. Eventually, I'll come back to run the second.

This was my first entry into the Resident Evil franchise, and although the control layout was slightly peculiar, it became natural within no time. The classic Resident Evil metroidvania loop of having to find items to open up passageways and obtain upgrades feels extremely satisfying, and is complemented greatly by both the smaller map size, shorter story, and obvious visual cues for where everything is used. I never found myself questioning where something was used for, but moreso, where I could find the obtainable piece which made exploration feel all the more rewarding. Similarly, the shorter runtime, with a slowly expanding map, meant that I was never put in a position where I had to try to remember the location and existence of a door from ten hours ago, just to use the key I found. 

The game also makes great use of the Tyrant, to help push you around the map by both giving you agency and restricting certain pathways, giving you just enough time to get used to your surroundings before introducing him. Despite this, the Tyrant still never feels as menacing as he could have since avoiding him is usually as simple as just moving in the opposite direction. 

The gunplay is also top notch, giving you an incentive to aim for headshots, but also not making it frustrating or too risky to do so. Aiming is simple, with precision increasing the longer you aim whilst still. This creates a decision for the player, is it better to be accurate, or is it better to be moving, and the answer is different for every situation. 

My biggest critique of this game would be the boss fights. Some include gimmicks, and some require you to hit weak spots or survive for a specific amount of time. The biggest issue with these different boss types, is it's not always clear which is which. Upon my first encounter with the gimmick boss, I found myself unloading several bullets into the enemy before my character played a voice line instructing me on how to activate the gimmick. Some of the boss fights also feel as though they are designed with the implementation of dodging in mind. This is great, except for the fact that there is no dodge or evade mechanic in the game. 

Once completing your first playthrough as Leon you unlock the option to do a "2nd Run" with Claire (I am not sure how this works for if you do your first run as Claire). This feels like a nice next chapter in the game, as it is told to you that the 2nd run will include alternate scenarios and an extended ending. Upon beginning this run, however, it becomes increasingly obvious that aside to the accompanying character, and one or two bosses, the game is either extremely similar or even just exactly the same in most segments. 

Weapons are different and some different doors are unlocked, however you will replay the same objects, in the same locations making it feel as though the game is dragging on slightly. The repetitive nature of this playthrough may make you cut corners, and approach the game with more of a speedrunner's mindset, which, although frustrating for some people, can also feel refreshing after slogging yourself around the first playthrough, attempting to discover where to find all the necessary items. 

Ultimately, my playthrough as Claire did feel significantly easier, which I believe is a consequence of spending less time exploring and therefore conserving ammo only for when extremely necessary to the main objective. During this run, the bosses also felt significantly less clunky to outmanoeuvre, however this was instead replaced with them all feeling significantly less difficult and intense. 


The extended ending given with the 2nd Run is nice, and I definitely do believe playing through both runs is required to fully experience the story, however the repetitive nature of the two playthroughs does dampen the experience.

Resident Evil 2 is a great game, however there are some elements of both the story and gameplay that I feel slightly missed the mark. It may just be that my expectations were not set properly as this was my first entry into the Resident Evil franchise, but I can safely say that I did still enjoy my time with it, and look forward to completing reruns of the campaign again in the future.

This is a full blown VR title now! Resident Evil 2 is probably my favorite of the series. A total classic that has been remastered with fantastic graphics. Credit to PrayDog for his VR mod with damn near perfect controls. Enhances the game significantly if you like virtual reality. While Resident Evil is mostly a monster game, the second chapter of the series proves to be mostly a zombie title. A must play for horror fans.

VR Mod instructions:

Download the mod from the Github link - https://github.com/praydog/REFramework/releases

Simply find your copy of Resident Evil 2 in Steam, view its properties and drag the mod files right into its game folder.

Launch Steam VR

Launch Resident Evil 2 from the Steam VR Menu

The final part is a little tricky but not too bad, on your left wrist there is a hidden VR menu that you can play around with rotating your wrist to find. You should be able to enable first person mode and VR from this menu. The menu is also accessible in the upper left hand corner of your monitor out of VR.

Last note - If you pick Leon, there is one bug where you will only see Leon's extremities in your left eye for the first 5-10 minutes of the game. Upon arriving at the police station and changing into your police cloths, the game corrects this bug and the rest of the title plays out flawlessly.

Didn't care that much for the "Ghost Survivors" add on, nor the "Tofu Survivors". Full disclosure I did not complete the "Cat Ears" challenge and only ran 2 of the 5 Tofu runs.

I would highly recommend the game to anyone, but if you are a completionist, expect to encounter some true frustration with some of the in-game records.

Capcom's remake of Resident Evil 2 stands as a shining example of how to modernize a classic while staying true to the essence that made the original a genre-defining masterpiece. Released in 2019, Resident Evil 2 Remake takes players back to Raccoon City with stunning visuals, refined gameplay mechanics, and a renewed sense of terror, delivering an unforgettable survival horror experience.

From the outset, the game impresses with its exceptional graphics and attention to detail. The atmospheric lighting, highly detailed character models, and gruesome environments contribute to a visually stunning and immersive reimagining of the iconic locations from the original game. The switch to the over-the-shoulder third-person perspective enhances both the horror and the action elements, creating a more dynamic and engaging experience.

Resident Evil 2 Remake successfully captures the tension and dread that defined the survival horror genre. The revamped audio design, including hauntingly atmospheric music and spine-chilling sound effects, intensifies the sense of unease as players navigate the labyrinthine halls of the Raccoon City Police Department. The pacing is masterfully executed, with moments of quiet exploration building up to heart-pounding encounters with the nightmarish creatures that inhabit the city.

The narrative, while faithful to the core of the original game, benefits from expanded storytelling and character development. Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield are brought to life with convincing performances, and the intertwining campaigns offer players a fresh perspective on the unfolding nightmare. The addition of new subplots and twists adds depth to the overall narrative without losing the essence of the original storyline.

Gameplay mechanics have been modernized to cater to contemporary gaming expectations. The inventory system, puzzle designs, and combat controls have all received thoughtful updates. The strategic use of limited resources, the clever level design, and the relentless pursuit of terrifying enemies contribute to an experience that perfectly balances survival horror with moments of intense action.

The replay value is high, with multiple campaigns, unlockable content, and additional difficulty levels providing incentives for multiple playthroughs. The implementation of the "Raccoon City Incident Report" system encourages players to explore and master the game, offering a rewarding sense of accomplishment.

While Resident Evil 2 Remake is a near-perfect experience, some might argue that certain segments could be more challenging, and the absence of the original's live-action FMV sequences could be missed by nostalgic fans. However, these are minor concerns in the grand scope of an otherwise exceptional game.

In conclusion, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a triumphant reimagining of a survival horror classic. It successfully blends modern gaming technology with the essence of the original, delivering a gripping, atmospheric, and unforgettable experience. Capcom's commitment to honoring the legacy of Resident Evil while pushing the series forward has resulted in a game that stands tall as one of the finest examples of survival horror in the gaming industry.

Resident Evil 2 is a masterful reimagining of a classic, blending nostalgia with modern gaming sensibilities. The story captivates with its intense, suspenseful narrative, earning a solid 8 out of 10. It brilliantly keeps you on the edge of your seat without revealing too much, ensuring a thrilling experience full of surprises.

The gameplay is commendable, meriting a 7 out of 10. It strikes a balance between challenging and accessible, offering enough difficulty to keep veterans engaged while still being welcoming to newcomers. The controls are responsive, and the game mechanics are well thought out, contributing to a satisfying survival horror experience.

Graphically, Resident Evil 2 is a visual feast. The attention to detail in the environments and character models is outstanding, with lighting and textures that create an immersive, eerie atmosphere. It's a significant step up from the original, and I'd rate the graphics a 9 out of 10. The game consistently impresses with its visuals, making every moment in its world both terrifying and beautiful.

Overall, Resident Evil 2 is a remarkable achievement that revives and enhances a beloved classic for the modern era.

9/10. This RE2 remake is a good story and a solid game. I loved the cinematics and overall art style direction. Unlocking a new area, key, or defeating a boss always feels fresh in this game. The designers of the game had an appreciation for beauty especially in the statues, art, and details that went into this. The aesthetics are a kind of heightened Americana type that I wish the US was more like (consistently). The characters are attractive, especially the women such as Ada, which is something that Western games are not doing as well with lately. The story telling left me with nothing else to be desired. The romance was hot. The boss fights are enjoyable. The game has a bit too many puzzles imo, but those can also be rewarding to solve. I have criticisms of many of the puzzles however, especially because some are so convoluted and tedious to figure out on your own that it will have you relying on online sources. Nevertheless, it is a charming survival horror game. I thought it kind of like Dead Space game but in a contemporary setting, but of course, RE inspired that. It was difficult for me given the limited health, ammo, and time-consuming inventory management, so I bought the DLC because it's more fun to have an MP5 with infinite ammo. Would still suggest that route. The dark environments, jump scares, and powerful enemies still frightened me. I considered it scary so that's good horror in my book. If you're a trophy hunter, most of the trophies are fair and not too obscure. You can finish the game in under 10 hours, so it is a short game, but it does have decent replayability as another character. All in all, I would certainly suggest it.

The map is your best friend. Check every door to make backtracking easy.

Keeping a cheat sheet is recommended, since some combinations/instructions are not stored in the files you always carry around. This is especially helpful for subsequent playthroughs since the answers still work without finding the clues.

You can and should examine the items in your inventory. Sometimes the object name changes, making it easier use or identify. For example to open a box, you'll have to spin it around and find the interact command.

When plot items have been used everywhere possible, they will display a check mark in the bottom part of their icon. There is no record/achievement for keeping all the items, so feel free to discard it once it's used.

Favor walking over running unless you're being chased or know an area is safe, enemies can track you by sound. Lickers and trenchcoat man use it the most, but even basic zombies become way easier to sneak by if they aren't already alerted the instant you enter a room.

There's not too much need to hoard blue herbs as a poison cure. It's a fairly nasty ailment, but only one enemy applies it during a relatively short segment of the sewers and you can even mostly avoid that with a defensive item. Maybe keep at least 1 until you're past that part, but generally the defensive buff you get from combining them with a red herb is pretty substantial and worth using.

The boards you find will permanently stop zombies from coming through a window. They are only for the first floor windows of the police station, so put them away if you're going to the second or third.

While some items stack or can be combined, there are limits for each one. Almost all typewriters are next to storage boxes, so clear up some inventory space for new things. Try one healing item, one or two guns, and maybe a knife, but even that's a lot early on.

Knives degrade slowly when you land attacks. Knives have a durability bar in your inventory menu, a durability icon when in use, and make a sound to let you know when they break.

Knives can be used to test if a corpse on the ground is still alive. Aim at their legs when you poke them, since they can grab and bite you directly from the floor.

Secondary weapons (Grenades, Flash bangs, and Knives) can save you from a grab attack, unless you're grabbed from behind. Make sure to equip the one you want if you expect to get grabbed.

After knives are used in defense, they can be retrieved after taking down that zombie. Knife durability will be reduced by 1/3 each time you use it to escape. Also, zombies can potentially wake up even after retrieving the knife.

Stunning zombies to get by is often more important than killing them. Headshots work well on Standard difficulty, but shooting kneecaps to trip them is recommended for Hardcore.

Sometimes a zombie's head will explode, which means you landed a critical hit. These are rare for pistols and submachine guns, but common for certain high powered weapons and ammo.

Zombies can open (unlocked) doors after banging on them a couple times, with save rooms being the main exception.

Generally speaking, Leon has an easier time dealing with zombies, and Claire has an easier time with bosses.

Certain records/achievements require you to play the game multiple times with both characters, so don't expect to find everything the first time.

Mr Raccoon statues can only be shot once and will never return. While the toy's red base remains in game, it's a good idea to jot down the room's name so you can focus on the rest.

Once a licker screams/attacks, either bolt for the nearest door or kill them. Weapons with stopping power are recommended.

If a dude in a hat and trench coat shows up, save your ammo and run. I hear he's slightly faster on Hardcore.

[h3][b]General Info[/b][/h3]
This is a Resident Evil 2 REmake which features a graphical rebuild and changing of certain story elements to streamline game play. There are basically two "stories" that you can choose from, though the basic premise of the story is roughly the same: You can play as Leon Kennedy through the first day on the job of the Raccoon Police Department, or as Claire Redfield as she searches for her brother.

[h3][b]My Thoughts[/b][/h3]
This game has a very different vibe to the original Resident Evil 2, that's not necessarily a bad thing since even though the original was extremely well made, the controls, pacing, and fixed camera are not for everyone. This REmake does an exceptional job of bringing the game into the more modern era of gaming. I personally would have loved a dodge in the game, but that's just me being a little picky. 

The game looks beautiful, has some fun puzzle elements (though nothing quite like the first Resident Evil game with the bizarrely constructed manor), and introduces game play elements and features that provide a lot of quality of life improvement (being able to expand your inventory blessedly being one of them).

[h3][b]Recommendation[/b][/h3]
If you are a fan of the Resident Evil series for it's story telling, and you do not mind a shift in game play style to something that would be considered more action oriented, then this is a game that you will likely have a lot of fun playing. If you prefer the puzzle elements, tension, controls, and pacing of the original games then the changes they have made to modernize the game may not necessarily sit well with you. In my personal opinion, I think they game is amazing and definitely worth playing through. If price is a consideration, wait for the Steam sales that occur pretty often to pick it up, but the value for the money spent is there.

I initially had a somewhat lukewarm opinion of the remake after my first playthrough, but which each subsequent playthrough I began appreciate the game more and more. With each run it always felt I was learning something new, whether it was a combat trick or familiarity with the level design. The game feels satisfying to play and I always felt in control of the situation, with deaths typically being the result of poor planning on my part. The game is paced well enough that I never felt fully comfortable with my ever dwindling supplies. Gunplay is gratifying due to good sound effects and impact on the enemies. Enemies have a reasonable amount of health on all playthroughs being relatively easy to kill but naturally at the cost of your limited ammo supply.

As far as gameplay I have only several complaints: Mr. X is stressful at first but eventually he just becomes a chore, either forcing you to expend ammo/health to get past him or having to take a long detour to get right back to where you were. There isn't a lot of good enemy variety in the game- of the new enemy types distinct from re1 they are mostly annoying to get around rather than exciting. The boss fights are mostly good except the 2nd form that relies on a gimmick that is infuriating to play around and can often result in instant death. Segments where you play as other characters is novel at first but become bothersome on repeat runs. I wish running was quicker but I understand why it isn't.

The presentation is great. Zombies come apart with each bullet/slash and the atmosphere is tense throughout most of the game. The game isn't as mysterious or memorable as re1's mansion but the police station does more than enough to keep me engaged while exploring every nook and cranny largely in part due to lighting and sound design. Voice acting is good and character models are excellent. Plot strikes a good balance between learning about the underlying cause/circumstances of the zombies and Leon and Claire as characters.

Achievements are fairly doable since there are fewer instant death scenarios than re1 and S+ runs allow a small amount of saves rather than none at all. The main issue are the achievements associated with the extra modes, though I found that they had enough leeway that I could complete them with 2-3 tries.

"Resident Evil 2 Remake" is a masterful reimagining of the 1998 horror classic, offering a deep and engaging experience that pays homage to the original while refining and expanding upon it for a modern audience. Here's an extensive review of why this game is a must-play.

Visual Overhaul and Atmosphere:
The most immediately noticeable improvement in the "Resident Evil 2 Remake" is the visual upgrade. Utilizing the RE Engine, the game presents a darkly beautiful and terrifyingly realistic Raccoon City, with detailed environments, atmospheric lighting, and grotesquely lifelike zombies. The police station, the game's primary locale, is a character in itself, with its intricate architecture now fully realized in stunning high-definition, making the exploration both awe-inspiring and horrifying.

Gameplay Enhancements:
The remake abandons the original's fixed camera angles for a modern over-the-shoulder perspective, significantly updating the game's playability without sacrificing the claustrophobic feel that fans loved. This change, coupled with refined shooting mechanics, makes combat more engaging, and the need to conserve ammunition adds a strategic layer to every encounter.

Sound Design:
Sound plays a crucial role in establishing the game's chilling atmosphere. The moans of zombies, the echo of distant gunfire, and the character's footsteps reverberating through the halls create an immersive and nerve-wracking audio experience. The game's soundtrack is carefully used to enhance key moments, adding to the tension and release during gameplay.

Narrative and Dual Campaigns:
"Resident Evil 2 Remake" features two parallel campaigns with protagonists Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield, each offering a distinct storyline and unique gameplay experiences. This dual approach not only provides different perspectives on the outbreak but also increases replayability, as players uncover the full story by playing through both characters' eyes.

Survival Horror Elements:
True to the series' roots, the game emphasizes survival horror elements. Resource management is critical, with limited inventory space and scarce supplies forcing players to make tough decisions about what to carry. The puzzles, a staple of the original, return with a fresh twist, requiring players to explore and interact with their environment thoughtfully.

Enemy Variety and AI:
The zombies in "Resident Evil 2 Remake" are not the only threat. The game introduces a variety of enemies, each with unique behaviors and weaknesses, including the iconic and relentless Tyrant, known as Mr. X. The AI is unpredictable, making each playthrough a unique challenge.

Character Development:
The characters in the "Resident Evil 2 Remake" are more developed, with expanded backstories and motivations. Leon and Claire are more fleshed out, making players more invested in their survival and journey. The supporting cast also benefits from this attention to detail, adding depth to the game's narrative.

Modernized Controls and Interface:
The controls have been modernized, making the game more accessible to newcomers while remaining challenging enough for veterans. The user interface is sleek and intuitive, ensuring that players spend less time wrestling with menus and more time enjoying the gameplay.

Replayability:
Beyond the dual campaigns, "Resident Evil 2 Remake" offers unlockable modes, secrets, and difficulty levels that encourage multiple playthroughs. The game rewards exploration and mastery, enticing players to return to Raccoon City again and again.

In conclusion, the "Resident Evil 2 Remake" is a triumphant revival of a classic game. It captures the essence of the original while improving upon it in every way, from graphics to gameplay to story. The game manages to be both nostalgic and fresh, providing an experience that is accessible to newcomers and deeply satisfying for long-time fans. Whether you're looking for a terrifying horror experience, a challenging survival game, or simply a well-crafted story, "Resident Evil 2 Remake" delivers on all fronts and stands as a benchmark for how to do a video game remake right.

The A story for this game is amazing. The art museum turned RPD is one of, if not the best location in gaming history, and although the later locations like the parking lot, sewers and laboratory are weaker, they're still fun, and you do get to revisit the RPD twice throughout the story, one of the times being optional. B story is also great fun with a different starting point, different item locations, and different, more difficult enemy placements.

I will warn you, B story can be VERY irritating if you active Mr. X early. To avoid this, don't enter the S.T.A.R.S Office Hallway past the locker and shower room where you use the valve to stop the steam. It'll stop Mr. X from spawning in until you're ready to go to the S.T.A.R.S Office and grab the battery for the bomb. Try and do everything you can possibly do before then so that when you do finally have to grab the battery and active Mr. X, you'll have a good amount of rooms open and you'll have a much easier time looping and losing Mr. X.

Whether this game is better than the Original or not is up to personal opinion. As much as I love this games new gameplay, I feel the Original does a better job at differentiating the A and B stories, a better job at rewarding the player for planning things out ahead of time, and overall just has way better writing compared to this Remake. I think the writing of it is where this game fumbles the most as a Remake. Aside from that, I overall really enjoy this game both as a game in general and as a Remake.

Gameplay-wise, it is extremely fun to play, even upon replays. Highly recommended, however there're a few things to note:

1. While there are enough differences between Leon [1st run] & Claire [2nd run] that you should play both, there aren't enough differences to justify playing Claire [1st run] & Leon [2nd run] on top of that, or vise versa. So if you're not keen on replaying the game, just choose 1 set & ignore the other. That being said, I did all versions of the scenarios multiple times over as I enjoy the gameplay.

2. Only buy the deluxe edition if you're interested in the costumes it provides or the soundtrack swap, the additional weapon is not worth it. The soundtrack swap in particular is a setting that must be toggled manually, otherwise it won't be present during your playthrough. Music comparisons are all subjective in nature, but there are some tracks that the remake does better (countdown sequences for both characters, 4th survivor), while some that better in the original, or in some cases only present in the original (Main hall, save rooms, library). As the ghost survivors are entirely native to this remake, there is no original version soundtrack swap in those scenarios.

• [u]Stunning Graphics[/u]: Resident Evil 2 Remake impresses with its breathtaking visuals, from the detailed character models to the hauntingly atmospheric environments.

• [u]Terrifying Atmosphere[/u]: The game masterfully maintains a tense and frightening atmosphere, creating a true survival horror experience that keeps players on the edge of their seats.

• [u]Reimagined Classic[/u]: The remake successfully captures the essence of the original Resident Evil 2 while modernizing gameplay mechanics, making it accessible to both nostalgic fans and new players.

• [u]Engaging Puzzles[/u]: Well-designed puzzles add an extra layer of challenge and depth to the game, requiring players to use their wits and explore the environment.

• [u]Compelling Storyline[/u]: The narrative is expertly crafted, drawing players into a gripping story filled with suspense, intrigue, and memorable characters.

• [u]Multiple Playthroughs[/u]: With different scenarios for both Leon and Claire, each playthrough offers a fresh experience, encouraging replayability and exploration of alternate story paths.

• [u]Limited Enemy Variety[/u]: While the game excels in creating terrifying zombies, the lack of diverse enemy types may make some encounters feel repetitive over extended play sessions.

• [u]Limited Exploration in Some Areas[/u]: Certain areas may feel restricted in terms of exploration, limiting the player's ability to fully immerse themselves in the detailed environments.

[h1]Resident Evil 2: A Remake Fans Have Been Asking For[/h1]

[b]Resident Evil 2[/b] is a remake of the 1998 classic that was released on the PlayStation. Fans had long been clamoring for a remake because while the original game was still enjoyable, both its graphics and gameplay had become outdated. The remake aimed to offer a fresh experience to both new and old fans of the Resident Evil franchise. Utilizing the same engine as Resident Evil 7, [b]Resident Evil 2[/b] attempted to recapture the essence of the original while providing modern visuals and maintaining its roots in survival horror.

In this game, players take on the roles of either Leon S. Kennedy on his first day as a police officer or Claire Redfield in search of her brother, both set within the Raccoon Police Station. [b]Resident Evil 2[/b] features two scenarios, denoted as A and B scenarios, which can be played by two different characters, resulting in a total of four campaigns that can be completed. While the story doesn't differ significantly based on the character you choose, the narrative is closely tied to the scenarios. It's enjoyable to see the different perspectives and interactions of the characters with their environment, and the canon story can be interpreted by the player, as the final outcome doesn't hold much bearing on the overarching story.

With [b]Resident Evil 2[/b], after venturing into more action-oriented gameplay in Resident Evil 4 and returning to old-school horror in Resident Evil 7, Capcom successfully recaptured the essence of what made the Resident Evil franchise memorable. The remake intensifies the experience compared to the original, especially with the introduction of Mr. X (T-00), a towering and relentless pursuer who chases you for a significant portion of the game, whereas in the original, he only appears in B scenarios. The zombies were also redesigned to be more in line with the original Resident Evil 2. Since Resident Evil 4, shooting zombies in the head has been the most effective method to eliminate them, and that still holds true in modern Resident Evil games. However, the remake adopts the classic approach from the original Resident Evil games where zombies are not easily dispatched, and headshots may lead to critical hits and instant kills, but occurs very rarely. It's often preferred to conserve ammo and avoiding unnecessary combat, particularly because Resident Evil 2 doesn't provide generous supplies like more recent entries. The horror element is maintained by the constant threat of Mr. X, zombies that are difficult to kill, and a scarcity of resources that require careful management.

[b]Resident Evil 2[/b] also incorporates puzzles and hidden items that players can discover. Solving these puzzles and finding hidden items provides valuable rewards, such as weapon upgrades or entirely new weapons. It's worth the effort to solve these puzzles since it allows you to experiment with different weapons. Notably, Leon and Claire have different sets of weapons, which prevents the game from becoming repetitive. Resources found in the environment often come in raw materials, allowing you to craft your preferred type of ammo or healing items. The return of the item box, a staple in the Resident Evil series, plays a crucial role in resource management, as you must save and conserve your limited supplies.

A noteworthy addition to combat in [b]Resident Evil 2[/b] is the use of the knife. While the knife has been an important weapon in various Resident Evil games, it plays a critical role in [b]Resident Evil 2[/b], particularly when dealing with zombie bites. The knife can be used to avoid damage and push zombies away, but it has limited durability and is quite rare to find. Once used, it can only be recovered by defeating the zombie that has it, which may require using additional ammo. This creates a balance between protecting yourself from zombie bites and conserving precious ammunition.

To the best of my recollection, [b]Resident Evil 2[/b] does not have any significant downsides. While Mr. X's presence can become more of an annoyance than a true threat as you become familiar with the game, he can also be avoided. The game may start to feel repetitive if you play it multiple times to complete both scenarios with different characters without taking breaks. At times, [b]Resident Evil 2[/b] might feel too similar to the original, to the point where it could be seen as a cash grab with minimal changes, but it's a well-deserved remake.

In summary, [b]Resident Evil 2[/b] is a solid remake of the original Resident Evil 2 (1998) that remains faithful to its roots. Players who are more accustomed to modern Resident Evil titles might struggle to adapt to the gameplay mechanics of [b]Resident Evil 2[/b], but it serves as a great entry point for understanding what made the Resident Evil series great in its early days.

It lives up to its rating. RE2 is a masterpiece, fun to watch and fun to play. With utterly spectacular graphics powered by the best engine of the last decade (also see DMC5 and SF6), RE2 delivers a compact and replayable loop of terror, tension, action and exhilaration. You pick between the male and the female protagonists, and try to survive in the spooky police precinct of the infested Raccoon City of 1998.

Perfected after two decades of practice, the Resident Evil formula delivers to the max. The plot is mercifully simple, the protagonist good-looking, and the action tense. Most of all, the atmosphere is one of gorgeous pervasive oppression and brooding menace. Best played in the dark, RE2 can genuinely get to you.

From a technical perspective, the RE engine never ceases to amaze. It runs great, loads fast, and the models and the lighting look terrific.

In terms of gameplay, you are back to basics polished to the max. You explore a tight space room by room, solving simple puzzles and shuddering before turning every corner.

Each of the two characters has two slightly tweaked scenarios. And if you complete all four versions of the game, you can try to beat the hardcore difficulty, or to get the "S" rating by speed-running. RE2 has something for everyone, from the casuals to the pros.

10/10 - a genuine masterpiece, highlighting both the cinematic potential of gaming as an art, and the sheer fun of carefully calibrated gameplay. If you had to play only one Resident Evil, this is probably the one. But keep in mind that the other RE-engine RE titles are also excellent; some of them close to or on par with RE2...

[h1] Resident Evil 2 Remake: A Faithful Return to PS2 Horror [/h1]

You know you're playing a good Resident Evil game when you need to keep a pen and a piece of scrap paper close at hand. Sitting on the first open page of my notepad are diagrams, numbers, three-letter codes, riddles, safe combinations, and cryptic notes. This is the frantic, stream-of-consciousness note-taking of someone deep down a Resident Evil rabbit hole. As an old-school Resident Evil fan, I couldn't be happier.

Calling this modern Resident Evil 2 a remake feels like an undersell. It's a faithful recreation of the 1998 survival horror classic, but it has been rebuilt completely from the ground up. From detailed character models and animations to the glistening entrails of what used to be a cop, this game looks incredible.

Despite the change from fixed camera angles to a third-person over-the-shoulder perspective, the layout maintains its claustrophobic and oppressive atmosphere. The game ensures you micromanage every detail - exploring, checking your map, examining items, and gathering clues. This meticulous attention to detail is a hallmark of classic Resident Evil games, and it's brilliantly upheld here.

Resident Evil 2 presents two different campaigns depending on whether you choose rookie cop Leon S. Kennedy or college student Claire Redfield. Both are unique experiences, introducing you to different characters, enemies, and weapons. After completing one character's campaign, you can dive into the "2nd Run," a follow-up with the other character that changes the story and gameplay. This non-linear approach keeps the game fresh and challenging, even on subsequent playthroughs.

As you explore, manage limited resources, and solve puzzles, the game maintains a constant tension, balancing the thrill of well-aimed headshots with the need to flee when bullets run low. There's even a sadistic pleasure in disabling zombies one limb at a time. This Resident Evil retains the spirit of the original while updating the gameplay to contemporary standards.

The Tyrant T-00, a formidable foe, intermittently stalks you, adding an element of unpredictability. The risk-reward dynamic of resource management and knowing when to backtrack through infested areas stays true to the classic formula.

This Resident Evil 2 remake is a true classic, blending nostalgia and modern survival horror flawlessly. It retains the heart of the original while embracing new possibilities. Just remember to bring that pen and paper - you're in for a chilling, unforgettable experience.

It is an absolutely great remake and it has successfully "improved and refreshed an absolute classic of this franchise while keeping the original atmosphere intact".

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3162114080

And for those who are not familiar with the original, this is a proper survival horror - really tense and scary ambiance and tight-spaced level design with great sound effects. You never have much ammo or resources, and you have to figure out almost everything for yourself. It is just incredibly immersive.

The police station part takes up most of the game, and it is clearly the best part of it, with great map design and a lot to explore (both the necessary parts and the optional parts if you want to be better prepared for the following sections), including some really nerve-wracking enemies, like the lickers and Mr. X towards the end that really make you stop what you're doing and plan out your route beforehand.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3045477281

The sewers part stretches a bit too long but it is still well done, with puzzles keeping it quite interesting, and it is a decent connection to the finale which is also very interesting, but that's the part where it rather takes on the action horror genre - which it also executed really well.

The characters are very memorable, with the very first inclusion of the icon Leon Kennedy himself, as well as Claire and Ada, who also appears later in the franchise, and are one of the most loved characters.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3166906558

Being able to play two different versions of the story that are also different themselves depending if it's the player's first or second playthrough is also very interesting and makes it worth replaying it, even more than once.
I would have loved to see more difference in their two stories though (as how would Leon's actions affect Claire's story and vice versa), but I believe I'm asking for too much there.
The extra modes, or the "future that could have been" stories of characters that you cross paths with during the original story are very good, but they present more of a challenge for those that would like to try some harder difficulty gameplay than a story that has somewhat of an impact on the original one.

A great game, worth both your money and your time, as it will keep you hooked even after multiple playthroughs.

A terrifying atmospheric remake of one of (if not the) greatest survival horror games of all time.

Though I never played the original RE2, I have heard this kept the spirit of the game alive while bringing it up to the modern standards of a survival horror game. The over the shoulder view, atmosphere, sound design, and set pieces make this a truly terrifying experience. It's not even the "jump scare" moments but the anxiety you get waiting for something to happen. It kept me on my toes the entire time. This game kept the puzzles alive as well, which was fun and a nice break from the action. The enemies felt for more varied than the first two games (RE1 and RE0), which was nice. The boss fights were not overly complicated and changed up the mechanics each time which was nice. It kept things feeling fresh. The overall combat just felt really good. Ammo, while not completely scarce, was limited and made you think about how to tackle each encounter which I really enjoyed. 

I played entirely on Steam Deck and it played flawlessly. I had it set to high/medium mix graphics, and locked it to 40fps and 40hz refresh rate. It took me a little under 12.5 hours to complete.

Overall, my favorite in the franchise so far. I unfortunately never played the original, but if it is anything close to this I'm sure it is fantastic. Highly recommend for anyone wanting to get into the RE world. Enjoyed it every step of the way.

I bought RE 2 Remake a couple of years back and played it for a little while and then didn’t touch it up until a couple of days back. In a way I am disappointed that I didn’t finish the game when I first got it because it turned out to be a great horror experience.

The story of the game is not anything special, it’s a pretty standard, monstrous virus that got out of a pharmaceutical lab and now it’s a hell on earth situation. Instead the characters are the ones that shine the most, even though there were some issues which I will address in a bit. Also, the writing is not the best, then again I am not sure if some of the dialogue sounds bad on purpose or not due to the game being originally released in 1998 and Capcom wanted to act self aware. The issue that I mentioned a few lines above concerns the voice actor of Leon, he just sounds like he is reading off of a script. Something messed up will happen or Mr.X would pop up and in the most calm and almost brain dead way he will say; “You bastard”, “What the ♥♥♥♥”. I mean, he has never seen anything like this, and he acts like he has dealt with zombies in the past at least three times a week. But still, it does not sound like an experienced person in the field, the voice actor just reads what is in front of him. It really seemed like every other voice actor put in effort in their character, except for Leon. Even though I enjoyed the Leon playthrough, his voice acting really pulled me out of the game from time to time.
Thankfully, that was not the case for Claire’s voice actress, she did a really good job throughout the whole story and I ended up enjoying it more than Leon’s story.

There are reasons to replay the game, since you can choose which character you play as, and after you’re done with their story, you can choose to play the 2nd run with the other, which will have you play parts of the story that were happening alongside your first playthrough. Although, I have to mention that parts of the story don’t really stick, meaning that something that you did in your first playthrough, you somehow also do it with the second character, this was probably done due to budgeting, I don’t think it can be justified any other way. 
[spoiler]Although I enjoyed the story on both my playthroughs, I have to admit that the sewers were the least interesting place and felt like a chore to get through.[/spoiler] Also, it has to be mentioned that in order to get the true ending you have to do the 2nd run with the character you chose not to play with on your first playthrough. [spoiler]I felt that the ending on my first playthrough was very abrupt but it made sense after completing the 2nd run, which also had two extra boss fights.[/spoiler]

There are also some speedrun story episodes that you can play. I personally did not play them since that is not something that I enjoy.


Gameplay wise, it seems that Capcom has mixed a few of old school mechanics with some more modern ones, which in a way felt refreshing and not repetitive (Talking about the inventory system and how it works, and also the animations when you interact with items and unlocking doors). The way that zombies work in this game - meaning that a single bullet in the head will not kill them - made me more conscious about how many bullets I had left and whether it was worth it for me to engage or not. Even though it might seem tiring in the beginning, I personally enjoyed it and thought that it added a bit of suspense every now and then when things were a bit too calm. 
I enjoyed the weapon choices more in Leon’s story than I did in Claire’s (2nd Run), it just seemed to me that she did not have as powerful weapons as Leon did. Leon had access to his service pistol, a shotgun,[spoiler] a magnum and a flamethrower towards the end of the game.[/spoiler] Claire’s weapons were her personal pistol, which if modified later in the story to take more powerful ammo (a snub revolver), another bit more powerful revolver, another pistol, a grenade launcher which shot flame or acid rounds, a MAC-10, [spoiler]and towards the end of the game a glorified taser gun.[/spoiler]

Personally I think that the game had an excellent soundtrack and sound design. The zombies sounded terrifying with growls and high pitched screeches and screams which really caught you off guard at times. I cannot talk about sound design without mentioning Mr.X with his loud thumping chasing you around in the police station, while also playing his theme in the background which really gets your blood pumping. The gunshots sounded very appropriate for the weapon you were firing, and the impact sound on the zombies were meaty and had depth to it.

The game seems to look beautiful despite the settings you set it on and it ran perfectly on my computer. Despite a few awkward face animations, the overall movement and expressions of the characters was really well done. The variations of zombies all look really well done in the way they move and act and how they look, especially the creepy as ♥♥♥♥ lickers.

I played the entirety of the game on Linux and had the same performance as my Windows machine, which I personally find to be a big plus. So, don’t hesitate to buy this if you have a Linux machine or have a Steam Deck.

Overall, I had a really good time with RE 2 Remake and I cannot wait to play the rest of the installments in the RE world. The game goes on sale quite frequently, but I personally find the asking price to be fairly reasonable for what you get.

TLDRL: It was a great horror experience with a mediocre story, really fun gameplay and an amazing soundtrack. It has some flaws every now and then, but they might not bother you personally.

"Resident Evil 2 Remake" on PC is a shining example of how to breathe new life into a classic title while staying true to the franchise's roots. This reimagining of the survival horror classic surpasses expectations and stands as a testament to what can be achieved in the world of game remakes.

Graphics and Visuals (5/5):
The graphical prowess of "Resident Evil 2 Remake" on PC is nothing short of stunning. The game's RE Engine showcases the terrifying atmosphere of Raccoon City with breathtaking detail. Character models, environments, and grotesque creatures are meticulously designed, immersing players in a nightmarish world. The attention to detail in the gore and environmental storytelling is a testament to Capcom's commitment to horror aesthetics.

Gameplay (4.5/5):
The gameplay seamlessly blends elements of classic survival horror with modern controls. The over-the-shoulder perspective provides an immersive experience, making every encounter with zombies, lickers, and other monstrosities a heart-pounding experience. Resource management and exploration remain core to the Resident Evil experience, delivering a rewarding sense of tension and achievement. The only minor drawback is that some purists might miss the tank controls of the original.

Story and Characters (5/5):
"Resident Evil 2 Remake" faithfully recreates the iconic storyline while introducing subtle narrative enhancements that add depth to beloved characters like Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield. The intertwining storylines of the two protagonists keep players engaged throughout. The pacing and storytelling are masterfully executed, delivering an emotionally charged narrative that keeps you invested from start to finish.

Horror Atmosphere (5/5):
The game's true triumph lies in its ability to terrify. The eerie, dimly lit environments, spine-chilling sound design, and relentless pursuit of Mr. X create an atmosphere of constant dread. The fear of what lurks around each corner is palpable, and the game keeps you on edge throughout. The use of audio cues, shadows, and unsettling environmental details make every step a test of nerves.

PC Optimization (4.5/5):
On the PC platform, "Resident Evil 2 Remake" shines even brighter with its enhanced graphics options, support for high refresh rates, and compatibility with a wide range of peripherals. It runs smoothly on most systems, but a slightly higher system demand might be required for players looking to max out the graphical settings.

Overall, "Resident Evil 2 Remake" on PC is a modern masterpiece that successfully reimagines a classic while preserving the essence of what made the original game a beloved horror experience. With its stunning visuals, terrifying atmosphere, and superb gameplay, it stands as one of the best entries in the Resident Evil series and a must-play title for fans of survival horror and newcomers alike.

Directions:

After getting 100% completion in Resident Evil 2 Remake, it's time to finally review it. First of all, the story is really good. You get two scenarios, which offer a lot of replayability, only one of the scenarios is canon though. I think I prefer Claire's side of the story more than Leon's, but their stories tie together nicely in the end. The gameplay is very fun; the first playthrough was scary, and you'll run out of ammo often if you're not careful. I'd recommend starting with Leon's story because it's more intense, primarily since the Shotgun is less powerful than the Grenade Launcher. Resident Evil 2 Remake — Review

Resident Evil 2 Remake is a great example of how to modernize a classic, though not without a few stumbles along the way. It captures the spirit of the original while delivering updated visuals, improved controls, and a tense survival atmosphere that can still make your heart race.

On the positive side, the presentation is outstanding. The RE Engine brings Raccoon City to life with stunning lighting, realistic gore, and an unsettling sense of dread. The sound design deserves special credit — every distant growl, creaking door, and echoing footstep keeps you on edge. Both Leon and Claire’s campaigns are strong, each offering unique perspectives that make multiple playthroughs worthwhile.

However, the pacing and structure can sometimes feel uneven. Certain sections — especially during the second scenario — reuse too much content, and some puzzles or encounters lose their tension after repetition. The inventory system, while faithful to the original, can feel restrictive rather than strategic at times. Also, the AI behavior of enemies like Mr. X can be more frustrating than scary in some areas.

Still, even with its flaws, Resident Evil 2 Remake stands as one of the better modern survival horror titles. It’s polished, atmospheric, and respectful to its roots — though it occasionally struggles to balance nostalgia with innovation.
7.5/10 — a strong remake that shines most of the time, even if it doesn’t always bite as hard as it should.

The first three entries of Resident Evil were among my favorite games for PS1. They were scary and brutal, and I loved them for that. When I saw that Capcom is releasing a remake of RE2, I knew I'll just have to buy it.
Resident Evil 2 offers the player a choice between two characters at the beginning of the game. Both characters (Leon and Claire) have a similar campaign, but there are some differences which make the game worth completing twice. The story takes place in zombie-infested Raccoon City, shortly after the events from the first Resident Evil game. Like in any true survival horror, your main goal is to survive while struggling to make every bullet count.
It's quite obvious right from the bat that this is a remake of the highest quality. The graphics and visual effects are truly outstanding and every movement seems natural and smooth. I don't think I've ever seen more "realistic" zombies in any game or even a movie. The music and sound effects are also impressive, on par with the graphics. Despite using dynamic camera, the game still manages to capture the characteristic creepy atmosphere from the original. Some new mechanics have been introduced (like the ability to board up the windows) and they blend in pretty nicely. Although you can find a variety of weapons and ways to upgrade them, you'll always be short on ammunition. This creates a feeling of constant dread in the player and makes the game incredibly interesting. The storyline is very engaging and I've often found myself chained to the chair, unable to stop playing. There are also a couple of bonus game modes which unlock after finishing the main storyline, but nothing notable story-wise. Incredibly, I didn't notice a single bug during both of my playthroughs - my respect to the developers. My only remark would be aimed at the boss fights, which are fairly scripted and sometimes tend to be annoying. I'd also like to see more story-oriented content added, but that would probably be an overkill.

I had high expectations, but this remake is really excellent. Hands down one of the best horror games ever made.
