========================================================

While this remake of Resident Evil 2 might not be the greatest survival horror game of all time (there are some other great contenders for this title that I believe surpass RE2make), it is THE definitive survival horror game for people who are unfamiliar with the genre.

Pros:
- a very faithful yet at the same time modern recreation of every iconic location of the original game
- smooth and precise over-the-shoulder gameplay with resource management that's very easy to grasp but requires the player to keep paying attention at their ammo and such at all times
- simple puzzle solving embedded in some of the most clever level design I've seen in a game of this type
- a completely seamless experience in which you can go from the very starting point all the way to the end without a single loading time
- a lot of replayability thanks to the various playable scenarios, difficulty settings
- good scares here and there but nothing that would cause a panic attack either meaning the player can keep focusing on playing the game without fearing for cheap jumpscares and such
- incredibly beautiful graphics that still hold up a few years later (with ray-tracing and FSR support!)
- lots of graphical options as well as great optimisation make this game playable even on weaker hardware while keeping acceptable performances and graphics quality
- the in-game logic is not tied to the framerate meaning you can go way beyond 60FPS without fear of breaking the game (remember Alien Isolation?)
- a very active modding community over at [url=https://www.nexusmods.com/residentevil22019]Nexusmods[/url] (NSFW warning)

Cons:
- unlockables don't feel rewarding enough aside from the 2nd run campaigns (for example, a game mode with fixed camera and tank controls would've been cool)
- the inclusion of ray-tracing feels very superficial and almost non-existent in places, and drags performances way down on AMD GPUs
- in some places, Leon/Claire's model doesn't cast shadows for some reason even with ray-tracing enabled, seems like a pretty big oversight considering how good this game looks
- all RE Engine games could use a proper benchmark mode, if you're gonna put so many graphical options in the game you should give players a way to test the performances without having to go in-game
- the classic RE2 OST is a DLC :(

Overall:
The Resident Evil 2 Remake is a great way of introducing anyone to both the survival horror genre and the Resident Evil franchise, perhaps the best game for this actually.
It doesn't require any prior knowledge of the RE series to get into it as the story is told from the perspective of characters who were completely new at the time the original RE2 was released (Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield), and it teaches the usual gameplay mechanics from both classic and modern RE games through gameplay naturally instead of forcing tutorials down your throat like most games do nowadays, which is a green flag when it comes to game design.
While some other games are probably objectively better, you still get a nearly flawless survival horror experience with great main characters, great gameplay, some puzzles here and there, completely re-imagined level design that keeps iconic locations and landmarks intact, and some of the most legendary bosses in the franchise.
RE2 is easily a 9/10 in my book, and a must-play for anyone old enough to handle gruesome stuff. :)

Title: "Resident Evil 2 Remake: Survival Horror's Greatest Hits Reimagined"

Review:
If Resident Evil 2 Remake were a movie, it would be the blockbuster hit of the summer – the kind of film you watch with one eye closed and the other peeking through your fingers. Capcom's reimagining of this survival horror classic is like a love letter to fans of the original, with all the thrills, chills, and zombie kills you could ask for.

Let's start with the dynamic duo at the heart of the game: Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield. These two are like the Batman and Robin of zombie-infested Raccoon City, armed with nothing but their wits and a trusty arsenal of weapons. Watching them navigate the city's twisted streets is like watching a masterclass in zombie survival – if that masterclass also involved a lot of screaming and running for your life.

But the real star of the show is the game's setting: the iconic Raccoon City Police Department. From its dimly lit corridors to its blood-spattered walls, every inch of this haunted house of horrors is dripping with atmosphere. It's like stepping into a nightmare version of your childhood police station – assuming your childhood police station was overrun by the undead and filled with puzzles straight out of a cryptographer's worst nightmare.

And let's not forget about the zombies themselves. These guys are like the Energizer bunnies of the undead world, with an endless supply of energy and a serious case of the munchies. Whether you're blowing their heads off with a shotgun or dodging their outstretched arms like a seasoned matador, there's never a dull moment when you're up against these brain-hungry baddies.

Of course, no Resident Evil game would be complete without its fair share of puzzles, and RE2 Remake doesn't disappoint. From deciphering cryptic codes to hunting down elusive keys, there's always something to keep your brain scratching while your trigger finger gets a workout.

In conclusion, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a spine-tingling thrill ride from start to finish. With its heart-stopping action, hair-raising scares, and enough zombie guts to fill a swimming pool, it's a must-play for any survival horror fan. Just don't forget to pack your courage – you're gonna need it.

Rating: ★★★★★ (5/5)

Resident Evil 2 Remake is an absolute triumph in the world of survival horror gaming. Capcom has taken a beloved classic and breathed new life into it, crafting an experience that both honors the original and sets a new standard for the genre.

From the moment I stepped into the iconic Raccoon City Police Department, I was captivated by the attention to detail and the breathtaking visuals. The level of realism in the environments is astonishing, making every corner of the police station feel hauntingly atmospheric. The lighting effects, shadows, and particle systems work together to create an immersive and spine-chilling atmosphere that keeps you on the edge of your seat.

The gameplay mechanics have been expertly modernized while retaining the essence of the original's tension and fear. The over-the-shoulder perspective adds an intimate connection to the characters, making every encounter with the undead an intense and heart-pounding affair. The updated controls are intuitive, ensuring that even newcomers to the series can dive right in without feeling overwhelmed.

One of the game's standout features is the meticulously designed puzzles that seamlessly blend with the narrative. Solving puzzles to unlock new areas or acquire essential items adds a layer of intellectual engagement that complements the relentless survival horror gameplay. The balance between combat, exploration, and puzzle-solving is finely tuned, ensuring that you're always challenged and invested in the unfolding story.

Speaking of the story, Resident Evil 2 Remake expertly weaves together the narratives of Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield, two iconic characters facing a nightmarish outbreak. The character development is exceptional, and the voice acting and facial animations breathe life into every interaction. I found myself genuinely caring about the protagonists and their struggles, making each narrow escape and moment of triumph all the more rewarding.

The sound design is another area where the game truly shines. From the distant moans of zombies to the creaking of floorboards, every sound draws you deeper into the world of horror. The unsettling soundtrack accentuates the tension, enhancing the overall experience and making every encounter an adrenaline-fueled event.

In conclusion, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a monumental achievement that revitalizes a classic while setting a new standard for survival horror gaming. With its stunning visuals, refined gameplay mechanics, engaging puzzles, and compelling narrative, this game is a must-play for both long-time fans of the series and newcomers alike. Capcom has truly outdone themselves, creating an unforgettable journey through Raccoon City's nightmarish apocalypse.

Although I will always believe that the Resident Evil franchise is silly (anyone who plays any of these games for long enough will be able to tell), this game has ended up meaning a lot to me.

I played this game with a person that I will never be able to explain to anyone. I always try to talk about things and express myself regarding them, yet this person has been able to make me feel things I thought were impossible. I will never forget these memories. If you are reading this, thank you for everything.

Playing through this game was complicated for me, as it was my first ever RE experience, and I played it on Hardcore, as the person I played the game with told me it was really easy. I'll have to admit, it was easy, but it was also really annoying. Its combat system feels janky and unrewarding; the saves and their placement are not always the best; its map design can be quite tedious to walk through; yet, I still really liked the game.

With this game, I've realized that our enjoyment is definitely defined by more than things such as graphics, gameplay, storyline, etc. A game is an experience, after all, and all of our experiences are specially woven into our lives by all the factors that surround them. Although we all play the same game, it's different for all of us. Isn't that the magic of life?

Regardless of the silly story, characters, events, dialogues, items, etc., I enjoyed this experience a lot. It is not always possible to enjoy experiences like these. To whoever is reading this, please try to realize the beauty of living and the world around you. Even during the worst of times, there's still going to be at least one thing to be grateful for: having the possibility of living one more day. To live one more day means having hope. One cannot lose all hope unless one wants to lose the meaning of living.

I am writing this review as an ode to hope. Watching myself play parts of this game, laughing and screaming, and ultimately loving someone, has made me realize just how much I have enjoyed my life. Although the moments in which everything seems calm and beautiful are fleeting or ephemeral, it is important to always strive to have more of them.

To whoever is reading this, if there's anything that you want to do with your life that you are scared of trying, please go out and do so immediately. It is fear that limits our capacity to live. Try living a little more every day. Get a new hobby, read a new book, try a new game, or talk to that girl or guy that you've been interested in for a long time. At the end of the day, what matters is that you tried. We always have to, and we always have to continue trying. To live is to try.

I hope that you are having a great day.
For us, the future, love, hope, and obviously, life.

Resident Evil 2 (2019) is a remake of the original Resident Evil 2 released in 1998. Take the role of Leon Kennedy, a cop-in-training being transferred to the Raccoon City Police Department. As he arrives in Raccoon City, he'll notice that a violent outbreak has ravaged the city, turning citizens into infected zombies and regular animals into deadly creatures. Carefully manage your resources and navigate through the police department and other hidden aspects of Raccoon City to uncover the mysterious origin of the outbreak and put an end to it before all hope is lost.

RE2 is a survival horror game focused around inventory management and puzzle solving. Leon has a very limited inventory meaning as you traverse environments you'll have to make choices and sacrifices on what items you'll carry with you, what items you'll come back for, and what items you'll have to leave behind. You'll always carry some weapons and ammo, but not too much because you'll learn pretty quickly that these zombies are resilient, and your best path forward is often by dodging the zombies completely. Health supplies are also limited though, so risking leaving zombies alive can put your health at a risk and leave you wounded for long periods of time. RE2 is definitely difficult, as you won't be able to just sprint through and gun down anything in your path. Careful routing and resource management will be key to getting you out of your predicaments.

RE2 is pretty scary at times as well, though I would say the focus is less on scares and more on tension-building. You're constantly surrounded or being stalked by creatures whose only purpose is to turn you into  mush as you walk around these dimly-lit environments that are eerily quiet after the human population has abandoned them. While Raccoon City and the other areas you'll explore are unsettling set pieces, I couldn't help but also be fascinated by the visuals throughout. The RE Engine used to power the graphics of this game is an absolute monster and delivers some stunning details, both in cutscenes and in gameplay. 

Once you've finished the story there's a lot of reason to revisit the game. Re-play the story as Claire Redfield, the secondary main character of RE2 that Leon frequently encounters, and see what she was up to while Leon was exploring the police department. Play the New Game+ variants of their storylines to unlock the true ending. Try out the hardcore difficulties that limit how often you can save and increase the danger of enemies. Check out the extra scenarios, little side stories about how the outbreak affected other people in Raccoon City. The modding scene for RE2 is also pretty solid, I did a couple extra playthroughs of the game with mods enabled and there were some absolutely fantastic graphics and gameplay mods.

RE2 is a fantastic display of how a remake should be done. Taking the base game and completely rebuilding it as if it were released in the modern-day, while still retaining what made it special at release. It's got a great balance between horror, action, and puzzles that will make it an intense but enjoyable experience from start to finish. I highly recommend picking up RE2, especially when it goes on sale and especially in the bundle that includes the RE3 remake as well.

One of the best horror games I've ever played. The visuals and audio are perfect. The gun play feels perfect on controller. The game is mature and grounded without trying too hard to be too gritty or overly realistic. The plot has a consistent through line and isn't trying to be overly complicated to seem smarter than it actually is like many games and movies these days. It knows what it is and it's doing it well. 

I'll also add that I did not play much of the original as I disliked the fixed camera aspect of the game. The 3rd person experience feels perfect in my opinion, as I see the original fixed camera angle as a bit of a misstep that probably only came about due to the hardware limitations of the time. I've also just completed Leon's story and plan on revisiting the other story at a later time. I'm also coming at this game as a someone that isn't a mega fan of the series and more of a casual enjoyer, having only previously beaten 4. 

My nits - obviously this game isn't 100% perfect as every game will have SOMETHING to criticize. I have to get this out of the way and just say that I think Mr. X sort of ruins every part of the game that he's in. He just kills the pacing and there is one part where the game just grinds to a halt because of him in a critical moment. I tried to find arguments to justify him being there and even if I go with the "it adds suspense and tension" take, it still doesn't hold up for me. I've heard that he isn't as bad on multiple play-throughs once you're kind of used to him, but I imagine the majority of players are only playing the game once. He's a pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ part of the game and I'm not just saying this because he adds difficulty or makes it scary or anything like that, but because he effects pacing in such an intrusive way. I can only imagine that he killed the game for many first time players and they just stopped playing because of him. 

[spoiler] Another gripe is the lack of closure in Leon's ending. I get that you're supposed to play the game twice to get different perspectives, but I felt like the ending could have been longer with some things explicitly shown instead of left to our imaginations. While I thought the reunion with Claire was a good tie back to the beginning of the game, it felt hollow because he doesn't really go through anything with her the way you do Ada. The story doesn't really let you care about her at all until you play from her perspective (I assume). In a way, I felt like the ending could have been better without her even though I get that they are likely trying to tie their endings together in one scene. I felt like we also needed a scene of Umbrella collapsing or exploding and a shot of Raccoon City at the end and I didn't get that which was kind of disappointing. I was even kind of hoping to possibly leave from the police station and find a car out of town as the train feels a bit too deus-ex-machina in my opinion. Why is there an underground bullet train to umbrella and where does it even go??? Maybe some of this will be answered in multiple playthroughs so forgive me if I'm jumping the gun too much here. [/spoiler]

That being said, this is a 10/10 experience. The game runs flawlessly at 4K with my 3060ti and doesn't have the "bad port syndrome" that a lot Japanese games have. Overall, it's one of the most gripping games I've ever played and it was grounded enough to suspend disbelief and get really into both the characters and the world. Definitely looking forward to eventually playing this a second time and hoping that the other games in the series are anywhere close to as good as this when I decide to play them.

TL;DR: This game needs really thick nostalgia glasses to look good. 

Long version: I haven't played the original, so I was coming into this unbiased. I was immediately drawn in by the incredibly immersive, well paced start of the game, with the terrific ambiance of the zombie attacked building; I will give credit where credit is due, this game did an amazing job in the ambiance, I felt more immersed and stressed than I did in Dead Space or in TLOU. But then, unfortunately, the gameplay happened. 

Everything about it is illogical and poorly implemented - starting from the fact that apparently shooting a zombie in the eye, into the brain, from point-blank range 4 consecutive times is not effective enough to kill it, coming through a couple of unnecessary "ticking clocks" in some situations (a big, unkillable enemy teleporting out of nowhere in a room next to you and chasing you is not a way to make the haunting atmosphere more intense, it's a way for me to uninstall in laughter at the bad design) and all the way through ALL THE RIDICULOUS PUZZLES. And they are ridiculous. 

Don't take me wrong, a well implemented, rational puzzle is a good way to provide a much needed smoothness in the pacing of a game of this kind, give some breathing room, but the puzzle must have the semblance of sense to not break any illusion of verisimilitude. Why are there multiple doors with different pretty symbols in a damn police station? How does a badge get into a bejewelled box unlocked through a crystal on a scepter held by a statue that is missing its left hand? Why do I need a knife to just remove some half-assed duct tape off a board? Why do I need to get a damn card to open a garage door to get out when literally any window would have the same function? 

This also kinda swings back to another weaksauce point, which is the plot - it's nonsensical, and any attempts to justify puzzles using the plot as an excuse somehow make both of them worse. The dialogue is cringy and unnatural. 

I really cannot stress how great the atmosphere is, and as such how tremendously worse every other aspect of the game is to manage to completely ruin that.

P.S. I could also write an essay on all the QoL improvements that are supposed to be in any modern game worth even a single buck, like a free saving system and inventory space that isn't convoluted for the sake of being convoluted, but I feel like I already overspent by buying this on a deep sale and don't want to feel like I am wasting something further on the game by writing more. But I could. 

P.S.S. After finishing the game (I.e. true ending, B run with the other character)so I can kinda feel like I am making my money's worth, no, I don't want to change my review one bit. If anything, my opinion of it is worse, there was nothing redeeming about the second run and the "different perspective" as elements that made no sense to repeat themselves repeated themselves, and everything annoying I stressed above was actually even more underlined. I don't know which is the best 3rd person action horror game, but this is definitely not even close to being there.

RE2 Remake does some things really well, but it also does some things really wrong, in my opinion. I'll focus more on the negatives.

I'm a longtime fan of the series, I replayed the classic fixed camera trilogy multiple times, as well as the original RE4 and RE1 Remake. All absolutely phenomenal games. RE2 Remake is no different, it's still a mindblowingly good game. The presentation is great, game structure and level design is fun and interesting, characters feel alive and have their own personality, monsters look intimidating. Survival aspect is definitely here, as it should be.

However... it's definitely not flawless. Some of those flaws are unfortunately really noticeable. I'm not sure how universal my criticism is, but that's how I'm feeling going through the game (Currently near the end of Claire 2nd) so I have to be honest about it.

-SPOILERS AHEAD-

1) Tyrant. As great as he is, unfortunately he starts being really obnoxious after a while. He shows up mainly in the police station but the thing is... the corridors there are usually very narrow and he's programmed to always grab you by the neck and toss you back during your attempt to outmaneuver him. You can flash him, but in case you're out of grenades you're most likely gonna be forced to backtrack and deal with him first before progressing. During the first few hours, it's not that bothersome and it's really cool, it really is a genuinely great concept... but after dealing with his bs for a few more hours I started feeling like I just want to be done with him for good. He just stops being a fun mechanic after a while, sadly.

2) Bossfights are... not great. It's mostly due to clunky movement of the protagonists. There's no dodge in the game and bosses often use wide arch swings that cover A LOT of area and it's really difficult to get out of the way sometimes. Leon and Claire can hold three weapons, few bags of ammo, 3 sprays and a giant cogwheel at the same time but they cannot... duck in time? Come on bruh. The audio-visual design of those encounters is great, don't get me wrong, but the fights themselves are often annoying.

3) Lickers don't have their unique breathing noise from the original RE2 anymore. It was replaced by the most generic hissing "I'm an evil animal" sound of all time. That... I just simply cannot forgive. They're much more dangerous in the remake, but they were FAR more intimidating and scary in the original.

4) Scenarios don't make any sense. Here's how it works... After you beat the first scenario for one of the characters, for example Leon, then you unlock the 2nd scenario for Claire and vice versa. Completing 1st Claire scenario unlocks the 2nd scenario for Leon. You'd think that means you'll be doing things in the same timeline. Right? Wrong. The events don't match, whatsoever. There are some differences, especially when it comes to door locks, key items and the order of visiting crucial rooms but some things are exactly the same, when they shouldn't be. Tyrant shows up in the exact same way for both characters in both scenarios. You'll know exactly what I mean when you see it if you decide to play.

5) You can literally buy all in-game rewards with real money. I don't have to elaborate further why this is utterly stupid and shouldn't exist.

That's it. Those are the most glaring issues for me personally. RE2 Remake is still a very good game and I have a lot of fun with it, and I'll keep playing it until completion, hopefully (which in itself is already much more than I can say about many AAA games) but at the end of the day I still think RE1 Remake did a better job overall. RE1 Remake is pretty much a perfect game in my opinion. RE2 Remake is close to being on the same level, but it's not.

I still recommend it, because like I said in the beginning, it's still a fantastic game.

From the moment I stepped foot into the dark, desolate streets of Raccoon City, I was spellbound by the stunning graphics and attention to detail. Every corner of the city is beautifully rendered, with eerie lighting, haunting shadows, and atmospheric effects that contribute to a palpable sense of dread. Character models are incredibly realistic, showing off the emotions of fear and exhaustion etched on their faces as they fight for survival. The grotesque and terrifying designs of the various zombies and monsters are nothing short of impressive, giving players a sense of constant unease.

Gameplay:
The gameplay in Resident Evil 2 Remake flawlessly blends classic survival horror mechanics with modern sensibilities. The third-person perspective places you right in the thick of the action, making every encounter with the undead a heart-pounding experience. The scarcity of resources forces players to make crucial decisions about when to fight and when to evade, adding a strategic layer to the gameplay. Furthermore, the puzzles scattered throughout the game are ingeniously designed, striking the perfect balance between challenge and reward.

Story and Atmosphere:
Resident Evil 2 Remake is a masterclass in crafting a gripping narrative. The story remains faithful to the original but is skillfully expanded upon to give more depth to the characters and their motivations. Claire Redfield and Leon Kennedy, the iconic protagonists, are expertly portrayed, making you genuinely care about their plight in this nightmarish setting. Additionally, the game's atmosphere is thick with tension and dread, aided by the hauntingly atmospheric soundtrack that intensifies the overall experience.

Level Design:
The level design in Resident Evil 2 Remake is a testament to the developers' creativity. Each area is meticulously crafted, offering a perfect balance of exploration and danger. The police station, in particular, is a masterpiece of architectural ingenuity, with interconnected rooms and secret passageways that keep players on their toes. Additionally, the varying environments, from the dimly lit sewers to the foreboding underground laboratories, maintain the feeling of a living, breathing nightmare.

Replayability:
Despite completing the game multiple times, I find myself eager to revisit Raccoon City again and again. The game's branching paths, multiple difficulty modes, and unlockable content provide excellent replay value. Furthermore, the introduction of the "2nd Run" feature, offering a fresh perspective on the story, encourages players to dive back into the terrifying world of Resident Evil 2 Remake.

Conclusion:
In conclusion, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a triumphant return to survival horror greatness. Capcom has revitalized a beloved classic, presenting it in a way that will both thrill longtime fans and captivate newcomers. With its top-notch graphics, pulse-pounding game play, engrossing story, and haunting atmosphere, this game stands as a prime example of how to remake a classic while preserving its soul. Whether you're a veteran of the original or new to the series, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a must-play title that will leave you breathless and begging for more.

ㅤResident Evil 2 isn't your standard zombie game; don't make the mistake of thinking it's another horde shooter where the large majority of zombies die in a bullet or two, because they don't. A single zombie can take upwards of 15 bullets to fully die, which is far from sustainable in a game where ammo is as scarce as it is. You have to choose whether to shoot them in the head once to stun them and squeeze by, or spend the ammo on killing them if you think they're gonna be a recurring threat.
ㅤThe puzzles are fine, they're nowhere near as [i]puzzling[/i] as the ones in Resident Evil 1 HD (albeit the hint to the knight puzzle solution in that game is literally nonexistent). They always boil down to one of three things: "Bring this key from one side of the building to the door on the other", trial & error until the thing happens, or a 3 digit combination that can easily be written down and regurgitated on repeat playthroughs.
ㅤSpeaking of repeat playthroughs, there are "2nd Run" variants of each character's story. In the original Resident Evil 2, you'd play your first run as one character (e.g. Claire A) and then you'd play your second run as the other character (e.g. Leon B) and events from your first run would carry over to the second. It's genuinely a cool idea for replayability, but it's where the remake really drops the ball. 2nd runs in the remake are mostly identical to 1st runs. You start in a different place but still run through the game mostly the same as the 1st run, just with item and enemy positions scrambled. Some 3 digit combinations are also changed, but you can just write those down too. You also get a "secret" final boss and ending for beating the 2nd run, which is by far the most substantial difference. Overall, I'd say 2nd runs are only really worth doing once, unless you're going for 100% completion, at which point may God save your soul, for Adaptive Difficulty will do everything in its spiteful power to ♥♥♥♥ up your day.
ㅤAdaptive Difficulty is by far my biggest gripe with the game. It makes fighting zombies very annoying, especially on challenge/completionist runs where you know what you're doing. You could be as precise and deliberate with your headshots as you want, it doesn't matter. You'll still get screwed over by a single zombie with a skull that's apparently thicker than the Berlin Wall. It ups the difficulty (deal less and take more damage) if you're doing well (hitting shots, getting lots of ammo), and makes it easier (deal more and take less damage) if you're doing poorly (missing shots). Basically, it punishes you for doing well and rewards you for playing like ♥♥♥♥. It makes sense, if you're huffing Sharpie fumes, maybe. It's just so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ frustrating when I headshot a zombie and it gets stunned just fine, only for another zombie a few minutes later to eat five bullets, charge me anyway, and instantly put me within inches of my life. It does not feel like my own fault, it feels like I'm having a prank played on me.
ㅤOverall, I'd give it something like an 8/10. It's fun when I'm not doing a challenge run on Hardcore where a zombie withstanding ten thousand shots to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ head doesn't undo about 30 minutes of progress, but when I am it's relentlessly frustrating. Fantastic game. It's my personal favorite Resident Evil, and one of my favorite games to replay as a whole

Graphics

This game has some of the best real-time cutscenes I've ever seen, and some insane detail. The gore is very graphic too. One minor complaint though: the use of screen-space reflections. Turn those off

Gameplay

Gameplay feels like an improved version of Resident Evil 4, with updated controls. I enjoy the mechanic of zombies being nearly impossible to kill, and having to learn to exploit i-frames to beat them. G-Mutants and Ivies are also cool. Lickers are cool if they aren't alone, but if they are, they feel trivial to beat. Mr. X is awesome with how he pursues you unscripted, but sadly he can be easily cheesed. The interconnectedness is another great mechanic, allowing you to explore for optional loot. Bossfights are the biggest highlight, my favorite probably being the Super Tyrant. It feels awesome to dodge or stun him by the skin of my teeth 

Audio

The audio is nice, each enemy has a distinct battle-cry, so you always know how to approach a situation. All the characters have great voice acting. The soundtrack is somewhat lacking, but the highs are high. Mr X's theme feels like that of impending doom. And the lab escape theme (for both Leon and Claire) is also pretty intense. The Super Tyrant theme is the best in my opinion, helping make the boss feel like an epic battle. The credits song is also really good, feeling faithful to 90s grunge

Downsides

There is a severe lack of variety between Leon and Claire and the A and B scenarios. There's some change at the police station in the B scenarios, but then it falls flat. Also, the ending feels out of place? Like Sherry saw both her parents die, and then goes on about getting adopted and buying pets. Weird. There was also no buildup to Code Veronica or RE4 either. Not sure if the former is going to get remade, but the latter was. Anyways, these issues still aren't the end of the world, just a bummer

I recently had the opportunity to play the iconic game "Resident Evil 2," and it was an unforgettable gaming experience. As a fan of survival horror games, I had heard a lot about the title's immersive gameplay and chilling atmosphere. Needless to say, it did not disappoint.

From the moment I started the game, I was drawn into the dark and eerie world of Raccoon City. The game's graphics were incredibly realistic, and the attention to detail in the environment was astonishing. The dimly lit corridors, the haunting sound effects, and the suspenseful music created an atmosphere that kept me on the edge of my seat throughout the entire gameplay.

One of the standout aspects of the game was the well-crafted storyline and character development. I appreciated the depth of the protagonists, Leon and Claire, and their journey through the zombie-infested city. Their encounters with various mutated creatures and the sinister Umbrella Corporation added an extra layer of intrigue to the plot.

The gameplay itself was challenging but rewarding. The scarcity of resources and limited ammunition forced me to carefully plan my every move. The puzzles scattered across the game provided a welcomed break from the constant tension, making me feel like a true survivor trying to uncover the city's dark secrets.

Despite the chilling atmosphere and intense gameplay, I couldn't help but admire the game's design and craftsmanship. The attention to detail in the character animations, the hauntingly beautiful visuals, and the well-crafted narrative all contributed to making "Resident Evil 2" an exceptional gaming masterpiece.

In conclusion, "Resident Evil 2" is a must-play for any survival horror enthusiast. It successfully captures the essence of fear and excitement, leaving players with a sense of accomplishment and a lasting impression. This gaming experience will undoubtedly stay with me for a long time, and I can't wait to immerse myself in the world of Raccoon City again.

I must say I really loved this game. The overriding feeling was that I always I had just the right amount of resources left to keep going; it's an incredibly difficult balance to strike, as most of the time games and up giving you far too much or too little. It's painstakingly crafted, with enemies, puzzles and resources arranged perfectly. It always felt fair, never harsh for the sake of being harsh. 

It had an incredible sense of fun, concise resource management and satisfying problem solving. Crafting was kept simple and to a minimum, just like it should be, and the same goes for weapon customization. The art direction and mechanics were god tier, and teams of voice actors/body/face models were excellent. 

My biggest gripe was Mr X. I appreciated how he spiced things up and forced you to draw on your knowledge of the map and improvise, but I would have preferred if he was only there for a small section, instead of totally inverting the game. A little goes a long way after all. It's not a big deal on PC, as there is a mod to remove him, which I did after leaving the police station.
Initially I also wasn't a huge fan of the sewers, nor the lab, but after subsequent playthroughs they did feel a bit better. 

A lot of people complained about the adaptive difficulty, but I liked it as it prevented the game from becoming too easy once I got better. There is also a mod to remove this feature if you don't like it. 

9/10

Oh man, Resident Evil 2 is one of the best games of all time, and it's also one of my favorite games. So, what about its remake?

They managed to rework this game in a masterful way and thus showed modern players what a real survival horror is!

Excellent gameplay, amazingly recreated locations, atmosphere, gunplay feels very nice, and controlling the character is a pleasure! The plot is almost the same, just as nice, and so are the characters! And of course the puzzles. Here I have to give credit to the remake since the puzzles here are objectively better than in the original; in the original they were also good, but there they were mostly search ones; here it is the same, but here you actually have to solve the puzzles, something that was not so much in the original.

I also like the fact that here, of course, as in the original, you need to save resources, but here it is felt more strongly since ordinary enemies like zombies here are very tanky, and this is cool since it makes you avoid them as much as possible. And of course the boss fights themselves are much better here, since in the original you basically just stand and shoot (well, this was the case for all classic survival horror games at that time, like Silent Hill as an example). I also really like Mr. X here; he now walks almost all over the station! (Though it was neat that in the original he was only in the B scenario.)

But for me, there are 2 major cons here: First con: almost complete absence of a soundtrack. The original RE2 is famous for its amazing soundtracks that set the right tone, and in the remake there are a couple of reworked compositions that sound cool, but it's just a couple; 95 percent of the game has no soundtrack, so I advise you to play the remake with the original soundtrack by buying the DLC (by the way, it would be nice if it were free).

Second con: the original had a unique scenario system that gave more replayability; what you did in playthrough A can affect playthrough B, and so of course there were alternative scenarios like you could play Leon A and Claire B and vice versa that had some unique differences, such as different boss fights, items in different places, and unique differences in the plot, and it was very cool. Yes, it was not super consistent, but it gave you the possibility to experience what the other character was doing at that moment. In the remake, this is simply not there, like they tried but it sucked because they weren't planning it initially; that was just an afterthought after receiving a backlash. Also, the nearly complete lack of Leon's and Claire's interactions was pretty sad.

Perhaps I have some other small nitpicks to the game, but it does not matter. Except that I don't like Chief Irons; in the original he seemed normal but gave off such a creepy and mysterious vibe, and then you read his diary and understand what a creepy and terrible person he is. That was great. In the remake, he just feels like an angry douchebag.

But, as a game in general, this is one of the best survival horror games, probably the best at the moment! The game is really well-crafted, forcing you to explore locations, soak up the atmosphere, solve puzzles, and there are so many different unique moments. A must play!

Been a fan since I was 9 years old back in 1998 when I played the original RE2 for the first time. When I heard we were finally getting a remake I held my breath. Myself, among thousands of others petitioned Capcom for about 10 years to give this to us, and it does not disappoint.
My take:  It is a faithful remake to the original. I think what a lot of people leaving negative reviews don't understand is this was never supposed to be an exact replica of the original. There are some missing enemies like crows and giant spiders, but these are enemies that didnt make much of an impact in the OG games anyway. The only reason crows were there was it worked better in that type of game. Imagine trying to shoot 6 crows buzzing around your head with the controls in RE2 Remake? No thanks. And the spiders can get lost too. They were only in I think 2 areas and were ammo sinks anyways for no reason.
Some areas are missing or different, but I honestly think its for the better as those areas get replaced with new ones. This game is an easy 8+ hour game for casual players with lots of re-play ability and secret modes/items to unlock. The original game was like 2-3hrs casually playing. There is far more to this remake than people realize.

Nostalgia can be very blinding so I did my best to go into this game with a renewed look on the story and it surpassed my expectations. 10/10 amazing remake from the small portion of Capcom that gave RE2 the love it deserved.

After playing through my A Run (With Leon), I was very impressed with Resident Evil 2. It is an impressive survival horror game that is a joy from start to finish. Everything from the puzzles to the exploration were excellently paced meaning there was never a dull moment. As a precursor, this is my first Resident Evil, (after a failed attempt at playing the RE 1 Remaster) so I cannot compare it to the original or any other games in the series beyond what I’ve seen others talk about. From what I have heard, there is cut content from the original RE 2, but for a newcomer, this isn’t much of a bother. I would much rather take the updated graphics and quality of life improvements at the cost of a marginally worse, but still great story. And Leon’s story was exciting. Leon is a rookie cop driven to prove his worth within the force. Upon arriving in Racoon City, he is greeted with a zombie virus that has infected the entire city. He seeks refuge within the police station where he begins to plan his escape out of the city. It is here where you spend a majority of the game, completing puzzles and unlocking rooms in order to help you escape. The puzzles strike a perfect balance between difficulties. I wouldn’t say any were unsolvable, but there were some that required thought and thorough exploration of the map. The police station itself was fun to get lost in, despite the ever present backtracking you must do in order to escape. Progression feels natural as you slowly unlock each room in the station.I would have appreciated more NPC interaction and overall world building, but I suppose the feeling of isolation was intentional in order to keep the player on edge. This was one of the few games I’ve played that really kept me in suspense throughout its entire run time. The scarcity of ammo and lack of a direct manual save meant that each encounter must be met with caution. The gore and lighting also do an incredible job at amplifying this feeling of tension. This game is beautiful and is best played on low brightness in my opinion; it is a small addition to the game that can transform the atmosphere. After you escape the Police Station, you team up with a woman named Ada and the two of you work together to find out the cause of this virus. It is an interesting story of corporate greed that is easy to follow on the surface, but you can’t help but feel like you aren’t being told the whole story. The story isn’t deep by any means, but you really do feel like you’re missing a part of the story by not playing Resident Evil 1. It expects you to know a little bit about Resident Evil 1, which to my knowledge deals with the very beginning of the outbreak. It isn’t a deal breaker, but I wish they spent more time on exposition in the form of audio logs or journals because I don’t expect them to remaster the 1st game any time soon. I enjoyed this second part of the game. It was more linear and story driven which was a nice juxtaposition to the equally entertaining exploration of the Police Station. I found the boss fights to be pretty underwhelming. There were two of them and they honestly felt pretty clunky. The movement in the game is pretty slow and realistic and in the context of fighting giant monsters, just doesn’t make sense. The movement isn’t bad by any means, I just don’t think it fit well with the high intensity of the boss fights

I am a little disappointed at the lack of replayability in this game. I am a little unmotivated to play through Claire’s run as it revisits many of the same sites of the first run. Resident Evil 2 Remake is a great showcase of how remake of classic video games can deliver the same (or even better) fun that the original had in the past. It is an excellent upgrade on every fronts.

RE engine, used since RE7, is a major factor in terms of graphics. The game looks great compared to other modern titles. From lighting to textures and animations are all good and run nicely. Even on low & old hardware such as mine (that still used DX11) can run the game fairly smooth. It’s regrettable now that Capcom decides to change the system requirements to compensate for newer hardware with Ray Tracing options.

The devs took so much care and attention with this remake. They didn’t just change everything to be more in line with modern shooting games. They pick and choose features and details taken from the original that resonate more with players. They keep most of the slow and intense horror atmosphere from the original, while also update things that didn’t age well or can be improved. Things such as slow and hard to kill zombies, scarce ammo, inventory management, save system, or even intricate puzzles are making a return. Tank controls & fixed camera angles are removed entirely. It is enjoyable even for fans who didn’t touch games from that era.

In the main campaign you can play as 2 different characters going through (almost) same events and locations. Leon & Claire each has their own stories that are worth playing in any order, much like the original. Both explore a few of the same locations while also offered different objectives, details, secrets & weapons. The remake also offered some scenarios and survival mode for players who want to enjoy more after the finish the main story. It is a complete package.

The game was enjoyable from start to finish. It didn’t frustrate you with backtracking, dead ends, missing puzzles, etc. You can progress through the story with relative ease without worrying much about getting lost or looking up online for clues & walkthrough. There are also plenty of consumables and upgrades for players. The map also features hints and indicators for items that you came across or missed during the campaign.

Overall, I really enjoyed my time with RE2 Remake. It is a solid remake of an already great title in the survival horror genre.

My first review was extremely brief so I figured I'd do this game a solid and review it with utmost detail.  I know Resident Evil games have been done-to-death.  There have been many sequels, prequels, spin-offs, movies, TV series, VR simulators, and walking simulators of it over the years (Resident Evil: Survivor).  And it's easy for one to think "stupid Capcom doesn't need any more money- it's all the same crap". That IS true for some Resident Evil sequels- some of them ARE crap part 5 for example.  You're in Africa and you play as Chris Redfield: The Lamest Protagonist Ever.  Sheva is surprisingly more interesting.  "Chris are you okay?  You gotta be careful!" "Chris are you okay?  You gotta be careful!" God Sheva SHUT UP.  Where are the zombies?  I'm fighting mutated tribesman?  The final boss is Albert Wesker?  This game did not age well.  (Part 5 remake is gonna suck a**)

But in 2018 when Capcom announced that a Resident Evil 2 remake was in the works I was f****** STOKED.  

It's been out for 4 years now and I still play this like once a week.  Now that's re-playability.

The roadmap for this remake was already laid out for the developers (the 1998 game was a masterpiece).  Guns, chicks, rookie cops, zombies, viruses, mutants, resource management, the london symphony orchestra- all a blueprint for what could be the greatest remake in the history of remakes.  All they had to do was pull it off.

At a time when games are abysmally woke, unfinished, buggy, pay-to-win, and straight up greedy, here comes Resident Evil 2 remake to PULL DOWN THEIR PANTS AND S*** ON ALL OF THEM!

First off, it's extremely well-balanced.  The game is generous enough to give you exactly what you need, but not so much that it's boring because it will IMMEDIATELY challenge you with those said items.  Some kind of built-in AI that actively adjusts the difficulty by analyzing what you have.  This dynamically changes your run, and will force you to adapt.  And when it sees you're getting too much help- it throws you a curveball.

Playthrough after playthrough I've found that every interaction is different.  Sure monsters may appear in the same room as last time, but no two interactions are the same.  Repetitive but not tedious.  Difficult but not impossible.  

Resident Evil 2 differs from other survival horrors in that it actively changes.  It's also fair- it only punishes you when you do something stupid.  It doesn't punish you for no f****** reason like the Amnesia series games.

Maybe you'll play the classic 1st Scenario: all guns all items readily available and playthrough is reminiscent of your memories of the game as a kid, instinctively running down those corridors trying to remember what you did back then.

Maybe you want to go asymmetrical and play the 2nd Scenario: all item locations have been juxtaposed and Mr X keeps the adrenaline pumping as you literally have no time to manage your inventory.  GET OUT OF THE DAMN WAY!  I love it.

The story stays true to the original, it's exactly the same.  I mean EXACTLY like it even takes place in 1998.  That's good: I hate when they try to modernize the media to appeal to a younger audience. The younger audience is stupid.  The younger audience plays GTA V.  The younger audience doesn't know their a** from a hole in the ground.  But developers ALWAYS cave and thus ALWAYS butcher the legacy game to appeal to the younger audience, because they know these youngsters will throw money at it if it features Ariana Grande as the soundtrack.  If the in-game characters use TikTok.  If the main protagonist has a vag***.  (Hey I'm all for female protagonists don't get me wrong- I love me some ladies.  But it become extremely tiresome though because the women are always social justice warriors).  Claire is not a social justice warrior (thank God), she's just a lost chick trying to find her brother. 

The problem is when you modernize the remake too much it doesn't stay true to the original media.  It becomes a different animal.  You end up with a sh**y movie called "The Departed" where all the gangsters have cell phones and whack eachother in-between phone calls.  Maybe I'm rambling but you can't always expect a franchise to change their core product just to appeal to the stupid minority.

And fortunately, that's NOT the case with this installment.  

The only thing that HAS changed, and for the better I'm sure most players would agree, is the fixed camera angles.  They completely ditched the fixed camera angles and went full-on Dead Space 3rd-person perspective.  For it's time the fixed camera angles worked- but it's not appropriate for the 2019 remake.  With better tech comes the potential for better gameplay.  They saw an opportunity and they took it.  So the fixed-camera angles were layed to rest.

Some would argue "it's not the same game then".  True, but tell me this: have you played Resident Evil 1 remake?  It's boring as f*** am I right?  They kept the fixed camera angles in that game and it completely ruined it!  Slowed the entire pace of the game, those door animations are so tedious to watch OMFG just kill me now.  I'm falling asleep over here.

They've also added "Challenge Modes" that weren't in the original game: Reach the end of the map playing as various NPC's from the base game.  It's basically an obstacle course.  Super difficult.  Complete these missions and you unlock rewards like infinite ammo and character accessories. 

I could go on for days but to keep it brief Resident Evil 2 remake is a schematic for everything a good remake SHOULD be.  They covered all the bases.  Left nothing to be desired.  This game has everything.  It leaves you feeling full.  Like you just ate a steak dinner with a glass of fine wine.

Buy it at full price or sale price it doesn't matter.

The original RE2 is considered one of the best games of it's generation, and this remake does it justice.  It feels like that game while adding new twists, turns, and unexpected things.  It is a great 3rd person survival horror game.  

It also has pretty good replayability.  There are 2 characters that you can play as: Leon or Claire.  About 75% of the game is identical between the 2 characters, but there are some interesting differences in that remaining 25%.  There are different story elements, characters, stages, and weapons that they use.  As such, I recommend you play through the game with both characters so you can experience the whole story.  

After you beat the game, you can then do a 2nd turn for both characters.  This is a fun and challenging mode because they locations of items and enemies are different, and the entry point into the 1st stage (Police Station) is different, meaning you have to completely rethink your route.  Finally, there are extra modes, which are basically time trial affairs.  I enjoyed all of them as well.

Just finished my playthrough of Leon and I have to say this one was very enjoyable. For context, I never played the original so this review is unbiased in that regard.

This game functions very similar to RE:0 in terms of its puzzle layout - Central location at the start with a mix of puzzle and combat, with more action towards the end of the run. I tend to prefer the starting puzzle sections more than the combat/action but it still carried me through with story.

Characters are fun and voice actors do a good job (better than previous entries). Story is great and paced very well. However, noticeably absent is extra flavour text that you could read by inspecting point of interest in earlier entries (RE:HD and RE:0) - Perhaps this is a theme with the newer games but it was missed.

Combat and Inventory mechanics were great! This game being modern means it can learn from previous entries and do it's best to present the best of both worlds of challenge and ease of use. One thing that did stand out is the ability to perform critical shots, that wasnt present in the locked off camera games. Free aim allows for headshots, meaning that the 'lock-on' button is void. I often found myself rarely using the shotgun and just using the pistol for headshots (unlike HD or 0). The chase sections were some of the most fear inducing that I've experienced in resident evil so far! Made the puzzle solving in certain sections so much more thrilling.

The boss fights were so much more interactive and intuitive. What previous entries lacked, RE:2 makes up for! Bosses have multiple stages, well designed attacks and you can tell if you're damaging it or not. 

Overall, a solid entry in the series without much to complain about.

The gameplay is mostly the same, there is alot less ammo and more gun types - which does switch things up. This adds to Claires gameplay being more stealthy than Leons 'run and gun' style. Resident Evil 2, the highly anticipated remake of the classic survival horror game, delivers an unforgettable experience that seamlessly blends nostalgia with modern gaming. From its stunning graphics and immersive sound design to its gripping storyline, this game takes players on a chilling adventure through the zombie-infested streets of Raccoon City.

The graphics in Resident Evil 2 are nothing short of breathtaking. The level of detail in both the environments and character models is exceptional, creating a hauntingly realistic atmosphere. The dark and dilapidated hallways, the grotesque creatures, and the atmospheric lighting combine to intensify the feeling of dread and unease. The attention to detail is commendable, capturing the essence of the original while utilizing the power of current-generation hardware to bring the horror to life.

Sound plays a crucial role in setting the tense and eerie tone of Resident Evil 2. The ambient noises, such as distant groans and creaking floors, keep players constantly on edge, heightening the suspense. The chilling soundtrack perfectly complements the gameplay, enhancing the sense of impending danger. From the horrifying screeches of the undead to the echoing gunshots, the sound design contributes significantly to the overall immersion and spine-chilling experience.

The game's story is a compelling narrative that draws players into a desperate struggle for survival. Set during the outbreak of the T-virus, players take on the roles of rookie police officer Leon S. Kennedy and college student Claire Redfield. As they navigate the labyrinthine hallways of the Raccoon City Police Department, uncovering dark secrets and encountering terrifying creatures, their intertwined stories unravel, creating a captivating and suspenseful plot. The well-crafted characters and their motivations add depth to the narrative, keeping players invested in their fates.

Resident Evil 2 excels in creating a sense of vulnerability and tension. The limited resources and relentless enemies force players to make strategic decisions, adding an extra layer of intensity to the gameplay. The puzzles scattered throughout the game provide a welcome break from the constant threat of danger, adding a cerebral element that complements the survival horror experience.

However, Resident Evil 2 is not without its flaws. Some players may find the controls slightly clunky, especially during intense combat scenarios. Additionally, while the game offers multiple playthroughs and branching storylines, the overall replay value may be limited for those who have experienced the original release.

In conclusion, Resident Evil 2 is a masterful remake that successfully revitalizes a beloved classic. With its stunning graphics, immersive sound design, gripping storyline, and intense gameplay, it offers a truly unforgettable horror experience. Despite a few minor shortcomings, the game's strengths far outweigh its weaknesses.

Pretty decent modern remake, but obviously doesn't replace the original RE2.

Zombies taking multiple headshots to down definitely can throw off new players that have the usual mindset of other zombie games where headshots are fatal, making early situations much more tense giving that original RE situation of deciding whether or not to spend a chunk of resources killing one zombie, or spend little or none just to get through. MR. X chasing down the player is also a great idea added to the remake as it gives players the incentive to rush or slow things down to avoid making too much noise.

Unfortunately the few gripes I have are things that are present in the OG that aren't in the remake. The remake's multiple scenarios are pretty much the same storywise going for a more "canon" event, compared to the original where each scenario had unique endings and would sometimes have different areas that weren't accessible in other scenarios. OG scenarios also had sections with small decisions that could affect the following scenario, which is not present in the remake. When it also comes to the remake's stories, some stuff don't make sense like the inconsistent character death of one of the characters.

Because of this remake, I see these modern remakes of RE to be more like a reboot to the series with what has changed from the original.

This is a really great update to one of my favourite Resident Evil games. There's a new over-the-shoulder control scheme that feels much more like a modern video game, and it keeps the same tense exploration and puzzle solving that made me fall in love with the original in the late 90s.

Zombies feel much more menacing and can sometimes take a handful of bullets to take down, only to get back up 20 seconds later. The way enemies react to your bullets is shockingly brutal—zombies will even crawl around without arms or legs until you eliminate them for good. Other iconic enemies like Lickers and Mr. X make their return, and I really like new, terrifying ways they’ve implemented them into the remake.

Classic locations like the Police Station and Umbrella Lab are updated with new passages and doorways that lead to other familiar sections, and I really enjoy the new altered layouts to make more logical sense. I do wish that some extended sections, like the Sewers, were a little less tedious though. But this is a great remake that Resident Evil fans are going to love playing through again, and it’s a game that newcomers will ultimately enjoy as well.

[b] Setting & Writing: [/b]
Resident Evil 2: Remake takes place in notorious Raccoon City. You start the game as Leon Kennedy or Claire Redfield. Leon is on his way to the city to start his first day as a Raccoon City Police officer (RCPD) and Claire is on her way to find her brother Chris who is part of the RCPD. Their paths intersect just outside of the city where they witness their first encounter with the epidemic that has been spreading through Raccoon City. Chaos ensues as the protagonist find out how the epidemic started to spread, who started it, and the nightmare they’re living through to make it out alive. The game has three distinct acts, notable by location. If you’re a veteran to the game, you know the story and you know the bad guy. For newcomers, expect a exciting yet cliché story. What makes it work is that it never overstays its welcome and the story just keeps pulling you along, so you don’t have to think too long on non-sensical situations.

[b] Gameplay system & Bosses: [/b]
RE2: Remake implements the popular over the shoulder third-person view camera. The resident evil team first implemented this type of control and gameplay back in Resident Evil 4. This was such a popular design choice by the team that it stayed around up until Resident Evil 7, which was the first time the team decided to go to first-person view. Another staple to the story are the puzzles. Essentially, the Resident Evil series were escape rooms before they became a fad (fight me). To progress your way through the story you may find little trinkets and codes that will continue to open up your way forward. Sometimes there’s a little bit of backtracking, but what’s nice is that you have an unintrusive goal list that generally tells you what you need to do. On top of that, the map system marks areas that you haven’t been to yet, allowing you to do further investigation if necessary. The shooting mechanic in RE2 is very risky as you don’t know when you might get more ammo. This leans into the survival horror aspect of the game. Resources are purposefully limited, making you concentrate on each shot taken. Ammo economy is slightly more forgiving on the lighter difficulties, but you feel it none the less. Being frugal with your ammo leads to rewards such as having it for boss fights! Boss fights hurt if you make the wrong move. They hit like a ton of bricks. Granted, they move so slooowww. Having more resources at your behest makes them easier to deal with.   

[b] Quest, Mini-games & Challenges: [/b] 
There’s one main quest of the game and its simple, make it out alive. Everything you do are building block to that singular main goal. Yes, there will be little things you pick up during the story. But Leon and Claire are to make it out of Raccoon City alive. Now after playing through the game enough (because it does go by quick) you realize that this game can be speed-ran. Through speed running the game you get the most exclusive treats. This incentives learning all the puzzles, killing only what is necessary, and optimal pathing. Outside of this, RE2: Remake offers DLCs that add more story beats to the information you’ve gathered within the story.  

[b] Miscellaneous (art, music, etc.): [/b]
RE2 utilizes RE: Engine. This graphics engine has catapulted Capcom into a renaissance. Everything is beautiful, everything feels optimized, and it just works. The team knows how to set the atmosphere and utilizes the power of RE Engine to accomplish that. On top of the sound design makes your trek though survival ominous and spooky.

I was born a little too late to play the OG Resident Evil games back in the PS1 era. It wasn't until I was 12 or 13 years old that my parents bought me Resident Evil 4 for the GameCube after I wrote them an essay arguing that I was mature enough for the graphic violence and it wouldn't turn me into a poorly adjusted adult. I freaking loved that game. I never told them about the nightmares it gave me, though.

Then RE5 came out on the 360 a few years later and I was not a fan. I dabbled in other RE games after that, like Umbrella Chronicles for the Wii, but I resigned myself to having missed the true glory days of the franchise, catching it's last gasp of the brilliance that was RE4. Then Capcom stopped playing games and released this amazing remake, which just oozes with dread, squishy zombie gore, and a deliciously oppressive atmosphere. I also really enjoyed the story (which I know is intentionally campy as hell, but I was pretty lore-ignorant before playing this game).

Anyway, the game is technically polished (from my experience), looks gorgeous, and runs well. What else can I ask for?

Resident Evil 2 on the N64 was the first one I could actually play "as intended." Never got further than the police station, but you'd better believe that when I heard about the remake, I bought and got 100% on it!

PROS
+Multiple improvements over the 1998 version. Kendo's misogyny has been replaced with a tragic micro-story, Ada has a better cover story, the Tyrant is much more intimidating, and the player's interactions with other characters (especially Marvin and Ben) are far more realistic.
+I know the REngine has been praised to death, but holy cow does it deserve it! Even on low-medium graphics, pretty much everything looks incredibly realistic!
+Whereas RE2's story changed based on which character you played as first, RE2R's has a defined story for Leon and Claire. The gameplay will change based on who you play as first, but the story will largely remain the same. By the way, the story is also greatly improved over the original.
+The voice acting is phenomenal. Leon balances the line of idealistic, "happy" rookie cop in deep poop, Marvin's every breath sounds pained, Ada's disregard for Leon slowly fades over the course of the game, Annette is pretty much perfect in every one of her scenes, and Claire really brings the emotion when she needs to. Also, the hyper-scared/frustrated/angry lines for Leon and Claire are 10/10.
+The setting of Raccoon City is phenomenal. Act 1's location has an overwhelming presence, Act 2's is dirty, gross, and uncomfortable, and Act 3's takes great inspiration from the movies, which I personally prefer over the original.
+Classic pains-in-the-ass like the Lickers and Dogs remain, while more silly creatures from the 1998 version like the giant spiders were wisely removed.
+The gameplay is a great reminder of what survival horror is supposed to be. Any time I wanted to move to progress the story, I would first map out my route, identify known obstacles, predict new threats, and grab a loadout for that single step. I'd then do that step (or die trying and start planning all over again), return to a safe zone, and start planning my next step. Inventory space is just as key in this as it was in RE2, making this very difficult, but very rewarding!
+The change to an RE4-style over-the-shoulder perspective greatly improves the gameplay over the original.
+The secondary-weapon system is a great addition of weapons while forcing each successful zombie attack to be another resource decision: do I spend this knife and save some health, or do I take the hit because I'm low on knives?
+The map is familiar to its 1998 version without being an exact copy, which greatly helps return players have a good experience.
+Zombies are actually scary again! There's no feeling like desperately trying to drop one who just refuses to die while he inches closer to you!
+The Tyrant, aka Mr. X, has far exceeded Nemesis from either the original or remake of RE3 as the best ongoing antagonist of the Resident Evil franchise. His constant presence is felt no matter where you go, and has some fantastic scares throughout the game, both in jump-scares and in entrances. His character is further felt in his increasing aggression as he suffers various setbacks throughout the game, and fighting him feels like fighting The Terminator. Not to mention: his face is just disturbing.
+Reading the notes is genuinely rewarding. Between giving hints for where to go/what to do, explaining apparent inconsistencies, and telling tragic stories, they add a great deal to the atmosphere of the game.
+Fun rewards for beating the game at higher difficulties, including infinite-ammo weapons!
+The 4th Survivor returns, posing a great challenge that feels akin to a New Game+ speedrun!
+Even better: the return of the Tofu Survivor!
+Even even better: you can run through the Tofu Survivor as other wonderful Japanese delicacies!
+Mods!
+Flamethrowers!
+DLC: The Original Sounds Pack is one of my favorite DLCs of all time. While the remake has better music for the boss fights, the original soundtrack has far better atmosphere for the entire game.
+DLC: Other options are worth a mention: the costumes are great (especially the Noir costumes) and the Samurai Edges help in the early game, but are well-replaced by the late-game handguns.
+DLC: The Lost Survivors provide some great challenge runs for players who have beaten the game, ultimately unlocking a Nazi Zombies-style survival mode! Great fun!

CONS
-My first playthrough for this was as Leon on Hardcore, and no matter what I did, I would always end up soft-locked near the end of Act 2, unable to handle the five or so G-Adults without dying. After beating Claire's playthrough, I was able to barely scrape through with only a grenade left thanks to liberal use of the now-unlocked infinite knife. While Claire on Hardcore is pretty doable, Leon is pretty much impossible without using speedrunner-level dodging or bonus weapons.
-DLC: While I like the Samurai Edges, they do technically provide an early-game advantage, if you care about that sort of thing.

Resident Evil 2 (2019) - A Classic Reimagined:

The release of the Resident Evil 2 Remake in 2019 brought to life the iconic survival horror experience of the original 1998 game in a stunning new way. While the two games share a core storyline and setting, the Remake masterfully modernizes and expands upon the classic, paying homage to its predecessor while offering fresh thrills for both longtime fans and newcomers.

Storyline and Setting:
Both games share the fundamental premise of a zombie outbreak engulfing Raccoon City. Players step into the shoes of rookie police officer Leon S. Kennedy and college student Claire Redfield as they navigate the chaos and uncover the sinister secrets behind the catastrophe. The core narrative remains intact, although the Remake adds more depth and nuance to character interactions and plot developments.

Locations:
Key locations from the original game, such as the Raccoon City Police Department (R.P.D.) and the underground Umbrella Laboratory, are meticulously recreated in the Remake. Fans of the original will recognize the layouts, puzzles, and challenges, while enjoying updated visuals and immersive environments that enhance the horror experience.

Puzzles and Exploration:
Both versions of Resident Evil 2 incorporate intricate puzzles and exploration elements that are integral to the gameplay. While the Remake retains many of the classic puzzles, it also introduces new ones that fit seamlessly into the redesigned environments. This blend of nostalgia and novelty keeps players engaged and challenged.

Enemies and Survival:
The iconic enemies from the original, such as the gruesome Lickers and hulking Tyrant, make their return in the Remake, retaining their ability to terrify players. The survival mechanics—limited resources, inventory management, and the need to strategize—are preserved, giving players a sense of vulnerability and tension that defines the franchise.

Tense Atmosphere
Both games excel in building an oppressive and tense atmosphere. Dark corridors, eerie soundscapes, and unexpected encounters contribute to a feeling of dread throughout the journey. The Remake elevates this atmosphere through advanced graphics, sound design, and lighting effects, intensifying the horror.

Unlockables and Extra Modes:
Just like the original, the Remake offers players additional content upon completion, including new scenarios and gameplay modes. This pays tribute to the tradition of rewarding players for their dedication while enhancing replayability.

Conclusion:
The Resident Evil 2 Remake successfully captures the essence of the original while modernizing it for contemporary audiences. By preserving key elements such as storyline, locations, puzzles, and survival mechanics, it ensures that players can relive the classic experience while enjoying updated visuals and refined gameplay. The similarities between the two games demonstrate the enduring appeal of Resident Evil 2's core concepts and its ability to captivate new and old fans alike. Whether you're a fan of the original or a newcomer to the franchise, the Resident Evil 2 Remake stands as a remarkable testament to the timeless allure of survival horror.

[h1]RESIDENT EVIL 2 REVIEW[/h1]

[h3]GAMEPLAY - 9/10[/h3]
Resident Evil 2 was the first game in the franchise that I played. The game has most elements of the survival horror genre that you'd expect, along with a good story. There's also a sense of resource preservation, as you have to manage your resources and inventory space. There's a constant feeling of being on edge with Mr. X stalking the ♥♥♥♥ out of you throughout most of the game. The puzzles are pretty solid—neither too easy nor too hard. The game also has an element of replayability, as it seems to encourage you to get every piece of content out of it. If you're an achievement hunter, then you'll probably find some of the achievements tedious and annoying, since some of them require you to either look online or load saves over and over. Overall, I'd give the gameplay a solid 9/10, as the game loop hooked me within just my first 30 minutes of playing.

[h3]GRAPHICS - 10/10[/h3]
To be honest, there's not much to say about the graphics. They're some of the best you'll see, and you really don't need an insane GPU or setup to experience them at their best. CAPCOM just has a really solid engine with amazing lighting and shadow work. They also did a really good job on character animation—some of the best I've seen in modern gaming—even holding up in 2025. So yeah, I'd rate the graphics a solid 10/10.

[h3]ATMOSPHERE & SOUND - 10/10[/h3]
Now onto one of my favorite aspects of the game. I'd recommend playing this with a nice pair of headphones, as the atmosphere in this game is peak. I personally believe that the RE series in general has some of the best ambiance in all of survival horror, or possibly even gaming. If I'm playing a game multiple times, I usually turn on music or just kind of speed-run it. But the ambiance here is so good that I was locked in for all my playthroughs. I'd rate it a solid 10/10 on atmosphere and sound design, including the OST. The Resident Evil games just do such a good job with their OSTs.

[h3]STORY - 8/10[/h3]
The Resident Evil franchise just so happens to be on of my favorite video game timelines/storylines. The Resident Evil franchise doesn't craft the best story in my opinion, but I think it creates a really unique and cool world that you haven't really seen before in the Biopunk genre, especially in video games. I'd give the story of RE 2 a solid 8/10, since it isn't my favorite single game out of the franchise yet.

[h3]Final Thoughts - 9/10[/h3]
The Resident Evil series doesn't have the greatest story or writing, but there's just something about it that I hold near and dear to my heart. If you're not interested in the lore of the series, I believe you can still get something out of playing it since the games themselves can be played without prior knowledge and are just fun all around. So if you're looking for a fun survival horror game to play. [u]Buy it on a sale and have fun![/u]

If you have nerves of steel, definitely get this game!
