[h1] Review[/h1] 
Initially I was absolutely not interested in seeing a remake of a game I already played. When I played the demo back then I was really surprised how the game turned out to be. I really liked it although I still wished that they would port the original on steam too.

[u]Gameplay[/u]
This time the perspective is switched from fixed camera angles or first-person view to a third person angle. I love change that’s neat. Especially how the controls work, your character is not moving in any way stiff anymore not that I disliked the control scheme in any RE before.

Also, the puzzle nature of the gameplay is back, you run around and find obstacles and try to overcome them, mostly by punching in codes or finding an item, like a key(card) or a valve. Although more “complex” text puzzles of the original are gone. Still this gameplay was always what I liked, coupled together with the enemies and resource management. Which fight should I pick, should I risk a health item or ammo, or reload an old save? Veteran mode is this time the only one that has limited saves via cartridges again. I like that there is a challenging but not overly difficult veteran mode, although there is no difficulty above that.

Combat is fun due to the extra challenges of manually aiming at zombies heads or other enemies that are out there.  They move unpredictable making it absolutely not an easy task. They took again the system with the personal defence weapons from RE1 remake, so the protagonist will stab someone and lose a knife if getting grabbed from the front.

You also find on your way upgrades for your weapons or completely new ones, along with a remake and improvement of the old games level design. Its very familiar but still completely different, especially in the lategame. I found the game absolutely fun from start to finish and cannot really complain much, aside maybe that the backtracking can be a bit too much and the feature that helps you highlight rooms which you completely cleared makes the game a bit too easy on the exploring. I rather wish it would only highlight either main quest items or only being on easy difficulty. S Rank will take you on highest difficulty 2 hours and 30 minutes. My first play through took me closer to 8 hours for a single character. Good length, not too short but not too long.

There are also a few challenges that unlock cosmetics (but there are barely any) or artwork and a couple of extra modes added on. Those extra modes are a minigame that brings you through mostly already seen places and is more combat focused by delivering a mini story. Neat. Sadly extra coop mode or some kind of mercenary mode the franchise is known for. Oh well.

[u]Story[/u]
As in the original you can play through the game as either Leon or Claire. They have some different story aspects but play through most of the same areas. I would say about slightly over 1/3 of their storyline and gameplay is different. You also have the A and B route again, which changes almost nothing in the whole game, I even have the assumption that it changes less than the original did. Main difference is only the new main pistol as mostly ammo for that one will spawn and the starting area of the game. Some puzzles have barely changed and just make the game a bit shorter. This is an aspect they could have just skipped and probably added only so original fanboys are not mad that it didn’t got included.

[u]Sound[/u]
A bit of a let down is the OST. They played it very save by making the OST less interesting. like the original and instead made it much more environmental, save aside a few tracks. Its definitely fine but not that memorable.

Game is available again in a ton of different dubbed languages. Also, the indoor sound design is really neat and the whole SFX they use was my highlight.

[u]Graphics[/u]
You can tweak a lot on the graphical settings. I especially love and give them kudos for actually showing pictures that resemble various effects. In literally all games I deactivate lens flares and bloom, but the pictures showed me an effect I liked so kept it. Neat stuff!

To the graphics itself, the game can run on a potato but offers scaling that you can have problems even with very modern hardware. Its great that they added this amount of customization. Its not the best looking game, but full of details and little animation quirks, like when zombies are about to grab you but you kill them in the same moment they fall against you while the protagonist pushes them off their body or they try to dodge them.

[u]Conclusion/TL;DR[/u]
I really absolutely enjoyed my playthrough. It’s a short game with lots of replay value which I absolutely like. The remake stays somewhat true to the original but offers so many new ideas and environments making it a must play for people who liked the ps1 game. The only downsides I have are a few nitpicks which are overshadowed by the fun core gameplay loop.

Despite cut content and the lame way they handled the zapping system from the original, this game holds up as the modern gold standard for survival horror. I genuinely don't think Capcom has lived up to what they pulled off with this game since, the RE3 remake was plain bad, RE8 was an action horror like RE4, and RE4R is back to linear action horror, and is considerably more janky than this game.

But this game? This game feels like an extension of everything good about 2002's RE1 remake. Resources are scarce and enemies are tough, so getting through the game requires a combination of planning and careful consideration of when and where to use your ammo. The game is fairly challenging, without being too over the top or cheap like RE8's VoS mode or the other ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ meme difficulties RE games have been adding in recent years (not including RE7 Madhouse, that's actually well made.) Beating the game isn't too hard, but beating it quickly, or achieving challenge runs, will test your map and enemy knowledge, as well as your ability to stay calm and plan a route. Getting that S+ takes raw skill and practice, it feels fair and getting the S+ rewards feels earned, it's just excellent.

The enemy roster is a bit smaller than the original, but every enemy type poses a unique threat relative to the others, and the way they're used in the extra modes really forces you to understand their mechanics. Additionally, as mentioned, the A/B scenarios have been gutted in favor of what is essentially just an arrange mode that's the same for both characters. It's sad to see the system gone, but overall this remake holds up as a solid survival horror game, something other games should be held to as a standard of quality. 

Highly, highly recommend any RE or Survival Horror fan play this at least once.

Each room and corridor has a story to tell, and uncovering the mysteries of the police station is a rewarding and immersive experience.

Whether it's a creature crashing through a window, a sudden encounter in the dark, or a menacing figure lurking just out of sight, you'll find yourself gasping for breath and clinging to your sanity.

In conclusion, Resident Evil 2 is a harrowing descent into the realm of survival horror that will leave you trembling in the face of relentless terror. Its atmospheric setting, nightmarish creatures, and nerve-shredding gameplay combine to create an experience that will haunt your nightmares long after you turn off the game. I'm going to straight up say that this remake is amazing, but there are some questionable design decisions which do lower its overall quality.

The good:[list]
[*]Incomparably more atmospheric that the original. By default there's almost no music, aside from safe rooms, not even ambient tracks, just sounds of the surroundings, and it works really well. I'd say it's the most atmospheric RE next to RE7. 
[*]Storywise it's a bit more down to earth, realistic, dramatic, and has a bit more sense. Dialogues are more natural. The building layouts are more logical and realistic.
[*]Much harder than the original. The zombies are more dangerous and bullet spongy. In RE2 you had so much ammo you could clear entire groups of zombies without much trouble. Here, not so much.
[*]Mr. X is probably the largest improvement. Instead of being relegated to scripted appearances during which he was barely a thread and easy to ignore, here he wanders around the entire RPD, patrolling it looking for you. His loud *thump thump* stomping sounds are fantastic.[/list]

Many QoL features are taken straight out of RE1 Remake and improved, as well as other additions:[list]
[*]Rooms with/without items are marked on the map. 
[*]Defensive Items return, now called Sub Weapons, and can be used offensively.
[*]You can enable the original RE2 soundtrack if you so please.
[*]An orphanage chapter was added. The orphanage was only briefly touched upon in a document found in the original game.[/list]

These changes show the dedication and love of the developers towards the source material.

The mid:[list]
[*]Character movement speed is painfully slow. Almost as bad as Fatal Frame/Project Zero. It's more shuffling than moving.
[*]Leon and Claire are moaning so much when """running""" you'd think they're """running""" a marathon.
[*]Leon and Claire's comments during combat can be grating at times.[/list]

The bad:
The design decisions I wrote about earlier.[list]
[*]The game is pulling wool over the player’s eyes in regards to some of the mechanics, i.e. it's easier than it appears. Other RE games also have them, but not to this extent: in RE2 Remake having the knowledge of its inner workings massively improves your gameplay potential. For example, you cannot die on any difficulty if you’re not in Danger state, not counting instant death attacks. The knowledge of this alone helps you save a ton of herbs for the future. It also makes the R+B mix, which reduces damage taken by half for 3 minutes, much more valuable than a full heal R+G on Hardcore difficulty. What’s more, some weapons deal either reduced or increased damage against specific enemies, e.g. Leon’s shotgun is great against zombies and dogs, but is pretty crap against anything else. Furthermore, there are 2 boss fights [spoiler](G2 and Super Tyrant)[/spoiler] which seem cheap and frustrating, but which become very simple once you know the mechanics behind them.
[*]The inconsistency in zombie durability. I get it, they want you to kill zombies only in high traffic areas, and shoot to stagger to avoid others. Except attempting to stagger sometimes takes 3 head/leg shots, sometimes 10, sometimes even more. You’re still wasting a lot of ammo. Trying to avoid entirely is extremely risky, since corridors can be tight and zombies can double lunge at you. Yes, you have Sub Weapons, but there aren’t that many of them and you want to save grenades for bosses or large groups of zombies, instead of lone ones. On the other hand, for Leon, once you get the shotgun, zombies stop being a threat almost entirely, since he can decapitate them 100% of the time with it. The balance is really weird and ruins the resource management part. People complain about RE3 Remake, but at least it's more consistent there.[/list]

The above forces players to metagame almost to extreme levels on Hardcore difficulty.

Last, but not least: the biggest bone of contention among fans is the A/B scenario system. It was the best feature of the original, but in RE2R they neutered it rather significantly:[list]
[*]You do not have any impact on B scenario via A.
[*]All the puzzles are the same, some of them have slightly different solutions.
[*]Bosses are the same with the exception of last two.
[*]Storywise it’s almost the same like in the original. Claire meets Leon only twice, at the beginning and at the end.
[*]The biggest gameplay difference are that each scenario has access to a few different areas which the other has not.[/list]

Other stuff:[list]
[*]I tried 4th Survivor/Ghost Survivors and didn't bother finishing it. A trial & error speedrun mode. These kind of modes are a mistake of nature, a complete anti-thesis to what the game is about. Same with RE7's Ethan Must Die. At best they are a get-achievement-never-touch-again deal. It could work in RE4, 5, or 6, but not here.
[*]I don’t care about them cutting the giant spiders or moths, for me they never felt like they belonged in RE2.[/list]

Resident Evil 2 Remake is a fantastic game that brings the classic survival horror experience to a modern audience. The game is a reimagining of the 1998 PlayStation classic, but with updated graphics, sound design, and gameplay mechanics that make it a must-play for fans of the genre.

The game takes place in the zombie-infested city of Raccoon City, where players take control of rookie cop Leon S. The story is well-written and engaging, with plenty of twists and turns to keep players on their toes.

The graphics are top-notch, with detailed character models, realistic lighting, and atmospheric environments that really capture the feeling of a city overrun by the undead. The sound design is equally impressive, with creepy ambient noises and the guttural moans of zombies adding to the tension.

The gameplay is where Resident Evil 2 Remake really shines. The game retains the classic survival horror gameplay of the original, with limited resources, tense combat, and puzzle-solving elements. However, it also adds modern touches like a dynamic camera system, improved controls, and new enemy types that keep the gameplay fresh and exciting.

One of the game's best features is the "zapping" system, which allows players to switch between Leon and Claire's campaigns, each with their own unique storylines and challenges. This adds a lot of replay value to the game, as players can experience the story from different perspectives and uncover new secrets.

Overall, Resident Evil 2 Remake is an excellent game that successfully modernizes the classic survival horror formula while staying true to its roots. It's a must-play for fans of the genre and a great entry point for newcomers.

RESIDENT EVIL 2 REMAKE REVIEW
*Warning: This review contains spoilers*

I’m not familiar with the franchise since I haven’t watched nor played anything Resident Evil prior to playing this game so this review is from the lens of a newcomer. The first thing I noticed about the game is the beautiful graphics and rendering. Just from the first scene alone, I already noticed just how good it looks. It does the perfect job of capturing real life through the graphics while making sure the player is still reminded that it’s still a video game. The character models of Claire and Leon in particular are remarkable. Their clothing, physics, movement, expressions etc. are satisfying to witness. Another noteworthy aspect is the lighting. Even if most of the game is set at night, it didn’t stop the developers from making sure that the lighting is beautiful, realistic and intentional. It’s noticeable especially every time light appears and disappears in a room. There are zombie video games out there that don’t have scary zombies that make you scared and  make you want to avoid them, but this game is not like that at all. Every time I witness a zombie or a licker, I do my best to avoid them because they look the part and sound the part as well. Not to mention, the gore in the game didn’t slack off as well. Moving onto the gameplay, I am very particular and critical about movement and the movement in this game did not disappoint. The way the characters walk, run and manoeuvre themselves is, once again, very realistic while being smooth and satisfying. I can say the same thing about how they use the weapons and shoot their guns. Technical aspects aside, I really like how the ammo, grenades, herbs etc. are limited because it challenges the players to be tactical about when to use them. I also like the mind-exercising puzzles, since the game is first set in a police station that was formerly a museum. Though, I do have to note that it was a bit out of place that one of the puzzles required chess pieces in a particular order since it was in an underground laboratory. The game never has a dull moment because there is always something to do. Before starting the game, the player is given the option to start the game off with either Claire or Leon first, which I think is great that you can choose since there are people out there who prefer to start off the game with their preferred character first. It’s also a nice touch that despite the fact that they had similar storylines and gameplay, they had their distinct differences. I appreciate when video games make you feel immersed in the storyline and in the world of the video game immediately so I was pleased when the game didn’t beat around the bush and started off the first scene with a zombie attack. I’m not gonna lie, I did wish that the game explored Claire and Leon as people more, but I was satisfied with what the game showed. I like how the two protagonists had their own supporting character, Claire had Sherry and Leon had Ada. It was also cool that the player was able to shortly play with the said supporting characters as well. I personally prefer Claire and Sherry’s story to Leon and Ada’s but that may just be me being jealous about Ada kissing Leon. Anyway, to summarize my thoughts the game is overall not perfect but it’s definitely amazing and I can’t wait to play all of the RE games post RE 2. I’d say you get more than your money’s worth as well.

A stellar remake of a survival horror classic. Resident Evil 2 is the perfect game to get into the franchise with, as Raccoon City is an outbreak that defines all the events from the Spencer Mansion to Miranda's mold-infected cult.

PROS

* The origins of Leon Scott Kennedy, the best protagonist in Resident Evil. Treasure his appearance in this game as a terrified newcomer to virus outbreaks, before he returns in 4 as a veteran trained by the US government.
* Modernized third-person gameplay that sticks true to Resident Evil's core as a survival horror.
* The atmosphere has been greatly improved. The hallways are dark and moody, rain pours into the buildings through windows and floods out rooms, several shutters and doors are closed and barricaded, and you get the undeniable feeling of a safe zone that has fallen to the monsters a long time ago.
* Terrifying monsters. The sheer durability and unpredictability of the regular zombies forces you to aim for the head or kneecaps, choose your encounters, and avoid getting swarmed in tight rooms. The Tyrant is one of the best stalker enemies in video games, having been improved from set encounters in the original to constantly stalking you throughout the police station, ready to Falcon Punch you to death.

CONS

* The police station is where the gameplay shines the most, as the pacing is on-point and there are multiple ways you can explore. The sewers and lab, by comparison, can feel much more linear and stretched-out.
* The Zapping System is not nearly as well-implemented as it was in the original. Run B, with the exception of the opening and ending, has very little differences from Run A outside of puzzle solutions being changed, so the main difference comes in whether you choose Leon or Claire. This also results in plot holes such as characters being in two places at once. Granted, the developers weren't able to make the deviations they wanted due to running out of time, so I'll give a pass there.

With excellent horror segments and a wonderful return to survival horror mechanics it's a breath of fresh air in a field of stale modern horror games.

The zombies are a constant threat, seemingly never dying unless you completely destroy their heads. It is quite handy there's a fun dismemberment system in place so you can instead choose to remove a zombie's legs and save ammo instead of killing him outright and use up precious shotgun shells or the always fun to use grenades.

The level design loops around in interesting ways and opening up shortcuts feels rewarding.

A couple of negative points are the fact you need to play the game twice in order to see the actual ending and the bonus content is severely lacking. RE2 is a rare gem, a game that every horror fan should play. It is also by far the best horror game I have ever played. The game contained so many good things that it is impossible to list them all in this review, but just to name a few:
-The zombies in RE2 are my all-time favorite video game zombies. They were very unpredictable in their actions and they moved exactly in the same way as I imagine real-life zombies would move. The zombies were also very "soft", you could dismember zombies or even split them into half with well-placed shots. Another great thing was that corpses didn't disappear (or if they did, it meant that they were lurching around somewhere nearby), which always kept me on my toes as I was afraid that they might wake up again. As a context for this, it was common in the game that zombies you thought you had killed weren't actually dead.
-Mr X was scary as hell. I really liked that he was actually walking around the police station searching for you, and not just appearing out of nowhere through some pre-defined triggers. Hearing his footsteps made my heart beat faster every time, especially if the footsteps got louder and louder.
-Story was very good, and it was worth playing the 2nd run as the other main character to get the entire story revealed.
-The map system was fluent and intuitive.
-The game was balanced really well: I never felt overpowered and I barely had enough ammo for almost the entirety of the game, which was perfect for a survival horror game.
-The graphics were top-notch (the lighting and facial animations in particular).

There are parts of this game I love. But there are a few aspects that absolutely ruin it for me. Enemies are bullet sponges- on standard difficulty, one of the first zombies I came across took 8 shots to the head to die. This is a problem, because ammo is very scarce, and it's common that you'll be stuck at one end of a narrow hallway with several enemies between you and your destination. When you run out of ammo, that's basically the end of your options- the only melee attack is your knife, which rapidly runs out of durability (each knife kills 2-3 zombies before breaking, if you don't first weaken them with ranged attacks) and knives are just as scarce as ammo, with only a handful being found in game. There is no push/kick ability to knock enemies away, and if you have no knife or grenades grapples are unpreventable and inescapable. There's a reason all of these aspects have been changed in later games in the series- they're obnoxious, artificial padding and they turn what could be a great game into a frustrating experience.
I'm sure this game is nostalgic for a lot of people, and I'm sure for a lot of people these things aren't issues. But I can say that this game is absolutely not for everyone.

The short: This is a good. You should play it.

The long: This is a good stand-in for the original RE2 if you're not one of the lucky people who owns the classic game or if you prefer the over-the-shoulder, shooter style of RE4.

The game is much more repetitive than the classic game with the A scenarios for Leon and Claire being almost identical, and the B scenarios follow the same pattern. This isn't a bad thing, but it feels a little lackluster to choose a different character and have the only changes being some weapons and a different NPC. However, the B scenario is well-worth the time which means that you'll have to play the game at least twice. That means the playtime is pretty decent.

The gameplay is the typical, fun shooter with an emphasis on resource scarcity to bring in the survival horror mechanics. The multitude of dead bodies will leave you on the edge of your seat as you make your way through the dark halls of the RPD since some will rise from the dead and others may not.

Speaking of! The RPD is a beautiful and memorable setting. In contrast though, I find the others less-than-enthusing. The sewers overstay their welcome for me, and NEST is just meh. The worst part is that the RE Engine (while gorgeous) suffers with its lighting and reflections in this entry. It's not enough that it makes the game look bad, but with RE3 and RE4 Remakes, this just pales in comparison. It should though since it's older.

Verdict: I would buy it if you're a fan of Resident Evil or you're looking to get into survival horror titles regardless of whether it's on sale or not. If you're more a fan of tank controls and fixed cameras or the high-octane action of RE5, maybe wait for a sale.

It's with a heavy heart that I have to put an enormous asterisk on this recommendation.

Is this game good? Yes. Absolutely shines as a remake. It really does capture the spirit of the old tank-control style classic with some modern QoL and third person shooter flair. Not to mention the story canon has been tightened up a bit to undo the lore dissonance provided by the Darkside Chronicles version of events.

Is this what Resident Evil gameplay should be going forward? That's a can of worms that I'm just about to open.

Despite the criticisms levied to more action oriented games like RE5 and RE6, I don't believe it's the action that has been holding back the franchise. RE7 pushed the survival and horror back into the fold and the reception has brought forth a bold belief that RE7 and this game should be the new standard going forward.

And I just can't agree that's the answer.

This remake, for all its charm and elegance, is also rife with its share of sticking points that make it less appealing to replay than a game like its later renditions. It's bizarre to hear folks harp on about the puzzles and exploration, then have that interrupted on the regular by an unkillable monstrosity. And once you've solved the puzzles once, it would feel weird to have the bulk of your experience be solving them again with few changes, if any. It's odd to me to have folks lambaste the action elements of older RE's, then become content in a system where dead enemies just get back up in the middle of the back and forth of exploring. I'm of the mind that a lot of Resident Evil's flavor comes from its action. The kind of game where fighting a giant mutant snake, spider, or shark is an expected and welcome highlight. In a game where your health pool is small, there's something rewarding about getting through a messy and uncontrolled encounter without taking a hit or blowing too much precious ammo, but there's no reward to unloading 5 rounds into a zombie's head and having them still come back to life, or making the unfair decision to waste some of said ammo to stun the unkillable monster in lieu of having to make a lap around the police station, knowing that the ammo would be better saved for the actual boss fight with said monster.

Overall, I'm glad we got RE7 and RE2R. The games are good and they do what they intended very well. But to say that this should be the model for the series could be argued against.

You will be actively seeking ways to minimise resource spent for survival, as if you are hunting for steam sales ...

Never played an RE game before, and I have to admit that it was pretty good. The game encourages careful play with calculated risks, heavily discouraging wasting bullets or going in guns blazing. Generally smooth mechanics, although the age of the original mechanics sometimes showed through, such as the lack of hand to hand combat or low mobility in general. It did quite well with the mechanics that it did have though.
The remake itself is great, very well optimised for older systems and could run very well on my R5 3500/1600S system, even if I had to turn down a few settings from max to high. The game looked and played great, no complaints there.
As for the story and characters, they were alright. Might have been groundbreaking at the time of the original's release, but they feel a bit corny and cliched in a modern context. There wasn't anything in there that really surprised me or jumped out to me as amazing, but it was fairly well rounded in general.
There are of course, the usual complaints - inventory management was pretty annoying, and the fact that each scrub zombie needed anywhere between 3-6 head-shots (depending on whether or not they get back up) was pretty cumbersome, forcing you to skip most zombies and kill only the ones that really block progress.
Overall, it's a pretty strong recommend from me, and I'd rate it around 8/10. Good game even for those who aren't into horror.

tl;dr on the surface, it's a good game, marred by a few very bad game design choices. If you're looking for the good ol RE experience, and you retained your standards for what this series is, look elsewhere. This game's made for a new generation. You're not the target audience anymore.

 Under the hood this games just fine, the combats good, its pretty, sound design is great. Controls are a tiny bit sluggish situationally in actually moving the characters but they work just fine in most cases. I rarely miss headshots, aiming is tight. Enemies visually are designed great. The problems though start from certain design choices. It suffers from falling into the trap that lot of modern game studios fall into and that is limitations/annoyance = challenge and difficulty. I'll preface this by saying, this game isn't hard by any means because that's the usual damage control of defenders of any series is to call the player bad so you dont have to address the flaws pointed out. 

No, RE2 remake and games in the series made like it, suffers a lot from what a lotta people call "artificial difficulty". The lickers are a great example. Stealth in most cases is fine, The main strategy here is to avoid them altogether by being stealthy, Dont shoot, dont run, sure thats fine. Until its not. The lickers can roam right into your way blocking your path, will stalk you to the end of the hallway, scriptedly change when going in certain rooms (stars office is the first example of this, if you walk under it without going in it doesnt change positions) Maybe I got unlucky but their design seems to be more centered around just never fighting them which is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. In my encounters with them if they DID manage to hit me I was basically stunlocked, basically stuck in a loop of heal until you run out. This would be ok if like in past titles you could reload weapons in the menu but they made the stupid choice of "limitations=good design". So naturally your next choice after you run out of shotgun (despite 4 clean shots to the lickers dome), is to go to the handgun. Good luck, it ignores handgun stun and just claws you anyway. Your only choice becomes learn their movement and go around them and hope their pathfinding doesnt get in your way.

Mr.X is another dinosaur in the room entirely. There is nothing I despise more than having a constant reminder following me around that, god forbid i do anything because stalker is waiting around the corner to police me being able to play the game. Mr.X does not add any element of fear, he doesn't add challenge, its an annoyance. If this character is scary to you I don't know what to tell you. no its just there to limit the player and control how they play, I despise this. If I didnt make the mistake of going afk while leaving the game on I'd refund this game. Maybe i'll look into modding this enemy out because this enemy literally ruins my want to play.

My perspective on Resident Evil may be different to most: I’ve heard how great the game was over the last decade and have watched the show before I played the game myself. Therefore, I have a view that I am prepared to receive clown awards for; Resident Evil is an objectively good game – but one that I subjectively did not enjoy – and one that is most definitely overrated from the genre-defining masterpiece I had heard it to be. This review contains minor spoilers.

Story

Resident Evil 2 is a survival horror game developed and published by Capcom. The game is set in Raccoon City, a midwestern American city that has been overrun by a zombie outbreak caused by the Umbrella Corporation's T-virus. The game follows two protagonists, rookie police officer Leon S. Kennedy and college student Claire Redfield, as they try to survive and escape the city. The story is divided into two separate campaigns, with Leon's and Claire's stories intersecting and overlapping at various points. As Leon and Claire make their way through the city, they encounter a variety of enemies, including zombies, mutated creatures, and other survivors who may or may not be trustworthy. Along the way, they also discover the truth behind the outbreak and the role that (really hope rytox isnt reading this review) Umbrella Corporation played in causing it. The game's story is further complicated by the presence of various branching paths and multiple endings, depending on the choices the player makes throughout the game. This adds an extra layer of tension and unpredictability to the already intense survival horror gameplay. Overall, Resident Evil 2 is a thrilling and terrifying tale of survival against impossible odds in a world overrun by the undead. The game's compelling story, memorable characters, and innovative gameplay mechanics have made it a classic of the survival horror genre.

Gameplay

Whilst I recognise RE is a remaster of a remaster of a 1999 last last gen video game, gameplay wise it holds up. I loved the way your character moves in combat – especially when running through infected – rather than them getting near you and instantly attacking, their attacks felt fair, and it is possible to weave in and out of their paths in a way many games simply do not allow you to. The zombie enemies smartly flanked and called out their intentions to allies, with general combat difficulty and encounters appearing well crafted and balanced. Movement is generally dynamic, and the flexibility of crafting was well done, along with the upgrade system of your character stats or your weapons at a workbench through items collected in the game world. Having to watch every single weapon upgrade animation – some of which were literally just Leon rubbing the gun with a cloth – got quickly annoying though. I enjoyed scavenging for supplies, but the gameplay sandbox simply never demanded enough of me to use most of them – so I was almost always full on what I had crafted and how much I could store. Shooting was setting-accurate but frustrating to engage with, yet I got through it as it was simply the most efficient way of playing as stealth just wasn’t worth the effort due to the soft cover system being too finicky. The game had a fair balance between combat and puzzle / traversal sections, though I would have liked to see just something else to vary things up; there was no side content outside of collectibles for the sake of achievements.


Graphics and Performance

The game looks good for one that is originally based off a PS1 title, and it holds up well even now in 2023. The variety of graphics settings were shocking – so much so that I just set a preset and was happy enough with that. I do not believe it is as bad as the Internet narrative has shown; we know that games are getting more VRAM intensive, and it’s clear that many people simply do not understand the right settings to use for their system. In my experience, outside of numerous crashes, the port ran well on high settings with the only real negative being occasional stutters. There are obviously areas where this port can be improved, but so long as you are reasonable, it’s a perfectly playable experience.

Overall

My conclusion here is the same as what I said initially: Resident Evil is a good game, but not much more. It does everything well enough but did nothing great enough to truly be of note. To me, this title is massively overrated from what I had expected it to be; whilst others may enjoy it, I simply cannot recommend it. Maybe I will just fall into the minority group of people who prefers RE Village…

REmake 2 perhaps is the best form of remakes. Whilst REmake 3 lacked either vision, or funds, or time, or motivation - REmake 2 felt like a bona fide attempt to bring the classic game to modern computers. And it largely succeeds. Largely, because it cuts down on a lot of things that makes the RE2 unique. The trade off is that the game feels more straightforward on a single run. You can check off most of the story boxes and have a good idea what's going on in a single run, then play the 2nd Run just to see what minor story beat you missed. But because REmake 2's idea of a second run is quite literally the same game with not much added in sans different variables of engagement, it's hard to really convince oneself to do it. The option is there, so that's value, but whether it's done right is subjective. 

But I think most of the value is in the 1st run anyway. I loved that Capcom could marry in the puzzle-heavy gameplay of the old REs whilst retaining a modern feel and layout. RPD has been made well here, which makes me wish I could explore Spencer's Mansion in REmake 2 as a DLC. I'm rambling. Cut it short, good game. Play it. Then play REmake 4.

Resident Evil 2 (2019) is a perfect example of a remake that successfully adapts to modern game standards while keeping the original Resident Evil experience alive.

The game is set around a zombie outbreak in Raccoon City, released by the Umbrella Company, which developed several zombie viruses to be used as biological weapon. You can play as one of two main characters, Leon or Claire, who get trapped in the police station of Raccoon City. They then need to solve puzzles, fight zombies and unravel the mystery around Umbrella and the zombie virus.

I can't say much about balance as I only know how the game worked for me personally, but I was amazed how well it worked. As a Survival Horror game, you constantly struggle with ressources - mainly ammo. There were a few parts in which I completely ran out of ammo and had to progress further while completely changing my playstyle. While this was an intense experience it didn't make the game impossible and I could always recover myself.

Another part I really enjoyed was exploring the map and solving the nested puzzles, which often had their own really enjoyable mini games as the portable safes or some wave-syncing hacking device.

Lastly combat is the third big part in the game and also incredibly satisfying as the guns feel very responsive and the zombies are animated physically. You can even shoot at their legs to make them faceplant and continue crawling at you.

There is a part in the game in which you are searched and chased for by an undying monster while you need to continue exploring and solving puzzles in the police station. As you know most of the station very well at that time, its maybe a nice idea to push the player to hurry a bit, but for me it felt very annoying after just a few minutes, when the horror effect was gone.

Speaking of horror, the game delivers a very decent horror atmosphere with occasional gory scenes and some good, yet sometimes very predictable jump scares. However the game managed to scare me even when I knew that this zombie hanging at the ceiling will drop at some point in the game, because it distracted me with another heavy enemy just before that.

After playing the game the first time as Leon, I expected Claired story to be significantly different. It turned out, that the story itself is different, but with the same levels and puzzles most of the time. As I met Claire outside of the police station in Leons story, I wondered what she did in the meantime, but in her story she was inside the station and Leon outside - so, yeah, I was a bit disappointed about that.

All in all, everything in the game was fun. Walking around, shooting at zombies, playing with puzzles, collecting and organizing ressources. The sound and graphics build a great atmosphere and the story is worth uncovering.

Definitely play this game if you are not too scared of dark rooms and zombies.

Every time you encounter a zombie, you have to wonder if it would be wiser to take it out, using up some of your precious ammo, or try to run around it, potentially taking some damage in the process (hint: shooting their legs off works wonders). In addition to the great combat, the inventory management is some of the best I've seen. Every time you arrive at an item box, you have to think about what you plan to do, what you need to get it done, and if you'll have enough room left over to pick up other items you might need if you take everything you want to take. It's phenomenal. It's short, but it has tons of replayability.

If you are in any way interested in this game, then I would HIGHLY encourage you to at least play the demo, since that's free. This game gets a huge recommendation from me.

Just when you think you know what's coming, the game throws a curveball that will leave you reeling. Never in my life have I liked a stalker-type enemy in a survival horror game, and yet they pulled it off too; Mr. X is plenty scary, and almost never frustrating. The game rarely goes out of its way to outright screw you over, but it regularly tests your ability to keep your cool. All in all, this is an easy recommendation if you're looking for a good horror game. Easily one of my favorites in this genre, and an incredible revelation that rekindled my enthusiasm for classic survival horror.

I played the original game 2 decades ago on PC, then on PSP, and now comes the remaster. I remember most of it, the biggest difference in the new game would be removing the ink ribbon for the printer, which was an essential and limited item to save in the original. I got the idea, most games feature autosave, RE 2 already restrained save place, limit the save would be too unfriendly for players nowadays, yet it also lowered the difficulty.

I chose Leon's story for the run. His part relates Ada and Claire's part is with Sherry, though both protagonists share the same Police Station walkthrough. Leon's story starts at a gas station, he and Claire were separated by an explosion. When I made it to the Police Station I'm glad to see it in HD, everything was familiar yet not totally the same. Licker appeared much later, the bookshelf puzzle has changed with a locked jack, the broken window can be fixed, open lockers and safes for equipment or extra storage, and that red light room for photos is not essential. There are also classic moments like that poor Police guy yelled for help and Leon was only able to get [spoiler]half of him out[/spoiler]. 

I enjoyed all the new content. Starting from sewing, being chased by a mutant gator creature ends with some action that is well executed. The parking lot requires a bit of distance running - the map is extremely useful, it clearly indicates all the items as well as locked doors and puzzles to be solved with different layers for player to browse. The underground lab is a surprise - with a botanic garden and new enemy type, new puzzles including making a reagent for sprinkler to kill the plants, I enjoyed those new experiences as well as the actions. I don't feel much of the horror even chased by Mr. X who can't be killed, probably because I'm a chicken and I chose the easiest Assist Mode lol, I especially regret that William is too easy to take down at the end.

The new RE 2 is a beautiful extended version tribute to the original, took me 6.5 hours for the first run and a DLC about a gun store owner making his way out. I'll try Claire's part of the story later. Kudos to CAPCOM.

Case in point, when you play as a fully dis-empowered character for one chapter, it serves as a great shake-up on your first playthrough, and on the second -- an annoying, un-skippable filler episode in your second or third playthrough.

I'll still recommend this game for its sheer quality of survival-horror gameplay, with the  first time experience providing palpable tension and exploration. 

Just stick to two play-throughs and let that great experience live in your mind.

I enjoyed this game way more than I thought I would. I usually shy away from horror games, but this felt more like a thriller with unrealistic body horror. Although it seems like a shooting game, it's more like an escape-room-mazelike resource management puzzle game. The combat is key of course, but on mouse and keyboard it isn't challenging by itself. The main joy came from slowly unlocking and learning a map until you've mastered it and visited all locations.

This game is very good at creating tension. First off is the resource crunch. I fought every enemy at first, but soon realised that there just isn't enough ammo to do it. Luckily, zombies can be easily juked by running and changing direction. However, running draws the attention of lickers, who appear in certain areas of the police station and are very dangerous. They can be avoided by walking quietly, but at times that's just not in the cards. As such, I ended up offloading my recouped ammo anyway whenever I saw one of these guys.

Just when I got comfortable with the first area, the freaking Terminator showed up. This is an invincible guy who stalked me through the map and punched me to death when I got cornered. He appeared at the perfect time to keep me from falling into complacency. At one crucial point when I was running from multiple zombies and the stalker guy through a licker hallway, a second licker appeared. It was a miracle I survived, since a desperate and very lucky grenade toss managed to kill both lickers and stun the stalker simultaneously.

That's just the first area of the game though. There were two more areas which were a bit less intricate, but I found them challenging enough. The ammo crunch lasted till the end, as I had little to spare for the final boss fight.

The story wasn't too interesting (I played through the Leon campaign), just a straightforward survival plot. Leon came off as a reliable dude in one scene and as a naive but hypercompetent greenhorn in the next. The environmental and note-based substories were pretty good for immersion.

I found the English voice acting to be annoying just because the player character would keep swearing at stuff just a tad too aggressively. I checked out other languages and found the German and Japanese voices to be pretty decent.

Overall though it was a good experience. The simple story worked well with the gameplay elements. The tension rarely let up for long. I don't know if I'll return for Claire's side of the story, but I enjoyed my time with it.

Unfortunately, I don't get the hype. Maybe it's because I'm not viewing this game through nostalgia-tinted glasses; I didn't join the RE fan wagon until RE 5 was announced and when I visited the previous games, they were all kinda outdated (except for RE 4).

Pros:
- RE 2 is beautiful to look at, high graphical fidelity and very strong art design/aesthetic.
- This game has fantastic sound design, probably the best I've seen (or heard HAHAHA) in recent memory.
- The slower, more thoughtful pace with puzzles and backtracking is kinda nice.

Cons:
- The game's challenge/difficulty comes from three things: low resources (healing items/ammo), bullet sponge enemies, and narrow corridors that keep you from avoiding said enemies. This feels frustrating and cheap.
- The camera struggles to cope with these tight corridors.
- Mr. X isn't scary, he's annoying, and he turns backtracking into a chore.
- The voice acting is mediocre.
- Unacceptable that they removed the whole concept of a B scenario. Why would I play through the same thing again?

If you must get it, get it on sale.

I bounced off this game hard when I first tried it, due to a combination of factors, but I decided to revisit it after playing through RE4 remake, and I completed it in one feverish sitting.

A lot's been said about what this game does right, so I'll focus on the things that stood out to me.
-The zombie shooting is industry-leading in my opinion.  Other games let you do more damage to a zombie's body or are more action-packed, but RE2 really hits a sweet spot between gruesome damage, enemy reactivity, and atmosphere that results in every fight having this feeling of tension and horror as heads snap back and flesh is blasted from bone but they just keep coming.  The combat has a methodical pace that really works in the game's favour, with every bullet being an uncertain experiment, hoping this is the one that puts your enemy down as you start to backpedal.  I usually get numbed to the violence of zombie-slaying pretty quickly in games that feature them, but RE2 persistently unsettled me.
-Claire's story was unexpectedly impactful - I've played a looot of resident evil games and this isn't a franchise I come to for stories that make me feel something, but there was a simple yet well-executed setup and payoff here that has left a lingering emotional impression.  Pleasantly surprised here.
-The map is fantastic.  More games that involve backtracking [i]need[/i] to take some lessons from the exhaustive, thorough, and helpful information presented by RE2's highly-readable map screen.

That said, I do have some lingering gripes - the problems that pushed me away from the game in the first place are still there, I'm just glad I pushed through them this time.
-I understand people love the Mr. X pursuit mechanic but it just struck me as frustrating.  You don't have any options to deal with him the way you have options to, say, deal with the xenomorph in Alien: Isolation, you can't hide or use traps or anything like that, once you wind up in the same room as him, you need to run and hope, or just beeline to a safehouse.  If encountering him was more rare, having no option but to run for your life would've been exciting, but once he's introduced, he's ever-present until you leave the police station.  Even then I wouldn't have minded too much if he didn't cheat.  I think he must teleport if he gets too far away so he's always nearby, because I would try to play smart, note his position in the police station, and do stuff away from him, only to have him appear on top of me out of nowhere while I was in the middle of something, forcing me to go on another time consuming safehouse run.  It just wore out its welcome quickly.
-I don't think the lickers in this game work, and you run into a lot of them.  The game encourages you to exploit their blindness and sneak past them, but the hallways are tight, and when I've seen one on a ceiling, I've only managed to sneak past by walking maybe twice.  They always seem to detect me despite my best efforts, resulting in a fight that invariably chews through a lot of ammunition that I can't get back.  I had a much better time with the blind enemies in RE4.

The conclusion here is that I'm really happy I pushed through my gripes with this one and finished it, because holy hell is this a good game.  Heartily recommended to anyone that loves survival horror, and if you're having trouble with Mr. X, my advice is to focus on advancing the story until he's no longer an issue, because it's worth persisting.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is a reimagining of the classic survival horror game originally released in 1998. Developed by Capcom, this modern remake features updated graphics, new gameplay mechanics, and a reworked storyline that stays true to the original while also offering new twists and surprises.

One of the first things that stands out about Resident Evil 2 Remake is its stunning graphics. The game features incredibly detailed environments, character models, and visual effects that create a hauntingly beautiful atmosphere. The game's sound design is equally impressive, with an eerie soundtrack and terrifying sound effects that help build tension and create a sense of dread.

The game is split into two different campaigns, one for protagonist Leon S. Kennedy and one for Claire Redfield, both of whom are trying to survive a zombie outbreak in Raccoon City. The two campaigns offer different perspectives on the story and feature unique gameplay elements that make each one feel distinct. Players can also unlock a third campaign after completing both Leon and Claire's storylines, featuring a new character named Ada Wong.

In terms of gameplay, Resident Evil 2 Remake delivers a solid experience. The game combines elements of survival horror and action, with players having to scavenge for resources while also fighting off hordes of enemies. The game's puzzles are also well-designed, providing a good challenge without being frustrating. The game's combat is visceral and satisfying, with a variety of weapons and upgrades available to customize your playstyle.

The game's story is engaging and well-written, with plenty of twists and turns to keep players on the edge of their seats. The game's narrative is also tied into the wider Resident Evil universe, with nods to previous games and characters making appearances throughout. Without giving away too much, the game's ending sets up some interesting possibilities for future installments in the series.

One of the most impressive aspects of Resident Evil 2 Remake is its level design. The game takes place in and around the Raccoon City Police Department, which has been overrun by zombies and other monsters. The level design is expertly crafted, with each area offering a unique gameplay experience. From the dark, claustrophobic hallways of the police station to the wide-open streets outside, each area is designed to keep players on their toes and provide a sense of danger and tension.

One potential downside to Resident Evil 2 Remake is its difficulty. While the game can be played on a variety of difficulty levels, even the normal difficulty can be quite challenging at times. Some players may find themselves getting frustrated at the game's more difficult sections, which require precise timing and quick reflexes. However, for those who enjoy a good challenge, the game's difficulty is a plus.

Another potential issue with Resident Evil 2 Remake is its length. The game can be completed in around 8-10 hours, which may disappoint some players who were expecting a longer experience. However, the game's high replayability factor makes up for this, with players able to unlock new game modes and items by completing the game multiple times.

Overall, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a fantastic reimagining of the classic survival horror game. With its stunning graphics, well-crafted level design, engaging story, and solid gameplay, the game is sure to please both long-time fans and newcomers alike. While its difficulty and length may be an issue for some players, these minor flaws are more than outweighed by the game's strengths. If you're a fan of survival horror games, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a must-play title that delivers a chilling and unforgettable experience.

I’ve had the Resident Evil 2 remake sitting on my hard drive for years, but only after playing the RE4 remake demo I got excited enough to finally play it. It’s also the first full RE game I ever played (I did watch some of the pretty terrible movies ages ago). And what a pleasant (well, sometimes rather unpleasant) surprise it has been! After adjusting to the very slow movement speed I found it to be a superbly crafted, tight experience. The RE Engine excels at rendering flashlight lit interiors, overall the visual quality of textures and assets is great and the game runs very smoothly. I took it slow, played very methodically, at least until the unkillable Tyrant shows up who introduces an element of chaos. I hate him! But I also see why he is necessary for the game. Finding all secrets, even going back willingly to that hellhole of a police station just to pick up some extras, while listening to those booming footsteps was both nerve wrecking and satisfying. After finishing the first run with Leon, which took me about 12 hours, I immediately started the second run with Claire and was delighted by the Kurosawa like second perspective on the same events. The level designers have done a good job when the player is happy to revisit the same, now familiar locations, because it gives him/her a feeling of competence and secret knowledge. The second run took me about 6.5 hours. My only complaint would be that the two stories don’t connect as well as they should because some puzzles must be done twice (statue puzzle, killing the plants etc.) which – among other minor events - contradicts the parallel timelines. That’s a wasted chance to make the game even cleverer. I also raised an eyebrow that Leon gets to be kissed by the hot Asian woman while Claire has to assume the role of the substitute mother. but I guess in B movie plots you can’t expect the formula to be broken. I recommend this to players who can stomach the horror violence (some parts are really disgusting) and prefer a tense atmosphere to frantic shootouts. 8/10

Having not played the original, and only recently playing the original RE4, so far I really enjoy this game.

Basically, from what I can tell, RE inspired the modern concept of an escape room. This game is basically that: running back and forth looking for pieces of various puzzles. While running back and forth scary things come out to get you.

The controls feel nice and the rooms are all very detailed. It's pretty creepy but without overly excessive jump scares.

A lot of the game comes down to inventory management which can be a little frustrating. Another frustrating thing is figuring out what pieces go with what puzzles: is this a handle for this jack? Or for that mechanical door?

One annoying thing is that upon every launch I'm asked if I want to enable HDR and I'm also displayed a list of all the DLC that I have "just installed". After a dozen launches there is clearly something broken with the game. HDR is also a bust and makes the game unplayable on my machine. The game also likes to jump between fullscreen and a smaller window mode occasionally during startup and shutdown. These are more issues with the RE Engine than RE2R itself.

Update: I beat the game after about 9 hours. For the final battle I had plenty of ammo and healing items. I think I missed two guns but the game was still fine without them.

A bit of a spoiler: The game has three separate "levels" where once you get to them you can't go back. The narrative does tell you when this happens, but it's definitely three very distinct places. It does feel like it slightly breaks the immersion, since you're otherwise running back and forth so much between shared locations.

Is Resident Evil 2 the best game I've ever played? Well it's definitely one of them!

Resident Evil 2 is a third person survival horror/shooter and is probably one of the scariest games out there. You play as Leon Kennedy, a cop who just started his job at the Raccoon City Police Department, however his night does not go as planned as the city has been taken over by the infected citizens.

The gameplay: (9/10) Throughout the game you are armed with weapons and tools to escape a horde of zombies, lickers, and dogs, however along the way you can collect herbs and first aid spray to heal your character when wounded. The game also shows a decent level of crafting/combining items to make special tools to aid your quest in surviving.

The music: (7/10) Whilst trying to not to die there is a soundtrack throughout the different areas you explore. It's mostly ambient drones and such but there is some amount of character behind it. But it was not able to match the original soundtrack from Resident Evil 2 (1998), and that was a huge deciding factor in what I thought of it. Plus in the DLCs there is one that costs about $3 that allows you to change the music and sounds to the Resident Evil 2 (1998) music and sounds.

The maps: (10/10) Even though I never played the original game, I can still understand that most of the maps in Resident Evil 2 (2019) were in the original and were certainly faithful to people who played it back then. The beauty and story in each room was perfect and the design was something a lot of games needed to feel immersive.

The graphics: (10/10) The cutscenes were so smooth and detailed it felt like it was actually happening at times, and the times we got to see the city streets were so exquisite I would just stop to look at it. Lighting was so realistic that I just wanted to keep playing and playing this beautiful game.

After playing this game for the past few days, I have really gotten to experience the amazing Resident Evil franchise, and when I'm done with Resident Evil 2 I will try to complete Resident Evil 7 and I might also do a review there too.

~SPOILER FREE REVIEW~

Story: You play as one of two characters, Leon or Claire and you guys are in the middle of a zombie outbreak. Gotta survive, figure out what's going on, fight monsters etc etc - zombie game shenanigans. The story was fun, it was good. True ending was nice. I do have problems however in the replayability part which I will talk about later. 

Gameplay: Hey! You like survival horror? Well, this is the game for you. Manage your inventory, use healing items, guns with limited ammo, then you have the puzzle solving elements every single RE game has and you got a pretty cool game.

Graphics - RE Engine make stunning games. Not gonna lie, but it looks really really good. The graphics of the newer resident evil games are just awesome, close to realism, but not too close. It almost feels like I am watching a movie during cutscenes.

Platinum or 100% Journey: For those people who want to 100% complete this game, or get all the achievements, I will say that this game is pretty much worth it. For your sanity? I don't think so. The main game is actually fairly easy if you plan it right. It took me around 3 playthroughs but if you wanna be hardcore, it would take you 2 playthroughs as each character and to get a majority of the achievements. But why is it bad for your sanity? Well, the extra modes. There are many extra modes, but I particularly hate only 3 of them. More on that later. The document, Mr. Raccoon and the safe's run can be done in pretty much 2 playthroughs. IF however, you want the No healing, No Item Box and also the Beat the game in under 14,000 steps achievement, you're gonna have to play this again, and again, and again, unless ofcourse, you're a badass and play with everything in one hardcore playthrough. This platinum is pretty OK, it isn't really that hard until the extra modes. 

Now for the parts I have issues with:

Extra modes - Don't get me wrong, I loved the extra modes. It was really fun. I just hate the BS in the 3 extra modes which I will talk about.

The 4th Survivor: No spoilers again - but - Sometimes, the AI really wants to *beep* you over, and you can't do anything about it. I can dodge zombies consistently, but then the game is like OH WHAT? YOU DARE CHALLENGE ME? OK COOL, I'LL MAKE SURE YOU GET A REALITY CHECK AND MAKES THE ZOMBIE GRAB ME like.. I can pull it off 6 times out of 10 times just because the AI wants to make me waste my resources. Next, CAN YOU STOP PUTTING SO MANY ENEMIES IN SUCH CRAMPED SPOTS? It is mad annoying when you have to restart and go through the area where you have like so many enemies just cramped up. Next, for those enemies who grab you (basically everyone but I am specifically talking about the BIG MONSTERS), why is it that, when two of you guys are there, one grabs me, I counter, and then, the other grabs me, I tank it, and AGAIN THE FIRST GUY GRABS ME? AND I AM IN A CONSTANT LOOP OF GRABBINESS???? LET ME GO THROUGH DAMN IT!  Anyways, that was not the worst, the worst, is yet to come.

Ghost survivor? I don't remember the name but it's basically the same thing - Military boi gotta extract. I hate this mode. I have made it to the end, 5 times, only to be grabbed by the same BIG MONSTER, who I counter with a grenade, and IT HAS THE AUDACITY TO GRAB ME AGAIN, AFTER THE GRENADE EXPLODES, AND BY THAT TIME, THE ARMORED ZOMBIES WHICH I BASICALLY KITED LIKE SO FAR AWAY, COMES UP AND GRABS ME THE SECOND I'M DROPPED AND ABLE TO MOVE, AND KILLS ME. AMAZING. 5 TIMES! IT IS NOT A COINCIDENCE, THE AI IS SO INCONSISTENT. The main reason I beat this mode was the fact that the BIG MONSTER did not grab me a second time and I just walked away and beat the mode. 

And finally, No Way Out - Simple objective: Kill 100 Zombies.... (In a cramped up gas station, with an infinite ammo pistol, with increasingly challenging enemies showing up, with weapon drops which can help you, low inventory space, poison zombies, armored zombies and more) This mode is brutal. I can't believe I beat it and survived. I kinda enjoyed this mode but I still hate this mode because of how unpredictable the AI is. If zombie wants to go away from you when you are shooting, it will go away, it won't come to you. This becomes really frustrating when you need to get the items from a backpack, but the zombie is like NOPE, I WILL HANG OUT WITH THE BOIS HERE, NO WAY YOU GETTING THE ITEMS FROM THIS PACK. Also *beep* THE PISTOL. IT TAKES 3-5 SHOTS TO KILL ZOMBIES AND YOU HAVE 9 BULLETS IN THE MAG LIKE NICE!!!  

And the last thing I do not like, is the replayability - THE WHAT? GLEN, ARE YOU OUTTA YOUR MIND? THIS HAS INSANE REPLAYABILITY. You would be right, however, hear me out. You have two characters to play as: Leon and Claire, cool. You have two scenarios, A and B, cool. But the issue lies here. Why is it that, when you play a different scenario, the doors and the things which you unlocked in the other scenario, are still locked? I understand that you want to get the players to play it for longer and all. Cool. But you guys are literally in the same building. Next, WHY is it that the bosses you fight, are also alive? Didn't you kill them in the previous scenario? And since the B scenario is about the other character's side of the story, I think they would have pretty much ran around doing other stuff and solving different puzzles while basically avoiding the same enemies and going through the same doors which should be unlocked? Also, why visit the exact same areas? I get it that you have to run through the areas, coz, you are in the same building, but I do not want to just keep solving the same puzzles (with a slight variation) to get to the exact same areas which have and should already be unlocked! Apart from Claire's segment and Leon's segment being a bit different, and taking somewhat different paths, everything is pretty much the same, eventually bringing you back to the same place and all you are doing is the same thing but with a different character and different weapons. Well Glen, what do you suggest? I'd say, make it so, the player in different scenarios gets a different experience while staying true to the area. In the sense, hey lets make it so, that if you unlock this door, it stays unlocked for the other character. Make it so, that when you go to the areas where you have to go, they go to different parts of the area and not through the same areas again, you open different doors which are exclusive to the other character's segments. Make different puzzles, have different bosses, do something. Just by making it so that you have a different character, with different guns, a slightly different path and a slightly different story, is not it. Also, another unpopular idea, make it so that if you have scenarios, the characters eventually meet in the area? You guys are pretty much running through the same area, just make the characters meet each other during running and then probably make them team up or like do different objectives (like Dead Space). The game just becomes bland and boring after a while as it is just, the same thing. Change something. Especially if you want to 100% complete the game, this game in terms of replayability becomes so repetitive because you have to at least play through the game like 6 times. 6 TIMES. PSN PROFILES GUIDE HAS IT AT 6 TIMES. WHY SHOULD ONE GUY PLAY THROUGH THE SAME THING LIKE 6 TIMES? If it was an RPG with different endings, cool, 6 times is pretty normal, BUT 6 TIMES IN RE2 WITH THE SAME AREAS AND DOING THE SAME STUFF WITH A DIFFERENT CHARACTER? NO THANKS. I know its a pretty old game, but those are my criticisms. 

Now, I know I am being a bit harsh, but overall, I really enjoyed the game, it was all part of the experience.

FINAL VERDICT - 8/10 - GOOD

PLATINUM OR 100% ACHIEVEMENT DIFFICULTY - 6/10 - MEDIOCRE CHALLENGE

A very good remake and a must buy for people who want a good remake

Killer remake that stays VERY faithful to the original game. If you've played the original RE2 on PS1, Dreamcast, or Gamecube, then a lot of the puzzles and map layout should already be familiar. Excellent, beautifully refined gameplay and truly next-level visuals and sound. Game is well optimized for how awesome it looks. Truly excellent graphics with a really powerful engine backing it up. One of the best and highest quality games I've ever played, remake or no. 

RE2 Remake is very much its own game with much more modern design. There are definitely some liberties taken and it's not a 1:1 scene-by-scene remake. It's fresh and new and tells the story with modern technology and gameplay. Sometimes when remakes stray away from the source material it's a bad thing. However the changes here are done in such amazing quality that IMO it is a far superior game to the original. If not one of the best games of its type EVER. 

With the newest update Dx12 is forced with Dx11 removed entirely which can be an issue for those on older video cards. Dx12 has always run worse, and with the RTX update the game's original SSR reflections are broken. This takes many cards like the mid-to-high end GeForce 10 series from being able to max the game comfortably to medium settings with broken visuals. I played through the first time using DigitalFoundry's optimized settings at 1440p 60FPS average on a GTX1070Ti. My 1080Ti I bought used just for this title could comfortably max it at 1440p with AA and lock my FreeSync limit of 72FPS most of the time. With forced Dx12 these settings are barely playable. Luckily Capcom have allowed the option to download the older pre-RTX build of the game. This should be the preferred option for anyone that doesn't intend to enable the RTX features.

All that said, if you have an appropriate video card the RTX update is excellent. Raytraced reflections totally replace the broken SSR and give a much more accurate image. Likewise the other Raytracing elements are very tasteful and subtle and have a relatively tame performance impact. With my new 3080 10GB I can comfortably max the game at 4K DLDSR with RTX at High and still lock my 72FPS limit with room to spare. So if you have the hardware, the update is definitely worth it and very reasonable to run.

This is a very nice remake/reimagining of the classic Resident Evil 2. While the changes done to the gameplay are substantial and may irk some fans of the original, I found them to be very tastefully implemented, retaining most if not all of the atmosphere of the first game and showcasing the qualities that made it such a classic, while simultaneously taking advantage of the progress made in game design since the release of the original and removing most of the interface related frustrations that would keep both new and returning players from fully delving into the experience. 

I say that as someone who played through Resident Evil 2 numerous times back in the day. I am deeply familiar with the gameplay of the original and I know there are some tense moments that arise from the way that it is designed. I also know that for every such moment, there are lenghty sections of frustration and tedium born of the same game design, and I wouldn't fault anyone who is used to the sensibilities of modern game design for not having the patience for it. Frankly, I don't think I would have either.

The only thing I would have liked to see done differently is the second playthrough as Claire. While the narrative, as told when playing as Leon, does not tell us much about what Claire is actually doing, it is implying that her story is running parallel to his, and that they intertwine at certain junctions. This illusion quickly falls apart as soon as you get in to Claires playthrough. After the intro where the two are seperated, Leons story goes on for around an hour before you meet up again, while playing as Claire sees you just run down a corridor and around a corner and there's the same meet up scene. From that point on, 90% of Claires playthrough is basically an alternate version of the Leon playthrough, with some smaller sections and events changed around a bit, rather than its own seperate story. The things you do as Claire could not coincide with the things you do as Leon, as they are largely solving the same puzzles in the same locations. I think it's a bit of a missed opportunity where the devs could have gone beyond the scope of the original, making Claires story actually make sense in relation to Leons. Would they have done that, it would easily have raised the score to a 9.

An awesome remake of a classic, the gore, the atmosphere, the horror, all good. 

Gameplay wise, its pretty solid, unlike the likes of RE4 or RE8, this game is focused more on survival horror, which is why ammo is far more limited, you have to value your ammo, cant go around shooting all enemies down or you WILL run out, this is worsen by how durable the zombies are, so you gotta be smart on how you approach each problem, speaking off, theres quite a few puzzles, which are pretty simple and fun to solve. 

The game has tons of replayability, has you unlock the various challenges available on the Records section, which grant you special weapons, concept art and models to see the various characters, weapons and monsters in the game.

One of the big bad guys in this game is the Tyrant, he will be an intimidating force in your runs, has an unstoppable monster that chases you around the RPD, when you hear those loud footsteps, its time to run. 

You will also unlock extra modes, which focus on short yet challenging scenarios, one being the 4th Survivor, and the DLC Ghost Survivors, which includes an Horde Mode of 100 zombies, theres also a variant of the 4th survivor, but wont spoil the surprise of that one ;)

Both of the main characters, Leon and Claire come with their own set of weapons, so how you play either of the two will be different. 

Sadly, here comes my one mayor complain of this game, the A and B scenarios, in the original game, what you did in scenario A would affect certain things in B, but in this game, both scenarios are completely independent from each other, having no effect what you do in the other, the scenarios are also nearly identical regardless of who you play, with the only variables being the weapons, certain sections, and the final boss, nearly everything else is the same, which is a sad thing.

Another problem with this, is the story, it makes no sense, on their own, sure, but when you play both scenarios, it doesnt make sense, and the protagonists have barely any interaction with the other, and both fight the same bosses and see the same events in different ways, which basically looks like both characters live on parallel dimensions. 

Besides that, the game is excellent and definitely a recommend that any RE fan should play.

As someone who never played the original, this was a real surprise. I put it off for a while despite really enjoying 7 & 8 but finally sucked it up and bought it on sale. The puzzles are fun and the story really easy to follow whilst not for even a second becoming dull!

The gunplay is simple but functional and fits the horror theme and sense of desperate survival well. A trap too many horrors fall into is the eventuality of becoming overpowered, which Resident Evil 2 doesn't.

The horror of the game is well balanced with there being a few sudden scares here and there. What really shines though throughout the series is the lingering anxiety of always being hunted, especially as Mr X makes an appearance. Throughout both stories you never truly feel safe, the game dangles sanctuary over your head for something to look forward to but that solitude is short lived as you are forced back into danger in an attempt to escape.

My main and almost only disappointment was it's length. Though you do get to experience it both through the eyes of two different characters as well as with alternative scenarios, the difference between these is very very slim and after a few playthroughs it does become quite stale, something I experienced over my 6 playthroughs for the 100%. Another small thing for me was not being able to pick up ammo and load it directly into your weapon. You need a slot free to put it in then manually reload it. This led to me quite frequently having to discard items (which you can't get back) to reload a few shells and be left with an empty slot. I was surprised that I couldn't combine them with the weapon to save the hassle.

The extra scenarios are just as good as previous titles and add that little bit extra to do which honestly I think really helped split the main game up when I was doing a total of 6 runs between the Leon and Claire.

Overall, I dig it. I can't wait to play the next and I wish I'd picked this up sooner.

Hey there, it's the Earl of Trash, back again with a review of Resident Evil 2. Now, I know what you're thinking - another zombie game? How original. But let me tell you, my corporate comrades, this game is something special.

First of all, the graphics are top-notch. The attention to detail is insane - from the blood spatter on the walls to the grotesque deformities of the zombies themselves, everything looks so realistic that you'll forget you're playing a game.

But what really sets Resident Evil 2 apart is the atmosphere. It's so dark and creepy that you'll be jumping out of your seat at every turn. And the sound design? Oh man, it's like something out of a horror movie. The creaking of the doors, the shuffling of the zombies, the eerie music - it all adds up to create a truly terrifying experience.

And the gameplay? It's intense, to say the least. You're constantly on edge, never knowing when a zombie is going to come out of nowhere and try to munch on your brains. But that's what makes it so satisfying when you finally take them down. And the puzzles? They're challenging, but not so difficult that you'll want to throw your controller across the room.

Now, I will say that this game is not for the faint of heart. It's gory, it's scary, and it's definitely not suitable for young children or anyone who's easily spooked. But if you're a fan of horror and survival games, then Resident Evil 2 is an absolute must-play.

All in all, I highly recommend Resident Evil 2. It's a game that will keep you on the edge of your seat from start to finish, and it's an experience that you won't soon forget. So grab your weapons and get ready to fight for survival - because in this game, the zombies aren't going to go down without a fight.

Here are some reasons to play Resident Evil 2:

You'll get to experience the thrill of being trapped in a city overrun by zombies, just like in real life.

You'll learn valuable survival skills, like how to effectively use a knife to defend yourself from hordes of undead creatures.
