You'll get to scream like a little girl (or boy) when a zombie suddenly jumps out at you from around the corner. It's therapeutic, trust me.

You'll get to relive the nostalgia of playing a classic game that scared the pants off you as a kid.

You'll get to witness some truly bizarre and disturbing creatures, like the Lickers, which are essentially giant, skinless tongues with legs. Who wouldn't want to see that?

You'll get to experience the satisfaction of blasting a zombie's head off with a shotgun. It's the little things in life, you know?

You'll get to join the ranks of Resident Evil fans who have been terrorized by this franchise for decades. It's like a badge of honor.

Finally, you'll get to prove to yourself (and your friends) that you have what it takes to survive a zombie apocalypse. Or, you know, a video game simulation of one.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is, without a doubt, one of the best remakes of all time. Capcom has truly outdone themselves with this one. As a long-time fan of the series, I can confidently say that this game is an absolute masterpiece.

The graphics are stunning, the controls are tight and responsive, and the sound design is excellent. But what really makes this game stand out is the way it manages to capture the essence of the original while still feeling fresh and new.

The updated storyline and characters are expertly crafted, and the addition of new areas and enemies really helps to keep the gameplay exciting and unpredictable. The puzzles are challenging without being frustrating, and the overall pacing of the game is just perfect.

One of my favorite things about Resident Evil 2 Remake is how it manages to create a real sense of tension and dread throughout the entire game. The zombies are genuinely scary, and the limited ammo and health resources really force you to think strategically about how you approach each encounter.

All in all, I would highly recommend Resident Evil 2 Remake to anyone who is a fan of the series, or even to those who are just looking for an excellent survival horror game. This is one of my favorite games of all time, and I would give it a solid 10/10 rating.

Really good. As someone who played a lot of REmake back when it came out on Gamecube, I didn't think I'd like the 3rd person perspective, but they pulled it off really well.

It's nothing like RE4, 5 or 6 which run you through a linear gauntlet of enemies to mow down with plenty of ammo. No, this game doesn't give you nearly enough ammo to kill everything, and is anything but linear. 

Just like the games prior to RE4, you have to decide whether each monster is worth killing, or if they should be evaded entirely. Much of the game is about planning your routes, i.e. taking a shortcut versus the safer route, and managing your inventory so that you have space for the item you're looking for, but are still equipped well enough to get to your destination alive.

What's great about the 3rd person perspective is that you can decide where to shoot a zombie depending on whether you intend to spend the ammo to kill them for good, or stun them just long enough for you to bolt past them. 

What I particularly love is that this game will mix things up when you least expect it, but it knows when to discard a game mechanic before it becomes stale. It excels at pacing itself slowly the same way as RE4 does at pacing itself fast.

The only glaring flaw is that you can easily miss clues or key items, i.e. item located in a part of a room you didn't know existed because maps don't really take furniture under account, or don't realize that a certain [i]officer's notebook[/i] has a second page (I had to look up a few of these, but personally I didn't find that doing so spoiled any meaningful amount of content). Then again, that's part of the old-school RE charm.

As someone who has never had prior experience to any of the Resident Evil games, this was an amazing great to start off the series. I had never really gotten into any survival horror games, and so the first few hours playing the game was a struggle. Prior to playing this game, I've heard about the reviews of the game, and for the most part the reception of the game was pretty positive. So for me, I'll list a few of the pros and the cons that I personally felt while playing this game!

Pros:
- Amazing atmosphere
- Amazing graphics
- Great feeling controls
- Great story-building

Cons:
- The second run was a tad disappointing
- Some of the map layout (the sewers) felt confusing to view

For my pros, the game personally for me (especially on the first run through blind) was incredibly terrifying. Walking through the lonely and dark halls of RPD had a psychological horror aspect to it, and a few of the creatures that lurked around those halls made it that more intense. As someone who doesn't typically play single-player games, seeing the great attention to detail anywhere you went was a great spice. It really added to the overall atmosphere and I appreciate the amount of effort that was put into each layer of the game. The story of RE 2 fascinated me and actually led to me watching and reading the different aspects of the RE universe, and so it's thanks to this game for captivating me into the narrative.

As for cons, the biggest con for me was the second run of this game. I was very excited to see how Leon and Claire's stories would play out considering that they are supposed to happen simultaneously; however, I was met with disappointment when I realized that (with the exception of the beginning) the second run was basically the exact same as the first run through. I wish there had been moments where you can see how Leon's story impacts how Claire's story goes. I did read that Capcom weren't planning on a B route, and only did so because of the backlash they received; however, if you're going to do it, do it right.

3rd game with playing the franchise timeline of events. I only played Leon's side of the story and I know there are different things between him and Claire, but that additional side of the story will be for future me when I want my survival horror fix again. I have not played the original and I am going to treat this review as if the original did not exist and compare to other RE games available on steam.

The Good: 
The graphics are amazing and genuinely had a sense of terror in some parts of the game. I did jump a couple times and it wasn't even a jump scare, i was just on the edge of my seat. The environments are incredibly detailed and the sound design is amazing. Enemies sound terrifying and the lighting is just enough to take in what is necessary. I genuinely enjoyed the interactions of the characters in this story and felt more real compared to the last two games (0 and 1). I enjoyed the puzzles and how the backtracking felt just like enough, not annoying but still enjoyable having things change and going back for a reward, It did not feel like a chore for the reward. 

The Bad:
I would say the only bad thing for me that bothered me a little bit was the repetition of SFX of our protagonist, Every time Leon got hurt or even poisoned, he made sure you knew! It bothered me a little how frequent he would make a comment but hey, I'd be vocal too if I was in pain. But it is the use of the same SFX of pain that got annoying. In the final boss I got hit quite a bit and just heard the same sound of pain over and over. Perhaps since I just played 0 and 1, once I got to the lab it felt quite boring... I got the same exact formula in the past two games. big building -> Underground facility -> lab. So it felt a little overdone but that is probably my binge playing of the series talking. Stand alone, it was great.

The Ugly:
Simply the ghost stories as additional content, It felt lazy just to have some speed run challenge. The reason I was upset about it was high expectations so it was my fault. I thought it was going to be 20-30 mins of a small RE story that had cinematics and to show more of the world you are in and how Umbrella affected the general population of raccoon city. I wanted that. That is not what I got. It was just a copy and paste of areas you have already been in and just shooting zombies with the "story" being a paragraph of text before you load into the game.

Conclusion:
The main story is amazing and should be considered a work of art and is a very effective horror game even to the experienced player to horror. The additional content was highly disappointing to me. You can be a fan of survival horror and not like RE universe to enjoy this game. I give it a 8/10.

Alright, I'm not gonna lie, originally this review was a "Not Recommended" because of some tedious oversights this game has that make the overall experience less enjoyable to me (back & forth level design, obscure puzzles and "difficulty scaling").

Having completed the game though, I can pretty safely ignore most of these issues and admit that this game is really damn good. 

Resident Evil games have a tendency to be designed in such a spectacularly unique way that is simultaneously janky at worst, and esoterically genius at best. You have to change the way you approach videogames (shooters especially) when you play a game like this, because where a lot of other games will hold your hand through how to deal with certain enemies, Resident Evil will more often than not give you an enemy that feels unstoppable, but has a very clever way of dealing with it.

From a new player's POV, Resident Evil 2 is extremely daunting. Not knowing the map layout, how any of the puzzles work, or even how things are ordered and expected to be done can be an extremely daunting challenge, and something I personally was not prepared for when I played it for the first time (this was my first RE game). 

At its best, RE2 rewards you for exploring and testing the limits of what you know versus what you can do. Enemy design is intentionally bullet sponge-y, and you're not expected to always claw your way out of every situation - there's always an alternative that involves as little spending of resources as possible (usually by just avoiding enemies completely) [spoiler]and Mr. X (aka The Tyrant) reflects this design philosophy perfectly - it's an unkillable entity that will hunt you throughout the entire map once it spawns, and the only way you can avoid it is by outrunning it and hoping it loses track of where you went. You can't kill it, you can only avoid it, and to avoid it, you need to cleverly maneuver your way around it, and take paths that help it lose track of where you are, or where you're going. It's downright satisfying to be on the third floor of the police station and looking down at the Tyrant on the first floor, clueless to your presence, and hopelessly trying to track you down.[/spoiler]

At its worst, RE2 is a repetitive walking sim that has you moving between several areas you've already explored because there is SOMETHING you're missing, and you don't know what (on a first playthrough). Obviously you get to appreciate its charm more when you try again from the beginning, but I can understand the frustration that comes from someone trying the game out for the first time and having no idea what to do without relying on a guide.

Overall, I think it's a great RE game and a great entry point to the franchise. If you're interested in trying out RE games, this is a good step to get you used to how the rest of the franchise simultaneously deals and experiments with horror FPS, and just pure action.

2019's Resident Evil 2 remake is a fantastic game! I can't say that I'm much of a fan of the franchise (though I'm pretty sure that I've seen some of the movies in my teens). This is the first Resident Evil game I've played, and I gotta say, it's pretty much fantastic in every regard.

The player gets to choose the character between Leon Kennedy, a rookie cop at Raccoon City's Police Department, or Claire Redfield, a college student searching for her brother. Depending on the choice, the story mode is entirely different, though both stories take place in the same location. If I understand correctly, a second playthrough will change a few details and add another scene to the end. There are also some extra mode that I haven't tried yet.
My first playthrough of Claire's story took me a good 9h. Admittedly, I did quite a bit of backtracking to open all the lockers and such, so I'm sure a speedy player could shave off an hour or three. 

The gameplay revolves around exploring the RCPD's police station, later leading to some interesting nearby structures. Locations within the station are continuously unlocked by finding keys or tools that can open doors. You'll also find combinations for dial safes or lockers throughout the game, which will give you additional resources or rare weapon upgrades. The game is played in the third person and has excellent camera controls that didn't bother me even once. The shooting of monsters works pretty well and is satisfying, though this is most certainly more of a resource scarcity horror game than a shooter. A helpful map in the inventory menu indicates whether you have found everything in the various rooms. 

My only annoyance regarding the gameplay is the inventory management. While not as terrible as in some games, you will most likely run out of inventory frequently. Thankfully, there is a 'shared chest' where you can just dump stuff you don't need at the moment; this chest can be accessed from multiple locations. Also, an indicator symbol tells you if 'key times' have already been used as intended, so you won't have to carry a bunch of keys and such around that you won't need any more.

All in all, I found the gameplay incredibly engaging. Searching through the police station was fantastic (if at times a bit arcade-like, because, seriously, which police station has hidden medallion combination locks in their statues?). The enemies are well-developed and interesting to fight, and the Tyrant/Mr X is absolutely terrifying, even more so than the Alien from Alien: Isolation.

The graphics are generally gorgeous, though for some reason I regularly saw the low-resolution textures of writing for a few seconds before the high-resolution ones would load. Also, every time Claire smiled, her teeth would send me to Uncanny Valley. 

The characters and story are not exactly oscar-worthy, but they certainly work very well for their intended purpose. I found Claire a pretty cool protagonist (reminding me a bit of Lara Croft from the 2013 Tomb Raider reboot), and wouldn't mind seeing her again in another game. I haven't played as Leon yet, but he seemed a bit more generic to me. 

All in all I can highly recommend this game to anyone who doesn't have a heart condition or an uneasy stomach. I'd recommend buying it on sale, where it's typically offered for 10€ (likely the same in $; 75% off). The DLCs only add other outfits (and I think some of them are needed for a bunch of cosmetic mods, though RE2 doesn't seem to be a heavily moddable game).

I'm extremely disappointed to give this a thumbs down after reading so many overwhelmingly positive reviews. As someone who never played resident evil 2, I can't recommend this remake at the full price for it's okay 10 hours worth of content. here's a pros and cons list:

cons:
- Overall the game is short AND doesn't respect your time in that short time span! it's amazing how they've managed this.
- Annoying backtracking makes up half of the first play through. get to red door, can't open, play 2 hours more, get to green door, can't open, get red key, go back for red door, get stuck by orange door... ugh. such a waste of time. The game knows this because the "2nd" play-through as they call it is designed to be completed in only 5 hours (or even less). 
- Movement sucks. It was designed for consoles and controllers and even then it's sluggish. The controls could have been much smoother without affecting the horror aspect. Even resident evil 5 had better movement...
- Your character scans and shows all the items in the map as you pass by them. it's boring but also probably necessary because of how bad the movement and interactions are.
- There is no intuition to the puzzles. All of them are pretty much the same (find a code) you just have to run around for hours because the answer is usually on the other side of the map...
- Saving and inventory management is unnecessarily poorly designed and unavailable when you want it. Classic RE design
- The 2nd play-throughs are exceedingly boring and repetitive as both Leon and Claire walk through 90% of the same areas. The IDEA behind playing as another character and meeting at certain points is fine. It would have been great if 90% of Leon and Claire's play-through was different and only 10% the same. This should have been possible due to the story but I guess CAPCOM got lazy
- Too much content locked behind 2nd play-through and speed runs which already aren't interesting to play meaning you will probably never see this content
- Classic bullet sponge boss battles (Though RE:5 did this A LOT better imho)
- Did I mention backtracking? Ugh...

Pros:
+ Some really spooky jump scares specially because of the claustrophobic design of the map. It's not the most scary game but it keeps you on your toes and I like that about RE games. Can't stand too much horror myself
+ Good Graphics and lighting [in most cases]
+ Decent gun-play albeit limited in variety
+ The story is decent albeit sometimes cheesy

Overall, I can't recommend this game unless you're already a resident evil fan and can buy this for $10 USD. I had more fun with RE:5 (albeit in co-op only and it's probably very outdated in 2023) and RE:7 (which was also not worth full price at release). Hopefully, RE:4 remake will be better and personally can't wait for a RE:5 remake with proper co-op.

I'm neutral on the game. Was going to keep the review as "positive" because while having mixed feelings, it's still probably an "objectively good" game, but considering everyone showers it with praize, I'd rather make an effort to let people know: there are things in this game that you may severely dislike.
On one side they did their absolute best translating the Playstation 1 survival horror game into the modern age while keeping the original style, on the other side, I don't think I like the original style of Resident Evil survival horror. If they managed to nail the same atmosphere with the game being a more linear venture like RE4 I think it would be great, but with the game giving you ample opportunity to waste your time and resources, while also punishing you harshly for wasting them it means that a mess-up almost automatically turns into a re-load of a previous save. Running back and forth, finding the optimal route through the environment while juggling limited inventory space and resources is good for a PS1 game that has limited space and assets, but here it means the game becomes less about reaching your goal, but more about reaching your goal with acceptable usage of resources. You CAN continue after bringing the wrong stuff out of the safe zone and wasting all your good ammo and struggle to survive at a constant resource deficite, but it never stops feeling like it's not the intended way, but that you did this to yourself. Save-scumming very quickly becomes a more natural way to play for people who don't have the Police Station layout memorized from the PS1 days.
Also, the boss fights are nothing special, you just throw your inventory at them and the game while decently optimized has graphical glitches on certain GPUs with both Ray-tracing and SSR.
Can't say much about the story - even not having a PS1, I knew the story of RE2 for a long, long time before this came out.
Most of my crisisms are based on personal preference, but this is a personal review and I don't fool myself into thinking I'm so unique that nobody else may have the same preferences as i do.

REmake 2, much like is predecessor that came out 17 years prior only succeeds in building and expanding upon the original game.  But where the 2002 REmake of the original Resident Evil uses the same formula and gameplay and polishes them to a higher sheen with added beautiful graphics and new content.  REmake 2 actually gives an entire shift to the gameplay, while still staying faithful to the original.  

Now a 3rd person over the shoulder survival horror, somewhat in line with modern classics like Dead Space or The Last of Us.  However Resident Evil 2 pushes survival horror to its utmost.  Where every enemy comes at a cost, resource are truly scarce and you are always encouraged to think before fighting or running from any engagement.  Ammo is plentiful enough that you can kill most enemies, but never so much that you really feel safe doing so, especially if it's not efficiently. 

In classic Resident Evil fashion, exploration and puzzle solving is the primary focus, starting off in a police station full of zombies, your tasked with escaping and pursuing the depths of the story.  The graphics are gorgeous and gruesome, the puzzles are engaging, fun and thoughtful and exploration is absolutely excellent and perilous.  For any fans of the genre, RE2 is a must play.

Timed runs, limited saves, unlimited ammo weapons, and four bonus time trials to spice things up (with one bonus mode really have 6 different styles to it). One of the best things about Resident Evil 2 Remastered is that it has multiple scenarios, and you can play the game with different characters and perspectives, giving the player a chance to explore the game and the story in different ways.

Overall, Resident Evil 2 Remastered is a must-play for fans of the series and newcomers alike. It's a masterful horror game that has been expertly remastered to deliver the best possible experience. This is an interesting game overall there are both good and bad parts that create a conflicting experience. Starting off with the gameplay, which offers 2 different experiences. While the levels are the same the ways the characters deal with situations will be different. Claire gets more of the explosive weapons which helps deal with more single target enemies but bigger groups of enemies not so much. For Leon his weapons are the opposite, making it easier to kill groups of enemies while some of the tougher enemies are harder to deal with. While this does affect some sections of the game, overall there are not enough encounters to make much of a difference. The game mostly takes place in the police station along with the sewers and nest 1. The police station is a great location and is pretty well designed. After that the game feels like it is desperately trying to end. With each location feeling very short with only having to go an area at most 1 time sometimes 2 if you missed an item. Along with that the enemy variety is lacking severely with the base zombie making up most of the encounters. While there are lickers, dogs, G-mutants, and plant zombies these are only for a few sections of the game that make them easy to pass through and forget. The main complaint I have with the game is the storyline and the unique 2nd run mechanic. While the story of each character is fine there are 3 occurrences where the characters meet each other and aside from that don’t interact at all. Despite the 2nd run mechanic which allows you to play the other character’s story while the first one is going on. Which plays the exact same experiences as the 1st run with just some minor changes to item placements and locations. Which ruins the design due to just playing the same game over again with no significant changes despite the unique characters associated with each story. The only thing new is the true ending to the game which just ends up being like a 3 minute long shooting section that just ends the game. Along with that the story doesn’t mention anything about the T-virus despite it being the driving force of the game. Instead it focuses on the G-virus which affects just the main boss of the game along with some enemies you encounter. Which might confuse people on what is really going on in the game. Along with the main game there are unique survivor stories that you can play through that either show events that could or would have happened had certain things not occurred. These are fun for the most part but certain sections of the levels feel like an enemy dump that you have to luck through to survive. The main level in the 4th survivor where you basically run an obstacle course has Hunk as you try to escape going through a majority of the rooms/levels in the game. This is expanded with the Tofu survivor, which are 5 unique characters that have different items while they try to make it through the same course. Overall, the gameplay in Resident Evil 2 is pretty good along with the experiences they encounter along the way. While it is disappointing that the story and 2nd run are huge letdowns that hurt the replay ability. In the end, this is a fun game that is worth your time if you have liked the series up to this point and overall 6/10.

If you've ever wondered why it seems like headshots take so long to kill a zombie, that's because it's entirely up to random chance. The most reliable way to kill them is to knock out their legs and slash them with a knife until they die. However, knives are an even more limited resource than ammunition, and break faster than a pencil being used as a crowbar.

I know that they don't want you to kill all the zombies, and that you're supposed to avoid combat unless it's necessary, but they could have gone about that by making ammunition incredibly rare, but potent. Instead they put it everywhere but made it useless. It's such a simple change that could've saved this game in my eyes, but they're not gonna change it.

Full disclosure: I have not played the original, and I don't really plan on it. From what I have heard, unlike 3, RE2 Remake didn't really cut anything out, and what this means is that what you get is a true remake of the original. What resulted is a really great game. The length of the main campaign seems to be pretty standard for Resident Evil games at around 9-10 hours, and after your first journey in Raccoon City, there is tons of alternate, additive, and bonus content to play through. The amount of stuff they fit in this game when compared to RE3 is truly astounding, and this is definitely worth a buy, but be aware that, unlike most Resident Evil games, this one can legitimately be a bit intense and scary, so if that isn't your thing, then maybe try somewhere else.

Capcom first released Resident Evil 2 on the PSOne back in 1998. At the time it was one of the best titles in the series. It proved the turning point for the survival horror genre and many experts think that it’s going to become the new PS4 cover image. And with the game currently being available via download only, fans can enjoy the game on the cheap, even compared to its classic counterpart.

As for Resident Evil 2 Remastered itself, it has received a rather mixed reaction from fans. It’s never going to appeal to everyone and, as a result, those who dislike it will probably hate it too. But that’s unlikely to stop people from trying it for themselves. Resident Evil 2 Remastered is an HD version of the PSOne classic and the end result is extremely impressive. You get full motion graphics and improved textures while also boasting a more authentic Resident Evil 2 experience. However, to go along with the additional bells and whistles there are some minor changes to the game, most notably an alteration of the original game’s story and a slightly different control system. The core gameplay remains the same but it’s the new additions that truly impress.

It looks fantastic and, in many respects, it feels much more modern and current than its 19 year-old predecessor. The entire game is saved in an impressive high-definition format that uses many of the PlayStation 4’s unique graphical features to enhance the game in all the right ways. So, in a lot of ways, Resident Evil 2 Remastered feels like a brand new game. Despite the game being nearly 20 years old, it still has all the ingredients for a modern, scary survival horror title. On top of that it’s also rather addictive, something which anyone who enjoys the genre will surely agree with. But where Resident Evil 2 Remastered feels like a standout is its gameplay mechanics and gameplay. It’s very intuitive and the controls work exactly as you’d expect them to. That’s thanks to the development team working directly with Capcom to create a hardcore and well-polished experience. Even now, many years after its release, the game still stands up to scrutiny and that’s why many consider it one of the best horror titles ever made. But unfortunately the same cannot be said for the title’s graphics, which can at times feel a little out of date.

Visuals are just disappointing sometimes and the main protagonist, Leon Kennedy, often looks a little out of date in comparison with the majority of other characters. The RE Engine has been very effective at building a beautifully detailed world, so much so that it even gives us a chance to explore certain areas of the real-world beyond the game’s premises. In the original, we saw areas such as London and other various locations. Here in the remaster, we get to explore areas such as Washington D.C. The whole thing looks absolutely fantastic. There are also a whole host of interactive objects dotted around which you can interact with using your menu system.

Sound design could be better and, as a result, some textures could be sharper. However, the whole package is otherwise great and it’s a credit to Capcom and Bluepoint Games that the game hasn’t aged badly. The only major issue with Resident Evil 2 Remastered is the endgame. While the whole game has multiple endings, the final chapter doesn’t have one. Although there’s more to the final part of the game than meets the eye, it also ends up feeling rather disappointing. A simple mission to escort a doctor to his plane only to get blown up and later find that the mission was, in fact, a set-up is the biggest blow to the title. It’s a little unfair that a PSOne classic has to suffer because of Resident Evil 2 Remastered.
After all, i had a lot of fun playing Resident Evil 2 back in the day. However, it’s really unfortunate that it isn’t nearly as memorable for the modern audience and could easily have done with another few years of maintenance. Overall, Resident Evil 2 Remastered is the game that fans have been waiting for and it’s a fantastic example of how a classic game can be remastered and updated for modern audiences without losing anything of its charm. It’s highly recommended that you take the plunge and pick up the game for the PS4 and PC.

-ability to be modded (which honestly. Squirrelies/RE2REmakeSRT is a must)
-huge learning curve which can be rewarding (learning about difficulty adjustment and physics mechanics)

Cons:
-terrible sound design. Enemy is audible at the same dynamic regardless of its distance from you
-horrible movement controls, there's like a slow input/output reaction for walking/running/menuing
-can't access menu or gain control of character until certain things play out. Example: if you get bitten by a zombie, you can't immediately open menu and heal, you'd have to wait until the zombie finishes the entire attack animation. So let's say you wait as your character is getting up and recovering but you don't know when the menu is available but you're hoping to open it ASAP by spamming menu. It's a really frustrating ♥♥♥♥♥♥ mechanic
-difficulty adjustment (DA) honestly ruins the game. You are essentially punished for playing the game. By picking up weapons, healing, and dealing damage to enemies, DA is increased so certain bothersome enemies like lickers will be more aggressive (run faster, aggro quicker, lunge farther, etc)
-there is no way to pause the game while going through certain animations like being bitten by zombies, grabbed by lickers or ivys, or being punched by Mr. X and while recovering by rolling around on the floor. -speaking of wonky physics, when you are on the floor recovering, your character doesn't stay in a static spot. Instead you are free wheeling to anything that can push you. Great game with excellent graphics and incredibly optimized PC Port.
RE2 Remake is one of the games that redefined modern Capcom games alongside DMC5.

They did an excellent job with the character designs, the representation of the map and exploration based on the original game and adapting the controls to the new modern look and camera control.
It's a good game, offers good challenge and requires exploring a lot. It takes the survivor horror genre as is should, being limited in resources like health and ammo and requiring deep exploration to unlock new areas to progress. The game doesn't tell anything and doesn't indicate where to go or what you should do, it's all about surviving on your own and grabbing new information from items.

The graphics and cinematography of the game are really good and show the power of the RE Engine, but the most impressive of all is how optimized the game is.
It ran incredibly well here with super smooth frame rates at 1440p 60fps, everything maxed out on a RTX 2060 Super. Everything looks amazing and the graphics menu is very complete with several options to choose.
I didn't encounter any frame rate drops, stutters or bugs. Very polished and flawless experience.
The engine also scales incredibly well from really high-end hardware running everything maxed out to low end hardware running at lower settings but still being acceptable.

My only complaint is that the game is very short. Took me about 4h to beat the first time with Leon and 2.5h to beat the second time with Claire. If you count the pause time, messing with menus, cutscenes and replaying some sections after dying, both playthroughs took a total of 10 hours for me.
It's interesting to be able to play as two characters. Everything is mostly the same with a few changes but I find it necessary to play with both Claire and Leon in order to fully understand the story. 
Playing Route A with a character then Route B with the other is recommended.
There are also a few free DLCs that should add an hour or two more.

If you like speedrunning, RE2 Remake is basically built around this and gives incentives to the player to finish the campaign as fast as possible to get higher rank at the end.

The game is very polished and a high quality experience. Just beware that it's very short.
I recommend buying when it's on sale.

My second RE, survival horror, and horror-in-general game after REmake, and it's fantastic! It's interesting how, in spite of the over-the-shoulder camera and precision aiming, this game still feels like a natural continuation and escalation of REmake, a by now 20 year old game. You'd expect, given the change in orientation, that this game would be more action oriented, but the zombies this time around are tanker, have longer reaches, and move erratically. In REmake, the bog standard zombie became, at a point, more of an annoyance as you clear the convenient hallways and learn to circumvent any threats. I'm not joking when I say that by the last hour of the game every zombie still felt like a threat. Also, lickers? Scariest design ever. Not too difficult to deal with solo (though I never killed one, just learned to walk around it) but when a zombie or (god forbid) Mr. X comes into the room it becomes a very dangerous game of chicken. For anyone who hasn't played, I recommend both paths-they are meaningfully different in both progression and plot-and remember: don't kill every zombie you see. You'll need to conserve the ammo; a shot to the head should stun it long enough to run past. Good luck.

Let’s get this out of the way: Resident Evil 2 is the best game in Capcom’s long-running survival horror series and possibly the greatest example of the genre ever produced. Released in 1998, two years after the agenda-setting Resident Evil, it introduced the iconic characters Leon Kennedy, Claire Redfield and Ada Wong. It had wonderfully horrible monsters (the tongue-lashing Lickers, the hideously mutated William Birkin, the indomitable Mr X), and it boasted a brilliant set-piece location, the Racoon City police department, housed within a scary old art gallery.

Now, 20 years later, Capcom has taken the game by the scruff of its neck, fully updated the visuals and controls, and reshuffled the narrative structure to deliver a contemporary horror experience that plays like our blood-tinted memories of the original. There’s been a zombifying outbreak in Raccoon City and two characters, rookie cop Leon and student Claire, find themselves trapped in the seemingly abandoned police station, trying to work out what has happened while fighting off the greedy and persistent undead. As we encounter reams of mutated scientists and endless documents about synthetic viruses, it becomes clear that local employer Umbrella Corp has been a very naughty pharmaceutical megacorp.

Every location in the game is, in fact, a giant and enthralling escape room, in which fiendish puzzles involving weird gems and gadgets and complex sequences of numbers and rotations reveal keys to the next locked area. The ultimate brainteaser, however, is inventory management. Ammo is strictly rationed, so every encounter is fraught with deadly peril (although a new assisted mode makes things more palatable for newcomers, offering unlimited saves and easier aiming).

Ultimately, the Resident Evil 2 remake is a reminder of how beautifully crafted survival horror games were in their heyday. From a terrifying orphanage to the festering sewers beneath the city, the feel of the action is always perfectly matched with the aesthetics of the setting. The rhythm, gradually building from many minutes of quiet exploration and puzzle-solving to gigantic, pulverising boss battles, is exact and beautiful.

After watching a few of my favorite gaming channels mention the RE4 remake coming out in March 2023 and how excited they all seemed to be about it, I decided to give Resident Evil a try for my self. I was not sure where to start, but did not want to go all the way back to the beginning, just far enough to learn the story line and also get some decent graphics and game play. After watching some videos on the different versions available I decided RE2 would be the logical place to start.

RE2 provides both decent graphics and solid game play...albeit a little short of a game maybe. The graphics are good compared to some videos I watched of the original game so no complaints there The cut scenes are all well done as is the voice acting for the most part. The controls are easy enough to learn although a little clunky in spots. The areas and rooms are very well rendered, but there is not much interaction with about 90% of what you see. Nothing moves unless you need it or have to kill it - which I found a bit bland. Still game play is good and the puzzles you need to solve to progress the game are fun and make sense...again, for the most part.

The best part of the game for me was the ambiance...especially when you first start playing. The music and sound really drew me in. If you play it in the dark it can definitely give you some chills and get pretty creepy now and then. More than once I was startled while playing the game too. My laptop has a pretty good sounds system so the spacial effects were pretty cool. But if you want really want an experience, playing wearing headphones would probably be very cool and something I wish I had tried as I look back now.

In the end the story is well told so I feel like I understand what is going on so when I play RE3 and eventually RE4, there should be no surprises and everything will make sense. If I were to compare it to a game I played recently it would be Control. However, Control was a much better game IMO. Still Enjoyed RE2, especially considering the price I paid. I have no desire to replay the game even though they do provide a follow up "2nd Run" version that is unlocked after you play though once - but once is enough for me.  I might come back and play it later, but would probably play Control a second time first. Still...I can recommend the game if you are a fan of the genre and want the Resident Evil experience.

I managed to solve most of the puzzles in one go without issue, they could have been better in that regard. Resident Evil is at its best when it forces you to think about a solution to a puzzle, looking for hints, connecting the dots, and rationalizing an answer. As a kid, Resident Evil 2 on PS1 was my introduction to the series.  At the time, the graphics were absolutely cutting-edge and the game was too scary for me to play alone, but an extremely satisfying experience beginning to end.  This remake perfectly encapsulates that experience but in a completely modernized translation that IMHO takes absolutely nothing away from the original, and only adds.  The graphics are amazing (it's like you're playing in a cut scene the entire game, they are simply phenomenal), the story is amazing, even the voice acting is pretty damn good.

I can't say the game terrified me as much as it did when I was a kid, simply because I'm no longer prone to that sort of thing as I once was, but it still MORE than makes up for that fact by providing endless jump-scares, chase sequences, and an absolutely perfect score to fit the tone of what is going on.  

I played my first run through on hardcore mode, and I would HIGHLY recommend doing so if, like me, you were a die-hard fan as a kid and want to feel a similar level of challenge and anxiety as you felt back then.  You are always at the edge of your seat fighting for your life to get to the next location, often clearing parts of the game with no health or ammo left, but the game does an impressive job of always giving you just BARELY enough to get by - really amplifying the "survival-horror" experience.

If you want to just play it as an action game and get through the story, definitely play normal or assisted as hardcore can be extremely frustrating at certain points.  I played as Leon first on hardcore and the 2nd game as Claire on normal, and the difference was absolutely night and day, no comparison.

Anyways, to sum it up and reiterate, this game is freakin' amazing and takes a classic and makes it near-perfect to today's standards.  Highly recommended whether or not you played the original, it's the best game I've played in a LONG time.  But, if you WERE a fan of the original, DO NOT deprive yourself of this experience, it's simply stunning.

It's with some embarrassment that it was this game - not RE:Village, which I had finished mere days before and which is structurally similar (both running on the RE engine), nor the New Game+++++ completions of RE4 across multiple platforms and decades i've previously enjoyed - no, it was RE2make which made me realise that Resident Evil games are made to be replayed. This is true not only normatively (i.e playing RE4 for the n+1th time is still great fun), but also descriptively - as evidenced by achievements, alternative NG+ level design, unlockables etc etc, which are at a frankly absurd high across RE2make and RE8. 

The fact that this - like many other RE games - is meant to be replayed means that the experience the second time around is very different to the first. Being aware of the differences in gameplay in the earlier games of the series, but having just gunned my way through RE8, my subconscious expectations were a little out of whack; instead of an attache case, sprawling environments, waves of enemies which stay dead when you kill them, and enough ammo to kill God, I got claustrophobic hallways, bullet-sponge common enemies, and the most obnoxious inventory system on Earth, which forced me to constantly retrace my steps through hallways with zombies which probably aren't dead and i've only got one more clip remaining in my handgun oh god oh god-

But then, about 3/4 of the way through (as you arrive at [spoiler]the contractually obliged secret laboratory[/spoiler]), you realise that you are carrying more than enough ammo, a hospital's worth of pharmaceuticals, and a handful of 'boss-reserved' weapons for anything even slightly challenging the game might throw at you. At this point you might as well be no-clipping, if not for the various puzzles in between you and the finish line which still need grinding through. Here's the thing, though: even on the second playthrough (needed to get the 'true ending', after a deeply underwhelming final-final boss), that feeling carries over. You know the hallways, the ammo spawns, and the arm length of the zombies; the mechanics are clear, fear goes out the window, and now it's your time to speedrun, just as you might have been doing for every other game in the series - except now you get your haste rewarded with achievements and concept art. Good job, but if you wanted to experience that creeping terror again, then good luck; the mechanics are laid bare almost immediately, and once you know them you can't un-know them.

All this is to say: yeah, the game's pretty good. If you're a fan of survival horror it's certainly better than RE1 (a game I have still not finished and maybe never will, sue me), and if this is one of your first experiences to the earlier Resident Evil games (before they leaned into the action horror B-movie thing), you could certainly do worse; the main gripe I have with it is that some of the mechanics - like the aforementioned inventory system - are heavily dated, but then I suppose it did still do its job in making me go down corridors I didn't really want to go down. That, and the fact that the dialogue and voice acting are probably the single biggest immersion-breaker going. Yes, I understand that this is a RE game and there's an element of parody, even self-deprecation, and I myself have recognised that bad voice acting is a staple of the series; I also understand that just because a game is taking itself relatively (compared to RE4+, anyway) seriously, it doesn't mean there isn't room for laughing at dodgy voice lines - but wherever that line is it was crossed almost immediately, as black holes of charisma Leon and Claire engage in some truly, truly terrible conversation, with each other and with other characters. It's enough to make you wish a big burly man in a trenchcoat and fedora would put an end to your misery.

Also, I just have to say it: I don't know whether it's just because this game has been out for two years and so the surprise was 'mildly' (heavily) spoiled, but Mr. X/Tyrant - while a decent enough mechanic - is simply not that scary. Sure, I did jump out of my skin the couple of times I opened a door and he was right there, but 'oversized bloke who got lost finding his way to the noir mystery film walks loudly and tries to punch you really hard' becomes old, even annoying, very quickly - to the point where the protagonists themselves were quipping on how he kept showing up.

Graphics are gorgeous, as well as details with animations - when Claire radios someone while not in a cut-scene, she actually pulls the radio off her hip, holds it up, then lowers it back down and clasps in back in. Stuff like that really deepens the immersion.

I do think the Police Station is the strongest area. The Sewers are a good area, and the lab is okay. I mostly found the lab annoying as it seems to just throw everything at you since it's the end of the game, rather than the meticulous pacing and planning of the police station. 

The boss battles suck, Mr. X is the only cool "boss". Fighting the rest of the bosses is as much about running around, waiting for an opening, getting 5 shots in, then repeat. They're great cinematic bosses, and when played on the normal difficulty they're not annoying in the way that you keep dying, they're just tedious. The only one that had a really good sense of tension was the one near the storage crate with the crane.

Overall, I do recommend this game as the Police Station pacing is a masterclass in atmosphere, puzzles and map design. After that, the game doesn't fall off, but it definitely has a tough time keeping up with the standard established in the beginning.

In 2019, following the 2002 release of the first Resident Evil remake, Capcom has finally pursued another proper and innovative recreation of one of their most cherished entries. It's the sequel to the 1996 installment with newer protagonists, villains, locations, and scarier outbreak after the Arklay Mountains incident. It follows Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield on their quest to not only survive the truest horrors of Raccoon City but uncover the causes of the zombie invasion. Along their journey, they meet potential allies and foes with similar or questionable intentions.

Firstly, let's address the elephant. It clearly has certain differences compared to its original version but not nearly enough to make it unenjoyable. If you've already played this sequel then you'll be surprised about Capcom's faithfulness and creativity with its content. It's truly the remake longtime fans deserved and would've already been amazing had this been released at the time of its 2002 predecessor. It's so visually and mechanically alluring that it outperforms expectations from its earlier advertisements.

Upon starting the game, players are now given the options between selecting Leon and Claire. Their stories unfold similarly but with newer and expanded events that weren't present in the original version. Regardless which character is selected, they're immediately thrown into the world of survival horror and prepared through a dire situation. Once the chaos escalates they're taken to familiar locations in Raccoon City before reaching their presumed final destination. These moments would make the most hardcore fans joyful while seeing these areas rebuilt and expanded.

Similarly to previous entries, it's a third-person experience but not with cover-based mechanics. Instead, it emphasizes true survival-horror by forcing players to strategically use their wits and resources while controlling characters. The format is similar to Resident Evil's fancy formula but with more realistic details. Now, your knife will easily break after extensive usage, certain enemies will literally fall apart depending on their physical damages, playable characters will react to their surroundings even while endangered, and other surprises that elevates the experience.

The story remains as it's been remembered but clearly modernized with changes to certain situations and outcomes. Leon and Claire will meet whoever in their stories as before but with newer interactions and events. Their objectives are also similar but also given special treatments so they're never repetitive and ridiculous. But the biggest alteration, and addition, is the reintroduction of Mr. X as the main stalker enemy in their stories. Until they're given chances to finally evade and potentially defeat this humanoid monster, they're forced to constantly avoid contact as it patrols everywhere.

But its story and characters wouldn't have more impact without its cast and direction. Every portrayal of familiar characters are fully committed and compelling. Compared to the original, Capcom has given this game an outright cinematic presentation that'll leave anyone amazed. It's a massive improvement that feels like a love-letter to its original fans and private invitation for newer players that missed the first time. There's never a shortage of enjoyment watching greatly voiced characters in greatly written events progressively worsening.

If there's any flaws, it's slightly lacking replay value with certain modes unseen from its 1998 version. There's no Extreme Battle or even fully explored stories featuring newer characters in special minigames. In exchange there's other bonus content that could be unlocked after completing tasks. Although more content would've greatly benefitted the game it's still enjoyable even for those only interested with the story. Passionate fans could still find this worth their time, energy, and money.

It's a fortunate remake that's fortunately rewarding.

[b]REmake 2, ditching the classic gameplay to please the modern audience.[/b]

As a remake, it's fine.
The redesign and remix of the maps and certain events are pretty cool, and gives people who've played the original nice surprises just when they think they already know what happens next because they've played the classic.
The story doesn't change much here no matter which character you pick to play as first, whereas in the original it changes heavily, like which bosses you fight aside from each route's final bosses. Even certain items you grab or don't grab in the first playthrough originally affected the second, but here it doesn't matter.
You can't examine the various props within the map anymore, so a lot of the charm in seeing the pictures and reading the protagonist's thoughts is either lost or more easily missed.
There is a lot of cut content, namely the lack of classic enemies like the giant spiders, moths, crows, and naked zombies. The animals were cut apparently because they'd look "too silly" and be "really, really hard" to add into a game with "scanned faces, motion-captured actors, photorealistic environments" according to one of the producers. The naked zombies were redesigned to actually be pretty terrifying enemies, and would have fit very appropriately on the later half of the base game, but they just stuffed that enemy into the bonus modes of the game.

The difficulty balancing is pretty obnoxious.
You can either play on Easy, Normal, or Very Hard. It's only on Very Hard—where zombies are annoyingly tanky—that you're allowed to experience the classic Resident Evil ink ribbon mechanic. On the first two difficulty settings though, you can just abuse the infinite saves and auto-saves.
There's also the matter of the adaptive difficulty thing that's been around since Resident Evil 4 where you get rewarded for being bad, and punished for being good. For example, you get more ammo the more shots you miss and damage you take, whereas you get less if you land hits and avoid damage. You can be as bad at the game as you want and the game will get easier for you for the most part. The only way to keep the difficulty stable is to load a save file and abuse that, or play on Very Hard where there's little change that happens no matter how good or bad you do, aside maybe from the damage you take.
None of this really matters if you play casually though.

Any boss fight in the classic RE games where you just shoot it until it dies have always been either boring or outright terrible.
Most of the boss fights in this game are pretty bad if just because the only way to "dodge" attacks is to do some weird swerve, just run away, or exploit their AI to bait out attacks that you can just take two step backs from. There are only two "okay" boss fights in the game out of the half-dozen because they actually have a lot of weakspots that stagger the boss when shot enough times, or the dodging is simply a matter of running to the side because they finally gave you enough room to do so.

Outside of the two easy difficulty settings, the survival horror part is pretty great.
Resources are very limited, so you really shouldn't be trying to kill everything, even though you technically could with some min-maxing.
Basic zombies are extremely threatening in the sense that they can eat up your resources if you don't make your shots count and/or plan an escape route. Maybe they'll get too close and grab you when you're still trying to aim at their wobbling heads, or you rushed a hallway and weren't careful of the possibility that there was one ready to grab you at the next corner.
Zombies being tanky isn't anything new to the series, but they shouldn't be able to take 10 whole handgun bullets to the head and still stand up. Even in the railshooter RE games, the zombies take less than half a dozen headshots to kill, or a single targeted shot in an extremely small part of their head for a critical one-shot. In the CG movies, they actually die to single headshots, and even Leon himself suggests to shoot them in the head in those. 
You can still do cheeky kills with the knife like in the original, but the knife has durability now and you can find multiples, and knife kills can only be reliably done when the zombie is on the ground.

There are practically no loading screens in the game, so going anywhere up until the last map can be seamless. The game also keeps track of every damage you've dealt to the zombies, so no matter how far you've progressed, the damage dealt remains the same down to the exact position they were killed at for the entire game.
This seamless mechanic thing also means it's easy to exploit some enemies since they're not allowed to enter some rooms; you can go to a room, wait for the monster to walk away from the room it can't enter, go back to shoot them, and repeat.

As its own game, it's pretty great. The "remake" part just makes me wonder if they're just trying to bank on the name.

First off, and probably the least debatable thing about this game is that the graphics look stunning. As someone who has never played a game in this series besides a small bit of RE 7: Biohazard at a friend's house after it came out, this game looks really damn good. Characters, environments, and enemies aside all look absolutely stunning compared to what I’ve seen from the original, of course. This game excels at making you feel immersed as you explore the station, with a constant sense of nervousness in your mind. 

I should say before I continue, that I do not normally play games in the horror genre, but this game scares me the same way John Carpenter's “The Thing” does, with a sense of dread and fear being ever constant. Jump scares might grab the sudden moment, but as you creep through dark hallways, sewers, and an underground laboratory, you will feel that dread. I can only imagine how it feels on hardcore, but for my first play through, normal did give me a bit of a challenge, but nothing I felt cheated about, unfair, or BS. 

Game play wise I’ve read how some people dislike the annoyance of zombies being more tanky, taking multiple headshots to knock down, or randomly getting their heads blown off to not get back up, but have to disagree with it hindering the game. The chance of a guaranteed kill or a more long lasting threat makes each encounter provoke your fight or flight, as the wrong mistake will quickly be your last. Each variety of enemy provides new challenges to overcome and forces you to change up your play style so that you can come out on top, helping feed the fear into your mind. Puzzles all felt fair, as they could be a good thought provoker, but never forced me to look up a guide or rub my head in frustration. 

My favorite part of the game is the ability to explore your surroundings and the power of map usage. Especially as you progress into the game and encounter bigger and badder enemies  . Exploration isn’t a requirement but you will quickly find your resources scarce if you don’t take time to look around, and explore your surroundings. It was so fun for me that I couldn’t let myself leave a room unexplored, even with present danger hot on my ass. The inventory system also pressures you into moderation and regulation of what you hold onto and what to store, forcing you to make decisions on what you carry into key moments. 

Overall, this game might not please everyone, but I very quickly have put this pretty high up on games that I enjoy and would recommend to others. I am very much looking forward to playing this game more, and even trying for some of the harder achievements to try and 100% this game, but I know that’ll be a pain.

1) buy this game. I got it on sale, but after having played it, I would've easily spent $40 on it if I knew how much I'd love it. I'm a bit new to horror games. I have played games before that really got my adrenaline pumping, but only recently bought some actual horror games. I have to say RE2 is one of the best games I've ever played overall. Gave me the greatest thrills I've had from any media in a long time.

You get two different characters to play as for the main story line, and there's some "extras" too which includes some bonus content with other characters. These are not story-centered, and are just time trials essentially, so I only recommend checking those out after finishing one or both of the main story lines. I've only finished Leon's story, and I'm looking forward to starting Claire's sometime. It took me about 14.5 hours to get through Leon's story, in a little over 2 weeks, which is longer than many people take. You could speed run the whole thing in a few hours it seems, based on the grades you can see at the end. But I wouldn't encourage trying to finish the game as fast as possible. I don't believe there's any reward for an A or B grade (I could be wrong, I didn't get a grade lol). This game has loads of little secrets and puzzles scattered throughout and across (hint) all the spaces you play in, and personally, I loved solving each and every one of them to figure out how to progress the story, but also to get more useful items like ammo (which can be really scarce at times) or useful gadgets. The puzzles are not too difficult, but also not super easy and require some degree of backtracking through previous areas at times, but the game keeps things interesting during many of those backtracking moments. Overall, the aesthetic of the game world is very creepy and unsettling. You rarely feel safe when you play this game. It's made even worse if you happen to be finding your way in the dark with nothing but 3 rounds. This is NOT a run-and-gun game.
 
View this game as a challenge. A mental challenge, and a survival challenge. If you want the ideal experience, play it like I outlined in my list above, for maximum immersion, and don't look anything up!

From the perspective of someone who has not played the original, the resident evil 2 remake is without a doubt one of the best games of the eighth generation and personally it is my favorite survival horror game that I have played so far. I understand that many RE fans prefer fixed camera angles as this can orchestrate tension by limiting the player's field of vision. However, I prefer the over-the-shoulder approach present in the remake and the likes of Resident Evil 4.

While the story is not exactly Shakespeare it is surprisingly classy, especially considering the context of resident evil as a series. The voice acting is great and both stories, whether you decide to play as Claire or Leon, are equally compelling and interesting. There is a particular scene involving a gun store owner that I will not spoil, it was very emotional and surprised me considering Resident Evil's campy nature. The presentation is simply outstanding no matter what segment of the game you are in. It is without a doubt one of the best-looking games I have ever played and runs beautifully on PC at 120 fps with no dips or slowdown.

The gameplay has the perfect balance of horror and action for a resident evil game ammunition is sparse however you will have more than enough so long as you play conservatively. The environments particularly the rpd police station are wonderfully designed offering plenty of puzzles, backtracking opportunities, and terrifying encounters, especially with the lickers and the stalking tyrant who in my case always threw a wrench in my plans once I was semi-comfortable navigating the environment.

Overall, the level design is outstanding however, I would argue that the sewer and lab segments, while strong, are much less interesting than the police station and are far too linear in design, playing the same on each subsequent play-through. The boss fights were very mediocre lacking impact/responsiveness from player damage. The boss following the sewer segment is particularly bad and the giant crocodile quick-time event is hilariously bad and feels like something out of resident evil 5 or 6. The final bosses are the strongest, however, they offered little tension offering a dramatic action sequence payoff, which I would say is earned by the game's later segments.

In conclusion, I cannot recommend this game enough, especially to newcomers to the series or the survival horror genre.

Resident Evil 2 Remake:
Oh how I despair, this game to me is a perfect example of whats wrong with the current state of the games industry, it's like someone said "let's take what was probably the genre defining game of the series, and turn it into a bland middle of the road shooter that only just about pays lip service to the original."
For this review i'll be referencing back to the original several times.

Gameplay:
First and quite obviously, its pretty much a different game with a resi 2 skin over the top of it. The tank controls and fixed cameras are replaced with the 3rd person movement and cam that's been used since Resi 4, Whilst I have no real issue with the replacement of the tank controls (it worked perfectly fine when they replaced them in the gamecube version of the original Resident Evil), its the 3rd person camera that really disappoints me. 
The fixed camera of the original gave a feel that you were watching the game play out through CCTV, rather than playing as Leon/Claire, which to me, added to the games constant sense of overbearing dread. This has since been replaced with the cheap jump scare of a zombie grabbing you from behind, because of the 3rd person cam. To me, hearing a zombie that you knew was there, but couldn't see because of the fixed cam, was far more panic inducing, which in my opinion makes for a better horror game, yes there was a few jump scares in the original, but it wasn't constant, to the point where it was more annoying than actually scary like it is now. Also, making the zombies need to be shot about 7 times in the head just to make the game artificially harder is dumb, yes you can shoot them once then run past, but 9/10 times they'll still grab you, they didn't even put in some kind of dodge mechanic, which has been pretty standard for TPS games for like that last 20 years....

Now let's talk about what's been cut from this version. [spoiler]
First, no crows, no giant spiders, no moth boss (just, why???), the symbiote boss has now been turned into an enemy you fight repeatedly, and is more of a chore than anything else. The alligator has been changed from a pretty iconic scene in the original (where you could choose to fight it, or run and drop the gas canister and kill it in a cinematic reference to jaws, to a 10 second run where it automatically bites a gas pipe, you kill it, you forget about it and you move on (boring, dull, pretty much how i felt about this game from that point forwards)
However, The biggest screw you to fans of the original game, comes when you realize that what you do in one characters game, no longer affects the others. For example you could choose to leave the hip pouches in Leons game, so that Claire could pick them up (as she desperately needed them, since she only had 6 inventory spaces at the start of the game.) [/spoiler]

Sound:
The sound effects of the game are the best thing about this game, I have nothing bad to say about them. The dialogue on the other hand, Jeez, was Leon the only character they paid a professional voice actor for? whoever voiced Claire sounded like they'd been pulled out of an amateur improv night, with no idea howto emote, she sounds like shes on vacation at Daytona Beach rather than in the middle of a zombie apocalypse.

Graphics:
I don't care about graphics at the best of times, but it's remakes like this in particular that really irk me, The original was a specific art style to fit with what they were making at the time, the gameplay was definitely what they put more of their attention towards. This remake however, I whole heartidly believe they put the graphics first, everything else came second, and the gameplay has obviously suffered because of that.

In Conclusion:
This games is at best 4.5/10

RE:2 Remaster - My Afterthoughts
I really only give this a thumbs up as RE is one of my favorite series from my console days. This however is starting to change very quickly in these lackluster "remasters"

The good - nostalgia, zombies, decent story.
The bad - they've changed lots of things from the original - zombie bullet sponges
The annoying - the game is basically one big jump scare hallway, the reworked Sherry scene is absolutely atrocious.

My biggest gripe:
Predictable and scripted to follow ABC -> XYZ
The formula remains the same even 20 years later...

If I had to sum up Resident Evil simply: Tedious and predictable and heavily scripted.

My biggest gripe, honestly, with much of the Resident Evil series (and quite a few games). Granted I haven't played Village yet, maybe they've changed the formula.

There is absolutely 0 unpredictability or randomness.

You want to brand a game survival horror - or make a name for your game for speed running? Make things random, make things change - force the player to adapt on the fly.

Unfortunately:
Everything is always and will always be in the exact same location it is meant to be. It will never change unless changed directly by the player (EG: forcing a zombie to a different location by baiting them).

Mr X always knows where you are while pretending to "hunt" for the player - step into a safe area and he just wanders off. Lickers always know where you are while pretending to be blind. Make a bit of noise or throw a grenade, they always know the location of the player.

This doesn't stand up against the sad state of survivor stories' which are basically long scripted hallways. (though surprisingly only one of them has any true chance for randomness)

You want to make speedruns more meaningful? But most importantly, replayability more meaningful? Make a multitude of things random: for example; 2 or 3 zombies in a hallway instead of only 1, forcing the player to adapt. Randomly change locations of items and herbs and secondary items so they have to adapt and change tactics. Scatter those zombies out or cluster them together so a player isn't always expecting the same formula around every single corner every single time.
Whatever happened to the A/B scenarios?

Sadly in the past 25 years of playing Resident Evil games, I've yet to find much of this true (with the exception of RE:5/6's coop modes which had some semblance of randomness to them but were still mostly scripted ABC -> XYZ)

I finally forced myself to finish the game.
I was surprised to find my "2nd run" to be completing all the same tasks as my first run counterpart yet informing the player that "they must have got here first" - but clearly nothing that was completed carried over. A very disappointing outcome to my surprise.

I really expected more... After 25 years...

This game is unusually short compared to the other 3 games I've played (RE7, VILLAGE, RE1) but it doesn't suffer from it. So, I don't exactly have any comparisons between REmake & original. I've heard that the REmake is very faithful to the original though, but cannot confirm or deny.

Resident Evil 2's main 2 characters are very good. I played as Leon in my playthrough, & he is great! This game really makes you love him. Claire Redfield doesn't appear very much in Leon's story, so I can't speak much of her, but from the little she is in, she is cool as well!
No matter which character you choose to play in your first run, I highly recommend you either play a second run as the other character, or watch a playthrough of the other characters story. Overall, RE2 REmake is a great game, the shorter playtime is more than made up for with the great environments & the detail within them, and also the fact that there is 2 different stories to play through means that the game is twice as long as it first is, even if your second playthrough is most of the same areas.

It is not easy to approach a remake of one of the most influencial games on history. One of the games that has shaped not only their genre, but any other game that came after it, and also the way stories are told in videogames.
Some would say that a remake for this game is not even needed, as games like RE 2 manage to stay relevant as a gaming experience regardless of age and can still be played and enjoyed as they were designed in the first place. I'm not sure what to think about this, but however is the outcome of this thought, I can assure that, as far as remakes go, this a very solid one.
RE 2 remake achieves something truly difficult that many other remakes from older games can't reach: stay close to the original in the essence, but updating every other aspect and improving it. It is very hard to identify and isolate the essence of a game, and it is even harder to do it on a game with the importance of RE 2, but here Capcom has succeed, and it is able to present a very close experience to the original but in spirit, not in pure form. 
A lot of things have changed from the original: The camera, the inventory, even the story...but it stays close to the spirit of RE 2 in the way it manages the sense of fear, caution and mixing moments of pure anxiety and discomfort with the calm exploration and mistery solving puzzles that made the saga stand out. 
A surprising success from Capcom, which tends to stray away from the right formula in some of the RE games, even if the last ones (RE 7,8) seem to have found again the good path.
This is a game that needs to be played if you have played the old RE 2, but also if you want to experience Racoon City for the first time.

Overview:
Loved every second of it!
It remains true to the original version. Deeply respects it and even add new content to it. Although they've removed, but replaced some plot elements, which i wasn't really a big fan. Sound effect are incredibly well made. It gives a lot of creep vibes and works well with the enviroment. The only thing, which i kinda disliked is it was the safe room theme. It wasn't as loud as it should've been. Graphics are amazing and gruesome.
Optimization is demanding, but you're "able" to play it even with a bad PC. (Here's a tip, lower it to "quailty" or "balanced". Put the graphics to 0 GB vram usage, but make the resolution 1280x1024 or better, so it doesn't get blurry and pixely. Increase every light effect to max or turn it on, but don't touch the shadow effects. With all this you aren't gonna lagg spikes or experience FPS drop, but the game gonna look decent.)
Bonus content are somewhat fun, but nothing breath taking. The game itself has a huge replayability with customes. This  game is the speedrunners dream.

Characters:
-Leon S. Kennedy: Remained true to it's original version. The naive rookie without any specific field training.
-Claire Redfield: She felt more natural, than Leon. Her personality shows the caring good big sister/mother vibes. Not just in Code Veronica or Degenerations. I loved the scene where she tried to flirt with Leon. (Cause she was lil' bit boy crazy)
-Ada Wong: The whole FBI cover up story felt stupid in my opinion. Her character remained true to her original one. The sassy narcistic "b!tch in a red dress". Her gadget felt way too high tech during it's time...
-William Birkin: Felt the same, except his voice was more younger.
-Sherry Birkin: Remained the same, but felt more natural.
-Anette Birkin: Her character was way superior, than it's original one.
-Marvin Baranagh: Lived more, than he should've been, which was a nice addtion, but his death scene wasn't that much of a big deal as in the original. The way how he got the T-virus infection was unbeliveable...
-Robert Kendo: I didn't like it at all...
-Hunk: The Grimreaper is the same. Misterious badass boss, 

Places:
-Gas Station is okay intro to the game, but not as good as Jack's Bar...
-The R.P.D. Station got expanded with a third floor, which is incredible, cause it was a museum in the first place. You can see what Irons covered up the unwanted investigators. The dark coridors makes more sense, cause after all electricity shouldn't work, after the attack of zombie hordes. The addtional bathrooms are a welcomed change, since we didn't get any in the original. Blocked hallways makes more sense, since the officers treated civilans who got infected and probably spread the virus inside the building. 
-The orphanage was a nice touch and gave the 90's vibe.  
-The sewers were expanded as well in a good scary way, but it felt more like a 2000's design.
-On the other hand i simply hated the lab (NEST) desgin. It felt more modern and unfilled. The original wasn't, that huge neihter, but i felt more natural during it's time (late 90's tech). 

Creatures: 
-Zombies are tough as hell (atleast in hardcore), they function as bullet sponges, which indicates why you should stun them, instead of wipe the floor with them.
-Lickers are scary as f**k, but a little daily knife work can do the trick or a flashbang. The music what they got paired with was spine chlling.
-G-Adults are scary and the reason behind that, cause they can emerge from the water. They're annoying, but you're able to dodge them. I was a good addtion to the game. It was present in the original in Leon A/Claire B and in Outbreak #1.
-Ivy creatures are rewamped to be zombies who got in contact with the Plant 43. I mean they weren't that scary, but the music was so terrifing with their moaning.
-Cerebruses were as annoying as in the original, but in Claire A campagin felt they aren't really present. 
-Mr. X (T-00 Tyrant) wasn't that big of a deal for me, not even Leon B hardcore. I could easily avoid him.
-Giant spiders: They've got removed, but replaced with G-Adults!
-Crows: Again they aren't present! 

Boss fights:
-Super T-00 Tyrant (Mr.X) was kinda "hard". The only reason why i say this is, beacuse of the old school one shot move, but in the end, if you had a flashbang or grenades it could do the trick for you.
-Aligator "fight" was just as bad, if not worse in the original.
-G-1 Birkin boss fight was better, than the original, but just as easy as in the OG version.
-G-2 Birkin was good, but kinda easy with both protagonist.
-G-3 Birkin, honestly was kinda enjoyable.
-G-4 was scrapped, which is unfortunate
-G-5 Birkin was the same, just as in the original. An epilogue "boss" fight.

Puzzles:
Usually Resident Evil puzzle aren't hard, but they felt good enough for me!

Summary:
It's a must have for every Resident Evil (Biohazard) fan. It's a gem! Although i still prefer the fixed camera angles, rather than third person (TPS) point of view [second person (SPS)].

I had no problem with the original's control scheme and camera angles but I prefer the remake's more than the original's. I also had more thrill playing the remake more than the original, as it was more stressful but in a good, fun way.

One of the best survival horror games. Semi linear level design, great enemy design, outstanding atmosphere. The puzzles are a bit on the easier side but that is normal for Resident Evil games and i don't know how i should feel about the dynamic difficulty scaling (if you do too well, enemies take more shots to kill so there is artificial scarcity), but those are nitpicks for an otherwise flawless game.
