RE2 is the first Resident Evil game I've ever played, and I was delightfully surprised (although not shocked, after seeing the huge boom it had in popularity when it released).

Although the plot is generally simple, it makes up for it in atmosphere and the puzzles it implements.

The puzzles are satisfying to complete, and I very rarely found myself wanting to quit when I encountered one. They aren't super hard either, and a keen eye can spot the tools and answers needed to progress.

The gunplay is alright. I can't say it's overly revolutionary, and I felt it's quite standard for an over-the-shoulder shooter. 

The scavenging and items system is alright as well, and the game supplies you with just enough to keep you on your feet, but not enough to allow you to blow through the hordes.

The movement feels a bit sluggish (yes, I'm aware this is a Survival Horror, and this is a common tool used), but with characters like Leon, it makes me groan when they just briskly speed walk to get around.

The general production quality of the entire game is great too, and the team at Capcom really put their best in for RE2's reprisal.

My only gripe I have is the similarities between Claire and Leon's stories. I get there's the whole "Oooh different accounts of events ooh", but it felt super lazy just nearly copy+pasting Leon's story into Claire's, with some characters being replaced/new areas being put into play.

Overly, I have little to no issues with RE2, and I had a fun time running through it, and I think you would too.

While the game is fun at times and it has some really next-gen gaming moments - like when characters mumble to themselves during combat - the core game design here feels archaic. That could've still made the experience pleasurable, if the game didn't forces me to finish it four times in order to get the full story. 

On the Normal, the only real threats are bosses, who feel unfair in the worst possible way. It feels like fighting a truck full of HP that can two-shot you at any moment. They don't challenge you with interesting mechanics - they are just huge, annoying bullet spunges. 

Normal enemies are just obstacles on the way, as you always have enough resources to get rid of them, which in turn removes the "survival" part of the game. And this is where the problem rears its head: with enemy design like this, action stops being fun too, as combat becomes repetitive and boring. 

Switching to Assisted sounded like a better fit for me, but the autoaim was so strong, that often times it made me miss. I couldn't find any settings to tune my Assisted experience, which disappointed me. All I wanted was weaker enemies that reanimate less often, so I could've at least had fewer obstacles on the way.

The cherry on top? I don't get to see the full story, because I don't have time to waste. I was excited to play the other campaign in the game, thinking it would show me what the other character to the one I picked was doing while I was dealing with obstacles. 

However, turns out my expectations are unrealistic, because in order to get that, I need to beat the game a total of four times. This is plainly stated extraordinarily retarded. I may have patience for bad enemy design, but I will never promote a game that does not appreciate it's players time.

Probably one of the best games I've played this year. The scare factor does suffer on replays, but learning the mechanics of the game and figuring out how to do everything more efficiently on each run feels very satisfying. All of the upgrades feel empowering and are worth going out of your way to collect. The early game is defined by a lot of survivalist decision making; conserving ammo and figuring out to efficiently take out threats (or avoid them entirely) is necessary for progression This never entirely goes away, but if you're smart and conservative with your resources the end game will feel more like an action movie. Some people may not like this, but I enjoy it very much as it is satisfying to watch the characters grow stronger instead of remaining victims. I haven't tried the game on Hardcore Difficulty yet, but Standard feels fairly balanced.

I'd happily recommend this game for anyone looking for a scary, challenging experience. But if you're like me and are more used to traditional FPS games, you should know going in that this is a very different experience. I've put some advice down below to help out newbies, feel free to take a read if you 'd like;

- Resource Conservation and learning when to pick your battles is really important. Ammo and healing are in short supply and you're going to want to conserve both for the later levels where enemies can get really nasty. A good rule of thumb, is that if you can avoid a fight or simply run past the threat, that is probably the best option. Only kill zombies if they are a direct threat, or if you know that you will be returning to the location often.
- A lot of zombie media tells you that always aim for the head. This mentality is not a good one in this game. Your starter weapon, even when fully upgraded, is not going to be powerful enough to kill a zombie with one headshot. Killing them this way can take up to twelve bullets, which is a huge ammo drain. Instead, focus on shooting limbs in order to incapacitate them and move past. I'd recommend starting with the legs since this will slow them down by a lot and help you get past them without using as much ammo.
- Using the sub-weapons like the combat knife and the flash bombs are essential, as both will help save on ammo and can be used when you're about to be bitten to get the zombies off of you and thus avoid having to use healing items. A good combo is to shoot a zombie's leg off and then move in with the combat knife to finish them off. Flashbombs are useful to disorient zombies and thus either run away or get a good shot in. Grenades are really helpful against hordes, or to do a lot of damage against bosses and elite mobs.
- If you use a combat knife to get a zombie off of you, remember to retrieve it from their corpse once you kill them. Combat knives can be used multiple times.
- If you're not sure if a zombie is dead or not, stabbing them is usually a better way to tell instead of wasting a bullet. Don't worry too much if a combat knife breaks. There are plenty scattered throughout the game and losing one is always better than wasting ammo.
- While it might be tempting to use stronger weapons like the shotgun or the flare gun to clear out weak zombies, this isn't always the best strategy. There are a lot of tougher enemies later on in the game that you will want to finish off fast, and preserving ammo for stronger weapons is essential for doing that. Only use a strong weapon on a weak enemy if you will be coming back to that location later and if you have a large stockpile, and if you do decide to kill them make it a headshot.

I hope that this advice is useful for you guys. Happy Hunting!

I've put sufficient time into the Resident Evil 2 Remake. Obviously I had conflicting feelings about the experience as I did not write a review about it right away.

On the record, the game looks stellar and utilizes the correct amount of shadows and darkness to add to the unsettling atmosphere. You really have to use the flash light to be at the top of your game. Additionally the foot falls,scamperings,and groans of creatures and undead increase and decrease in relation to how close and far away they are from your vicinity. These are very subtle touches but add a lot to the overall experience.

It likewise feels good to pull off critical gun-shots with the appropriate head-splattering results
or to discover that one item which will allow you to progress just a little further into whatever
evil residence you are exploring at the moment!

However,sometimes there are a few too many puzzles and a bit too much when it comes to back-tracking. Staples of the series to be sure but for some odd reason I found it more difficult to navigate through the police station or Raccoon city sewers than the Spencer Mansion or whatever other new locales came after the classic trilogy.

If you are afraid the characters in this remake are poorly represented compared to their earlier depictions rest assured this is not the case. Leon,Claire,and Ada have never been more themselves and even side characters like the Berkins and police chief Irons are all faithfully recreated.

Granted,sacrifices must always be made. A particular memorable boss fight is reduced to a quick-time cinematic and the "alternate scenarios" got nerfed. Yes,things are slightly different if you go thru the game as Leon or Claire a second time but there are not as many rewards and additional story content for doing so. (Not to mention there's a stealth segment with Sherry that drove me up the wall. It's doable but only via repeated trial and error. I'll level with you,I'm not the greatest at the hide & sneak style of gameplay!)

Luckily RE 2 R does have the usual bonus modes you would expect as well as "ghost survivors" which allows you to complete what-if scenarios with a few of the more memorable side characters. My point of contention is said characters are restricted to their locked-in progression paths so you do not get the freedom of choice that you would in "mercenaries" or "raid mode".

Overall I believe RE2 R is "almost" as good of a remake as the one done for its' progenitor but there's just something RE1 R had that's missing here. Could it be the pre-rendered backgrounds,forced perspective,and additional artistic flourishes gave the mansion more of a memorable appeal than Raccoon city as a whole? Can there really be "too much" of a good thing when it comes to puzzles,macguffins,and items that need to be inserted into "other" items? (Whilst Mr X stalks you relentlessly as you go about your prolonged scavenger hunts!) Perhaps that is the case or just personal tastes. 

Regardless,this is one of the better Resident Evil Entries. I'd say it is a safe purchase if you prefer the lore in the original trilogy and you want a mostly faithful adaptation of RE2 that strays from the source material ever so briefly before getting back on track......

Pros

+The developers cared

+A respectful sincere tribute to RE2 even if it is not a 1/1 remake.

+Characters are faithfully recreated (Overall)

+Moment to moment gameplay and movement are smooth and responsive.

+Additional content to complete after the main campaign is finished. (Ghost survivors,etc.)

+Being able to board up windows adds a new strategic element that makes sense in the context of the setting.


Neutrals

+/- Plenty of puzzles and macguffins if that is what you missed about the more methodically paced originals.

+/- Lotsa backtracking and even a stealth section thrown in.

Cons

-Don't misunderstand me,the inclusion of Mr. X is fantastic "but" it can sometimes be annoying to dodge around him whilst scavenging for a key item or trying to solve a puzzle! (Woah X,NO! Please DON'T give it to me!)

-No moths,spiders,or ravens (It should be mentioned for every old enemy yeeted a new one was added or is a modified updated version. Kudos for that!)

-"Alternate paths" nerf. 

-No mode allowing you to select your preferred characters.
(Beyond variants of Tofu in that specific mode.)

-Despite its' technical prowess it lacks some of the authentic charm of RE1 R.

I have to mark yes on recommendations solely because there's no middle-of-the-road option when it comes to an overall review. To summarize my point bluntly, the game is a recommend, but only at or below $20. 

The game is in a very awkward place when it comes to both its positives and negatives as I'll list out:

[b] Positives:[/b] [list]
[*] Beautiful graphics
[*] A good build-up of atmosphere and tension through the early game
[*] An absolute wonderful first playthrough
[*] Intense pursuer chases in the police station
[/list]
[b] Negatives:[/b] [list]
[*] General enjoyment quickly falls off with repeat playthroughs, particularly because [b]all scenarios play out very close to the same, albeit with a different "middle part" starting at the first boss fight and intermission between the police station and sewers, and a different end boss[/b]
[*] B scenarios play out exactly the same as the A scenarios, just 10 minutes ahead of the A scenario, and with slightly different item placement
[*] The pursuer immediately loses his presence after the police station, and only reappears very briefly in small spurts (In Leon's campaign)
[/list]

These are my [b]very[/b] brief thoughts on hard positives and negatives for REmake2. My other thoughts are a little less precise, but I wanted to mention them. The game has a weird middle ground being struck between being close to the original, but also distancing itself well away from the original to effectively do its own thing. It's undeniable to see what was cut just through a watch of the original PS1 game, though I feel like the game is in a place where it should have gone fully in one direction or another, and the scenarios are the biggest stickler for me. As I mentioned before, the first playthrough is something else, but as soon as you play the other character's A or B scenarios, you'll see just how worthless of an addition the concept is.

The extra scenarios really needed further fleshing out to warrant their existence, if not being reworked altogether to serve a better placement in the remake. To me, this feels like lost potential to not fully dive into the idea of diverging paths that was presented in the original where Leon or Claire ended up taking a different path at the beginning and it affecting the story events, even if in a minor way. It feels tacked on, especially considering just how much everything else has changed from the original.

As for difficulty, REmake2 has adopted the idea that zombies shouldn't be meant to kill, at least not without taking ample time to down them. Even on Standard difficulty, you'll commonly make 3 shots minimum to the head to down a zombie, and typically the best way to make sure they stay dead is to use your (now perishable) knife on them until they do the telltale dying spasm or fail to respond to your knifing after 3 or so swipes. (Hint: The knife's damage works on FPS, where the higher it is, the more damage it does. If your machine can handle it, you could unironically solo the first boss just using knife swings. It's remarkably silly.) It is a bit of a pain that the only way to make a confirmed kill with a shotgun is to be close enough that the barrel is sticking in their mouth, blowing open their head like a pinata, though permanently dealing with zombies through frequent knifings helps avoid wasting ammo.

As for the extra modes, they're OK. Not great, not bad, not terrible. Majority of them are just running from point A to point B, with Hunk and the tofu modes returning where you run from the sewers back through to the front of the police station. Standout mode is a holdout in the gas station at the very beginning where you have to survive past 100 zombies in waves. Again, it's alright.

Finally, the most worthless point of discussion, the achievements: they're fine. It's just a bit of a slog to run through the campaigns as often as you do to 100% the game, though I know better than to seriously criticize the game for that. As I said, the game is a recommend and a good time through, though I can't comfortably recommend it at $40. I wish they either stayed closer to the original or strayed further away from it to do more of their own thing.

Resident Evil 2 is a fantastic survival horror game with a good story, really nice character animations and very unique mechanics that always keep you on your toes. The puzzles aren't difficult enough to be frustrating but remain interesting throughout, and the map is great to explore and re-tread much like you would do in a Metroidvania game.

I actually also really like the UI in this game, it makes known information available readily and is easy to use quickly which really helps with the pace of the game as you don't end up spending loads of time in menus. 

You are free to approach gameplay in different ways, though generally avoiding combat if possible is a good idea due to limited resources and durable enemies. This management of time against resources is the core challenge of the game and keeps the experience engaging. 

In terms of negatives, I think the boss fights - while well presented - don't benefit from the intentionally clunky controls and evading their attacks does not feel intuitive without the presence of any sort of dodging.  That's not to say I think the shooting should be easier or that your character could be more agile since I think these design choices work well for the majority of the game. Secondly, I was a bit confused by the 2nd playthrough with the other character, as it does not make it clear what the 'canon' version of the story is - if there even is one.

Overall, I definitely recommend playing this especially for the low price tag you can often find it for. It may not take that long to complete the main story with 2 characters (~12 hours) but it's all time well spent.

Great game. Resi 2 was my fav of the series growing up, It was great to be back in familiar surroundings!

It had been 17 years between REmake 1 and 2, whilst fans had been asking for a resi 2 remake for years did it come too late? The gaming landscape has changed dramatically since REmake 1 and even resi had been through several identity crises, would capcom fumble what many fans consider to be the greatest resi ever? 

No, they did not fumble and quite possibly they delivered what is easily the best modern resi and could even be the best resi of all time. 

Now before we begin, this game is a radical departure from the orginal REmake. Whilst REmake 1 is more in-line with the original resi 1, this game goes for a more resi 4 over the shoulder perspective which was already considered at the time to be quite a drastic change considered resi 7 was a 1st person game. Because of this change there is a small majority of the fan base that still prefer the old school style of resi 2 and I do think both games are worthy of the resi 2 name, this is not like REmake 1 which I think is vastly superior to the original that it could replace it but I do still prefer the REmake of resi 2 over the original, now that's out of the way let's get into the review. 

Pro 

The police station is potentially the strongest RE level ever crafted, it has beautifully intertwined corridors and doors, shortcuts, secrets and more. The other main areas are still top tier as well but the police station stands out as the best level capcom have ever put in a resident evil game. 

3rd person perspective that isn't an action game, I can't get over how they perfectly managed to recapture the horror of having a zombie blocking your path, even in a fully 3d space which makes dodging easier they still made zombies a threat and scary. Crazy to say zombies in a game are a scary foe especially considering how many games have zombies in them now. 

Graphics are incredible, I love the RE engine so much and it's my favourite engine only really matched by the fox engine by its stability and beauty.


Combat is amazing, this is not an action nor is it a zombie shooter despite being a game in which you shoot zombies. Every zombie is a puzzle and you are given weapons to deal with that puzzle, much like crimson heads in REmake 1, zombies will stand up randomly after being put down, might be right away or might be hours in your playthrough. This makes an interesting dynamic and makes ammo management more interesting, do you sit a zombie down using the plentiful pistol ammo or do you use the more rare shotgun ammo? 

Puzzles are fun and not frustrating and not super obtuse, this game streamlines a lot of stuff and puzzles are one of them, they are good enough to make you think for a second but they will not stop a playthrough or cause you to consult a guide. 

Two iconic protagonists to choose from, both with different weapons and story paths, they also included the 'B side' from the og resi 2 but it's not perfect and we will come back to that. 

A modern retelling of the resi 2 story with better writing and more indepth characters, all the side characters get a glow up and Leon, Claire and Ada have never looked better. It's still cheesy but they perfectly balance the serious tone with the cheese 

GOD tier ost and even better you can listen to the og ost which is also god tier (via dlc) 

Leon is best daddy 

Cons 

They did cut some content from the original game and we lost some enemy variety, gone are some bosses (rip big moth) and locations. 

The B side of the story feels rushed abd tacked on (because it literally was.) You can't share weapons between Claire and Leon and there isn't much difference between the first and 2nd run except for some remixed puzzles and an extra boss at the end. I'm thankful they did include the B side but it was better executed in the original. 

As mentioned enemy variety took a big hit, it seems at some stage other enemies had been planned as you can see spider webs in the sewers but ultimately they have about 5 enemies, not including bosses and whilst this seems enough repeated playthroughs you start getting a bit bored of them. 

Conclusion 

Capcom have made another resident evil classic, this is a game that will be talked about for years to come much like REmake 1 was. In my head it's a constant battle between REmake 1, 2 and 4 as to which is the best Resi game.

A fantastic game. I have never played the original RE2, having started the series with RE4, so I cannot comment on how well this game reinvents its classic roots, but I can say this is a game that simply stands on its own as a great and modern entry into the series. 

This game feels great to play (taking a leaf out of the book of games like Dead Space for its movement, rather than the tank controls of yesteryear), looks genuinely amazing most of the time, and above all has superb level design. Out of the core pillars of this game's design - satisfying gunplay; the survival horror aspect where you really do need to carefully save ammo; and the level lay-out and the puzzles, respectively - it is the third aspect, i.e. the way the progression through the environments is built up, that made me fall in love with the game. 

The game nails this part especially in the first environment, which is the police station. You end up knowing it by the back of your hand, especially after you go through it again on the second playthrough (which, much like in Nier: Automata, is effectively an abbreviated playthrough with the other character), and there is a real sense that the level designers were geniuses as you gradually gain the tools to enter rooms you had to leave by the wayside earlier, or unlock certain items within rooms that have been taunting you for the last hour. It's probably a bad idea to compare every single game with the Dark Souls series, but just like in those games, there is always another option for where to go, always another thread to follow if you get stuck at a certain part or can't overcome a certain enemy. You have to get through a hallway that features a powerful enemy, and you don't have the ammo for it? Opening the map and looking at the places left to uncover most likely leads in another direction where you will find precisely the type of ammo you need. 

Honestly, at times it felt almost magical how well the game was paced in terms of its doling out of items. There were times when I was desperate for ammo, and the game somehow gave me exactly what I needed if I looked a bit further off the beaten path. This wasn't a case of enemies dropping more ammo like would have happened in RE4, by the way (enemies don't drop anything in this game, aside from the knives you have just stuck into them): it's a case of the amount of ammo and items in this game being calibrated extremely well to the needs of the player and the challenges presented.

Of course, this game wasn't perfect, and the few gripes I have with it come from the parts where this design philosophy breaks down a bit. First of all, I found the second playthrough (with the other character) not to be all that well done. It starts off promising, launching you past the introductory sequences, but then you realise that not only this means you have less time to prepare for some of the structural obstacles that haunt your every step in the game, which makes the opening of run two needlessly punishing, the other problem is that after a while you realize most of the later game is unchanged. Yes, Leon and Claire to go off in different directions, and so there is one environment they don't share at all, but but for the most part the last 3 - 4 hours of a 6-hour second run felt like I was going through the exact same motions again. This is extra unfortunate because the second half of the game is not nearly as strong in terms of level design as the police station. Although it has to be said, this gripe only exists because the police station is so perfectly designed that it is rude to expect the whole game to maintain that level of design artistry.

Secondly, perhaps in part because I was rushing a bit with Leon on my second playthrough, I ended up at the final bossfight with almost no ammo. I believed the game would give me some, but it sort of didn't. It made the final boss fight very tedious, because I basically had to survive until a scripted event would play, but the boss has a one-hit kill move that is quite tough to avoid if you do not have ammo to stun them, and the cutscenes in this game are unskippable, so I had to watch the cutscene before the fight like four times before getting through it. 

Finally, the story is nonsensical in that hand-wavey anime sort of way. These characters are as far removed from actual human beings as they can be in many of the scenes. There are some really dangerous enemies in this game, and seeing the main characters basically shrug and laugh at them when they met them in cutscenes was kind of funny, and broke the tension in a positive way for me, but it was still jarring at times. Also, the game expects you to care about the relations the characters supposedly have grow between them throughout the game, but there is almost zero attention paid to actually building up these interactions, and none of the characters' motivations make any sense at all. This may well have been a legacy burden of the original game that they had to abide by, but it still made the cutscenes almost boring to watch. It's a shame too, because this game has absolutely incredible production values, and so the cutscenes are well-rendered, and very well-acted and voiced. 

I've written three long paragraphs here about some issues I had with the game, which is probably unfair. The truth of it is this game is absolutely fantastic. The first half of it ranks among some of the best gaming experiences I've had in years in terms of level design, atmosphere building, and setpieces to get through. However, it is also true that the second half of the game does see the quality drop off a bit (even if it remains a great game throughout on the whole), and the second run compounds this issue by shortening the arc of the police station and making you go through the inferior second half fully. All of these complaints represent only small blemishes on a gaming experience that is absolutely not to be missed, however. If you're thinking about getting this game, do so; it'll be worth your while.

[h1] Survival Horror Is Back To Racoon City! [/h1] 
Resident Evil 2 is a 2019 survival horror game developed and published by Capcom. A remake of the 1998 game Resident Evil 2. Players control rookie police officer Leon S. Kennedy and college student Claire Redfield as they attempt to escape Raccoon City during a viral outbreak that transforms the citizens into zombies and other creatures.

        [td]With terrifying hallways of the Racoon City police department, to the laboratory of Umbrella; the lighting and atmosphere is absolutely haunting. Many areas tell a haunting story of struggle and panic. I love the design of every area in this game. It’s so claustrophobic and terrifying. The enemy designs are flawless, actually just perfection! Also the zombies are the scariest I've ever seen in a video game. The UI is also clean and really easy to navigate. The in-game map is so useful. Any item you don’t pick up is marked on the map, so you will never forget where items are. That’s such a welcome addition to any survival game. Also the UI for the map just looks amazing, and user friendly.[/td]
    [/tr]

The zombies (and other enemies) can be bullet spongy and can pull a few surprises on you. You will encounter many item puzzles, for example keys, a handle for a valve, and more. Also many items to help you on your journey. Healing items and finding pouches to increase your space will be a lifesaver! Exploration is everything in this game. So do not rush and take your time. Safe rooms are also a blessing and a returning feature from the original game. The safe room is, well, a safe room. No monsters can come in and hurt you. There are many types of horrible creatures to fight through. Ranging from your normal zombies, dogs, G virus creatures, and much more! The game uses the third perspective so that the camera is directly behind the character, and I consider this camera very suitable for this type of game. The horror in the game combines psychological and jumpscare, especially in terms of sounds when you hear the giant's footsteps chasing you and you can't do anything about it except run for your life. TL;DR: This game is extremely well optimized, holds up graphically three years later, and has some scary, fun gameplay. But the 2nd run that is unlocked after beating the game lacks creativity and makes no sense.

Traditionally, the word “remaster” gets associated with cash grabs, especially among console players. Remakes, however, can be a means to modernize an older game and bring it to a new generation. I view it kind of like art restoration, especially with fantastic examples like Bluepoints Demon’s Souls and Shadow of the Colossus remakes. This is another one added to my list of great remakes that I’m glad were made. Few older games can be seen as outdated as the original Resident Evil games, but the story and atmosphere are there, and now everyone can either enjoy it for the first time or all over again in a completely new experience.

Performance
This game ran fantastic on both my PC with a GTX 1080 at 1440p resolution as well as on my steam deck. Unlike games of the last couple of years, frames stayed above 100 throughout my playthrough, cutscenes ran great, and my CPU never even hit 70 C. This game is wonderfully optimized. With recent games struggling to be well optimized on even the best gaming PCs, such as Cyberpunk or the frame rate issues of Elden Ring, it was a breath of fresh air to boot this up and get 100+ fps in a beautiful looking game from the start. Even though this game is 3 years old now, it had been so long since a game looking this good had run this smooth, and it’s too bad it stands out like that. It reminded me of playing Rise of the Tomb Raider or The Witcher 3 when I first built my PC and being so satisfied with the results. No complaints here.

Atmosphere
I had a couple friends tell me they didn’t finish this game because they got too scared. I found that hard to believe because I felt that a first person experience would be much scarier. But they were right, it is quite scary. It does a good job of keeping you guessing as to whether this dead body is going to come back to life or not. The fear level really gets increased when you start getting chased by a large man, and your only indication as to where he may be are his loud footprints in the distance. He tends to show up at the worst moments and really causes the player to scramble to finish what they were doing.

Story
There are two runs to this game, and they need to be discussed individually. The first run will be your first playthrough, and you will pick either Leon or Claire to play (I picked Leon). My first playthrough was awesome, and I'd give it a 10/10. It was fun, scary, and action packed. The dialogue isn't always great, but the voice actors are much better than the RE1 remaster. By the end of my first run, I couldn't wait to start the 2nd run. This is where my biggest issue with the game comes in.

Occasionally, you'll run into Claire during the first playthrough, but she is always separated by a locked door or something. The 2nd run allows you to play as the second character and see what they were up to during the whole game. The ending of the first run even alludes to more that was happening, and you have to play the 2nd run in order to get the true ending. After I beat the 1st run, I couldn't wait to start it up as Claire and see things from the other side of what I was doing. If you choose to play the 2nd run, prepare to be very disappointed and confused.

You see, Capcom decided that while some cutscenes coincide between the two characters, just about everything else will make no sense. Claire enters the RCPD after Leon has left. Everything Leon had done in the 1st run should be visible and obvious. Not so. All doors are locked again, all puzzles must be solved again, and all keys must be found again, including those that should currently be in Leon's pocket. Some walls even need to be blown up again. The only difference between the two runs are the cutscenes. Some puzzles are altered, but you're going to be doing variations of what you already did, going to the same places you already were, even fight the same bosses in the same way as before. I cannot emphasize enough how much sense this does not make.

This could be considered a minor gripe, seeing as the 2nd run is optional (unless you want the true ending), but play through the 1st run and you'll see that they bait you into another playthrough by teasing you with Claire and hinting that she's up to something as well. It's unfortunate, but while the 1st run is fantastic and I highly recommend it, the 2nd run lacks all creativity and makes absolutely no sense. Capcom either assumed the player would be stupid or just blatantly did not care. Honestly, if they had made the 2nd run significantly shorter but let me do new things, or even just let what Leon did before be plain and visible, I would have no problem. But we're talking a character will die one way in the 1st run and a complete other way in the 2nd run. These are basics of story writing, and they got it all wrong, and I am annoyed. If RE3 Remake has a 2nd run, I will not be playing it.

Anyways, 1st run is highly recommended. I purchased it for $20 a few years ago and it was definitely worth that.

Don't let the timestamp of 7 hours fool you⁠—I actually have this game on PS4 Pro as well, where I've beaten it three times (once with Leon, twice with Claire). I just happened to pick this up on sale alongside Resident Evil 3 and ended up doing a new playthrough as Leon.

To put it bluntly, the Resident Evil 2 remake is superb. Highly desired by the fan base for ages, it did not disappoint; everything, from the graphics to the gameplay to the acting and story, is just astonishingly good. The RE Engine is amazing, this game already looked and played well on PS4 Pro at a sweet 60 fps looking beautiful, and it just looks even better running on an RTX 2060 at 90-120 fps on max settings (1080p resolution). Seriously, if this came out next year, nobody would bat an eye.

It's not easy to modernize a classic, but Resident Evil 2 ticks all the checkboxes. The over-the-shoulder gameplay was received with some skepticism when the game was first announced, but it works wonderfully and still retains the tense survival horror of the original. The zombies are actually scary, for the first time in a long while! Even a single zombie can be cause for concern despite the fact that it essentially plays like a shooter, although the fact that damage feels essentially randomized and the zombies can take quite a wallop to take down can be somewhat annoying, but it's part of the balancing to keep it tense. (Pro tip: shoot them in the legs instead, they're much less dangerous crawling around!)

Of course, the big star of the game is the Tyrant a.k.a. Mr. X, the "stalker" enemy that chases you around for a good part of the runthrough (even more so in the 2nd run modes you unlock after beating the game with each character in normal mode). Mr. X is endlessly intimidating and, even after four whole playthroughs and essentially memorizing the game, can still quicken my heartbeat in the right conditions. More so, it never feels cheap or like it's cheating, which is a plus as these types of enemies can easily end up feeling overpowered.

It's not all perfect⁠—the first third is absolutely the pinnacle of the game (not that the rest is bad, it just becomes more action-y, which I personally don't mind as it makes you feel like you're properly progressing and becoming a badass zombie killer) and the puzzles aren't exactly headscratchers most of the time⁠—, but it's arguably as close to it as this remake could've been.

As close to my heart as Resident Evil 4 is, Resident Evil 2 might actually be my favorite now, as it perfectly balances the survival horror of older entries with the gameplay of Resident Evils 4 to 6. Absolutely a must play if you can handle the horror.

[h1] Wow...where to begin. [/h1]

Resident Evil 2 shows us how remakes should look like. There is a good reason why rewiews are overwhelmingly positive - it's because the game makes both fans of the old school, original RE games, as well as newcomers to the series (like myself) happy. Modern third-person shooter mechanics get combined with classic puzzles without being a convoluted mess; rather, they complement each other beautifully. But let's get into some details:

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
The game can be separated into three big sections; the first third of the game is spent inside the Raccoon Police Station. And this is where you find the classic RE puzzles. Locked doors with spades, hearts and diamonds engraved into them, and corresponding keys wanting to be found. A gas leak, which needs you to find a valve, a statue which you need to hand a book so it releases the cepter it's holding, the list goes on. While this may sound tedious on paper, the execution is done VERY well. After all, you're not just running around in an empty building - you need to watch your step, as behind every corner danger might be lurking! 
What really enhances gameplay is our next big point: 

[h1] Difficulty [/h1] 
The way this game handles difficulty is phenomenal. It is far, FAR more than just a health slider for enemies (though enemies ARE tougher or weaker depening on the difficulty). When playing the game for the first time, you will likely find yourself short on ammunition...pretty much all the time. Enemies seem to be everywhere, and it might look like zombies refuse to stay down for good most of the time. The locked doors Imentioned, paired with safes and locks you don't have the combination for right away don't exactly help your cause. So why is this a good thing, again? Because the game is only as difficult as your ability to adapt. This isn't the kind of "we're simply throwing more and more enemies your way" difficulty, but rather the approach Dark Souls takes (yes, I compared the game to Dark Souls, I'm sorry and I promise I'm not a game journalist): difficulty comes from your lack of knowledge. When playing the game for a second time, you'll know where the enemies are, you'll know what the safe combinations are, you know what to expect from each boss fight. And THAT is where a lot of the fun comes from: learning how the game works, learning which enemies to take out and which to simply run past, where you find key items and so on. A very rewarding, almost rouge-like experience. In addition, standard mode has adaptive difficulty; if the game notices you're struggling, it goes a bit more easy on you. Enemies have lower health, move more slowly and sometimes they don't even show up in the first place. On the flipside, if you're doing well, are always in good health and loaded with ammo, the training wheels come off, bit by bit.

[h1] Story [/h1]
RE2 tells the story of two survivors: Claire and Leon. No matter which one you decide to play first (personally I recommend Leon), you're going to - as the game puts it - experience the nightmare first hand. Be it Leon, who slowly uncovers who or what is behind the zombie outbreak or Claire, who, after finding out her brother wasn't in town originally had no reason to stick around, takes a detour to help a very special person she met along the way. While the story stays faithful to the original for the most part, some details and characters were changed, most of which help show how grim things really are in Raccoon City. [spoiler] Looking at you, Kendo. :( [/spoiler]

[h1] Conclusio [/h1] 
I cannot recommend this game enough. You'll be scared, you'll be disgusted, you might even get frustrated - but at the end of the day, you will probably agree with me that this game is well worth the time and money. 

[h1] Post Sciptum [/h1]
I said you'll be disgusted and scared, and rightfully so, the game really doesn't hold back to both show and tell you horrible depravities. But all the zombies, mutated monsters and infuritating emails left by corrupt policemen and rithless scientists pale in comparison to one, single note you can find while playing as Sherry or Claire. It's a diary entry on a table next to a typewriter in Iron's taxydermy room, in the orphanage. This one note...really messed me up. It's not very long but it cuts a lot deeper than anything else I've seen in this game, heck maybe even in ANY game. I will not spoil it here, if you know, you know, if you don't you can search for it yourself. But once you find it...maybe it's best you don't read it.

The first one of these other than 4 to really hold my attention. I've tried relentlessly to properly get into the series and usually get bounced off by one thing or another. This still has the fundamental problems I have with the series, but it's enough of a rollercoaster-ified, steroid-pumped execution of the formula that I can overlook them.

On the positive, the game looks unreal levels of fantastic. The zombies deform and show damage well, the whole of the game's visuals are polished to a mirror shine, and there's a burger in the opening cutscene that is more visually appealing to me than most pornography. Claire and Leon are also in the game, though this is a substantially less yass-ified version of Leon than the later games present. Still, I like him. 

Gunplay is deeply satisfying, which is odd considering that this is a game where you actually shouldn't be shooting a good percentage of the time. Puzzles are good, movement is solid though I think dodging in bossfights is a bit of an annoyance, and the pacing is phenomenal. This is a series made by consumate pros, and this is some real top-shelf work.

I think most of my problems are things that are fundamental to the series and I don't know that even the level to which I enjoyed this entry made me like the series more. 

The target audience for any given Resident Evil game is somebody who has already played it. If you're new and trying to blast through and finish, the game is hard enough (by design, it should be that way) that this won't be possible unless you know what you're doing. If you're trying to be thorough and pick up all the items you can in a playthrough, you're likely to get bled of ammo and healing quite quickly when you go back to previous areas that have been repopulated. On your first playthrough or two, you are guaranteed to run up against the final boss either underpowered or dry of resources. The boss isn't some absolute torture chamber, but bosses in general have a bad habit of showing up in situations where you're going through famine and not feast.

Again, I don't know that these things could really be toned down in such a way as would please me without losing some of the fundamental appeal and identity of the series. If you can't really bone yourself, there isn't as much tension to missing shots or having to weigh whether to fight an enemy or not. For the record, every playthrough of the game after the first is much smoother and more enjoyable, but you never manage to recapture the tension of entropy and discovery that the first playthrough provides. The game is at it's best when it is being the meanest to you, the game is also at it's most frustrating when that is happening. I think with this sort of relationship in mind, a lot of your enjoyment of this game will depend on how willing you are to be at least slightly antagonized at all times by the developers. I don't hate it, but there are times where this game does grind my gears.

Overall, it is totally worth your time. Near-infinite replay value and a ton of bang for your buck, but if you aren't sold on the formula of Resident Evil as a whole, I don't think it does anything that will change your mind. If you're only partially sold, if you really liked 4 or 8 and have struggled to get into the rest of the series, I think this one does enough to justify the purchase without being the knight in shining armor you were looking for that makes the hype make sense.

It does have Claire though. And Leon. And a burger. ♥♥♥♥, that was a sexy burger.

Here are just a few of the things that I love about the game. (SPOILERS AHEAD)

Zombies and Gunplay

As you traverse through the police station and other places, you'll find zombies everywhere. At first you might just want to mow them down. However, Resident Evil 2 creates tense situations by strategically limiting the amount of ammo you can pick up in certain areas as well as the actual potency of your bullets. Your first gun, the Matilda (if you play as Leon), is your starter pistol. However, as you shoot past rooms and hallways filled with zombies, you find that the Matilda is not dependable at all. Like many guns in this game, it takes a while to become fully accurate and you can easily miss a couple shots as a zombie sways back and forth as it runs to you. If you're lucky, some zombies can be taken down with a single bullet with a critical headshot, while others seem to eat your entire magazine without a sweat. Even when you take down a zombie, its lifeless body is by no means an indicator that you won the battle. Some zombies can pretend to be dead, but spring to life as you run by to bite you in the ankle. Over time, you realize that conserving ammunition is the most important part of the game. Shooting zombies enough to knock them back or dismember them becomes your main strategy, but also has the downside of giving you less assurance that zombies won't be waiting in a room when you come back. As you progress through the game, you will get more and more weapons, but the game's reluctance you give you an abundance of ammunition guarantees that you will stray away from using precious ammo for heavy hitting guns unless you are in an emergency. While all of these aspects to gunplay might not seem fun in a typical shooter, it's inclusion in a survival horror game is what makes Resident Evil 2 so much fun to play. 

Exploration

This part of the game will take up the bulk of your time. From finding a specific key to open a door to encountering a puzzle to progress to the next area, exploring is paramount to surviving in Raccoon City. The layouts of the police station and other locations are cleverly designed to indirectly help you progress through the game. But it is by no means linear. Getting a key in one area might give you a combination that allows you open a locker with a useful item. The only problem might be that that item is located on the other side of the map. Putting an emphasis on exploration causes people to stray away from playing the game linearly because checking every nook and cranny to collect every item gives you such a big advantage over just cruising through the story. Even after you leave an area seemingly for the last time, extremely perspective explorers can find ways to go back to old locations, using new items to open doors and unlock treasures that you saw before, but couldn't open. Especially in Hardcore difficulty, getting that extra healing item in some optional room or another magazine of pistol ammo might be the difference between life and death. Luckily, there are plenty of safe rooms to give you a break from the zombie hoards.

Item Management

Many games have an inventory, but Resident Evil 2's inventory system is designed in a way that only helps to service the game and its aspect of survival horror. While many games give you an unrealistically large or even infinite amount of inventory space, Resident Evil 2 starts you off with only 8 item spots, with (optional) opportunities to upgrade inventory space by a maximum of 8 spots. Every object takes up at least 1 spot and some can even take 2. Even important items (like keys and medallions) share this criminally small inventory. This makes you think carefully about which items you take from the global item box. Having a lot of ammo could be helpful, but so could healing items and sub weapons (which are weapons that protect you from an enemy once). Finding a key item with a full inventory means you have to decide between discarding a useful item or running through zombie infested rooms to the nearest item box to make space. At times, the lack of a larger inventory can seem detrimental to the game's enjoyment, but the decision to heavily limit inventory space creates the tension and important decision making that keeps a perfect survival horror game from becoming an arcade-y shoot-em-up.

Mr. X

Mr. X serves as the main stalker antagonist during your time in Raccoon City, even if he doesn't show up for the whole game. When you finally activate the checkpoint where you meet him, you will find that he will not stop chasing and looking for you until you complete that entire section of the game. For people playing the game for the first time, this continuous threat will impede their progress for hours at a time. Maybe you need to accomplish a task where you're stuck in one place. Well, Mr. X will make sure that you won't be able to do all of it in one go. Sometimes even running from him is a bad idea, as you might just run into the territory of a licker. When this happens, you have to go slow enough to not wake the licker while also hoping Mr. X won't close the distance between you. This tyrant's loud footsteps and music will keep you on your heels, making you hope that the door that he opens next isn't the one right next to you. While he cannot be killed, hitting him with enough firepower can temporarily disable him and buy you time to do what you need to do. Also, save rooms are safe from him, giving you time to change your underwear and lower your heart rate. While Mr. X was considered the most "vanilla" of the stalker types in the original games, his implementation in this game makes him both a terrifying being and a source of extreme dread. I would even argue that he is far more terrifying than Nemesis in Resident Evil 3 Remake, which was a far more scary tyrant in the original.

Story and Characters

Even if the story wasn't good, the gameplay more than compensates for it. However, I enjoyed this story from beginning to end. Right at the beginning, we get to see what kind of people Leon and Claire truly are. Leon Kennedy is just a cop with a heart of gold who is willing to do anything to protect the citizens of Raccoon City. Claire Redfield, on the other hand, is a normal citizen who is forced into the zombie infested city to look for her brother. Both of these people unknowingly involve themselves into the zombie apocalypse and the overall hidden conspiracy. Leon is forced to grow up from his perfect ideals. he has to sacrifice his superior police officer in order to find a way to escape the police station. He even has to kill fellow police officers who turned into zombies. His sense of justice never wavers and I was drawn close to him and was rooting for him from start to end. On the other hand, Claire is a caring individual with little to no experience with a gun or killing zombies. She's forced to learn quick as she uncovers a mystery that stretches past a virus outbreak and goes out of her way to rescue another person. While I did enjoy Leon's story more, I really liked both. I also liked how the game offers A and B scenarios so you can see what happened to the other character while you were away killing zombies and solving puzzles. While some of the events overlap, it creates enough cohesion and offers different versions of events to make you want to play the A and B scenarios for both Leon and Claire.

Overall

Resident Evil 2 was possibly the best free game I ever got. I would even say that it's my favorite game ever. It's what got me into the survival horror genre and also helped me get over my fear of horror games and movies. Everything about this game is amazing and I'm already eagerly waiting for Resident Evil 4 Remake to come out. Anything with Leon Kennedy in it is going to be a blast to play and I cannot wait for more Resident Evil awesomeness.

I never played the original Resident Evil 2, so this remake was my first exposure to the story, with basically no context for anything going in. With that out of the way, this is a fantastic game, and it feels like it very much exemplifies the tenets of survival horror, while still being an impressively modern game in terms of mechanics, graphics, and general feel. The RE Engine is absolutely magical here, a rock-solid base for a remake that feels incredibly fresh in a modern context. Controls are tight and highly responsive, and though there are plenty of moments where the game catches you off-guard to maximize your stress levels, I never felt that anything was necessarily unfair. You can either battle or run your way out of just about anything, and the moment-to-moment decision-making in that regard has real, logical consequences. The two campaigns are an interesting gameplay decision (that I know was taken straight from the original), and they were different enough to feel worthwhile while using the same assets and general progression. 2nd Run made this much faster, too, streamlining exploration and cutting some of the fat given that you've already played through the game once. A personal gripe is that I absolutely hated the chase sequences with Tyrant - they make it basically impossible to explore at your own pace, which I understand is the point, but I was frustrated at having to rush through the police station in both campaigns once that big bastard showed up, not knowing if I'd have the chance to come back later. The boss fights all felt intuitive, even if the end-game ones were stupid hard in some regards, but they were satisfying once you finally got the hang of them and could get through them. Overall, setting aside the question of how faithful a remake it is, RE2 is a fantastic game, emblematic of the genre, and an extremely fun ride start to finish.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

Resident Evil 2 is my first Resident Evil game. I never thought I’d like the serious as I’m not big on horror, but what I got, and I know this may make some people mad, is a really good Luigi’s Mansion game. Yes, I know Resident Evil is years older than Luigi’s Mansion, but I played Luigi’s Mansion years before I played this. Take Luigi’s Mansion, swap the ghosts for Zombies, the Poltergust for guns, and add in a lot more blood and gore and you’ve got yourself Resident Evil 2.

While the story was interesting enough, the actual dialog and writing often felt stiff and awkward, but this really feels like a game you play for the gameplay rather than the story. Like Luigi’s Mansion, you go from room to room exploring a [strike]haunted house[/strike] infected police station solving puzzles and finding items to get to new rooms where you can solve more puzzles and get more items. It’s a really fun gameplay loop. Resident Evil 2 does a really good job of guiding you through your exploration of the map. I was never 100% sure where I needed to go, but I never felt lost enough that I needed to look up a guide to progress. 

Having to deal with the zombies was annoying at times, especially when you walk through a door to instantly die to a zombie waiting directly on the other side making you sit through a way too long dying animation and lose 5-10 minutes of progress, but it definitely added to the atmosphere and the game really would not have been the same without them.

I also was not a fan of the way inventory works. I totally getting to limit the amount of healing items and ammo to make the game more spooky, but limiting the amount of key items you can hold seems more like an annoyance. It just meant backtracking through areas I had already cleared out to get to a chest to swap out items. I think it would have been better to let the character hold all the key items, but only a few stacks of ammo, maybe one per gun type, and one or two healing items.

The game ran pretty well, but I would have random lag that would drop me down to 20-30 fps for several minutes at a time and sometimes a lag spike would occur when switching rooms.

Overall Resident Evil 2 was a lot of fun and I’m glad I gave it a shot. It’s not at all what I was expecting, but it is really good. I think it’s neat that I can now go back and reexperience the game as the other character, but I don’t think I’ll do that just yet. Maybe for Halloween this year.

The storylines aren’t complicated — you could almost fit them on a sticky note — but that’s not really the point. What makes Resident Evil shine is the atmosphere, the puzzles, the resource management, and the constant feeling of pushing forward on a mission in the middle of a hellscape.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is a phenomenal game which offers a large amount of content for the price that you pay for it. It is one of those games where you will truly get your money's worth, especially when it goes on sale.

First of all there are two campaigns, Claire and Leon. They are similar but different in a multitude of ways, different endings, different parts of the Police Station you can access, different weapons, but once you play your second playthrough as the opposite character from your starting one, you'll notice that some parts of the game are more or less the same. 

The game looks amazing, the amount of detail the graphic designers put into the police station and other set pieces to make the game look realistic is outstanding, there are so many small and fine details that are easy to miss but if you just take a moment to appreciate it, you'll notice the real love that went into this game.

Combat is pretty decent, but if you go around trying to permanently put down every zombie you see, you'll run out of ammo fast. There is only a set limit of how much ammo you can obtain each playthrough, enemies do not drop extra ammo upon killing them, which players might be used to if they've come from playing the 4-6 games. The part that makes the game proper survival horror, is knowing when to fight and when to run, consider saving your ammo for when you truly need it.

The puzzles are great and I personally don't think the backtracking in this game feels as tedious as it does in most games, mainly due to the fact that you might think you've cleared an area but something has changed whilst you've been away or some random zombie has decided to go for a wander and now he's there to contend with. The puzzles themselves aren't necessarily difficult but as long as you keep ample inventory space, you'll be fine. 

The story is pretty decent, it's really just about surviving and trying to get out of the City and more revelations reveal themselves about the origin of the breakout and what not as you progress; as well as different files dotted around the map to give you some context and some world building, but in terms of storytelling it's definitely not on the same level as something like Death Stranding or Detroit Become Human.

I only had one gripe with the game and it wasn't consistent all the way through, sometimes you do just get slapped with special infected or a copious unmanageable mount of Zombies at one time, and you can easily be stun locked if you're not careful. 

It's also worth noting that after completing the game you unlocked "2nd Run" mode, which basically is the same game but the items are in different places and certain things play out differently, it gives the game excellent replayability as you won't know the locations of all the items you got in your first playthrough. More games should learn from this.

Another fantastic feature is the "Records" bonus content, where you get three short scenarios about three different characters from the game that aren't really expanded upon. Most developers/publishers would have released this as a paid DLC, but it's completely FREE and in the game, giving you some new characters to play with a new scenario to play out. So there's some extra content after you finish the main campaigns, once or twice.

Overall, Resident Evil 2 is a testament to how games that were limited by their technology at the time can be remade into near perfection. This is how the game was meant to be played and any developer, in my opinion, that remakes a game that does not fit this standard of remake that Resident Evil 2 offers, shouldn't bother making it. 

9/10, you will absolutely not regret this purchase.

There are a lot of reviews, so I'll just mention what isn't talked about enough, I think.

The core game is good, and you can actually not only play as both Leon and Claire (the dfference is mostly their weapons), but there's also a second playthrough with new cutscenes, new parts of the locations (unavailable before), new enemies, another ending, and you get to play as another character. Yes, most of the game during the second playthrough stays the same, but the changes overall make it a good experience. And since you can play as different characters, there are two options: first playthrough as Leon, the second as Clair and vice verse. And both playthroughs will take you at least 10 hours unless you have a walkthrough.

There's also a ghost survivors mode, which reuses the game locations and lets you go in an absolutely linear path fighting A LOT of zombies. I didn't like it at all - too much action in a game that is essentially about story, puzzles and survival, and camera+controls don't really work well for that kind of gameplay. What's the point of this mode when there's Killing Floor, Day Z, World War Z, Left 4 Dead and many other coop/solo zombie shooters? But it's still a nice bonus to the main game, and maybe you will spend a few more hours there.

And, of course, if you want to beat hardcore mode with S rank, that's a few more playthroughs because the game can be pretty punishing even to the smallest mistakes. But then again, I believe the majority would just play it on standard difficulty for the story, and the game is totally worth it.

The Resident Evil 2 REmake is well deserving of all the praise it’s received so far. It’s a fantastic survival horror game and between the claustrophobic environments, slow but durable hordes and the unrelenting predator that is Mr. X this game is filled to the brim with adrenaline pumping tension. 

With scarce resources and risky combat, RE2R is both fun and challenging and extremely replayable. You’re encouraged to play the game over and over again for various challenges and there are multiple bonus chapters where you get to play “What If” scenarios of other potential survivors. 

Claire and Leon each have their own unique set of weapons which allow for different strategies when dealing with the hordes. That said however, story-wise they both go through the same major plot beats with only their supporting cast and final bosses changing depending on who you play as. 

Out of the two protagonists I would say Claire’s story is stronger in this game than Leon’s. Don’t get me wrong I love the guy but if RE4 is his game then I don’t think it’s unfair to say Claire steals the spotlight here. I feel that this could have been evened out more if the B Scenarios were more fleshed out as they do not merge the two stories together cohesively. 

The B Scenarios do not provide insight as to what either Claire or Leon are doing while the other is engaged in their A Scenario as they have no unique storyline. It’s just a harder version of their A Scenario’s with a different way they entered the Police Station in the beginning and although some of the puzzle solutions have changed, the bosses are the same. They’re fun to play but it feels like a missed opportunity to do something more and craft a fuller plotline. 

The music is fantastic and the sound design keeps that tension up all throughout the game. I’d also recommend checking out the DLC at your own discretion as I loved playing through the game again with the original Resident Evil 2’s soundtrack and there are a lot of fun costumes to check out! 

A true modern gem, if you’re looking for a new survival horror game to play you don’t want to miss out on this game.

That's not even the least of your worries as ammo can be hard to come by, and killing every zombie you come across will surely leave you wishing you hadn't when you find yourself backed into a corner in one of the boss fights that will bring your speed-run to a standstill.  Ada's section was good, and its cool how Mr.X made an appearance that did not feel out of place in a short segment. 
Sherry's segment is probably one of, if not the best stealth section I have played in a game in the last 2 years at least.
Claire's portions are impressive due to her having no official  training or being part of any organization yet receiving training from Chris ( canonically). Her wanting to help and take care of Sherry also fits in her character knowing that she and Chris had no parents growing up either it would make sense for her to want to help. 

The game play itself is  as follows: 

The RPD feels thrilling, its a maze but in a good way, you feel like you finally know your way around it after exploring it for hours only to run into a corridor you've ran into a hundred of times and get hit by a licker-zombie- Mr X combo and expire. The sewer section and the second Birkin fight can go drink bleach.

Not only do you get the thing-a-ma-jig to get the lights back on faster but you also fight Birkin for what feels like an eternity. So I ended up going back to the beta tab Dx11 version (thank you for adding this Capcom), and after some serious tweaking of the settings I found a configuration I'm happy with. I recommend trying out different anti aliasing options and testing which you like best, and you might also want to try setting the color configuration to REC7 instead of the standard SRGB. SRGB makes the game very bright and pale. REC7 is more vibrant and darker, and if you set up your brightness properly it won't drown out detail either.

[h1]Resident Evil 2[/h1]
A RE-imagining of the third-Person, survival horror behemoth, that is Resident Evil 2. This rendition is an authentic old-school experience in the modern era of gaming. It brings the classic quirks and charms of the original into Capcom's new RE Engine that significantly improves the visual and audio fidelity alongside mechanical refinements and more, resulting in frightening moment-to-moment confrontations, great atmospheric tension, and a plethora of scares. 

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
The visuals are astonishingly photorealistic. The art department nailed everything from the design and creation of assets to the texturing and lighting of the environment. Everything feels meticulously designed with tons of passion for not only Resident Evil but also horror as a genre, resulting in exploration and confrontations being unsettling, captivating, and fulfilling.

The zombies are terrifying and distinctive enough to avoid feeling generic or repetitive. Whether it is a recently transformed victim, an infected creature, or the Tyrant himself, a characteristic they all share is the frightening and impressive designs. From NPCs to the police force or your two main characters, the models look great and are recognizable. 

[h1]Soundtrack[/h1]
Audibly the game sounds incredible in just about every way. For example, the weaponry, from reloading your magazine to blasting a zombie's head off, does not get stale because of how realistic and satisfying it sounds. That is if you can distract yourself from the spine-chilling zombie groans and ambient noises. Which is enhanced by the soundtrack as it keeps you on your toes by eeriness or an intense moment. Amidst all, the voice actors portray their feelings and intentions through interactions and voice lines encompassing despair and distress to heartfelt moments.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Through gameplay, most of the "old-school" qualities come into play, as it plays like a third-person horror game from that era when the original was released, but with a modern twist. 
Rather than revamping the formula, Capcom decided to stick true to the original, which is fine, and possibly preferred by many. That does, however, mean that the kinks and quirks also remain.

Exploration and inventory management are among the most vital aspects of the gameplay loop. Resources are scarce and thus require you to think twice about what you take with you and when to use it, or whether to blast a zombie to bits or try to run away. It incentivizes exploration as this is where you can find resources such as ammunition, medkits, clues, notes, and upgrades for your guns or inventory. Exploration is further encouraged through the thrilling and stunning visuals that Racoon City has and ultimately makes it enjoyable. 

Backtracking is also a massive part of Resident Evil 2, Whether because of an item you need to progress the story, complete a previously inaccessible puzzle, a lack of inventory storage, or Mr. X forcefully causing you to retreat to the nearest safe zone. Luckily, the Map layout is easily readable and manageable, but that does not stop it from occasionally becoming a drag or a nuisance.

I also found Mr. X to be incredibly obnoxious, which he is intended to be. But to the extent that I felt it was hurting my enjoyment of the game as well as not being fond of the early stage inventory storage limit finding it obtrusive rather than a mechanic to work around. It, however, slowly becomes a null issue later on. 

Combat is incredibly satisfying and entertaining, whether you are conservative with your ammunition and try to avoid using it or being trigger-happy mowing down every zombie you path into. Zombies are a bit hard to take down and require a respectable amount of bullets to finish off, although it is possible to slow and immobilize them by either shooting at their limbs or utilizing a flashbang. They do manage to avoid feeling bullet spongey.

That is, however, the polar opposite of boss fights. They generally feel extremely clunky, unfun, bullet spongey, and frustrating. They are memorable, but not because of the battle itself. But because of the visual design of the bosses and the soundtrack that comes with it. That is where the art and audio department carries the moment and makes it memorable. 

[h1]Story[/h1]
A virus engulfs raccoon city, causing chaos amongst its citizens, as its victims arise as flesh-eating zombies that roam the streets. The story revolves around Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield. They have different motives and intentions but ultimately are intertwined in the overarching story. Claire is on the hunt for her missing brother, Chris Redfield, whereas Leon Kennedy is a new police officer who has his precinct completely wiped and tries to get to the bottom of what happened and who caused it.

It is at heart, a Resident Evil story and by no means perfect, nor does it pretend to be. There is, however, plenty of character and fun to behold within it. It may be as cheesy and cliche as it comes, but it is incredibly entertaining to witness Claire and Leon’s stories play out.

[h1]Additional Note(s):[/h1]
Resident Evil 2 can be considered a short game, but has replayability alongside Bonus content such as additional events, bonus missions, unlockables, and more.

[h1] Final Thoughts [/h1]
A faithful RE-imagining worthy of being played by newcomers and veteran fans of the series. It is visually and audibly stunning with a cheesy, albeit memorable story and characters. Action is satisfying and fun while still being a tension-filled survival horror game. The minor issues I have are the clunky boss fights and how incredibly intrusive Mr. X can feel, but despite that, I highly recommend playing it.

Does the original justice, beautifully remade and lots of other playable/unlockable content added to make it even more replayable. 

Visually the game is stunning on highest graphic settings, apart from some odd facial animations, weird hair movement and the occassional ragdoll physics going insane it's a very beautifull game.

Soundwise it's perfect, the atmosphere is well built. From the zombies moaning outside the station, the eerie quiet being disturbed by loud foodsteps by your tyrant friend and the very decent voice acting. The oneliners and cheesy dialogue are cringy but too few to complain about.

Gameplay, it's ridiculousy good. The shooting is great, the puzzles are okay (imo much better than the original) and movement feels fluent. The only annoying part I felt was the lack of any dodge ability since you can get grablocked by enemies, especially bosses where you take an extra hit just because the hit animation needs to do it's thing before you're allowed to move again.

In conclusion, the RE2 remake does so many things right that those little hickups won't ruin your experience. 
It took me about 14 hours to finish Leon A and Claire B and still have to check the survivor mode and Claire A/Leon B so you'll definitely won't regret getting this (I got this during the sale and well worth it).

More than three years later, Resident Evil 2 remains the blueprint for any developer looking to remake a classic title. Successfully modernising the 1998 survival horror game for fans and newcomers, there's no doubting its sustained quality.

I hadn’t played the original Resident Evil 2 since its release 20 years ago and only remembered the broadest of strokes.
I knew it largely took place in a police station, the lickers were introduced, and the giant spiders in the sewers were a nightmare. 
If a similar amount of time has passed for you, or if you’ve never played it, it might not be apparent what an enormous improvement this remake is unless you look at it side by side with the original. 

Crucially, inventory and ammunition management is still a key part of Resident Evil 2 gameplay. 
This is real survival horror, where it always seems like you’re just barely scraping by with enough ammo and healing items. You can’t carry everything you find with you, so what you should store and what you should carry is a battle constantly being waged in your mind.
Those quality-of-life improvements I mentioned include automatically updating your maps to let you know if a room has been cleared of items or if you missed something, frequent and unlimited save points, and freedom from the infamous barrage of loading screens. 
All of those are very much appreciated when exploring Raccoon City.

Tension has been elevated by the excellent sound design. 
Very little music accompanies gameplay, which leaves plenty of room for creaking doors, thunder and rain, the moans of the undead somewhere just out of sight, and heavy footsteps of something sinister in the next room over.
Capcom did a fantastic job of resurrecting all the best parts of the classic Resident Evil 2 and making them look, sound, and play like a 2019 game. 
If you’re of the mind that the series had lost its way for a while there, this game is very much a return to form. The zombie combat is satisfying and exploring the dilapidated ruins of Raccoon City is a thrill.
