[h1]Resident Evil 2 (2019)[/h1]

Resident Evil 2 (2019) is a remake based off the 1998 game, improving on the game both visually and mechanically. Although the game's writing takes different strides from its original counterpart, RE2R did really well to improve and update its gameplay by emphasizing durable enemies with distinct weaknesses and item/resource management.

[u]Story + Characters (Possible Spoilers!)[/u]

[spoiler]Out of the two storylines, I think Claire's storyline is much stronger considering that she has a lot of interactions with Sherry and Annette who are two important characters in this story. I just wished she had a lot more time to develop her relationship with Sherry because it feels awfully rushed. She really goes beyond for a girl who she just met, even if she's a little kid. Although, I did find Claire's character to be improved in this remake as she was just as likable in the original and was often humanized even more in her interactions with Sherry.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Leon's story is fine for what it is. His story goes from "trying to get out of the city" to helping Ada with her investigation into Umbrella (which is later just a front so she can get a sample of the G virus) with intentions to save the city in any way he can. Nothing special, but it was awesome to see Leon slowly grow out of his naive rookie cop shell and into the bad**s he would eventually become.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]On a negative note, there is no A/B scenario here where the story actually changes depending on who you played first like OG RE2 which means the scenes from the 2nd Run of each character's playthrough will always be the same as their 1st. Also the story cutscenes have some inconsistencies to them like G3 appearing to Leon and Claire in the same area or both of them going through each setting without seeing each other, let alone acknowledging each others' existences (outside of the intro and one early scene) until the very end of the story. Even with my first playthroughs on PS4, these inconsistencies were very noticeable.[/spoiler]

[u]Gameplay[/u]

Resident Evil 2 (2019) is up there in the ranks for being one of the most fun RE games I have played and this is mostly due to the fact that gameplay is very balanced.

RE2R is one of the most management intensive RE games that emphasize on Items & Resources. The inventory can often be filled up quickly even if you have the max amount of slots. With the variable of enemies, RE2R teaches you to only bring what you need because you still need room to grab key items and additional resources that will be essential going forward. Puzzles take some decent thinking (especially near the end) and are fairly abundant.

Enemies are durable but have weaknesses which can be exploited through ammo types or weapons. On higher difficulties, there is often not enough ammo for every enemy so you'll have to consider running past or just hit stunning them.

Each character has a unique play style to them through the weapons they claim: [spoiler]Leon has access to the Shotgun, Magnum, and Flamethrower while Claire can use the Grenade Launcher, Submachine Gun, and Spark Gun.[/spoiler]

Controls are refined, compared to the original. Instead of tank controls and fixed cameras, RE2R runs a third-person view similar to RE4 and anyone can get used to the controls relatively quickly. Very casual friendly.

RE2R has decent replayability thanks to the 2nd Run which changes up some of the game's item placements and enemy encounters (mostly in the beginning) and also comes with extra modes such as [spoiler]4th Survivor[/spoiler] and [spoiler]Ghost Survivors[/spoiler] .

[u]Graphics & Sound[/u]

RE2R's graphics hold up exquisitely, thanks to the RE engine. Many of the details of the RPD station and other design levels are visually impressive and the atmosphere of horror is prominent in many settings that you will find yourself in. Gore is highly detailed as wounds from monsters can be seen in relatively gruesome fashion - some of the best gore details in any Resident Evil game.

While not all the soundtrack isn't remade versions of the original soundtrack (which some would have preferred, including me), the remake's soundtrack still does its job for when its music is present in settings that range from tense encounters with monsters to poignant interactions between characters.

[u]Conclusion[/u]

At the end of this review, I have to mention some of the cut OG content/downgrades unfortunately because this is ultimately a remake of the original game and as a result, comparisons are bound to happen:

No Spiders, Crows, Evolved Lickers, Giant Moths, Ivy Plants (replaced by Ivy Zombies).
The MAJOR cut of the A/B scenario along with the zapping system. 
The Bowgun weapon.
The Marshaling Yard was cut and NEST was downgraded to three pathways & a one-time use elevator.
Some radio interactions between Leon and Claire.

This game could have been an easy 10/10 but those cuts really do hurt it because it takes out a bit of replayability and depth from the game.

Despite that, Resident Evil 2 (2019) is a solid addition to the Resident Evil series and maintains its identity by remaining relatively truthful to the original RE2. Even with some of its cuts, RE2R compensates by improving on the original through gameplay, character development, visuals/design, controls, and sound effects. Would recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of the survival horror genre and/or zombie games.

Perfect example of how to remaster a game properly. Resident Evil 2 pays tribute, & surpasses it's original version from 1998.

Graphics: Hands down one of the most detailed looking games ever. Character models, backgrounds, lighting, shadows, reflections are all beautiful. Enemies look gruesome & terrifying. Amazing how far games have come since the original came out in 1998.

Sound: Sound effects are great. Zombies sound scary, as well as the other enemies. Weapons sound punchy. Voice acting is good, especially when you compare to the original. I personally am not a fan of the new soundtrack, so I prefer to switch to the original version. The music is the only thing in the game where I prefer the original over the remaster.

Controls: I was initially very worried about the controls while watching game play footage before the game was released. However, I was surprised at how responsive they actually are. The days of fixed camera angles & tank controls are gone. Camera remains behind the player, & never becomes an issue (unlike the Resident Evil 3 remaster). Aiming is nice & smooth.

Fun Factor: This game has a very high replay value. Resident Evil 2 on Playstation 1 was always my favorite RE, but this remaster has now taken it's place. Truly remarkable what Capcom did with Resident Evil 2. I can't recommend enough.

Overall  experience for me = 8/10 - For the type of game Resident Evil games are. If you are new to Resident Evil, you need to understand that these games have always been puzzle, exploration, and inventory management games. Combat is not the main focus of these games, so if you are going into them thinking you are going to go on a zombie murder spree.....you may want to reconsider. At any rate, here is my personal scoring of some key areas.

Music/Atmosphere = 10/10 - Not much to else to say, this is the bread and butter of the series. If you are not tense while playing, then the game really isn't doing what it was meant to do.

Combat = 5/10 - Very basic combat as far as guns go. Not great, not bad. It's perfectly adequate for Resident Evil. The main focus is on whether or not combat is "worth the resources" rather than how many zombies you can kill.

Story = 5/10 - Typical cheesy/average resident evil story. The story is enough to keep you interested, but don't expect anything mind blowing.

Graphics = 8/10  - Game looks great. There are low res textures on random junk, but who really cares about how detailed your can of soda is? 

Controls/Movement = 7/10 - Key mapping is nice, but controlling the character just kind of feels clunky. This is intentional because they need to make running away somewhat risky. The awkward turning and slow running makes the game more scary, but I still found it kind of annoying.

Puzzles = 7/10 - Decent puzzles, not nearly as ridiculous as the original REmake. Just find the object and stick it somewhere for the most part. Nothing that requires 5000 IQ to solve. Just enough to keep you engaged.

Interface = 8/10 - Everything is fairly clean and works well, kind of wished there was a more detailed quest tracker. When areas are cleared of useful items they turn blue on your map. If this didn't exist, I think the games would be frustrating to play, because there is already enough backtracking as it is.

Resident Evil 2: Remake is a fun and tension filled homage to classic Resident Evil games with an excellent modern twist.

+Pros

+Gameplay
Instead of the fixed camera angles the first RE2 had this version is updated into a 3rd person perspective allowing for a more organic and natural feel for gameplay. Despite the perspective changes you’ll often find the game to still be quite claustrophobic as many zombies will try and snuggle up with you while in a small corridor so no worries there.

Shooting is the same in this game as the other Resident Evil titles so make sure to position yourself carefully and aim for the head so you suddenly don’t find yourself with a chunk of your flesh missing.

The game also allows you to be a little creative when dealing with zombies. So say you want to shoot them but don’t want to use too much ammo, you can also shoot them in the legs and disable them so it’s easier to run away and trust me it’s quite fun to do.

Still though, running away is still the most optimal way to play the game as ammo and healing items are worth their weight in gold, especially on hardcore difficulty, and it’s best not to waste them by fighting every zombie you come across.

You’ll also find various puzzles you’ll need to solve in order to progress through the game. The best addition to this game is that whenever you fully explore a room, the room will then be colored blue telling you that all possible items have been retrieved so if you ever want to find out where to probably check out next just check your map and you’re on your way.

All in all, the gameplay is fantastic and definitely can keep you on edge throughout your entire playtime.

+Audio
This game is absolutely meant to be experienced with headphones as it really adds to the horror factor hearing the zombies constantly banging their hands on windows and doors trying to break into the police station and it also helps gameplay wise when a zombie you thought was dead suddenly starts snarling back to life.


+Graphics
The game looks absolutely gorgeous as you’ll soon find out that with every bullet you put inside a zombies dome the blood and character models on the zombies look both beautiful and terrifying at the same time.

The lighting is also top notch as most of the areas you’ll explore are very dark and you’ll make use of a flashlight in order to navigate and it can be seen that a lot of effort has been made to make sure it looks both good and is functional for gameplay.

Facial animations during cutscenes and the environment you’ll explore is also well polished and pleasing to the eyes.

+Story
Just by examining a general overview of the entire story so far and all the lore the Resident Evil series has established so far it can be seen as a little convoluted and ridiculous even for people who are long time fans of the series.

However, seeing as how the story has just relatively begun, the story is more simplistic and easier to follow as well as a few changes being made in this game to streamline the action.

-Cons

-Slight Inconsistencies With the Story
As you do get to play as both Claire and Leon in the game it can lead to a few slight problems with the continuity in the story.

For example, who got into the police station first? Who met Sherry first? Are there multiple Mr. X’s?

Small stuff like that that continues to make the timeline a bit skewed here and there.

-Overall Very Short
The actual game itself is very short as it would only take me about 13 hours to fully complete both Leon A and Claire B and that includes running around getting all of the collectibles. If you play on hardcore difficulty it may take you a bit longer but for a standard playthough you should be able to beat the game relatively quickly.

Now while there is replay value in playing throughout all the different routes if you’re a one time playthrough kind of person, you may lose some value in this game.

Final Verdict:(9/10)
Resident Evil 2: Remake works both as a fun action/zombie game and tension filled, survival horror as you’ll constantly be on your toes as zombies will barge through doors and windows to get a taste of your delicious meaty flesh. Story is also easy enough to understand so anybody can dive right in without any prior knowledge as to who these people are and how they stand in the franchise.


All in all, if you’re like me and just want to find out what all the fuss was about it’s definitely worth a pick up at full price and for long time fans you’ll feel right at home

RE2 Remake is an incredibly fun and gorgeous game, a true beacon of quality in our over-saturated market of live-service, AAA, heavily monetized virtual entertainment. The original game is rather faithfully recreated here along with a lot of new and truly inspired content that really adds to the overall experience. I remember the OG Resi 2 very fondly but I was always too young and scared to play it much. I was very excited for this remake and let me tell you, I am absolutely blown away by how much love they put into this project. 

Playing the game is kind of relaxing and soothing in a weird way, once you get things down. The initial playthrough is very good, very spooky, but of course very short. Once you finish the B side and get the true ending, taking your time ends in roughly 8-10 hours of content. But the game is meant to be replayed and there are rewards for completing certain things. However the meat of the game is simply playing and enjoying the second by second flow of gameplay. 

RE2make takes place in several locations: the RPD, the sewers and city, labs beneath. The game is subtly but discreetly divided into roughly 3-4 segments per character. RPD takes the bulk of time but is the most fun to explore and cleverly designed. Think of a Dark Souls level where the location slowly opens up as you unlock shortcuts. Each area centers around a puzzle unique to its location and to be honest, they're not as much puzzles as item fetch quests. Which is fine because the focus of the game is navigating the environment and dealing with threats. 

Threatening as they may be in bulk, zombies will never be your greatest enemy. However, the tight corners and cramped hallways will usually ensure some level of discomfort. The major hurdles early on are the limited inventory space and the lack of ammo/healing items. Once you get a nice stock, its easy to feel a false sense of security. That is until the game throws Mr. X at you. I'm assuming in 2022 everybody knows about Mr. X, but if you don't then [b]spoiler alert[/b] he's a giant unkillable monster that stalks you throughout the latter half of the RPD. I wish he were in the game a lot more but I understand his placement, its perfect. You spend early game learning the layout of the station before he's unleashed upon you. Then he can show up at anytime almost anywhere in the RPD, barring safe areas. He's essentially an aggressive NPC that you can hide from and outsmart, but the longer you stay hidden the more relentless and quick he will be. He is a big part of what makes this game so amazing. 

My other personal favorite part of this game are the boss fights, which may be a controversial opinion to some. I think they're ****ing awesome, each one is fun and unique, not too difficult on normal. The tools to kill them are almost always in their arena and a few have gimmicks but honestly I look forward to them every single time, especially G3, Mr. X, and the final boss. 

The game has extra modes and stuff, pretty fun but not my cup of tea. This is one of the few titles where I've bought pretty much all the "DLC," ESPECIALLY the original soundtrack. I even appreciate being able to buy the unlockables because I'm a dirty cheater and a filthy casual, and I NEED the infinite ammo weapons to even beat Hardcore. But I digress. 

If you enjoy Resident Evil, survival horror, great games, or cute college girls with grenade launchers, then you probably owe it to yourself to play this. I avoided talking about the plot because I'm extremely biased and I think the story of Resident Evil is amazing B-horror, but this title stands out as being particularly believable and realistic. The graphics are so good but that's not my forte, and the music is too but same kinda thing. Like I said, if you truly love excellent and fun games then this is right up your alley; you may even get a kick out of scaring yourself to death.

You're stuck in Racoon City in an infected infested police station. What seems to be a normal day turns out to be a dark one now that a devastating pandemic is now killing lives and destroying all properties. You can choose to play as either Leon, a rookie officer of the force, or Claire, a freelancer trying to find her missing brother, and experience their tale about what's happening over there.

Both have different perspectives and stories that you can experience in two runs or playthrough. I like Leon's story more than Claire since ya can't feel for the guy for having one hell of a first day on the job. Even that, at the end how he views the world seems to be upside down now. Claire is okay, and have some scary moments and also endearing ones in her story. Both have interesting stories that intertwined to reveal a dark secret in the city.

Talking about the story, I didn't expect it to be story and cinematic driven, unlike its predecessor, Resident Evil Remake which is more faithful and also more fleshed out than the original. RE1 Remake has an interesting story but is not cinematic. But here, everything is presented like a movie. Which is a plus.

The horror aspect is a return to form, like how it is in the original. I didn't play RE2 OG unlike the first game so I don't know the differences. But what I can compare is from past games especially RE4, 5, and 6, and how different, and astray it was from the horror aspect from before. Every corner in this game is scary. Zombies running the places have realistic animations, like sometimes taken aback from your shots. You can dismember parts of the zombie. And their realistic movements can be difficult for you to aim and shoot. Every bullet counts and every zombie felt like a boss fight.

Which brings to the main thing that for me is the most scary thing in the game that is Mr. X. Mr X will hunt you down in that station and will not stop. You cannot kill him. You will always hear his footsteps. And the best way to do if having an encounter with him is RUN. Mr X chasing me is the scariest and funnest shet I've ever experience.

Which brings to what you actually do in that place and how to get out. The station you're stuck in are designed to have keys and puzzles for you to solve. Other than shooting zombies, you'll need to know when to spend your bullets so that the place where you have to go isn't that hard to go through with enough bullets. Every puzzles are fun and can be challenging. And also the station is very intricately designed with winding paths and more puzzles to solve.

The soundtrack is good. I like the licensed song.

With that being said, this is Resident Evil in its roots. A classic experience that RE gave during its initial lifetime. It's not as action packed like the recent installments or other zombire games like Left 4 Dead or Dead Island. It is survival horror at its finest. 

Overall, being scared has never been more fun.

There isn’t much I can say about this game that hasn’t been said already. This game is an absolute technical marvel. The environments are designed to perfection, the graphics are sharp, the atmosphere is eerie and unsettling, and the structure behind the objectives and the map system is very smart and intuitive. The presentation is unrivaled in how cinematic and immersive it is. The character animations are so expertly crafted with palpable love and care. For instance, there’s a part in Leon’s campaign where you climb a manhole ladder and lift the cover off so you can emerge into a parking lot; however, before you lift off the cover, Leon licks his lips and takes a second before proceeding with the action. Admittedly, this sounds like a throwaway point on paper, but this scene really hammered home the anxiety that I and many other players felt during our first playthrough of this game. This game feeds on your anxiety, stress, and fear of the unknown. Opening doors, turning corners, uncovering new areas - they all feel like such monumental tasks when you first play because you don’t know what to expect. I was trying to brace myself for whatever was coming next when I decided to climb that ladder, so Leon taking a second to lick his lips and brace himself just like I did was just the kind of immersion this game excels at with flying colors.

To keep this brief, I give this game an 8.5/10. The only weak point for me was the narrative and its structure. Playing the game once as either Leon or Claire is fine (I found Claire’s narrative to be more gripping), but you really need to play the game a second time as the other character to unlock the “true” ending. Otherwise you’ll be left with a very weak ending that kind of just abruptly cuts off. There are also narrative inconsistencies between the two campaigns. For example, if you play as Leon and fight the first boss fight, you end up trashing the place and leaving obvious marks signaling that a battle has taken place. When you go through it again as Claire however, you end up fighting the same boss in the same area as if Leon never had fought him. I understand if you play as Claire first or Leon first, their campaigns should play out as if you’re going through that scenario for the first time. However, when you play as the other character second, maybe some boss fights should be skipped and only the wreckage left from the battle should remain to signal that the other character had already taken care of it. It would have made for a much more solid and cohesive narrative experience. I say this because if you play as Claire after Leon, you can find notes left by Leon for Claire indicating that he is ahead and has already gone through what Claire is going through. Same thing if you play as Claire first and play as Leon second, only their positions are switched.

Again, the game overall is a beautiful experience. Truly a terrifying journey upon first playthrough, and a very thrilling and curious puzzle to unravel and uncover on repeated playthroughs. Had me at the edge of my seat the whole way through, and playing this at night in the dark for the first time is an experience I won’t soon forget. I can’t sing its praises enough; what a masterful game this is.

On DX12, I'd get lag spikes when walking through doors/loading new areas whatever you want to call it. DX11 always ran pretty flawlessly. I am however happy to report that now the DX12 version is running with none of these issues present for me. I'm on an older 1070 based rig, and the game always ran, and always ran absolutely perfectly in the DX11 mode, but now it seems to run just fine in the new DX12 implementation as well. I hope that's good news for some of you. Give the new version a go and see how it performs for you!

Although I was unable to make any significant tests myself and the game still runs at well above playable fps for me, anyone still running something like a GTX 1060 or RX 580 (two GPUs that are more than capable of running this game at 1080p/60 with all settings cranked to max) will most likely have some trouble maintaining stable performance. Moreover, the update also introduced FSR 1.0, when FSR 2.0 already exists and provides significantly better image quality over its predecessor. So not only is performance worse in this new update, players must now use poor upscaling technology, with blurry edges, ghosting and other artifacts, to achieve the performance they would otherwise be able to get on DX11, which was senselessly removed in this latest update.

This was the first Resident Evil game I've ever played. I had heard a lot of good and bad about the series. I was somewhat aware of the "downfall" associated with RE5 and 6. But I can't really speak for them, let alone the rest of the franchise... But this game... This game is a treat.

Amazing, spectacular, oppressive. It gets so much right. My first playthrough was Leon on Hardcore difficulty (altho I recommend playing Claire first). Hardcore is absolutely the way to play the game. Even if it's your first time. The anxiety of entering the next room. Low on ammo, no more heals. It's extremely dark, and your flashlight can only illuminate so much. The growls of the zombies surrounding you. *That* lingering threat. Gets the blood pumping.

Atmosphere - This deserves a mention for sure. It's incredible. From the moment I walked into the opening gas station level, I instantly realized this was something else. The lighting, graphics, the setting. Everything comes together in such a great package.

Levels - I've always loved metroidvania style games. And this is no exception. Picking up an item that's seemingly unimportant, but later comes in handy is gratifying. Who doesn't love to have the lightbulb go off "Oh I need to go grab X for this". It's great. There's just enough layered to have you revisit areas multiple times. Each encounter being more tense than the last.

Enemies - A zombie slowly shambles towards you. You dump an entire magazine into its head. Careful not to miss a shot of precious ammo. It falls to the ground. You feel your shoulders relax as you reload and begin to proceed. Big mistake, as it rises again to grab you. This game absolutely nails the threat of a zombie. You are in small rooms, surrounded by them. Nowhere to run, and they don't go down easily... There are more enemies than just a zombie, and they are all interesting in their own unique way.

Bosses - Not the greatest. I can't think of any that was simply unenjoyable. Even if they were all simplistic *shoot the orange spot*.

Mr. X - If you know nothing about this game, stop reading right here and go buy it. Seriously, the less you know, the better the experience.... Bam, Mr. X gonna give it to ya. This guy single handily raises the entire game to top notch. The moment he enters the game, everything changes. You were probably relaxed and thought you had solved the game. Zombies aren't so bad anymore, Lickers? Not a problem. I've already cleared and boarded everything up. Then he hits you. Like a stack of bricks. You can't breathe because those heavy footsteps close in. This guy is relentless. His presence is exactly the fire needed to reapply tension. "Dread" is the best word to describe him.

Final thoughts - Damn what a game. I loved both playthroughs, and I think hardcore is very well balanced. Easy recommend. It's not without flaws, but those that exist feel rather mundane compared to the whole experience.

Eh. It's a pretty good remake, Resident Evil 2's story with Resident Evil 4/5's gameplay style, along with the newer RE7/RE8 item management. I don't mind the 3rd person camera. It takes away that "suspenseful" movie-like classic RE Camera (as RE4 onward has) but the game is nearly infinitely more accessible that way. 
Accessible, but still pretty challenging, if not more so than the original game, to be honest. The tyrant actively stalks you across the map, impeding your progress. Zombies can overwhelm you, in tight spots and as large groups. Ammo is fairly plentiful but you'll still be swapping between weapons and using them strategically, so don't expect things to be a walk in the park. Characters also have different weapons across their different scenarios (and alternate scenarios), in effect shaking gameplay up that way as well.

It's pretty replayable, given that you get four different scenarios, 4th/Tofu Survivor minigames, and a DLC mode featuring four different "What if" scenario minigames. The achievements (and unlockables) also provide unique challenges to attempt on each of your runs. If you're looking for a fresh take on RE2, or found the original to be inaccessible, I highly suggest this game.

From the first cutscene you realise that this is a remake that is not messing about. Amazing recreations of all of the original game's location all rendered in beautiful full 3D - it's obvious this was a passion project as Capcom have not skimped on any part of this - played at night with 5.1 headphones, it's chuffing CHUFFING scary. There are some minor concessions to quality of life improvements (no need for type writer ribbons to save at a typewriter, for instance) although the  inventory system as always is just as infuriating as you remember it - so rare are the inventory-expanding hip-packs that finding one is akin to the rush of adding another swig to your Estus flask. Wow! I was super impressed with Resident Evil 2. While I'm still new-ish to the genre, this is still one of the best horror games of I've ever played. Also, it serves as THE defining example of what a modern remake should be. This game does so many things right. It looks great, it plays well, and it once again proves that Capcom is killing it within the AAA sphere.

The best aspect of this game is by far its level design. Every area you uncover feels rewarding and has been meticulously put together by a team that really wanted to get it right. You're forced to explore and backtrack through every nook and cranny of the environments in RE2. But you don't mind, because it's all so seamless and well designed! Other developers, take note!

Items are limited in this game, and so is your inventory space. What could've been an extremely frustrating system is instead very rewarding. You're required to plan ahead and think strategically - what are you taking with you to the next few rooms? Is it worth going back to a dangerous area to grab items you missed? It adds another layer to the mix and firmly cements this game to its survival horror roots. There are some puzzles you encounter that feel a little tedious, but there's nothing that takes you out of the experience too much.

The final boss was a little disappointing in my eyes but I can look past it. Overall, Resident Evil 2 is a very well-made game that's worth your time. This is a game that benefits from replayability, and I'm excited to go back and play as Claire now that I've got the first run under my belt. This is also a great choice for those who want to dip their toes into the horror genre - nothing too overbearing but it is a very tense experience from start to finish!

Absolutely recommend, if you're even remotely interested I say pull the trigger!

The game controls are vastly improved from the original version, but the game mechanics are still terrible. It is a fairly standard tradition of the “zombie survival” franchise that one shot to the head, or a broken neck, kills a “zombie.” The initiating scene features what appears to be four, possibly five, of the shambling dead. Clair has ten rounds of ammunition at the start. This would be enough, if every shot to the head were to kill one single “zombie,” but it is not. You could put ten rounds into the head of the FIRST zombie, and it would still get back up. The interchange to the second scene, after this, also, does not provide fresh ammunition.

Apparently Leon expects you to turn into Alice and kill them with your bare hands, because you've got one gun and no ammo. Ultimately, the point of the game is not to kill zombies. It's to knock them over and run. This does not strike me as “zombie survival horror.” It strikes me as “escape from zombies” horror.

The fight controls are, also, still, far too badly-communicated. There is no way to hand-to-hand combat the “zombies,” either. If there were a command that allowed you to stomp a downed one's head to destroy it, I'd be a little more forgiving of having to use 30% of your ammunition at the start of the game on even simply knocking it over. It's already challenge enough to have to hit it in the head three times to knock it down, on Normal no less, but the absence of a confirm-the-kill mechanic in the first scene, makes this too completely unenjoyable for me to want to bother with it.

The graphics are fantastic. Could this be a good game? It could.

Except that it isn't, because they made some truly moronic decisions about the mechanics of “fighting,” the shambling dead. I put fighting in quotation marks, because I don't see running like a coward to be the clear hallmark of a well-made survival game. I just don't. The hallmark of a well-made survival game is being able, from a practical standpoint, from the very first play-through, to kill everything that comes at you.

It shouldn't be easy. It shouldn't be remotely easy. It should, however, be possible, and should be possible enough that you don't run out of bloody ammunition on the first enemy without actually even killing them.

[h1] Hesitant Weevil 2 Recake [/h1]

The original will always be superior... but I still like Resident Evil 2 Remake... even if it's not exactly perfect.

Resident Evil 2 Remake starts off strong, with a grand opening and prime introduction. The first half is ALMOST on par with the original, the classic.
I loved the first few hours of the game as resources truly felt scarce & useful; you had to use each bullet smartly. No bullet to waste. The map felt huge, it was like an entire complex multi-level joyride. Each room felt distinct & useful; like they all served a purpose in general.
Puzzle items were also commonly scattered about nicely in amount, where you had to factor the possibility upon stumbling upon such on small journeys towards other goals. It made the resource management a lot heftier of a ponder, and a bigger prevalence. I love when I am craved to think smart in games, and punished when I don't; and the early parts did that absolutely wonderfully using the resource & inventory management systems. It meant that trips were not only planned with the routes in mind, but also the locations. Puzzles themselves were also smart & commonly spread about. I had to both mentally & physically prepare myself every single time. Love it!

Now, the latter parts? ehhhhhhhh. meh.
As much I loved the former first-half, after leaving the Police Station it all slowly falls apart like brittle old toilet paper.
After exiting the Police Station and entering the Morgue/Parking Lot/Prison Cells/Shooting Range it just kinda drops in quality all-over everywhere. 
Now the game becomes way too generous with items, especially bullets. In the latter-half I ended up finding so many bullets that they flooded my inventory and I had to savour most of them in the chest. The map also become way too lenient, as now rooms felt too straight-forward. It didn't feel multi-directional with sprawling multiple branching paths, instead it felt like a road guiding me along. Key puzzle items were also reduced, alongside fewer unique quality puzzles & puzzles as a whole. Sad.
I feel the game TRULY drops the cake when you enter the Sewers... and furthermore even steps on the cake when you enter the Lab. It's so sad, and pathetic; as the beginning of the game was absolutely striving!
Yet the balancing & pacing felt totally overhauled... but poorly.

I think a nice & easy way to fix this the abundance of ammo would be lowering the health of zombies overall, but also lowering the amount of ammo later on by a lot. If balanced well, then this would still cause an encouragement to kill bothersome zombies, but also amplify the resource-management. It could also further cause the mojo of "each shot counts" as a single miss would mean a much bigger drawback.


A minor complaint is also how the A & B stories entirely contradict each other. You'll kill the same character twice, alongside causing contradictions in your settings between the stories. It's really weird, as the classic Resident Evil 2 had no problem fitting both A & B together canonly without breaking each other completely. It feels like they tried implementing the same outcome of big story events in both stories, even though half of them previously had been divided between the two adventures. They really didn't need to do that.



[h1] Visual experience [/h1]

The camera in this game is... meh.
Gone is that beautiful stationary camera showcasing each room from their best most elegant & useful perspectives, reminiscent of the camera-angle of classic horror thrillers.
Now it's been "modernized" AKA downgraded, because The Last of Us did it and now every AAA needs to do the same apparently. There are times I had hard times seeing anything in-front of me, alike items & zombies, causing otherwise unnecessary rage.
Also when you're grabbed by a zombie the camera gets completely disoriented, meaning suddenly the camera snaps away and focuses on the showcasing the bite. Unnecessary but OK. However it also means that I can barely see anything around me as it happens, and when the animation is over my camera-angle often would never be the same as beforehand, meaning I'd usually just run into another zombie as I can't see anything.

The whole game also suffers from this really odd filter. It's like the entire game is dulled out with the "bleh" washed filter. Everything looks so dull & bare. It's hard to describe, but I'm not sure why they would do this, or why they wouldn't want you to turn it off. It could probably easily be fixed using ReShade... but I can't be bothered.

Many areas also have this odd choice of making the rooms COMPLETELY dark, to point where I could not see anything. This means that you have to rely on your puny-ass flashlight just to see anything right in-front of you. I don't like that.
It's this really odd modern-day trend of horror games that think "can't see = spoopy" which is absolutely not true. I would have no problem if the darkness was excluded to one big room, as it'd make it feel special & unique with a certain thrill-directed hinderance. But  that's not the case, as there's like 30 of those completely dark rooms.
Turning up the brightness doesn't help either, as it instead just adds this really dumb white filter, as if someone put a paper over your screen.

A minor complaint is also how the game treats corpses. There are times where I'd down a zombie, 'till it was completely motionless. You'd assume it's dead then, no? Incorrect. It'll most likely still grab your foot as you walk by, even if you shot it in the head like 4 times before walking past it. Dumb.
I think they could easily fix this by reintroducing the pool of blood appearing under zombies after you've killed them fully from the classic Resident Evil 2.



[h1] Music, or lack there of [/h1]

Another dumb-ass modern-day AAA horror game trope is no music. It's like they think having in-game music playing throughout it all would detract oneself from the thrill of the game, even it's completely nonsensical. I have no other idea of why they'd want to avoid adding music.
The classic Resident Evil trilogy had no problem with a constant beautiful soundtrack. The beautiful soundtrack of Resident Evil 2 only amplified its elegant horror & setting, with most iconic areas having personalized themes beautifully transitioning the setting into sounds as well.
But no, that's now gone. Sad.



[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

I'll continue to much rather recommend the original Resident Evil 2 over the remake to most people, as not only is there more refined game-play, camera, visuals, balance, story, and maps, but it also has a lot more charm.
However if you're interested in the remake at all then feel free to go on and buy it. Yet only expect 8 hours of fun from the first 4 hours from the beginning of each campaign -- beyond that? Eh.

If you end up loosing your will to continue playing after leaving the Police Station, then I won't blame you. The game only downfalls beyond that, and you won't ever reach the same peak again.

Sometimes, when I'm playing as Claire, I let Mr. X catch me, teehee!

For real tho, this is a helluva good game. Right up there with Dead Space as my favorite TPS horror games.

[h1]Should I get this game? Is it for me?[/h1]
[b]In case you're a newbie like me, and the phrase 'survival horror' means nothing to you,[/b] the general vibe of this game is a third person shooter with some light puzzles and a cheesy but charming story [b](if you're looking for an innovative narrative with complex character arcs, this is probably not gonna be your thing)[/b]. While it definitely has spooky atmospheres, It's not scary; the horror comes primarily from the 'survival' aspect: the stress of managing a limited inventory capacity, conserving ammo, and planning your route through the map. 

[h1]Gameplay. Tell me about the gameplay![/h1]
I adore the gameplay. Although the guns feel super fun and responsive, it's the context that makes it so engaging for me. Ammo is scarce. Healing items are scarce. Explosives and other gadgets are scarce. In other games, I would be hoarding these items and forgetting about them for the rest of the game; not here. The items make a huge difference, and it feels good to [i]actually need[/i] my items. 

The enemies are vicious, you die in around 3 hits, and unless you're going to bust out your most valuable guns and ammo, enemies won't die from dozens of your gunshots. Guns provide you with a way to stun your enemies so you can run past them without fear of getting lunged at. When I first bought this game, I refunded it because the gameplay flow was so foreign and intimidating, yet something drew me back into the challenge. I find it very satisfying to save ammo and run around enemies, because that helps me long-term, but shooting is also satisfying because it's a rare treat to do so. You get a variety of combat goodies if you search the map, too.

The exploration and discovery, along with the number of scripted events designed to catch you off guard will make your first playthrough quite terrifying. I have jumped at horror games before, but the threat of losing my progress when the game ambushed me with enemies made me truly [i]scream[/i]. 

[h1]Get to the point. Is it worth my money?[/h1]
Depends on the kind of person you are. The large hour count that you see on my review comes from around 11 full playthroughs, some time in the extra modes, and goofing around with the bonus weapons. [b]For my first blind playthrough? Around 5.5 hours[/b]; I was thorough, but also didn't know where anything was, and I missed plenty of items. [b]For everything after? Maybe 3.5 hours, 2 hours 20 minutes if I'm hustling[/b] (I'm no speedrunner lol). The game loses its novelty when you've memorized all the item locations and the order of where you need to go, but there's also something fun about familiarity and learning the game more. I felt a lot more badass on future runs, and the short length encouraged me to try for a better time and earn the bonus weapons by beating the game on the hardest difficulty with the highest rank. 

As you may know there are two different playable campaign characters, and besides their gun and movement differences, there are only around 3 sections where they explore their own exclusive map areas. After beating the campaign, you unlock a new game plus kinda thing which changes how the campaign begins and how it ends; it also shuffles around the locations of several key items and some enemies and other things. Besides some difficult bonus scenarios you can play from the main menu, this is the full extent of the game's novelty and I feel like that's worth mentioning if you aren't the type to replay games.

[h1]My verdict? A big thumbs up![/h1]

Resident Evil 2 (2019) brings stunning visuals and welcome dialogue changes, yet it struggles to capture the haunting atmosphere that defined its predecessor.

Let's start with the positives. From the moment you step into the desolate Raccoon City, the visuals in Resident Evil 2 Remake are nothing short of breathtaking. The attention to detail is awe-inspiring, from the dilapidated police station to the grotesque designs of the undead. The photorealistic environments and character models elevate the horror experience to new heights, immersing players in a world that feels disturbingly real.

The character redesigns are particularly noteworthy. Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield have been reimagined with meticulous detail, making them feel like genuine individuals facing an unimaginable nightmare. The transformation of iconic monsters like the Lickers and Mr. X is equally impressive. The complete overhaul of the Ivy plant monsters into the Ivy Zombies is a welcomed change.

The dialogue changes in Resident Evil 2 Remake also deserve praise. While the original game's script had its campy charm, the updated lines and voice acting bring a more mature and believable tone to the narrative. 

However, where Resident Evil 2 Remake falls short is in recapturing the eerie atmosphere that made the 1998 version a genre-defining experience. The original game's fixed camera angles, limited resources, and deliberately paced exploration created a palpable sense of dread and tension. In contrast, the remake, with its over-the-shoulder perspective and more action-oriented gameplay, sacrifices some of the original's atmospheric magic.

There are questionable design choices that are quite discordant in keeping this a remake. Inclusion of modern tech and sleek modern fashion is quite jarring. The city, sewers and police station design are very good but certain elements of the NEST look like they belong in a far future setting while other elements work well in a 90s enviroment.

The revamped sound design, while impressive, fails to replicate the spine-chilling ambiance of the original soundtrack. The haunting echoes of the police station and the menacing growls of the undead, while present, lack the same haunting resonance that lingered in the corridors of the 1998 classic. Thankfully, included for free, they give the option to change some of the tracks to the classics.

In conclusion, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a triumph in terms of modernizing the survival horror genre with its stunning visuals and refined dialogue. However, it struggles to capture the atmospheric brilliance of its predecessor. For those who appreciate the evolution of gaming and a fresh take on a beloved classic, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a must-play. However, for purists seeking the nostalgic terror of the 1998 release, the magic may be somewhat lost in the transition to a more contemporary gaming experience. While the Resident Evil 1 Remake made the original redundant the same cannot be said about Resident Evil 2 Remake.

Let me get this out of the way before I alienate anyone but if you love this game (of which I assume is many of you), then I have one thing to say: Good for you! I'm really glad you enjoyed the hell out of it on some level. It's a game that has a lot of love from people and I'm sure you can find someone to chat with endlessly about its qualities. And while we're at it, I honestly think this new era of Resident Evil has been a genuine boon to the franchise, inspiring both technological and artistic achievements across the board for the brand. Works like 7, R3 and Village have lit my senses on fire with the things they've pulled off, genuinely combing the tried and true formulas of game's past with surprisingly sophisticated storytelling chops that have been almost unheard of in a game series such as this known for its absolutely cheese.

But with all of that being said, I absolutely hated the remake of 2.

While there is technical polish, tight controls and classy presentations abound on this, the frankly teeth gnashing difficulty here just makes it a chore to play it. And look,  I'm not the sort of person who doesn't like hard games; I loved The Evil Within, a game with for more issues than this game and that thing was an absolute bone cruncher in terms of hard it was. But in contrast to that game to this one, TEW always kept you going forward while RE2R has you backtracking and backtracking and backtracking and backtracking endlessly on. Oh and big thanks to the genius in the development time who thought it would be a brilliant idea to make the standard zombie's rotting cranium as durable as reinforced concrete. Or making knives breakable while giving you as little ammo as possible. Or making the new voices of Leon and Ada about as bland as possible. Or going for some oddly weak audio design with the weaponry. Say what you will about the remake of 3 but at least it was snappy, tighter and to the point than this is.

To be frank, I didn't even play Claire's side of the story because my experience with Leon's was just so exhausting to me and I'm not in the mood to put myself through more torture. I'm still game for whatever things Capcom has planned for the franchise (such as DLC for Village and whatever they're going to do next for 9) but I'm writing this one off. Sorry guys.

Resident evil 2 is about A deadly virus taking over the residents of Raccoon City in September of 1998, plunging the city into chaos as flesh eating zombies are roaming the streets for survivors. You start the game as either Leon (a brand new cop going into Raccoon city for his first day as a cop) or Claire (The sister of the 1st games protagonist Chris Redfield. She a college student on her way to Raccoon city to find her missing brother who is a cop himself). Both of the characters have no idea that they would be on their way to a zombie infested city.  

Resident Evil 2 remake is an amazing reimagining of the original 1998 original game. 
There are some aspects of the original game that are better than the remake, for example, the A and B 
Scenarios in the remake are a huge disappointment. In the original game the A and B Scenarios were almost completely different campaigns from one another, and they have different boss fights. The remake however has minor differences to the A & B Scenario’s making the B Scenario leas impactful like in the Original, the only notable difference for the B Scenario in the remake is Claire and Leon get a different starting weapon than they have in the A Scenario, and the B Scenario has an extra boss fight at the end of the game. Another minor complaint I have is the music. Yes the music in remake is not bad, but the original soundtrack is simply iconic! I really dislike capcom's decision to put the original soundtrack in a paywall to add over the remakes music. 
The last nitpick/complaint I have is that for some reason Capcom removed the Giant Spiders in the sewers! 

What the remake does better than the original is it has a better story (more grounded and less campy), better combat and gameplay in general, the camera is actually behind you and not fixed, and it's a very beautiful game even on low settings.

Resident Evil 2 remake is an incredible remake that manages to keep it very true to what made the original game a hit, but also separates it from the original making it stand on its own as a great addition to the RE franchise! Without any spoilers, I recommend everyone play this game on hardcore, I feel as though adding checkpoints in a Resident Evil game kills the suspense, but I do agree that the checkpoint system is great for new comers to the franchise! 
Overall, I’d give this masterpiece of a game a 10/10 even with the missteps with the B Scenario’s of the game! Easy recommendation and my personal top 5 favorite games ever made

Resident Evil 2 (2019) – A Masterful Reimagining of a Classic

Resident Evil 2 (2019) is a stunning reimagining of the iconic survival horror classic that expertly blends nostalgia with modern gameplay mechanics. This remake not only honors the original game but elevates it to new heights, creating an experience that is both terrifying and captivating for both longtime fans and newcomers to the franchise.

From the moment you step into the dilapidated halls of RPD, the atmosphere is palpable. The game’s visuals are nothing short of breathtaking, showcasing meticulously crafted environments that are richly detailed and incredibly immersive. The lighting and sound design work together to create a sense of dread and tension that keeps you on the edge of your seat. Every creak and shadow feels alive, drawing players deeper into the haunting world of Resident Evil.

The gameplay mechanics have been beautifully updated while retaining the essence of survival horror. The over-the-shoulder camera perspective enhances the immersion, allowing for a more intimate and terrifying experience. The controls are responsive and intuitive, making it easier to navigate the environment, solve puzzles, and engage in tense combat against the terrifying foes that lurk in the shadows.

Character development is another highlight of the remake. Players can choose to experience the story from the perspectives of both Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield, each offering a unique narrative and gameplay experience. The voice acting and character animations are top-notch, bringing depth to the characters and making their struggles feel authentic and relatable.

One of the standout features is the redesigned Zombified enemies. The AI is smarter and more relentless, creating intense encounters that require strategy and resource management. Every encounter feels meaningful, and the threat of running out of ammunition or health keeps players engaged and on their toes. The incorporation of Mr. X as an ever-present threat adds a layer of tension that heightens the horror experience, forcing players to think carefully about their choices and movements.

Puzzles and exploration are thoughtfully integrated into the gameplay, encouraging players to investigate every nook and cranny of Raccoon City. The remake successfully maintains the sense of discovery that defined the original while introducing new elements that keep the experience fresh and engaging.

Furthermore, the game features a variety of modes and challenges that enhance replayability. After completing the story, players can dive into the “The 4th Survivor” mode and the “Tofu Survivor” mode, providing additional layers of challenge for those looking to test their skills.

In summary, Resident Evil 2 (2019) is a masterful reimagining that captures the essence of the original while successfully modernizing it for a new generation. With its stunning visuals, immersive gameplay, and expertly crafted atmosphere, it stands as a shining example of how to honor a classic while pushing the boundaries of the genre. Whether you’re a longtime fan or a newcomer to survival horror, this game is an essential experience that will leave you breathless and wanting more. Prepare for an unforgettable journey through Raccoon City!

This breathed new life into the game for me, as every mod made my playthroughs feel different. The improved graphical and lighting(REshade) quality only sweetened the deal. 

In closing, my primary gripe with the game was the 2nd run scenario being nearly identical to the 1st scenario. I recommend this game only because is a good tribute of the older version of the iconic Resident Evil 2.

I played the original Resident Evil 2 back in the 2000's and that game was astonishing, not only for the survival horror part, but the plot, story, script, puzzles, resourse managment, among other stuff, were taken very serious and they delivered a product with such high quality. Even the old CGI still looks good on these days and the art direction which, at least for me, still looks better than the remake.

Now, talking about the Resident Evil 2 Remake. The graphics are top notch, the remake of the police station looks insane and the recreation of some areas are incredible (for example the laboratories, where you can see that they did a good research of how should look and which equipments should be in it) . The combat system is way more efficient than before (Third person shooter like RE4), the inventory is way bigger, the sound of the game, how they made the new Ada, Leon, Claire (I prefer the old one) and other characters is simply incredible; another good thing is the mods that you can find of this game... and hey, that's all. The rest is not that good.


[h1] SPOILER ALERT ON THIS PART:[/h1]
------------------------------------------------

[b]Notes:[/b]

* This review is a comparison between both versions, reviewing what I like and what I despite.
* I watched recently some gameplays of the old RE2 to refresh my memories about this.
* The points of interest are only to make a direct comparison between both versions and not to tell you, for example, a summary of the story or any other aspect.

[b]The Story[/b]

The story used to be very rich in dialogs and it did a very good job making the background for the game on the old version. Every character was very distinctive, the game was very explicit with the "Umbrella's incident", there was a lot of mistery behind everything, but also like they were very open to tell you what was happening there. It was understandable how the characters get attached and how they become friendly. Even the bad guys are way more developed compared to the 2019 version. So for the remake, the omitted a lot of details and dialogs from the original and they focused more on the action or the survival instead. Back then, the story used to be coherent after you play both scenarios but on this one... the worst part for me, is that there is a Mr.X that dies quickly on Claire's campaign and one on Leon's campaign that is very persistent and dies at the end. It's like Leon and Claire were in 2 separated police stations with 2 Mr.X each one. It doesn't have any sense at all. It feels like they made this game in a rush... I won't give more details about this but that is just one part of the issues of this game related to the story. Old RE2 feels more for mature audience than this one.

[b]Mr.X on the Police Station[/b]

Having in mind that the story has big flaws, especially how the Mr.X is involved on this, I'll talk about his appearance in this game. This enemy is awesome and is lurking the police station to kill any witness, which is basiclly you. The player must find a way out to avoid conflict with this enemy. The sound of him is creepy and builds tension. It's very funny having him trying to kill you. Thing is that it seems that they focused too much on that and they made a lot of mistakes on other parts. How they made this enemy was a nice touch.

[b]Absense of main characters gore[/b]

Goodbye to the gore on this game. I'm not gonna lie, there is a lot of gore on the zombies, characters on the story like the journalist or the police man on the gate, blood everywhere, but... they never rip appart Leon or Claire. Lickers can't decapitate the main characters like the old version and it feels like a child game. No more gore like Resident Evil 4 where the player can watch Leon die in brutal ways... What is happened with the explicit gore?? If I want to play a game without gore I would be playing other stuff.

[b]Second Scenarios[/b]

If you are new to RE2 then you must know that the game consist on 4 different campaigns. If you start with Leon, second scenario is Claire and if you start with Claire, second scenario is Leon. Second scenarios were made to fill the holes on the plot when the other character is helping you through the story on the main campaign, so at the end, it would make more sense of how the situation developed from 2 different points of view. The remake version, instead of making it more complex or way more developed, delivers a campaign where each scenario seems to be separated from the other survivor's perspective, which was supposed to be helping you on some areas. Items can't be shared by storing it on the inventory box like the old version. Second scenario used to be where Mr.X make his appereance on the police station, so only one survivor used to witness him. Now both see him on the story but apparently there is a Mr.X that dies at the end and a Mr.X that dies on an elevator (sorry for repeating this but is very dissapointing).

[b]Dark Areas[/b]

Capcom with the RE Engine made a good job with the shadow casting, lighting, shaders, ambient occlusion, reflections and other effects that makes the experience more real and more believable on every part of the game. The visuals of this game was not only achieved by the Capcom's RE Engine, there were more companies and software involved (you can see it on the credits). So, yeah they basiclly show us a new whole set with dark areas where you can use the flashlight and it looks fantastic and creepy, but in my opinion was like "hey why they made so many dark areas? I hope they don't think that this actually scares people". Like half of the areas that you visit on the game are now set with no lights or are darker in order that the character make use of the flashlight. If the intention was to create more tension or an atmosphere that scares players then they failed because is not necesary. One of the best examples of it is Alien Isolation, complete full of light corridors but you are always scared to run or to do any kind of noise. The old RE2 used to show illuminated areas that were even more scarier than the ones of this game. In my opinion, they had more options with this engine but they don't make advantage of that and they just come up with making the game darker.

I was expecting a game way more bigger, more explanations to everything, even more areas to explore or to get confused, more puzzles. On 2017 Capcom stated that they wouldn't be using the same voice actors of the old RE2 for the remake and also said that they would be including a lot of new dialogs... Didn't happen. That's why I say, I recommend this game because is a good tribute.

The final question would be: Capcom, if you have no space restrictions compared to the old times to create a masterpiece, why don't you make a good extended and more explanatory version of a game? instead of making it shorter or more appropiate for the audience. If you want to make a game for a new audience, then create something new. A new horror IP would be a good idea for starters...

I would recommend you to play the old version before this one which is way better. Despite that, you will enjoy this game.

9.5/10 - EXCELLENT but can be frustrating at times.

Price I paid: $12 (for the Deluxe Edition)

Pros:
+3rd person over-the-shoulder perspective is the BEST for these types of games, IMO.
+Fantastic graphics and animations.
+Very gory and the dismemberment mechanics are quite dynamic; e.g. you can shoot arms/legs off of zombies and they'll behave differently.
+Puzzles are pretty fun to solve.
+Dialogue and voice acting is pretty great (especially for a Resident Evil game).
+Replayability; I keep trying to improve my performance!
+Keeps you on edge the entire time (at least during your first playthrough).
+No quick-time-events!
+Thorough exploration is rewarding and so is rushing (want all the weapons/upgrades or think can you make it with the bare essentials? Either way is fun.)
+Bonus game modes are fun, especially the one where you have to [spoiler] kill 100 zombies without dying. [/spoiler]
+Unlockables: costumes, infinite ammo, concept art, etc.
+Speedrunning / stat-tracking.
+Mods (haven't used any, personally).

Cons:
-Extremely frustrating at times.
-Can be really confusing (Where do I go [again]? What do I use this item for? Did I miss something?).
-Stupid checkpoints (e.g. did you die AFTER solving a puzzle and watching a cutscene? Great! Solve/watch/try it again!)
-Luck is significant (e.g. you can get an insta-kill or end up using an entire clip on the same zombie, even with perfect aim).
-Combat knives break after very few uses (I think that a pocket knife or screwdriver would have been better at first, then you can upgrade to a much stronger combat knife midway through the game - just a thought).
-Despite the gorgeous and gruesome graphics, lack of blood splatter/trails can ruin immersion (e.g. thought you killed that zombie after you blew off his legs? Nope! He crawled away!... but where did he go? All you see is a few drips where you shot him.)
-Inventory management can be outright stupid!!! (Are you dying, have no space in your inventory and come across a health item? Gotta decide what you need the least [probably ammo] so you can throw it away, place the health item its place and then use it!) This should have been fixed immediately but never will be!
-Absurdly redundant! Not in a horrible way, but more of an immersion-breaking way (e.g. beat the game with [spoiler] Leon [/spoiler] and excited to play as [spoiler] Claire [/spoiler] or vice-versa? You'll end up doing essentially the same exact thing, even solving the same exact puzzles and taking the same exact paths! It kind of ruins the story IMO).
-Not that many models (i.e. enemies; there's a zombie with a scary mouth, a zombie without a nose, a black zombie, an asian zombie, some wearing cop uniforms, some in armor, some that look exactly the same with [spoiler] white eyes and some purple gas coming out their mouth [/spoiler], a [spoiler] plant [/spoiler] zombie and that's about it. A little more variety would be greatly appreciated!
-Zombies with their eyes/ears blown off can still have perfect perception (it would have been cool if they behaved like [spoiler] lickers, who are blind but can detect you if they smell/hear you.) [/spoiler]
-Enemies never drop anything! (Yes, scarcity adds to the horror factor but you would think that you'd find at least a single bullet on a cop zombie or maybe even a flash/frag grenade on the armored ones, right?)
[spoiler] -Laser sight is only available on one weapon for either Leon/Claire (I think); considering that RE4 was my favorite, this is kinda disappointing. I would have hoped this would have been an unlockable for a 2nd/3rd playthrough, but it isn't. [/spoiler]
- Apparently you can $$$ BUY cheats $$$ that you'd otherwise unlock by doing difficult tasks... that's just lame.

A brilliant re-envisioning of the PS1 classic.  It's got the atmosphere, the scares, the puzzles, and all the survival horror goodness made more playable for the modern era.  The gameplay has been updated to the third-person shooter style that has become the series standard since RE4, and the graphics are top notch.  My only criticisms would be:

- The limited inventory.  I know this is a staple of the genre but the amount of space individual items takes up seems totally arbitrary and it just necessitates backtracking.  Could have done without it.

- The boss fights.  The bosses look cool but generally every boss fight is the same.  Run away, turn around, shoot weak spot.  Run away, turn around, shoot weak spot.  Repeat.  The deliberately slow and clunky controls do not help the matter.

- The "2nd run" options that take the place of a NG+ mode and theoretically continue the story are too similar gameplay wise to the original campaign and don't really make sense story-wise.  I couldn't motivate myself to finish the 2nd playthrough even though you need to in order to see the "true" ending.

Still, even if you only play the main campaign, it's still an excellent experience and very much worth your time, not just for survival horror fans but for all gamers.

This is by far my most favourite Resident Evil game ever. I played the original as a kid on the N64 and simply just fell in love with horror and zombie shooter games ever since. The remake version may have some alterations from the original that changed the story plot in a few ways, but the majority of the Resident Evil lore pretty much stays intact. If you're looking for a zombie shooter game experience that really emphasises on horror, survival and resource management, this is definitely a game worth playing.

Gameplay
RE2 Remake is an over-the-shoulder style third person shooter that involves resource management and a lot of puzzle solving to navigate your way through an overran city. The gun-play isn't too bad and it's very similar to other third person titles. But don't go expecting headshots to easily kill a common zombie. Inventory management is also highly encouraged in RE2, and the game teaches you that early on when you start off the story with very limited resources and inventory space. Puzzles are also very well implemented, with hints and pieces cleverly scattered throughout the environment. Furthermore, puzzles were also made in a way to emphasis the mysteriousness of Resident Evil's backstory, which really does make you curious more about the lore.

Graphics and Environment
Game graphics are simply just amazing, as expected from AAA titles nowadays utilising physically-based rendering. The atmosphere and environment was modelled and rendered exceptionally well to convey the horror elements of a zombie apocalypse. Details such as blood stains, bullet holes, barricades and abandoned belongings really conveys the citizens' desperate attempts at defending themselves from the zombies, and makes you wonder what their final moments were like. The darkness in some areas, especially during your first playthrough, really puts you on edge to always have your handgun pointed in a "ready-to-shoot" stance, expecting a infected zombie to attack you at any moment.

Replay Value
There are 4 routes in total for the RE2 Remake's main story campaign; Leon A & B, Claire A & B. You can either choose to play as Leon or Claire, and experience each of their own story path on how they managed to survive the T-virus outbreak that completely devastated Raccoon City. Each route features it's own distinctive routes and exclusive firearms to use, which also helps to refresh the experience. Furthermore, if you do get bored of the main story campaign, you can also experience RE2's minigames in the 4th Survivor free DLC.

Mods
As expected from a PC game, Resident Evil also features a very dedicated modding community. If you do ever get bored of the game, there's plenty of easy to install community-made mods that can really spice up your experience.

Everything about this game, from the mechanics, to the level design, pacing, graphics, writing, etc. is perfection. One of my favorite mechanical improvements over previous Resident Evil games is that you must sacrifice a secondary item (eg knife or grenade) to shake off an enemy. Between this and the dramatically limited ammo supply that forces you to choose which monsters to kill and which to avoid, every single zombie in this game becomes an interesting encounter.

Add to this the surprising quality of the dialogue and motion-capture acting, and you have my favorite Resident Evil game of all time.

I dearly hope that this game is not a flash in the pan for Capcom and they continue to pursue this kind of excellence in future Resident Evil titles.

I think they did a great job remaking Resident Evil 2. From the scenarios to the extra content, and many features of the original game expanded on, redone to improve and add to the experience. I love so many things about this game and even after beating it there are many reasons to keep coming back to it.

Cons:
• Pacing in latter half of game suffers - Police Station 10/10, Sewer 8/10, Lab 6/10
• Atmosphere declines in quality in latter half of the game - the Lab is underwhelming and lacks spook/creep
• Mr X feels out of place outside of the Police Station (in both gameplay and mood)
• Music is lacking throughout - which is a crime considering RE2 Classic has one of the best scores in gaming
• Music in latter half of the game is comprised of cliche "loud" action tracks that are unimaginative and forgettable

Pros:
• Superb graphics
• Mood in Police Station is sombre, creepy and nostalgic - they knocked it out of the park here
• The atmospheric music (what little there is of it) is excellent in the first half of the game
• The zombie action is peerless - it's never been done better, anywhere, ever
• Zombies full of character and surprises - stumbling into furniture, crawling across desks, and dismembered by weapons they continue to crawl at you - 10/10
• Mr X adds pressure in just the right way - forcing you into harms way as you flee - this works expertly in the Police Station but is poorly implemented in the Lab

Conclusion:
It's a schizophrenic game - the first half is an expertly curated survival horror game set in one of the most tangible haunted-houses ever seen in gaming - but the latter half feels like it was developed by teenagers.

There is a distinct split in the fanbase between this and the 1998 original, and having been a life-long fan of the original, I was nervous to even try this. 

After a few blind runs, breaking to play the original again, and coming back for comparison, I find that there are some pros and cons, but nostalgia is largely driving the superfluous complaints such as Mr. X not having two flaming arms (I prefer is remade look, honestly).

My first playthrough, I went slow and took in the beautifully rendered versions of the RPD halls I spent so much time in as a kid. I didn't use puzzle guides, and I just let it flow naturally. That turned into pushing for speed runs, optimizing gameplay as much as possible, and generally playing through runs over and over again. I'm still not finished doing that 42.4 hours into it. 

After playing the original and coming back to this, I find that I much prefer the pacing, boss-battle layouts, storytelling, and gameplay of this reimagining. It's not without its flaws, but I always felt like, even when I was stuck, progression was right around the corner. If I failed, it was because of my own actions. Every success felt meaningful, whether it was leaving the right zombies and taking out seemingly pointless ones that would turn out to be a nuisance later, or if it was overcoming the super tyrant. Every decision had an impact, but there was always a way to fix bad decisions with a little work or clever thinking. 

In the original Claire A run, I kept preparing for boss fights that were teased but never popped up, then had multiple back-to-back boss fights in the end sequence, was left stuck by things that weren't puzzling but poorly presented on a couple of occasions, and when it ended, despite taking much longer, it felt short for a run. I get that it's made for A/B runs, like the 2019 version, but you can pick any single run and feel as if you got a full campaign experience in the 2019 version. Perfect for doing a quick and fulfilling run after work or on a weekend, but if you prefer a longer experience with all angles covered, the opposite runs are there, too. That, and if I was stuck, it wasn't because of a poorly presented key feature in a corner or other nonsense. It was because I wasn't doing something right. 

Then, there's the extra content. '98 had an impressive amount of content for the time, and even more than a lot of AAAs of this time period, but 2019 kicks it up a notch. Not only are the classic Hunk and Tofu modes available, but Tofu gets different variations, and there are all-new original sequences that go into detail about side-characters that never get fleshed out in either version's main story. These are challenging and fun, but they add to the lore, too. Once I've played through and mastered every main scenario, I look forward to truly tearing those apart. 

For combat, I love that the modern setup maintains the tension that fixed angles and tank controls built in the 90's while being far tighter and more engaging. Combat is harder but more rewarding, and you have to actually think before you start snapping off shots. A lot of folks said items were rare in the original, but I went through the RPD wiping out every enemy in sight without ever worrying about ammo. In the remake, I was bothering to make my shots count and strategically targeting different enemies in different ways depending on the situation, and I was never flush with ammo until right before the final fight thanks to my careful gameplay throughout. It wasn't just to horde, either. Leaving enemies (or not) had real consequences later on that fueled each decision. That final run to the finish line was a rewarding Rambo-style romp with all the ammo I'd saved leading up to it, and it was a great thrill to finish my very first run that way after being uptight the whole time.

Mr. X is also a big talking point, and I love how he's implemented. It would be nice to have an X-free run first like in the original, but he was implemented well in this game's 4 story scenarios, and he doesn't feel too overbearing in any bad ways. In fact, once you  know the routes and your goals, you won't see him for more than 10 minutes of any complete run (going slowly). Those short spats of unscripted chases through large areas sure are tense, though. This is better in my opinion than the scripted popups of the original's B scenarios, and he just functions better overall.

The only cons I have against this version is that the A/B scenarios share boss fights and puzzles. They still present different sides of the story, but the continuity errors are distracting. However, they do make speed runs easier since you don't need to learn different story placements or combat strategies  for the most part.  Also, while the soundtrack is great, I'd prefer the original or a remix of the original without having to pay extra for the privilege. Given the rest of the DLC was handled properly, that's forgivable, though. 

It was awesome to dive into Raccoon City as a kid with the '98 version and countless lasting memories stemmed from it, and I'm happy that Capcom not only brought that feeling back in new and exciting ways for adults who grew up with it like me, but also made some major improvements that just make it a better game. 

I'll still occasionally go back to my old bread and butter for the tank controls and nostalgia, but RE2Make has taken the crown as my go-to RE experience despite the relatively minor flaws.
