If you wanna play a legit remake that truly pays homage to the original Resident Evil 2, while keeping it modern and enough to stand out on it's own then this is the game you should be playing. I'd recommend this game to anyone who has played the original sometime in their life. Even if you haven't? Give this one a try over Resident Evil 3 remake. 

Immediately, just loading up the game and you get drawn in by the amazing cutscene of the truck driver, and depending on which protagonist you pick - Leon, or Claire, you get to witness sort of different intros. I find both stories for the characters to be very much like the original, with some twists here and there. The game for starters is really beautiful. Leon and Claire themselves are at their best yet in the series (even if it's a remake and not like a sequel game). They both look amazing. And you truly do feel connected to these characters. I think what I enjoy the most about the remake is how human they made both Leon and Claire feel compared to their 90's counterparts that felt more...out of place, and just not relatable. 

Raccoon City looks awesome, even if it's outbreak state. The RPD is spooky, but so much more believable in terms of you know some weird and crazy stuff has happened there. Pretty much every location throughout the game has been expanded, and made to feel more like believable in terms of the atmosphere. You truly at times just get amazed in the detail of each location you visit. The ambience, and sometimes almost eerie feeling of it all. I think they truly spent a lot of time crafting this world for us OG fans and new RE fans to get truly lost in.

The story itself isn't much different in terms of the OG. Some tweaks here and there. You do have count stories and such much like the original where you can play it differently. As in if you went to the Police Station the original way through the city, in your next play-through you could essentially have it start you immediately at the RPD but on a different path. In the end in my opinion, it doesn't really matter which one you play or like the most. I feel both are able to make for an enjoyable playing experience for OG fans and new RE fans alike.

Now, as for the zombies and enemies you come across in this game..in my opinion? They are done so well that at times, you feel like they rent spent time on making the zombies feel well..like zombies. The Cerberus hounds, Lickers, Planet Monsters, and even the Alligator are truly much more frightening in this remake. The only enemy I'm afraid you won't see are the giant spiders. I'm not sure if their missing is truly a bad thing? Even though they were a part of the original in the sewers..I personally didn't mind their absence. It's truly something you don't really pay much attention. Oh, and the G-Spawns are truly so icky and probably so well done. There are times in the sewers I just felt extremely icky and uneasy because of them.

Of course, we can't talk about Resident Evil 2 without talking about Mr. X. Truly one Capcom's most known villains in Resident Evil history. Though, I feel the remake truly makes him shine and standout the best he ever has. I feel up until you meet him in the game, everything seems to be quite easy in terms of navigating the police station. It isn't until his appearance, where you then realize he truly is unstoppable and will stalk you throughout the entire half of the game (if you're Claire he meets a more early demise than with Leon). I think his presence is truly nerve-wracking at times because you have to think about each time you enter a room on how long you're gonna stay there, making less noise, and being able to get out in time before he barges his way and finds you. It's more calculated and you truly feel like you're always having to avoid him and I kind of like that. 

I also think Sherry this time around is more likeable as well. In the original (though it was the 90s and character development wasn't really a huge spread out thing in the gaming world). I tend to find the presence of her character, and when you plat her in Claire's scenario more exciting and honestly? Terrifying. Chief Brian Irons is truly one sick character in the series. And that's saying a lot considering this serious is notorious for messed up characters. Her and Claire's connection I feel is more believable than in the original where in the OG it felt like Claire was just immediately must protect Sherry without any real character bonding. As where in the remake, we see Claire kind of becoming curious about Sherry and her parents, and why she's alone and to even at the half way point realizing she needs to care for this character because her parents sure haven't..or can't. 

As for Leon and Ada? I feel their relationship is more comical, but interesting in this remake. Ada from the get go is very intriguing and very alluring. Leon is immediately curious himself, and it's obvious why. I think their short time together in the game you kind of see two character at the opposite sides of the tracks, but in a way by fate, have sort similar goals (even though Ada's are more profit and personal gain). They, in the end, just wanna survive. I also think allowing their characters to experience the act of betrayal but in a way knowing if it weren't for each other? They wouldn't have gotten that far as they had so in the end they needed each other. Ada is also much more likeable in the remake as well. 

A couple of more things to end this off since I've typed quite a bit already... William and Annette themselves feel more real, and are well thought out and done this time around. I also think much like the OG, we get two versions of Annette is both stories with Leon and Claire. Leon getting the more shrug-offish and you won't take me alive. Where as with Claire, we see a more open, but guarded and determined character. I think it was nice seeing both variations because we got to see how Anette reacted to two different characters, along with their counterparts being one: her daughter. And the other being Ada who she was immediately weary of as where Leon wasn't as quick to catch on.

William himself is a unique character/antagonist. I think his entrance in the remake is one of the more spooky character entrances in the series. It could be maybe in the 90s, unless you were playing Silent Hill or something..games to me weren't all that scary. But then again, I've always been an avid horror fan so scaring me isn't as easy. But, I find William to be one of the more terrifying antagonist in the series. Even more than the remake Nemesis because at least with William, it feels fresh and more haunting to see. Especially after his transformations where as with Nemesis the in the 3rd remake, he just feels kind of like an obstacle and not really scary in terms of his original counterpart. 

I'd say as for cons for me? It'd be the lack of story development of the side characters. Yes, they were eventually thrown into those weird DLC games. But, they really weren't there to be canonically accurate. Other than Hunk's story of course. I would have liked to have seen them all get a better redemption, along with Marvin. He truly should have had a DLC. It would have been nice to have seen his character before Leon and Claire had made it to the station. Though, in the 3rd remake, we do find out how he ends up in the condition he is in the 2nd game so that was cool I guess? But it shouldn't have took another game to have known, or seen that in my opinion.

Anyway, to sum it up: I highly recommend this game for any OG RE fan to any person wanting to get into the series and maybe you've played the RE 1 remake from years ago. It's a real good start, and I truly don't think you need to the play the OG one to enjoy this game. I feel they did a great job at recapturing the game, and giving you the story with a modern update and appeal so it doesn't feel dated like the PlayStation Era counterpart.

[h1] A Different Game, A Different Beast Altogether [/h1]

Resident Evil 2 is one of the best games ever made. It's legacy knows no bounds and is rightfully responsible for the Resident Evil franchise to have found such great success. It was the first in a long line of cheesy, fun, gripping games.

Resident Evil 2, this game, the remake, is/was a difficult game for me to properly analyze. While it does some things better than the original (namely in the mechanics of gameplay, graphics is a no duh and with it atmosphere), but it also screws other stuff up, but not in a way that would ever make me want to say this game is awful.

[h1] The Good [/h1]

The return of survival horror has truly been a delight. Resident Evil 7 was a proper return to form, and this remake of RE2 continues the tradition. Say what you will about whether it is or isn't survival horror, the point is that you have little HP, little ammunition, limited inventory space, a whole lotta crap to grab and chug around, and lots of undead who want to eat you alive. THAT is what survival horror is all about, and this game certainly meets that head on.

However, the gameplay has been spiced up from the original RE2, now with the over-the-shoulder camera popularized by this game's predecessor RE4, the knife save from RE1 remake, and a more thoughtful approach to crafting health and ammo. The beasts of the Umbrella corporation are tougher than they've ever been, taking bullet after bullet after bullet in the head, and can easily over-whelm you. Note that this isn't poor design for a game that's SUPPOSED to be about NOT killing EVERYTHING and instead managing your resources, picking your paths, and doing everything you can to AVOID as many negative situations as possible. You get used to it, and learn some rather clever tricks along the way to make your game session easier, faster, and over-all more enjoyable.

Puzzles are here, and they aren't too easy but also not too hard. They are right in the middle. Well, most of them. Some of them really are too simple, whereas others can take quite some time to solve (I'm looking at you wiring puzzle).

The police station has gotten a bit of a redesign since the last time gamers saw it, and I would say it is for the better. There's plenty to do, and it all winds up and around nicely. The same can be said about the sewers, which in the original RE2, was but a very small, insignificant and mostly unmemorable location if it wasn't for the giant alligator. I quite like what they have done to the sewers, in terms of its layout and design.

The story is less campy and the characters have some more charm and "professionalism" in their performance, and in some ways, I consider it better than the original. In others...well...let's just say...despite OG RE2 being hella campy and goofy at times...I'd rather have the original than the new one. More like a splice of the two. More on that later.

On top of all this, there's a good amount of additional content to play, including the 4th survivor and even the Tofu mini-game as well, returning from the classic RE2. Everything else is new, and puts a fresh spin on the game (for better and worse).

[h1] The Bad [/h1]

While the story has some good bits, it starts to fall apart when you play both Leon and Claire's stories back to back. They fight the same bosses, in the same rooms, in the exact same way, besides 1 or 2 other bosses and the final spoiler boss (at least that has remained in-tact). In the original RE2, depending on who you played first, would have an effect on the story of the character, resulting in them having to fight different bosses, find items in different locations, and over-all have a much different progression than your first playthrough (along side alternate story bits). Most of this remains true, except the story and boss part. The character's leave notes to each other, whereas in the original RE2 they would have actually spoken to one another, whether it was via radio or in person. Nope, not here.

While I never really disliked Mr. X's greater inclusion here, constantly chasing down the player, in fact I kinda like his inclusion (there's a lot of ways to get around him and if you "git gud" he's honestly not that big of an issue), I recognize some glaring problems with him. He is a complete pace breaker, and forces the player to accommodate for him, which can lead to unintended, frustrating experiences. You could say that's a good thing in a survival horror game, but it would be nice if he was a little more scripted and not constantly up your ass. Too much time is spent with the player waiting in rooms or taking the long way around just so you don't have to deal with him, and that would be my biggest gripe. Unless you're a speed running pro, Mr. X is gonna bring your game to a grinding halt, and I can see why people wouldn't like that about this remake.

The laboratory section of this remake of RE2 is small, short, and lack-luster compared to the original. I found the lab design of the original RE2 better than the remake, because it had more interesting rooms and more varied monsters to fight. I also miss the giant venus fly-trap plant monsters. Instead, we have zombies with vines all over them and you gotta shoot these sacs on them to kill them or burn them to death. Honestly you could keep the same mechanics but just, visually, aesthetically turn them into actual plant monsters, like they were before.


[h1] The Ugly [/h1]

Zombies taking so many shots to the head is kind of annoying. Granted, I know how to make my life easy (shoot legs till they break, knife to death), but that takes an awful lot of time. I'd rather there be MORE zombies that you can kill faster than fewer zombies who take a million shots to kill. The police station does feel a little too...empty...sometimes.

The police chief is a mockery of what he used to be. All that charm and mysteriousness about him is all gone. I mean sure, he was a one of character, but I much prefer the "bad guy pretending to be a good guy" shtick more than "I'm literally just an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" shtick. Why is this here and not in the "the bad" category? Because it's not bad...it just feels lame in comparison to the original. The game isn't any worse with the police chief's new characterization, it works in the plot, consistent with his "new character," and still establishes him as a villain. It's just UGLY.

The beginning section of the game, in the streets of Raccoon City, is WAY too damn short. In the original, it was a prime time to teach the player that you can't actually kill every zombie without taking some serious damage, or dying outright. It was the perfect place to teach the player to run away, and pick your paths to avoid confrontations. This rendition of RE2 actually has ALL of those sections present, but splits them around in different places, so you actually end up taking more "familiar" routes LATER in the game than earlier. I don't know how to feel about this change.

[h1] Verdict [/h1]

Resident Evil 2 Remake is...different than the original in ways that make me look at it with a different perspective than, say, RE1 remake, which is a bonafide improvement over the original. For this game, you have to approach it from the perspective of "Resident Evil 2, but re-imagined." It's a bit more than a remake. It is faithful enough to its source material, but it's wrapped together nicely enough with new designs, features, and direction that I don't walk away feeling upset.

Over-all solid game, and I'll probably play it again in the future. It also has lots of mod support, so that's a plus too!

They dropped certain aspects of the original like how choices in one route will impact the other route, but overall the game is very enjoyable and keeps true to the spirit of the original Resident Evil 2. Easily one of the best installments in the whole series.

This is by far one the most enjoyable, yet unapologetically difficult games I have ever played in my life. This is a game that completely breaks normal gaming conventions to offer its players a refreshing game play experience that players wont find anywhere else. It is hard, it is terrifying, and it is beautiful. It is truly difficult to find anything negative to say about this game. 

If I were to describe this game in one sentence, I would describe it as a resource management, escape room style puzzle-solving survival horror game. The gist of the game is that you run around a giant map solving progression puzzles that allow to access new areas and collect new progression items. Its like a 3D MetroidVania game on steroids. The scope of the map is truly astonishing. Just when you think it can't get any bigger, you discover an entirely new area of the map. There's a lot of backtracking in this game, but the back tracking doesn't feel cumbersome. Every area offers unique challenges that force the player to strategically navigate through the map. Add that with the constantly evolving hellscape and you've got a winning recipe for audience engagement. I'll talk more about that later.

There's so many things this game does to create an effective horror experience that it's hard to list them concisely. Firstly, ammo and resources are scarce and finite. Every bullet you shoot is a bullet that you're never going to get back. Every hit that you take is a hit that you're going to have to waste a healing item on. At no point will you ever have more resources than you need. Whereas most games focus on shooting your way through hoards of enemies, this one forces the player to choose very carefully which enemies they are going to kill and which ones they will let live. This game generally tends to prioritize avoidance over combat. If you run through a hallway that is filled with enemies, chances are you're going to have to go through that hallway again at some point, and if you didn't kill the enemies the first time, they'll still be waiting for you when you come back. As tempting as it is to kill every enemy, bullets are a rare commodity, and you'll find yourself in a really bad situation if don't have bullets when you really need them. Alternatively, you may find yourself wishing you had killed an enemy the first time you went through an area as opposed to the second or third time. It's a tough call to make. 

Lots of the horror comes from the fact that players must force themselves into the most soul-crushingly terrifying situations imaginable in order progress through certain areas. There's an overwhelming dread as you arduously navigate through tight corridors with nothing but a few bullets between you and the monsters. Often, the player must force themself to backtrack through hostile areas to collect items that they either didn't have room for, or previously didn't have access to. You will repeatedly be force to make decisions on whether to trek through hostile areas for a second time to collect something, or to abandon that already scarce resource that could save you in the long run.  

All of this is made worse by the hellish creatures that work their way into the map throughout the game. If you thought getting through an area once was tough, wait till you come back an hour later when the halls are littered with near-invincible monsters that chase you for making too much noise. This means no more bullets and no more running. Every path has to be strategically planned to get you from one point to another without all chaos breaking loose. To add insult to injury, there's a giant 8 ft tall indestructible monster that is perpetually searching for you throughout the game map. It actively listens for running and weapon fire, and patrols near key items, incomplete puzzles, and areas of high traffic. 

The pacing of this game is uniquely perfect. When developing a game, the goal of pacing in is often  to keep the player on their toes by meticulously crafting a series of fast paced experiences that quickly and seamlessly transition through one another. On the contrary, this game creates memorable moments through slower, yet equally engaging gameplay. As mentioned previously, the horror in this game is the slow, arduous kind; the kind that aims to cripple it's players with fear in such a way that every fiber of their soul wants to stop progressing. This style of horror is perfectly suited for the slower pacing of RE2. This pacing highlights moments of intensity and allows the game to breath so the player can fully appreciate everything this game has to offer. 

Just when you thought it couldn't get any better, this game has four different game modes which are all worth playing. It effectively quadruples the length of an already gigantic game. These game modes are like a remix of each other. Some start you in different areas, and some give you access to different weapons/ progression items. As arbitrary as these changes may sound, they actually end up changing the game quite significantly. The order in which you collect certain progression items changes which in turn forces you to use your knowledge of the map from previous playthroughs  to determine how to progress. You end up visiting different areas, fighting different bosses, etc;

Finally, this game is stunningly beautiful. The graphics are crisp, clean, and polished. Even on lower graphics settings, this game looks amazing. While I could ramble on about lighting, textures, movement, etc, the game speaks for itself. If you want to see what the graphics are like, check out the trailer. 

In conclusion, there's no singular thing that makes this game great. It's the culmination of all these things that work together to create an immersively enjoyable experience. If you play this game and determine that you like it, go ahead and play RE3 Remake. It's spiritually very similar, but with less emphasis on horror and puzzle solving, and more emphasis on combat. If you didn't like the balancing of RE2 Remake, you'll likely enjoy the balancing of RE3 Remake.

Almost everything you hoped this REmake would be.  Almost.  

There are really only a few minor quibbles I have with this game.  I'm not really hung up on tradition.  I was never a part of "The Split" in the fanbase when Resident Evil 4 came out, and other people loved or hated it and the direction the series took afterwards.  I find these opinions are largely dependent on what game they played first.  I got S-Ranks across the board in the old games, and I liked most of the new games just fine.  

Even though this is a REmake, I'm not doing an exhaustive analysis.  The original RE:2 was my favorite, and this is outstanding.  If that's all you needed to know, go buy it.  What follows are just a few minor design issues I found that stood out.  

First of all, maybe I've been spoiled by the likes of heavily-modded Fallout games, but I find absolutely no reason why random zombies will sometimes take around five to seven headshots to completely kill.  If I had sh*t aim, and they were all bodyshots, I'd completely understand that, but the hidden "crit" system is vague and unnecessary.  The game utilizes a sort of steady-aim mechanic, where you are rewarded with extra flat damage when standing perfectly still and aiming for a couple seconds, with a supposedly(?) increased chance to completely explode the head in a gratifying shower of gore.  Ostensibly this is to reward players with good aim and positioning skills with more damage, but with the exception of perhaps one of the pistols, I found the payoff so rare it wasn't worth thinking about. 

My next minor gripe is the famous Mr. X, who at one point will stalk you through the police station.  He does actually look for you, by the way, it's not just a sound effect from another area as you hear him stomping around, though he does teleport to certain "blocks" of the map geometry to keep up with you.  This can be a minor nuisance because if you sprint across the map to leave him behind, sometimes he'll pop up in front of you instead.  But mostly my gripe is just how safe you are.  

Because of how the map is designed, there are numerous areas where it would "feel cheap" if Mr. X could get you, such as most areas where there are typewriters.  Other areas he ignores are where it would be basically impossible to avoid him, probably to avoid complaints from the playerbase after.  I found this flaccid design of his patrol system to be increasingly annoying as I discovered more and more spots where I could simply hang out, and break immersion for myself listening to him clomp around ineffectually looking for me.  Tough sh*t, Boss, I got magic doors.    

So, RE:2 was basically famous for the "2nd Run" mechanics, i.e. when you finish the game with one character, you play it with the other to see what they were up to all that time.  In the original you had to play the game at least four times to see the complete story.  

Well, not here.  The mechanic still exists of course.  The game is tougher on 2nd runs, with some minor changes to the weapons, mechanics, and puzzles.  But it's really just a RE-shuffling of content you've already seen.  Unless you're just itching for more of the game (which is entirely possible), there's NO story-driven reason to do these runs, except for the alternate ending.  

"Emergency Defense" items reappear from previous REmakes, and they include the knife this time around.  Knives are especially fragile, except obviously the "infinite" one you can unlock by shooting all the little Raccoon statues in the game.  I don't mind the knife having durability, but it drastically changes the rest of the game's combat in one major way: ammo.  

For people who were never obsessive enough to do it, knife-only or heavily assisted runs (such as shooting a zombie in the kneecaps and then finishing them with the knife) were a thing for a long, long time.  A staple of more advanced runs, even. By giving knives durability, locking players out of the eccentric and masochistic option, the game in turn has to make absolutely sure that the experience has enough ammunition and healing items to get through ALL difficulties of the game, and then scale that math down across them.  To use the extremely technical industry term, that means you have "a f*ck-ton of ammo," if you're comparing this to a more traditional survival horror experience.  

Now, I love action horror at least as much as survival horror, but between natural ammunition spawns and mixable gunpowders, you can probably kill everything in the game twice over, unless you're a spray-and-pray youtuber.  This completely removes one of the primary crucial decisions of survival horror - to shoot, or go around?  I would say that for most people whose anxiety scales with atmosphere, they may not even notice this shift.  But for the rest of us, it really ramps down the intensity.   

Finally, let's talk about those unlocks.  Classic RE games rewarded you for beating the game on better ranks to unlock costumes, infinite weapons, etc.  But this time around the system falls flat.  It still has those items, of course, including the 4th Survivor Hunk's mode.  But you get all of them by either casual runs on Standard difficulty, or S-Ranks.  There's NOTHING inbetween.  Don't get me wrong, a lot of people will probably delight in the fact that the system is still there at all, but most people who have played the original are 35+ years old by now, we're not interested nor have the time to repeatedly practice the game until we beat it in under TWO HOURS just to have that bit of extra fun when the game is no longer a challenge in the first place.

What I love most about RE2 is it's ability to make you feel scared without relying on cheap jumpscares and cliche tropes such as 'the darkness'. Instead, RE2 focuses on making you tense - REALLY tense. I was never truly 'afraid' of anything, instead I found myself crying in terror at the occasional small hordes of zombies I had to squeeze past in narrow hallways, or the scariest of all, Mr X. He is one of the main improvements that puts this remake above the original, besides the obvious graphical and technical enhancements. He is simply an invincible TANK of man that stalks you very loudly, and very quickly while all at the same time, you are attempting to dodge zombies and other abominations. The tension this creates is nearly indescribable, but just know it made me audibly gasp multiple times and stand out of my seat. He appears multiple times throughout the game, sadly though the tension created the first time he appears never reaches the same height again for the duration of the game.

Luckily, RE2 has a brilliant story to fill the gap provided by a slowly-deteriorating-in-tension Mr X. Without spoiling anything, you get to play as either Leon or Claire. Leon is a police officer, and Claire is just a civilian looking for her brother. While both characters each have their own motivations, the story that takes place for each is roughly the same; Although, there is some unique deviation depending on the character you play as (such as new areas, new characters, and as a result of different motivations, a different main objective). On top of this, upon beating the game you are rewarded with a second playthrough for the corresponding character that starts of slightly different and has you facing the same threats with increased difficulty and timing. Puzzle solutions and item placements are also changed as to keep you on your toes. This, and the optional challenges and unlocks provides hours of gameplay to ensure your money is well spent.

Overall, RE2 is a genuine masterpiece deserving of the love it gets. If you're new to the horror genre, a veteran, or even if this is your first Resident Evil or the last - you seriously can't go wrong buying this game.

Good game, with some frustrating design choices. First, the good. The game looks amazing, and does a great job freaking you out. There are times where I literally had a hard time controlling my mouse. I've tried to limit how much I look online, so I'm surprised, and it does a excellent job of that. Some of it is predictable, but for the most part you just don't know what's coming on your first play through. It greatly succeeds as a horror game.

Now, the bad. The boss choices and what it takes to kill pretty much any enemy is just really bad. The weapons all feel like they have no power. Why am I shooting a zombie up to 12 times in the head? You will read about people defending this mechanic, but don't believe it. It's ridiculous and a bad design choice. There should be a reward for accuracy, even if it's a space the size of quarter on their brain stem there should be a way to down them quickly. As it sits, there's no reward in his game for accuracy. You can shoot a leg off to make them crawl to save ammo, but in most cases the area is to tight to get past them and they can still grab you. At a minimum, there should be a finishing move to kill them off while on the ground. 

Now, the bosses, and mini bosses. None of the boss fights feel good. You pretty much just get smacked around until you pour enough ammo into them to bring them down. Mostly because our hero's run like they are slow jogging. Another stupid design choice. Why are these hero's that are in such good shape, jogging like they are 70 years old? There should be a run mechanic with a cool down. There's also an invincible enemy in the game, which very few games get right and this one didn't. So, I've got flame grenades, acid grenades, laser sighted handgun and and fully automatic weapon and I can't take it down? There's no armor plate on it's head, so rationally head shots should bring it down. Nope, head shots in this game are a non functional.

I know that sounds like a lot of complaining, but it really is a good game. It could have been great with a lot more thought into rewarding accuracy.

This review will not contain any grading system for the game besides the "Yes" recommendation that i initially gave. The review will also not comment on any of the DLC's that the store page offers or any of the game modes besides the main story. I have also not played the original Resident evil 2 so i will not be drawing any parallels between it and the remake.

                                                                     !!MINOR SPOILER WARNING!!

First i would like to inform anyone reading my review that at the point i'm writing this i have completed 2 runs with both playable characters on 2 different difficulties, Standard and Hardcore.

Optimization/Bugs:
As someone with a low-mid end PC (1050Ti, Ryzen 5 2400G, 16GB RAM/ 3200Mhz DDR40) i can safely say that the game runs smooth (60-80FPS) on medium settings. Framerate dips appeared only once in one of the police station hallways in the East Wing. 
The game seems to be almost bug-free as well, the only time i have encountered one being in my second playthrough with Claire (camera bug that prevented me from looking down), in the small transitional area (basketball field) between the station and the sewers.

Graphics/Aesthetic: 
From my point of view the game looks great. I had nothing to complain about the textures, lighting, or overall look. That being said your opinion may differ depending on the graphical settings you use, and the graphics quality you hope for.

Gameplay: 
This is the part of the game that made me want to write this review in the first place, since it gave me a lot of mixed feelings about the way the game is meant to be played and the design logic (or lack thereof in some cases) that went in the map/arena layout and shooting mechanics as well as in the puzzles and the inventory management.

First off, the map design. The game is split into 3 main areas, the Police Station, the Sewers and the Umbrella Lab, each with their corresponding boss fight. The first one (Police station) is in my opinion a balanced zone. The Station is split into 4 main zones, the West wing, the Main Hall, the East wing, and the Parking. While the Main Hall serves more as a Lobby than an actual zone, the West and East wings of the building are somewhat symmetrically complex with a decent amount of puzzles and shortcuts. The parking acts like a basement of sorts, and while solving the puzzles in there requires backtracking to the before mentioned zones, it still feels somewhat separate from the main building.
The second main area of the game, The Sewers, is needlessly frustrating in its layout while being quite simple at the same time. It is filled with huge rooms that connect different layers of the zone through elevators, and lead to dead ends in some cases. That combined with really though enemies that block your way means you will only be able to freely backtrack once you cleared the areas of mutants. If you're running low on resources, though luck, in that case you will need to either risk kiting the monsters while dodging their pretty unforeseeable hit boxes, or try and cheese their despawn/respawn mechanic by luring them to a ledge, then running past them before they respawn. To top it all off, this section of the game also features a mandatory key collecting puzzle that requires 4 different parts. One of those parts also acts as the key for a drawbridge and is the only key item with multiple uses in the Sewer section, leaving players that got confused by the map layout even more clueless, making them fear they might just be missing a non-existent pathway.
The third zone, the Umbrella Lab, is quite forgettable and simple when it comes to its layout. This time the lab is also split into 3  main sections, the west wing, the east wing, and a lobby of sorts connecting those 2 with long bridges, but all 3 sections are more ore less their own thing, with no reason to backtrack between them. The puzzles also seem to be easier than the ones in the first 2 zones.

Enemy design is the biggest problem i have with the game. The regular zombie seems to have a "temperamental" health bar, meaning it will either get its head split open with 2 bullets, or take an entire mag to the head and still get back up after being already downed 2 times. Non-boss special enemies seem to not suffer from this problem, although all of them can be easily dealt with in a playthrough with Claire , while being extremely challenging in one with Leon, mainly because of the different weapons the 2 protagonist acquire during the game. Bosses have gotten somewhat of a "Souls-like treatment" with their attacks being telegraphed by subtle queues, this being in the detriment of the player since the twitchy nature of their movement and the shifted (and close to the character) 3rd person perspective will most likely make you miss them. The attacks are also only proximity based, not time based, meaning you can freely spin in circles and have the boss follow you like a little puppy while at the same time not being able to shoot accurately, locking both of you in somewhat of a stalemate until you feel confident enough to make a move. All of this would be relatively fine, if it weren't for the extremely small arenas in which you will have to carry most of the boss battles. Using utility items like the knife on non-boss enemies is also quite a problem, since the regular zombie wont give you the option to escape all of its grab attacks every time, even if you have the utility necessary to do so in your inventory. The plant based mutants that replace the regular zombies in the lab are poorly designed in relation with map and the tips that the game gives you. While being vulnerable to fire and having a note that says "burn them to the ground", since they infinitely respawn in the areas you find them, it is much better to just stagger them with your flamethrower than to entirely kill them, saving lots of fuel.

Overall the game has no major issues, but manages to get quite frustrating by piling lots of small bad design decisions on top of each other during most of the playthrough.

My first introduction to the Resident Evil series and I'm not disappointed. I generally hate horror games because it's just long hours of stress but I enjoyed Dead Space 1 so I expected that I'd get used to it as I did with Dead Space. Luckily, RE2 is a very enjoyable experience and while it leans a little more towards the horror in the earlier areas, RE2 gradually settles into its more action direction. While not bad, I personally felt a bit disappointed in how quickly scares didn't affect me. However, the thrill of the chase is very much present constantly.

The inventory system and slow-paced movement against Michael Myers-fast, bullet-sponge zombies makes for a stressful yet fun experience. You're not meant to run and gun like an action hero. You're meant to conserve your resources and health in order to just barely scrape by. 

edit (first finished Leon run): on Standard difficulty, don't expect to use absolutely all of your inventory items. If you play correctly, you'll save up on so many resources that it'll feel a bit disappointing that you didn't get to use something as much as you would've liked.

A stunning remake and a must own, must play title. Honestly, when I heard they were doing this, I never thought it would live up to the original Resident Evil 2, but this surpasses it on every level.

Scary atmosphere, one map full of puzzles and mazes (go here, get this, open this, while evading zombies and being chased by Tryant, especially in early gameplay).
RE 2 Remake has solid gameplay. It's not a guns-blazing game like some of it's other title.  It really is a zombie-survival horror game. You are not overpowered, you have very limited ammo, some zombies are very hard to kill, some are unkillable you need to keep on running. 
Some zombies need you to time your running so you can get pass them, some you MUST NOT RUN at all and shoot, some you MUST ALWAYS run (unless you got shotgun on you, but that wont keep ya safe). 

The game needs you to make preparation, if you wanna go somewhere and it has zombies, you dont just go guns blazing. You check your ammo, you check your subweapon to counter the enemy's grapple.  You can roughly calculate how much damage you take (i.e 1 bite = 1 health), and you can calculate inventories you have to be prepared (i.e knife/medkit). The game asks you to wonder around, from place A, to go to B, then return to A, to get item to get to C. And repeat. It's kinda annoying if you think that way, but once you play the game, it's actually fun, and adrenaline pumping keeps you wanting for more!

my 2 gripes with the game are my personal gripes that seem the somewhat split between people who agree with me and disagree:

-Enemies wont stay dead.* You can put 10-15 rounds in an enemy zombies head before they finally die. However at the 5 bullet mark they usually fall to the ground, making them appear to have died. Unless their head actually explodes or their guts literally fall out, the zombie more than likely is playing dead, and will get up the next time you're passing the area.  (who has ever heard of zombies playing dead? Zombies with intelligence?) I don't like the design choice personally, but I'm sure the devs have their reason, and this fandom seems split on whether or not this was a good call. I personally hate this, but learned to live with it. 

-Forced replay to get full value. You remember pokemon gold vs silver? and how there were ever so slight differences, but you couldn't get every pokemon because some were missing? Not all, but just enough to annoy you that you were missing the other 10%? Well this game does it as well in the split story of two main characters. You choose to play as one of the two at the very beginning of the game and depending on who you choose you will miss out on ~15% of the game without any explanation as to why. I got angry that I was playing as Leon and couldn't find the heart Key to open up some of the rooms. Wasn't until I googled it that I was told I will never get access to these rooms, Likewise Claire will never gain access to the Spade rooms without any explanation as to why. So if you're like me, someone who keeps searching desperately thinking that you've missed something, you haven't, you've just wasted your time. I could spend hours replaying the game just to see whats in these rooms, but really why? Why not just let me into these rooms, or tell me in some way that the other character is needed for this area.

All in all it is what it is, a remake of a game, but I kinda wish there was more to justify the price associated with the price tag of a modern blockbuster.

[b]"Resident Evil 2" introduces one of the most classical survival horror games into the modern era of gaming and it does it pretty well. Everything is revised and redesigned but with huge respect to the aesthetics and the feel of the original game. Marvelous graphics, awesome sound design, great level design, imposing dark atmosphere, splatter situations, creepy enemies, well built puzzles and a fantastically crafted gameplay system for real survivors are some of its core elements. "Resident Evil 2" is a unique survival adventure full of agony and pain that you must experience.


Manometer: 9/10[/b]


The good
- Awesome graphics with detailed models, great dirty textures and fantastic atmospheric lighting. It also packs some high quality visual effects (fog, rain, volume lights, flares, explosions etc.). It is gorgeous.
- Fantastic level design. Racoon City's police department is one of the most iconic and well designed buildings I've seen. So many different qualities from room to room and floor to floor. So many places to discover.
- Imposing atmosphere. It is dark, rusty and creepy and it smells death. You will feel haunted and alone in this desperate attempt to survive.
- Great, well balanced gameplay that serves the survival experience. Exaggerations have no place here. You are not a killing machine and ammo is restricted. Every bullet counts and most of the time you will have to be quiet or hide in order to survive. Control mechanics are responsive and effective too. Although your character feels a little bit heavy with slow running, this is a wise and realistic choice that enhances the survival element.
- Incredible sound design with attention to detail. Horrific sounds, steps, screams but also environmental and ambient sounds give the game absolute realism and enhance the atmosphere. Main characters' sounds when they breath, struggle or they are in pain are great. Sound design is an important element to recognize the environment around you in order to survive. T-00's steps will haunt you for days.
- Nice direction and cinematography. Good flow with high quality cut scenes and some sceneries of great artistic value.
- Good, convincing voice acting.
- Zombies and enemy creatures are awesome. I liked this classic version of zombies that are slow but much more creepier. Bosses are also fantastically designed. T-00 is one of the coolest villains ever.
-  Great splatter effects. Bites, stabs, slaughters, blood and body parts are everywhere. The wounds on the bitten protagonists give an extra realism too.
- Amazing animations. Everything feels so realistic. How the characters walk when they are healthy, how they walk when they are injured, how they react to enemies' attacks. Everything feels right and convincing.
- Nice atmospheric music. I like the choice to keep it simple and subtle and let the environmental sound do the trick. Nevertheless when it is necessary music gives an extra boost.
- The main story is simple but interesting enough. Diaries, brochures and notes which you discover will gradually give you some extra information about the past of the city and the incidents that happened there.
- As part of the main story you will find two great mini levels that offer a slightly different experience and will let you take a break from the main characters' storyline.
- Puzzles are simplistic (you mostly collect items or search for hidden safes' combinations) but they are cleverly placed inside the levels in order to control your movement and the game's flow. Each puzzles guides you seamlessly to the next one.
- There are many hidden things scattered inside the police department that give an extra depth to the game (hidden rooms, weapons, messages etc.).
- You can play four slightly different playthroughs of the main story. Also the game packs a great amount of extra stuff. There are some well build survival modes, a gallery of interesting concept art images and a rich 3d models' gallery.
- Stats screen (with saves' counter and rating) after a playthrough challenge you to play it again and get better. Hardcore mode is a real nightmare and gives the game extra replayability. 
- Showing respect and keeping the original game's character, feel and core gameplay elements, the developers created something entirely fresh. This is how remakes should be done.

The bad
- Zombies movement and reactions are a little bit inconsistent. They can open some doors but they cannot walk through some others that are already open. They sometimes grab you from three meters away and sometimes they fail even if you are standing just next to them. This could be a realistic approach but has a negative impact on the gameplay. You feel like having less control over the game and that some things happen a little bit random.
- When you open a document or examine an object in a room the time stops entirely and you can sit there for hours even if you were chased by a hoard of zombies. I felt that a lot of times this ruined the pace and the vibe I was into.
- The main characters are cool but a little bit shallow. Without a solid backstory you cannot emotionally attach to them. If you really cared about them, the game could offer you even more emotions and agony.
- I expected that the second playthrough (with the other character) would be complementary to the first and entirely new. Although some things are new or made differently, it is absurd that you repeat procedures that is supposed to be already done by the first character. This is just inconsistent to the story and makes no sense. I expected something more.

The criticisms are valid when it comes to cut content between the four campaigns of the original. I agree that expectations there were missed. Even so, this game stands on its own very well. It delivers on scares, action, and good ole eyeball-monster killing goodness. Well worth the purchase.

I will preface this by saying: This isn't a good remake. It just isn't. 
Is it the worst remake I've seen? No, but it actually is a "re-imagining" of the original game. What does that mean? It isn't Resident Evil 2. It doesn't have the same story, characters or feel as the original. Sure, almost everything's there in name, but it's nothing like the original, and despite the original being a 1998 game, it does quite a few things obviously worse, most noticeably in the side characters. Though Claire has some issues too, she looks really weird in this game compared to her original appearance too. 
But that aside, the game does not have the A/B scenarios and Zapping from the original. For example what you do in your first playthrough as Claire has no bearing on your second playthrough as Leon unlike in the original where one would affect the other. Though they redesigned the first part of the game for the B run, everything else plays pretty much the except same, and moreover, none of the plot changes at all like in the original. Another thing is that Resident Evil 2 is a SEQUEL to Resident Evil 1, and this is made very obvious when you play the original, it's very much connected to the events of the first game, reinforced by Claire looking for her brother Chris Redfield, one of the main characters in RE1. The remake just kind of throws this all away and makes the plot seem like a self-contained thing.
There are also some plot things that make no sense in the remake, and I'll go so far to say that this game doesn't have a good story. If anyone says it does, it's simply not true. At best it's serviceable if you consider the game to be it's own thing.. and not a remake.

Now all that said, this is a great game! I've put almost up to 90 hours into this, unlocking all of the achievements for good reason. The base gameplay is very satisfying. Hardcore difficulty is pretty much perfectly balanced, and the gameplay itself is just very fun to master. Realizing that you can get by simply stunning enemies and running past instead of being expected to kill is such a gamechanger. The zombies are also very fun enemies, not because they're fun or satisfying to kill, but because they're legitimately dangerous, you can easily get grabbed if you're close, and they do a surprising amount of damage with a bite. This isn't at all frustrating, because it can be easily avoided with observant and good gameplay.

Trying to get S+ rank on either of the characters is actually a fun thing to try, because the game is actually pretty replayable, like RE always has been, this remake does that well despite lacking the distinct A/B runs and Zapping. Moreover it actually improves upon the extra content the original had like 4th Survivor. The remake also adds Ghost Survivors, more scenarios like 4th Survivor which drive up the challenge a lot more.

As for the DLC you can get it with the game.. it's okay if you're crazy for the game, but the thing I actually would recommend you get is the original soundtrack swap. The remake's soundtrack is a little.. lacking or just too muted in the actual game, playing with the original soundtrack actually adds a lot since it still holds up. Though if you don't want to spend that little extra, it's really not something to worry about.
Price-wise, I think even the deluxe edition is worth the full price, and if it's on sale, there's no reason to pass it up.

All in all, while don't think this should in any way replace the original game, and it's lacking as a remake.. It's a damn fine game on its own that's worth your time.

RE2 is a 2019 remake of the 1998 survival horror classic reimagined with a modern over-the-shoulder control scheme and a familiar but different story. Unlike the RE1 remake, this is a complete from-the-ground-up change from the source material, choosing to keep some elements the same while changing others entirely. 
The setting once again takes us to Raccoon City, this time within the city itself, as newcomers Leon S. Kennedy, a rookie cop arriving to his first day at work, and Claire Redfield, a college girl looking for her missing brother, as they find themselves in the middle of a city-wide viral outbreak. Every street and store is filled with zombies, and they are forced to find shelter in the now boarded up Raccoon City Police Station. Their only option left is to find a way to go deeper into the heart of the pandemic, and make it out to the other side alive.

Resident Evil 2 (2019) takes gameplay cues from Resident Evil 4 (2005) with the over-the-shoulder camera perspective and precision-based aiming, but also uses many survival horror elements such as inventory and resource management as well as puzzles to progress. The enemies are rebalanced from the original to be much sturdier to compensate for the easier perspective, with T-virus-zombies being much more resilient, staggering in their shambling that makes aiming more difficult and needing several headshots to put down for good. The puzzles aren't all that hard, but are still enjoyable to solve. The gameplay highlight is arguably the completely redone T-103 Tyrant miniboss, made into a stalker-type enemy. He will chase you through the entire RPD aside from save rooms, forcing you to pace yourself. 

The game has two scenarios for both characters, an A and B scenario, with Leon and Claire both having their separate experiences in the story differentiating them. The problem being that the A and B scenarios for both only really mix up some item placements and the order of cutscenes, but otherwise don't change much. Granted, the original 1998 PS1 game's 'zapping' system wasn't too much more intuitive, only affecting items and scenarios in a limited amount of sections if you didn't tackle them with one character by the time you played as the other, so it's not a giant loss. What IS a loss is the original method of the A and B scenario, as they're intended to be Leon and Claire going through the story at the same point in time, so their experiences and encounters in the original differ. In the Remake, they both encounter mostly the same bosses that the other should be dealing with at the same time, while only changing some minor elements like starting zones for each character and parts unique to Leon and Claire (Ada for Leon, Sherry for Claire). Some areas and enemies like the Web Spinners which returned from RE1 were cut as well.  While not the best remake, it is a competent game with enough content to enjoy to warrant playing. If the RE3 Remake only adapted 30% of the original game's content, then RE2 Remake at least covers 70%, which is adequate enough. All of this, at the very least, does not diminish the quality of RE2R as a game enough, unlike 3R, which even compared to this recycles many assets and is a technical downgrade in terms of model variety, animations, gore, etc.

Still, the game is an absolute must-play if you're starting out with survival horror, and want something to follow up the RE1 remake. Absolutely grab at full price, though it does also go on sale often during the Capcom publisher sales on Steam. You should still try the originals on GOG, even on easy mode, especially with how cheap they are, so you can experience both the classic and remake iterations of the story.

TL;DR For the most part I recommend this game for its gameplay and impressive graphics. However, as an old fan of the Resident Evil franchise, I'm 50/50 about this game in terms of storytelling, variety, character development and designs in comparison to the original. By those standards, I recommend the original Resident Evil 2 (or hell, the Darkside Chronicles retelling). But if you're solely looking for a scary game that makes survival your top priority, this is definitely for you.

I know I'm a tad bit late to be making this review. But I'm bored and have nothing else to do right now. I'll try not to make this super long, but I want to cover some things that everyone else seems to disregard in favour of green lighting this remake. This write-up is going to be centred mostly for long time fans of the franchise, or newcomers who are interested in knowing how consistent this game in regards to continuity nods from later games that take place after it in the story.

I will congratulate this game for simply being A remake of Resident Evil 2 as that has been a game in the entire Resident Evil franchise that a lot of us have wanted to see in modern graphics for years. Partially due to it being the introduction of fan favourite Leon Kennedy and sassy biker chick Claire Redfield, the sister of the first game's Chris Redfield. It's been a game that has been referenced in later titles and has had several games in the franchise based on the events from it, either as a spin-off or a retelling (Outbreak, Umbrella Chronicles, Darkside Chronicles, Operation Raccoon City, decent games I would recommend giving a try). However, it's come as a disappointment for a lot of us die hard fans who were excited to play this, largely due to the fact that they remove a lot of content and variety that the original had (weapons, enemies, unique designs, zapping system), and more importantly; messes up story events that ultimately ruin the continuity.

Character designs have faced some drastic changes, some for better and some for worst. Some of the designs are based on early concept art when the characters were being created for the original game, and while I can appreciate that they are being faithful to what was once going to be, some of it can be a bit unnecessary. A big fear everyone was dreading with this game was how the facial designs were going to be made as when Resident Evil 7 released and featured Chris Redfield at the end, his face looked nothing like how we've seen him in past games all because Capcom wanted to feature real face imports, and I can fortunately say that (for the most part) this isn't a problem in this game.

In terms of story, I could go on for hours about how this game ruins the continuity. While the original had no definitive canon path, it was highly believed that the Claire A and Leon B path held the most in canon as the events that occurred exclusively in that path are referenced or retold in later games and spin-offs. Unfortunately there is no A/B scenarios in this game and instead we have 1st/2nd runs that essentially place items and enemies elsewhere so we won't have to worry about locating them in the same place as the other character. The 1st/2nd runs are ultimately lacking though, as the only difference is who gets to meet Marvin at the beginning, and who gets to fight William Birkin in his final form, that's it. And you guessed it, this leaves a lot of contradicting events that overlap each other that make the game very VERY confusing, especially at the end with Annette Birkin, I won't spoil it, but when you play both paths it speaks for itself. And remember how I said the zapping system was removed? Yup, whatever you do in the 1st run will not carry over to the 2nd run, which was a massive bummer and was actually something a lot of us were prepared for as Capcom had announced years earlier that the zapping system was not going to make a return. I know the A/B scenarios are not mandatory, but when you're expecting a remake of Resident Evil 2 to release, you'd expect the people who are making them to be as faithful as possible to what made the game enjoyable. Honestly, I just wish they had made one designated segment for Claire and Leon and just decided "screw it, this ♥♥♥♥'s canon" because this has lead us down the exact same confusion now with Resident Evil 1 in terms of Chris and Jill's run not featuring Barry or Rebecca when the canon ending requires them both to have escaped but is impossible to obtain in-game, essentially putting us in the same confusion that the original had already cleared up.

Now I know what some of you are going to say. "If you don't like this re-imagining, then just go back to play the original." The problem with remakes is that they usually take priority in the canon, and if they're a bad remake, then that is a problem by itself (looking at you Metal Gear Solid Twin Snakes). So unless someone in Capcom says otherwise, we're stuck with Claire's awful redesign and all the plot holes that this remake has presented us with.

I apologise for the long rant I have made about this game's inconsistencies in this review. Ironically I would have said more, but due to Steam's text cap, I can only say so much. This game is no doubt wonderful as a survival horror. But as someone with more than a decade of knowledge surrounding the franchise, this remake did not live up to what I was hoping for, Darkside Chronicles' retelling is more faithful than this and that was short as hell. Some people will just praise the gameplay and only enjoy that part for the sake of its entertainment value, which is completely fine, but as I mentioned before, this review was mainly for the die hard fans or those who wanted to get invested in the story. So in a way, you can consider this to be a bit of warning for those who require details. And as such, you're welcome.

Never played the original but I think this game definitely stands on its own. The graphics, lighting, sound effects and character models are all incredible and feeling the bullet impact on the bodies of zombies adds so much immersion. The story is just entertaining enough to get you keep going and the puzzles aren't that hard to solve but the arrival of the fashionable "miniboss", Mr. X is when the game really shines. As soon as this undestructible force starts slowly chasing you, the tension cranks to 100. I almost got paranoid, expecting to those loud thuds from his footsteps while hurrying to solve one of the puzzles.
Also, I thought being able to replay the game a 2nd time as the other character would just be a model swap, but boy was I wrong. Capcom actually put the effort into making Leon and Claire's playthroughs unique enough to not feel repetitive. Presentation: (5/5) - Visually, this game is nearly flawless with fluid animations, extremely realistic humans and their facial expressions, horror-appropriate settings such as the police station, terrifying monster design. Even better is the sound design, especially when using headphones, making you feel uneasy and with the feeling of being followed (a particular shadowy figure with a hat and its associated footsteps being a highlight). Presentation is everything in a horror game, and this game delivers on this front.

Story/Dialogue (3/5) - Rather campy with somewhat forgettable characters that don't always have a great dynamic when they cross paths, some horror cliches, and a general story that serves the gameplay but is nothing to write home about. 

Gameplay (4.5/5) - Again, the presentation is what makes the game. That being said, the gameplay mechanics are very solid even though they are mainly design to expand on the horror. You can only save and access all inventory in a few specific 'safe rooms', your ammo is very scarce (you are discouraged from fighting most threats) ,and your very limited carrying capacity encourage risk taking - leaving a few things behind or not carrying something foolishly thinking you had no need for it. The shooting mechanics are far superior to the old Playstation games and help make boss battles very entertaining. The game is also intended to be played twice, once with each character, with enough variations and added difficulty on the second to keep you on your toes.

This was my best survival horror experience yet and I enjoyed it more than RE7 due to the enemy variety and more interesting locations. I played Claire A / Leon B and think that this path makes a lot of sense narrative wise. Claire however has better weapons imo.

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
[b]Resident Evil 2[/b] also known as [b]RE2[/b] released in 2019 with very positive reviews in Steam which has piqued my own interest to see if it lives up to the hype. The [b]RE2[/b] remake has promoted an improvement on everything in the original game with an improved camera, new story elements, new map layout, combat improvements, voice acting, and a graphical upgrade to finish off the list.

[h1]Pros and Cons[/h1]
[b]Pros[/b]
[list]
[*]Fantastic story with two playable characters that offer their own unique stories
[*]Fun survival horror gameplay
[*]Unique puzzles that provide a real challenge
[*]Beautiful graphics everywhere you go throughout Raccoon City
[/list]

[b]Cons[/b]
[list]
[*]Only minor issues that didn't affect gameplay
[/list]

[h1]Story[/h1]
September 1998, police rookie [b]Leon S. Kennedy[/b] received a rather weird call telling him to not come to work. Curious, he decides to go to [b]Raccoon City[/b] and upon arriving at a gas station, meets a university student named [b]Claire Redfield[/b]. When they reach the city, they find out that it’s crawling with zombies, and with little left to do, they head towards the police station where refugees are said to be held.

However, the two are separated when a nearby truck driver who was attacked earlier crashes his oil transport causing a fire between the two. Both [b]Leon[/b] and [b]Claire[/b] must travel separately by foot to reach the station and find a way to make it to safety.

[b]RE2[/b] is split up into two stories. [b]Leon[/b] and [b]Claire[/b] will have their own scenarios where they will fight the same enemies but may have different obstacles to deal with. You don’t have to play as both to understand the full story but each has their own unique story.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The gameplay for [b]RE2[/b] has been completely changed from the original, with improvements and new features added. The character movement and camera are in your control which is a huge improvement as you can control your aim without those awkward camera angles from the original.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2581653032
Combat has also been improved. While aiming at enemies you can take them out in three hits to the head so it’s best to aim there. However, [b]zombies[/b] won’t stay dead, some of them returning back to life after a few minutes. They can die if their head is blown off by a critical hit but you only have a random chance to get them. I recommend saving your ammo for the right occasion as just mindlessly shooting enemies won’t work as they may just come back. 

If you see one [b]zombie[/b], don’t even bother with it, just run past it even if there are two or three spread apart (keywords SPREAD APART). Ignore them until they are clumped together then you can shoot. This screenshot will show you a prime example of when it’s best to use your ammo.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2583515672
There are also some other enemies you will have to be careful around when fighting. [b]Zombie dogs[/b] for example will come back to life just like normal [b]zombies[/b]. Then, there are [b]lickers[/b] which can be trouble if not taken care of, for some reason though, when they die they are dead for good. Only forms of [b]zombies[/b] can come back to life it seems.

Then there is [b]Tyrant[/b], this thing will chase you throughout the game if you make noise with your gun, so be careful when shooting. I also recommend not even trying to fight [b]Tyrant[/b], as he is immune to anything you throw at him; he can be temporarily disabled if enough damage is inflicted on him but I don't recommend going for this strategy, retreat instead.

There is inventory management, weapons will usually take one inventory slot but upgraded ones will take two. Some items that are used for puzzle solving may also take a second slot, so be mindful of what you are carrying.

There will be moments where you will have to do some puzzle-solving and this is where you will have to start thinking and these provide a good challenge. I enjoyed how creative the puzzles were. My favorite puzzle is one where you had to obtain three medals to unlock a secret door. It was a clever approach that also had you solving a few smaller puzzles along the way.

[h1]Graphics and Performance[/h1]
[b]RE2[/b] is a beautiful game, [b]Raccoon City[/b] is honestly a creepy place that is crawling with the undead. Some areas may have something else lurking in the shadows providing plenty of suspense preparing yourself for things that may or may not be there.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2583515940
I tested the game on an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1060 3GB, AMD Ryzen 5 1500X Quad-Core Processor 3.50, with16 GB of RAM. I experienced a smooth 60 FPS running into no issues.

[b]Final Verdict[/b]
I am honestly impressed with what [b]RE2[/b] was able to provide. I found no issues with the game which is a rare thing for me to say. Even if you have already played the original [b]RE2[/b] I still recommend picking this up as the improvements made will feel like a completely different game compared to the original. It’s a gem of a game and one that I highly recommend for [b]RE[/b] and horror fans.

I want to mention that I didn't play the original and only played RE7 before so my perspective isn't anything related to nostalgia or the likes I was only looking for something along the line of action horror and heard about RE2.

Let's talk about the horror, it's much more about tension and a lot less about giving the player a scare so while I did get jump scared by a zombie that happened to be next to a corner almost all of them weren't intentionally placed there for that purpose. The core aspect of the game is about exploration and puzzle solving while fending off the local population of monsters and managing your resources to not run out of ammunition or healing. Exploration has a good amount of running around the same areas looking for key items and trying to play conservative with ammunition because resources are limited and precious. An important emphasis is placed on those limited resources so generally even if it's not required for progression exploring everything is a wise choice unless you know what you're doing. Something interesting is how the game keeps you on your toes pretty much the entire time increasing the danger as the story goes with the infamous Mr. X aggressively power-walking after you while you're frantically looking at where to go and what you have to do to get the hell out of this hellhole. There are safe rooms but otherwise the ambience is dreary and easily what makes the game so good. Also worth saying that puzzles aren't difficult and really simplistic but they add to the fun nonetheless and I don't think you need to pay that much attention to be able to play through this game without getting stuck it's pretty straightforward. 

Story-wise it's good, both Leon and Claire have their own path that will on occasion cross to kind of connect them together and establish a timeline of the events. Unfortunately, the gameplay mechanics, other modes, and the [b]MOVEMENT[/b] can be pretty bad. First, let me say: why isn't there a frickin dodge button? Or even a crouch button? And for those who say "It wasn't in the original game, duh" I'm not looking at this game as a comparison to the original, I'm looking at it as itself, and nothing else. There were many, many situations that I could have avoided taking damage if I could duck a foot in another direction, or if I could even stumble forward just a tiny bit. Turning is obnoxious, as if I need to spin in a giant circle to turn around. In a tightly packed corridor with a bunch of zombies, this means death. Boss fights especially are miserable. I never feel as if I'm really in control of the character. Also, the game shows in the intro and outro cutscenes that yes, Leon and Claire can indeed run. Except when their lives depend on it. Then they have to hobble around at half normal walking speed ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

Getting away from that, the story is very good and the characters are engaging. Again, I've never played a Resident Evil game before, but this story seems pretty establishing for a much larger, overarching story. This is probably why there's like 8 of these games now. One note about the story: This game really only has 1 1/2 campaigns. There's a couple differences between Leon and Claire's stories, but it's largely the same in certain areas. The 2nd runs are almost exactly the same as normal, but some puzzles are slightly different. I was kind of disappointed at this, but it was pretty good overall, just super repetitive. The game looks amazing in most places, except when textures decide to go into low-poly mode for no reason (but it's pretty rare).

Other notes: The bonus modes, at least the first two I played, are basically super limiting speedruns to see how much crap the game can throw at you until you get frustrated and give up. Mostly the scripted enemies that don't follow the normal game's rules were the most annoying (AKA lickers that attack you instantly once you hit a trigger, even if you were completely silent). Pretty underwhelming, but at least they weren't DLC, I guess.

All in all, you should buy this game for the main campaign, and that's about it. I'd definitely wait for a good sale, though. I'd probably give this game a 6/10. If the movement didn't suck it'd be a 8/10.
