TL;DR: If you don't have access to a copy of the original Resident Evil 2 (1998) release on the PSX, this is a very comparable experience while still providing plenty of nice changes.

[h1][b]Context[/b][/h1]

I played this game over the course of 4 streams, spanning about 10 hours of total playtime across 2 campaigns. I played through a single run of Leon A/Claire B[1] on the normal difficulty mode. I did not used enhanced/"cheat" weapons like the infinite ammo weapons you get after completing the game. This was my third playthrough of Leon's A campaign, so I knew pretty much all of the his scenario's content at this point. I finished his A campaign in just over 4 hours, and received an A rank for the trouble. Claire's B campaign, with which I had much less experience with, was finished in 4 hours & 39 seconds, but I only received a B rank. For the record, I have no experience playing any variation of the original Resident Evil 2 (1998) release. This was my first experience playing a [i]third-person[/i] Resident Evil game.[2] I paid for this game at full price during the week of its 2019 launch. 

[b][u]SPOILERS FOR RESIDENT EVIL 2 AND RESIDENT EVIL 2 REMAKE BELOW; READ AT YOUR OWN PERIL[/u][/b]


[h2][b]Narrative[/b][/h2]

Since this game is a remake of the long-beloved Resident Evil 2 (1998), it stands to reason that RE2R's story is much the same. I haven't played the original, but the basic building blocks of the story are all in place. Leon Kennedy is a rookie police officer that arrives in Raccoon City during the middle of a zombie pandemic, and Claire Redfield is the younger sister of Chris Redfield - one of the elite members of S.T.A.R.S. from Resident Evil 1 (1996). Along the way, they discover that the Umbrella corporation has unleashed the "T-virus" throughout the city, meanwhile a Tyrant-class bio-hazard known as "Mr. X" stalks them throughout the police department. Like in the previous 2 Resident Evil games, the general environment order is: Mansion, Underground, Laboratory. This is also where we get introduced to another Resident Evil mainstay: Ada Wong. She serves as both a foil to Leon as well as a potential love interest. Throughout the game, she gradually grows closer to Leon until she inevitably betrays him for the sake of her mysterious employers. At the same time, Dr. William Birkin has infected himself with the "G-Virus", and acts as the main antagonist for the duration of the game. Depending on which scenario you play in which order, either Leon or Claire will be the one to finish Birkin off at the back of the escape shuttle.

[h3][b]Gameplay[/b][/h3]

As expected of a 2019 remake of a beloved 1998 classic, RE2R uses modern technology to beautifully recreate the pre-rendered backgrounds of the original into a fully-explorable 3D space. Unlike the previous game's remake, RE2R utilizes a more modern control scheme to maneuver the character as opposed to the tank controls that the older games were built on. As such, the remake feels much more aligned with the later entries in the franchise, while also still keeping the horrific tone of the original trilogy. The remake also, like its 3D predecessors before it, does not include any forced camera angles. Some would argue that this removes some of the tense atmosphere from the experience, but I found it did justice. I was already a fan of the Dead Space series, so I was happy to have something akin to that game's tone. Overall, the survivor-horror experience remains intact with players having to explore the different levels scavenging for resources while defending against the undead. The game has a very interesting way of determining what resources you find using a scaling difficulty system. [3] As you progress, the game takes a dynamic tally of various statistics (e.g. number of shots fired, hits taken, items acquired, etc.). It uses these statistics to determine chances for critical shots, how much ammo you find, and how much damage you take from an attack. This remake also keeps the weapons upgrade system from the original, upgrades that are usually found through exploration and solving the multiple puzzles across the game's environments.

Puzzles range from finding critical items to progress the plot forward to simply finding key-codes to unlock safes/lockers. A personal favorite of mine was the challenge involving unlocking Leon's desk in the main office. There is a note left by the his lieutenant, Marvin Branagh, that tells Leon that he needs to look at the nameplates on his coworkers' desks in order to find the combinations to 2 locks on the table. The combinations are the first initials for each member of the team. This was a new addition to Resident Evil 2, and I felt like it added a nice touch of personality to the station overall. It was especially heartbreaking when reading the underside of the note revealed the words:
[i]"Be glad you're not here, rookie".[/i]
This moment of humanization was really touching, and was only elevated by the environment designers recreating the "Welcome Leon" banner hanging from the office ceiling. It helped sell the idea that these were real people suffering in a crisis, and that my late arrival as Leon was nothing short of happenstance.

Shooting in this game feels weighty enough, and the zombies react with very convincing recoil. The dynamic gibbing system the developers included add a sense of strategy to the game that wasn't present previously. In earlier titles, shooting/exploding a zombie would simply result in 3 states: Standing, Stunned, or Dead. If they were still standing, they could just as easily continue to approach you. If an enemy was stunned, the player has an opportunity to either run or continue attacking. Dead enemies would (typically) remain dead, prone on the ground or evaporating into goo. The addition of body parts being torn apart, thus affecting the enemy's movements and ability to attack, gives players more agency in decision-making. Someone could easily play this game by shooting off the legs of every zombie, and skirting past them. I imagine that a lot of speedrunners take advantage of the long recoil animation enemies suffer from when knocked to one foot. The limited inventory space present throughout the survival-horror genre continues to be present in this game, however it is nowhere near the level of OCD-inducing customization found in Resident Evil 4's attache case.

[h1][b]Overall Thoughts[/b][/h1]

This game is an excellent introduction to the franchise as a whole for people unfamiliar with the genre. However, if one desires to explore everything that Resident Evil has to offer, I would still suggest people start at Resident Evil 1 Remake. I have a review for that game [4] for those interested to read before they buy. For those wishing to explore Leon Kennedy or Claire Redfield as characters, however, this would be the best place to start. Leon is the main character of RE4, and Claire shows up as the lead heroine in Resident Evil Revelations 2. There is also a variety of non-game media featuring them, but I have not personally watched/read it.

[h1]Resident Evil 2 Remake does a curious thing where, unlike every single one of its predecessors, this one's an actual horror game.[/h1] 
Crazy, I know.

Resident Evil was always meant to be more Action than Horror. because Shinji Mikami hates being scared, instead using Horror as a backdrop, an aesthetic for the general puzzle-solving, inventory management and combat.
However the first game coined the phrase Survival Horror and this is the closest we've ever gotten to that. 

Inventory isn't restricted enough to be tedious, but not big enough to be unrealistic. There will be moments where you're low on Ammo and afraid to continue on without finding more. Shooting feels satisfying and rewards a methodical approach rather than spraying. The Boss fights are sadly no highlight, but Mr X makes up for it plenty. It's not too difficult on Normal, so everyone should be able to finish it with a little bit of elbow grease. 

The Police Station is a joy to explore, with shortcuts getting you around, puzzles to solve and excellent sound design. Everything is laid out in a way where along with your map, you won't really need a guide like in RE1 for instance.
Theres this general feeling of satisfaction and unease that will accompany you the entire 10 hours of the first campaigns runtime, allowing you to go in for seconds with different paths and story beats when you wanna come back to it again.

RE2RE (great name btw) is undoubtedly up there as one of the best Resident Evil games. Along with RE7, a great entry point and one that feels different than any other game in the franchise. Well-paced fun and wonderfully rendered zombie survival horror with a hearty dash of puzzle-solving.

To note, somehow the [i]Resident Evil[/i] games have passed me by, and before this one, I'd very recently only played [i]Resident Evil 4[/i]. When it comes to the handling, [i]Resident Evil 2[/i] shares more with the latter than the 1998 original ([spoiler]although don't expect everything that worked in 4 to be applicable to this game![/spoiler]). The various difficulty selections also give a nod to classic [i]Resident Evil[/i] for those looking for a more challenging approach.

The key thing is that this is survival horror, not a straight up zombie shooter. Inventory management (a stalwart of the classic games) makes a return, to add to this atmosphere, as well as a hefty number of puzzles to help you along the way and progress the plot. The area design is commendable and definitely is a key part of the game's feel.

Optimisation wise - It runs very smoothly on GTX 1060 with no further tweaking required.

Replayability - there are relatively minor differences in game experience depending on whether you pick Leon S Kennedy or Claire Redfield ([spoiler]namely weapon availability, item locations, areas unlocked, and mid-game plot[/spoiler]). The game mechanics do not differ substantially. As noted by the Results menu, there are various scenarios ([spoiler]but these are not substantially different to the main game, and B scenarios are unlocked on completion of an A run[/spoiler]).

Definitely a steal if on sale or if you wanted to start earlier in the [i]Resident Evil[/i] timeline with modern visuals.

Resident Evil 2 is a remake of the 1998 classic made from the ground up, but faithful to the original experience. Old mechanics and new improved combat makes this game worth a try. The story starts Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield, as they arrive to Racoon City which has an ongoing full on zombie invasion. The game has you picking between one of the two leads to complete the main campaign to obtain a character specific ending, after that you can opt for a second run with the character you did not play this will unlock a secret boss, the other character specific ending and provide the true ending for the game. 

Positives:
-True Survival Horror
-Crafting system 
-Amazing Story
-Great Combat
-Sound Design
-Good Character Development 
-A true remake
Neutral:
-Linear
-The game can feel short if you are a veteran of the genre 

Bottom Line: As you can see i could not point a single flaw, with this game and that is because it is a master class of the survival horror genre in video games. For players that want to start with the Resident Evil franchise or Survival horror games in general this is a good choice and one you certainly don't want to miss. 

Final Score: 10/10

I am a huge fan of the whole Resident Evil series. While I personally prefer the more action oriented installments (like 4,5,6) I really loved the classics too.

I wasn’t sure if Capcom will put out something great when bringing back the older games. Fortunately, they fully delivered with this one. The updated classic formula works really great.
There are no “tank controls” this time around like in the original RE2. Instead the game is comfortably played from the third person. Therefore, you might think shooting your way through every scenario should be pretty straightforward, especially since zombies are not as agaile as, let’s say Ganados from RE4.
However, Capcom still makes the game challenging – zombies can be quite durable and unpredictable. For example they move at a snail’s pace to make you let your guard down, only to lunge toward you from far away. Also, it does not always take the same amount of shots to kill one of them, and it may not always be clear if someone is truly out of the fight (as they can rise up from seemingly fatal wounds). You will have to figure out how to deal with this and adjust your tactics accordingly.

This creates a somewhat different and more methodical gameplay loop than in more fast-paced entries like RE 4, 5 or 6 (where it is more about efficiently dispatching a seemingly overwhelming but more predictable force of enemies, especially since you can suplex or punch dudes left and right). Still it is a satisfying loop nonetheless.

This is also a great game to showcase how a good remake can be made – it’s close enough to the original to bring out some nostalgia, but it is also quite different and modernized (both story and gameplay wise) which both veterans and newcomers can appreciate.
What is more, a wealth of free content and extra modes makes this a really game good investment (Hunk is back, Kendo rules etc.).
Overall, this game is a great title and a success, and proves that both slower and fast-paced Resident Evil games can happily co-exist.

The lighting in this game is gorgeous. Every map is eye candy.

I've played the remake of RE3 and it just doesn't compare to this game. In RE2, I had time to be fully immersed in the world, to really appreciate the work that went into recreating the familiar surroundings I loved so much from the original. In RE3, it just felt like a rushed project. Heck they reused environments from RE2 for gameplay in RE3, but didn't add anything new.  Everything in RE3 was Go Go Go! I felt nothing for the characters. In RE2, that segment with Sherry was genius. I was really afraid for her.

RE2 feels lengthy compared to RE3 because of the four different story modes. On top of the four main story scenarios there are bonus side stories we can play. RE3 was just that short main campaign, (which, let's be frank, was mostly monsters shoving things down Jill's throat) and the multiplayer bs that the developers shoved down OUR throats. Had it been a good multiplayer experience, I may have forgiven the short, obviously rushed story mode. But it wasn't. Sad panda is sad.

Some games define a generation. Some shape your childhood. And some, like the original Resident Evil 2 in 1998, take the gaming world by storm and become unforgettable classics. For many players — myself included — the original was one of those rare games: endlessly replayable, brilliantly atmospheric, and capable of lodging itself permanently into your memory.
So naturally, when CAPCOM announced a full remake decades later, feelings were mixed — excitement tangled with apprehension. Why remake something that was already so good? Could any modern reinterpretation possibly live up to the legacy of a PlayStation 1 icon? These were reasonable worries, and you carried them into launch day.
And yet…
Launch day arrived, and Resident Evil 2 Remake didn’t just meet expectations — it shattered them.

🎮 A Remake That Respects the Past While Perfecting the Present
From the moment the game boots up, it becomes obvious that CAPCOM approached this remake with a mixture of reverence and bold creativity. They didn’t attempt to simply duplicate the past. Instead, they asked:
“What made the original magical — and how can we make those moments even better?”
The result is a reimagining that feels both faithfully familiar and astonishingly new. The tight corridors, the crackling tension, the sense of dread around every corner — all of it is there, but amplified through cutting‑edge design, technology, and sound.

🎨 A Visual Overhaul That Borders on the Unbelievable
Your first reaction says it all: utter astonishment.
The graphics are jaw‑dropping — a staggering leap from 1998 while still retaining the visual soul of the original game.
• Every shadow feels threatening.
• Every pool of water on the RPD floors glistens with eerie detail.
• Every zombie looks disturbingly human.
• Every environment looks like a living (or dying) space rather than a backdrop.
CAPCOM didn’t just upgrade textures — they rebuilt Raccoon City into a fully modern survival-horror world.

🔥 Storytelling: Familiar Yet Fresh
One of the most impressive achievements of the remake is how it retells the same beloved story while adding clever twists that challenge returning fans. It is recognisably the same journey, the same characters, the same terror — but updated with:
• new events,
• improved pacing,
• expanded dialogue,
• and more cinematic tension.
For longtime fans, this feels like coming home to a place you once knew, only to discover new rooms you never realised were there.
For newcomers, the remake offers a polished, gripping experience that stands completely on its own.

😱 Suspense That Grabs You and Won't Let Go
The remake captures — and often surpasses — the atmosphere that defined the original:
• The creak of distant footsteps.
• The heavy breathing of zombies hidden around corners.
• The unnerving silence broken by sudden chaos.
• And of course… the relentless, unforgettable presence of Mr X.
This isn’t just a horror game — it’s an experience. A deliberately engineered emotional rollercoaster that keeps your pulse elevated and your nerves wired.

🎧 Sound, Lighting, and Atmosphere: Horror at Its Finest
If the visuals are impressive, the audio is nothing short of spectacular. Every groan, every gunshot, every thunderstorm rumble contributes to a sense of total immersion.
The lighting design deserves special praise too: dynamic, realistic, and constantly playing tricks on your imagination. Few games manage to make turning a single corner feel like such a monumental act of bravery.

❤️ A Love Letter to Fans Old and New
What makes this remake extraordinary is how it manages to please two very different groups:
• Veterans who adored the 1998 classic
• New players experiencing the story for the first time
Each group gets something special.
Each group gets moments that feel designed just for them.
This dual‑approach design is rare — and a testament to CAPCOM’s understanding of what made the original a masterpiece.

🏆 CAPCOM’s Triumph
My conclusion mirrors the sentiment shared by players and critics across the world:
CAPCOM didn’t just remake a classic — they elevated it.
They proved that a remake can be:
• respectful
• ambitious
• innovative
• emotional
• and utterly unforgettable.
 
This is a remake done right.
A standard for all future remakes.
A milestone in survival horror history.

🦕 And What About Dino Crisis?
My closing thought is one shared by thousands of fans:
If CAPCOM can remake Resident Evil 2 this well… what about Dino Crisis?
With the RE Engine capable of such mastery, the idea is undeniably thrilling.
Only time will tell — but if they ever greenlight it, the gaming world will be watching.

⭐ Final Verdict
Resident Evil 2 Remake is not just a great game — it’s a restored classic, a modern masterpiece, and proof that CAPCOM understands the art of fear, nostalgia, and reinvention.
Well done CAPCOM, indeed.

It took me years to get into it properly, survival horror as a genre overall, but Resident Evil 2 specifically. I played 7 first and loved pretty much every second, the game that really demonstrated just how immersive, tense, scary, and compelling survival horror as a genre can be. This was quickly followed by Dead Space, Alien Isolation, Evil Within 1 and 2 and so on. I started and played RE2 a few times over the years but never really appreciated or even finished it, until now. 

Yes, my favourite RE games are still 7 and 4 Remake but Resident Evil 2 is still a masterpiece of the genre,  its level design and layout, its incredible gameplay loop of exploration, puzzles and re-exploring previously locked areas, Mr. X relentlessly following you, it flows together so smoothly. The phenomenally tense gameplay of having to wait and focus the reticle as zombies shuffle towards you, needing to wait to see if you shot enough bullets to actually put it down or whether it's just gonna get back up, the ammo and supplies economy, figuring out what you need and what you should store for later, it's all excellent. 

From a purely technical perspective Resident Evil 2 Remake is excellent, as these games usually are. The lighting is great, the sound design is fantastic, and the optimization is some of the best in the industry. even 7 years later this game shines in every aspect, the only thing that has aged in any way, marginally, is the faces and facial expressions, but it's barely noticeable. 

Yes of course Leon is much cooler in 4, yes the story is campy, but that's just Resident Evil, and always has been, more or less. Sure, Silent Hill is much more intelligent and deeply frightening and serious, sure it's tonally much more coherent and tight, of course Dead Space is more immersive and more impressive from a visual artstyle perspective, but that's not the point. Silent Hill is genuinely haunting, and. by design, really not that fun to play, intentionally so. Resident Evil is just fun man, even at its scariest and most tense, it's still a blast to experience, and that's why Resident Evil is still so beloved so many years later, and why the franchise has so many loyal fans.

It may be my favorite Resident Evil game.

The first time I played this game, I decided to do both of my side A and side B on Hardcore. This is to really drive in the survival aspect of the game and make me think hard on resource management and routing. A good portion of the runs were spent in circles and dying just to get bonus items.

The game has some interesting choices for design. I managed to miss notes I needed in a "full-cleared" room to finish my Side B run (I never would have found them due to circumstances with Side B and being on Hardcore). The camera control can be taken away from you in small instances that feels super clunky. The bosses can feel quite tanky, possibly due to the adjusted difficulty which rewards you for playing poorly and punishes you for playing well (diminishing having difficulty choices to begin with). The knife is a bit insane for damage output (apparently even more so if you have a higher FPS) which makes it's priority for bosses kind of dumb. And there are gimmick sections that are more of a time sink than anything else.

With the bad out of the way, the game is really fun if you're into routing and resource management. There are effectively 4 different campaigns to play, giving a lot of replay value (there's also some bonus mini-campaign content, even if I wasn't as big into those). Trying to optimize routes and learning how to avoid enemies is something I've been enjoying with each run. The game also lends well to randomizer and modded content, letting me replay in even more ways (though, I wouldn't recommend this game if it wasn't worth playing without mods).

Your movement isn't superhuman or super smooth. You have be careful how close you get to enemies and plan your movement, which I really enjoy. Getting attacked by zombies I can't always break away from on a whim leads to encounters feeling intimidating and tense as I have to plan and scramble for an escape. Some moments where you can take advantage of i-frames because of things like you're on a ladder feels cheap, but it's not a deal breaker. The enemy variety is also pretty good, making how you should respond differently to a situation even more enjoyable. I enjoy have to improvise at times and not have everything be super predictable (though, adjusted difficulty isn't what I would want for this).

If you want an action based experience, this probably isn't the game for you. If you want to feel like you're surviving a horrible zombie outbreak as you escape from a police department, you might want to check this out.

Wonderful, tense horror game that plays a bit like a survival/horror take on a metroidvania. Incredible sound design (wear headphones if possible) and great replay value are key selling points.

The main downside is that the first part of the game (Police Station) is easily the best part. Not going to spoil anything, but it really doesn't re-capture that level's execution of metroidvania-style design mixed with horror and planning. The big thing that sets RE2R apart from other metroidvania games is the planning involved. You'll be thinking about where zombies are, where the next puzzle pieces are, how much to bring with you (not too much, as you need to be able to carry the spoils back with you), and which zombies to shoot to conserve ammo properly. It gets you into this mindset that I haven't seen many other games pull off. If you liked Resident Evil Revelations or RE3R, you'll love this game. 

If you want the game to be easier, run at higher framerates and use the knife. It's legitimately overpowered, as the damage is calculated based on the number of frames where the knife is colliding with the enemy. It feels like it's balanced for 60 fps, as when running at 144 frames, I could pretty much destroy bosses and tougher enemies by just downing them once then slashing with gusto.

My favorite resident evil game... REmade.

During the start of the pandemic I went through a bit of my unplayed/unfinished backlog of games, and so I booted up my vita and remembered I never beat the ps1 version of RE I've had for years... Immediately I fell in love with the horrible voice acting and surprisingly solid metroidvania-esque exploration based gameplay that still mostly holds up today. After beating Jill's route I bought the PS1 version of RE2 and this went on sale around the same time last year.

TL;DR this game is amazing, but there's enough difference to make both it and the original worth playing for anyone who enjoys horror games.

RE2 for the PS1 is a masterpeice. So much is improved from RE1; the voice acting's decent not great but it fits the mood and I could at least hear some of the emotion in the character's voices. The gameplay is so solid i immediately started Claire's 1st run after beating Leon's and I finished almost as quickly.
The graphics while not good by today's standard let your brain fill in the gaps and really set the mood well, especially on a vita screen. the music and sound design is amazing, incredibly memorable and made the suspense 10x more effective.
the ps1 game is a must play for anyone who enjoys retro games, horror games, or exploration based games. 
I suggest playing it on a handheld or tablet though, due to the compressed ps1 backgrounds looking WAY better on a smaller screen.

I genuinely hope Capcom decides to make a classic RE trilogy collection and put it on steam and modern consoles. they all have enough to offer and with ps1 title not currently on the ps5 AFAIK not having a reliable and accessible way of purchasing them only leads to piracy.

Now onto the REmake... it's not at all similar in anything other than story, but that's NOT a bad thing, its just different.
gameplay wise this feels more polished and like a triple A title, it's best suited for controller imo so I used one of the gyro aim configs and had a blast (pun intended).
 the graphics and scenery is BEAUTIFUL, but also very VERY gross. in order to really drive home the horror of the original that can't really be replicated in a game as realistic looking as this Capcom made some of the creepiest gore I've seen in a game.
soundwise though this game falls off... quite a bit. the original OST mode helps, but most people won't play the game with it. with it off there's like 0 music which while realistic made any suspense they tried to do fall flat,yes Mr. X does have his own theme but music can do so much more. IMO they should've recreated the OST and had it play in the areas without many zombies like that big main room of the RPD.

Imagine this: you get used to the RPD theme in the area where Marvin is and when you return from the underground section it's not there, just pure silence when you hear the growling of a zombie and see marvin's turned. immediately so much more impactful.

but even with all that i still think this the an amazing REimagining of a classic. both are very deserving of a playthrough.

[h1] Information / Review English [/h1]

[h1] Gameplay / Story [/h1]

The opening credits show a trucker driving a tanker at night while eating a hamburger. After he hits a figure with his vehicle, he stops his vehicle and gets out to see what he has detected with his vehicle. The figure lying on the street is a woman's corpse who turns out to be a zombie and attacks the truck driver after he tries to examine her. The actual game then begins with the prologue. The two player characters are each on their way to the fictional city of Raccoon City. Leon S. Kennedy to take up his post as a policeman at the local police station and Claire Redfield to look for her missing brother Chris, who was with the S.T.A.R.S. was active. The played character stops in front of the city at a gas station, which the player has to investigate. It turns out that there are zombies in it and when leaving the gas station, the character meets the other character. Together they then flee from the zombies at the gas station and continue their way together in the car to Raccoon City. Once in town, they drive to the police station, where the tanker truck from the intro hits at high speed and causes an accident. The two main characters are separated by burning vehicles and hordes of zombies. Now the played character has to be surrounded by zombies and navigated to the police station, the gate of which has to be locked from the inside.

In contrast to the original, the remake is played from the perspective of the pursuer. At the beginning the player has the choice between two characters: Leon S. Kennedy or Claire Redfield. Depending on the chosen character, some parts of the game are a little different. In addition, after playing through the game for the first time, the game can be started in a so-called "B scenario", which has further differences in the course of the game. The player has to solve various puzzles in the course of the game. Different keys and objects have to be collected and in some cases combined or used in the right place in order to make progress. You are constantly pursued and threatened by various zombies, while only limited resources such as ammunition and medicines are available. As in the original game, saving is limited in the higher level of difficulty. Color ribbons can then be found in the game world, which can be used once for saving on a typewriter. Objects can be moved from the limited inventory to a chest, the contents of which can be accessed from different storage rooms. When you have played through the two different scenarios, you also unlock the additional mode The 4th Survivor, in which you have to escape the sewer through the police station with the character Hunk. If you manage this challenge, you can also do the bonus mission The Tofu Survivor. The course is the same as in The 4th Survivor, with the difference that the game character is a man-sized chunk of tofu with only knives and a small number of medicinal plants at his disposal.

[h1] Gameplay / Geschichte [/h1]

Der Vorspann zeigt, wie nachts ein Trucker mit einem Tanklaster fährt und dabei einen Hamburger isst. Das eigentliche Spiel beginnt anschließend mit dem Prolog. Die beiden Spielercharaktere sind jeweils auf dem Weg in die fiktive Stadt Raccoon City. Leon S. Kennedy, um seine Stelle als Polizist im örtlichen Polizeirevier anzutreten, und Claire Redfield, um nach ihrem vermissten Bruder Chris zu suchen, welcher in der Spezialeinheit S.T.A.R.S. tätig war. Der gespielte Charakter hält vor der Stadt an einer Tankstelle, die der Spieler untersuchen muss. Es stellt sich heraus, dass sich Zombies darin aufhalten und beim Verlassen der Tankstelle trifft die Spielfigur auf den jeweils anderen Spielcharakter. Gemeinsam flüchten die beiden anschließend vor den Zombies an der Tankstelle und setzen ihren Weg zusammen im Auto nach Raccoon City fort. In der Stadt angekommen, fahren sie zum Polizeirevier, wo der Tanklaster aus dem Intro mit hoher Geschwindigkeit angefahren kommt und einen Unfall verursacht. Die beiden Hauptcharaktere werden durch brennende Fahrzeuge und Zombiehorden getrennt. Nun muss der gespielte Charakter von Zombies umgeben in das Polizeirevier navigiert werden, dessen Tor man von innen verriegelt. 

Das Remake wird im Gegensatz zum Original in der Verfolgerperspektive gespielt. Der Spieler hat zu Beginn die Wahl zwischen zwei Charakteren: Leon S. Kennedy oder Claire Redfield. Je nach gewähltem Charakter verlaufen einige Teile des Spiels etwas anders. Zudem kann das Spiel nach erstmaligem Durchspielen in einem sogenannten „B-Szenario“ gestartet werden, welches nochmal weitere Unterschiede im Spielverlauf aufweist. Der Spieler muss im Verlauf des Spiels diverse Rätsel lösen. Dabei müssen verschiedene Schlüssel und Gegenstände gesammelt und zum Teil kombiniert oder an der richtigen Stelle eingesetzt werden, um Fortschritt zu erzielen. Man wird dabei ständig von unterschiedlichen Zombies verfolgt und bedroht, während nur begrenzte Ressourcen wie Munition und Heilmittel zur Verfügung stehen. Im höheren Schwierigkeitsgrad wird zudem wie im Original-Spiel das Speichern begrenzt. Es können dann Farbbänder in der Spielwelt gefunden werden, welche man einmalig zum Speichern an einer Schreibmaschine einsetzen kann. Gegenstände können aus dem begrenzten Inventar in eine Truhe ausgelagert werden, auf deren Inhalt übergreifend von verschiedenen Speicherräumen zugegriffen werden kann. Wenn man die beiden verschiedenen Szenarios durchgespielt hat, schaltet man außerdem den zusätzlichen Modus The 4th Survivor frei, in welchem man mit dem Charakter Hunk aus der Kanalisation durch das Polizeirevier entkommen muss. Schafft man diese Herausforderung, so kann man zudem noch die Bonusmission The Tofu Survivor bestreiten. Der Verlauf ist darin der gleiche wie bei The 4th Survivor, mit dem Unterschied, dass der Spielcharakter ein mannshoher Tofu-Brocken ist, dem ausschließlich Messer und eine geringe Anzahl Heilpflanzen zur Verfügung stehen.

Great remake. Nuff said.
It basically did everything I had wanted RE1 Remaster to improve (no loading doors for one, better and clearer map with reminders, more inventory space, free moving camera, obviously graphics, better saving system, some auto saves at least, less pointless backtracking, better story and voice acting, etc.).
The one thing I'm still not super hyped about is the uselessness of the standard pistol, even upgraded. On Normal even regular zombies just can't be taken out with it, unless you get a lucky "crit", so their head explodes. Since there is no possibility to set corpses on fire anymore (unless you have the flamethrower later on with Leon or Clair's grenade launcher with incendiary ammo), you face the possibility of endlessly contesting with reviving basic enemies. Not as terrible if you're on a 2nd playthrough and know what you're doing, but especially during chase scenes unnecessary stress. God bless the shotgun and magnum though.

As for the story: It's actually involving. Your basic playthrough is either as Leon or Claire. Both play through the same levels, but have some deviating story arcs, but gameplay-wise apart from 1 or 2 different boss encounters and obviously different lines of dialogue it's basically the same gameplay. When you beat the game with one of them, you can also start a "2nd run" with the other character, basically a more condensed and a little bit harder version of the game with an alternative beginning, some rearranged enemies, puzzles, etc.
But overall the story, again, stays the same for each character. But you get the "true ending".
After you've done that you also unlock the "4th survivor" mode, which is where I just couldn't bother anymore.
It's a time trial survival run to the extraction zone. You have limited ammo, limited healing and a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of enemies, you basically need to avoid as much as possible, because, well, you don't have much ammo. It's frantic and imho just not very fun. It is the polar opposite to the methodical, careful approach of the main game (that only gets really hectic when you have to escape Mr. X or when you fight a boss, both things not being the game's stronges points imho).
There is no saving, no checkpoints, you just have to "learn" the route and how to deal with each section and hope you can make it. Especially Mr. X and the lickers here are a real pain in the ass, since, again, the pistol is basically useless if you run out of ammo for all other guns. And lickers are even bigger bullet sponges than regular enemies.
IF you can beat that (because I sure as hell can't) you unlock the "Tofu Survivor" mode, a callback to the original, where all you get is a few knives. Have fun beating that.
The "ghost survivor" stories are even more of that ... just alternative stories for characters you "meet" along the way.
Not very engaging in my opinion, but whatever.
I'd have liked to play as the Tyrant for instance. Carefully listening to noises in the police station to corner your prey. Should be possible with an AI opponent (or maybe more), but nah.

All in all this is still easily a 9/10

Edit: Some negative reviews bemoan the fact that the 2 playthroughs are practically identical. They're not. Weapons and story are different (at least on 2nd run, which is the standard way to play the 2nd playthrough). One caveat is that the 2 character playthroughs contradict each other a bit. It's not like you're just viewing the happenings through someone else's eyes. If you play as Claire (2nd run) after you've played through as Leon it is obvious the "AI Leon" hasn't just experienced what you've experienced as Leon. Things don't add up in the same way (especially the helicopter or simply all the boss battles).
I've also read people are annoyed by how little ammo you get. I've played through the game on normal and while I wasn't usually loaded on ammo it's always been more than enough to handle everything (and I've wasted A TON of ammo). On Easy you get more than enough ammo and enemies are weaker ... even in 2nd run.

I've so far only played through Leon's story, but it is so worth going back and replaying as Claire and then playing the second play through for both to get the "real" ending. Not sure how long it'll take me the second time through now that the new game adrenaline has worn off, though, because holy cow all the monsters you fight are terrifying, especially when they come from places you least expect. If you want a scary game, just know that almost two hours of my game play was spent not actually playing, but reading the map over and over to find the quickest way to make it to my next objective, while subsequently running past all the zombies. I got this game on sale, but I would've gladly payed full price, it is just that good.

Unpopular opinion: I didn't really like the game.   I know everyone is different, and I respect how many people really enjoyed the game it just wasn't for me.  THESE THINGS MIGHT NOT BOTHER YOU and I don't want to dishearten anyone or convince anyone to purchase or not purchase the game. 

I will note, deep love for Resident Evil 7 & 8 does NOT translate to loving this game.

I had two main issues with the game that you might (or might not) wish to consider when deciding whether or not to purchase the game:
1) Lacks replay-ability.  
This makes half the game not so fun.  Once you go through as one hero, you can play through as the other hero in the SAME EXACT LOCATIONS.  Some of the pathing is slightly different, and you get to experience other guns, but I really wish there had been two different stories and experiences these heroes had.  It just detracts from the story completely when OBVIOUSLY Claire wasn't with Leon inside and vice versa.  I don't even see the purpose of having another hero, why not another playthrough?  it was slightly misleading for me.
2) Ammo scarcity made the game just not fun. 
 It is HORRIBLE the lack of ammo you are given.  There are areas where mobs can respawn infinitely.  There are ways to stop this but not enough resources to stop them all.  I found the lack of ammo annoying and detracting from the experience and ambiance of the game.  I like being engrossed in games and being annoyed for over half the time really made this a chore at times to play.  I will also note that I am a FPS gamer so I did NOT waste more than a handful of bullets the entire run through and still had a negative experience.  I DID run from many enemies as is intended, I killed only those in locations with very narrow corridors I had to revisit and still had an issue.  It made the game really not fun for me.  You might like this, but I did not at all and it strongly deters me from trying other resident evil games that were created before RE7.  

If you LOVE original Resident Evil games, don't mind the second story line being very unoriginal and don't mind having only enough bullets to kill 10% of mobs, then you may have a completely different experience than I did and I hope you have fun playing this game!

Resident Evil 2 is an example of a perfect remake. It holds true to the vision of the original, while bringing a very dated classic to the modern day. Leon and Claire are classic characters in the Resident Evil mythos, and they're better here than in almost any other iteration. The game looks, plays, and feels fantastic.

The overrun Raccoon City Police Department is the location the majority of the game takes place, and it is truly a place of nightmares. You're rarely ever safe within or without its walls. Enemies you've long thought dead may stand back up hours later, and supplies can be scarce. More than once your best bet will be to simply run for your life. The atmosphere is uniquely terrifying, and the game doesn't relent for the first several hours. 

In the later acts the game can dip into a more action oriented style, but after hours of being on the defensive, this can be a welcome shift in power. Ensure you play through both Leon and Claire's paths to get the full experience.

Resident Evil 2, is a third person Survival Horror remake of the the original game of the same name from 1998. It is also an excellent example of Remaking, rather than an HD Remaster, much like Resident Evil 1's remake. Player's returning from either playing the original RE2 or having finished RE1's remake will notice some significant gameplay differences. However, I submit that RE2 remains an excellent addition to both the Resident Evil series, as well as the Survival Horror genre.

Like with RE1, RE2 has you thrust into a dark and mysterious environment while playing as one of 2 possible protagonists. In this case, out resident floppy haired hero is Leon Kennedy, taking over for Chris, who is a rookie police officer just arriving to Raccoon City. Chris's sister, Claire Redfield, is our action girl heroine, who has come to investigate her brother's disappearance.

In terms of your experience, both characters have similar stories travelling through the same areas, though there are some departures. Like with RE1, each character has their own supporting characters. Leon is assisted by the mysterious agent Ada Wong, who is looking to uncover evidence of the start of the horrific events occurring in Raccoon City. Claire will be doing all she can to help Sherry Birken, who herself has a strange connection to forces behind the viral outbreak.

Both stories are good, and I commend RE2 for having them actually diverge, even if they only so at certain places. RE1, while having 2 characters, did not have their stories truly differ beyond a few moments and some gameplay changes. RE2's changes, while also not incredibly large, are still noticeably greater. Apart from story and the few differences in locations, Leon and Claire play primarily the same but with a different set of weapons for each character.

Leon will tote a semi-automatic pistol, the shotgun (a series mainstay), a magnum (whose ammo you will hoard like a gunpowder addicted trash panda), and Resident Evil's Chemical Thrower (A flamethrower by any other name burns as crisp). I don't count the Rocket Launcher because you only get it for the last fight, as you did in RE1.

Claire has a six-shot revolver, the grenade launcher (another returning weapon), her own semi-automatic pistol, a sub-machine gun (who RE4 fans will rejoice to find), and the Sparkshot (an industrial taser that looks like it was designed by dewalt).

Both characters can make use of Knives and Grenades, which work both as regular weapons and as defensive items, as with RE1. I really enjoyed this change, and found myself using the sub-weapons far more frequently than I might normally because of this dual purpose.

All the weapons are fun to use, and RE2's more action focused game-play is happy for that. Nearly every weapon can also be upgraded by carefully searching, as can extra ammunition. You can also find gunpowder, any two of which can be combined, as with herbs, to produce ammo of various types. If you play cautiously, as I do, and use items like the knife to dispatch downed enemies, you'll likely end up with more ammo than you truly need by the end of the game.

Speaking of gameplay, I feel I can finally move on to the meat of RE2's experience. RE2 is set in third person, taking its notes from RE4 which started the trend. I feel a little sad about this, since RE1's remake kept the original game's fixed camera angles. This allowed RE1 to use pre-rendered back grounds, which look great to this day. RE2, on the other hand, had to make a change with its new perspective.

Without the fixed camera angles you cannot ensure the player sees precisely what you want, so some of the drama and mystery is lost. Now Leon and Claire can orient the camera and peek around a corner to see an enemy. You can even move and shoot simultaneously (which is a bigger deal than you might think). In my RE1, I noted that the fixed angles were great for imposing a sense of looming evil and added some wonderful dramatic views for the player. RE2 makes up the difference in dread with several key features.

First, while you have far greater control, you will now face more enemies and will also feel more anxious trying to track and move around them all. Second, the use of light (or lack there of) is great, as are the "feigning death" zombies. RE2 is chock-a-block with surprise encounters too. Third, and most important, RE2 has some of the best sound design for horror I have experienced in a long while. Moving around the Police Station, in particular, can be truly frightening. Each sound is a potential signal of some threat moving around. The creaking, dripping, groaning building constantly builds a sense of foreboding decay and looming threat. This is then compounded by some of the new enemies in RE2's roster.

Apart from you bog standard zombies and zombie dogs, RE2 introduces the Licker, and evolved form of RE1's crimson heads. These enemies are tough, and I found myself breaking away from the pistol to the shotgun to dispatch them everytime they showed up. Their ability to crawl on walls, their disturbing movement patterns, and leaping attacks are all really threatening and creepy. They are also blind, adding an interesting new dimension to evading them, should dispatching them with hot lead or high ordinance not do the job.

You will also meet malformed mutant sewer beasties, which I preferred to avoid and evade than fight, and plant based Ivy zombies, which take a page, again, out RE4's book, being very similar to Regenerators. I do like that they are weak to fire, which makes them feel more unique as an enemy. I wish more enemies were likes this. I also which targeting heads did more substantial damage. Given the freedom to aim, I would have thought that aiming for the head would have made a greater difference. Shooting different areas does do different amounts of damage, and shooting specific areas also has a chance to explode or remove those parts on regular zombies. Still, I would have like to see my marksmanship a little more highly rewarded.

However, the best enemies in the game are the Tyrant Pursuer, "Mr.X", and Mutant Murder Machine, "G". Mr.X in particular gives an all star performance as a pursuit type enemy, constantly chasing the player. While searching he moved from room to room, and his heavy footfalls can be heard. What is incredible is that he truly does move between rooms, exploring the map simultaneously to the player, and can be lead to different areas. This adds a new dimension both to the already stellar sound, but also to the urgency as you search for items and solve puzzles. It also acts as a counter the Licker's who can only be avoided while moving slowly.

All of this helps to set the stage for RE2's Horror themed action storyline, which I greatly enjoyed. Much like other titles, their is a certain B-movie feel, though RE2 does feel a little less campy. I would have like to have a few more quippy lines, or weird campy writing as opposed to some the swearing. It isn't that I am opposed to the swearing, I just like the quirkiness that some of the older titles liked to have. All that said, it is a fun horror movie vibe, with some wonderful ambience (I like the quiet lonely bits in places), brilliant set pieces, and some good action, puzzles, and investigation. There are a total of 4 scenarios (2 for each character), and you will need to beat at least one of the first scenarios to get the second scenario with the true end.

On one final note, RE2 does have one terrible, abysmal flaw that almost had me quit the game. Half way through my first run the game repeatedly crashed. This required me to investigate a fix online (updating video drivers, altering the configuration text file, and dropping my graphics settings). If you decide to pick up RE2, understand that while the game is fun the engine is made for high end performance, and that you may also need to do this same sort of fiddling.

Every once in a while you play a game that completely changes your entire outlook towards a certain genre of games, Resident Evil 2 Remake was that game for me. Horror/Survival Horror games have never been my cup of tea but after playing this brilliant gem my perspective has definitely been changed.

The game gives you the choice of picking one of the two main characters to play first - Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield. Depending on whom you pick first the cutscenes and the order of the stuff you do change but nothing major. The game encourages atleast two playthroughs once with each character. A horror game lives and dies by its sound design so i am happy to say that this game has one of the best sound design i have ever heard. The thumping footsteps of Mr.X, the screeching screams of the infected and the diverse environmental soundscape  further raises the sky high tension present throughout the game. The voice acting are well done with some of the cutscenes being absolutely mindblowing especially the opening cutscene which uses photogrammetry technology to make a fkn burger look lifelike. The overall graphics are top notch as well, with a stellar lighting system further immersing the player into it's gripping atmosphere.

The main gameplay loop consists of solving various puzzles to gain access to new areas as well as new routes or shortcuts to previously accessed areas, while trying to avoid the infected because of the scarce resources the player has. The inventory you start with is very limited forcing you to make important decisions regarding what to prioritise, which further raises the stakes. The level design of the main area i.e. Racoon City Police Station is one of the best i have ever seen. Never had I thought a simple police station in a video game would be so interesting to explore since its looping and interconnected paths make it feel like a real lived in place rather than level in a video game. All of the puzzles are really well made and pretty intuitive since the solutions always made sense. And lastly how can we forget about the star of the show Mr.X, his presence in the game takes it from a pretty good game to a fkn masterpiece. I further do not want to spoil the heart wrenching encounters you will have with him so i suggest that you experience them for yourselves.

The story is nothing to write home about but it definitely does not detract from the overall experience since the gameplay more than makes up for it. The fans of the original will definitely love this as it faithfully recaptures the magic that was present in the original. This game has definitely shattered my preconceived notions about this franchise as well as the genre as a whole that i cannot wait to try their other games as well.

Resident Evil 2 is the first real remake of the classic series. Rather than being "remastered," this Resident Evil 2 provides a fresh take on the an original classic. Yes, you will notice some change in the storyline, but overall it remains relatively the same.

You're able to play as either Leon or Claire as they have their own independent stories that merge over time. The bosses and B.O.W's have received a massive overhaul in appearance and abilities that give this classic a new spin. There are additional optional features that you are able to unlock after completing certain quests resulting in infinite ammo weapons (or you can just buy the upgrade directly, its your choice really.)

After completing the game, it does unlock the Hardcore mode where you take your skills to a whole new level. With unlimited ammo weaponry, its still relatively challenging giving you that same level of excitement ans suspense.

The game also includes a Mercenaries mode that really allows users to relive the classics. Capcom was nice enough to even throw in the original Tofu character.

Overall, this is a wonderful remake and a great installment into the series. You definitely get what you pay for as the storyline has plenty of hours on either side. Well done Capcom.

Following from my enthusiastic experience with the original Resident Evil Remake, i decided to play the remake of the second game to continue my journey in the series.

Resident Evil 2 gets so many things right that it is almost hard to believe. The atmosphere is tense (expecially thanks to the incredible lightning effects), getting around any corner can always hide an unexpected enemy encounter. Mr. X alone gest so much stress on the player that it makes the rest of the game look (almost) innocent.

Coming from the original, it took me some time to get used to the dinamic movement and aiming, but it's no traumatic change, instead it benefits immersion. Difficulty-wise, it would have been cool to have a standard mode WITH the ink ribbons, expecially for new players looking for a taste of the original experience without the need for expertise it requires.

Story is fun, i much preferred Leon's, but it is not really the strongest point of the experience. That is Level Design.
Resident Evil 2 is built in such a way that it suits exploration, speedrun, horror, survival, and whatnot all depending on the player's knowledge and ability. It is versatile, and that is maybe why i played through it 4 times, always finding new approaches and ways to experience this incredible remake.

As for the original one, I say to newcomers "Don't be scared!". Well, of course you will be scared, but there is really so much to enjoy here that it would be a sin not to play this game.
Stunning Visuals. Great Atmosphere. Immersive Gameplay. Lastly, a great third person zombie shooter you can count on having a good time in.

[h1][u]A Brief Introduction[/u][/h1]
Resident Evil 2: Remake is a complete and full, true remake of the original Resident Evil 2 that dropped seemingly out of nowhere in early 2019. It has since received numerous accolades from players and solidified Mr. X as a recognizable household villain, infamous for punching streamers on Twitch that have no spatial awareness. Is RE2 worth the hype? Let’s find out.

[h1][u]In-Depth Analysis[/u][/h1]
[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Resident Evil 2: Remake is a proper modernization of the core Resident Evil mechanics that have become dragged down by age and clunkiness. Ammo isn’t a hot commodity, healing and resources are limited, and inventory space is very small. What RE2 does right is properly add to these outdated restrictions with a modern touch that heavily rewards backtracking and thorough exploration.

The key additions to the survival horror formula are gunpowder and hip pouches. These items can be found scattered around the world, of course in limited quantities. Gunpowder varieties can be combined in different ways to provide different kinds of ammunition, with rarer gunpowder types providing better resulting ammo. This allows the player to temporarily and selectively circumvent normal ammo restrictions to obtain more of it. Hip pouches are even rarer, and always hidden behind locks and safes, but when obtained boost the inventory space by two, making them very motivating to seek out. Now players are not irritated by heavily squeezed inventory space, but still need to overcome adversity to achieve this. It is not handed to them easily.

As for gameplay, RE2 features unrestricted over-the-shoulder third person shooter action, a sharp departure from the fixed camera angles the original game is known for. This is nothing but a boon to the experience, as being able to appreciate how many enemies are trying to box you in is easier with the freed camera, and a player must be able to actually aim to fight off zombies. 

However, the undead don’t really need working bodies to keep trooping along, so the gamer instinct to aim for the head won’t always yield results. Zombies don’t need a fully functioning brain, headshots only work if you can take the whole head off. Instead, shooting off limbs to disable zombies or at least temporarily stagger them long enough to sprint past are the core elements of this game. While you can just fire willy nilly into a crowd and hope for the best, more punishing enemies like Lickers or the infamous Mr. X will not oblige your reckless play and will quickly (and involuntarily) make you join the undead horde. You need to play smart, not aggressive.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2509878828
The famous Mr. X only plays a prominent role in the first area of the game, the Police Station, but he is an omnipresent nuisance to your plans that forces you to consider your actions ahead of time, lest he corner you with a Licker or more zombies than you can handle before he pummels you to death. His constant thudding footsteps and the sounds of doors being kicked open will hound both Leon and Claire as they try to get out of town.

RE2 features puzzles, just like all Resident Evil games, but thankfully these puzzles are all fun brain teasers that don’t require extensive mind-wracking to figure out, unlike the original trilogy of RE games. Still, many of them seem to be the player solving a problem that really just shouldn’t exist in the first place, like a sewer door locked by six circuit breakers sealed by a riddle and chess pieces. The concept is so outlandish it breaks even the suspension of disbelief, but thankfully not by much.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2509882465
[h1]Story[/h1]
The player steps into the shoes of either Leon Kennedy or Claire Redfield as they are attacked by undead, and try to get to the bottom of the situation. You can choose from two distinct campaigns to play through the game with, and while both share the same major areas, the way they progress through them is changed, each character has areas unique to only their campaign, and a few enemy or item placements are changed up. 

This is welcome replay value, further enhanced by the Second Run feature, which lets you replay the two routes with completely different item and enemy placements, the progression of rooms in the Police Department is dramatically changed, and Mr. X shows up far earlier in the game to start causing problems.

From start to finish, the story is engaging and motivating, dealing with the grasp Umbrella Corporation truly has on the city, the T-Virus, and the mysterious G-Virus that makes the T-Virus look like child’s play. There’s never a dull moment.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
RE2 looks amazing. Environments are extensively detailed, decorations and architecture are beautiful, the models of enemy and ally alike are impressive, and the game constantly delivers. The attention to animation detail is also noteworthy, as RE2 captures the twitchy, spastic nature of the undead, and the  bloody splitting of limbs. Mr. X lumbers around, persistently power walking towards you on sight. Bosses especially have just as much visual spectacle as gameplay, their attacks damaging the environment around them, their aggressive presence…. the whole experience is simply difficult to explain. It’s the same quality of visual action I’d expect from a stellar sci-fi movie, not a game.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2509883255
[h1]Audio[/h1]
The musical score is the other half of the presentation of the game, pairing with the visuals to create nervous tension in dark hallways, a calm sense of safety in saferooms, or a grand sense of urgency and awe when facing down Mr. X or William Birkin in one of their various iterations. The bellowing brass, chorus choir, hard beats, the roars of the enemy, explosions all around; these give an unparalleled sense of “This is it. This is a FIGHT.” that you rarely get these days from non-heavy action games like Dark Souls. Even if fights like the Super Tyrant weren't mechanically impressive, they will stay in my mind for a long time for sheer memorability and spectacle alone.

[h1]Technical[/h1]
[u]GeForce RTX 2060 6GB | AMD Ryzen 9 | 16GB | Windows 10 [/u]
I could easily get over 120 frames on mostly maximum settings. The graphical settings are a bit strange, displaying the VRAM and giving you the option to dedicate way more memory than you need to just textures. But if you don’t try to overkill your own game, it should run fine on most hardware.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
[h1][u]An Essential Experience[/u][/h1]
Resident Evil 2: Remake is a phenomenal game that provides both tenseness and intensity at the same time, through its excellent mechanics, gunplay, rewarding exploration, and sense of excitement that is difficult to find in a single game. The high replayability with two campaigns, both featuring modified second playthroughs, is just icing on the cake for content to give more bang for your buck.

The free DLC even includes four more challenge run / campaign hybrids for people that find themselves hooked like I did. 
Unless you sadly can’t run it, there’s no reason you shouldn’t grab yourself a copy of Resident Evil 2: Remake during the next sale, or even potentially at full price.

Resident Evil 2 a third person survival horror and a remake of the 1998 game of the same name.
The remake features modern graphics and gameplay, so no tank controls or fixed camera angles.
The story takes place two months after the events of Resident Evil. Most citizens of Raccoon City have been turned into zombies.
The game features 2 scenarios, the Leon or Claire scenario.
Leon S. Kennedy is on its way to Raccon City to start his job as a cop in the RCPD (Raccon City Police Department), while Claire Redfield is on her way there to search for her brother Chris. The game starts at a gas station outside of the city, where both protagonists meet each other. They are now driving together but it will not take long and both get seperated after arriving in Raccon City.
Both scenarios features the same areas but with different paths, the enemies and the puzzles are also the same. But both characters have different goals, different NPCS and different weapons.
The duration of the first playthrough is around 8 hours.

I wanted to like this game, and the RE3 remake after it. Heck even get into the RE franchise more. But after a short time, I just couldn't with my overbearing disappointment with them. (This is a bit of a combined review of RE3& RE2 remake fyi, mostly RE2)

In short:
The two new remakes are incredibly stunning in visuals, BUT having an ungodly slow run speed. Weapons do no damage. Combat just not being fun. Deteriorates you from wanting to explore. Item management being a nuisence rather than being a fun, or even a decent part of the game. All in one package, making the games incredibly boring. I cannot recomment anyone buying any of these at full price, or at all. I say that with a heavy heart. I wanted to like these.


----More in detail-----

I recently played through RE4 on the gamecube, and I had a lot of fun playing it. I even did a full new game+ of RE4 right after it even though I didn't intend to do it, nor is that common of me to do so, but alas I did it while still enjoying myself. But RE3 & RE2 in comparison was just disappointing. I almost never ask for refunds for games, but these made me want one almost immediately. RE3 and 2 felt like everything from RE4, but worse in every area except from looks. 

RE2's introdution is actually quite nice. It is truly interessting and gives a good amount of immersion. However it doesn't set you up to something all that exciting. You just investigate a small area, then try to get into the police department. Now lets take RE4 as a comparison. You get a short briefing on whats going on and what you need to do. You're taken to a remote village for a rescue mission. The locals turn on you, and rather quickly you have to fend off against a whole village while despirately scavenging the villlage for resources. The guns and mechanics makes fending off a horde fun, manageble, and engaging. Back to RE2, you get a gun, leave small area, and run past some zombies to get to a safer place, big whoop. The introduction gets carried a lot by simply looking great, but it falls short on being engaging with gameplay.

Secondly, the gameplay is really boring. You run around at the speed of a slog while having to cover a short amount of distance. Which ultimately ends up feeling like an eternity due to your lack of speed. I could've probably gotten through the whole village + farm part in RE4 by the time you've jogged to the third floor of the R.P.D in RE2. The gun is a literal peashooter in both RE3 and RE2 and you cant even fire it in rapid successions even if you wanted. That is before any possible upgrades. The only reward for killing zombies is that you dont have to face them anymore. Which albeit really advantageous and good, though the zombies aren't even fun to kill in first place. Why are they not fun to kill? Again, literal peashooter and you constantly have to make sure they are actually dead. While making a lot of sense, but is it fun? Not to most I would imadgine. So much so that you start to question "why bother?" And in RE3 there is a whole nother gameplay nuisance. That being getting grabbed by zombies. Once grabbed, you are going to get bit. That is tradition. But when you get a button prompt that makes you believe you can get them off you, only for it to not seemingly to anything? THAT'S just misleading. Although you later find out that it simply mitigates damage taken, and in previous games, why even have it there in the first place? Where I once again have to ask myself "Is this fun?", for me to then give a resounding "NO".

Lastly, the items. 10 or so slots that fills up at the blink of an eye? Gee whiz! Sounds like fun to me!...... Although an iconic part of the RE franchise, having to suddenly have a full inventory, run back to the item storage box, and then back to the place you wanted to lot is just poor game design. Rinse and repeat too bear in mind. This isn't 199X anymore. And even by that time, I can't see that being much fun. With the addition of making it seem like you can pick up a lot more than you can actually pick up, the whole package ultimately deteriorates you from wanting to explore and loot areas as a whole. It's funny to me since one of my favorite franchises is basically item management the series. However RE4 did leagues better here, even made it satisfying too (search up Resident 4 Inventory ASMR, and you'll get what I mean). RE4 is more action focused sure, but I dont see much of a reason to be that strict and faithful when its not even fun. I wouldn't even have wanted that big of an upgrade to your inventory. Just 2, maybe even 4 inventory slots more from the get go. The item pouch increasing the same amount as before, and 10 slots being standard on hardcore. 

In conclution, these remakes (except the 1st one) seem too strict and too faithful to the original. While that often being a good thing, in this case its just feels outdated and redundant. And if you've already played something better, I hardly see a point to pick this up. Much less at full price. These (RE3&2) just seem like resident evil games with all the fun parts sucked out of it. Seemingly forgetting that its supposed to be a game. Its supposed to be fun ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥! These are legit a contender for the worst games I've ever played out of my 60+ games I've played to completion. I'd rather have a bad game out of the get go, than that of a painstakingly boring one. Because with the obvious bad one, I dont have to waste time figuring out if its a waste of time, money, or having to think about the possibility of has some promise later on.

After 43 hours, over 11 playthroughs and every achievement/record in the game unlocked, I can wholeheartedly say that this is hands down the best remake of any video-game, period, and has quickly risen into the ranks amongst my favourite games of all time.

I don't think I've ever had an experience that so effectively managed to make me simultaneously want to explore every inch of its environment, whilst at the same time being absolutely terrified to go anywhere outside of the comfort of the safe rooms. This game just understands horror, in every aspect, and there were numerous occasions that made my heart race like absolute crazy, even from menial things such as sound cues, lighting or ambience.
I truly could go on about this game for hours. I considered starting a YouTube channel just to write and record a video essay on why I love this game so much. But to stick with Steam's restrictions, here are, in my opinion, the things this game does incredibly:

- [u] Atmosphere And Ambience [/u]
This game mixes survival horror and action in the most perfect of ways, without ever feeling like the action-movie-oriented entries later down in the franchise. Every corner of RPD has atmosphere in spades, all accompanied by haunting ambience, faint background noises off in the distance, and a substantial lack of cliched horror movie-esque sounds/music
- [u] Exploration And Collecting [/u]
The level in which this game is crafted to prod the player's ingenuity and make them think about things such as item-management, crafting, storage and route-planning on a consistent basis without just throwing you bags of ammunition and healing items, is utterly masterful. Every room in both RPD and beyond serves a purpose, and 99% of them feature something you can come back to once something has been obtained later on down the line. I can't even describe the pure rush of euphoria I got on numerous occasions when I'd find an item near the middle/end portions of the game that let me go all the way back to the starting areas and finally reach something I'd been clueless on how to get for ages. By the end of my second playthrough I knew the police station inside and out. The game is perfect at making you need to remember rooms and play methodically to survive, even if you know the map like the back of your hand
- [u] Character And Worldbuilding [/u]
It's been said by many a reviewer that Leon and Claire are the best performed and most believably portrayed in this game more than any other of their appearances in the series, while a few argue that Leon's clueless baby-faced persona doesn't remotely compare to his roundhouse-kicking bomber jacket-wearing badassery of RE4. Personally, I think Leon and Claire are two of the most well-written and joyfully performed protagonists of any game I've ever played. The two so perfectly capture the attitude and confidence of two innocent bystanders that got caught in an unlucky situation that changed them for the better. Leon arriving as a clueless rookie that just wants to get everyone out alive, and ending the game as a confident vengence-fuelled hero that wants answers from the company he feels betrayed by. Claire starting off as an innocent teenager wanting to find her brother, before ending the game as a confident and motivated pseudo-parent to a girl that entrusted her life into her. Through the entire experience I cared thoroughly about both characters equally [spoiler] and found the true ending incredibly heartwarming and satisfying [/spoiler]
- [u] Mr X [/u]
This beautiful beast gets his own section, because he truly, for me, took the overall experience of this game from a solid 9 to an easy 10 single handedly. Purely through presentation, behaviour, AI, and his terrifying presence throughout the game. Without him here, subsequent playthroughs likely would've gotten very repetitive, and I would've felt very little desire to keep coming back to this game as consistently as I did, but being able to return to RPD and have to complete a whole new set of puzzles and exploratory segments while an unstoppable brute with absurd damage audibly chases after you is the most heart-pounding feeling I've ever experienced. Just being in the middle of a puzzle you really need to finish, or looting a room with only one entrance, only to hear muffled footsteps either above you, below you, or right outside the door, is a feeling I find almost impossible to describe (considering I was playing with surround headphones too, the adrenaline skyrocketed on numerous occasions). Even if you have the tools to deal with him, and even if you truly feel like you could take him in a fight, don't. Ammo will be wasted and you'll only spare yourself around 30 seconds before he gets right back up. Somehow in a game featuring miniguns, grenade launchers and electricity blasters, the mere presence of Mr X so perfectly encapsulates a feeling of utter helpless, and the bass drop accompanying his utterly stomach-sinking theme will never not make my heart race, even 11 playthroughs in.

I truly can't tell you a single thing I actively dislike about this game. Gun to my head I sometimes think the zombies soak up too much bullets, and I kinda wish Mr X wasn't as scripted/scarce in some areas (i.e the [spoiler] NEST section where he smashes through the window of the greenhouse [/spoiler]

Also, despite all the memes and how beloved Mr. X is, in the end he just becomes more of an nuisance rather than an terrifying obstacle in your path.
 
 Sadly, there honestly isn’t an whole lot of replay value outside of playing the A and B scenarios for both characters on the other three difficulties. There is 4th Survivor mode where you play as HUNK, everyone’s favorite Umbrella Agent from the series as you navigate your way past every enemy in the game on this tight corridor gauntlet. Beating it will unlock Tofu Survivor where you’ll play as Elite Operative, Tofu instead of HUNK and running through that will unlock his other teammates from the squadron. Ghost Survivors is another one that will occupy your time for a bit for the collectibles and challenges but at it’s core it is essentially just 4th survivor but other characters who’ve died in the game on an what if scenario of if they did live during the Racoon City Outbreak. Sadly, there isn’t really any dialogue or story outside of an small cutscene that is still framed and in black and white or the loading screen telling you the synopsis on what this is about.

 If you’re an fan of the series you’ll enjoy it for what it is but if you come into this with an high expectation of terrific storytelling, great character development and stunning visuals and fast gameplay. Then this game will not be for you. Story is pretty meh, no real development outside of maybe both protagonists being more brave and or less scared throughout the game. The game is pretty well… pretty and it is stunning to see this old game in the modern RE Engine but the gameplay side of thing’s is deliberately more slow paced compared to its older entries from RE 4 onwards, no dodging and no punching/kicking or germen suplexing zombies. You can not aim and move if you aim down sights to focus not only will it take a bit of time to have the reticle focus into an more precise and critical shot but your character will be stuck in place for all other foes to get close towards. Patience is the name of the game and strategy is optimal to live and get by each stage, that means ammo and slot management for your inventory, the pro’s to fighting is if you kill that zombie he will not hinder you during your backtracking for puzzles or collectibles. The con is less ammo and time loss for running the game under 2 hours. Sometimes running away is the quicker and best option, especially if you know you’ll never be back over there anyways. 

 All in all. If you’re an fan of the series or maybe classic survival horror then this is the game for you. If you’re not any of those but have been told good things and or are interested in the series or genre then I implore you to give this gem a try. Just know what you’re getting into first and take your time for the first time till you get the hang of it all because if you run and gun like other games allow you to do, you’ll get punished for it.
