A masterpiece of action and horror although not without its weak parts, it’s mostly stunning to look at and mostly great to play.  

The graphics are great, using light and particle effects to good effect and the levels look good with varying amounts of disrepair, although some of the textures are really low resolution for some reason. The limited direction cues, convoluted key hunts, maze like structure and involving puzzles with tough, endless enemies does make the gameplay a bit slow and repetitive at times, but adds to the difficulty and the tension as you never know what’s around the corner.  Having to manage limited resources in a small inventory starts off annoying, but does mean each decision has a greater impact and isn’t that bad towards the end. 

The characters and the monsters look good and as iconic as they are, they don’t actually have much ‘character’ to them in this game.  The overall premise is a bit daft, running around a museum/police station finding elegant keys to elaborate locks and exploring massive secret underground laboratories, but that’s part of Resident Evil’s charm.  The inability to dodge most attacks and the weakness of the weapons are questionable choices, but I guess this is a throwback to the original.  The boss fights are good fun, although the final ones throw away all sense of realism, the additional playthrough was a bit underwhelming, and I really didn’t like the bonus “time attack” modes.  There also isn’t much in the way of sound effects or music in the main game.

Resident Evil 2(2019) is a remake of the Resident Evil 2(1998). This is a long overdue project since 2002's incredible remake of the original Resident Evil. This is an huge opportunity to revisit one of the calssic games for the veterans and a great game for those who never played the original. 
As someone who never played original RE2, because I don't really want fiddle with PS1 emulation or search for original hardware to play it, so I have no first-hand experience seeing differences between original and remake.

The story takes place in Raccoon City. A small american town, that became a epicentre of the horrible outbreak of the unknown virus, that turns people into flesh eating, unstoppable monsters. Without knowing this, a rookie police officer Leon S. Kennedy, and college student Claire Redfield, come into this nightmare, where they find the reason behind this epidemic and stop it's spread, while trying to get out of there alive. Before starting a new game, you choose who are you going to play as, and your choice will change some story elements and each character have their own unique equipment and rooms they access. Depending on who chose to play as first will open you an ability to play through the game second time as different character, following the footsteps of your first character. This is cute gimmick, that increases replayability and gives more content to experience. That being said the main bits of the plot are the same. You get trapped in the police station, get out throught the sewers, find the Umbrella lab and get out of there before it self-destructs
Now the plot is not the best part of RE games, they always lacked deeper emotional or philosophycal stakes of something like Silent Hill, instead leaning into it's action roots with stupid dialog, that tries to be either so unfunny that it becomes funny in the proccess, or so overly serious that it's, again, causes only laughter. That being said, this is AAA game from 2019, so I don't thimk Capcom could get away with cheesy dialog performed by two puppets, so direction it took is atually quite serious. The few characters you meet are actually great. The mysterious Ada Wong, who manipulates everything and everyone to get what she needs. Chief of the police Irons, who is perfectly portrayed as a total scumbag of a character. Even little girl Sherry doesn't come off as annoying. And there are some genuienly great cutscenes, that are entertaining to watch, and can be skipped on repeat playthroughs. That cutscene with Kendo was just something else< almost cried at that.

The game is build on the Capcom's own proprietary RE engine, that was developed for RE7. At it looks great. When it comes to the visuals of this game, I have actually no complaints. That characters look incredibly detailed and realistic. The levels are great and filled with all sorts of detailes. And to top it all off, the game is very well optimised. There are a lot of options you can tinker with to get the possible picture with the least amount of impact to the performance and I really appreciate that Capcom actually put so much care into the PC port of the game.

I think the biggest challenge of this reamake would be translating the core gamelay features of the original, without alienating new players and not changing it so much that it pisses off old ones. Again, I haven't played the original, but what we have here is great. In REmake with it's controls and systems you fighting against you own limitations, when it comes to small invertory space and controls, and how helpless you felt against monsters. Now in RE@make we have the third-person camera that was implemented by the RE games since RE4, which in a way helps with putting you face to face with enemies, but might take away some athmosphere, and modern controls, that all of the modern players are familiar with will not give the same sense of helplessness that older titles would have. But I think in RE2make, even if it is more comfortable to play, it still punishes you very, very hard by putting you constantly into dangerous situations that you have no safe way to get out of. There are so many damn zmbies in this game, AND THEY JUST WON"T DIE! The game gives you just enough resources to get by, but if you blow all of your ammo and healing items in the first couple of rooms, you will have even harder time later when you face much more threatening enemies and even more dangerous situations. So with your superior movement and control, you have to outsmart your enemies and avoid them when possible. Save yourself some ammo, hold onto your herbs and sprays until you need them and pray to your god to have enough ammo for the next section. And while shooting is much easier than the originals with their own systems, aiming and shooting is not enough, most of the guns require you to stand still and focus your aim to get that perfect, accurate shot. The game thread the path between action and horror very well, so you have your shooting moments, and your scary horror moments, but only if you play your cards right, because you don't want to get stuck in a room with two lickers without ammo for your most powerful gun, that you blew on some random zmbie that annoyed couple of rooms ago. And with how much tension and anxiety the game builds andnight somehow comfortable with your position in the game, they just drop unkillable Mr. X on you, and he's gonna give it to ya.

So yeah, I'm actually kind of surprised how well RE2Make plays. It is a very well made game on it's own even without it's legacy as a remake. New players will definetely enjoythemselves if they enjoy this brand of horro and gameplay that constantly stresses you out and puts you into uncomfortable situations. And it's also full of content. Not only you get two full campaigns that play differently depending on which character you pick, you also get some bonus modes like The 4th survivor and The Tofu Survivor. you also can get some small episodes as DLC that show stories of other survivors of Raccoon City. And the there are challenges, like playing through the game without saves, or speedrunning it to get some bonuses like new cool weapons. RE2make is a great game that will satisfy fans of survival-horror.

Overall a very fun game. Replays are very short, there's a lot to criticize in terms of visuals, the soundtrack isn't very good but at least isn't noticeably bad either (just lacks the proper RE atmosphere) and can be replaced with the optional DLC for the original (which is more effective at putting you on edge) and the game tries to nickel-and-dime you over every tiny bit of bonus content in the form of outfits (many of which would be better served by giving you, idk, classic versions of their outfits or remakes of the original bonus outfits), but as a complete experience this is a very, very fun game to play through.

Zombies take forever to shoot in the head, which kind of takes you out of it, but it's somewhat understandable given that the game doesn't want to overwhelm you with dozens of zombies all respawning too much. This isn't exactly an ammo management game, at least not on the lower difficulties, but you do still have to watch you don't waste it all or you might start to have trouble with bosses in the game.

Ignoring all of those problems, though, I'd easily recommend the game. RE3's remake was disappointing by comparison, I can say that with certainty after playing it. It just felt so abhorrently short and the few sections where Nemesis chases you is far more annoying than dealing with Mr. X who is more of a slow menace, extending gameplay and giving a looming threat as you wander the police station, rather than what the Nemesis does where he just constantly pressures you and easily wipes the floor with you after just a few hits.

As someone who never got to play the original RE2, honestly barely even being aware of its existence for most of my life (saw 1, owned 3, beat 4, 5 and 6 as well as spin-offs like Operation Raccoon City, Outbreak, Revelations 1, blech, and Revelations 2, which was great), it was a really satisfying way to experience it with a more modernized approach. In a lot of ways it reminds me of RE4, my favorite of the series, but only in terms of general gameplay. There aren't any quicktime events that I can think of (thankfully) and the game isn't very campy in a fun way or action-y to the same degree that you'd see in 4-6, it's definitely more horror in tone, but I still can't help but draw comparisons because of the basic combat gameplay. I've always enjoyed this style of gameplay and it's why I never hated 5 or 6 for their many other failings. They're just fun games and they did gameplay right. Period.

I've actually recently heard the comparison that Capcom has just been remaking Revelations 2 over and over again and is hoping we won't notice and... they might be right about that, but that's not a problem for me, because I loved Revelations 2.

But back to RE2:R. If you want a real horror experience with the game, I recommend the optional soundtrack and to play on normal or higher, rather than Assisted. For me, I got through most of that but felt I just enjoyed the game more with Assisted (aim assist off, though, blech) and the default, bland soundtrack. I've always been a Resident Evil and general survival horror fan, so I was super excited to play this one. I will be basing much of this review off of both the original Resident Evil 2 and cutting it into four categories: Graphics, Audio, Gameplay, and Story. I will also be ignoring The 4th Survivor, The Tofu Survivor, and The Ghost Survivors, as they simply act as extra modes to have fun with and don't have any notable effect on the story or gameplay.

[b] WARNING: I will give my thoughts on every aspect of this game, and therefore will talk about story spoilers. Important mid-to-late game information will be censored if you don't want to see them. [/b]

[h1] Graphics [/h1]

The graphics in this game are absolutely unrivaled, to put it simply. The lighting perfectly compliments the claustrophobic and dark atmosphere of the game, as well as really bumping up the horror. Every single character was based on a real person, and they all look different and unique, to the point of looking real at times. Enemies are also incredibly detailed, especially the zombies. There are gender and race differences among zombies, which definitely add to realism the game was trying to emulate. Lickers look weird and horrifying, which is a perfect fit. [spoiler] Mr. X is wildly improved, both in behavior and visuals. He now sports a fresh hat, and somehow seems like an even bigger threat than his original introduction. [/spoiler] I won't discuss bosses in this category, but note that I love how they look in this game.

[h1] Audio [/h1]

Audio in this game is similarly great, especially in gunshots. Capcom clearly put detail into every sound, with subtle echoes in more spacious rooms and tighter pops in smaller rooms. The pained moans of zombies, banshee screeches of Lickers, echoed barks of the Cerberus, the [spoiler] resonant stomps of the Tyrant, [/spoiler] and the [spoiler] satisfying pops when shooting at Birkin's giant eyes [/spoiler] fit them all perfectly.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]

Rather than the tanky, fixed-camera controls of the original, RE2 went for a sleeker, over-the-shoulder camera angle, with new-gen 3D movement controls. Considering the state of current-gen gameplay, the 3rd person view was very well done, and I was quickly able to get used to it. 
Gunplay is unique and well-handled, as well as effective at not making me feel too weak at any points. I could confidently walk into a room with 3-4 zombies, knowing I can keep my distance, stagger them with a few handgun rounds, and finish them off one-by-one. During boss fights, you are given resource restocks that can single-handedly take the boss down, which not only worries you less, but also gives you a hint of "hey, this is going to be a really difficult fight, so we gave you some extra ammo!"

[h1] Story [/h1]

The story wasn't much to write home about, but also not that bad. It was heavily based on the original story, with some extra focus on [spoiler] William and Annette Birkin, the game's main antagonists. [/spoiler] The story drives itself forward, and ties events together somewhat well. One specific instance, however, has been bugging me since my playthrough. Why are the [spoiler] first and second playthroughs not connected? The 2nd campaign should be what the other protagonist is doing, and fighting the same boss fights and doing the same things in the RPD seemed really cheap on Capcom's part. [/spoiler] Overall, I didn't find anything overly offensive, so it gets a pass from me.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1] 

Overall, this game is absolutely phenomenal. It over time became my 2nd favorite Resident Evil game (behind Resident Evil: Village, which I personally thought was an absolute masterpiece looking past the minor flaws), and if you have the opportunity to, buy it. You won't be disappointed. For my final verdict, I rate this game:

[h2] 9/10 [/h2]

[i]Resident Evil 2[/i] is a testament to how the franchise has really developed a healthy balance between action and survival horror. What we’ve got here is a fantastic remake of an already amazing game, implementing tight controls and beautiful detail without harming the survival horror integrity of the original title. This game is a love letter to the franchise and embraces its roots harmoniously. I enjoy the original titles, but it feels so good to play them with modern polish and no alienating quirks. [i]Resident Evil 2[/i] is the perfect representation of why the original RE titles are still adored today.

[h1]The Classic “RE Formula”[/h1]
The amazing balancing act of managing resources with inventory space is probably the best it’s ever been in [i]Resident Evil 2[/i]. I love constantly having to decide how much I should bring to defend myself from threats, while also having to leave spaces open for the potential of new items. This resource management is exhilarating in your first playthrough, as you have no idea what each room could contain, but it’s even better in later playthroughs, as advanced knowledge of the building’s loot gives you more options as to how you approach a situation, and thanks to the amazingly interconnected level design and large variety of weapons, there's plenty of ways to confront the game’s enemies.

They’ve captured the survival horror aspect amazingly well in this one too. There’s more control granted to the player than ever before, shooting and movement are extremely fluid and easy to perform now, but the player still feels often horrifically overwhelmed. Zombies are still absolute tanks, only the most powerful weapons can reliably kill them, providing additional strategy as to whether it’s worth fighting a zombie, or just stunning them and running away. It’s a brilliant balance of control and terror that permeates most of the game, but there are a couple occasions it’s thrown off balance. The Sherry & Ada sections are far more focused on terrorising the player, and although they’re alright overall, they become increasingly tedious as they play out exactly the same every single time.


I really appreciate just how many options are provided to the player with the most basic tools. There's a couple small touches that really ramp up this feeling, such as shooting limbs off of zombies to hinder their offensive, providing a multitude of solutions to the undead menace. This is where the crafting system really comes into effect, the player is free to balance their resources for the items they need more than others, offering a lot of customisation for what weapons the player wants to rely on. It opens the field for replayability too, there's  plenty of options to try new strats, and modifiers that can alter the game completely, I highly recommend a “no-box” run. This variety is only limited once you hit a boss fight, which are often nothing more than HP sponges. They’re a mixed bag, some can be fun to fight while others infuriating (crane boss), but I do think all of them go on for just a bit too long.

[h1]Racoon Police Station[/h1]
I think what stands out most in [i]Resident Evil 2[/i] is its creative setting like no other. The former art museum turned police station makes for a jarring building layout (what police station has a library and a clock tower?), making it all the more interesting to explore. It’s such a weird contrast as you explore this building that almost makes sense, but it’s all beautifully interconnected that traversing the environment is quite easy. Every room felt like it needed to be visited twice due to its quantity of detail. Hunting for secrets and finding new keys as you slowly master the layout of the RPD’s headquarters was the best feeling that this game gave me.

The police station also let’s [i]Capcom[/i] once again flex their incredible RE Engine. This game looks insane, the brief glimpses you see of the city in the intro are incredibly detailed, with the hoards of flames and meticulous car wreckages immediately selling the danger you now face. Then, when you finally step inside, they out-do themselves with how insanely detailed each room is. The elegance of the main hall, the comradery of the West Office contrasting it’s current decay, the segregated pristine status of the S.T.A.R.S Office, each room has been lovingly crafted with so much care to inform you the lives that once played out in this station. The environmental storytelling is impeccable both within files and in the world itself, and it integrates perfectly with the gameplay, as the player is encouraged to search these environments from head to toe for precious resources.

The police station is so insanely high quality that it eventually hurts the rest of the game. You spend a majority of your time in the building, and there’s an amazing amount of content to uncover there, that when you’re eventually forced to leave the building it becomes quite depressing. Later areas in the game are of a remarkable quality and introduce their own charms, but after riding off the coattails of such an excellent area, it can feel like a bit of a downhill slope from there.

[h1]A (Mostly) Faithful Remake[/h1]
This is one of the most impressive remakes I’ve ever played, it’s insane how much love has gone into capturing the feel of the original 98’ classic, the protagonists are a huge part of that. Claire and Leon feel so unique from one another, they’ve got access to very different weapons and branching storylines that take them to differing areas and encounters, but I think their in-game mannerisms really sell their characters. It’s great hearing their reactions to just how tough a zombie can be in the middle of gameplay. Their actual cutscene dialogue is rather dull along with most characters, and makes for a mostly serviceable story at best, but those natural callouts and witticisms in game felt very at home with the tone of the game.

I’m glad [i]Capcom[/i] was willing to take the risk of altering the original game for the better. The police station has received some huge layout changes that help sell it as a more lived in building and fixes traversal issues. The most notable addition is the stairs in the main hall, which feel so natural in the environment now that it’s amazing to think they once weren’t there. There’s even just new rooms and areas all together, with the third floor of the building being far more fleshed out and connected. The most interesting modification would have to be the increased relevance played on the Tyrant encounters, a small event turned terrorising stalker whose constant presence causes exhilarating chaos throughout each run through the game.

The one thing I found myself missing was the original games “B scenarios.” The remake offers a compromise in the 2nd run system, allowing you to play the other character’s scenario with various challenging modifications, much like [i]Resident Evil 7’s[/i] madhouse difficulty. This is a fun challenge, it’s great seeing areas you once knew become a bit more unpredictable, but it’s mostly just the same campaign which is a bit of a shame. It would’ve been nice to see Claire’s actions have an impact on Leon’s campaign or vice-versa, but with no differences in their campaign or interactions other than a couple cutscenes or written letters, the campaigns feel very disconnected as they create a weird “pseudo-canon” that doesn’t make any sense with the games overall events.

[h1]9/10[/h1]
[i]Resident Evil 2[/i] is a fantastic game that takes the best qualities of both the old and new titles from the series. Despite a couple missteps, the title stands as a brilliant remake of an old classic and one of the strongest games in the series.

Don't let the playtime fool you, I already beat the game on console twice and both times I loved it. This was my first proper delve into the RE games and I enjoyed every second of it.

The gameplay is great, the story is really good and sometimes feels like something akin to Aliens in that there are action elements within but it still puts horror center stage for the most part. The locations are memorable and carry such a foreboding and anxiety inducing feeling that you'll be hesitant to go down most corridors out of fear of what may be down there. The soundtrack is nice and atmospheric but for me personally I chose to get the original score add-on and had that playing from start to finish instead. Overall, even though it's from the PS1 era, the music still fits within this remake of the game and I feel it helps with the atmosphere for most of the locations, the RCPD building especially.

The combat is solid, though you may wish to conserve ammo, especially on harder difficulties as there's only so much you can find on the maps (I did a playthrough on hard once and by the time I reached the first major boss fight of the game I barely had enough ammo to get through it. So if you're playing on Hard or above, save your ammo and plan accordingly).

Graphics-wise the game is stunning. I had originally played this on the PS4 and thought it looked good then but the PC version is like night and day. The details on the zombies as bits of them are blown off, the rain, the environments, the character models, they all had serious time and care put into their designs and it shows. 

There are puzzles in the game (as is the staple with RE games from what I understand) and while they can be challenging, they're not impossible and you can figure them out without feeling the need to rage quit.

In terms of how it runs on PC, I've yet to have any issues. Haven't come across any game breaking bugs or glitches, no crashes of any kind, nor any frame rate drops. Overall the game runs like a well oiled engine on the PC.

There's tons of replayability with bonus content unlocked through things such has how fast you beat the main story and in which difficulty, or how many certain enemy types you kill, etc. The bonus content can also be bought as DLC too but it's optional, thankfully, as you can just unlock it through gameplay as mentioned.

In closing, RE 2: Remake is well worth the price. Either get it now or wait for a sale, it's up to you. But definitely make this a game to add to your library at some point.

What I liked:

It has the creepy tension of the original Resident Evil games, with lots of rooms to explore and puzzles to solve. The environments are all fantastic and fleshed out. The cinematic cut scenes are all pretty seamless, making it feel like an interactive story. You never really feel "safe" in the game, even though, at times, you know you are. They throw just enough at you to keep you on edge pretty much all the time which keeps you immersed. The graphics are nice, and all the animations are fluid. The way the zombies stagger around makes it more difficult to head shot them, which is challenging and realistic, I suppose. I think the resources are spread around fairly, at least on average difficulty. If you're too aggressive you'll feel the pain of lacking ammo later in the game. If you're not cautious you'll wish you had more healing herbs. Extra weapons are just difficult enough to get that you feel rewarded for doing so. You have to do some planning and strategizing at times in order to carry around your essential items. All of these factors add layers to the overall challenge, which is to survive, and escape. 

What I didn't like:

You have a frustrating lack of control over how the character responds to close contact with zombies. Once they're within your personal bubble you're forced to watch a cookie-cutter cut scene of the zombie biting your neck. If you have a knife or something you can hit space bar which alters the cut scene, but it forces you to waste a resource in the process which is barely any better than letting the zombie take a bite. Even toward the end of the play through, many hours into it, I still found myself mashing buttons wishing my character would respond the way I would in real life -- pushing, kicking, dodging, ANYTHING other than haplessly letting themselves get bit. I understand why they made the game the way they did -- to remove enough control to keep it challenging and resource-focused, and it works. But I think they could strive for a better technique. I would have enjoyed the game more if, say, the zombies were deadlier -- like maybe a single bite is either deadly, or toxic -- but my character could maybe shove them away or disable them somehow. But these zombies are magically capable of getting shot half a dozen times in the brain stem and they keep going, retaining their wild hunger, vision, and control over their body. The fact that a zombie can take so many bullets to the brain and be unfazed is even less realistic than the concept of zombies in the first place which is the one thing that detracts from the immersion the most.

Also, some of the puzzles were too easy. They're made out to feel like a National Treasure type of mystery, but all you have to do is pull up a menu and the answer is right there. Kind of removes the whole "puzzle" part of the puzzle. 

I don't think they switched things up quite enough for the "second run" to fully warrant another play-through. They came close, but for me the reward just wasn't there toward the end of the second play through and I (thus far) have not felt compelled to get over the hump.

Conclusion: I would give this game a 6 out of 10. Buy it on sale and enjoy it for what it is. Try not to think about what it could have been. Play it at night with headphones and enjoy the immersion.

I usually am not aware how to start reviews, however this is my first Capcom game, which i loved with its entirety. Unfortunately, i've not played other RE games, but since this one was enjoyable i've decided to pre-order RE8, along with RE7, therefore i will be able to experience most of the RE franchise. The game had a few flaws, which i will elaborate shortly.
P.S i had nothing to do since its curfew, so i finished the entire game, with its 4 endings, in 2 days!

Graphics:
Now, as mentioned i have not played the original, however, since this is the remake i basically witnessed the original game. Usually, when it comes to old games i have urge to play them, but the graphical issues and mechanics are shoving me back. For instance i've bought witcher 1, but its way too long and mechanics are messy, thus i have not even played it. The same thing goes to RE2, that is basically the reason why i did not play original(nor other versions) and went straight to the remake. Let me lengthen the graphical review a bit more... Amazingly and neatly done, i would go as far to say that even in 2021 we have not gotten such games! Zombies are well detailed along with cut-scenes, Main characters are beautifully created. Man, the RE engine really did an amazing job. When it comes to Graphics card, it did not have any problem with mine and i use 1050TI, which is one of the worst 10 series cards, I could play on medium and even with these settings it looked gorgeous!

Story:
I certainly don't want to spoil anything from the story, thereby i will give you a Warning! When it came down to story line i was a little disappointed in advance, i dont know why but i have that weird habit... but then i played it and oh well it was amazing! loved every single second of it. However, as i mentioned "flaws" thing is... you have to play the game 3 times, at least. Firstly, you have to finish Leon's or Claire's part then you have to finish either of them on the 2nd run in order to get the "true ending". Personally, i played 4 times and finished it all of the times. At the beginning i could not understand a thing, but then i got used to mechanics and other things. I got decent at it, in fact i even finished the second run in 2hrs and 40 minutes! If you wanna understand what Claire was doing while Leon was in the police station (or vise versa) you should definitely play the second run, along with both characters, because the story line in messy but yet profound. P.S boss fights are rather easy even on standard mode, but you can always change your mind and play on hardcore mode. One good thing is that, if you find hardcore/standard mode hard, and you end up dying quite a lot of times, the game tells you and lets you choose to switch to assisted mode, which is easier and wont be as complicated, if you are here for the story just choose assisted. Lastly, I only got jumpscared (in general scared) twice, so i guess its not that scary afterall.

Extra Game Modes:
You attain those modes after finishing the game, which i highly recommend you to do. Now, i've only played 2 of these DLCs (which are free as long as i know), although they are extremely hard... imagine playing Doom Eternal on Ultra Nightmare, but in a slowmotion. When you die it resets itself and you start from the beginning. I said its hard, because there are a lot of zombies and in certain occasions you have to go through narrowed passages, or through a bus, which makes everything twice as hard, Despite random loot zombies and "candy vending machines", from which you are able to get bullets, heal and etc, it is still hard. It is not impossible, but be ready to endure the frustration after dying over and over again. What these DLCs bring? you may ask, well they give additional information about certain characters, which you have come across during the gameplay. However, these DLCs are, apparently for me, rather confusing. Forgot to mention, there is no checkpoint in those DLCs. People like to use Cheats to finish them, but i could not figure out how to use cheats, thus i did not play all of the additional content  that the game offered. However you can win the game in less than 4 hrs to get the S rank, with that rank you get a pistol with infinite ammos. 

Flaws:

Resident Evil 2 introduces us to rookie cop Leon Kennedy who arrives in Raccoon City at the height of a devastating zombie outbreak and is tasked with uncovering the secret behind the accidental release of a viral biological weapon called the T-Virus.

I've never played Resident Evil franchise before the last week. Started from Zero and worked my way up. This time I gave Hardcore mode a shot on a first playthrough and I got a balanced, challenging experience that's extremely difficult to find in today's mass-consumer industry. This game was also a huge breath of fresh air as it's pure action and fun with its premise, gameplay and story not compromised by modern social justice and political issues.  

While puzzles where easier and more accessible than those found in Zero and REmake, I have greatly enjoyed  the concept of this game, which is a third person action game set in a puzzle-filled maze where we progress by solving mysteries, finding keys and items which is very much like an old style point-and-click adventure game. Resident Evil 2 is an amazing, one-of-a-kind hybrid of genres. 

Unfortunately, this game isn't scary aside from a couple of jump-scares. What it does with its enemy, combat design and ammo scarcity, however, is keeping you on the edge for a fair amount of  time as you progress into the unknown with limited supplies and saves. The tension can be there. I especially enjoyed having to deal with not only rooms and corridors packed of regular enemies, but also a special entity that is stalking you around the maze. Sadly it was a fairly short segment. 

I liked how I had to manage my limited inventory space and how I constantly had to make decisions and carry on with them. There is still that possibility to screw yourself up in the middle of a playthrough if you mismanage your resources, something which is just not found in games now. With all the bloatware games out there , here not once I felt punished for missing out on finding an item or not fully clearing a room and not picking everything up like a kleptomaniac as prioritizing and making sacrifices is part of the experience. 

I normally don't, but I am looking forward to replaying this as my memories fade. It is very unfortunate that once you figure out how to deal with the AI and get familiar with the map layout you can start breezing through the game without ever feeling threatened, hence I'll give some time before second playthough. 

Graphics and sound design are phenomenal. Texture are of very high resolution, lighting is great and does a good job in creating a dreadful atmosphere. Main character models are of beautiful, aesthetic people who are pleasant to look at with very well animated rigs and expressions. I am fed up of actors and models being uglified on purpose in western games but RE2 does a reverse and main cast contrasting with the antagonists really emphasizes the "good versus evil" vibe. Enemies are gruesome and some of the best undead I have seen in a game. One really has to appreciate how designers made the models change as they receive damage. I can say this the best-looking game I have played. Voice acting was really good and 180 to a typical English dub of a Japanese game, although sometimes you could tell that actors / designers failed to capture the tension of the moment, especially during combat "barks."  
Game is very well optimized. I was able to max it out for consistent 90+ fps on 2080 ti and i7 9700k. Stuttering happens due to the engine loading assets and scripts (which is one way you can tell that there is something about to happen / jump at you..). Fps drops were seen only in one or two particle-heavy cutscenes. 

Given the state of modern gaming I can't help not to give it 10/10. I just can't find a flaw and I hope to play more games like this in the future. Games that respect me, expect me to stop (or sometimes keep moving) and think and offer a challenge testing both gaming skills and being able to put things together. 

Again, my biggest issue with the game was that it just wasn't scary. Attentive player will quickly realize how things work, what to expect and how to avoid most danger which greatly impacts the threat factor. I didn't like a lackluster ending without closure (keep in mind I have only played single playthrough of Leon so far and there alternate characters with additional story tidbits).

I strongly urge anyone playing this to give themselves a favor and just go Hardcore right off the bat. And do not touch walkthroughs. I did once with the weapons case, ashamed to admit...

[h1][b]About The Game:[/b][/h1]
Biohazard 2: Remake is an attempt at faithfully remastering and remaking the original game released on Playstation back in 1998. Developed and Published by none other than the company who originally released the game all those years ago Capcom.

The game is a Survival Horror experience tailored towards newer audiences who may have been unable to enjoy the original game as it were back in 1998.

[b]Full Disclosure:[/b] I am a massive fan of the original 3 games and Biohazard 2 I consider to be an absolute masterpiece and my favourite in the series.

[h1][b]Enter the world of survival horror! Good luck![/b][/h1]

[h1][b]The Story:[/b][/h1]
The story is practically identical to that of the original game (with slight differences and variations.

You play as 1 of 2 different survivors facing the horrors that was once a bustling city in the heart of the United States known as Raccoon City, however this city has a dark secret known only to those who are in on the massive cover-up. Those people have been working closely with a group of scientists to design a new way of warfare, the creation of super weapons that, unlike humans will stop at nothing to achieve their goals. Bio-Weapons known as Tyrants, these genetically enhanced human-like weapons are among the many experiments that the Umbrella organisation have been developing in secret below the city streets.

Our main protagonists are in Raccoon City for their own reasons and just so happen to become a victim of circumstance:

[b]Leon Scott Kennedy[/b] a rookie police officer about to start his first shift at the Raccoon Police Department.

[b]Claire Redfield[/b] a teenage woman in search of her missing brother who once worked at the Raccoon City Police Department. 

Their original purpose for being there? Now completely out the window and a new purpose begins, to survive the night alive. However along the way they begin unravelling the hidden secret that lurks just below the city streets that they never intended to find.



[h1][b]The Gameplay:[/b][/h1]
The gameplay is quite simple when all things are considered, you must try and avoid zombies and all other forms of monsters that are unleashed upon the Raccoon City streets and buildings. Along the way you will encounter a number of interesting individuals that all have their own troubles and reasons for being in Raccoon City at the time.

To escape the city our protagonists must complete objectives, solve puzzles, duck, dodge and weave through hordes of the undead and of course shoot the occasional enemy along the way. However ammo conservation is paramount in a world filled with the undead but not a lot of ammo to waste.

The game is played in a Third Person perspective, the camera is placed behind the shoulder of our protagonist and you control them as you would any other game. Unlike in the original static camera angles are unfortunately gone.

Ammunition creation is back now, a returning feature that was original placed in the original Biohazard 3: Last Escape game that went MIA for a long time due to unpopularity with the fans. While playing our protagonists will find gun powder in which they can combine together to create ammunition for different firearms throughout the game.

Another returning feature from older games is the return of defensive items/weapons. Knives, Fragmentation Grenades and Flash Bang grenades all make a return for our protagonists to use when they're in a bind and need to make a quick exit or get out of the grasp of a monsters hands,

The Tyrant (aka. Mr.X) is now a dangerous and unpredictable force that is not to be taken lightly. The Tyrant will stalk the protagonist throughout the game. It is unpredictable and can turn up just about anywhere. Shooting it is only wasting your already small ammunition pool. [b]RUN![/b]

The boss fights in this remaster/remake have had an overhaul. They are now similar to modern game bosses with weak points in order to put the boss down.



[h1][b]The Verdict:[/b][/h1]
The Biohazard 2 Remake is an absolutely fantastic recreation of the original game that is already an absolute masterpiece. This game was very clearly created with a lot of heart, tonnes of passion and a strong drive to please the fans of the original game.

The graphics are absolutely stunning, fantastically compliment the atmosphere and definitely add a lot to the game There is so much detail in the world, in the models and in everything else about this game. Enemy dismemberment is absolutely amazing and weapons feel weighty like they would actually cause the damage you see on the enemies when you shoot them.

The amount of time and effort that was put into trying to please the fans in this remake is definitely apparent throughout gameplay and it must not be understated that it's greatly appreciated by a huge fan of the original.

However I cannot just praise this game as there's so much that is missing from this remake/remaster that made the original so special and so memorable to me as a fan.

There are area's of the original game that have been completely cut and are absent. Area's like the run through the Raccoon City streets at the beginning of the game have been made smaller, certain sections of the Hive have been cut (for example the giant plant between the upper and lower area of the Hive is now gone completely) and many other memorable areas.

Certain enemies are completely absent as well. The moths from the original game are no longer in the Hive and the Crows are no longer in the RPD or on the streets of Raccoon City, the Ivy's are still present, however have been overhauled (I would've preferred the originals). 

Now let's talk about the B scenario's for Leon and Claire.... Here's where I am going to deduct the most points. The original game had 4 very different scenario's that each of the characters could go through. Leon and Claire would encounter each other in the game in different area's each time, they would perform different actions each time and the game would end differently on each of the 4 scenario's. 

Many events that happened in the B scenario are completely gone, many of the area's that were in the B scenario are completely gone and a lot of the replayability from the B scenario are now absent. This is a major issue and I absolutely know why it was done. Capcom didn't want to delay the game and allow the developers time to make the game an absolute recreation. It was done in the vain of making money. This disappoints us fans of the original very highly and as such it will greatly affect the rating I can give this remake.



[h1][b]Final Thoughts:[/b][/h1]
While I do love this remake and I think that it does a very solid job of pleasing the fans, it lacks so much of the charm and replayability of the original game. I am very grateful that this game got the remake treatment, but it deserved better than it got. It's still a fantastic ride, and I still recommend people give it a try. But it's not what I had hoped for as a fan of the original.

The butchering of the B scenario's hurts me to the core greatly as a fan. The removal of enemy types and area's from the game hurts the replayability and the authenticity of the game as a faithful recreation of the original.

Overall though it's still a good remake and still deserves to be considered highly among us fans as a job well done on the team behind it. They deserve commendation for their efforts.



[h1][b]Final Rating?: 7/10[/b][/h1]
The effort that was put here is not to be understated. There was so much passion here from the developers, there's so many little details that most people wouldn't notice on a normal runthrough (or even on their first run through of the game). The developers behind this remake obviously wanted to make the fans happy.

I only wish that Capcom had given their developers more time to fully recreate the original game and given it the full remaster it deserved.

This makes moment to moment gameplay very interesting when you have to weigh up if using the precious grenade ammo is worth it when you could try to run away. At later points it introduces more dangerous enemies, which keeps the difficulty high and adds a fear of the unknown when re visiting areas as you don't know if there could be a new horror waiting around the corner.

It also has very good graphics (if you don't like blood and guts that would be a valid reason for not playing, the gore is detailed and gruesome) and a wide range of unlocks and bonus stories. I really liked it, I would highly recommend it.

[h1]Short Version[/h1]
[quote=VideoMortals]Resident Evil 2 is a perfect remake in every way. With an authentic storytelling in an environment of stunning graphics, RE2 is replayable and for sure, enjoyable! Just make sure they're dead for good.[/quote]

[h1]Long Version[/h1]

[b]Graphics : [/b]That is the key feature they aimed for in this title, and it's fair and reasonable to say that it worked really, really well for them. The game looks just breathtaking! The level design is real simple, yet still crowded and full in it's own trend (in a good way of course) The character design is just perfect. I was amazed by that actually, they look so good. Overall I was very much satisfied in terms of world graphics, Racoon city looks really good. The game itself storywise is, with some exceptions, pretty much the same as the generic Resident Evil 2 we all loved as a kid but the graphics, man they are just an awesome step up in this. (We will come back to story in a second) They offer us a great Resident Evil 2 remake with really good graphics you can't get enough of and it's just too much fun to play it this way. If you loved the original Resident Evil 2, this will make your life joyful, the graphics are THAT good. As a result, graphics, of course, passes ✔

[b]Gameplay : [/b]The new mechanics they installed in this is fairly great. The simplified inventory offers the perfect inventory management for you. It's pretty easy to navigate through menus, which is a really great thing if you're like me, the kind of player who likes to read every single thing they collect. Roaming through the Racoon City is really simple, since the combat is just super easy. Just run, run and run, well and sometimes shoot. Joke aside, the game offers a decent combat, in a beginner friendly manner. Even your fights with the main boss, Nemesis, are actually pretty easy as long as you understand his movement and attacks.
What I'm saying is, gameplay in RE2 is the best single thing I've seen all year in gaming. Amazing. Pass, pass, pass! ✔

[b]Open World : [/b]Re2 remake offers a fair amount of land for you to discover and rewards you for doing so. From weapon mods to herbs, medicine to tools, the game offers you a lot, just for exploring the magnificent Racoon City, and most importantly the magical police station. Yes, your map is limited and the world is not "open" per se, but you're totally free to create your own route and explore on your own and that's just enough in a horror game if you ask me. Still, for the integrity of this review, I will not be adding this section to my verdict. Open world, not included ❓

[b]Sound : [/b]Outstanding. Best sound in gaming this year, no questions asked for me. Just listen the originals, just amazing. Pass, of course pass ✔

[b]Replayibility/Story : [/b]I might sound like a fanboy here, but this is also a "great" section. The game has 2 main stories, for your 2 main characters. Both Claire and Leon stories are actually pretty similar in terms of ongoing action, you basically shoot zombies regardless of the story you're playing. But, they also are really different in the same time. The Claire A story is great on it's own, and full of joy, still in the end, game doesn't just end there, it gives you a half ending and makes you wanna play the other story even if it's just to kill that guy again and reach the actual ending. Plus, the game offers an amazing endgame points system, which simply rewards you for finishing it many times. You can get skins, you can get unlimited ammo, an infinite rocket launcher that basically lets you destroy Mr X and make fun of the little fella. Anyways, if I wasn't clear, yes, it's a pass. ✔

[b]In the end our results will look like this :[/b]
[b]Graphics : ✔[/b]
[b]Gameplay : ✔[/b]
[b]Open World : ❓[/b]
[b]Sound : ✔[/b]
[b]Replayibility/Story : ✔[/b]

This game is fun until you get into hardcore mode. The weakest of zombies turn into literal bullet sponges. The RNG at hardcore is actually stupid and poorly thought out. The same zombie will take 2 headshots to crit kill at one instance, and then 8 in another. This points to RNG, and RNG in shooting games is a lazy way of increasing difficulty. In the original, one of the funner parts of the game was figuring out in which instance you should run away and when you should try to drop a zombie. And why does it take 8 headshots to drop anything anyways.  I'm no gun or head trauma expert, but I feel like 6 consecutive shots at a head (even with a little 9mm) would disintegrate the entire cranium, so I just don't understand the rationale behind this inclusion. RNG on a zombie game? I just really don't understand. It's lazy. Instead of reprogramming these modes to add in more zombies/zombie types/horde varieties, they just made it harder to kill what was already there. 
The equivalent of this would be if you went to a restaurant and ordered a 12 oz ribeye, and they brought out an 8 oz and 4oz ribeye. You technically got what you ordered, but the experience isn't going to be as great it should have been.
This game literally could have been a genre redefining moment for Capcom and Resident Evil, but it just turned out to be REVII Biohazard with a RE2 skin. 
Time and time again, I've exepcted this company to bust out with a "zombie dark souls" type game that completely revolutionizes the way zombie games are packaged, but instead, in typical Capcom fashion, we end up with a "run away from the zombies in skintight clothing" simulator. 
It feels just like any other 3rd person shooter, at this point.

So far, I’ve played all TPP Resident Evil games starting from RE4 up to RE Revelations 2, and I’ve never been fond of the older entries with fixed camera. I knew many hardcore fans preferred the old ones, saying these were the real horror games and not action games. Hearing that Resident Evil 2 is being remastered, and it will be a TPP game, I just had to add it to my shopping list. And I’m glad I did.

Claire Redfield is my favourite character in the RE – this is the first RE character I’ve ever controlled and I just couldn’t help succumb to her personality and charm, so she was the man reason I wanted to try out RE2 after skipping RE7. I also grew attached to Leon Kennedy while playing RE4 and RE6 and he is by far the most likable male protagonist in the TPP RE games. So, as a non-hardcore RE player, I was really curious about their origins but I’ve never wanted to play the old RE2 for PS1. Now I had the chance.

RE2 is the best RE entry I’ve ever played. The only problem is, that it is way too damn scary for me at times, and I just can’t get myself to play for too long. And it is due to its enhanced realism. Naturally, it has the best graphics, but I also love the mechanics transferred from the previous entries and further improved in this one.

Of course, enhanced graphics quality makes the BOWs more terrifying, however, what makes this game a really horrific experience is the use of light (or rather the lack of it), shadows and space, and silence. A zombie is one thing but a zombie you can’t see until it’s too late with just barely enough space to put up a fight, the presence of which Is only realised when it growls behind your back is another level. [spoiler]And this is long before you have your first encounter with Mr. X. Damn this guy caused me so much stress I felt like I had PTSD after switching the game off to rest. Although he isn’t really much of a threat, and managed to trap and kill me just once or twice, the level designers really know how to make you anxious and paranoid about this guy![/spoiler]

The most notorious mechanics of the game is the vast weapon sway. So far I’ve only played as Claire, but I’m pretty sure it applies to Leon too. And this is understandable, Claire being a college student, and Leon being just a rookie cop, would be highly unlikely to aim and shoot firearms like a Navy Seal. This only multiplies the amount of stress, knowing that you have strictly limited ammo and you’ve just wasted two bullets missing a zombie from less than 3 meters.

Furthermore, unlike in RE6, the interface is minimalistic, simple, and clear. You can navigate through inventory, documents and map seamlessly, swiftly and effortlessly. This was a problem in some of the previous games, so this is a major improvement. It’s never been that good, in my opinion.

Finally, what makes the game even more atmospheric and immersive, are Claire’s and Leon’s displays of emotions in reaction to what’s happening ([spoiler]e.g. verbal irritation when the player struggles with fighting off BOWs or reloading weapons[/spoiler]).

I’m only just past the sewer sequence with Claire and I haven’t seen the whole game yet, but I already know I won’t be disappointed with it. It’s just a great horror game, apparently too good for me, because I’m too anxious to play it, so I progress really slowly. But don’t mind me, try it yourself!

RE2 Remake is not only a tribute to the saga, but also a teaching of how to make a remake. This might be the greatest remake I've ever played so far. A very good example of what remake should be. Back to over the shoulder formula of RE 4-5-6 with the atmosphere of the first 3 games. Amazing in almost every aspect. You have to complete both parts to see the real ending of the game. Even after completing the 2 parts of the game you can still play it again with the new unlocked diffuclty level; Nightmare. 

In this diffuclty level everything becomes much more tense and that makes a new more challenging and fun experience. Also makes you feel the thrill of being a survivor like never before, as each bullet shot, each item found, and each decision taken, can make the difference between life and death. Simply put, remake or not, this is survival horror at its best.

 Unfortunately, a single playthrough is slight at about 8 hours, but every minute is oozing with quality.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is a solid take on the original game that brings the nightmare of Raccoon City to a new generation.  There is a lot of content missing in this version of Resident Evil 2 in comparison to the original.  It feels like the developers chose to "cut out the fat" and keep only the areas of the game that truly felt intertwined with the narrative.  To balance this, however, they also brought cut content from the original RE2 to life, which is an awesome thing to see.

This is such a solid remake that I would give it a 9/10 were it not for a few key things I really did not enjoy:

1.) Mr. X/The Pursuing Tyrant can get [i]very[/i] annoying while you are trying to solve puzzles and learn the layout of the RPD for the first time.  I can completely see what they were going for, and I like the idea.  But, I think he lingers in the same area for too long, even after losing sight of you.  That caused me a lot of frustration rather than horror.  He felt more like nuisance, rather than a dynamic enemy I was supposed to fear.  Granted, as I moved on to Claire B etc., he had more of his intended effect simply because I knew where I was going and could try to avoid him, creating some tense moments where he would interrupt my planned route and I'd have to take a detour.  But, that initial impression while I was still trying to get my bearings really soured him for me.

2.) The crane boss (players will know the one) gives you such little room to maneuver that it is frustrating instead of scary.  I understand the idea behind giving the player less room so they feel trapped, but the player has no dodge button.  So, some attacks are pretty much impossible to avoid unless you get lucky.  A bigger boss arena would have made it significantly more fun.

3.) The 4 scenario system didn't need to stay.  I played all 4 (Leon A/Claire B, Claire A/Leon B), and there are little to no significant differences between the first and second scenario pair.  While the original RE2’s 4 scenarios had some distinctly different moments, in this remake it just feels like you're playing the same game in the opposite order, as if you're going from Leon A/Claire B -> Claire B/Leon A, or vice versa.  There are barely any noteworthy differences, so I don’t understand why they kept it other than for a throwback.  It worked in the original game for the replay value, but doesn't serve much purpose this time around.  I would have preferred just 2 scenarios, one Leon and one Claire.  That way, they could have put more time into making them distinctly different with set points of intersection where Leon and Claire's events overlap, similarly to the intertwining character stories in Resident Evil 6.

4.) The extra modes are not worth the ridiculous amount of effort it takes to complete them.  I got excited when I initially saw them, thinking they would be short glimpses into the lives of certain side characters in the game (especially [spoiler] Hunk! [/spoiler]).  But, all of them are just brutally difficult escape missions, the majority of which are non-canon what-ifs...  I really wish the developers had put their resources towards creating fewer high quality pieces of extra content with canon story like Ada's unlockable campaign from RE4 or Chris's "Not a Hero" campaign in RE7.  Instead they spread the content thin into a handful of extras that feel like low effort copy pastes.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is a very high quality entry to the series that streamlines a lot of things the original brought to the table.  Despite having a few notable flaws, I truly enjoyed my time back in Raccoon City.

While I have played the more modern style of resident evil games that exists in resident evil 4 and resident evil 5, I have not played the original resident evil or the original resident evil 2. This review is about how I, a casual fan of the series, experienced the remake. This remake is incredibly well done.

The environment and ambience in all stages of the game is amazing. The only thing that is somewhat of a blemish in this area is the cheesy voice lines from Leon and Claire. However, other moments, such as the first time you walk down the watery hallway and the first time you see a Licker, are intense and terrifying. These moments create a very powerful fear of what's around the corner, which is much easier said than done. I think all horror games should strive to create this emotion in the player, and very few are successful at this. Amnesia: the Dark Descent is the best example of a game that makes you afraid, and while the Remake does not go to Amnesia levels, it played its cards as a zombie game very well.

Puzzles are not difficult and the process of running through the map and gathering puzzle pieces to put together to make progress is a time-tested way to keep the player entertained and having fun. Old school resident evil games operate with this method at their core, and it works out very well. Bonus puzzles that are not necessary to continue the game but offer very helpful resources also entice the player to keep looking in every nook and cranny and experience all that the game has to offer.
Overall, I really enjoyed this game and didn't find too many flaws.

This is by far my most favourite Resident Evil game ever. I played the original as a kid on the N64 and simply just fell in love with horror and zombie shooter games ever since. The remake version may have some alterations from the original that changed the story plot in a few ways, but the majority of the Resident Evil lore pretty much stays intact. If you're looking for a zombie shooter game experience that really emphasises on horror, survival and resource management, this is definitely a game worth playing.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
RE2 Remake is an over-the-shoulder style third person shooter that involves resource management and a lot of puzzle solving to navigate your way through an overran city. The gun-play isn't too bad and it's very similar to other third person titles. But don't go expecting headshots to easily kill a common zombie. Inventory management is also highly encouraged in RE2, and the game teaches you that early on when you start off the story with very limited resources and inventory space. Puzzles are also very well implemented, with hints and pieces cleverly scattered throughout the environment. Furthermore, puzzles were also made in a way to emphasis the mysteriousness of Resident Evil's backstory, which really does make you curious more about the lore.

[h1]Graphics and Environment[/h1]
Game graphics are simply just amazing, as expected from AAA titles nowadays utilising physically-based rendering. The atmosphere and environment was modelled and rendered exceptionally well to convey the horror elements of a zombie apocalypse. Details such as blood stains, bullet holes, barricades and abandoned belongings really conveys the citizens' desperate attempts at defending themselves from the zombies, and makes you wonder what their final moments were like. The darkness in some areas, especially during your first playthrough, really puts you on edge to always have your handgun pointed in a "ready-to-shoot" stance, expecting a infected zombie to attack you at any moment. 

[h1]Replay Value[/h1]
There are 4 routes in total for the RE2 Remake's main story campaign; Leon A & B, Claire A & B. You can either choose to play as Leon or Claire, and experience each of their own story path on how they managed to survive the T-virus outbreak that completely devastated Raccoon City. Each route features it's own distinctive routes and exclusive firearms to use, which also helps to refresh the experience. Furthermore, if you do get bored of the main story campaign, you can also experience RE2's minigames in the 4th Survivor free DLC.

[h1]Mods[/h1]
As expected from a PC game, Resident Evil also features a very dedicated modding community. If you do ever get bored of the game, there's plenty of easy to install community-made mods that can really spice up your experience.

At the time of this review I am only 9 hours into the game, and know that I really wanted to enjoy this game going in, but I constantly find myself struggling to like the game, for a few main reasons. 

Reason 1: the Map is often times too small, not in its span, but it's layout, for example, when in rooms with zombies or other enemies, it is almost impossible to avoid taking damage when attacked, as the rooms and hallways are so narrow you cannot walk far enough around the zombies to avoid being hit. 

Reason 2: Why is there no simple dodge function? I understand that this game is trying to be as true to the original as possible, but when you add AI to a game that is as challenging as it is in this game, I believe a dodge mechanic would be called for, without a dodge mechanic it makes it almost impossible for the player to be able to avoid incoming sweeping attacks from enemies such as "William", and the "Tyrant". 

Reason 3: the third person camera leaves much to be desired, as at points in the game I have turned corners, only to come face to face with enemies, all because the third person camera has snagged on objects such as walls, plants, and junk, and not followed Leon around the corner, at certain times objects have even blocked the third person camera while aiming the gun making it impossible to shoot what I am aiming at, A simple fix to this problem could have been to simply make the camera turn First person but only while aiming a gun, which would allowed for better camera work, in my honest opinion. 

All these problems combined make the game for me feel like a absolute chore to play, I have not at the time of this review found the game fun to play, (even though once again I really wanted to going into the review), but if you did enjoy this game then I am happy that you did, but it may just be that this is not the game for me.

I don't care if you have literally only heard the name "Resident Evil" in PASSING. THIS game MUST be in your library and I feel obligated to explain why in detail, but

     Tl;Dr - It's a well-optimized, beautiful, Heart-racing, suspenseful, terrifying horror game that blends absolute anxiety & fear with puzzles with memorable maps, that even ENCOURAGES multiple (speed)runs.

The first things that caught my attention right away was the graphical detail, artstyle, and optimization. Even on lower-end settings the game has VERY solid performance, and amazing graphical detail. You'd expect a game that is this detailed and beautiful would be at least 50+GB after being conditioned to just accept game companies to shaft you with abhorrent unoptimization. When the RE2 remake was announced, Capcom devs said "we do it". And they did.

I grew up with the original three Resident Evils along with a bit of CODE: Veronica (I used a relative's Dreamcast to play it, but never got around to finishing it). I don't like RE4 because I don't find it a good survival horror game, it's a good action game but I don't think it's really *Resident Evil*. I loved the first half of RE7, and found the second half (was it a "half" point?) passable -- the former was a true return to form for the series, even if at a different perspective for the player in its gameplay. To be clear, I'm laying out my opinions on other games in the series so you can see where I stand with it, so that if yours are anything like mine, you know there's a good chance that your opinion after you play the RE2 remake reflects mine as well.

To me, you see, Resident Evil isn't about the T-virus or Umbrella corporation, or dragging on plot threads about tired characters that should've ended over a decade ago, or getting thrilled over whether Chris manages to convince Leon to help continue the Redfield bloodline. To me, Resident Evil is about exploring places with weird layouts and intricate architecture, solving bizarrely placed puzzles to progress, while constantly making tough resource management decisions to try and survive the threat of strange, frightening creatures: should I spend my ammunition that I may need later to make that zombie-infested hallway safe, or should I try to run through them, risking my health and thus my even scarcer healing items, assuming I don't give up my life? Should I spend this ink ribbon to save the game now, or should I save it for later when things get tougher, and risk losing precious progress forever if something goes horribly wrong?

The constant need to make all these decisions creates [b]tension[/b]. To me, this is the core of Resident Evil. 

And I am happy to inform you that the Resident Evil 2 remake delivers. Not only does it deliver this tension, it also delivers other things that made the original great, such as the sadistic pleasure of mutilating zombies to your heart's (ha) content, and such as the subtle film noir atmosphere (although that would be better achieved with a soundtrack closer to the original, as opposed to the more ambient one we get in the remake -- this is relegated to DLC; I find it almost [i]criminal[/i] that the original menu sounds are exclusive to the DLC and not default in the remake, as well as the also DLC-exclusive "Resident Evil 2" voice when you start the game being changed from the original, ominous one, the replacement being a bit cringe-inducing). It's joyful to see Capcom take the Resident Evil 4-style gameplay and make an outstanding, real Resident Evil game around it.

I have a couple more complaints about the remake; the length of my description is for detail, not because of great relevance: the first thing, I think, is that there should've been a way to have limited ink-ribbon saves in the standard difficulty. This would've emulated the difficulty of the original perfectly. The standard difficulty is too easy with infinite saves; needing ink ribbons would lend it a bit more of that tension for newcomers. Currently, the only way to have limited saves is in hardcore mode, and that is, and I'm not afraid to admit it, [i]too difficult[/i]. With all the difficulty elements together (tougher and more numerous enemies, less health, scarcer ammunition...), the game becomes [i]too[/i] tense, and ventures into the realm of frustration and stress. The devs aren't playing around with the naming here: hardcore mode is clearly intended for players who want a real challenge in their second playthrough. I just feel that there should've been a difficulty option that stood somewhere between standard and hardcore, intended for a first playthrough. 

[b]Yet, I think hardcore is still the best way to experience the new RE2.[/b] If you're not careful with the risks you take and parsimonious with your usage of resources (and let me reiterate: saves are a resource), the game will kick your ass without consideration for whether you're doing well at it or not.

This brings me to the second blemish I find with the game, and that is the bosses: they can be quite bullet spongy, and if you're too low on resources, or wasted your saves way too far before getting to them (or simply before making good preparations), you will get frustrated, and you may even have to consider restarting the game. This is, of course, not considering the standard difficulty, where infinite saves trivialize these issues.

At the end of the day, though, RE2 really delivers. The original RE2 is nearest and dearest to me (despite my finding REmake to be """objectively""" better, the quintessential old-school survival horror). It's a game that is sacred to me, having been my first acquaintance with the series, and one that brings warm fuzzy feelings of childhood nostalgia whenever I play it. The remake does a great job at mixing things up while preserving everything that was [i]iconic[/i]. The memory of the old police station layout is seared into your brain, and you will find many things as you remember them, but the layout is not quite as you recall. You will still have to get acquainted with it. Routes are perfectly designed to direct you in a clear progression inside the station and its whereabouts, and once you clear out and explore all of it, new objectives, new threats and new paths are thrown in, and you must adapt. It's all subtly changed from the original, but this is perfect Resident Evil design as you remember it: at its best.

Anyway, finishing remarks: the ideas here are scattered around and I put too much emphasis in (somewhat) minor negative things about the game... but then again I'm kinda sleepy and I'm not going to lose more sleep over a review, lol.

Either way, I HIGHLY recommend this game. If REmake is the quintessential old-school survival horror, RE2 remake is something of a masterpiece in adapting that perfect adventure game-like design to a modern horror game with modern mechanics and graphics.

I grew up with Resident Evil. I fondly remember being 9 years old playing my friend's older brother's PS1 and trying out his creepy game called Resident Evil 2. Thinking we had started his save file, we played for less than 60 seconds before things got too intense. For years I had proudly told my friends that I got to the part where everything was on fire and you were surrounded by cars and zombies. Little did I know that was the very beginning of the game. Years later I decided to get Code Veronica for my Dreamcast, and my love for that spread to the Dreamcast ports of RE2, RE3, and then the Gamecube releases, and every mainline title ever since.

Resident Evil 2 (2019) isn't a scene-for-scene remake; It is very much a modern third-person shooter/survival horror game that has all the benefits of a AAA title for the current gen, but has a familiar story path and characters with subtle nods to the original game. While I have no issues with games that essentially copy and paste the environment, characters, and story with higher res textures and updated character models, when done correctly I think Capcom's approach here with RE2 2019 is a great way to remake a game.

There wouldn't be a head left after that many dome shots.  What is the point of a gun if it does almost nothing?

While limited ammo is inherent to RE2, making every enemy into possibly a massive RNG-based bullet sponge on top of that is unforgivable.  The point of rare ammo is to create a feeling of contrast.  When you're flush with ammo you're supposed to be powerful and dominant... when you're low on ammo you are vulnerable and weak.  This creates periods of tension interspersed with periods of revenge.  Without the release of the revenge period the tension period loses any meaning and becomes mundane.   Tension dissipates because every encounter becomes a quasi-puzzle game about exploiting the pathing and AI of the zombies to bypass them with minimal shooting... completely destroying the suspension of disbelief.   There is no release of tension revenge period because most ammo types are so ineffectual and random you feel like an idiot for even bothering to try to kill anything.

If they wanted to make this game right:

1.  Enemies would actually stagger reliably when you headshot/leg shot, like they did in RE4.
2.  Regular zombies would actually die in one or two headshots instead of a random amount between 1 and 30.  Again like RE4.  Some zombies might even be able to survive without a head, but they wander around randomly and maybe fight with other zombies they run into rather than pathing toward you.  This would add some dimension to the zombie gameplay.
3.  Regular zombies would move faster within lunge range, making headshot misses more likely and regular zombies more dangerous rather than simply annoyances.
4.  Rather than relying on regular zombies to drain your ammo, let the player actually merc the regular zombies reliably and simply place large hordes or dedicated bullet sponge enemies at points where the designers want the player to be drained of ammo and have to run for their life.
5. Not remove all the text descriptions from the game.   Why not leave the old school flavor in?  It costs almost nothing in dev time.
