Resident Evil 2 ( 2019 Remake)

A horror/action game that sets the tone for the Resident Evil Universe (as RE7 is in FP). You follow the story of fan favourite’s Leon and Claire. The gameplay is what you’d expect for a series known for its survival horror aspect of gameplay. Ammo is scarce and you have to craft them, and so are herbs and healing items. They each have their different types of crafting which depends on what you need best. The game really forces you to think like a survivor, try to save ammo when can and think ahead about the future. The combat is slow paced but somewhat realistic (when compared to the previous instalments where your character literally just stands still when shooting or reloading). Your characters are competent but they do feel amateur as you are playing a rookie cop and a college girl. The zombies actually feel like zombies as they stumble around, react to gunshots and may very well still be alive even if you’ve knocked them down on the ground, motionless. You can use many weapons with many upgrades acquired along the way in addition to sub weapons to take multiple types of enemies out according to what they are, and how they respond to you. The map uses the hardgating system where you’d have to collect a certain item to reach, but it helps players get used to it as they return to many previous spots multiple times as they reach multiple destinations, with different items held each time for different goals and triggers (some required to progress the game and some just to better equip your character). The puzzles are quite underwhelming for a Resident Evil game but they’re still good nonetheless. Overall, a fun horror experience thats both challenging yet fun.

Let me start off by saying that Resident Evil 7 was the first Resident Evil game I owned and played, of which I plan on going back to and playing again.  I bought this game afterwards due to such positive reviews and really liked it - until I got to the part of the story where an invincible man (so named Mr. X apparently) indefinitely follows you around the whole game.  I, not being aware of this person and his invincibility, wasted all of my ammunition on him thinking he was some sort of boss encounter, only to find that you cannot kill him but instead only disable him.  It also so happened that I had screwed up my save points somehow so that the only save I had was the one preceding the event of me depleting all of my ammunition.  

Anyhow, ammunition and screwed up save aside, I found the game challenging enough without this Mr. X following me throughout the entire game.  Is it possible that maybe this is not the case and I might eventually get to a point where I can get rid of him?

Mr. X aside, everything about this game I found to be of excellent quality, including some of the minigames. If you are like me and find this to not at all be very much fun, then avoid it and maybe pick up Resident Evil 7.  Be warned though, there is a bit of following in Resident Evil 7 but not nearly to the extent found in this game (they usually search for you rather than knowing where you are at all times like Mr. X).

Note: I also found the RNG aspect annoying in regards to killing enemies. An absolutely fantastic game. I had never played any other Resident Evil other than RE7 before this, and this vastly exceeded my expectations. It's less overly scripted than RE7, with some of the most fluid and organic-feeling game design and the best implementation of zombies I've seen in a video game. How many bullets does it take to kill a zombie? Who knows! It could take 3, it could take 20 - and you've got very little ammo to use on them. It adds this tension to its metroidvania-style puzzles that I've never seen in another game - any zombie you leave or kill or whatever else [b]will always be there from now on[/b], so there's that constant thought in the back of your head that they'll get up and lunge at you no matter how many bullets you used. You memorize the location of that one hallway where you ran out of ammo and left 5 zombies to shamble around, and figure out alternate routes on the fly. This feels super rewarding and is a puzzle in and of itself. It's a puzzle that [b]you[/b] made as you just played the game.

Things do get easier as the game progresses and you learn how the different enemies move, but then juuust as you figure things out, the game throws more at you to make sure it doesn't get boring.

It's not perfect, though. Boss battles are tiring and feel antithetical to the general feel of the rest of the game. After learning how the zombies worked at the beginning of the game, the first boss totally threw me off guard since you're basically just supposed to pump bullets into him to whittle down your resources. After conserving so much ammo, it feels wrong (which was probably on purpose :P ). Some bosses also get really scripted and janky in places, but those sections are pretty short.

So yeah, a fantastic game for people who like survival horror, or who just like really well-designed games. I just think the boss battles don't really fit the style of the rest of the game. I know why they're there, but I'm hoping they put a little more work into them in future games/remakes in the series. Also, I have now bought almost every RE game on Steam because I desperately want every game I play to just be more of [b]this.[/b]

[i][h1] Outstanding remake of a fairly good classic [/h1][/i]
To be fair, I've never played the original RE trilogy or RE0, my first was RE4 which still is my favourite video game of all time. So naturally I compare every other RE game to it.
That said, I'll tell you why this game is amazing and disappointing at the same time.
Let's start with gameplay features and pros-
-RE2 looks absolutely phenomenal, to me honestly it looks next gen (for the most part) and complementing to it, runs beautifully even on low end gpus. This is clearly RE Engine at its best. 
-The remake is made in such a way that everything just combines naturally- the atmosphere of the game is off the charts, the transition between scenarios, the cutscenes, exploration and puzzles, all appear very natural. There's no hand holding, no cheap jumpscare or scripted zombie encounter- you will have to explore cautiously and need to conserve ammo to survive and you WILL FEEL THE TENSION.
- The gunplay, hit impact, the zombie physics, all are amazingly done- the zombies here are totally the best zombie incarnation in any video game, period.
- Story is decent by which I mean it's much less crazy than any other part imo but that's not a bad thing as it complements well with the mood. All the characters are fairly likeable too with good voice acting.
- Throughout the game you'll get various files to read which describe various other incidents that add to the lore, some describe the events prior to the outbreak, some even throws light at other RE characters, some are just plain horrifying diary entries. Also many cool ester eggs too! So make sure to read them!
- The MAP! this is your best friend throughout the game! You can survive without ammo but without your map you have no chance! So many reviewers do not mention this but I can't stress enough how important it is and the quality of life improvements that you won't even notice! Since your inventory slots are limited at the beginning you won't carry much but don't worry! All the items you've seen once gets registered on your map- you can check anytime where a particular item is once you've discovered it, It'll also indicate when there's no other item of interest in an area which is a small but amazing feature. This is how every survival game map should be!

I wish I could stop here but  I'll have to tell what I didn't like-
- DirectX implementation is weird. For me crashed quite often in dx11. At one point I could't even go to the main menu as it crashed before that. I had to manually edit the config file and use dx12 instead to solve this issue (after which it didn't crash a single time). So if you ever face such issue try changing from dx12 to 11 or vice versa. Also Screen space reflections and shadows have weird shimmering and dithering effect which look odd at times, only way to reduce it is to use TAA. These are mostly issues with the engine itself as I have seen this in RE7 too.
-The last 1/4th of the game falls flat in comparison the the other areas of the game- what made the RCPD great was the intricate level  design, there are multiple ways to enter a room- just traversal felt like a puzzle by itself which felt great but in comparison the last area is very linear and since you get most of the upgrades before that area it just feels like RE5 for that period. I know it's supposed to be a faithful remake still I wish they could've expanded the area like they did with the sewers. Atleast this section is small so it's not that bad.
- THE BOSS FIGHT. HAHA the boss fights suck- you can clearly feel this is direct 1:1 recreation of a 90s game just from the bossfights. It's simply put, not fun at all- not that they're difficult or anything (quite easy infact) it's just that every other post RE4 game did it way better. All I can say is that only Leon's last boss fight is kinda fun. I won't spoil how the fights go just don't get your hopes up for the fights.
- The 2nd Run where you play as the 2nd character (either Leon or Claire) is very lazily made. Except some areas and a very few puzzles, everything else is exactly the same as the normal campaign. It doesn't even make sense from the story point! I really wish they could've atleast changed the puzzles l rather than make us do the same stuff again atleast to connect both the timelines properly!
Nevertheless I'd say I kinda liked Claire's campaign story more than Leon's so that's a plus.
- Finally, the lack of extra content- after finishing both campaigns there's really not much to do. There's the ghost survivor missions which are basically the same campaign scenarios but with a different character (who are supposed to be dead in the campaign). It's pretty hardcore that really tests your skill and actually has 1 new enemy type but still it's basically the exact same areas. It's worth trying atleast once but no more. You also unlock the 4th survivor and Tofu survivor mode after beating the main game but it's exactly the same as ghost survivor just ever harder. (But hey atleast u get to hear the voice of Hunk and Tofu!) 
Well this was not actually a con as it doesn't affect the campaign itself but considering other RE games had so much post campaign, it's kinda disappointing. I really wish they add a co-op mode at some point.

Overall, it's a great single player game and more importantly an amazing  Resident Evil game.
I honestly didn't have this much fun in a RE game in a very long time. There were many disappointing factors as well but that doesn't make RE2 a game unworthy of high praise.
[b]Although, not a GOTY material still this is a very well crafted, enjoyable game with a heart and soul[/b]

On February 3rd 2026 Capcom released an update that removed Denuvo, a DRM which requires a costant internet connection, and replaced it with the Enigma Protector. This DRM is supposed to prevent "cheating" (any kind of modding of the game) and it's russian developed.
Tested by the Youtube channel Digital Foundry in the video "Resident Evil 4 PC: Is New DRM Impacting Game Performance?" has been found that the Enigma Protector DRM causes an average of -10% in framerate drops, with dips of -40% in certain scenarios, way more than the original Denuvo DRM.

This is not the first time that Capcom decided to put Enigma in some of their older games: RE Revelations suffered major backlash from customers because of the major dip in perfomance, so much so they had to remove Enigma from the game for good and recently they released the original Dino Crisis series on Steam, a quick scouring of the forum will reveal a lot of customers unhappy with the perfomance of said games. Why a 25 years old single player game that should run flawlessly on a phone had to be "protected" against "cheating" is everyone's guess, especially when you realise that a GOG version of both games was already available, without the Enigma Protector and without issues.

Here's my grievances with it:

-Retroactively degrading perfomances of a game or a product is an unethical and fundamentally anti-consumer practice that should be illegal. Imagine your car having less hp out of nowhere because the car company decided to update the software that way

-Capcom degraded the game for no reasons at all, Enigma Protector doesn't prevent cheats or mods in any capable way and it's openly mocked by the mod communities

-All Capcom's game that have been "protected" by Enigma suffered of significant perfomance loss and the DRM can be easily removed by the cracking scene. The customer is therefore presented with this funny scenario: would you rather download the game for free or pay money for a degraded version that runs worst than the pirated copy?

-There's a very likely possibility that in future all Capcom's games will eventually incorporate the Enigma DRM years after launch, the system that you used to play them could eventually not being capable of the same perfomance as before, forcing some to spend money on very costly upgrades (due to the AI craze)

-The DRM is russian developed, profits from the company are most likely to be used in the ongoing russian invasion of Ukraine. This is not only unethical per-se but raises security questions for all the countries where the governments are actively funding the ukranian defense: Russia is well known to use cyber warfare against its enemies, I personally don't want anything russian developed in my system

-Enigma Protector devs in the past have behaved very unprofessionally, mocking and insulting whoever questioned the validity of their practices and their work, raising more than one red flag on the true purpose of their work and their true intent

I don't know who and why at Capcom signed a contract for this to happen but they clearly got scammed and it's time for them cope with it. I will leave a negative review on all my Capcom products and maybe I will revert them if they abandon Enigma altogether. Just maybe though, I'm kind of fed up on AAA publishers malpractices.

It feels like you're playing the original RE2 but at the same it doesn't, it's a completely different game all together, not just in mechanics but in level design and game progression.  If you've played RE1make you'd understand what I mean but instead of being a complete upgrade like RE1make was, RE2make is more fitting of being a side-grade and whether you like the original or the remake better is honestly just preference.  

One of the biggest differences is that Leon/Claire A route and Leon/Claire B route doesn't exist anymore and instead you play through Leon's and Claire's stories who don't connect at all unlike the original; a '2nd run' exists where you skip the majority of the first parts of the game and progress through the game slightly differently but you still fight the exact same bosses and still has the exact same story.  It's lazy in a sense that they didn't bother to separate the gameplay and connect the story of Leon's and Claire's stories and separate them into 4 routes that are all completely different games like the original but in return we receive a very high quality 1st playthrough and a slightly altered 2nd playthrough that isn't all that much different, nonetheless it's still disappointing as I was looking forward to playing a completely different game with Claire, new bosses and all but was faced with playing the exact same Campaign Leon had.  All this is only an issue though if you've played the original in the first place since a very high quality first playthrough is more fitting for present day games as most players don't play past a first playthrough.

With Leon/Claire B route not existing, which were the routes Mr. X was exclusive to, we instead have Mr. X appearing regardless of 1st playthrough or 2nd. I'm all for this change since it means everyone, including 
casual players get to experience Mr. X and unlike the original where he was a useless, walking ammo box, in this game he's an actual threat.  It's not so much that he, himself is a threat since he's so slow but moreso him making everything around you more of a threat since his persistant chasing will cause you to play more reckless and be damaged more frequently by zombies and lickers.

Among other things the remake did that I don't like; enemy variety has been extremely reduced and a bit of a nitpicky thing is they made the crocodile battle which was the scariest thing to 4 y/o me into a boring cinematic battle.  Finally, I prefer fixed camera angles and tank controls for RE games but this is a very niche preference that many modern gamers wouldn't understand.

Other than that, the original may offer more content but the single playthrough RE2make  offers is a way higher quality than any of the single routes that the original has and none of these issues apply to anyone who hasn't played it.  If you have played the original though the feeling does linger that there is missing content and it hits even more since the game is so good and you know there could have been more but better this than no remake at all.  Honestly, I recommend everyone to play both this remake and the original since along with RE1make, RE2 and RE2make in my opinion are some of the best games ever made.  Oh yes, I forgot to mention the story? Who plays RE for story?

[h1]KitKat Reviews #7[/h1] 
[h1]Resident Evil 2 (2019)[/h1] 

[h1]Game Plot:[/h1] 
This game takes us to Racoon City in 1998, where we follow two people's events that are also two sides of the same coin. We follow Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield as they meet up at a gas station, they encountered their first experience with the zombie-like people later known as the T – Virus. Having met and escaped in a police officer vehicle, Leon is a Rookie Police Officer, and Claire is a College Student. As soon as they make it into the city, they notice that the city has entirely been evacuated or the whole city has turned into zombies. As a hoard of zombies blocks them, a truck loses control and rolls on its side, hitting the police vehicle. Claire and Leon notice that the truck was a gasoline hauler, so they got out as fast as they could from the car just in time for the truck to explode despite the hoard of zombies. Despite the fact they were alive, they were separated, and then the story develops for each character. They both make their way to the Police Department and fight of the night as they face the terrors from the infamous Umbrella Corporation.  

[h1]Personal Opinion About Plot:[/h1] 
During the Pandemic (12/24/2020 when I write this), this was the best game to start the year. Having played both stories and both situations, I've concluded this is a great game to have others join in your gameplay, to sit back and enjoy. I played this with my family members, every moment, and every panic attack I got from this game was truly cherished. Above all, you want to hear the relation to RE2 the original, which I'll have to report back later as I will play RE2 the original on the PS3. I cannot compare the two right now. Overall, the story is likable, enjoyable, and can be discussed later on because of the cliffhangers and unknown parts of the story.

[h1]Game Gameplay:[/h1]
The 1998 version of Resident Evil 2 game uses tank controls and fixed camera angles. The remake features "over-the-shoulder" third-person shooter gameplay like Resident Evil 4 and more recent games in the series that allows players the option to move while using their weapons, similar to Resident Evil 6. The assisted and standard difficulties mode deviates from the original by featuring autosaves and allowing players to save as often as they would like inside safe rooms. If the player chooses to play on "Hardcore" difficulty, players will be required to collect and use a finite number of ink ribbons to save the game's progress, much like in the original game.
While exploring the police station, players can find and pick up items that can help them survive and escape. Certain items, such as herbs and gun powder can be combined to make healing items and ammunition. Items can also be inspected for clues gaining access to certain areas or items hidden throughout the game and can be discarded after use.
Overall combat varies depending on difficultly. Assisted difficulty allows aim assist and health recovery along with weaker enemies while hardcore difficulty has stronger enemies and has scarce ammo for players to find. Combat will also vary depending on who players are fighting. Enemies will generally come after players after they are spotted and can be killed or crippled to slow the down. Zombies will attempt to break into the station through windows but can be stopped if the windows are boarded up beforehand. Certain enemies must be fought in order to progress through the game and cannot be avoided.

[h1]Personal Opinion About Gameplay:[/h1]
Overall, the features that went in the game were much like any other Resident Evil game. Of course, shooting and puzzle-solving have returned with a vengeance from Resident Evil 7. The style of gameplay with the environment, music, etc., turns this game into an excellent immersive experience, but for my parents, it was more like a movie because they weren't playing, of course, lol.

[h1]Personal Opinion on Graphics:[/h1] 
As I make my way through the horror game, this is by far the best game I've experimented with these edge breaking graphics. The detail used to make the simplest object to the way you shoot zombies and the way their body parts all have different reactions to the different shoots from the guns. Everything is so clean and pristine. There RE Engine is the best engine in the horror community! 

[h1]Personal Opinion on Sound Design:[/h1]  
Compared to Resident Evil 7, I'm sad to say that the music score has a few likable soundtracks, but the music is appropriate to the producers' environment. They made music for background environment properties. Resident Evil 7 tells stories about what type of a situation you're in and when to panic, and when to run. Each environment that its theme, and each boss had their soundtrack that was up-close and in person. Here we have Resident Evil 2, which changes from the first person to the third person. This brings too many environmental soundtracks. The only in-person and familiar panic soundtrack is Mr. X's theme, "Black Impact." Other than that, AMAZING ON 7.1 SURROUND.

[h1]Things needed to be Fixed like Bugs:[/h1]
Nah, no bugs! Only a few things you can do with enemy's that suspicious but, all's well!

[h1]Final Thoughts:[/h1] 
This a great test on their RE Engine and adds a step forward in their games. I'm looking forward to the series they are making and the new game they are releasing soon!

First of all, I've never played the original Resident Evil 2, but I've played many of the other ones, namely 4, 5, and 6. Honestly going into it I wasn't expecting much, but I ended up being completely blown away by this game. RE2 Remake is the standard that all remakes should adhere by. The entire game just felt so reminiscent of older PS1 games yet completely invigorated and modern. 

What I liked most about it was it didn't try to be more than what it was. The levels weren't gigantic, but packed to the brim with detail. The puzzles were fantastic, the pacing was good, and the jumpscares felt appropriate. Most of all, the atmosphere and feeling of the levels were fantastic. It felt like the developers put a lot of love and passion into every inch of the game. 

The only negative thing I have to say about RE2 is that it was too short. The initial campaign can be finished in about 8-10 hours, and the rest of the content mostly came from doing the same campaign but harder. Personally, after I experienced it the first time, the magic felt somewhat lost, and I was not motivated to complete the post-game content. 

Overall, a must play for RE lovers, zombie apocalypse lovers, video game lovers.

A primera vista este juego tiene muchos elementos cautivantes: El motor es espectacular, la gráfica y el ambiente son atrapantes y las cinemáticas definitivamente le aportan una connotación más profesional en comparación a la versión anterior de 1998 (muy criticada por sus "actuaciones". La primera impresión que te deja este juego puede llegar a ser intimidante en el buen y mal sentido. Es reconfortante y desolador reconocer los antiguos pasillos y ser testigo de los maravillosos cambios que el nuevo motor se luce en renderizar. Esta delicia definitivamente se acentúa si ya se ha jugado a los originales. Para personas nuevas a la franquicia entiendo que no hay mucho nuevo que ver aquí más que el legado de la marca Resident Evil.

Y es por esto que debo advertir que el grave problema de este juego, es que cuando se pasa esa etapa inicial de admiración y horror del bueno (gran trabajo de ambiente); viene una segunda etapa de frustración por como han envejecido ciertas mecánicas del survival horror. Para veteranos de este género todo ésto no es nada nuevo, pero para los recién llegados; la mayoría del gameplay en este caso se trata de un ejercicio de prueba y error cada vez que se descubre un objeto importante y un lugar nuevo -donde más que asustado puede que provoque aburrimiento de tener que recargar tu fila una y otra vez por un sinfín de situaciones ridículas e injustas que pueden provocar un gameover por un solo error incluso en dificultad estándard-. Para más remate los enemigos son tremendamente rescilientes hasta decir basta, los recursos son sadísticamente escasos, y los pasos audiblemente auguriosos de cierto personaje que comenzará a frustrar tus planes se vuelven psicológicamente pesados; por eso es que siepre va a ser recomendable no tratar este juego como un festín de balaceras y disfrutarlo por lo que es. 

El tecer paso, es que una vez que se superan las frustraciones y (haz tenido la paciencia de) aprender de memoria estas injustas papas y todas las maleterías del juego, es posible evitar muchas de las trampas (e incluso disfrutar de todas esa basura) que te plantean cualquiera de las dos campañas, que dicho sea de paso -y aquí se cae de tropezón el juego- son prácticamente lo mismo a excepción de ciertos lugares y eventos. 

Y es que debo quejarme de que los puzzles son los mismos para ambos personajes (con ligeras diferencias en el escenario "B")..."Rutas secundarias" llamadas aquí; que, a propósito, son un despropósito. La cohesión de los eventos está muy mal trabajado en comparación a la versión original de PSX, y si jugaste el original esta falta de atención al detalle te chocará bastante.

De todas maneras y para concluir; para fans de la serie, es posible que caigan en el cuarto paso del vicio de hacer speedrunning. Para casuales, es igual un tremendo juego e indiscutiblemente memorable por diversas razones. Sólo estén advertidos: este juega peca de tener linaje de la vieja escuela, ya que avanzar no se trata de entrar como rambo disparando a cada habitación, si no de medir tus acciones y ser silencioso en tus pasos. Correr muchas veces es LA OPCIÓN.

Como nota al pié, acotar que los minijuegos también son tremendamente adictivos pero aún no los completo todos (mis 90+ horas de juego se atribuyen a querer completar las campañas con calificación S+ para desbloquear todas las armas). Incluso fuera de la campaña encontrarás mucho replay value aquí si eres paciente.  El tener que comprar la música original (y los trajes adicionales también, EN SERIO CAPCOM?) me parece un insulto si y no puedo dejar pasarlo. 

En fin, un tyrant que se teletransporta por la estación y te encuentra igual en la misma habitación que un licker/10.

This is a new review after playing "Leon 2nd run". My score dropped since then so by my good morals I had to update it.

[code]𝐐𝐔𝐈𝐂𝐊 𝐑𝐄𝐒𝐔𝐌𝐄[/code]

I approve the game, but some new things may feel sacrilegeous like the "Ghost Survivors". Bugs like teleporting lickers or a nonsensical second scenario are on the list. While the majority of the gameplay does a great job, I can see the new stuff acting up (such as mediocre boss fights) thus compromising it a bit for me. [u]Only the first scenario acts as the main now[/u] they won't interact as the original did, making it look silly.

[b]YES:[/b] I know the remake can't just copy and paste things. Remember the classic CGI when Leon finds a Licker? This time, they wanted you to be blown away while he slowly moves on the ceiling, no cutscenes. While I understand this is awesome, I had 2 immersion breaking bugs during that momment.

They still managed to revitalize the series better with this attempt than the first person one. I don't like the new one always using cheap sexism to sell Resident Evil. So I don't know if the remake was really that good for me, or I'm just amazed that they didn't screw this up.

[h1]What survived the remake?[/h1]

[code]𝐌𝐀𝐈𝐍 𝐂𝐇𝐀𝐑𝐀𝐂𝐓𝐄𝐑𝐒[/code]

I couldn't stand Leon's double chin and Claire's baby face model so a very talented modder called "Chiarav1" did a great job adding Leon from RE4 and Claire's DC faces for the Fluffy manager. You may want to fix faces but their personalities are good enough by design. Claire’s is now more expressive (not like it was on Veronica’s) and Leon still is that likeable smooth badass. Now, about the new survivors characters, they're so unecessary it feels like just fast fun. Capcom should've used the resources to create better second scenarios instead. Bummer.

The Fourth Survivor was the best for me in the old game, a bonus intruder in the story. Ironically he didn’t survive the remake much - he looks right but his personality doesn't, he talks too much now and with low-quality nonsense. His extra mission is free at least, it still is an integral part of the post game so that’s something positive there. They could have charged you 20 bucks for that but they didn't, community would burn them. 

His timed bonus mission still is fast, a clusterf𝕦𝕔k of monster madness, that’s what matters.

[code]𝐅𝐄𝐄𝐋𝐈𝐍𝐆𝐒[/code]

The classic RE2 music was great as I remember it vividly, depressing with a desolate and hopeless atmosphere. The vibes were nostalgic but also very tense and fearful during action. I used to have nightmares when I was younger, trying to run away from Mr X and never really scaping. I don't know why but the original vibes survived much better in the first run scenario. 

The best points that did so, have been intensified with great FX and graphics rather than just remastering music. The classic tunes became more of a ambience hint now, rather than live emotion. This is a good and bad thing at the same time.

[code]𝐁𝐑𝐀𝐈𝐍𝐒[/code]

Puzzles were one thing that made RE2 known for its cleanse originality. You ask non-gamer people about the Queen and Bishop spark plugs they probably heard about it somewhere. The story still looks like a 1998 event, they preserved it quite well. The devs managed to fit in new ones just as classy, while preserving all the old sacred stuff. Remember this is a third person game now, things like removing a capacitor and placing it somewhere else is in, but they did so with nice sophisticated class. The frequency modulator was my favorite new puzzle so far, gotta use it to believe it. If everything looked the same, in this case it would be the ruin of the remake.

[code]𝐒𝐓𝐎𝐑𝐘[/code]

If RE2 story was a real situation, it would have been like a WW II holocaust or hundreds of Twin Towers death toll scenario and shocking and awe. Now everything has been augmented and the conspiracy is believable, rich people doing stupid things for the lack of better things to do, this world can really be “infected” by hypocrites as real world’s events can tell.

They managed to give even more life to side characters, when dialogue works. The chief of police for example is perfectly portrayed as an insane, power-hungry sick bastard with good writing and voice acting. The doctor’s wife is the one holding the best of it, at showing weirdness off. The people involved in the corruption that led the crisis are creepier than the immense barrage of sheat hitting Racoon city.

The original climax and the original ending wasn’t all that happy for the characters and the music helped to darken my heart. I'm sad to report that this isn't exactly what they did with the remake, specially on the second-run. They even had the AUDACITY to remove Leon finding Claire in the STARS room, actually, scenarios won't really interact with each other.

The original composer Shusaku Uchiyama worked on the remake, a couple others from RE4’s too so they tried hard, but the second run feels rushed, killing essential vibes of "meanwhile" story progression.

[h1]The bad[/h1]

The uninspired Capcom I despise also made it through the remake. A few dumb dialogs and Power Rangers body actors trying to look human. It is not happening all the time and not with everyone, but when it shows up I can tell. Leon and Claire loves to do commentaries that just won't match the horror of the moment, trying to induce dumb memes I guess.

They had to fix some old plot holes, such as the scientist getting shot at and one of his experiments falling over his wounded shoulder. Great! But you don’t replace it with even crappier excuses and low effort dialogue that won't match things. The 2nd run used to be a misterious game, with interesting secrets. 90% of it is gone now.

Another flaw I can’t forgive is the lack of parrying in this game. You can’t even crouch, not even Leon and the man is the world’s best cop. Two dimensions mannequin, when crazy sh𝕚𝕥 is happening just run and hope for the best. I know bosses are needed but at least let us dodge attacks.

They had to stretch the Racoon City’s sewers part and it was the best part of the remake.

But every G boss encounter after the first one was bad. The container platform was the worst of them all, maybe unfinished, just not right. Some stuff like that feels out of place, not because they're new but because they're unintuitive at best.

[h1]WTF graphics[/h1]

[code]𝐀𝐓𝐓𝐄𝐍𝐓𝐈𝐎𝐍 𝐓𝐎 𝐃𝐄𝐓𝐀𝐈𝐋𝐒[/code]

Every statue is a perfect replica of the original, most corridors, most rooms, most textures have been replicated, the original atmosphere reigns. Anew of course, but faithfully done so.

The further you advance, the dirtier you’ll get. That half bite you had in there will stay for a lot of time with you. Immersing your legs into that mass of sh𝕚𝕥 will also stay with you for a lot of time. That zombie you had to melt with acid will still be frying there in pieces, even after reloading the game. Some enemies will keep reviving if you kill them wrongly. Water looks like real water, the rain pierces my soul, the sound effects haunt my mind and trigger intense sound paranoia, the in-game body animation is more convincing than cutscenes… They managed to make dumb zombies scary again, with perfect state-of-the-art impersonation, specially when they take the bullets.

[h1]Final score: 7/10 [/h1]

I found this game to be quite fun; though was a bit disappointed in some aspects of the gameplay. Let's start with the good: intriguing story, great bosses and scary zombies, and best of all, the visuals. Compared to other games, the visuals are a tier higher. Every scene is cinematic; same with the gameplay. Though many aspects of the game was astounding, I found the story to be a bit repetitive, especially when you finished the game the first time and switched to the perspective of the other character. When I first entered the game, I expected the story to show different perspectives while occasionally bumping to Claire/Leon. I was quite excited in my first playthrough, seeing Claire on the other side of the police fence made me hope that I could get into her perspective later. Indeed, it did, only after you finished the 1st story and went towards the second run. However, as you proceeded through the story, you realized that each character was practically doing the same exact objectives each time, but just had a little twisted main story. I've done both the Leon A and Claire B scenarios, and I have to say this is about as perfect of a remake (or re-imaging) as you can get.  The story is faithful to the original, but with much better voice acting, and paired with modern graphics. Speaking of, the graphics in this game are fantastic, and they are well optimized. My machine (i5 6600, 16gig ram, GeForce 1060 6gb) ran this game at max settings, and consistent 60fps at 1600x1200 resolution. Capcom created a thing of beauty with the RE engine.

It is also quite scary, with many ambient sounds, shadows, lighting, and the music cues. You have to conserve ammo and resources as Zombies take a lot of bullets, and then you eventually have to contend with Mr.X. Play in the dark and with headphones for the best experience.

As for content, there is plenty here. You can play both the Claire or Leon campaigns. Both follow similar paths, but tell a slightly different story, have different items, weapons, ect. You need to complete both to get the "true" ending.
After that, there are various "Survivor" challenges to complete with new characters, in addition to unlocks for new costumes, collectibles,  ect. 

There was plenty of content here to justify a $60 purchase, but now that the game can readily be bought for <$20 its a steal. A must buy for any RE fan, fan of horror/survival games, or the zombie genre in general.

After playing all of the resident evil games on steam and emulated versions of the original 0,1,2,3, and code Veronica, this is a fairly scary and fun game.

When [i]Resident Evil 2[/i] released in 1998 I wasn't born, and I never played the original game. I have no nostalgia for it, and I went into this experience completely blind. That being said, this is one of the best games I have ever played. 

[i]Resident Evil 2[/i] is stunning, and extremely fun. When I randomly decided to pick this game up I never would've expected that I would end up beating it two or three times, or that it would become one of my favorite games. However, it is, and that's because everything here is so smooth and well done. The graphics are beautiful, the combat is exciting and extremely tactical, and the puzzles are just enough to provide a short break from the action. Different items are perfectly placed around the environments to keep you moving back and fourth while having to avoid the infected and Mr. X. 

For others who are going into the game blind, [i]Resident Evil 2[/i] is a survival horror game. So, although you'll see zombies walking around the police station, it's important that you pick and choose which you eliminate and which you tactically slide by. Additionally, this isn't an on-rails linear experience; there are multiple puzzles for you to solve around the police station, and you'll need to wander around clearing rooms, finding new key items, and figuring out how they can help you clean up any messes that are halting your progress. 

On the first playthough the scares were thrilling, but never anything crazy. In fact, [i]Resident Evil 2[/i]'s fear factor comes more from the constant tension of Mr. X won't leave you alone and chasing you around than from jump scares. [i]Resident Evil 2[/i] is so fantastic that it doesn't need to be scary to be good. Additionally, there is so much replayability here; you can play through the game as Leon or Claire first; the two have slightly different stories and the difference is certain enough to warrant beating the game as each of them once. Furthermore, once you beat the game for the first time you unlock a second scenario that you can play as either Claire or Leon, so there are really four different playthroughs you can have here as well as different difficulties you can play on. 

Four playthroughs seems like it could become repetitive, however, I will say that my second playthrough only took me four hours, that's nearly four hours faster than my first, and I'm sure it only gets easier the more you play. 

Outside of the main story there is still more content in the form of multiple different short-stories you can play through. These are a fun little addition, and you can challenge yourself to complete them in fast times. Collectible wise, throughout the main story there are little bobble-heads hidden for you to find and destroy- you can't go back to find them, but secondary playthroughs keep your collectible progress from previous runs. Completing harder difficulties and challenges rewards you with new weapons that break the game, allowing you to take your victory lap on this nightmare sittuation.

Honestly this is one of the best games I've ever played. I've never been a horror fan, and I had never played a [i]Resident Evil[/i] game before, but I had an absolute blast with the game. I'd highly recommend it to anyone; it's well worth the price for the amount of content packed in, and it's thrilling from start to finish with amazing incentive to replay countless times. I hope Capcom continues to remake [i]Resident Evil[/i] games in this style, or learns from the successes of this remake and implements them into the newest [i]Resident Evil[/i] titles.

Great remake with new way looking in-game mechanism. However if you played the original will feel nostalgic.

NOTE: It says my playtime is 4.9 hours at the time of writing this review, but this is not accurate as I normally play while offline. I have played through the game 5 or 6 times with both Leon and Claire, including hardcore mode, "B" modes etc.

Now for the review...

This game is one of the absolute best RE games and a perfect representation of what the series is about.

The classic elements of RE are there: exploration, puzzles, item management etc, but some comforts of modern gaming have been added eg the map shows objects you have interacted with on the map so you can remember where you need to take a certain key or puzzle item.

The atmosphere is perfect, it looks beautiful and the gameplay is so enjoyable it is hard decision to stop playing on the first couple of playthrough. The item management, hidden items, puzzles, and just trying to navigate your way safely through the environments is extremely satisfying.

As far as being a remake is concerned, the police station has been expanded quite a lot, and the sewers and lab have been completely overhauled. The overhaul of the sewers and lab might disappoint some who were hoping to see familiar places but a lot of work has gone into those areas and they are excellent and memorable parts of the game.

There are a few other changes here and there, some for the better, some for worse, but overall the experience is excellent.

This is the best RE game in many years (yes, better than 7 [which is a great game in it's own way], and way better than RE3 Remake). It perfectly captures the spirit of old school RE, which is a hard commodity to come by these days!

If you are considering buying RE2 Remake, do yourself a favour and don't watch any videos of the game and just play it so you spoil any of the exciting moments or secrets for yourself.

I am doing a complete run of all the Resident Evil games and as much as I enjoyed the ones leading to this addition to the series, I am thoroughly enjoying RE2 even more. The character hopping in mid-story is very enjoyable. The extra segment characters (little girl with Claire and woman with Leon) have skills and play style requirements unique to them, and enjoyably implemented. It took me 3 tries to get the additional achievement for the women, but only 2 for the little girl, apart from the one acquired for completing their segment. Even still, I did them both an extra time after for good measure. 

I have yet to get a grade of S+, but getting S is relatively easy. The controls are worlds better than RE Zero and RE Original, which is to be expected by the basis of their release. Even so, I find myself enjoying being able to aim and move with a much greater degree of control. The characters animations in these actions are also brilliantly done.

In all, Resident Evil 2 is a superb game, and I highly recommend it. The gore factor might put off the squeamish, but it will delight the zombie slayer in you.

I have fond memories as a teenager playing the Resident Evil games.  3 was always my favorite and I think that’s where the series should have ended.  I thought Code Veronica was ok at best and after 4, I just stopped playing.  The ability to tell a cohesive story basically collapsed after 3 and story matters more to me than anything else in games.  Which is why I can never recommend this game.

If all you want is a superior version of Resident Evil 2 as far as graphics go, well then this is the game for you and you’d be super pleased.  I was hoping they would redo the story to fix a variety of massive issues I have with the plot and actually make the Leon/Claire different routes feel connected.  None of that is fixed and I found combat decisions highly questionable, to the point that I found playing the actual game not fun at all…so that’s a problem.

I don’t understand why the combat design decisions were made the way they were…I found them nonsensical.  For starters you have no melee attack…you get disposable flashbangs, grenades, and knives that if you get into melee range you can use in a quick time even to push the zombies away.  No melee in a survival/horror game where you have little ammo is very problematic.  I found myself constantly having almost no ammo and then left with no way to defend myself.  There is also no dodge mechanic, so if you get close to any zombie you are basically just going to immediately get jumped on…how zombies can be more athletic than your main character is beyond me.  So in the end you are left with no ammo, no melee ability, and no way to dodge the zombies, and then the game puts you in extremely tight spaces with no room to maneuver so you basically just need to stack healing items because you have no other option then to get eaten constantly.  They also decided to make the zombies basically unkillable.  You can unload a shotgun into a zombies head and it’s still walking around fine.  You can shoot out their legs, but they’ll just crawl after you.  Again if you had melee this would be fine as you could shoot out the legs and then melee them to death…but you can’t so then you just have a bunch of crippled zombies blocking the narrow hallways…which again you can’t dodge.  This didn’t make the game scary, it just made it frustrating

The plot badly needed fixing and for some reason they decided not to.  The characters motivations just don’t make much sense.  Claire hasn’t heard from her bother in a long time…so travels to his city…then discovers it’s been overrun by zombies and then searches for him…eventually finding a letter saying he’s gone to Europe?  When I originally played RE2, it never really dawned on me how insane of a plot that is.  The central motivation for Claire is she is looking for her brother…probably any other plot would then have the end goal be Claire finds her brother dead, zombified, or alive…but no you literally find a letter saying he went to Europe and Claire just kind of shrugs and says oh well?  How ♥♥♥♥♥♥ of a brother is Chris Redfield that he doesn’t contact his family for months then flies to Europe…again not telling his family…while knowing Raccoon City is basically one giant bioweapon test facility.  Did it never occur to him that a family member might come looking for him and then immediately die?  Leon’s I guess makes slightly more sense as he’s a new police officer simply showing up to his first day on the job.  However, it’s also weird because Claire and Leon literally meet up, but then never see each other until the end of the game?  No one would ever write a story where you have two characters meet at the start of a story and then have them never interact again until briefly at the end.  It feels like this game was written by people with no concept of narrative design or character development.

The other thing I was desperately hoping they would fix is making the Claire/Leon paths the connected whole in an overall story.  They don’t even do that.  Both stories have you basically retreading the same path and solving the same puzzles as the other character.  This is weird…a competent story would have either 2 stories that are entirely separate or one story which can be viewed from two different perspectives…instead the same events happen to both characters…I think the one story 2 perspectives would have been the better option.  Leon’s story should be all about him discovering the Tyrant finding Ada and figuring out what is happening in this city.  Claire’s story should be about her being faced with William Brikin and her quest to find Sherry Brikin.  Clarie and Leon should meet up multiple times throughout the game to discuss what their goals are and then meet up in the umbrella labs, Leon to wipe out the virus and find a way to destroy the Tyrant and Claire to find a cure for Sherry.   Instead both have to deal with the Tyrant and Birkin while treading over each others paths, but never meeting, while the same events happen to both Claire and Leon.  It’s just very incompetent story telling.  

I will also say the characters reactions to events in the game…also just seemed strange…Maybe it was bad voice acting…but I don’t think so.  Claire and Leons dialogue doesn’t sound particularly scared of the zombies…or surprised…I feel I would be pretty shocked and terrified if zombies wiped out an entire city and were chasing me around.  When the Tyrant shows up at the police station…it’s not this big appearance and both Clarie/Leon just kind of shrug and say “what the hell is that thing.”  This is the major monster of the game that is relentlessly chasing the heroes and his entrance is basically a shrug of “oh well?”  Even Birkin who is a giant insane mess of a monster doesn’t cause Claire/Leon to have much of a reaction.  I just don’t understand.

Look, I’m not recommending a game with such poor narrative design.  The Resident Evil games are all in need of a massive redesign in narrative to tell a cohesive story…they dumped a ton of money into remaking this entire series…yet gave no thought to fixing the massive narrative problems in this series…it’s such a waste.

Amazing graphics, but the core gameplay is simply not fun.

• Enemies are bullet sponges.
 -> Zombies are slow-moving, presenting almost no challenge except the chore of carefully lining up 4-10 headshots with 2 seconds of refocusing between each shot.
 -> Lickers can be easily cheesed with doors, making them just slightly tougher bullet sponges
 -> Mr. X for some reason cannot enter a save room by breaking down a thin wooden door

• Combat is unsatisfying
 -> Aside from random critical hits, you rarely know for sure when an enemy is dead. In Dead Space, you can stomp an enemy until they're bits and pieces, and proceed with the confidence that they won't get back up, but in RE2, there's nothing to indicate that a "dead" enemy will not get back up and attack you as soon as you leave and re-enter a room.
 -> The melee is garbage. You're given a combat knife that might as well be plastic for how much damage it does and how fast it breaks. There are no unique moves you can pull off, just a basic sideways slash that does virtually no damage and that the enemies don't react to at all (no knockback/stagger).

• The inventory/puzzle system sucks.
 -> Found some weird key or lever? Well either waste a valuable inventory slot carrying it around for the next 20 minutes, or put it in your storage box and run all the way back to grab it when you find the right door/puzzle.

• Movement options are limited and don't feel responsive.
 -> If you run out of bullets or just don't want to fight zombies, your only option is running or walking around them. There is no rolling, dodging, crouching, jumping, or using props to trip them.
 -> The "sprint" is extremely slow, making backtracking more painful.
 -> Tight turns are sluggish to execute, making it difficult to run around larger groups of zombies.

• Cringey voice lines, lack of chemistry between the main characters, and occasionally bad facial animation.

If you're considering getting this game, just play Dead Space instead.

In 1998 I bought the original RE2 using all my baptism gift money. I literally went to the game store minutes after the ceremony, and used the only 50 bucks I’d just received to buy a brand new copy. I raced home to play it and opened the walkthrough guide from PSM, my favorite gaming magazine at the time, to be my constant companion. I barely ever got new games as a kid and this was a big deal. 

Even though the graphics were primitive by today’s standards, the characters imposed on top of pre-rendered backgrounds made for nothing else like it on Playstation at the time. Looking back now it would be easy to scoff at, but back then it was scary. Environments were nerve-racking. The odd tank controls and camera angles, the sound design, the character design, the perfectly timed jump scares when everything was quiet... it was all just awesome and kept you on edge constantly.

Fast forward twenty years and my initial impression is almost the same as with the original. The truck driver is still a fat slob but now I have to watch him eat a greasy cheeseburger before he gets it. Leon still has an early Beatles haircut for some reason. Graphics are stunning but also running flawlessly on a pretty average rig. I swear I had the weirdest deja-vu I’d ever experienced when I first got into the police department. It was like tons of memories that had been dormant for all those years fired off all at once. It was a truly unique feeling I don’t think I’d experienced yet in my time playing games, and it made me instantly wish for more remakes of great titles from my youth. I hadn’t even gotten into this game yet and already I loved it. 

Your average zombie, while slow and dopey in the 90s fashion (before they turned into Olympic sprinters in the early 2000s), are no walk in the park to deal with. They are built like tanks and can easily chew up your already limited ammo. They become even more formidable when grouped together in a narrow spot that makes running by them not an option. To make matters worse, they will often play dead after you put them down, waiting to grab a bite as you walk by later when you backtrack through the area. Even multiple headshots above the nose are not always enough to slow them down. In general it is best to leave them alone wherever possible and move around them, because they will clean you out of your inventory otherwise. That said, there are segments where you will wish you had thinned them out more before you had to come through again. Find the balance with your play style. You may very well want to reload a save more than once because you used too many rounds in a basic encounter, and you need plenty of ammo despite the fact that you find almost none. You are always down to your last few rounds and wondering how you are going to get through the next fight.

There are your other standard RE fare enemies and mini-bosses to deal with, and they have plenty of hit points too, but all this becomes complicated even more by the fact that you are constantly being pursued by the Tyrant. After a little ways into the story, he will reveal himself and follow you through virtually every part of the police station, and into later stages. You have to then complete your objectives, puzzle-solving, and looting, all while being inundated with tank zombies in corridors, running dogs and lickers, and while being tirelessly pursued by a giant in a trench coat who can one-shot you. It’s stressful as hell but still really fun. Then, factor in the other things that stuck out in memory from the first time, like being chased down a sewer by a giant crocodile only to come to a conveniently located explosive that you can use against him. It’s just a good time and hitting all the nostalgia notes the whole ride. 

Needless to say I recommend this to anyone who enjoyed the original, but someone going their first-ever run through will get a really faithful adaptation to the original in Capcom AAA form. There are some obvious differences but it’s reminiscent of the first in every meaningful way. This game was very close to me when I was a kid and playing the remake has been a trip down memory lane. I hope other game developers take note of its success and start masterfully rehashing some of the heavyweights from past decades.

Okay okay. It goes without saying that a remake of one of the best Resident Evils of all time is bound to be scary, but... Damn. I prefer said original, but Resident Evil 2 ups the ante and somehow manages to be even scarier than the base game. The denizens of the apocalyptic Raccoon City have been given one hell of a macabre facelift, the adoption of the over the shoulder perspective introduced in Resident Evil 4 means that you're closer than ever to the nightmarish zombies and monsters, the character of Chief Brian Irons is somehow even WORSE than he was in the vanilla game, The Tyrant that was once exclusive to the second scenario in vanilla makes his debut in the first scenario and now pursues you throughout the entire game, and when playing as Claire, you're treated to a certain setpiece which is so diabolical it needs to be seen to be believed.

From that description alone, Resident Evil 2 is worth buying if you want pure adrenaline soaked terror, not unlike Resident Evil's remake. However, there's also the fact as a game, it's just a solid companion piece to the original smash hit: The gameplay goes for a hybrid of Resident Evil 4's combat and perspective with Resident Evil VII: Biohazard's terrifying pacing and ammo conservation, and succeeds with flying colours: The controls feel reminiscent of 6's, but thankfully unlike 6's, they feel just right, as the circular movement only happens when you're running, you strafe whilst walking, and the FOV doesn't make me want to vomit. And yes, it feels just as good on Keyboard and Mouse as it does on a gamepad due to the button layout being identical to VII's. Graphically, it's up there with 5 and the aforementioned VII as the best looking of the lot, with the noir-like atmosphere of the rain and night skies setting a foreboding mood, and the various environments you visit being rundown, decayed and wrecked beyond belief. It does a great job at bringing the story of the Raccoon City Destruction Incident and Leon and Claire's efforts to escape to new life and introducing it to new players.

It is flawed however, some content has been cut out in the Remake, notably the Zapping System, and their absence is greatly felt if you've played the original. But still, Resident Evil 2 is still a damn fine survival horror game. It's a solid modernisation of a classic game, manages to be even scarier than said classic, and is highly recommended.

Resident Evil 2 is a great remake, and a worthy successor to the original. It's difficult, requires skill, patience, and planning, and provides a good variety of challenges considering its length. Among some of the best horror games I've ever played, this HD edition was not just entertaining, but suitably frightening. 

The graphical updates are top-notch, so that even during the gameplay it looks like it could be a live-action movie. Every character model is unique and memorable, while retaining a lot of the soul of the originals (such as in the design of individual zombies), and the levels are excellent for setting the atmosphere. From the first moment you pull out the flashlight to explore a dark section of the game, it already had me hooked, and I was being scared not just by the encounters, but the environment itself. By the end, you'll have lots of great images in your head of the various locales, and though the monsters aren't necessarily original; they still accomplish their purposes well.

Like the first game, I love exploring the wide-open spaces in this one. The first section is set in a police station, which has the elements of a museum in its architecture, and it's unbelievably immersive. Even better than the mansion of the original game in a lot of ways due to the amazing visuals and your ability to fully control the camera for investigation; yet it still feels like you're delving into a real structure. The puzzles this time around are a little more straight-forward, and serve more of a purpose in their presentation such that I was able to figure out pretty much everything without having to exhaust every possibility; and though there's locked doors and diverging paths, the levels are concise and effective. 

As for the gameplay, I mentioned that you're now in full control of the camera which makes movement and combat more enjoyable, while it still has a good balance in the management of resources and inventory. As the zombies are extremely durable, and there is quite a lot of them, you really have to make good use of your ammo and support tools to navigate. There's also a lot of new enemies, which are shared in a fairly relaxed way so that you won't get overwhelmed or bored as you explore; and the interesting dynamic of a 'constantly moving' enemy that can surprise you in any room. Best of all, when you finish the game, you can play an adjusted experience over again as the secondary character--where you'll see the rest of the plot, and you can tackle the levels with new weapons and strategies. The only problem I had on this front is Resident Evil's constant habit of having bad boss fights. They're really horrible in this game, mainly just meant to eat ammo, while you struggle with realizing how clunky a third-person over the shoulder experience is when it's all about guns. Furthermore, you have to fight essentially the same bosses repeatedly, made all the worse in the 2nd Game experience.

The story itself isn't much to speak about, as it's a little bit cheesy, but there's less reading than in the first and it doesn't seem as outlandish. However, the music is surprisingly good. It's atmospheric and chilling at points, while being exciting and heart-pumping for other portions. One of the stand-out aspects of this game is its soundtrack, considering my experiences with the other games have had nothing to say of it.

Once the main story is completed, there's also a few bonus missions where you return to the levels of the game, but you have to play as new characters with a limited array of items, and huge swarms of enemies. These "Ghost Survivor" missions also add in new enemy mechanics, and due to the use of blockages and positioning, have you racing to reach a specific point usually 'backwards' through the levels you did in the original story. These missions are incredibly difficult, and really push your skills to the test; which offers some survivability outside of the main narrative. Overall, it's an excellent game, and really does the series justice.

It really blows compared the original game and underwhelming especially after playing 7. First of all, why remake this game in the first place?  We're back to the zombies. Why? RE4 and 7 proved you can make a good RE game without zombies. Well whatever.

All the creepy music from the original RE2 on PS1 is gone and Leon has to, for some reason, add profanities while engaged in battle with zombies or seeing something grotesque. Why were either of these changes necessary? Seriously, what does Leon saying "♥♥♥♥ you" add? All it does is lower the tension. Here's a horror game 101 guys, the player character should just shut the hell up and let me do the reacting. Making the character react is the equivalent of a laugh track in a sitcom. Besides, it doesn't even make sense how confident he is while he tries to kill zombies. Did the people who made this game not know that this is Leon's first game and he's an inexperienced rookie cop? And what happened to the memorable police station Main Hall and Save Room themes from the first game? Marshaling Yard? Nowhere to be found. Just dead silence. The music has just become contextual. You know I can almost forgive this too, but every RE game has a friggin save room theme, it's a staple of the series. There actually is one and it's surprisingly really good, but it goes away after like 30 seconds. Why? WHY? I'm just imagining if the whole game had music like this, it would already be 100x better.

\And all the modernities really lower the tension too, which isn't really the game's fault per se, but in remaking it, you will take away a lot of the tension that comes with clunkier design. In RE2 for the PS1, the tank controls, sloppy aiming, door-opening sequences, and pre-rendered backgrounds/fixed camera angles added to the scariness, as did the grotesque depictions of zombies with very low resolution polygons. If I can aim and control like a dream and the zombies are comically gory, will the game be the same level of scariness? No. 

There's also this annoying thing where enemies break through doors. This basically makes it so you have to shoot them dead so they can leave you alone and you can actually focus on exploring. In the original game you could dodge the zombies in a particular room to conserve ammo. In this game, they're somehow able to track you down no matter what. It's such a radical departure from the original where a huge factor in the horror was making it to the next room without running into zombies.
 
This isn't to say RE2 isn't worth buying, just that I can't recommend it because it feels so neutered compared to the original. i guess if you don't know what you're missing, it's not so bad. Let me reiterate though, if you enjoyed the original RE2, you are NOT the target audience of this game. In fact, I'm not really sure who is the target audience. They're not going for the RE4 crowd because the game takes place in cramped, dark corridors instead of outdoors where you have a better ability to fight hordes of enemies; and they're not targeting the RE7 crowd either since that game had purposefully bad aiming and an interesting, mostly-invincible family of villains whose draw was that you're being hunted down by them. It seems more like they copied the scenario of RE2 to avoid doing any planning work, then slapped on modern shooting controls and called it a day, without realizing ANY of the needs to have psychological horror. To the creators of this game, let me just say old school Resident Evil is not about being able to see someone getting cut in half while his entrails are exposed, and it's not even really about shooting zombies, it's the feeling of pure dread and hopelessness at being one of the few survivors in a zombie-infected city, being trapped in giant manor that wants to kill you, and the need to push through to the end regardless.

A truly distressing yet enthralling zombie game that features involved gunplay, brisk puzzles, expertly composed labyrinths, and a beefcake with bad fashion sense who just won’t leave me alone. Despite my initial reluctance, RE2 turned out to be an intense display of the depth horror brings to methodical gameplay. Since completing the game, my newfound appreciation for the genre has inspired me to experience a litany of other fantastic titles that I had once very swiftly dismissed. Planning ahead, staying alert, and aiming carefully are generally essential to progression, but an explicit atmosphere adds intrinsic motivation for efficiently completing these tasks all while conquering your fears.

Picking your battles is an uncanny part of what gives RE2 its terror and tension beyond the scope of its gruesome presentation. Not often does a game featuring zombies and guns demand patience and restraint. Whether or not basic zombies remain directly frightening a few hours into the game, the threat they pose to your resources and future security makes them an obstacle worthy of consideration. Part of the initial learning curve comes from knowing that not every enemy has to die. The importance of wounding and kiting, especially in open or infrequently visited rooms, is a lesson that’s intriguingly contrary to the shooter staple of [i]‘all the undead must die’[/i]. Managing a tight budget via a physical inventory adds great intimacy to your condition and an eerie awareness of just how far you are from helplessness. Ammo conservation is a common tool used for suspense in shooters, but RE2 often makes taking a shot akin to a chess move.

The level design in RE2 is something to behold. Even without the uneasy atmosphere and high emotional stakes, navigating the interconnected police station would remain an absorbing excursion. As objectives are cleared, locked doors satisfyingly loop back into familiar locations. As the facility grows in complexity, so does the feeling of relief that comes with uncovering shortcuts. However, an infamous fedora-sporting bodybuilder will at some point begin testing those pathfinding skills. While his presence might be a tipping point for players still averted to horror themes, he adds an element of dire unpredictability to offset the danger of player complacency.

Upon further reflection, the sense of curiosity and self-preservation that RE2 evokes through fear mirrors the immersive moments found in many titles that don’t necessarily fall under the umbrella of horror games. I've come to realize the number of games that I’ve played that have omitted the polarizing genre-tag despite them containing plenty of definitively ‘scary’ gameplay segments. Discounting the horror genre would undermine the effort that it takes for any game to create impactful suspense. Gore or messy hallways might be one way of producing suspense, but RE2 has the intelligence to back up its presentation with suspenseful mechanics as well. For those who would prefer a lighter haunting, RE2 has an assisted difficulty mode. Even if a more complacent playthrough takes away from the core thrill, the story alone, with its movie-quality cutscenes, makes the game worth its time. Even if you regard horror games as 'not for me', I believe that anyone can enjoy if not appreciate the grip of RE2’s design.

[b]Intro[/b]
I've finished Resident Evil 5 and have played a few hours of Resi 4, both fairly recently, but beyond that I've only ever had a passing interesting in the series, so imagine my surprise when this remake of the second game in the series ends up being the single best purchase I've made in a long time.

[b]The Great:[/b]
++The game's survival horror based gameplay formula is [i]highly[/i] enjoyable. Item management, the constant juggling of the choice to either avoid enemies or to take them on, map exploration, puzzle solving and progression in upgrading your arsenal amounts to rewarding, addictive and interesting gameplay.
It's a proven formula that will hold up forever.
++All of the characters are really likeable (outside of antagonists which do a good job of being easily hated), especially the protagonists. Claire being one of the best characters I've played as in a game quite easily. And not just 'coz she's hot. This is compounded by...
+the fact that, for the most part, the voice acting is really good, even despite some awkward interchanges and corny dialogue. Claire's voice actress especially does a good job of playing the kick-ass heroine with a caring heart of gold, so you can believe it when she's pissed off by the actions of a certain individual,
and when she's doing her best to hold back tears when put in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ scenario involving another certain individual (no spoilers)

[b]The Good:[/b]
+Animations look great
+Besides some stuttering, the game runs really well and has lots of graphical options (including, unlike in RE7, being able to disable anti-aliasing). It came out last year and yet I'm playing it at 4K on an RTX2060 with only occassional dips below 60FPS at mostly high settings. Very respectable performance.
+The gore looks great and it feels rewarding as hell blowing limbs and heads apart
+The brief moments in each of the two campaigns where you play as someone else do well to mix up gameplay without lasting too long
+If you do both campaigns (which you really should, otherwise you're just missing out on half the game) the game's pretty well lengthed and there's a lot of reason to replay
+Weaponry feels satisfying
+A healthy amount of unlockables and extras

[b]The Okay/Not Too Big of a Deal:[/b]
-+The story is sort of 'eh'. Leon's campaign has some really predictable moments, and Claire has one or two, but some things I definitely didn't see coming... even if sometimes they were totally bogus. The Claire 'real-ending' was nice, though and I did legitimately care about the characters.
+-Emotive, realistic facial expressions help deliver dialogue but for some reason they're not always good. I noticed near the end of Claire's campaign especially that sometimes they look off, but they're usually well done and help deliver some corny dialogue.
-+This is certainly darker, gorier and more vulger than I imagine the original game ever was... whether that's a negative or not is up to you
+-The puzzles are okay. Some are tedious with backtracking, and some are braindead easy, but they're usually fine. I only got stuck on one (for about half an hour) because I somehow totally forgot you can examine items... a feature which had already come into play multiple times so I really have no idea how I forgot. 
-+Mr. X, the invincible being that hunts you down in key moments during both campaigns, is usually an intimidating threat that does nothing more than shake things up and keep you on your toes just as you were getting comfortable, which is a good thing. During my Leon campaign playthrough, he didn't bother me at all
and I enjoyed his inclusion. During my Claire playthrough however, I found him a bit annoying as he'd like to hang around me so I could barely get out of my safe room before getting knocked out, and on top of the increase in enemies around the station, he became more of a chore than an enjoyable challenge.
+-I'm kind of mixed about the sound design. It's not a bad sounding game, but it's not a particularly good sounding game either. The binaural audio doesn't really play much of a part in delivering an immersive sounding world. Mr. X for example sounds like he's stomping around right next to you behind a wall even
if he's floors above/below you.
-+Likewise, graphically, it's kind of average. There's some great lighting and reflections, but some of the liquid effects look dated, the environment's are often dull looking and despite the option for ultra high resolution textures, they still didn't really impress me all that much.
+-This isn't a particularly scary game at all. I had a few jumpscares at most during my playthroughs when an enemy was somewhere I didn't expect, but other than that it's not exactly up to the standards of a horror game. Whether that's an issue or not is up to you.
-+You really should be able to pick which defensive item to use in the moment you're groped by an enemy

[b]The Bad:[/b]
-The game stutters on 16GB RAM and with graphical settings that use less than my max VRAM
-Some of the dialogue between characters is a bit odd and awkward. It's not all that common but I definitely noticed it from time to time. There's also a few moments of total cheese, seemingly added on top of the usually decent writing, to keep with RE tradition... "It's secret weapon time.", anyone?
-The animations look great but that doesn't mean they tie in with movement perfectly. As a result movement isn't as smooth as it should be.
-The soundtrack is totally forgettable. It's either silent, quiet and dull, or in the two times where I really actually noticed it (during bossfights and whenever Mr. X is on your tail), just simply bad.

[b]The Horrible:[/b]
--I've never been annoyed by backtracking in games until now. Considering how slow your character is (I get why; it's so enemies are actually a threat), having to revisit the same locations over and over if you're stupid like me because you forgot to pick up an important item or much often,
didn't have the space in your inventory to pick up an item, or even more common; because you previously couldn't access somewhere near that location until you found a specific item/did a specific action, can get really tedious. A problem even more when Mr. X is on your tail and when enemies like lickers and zombies
spawn in to slow things down even further. It was mostly a problem with me, and it didn't really start annoying me until my Claire playthrough, but nevertheless, what is simultaneously one of the best things about the game (map exploration) is also the worst thing about the game.
--I assumed Leon and Claire's campaigns would tie in fluidly and cleverly, where you'd see one person's actions impact the other's, but that never really happened. I don't know which elements of each campaign are canon, but they simply can't both be due to the constant overlap in actions. Only rarely did someone else's
actions seem to impact the other's. 'Horrible' is an exaggeration, but it's certainly disappointing.
--The ghost survivor stories are pretty lame. They're basically story-less, total action oriented, difficult reuses of the proper game's maps. Aside from the first paragraph as it loads, the 'what-if' idea is essentially completely removed. I thought they'd be unique gameplay scenarios but nah, they're all similar and lame. If you like them that's great, but they're not what I expected nor do I find them enjoyable.

I've never had a game have so many note-worthy, mixed bag things that fit under the 'The Okay/Not Too Big of a Deal' category before, but still better than falling under the ones below! Never played a survival horror game before? Well, here's a good way to start!
