[h1]Plot[/h1]
On July 23, 1998, Bravo Team was sent to investigate a series of cannibalistic murdering occurring near Arklay Mountains outside of Racoon City. After not hearing from Bravo Team, S.T.A.R.S (Special Tactical and Rescue Force) sends its Alpha Team to search for them, upon near arriving at the scene, the helicopter suffers an engine failure and crash into the mountain. After this strange malfunction, Alpha Team decides to search on foot only to find the derelict helicopter of Bravo Team crashed in the ground along with the dead body of the pilot. While still looking for answers Alpha Team is attacked by a bunch of wild dogs the bullets oddly don't seem to have any effect on the animals, the only alternative at that moment was to rush to a mansion at far sight.

Only four members of the Alpha Team manage to survive, stumbled upon the mansion, the captain of the unit decides to separates and search for Alpha Team missing member. The building seemed to be like a mase, the architecture was unique but overrun with creatures inside trying to attack any living creature. Alpha Team learned that there was a laboratory conducted by the International Farmaceutical Umbrella Corporation, but something went wrong; a virus had escaped the labs, the whole mansion was put on lockdown, polluting the entire complex. All inhabitants, which included Umbrella researchers, were infected from the virus and were (due to the viral nature) degraded into "zombies". Some who had yet to have fully succumbed to the effects of the virus were killed either by suicide, by Umbrella's security team when trying to escape the mansion, or by the B.O.W's that had escaped their confinement. 

The building was designed to be a laboratory to test a new drug that would breakthrough modern warfare, and in case something went wrong the entire staff were to be confined inside the mansion so that nobody could leaky any information about the project. After learning all of this, Alpha Team decided to blow the mansion and warn S.T.A.R.S. It was too late the cannibalistic attacks were occurring months before B's and A team investigation. The return of the four S.T.A.R.S. veterans caused a serious problem to the company's control of Raccoon City. Umbrella was able to slow down any official police investigation due to their control over the Mayor and Chief of Police and also made plans to assassinate the S.T.A.R.S. officers if they were to be found conducting an unofficial investigation. S.T.A.R.S. itself was shut down and replaced with Raccoon S.W.A.T. 

The virus made its way to Raccoon City in less than two months, having a population with over 100.000 residents, little could the citizen do, one night they went to sleep in a peaceful town only to wake up in hell.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Resident Evil 2 Remake uses almost the same engine as Resident Evil 7 (RE> Engine), the movements are fluent and well made for the Remake version, which allows the players to feel very comfortable about combat. The zombies play a major factor with AI implemented which will make you decide to run past a zombie or take It down, features such as photorealistic visuals are possible; enemies react in real-time taking instant visible damage, limbs can be ripped off from enemies, staggering the zombies plays a big role in here, you can either shot It in any part of its body and wait for the draw back effect or shot one of its legs until It rip off.

The game uses the same over-the-shoulder view from Resident Evil 4 through Resident Evil 6, for instance, the character control resembles that of Resident Evil 6, with the player being able to move freely toward any direction without needing to face it first. The player can also move while aiming, but that will increase the weapon's spread, although some of the weapons are exempt from this mechanic.

The inventory starts with 8 slots but can be expanded to the maximum of 20 slots by collecting the Hip Pouches scattered throughout the game. Certain weapons found in the game take up two inventory slots while others only may take one, before upgrades are applied. 

Knives in this game have a durability rate, similar to the non-knife player, so you cant use your knife all the time, you need to know when and where to use it and cannot melee zombies after stunning them or putting them on the ground. Another feature which was included in Resident Evil is the return of defensive items. If the character is grabbed by an enemy and they have a defensive weapon in their inventory, a prompt will show up on-screen and if pressed the item will be used as a defence weapon which shakes the enemy of the player. (If you use your knife as a defence item in enemies, including the boss, you need to defeat It to get it back.)

Like previously games, there're RANKS when you finish the game, the faster you do It higher It'll be, so where's the thing, for you to unlock new weapons you need to beat the games as fast as possible, simple as that, but remember the Machine Gun and Rocket Missile from the classic? Yes, the BIG BOYS, well for you to get those you need to beat the game in Hardcore mode. The requirements for S+ Hardcore are pretty intense:
3 saves or less (with no auto-save)
No infinite weapons (except for the infinite durability combat knife)
Must be completed in under two hours and thirty minutes for the A campaigns, or under 2 hours in B scenarios.

You need to speedrun the game, which will mentally push you.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
Thanks to major graphical improvements with the help of the RE Engine, items, characters, enemies, objects, and even the environment itself have photorealistic rendering and visuals. Unlike in the original 1998 release where the Raccoon Police Station's hallways and rooms are lit, the 2019 remake instead turns the precinct's hallways and some locations far darker, giving it a chilling and intense atmosphere as the player traverses them. The shadows were greatly improved as well, as opposed to the original's shadows being a small dark translucent circle beneath the characters or enemies.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2433043658
[h1]Extra Mode[/h1]
Resident Evil 2's campaigns are structured out through isolated scenarios. After finishing the story for the first character, a new option in the main menu called New Game (2nd Run) will open up. The first character you pick will essentially be the lead of the story, with the other protagonist experiencing their own encounters as they tie up the overall plot's loose ends. While both characters will experience similar events and explore the same locations, the choices and impact of each scenario are totally isolated from one another.

There are also 4 extra modes, which tells what would happen in an alternative universe in which those characters are set. 

[h1]Overall[/h1]
Resident Evil 2 Remake is very well made and honours the classic, without a doubt one of the best Remake ever made, I highly recommend this game for players who like the genre.

I have never been a fan of horror. Not when I was little and not now as a 21 year old adult. It's just not for me. Which is why I had to write this review. If you told me I'd finish a horror game like Resident Evil 2 a year ago I wouldn't believe it. But here I am at around 40 hours playtime with two full playthroughs and the true ending unlocked. Not because I've conquered my fears of horror, at least not yet, rather it was an amazingly terrifying yet thrilling experience from start to finish.

The slow transition of creeping through the cold dark hallways of the Police Station in fear of disturbing the dead to trudging through sewer sludge and mutants on a hellbent heroic mission to storming out of a self destructing underground base mowing down any undead freaks in my way with an epic boss battle conclusion was an exhilarating and oddly natural pace to experience. I enjoyed this type of non-linear level design, the chance to go back to old areas to encounter new enemies, new puzzles, new areas, and the most satisfying of them all, new loot. 

The absolute emotional levels this game can take on you is bizarre. You can feel like an invincible slaying machine if you have the skill and loot for it or be absolutely petrified when low on ammo and health and you hear a certain you know who's boots get louder and louder searching for you. The dopamine release that you get for solving puzzles or finding that cursed part you needed to fix the damn doohickey is on another level of its own. Not to mention the boss fights, yes boss fights, this game has. Each one more epic than the last.

Okay, sure the gameplay sounds great but what about the story? Which was actually my favorite part. You can play as either rookie cop Leon Kennedy or college girl Claire Redfield. Some noob nobody and some frat girl you might think? Wrong. These two characters are some of the most badass, balls of steel, down to earth people I've ever seen exist. 

The basis is, for the primary playthrough, you're rookie cop Leon Kennedy returning to his hometown, Raccoon City, for his first day on the job as a city police officer. That is until he arrives in town with a full on infestation of zombies, mutants, and other horrors. The rookie then takes matters into his own hands and decides to get to the bottom of what's happening in his city with the help of his new friend, Claire Redfield. Together, they are but two of the few survivors left in the now city of the dead. The absolute journey these two go on in just one night blows my mind in how much they were able to accomplish. And what a hell of a night it was.

The game has amazing graphics, great voice acting, fantastic gameplay, natural pacing, a good story, deep lore, and lovable characters. The only cons I could find was that the two playthroughs don't make sense together. Separate, they're great. But when you start to compare them is when you start running into continuity issues. 

Also, this game is hardcore. There is absolutely no hand holding. The most the game gives you is an assisted mode which helps you out with more loot and weaker enemies but that's it. The puzzles can be extremely hard for new comers and playing hide and go seek with Mr. X while not knowing what on earth you're looking for, or if you do where the hell it is, can be rather intimidating. But if you manage to solve it all, kudos. Or get help from a guide or friend like I did, makes the whole experience more enjoyable rather than frustrating in my opinion.

All in all, amazing game. The price tag is well worth for getting at least two playthroughs, because Claire and Leon's are both fairly different, or even more for different scenarios, dialogue, achievements, extra modes, DLC, etc. I was lucky enough to pick it up on sale for twenty dollars. 

Nonetheless, this is a game like no other I've experienced in my decade plus of playing video games. It'll be one to remember for me, which is why I'm going to give this game a 9/10. It was horrifically action packed and I loved and hated every moment of it.

I wasn't a fan of the original RE2 but I enjoyed this remake. I found the controls solid, music phenomenal, and graphics excellent. Resource management is done well; you'll find yourself stressing over losing a knife or missing a shot. Some decent tense moments and surprises. The 'Map System' is very helpful during a first play-through, but should have been removed in harder difficulties. Puzzles were not challenging, but were not comically simple.

It's clear the developers wanted to create a game to replay again and again, but the challenge does not significantly change enough to create a new unique experience. Difficulty 'Hardcore' does not live up to the name. The survival/action aspect of the game hardly alters; instead the player is just presented with less inventory space and limiting saves (the player still gets over a dozen, far more 'saves' than you'll reasonably need when you're ready to attempt a harder difficulty). 

Characters lack development, but Claire and Leon are still likeable (Leon is written as a young and idealistic greenhorn policeman, Claire as a sensitive but scrappy tough-as-nails college student). Claire's fearlessness in the lab is my favorite scene (G3). After a few hours of playing, I noticed the game is largely just a fetch-quest (need to find a thing to move to another area, where you need to find another thing, etc.). The game is great and I would certainly recommend it, but the lack of character development, little variety in challenge, and fetch-questing would be the main reasons I wouldn't consider it one of my favorites.

The RE2 remake is a really fantastic game. It had me on the edge of my seat and, for some parts, had me genuinely jumping out of fear (looking at you Mr. X). The graphics are really beautiful and you don’t need a beefy PC to run it; I ran it on an Intel i5-8250 processor with Intel UHD 620 graphics (admittedly, you have to play  a little lower than you would like but definitely still playable and gorgeous either way so don’t be turned away if you don’t have a monster of a PC to play it with). The characters are all designed beautifully as well.

After completing the main story, which you can do as Claire or Leon, you can then play through a Bit scenario where you play as the opposite character to see what they were doing while you were busy (and also get access to items/areas you couldn’t before). The story is really amazing, and a lot of fun (especially in the RPD, there’s a lot to do there and it’s very immersive and tense at times). After playing through the main story and B scenario though, there isn’t much to replay, even if you do the other character in a new game as many of it doesn’t change besides a few certain things. 

If you look carefully, you can also see hints towards the other RE games, too (say RE: Outbreak.. hopefully a remake or even a remaster of that will come soon too :) )

[h1] ▀▄▀▄▀▄ Resident Evil 2 ▄▀▄▀▄▀ [/h1]

[u][b]TL,DR Review[/b][/u]

Raccoon City has never felt more realized here in the remake of Resident Evil 2 with exceptional visuals of the RE Engine. Play as Leon or Claire and navigate the RC Police station while surviving the outbreak of the T-virus and the relentless pursuit from Mr. X.

[u][b]Full Review[/b][/u]

September 1998 is known as the catalyst for the entire Resident Evil universe with the T-Virus incident in Racoon City. As time goes on, it's revealed throughout the series that this is only the first in many macabre creations by the Umbrella corporation. Here in RE2, you get to experience the chaos of the outbreak in Racoon City through the eyes of Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield. A chance zombie encounter at a gas station in the outskirts of the city takes both characters to the Racoon City Police Department for different reasons, not realizing the horrors that await.

Resident Evil 2 returned in 2019 as a full remake using the RE Engine with completely new assets (other than a few from RE7), reworked story, different game-play and new voice actors for the cast with addition of face scan models hired for each character in the game. Visually it looks fantastic and the RCPD has never felt more realized and lighting adding a foreboding mood to to the less well-lit parts of the map. Enemies also look great with the shambling corpses of zombies caked in the fresh blood of recent victims and their glossy dead eyes reflecting in the light as they shamble towards you. 

Game-play has been retooled from RE7 to something more like RE4 or RE5 with a 3rd person perspective but feels more rapid and less stiff compared to those 2 games. Zombies in RE2 have been worked to become a genuine threat, a rare thing even now. Zombies can take significant damage depending what difficulty level you play at and can still come after you even if you remove their limbs with the dismemberment system at play. When grouped together in close quarters, there is a real risk of getting a game over. You also of course have to deal with Mr. X, a bio-weapon created by Umbrella that was let loose on the police force as a field test. When you encounter him, he's virtually invincible with the ability to move around the map in search of the player. While you can burn up your ammo to fight him, it's ultimately a waste of resources for other threats you'll need face later on. Keep your distance and be prepared to move as his stomping footsteps edge closer to your location. 

Puzzles are what you would expect from Resident Evil, with getting one object from A to B without getting torn apart by lickers or something like creating a mixture to progress further in a level. Claire and Leon both have some diverging paths in the story that will take to different parts of the RCPD and eventually completely different parts specific to one or the other. Both are a lot of fun to experience since you also get different weapons to find\use as well as different enemies to encounter.

Since I'm writing this after some time beyond the release of RE3 remake, I'd like to talk about some comparisons of that game compared to this one. RE2 is a slower, more methodical game that is very rooted in traditional survival horror. It's pacing and campaign structure reflect that with extended periods of downtime, it also has post-game content that some people value more than others. We're taking wave-based or speed-running options that some players will enjoy. RE3 remake doesn't have these game modes but options for more difficulty options that change enemy behavior and positioning with more health and damage output as well as different item placement. The game-play of RE3 is also much faster with a lot less downtime and a shorter action-packed campaign for it, unlocks are also much easier to achieve with no penalty for using certain items unlike RE2. I find that the campaigns of both of these remakes were fantastic and complement each other much like the original games did back in the late 90s, ignore the rhetoric and enjoy them both for their different experiences of the outbreak. Resident Evil: Resistance does come with RE3 but I'll save my thoughts for that in its own review.

RE2 remake really is an amazing return to form since the somewhat divisive experience of RE7, its game-play was a lot of fun while realizing Racoon City in a way that many of us imagined when playing the original. The demo is available for those who are new to the series but for anyone who has interest in the genre, this is an obvious recommendation and you owe it to yourself to check it out.

I have to say, this is the best Resident Evil game I have ever played.
I'm a fan of the franchise since the PSOne, and this remake really brings the essence of Resident Evil: survival horror, puzzle solutions and resource management.
The environment, the soundtrack, the voice-acting, the mechanics, the story, the puzzles: this game is absolutely superb.

Many people don't like the fact of going back and forth in the Police Department, but that is the fun part of the game for me, since everytime I go back to a room to pick up something I left previously, I find a zombie that wasn't there.
Each corridor made me listen carefully for lickers' screeches. Having to run around the map looking for a puzzle piece with Mr X in my tail is such a thrill.

There are issues with it, of course. To me, personally, the first half (RPD & Prison) was much better than the second half (Sewers & NEST). This might be because I was so excited in the beginning, but it drags a little bit.
Indeed, some parts are cheesy, but this is not new for Capcom (hence "you almost became a Jill sandwich", from RE1).

Another thing I loved about this game was how the characters feel alive now, and not talking polygons like in the 90s.
Officer Marvin, Robert Kendo, Chief Irons, Annette & William Birkin... They are fully-realized characters now. I loved this.
Leon is not an idiot like he was in RE4 (sorry, unpopular opinion, I know), Claire is so much more interesting and loving this time round, and Sherry also had improvements.

Overall, this game is a masterpiece. Resident Evil at its best.

[h1]This is how to do a remake[/h1]

[list]
[u]What I liked about the game[/u] 

[*]	I like how you can play as two different characters (Leon and Claire).

[*]	I thought it was a good idea to remake the game with an over-the-shoulder perceptive instead of those fixed camera angles and tank controls. 

[*]	Tons of challenges to complete and unlockables.

[*]	Wants you completed the first campaign, you unlock the second where you play as the other character.  The second campaign changes some things around and adds new areas to explore and new characters. 

[*]	There are some really good extra game modes, like “What if” scenarios, 4th survivor, and for a laugh Tofu survivor. 

[*]	The characters are really likable and well voice acted. 

[*]	Awesome boss fights. 

[*]	Nice selection of weapons which feel good when fired. I like how each character has a different load-out.

[*]	I really liked the changes they made to Sherry’s and Ada Wong levels, especially Sherry’s.   

[u]What I disliked or was disappointed with[/u]
 
[*]	Some of the enemies from the original game were cut, like the spiders and the giant moths. 

[*]	I wish the puzzles were a bit more challenging. 

[*]	Wasn’t keen on the idea of having knife durability. I didn’t mind the idea of being able to use the knife or grenade to stop getting bitten. 

[*]	I wish they made more changes to the second campaign. I would have liked to have seen some new puzzles and more areas to explore, especially at the NEST level. 

[*]	I remember in the original game that Mr X only appeared in the second play-through. I wish they kept it the same with the remake, just to make the second play-through feel different. 

[*]	They could have made the game a bit scarier, although people who haven’t played the original game might find this game quite scary, especially when Mr X is chasing after you.   

[/list]

Conclusion

I really enjoyed the remake of Resident Evil 2. I thought it was a good idea to remake the game with an over-the-shoulder perspective. I was a bit disappointed with some of the content they cut out of the game, but there is a lot of unlockable content and challenges. I also wished they changed more things around and added more content in the second play-through, because it felt for the most part too similar to the first play-through. If you liked the original resident evil 2 or the other games in the series then I highly recommend you buy this game.

I don't know what I was expecting after having played the original version several times, but, this... is Resident Evil 2. Feels about as solid of a remake as the update they did on Resident Evil 1 back in the Gamecube days, except with more modern QOL and obviously higher resolutions on everything. Played Leon A/Claire B on Normal, apparently I had DLC unlocking all of the bonus stuff right away, which is nice as I have no intention of attempting to speedrun Hardcore mode to get those things, although I did not use them on my first runs (but I did storm through Claire A/Leon B with full goofballs weapons). I can and do appreciate the changes to some of the bosses, but mostly during my playthrough I just kept thinking "wow, I remember this from the N64... and this too... and this", and that sounds like I'm being facetious or flippant about what a great job this update did, but I guess I'm just sort of misunderstanding that this WAS a remake and not just a thematic re-marketing of an old brand with a new spin. It should be noted that the second run aka B campaigns are nearly identical storywise to the A versions in this release, which is odd to drop what appear to have been major differences in events from the old game. I suppose they wanted to establish what was meant to be canon, so, you won't see an uninfected Sherry who has a sample of the virus in her pendant that gets stolen. After playing a few other game remakes "for the first time" like Luigi's Mansion and Majora's Mask, it's nice to see one that doesn't trip over its own attempts to get better. As far as handheld playing goes, the GPD Win Max runs this game acceptably.  Performance Preset gets it to around 25-40 fps throughout the entire game which is great.  I am so happy I can play both this and the remake of RE3 on a handheld.  

- The Bad

Intel Graphics Optimization.  The flashing assets with running this on the Win Max's Intel Iris Plus Graphics really looks rough.  Having stairs, floors, and ladders constantly flashing really makes me glad I don't suffer from seizures.  But I can put up with it for portable RE2Make. As of this writing, I have only played RE0, RE1 (both HD) and RE7 before RE2 Remake. At first I really could not enjoy it as much because it was too damn difficult - mostly because zombies were bullet sponges and Mr X. But having played for about 96 hours now according to Steam, I have had a new found appreciation for the game. I have replayed this game for more than 10 times (mostly Claire's campaign because I am a simp), and the subsequent replays were not as difficult because 1) I was more familiar with enemy movements and spawn locations, and 2) I have unlocked every weapon and infinite ammo as well. The hardest and most frustrating periods I had were when I was trying to get S+ rank for both campaigns, it was a freaking chore and I grew some grey hair just for trying. After that, everything was a bliss. It was fun to trial and error here and there, to see the zombies suffer as they have made me suffer. Everyone knows how great this game is, so let us talk about what I absolutely hate about it.

1) The death animations. When you are dying, an animation will play out e.g. a zombie biting your flesh out or an Ivy flytrapping your head. That is cool and all, but they are UNSKIPPABLE. Like. . .why? These animations are long, and yes I get it...the deaths are horrendous and I screwed up. It was cool seeing it once or twice, but when I am not a mission to complete the game, that 10 seconds of animation is a waste of my time and an insult to my patience. I died a lot of times and I wish I did not need to waste time seeing every death animation repeatedly. This is one of the biggest flaws of the game. It may seem like a small thing, but it is honestly very annoying and can impact your mental health.

2) The clunky controls. Simply put, you cannot perform strafe movement in this game. When you hit the A or D key, your character simply turns left or right completely. That is a no go for me because that is what the mouse is for, to turn your character to whichever direction you want. You CAN do slight strafe movements, but that is only when you are walking/running forward or aiming. I would not have had much of an issue with this if the game did not have such combat elements. However, the game does have combat elements and therefore it makes no sense that the character movements cannot be as fluid as they should be. It is as though the game developers never played an FPS game in their lives, or even TPS like PUBG or similar. You cannot use the "it makes the game scarier when you are more restricted" card here because I will rebut with "why not just have the character go into shock for every enemy encounter, even scarier right?". 

3) Discarding items instead of being able to drop them. I had the same issue regarding this with RE7 (and RE1 as well). It is 2019 and I do not understand why this is still a part of the game mechanics. I know item management is integral to a Resident Evil gameplay, but this just does not make sense. It feels stupid and irritating. 

Lastly, the A and B scenarios for Claire and Leon are practically the exact same thing, save for B having a slightly different opening and being a little more difficult at first. I felt that it was weird, but I was able to accept both scenarios as alternate realities instead of a linking narrative. Since I did not play the original 1998 version, I had no emotional attachment to anything so I did not share the anger that many fans had over this issue. However, after reading up and watching some gameplay videos, I do agree that the developers should have put in more effort into the A and B scenarios. 

Otherwise, I think this game is as good as survival horror games get. I cannot wait for RE8.

P.S. Claire and Ada are so hot in this game. The developers totally chose the perfect models for these characters.

Never playing the ORIGINAL RE games, I was truly happy I could finally try it out with everything updated, and survival horror being one of, if not, my favorite genre to boot. There isn't much I could say you most likely have not heard. Graphics, amazing! Gun play, smooth and responsive. Sound design, truly breath taking (granted, as usual, I feel the guns themselves, could have had more kick, and bang, but what we got is serviceable). The atmosphere is on a whole other level and your first play through, will be truly special! I want more of this! This is why some say, "video games are a form of art". There is love and care built into this one and I truly appreciate the time they provided it! It really shows. 

So instead of why I love the game, because it is truly a work of art (as stated), I want to cover things that bothered me and, as a newbie going in, stuck out to me. Things that could have truly sent this game on to record breaking ratings (imo). 

The Story
It works. It takes its time to show up, but that is understandable. Even if you haven't played any RE, most likely you know the story, at least the beginning. That being said, if your brand new to the series, and love story driven games, this really isn't one. It picks up towards the end, but it is as simple as, stop the baddie. I was kind of hoping there would be a little more lore to dissect. Even in the files you find scattered around the world, come out to be disappointing, and there really isn't that many tbh. I would say half the files (I am counting any paper you can pick up), is usually the answer to a puzzle, tutorial for crafting, or just the final moments of an NPC. Not much else. Also, I am not marking down for this, but some characters just seem like there would have been some story to them. Instead, for example, one is explained by greed (money) and you move on. That's it. I just wish time was given to give these characters back stories. Have them interwoven into the main campaign a little bit, or explained in side areas. Leaving it up to the player to decide if the time is worth it to explore, or at least, as I said, files. Documenting their motives and goals, so you can understand the world and people, around you. 

Campaign A VS B
So the way this game truly works, you need to play two play through. Leon, or Claire A. This may sound confusing, but don't worry, the game just asks you who you would like to play with, Leon or Claire. You pick one, you start playing, that simple. However, when your done with that play through, you unlock campaign B. This confused me at first. So I'll explain, just in case. You want to go in actual order. Beating Leon A, you would then go to Claire B (A, B). I originally thought it would be, Leon A, to Claire A, but this is incorrect. This would have you replaying the same portion of the game, with no difference, besides the character running around on screen. So, as an example of my play through, I went, Leon A, to Claire B. This gets you the true ending, and a difference in play through. However, I believe canon is, Claire A, Leon B, if you want to go by that standard. I did not know this until after I beat the game. 
So after explaining all of that. I do have some issues. Playing through the B campaign has its differences, but not enough, imo. I thought they would be the same in locations, but not so much as puzzles, and bosses. It felt truly weird to replay the B campaign and basically follow the same story. Again, there are differences. Leon and Claire access a small portion in some locations that is unique to their play through. Not to sound needy, but I would have liked more. Different puzzles and bosses. As it stands, it felt like campaign A was canon... But then you play B, so, that's canon now? Campaign A, leaves notes around the games world (only two), so it seems you just missed them. However, going to other locations, it would seem the other character had not arrived yet. I know I am over thinking it, and asking a lot, but I would have gladly waited another year to have more alterations added, or at least have it blend better. Granted, you do get enough of a difference in story, to make it worth playing through a second time. Please do not get that confused. 

Enemy Health! 
My GOOOOOODNESS! These zombies are NO joke. Not sure what the G virus does, but it must THICC'N that skull. There were times I became really frustrated after putting 10 plus rounds into a zombie brain, for them to still get back up! I get Capcom wanted to make it scary, but this is more infuriating then anything else. Heck, cut our bullet count by half, and the zombies health. Killing a zombie in 1/4 shots, seems alright to me. But 10 plus, can really kill the immersion this game has going for it. Luckily this doesn't really INFECT the bosses too much. Outside the second to last boss on B campaign, every boss felt pretty good. I might get some flack here, but Invader Studio did it right with Daymare 1998. Most filler zombies ate 1/3 shots before going down. This felt good, and they placed ammo around accordingly. Don't get me wrong, on both games I was stacked by the end when it came to ammo. Still, After dropping 3/4 shots with a pistol, nub-tube a fool that fries them up, for them to still grab my leg (with no way to counter) and bite it as I walk by, can be irritating at best. I hope they address this in RE8, or the next remaster. 

Final Thoughts
In the end, RER2 is an amazing game! The Witcher could easily show other Pubs/Devs on how to make an open world RPG. While Capcom, RER2 can be a blueprint for survival horror! This takes time and effort and they truly dedicated both to make this masterpiece of a game! Survival, horror, action and adventure, you get it all here! Do yourself a favor, buy this game!

I actually didn't play RE1 and i did played RE2 and RE3 but very little, also 4 but i didn't got very far, all of those because the games belonged to friends and cousins, i didn't own a console until i was old, so i actually fully played RE5 because it was on PC and it was a good game but not spectacular in my opinion, so some years after 6 came out i bought it and while ⅔ of the campaign and story was horrible the gameplay was extremely good in my opinion, i loved mercenaries mode in 6.

So when they announced the reboot and went back to original gameplay i wasn't particularly interested, i figured they would just use the gameplay from the RE6 leon campaign which was the best from the last game. And I attributed the high reviews and general appraisal to nostalgic feelings on the fandom so i just had the game on my wishlist until it was on deep sale.

But my friend gave me a copy for my birthday so i decided to try it…

It was incredible. From the start the gameplay feels right and while I remembered my issues with limited inventory it actually never bothered me, because instead of being an arbitrary limitation on how many items you can carry at once it actually feels like a well thought out system in a well designed map in which each decision you take has weight.

I do have some criticism to the game, the “dynamic difficulty” makes some fights essentially random and while i understand the reasons behind the system, it still feels cheap that you are doing well and suddenly you are death because you reached the maximum difficulty and the zombies are at maximum alert, maximum health and your shoots do almost no damage. Then after you die and select continue you “suddenly” kill all zombies on one hit and get flooded by resources.

I felt that I was punished by playing the game right until my death and then insulted by the sudden drop in difficulty.

I want to think that there is a better way to do this, in dead space 2 which is basically the same game but in space the ammo and health pickups were influenced by your gameplay as well, but in that game when you played poorly and got hit a lot, you did get more health pickups but less ammo, forcing you to aim better and be less reckless in a way, if you were generally better you did get more and better ammo but less health, so it was still punishing if you got hit. I'm not saying that was perfect but in here it's a constant pain that zombies react randomly to your shoots.

To conclude, i don't feel the game suffers much from those issues because the game does feel designed around it and it does accomplish the objective of making you more weary of your surroundings so i still recommend this game.

Resident Evil 2 (2019): My first day in Raccoon City  

Intro:

The Resident Evil series (much like many a classic gaming IP) has passed me by until now.  I always knew they were the force that popularized the Survival Horror genre. But with the added caveat that they were full of meme-worthy voice acting,  dialogue, and music choices.  It also didn't help that (asides from RE4) the recent ones were either mediocre (RE5) or reportedly crap (RE6).  I only started taking note of the series around RE7 and started taking notice when RE2 Remake happened.  So here we are, my first Resident Evil game.  The awesome remake that continues Capcom's remarkable tracks record.  

It's pretty stupid when you think about it

Why does Ada Wong look like she stepped off a 1998 fashion catalog? Why is she wearing high heels in a situation where she would have to run often for long periods?  Mad Scientists injecting themselves with bioweapons that turn themselves and other people into monsters is perfectly rational and has no means of backfiring in any way.  Why doesn't Claire just call Chris? Cell phones existed in 1998 (while not cheap) and would cost less than just turning up at her brother's place of work. She could have just called the police station and asked. 

All of these aspects of RE2's story suggest an element of fun to the narrative.  None of these would make any sense in a realistic story.  There was no self-awareness (like the originals) RE2 would have been laughed out of the room.  But with a quiet hint of knowing absurdity, it works to the story's advantage.  It makes perfect sense that the police station was formerly a museum. And the emergency exit can be opened by finding three seals scattered around the police station. 

Going back and forth

RE2 is split into several large areas that have to be traversed often to collect the pieces required to solve puzzles.  To the player, it might seem like a bit of a daunting task. As you have no idea where anything is and are panicking thought of encountering more bloody zombies.  But through repeated backtracking (and finding the map), the player gradually becomes familiar with their environment, where the short cuts are what puzzles need to be solved. 

The player soon becomes intimate with their surroundings, how to save time and avoid the worst.  Considering your limited inventory space you will most likely have to go back anyway.  RE2's level design embraces the best kind of backtracking. The sort that doesn't waste the player time but works as a puzzle in of itself, one that the player has to solve through repeated interaction.  The player has to learn the map layout, to learn how to reach their destination without getting into trouble.
Could not be happier with this game.  RE:2 was one of the first games I played about 20 years ago and it's always been a favorite.  This remake is absolutely amazing.  The best RE since RE:4.

It's been a long time since I've found the motivation to replay a game's story mode--games are often long, life is often busy, and my backlog is growing faster than I can shrink it. But this game's second run system which turns your understanding of the game world inside out by sending you through it in a different way while telling a new (but connected) story within it tipped me over the edge. I beat it on my first run about a week prior, took some time off to beat Resident Evil 4 (a masterpiece in its own right), then came right back to this. I'm working through my second run, Claire's B campaign, on Hardcore mode this time, and it is intense, difficult, and even more terrifying than last time. I love it.

It takes all the strengths of classic Resident Evil, (the interconnected, puzzle-littered hallways of the police station will feel familiar to anyone who has braved Resident Evil 1 Remake's mansion--have you? It's also an incredible game!) but anything that might have even verged on tedious is cleaned up; the map marks rooms with things left to find and unsolved puzzles instead of asking you to memorize them, write them down or wander aimlessly. While the beautiful, cinematic fixed camera angles of that game will be missed, the crisp control of Leon and Claire's shooting and the increased action allowed in boss fights or more dramatic enemy encounters as a result of the over-the-shoulder camera feels like the full realization of what classic Resident Evil merely evoked with its more simplistic fights.

And the scares! It's not the most terrifying game ever made, but man is it tense. Mr. X has had volumes written about him, so I won't belabor the point, but he'll get his moments over you, as will many other enemies, sooner or later. I hope I never have to hear a set of loud footsteps approaching when I'm out at night. There's always just the right amount of ammo to make it possible to get around enemies but impossible to actually kill more than a few at a time. This combined with the ever evolving layout and paths around the station makes it an uneasy but immensely rewarding task to venture out of your save room.

This core gameplay loop of exploration, infrequent combat, and the occasional bombastic, brilliant, satisfying boss fight before the eventual return to peace makes it downright addicting for the ~8 hour length of your first campaign. It's tight and utterly devoid of chaff, and this is what makes the prospect of a second run with some changes so appealing--it's simultaneously satisfying and leaves you wanting more of it. That, to me, is the mark of a perfectly paced game, and the character switch takes such smart advantage of it that I wish more games focused on being tight, well-crafted, and replayable instead of big, big, big. The characters themselves are both easy to get attached to, too, and they each have their own arcs with a few unique supporting characters. Leon is immensely relatable, always seeming to say what I'm thinking, and Claire is both believable and likable as the unlikely hero of her story.

That's not to say it takes itself seriously all the time, of course. It's impossible for Resident Evil to totally shake off its B-movie charm, even with the insane production values of a game like this. The nine-foot-tall Mr. X dresses in a fedora and trench coat to blend in, for one. It could never avoid being hilarious. It's just that, like some of the best classic low-budget horror films (Evil Dead 1 comes to mind), this doesn't get in the way of its thrills, scares, or story. The gradual amping-up of the stakes and scope doesn't feel like a cheap or formulaic escalation, but a necessary and satisfying payoff. The narrative is just as gripping as any other part of the game, and every part of it gripped me harder than an angry Tyrant. It's rare that a game comes out which is simultaneously so focused and so crowdpleasing, so tough and so well-designed, so highly-produced and still so passionately made. It's been so long since I loved a game quite this much, but then again, it's been a long time since I played a game quite this good.

I was excited to finally play Resident Evil 2 Remake - I never got a chance to play the original (but saw it streamed) and the Remake came out when I couldn't quite afford it. 

[h1]I played RE2R to completion, and I agree that it is a solid successor to the original RE2[/h1]

[b]The survival horror elements are maintained near perfectly while converting to a modern 3rd person person shooter perspective versus the static camera styles of it's predecessors.[/b] The Police Station set within an aged museum with locked portions, barricaded hallways, sewer access, and paths to a secret lab feel very familiar while offering a new setting to explore. Combat is always a challenge until you master it while puzzles and exploration offers just enough deviations to the formula to keep game world fresh an interesting. If you have any reverence for the series or the genre, you will be satisfied with your purchase.

[h1]Given the choice to play Leon or Claire, your player makes a stop at a local gas station and comes across the grisly scene of undead humans cannibalizing living ones[/h1]

After escaping this threat, you meet the other player character, each with their reason for being there. You make your way to the police station before being forcibly split up. The police station was supposed to be the bastion of safety in this zombie outbreak, but it too has been overrun. [b]Your goal now, is to find out what happened to the police as both characters have ties to them and to make it out alive.[/b] Anybody who has played the RE games knows that something sinister is afoot.

[h1]From this point, the way out is via secret pathway to leads underground back out into the streets with less activity. This is easier said than done, as the pathway requires a convoluted process of finding three medallions locked inside stations only obtainable after completing a relatively simple puzzle with an unknown solutions[/h1]

[b]You need to explore the building, finding ammo, healing items, keys for special doors, alternate pathways, wooden boards to block zombies from breaking in, pouches to increase your inventory space, and items to open closed pathways such as door fuses, crankshafts, and a jack. The entire experience is a management of resources - making progress requires various "key" items, but doing so requires dealing with undead citizens and cops spread around the facility, that will certainly drain and eliminate your ammo reserves.[/b] In most cases until the end game, there is simply not enough ammo to deal with every zombie which can take anywhere from two to a dozen headshots, depending if you're lucky to get a critical hit. Basically, you can't rely on crits, but you can rely on your ability slow the down or move around rooms and hallways to avoid their deadly magnetic grabs alltogether. Yeah, it is very irritating how zombies command grab you from a distance as bullets barely have an effect on them while your character doesn't seems to understand the concept of dodging, but at least the game is built around that and expects you mitigate these situations. 

[h1]It isn't long before the near immortal Tyrant rears it's literal ugly head to chase and kill you[/h1]

[b]A tall, grey, lumbering muscular man-like experiment gone wrong (or possibly right) with the inexplicable ability to always find you and attempt to punch and grab you to death.[/b] Also known as Mr. X, this monster is strange - a tall beast with heavy footsteps, that isn't fast enough to run, but walks fast enough to catch up to you only by walking while Leon and Claire runs at full speed (though, for some reason, they don't understand the concept of sprinting either). He can't be killed, and can only be slowed down by wasting plenty of precious ammo to stun him for what seems like one or two minutes at best. Mr X is the ever looming threat as you make gradual progress through the station, forcing you to think on the fly as you back track, shoot him down, or take an new unfamiliar pathway. RE2R would be quite easy for many seasoned gamers if it wasn't for this semi-random threat.

[h1]The best part of the mainline games is properly maintaining your ammo and inventory, learning when to shoot and when to evade, and when to pick up an item or leave it for later.[/h1] Maybe you don't need that healing item if you could survive better. Maybe you can skip that room with ammo, gunpowder, or grenade to avoid enemies so you can more quickly make it to the next progress point. It feels good when you get to the midway point and near end point of a run and have more than enough ammo and gear to deal with the remaining threats or just straight up heal yourself through it. Because the zombie gameplay in RE2R feels a bit cheap sometimes, killing zombies doesn't feel quite as satisfying as it did in Resident Evil 1 or 4, unless you use explosives or get a random critical headshot. Even with the cheat weapons that have unlimited ammo, shooting a zombie in the face with 10+ minigun bullets will still not be enough to kill them sometimes. 

[h1]Resident Evil 2 Remake is a solid return to survival horror form, and looks good doing so.[/h1]
It challenged my gaming PC and made me upgrade it to get playable framerates. Mods make it look too, with professional looking weapon and player skins. I'm not very fast at these games, so [b]it took me about 8-10 hours per run (a first and second run for both characters).[/b] The extra modes were terrible in my opinion, taking a game about managing your ammo and dodging enemies and instead forcing you into tight corridors with nowhere to move, little ammo, and annoying gimmicks. I didn't finish a single one of them and I don't want to go back.

[h1]Despite my misgivings, RE2R, makes a high spot in my RE Tier list, though still don't exceed RE4 and 1 for me. If you want more survival horror, Resident Evil 2 Remake gives it to you[/h1]

Resident Evil 2 is a remake of a classic survival horror game from 1998, but fully remade and released in 2019.  It’s changed from the fixed camera angles of the original to a third-person view which is more familiar to players of Resident Evil 4 and beyond. 

As a remake, Resident Evil 2 had a massive legacy to live up to.  Resident Evil 2 was quite beloved, and the fact is, the remake has captured much of the classic design and style while still creating an improved experience for players.  

The story in Resident Evil 2 is similar to the original.  Claire Redfield and Leon Kennedy arrive at the police station in Racoon City and must try to find out what’s happened and escape with their lives.  Players can choose either character to start with, and both characters will have a slightly different path through the police station, though mostly it’s due to a different key being available to Claire and Leon as well as which secondary character they meet. 

The combat has also been improved, with the third person over the shoulder view being preferable to the strange fixed cameras of the original game, and the less said about the tank controls of the original game the better.  

However, the combat in Resident Evil 2 is not what players might expect.  Zombies are aggressive and players have limited resources to engage enemies.  I found on my first playthrough with Leon where I tried to shoot zombies I needed to get out of the way in the head, I was quickly running out of supplies.  

This creates a more tense situation, but after checking online I found that the better solution was to shoot zombies in the leg.  On the second playthrough with Claire, shooting zombies in the leg, and I was suddenly swimming in ammo by the end of that playthrough.  This is something that bothers me though because it feels wrong to not teach players the right way to play your game.  

If the designers wanted the leg to be a better spot to hit, that is fine.  However, correcting the players' misconceptions is important.  Shooting zombies in the head is a pretty universal trope, feels like the game designers were purposefully hiding something that could have been shared.  Or perhaps the leg takedowns are an unintended benefit.  

Much of Resident Evil 2 is about traversing the map and trying to solve small puzzles while dealing with the horde of zombies, and in this Resident Evil 2 does well.  The tension of the mounting horde is great, and the enemies who harass the player both feel dangerous, and manageable at different times, and players get the feeling there is danger around any corner because there usually is. 

The bosses too are great, even if it’s mostly the same enemy attacking the player over and over.  The feeling of a growing power differential between the player and the boss as it grows and becomes overwhelming is incredible and it’s a highlight of the entire game. 

One of the best parts of the original Resident Evil 2 was the ability to replay the game and see the same story with the other player.  This is possible in Resident Evil 2’s remake, however, I find this to be the big problem with Resident Evil 2.  I played as Leon the first time through and experienced the game as it was meant to be.  I was quite excited to play through the game a second time as Claire and see what has changed. 

The fact is, not much has changed in the second playthrough.  Claire entered through a different door, and there was a small amount of content to get to that door.  As mentioned the Claire and Leon have different keys so there’s approximately ten percent of the game that Claire sees that Leon won’t, and visa versa. 

The problem is for much of the rest of the game, Claire goes through very similar motions as if she was playing through the main story.  Claire has to open the same doors she would and fight the same bosses. 

Claire and Leon fight the same three of the same bosses in the same arenas.  While both characters have different weapons, it’s not a big enough change to make it a different experience.  Both characters do have a fourth boss that is unique to their playthrough and there is a final boss, at the end of the second playthrough, but having to fight the same bosses, characters, and enemy on a second playthrough doesn’t make for a better experience. 

What’s worse is that Claire and Leon rarely cross over.  I believe they only have three scenes where they can even see each other, and that limited amount of connection is made even weirder at the end of the adventure where they look at each other like they have made a connection.  Granted they both survived through horrible circumstances, but the way the playthroughs are set up and the limited time that our characters have spent together really make this a strange system.

And I realize that Claire and Leon were both playable in the original game, but in 2019, I would expect this to be improved.  Imagine if Claire saw some sign of Leon or Leon saw signs of Claire as they progressed through the game.  If the second playthrough had some moments where players would remember what happened on their first playthrough, or puzzles that had already been solved instead of made harder, players might have thought fondly of their original time. 

Instead, the second playthrough gimmick feels like a weak experience when it should have been one of the strongest parts of the game. 

Ultimately Resident Evil 2 is a great game.  It reminds people why this series was thought of as the very best in survival horror.  It’s a perfect example of how to remake a game and please both fans and new players, something that other games struggle with

Though I do think that Resident Evil 7 is my favorite game in the series so far, but Resident Evil 2 is solid, if flawed. 

On my arbitrary scale of arbitrariness, I’ll give this game a 

7/10  

It’s solid, but the second playthrough dulled the excitement of the first playthrough.  I felt like I was experiencing the game on a slightly different difficulty, not seeing a second story.  And I even found the second playthrough a bit easier at some points.

RE2 is truly a mixed bag of both really great and really terrible attributes, but one that overall manages to craft a solid and fun survival horror experience. 
The game takes place in the fictional Raccoon City after a zombie outbreak where players take control of both Leon and Claire who are tasked with escaping the city, finding out what happened, and rescuing any survivors. Overall, the story is GARBAGE! Granted, I don't blame the makers of this game too much as they obviously are remaking a game and thus are very restricted here, but still the narrative here is just terrible. Leon is an idiot for most of the campaign, there are far too many clashes of seriousness with cartoonishness, and there is virtually no character development. Every character seems to react to these events in stride, and have no lasting effects on their psyche. As a result every character just feels out of place and immersion shattering. Also, the second run has more plot holes than zombies in the game, witch is saying something! You often have to repeat certain events in this second playthrough that you already completed the first time around, even though it makes no sense, the same puzzles, the same enemies, and the same characters showing up even if their fates were solidified on the concurrently running first playthrough. It all just feels lazy, as in order to get the "true" ending you basically have to play the same game twice with a few minor gameplay differences. 
Luckily, the gameplay more than makes up for the story. Combat is some of the best I've seen in a survival horror game since Dead Space. Ammo is scarce, but there's usually enough to kill enemies and provide constant tension of resource management. Zombies move really well and interact with their surroundings in cool ways, like tripping over dead bodies and such. The shooting mechanics work well too, as they feel challenging, but not frustrating and clunky. Tyrant sequences also provide a much needed pacing uptick to the game and and help up the scares. The puzzles are also really well done. This is partly because there aren't too many puzzles per say as there are obstacles to progress, like doors that need to be unlocked (fairly inexplicably) or items that need to be acquired, but if you progress through the game it just kind of opens itself up to you as you often remember where you can use certain tools and keys and even if you don't the map will remind you. Resources are scarce but manageable as well, really balancing the tension well.
Graphically this game is very good looking, as both the environments and characters (with the exception of Claire's teeth) are really well designed an textured. The game also has a ton of well calibrated settings that help you get the most out of your PC's performance. Lighting is fantastic and atmospheric as well.
Sound is more of a mixed bag. On one hand, the zombies and FX sound great and spooky, Tyrant's footsteps are especially great as you can hear him in the building hunting you and it really adds to the tension. Music is solid too, although not memorable outside of the Tyrant sections. Voice acting on the other hand is pretty bad here. Granted, the material is terrible but Leon, Ada, and Sherry all stand out as being terrible on this end and really prevent you from immersing yourself in the game. Claire is serviceable and probably the only decent actor in the game, but she's not even particularly great either.
Technically, the RE Engine is really good, I can't think of a single glitch I experienced during the game and the only issue I encountered were texture pop ins when I examined some objects up close.
Once again, the gameplay more than makes up for the terrible story, and while it may not be a great game overall, it is a good game with a decent amount of replayability, making it worth the price tag IMO.

I remember being sceptical about this game but my friend told me that I have to buy assuring me that I am going to love it. Knowing that we both have similar taste I figured it must be good, and is it any good? No it's not good...IT'S AMAZING! Honestly this must be the best remake I have ever played! It sets a completely new standard for all remakes in my opinion! The gameplay, graphics, animations, sound, music, game mechanics and that horrible (in a positive way) atmosphere. I think it has everything what all Resident Evil fans want (old and new) and those unfamiliar with the franchise but like playing horror games. Naturally the gameplay has been updated to meet today's standards, yet not completely. It still keeps the essential things from the 90s like inventory management, backtracking, learning parts of the story from notes, etc. Your main characters to play are Leon and Claire, but depending on which one you pick, you follow parallel to path to the other protagonist, meaning that some areas will be accessed only by Leon or Claire as they are split for almost the entire game (only cross paths during cut-scenes or when one caught up the the other for a short time. So you are on your own which helps in building up that horrible atmosphere. Also add to it a limited amount of ammo and health regeneration items you can carry and you're almost ready to crap your pants. Almost, as there is something more which I am going to mention later.
Ok, so how does the game look? It looks brilliant! The shadows, lights, textures, rain, wet textures, particles, the way everything moves is just amazing! There's one extra thing with zombie's animations, basically when you are far from them they seem to have this clunky, stop-motion like animations. Some people say it's a technical problem of the game's engine but I always thought this was intentional - a small wink to the old horror movies. Sound design is truly great, all the zombie sounds, jump scares and the music, all this helps to make you feel uneasy and wanna look over your shoulder. 
Time to mention the worse thing. A Tyrant called Mr. X. He or rather "it" is a real nightmare! imagine something like Arnold Schwarzenegger's T-800 from The Terminator movie looking for you. He can't be bargained with, he can't be reasoned with and will not stop, ever, until you are dead! Literally! The scariest thing about it is that Mr X is not scripted (apart from maybe 3 instances), he randomly walks around the entire area looking for you. It's also worth mentioning that it listens to the surroundings as well so if you make a lot of noise (for instance shooting a gun) expect it to show up in few moments. And you cannot kill it, only stun for approx 20 seconds but it's not worth it as it takes a lot of ammo to do it, so it's just better tot run away! Honestly it creates such a disturbing feeling as you constantly are watching your back and those footsteps when it approaches! Generally Mr. X is probably the best of the worse things in this game and that's really a huge positive because you are meant to feel that way!
To sum up, RE2make is a great game in general and truly the best remake to date. Not only with regards to the series but every game and I'm glad it proves that you can still remake a classic from the scratch instead of remastering it and still make it great. Well done Capcom!

This was the first Resident Evil game that I played and I have to say I was impressed. Graphics are excellent, production quality is very high, audio was strong, I didn't encounter any bugs and it supports modding. The game was a mix of problem solving and 3rd person shooting, which came as a bit of a surprise since I thought the RE games were more action oriented. That's not meant as a bad thing though. 

The only thing I didn't enjoy is a couple of the boss fights where you can't beat them, but just have to run around them VERY slowly while staying out of arm's reach on a tiny platform.

The campaign took about 7-8 hours to complete on the first run through but they cleverly encourage replays. Depending on whether you opt to play Claire or Leon, the story differs somewhat - quite substantially in the middle - and you meet different characters, get different cut scenes, etc. Once you complete the campaign for each character you get a second run with the opposite camera. The second run speeds through the first section of the game and then offers different puzzles, extra boss fights, and different endings. It creates a nice mixture of familiar (subsequent games took 3.5-4.5 hours to complete) with enough difference to make the replay worthwhile, occasionally using tricks to throw you off the expected path. It's a smart way to reuse locations but offer different challenges. There's easily 20-25 hours of play value here.

So far I've completed the Leon 1st run, Claire 1st run and Claire 2nd run. There are two more new game modes as far as I understand but I'm a bit RE'd out now and will come back to those later.

I came to Resident Evil 2 Remake for the survival horror—and left questioning everything I thought I knew about myself. The game is a masterpiece: beautifully grotesque environments, tight third-person combat, and a pacing loop that keeps your adrenaline pumping. Navigating the RPD with Leon felt tense and cinematic, but also, weirdly… comforting? Maybe it’s the police uniform. Maybe it’s the lighting. Maybe it’s something deeper I shouldn’t unpack in a Steam review.

As the game progressed, I found myself obsessing over character animations, noticing the subtle swish of fabric physics on Claire’s shorts—or Leon’s tactical gear. I thought it was just good game design, until I realized I was Googling mods at 3AM, and stumbled down a rabbit hole that began with “jiggle physics” and ended with “why does this wolf femboy have better character development than some JRPG protagonists?” Let’s just say RE2 opened more doors than the ones with electronic keycards.

All jokes aside, Capcom's remake is top-tier horror, with surprisingly tight controls and an even tighter fan art community (you’ve been warned). If you're into tension, beautifully reimagined classics, and discovering furry femboy fox OCs named "ShadowPawXX" while looking for costume mods… this game might change your life. Or at least your browser history.

The Remake for Resident Evil 2 follows in the Footsteps of "Resident Evil Remake", that means not only have graphic received an overhaul but, items are in different locations, puzzles, enemies and items have received an overhaul, etc...
While changing the formula from a fixed angle view to an over the shoulder camera (similar to the one used in Resident Evil 4, 5 and 6), making the gameplay more accessible for new players.

Resident Evil 2 brings the story of the journey of Claire Redfield (A college Student looking for her brother) and Leon Scott Kennedy (A Rookie cop on his first day working at the RPD) through the Raccoon City Police Department (RPD) building and Umbrella NEST labs. The Player selects either Leon or Claire as their character each one having a side character on their own campaign (a mysterious woman named Ada Wong in Leon's Campaign or a little Girl named Sherry Birkin in Claire's Campaign).

Resident Evil 2 Remake is an excellent survival horror experience where story telling prevails above mindless action.

[h1] Intro [/h1]
Resident Evil 2 Remake is a survival horror 3rd person shooter game. It takes place in Racoon City, a city infested with zombies and destruction. You play as either Leon S. Kennedy (A rookie cop on his first day on the job) or Claire Redfield (A sister looking for her brother in the city). Your goal and the story's main point is to survive and escape from Raccoon City, all while surviving the hellish monsters and dangerous situations you'll be facing. The game is not for the faint of heart and is quite gory and creepy. If you are weak to horror games, I would suggest trying the demo first before purchasing it to see if you can handle it because It can definitely be scary and unnerving to play. If you're not a  Resident Evil fan, this game is an excellent franchise entry point for you, as you don't need to know the story of the previous game to enjoy this one.


[h1] Gameplay & Mechanics [/h1]
When you start the game, you get to choose to either play as Leon or Claire, these two characters get different weapons and have different personalities. You can pick whoever you prefer, as you can play the other character after you finish the game. You can play the other character in scenario B. Scenario B is basically what the other character goes through the game while you're doing Scenario A with the first character you played. Meaning you'll be going through the same areas again, but with some things happening differently, and having different encounters. So, you won't miss out on anything if you start with either character. However, you need to complete both scenarios to get the game's final ending so keep that in mind.

The gameplay and shooting mechanics in RE2R are fantastic and are definitely a significant improvement on the original. The shooting feels satisfying and tight for a third-person shooter. Blowing zombies heads with your pistol or shotgun is always enjoyable and never really gets old. In the game you'll be getting different various weapons to deal with the enemies you face. The game offers many ways of dealing with the zombies or enemies you face. Depending on the difficulty that you play on, ammo is very important. If you don't conserve your ammunition, then it'll be challenging to deal with the threats you face, so one of the ways the game offers you to deal with this, is by ignoring some of the zombies or enemies you encounter by going around them and avoiding them, this provides a lot of flexibility in the game where you don't have to kill everything to progress, and that's always a welcome addition in any game. You can also shoot the zombies in specific areas like their legs/kneecaps to dismember them and immobilize them to conserve ammo because sometimes killing these zombies takes a lot of bullets to get the job done, so immobilizing them is an excellent way the game offers you to get around this issue. The game also has many puzzles that you would need to solve or find items to unlock them. RE2R is also a Metroidvania type of game, meaning you have to backtrack to areas you've been before multiple times because you either found a key to a door you couldn't unlock before or to get a specific item from a previous area you visited. 

You'll also be facing various enemies that are not just human zombies. Enemies such as the lickers, zombie dogs, sewer monsters, etc. But the most critical and most menacing enemy you'll be facing is "Mr. X." He will be by far the scariest enemy you'll be facing. You'll have to deal with him constantly because he will be chasing you in a lot of parts of the game, and I can't tell you how distressing it is to hear his footsteps while you're exploring and knowing he's a room behind you and has almost caught up with you. It definitely puts you on the edge of your seat and fills you with thrill as you try to avoid him as much as you can. This element adds another layer of horror to this game and a great one at that.

You will also have a limited inventory system that you can upgrade by exploring areas and finding upgrade items to increase your inventory capacity, but before you do that you will find yourself in many situations where you have to sacrifice an item you have for more ammo or for a healing item that you found but don't have space for, so the item management system in this game is pretty important, and you'll have to learn to deal with it from early on in the game. Weapons similarly can be upgraded by finding upgrade items for them behind locked safes and puzzles. Make sure to explore the area thoroughly before moving on to the next area because if you miss out on these upgrade items, you won't be getting them again later in the game.

To conclude this section, the gameplay and mechanics of RE2R complement the game perfectly and is a major improvement on the original Resident Evil 2.


[h1] Graphics & Sound [/h1]
The graphics in RE2R are fantastic. The RE Engine is perfectly tailored for this game, and it shows. From the lighting to texture details and overall, the whole atmosphere it gives off for the game. It definitely makes the game very atmospheric because of the engine, and I think the graphics are fantastic for this type of game. I easily remember the game creeping me out at many moments because of how realistic and creepy it looked. The blood and gore look very realistic that you can't help but appreciate how good the graphics are in RE2R. I also want to point out that the game is really well optimized and runs quite well. The graphics customization settings are excellent and very customizable while also detailing what each graphic option does.

The sound design in RE2R is also fantastic. The sound design is very atmospheric and complements the graphics so well. From the zombie moans to door creaks, and window sill shutters opening and closing. Everything sound-wise is excellent in the game and definitely makes you feel fully immersed in the environment. Playing this game with the lights turned off, and with a headphone will definitely give you a very fulfilling and creepy experience.


 [h1] The Bad Parts [/h1]
Now, my only critique about Resident Evil 2 Remake is the scenario B part of the game. Capcom has sadly not worked much on the scenario B part because it pales compared to the original RE2. When you play with the other character in scenario B, it barely feels any different from scenario A. You basically go almost through the same areas and the same enemies, making it feel like an unfulfilling experience and pretty much the same experience you had in scenario A, making the whole thing feel pointless. Had they done it the same way that the original RE2 did it, then it would have been unique and felt completely different. Sadly, Capcom didn't put all their efforts into this part of the game and just focused on scenario A only. I also found the boss battles in this game to be quite disappointing. They aren't challenging and are quite forgettable and easy to beat. I think Capcom should have put more emphasis on the boss battles and made them more enjoyable and memorable. Because as they are right now, they definitely are one of the worst parts of this game.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
All in all, RE2R is a fantastic game. I thoroughly enjoyed it and had many memorable moments in it. I easily recommend this game, especially if you're into survival horror games, and even if you're not, this game is still worth trying out because it might be something you'll enjoy. It's an unmissable experience, in my opinion, and is one of the best games that came out in 2019. It's also a fantastic remake that improved on the original in many ways; this is how remakes should be handled and made.

Resident Evil 2 when it came out back in 1998 was considered one of the best survival horror games of its time and 21 years later the best got better with the release of Resident Evil 2 Remake. RE2R took what made the original what it was and brought it into a new generation resulting in a game that is not only faithful to the original but adds things that expand and better the gameplay and story.

The story follows Rookie Cop Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield as they try to escape Raccoon City amid a zombie outbreak. You can play through each characters story in any order you like with a New Game + option to continue the story from the other characters point of view. This Remake also adds new side stories that you can play apart from the main campaign. The new map feature that shows you what items you're missing and where they are located keeps you wanting to explore the map and the quick inventory first seen in RE7 help keep the game moving at a quick pace. 

Resident Evil 2 Introduced the Tyrant also known as Mr. X and he is here with a vengeance in the Remake. A great enemy that knows where you are at all times and is always tracking you throughout the RPD Station. Mr. X mixed with the zombie outbreak and other enemies you will find throughout your playtime help to create a great tension and atmosphere to this game that helps it hold its title of one of the best survival horror games around. 

If you are a fan of the Resident Evil series or have played the original back in the day then you have already bought this but if you are new to the series or love Survival Horror games, the original was up there with Silent Hill 2 and is even better now with all the updates and features that were added to this game. Resident Evil has become a divisive series these days with the newer games being more action oriented but RE2R bring the series back to its roots of survival horror with limited ammo and health items.  It's about as perfect a remake you can get and nails all the things you would have wanted out of RE2 in 2019.

I was given the original release of Resident Evil 2 on my birthday as a gift back in the 90's.  I proceeded to install it on my trusty Pentium 3 PC. It's the quietness of hearing nothing but the eerie silence except for your own foot steps, then suddenly a loud crash as a zombie breaks through the window your are walking past.  I couldn't count the times I jumped out of my chair playing this game.  Even today, with all of the zombie genre games (which Resident Evil started) and copycats, there's not many like this series that are as good.  

This modern remake is absolutely worthy of the series and does great justice to the original.  As far as I can tell, it's stayed true to the original in just about every way.  The new graphics are stunning, the story line is just as great the suspense is just as gripping and the puzzles are just as satisfying.  I really feel alive playing this game.  I don't feel like I'm looking at a screen playing a game, I feel like I really am walking through Raccoon City Police Department trying to figure out the answers to the intriguing mysteries.  I am so happy I bought this game.  It brings back so many fond memories and I'm having so much fun experiencing the game again as an adult.  Thank you Capcom, you did good here.

+ Great visuals & lighting coupled with amazing level design. I heard that this remake changed little to nothing from the original's map & locations, which is even more amazing that everything still holds up decades later, only now with jaw-dropping visual updates.
