I’m glad it’s now all but universally accepted that “classic” [i]Resident Evil[/i] gameplay is kind of ♥♥♥♥. The best games in the series, [i]4[/i] and [i]7[/i], were the ones that reinvented the formula, and now with this remake, [i]2[/i] can join them, possibly at the very top. That’s not to say it completely abandons its roots – it’s still about escalating dread and resource management – but it no longer needs to use artificial movement and saving restrictions as a horror crutch. Instead, the presentation is gruesome and claustrophobic, jump scares (both natural and scripted) are skillfully executed, and there are multiple features that exist solely to prevent players from ever feeling truly safe.

The vital ingredient here is that even if this wasn’t a horror game, it would still be entertaining. There are no incidental enemy encounters; even the basic zombies have complex and organic behaviours and interactions. Furthermore, as nonsensical as the puzzles may be, they’re never annoying. There was a cost to all of this enhancement, however. The remake omits several enemy types and the beloved interweaving of its two campaigns. The narrative also largely failed to modernize; its plot and writing are serviceable, but its premise is distractingly stupid even by series standards. Finally, the music and sound effects are great, as is the voice acting…for everyone except the protagonists, strangely.

After years of waiting for a remake of Resident Evil 2 Capcom have finally delivered, so let's see if a classic can hold up in the modern era of remakes

PROS:
-Modern 3rd person movement controls
-RE7 inventory management
-Mr. X is terrifying
-Intense and spooky atmosphere
-Cool and upgradeable guns
-Beautiful graphics
-Tofu mode

CONS:
-Mr. X can get annoying after a while
-Story's a little on the campy side
-Zombie grabs can be a little inconsistent
-Healing items can only be used while they're in your inventory

As someone who has never played the original resident evil games Resident Evil 2's remake is solidly well made, the combination of a 3rd person viewpoint and inventory system taken from Resident Evil 7 makes for a fairly intuitive design that still manages to keep the tension high, just sitting at the box and debating what to take with me while I run around RPD really improved the experience especially when I ran out of ammo. This would've  made for a fine enough experience on it's own but part way in the game throws Mr. X at you and this guy is nothing to sneeze at, he eats your precious MAG rounds for breakfast and even when he does go down he's not dead, just stunned, forcing you to run from him on most occasions rather than taking him out which I think adds to the experience. Speaking of MAG ammo let's talk weapons, all of the base weapons you find throughout the game can be upgraded with parts you find behind puzzles or locks which range from fairly easy to kinda difficult, but most of these upgrades help increase the effectiveness of your arsenal and makes them look cooler as a side bonus. All of what I just mentioned wouldn't look nearly as good without the modern graphics and damn does this game look good, from the lighting to the characters and their guns this game nailed the graphics, there's something awe-inspiring and terrifying about seeing a licker rendered in full HD for the first time.

With all that I've said this game does have a couple of issues, for starters, Mr. X, while he is a terrifying relentless terminator, on subsequent playthroughs he tends to be more of an annoyance you have to work around rather than a serious threat, I think I spent more time huddled in the safe room waiting for him to pass than I did actually running away from him which makes him less scary once you understand how he works. On the opposite end of the spectrum the zombies seem a bit more unpredictable in their behavior, while the lurching to avoid my headshot is a good addition getting grabbed even though I'm clearly outrunning the zombie that's grabbing isn't, and it ends up becoming annoying when it happens seemingly at random, this becomes more of a problem due to the fact that you can't use healing items until they're in your inventory, granted this is a minor nitpick but I still find it annoying that I can't just pick up a healing spray off the shelf and use it, I have to pick it up, put it in my backpack and then use it, while this was probably intentional to provide a greater focus on inventory management it's still annoying. Taking a break from gameplay the story is a bit campy in my opinion, I know that historically Resident Evil plots aren't really known to be serious 100% of the time but here the occasional wisecrack just feels out of place, not to mention there's one character in particular who has 4-5 different death scenes which kind of ruins the experience when I'm hearing her death rattle for the umtheenth time.

Still despite my nitpicks if you like horror games or are a fan of Resident Evil I'd still recommend this game for the gameplay alone, there are a couple of decent scares and the gameplay alone I think is worth the money.

[list]
[*] Terrific map design and environments, with unique and memorable areas.
[*] Wonderful sound design that adds a TON of atmosphere in every single aspects. From the door squeak, footsteps, to the ambience and music in every sequences and areas. It is recommended that you play with surround headset
[*] Great story progression and character developments in the span of 8 hours 
[*] Great character design from the main characters, zombies, and bosses. Zombies and Mr. X's AI are great in adding tension and element of surprise in an already scary areas.
[*] Wonderful inventory and weapon systems that forces player to be creative and efficient in managing their inventory
[*] Great item/ammo placements. It gives the nuance of survival as items could feel scarce at times but at the same times, it always gives you something to get by.
[*] Technically speaking, the game runs flawlessly and gorgeously as a result of RE Engine wonderful photorealistic system. The difference between low settings and high settings are barely noticeable as both looked wonderful. 
[/list]

However, there are some things that isn't so great........like;
[list]
[*] The parallel stories system which gives a disconnected feeling between Leon and Claire story. As if both exists in a different dimensions because they only meet in the beginning and at the very end with no explanation on how they could solve the same puzzles in the same area and fighting the same boss without ever run into one another. However....

[*] Processor intensive engine causes frequents stutter in certain areas and freezes in-between areas. 
[*] Reduced contrast and desaturated graphics which isn't too big of a deal at first glance but once you apply a Reshade and FX mods, you'll see the huge difference in how a slight adjustments could hugely increases the visual experiences.

Resident Evil 2 Remake hits the same beats as the original but focuses on making the game more accessible to “modern” audiences, attempts to make the world a touch more believable and creates a dark atmosphere to traverse while trying to escape Raccoon City. 

	The biggest concern I had when this game was announced was the third person camera angles that would replace the original and notorious “fixed” camera angles that allowed the original three Resident Evil titles to bring fear to your screen and add tension. The remake manages to give players a strong sense of control by framing itself in third person but enemy placement, sound design and the map itself can still make your first play through a tense experience. The first time you turn a corner and look into a dark corridor illuminated only by your flashlight with every step made by your character emitting a wet footstep through the damp hallway the player will understand what type of game they are about to play; either finding themselves smile at the dark-design of the RPD’s interior or nervous to turn each corner.

	The Length of the game may be on the short side but that’s assuming your only goal is to beat the game and see it’s story play out once. Having two protagonist to choose from; both with different routes and items in each of their stories and a “Scenario B” included that alters the puzzle solutions and has the character start in a different area changing the route, grants players the opportunity to enjoy the game multiple times. Also many bonus modes are unlocked as you play the game and replaying in hopes of completing with a faster completion time is always a welcome challenge. 

	I highly recommend this title. I’ve purchased it on two different platforms and both times enjoyed collecting the items, getting all the trophies and trying to finish with a smaller completion time. Easily my favorite game released in 2019.

I beat [i]Resident Evil 2[/i] about half a year ago, but I got a little bored and set it aside for a while, maybe it just wasn’t the right moment. If I had written a review back then, I probably would have given it a lower score. But games aren’t movies; to get a true and complete impression, you need to invest time and explore the gameplay and its hidden mechanics.

The police station is by far the best and most enjoyable part of the game, offering plenty of options for dealing with zombies that bite really hard and escaping the relentless, Terminator-like pursuer. The sewers and the lab are fine but not particularly memorable, while the orphanage is an interesting and well-detailed location—I just wish I could have spent more time there.

Zombies feel relevant again, unpredictable, and genuinely dangerous. Capcom did an incredible job depicting the degeneration and destruction of human bodies. Visually, [i]RE2[/i] is stunning, I love the blue color palette, and the character design is phenomenal. That said, I didn’t really get the sense that the game was set in the late 1990s. The weapon design is fantastic as well, and I particularly enjoyed the Colt Single Action Army revolver—it was a lot of fun to use. Too bad there’s no spaghetti western poncho costume to go with it.

As I mentioned, the game gives players many choices, from melee weapons to a variety of firearms, along with the need to carefully plan routes or avoid close-range zombie bites. Still, I missed having a block or dodge button, which I think would have improved the boss fights. Speaking of which, lickers are the most ruthless and brutal enemies in the game. The bosses, on the other hand, are mediocre and sometimes frustrating, though it’s cool that they can be tricked or cheesed.

My biggest complaint is with the AB scenarios, they’re far too similar (almost identical) and narratively inconsistent. Instead of four campaigns, we essentially get one and a half.

I enjoyed [i]RE2[/i], it’s a great game, but I also find it a bit overrated. Interestingly, I personally think [i]RE7[/i] is the better game, even though I was hoping for something like [i]RE2[/i] when [i]RE7[/i] was first announced. Perhaps it’s because [i]RE7[/i] feels a bit fresher, whereas [i]RE2[/i] gives off a "been there, done that" vibe.

Rating: ★★★★☆

(Very good remake, even if I don't like all the changes)

============

Review:

I am quite critical about this game, because I have nostalgia for the original PS1 version of Resident Evil 2.

So I say this in advance - I think the remake is a very good game, even if my review might sound negative.

I recently played the original resident evil 2 so I could compare it and the remake on actual data instead of nostalgic memories.

============

Graphically the game is absolutely beautiful - everything looks really good. All the characters, monsters and areas are detailed. Lighting and shadows are also superb - I can't complain about anything, it just looks good.

The sounds.. again, very good. All the zombie moans, monster screams and environmental sounds like wind, cracking walls, banging windows are great and create atmosphere well.

The voice actors are actually good, which is a nice change since they tend to be on the bad side in RE games.

But the music.. that's a downgrade. The music is a lot more subtle or even non-existent - most of the time you probably won't even notice it. (Unless the Tyrant is in the same room)

Now this kind of works in the favor of the game, because you can hear the zombie moans and environmental sounds better when there's little music to distract you.

But still, I prefer the original game's music, because it boosts the atmosphere of the game, and creates a feeling of dread and suspense. And also basically tells you when you're in a safe room, something that's typical for the old RE games.

The thing is.. you CAN use the original music in the remake, but you have PAY for it. That's a kind of.. greedy and lame decision.

============

Well, what about the things I don't like?

Tyrant for one. Or Mr. X, however you want to call him.

Some people love him, some people hate him. I'm one of the latter ones.

He is scary the first time you play the game, yes I agree on that. But after you play the game again, try different character / scenario.. then he just becomes an annoyance. Like a speed bump, it's just not fun.

I very much prefer how he was in the original Resident Evil 2 - you had to face him several times before you could kill him,
but you could disable him every time. And you got bullets back if you did shoot him instead of just ran.

I really liked that - because the game gave you a choice - you could fight or run. And it wasn't just a waste of ammo if you chose to fight.

In the remake, shooting him is literally just a waste of ammo, because he will just get up in 20 seconds and continue like nothing happened.

The original game also had more areas than the remake - so some places were just cut. And the sewer area of the original is vastly superior - It's tedious in the remake, at least on your first run it can get confusing.

And well.. I know I'm in the minority here, but I'd actually prefer those fixed camera angles and tank controls over this. So it would work like Resident Evil Remastered - it would be more nostalgic for those that have played the original game.

This should be like an option or a DLC where you could switch the control scheme.

============

But yes, despite the obvious upgrades, I am slightly disappointed at the remake.

It is essentially a hybrid Resident Evil game that tries to please all RE fans in some way - but when you do it this way, no one is perfectly happy with it. (Well ok, maybe someone is..)

For the old survival horror fans it brings nostalgia in the form of areas, puzzles and inventory management, but that's about it.

For the fans of the action parts of the series it gives all them "shoot it in the eye" monsters, and similar controls for targeting and movement.

I have played nearly every RE game and I can see why they made these design decisions, but I still would have preferred it if they made the remake of RE 2 similar as the remaster of the first game.

============

But yes, overall it's a very good game, even if I'm personally a bit disappointed.

This is something you have to experience - at least once.

So I recommend you to get it from a sale, and play it slowly on your first run - exploring your surroundings thoroughly and getting immersed in the spooky setting.

============

Summary:

The Good 👍
+ Looks absolutely beautiful
+ Immersive sounds
+ Actually good voice actors
+ It still feels like Resident Evil 2
+ Good replayability, like the original.

The Bad  👎
- Doesn't give you a choice on how to deal with Tyrant
- Less areas than the original
- Non-existent music (and have to pay for the original music)

The graphics and game play are outstanding.  Intuitive player controls make playing with a mouse/key board or gaming controller a delight.  Great use of music and ambient sound to add shock value to most situations.

Pros:
-The game is a different horror experience than the original RE2, so older fans can appreciate this new take on the story.
-The game sounds AMAZING! The sound design (especially for the enemies) sends chills down your spine when you don't expect it. Highly recommend playing with headphones. 
-The voice actors did an excellent job making Leon and Claire sound very natural. 
-Looks great, love the small details scattered throughout each location.
-Loads of replay value

Cons:
-Again, this is a different take on RE2. I have played the original and I can see what the original did better versus what the remake did better. It isn't like REmake where it takes the original and makes EVERYTHING better about it. If you love the original RE2, definitely play this. If you love the new RE2, play the original when you're done.

-Riffing off my first point, the original had a more cohesive A/B scenario story. In this game, there are small plot holes left in because it does not commit to a true A/B scenario system like the original. If you are really into the story of the game,  it gets a little messy if you are figuring out how Leon's and Claire's story fit together at some parts. The boss fights also have this issue when moving from different scenarios. 

-The music in the original game was incredible, I recommend buying the original soundtrack swap and playing this RE2 with the new music. The score in the base game is alright but the original game's soundtrack boasts more tension.

Many reviews really focus on the fact that RE2 isn't like the original, but having played both games, it's completely okay. I see more of the things they changed be replaced with something just as good or even better. I feel like this was the biggest blunder for this remake, but if you can take that issue away, both scenarios are a solid experience. 

TL;DR
HIGHLY RECOMMEND, amazing game, loads of replay value, modern take on the original, buy the original soundtrack and play the game with headphones. Don't get so caught up with who to play first, but I loved ClaireA/LeonB ;)

My relationship to the RE franchise is small but substantial.  Up until the remake, I'd only played 3 of the mainline games (2, 4, 7) to completion.  I have fond memories of the experience with Resident Evil 2 for the PS1 and I won't lie, it almost certainly colored my opinions of this remake...not always for the positive.  But I will say right off the bat it IS a good game.  A VERY good game in fact.  It updates the experience for modern times while using design decisions that allow it to still retain the tense survival horror aspect of the original.

The first noticeable change for me was the update to a WASD control setup as from RE7, where the players were now given the full range of movement.  This was a decision I had wanted since RE4, and a contentious one in the fandom.  In both RE7 and here, Capcom have proven to have made the right decision in bucking against the expectations of the faithful!  Turns out the freedom of movement in this remake does little to detract from the survival horror atmosphere of the original.  Your character is still slow as molasses, so the new range of movement doesn't so much 'break' the game as it allows you more moment-to-moment options to deal with an immediate threat.  The aiming is also much more responsive, which is necessary as the majority of enemies are designed around precision aiming of specific 'weak spots'.  One of the few exceptions to this is also one of the most common.

The zombie plays by completely different rules from normal expectations.  Their damage intake is determined by a very wide RNG.  Getting them to the ground can take half a clip, but it you can end up spending an ENTIRE additional clip KEEPING them there...or you could get lucky and land an RNG crit on their head that blows it apart in one shot!  It's all random and leads to strategies of staggering them so you can run past or chopping off a leg with a combat knife attack when their on the ground or other means of managing them rather than standing in one place trying to kill them outright.

This leads to the main criticism I have with the new game.  Like the original, the zombies are the first-encounter enemies that front load the first part of the game: The Police Station and it is this part of the game that's the most engaging...and conversely, the rest of the game the least.  The Police Station makes up 1/3 of a playthrough in structure, with the rest being largely taken up by the Sewers and the Underground Lab, but a good 1/2 of the playthrough in practice.  This is because the remaining areas are smaller, and much more linear.

The sewers pretend at complexity with an obtuse level design that only hinders and frustrates as you wander around collecting chess pieces for a plot-door.  The labs meanwhile are compacted into three segregated sections that offers a few more moments for exploration, but still pales in comparison to the beginning hours of the game.

This is only exacerbated by the campaign structure of the game.  RE2 as a singular experience is incredibly short, easily being completed in less than five hours.  This is intentional as it initially offers two separate campaigns and then an additional two campaigns upon completion, all intended to offer different spins upon the same story...except it doesn't.  Once again, it's the Police Station that receives the most attention in these alternate playthroughs, with the sewers being almost completely unchanged and the lab changing things up only slightly in comparison.

The original alleviated this issue through item placement and inventory space.  Necessary items would often be scattered all around the environment, leading to much more backtracking and general exploration, while an initial inventory space of only six slots (with one upgrade to eight) required much stricter inventory discipline and would lead to extraneous items having to be left behind to be risked being picked up later or simply ignored.  In short, the original simply forced you to stick around the environments a lot longer, making them feel more memorable than they may otherwise have been.

While overall, the remake's decision to streamline these processes makes for a more enjoyable experience, it also makes the experience feel brief and light.  The lack of substantive changes among the later half of the alternate campaigns makes it feel somewhat repetitive.  Thankfully, there are a slew of alternate side experiences included, which I have yet to indulge in that may make up for the loss.

That being said, I'd say this game - outside of its heritage - is still a damned fine game and worth picking up for those who want a fun and faithful Resident Evil experience.  Maybe wait for a sale as the main meat of the campaigns might feel a little light compared to a full priced experience.

From the utter disappointments by Capcom over the start of the '10s, it was highly speculated the idea of remake of such a legendary classic would be trash too; contrary to popular belief however, Capcom remade this game the way it should be: scary.
Resident Evil 2 Remake follows a very close storyline to the original, therefore keeping its roots intact as a survival horror. Technological advancements have made amplified the horror factor to a notch, notably the gore that you previously saw as pixelated blood. The gameplay has been tweaked from the original to keep with the current style of playing (although its very possible to mod the game and bring the 'Tank-style controls' and the older camera perspective back); some elements, both from gameplay and story have been altered for increased realism. Story itself is a masterpiece, and you can feel more in-depth character of basically anyone you come across, including the player character you're controlling. The utilization and upgrading of RE Engine is spectacular, and is a huge leap from its predecessor, therefore you can enjoy the acute lighting you require to traverse through dark areas and basically keep yourself not being eaten alive by zombies. The enemy AI is where the jewel of the crown is for this game, to be precise. Gone are the days when you may seek refuge from enemy through getting to a door and pressing action key; be it a zombie or panic-inducing Mr. X; you cannot hide! (bless the developers for Safe Rooms like in the predecessor however!) That alone makes your blood pump faster and make quick decisions... some of which can be really fatal. Last but not the least, voice acting. As much as I miss the original's cheesy voice acting, this is where I felt it could've been better in the remake. While of course, the newer voices fit the characters better, but there is something from the original which I personally can't miss with the VA.

To sum it up, this felt exactly like how it was in 2001 (when my Dad got a PS1 copy of the game), except a lot more gore-y and HD. Whether you like the series or not, I'm sure you will not be disappointed with this one. Also, Rest in Peace, Paul Haddad.

[h1]A masterful reenactment of an all-time classic, Resident Evil 2 Remake is everything horror gaming has ever got right.[/h1]

Ah, who hasn’t played Resident Evil in our childhood? Who doesn’t remember walking the hallways of the Raccoon City Police Department, searching for the myriad of items required to sort out a puzzle in order to move forward all the while mowing down zombies with our pistol and carefully avoiding the despicable cunning of lickers? Resident Evil 2 holds a special place in most of our hearts and rightly so: while the first installment paved the way for others to follow, it fell to 2 and 3 to truly carry the franchise onwards to worldwide fame. The sheer scope, the masterful execution and the incomparable horror -for a 90s game- earned it a place among the greatest games of all time.

Fast forward some twenty years and we have its remake, and boy… is it good…

For newcomers to the series: You play as either Leon S. Kennedy or Claire Redfield -the famed Chris’ sister- who, after being left stranded in the streets of a virus-riddled Raccoon City, make haste to the Raccoon City Police Station, where according to a radio transmission they should be able to find shelter and whatever remains of human survivors. Upon reaching the damned station they realise that virtually every single person inside has turned, leaving them trapped into a building which resembles more of a trap rather than a shelter. Their purpose? To flee the damned station and city. In the course of their travails they will fend off wave after wave of murderous zombies, sneak around cunning blind (yet deadly!) beasts known as lickers and evade the sinister and relentless pursuer that is the Tyrant.

The Tyrant (also known as “Mr. X”) is the game’s signature antagonist. True enough, being just a bio-organic weapon (B.O.W.), the Tyrant possesses no will of its own and thus cannot compare in sheer evil to the true wrongdoers that created the disease that turned the hapless city into the living hell that we see it to be during the events of the game, yet his cold, calculated hunt for you that will see him smash through walls, balk at nothing, not even a shot to the head in his quest to hunt you down. Its ominous presence is there for you to feel even when the beast is not around: all-too pervasive footsteps around the station serve as a grim reminder of his patrols of the premises (which actually serve as a sound cue to alert you as to where he might be) and you are never again quite at ease in the game after he shows up for the first time. His behaviour evokes that of the original Resident Evil 3’s Nemesis’, yet unlike the eponymous beast of the remarkably beautiful third installment of the franchise, this one won’t stay down, not even after soaking a hail of bullets. It stumbles to the floor, replenishes his health and gets back up, ready to resume his deadly hunt. 

The joy of reliving (or in my case finally being able to complete for the very first time) Leon S. Kennedy’s and Ada Wong’s story, of getting to see horror unleashed by the hands of William Birkin, of seeing the relentless tyrant in action, of helping poor Sherry out as Claire... all recast and molded into a fully-fledged 2019 game both in graphics, acting and mechanics. Who hasn’t dreamt of this moment? Of this beautiful reckoning that a mixture of the old and the new has borne? It achieves this perfect concoction by delivering the very best experience the Resident Evil universe has thus far offered us.

While the game draws on the nostalgia factor aplenty, it appeals to both old-timers and newcomers alike. Indeed, I have recommended this game even to those who have yet to try a Resident Evil game at all, for it goes beyond being a great title in the franchise, it is simply put one of the best horror games out there. You just can’t begin to grasp the sheer horror I felt when leaving behind the safety of the main hall of the RPD station to tread its dark hallways filled with the undead, nor the dystopical sense of nerve-racking despair that filled me upon setting foot on the eerily immaculate and ominous hallways of NEST. Resident Evil 2 manages to convey all along its remarkable ride this sense of wrongness, of things gone awry, of distorted normality that shakes us to the very core. Everything is there… yet it isn’t anymore. Zombies still don their clothes from days, perhaps merely hours, ago, former cops who joined the ranks of the infected still wear their caps and their badges as they lurch towards you to get a bite at you, and the sinister corridors of the underground lab all reek of an everyday life suddenly brought to a halt. Normality has been torn apart and we delve among a sea of shadows from a past that was lost barely hours ago.

Something worth mentioning: the game’s essentially divided between two main campaigns: you either play as Leon or Claire as the main character (who gets to experience the bulk of the game’s events) and then you should have a go at the so-called “2nd run” as the other character. The difference between this “2nd run” and starting a game all over as the other character is that the 2nd run actually follows the footsteps of the other character as he or she goes on to follow a parallel path to the one you happened to choose as your main, getting to explore other areas and solving other puzzles previously unavailable to your other character. To top it off, each character has a vastly different story, which the outcome of the story differing drastically depending on whichever you choose to play as. Do note that to see the complete, true ending of the game you [i]must[/i] play a first run and then complete its corresponding second run as the other character.

Then, there’s the Survivors mode, which neatly lets you play as other characters you came across during the campaign, in a neat twist of fate that would have prevented them from meeting an untimely death. Most of these scenarios delve in the challenge department and are not for the faint-hearted. They, however, serve as a neat experience for whenever we finish the game and are still itching for more. The 4th survivor mission, unlocked after a full campaign played from start to finish, honours the all-time favourite Umbrella operative HUNK and with him, the beloved Tofu Survivor makes a comeback!

Note: While I have dozens of hours played at the time of this review, do note that the game takes approximately 10 hours to finish (that being 6 hours of the main character’s campaign and some other 4 of the other character’s 2nd run). I have raked some more in my drive to hunt all the achievements and score a 100% on this one, which I only try and do on those games which I truly loved playing.

Thus, Resident Evil 2 Remake is a horror masterpiece and a game you should definitely play. Do yourself a favour and grab it whenever you can.

[h1] A REmake Done Right [/h1]

Capcom has made a game that has become the gold standard for remakes, while I do believe it’s overhyped and it’s not THE masterpiece some people claim, I think it’s a fantastic game none the less and something us fans were dreaming for a looong time, they nailed pretty much everything with this title.

The 1998 version was already an improvement over the first one, the game felt bigger and better finished back then when compared to RE 1. If you’re a fan of the originals like I am you’ll still find its essence here, this a classic Resident Evil experience, inventory management, typewriters, limited itens, puzzles, the atmosphere, all masterfully done. They managed to improve and expand an already fantastic game while keeping it’s roots untouched, I really appreciate what they have accomplished here.  The game looks and feels amazing, the characters, the gore, the textures, the lighting, everything makes you feel like you’re there, controls and camera are a HUGE improvement over the original. The gunplay and physics are great, I love the way bodies react to the environment and damage, the weapons feel like they actually have a stopping power, shooting zombies with a shotgun is a blast (no pun intended), the sounds could be better.

The story is pretty much the same with minor differences, there are two scenarios for each of the main characters , A and B, and they play out differently depending on which character you start as, to fully experience the game’s plot and get the “true ending” you’re supposed to play one character’s A scenario and the other’s B scenario, they kinda fit together. Having played the original I noticed that some storylines were changed and others were dropped completely, nothing crazy, most of them were for the better as they expanded the story, there are still some plot holes though . 

The characters and their relationships also changed, here I found them much more dramatic and coherent, some of the things they added to the plot gave them an extra layer of personality, the side-characters are very compelling and sometimes they steal the show, even getting their own chapter. You’ll meet different people depending on who you’re playing as.

The enemies types you’ll encounter are more or less the same as in the original, one of the  differences is that now they look much more terrifying, even the standard zombies are more menacing this time around, mainly because of the detail level they put in the models, there’s a decent variety and they behave more naturally. The bosses and the special enemies are very unsettling, specially the Tyrant, [spoiler] since you can’t kill him [/spoiler], hearing his footsteps approaching while he searches for you and you’re trying to get an objetive completed will sure get your anxiety levels through the roof. 

It’s not a difficult game but it can be challenging in some situations. People used to RE or survival horror in general will have no problem getting the hang of it and beating everything in their own pace, maybe even get an S rate. New players might take some time getting used it, because of some classical RE mechanics like I mentioned before, but once you know what you’re doing you’re settled for pretty much any RE game. Although, if you’re playing in hardcore it’s a whole different ball game, specially if you’re trying to also get an S ranking, you’ll find that it is pretty much hell on earth, few items/ammo, more enemies and a single encounter can be fatal, not to mention the 1 hit kill bosses, I almost lost all my hair getting through some chapters in that difficulty, but totally worth the extra-hours and the stress in the end.

Talking about extra-hours, on top of the different campaign scenarios (A+B), the different difficulties and rankings, the game also features an alternative game mode called 4th survivor and a free dlc. 4th survivor is a minigame where you play as Hunk and have to complete his mission during the outbreak, the events in this scenario are canon. It’s a short but interesting campaign, giving insight into one of the game’s side stories. The free dlc is called “Ghost Survivors” and it features 4 stories with 4 different characters, following them as they try to escape the city, the dlc storylines play out the same way as the 4th survivor campaign, short, linear and entertaining, but they’re not considered canon to the game’s story. If you liked the game you’ll enjoy them.

This game is a great way to introduce new fans to the series and is a reward to the OG fans that endured RE 6, ORC and UC days. I want all my future RE titles to be exactly like this one.

Surely, this is the best of the Resident Evil remakes in Steam. The work put into it is amazing, and so is the devs' attention to detail. To capture the real survival-horror feeling, players should dive head-first in the hardcore difficulty. I first played it in the normal difficulty, and it is way too easy to stock up on ammo and health items. To get the most out of the experience, you can go ahead and play in the hardcore mode !

The story is not the best I've ever seen, but the writers made it amazingly well-told and tailored. Leon and Claire are always after something, and it's easy to get caught up in the world Capcom created; It's hard to put down the controller in your first playthrough. And even if you already beat the game, the unlockables are a fun reason to play on harder difficulties and aim for the S rating. A few extra modes are also included in the base game, and they're very fun to go through, because of how action-packed they are. If you played RE7, think of "Ethan Must Die".

Out of all the DLCs, the only one I think is worth paying for is the original soundtrack. Not because of nostalgia, but because, in the base game, music only plays when you first enter a save room or if you're on a boss fight. For most of the game, it's either complete silence or some very bland sounds. When you switch to the original soundtrack, if you're in a save room, a slow melody plays. When fighting an enemy, a bass-like sound plays, and so on. I think it suits the game better, and it's not really expensive. The other DLCs are either cosmetics or unlock all unlockables early on, but I don't know why anyone would want to pay for the unlockables since you can unlock all of them for free by playing the game.

This game has something to offer for all kinds of players. If you're only interested in a horror story, this is surely a great gateway to this genre, and should give you about 20 hours of content. If you're a completionist and want all achievements, you're looking at 50 hours of content. 

Either way, I strongly believe this game is one of the best on steam, and it's a steal on sales! Absolutely worth picking up!

My earliest memories of gaming include being completely terrified by Resident Evil 2. The puzzles and controls were a bit much for my tiny kid brain at the time so I just watched my brothers play it. But the impression the game left on me was undeniable. It is to me Le Grand K of horror video games.  Every zombie game and every horror game I played from that point on was weighed against these early images of shambling corpses and empty ammo clips. Nothing would stack up until Amnesia.
The Resident Evil 2 remake does all of these memories justice. This is not a nostalgia cash-in. It's a lovingly crafted, modern recreation of one of the greatest survival horror games ever created. I was stunned by how the modern visuals and gameplay could compensate for the near two decades of age I'd accumulated since the original in such a way that I could be as terrified playing now as I was when I was three feet tall. I was SURE the hilariously slow zombies and occasional jump scares wouldn't affect me. But then that first window shatters, that first licker drops down, or you're in a room with only one exit and the footsteps start sounding nearer. 

The visuals are gorgeous. The gameplay is smooth and smartly converted to a modern third person perspective. There are several challenge modes that follow the stories (more or less) of characters found throughout the main campaign. Ammo is precious and scarce like it should be in a horror game and there's a real chance you will run out of herbs at some point, too.

There are plenty of jump scares to make you jump out of your seat but the real name of the game is tension. Too many zombies, not enough ammo, and always being followed as you navigate the enormous museum-turned-police station to solve puzzles and escape in what must be the least practical ways possible.

11/10

In short, Resident Evil 2 Remake is my Game of the Year 2019. It hits all the right spots.

Resident Evil franchise actually took a few sharp turns over the years. The classic Resident Evil (0, 1, 2, 3, etc.) are survival horror featuring intense gameplay from limited supplies and slots. Inventory management, map design (Metroidvania-like) and puzzle solving are the core gameplay. Whereas the more recent Resident Evil (4, 5, 6 and Revelations series) are more action and shooter oriented. They are no longer survival horror but more of a third-person shooter. The latest of the franchise (in terms of story) Resident Evil 7, is completely different than its predecessors as a first-person shooter for the first time of the franchise. While merged shooting with similar code gameplay from classic Resident Evil, it features the horror atmosphere and sophisticated story that unravels itself as the game progresses, and even a much stronger character building making the plots no longer generic.

Back to Resident Evil 2 Remake, the game is completely overhauled with a new engine. New technologies enable the game to create grim atmosphere and surroundings making it far more immersive than the original, while keeping what makes a good and intense survival horror: limited resources, relentless enemies, jump scare, the urge of running etc. Combat is relatively slow-paced, but the game is still pretty intense. With a modern shooter system, players can surely go gun blazing, but you might need to think about your strategy on saving ammo and stuff, especially with enemies that don’t stay dead easily (use your knife wisely).

Map design is very interesting and is one of the best map designs I have ever seen. The game is a horror game that makes you want to runaway, however the map design makes you feel like exploring and gathering all the loots and secrets. Basically, when you get a new item, there are hints what you need to do next, unlike Resident Evil 1 which I felt completely lost and unable to process due to a lack of “hints”. The layout is complicated (not as complicated and unfriendly as Resident Evil 1) and you might get lost, but the map can always give tons of help. Also, the map design gives this game a lot of replayability. It is still fun to dive in more than once. As you get familiar with the map and enemy layouts, you will feel like a badass in the second or more times playthrough.

The story is a bit generic and there are a few nitpicking I want to point out. You need to play the game twice with different characters in order to reach the true ending. While it is not a problem, this design causes inconsistency in the story. Though with a few differences, you experience the same scenario twice. It doesn’t make sense in the story perspective since you have already done these things once with your first character. I know it is mostly due to how the original was designed, but the stories of two characters are supposed to happen in time order, instead of being like in parallel universes.  Another thing is the performance. The actress of Claire, though she is very cute, her performance is not that great as her expression is kind of stiff and the same most of the time. The voice actress of Ada Wong, correct me if I am wrong but it seems her accent slipped several times.

Anyway, this game is 10 out of 10 to me and I recommend it as a must-play.

This is one of those rare cases where, despite being a retro gaming/emulation enthusiast, I like the remake better than the original. Many remakes and reboots of classic games have disappointed me, but this one impressed me. Unlike the early Silent Hill titles, the fixed camera angles and tank controls of the original *didn't* contribute to the gameplay in a positive way; they were just technical limitations of the time. A remake that can be enjoyed by both newcomers and fans who have played the original, although OG RE2 fans will be able to appreciate and recognise all of the changes that have been made. RE2R is presented as two routes (one for Leon and Claire), and both paths are intended to be played back-to-back to get the full story. There is a lot of backtracking, key hunting, and simple puzzle-solving required, similar to the old games. At the higher difficulties such as Hardcore (which is intended to be the authentic Resident Evil experience), ammo and inventory management becomes a key factor. This is not RE5 or RE6 where you can gun down every zombie in your sights — saving bullets and running past avoidable enemies is a must because ammo is usually scarce.

Just like the original, the two protagonists will encounter different characters and slightly different boss encounters for some portions, and because of the different weapons available to both characters, your tactics and playstyle will change slightly. Claire for example, gets access to powerful ranged weapons. But Leon's strongest arsenal is mostly close-range. There is also a new sub-weapon mechanic similar to RE: Revelations 2. These can be used individually at any time like a normal weapon, or they can be used as a "last-ditch" defence against zombies that have grabbed you. This opens up new tactics that were previously impossible in the older games, such as deliberately allowing a zombie to grab you so that you can shove a grenade down their mouths. Flash grenades are the most important sub-weapon, use them wisely because they will save your butt.

Overall I really enjoyed the RE2 Remake. Not because of nostalgia, but because it's a solid example of how remakes should be done: A fresh coat of paint while still maintaining the foundations of what made the original so great.

One of the most successful remakes of all time, RE2 Remake brings back the essence of late'90s survival horrors with the 3rd person camera/shoulder aiming of RE4/5/6, wrapped up in mesmerizing HD graphics. But make no mistake about the camera angle : this IS a survival horror game. HD graphics with 1998 gameplay, simple as that; RE2 remake punishes you (hard, perhaps you'll even have to restart your game since the beginning) if you throw away your ammo and meds. The game is not easy and the zombies and enemies are hard to kill in Standard mode. Hardcore mode is nearly impossible without the infinite ammo weapons.

TIPS:

a) Map is your friend. Use it, continuously.
b) Not every zombie is supposed to be killed (this ain't RE 4 or 5, with tons of ammo). In fact, most zombies should be shot in the legs and/or dodged (which ain't easy since there's no dodge button/action. As I've said, this is an old-school game with limited mechanics- no pushing, kicking or punching either, only knifing, which adds extra-dated flavour).
c) Only use a green herb/spray if seriously injured-close to death (Danger). Playing injured (Caution) is natural in a survival horror game.
d) Discard items in your inventory as soon as possible and merge ammo.
e) Mr.X is unkillable; run like hell and only face him if absolutely necessary.
f) Map is your friend.
g) As I've said, this is an old-school game. Dying/reloading and a trial-and-error approach is natural. I recommend a "Claire Story" on Assist (Easy) to get the basics of the game, and then a Leon 2nd Run (canon) on Standard.
h) Map is your friend.

Not having played the original Resident Evil 2 on the GameCube, I went into Resident Evil 2 remake completely blind, not knowing what to expect of my first Resident Evil game: will it be good? Will it disappoint? Capcom has given me an experience that I will remember for a long time: the game is fun, creepy, has great sound design and voice acting, and is visually stunning. The two playable characters Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield are well written, and changes little bits of story depending who you’re playing (although not as much as I hoped). I enjoyed every single minute in the shoes of either the rookie cop, or the girl who is just looking for her brother.

Starting the game you have to choose between Leon or Claire and after that the survival horror begins. Starting the game you visit a petrol station, trying to get some fuel but you soon notice that something is not quite right. Lights are out, the place feels deserted and the car of the sheriff is just standing there; doors are unlocked, and not parked properly: something is wrong. After encountering the first zombie and killing it, you meet Claire or Leon, depending on who you’re playing. The place then is overrun by zombies forcing the couple to drive to Raccoon City, looking for answers, but the only thing they find are more questions. 

The game is a third person, story driven experience. Like in other RE titles there are puzzles to solve and key items to find, needed to make progress in the story and areas. There are enough areas to explore with supplies or key items to find, making it feel like every room or area actually is useful and no area is there ‘just because’. The areas are well designed with stunning graphics and sound design is incredible. The whole vibe in the game is always amazing, the environment and music and what not do their job: If the game wants you to be scared it creates the perfect setting and the same goes for when the game wants you to feel safe, for what short period that may be. The game is a real survival-horror experience. It has its scary moments and it nails the feeling that you’re just barely scraping by in this zombie infested city. Movement is good, shooting feels great and boss fights are fun enough, not too difficult or too easy. Frame rate is steady, I cannot remember that I had any frame drops.

Even though you can play as two characters, who do have different story lines, the two stories still feel a lot like the same storyline, which was kind of disappointing. After having finished my first run as Leon I immediately started playing again as Claire in the ‘2nd run’ option and I expected it to be different than Leon’s. Even though it kind of was, it wasn’t enough. It was still lots of fun though. The game has great replayability, whether you are trying to beat your high score (at the end of the game you get stats and you receive a ‘rank’), or unlock weapons, beat the game on a higher difficulty or just trying to get all achievements. The game also comes with some free extra DLC, which are fun at best but nothing too special. Furthermore the game’s story isn’t just told through dialogue and cutscenes, but also through the environment and files you can find in the game, making picking up and reading all the files worth your while.

Verdict: Resident Evil 2 Remake is a awesome survival horror game, with amazing graphics, sound design, voice acting and a steady frame rate. The characters are interesting and the gameplay feels good and responsive. Boss fights are fun and not too difficult and after having finished the game with a good and satisfying ending, replaying the game again is tons of fun. Whether it is for achievements or just for playing, the game stays fun and interesting. Maybe you’ll notice some details which you didn’t before, by picking a file that was hidden somewhere which you didn’t notice in your first run.

[quote][b]OVERVIEW[/b] ↴[/quote]
Resident Evil 2 is a very well done remake of an old-school survival horror game from 1998 under the same name, which tells us a story of rookie police officer Leon S. Kennedy and a college student Claire Redfield as they attempt to escape The Raccoon City after it's citizens are transformed by a unknown biological weapon secretly developed by the pharmaceutical company called Umbrella, while being chased by zombies, other monsters, and especially the Tyrant, who is dispatched to hunt down and kill any survivors, making it harder for two of our protagonists to find a way to escape the city. But somehow you gotta escape, so get to it!

[quote][b]GRAPHICS AND AUDIO[/b] ↴[/quote]
The quality of everything in this game is simply outstanding. To tell you the truth, saying that this game is beautiful, doesn't quite convey how it truly looks like. It's amazing how much of a great work was put into every single astonishing tiny piece for the whole surrounding you environment to make such a fantastic atmosphere, from the characters models to the monsters both terrifying and exquisitely detailed ones to the top notch polished animations that made the bloodstain patterns look very realistic and savage (as they should be)... for example when to your great satisfaction you shot a zombie in the head, which *coughs* might not happened a lot in my case. The attention to detail is out of this world and definitely setting a new bar for all other developers, especially when it comes to things like dead body collision, facial microexpressions or dismemberment mechanics. But if you add to it the haunting sound design and excellent voice-acting (I'm ignoring Ada's bland one and those cheesy one liners) which adds great depth and so much tension to the mood that drives the atmosphere into a completely another level of immersiveness. You'll get to experience a whole new layer of terrifying horror which you may like or not, it depends on your scary meter level.
 
[quote][b]GAMEPLAY[/b] ↴[/quote]
We get to experience two pretty similar scenarios where you need to start off by playing part A to unlock yourself part B. Players will have to carve their way through zombie infested police station, then straight to the putrid sewers, and after it to even more nightmares inducing places (uh-huh no spoilers). For those who somehow didn't figure it out yet, gameplay style in fact was made for us to favor extreme conservation of resources for when they truly gonna matter (but don't worry too much if you'll shoot zombie TWICE in the head... as Keanu said "Yeah, you gotta make sure.") like the big boss fights, or just simple unavoidable fights, but it also encourages us to be more thoughtful and creative in approaching enemies, and actually avoiding as many unnecessary fights as possible. Furthermore to help us out, the game focus also on exploration which turns out to be very rewarding and even more satisfying for those willing to risk it and who truly want to explore every single cranny, maybe check out all the lockers (that might've been a bad idea), try their hand on cracking those pesky locks, and examine bunch of items to reveal theirs precious secrets. We're not only getting rewarded with ever-needed resources, but aswell new weapons and most importantly my favourite: the additional inventory space. Believe me when I say that every single upgrade and your last bullet will be needed to make it through this horror alive, so better start looking and cut down on the complaining, because we don't loose resources here, we gain 'em. It's a survival game, you gotta survive! As one would do in a real life apocalypse after all, don't you think.

[quote][b]STORY[/b] ↴[/quote]
From the very beginning it's known that we're gonna play two solid and decently written parallel parts: Claire Redfield's and Leon S. Kennedy's, with each having it's own supporting characters that have defined personalities, one radically different side-story that happens in the middle, and their own unique final boss. It's completely our choice with which part we would like to start the story of our protagonists and The Raccoon City, a town torn through with seemingly unstoppable virus that is leaving it's residents either very much dead or turned into vicious monsters and the place where all paths will cross several times in this chaos infested city, whatever it will be between Claire and Leon, shady characters with their own agenda or the true masterminds behind this zombie outbreak. Put this all together and it makes for an engaging story from the start to the end, that will take more than just pure luck but a helluva lot of nerve to get through.

[quote][b]PERFORMANCE, BUGS AND GLITCHES[/b] ↴[/quote]
I have absolutely nothing to complain about when it comes to performance. I didn't experienced any bugs or problems at all... from what I can remember of the gory details.

[quote][b]CONCLUSION[/b] ↴[/quote]
RE2 can easily join ranks with those remakes that truly did an excellent job 'cause it lives up to it's expectations and deliveres a classical survival horror game while also keeping the original game theme intact which makes for an incredibly well done game that I find hard to believe for anyone not to like. It's a gem of old times brought back to live with one of the best modern technologies. Seriously, probably the best game remake that I've ever played and absolutely worth the time spend on it. Yes, this game can definitely keep you on the edge throughout your entire playtime, makes you enjoy it and most of all leave you proud that you didn’t cower away from the challenge. So whatever you feel better by buying this game on sale or not, doesn't change the fact that you should buy it.

Resident Evil 2 (2019) is a perfect example of how awesome old-school game design is compared to the open world bore-fests, looter shooter grindathons, and on-rails action movie wannabes we usually get nowadays.

How wonderfully freeing it is for the developers to have a little faith in their player's and not treat them like complete idiots. It's refreshing to play a modern game without all the Google Maps mongoloid nonsense telling me exactly where to go. There's only good old fashioned intelligent level design and environmental storytelling here folks.

I'm happy to see that Capcom can join FromSoftware on the extremely small pantheon of AAA developers who make single player games that are worth giving a damn about. To summarize, I overwhelmingly recommend this game to anyone who likes playing actually good single player games that have a genuine sense of adventure and discovery.

Game takes place in a couple of visually different areas but the best one is definitely the RPD, which has one of the best level design I ever experienced. It has just the right amount of puzzles to action, and makes the rest of the game afterwards(as it's the first area) look pretty shallow, until late sewer and laboratory, but those are filled with some other annoying "features" that make the experience far less enjoyable.

Boss fights are both a pro and a con in this case, some are really well done, but those where they went with the original small arena mechanic are suffering as your character isn't an agile one, and much more resembles the OG game in that regard, but enemies have super high speed attacks making them pretty hard to dodge unless you cheese their AI. The other problem with some boss fights is that they are a "one & done" type of deal, and you won't enjoy fighting them again in the next play through, making them pretty tedious on your next replay.

What I wish the game had more of is variation between different scenarios and characters, for the most part you're doing the same exact thing, perhaps in a slightly different order but it's the same thing over and over again, meaning replay value isn't as strong as it could be.

As for the "bonus modes", those were a complete miss for me, I didn't enjoy any of them, they all focus on speed running apart from one, which is a survival level, but either way, all of them are far too opposite from what I expected and got from the main game.

Now if Capcom stayed with this "formula" for their other games, that would be great, I'd really like another Revelations game but this time without linear levels for 90% of the game, and instead make them puzzle heavy like RPD.

Disclaimer: I never played the original PS1 version.

[b]TL;DR[/b] Resident Evil 2 is a return to form for survival horror games, keeping its gameplay simple, refined, and a joy to play. While a single run through the game is pretty short (~5-6 hours), there is enough incentive in the form of bonus modes, alternate story routes, and tight gameplay to justify the asking price and to keep you coming back for more. This is the most fun I have had playing a horror game in a long, long time.

[b]The Good:[/b]

Core Gameplay: The core gameplay is very simple, and its simplicity is its strength. You go from room to room, investigating leads, conserving resources, solving puzzles, and shooting zombies that get in your way. The game is fun, addictive, and satisfying.

Graphics: They are beautiful, nearly photo-realistic and run extremely well even on my old, low-end GPU. Animation is fantastic, and other than Claire's face edging toward the uncanny valley at times everything looks good and believable.

Atmosphere: The game achieves a consistently intense, chilling atmosphere. The music, lighting, enemies and sound designs all work very well together. The game is filled with slow, quiet moments walking through empty corridors with nothing but the sound of your foot steps accompanying you, punctuated with quick, intense, visceral action. It all works very well, and even after 40+ hours of gameplay I still found myself unsettled and occasionally jumping from my seat. You feel vulnerable at all times even later in the game when you get some heavy weaponry, thanks in part to a vague health system and a limited inventory size, forcing you to plan out your trips from the safe areas to explore.

Replayability: The game is infinitely replayable, and does not lose any of the fun between playthroughs. There are two characters you can play as that change the story considerably: Leon and Claire, and each character gets two slightly different runs through the story.

Extra Modes: The extra modes are a ton of fun and add a lot to the game if you tire of the main campaign. They are significantly more challenging than the campaign is though, so be prepared to die A LOT at first until you get the layout of each bonus mode. This can be rage fuel if you are not patient.

Horror/Fun Balance: The game walks a fine line between being fun and gamey and being scary. It manages to be tense and scary while also being a fun shooter. It avoids the pitfalls of horror games that may focus too much on horror to the detriment of being fun, and of horror games that try to be so fun and action-y that they forget to be scary.

Technically Impressive: I can not recall encountering a single bug or technical issue from my 50 hours of play time. The game is well programmed and runs smoothly.

Resource Management: Whether you are playing on standard or hardcore or even in the extra modes, the developers have done a great job of always making you feel short on ammo and health supplies. You really have to be smart with your use of ammo and other consumables or you will find yourself in a very hard spot. At no point does the lack of resources feel overwhelming though, there is always just enough to get by with a modicum of effort. This really enhances the atmosphere and the rewarding feeling that comes with progressing successfully through the game. I know how much of a balancing act it can be to pull this off, so major kudos to the developers on this one.

[b]The Bad:[/b]

The Story: It is very minimal, and does not stray too far from standard zombie movie plots. Characters are kind of wooden, including the main cast, and other characters are basically cartoon villains with unclear motivations. Dialogue ranges from okay to cringe ("you can adopt me and we will all live together!")

Bullet-Sponge Enemies: The damage rules, and amount of ammo necessary to kill zombies, are unclear and vary wildly. Sometimes you will get lucky and a single head shot will explode a zombie's head and kill them instantly. At other times, you can empty entire clips into one zombie's head and they will continue shambling towards you as if nothing is wrong. I can understand why they designed the game this way as it can make certain moments much more tense and unexpected between playthroughs, but it comes off as unfair a majority of the time.

[b]The Ugly:[/b]

Backtracking: There is a LOT of back tracking in this game, a symptom of poor level design. This is compacted by Mr. X who can be very annoying and inconvenient, chasing you away from areas you need to get to constantly. The map will be your best friend, marking key puzzles and color coding areas to let you know if you missed something or not.

Mr. X Himself: He was a bit of a mixed game mechanic for me. It is interesting, and certainly brings a new dynamic to the game, having an invulnerable hulking monster hunting and stalking you periodically through the game. On the other hand, he can be a persistent annoyance, running a train through the atmosphere making it more run and gun. It would have been better having his encounters random and end sooner. As it stands, he can be an annoying, predictable time sink that will not go away until you advance to certain parts of the game.

Ahhhh....That feeling you get when the best game of the year comes out in January. Sucks for all the other developers I guess. And beaten by "remake" no less. Damn! ...I actually didn't get around to playing this one until June, it was my first ever Resident Evil game which probably explains why I liked it so much more than the fan boys. I tried to play RE4, and I promise I will eventually complete it, but the controls and camera...ugh. I'm struggling. Same problem I had with RE1 Remastered, awful camera, I can't stand dying because my controls inverted because unbeknownst to me the camera flipped, and I ran right into some hungry zombie's teeth. Dying on accident on losing lots of progress sucks. THIS GAME however, they nailed it. Silky smooth over the shoulder movement, and the camera pans the way god intended it, and not up your ass when you back into a corner. The game also saves regularly so you don't stupid yourself. 

It takes place almost entirely in one building, but everything looks gorgeous and the soundscape is atmospheric delight. I literally cannot believe this game can look so good and run so well on my system compared with other games that don't look as nice and struggle to perform as well. The level of detail and nuance in the every single inch of the police station is just incredible. Mist from the rainstorm outside sprays in through open windows, blood drips down the sides of the wall and forms puddles on the floor, your flashlight is just bright enough to illuminate danger right in front of you but not enough to make you ever feel comfortable in the dark. Speaking of which the pacing is brilliant, I've played it many times through now and I noticed that the game's AI seems to perfectly balance challenging combat with eerie spooky downtime. On the normal difficult setting, you often feel like you have just enough resources to eek by, and it makes small victories seem so much more rewarding. They remastered everything but the dialog. Don't expect CDProjektRed, but the writing is decent and it doesn't take away from how brilliantly the directors and artists created true horror here. 

It is one of the scariest games I've played, which also explains why I loved it so much. It ranks up there with Alien: Isolation and System Shock 2. Unlike Prey, which is scary in a more cerebral way, this game is scary in that ♥♥♥♥ your pants way, which reminds me of Alien, especially in the sections when you're evading pursuers. The scarcity of resources builds tension and necessitates calculated, strategic thinking on the part of the player. You often have to backtrack, so you may be avoiding taking out a few zombies and saving bullets because zombies are easy to sneak by, only for a licker to show up the next time you pass through, and the licker is far harder and more dangerous to sneak by especially with zombies chasing you. Then the game really ramps things up when Mr X shows up and you have to backtrack through an area with zombies and lickers all because you wanted to save a few bullets and now they are useless in face of your relentless pursuer. I admit on paper it sounds kind of corny, but in the moment, in the dark, as the zombies growl in the distance and the heavy stomping foot steps draw closer and closer and the string quartet picks up and the door blasts open and you slink down into the corner as this gray giant ducks into the doorway. He seems to take up the whole room as he enters, cracks his knuckle,s and locks his gaze on you...AND...then you shoot off his hat and run like hell for a safe room!  

One thing that's really nice about this game is the way they mix up scenarios, so you can replay the game and while objectives are largely the same, the way you go about completing them and the location of key items is totally different. Also, the enemy placement changes, so the need for clean underwear remains, and even after dozens of hours this game is still terrifying and fun.

For those who have played the original Resident Evil 2, you might be able to understand why I have given this game a thumbs down. I have only played Leon Scenario A and Claire Scenario B at the moment (as I don't feel like continuing any further for the time being). Graphics are good no doubt, though "Screen Space Reflections" has still not been perfected even after over one year from the game's release. After playing a certain game for many hours, you tend to focus less on graphics and more on story/gameplay. That said, I will now summarize my reasons in points:

• RE2 remake has too few timeline interactions between Leon and Claire. The remake went backwards in where it shone in the past. (You can wiki about it for more detail regarding what I am talking about)

• In the old RE2, the starting time for A and B are sensibly around the same time. In the new one side B for some reason starts at the point where the helicoptor crashes (totally illogical).

• In the old RE2, the save system enables more consequential interactions between scenarios A and B. However in the new game, there is no inheriting save system, so your side A actions will cause no specific changes to side B whatsoever. (More detail on the internet).

• In the old game there are more essential variations in paths, there are boss changes throughout. For example, A would fight G1 G3 but side B would fight G2 and G4 etc, among other things.

• *SPOILERS* What really gets me is when Annette would appear on both sides A and B to trap Ada or Sherry in the dump and also appear before G3 fight and talk to both characters, and also like die twice. This is the breaking point for me, it breaks the side A vs side B story's coherence completely, and needless to say, is lazy and a bit excessive.

• I think Leon and Claire's interactions are not timely and as a result they lack the bonding they are supposed to have by the end of the game; and both side A and B boss fights and paths to take aren't showing any efforts to weave into each other but remains largely repetitive.


Overall, I think the story is sort of incoherent because of the accumulation of these little narrative details. Resident Evil 2:REMake(Get it?) is a new game with a familiar setting, a retelling of Resident Evil 2 from the ancient days of yore and the dingle-dingle-ding-diiiing-duuuuuu of the Playstation 1. Leon and Claire are visiting Raccoon City and things get out of hand due to that wacky Umbrella corporation. The iconic flaming city streets, rancid sewer, final lab and glorious police station are rendered in seamless 3D with full 360 character control, a moving camera and almost no loading screens. You can aim your gun and the excellent body-part damage system in this game makes every shot count. This is truly a brand new game in every sense except the story.

If you are reading this review I assume you've held back. Maybe you never got into Resident Evil at all. Maybe you are convinced Ye Olde Games Ofe Thee Past are better. You're waiting for a sale and really value your money, is even $20-30 too much for these darn rehashes from creatively bankrupt devs? I'm here to tell you yes, this game is very well made. It is highly entertaining and tightly polished. A satisfying experience where one can soak in a 4-10+ hour first blind playthrough and then go back again. They can go back as the other character for a largely new experience, they can try the slightly revamped B modes(which are more remixes now than a true second half), there's expanded survivor gauntlets including the free DLC Ghost Survivors. There is a lot of game here and in a clever design element the core game is very speed run friendly, encouraging you to replay it since it can occupy a gap in an afternoon. 

The core gameplay is simple. Explore and survive. Fight the undead. Encounter design and enemy placement is cunning in this game. Zombies have a great deal of smoke and mirrors invoked to keep you unsure as to whether they're truly dead or not, with experienced players learning the few reliable tells. More advanced foes are tough but fair, having great strengths and clear weaknesses, punishing the unobservant and unprepared. Anyone who has paid the slightest bit of attention to media around this game is probably aware of the Tyrant pursuer, Mr. X, who will ceaselessly chase the player at some points. With haunting environments and top tier graphic design this game has plenty of horror to spook you with.

So what can the player do, other than fumble helplessly and hope for the best? Resident Evil encourages you to aggressively prepare for and plan your routes. Explore thoroughly, make the best use of your supplies and know what you're doing. Pause, catch your breath and THINK! When you want to replay the game and get better clears, you need to have plans of action and execute them well. By default death will take you back to an autosave checkpoint and manual saves are free, with restrictions only appearing at your choice to pursue greater difficulties. You are free to be scared but not irritated. This makes the challenging, bombastic boss fights charming pretty much every time, and as you gain experience it's fascinating to peel back the layers and see what makes the animatronics work.

I recommend the game highly for the main story alone. You can expect a good long first run that is worth on sale price and extract as much value as you want from replays with strong incentive to do so, to get rewards and to master the game. So I'll wrap up with some thoughts on the gauntlet modes, 4th Survivor and Ghost Survivors, which abandon intricately crafted story and set piece staging in favor of heavy combat. They are bonus modes, not proper stories. 4th Survivor is pretty well done. It is a robust, challenging gauntlet with just enough give and take and fine execution to learn that makes things easier than they first appear. You are very generously armed yet will need it all to have a chance of survival. Tofu modes are amusing, though getting past Tofu to unlock the others felt draining and a bit luck-heavy to hold my interest. Ghost Survivors are entertaining and arguably the hardest content in the game, pushing the games combat systems to their absolute limit and often growing unfun due to it. When they are doing well they feel like tense combat tests and engaging live battle puzzles. When they're lousy you're just following a robotic run and hoping you aren't randomly grabbed, wasting your time. But hey, they're free and optional and clearly meant for players who want to push that hard.
