Resident Evil 2 is one of the better horror games out there in the market. This game is the complete remake of the original Resident Evil 2 released in 1998. This remake lives up to its expectation and delivered a classic survival horror game while keeping the theme of the original game intact. This remake will be enjoyed by both new players and the players who played the original one. 

[b]Game Type[/b]
Survival Horror (with gun play)

[b]Gameplay/View[/b]
Third Person View. You either play as Leon or Claire, the two protagonists in the game. You have to survive from enemies and complete puzzles to proceed towards the objective. 

[b]Difficulty[/b]
Have three difficulty settings suitable for both beginner and hardcore players.

[b]Game Length[/b]
Between 12 to 15 hrs for one campaign playthrough.

[b]Weapon Types[/b]
Pistol (4-5 variety of pistols), SMG, Shotgun, Grenade Launcher.  There are some exclusive weapons like rocket launcher, Machine gun etc. only available in certain boss fights.

[b]Items/ Equipment[/b]
There are many items or equipment which the player can gather in their walkthrough. Items ranges from Knife, Grenade, flashbang, herbs (for healing and curing any status like poison) and some other.

[b]Crafting and Inventory[/b]
Players can combine two items to create a new item that ranges from ammo, healing herbs.

[b]Exploration[/b]
The game encourages the players to explore the areas. A lot of mission items and special items/ equipment are scattered throughout the area and it is essential to explore the areas.

[b]Enemy Types/AI/Boss[/b]
Enemy AI is great. Loud noises from running, gunfire can attract enemies from a distance. There are quite a few enemy types/varieties ranging from zombies, dogs, lickers, swamp monsters and some others. In addition to normal enemies and zombies, the player is chased by special enemies in certain areas. In the early part of the game the infamous Tyrant (Mr X) will be stalking the player throughout the level in the early part. While some players may get frustrated, this chase/stalking of Mr X is a critical/ fundamental part of this game and the players will feel a sense of accomplishment once they manage to overcome this part. Boss fights are decent although there could have been some improvement. 


[b]Sound, Graphics and Atmosphere[/b]
All of them are excellent which when combined together recreate a true horror feeling among the players.

[b]Replay Value[/b]
Good replay ability value. The player had to complete the game twice to get the true ending. This has to be done with the two characters Leon and Claire. Note that the player had to do the second playthrough (entitled second run). There are certain modes like Survival modes, NPC scenarios which unlocks once a player completes a playthrough.

[b]Some advice and tips[/b]
Killing an enemy is not recommended unless absolutely necessary since ammo is scarce. (it takes a huge number of bullets to kill an enemy Crippling an enemy (shooting in the leg) is an effective way to conserve ammo and complete objectives faster. 
All the items/mission items should be checked and inspected since it can reveal new features which otherwise can be over looked. For example, a badge (used for unlocking locker) on proper inspection can change into a USB dongle that can be used to access a computer.

Inventory management is important since the number of inventory slots are limited and some items can occupy 2 slots. It is essential to keep at least 2-3 slots free before the player decides to investigate a particular area. It may happen that the player run out of inventory slots while coming in front of a mission item. The player can drop items/ammo to make space but those ammos and items are quite hard to come by.

The player had to backtrack a lot in this game so it is essential that the player gets accustomed with the map/area.
 A player can check on dead bodies/zombies using their knife (and not waste bullet) to check if they are actually dead or not. Otherwise the bodies can suddenly reanimate and can catch the player off guard.


There is no dodging in the game. The player must make each step with caution. Always keep a knife or two equipped so that if an enemy catches a player off guard, the player can snap out of the enemy grab/bite with their trusty knife.

[b]Final Verdict[/b]
9/10. Definitely recommended. Capcom have really showed us as how remakes are actually made!

Okay, now that we have an intro out of the way, let me tell you something more about this game. But first, let me tell you that I didn't play the original from 1998, neither did I play any of the 'old' RE games. I did, however, play the RE HD remaster a while back, and I did enjoy that game in a similar way that I enjoyed this one. So that will be me reference point.

Although I'm not that young being 31 years old, RE HD remaster felt like an oldschool game for me in a lot of ways, and so does the RE 2 despite being so recent. Limited inventory space, somewhat slow and clunky controls/movement, combat that isn't all that flashy, limited ammo, no autosaves and limited save numbers in hardcore mode and several other features that are not popular choices in modern game design filosophy anymore, are present here. And despite those choices are somehow against the player's comfort, they are perfect for a good survival horror, as they add to the experience of being just a weak and helpless human surrounded by countless atrocities. 

The atmosphere that RE 2 builds is really heavy, both in how the game is structured and how it is presented visually (and the visuals are great). The only thing  which is a bit lacking in that department is music, which isn't really memorable. The puzzles are not that hard, but engaging and adding another layer to the gameplay. There is a lot of backtracking, but while you revisit the same locations some new monsters show up to spice things up, and at some point of the game another layer of fear and stress is added to that, which I won't spoil. The story is just there, nothing too sophisticated similarly to RE movies, but it's enjoyable and sometimes even emotional. You get to play 2 characters, and their playthroughs have some differences. And after that, there is a '2nd run' option unlocked, which adds some more new things. So all in all, there are 4 playthroughs to be done and it's worth it to do them all - they did manage to surprise me more than once even after I've done the first two. So I played through the main game 4 times, and there are still some free DLCs which I didn't yet play - so I'd say it's a pretty good replay value.

I have to say, this game stressed me out a lot. But after all, that is the purpose of a survival horror, isn't it? If you're weak-minded, than don't play it. However, for the players that enjoy real survival horror games, I cannot do anything else than recommend RE 2!

The game itself stays faithful to the original with the storyline whilst also adding in extra lore notes and puzzles. A few areas are changed slightly, for better and for worse, however, is also awe-inspiring due to the beauty of the Resident Evil Engine.

While I have played the more modern style of resident evil games that exists in resident evil 4 and resident evil 5, I have not played the original resident evil or the original resident evil 2. This review is about how I, a casual fan of the series, experienced the remake. This remake is incredibly well done.

The environment and ambience in all stages of the game is amazing. The only thing that is somewhat of a blemish in this area is the cheesy voice lines from Leon and Claire. However, other moments, such as the first time you walk down the watery hallway and the first time you see a Licker, are intense and terrifying. These moments create a very powerful fear of what's around the corner, which is much easier said than done. I think all horror games should strive to create this emotion in the player, and very few are successful at this. Amnesia: the Dark Descent is the best example of a game that makes you afraid, and while the Remake does not go to Amnesia levels, it played its cards as a zombie game very well.

Puzzles are not difficult and the process of running through the map and gathering puzzle pieces to put together to make progress is a time-tested way to keep the player entertained and having fun. Old school resident evil games operate with this method at their core, and it works out very well. Bonus puzzles that are not necessary to continue the game but offer very helpful resources also entice the player to keep looking in every nook and cranny and experience all that the game has to offer.

The first resident evil that I played was resident evil 4, which is much more arcade combat than the survivalist take employed by resident evils 1-3 and the remakes. You are not a god, in fact you are a bytch, and I think it works well. Adjusting to the idea that I should avoid or impede zombies rather than exploding their heads with a suplex did take some time. There are times when for some reason, certain zombies just won't get stunned or blowing their legs off takes more bullets than expected. These times can be frustrating and it can make the player feel as though the game is cheating. I do think that this survivalist approach which forces the player to conserve ammo and to choose when and where to engage is entertaining and enjoyable to play. It is a different take on video games when most other games out there are force feeding ammunition down players' throats, holding the players' hand, and all people care about is how to kill enemies in an even more spectacular fashion than other games. It forces the player to be resourceful, which makes the player feel good after achieving this resourcefulness. Lastly, not pushing the player into combat at every turn lets some of the pressure off of the game for not having the best combat. Killing zombies isn't actually all that fun, and so encouraging the player not to do it all the time lets pressure off of the game for having not so entertaining combat. It is, after all, a horror game, and you should be afraid of the enemies. This remake achieves a good balance of the player's power in that you can obliterate zombies with a shotgun, but you can't kill them all, so you have to respect and fear them.

Enemy diversity is maintained well at a steady pace throughout the game. The player first learns how to deal with regular zombies, then lickers, then Mr. X, and then all of them at the same time, and then the plant enemies are introduced. Each enemy is a different puzzle in itself. The player has tools to deal with each enemy type effectively but must do so with guile and resourcefulness rather than shoot everything on the screen. The diversity in enemies keeps the game fresh and prevents the player from getting bored. Mr. X can be somewhat annoying when there is no time to solve the puzzle that is blocking progress because he keeps following the player around. Other than that, the enemies in the game look good, they are dangerous, and outplaying them is fun.

The story I don't have much comment on, as I am sure that the creators of the game would rather not have had the exact same story that was thought up over a couple decades ago. It is a little lacking, but back in the day they did not have gigabytes of space to work with. It gets the job done.

The graphics and visuals are outstanding. Sometimes Leon and Claire's faces look weird, but you aren't really looking at them all the time.

Weapon variety is enough to make the player feel like a badass. Upgrading the hip pouch makes the player feel good, for who doesn't like leveling up.

Having two scenarios gives the game some replay value, although having to play the game twice to get the full story is a little annoying. This problem is mostly a non-factor since the arsenal available to each character differs enough to keep the game fresh.

Overall, I really enjoyed this game and didn't find too many flaws. It's a great way to spend 20 or so hours, especially if you get the DLC. While I haven't played the DLC, I have heard that it is good.

A great remake.  I really enjoyed some of the old styles.  They kept a lot of things pure from before.  Limited inventory, limited ammo, and lots of puzzles.  Overall, a 10 of 10 remake.  Though I could not remember the older version that well anymore.

However, as a general Resident Evil fan...  5 of 10.  Allow me to explain.  They added the over the shoulder view.  Very necessary.  Inventory was a bit overly limited, but arguably enough.  Thus, I didn't include that in my grading.  Yet, they did not add a dodge, increase run speed, or allow melee outside of the knife.  These were some of the great upgrades from Resident Evil 5 and 6 that should have been added.  

I want to move at more than a leisurely jog.  I want a dodge, manual is nice.  A quick time event (QTE) dodge is ok, but I don't always trust developers on timing.  I'm really, really glad the QTE sequences from RE5 and RE6 were not added here.  The times were badly written, especially for RE6.  Ruined the replay ability for that game.  Melee from RE5 and especially RE6 was awesome though.  I was really sad not to see that here.

Lastly, as a side note I was super disappointed to see speed runs controlling ranking and replay, despite that being part of the original game as well.  While it is a thing, popular with some, I don't find it to be worth my time...  No pun intended there.  A better mix may have been accuracy, hits received (assuming there was a dodge), and enemies killed.  These are stats more based on skill rather than memorization or cheating.

Trash game and those who defend this game have never played an actual good Resident Evil game. Micro DLC available for real money purchase to cheese your way and hold your hand through the game. 100% RNG on if a zombie gets stunned or staggered by a pistol shot. The knife registers hits based on FPS which in most cases gives PC players an automatic advantage. Zombies who lunge for you can infinitely re-lunge at you if player is within distance on Hardcore. Didn't appreciate that both scenarios starts the exact same and are almost the same exact in both playthroughs including second scenarios. Lets talk about character movement speed, who the heck decided you run faster in caution? And who decided that only one playable character doesn't get that movement speed? To me if you were going to implement a mechanic like that then every character should get that treatment. Yes, I have played a Resident Evil game like Resident Evil HD Remaster where one character gets a slight advantage over another but if you're rebuilding/rebooting a franchise why not change that too? Too many inconstancies with movement in general especially for stair skating in RE2 Remake,.. I can literally stair skate 3 different ways (I seem to be alone on that opinion on why it's not good). Yes there is some cool speed tech tricks like quick turns, but to me in this situation I think that bad outweigh the good in this circumstance. 

One thing I appreciated (that most others did not) was the the different skins/outfits for each character. I enjoyed the toughness of the boss battles and them being almost always intense (without infinite death machines and rocket launchers). I appreciated how hard it was to unlock the OP special weapons until the micro transaction was added that allows you to obtain them all for $5. I appreciated the puzzles for the first two or three completions of the game, but after leaving the game and coming back months later I would have to open my cheat sheet because who reads files after the first playthrough? Resident Evil 2 Remake is the reimagination of the 1998 Resident Evil 2. You play as either Leon Scott Kennedy, or Claire Redfield, as they try to survive and escape from the zombie infested Raccoon City. Returning back to its survival horror roots, resources are scarce, and flight is most of the time preferred than fight, with various puzzles that required to be solved in order to progress. Unlike in the original game, this game will not have a tank like control, instead its more of the over the shoulder third person style of control, similar to RE 4, 5 and 6.

In game, not only zombies will be getting in your way, but along with zombified beasts, mutated experimented creatures, or worse, a bioengineered creature hellbent on just killing you. It's up to you to decide how to bypass these obstacles safely in order to progress. Similar to the original, there are two routes for each character, thought they just relabelled it as 1st run and 2nd run, unlike the scenario A and B labels given in the original game. By playing through both scenarios for both Leon and Claire, you will get to see the entire story, since some events in the 2nd run are not covered in the 1st run, along with how each of them survive Raccoon City.

This game does have some value in replayability, since it has two routes for each characters. Furthermore, this is cemented by unlockable weapons when completing any of the route under certain circumstances, in addition to the free DLC for Ghost Survivors, and the return of the classic side modes, Tofu and Hunk mini games. It also manages to recapture the old survival horror feeling instead of being gung ho like in RE 5 and 6. Unfortunately, the two routes mentioned earlier, while having some minor differences in events, is practically identical to each other. The DLC game modes, while being challenging, are pretty short in length, since they are mainly as a speedrun challenge.

Despite that, I would still heavily recommend this game. Sure it has some flaws, some stuffs from the original are missing here and the routes doesn't make sense, but it's still a great game. Get it if you can, you won't regret it.

Most of my time with the Resident Evil 2 Remake was spent in a state of frustration rather than fear. Between the tyrant that never leaves, certain enemies with unblockable attacks, no gauge on when something is dead (for good), and the countless errors in continuity across all the playthroughs – yeah, I’d say “frustration” about sums it up. There was, expectedly, an obvious love for the source material that drove each design choice made in the RE2 Remake. And it also drove sales. It was a fantastic gimmick, really. But it’s difficult to tell where that love ended and where laziness/time constraint/inability took over. There was enormous thought and ingenuity put into the mechanics and engine and all of that felt great and worked well, very well - but it’s in the application of these systems where the RE2 Remake really starts to waver. The entire game is riddled with good intentions executed poorly. A few examples include -

Ammo: They were correct to make ammo scarce. They were incorrect in making no discernable way to identify when something was dead (for good). The original did this (when something was dead for good, they used a blood pool as a tell). How can I save my precious resource if I don’t know when to stop shooting? Again, it’s frustrating. Not scary. Am I doomed to this ridiculous purgatory of playing a very tedious, and sometimes deceiving, waiting game to see if something gets back up? It’s not even difficult. It’s just an impediment. Jesus Christ, just die!

Mr. X: They were correct to have a hulking tyrant track me through the narrative. They were incorrect in making his existence a chore. Once you realize that the Tyrant can be knocked down (by wasting ammo) with a few rounds, his existence becomes more annoying and less frightening. Mr. X’s immortality is not what makes him scary. Him tracking you indefinitely is. But this too falls apart when you realize there are certain rooms (not just save rooms) that he decides, out of the kindness of his heart, not to enter. It’s a slightly more sophisticated game of Frogger – you’re safe in the median. I’m not saying that it would be good design for him to track you forever and anywhere. I’m saying that perhaps the design, as it currently stands, wasn’t too well thought out if he just lets you hang out and crack open a beer in certain areas. The game doesn’t seem conducive for hide-and-survive gameplay the way others – like Alien: Isolation – were. The entirety of Mr. X’s role feels like a minigame. An exhausting one. The gives no reward and can’t be beaten. 

Multiple Scenarios: They were correct to keep the multiple scenarios. They were incorrect in making them a mishmash of various continuity errors. This was easily the biggest failure of the entire remake. Both of RE2 Remake’s main scenarios cannot exist logically. Some characters die twice (and in different places). Some of the same puzzles still exist slightly altered, but locker combinations remain the same. Some bosses die in certain scenarios (and in different areas) and not in the other. Some item locations change, some stay the same, or some switch what they are. Some routes that lead to one place in one scenario change in another. Some notes left behind by characters generate magically - We know Leon didn’t write notes to Claire because we played a whole game as Leon and he never wrote them! Why are they here then? Do you think we’re stupid!? - This list goes on and on. Yes, the original RE2, a game from 1998, had a few continuity errors too. However, mostly both Leon and Claire’s night through Raccoon City could be taken as independent continuity. Not here. All scenarios both happen and don’t happen. There’s no arbiter of truth, no narrator to piece it together. The player is forced to draft continuity in their own mind. It shouldn’t be crazy to expect that this concept should have been improved in 2019 over a version from 1998. 

Not wanting to get too bogged down in negatives by turning this review into a spoiler-fest, anger-riddled mess, the game does manage to do several things right. None of it was original, for the most part, but it was a slick reincarnation of the excellent design that proceeded it. It’s classic 90s Resident Evil formula. These games are just good. They were then and they are now. There was undeniably a starvation for a modern, new game, in the old formula. And in that respect, the game achieved its goal. Minus the plaguing tank controls, and controversial fixed camera angles, the game does “feel” like classic Resident Evil. But, by comparison – counting all games pre-Resident Evil 4, as it’s primarily an action genre after that – it does fit-in. It’s not my favorite, obviously. But it fits. And that’s perhaps the best compliment I’m willing to give it. Of the same types of Resident Evil games, it’s not the worst either (Zero still holds that title by a healthy margin), as it still contains an expectedly high amount of polish. It’s hard to hate it – it is Resident Evil. But I found myself happier that it existed rather than being happy to play it. I experienced great potential, not a great game. 

What made it great was the mechanics and engine. What made it mediocre was all that was in-between. It’s a wonder, truly, how well-praised this game was. On the one hand, I’m happy for it, really, because of the potential I keep mentioning. More people should be exposed to these versions of Resident Evil. The better the reviews, the better sales, the more likelihood this type of Resident Evil will continue. To me, it is the *correct* way to do it. On the other hand, there is a contradiction – good intentions and solid ideas were mixed with poor implementation. The game got a pass on that. Perhaps that’s for the greater good? We can hold two thoughts in our head at once though. The game has issues, a lot of them.

In the Resident Evil pantheon of this type, I’d pass on this until you’ve experienced the others. At least in order. There is a better Resident Evil, of the same formula, available on Steam right now in the form of the Resident Evil 1 remaster. Yes, the graphics are older, and the camera angles are archaic, but the formula remains pure. The RE2 remake proved that beyond anything else. This is only the ghost of a good thing living on in a decent disguise. But it’s evidence – we can go back. 

The formula is pure. And I think the starvation for that formula is where the praise comes from. It’s coming from a good place, to be sure, but the game was no match for legends that came before it. Instead, the RE2 Remake is simply... acceptable?

RE2R was my first experience playing a Resident Evil game, after decades of only indirectly observing the sprawling mess that the franchise is. I'm a huge fan of Dead Space, and Resident Evil is very often regarded as an important part of that game's foundation, so fully modern remake unhindered by the limitations of the 90's and early 2000's appealed to me a great deal. Hardcore fans of the series seem divided on the remakes, but as a newcomer with no expectations of reliving my nostalgia, it really was an excellent experience.

Even on my half-upgraded-half-straining-with-age machine the graphics are gorgeous and run just fine, with no substantial slowdowns or choppiness, helped by the fact that the game tends to keep things claustrophobic and pit you against a small number of strong enemies rather than waves of weak ones, so there's never too much going on at once.

The story is Resident Evil. Like me you probably knew at least part of the story long before this remake ever came out. It's not exactly a nuanced exploration of complex characters and deep themes, but a simple story with great atmosphere and very good performances for all the significant characters.

The hardiness of the enemies - often requiring more than one headshot to bring down, let alone to make them stay down - and the frequent runaround and backtracking with various key puzzles and dodging your pock-faced teenage son as he stomps around the house wearing his trenchcoat and trilby can prove somewhat annoying for people like me who prefer to solve their horror problems with the thunderous roar of heavy ordinance, but that's ultimately a deliberate design choice rather than a fault.

Overall a very solid 8/10 game, would recommend, will play again.

Resident Evil 2 is, at its core, a puzzle game with zombies - and a very good one. It builds up suspense extremely well, keeping you engaged with the second-to-second gameplay even when there's no combat. And when you do have to draw your weapon, it is viscerally satisfying. The zombies soak up basic handgun bullets like sponges, adding to your sense of despair and urgency to survive. When you do manage to blow a zombie's head clean off, it's all the more rewarding. The game leaves you scouring every inch of the Police Station for ammunition and health kits, making sure you're always at risk of spending whatever you have in a single encounter. Among the threats you encounter, Mr. X is the best at instilling fear in the player. His ominous footsteps reintroduce fear into completed parts of the map that otherwise might get dull. Unfortunately, he can eventually become tedious if the player lingers too much without progressing and learns how to exploit his poor mobility. Still, I find he's a great addition for the general atmosphere of the game – and atmosphere is very much where this game excels the most. The graphics are some of the best I've seen, helping the player immerse themselves with the core of the game. The lighting is dramatic, with long shadows appearing intimidating around any corner. The environments are also filled with great detail that manages to tell stories of what transpired around the station in a way no amount of dialogue or exposition can. Any player can immediately recognize and appreciate the amount of polish that went into designing this game.

That being said, there are times when the game lulls a bit, particularly regarding backtracking. The movement is very slow, which does work well for early tense hallway exploring. However, not so much when the player begins settling into their surroundings and has to briskly jog across the entire Police Station, past the same corridors and dead enemies you've seen about 5 times already to develop a single roll of film. Another nitpick of mine is that Leon constantly groans when under full health. Walking down hallways without health (and no healing items anywhere in sight) entails hearing a lot of repeated grunts with little silence in between. It's a small detail, but it became a noticeable annoyance at certain parts. Simply increasing the interval in between would be enough to solve this.

Outside of gameplay and presentation, the game does have a few other glaring flaws. The writing has an air of cheap 90s horror, and this is probably by design. This would work better if the game had more of a tongue and cheek tone, but it doesn't. Instead, the 90s charm falls flat as it tries to sell us a cohesive world with serious threats and failed to truly convince me the stakes and drama of the plot. As a result, you have a story really isn't compelling on its own. To make matters worse, Leon's reactions to the horror around him mostly makes him seem like a massive dumbass. It especially gets worse 5 hours in when you've blasted around 100 zombie skulls into smithereens and he's *still* incredulous at the idea of a zombie walking in his general vicinity. I find that a lot of the main characters seem like the victims of a Jason slasher film, but instead of being expected to laugh or be shocked by their horrific deaths, you're supposed to care about them enough to prevent it. Finally, while I praise the game for its tension and pacing, I thought it lacked a deeper sense of dread and terror that really makes a horror game stand out. Perhaps this is just naturally the case with a game that emphasizes so much action, especially in the later half of the game.

To RE2's credit, there are times where the corny 90s vibe actually does land well with me. I like how Leon's character, while a bit dopey, has a naive sensibility that makes us sympathize with him as an underdog in the entire situation. His earnest, idealistic sense of justice stands in stark contrast with the world around him, and it brings much needed levity to the crushing atmosphere. And even the horror tropes that bleed into gameplay (i.e.: zombie lying on the ground actually isn't dead and attacks) are all very welcome additions to the tension despite their predictability. So even with its flaws, the narrative is still entertaining enough to be spectacle to justify the player's actions. It'll certainly keep your attention throughout the suspenseful and satisfying core of the game. It just doesn't excel where it could.

Overall, this game was very good and I recommend it to anyone looking for a polished survival horror experience. Just don't expect anything about the narrative to blow you away -- but you probably weren't if you know anything about many of the Resident Evils that came before it.

While not a perfect Remake, Resident Evil 2 in my opinion is the best game out of the three Resident Evil RE Engine games. 

I have poured so many hours into this game (50 hours last year, and 31 hours this year to finally complete most of the optional content) and it has been a blast every single time to replay this game. Its one of the few games that I've ever been excited to replay it and try to beat it in a faster time. 

There is also so much extra content in this game it's not even funny (4th Survivor, Tofu Survivor, Extra costumes, tons of unlockable costumes, the free 98 costumes and Ghost Survivors DLC, lots of concept art and such to unlock) it definitely has a lot going for it when it comes to replay value and bang for your buck. I honestly don't find the ghost survivors very fun (tons of trial and error and don't really add anything story wise. I don't think they are as well thought out as 4th Survivor) they are still a nice bonus to have and it's just cool to play as other characters. 

Graphics and visuals are still extremely beautiful, but it took me a reshade mod to actually appreciate the colors and fidelity, since the game default has this strange greyish filter over it and the difference is night and day. The horror atmosphere is so tense and amazing and it's some of the best I've ever experienced in the genre. Character models look great with some exceptions (Claires face sometimes becomes uncanny valley but most of the time she looks fine) and the redesigns I personally like. All the monsters look fantastic, especially Birkin and Mr X who are all very intimidating in this version. The gore is also phenomenal in this game, you can see every single muscle on a lot of the undead and Birkin and it's so gross that it's awesome. The dismemberment system is also fantastic and being able to blow/slice limbs off is super cool and a good strategy. The only downside I have is that when I try to run the game at higher framerates, the game begins to stutter and idk why (this doesn't happen to me on Resident Evil 3 Remake, I can play that over 120fps), idk if it's a game problem or a problem on my end, but the game still looks fantastic at 60fps. 

Gameplay is very smooth and responsive, I personally like playing Resident Evil on a controller but I'm sure it also runs very well on keyboard as well, and this style of OTS is personally my favorite. With how tough the enemies are, being able to move and shoot helps a ton. 180 turn is also a godsend, though this isn't new for the series. One of the biggest issues I have personally is dodging enemies (especially bosses) because enemies have large hitboxes/huge grab ranges because the game does not have a dodge. I also think that the zombies are a little too bullet spongey and I would have preferred if they toned it down a bit, but I can see that this was a deliberate decision to make them more of a threat instead of just enemies you run by easily like the original. The boss battles I think are also very hit or miss in this game, most of them just mainly bullet sponges (which they were like in the original too) with G2 Birkin being the only one with a slight puzzle element to it. Speaking of puzzles, the game has a decent amount of them and I think they are on par with the originals puzzles, so nothing too ground breaking here. 

Music is...almost non existent unless you buy the original soundtrack. That I think is the optimal way to play the game, the original soundtrack still holds up so damn good today and it fits this game so well, especially the save room theme which still has that chilling and haunting feeling. 

The game isn't perfect though, I think 2nd Playthrough Scenarios (B) are completely pointless and barely have any remixing done to them, plus the story inconsistencies kinda hurt their relation to the A plot (fighting the same bosses, people dying in two different places, etc), some of the voice acting is really cheesy (sometimes even cheesier than the original). Zombies being able to turn 180 degrees is kinda BS sometimes. The removal of the zapping system kinda sucks. While they did change the aesthetic of some locations, I actually like the remakes interpretation of them. 

Resident Evil 2 Remake is definitely a must buy for any fan of the series and is personally my favorite game in the series. While not a 1:1 remake of the original, it does it's damnest to keep the spirit of the original and succeeds with flying colors. One of the best games of 2019, check it out.

The Resident Evil franchise has gone through a series of changes throughout its years of survival horror. Whether it be changing from tank controls, to swapping enemy types from zombies to merely “infected” enemies capable of wielding forms of weapons. The franchise’s downward spiral however reached its end once the reimagining of Resident Evil 7; a new style of survival horror down in a first person perspective and once again being placed in a claustrophobic household recalling the mansion in the first game.
	Resident Evil 2 remake returns to a survival horror style of gameplay while updating tank controls to over-the-shoulder 3rd person gameplay. While introducing better controls and incredible up-to-date graphics to revive the original games once again. The gameplay is revitalizing as the horror elements have been updosed through incredible lighting and subtle sounds that will have you pointing your firearms in the shadows. The zombies feel more life-like than ever as they stumble in your direction sporadically dodging your precious ammunition. The BOW’s are more challenging than before as they require a specific touch to each of their weaknesses and if not approached carefully, will lead to your demise. All of this however is shadowed to how incredibly well done the Mr. X tyrant proceeds to stalk you throughout the police department, causing several fight or flight scenarios and constantly building tension while trying to discover the secrets being discovered through Raccoon City.
	Its faults are not enough to bring down the game as much as some have to say for it. It could have had a more intricate story or differentiation between the Leon/Claire story besides a few weapons, however it still holds to its title. Resident Evil 2 remake reintroduces a style of survival horror that has needed to be introduced into gaming for some time, and although the game still has some faults, it provides a game worth being invested into and discovering all of its secrets.
I love this remake.

Wonderful remake. It captures the essence of the original quite well. The fact that A and B Story are still present, as well as the true ending, nakes it all the more worthwhile.

The game feels much more tense than the original. Music and ambience, as well as scenic design and attention to detail, enhance the entire experience and make it much more immersive.

Some enemies have become much greater challenges than before, especially due to the new control scheme which gives the player much more freedom in aiming. If one is used to auto-aiming and suddenly having to shoot manually, the difficulty curve is much steeper. There is an assisted mode for this, which locks on to targets, but it does make the game too easy at times. Due to adaptive difficulty, this is not too prominent and only really exposes itself in retrospect.

The new threat of Mr. X added a whole new dimension of horror to the game, as his heavy footsteps can be heard throughout almost the entire wing the player is present it, in conjunction with the wonderful sound desing this makes for an excellent fear factor, as I more than once cowered in a place i deemed "out of sight" enough only to be ambushed by an enemy that is unkillable and able to open doors.

I strongly disliked the X encounters with Claire, for some reason they always felt much more extreme than the encounters with Leon.

The remodeled G is a wonderful sight to behold, and at the same time easier and more difficult to handle, compared to his past self. His weak sopts are much harder to hit, but seem to damage him more.
His encounters are more varied and react to yor behavior, at least a little. Stage four is wonderfully horrifying, as I remembered some sort of four legged toothy creature and was greeted with a gigantic hulk of arms, claws and eyes, which is not as fast but can jump and charge, which requires more precise movement, but not as much. I am unsure if G4 even has a weak point, as I was wailing on it with a minigun that seemed to n barely enough damage to keep it at bay.

All in all, a thrilling experience which I can only recommend. Those remembering the original will have a lot of nostalgia when playing, which may or may not overlap the fear and tension, while new players can easily get into it as the story - as before - starts with you knowing nothing and requiring you to find out everything for yourself.

Final note:
Cutscenes can be skipped, so if you are really just into it for "fun", there is no need to follow all details of the story - but I can only recommend not to skip. Story is well adapted and rewritten.

Horror games are toxic creations. It doesn’t matter what kind of horror they’re striving for half the time. Even the most predictable jump scares tend to spook the bejeezus out of me. And yet, I continuously punish my senses by suffering through horror games. 

But I have a rule - the quality of the game has to be worth the anxiety that will inevitably consume me.

This time around, I played Capcom’s remake of 1998 classic Resident Evil 2. Fortunately, this remake passed my quality requirements by a large margin and proved to be one of my favorite games released in 2019. And that’s despite feeling me with an overwhelming sense of dread from start to finish. Resident Evil 2’s tense atmosphere, gruesome visuals and satisfying gameplay all come together to create an exhausting, exhilarating and memorable survival horror experience.

Premise and Storytelling

I’m aware this is a remake of a game from 1998 and most of you probably already know the premise, but as someone who has not played the original, I’ll outline the premise for my fellow Resident Evil noobies out there.

Resident Evil 2 takes place in 1998 in Raccoon City just after the viral outbreak of the T-Virus, a bioweapon developed by the super evil Umbrella Corporation. There are two campaigns where you experience the story from the perspective of two different characters: Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield. As both of these characters, you find yourself trapped in the Raccoon City Police Department trying to figure out what the HELL is going on and how to get out of there as soon as possible - all while being stalked by the unstoppable Mr. X.

The story is a good time but not the start of the show by any means. It’s campy yet engaging, with fine voice acting throughout. There is increasing urgency as you play through the title, particularly after Mr. X is introduced. The characters that you play as have different motives for being in their situation and give each campaign its own flavor. Leon is a rookie Raccoon City Police Officer walking into the outbreak on his first day on the job. Claire Redfield, on the other hand, is a civilian searching for her brother Chris who has not been heard from for a few days. Leon is duty driven, and Claire has family on the line and is more driven by personal motives. 

I have only completed Leon’s campaign thus far, but have begun to dabble in Claire’s. While both campaigns start the same way, they do divert at certain points. I have been a little disappointed that Capcom didn’t do a better job with continuity. Instead of it being one story from two different people’s perspectives, it often just mixes up character locations to suit the story for each campaign. This means that when Leon should be in the police station while Claire is outside, it just ends up being the opposite. This dampened my drive to play as Claire after finishing up my time with Leon. It doesn’t ruin the actual fun of the game, but it does feel like a missed opportunity.

Gameplay and Graphics

Resident Evil 2 has undergone quite a change since it was first released in 1998. There is nary a blocky character to be found in Capcom’s RE Engine - unless you wear the right skin, of course. On the gameplay front, Capcom took the locked camera and tank controls of the original, pounded them to a fine ash, and reformed it into the third person shooter style that was first introduced to the series in Resident Evil 4. The beauty of this remake is that for me, a guy who never played the original, it feels brand new out of 2019 as opposed to a remake of a game in 1998 - and I’ve heard the same thing from many who did play the original. 

The Police Station and other locations in the game are highly detailed, and the feeling of traveling throughout the police station without a single loading screen makes for a relentlessly stressful and engaging experience. While there are safe rooms where you can take a breather and plan your next move, Mr. X is stalking you throughout the rest. His AI is literally looking for you on each floor of the police station from the moment he first appears, and his footsteps can be heard throughout the police station as he stomps and slams through doors to find you. I hope more remakes strive to find this balance of modernizing the original while retaining the essence of what made the original special to begin with. Resident Evil 2 may have set the bar.

The moment to moment gameplay in Resident Evil 2 is a mix of puzzle solving and survival horror. As is Resident Evil tradition, you often need to find various puzzle pieces throughout one location in order to move forward into the next. This is definitely the case in Resident Evil 2. Fans of the series might love this stuff, but I find this element repetitive. I don’t love backtracking, but I know it’s one of the defining features in a Resident Evil game.

From start to finish during Leon’s campaign, I felt incredibly low on resources. The Raccoon City Police Department is a cramped, dimly lit and dangerous place. Disturbingly, despite being THE Police Station in a metropolitan area, it is seriously lacking in ammunition. There are never enough green herbs, either. This title takes advantage of that and demands that you are careful with the little resources you have to survive the game. Just as soon as I feel like I have truly stocked up on ammo, it is all stripped away from me in one bloody shootout or close encounter with Mr. X, and I’m back where I started. Scared, and alone. 

It was a careful balancing act of not wasting ANY item that the game. I would wager that roughly half of the tension I felt in the game was tied to trying to not waste resources. I think Capcom did an excellent job of giving the player just enough resources to keep the player on their toes, while still ensuring there are enough to finish the game. Regardless of the last fight you were in, you have to continue the game and there are a finite number of resources that you can rely on. This exact thought process is what kept me hooked to the flow of this remake’s gameplay, and what makes it a blast.

Sound and Voice

Capcom succeeded in traumatizing me.

Throughout every area in the game, haunting ambient noises follow your path. Moans. Pipes groaning. Wood creaking. Scratching in the walls. Your own heart pounding in your chest. There’s a steady amount of unease as you play through the game, and it carries into every environment you come across in the game.

The worst part is that all of that is true before the best and worst sound in the game makes itself known. That’s right - Mr. X’s big ‘ol boots stomping down the hall, kicking in doors on his way to kicking your ass. Every single time that man’s boot touches the floor, it shakes my brain. You can tell when he’s above you, when he’s beside you, when he’s directly BEHIND YOU. I’ll tell you what, guys - it’s a tough time out there. 

But don’t you worry - Leon and Claire have loud feet themselves. Possibly the loudest feet, in fact. As soon as you start running, no matter where you are, Mr. X can hear you. And he is coming.

Fortunately, once you stop running and decide to shoot your way through all of the horror, it sounds beautiful. Every gunshot and explosive packs the right amount of punch, and getting that glorious explosive headshot on a zombie is visceral and deeply satisfying.

Rating: 9/10 - Worth It At Full Price

The gist of it is that if you enjoy the Resident Evil series, zombie games or media, or are simply looking for some quality horror - this is a game worth buying. For most, it gives around 10 hours of gameplay for one of the campaigns. With two campaigns, 2nd run versions of each campaign, and a few extra missions sprinkled on top, you receive a lot of gameplay when you buy Resident Evil 2. You can often find it on sale if you are patient enough to wait for the next console or Steam sale, so you can easily add to that value.

What a game!  My full breakdown:

GRAPHICS:  Realistic facial expressions, environments loaded with personality (just like the original PS1), great detail in everything ranging from the monsters to the weapons.  The game looks too sweet at 1440p, 144 fps.

SOUND:  This to me is the key element of any horror game.  The eerie sound of silence mashed up against a subtle air vent rustling, or was that a monster growling........?  Uh oh, better approach that corner carefully in case something tries to eat me.  The score kicks up in intensity when you engage in battle, which further fills the situation with dread.  The only negative I can say about the sound is the voice acting (or should I say script) almost sounds like a teenager wrote it at times.  The voice work itself is great, but there's waaaaay too much swearing to the point where it just feels overplayed.  A good "F-you" can give a situation that needed punch, but it loses meaning when it gets thrown out every other sentence.

GAMEPLAY:  The most important part of any game.  This being a remake of the original RE2, comparisons will naturally be made here.  Gone are the tank controls, in favor of the RE4 style over-the-shoulder view.  Therefore, combat is more particular and aiming based, allowing the user to perform head shots, or slice off limbs, or come up with other creative ways to stop the undead.  The overall environmental layout mirrors that of RE2, puzzles and everything, though they do kind of hold your hand in some spots to guide you to the next objective.  Controller and keyboard/mouse options both play wonderfully.  Added is a much welcomed "Assist Mode" that can help players recover health automatically over time, aim assist in hitting critical areas on enemies, and generally easier difficulty.  For those who enjoy punishment though, the Hardcore difficulty gives players just enough ammo, health items, save opportunities, and harder enemies to get through to claim victory.  The end of each game is graded based on the difficulty, time, and number of times saved on a scale of C through S+.  Obviously getting that S+ will earn you better goodies if you're skilled enough to achieve it.

REPLAY:  As you can see by the number of hours I poured into this game, there's a lot to see and do!  Being  a master at it, I'm now able to get through the game on Hardcore difficulty in less than 2 hours, but my first playthrough was closer to 7 hours.  There are 4 different scenarios in the main campaign to play through, so you can see where all that time goes.   After the main campaign, there are additional Ghost Survivor challenges to complete, as well as weekly challenges issued by Capcom.  To fully 100% the game, you're tasked with performing certain challenges to unlock all the artwork, character models, and infinite weapons.  Some challenges are as easy as "Shoot a zombie in the head 10 times" or as hard as "Get S+ rank on Hardcore mode".  

So who is this game for?  Anyone who likes the Resident Evil series, newbies who have no idea what Resident Evil is but lover horror, and even those folks who are terrible at third person shooters (thanks Assist Mode!).  There's something for everyone here.  Truly a masterfully crafted game.

This is a fantastic remake and a worthy successor to the original.  The gameplay is modernized without taking away from the atmosphere and dread, a feat I didn't think was possible.  The graphics and sound design are excellent.  Play it in the dark with headphones on if you want to ramp up the tension.  

Two quibbles, and they are minor.  First, there is no dodge mechanic when trying to run past zombies, and "sprint" is a mild jog at best.  The lack of dodge is especially jarring if you've played the RE3 Remake and have gotten used to that little dodge roll saving your skin.  

Second, the A/B scenaries (or New Game and New Game 2nd as it appears in the menu).  While much of their narrative does dove-tail nicely, the illusion of dual paths falls apart spectacularly, and not just because all the puzzles reset and have their solutions changed.  Barring their final fights, Claire and Leon fight the *exact same bosses* in the *exact same places*.  It... doesn't make any sense, and I really wish they'd done something as simple as swap bosses into different arenas so as to pretend these are the *exact same* battles  happening again.  

Those two things aside, I highly recommend this title to any Resident Evil fan, old or newcomer.

Pros:
+Game is a true survival game; ammo is scarce, so sometimes an ankle shot and a run is your best choice.

+Zombies have multiple ways of attacking. They'll even come at you crawling on the ground!
+The Tyrant, aka Mr. X, keeps stalking you, it's truly terrifying and it keeps you on your toes.
+Blowing up zombie heads with a satisfying squelch!
+The is a lot of good (unlike the original) voice acting and it triggers naturally in gameplay!
+Epic bossfights that are super intimidating but not too hard : just hard enough (on normal difficulty).
+Examining items up close to open them or find details, or just for fun.
+Campaign has some welcome surprises (hacking with one side character and sneaking around with another)
+Story is super cheesy like a horror B-movie but in a good way and it's entertaining.

+Ada Wong is hot.

Cons:
-Some boss fights were a bit repetitive and not all that memorable.
-A little too much gross stuff all over the place. (sewers especially, yuck)
-Lickers. Just... everything about them. You can't sneak-move so you can't exploit their blindness either.
-Side-stories are lame. There's no dialog or voice-over of any kind, so the characters have no life to them. It's only for shooting more zombies, or rather speeding past them.
-No co-op. It was pretty awesome in RE5 (although not much else was).
-The number of bullets zombies take is ludicrous and arbitrary. Sometimes 2 shots blows up a head, or 12.
-Mr X doesn't want to go into save rooms. Would have made more sense for the doors to be lockable and impenetrable to block him off instead. 
-Second playthrough only has you visit a couple of new rooms. Otherwise, as well as in side-stories, you're mostly just retreading old ground. It also has a weird alternate reality thing going on.
-If you run out of ammo and there's a narrow passage filled with zombies, you're pretty much screwed! 
-Police chief is a total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, jeez. How can you work for this guy Leon???

Bottom Line :
Possibly the best Resident Evil I've every played! RE4 is a close second, mostly due to annoying QTEs.

Highly recommended for anyone!

I went into this not expecting much more than a bland semi-enjoyable single player experience with a touch of horror I've come to expect from Resident Evil in recent years but I was really surprised by the quality of this project and I wanted to talk about it.

Even though this is considered a "remake" this is definitely not the same game as the original at all. There's tons of new content and the whole map is basically remade, none of the items retain their previous locations (besides maybe 1 I can think of off the top of my head) also none of the puzzles are the same. The map changes are really incredible, especially the Lab and Sewers. These areas were finally fully fleshed out and turned into the places they imagined them to be in 1998, RIP Train yard though. The characters were beautifully remade and look fantastic! The graphics are very life like due to photo scanning real objects that are used as models (like the burger in the intro). The sound design is very accurate with their binaural sound design that makes sound feel more 3D. The story remains relatively similar with some minor changes. One thing I wish they did was have Leon and Claire in contact with each other more often. This is a missed opportunity IMO, especially since the original had them working together a lot and their goals were more apparent. Claire was looking for her brother that punches rocks for a living and Leon wanted to help save everyone that he could. They worked together to get things done. In this reimagining it feels like each characters story is isolated and selfish a endeavor more than a common goal. The goal remains the same however but it is not really executed on until later. This game is actually scary! (crazy right?) The new rendition of the zombie is the best in the series, by far. They stumble and trip all over the place. I was pretty surprised at how hard they were to take down and makes them feel like an obstacle more than just a chore like previous entries. It really brings back a lot of the survival horror aspects of the game deciding If It's worth spending ammo or just running by since It can take an entire pistol mag to down 1 zombie if you so choose, most of the time It's better to just shoot a leg off and keep moving. That brings me to the dismemberment system. This tech is awesome! If you shoot a certain limb consecutively it will eventually fall off and limits the zombie, for instance, if you shoot the arms off a zombie it can no longer grab and if you shoot the legs it won't be able to walk anymore and can only grab your ankles. This system is a welcomed addition and adds a lot more depth to each encounter, not to mention the animation of the rotting arm / leg slowly disintegrating off their body looks amazing in the most disgusting way. [spoiler] Mr. X makes his return seemingly coming out of no where at all times and following your every move. You'll know by the music that plays when he's around. He stomps around the R.P.D looking for you and tracks you by sounds you make. He is actually walking around too, you're not just hearing a sound effect of his footsteps, you can sneak up behind him if you're quiet enough and watch how he searches every nook and cranny for you. He's a very scary seemingly impenetrable force that will keep you anxious for when he's going to pop out next... that being said, I can see how he could be a bit annoying for some players, he kinda over stays his welcome at certain points and then doesn't appear at all for others. [/spoiler] The attention to detail is what really sets this game apart The beginning sequence when Claire ducks down so Leon can shoot the zombie behind her, the picture of Rebecca in Wesker's desk and the "Wellcome Leon" sign with the extra L on a near by desk just name a few. 

Overall, this game is beautiful and the best entry in the series in a long time.

A great remake of a great game and a worthy addition for the Remake Age of gaming we're currently living in.

I still remember most of the original from 1998 and if we're nitpicking I could list a lot of differences. But this is a remake, a reimagining for a modern age (naysayers just might call this dumbing down) and Capcom did an excellent job. A remake for the textbooks. It seems Capcom took all the best bits from various Resident Evil games and mashed them all together into one giant, savory and tasty sweet potato mash.

The visuals are top notch. The new RE Engine works wonders, scales well with options, is incredibly well optimized (I've had absolutely no technical issues with the game, not a single bug or a glitch, played on i7-7700, RTX2070, 32GB RAM and an SSD) and breathes life into the characters, monsters and human, and environments which are now packed with details. From sewers full of garbage and subtle writing on the chalkboards to the horribly gazing and blinking eyes on the G Monster. Lighting deserves a special mention and really brings the tension in. Characters are highly polished, move and act like normal human beings (still in the uncanny valley, no doubt there, but they're very well done) and facial animations are great.

Audio, ambient sounds and voices are impeccably done, but there's that little something missing about the music. It lacks those fear inducing strings that the original had for an added layer of stress. 

Gameplay mechanics are updated for the new generations and they're brilliant. The characters are not pieces of concrete slab on wheels, but move and respond with brisk pace. The aiming mechanics are improved, meaning you can actually aim (you couldn't in the original) which makes applying excessive high velocity blunt trauma to zombies very satisfying. Don't expect them to go down quickly though. With the improved aiming come improved, resilient zombie bullet sponges. They can absorb a lot, even on the easiest difficulty, but shooting them in the arms and legs takes them off, leaving them armless or crawling and making them easier to avoid. The inventory management is pretty much the same, fiddly with limited item slots that are upgradeable with inventory bags, if you find them. Each character has different weapons that can be fitted with modifications, but some of them increase the space the weapon occupies in the inventory. The bizzare puzzles with door hunting, jeweled boxes, weird keys and lost medallions are still here, but are not a large hindrance to progress. Everything is clearly marked and written, just open your eyes. Mr. X, a greyish terminator wannabe, pops out at inopportune moments making your life a bit more stressfull and cementing his echoey footsteps in your mind. He can be brought down temporarily, but at great cost to your inventory, if you have it to begin with. Easier to run and find another path. The Lickers are still the scariest product of Resident Evil's minds.

There are 2 main stories, Leon and Claire. Finishing them opens up the 2nd run stories, which are slightly different with different main item placements. There's also an unlockable 3rd story (absolutely worth it to finish this just for the bonuses you get) after doing the main ones. The story itself is ok, it's satisfying, it's fun to follow, but it's not any kind of remarkable accomplishment. The entire Resident Evil story is pretty much a convoluted mess. To quote one character from the game, "Nothing dies down here". It's well worth finishing both normal stories and second runs, they're different enough and you'll get a few new angles on the story. And the game is made to be played multiple times. As you learn the map layouts and key item placements, and you'll need that knowledge if you're planning to finish the stories with an S rank, you'll see your game completion times go down. There are 3 difficulty modes, Assisted (which makes the game rather easy even if you have no experience), Standard (normal mode) and Hardcore. Hardcore features significant changes. There's no autosave, you need to find ink ribbons to be able to save normally and the enemies are tougher. But even hardcore shouldn't be much of an issue when you're armed with knowledge from your past runs.

A free DLC, Ghost Survivors, was added to the game, adding 4 new what if stories featuring some side characters from the main game. They're somewhat short runs, slightly more action oriented get from point A to point B, but are fun and each one adds a different obstacle, like exploding poison zombies.

A great survival horror game, slightly toned down on the horror, but updated for a faster, modern age with slick visuals and controls, still retaining everything that made the original such a remarkable game. Well worth a play and if you've waited this long to get it, you can find it rather often on a great discount, putting the price around €20.

Take a peek inside the newly opened [url=https://steamcommunity.com/groups/thecabinetofcuriosities/discussions/0/2272575584124463561/][b]Cabinet of Curiosities[/b][/url] if you like to walk off the beaten path and only sometimes return to the main roads. You might find something worth exploring. And if you do, thank you for the visit.

[url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/30168383][b]Follow the Average Achievement Hunter Curator for reviews and useful information on Steam achievements[/b][/url]: There's a few collectible achievements, a few missables (defeat a boss with x timer left, finish the game without opening an item box and a few more) and 2 hardcore/speedrun achievements (they can be combined, if you're good). I can't judge how hard the speedruns are going to be for you (as of writing, I've done the Assisted speedrun as a test run in around 2 hours 30 minutes and I've done Claire's story on Hardcore), that depends on your patience and willingness to learn the layout of the game, but they're not super easy and if speedrunning's not your thing, the S rank times might be cutting it close. Everything in the normal game can be done on Assisted difficulty which makes the game a much more casual stroll, but speedruns need to be done on Standard or Hardcore. The 4th Survivor extra story and No Way Out from The Ghost Survivors are rather tough and will definitely need a few tries, even if you check a video walkthrough.

[h1] Disclaimer: Despite the negative review, this is more of a neutral review. Due to Steam's "Yes/No" choices, I am inclined to say "No" instead of "Yes". However, do keep in mind this is by the tiniest of margins [/h1]

To summarize the review very briefly, I have only one thing to say, really.
[b] It is a good game. It is a bad remake. [/b]

First, I will describe the positives and negatives of the game without referencing the original Resident Evil 2.
Then, I will look at things that Remake improves over the original and likewise, things that Remake did worse.
Let's begin

Positives:
1. Graphics and majority of things to do with graphics. 
To me, graphics are among the least important things. To some, they are not. RE2R looks great from visual perspective. I have nothing else to say really, it's just very pleasing to look at, yes.
2. Gameplay that (for the most part) manages to combine some of the REmake (2002) elements such as defensive items and over-the-shoulder camera of RE4 (2005).
3. A very good implementation (probably one of the few times where it was not annoying) of an unkillable stalker enemy archetype. Mr. X is the highlight of the game, for good reasons, too. 

Negatives:
1. Extremely low replayability, even if you decide to ignore the original. More on that in the section where I compare 1998 and 2019 RE2. The only DLCs for extra replay value the game's got are 4 extremely short-ish DLCs, one extra game mode with HUNK and that was it.

That's about it for the first part. You will see that the list is relatively short, because to me, looking at RE2 2019 without comparing it to the original is impossible.

Let's talk in comparison now. 
What REmake 2 did better:
1. Added realism to some aspects of the story (but then decided to weirdly crank up the awkward "comedy" in some others), case in point: 
[spoiler] The scene of HUNK and his team ambushing Birkin. Excellently crafted scene, improved vastly compared to the original, whilst not taking away the charm of the original and on the other hand, the final escape scene, where the trio exchange extremely out of touch remarks, when Sherry says "You guys can adopt me". Darkside Chronicles did that part so much better, I do not know why they felt the need to make it so painfully awkward. [/spoiler]
2. The zombies and their sheer sturdiness. If you have seen RE3 1999 intro, you saw those zombies not dying and thinking to yourself "Just shoot them in the head, you fools!". Once you try it here, you quickly realize this is not an ultimate solution. Whether intentional or not, this really helps justify the deaths of the entire RPD force to "just zombies"
3. The orphanage addition. Probably the highlight of the remake and my personal favorite lore place in the RE2R. Exceptionally creepy, because once you realise the true idea of that place, the horror dawns on you. Well done for the most part, from lore standpoint. 

From here on out, though, I will start listing things where Remake goes wrong.
1. Let's address the elephant in the room, the branching scenarios are nuked. Completely. There is almost no difference, there no longer exists an idea of Leon A / Claire B or Claire A / Leon B branching. It's essentially cut out and the "2nd" scenario, if you can call it that, is essentially unchanged, regardless of who you play. Yes, you get occasional notes from the other character, but there is no alteration of the story of any kind.

You will think "Oh, but that's not a big deal", and in reality, it is — why did RE (2002) manage to keep all the details in down to every last thing (almost) and RE2 2019 suddenly can't do that? 
Subtle jab from the author here, it's this kind of attitude that led to the disaster that was RE3 2020. 

2. Very subjective, but as the time goes on, undeniably present downgrade of the main cast. I wouldn't know how to even call it, but essentially almost every main character in RE2 and RE3 remakes is somehow altered to look like a parody of themselves.

While we are at the topic of character consistency, if you played RE4R, you know that game tries to sell Leon as this man who's traumatised, yet, if you observe him in RE2R, he seems to just not care. Whether this is a coping method of some kind or not, it does not go well with how much the game tries to portray him as a traumatized person, who tried to save people and failed, thus getting wracked with guilt. 

Long story short, the modern writing of the remakes is somehow worse and less interesting than the originals, which are said to be lacking in that department. 
I could write a thesis on that, but generally speaking, somehow RE2R and RE3R became cheesier than the originals (excluding the very first RE1) and people that used to take jabs at the latter, are now praising the former for... the same cheesiness, just with a different flavor.

3. This one is far less subjective and a continuation of one of the points from the negatives part above.
Let's just say RE2R did not bring enough to the table to make it stand out as a good remake. 
Refer to RE 2002 where they introduce crimson heads, that dramatically alter the way you are meant to be playing. You can no longer gun down every zombie and be home-free, in that game you had to either be fast with your moves or risk having them come back as much scarier Crimson Heads and even though you could outrun them, the creeping fear of them just being able to come back was enough to make you want to reconsider, especially on higher difficulties. 

What did RE2R bring in terms of genuinely new things to the table? Defense items are an idea copypasted almost entirely from the same RE1 2002 that I just mentioned.

4. Second biggest downgrade that is almost undeniable - the atmosphere, that was well crafted with sounds, soundtrack AND ambience is ENTIRELY gone in Remakes. You get a "realistic" atmosphere, but it is null compared to the original, where you have the wind howls mixed in with the cries of the undead, alongside dreadful music that played, really adding to that tension. NONE of that is present in the Remake, which is probably one of the biggest objective downgrades, in which remakes flat out lose to originals.

5. The biggest flaw of them all, when compared to the original is the sheer potential that COULD have been, if the game was not rushed or just made in a rush (because that's what it feels like). 

Extended scenario system, added cameos of characters from other RE games (Outbreak comes to mind first and foremost), improved gameplay mechanics that would drastically alter how you are meant to navigate the precinct. The possibilites were all there and instead we got the bare minimum.

In essence, when you look at it and realize how much community let Capcom get away with in RE2R, the disappointment, that was RE3R, makes sense, alongside the current mainstream line (RE7-RE8)

What's the best way to summarize this game then? 
If you are a hardcore fan, who grew up on the classics and was looking forward for a grand remake, where things would just be NEXT level, you will most likely be left with a sour aftertaste, like you've been cheated out of something.
If you are new to the series, this makes for a decent enough game that earns your money.
If you are casual to the series and are indifferent to the changes made, you can still enjoy this game.

As for me, I will quote what I already wrote, I think it is a good game, but a bad remake.

In a world where a lethal virus turns people into rotten beasts that roam around the dead cities while screeching at their top of their lungs, I boot up Resident Evil 2 Remake where things look a bit more hopeful so far. Such a beautiful game! You can spend hours scrutinizing the detailed, perfectly underlit, somewhat open-ended environments and smooth models. Just make sure to keep an eye on the wandering Inspector Gadget who would punch your teeth out without a second thought should you stop paying attention. I also loved the famous transforming boss, Doctor Birkin, another perfectly carried over classic RE design.

I always felt bad for the poor sod. While nailing the big attractions, the remake is all about details, like that separate animation for the rare occurrence when two zombies grab you at once! Cool, eh? I appreciate it when developers put thought into such seemingly unimportant stuff. Of course, none of this would matter if it didn't look and control so well. The gunplay, in particular, is almost too comfy for a horror game. And it was one of the several reasons, first of which is my own lack of balls, why I personally didn't find my experience that scary.

The game is Intense in all the right places, yes, but not very oppressive in tone. Maybe the absence of cinematic camera angles plays its role, too. It may sound blasphemous, but I wouldn't mind more jumpscares, in general, and additional surprise monster spawns while backtracking, just to put on some more pressure and to drain the excess of ammo. To boot, the typewriters are on every corner, there are autosaves every couple of minutes... you get the picture, I robbed myself by playing on Normal. But go easy on me, this was the first more or less classic Resident Evil I played since the third one came out! I wasn't even sure if I still got it. Boy, did this one crack my dusty shell.

Either way, the peculiar atmosphere of a zany zombie flick is still there and this is what actually counts, in my opinion. And don’t get me wrong - the game wasn't too easy, just not soul-crushingly brutal. The original never was, too, but this one is a great deal more accessible to the general public, which is fine by me. Want a deeper horror experience that is somewhat closer to the originals? Play it on Hardcore, they even got Ink Ribbons there. I'm such a chicken for avoiding it. But hey, that would be a great reason to replay the game after a few years! Ultimately, I enjoyed it as a fun, complex action-adventure. It's a different take with a different vibe, but the same [mostly] unerring  formula. Polished, clean, classy... mwa!

What i liked:

Absolutely one of the coolest game worlds I've ever had the pleasure of exploring. The atmosphere is mysterious and ominous, and immersing yourself is easy. I'm not even a usual fan of survival horror games, but this was enjoyable all the way through.

The puzzles are rewarding and none of them are too hard. I love the way the game teases you with something locked behind a glass case or prison bars, and then makes you go out into the rest of the level to look for the way in, all while fighting zombies/running for your life. When you finally get to go back and collect that weapon it gives a serious feeling of accomplishment and reward. 

The bad stuff:

There is rarely anything in this game that makes me wish for a change.  One of the only things I didn't like in this game was that once you pick a difficulty you can only adjust it downwards after that. If you die a lot to one enemy the game will prompt you to lower your difficulty to assisted, and then you're stuck on assisted for the rest of your save file. This is a pretty annoying feature, but not game ruining or anything. This is pretty much the only reason it's not a 10/10. 

Another issue is how slow your character moves, but I don't know if I'd really call it an issue, because it's intended.
