Far less flamboyant than the later entries, RE2 takes us back to those simple days when Leon wasn't an unstoppable somersaulting action hero, and merely a few zombie bites could put him down for the count.  This is [i]true[/i] survival horror (not that I have a problem with action RE; actually, I friggin' love it).  Movement is slow and cumbersome.  Ammo is limited.  Even knives -- I primarily used mine to fillet downed zombos and save shells -- break readily, and unless you play it close, it's easy to be left with [i]nothing[/i].  The creatures in this game are complete bullet sponges, so stay calm and watch your aim!  It's no mean feat to center your reticle on the noggin of a shuffling undead when he's swinging it around like Will Smith in the [i]Fresh Prince of Bel Air[/i] opening.  

What you've probably heard most about is Mr. X: an unkillable, wrinkly terminator guy in a cute detective hat who pursues you, slow-stridin' Jason Vorhees-style, through select portions of the game.  If you've played Haunting Ground or Clocktower 3, it's nothing quite so elaborate; you can't hide behind credenzas or distract him with fine chocolates, only run away (and smack-dab into the claws of a licker), and if he catches you, he simply karate punches you into the afterlife with his big meaty fist.  [b]Hi-yah![/b]  It's that stressful kind of fun that opens up your adrenal glands and makes you scream "I hate it!  I hate it!" like a small, spoiled child.  But you love it, really, because it makes you feel [i]alive[/i] inside, and that's what these games are all about.  Watching your brother/friend play is just as engrossing as playing yourself.

If you're an RE fan, make sure to go through both segments.  They're pretty similar, but each has its own supporting characters, one radically different side-story in the middle, and a unique final boss.  If for some reason you can only play [i]one[/i], pick Claire's.  It's got the most meat.

Speaking of meat, the opening shot in this game?  It's a super close-up of the most disgusting, detailed, squishiest, greasiest fast food burger I've seen in a video game.  That's got to be a first!

Ok, I feel this review is relevant to all the recent Resident Evil remakes, beginning with 2 in 2019. They are all good games. They are all even good Resident Evil games. Are they replacements for the original Resident Evil games? No, they are not. That doesn’t mean you can’t still love and enjoy them for what they are.

Understand, these remakes are not like the Dead Space remake of 2023. That game is so perfect a remake, that there really is no reason to ever play the original Dead Space unless you miss the original voice actors for Hammond and Kendra. Everything about the Dead Space remake is better than the original. That is not the case with the Resident Evil remakes.

It really comes down to what kind of Resident Evil gamer you are. Do you like the running and gunning Survival Action of OG Resident Evil 4, 5 and 6? Then you will really like the new remakes and probably not play the originals, if you ever did. However, do you love the puzzles, keys, clues and Survival Horror of the originals? Then you probably won’t really like the remakes. While the (currently) 3 remakes do still have those aspects, they are not nearly as prevalent as they were in the originals. While the Resident Evil 2 and 4 remakes have expanded the environments and even added a few new places, Resident Evil 3 remake actually took places away, most notably the Clock Tower area. I did appreciate that you got to play as Carlos more than once, and the Hospital was expanded to more than just 3 rather small areas, but I did miss the Clock Tower. I do know why they took it out, because it was an area that was purely OG puzzle and keys. Didn’t really fit the new direction of the remakes. So, I understand why people are complaining about that. The ones that complain about all the Nemesis events being scripted apparently don’t remember that ALL of the Nemesis events in the original are scripted too. Look at and any decent walkthrough of the original game, or the wiki. They can tell you where all the encounters are going to be and what prize you can get from Nemmy when you put him down, temporarily. So I don’t get that complaint.

Still, the remakes are very good games. You just need to take a few minutes and figure out what part of the Resident Evil games you loved the most, and play those versions.

The Remake is a remarkable improvement over the outdated original game. 
It is the pinnacle for the Resident Evil series, where most of the mechanics and atmosphere have been enhanced beyond a mere graphical update. 
This game is accessible to all audiences, regardless having played any Resident Evil title in the past. 

[h1]Positives[/h1]
(+) [b]Gameplay[/b]
The aiming system has been made to fit modern standards, where precision and player movement is possible. Having the game in third person relieves the claustrophobic nature of the original game and grants freedom to the player. Although some of the puzzles can be tedious, they provide another engaging challenge. 

(+) [b]Graphics[/b]
The graphics are marvellous for 2019 and is optimised for most systems. However, the game does benefit from running on a 60fps cap due to scripting and event triggers. 

(+) [b]Atmosphere[/b]
Although the Original game’s music is much more eerie, the dark corridors of this game create a tense world where danger lurks everywhere. The lack of resources and inventory space adds urgency to decision-making. 


[h1]Negatives[/h1]
(-) [b]Obvious Gameplay Padding[/b]
The Secondary runs are mostly the same with minor tweaks to events, item locations and guns. There is hardly any intertwining between Leon and Claire’s story. 
Ada’s segment is a Point-And-Click adventure to bloat the game an extra 20 minutes. 

(-) [b]Forced Stealth[/b]
It is an effortless way to add tension and is a truly terrible gameplay mechanic. 

(-) [b]Random Elements[/b]
Random elements of the game become apparent and frustrating during Hardcore runs, where a misstep can lead to replaying an entire chapter. 
These include zombie spawn locations, number of bullets to kill enemies, stuns and enemy attack patterns. 

(-) [b]Poor DLC implementation[/b] 
The Original game’s soundtrack is much more eerie and terrifying than the Remake’s soundtrack. However, it can only be unlocked through DLC when it should have been in the base game for free. 

(-) [b]Minor Settings Bugs[/b]
There is no monitor selection for multiple-monitor set-ups. The game will automatically run the game on the primary display. Although this can be worked around by changing your primary display, it can be annoying. 
HDR increases the saturation on everything in the monitor. This makes the steam overlay and applications appear neon-like.

Videogame remasters are very proliferate, but actual, full remakes are rare. Not for the Resident Evil series, though. Capcom has, for better or worse, milked this franchise for years and more than once rather than advancing the storyline they've engaged into retelling the same story through different perspectives (e.g. Operation Raccoon City) or through a different kind of gameplay (e.g. Umbrella Chronicles). The first actual remake was for the original game, which got a remake for the Gamecube, which was later remastered for newer generations.

That REmake did things right. It took the original concept, setting, story and characters and updated them for the then-current technology. The only thing that didn't really change much was the gameplay style, with static cameras, exploration and tank controls. But, after Resident Evil 4, the gameplay in the series changed. It became more action-focused, it relied less in exploration and used an over-the-shoulder camera that became the standard not just in the series, but in the industry for most action titles.

This new remake is a bit of a mix. It takes the RE4-style camera, control and gunplay but keeps the exploration-focused 3D metroidvania style from the classic games with more focus on survival than action. For the most part, it works wonderfully, but if you're too used to action games you're gonna have a bit of a hard time adapting. Enemies are fast, but your character isn't. Ammo is scarce and enemies are tough, so you can't solve all your problems by shooting like a gun-totting maniac. You need to conserve ammo and get really good at headshots in order to survive. You need to figure out what's the better weapon for every ocassion and you have to swallow your pride and learn to run.

One major gimmick of the game is Mr. X. While this character, a tall, implacable, seemingly invincible strongman was merely a bit of a mini boss that would ocassionally show up in scripted sequences throughout one of the game's two scenarios, here he shows up in both and he can be terrifying. He will randomly show up when you least expect him and follow you until you manage to lose him or stall him. It can get a bit aggravating, though, when you're trying to just pick up an item or do a puzzle and he shows up and forces you to run away. But as soon as you learn your way through the map and use it to your advantage, you can do well without getting too frustrated. Besides, he only shows up in certain sections of the game, so you have more freedom to explore in the rest.

The game does a great job of working on its own and as a remake. If you're not familiar with the franchise, this is a good starting point. The game expects you to be familiar with either the first game or the original RE2, but it really doeesn't matter if you're not. The story is simple enough (there's a zombie apocalypse in town and you need to find a way to escape), so there's no room for confusion.

A possible low point is that the two-scenario model of the original game is not as deep here. The original game had you pick one of the scenarios to start and once you finished you'd play the second one, while actions taken in the first one would affect the second one (you could make things easier for your first character and harder for the second character or viceversa, depending on your choices). Your characters would also ocassionally meet or talk throughout the story and sometimes travel through entirely different areas. If you reversed your original choice and played with the characters in the opposite order you'd have new differences in each scenario. In here, though, this is all very minimal. The paths taken in both scenarios are almost identical, your characters only meet once before the end and your actions in the first scenario are irrelevant to the second.

There are still enough differences between both characters to keep things fresh, of course. Like in the original, playing as each protagonist will have you meet different characters, using different weapons, engaging in different puzzles and ocassionally fighting different bosses.

Despite the scenario issue, there's a lot of replayability here. Certain challenges will help you unlock powerful weapons and new costumes. There are also a bunch of cosmetic unlockables like concept art and models that can be obtained by reaching certain milestones and goals. Plus, there are a couple of extra unlockable modes, each with their own characters to play as and their own goals. There are dozens of hours of fun to be had.

Graphically, it's quite impressive. The lighting, sound and design give the game a creepy atmosphere that no game in the series has managed before. It also runs quite well in middle-of-the-run PCs. It certainly runs better than RE7, despite using the same engine and having a few larger areas.

This is just an amazing game. If you played the original you pretty much know what to expect with this game except with better graphics, new puzzles, new areas and more. I won't spoil appearances and such, but know that it's very faithful to the original game.

Pros
+ Great survival horror gameplay. It's a third person game which on the first playthrough will have you thinking about ammo consumption, what zombies to skip, how to approach enemies, saving your healing items, etc. and even better if you play it on hardcore mode you will have to think where to save because you need to use ink ribbons to do so. I believe it's pretty hard to get softlocked in this game in hardcore mode, but still, you have to think about what you're doing in general to not screw it up. If you want a chill experience and you just want to enjoy the story then you can play the game on assisted mode which is equivalent to a very-easy mode. Other than that, you can play the game on Standard or on Hardcore difficulty.
+ Decent puzzles. They're not annoying and you will have to think a little in order to solve them (not too much actually.)
+ Replayability. The replay value in this game is awesome. You have four main game modes: Claire A, Claire B, Leon A, and Leon B which are all similar but will keep you entertained for a while if you liked the gameplay. You also have the Ghost Survivors extra modes which will test your capabilities and decisions.
+ Graphics. This game is really beautiful. It's powered by the amazing RE engine. Not much more to say. This game looks amazing!
+ Voice Acting. No, you won't hear the original RE2 voice actors with their cheesy lines (which I absolutely loved.) This game's dialogue has been fully rewritten and the new voice acting is superb in my opinion. There are still some cheesy lines but I really enjoyed it.

Cons
- Music. This is my own subjective opinion. I didn't like the new soundtrack at all. To me it felt like the new music was just filler music with absolutely no soul. Save music room has been toned down and in some places it's non-existent, HOWEVER, if you have the DLC you can switch to the original soundtrack which also adds the original sound design (menus and all) which is great if you don't like the new music and sound palette.

Conclusion
This game is not also true to the original, but it also adds new elements that were not in the original such as really good voice acting, new gameplay mechanics, and new story elements. If you loved the original RE2 then I'm pretty sure you will have a blast playing this game because this game is just pure nostalgia, only prettier. If you are new to the series, you will also probably really enjoy this game. Just be sure to read what happened in the original game, or better, if you can afford it play the original one before. Go buy the game! It's awesome, trust me!

First of all, the zombies in this game are fantastic. They're slow and clumsy, but manage to keep you on edge by being completely unpredictable and almost impossible to kill. Combine that with the cramped hallways and barely lit rooms, and you've got yourself a tense atmosphere that leaves you constantly thinking on your toes. While many games give you hordes of zombies, this game makes it worrying enough to see two of them.

The limited inventory space, items and save points that are scattered around the map, the cramped hallways, bullet-sponge zombies combined with limited ammo create this air of tension and keep you constantly making decisions. The maze-like structure of the map have you planning routes, and as you go through the game you start to familiarise yourself with the police station - the safest rooms, the hallways you dread. The map effectively becomes its own character as you uncover its secrets and history. And Mr X of course. Consistently hearing him, planning around him, dreading him. 

Gameplay-wise, the only thing I don't like is the boss fights, and frankly, I wish this game had none of them (or far fewer) as they kind of go against the whole philosophy of the game. I would recommend to stick with them though, because it's worth it.

The game's story isn't perfect. It's got some weaker, campier parts but I understand that it is trying to keep to the original game and there are plenty of genuinely good moments mixed in as well. The timelines of the two main characters are a bit confusing (you [i] have [/i] to play both storylines to get the full experience), and I wish Leon and Claire interacted with each other more, but overall a really, really solid survival horror game. Probably the best zombie game I've played.

[h1]An Outstanding Remake[/h1]

[i]A deadly virus engulfs the residents of Raccoon City in September of 1998, plunging the city into chaos as flesh eating zombies roam the streets for survivors. An unparalleled adrenaline rush, gripping storyline, and unimaginable horrors await you. Witness the return of Resident Evil 2.[/i]

[h2]Story[/h2]
Leon and Claire arrive in Raccoon City on the same night and quickly find the city in chaos, overrun with zombies. After briefly meeting, they are separated but continue working to escape the city while uncovering what happened.

Inside the Raccoon City Police Department, they discover that most officers have been killed, and clues point to Umbrella as the cause of the outbreak. The virus spread after a biological experiment went wrong in the Umbrella underground laboratory (Nest) beneath the city.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Resident Evil 2 (2019) is a third-person survival horror remake of the 1998 game. This remake reimagines the gameplay and story for modern audiences. The tank controls and the fixed camera angles are replaced with a dynamic, over-the-shoulder view that zooms in while aiming.

At the start of the game, you choose between two main characters: Leon S. Kennedy or Claire Redfield. This choice changes how the whole game plays out—you’ll see different stories, explore different areas, use different weapons, and even face a different final boss depending on who you pick.

Each character has their own partner: Leon teams up with Ada Wong, a secretive government agent investigating the shady Umbrella Corporation. Claire, on the other hand, works with Sherry Birkin, a young girl being hunted by a terrifying creature.

The game focuses on exploring and managing your supplies carefully. You’ll move through connected areas, searching for important items like ammo, healing herbs, and puzzle pieces that help you move forward. You can inspect items in detail to find hidden clues, combine things like mixing herbs for stronger healing or gunpowder for ammo. Once an item has served its purpose, it can be safely discarded to free up space.

Each character has their own set of weapons. Leon uses guns like a shotgun, magnum, and flamethrower, while Claire wields a grenade launcher, submachine gun, and her special “Spark Shot” weapon. Both start with a basic handgun that can be upgraded over time.

For up-close fights, you can also find backup weapons like combat knives and grenades (either regular or stun types). These can help you escape when grabbed or deal extra damage in a pinch.

[h2]Enemies & Bosses[/h2]
Zombies are the most common threat you’ll face. They’re slow but unpredictable, staggering in erratic patterns that make them difficult to hit. If they manage to grab you, they’ll try to sink their teeth in—and don’t assume they’re down for good just because they’ve fallen. Unless you destroy the head, there’s always a chance they’ll get back up.

Lickers are a much deadlier foe. Though blind, their heightened hearing makes even the faintest sound dangerous. They’re far faster than standard zombies, able to lash out with their long, whip-like tongues or slash viciously with their claws. Their attacks hit hard, and they can leap great distances to close the gap. Taking one down requires significant firepower.

Throughout the game, you’ll encounter several boss battles, each one testing your reflexes and aim. Most bosses feature exposed weak points that must be targeted while you dodge powerful, clearly telegraphed attacks.

The Tyrant is a constant, looming presence. A relentless and invincible B.O.W. which can only be staggered or temporarily incapacitated. The Tyrant relentlessly stalks you through most areas, forcing you to rely on stealth, careful listening, and strategic movement. Only safe rooms offer brief respite as you gather the items and solve the puzzles needed to progress.

These are just a few examples of the enemies you face.

[h2]Environment & Scares[/h2]
The game world might seem straightforward at first, but it’s cleverly built so that different areas connect back to each other in surprising ways. This looping design keeps exploration interesting and makes the world feel more real.

The horror really comes through in the level design—tight hallways, cramped rooms, and low lighting make it easy to feel trapped as enemies close in on you. Most of the time, you’ll be moving through dark, shadowy areas with only your flashlight to guide the way, which adds a constant feeling of tension and unease.

Adding to the fear is the Tyrant, a massive enemy who never stops hunting you. You’ll often hear his heavy footsteps echoing down the hall, forcing you to think fast—run or try to hide?

Exploring the environment is made easier by an excellent map system. Rooms that still have items to find show up in red, and once you’ve collected everything, they turn blue to show they’re cleared. When your inventory is full, uncollected items are automatically marked on the map for later retrieval. Doors are clearly labeled too—red for locked, blue for unlocked, and special key symbols (like a Spade or Club) show what key you’ll need. It’s an incredibly smart system that helps you keep track of what’s left to do and where to go next. Simply put, the map is one of the game’s best features.

[h2]Visual Design & Sound Design[/h2]
One of the most unforgettable parts of the game is the Tyrant himself—both in how he looks and how he sounds. Dressed entirely in black—a heavy trench coat, combat boots, gloves, and a wide-brimmed hat. His pale, wrinkled skin and hollow lifeless white eyes really evoke a sense of unnatural menace. His movement is stale and decisive, with loud, metallic footsteps echoing through the halls, letting you know he’s getting closer long before you see him. The music intensifies when he’s nearby, cranking up the tension. Every time you run into him, it feels personal, nerve-racking, and genuinely scary.

The game’s visuals go far beyond just creating atmosphere. Enemy damage looks and feels realistic—bullets rip through flesh, and you can even blow off limbs, which changes how enemies move and attack. This attention to detail makes every shot feel powerful and satisfying.

Your health is shown through a small heart rate monitor in the inventory menu, giving you a subtle, realistic way to tell how hurt your character is without breaking immersion.

[h2]Constructive Criticism[/h2]
There’s little to criticize overall, though in certain encounters I found myself wishing for a dodge mechanic.

[h2]The Verdict[/h2]
Resident Evil 2 Remake is a brilliant reimagining of a classic and easily one of the best games in the series. The story and characters are engaging, and playing through both Leon’s and Claire’s campaigns gives you fresh perspectives, so each playthrough feels unique.

Combat is satisfying and impactful—every weapon feels different, responsive, and powerful. Ammo is limited, so every shot matters, making battles tense and exciting. The Tyrant stands out as the game’s most terrifying and memorable enemy, always keeping you on edge. The crafting system is simple but rewarding, letting you combine items and plan strategies without slowing down the action.

Exploration is a real highlight. Smart level design and a user-friendly map make collecting items, solving puzzles, and navigating interconnected areas both satisfying and immersive. The game world feels alive, and discovering its secrets is genuinely fun.

In short, Resident Evil 2 Remake perfectly balances horror, action, and strategy, delivering a thrilling, tense, and unforgettable experience from beginning to end.

Resident Evil 2 is a fantastic survival horror game that understands the true meaning of survival horror. Unlike Resident Evil 5 & 6, this game makes you save your ammo and strategize each play with the constant swarm of zombies and other enemies including Dogs, Lickers, Plant 43 Zombies, Lesser G Monsters, and even the bosses such as The Tyrant (MR. X) and G-Virus infected William Birkin. 

With the constant fear of the unknown and further developing evil within Resident Evil 2, it has an even further escalated fear and intensity built through the games fantastic location of the RPD, Sewers, Umbrella research facility and a continuously unsettling atmosphere built through the games stellar lighting.

Capcom and other game developers also remembered what Resident Evil is within RE2, Due to the constant savory and conservation of ammo and further resources, making it feel like Resident Evil is finally back to it's routes of terrifying Survival horror, rather than fully fledged dark and gritty action games (unlike Resident Evil 5, 6 and to a certain degree Resident Evil 7: Biohazard). With a constant sense of terror and danger, progression through the game is made more difficult yet investing with the games puzzles scattered through out whether they're to reveal and obtain items and or attachments for weapons, or to progress through the story. A great example of this is the particularly frustrating yet clever chess piece combination door fuse system found in both playthroughs (Leon A and Claire B, or Claire A and Leon B), before entering the Umbrella lab underneath Raccoon City.

Sadly, the game did every now and then suffer from a few texture issues and glitches within the game that made gameplay either hysterical or particularly frustrating.

None the less, Resident Evil 2 is an almost perfect remake of an iconic and already phenomenal game released in 1998. While the game feels familiar and is much the same as its original, it adds a unique flair through its new and improved graphics and gameplay style while also being its own thing that feels like more of a re imagining than a remake. Terrifying, complex and incredibly fun, Resident Evil 2 is a return to form for the beloved Resident Evil series that I have loved since I was a young boy. It stands on a pedestal to join the greats within the franchise and shows fans that even with a few hiccups, Resident Evil is here to stay and will always pull through to deliver a truly horrifying video game experience.

[b]Resident Evil 2 is both terrifying and addictive as it can be.[/b]

The dead have risen, as fuzzy memories being brought back to life, and all the associated nightmares are now flooding back.
Nostalgia may entice old fans, but the entire experience in Resident Evil 2 is a brand new one that surprises from start to end.

The plot are almost brand new. Rookie cop Leon and college student Claire (sister of Chris Redfield); regardless of whose charecter you choose, there is little doubt that a feeling of dread is ever present in this new iteration of the infamous city.  All the rain, dirt, grime, and blood permeates through the surfaces, and it is no coincidence that you will never feel quite safe. Something has gone terribly wrong, and you are living it with each and every tentative step you take.

Smart use of your limited resources, knowing when to fight and when to run, and preparing for upcoming encounters can be the difference between getting past a gauntlet of zombies, and staring at the “You Are Dead” screens over and over again. Headshots no longer guarantee your safety, and the struggle intensifies when Mr. X decides to show up and ruin your day.

Of course, it would not be Resident Evil without some puzzles. From collecting chess pieces to opening ancient passageways with medallions, these are not exactly headscratchers, but they belong here in true Resident Evil fashion.

Seeing the gnarling jaws and slithering guts of the dead up close, one cannot help but admire the amount of work and dedication of the developers in making such a realistic representation of guts and gore, while simultaneously fearing for your life.

Resident Evil 2 is a perfect love letter to all the hardcore fans of the survival horror classic, and an impressive entry for newcomers to enjoy all that made the original so special. This is the definitive entry to represent survival horror, and Resident Evil 2 continues the course of making Resident Evil special again.

A pretty solid game that nails all the right aspects of the Survival Horror genre and wraps them up in an all around pleasant package in terms of graphics, music and gameplay.
Resident Evil 2 (2019) continues the trend of the franchise of abandoning the "action" aspects for a return to the roots of the "survival" aspect. As the player navigates through the story and faces the horrors of a zombie outbreak in a masterfully portrayed urban setting, resources and ammo will be few and scattered around, adding to the feeling of uncertainty and dread. A feeling that will be intensified by the fact that, for a significant part of the game, the player controlled character will be stalked by an unstoppable monster, with no way of permanently getting him out ouf the way. 

The story follows that of the original RE2, but it's more polished, and has a more "real" feeling to it, thanks also to the excellent voice acting. Characters and setting are well designed, with great attention to detail.

The game offers a solid replayability value. The two main characters have slightly different storylines and carry different weaponry. Each of them can also play a second run which follows a slightly different scenario with different item and enemy placements. In addition to this, there are a several extra game modes, shorter than the main story but peculiar in their own way, featuring other characters. There is also a set of in-game achievements that unlock game modes, concept art and character models (in addition, of course, to the common Steam achievements).

This is definitely a game I would recommend, especially to fans of the survival horror genre.

It's not that spooky like RE7 or Outlast obviously (since it's in 3rd person).

GRAPHICS: Feels like watching a movie. Its graphics are spectacular! So is its physics! I don't remember a game in which characters walk thorough stairs without bugs. Zombies' physics are very particular as well in my opinion (though I've never seen a real one). Nice cinematic/cut-scenes as well. To be fair about it, I gotta say characters' lips move badly though, but that wasn't a big deal for me.

GAMEPLAY: It has inventory slots like RE7 (not like RE4), and I personally find it exciting for such a survival game. Also there's a stash in safehouses you can store your items in, so don't be worried about managing your stuff. It also has manual saving, which can be written via those popular type-writers found in safehouses. Saving system works a bit differently in each game difficulty you choose.
The shooting system is smooth and great. You have to use your ammo a little efficiently though (well it's a survival game).
You don't have a scaled health bar, neither the zombies even bosses have. BUT your health has three steps: Fine, Caution, Danger and there are healing and craft-healing items to recover your health... not like CallOfDuty that screen turns red, you hide behind a tree, and there you go, you're healthy now.
Everything looks so well detailed, for instance you can find the corpse of a zombie wherever you've killed it whenever you're back.
Things in this game feel realistic. Except for zombies... I guess...

STORY: This makes the game replayable when you can experience the story from 2 perspectives (Leon or Claire) with their own different features (like RE4), though most of the story will be the same in both, but there are enough new things and characters to keep you entertained. Also you can have a second scenario (2nd run) for both Leon and Claire where there are very little bit changes in gameplay.
There are Extra game modes (free DLCs) which you can play after finishing the main story. So you can finish the game 4 times and experience some different things each time!

Lacks: Its achievements/trophies may make you feel bored if you care about them; you have to play the game at least thrice to get 100%.

Just gonna throw this out here: I'm a newcomer / foreigner to the Resident Evil franchise and my friends have been banging on about it for quite a while. So when it was on sale I decided to pick it because it looked like a fun 3rd person survival horror.

So in terms of gameplay its a mash of survival horror, puzzle solving and a bit of stealth mixed in I would say. The gameplay is probably the best reason to buy this game. Its no joke its really good. A similar game that came to my mind when playing this was Luigi's Mansion for the GameCube and yes it did come out before it, but the original game also came out before I was born so there's that. The gameplay revolves around a main objective that has sub-objectives (usually obstacles blocking your path) and your job is to find a way to get to the next area while cautiously capping zombies and other biological terrors and solving elaborate puzzles. I have mixed feelings on the Tyrant. On one hand he is crazy scary when he's first introduced with no cutscene, my first instinct was to duck in a saferoom and granted he doesn't enter those. He becomes a nuisance as his thunderous footsteps echo throughout the building. Sometimes he could be on a different floor or outside of the room you're in but you could never tell which I guess is both a good and bad thing I suppose. As for graphics, they are top notch with beautifully rendered models and outstanding gore effects that a lot of work went into. There is however a grey filter that ever so slightly washes over the screen but this can be reduced in the settings menu.

The story centers around 2 main protagonists, Clair Redfield and Leon Kennedy. I can come to a reasonable conclusion that you don't need prior context of the story from earlier Resident Evil games. Leon, a rookie cop arrives late to his new job at Raccoon City and Clair who's failed attempts to contact her brother attempts to visit her in person. I have played through both scenarios A and B for both characters for a combined run of 4 playthroughs and never once had I been disinterested in the game.

There are some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ though that are absolutely not deal breakers. First I have to say is the mobility which is kinda sluggish especially around stairs and because of the game mechanic where you can't counter on stairs making evasion difficult. There's also a few obscure puzzles and the 2nd boss fight in the game that was also a pain to deal with, even after many playthroughs.

There's a plentiful amount of endgame content that aren't locked behind DLC. The DLC advertised on the storepage is weapon skins, character models and an unlock everything pass.

Final score is gonna be a strong 9.5 and is probably the best game I have played in the last 10 years and this isn't an understatement! Clearly a masterpiece.

Incredible. One of the best games of 2019, possibly the best remake ever made.

“Resident Evil 2” was a classic back in the day, when it was a staple of the original PlayStation's line-up. The 2019 remake not only re-affirms how deserving the title is of that status, but positions the series for an unprecedented level of success in the current gaming landscape. 

The plot is much the same as the original, as are the locations, puzzles, and methods of progression. The characters are all here. There are changes to how the A & B scenarios play out and interact with each other, but I'm not convinced that's an altogether bad thing. The game looks and sounds amazing. Lighting is gorgeous. Models, rendering and mo-cap are on freakin' point. The dialogue is still nothing to write home about, but the voice-acting is very good. 

And the doors... Doors remain a signature element of the experience, but their contribution to said experience is fundamentally different now. Lickers are still terrifying AF. Mr. X is more intimidating than irritating; his inclusion instills a welcome sense of urgency in certain sections of the game. The zombies manage to do most of the heavy lifting in the 'scary creatures' department (not altogether true in the original) and that's awesome. Even without zombies and lickers and other things, the locations inspire creepiness on their own. Atmosphere: the game drips with it. 

What the game does not drip with is music and I'm undecided on how I feel about that. On the one hand, music can be a force-multiplier for mood. There are definitely scenes that felt as though they could have been greatly enhanced with the inclusion of specific musical pieces to heighten drama/tension/anxiety. On the other, there's a certain kind of unsettled-feeling that comes from being forced to listen to what's going on in your surroundings without distractions. With no musical intrusions to overwrite the creaking floorboards, pattering rain on the windows, groans of nearby zombies, the sense of immersion offered thereby is unparalleled.

“RE2: Remake” opts for a dynamic difficulty adjustment (DDA), meaning the game will assess your performance and progress, then increase or decrease enemy behavior and durability accordingly. Having a hard time? Enemies become slower and take more damage from your attacks. Doing really well? Now enemies are quicker, less predictable and take less damage from you. Another change: POV. The remake really benefits from the 'over-the-shoulder' camera as opposed to the fixed camera/environment combo of the original game. Now you can better see what's in front of you, but you're still at the mercy of whatever may be creeping up behind you.

While that change in perspective adds a great deal to the perception of game play, it's not enough to shake the dismal movement controls. I understand wanting to limit player options in the movement category as it can induce a feeling of desperation not possible to achieve in any other way. Too much control or recourse in those close-encounter situations diminishes (or outright dispels) the sense of dread or anxiety so crucial to sustaining horror. Also, 'dodges' can be hella difficult to code/implement correctly. But when you've seen someone posses the requisite agility to climb over a pile of debris or squeeze through a window or shimmy under a narrow opening in a shutter door... only to then watch that same person struggle to turn a corner in a hallway or unsuccessfully navigate a series of upright shelves in a timely manner because some invisible part of their body is sticking to one of the shelves... 

This brings me to my only real sticking point with the game: driving an upright brick. The player is just fast enough to escape or outrun many enemies they'll have to engage, as long as the player is deliberate in movement choice and exercises environmental awareness. That approach is perfect for helping create/maintain tension. In other words, the remake preserved the ratio of enemy:player movement speed, which is fantastic. What is not fantastic is feeling like you're trying to maneuver a big block of tofu in a narrow doorway, when said block of tofu is invariably more interested in sliding across the door onto the wall rather than passing through the open doorway right in front of it. 

Seriously, guys? All these dynamite changes to the core mechanics of the original game, even abandoning the 'tank' style movement orientation for a more intuitive control scheme, and you still leave the character's model collision as wonky as the original? You got a 'pass' on that in the original because you were inventing the genre. But to do that now? DELIBERATELY? It's exasperating.  

Equally exasperating: the DLCs. Their inclusion was pretty great, but they felt like they should have been cooler than they actually were. Exception: the 4th Survivor is AWESOME (possibly my favorite section of the game). Finishing that run will leave you feeling like a f*cking champion. The rest of the “Ghost Survivors” add ons were too inconsistent, however. One run through may result in failure at the second room, while the very next attempt yields success with no damage and minimal shots fired. It's one thing for the game to change the placement and behavior of enemies; to do so is in-line with the stated purpose of DDA. This makes the game more challenging which in turn increases the feeling of satisfaction and accomplishment when you finally complete the scenario. 

The trouble with the Ghost Survivors is they're often over-tuned. Sometimes those DDA changes require the player to make fundamental alterations to execution with NO commensurate adjustment of resources.  For example: there are four enemies in the room. You need to get to the other side. You probably can't dodge/run past all of them and you'll be effectively forced into combat with two of them. Here are 8 bullets. Figure it out. Maybe you do, maybe you don't. Those 8 bullets are enough to deal with the two enemies you're being 'forced' to fight, since each enemy is likely to take 3, possibly four rounds to stun/dismember. Two or three attempts later, you come back into the same room. But this time, due to changes in positioning and behavior, you're forced to fight all four enemies... with the same 8 bullets you had the first time through. That's not a challenge so much as the game giving you a big ol' middle finger. 

The changes themselves are good, provided the player is properly provisioned. Otherwise... it just sucks. Don't get me wrong: the Ghost Survivors are absolutely worth checking out. They just might not be worth banging your head against the wall in order to complete. At least accept a warning for how much abuse you're likely to take and plan accordingly.

9/10, two thumbs up all day long. Easy recommend. Eager to see how much RE3 benefits from a similar level of TLC.

It may be unbelievable, but Capcom actually did it: they crafted an over-the-shoulder RE experience without replicating the tropes of RE4/5/6. And it’s not just any RE game: it’s the complete remake / reimagination of what is considered to be one of the best in the series: Resident Evil 2. People have been dying to get their hands on it for a very long time, ever since any so little information regarding potential development has been revealed and a 1-shot demo later, the full thing finally made its way onto PC, X1 and PS4 in January of 2019: could there be a better way to start a new year in video game industry? And though I only got to dive in myself a year later, I can only imagine the look of joy on everyone’s faces when they fired it up on release day: I honestly don’t even know where to begin.

Unlike the 2002 remake, this one is leaning more towards a reimagination, rather than the former. You’ll be seeing familiar places, but in a different order and redesigned to some degree. Either way, the atmosphere is excellent through and through, all created by the photorealistic RE engine (as previously showcased in RE7) with fancy lighting effects, shadow play and a subtle soundtrack, though it is arguably weaker than the original and just less memorable in general. As for attention to detail, Capcom really went all out: you’ll see Leon / Claire facial expressions of  aching pain, Lickers being more sound-oriented, zombies featuring more hitzones, the list goes on and on. The controls are smooth, the animation work is slick and there are no door loading screens to interrupt the flow of the game, it’s just wonderful. And with all the options in the graphics menu, it’s easy to adjust the settings to your system, thus avoiding performance issues. Did I mention you could skip all cutscenes, at any time? 

Moving on with the changes in the game, there is tons. For starters, it’s not just the same with an OTS camera and improved graphics: there are new puzzles, new areas, some expanded (the sewers), some reworked and with mechanics first introduced in RE3, such as gunpowder mixing and 180° turns, though all that existed in RE7 as well. Remember the defense items from 2002? Yup, it’s all here: grenades, flashbangs, knives, you name it. However, you are free to use them whenever you feel like and not just during an attack. The gun parts have too met some changes: certain guns get more than one, they can take up an extra slot, they are always detachable and both characters can find them, so it’s no longer exclusive to Leon alone. Unlike the weapon slots in RE7, there is no preoccupied inventory space that can only be used for specific items so that’s yet another convenient, little change. Speaking of inventory, it does get increasingly bigger by finding pouches scattered throughout the game and their amount depends on the difficulty you are playing at. Oh yeah, the difficulty settings: no, the hardest does not have to be unlocked by playing on Normal first, a trend in modern games I really want to disappear. And if you always wanted RE2 to be hard, then Hardcore is the setting to go with: resources are scarce, the enemies hit hard and saving is done the old-fashioned way with ink ribbons, as it should be. In my opinion, the original never required you to try and manage your items as they were always plentiful and the actual Hard setting wasn’t included on PS1, the platform I first played it on. But here, you’ll be holding onto every bullet you have in your clip and think twice before you shoot: if that’s not survival horror at its finest, I don’t know what is. The Ada / Sherry segments are completely new and with their own mechanics to add some variation, but admittedly still not as exciting as our main heroes, especially Sherry’s part may not be everyone’s cup of tea. And last but not least, the voice acting: it feels more natural and not as exaggerated, I don’t think the 90’s cheese would go well with the rest of the game so I’m happy with these changes. 

I’ve clocked in about 14 playthroughs total, meeting all the necessary requirements to unlock the overpowered guns with unlimited ammo, filling out the ranking chart and battling my way through the extra modes, do I need to point out how much replay value it contains? And yes, the B scenario might not be as good as in the original due to the lack of its zapping system, but it’s “unique enough” to squeeze out more hours of gameplay, despite the rushed intro and G5 as the only extra boss. Additionally, you have access to the free Ghost Survivors DLC, it functions in the same vein as the Hunk / Tofu but with unlockable accessories, which I really would love a lot more if they were usable in the main game. And how could you forget about the mod support, who wouldn’t want to dress up Claire in a bunny suit and have her run through the zombie apocalypse with jiggly physics? But I’m getting a little sidetracked :’)

Was there anything I think should have been done better? Well, the idea of Mr. X being a predator pursuing the player sure is a shocker first time around, but becomes ultimately redundant when you find out how exploitable and how little of an obstacle he really is, it’s like it feels tacked on. Death animations, as awesome as they might be, should be either skippable or pausable, I don’t want to wait for it to finish everytime I die. On a side note, Ghost Survivors really needed a RESTART option, quitting to the main menu whenever you thought you did horrible was lame. Instant death enemies are the only reason I wouldn’t recommend to start the game on Hardcore, as it might force unaware players to replay longer bits over and over. 

Capcom has been killing it during the last few years and RE2R is no exception, it seems their greatest strength is in reshaping old gems that already have a dedicated fanbase and with all the new modern features, it would win a lot of new fans as well. And enough fans gather it did so now we’re eagerly waiting for the remake of my personal all-time favorite to drop: Resident Evil 3.

A pretty great game, and a candidate for best remake. A few key pros to discuss:

A faithful retelling of a classic survival horror scenario
Excellent difficulty curve. Provides just enough resources and clues to keep going but not so much that it feels like a mindless drudge.
Highly optimized. Can run well on a variety of configurations, and looks great as well.
Great sound design.
Extra "what if?" scenarios and minigames that add a bit of depth to the established universe, as well as extra playtime and value.

Some cons:

It varies quite a bit from the original in the sense that there are some continuity issues when playing each scenario from A to B.
Not as much variation between scenarios as there could have been, especially with Mr. X being in both scenario A and B.


Overall, I would recommend this game. It played flawlessly on a Ryzen 5 1600 with a Vega 56 and 16gb of RAM. Recent replays on a Ryzen 5 3600 with faster memory have put me past the 144 FPS threshold, so those seeking to run the game at 1080 with very high framerates should have an easy time with appropriate components.

William Jennings Bryan (March 19, 1860 – July 26, 1925) was an American orator and politician from Nebraska. Beginning in 1896, he emerged as a dominant force in the Democratic Party, running three times as the party's nominee for President of the United States in the 1896, 1900, and 1908 elections. He also served in the United States House of Representatives and as the United States Secretary of State under Woodrow Wilson. Just before his death, he gained national attention for attacking the teaching of evolution in the Scopes Trial. Because of his faith in the wisdom of the common people, he was often called "The Great Commoner".[1]

Born and raised in Illinois, Bryan moved to Nebraska in the 1880s. He won election to the House of Representatives in the 1890 elections, serving two terms before making an unsuccessful run for the Senate in 1894. At the 1896 Democratic National Convention, Bryan delivered his "Cross of Gold speech" which attacked the gold standard and the eastern moneyed interests and crusaded for inflationary policies built around the expanded coinage of silver coins. In a repudiation of incumbent President Grover Cleveland and his conservative Bourbon Democrats, the Democratic convention nominated Bryan for president, making Bryan the youngest major party presidential nominee in U.S. history. Subsequently, Bryan was also nominated for president by the left-wing Populist Party, and many Populists would eventually follow Bryan into the Democratic Party. In the intensely fought 1896 presidential election, Republican nominee William McKinley emerged triumphant. Bryan gained fame as an orator, as he invented the national stumping tour when he reached an audience of 5 million people in 27 states in 1896.

Bryan retained control of the Democratic Party and won the presidential nomination again in 1900. In the aftermath of the Spanish–American War, Bryan became a fierce opponent of American imperialism and much of his campaign centered on that issue. In the election, McKinley again defeated Bryan, winning several Western states that Bryan had won in 1896. Bryan's influence in the party weakened after the 1900 election and the Democrats nominated the conservative Alton B. Parker in the 1904 presidential election. Bryan regained his stature in the party after Parker's resounding defeat by Theodore Roosevelt and voters from both parties increasingly embraced the progressive reforms that had long been championed by Bryan. Bryan won his party's nomination in the 1908 presidential election, but he was defeated by Roosevelt's chosen successor, William Howard Taft. Along with Henry Clay, Bryan is one of the two individuals who never won a presidential election despite receiving electoral votes in three separate presidential elections held after the ratification of the Twelfth Amendment.

Capcom's remake of Resident Evil 2 is something that overall left me feeling underwhelmed. The problems with the game lie with its outdated gameplay and many other issues.

To go further into it the main issue with this game is replayability, I must confess whilst you can clearly see I have put a decent number of hours into this game this was mostly due to me trying my best to like the game. You purchase a game and you try to get your moneys worth, whilst I tried to do that I can't say I have many fond moments playing this game. The game clearly lacks proper different scenarios of the original, hence why replayability isn't that good then the issue of familiarity the game doesn't change from one play through to the next. Essentially the only real reason to replay the game is to speedrun, but we all know that the vast majority aren't doing that and it is just a very small niché portion of the playerbase who do the speedruns.

Gameplay, the gameplay isn't fun it leaves a lot to be desired you will go from 1 zombie tanking 10 shots to the face and then maybe the next only taking 1 for it to be downed. Due to that issue it makes gun gameplay feel very underwhelming almost as if you're firing a pea shooter. I think it make sense to mention DA (Difficulty Adjustment) this a somewhat good thing to have, but I think for the most part that you shouldn't be turning a bog standard zombie into a bullet sponge when you're constantly tagging the head. DA works in the fashion that If you're cruising through the game easily and collecting a lot of resources that a potential boss fight will take even more damage (that's fine by me) and this also applies to zombies and other enemies. Final thing to say about the gameplay, I feel as if the game focuses too heavily on hide and seek instead of taking enemies down i.e. do you bother wasting 15 bullets to kill one zombie or do you just flinch it and run past to me I don't find it fun doing that.

Now onto controls, I get the fact that Capcom are wanting to appeal to both sides of a nostalgic audience and a new one but how can the controls be so janky and awful? The character moves at a snail pace and I'll get into that later and the game has a fair amount of stupid things in place which haven't been fixed. For example, Claire when damaged down to caution she runs faster than intended then the issue with stupid things such as aiming in and out whilst going down stairs to move faster. Granted, I'm definitely nit picking with that, but any other huge triple A game you would expect to see things that weren't intended to be there removed what's the difference for Capcom who couldn't even give us two completely different stories with unique bosses for each character!?

Length of the both stories are abysmal and I can delve into this further, whilst your first playthrough might be a bit longer this is very common because you've not figured out the puzzles yet. What happens when you've played the game you know the puzzles and all the locations, you end up with a very short game both stories can easily be completed in a few hours Claire 2 hours and Leon 2 hours and a bit. Now, take out the inventory management and constant back tracking how long would the game be then? Yes, that's right the game duration is fabricated with constant back tracking for items and dealing with what items to hold it's so so silly for a 2019 game to be this outdated. 

So I somewhat touched upon this next issue a little bit, the game lacks variety of enemies when you compare it to the original there is obviously a fair chunk of enemies missing. The question is why? We pay the premium price year in and out and we can't get more than a Zombie, Dog, Licker, Ivy and G-Type enemy and some of those enemies you only encounter a couple of times.

Final thing to somewhat trash the game on, animations and sound effects whilst the majority it is good there are 2 things that annoy me. How can you possibly have 5 or more different handguns and they all have the same sound effect!? Absolutely lazy! The animation issue I have is with the guns, I previously stated that gun gameplay feels underwhelming well the animation recoil etc pretty much ties in with how lacklustre that is.

There are definitely reasons to buy the game, but for me its a big no! The game is a play it once and be done with it, I tried to make more of it but I can't really same anything other than I wasted hours trying to like it like the majority of reviews. A trend you will find is a lot of people rating the game positively haven't played it for a long time. The game does atmosphere correct and it does a fair job on giving all the nods to the original but I'm sorry there is just far too much wrong with this game.

If you were a fan of RE2 back in the day, playing this remake (or re-imagining, which I feel is a more apt description) is like spending time with an old friend you haven’t seen for two decades and finding the things you loved about them have flourished over time. It’s a textbook example of how to do a remake of a classic game right, nailing the nostalgia factor and doing near-flawless justice to the original with some creative additions to the presentation and story that pay homage to the source material while building upon its foundation. The RE Engine runs incredibly well and is a testament to what Capcom can accomplish when they really put their backs into it - the graphics & animations are gorgeous and the optimization is top-notch, featuring outstanding performance, very few bugs or glitches, and great ease of modding (with hundreds of fan-made mods ranging from humorous to smutty to enhancing, including one that allows the game to be played in first-person perspective à la RE7). The over-the-shoulder camera, fluid movements, and tight gunplay are brilliantly executed (no more fixed camera angles or stopping to aim or turn), and little flourishes such as the camera zooming in and shaking when you’re grabbed by an enemy really add to the game’s horror and sense of immersion. Audio is also incredible and highly detailed - the score complements the game’s thick atmosphere while paying homage to the original’s, little audio touches like bullets hitting zombie flesh are very satisfying, and the way ambient sounds reverberate through their environment are realistic and add to an already engaging experience.

The story here is essentially the same as the original's, save for some subtle, well-implemented changes that modernize it and give the characters - especially many of the supporting ones - a lot more depth. There are four variations of the campaign, including Leon’s and Claire’s intertwining A and B stories (which are largely the same but have enough differing scenes, characters, areas, and weapons to make them worth playing through), in addition to the Hunk survival mode, and though an arcade mode à la Mercenaries from RE5 & RE6 would've been a lot of fun and bolstered the replay value, there is just so much here to love for old fans and newcomers alike as well as a lot to look forward to with the upcoming RE3 remake and a potential RE4 remake in the future. This comes with my highest recommendation as a top contender for 2019's GOTY and one of the best videogame remakes ever created.

I feel torn with writing this review. With remakes I usually put in my opinion about how the remake removed something or added something and how that made it better or worse. This game, its something new all together.

This is a zombie survival game where you'll find yourself rationing rounds and health items. There are puzzles which are relatively easy to solve (at least for me) in order to progress through the story. There are two main characters, Leon and Claire, whom you pick at the start and have the option to play as the other in a slightly altered more difficult second play-through. You are also stalked by the ever-vigilant Mr. X in both scenarios.

Now for my analysis on remakes and RE2. (spoilers ahead)

Usually when I play remakes, they don't feel like a completely different game. Sure graphics are done differently or maybe items have been moved to different areas but the narrative always seems to be the same as the original.  The RE2 remake feels almost completely different while maintaining the same narrative and making some things feel better explained. It is honestly what I always wanted in a remake. The original had a lot of weird little things I had always wanted to explained differently or at least better and to my surprise the remake hit almost everything on the head with creepy precision. Annoying as it was I loved how Mr. X was a constant threat (there were a few scripted moments but they felt seamless with everything else). I appreciated how Annette (Sherry's mother) while just as twisted as the original has some redeeming qualities to her even if they come at her end. Chief Irons got his creepiness cranked to eleven and far out-weights his original.  Now I am not saying that the original is not worth playing, I feel it still is if only to appreciate a remake of this quality.

Being someone who grew up with the previous generation of videogames (early 90s-late 2010s), I'm extremely wary of amything that falls within the "remake" group, since I find the concept a mere excuse to justify the lack of fantasy and originality that pervades the movie and videogaming industry nowadays. However, Resident Evil 2 managed to make me change my mind, although partially, about this.

RE2 Remake is very likely what Capcom and all fans of the series wanted it to be if they'd had today's technology back in 1998. Everything has been remade in order to give the player a genuine feeling of fear and leaping into uncharted ground, but most importantly I like the way the main characters were revisited: we no longer have Leon and Clair bumping into and strolling around Raccon City with a badass attitude, but they're genuinely taken aback by all the ongoing mess in the city - and dialogues and face expressions hugely help in delivering this to the player.
I've also highly appreciated the idea to set all the places from scratch, in order to detach the remake from the original game as much as possible.

I can only recommend this game, but you should play the original one still!

A much more thrilling, improved and breathtaking remake of a survival-horror classic that is already a masterpiece.

Resident Evil 2 (2019) reminds us of how the survival-horror scene was started when the original came out in 1998: intense atmosphere, heart-racing story, terrifying and uniquely designed monsters, lack of ammo and aid, cease of action-packed sequence, more puzzle-solving levels, etc. 

Compared to the original, RE2 Remake has improved in every aspects, from game play, to visuals, audio and acting. The graphic looks stunningly beautiful. Characters, from both main protagonists - Leon, Claire, to minor characters, such as the burger-eating truck driver; all have extremely detailed and realistic design and facial animations. The over-the-shoulder camera angle and character movement made the game play so much smoother and immersive. Combat is rather simple. but satisfying thanks to realistic audio design and reload animation. 

However, there are elements that could be improved further. For example, puzzles could be more challenging and variable. Voice acting is decent, but some of the dialogue are slightly cringe-worthy and end up being unfunny, dried one-line jokes. Both of Leon and Claire scenarios could have been linked closer by implementing details caused by player's choices. To illustrate: some puzzles that were solved by Leon, could have been removed and replaced with new ones instead of being reused in Claire's play through. 

Overall, this is a topnotch and incredible retold version of an already awesome survival-horror classic. - 8/10

Resident Evil 2 Remake was an easy top 5 for me of 2019 (even have it on PS4 and spent 100+ hrs easy on it since launch). To call it the greatest remake though would be throwing the remake of 1 under the bus sadly but I cannot find a better way to enjoy RE2R from the sheer design of it all. As games become more and more packed with tedious quests, big terrain with little substance and weak combat mechanics that create a void of time sinking and numbs the brain, RE2R comes in and says "I got replay value, great combat, intricate level design and fan service done tastefully well." I have played the original for comparison and while I respect it a good deal (being a big fan of Hideki "Blocked You" Kamiya's directorial work) and even seeing better aspects like scenarios done well, RE2R just has alot to it that feels better overall if some parts a lateral move at worst. Let's get to the nitty gritty though:

Graphics: Game looks great. Not a big graphics fan and prefer art that will hold up over the passage of time, but the RE Engine might be my new favorite engine from any game company. It sacrifices super high fidelity for performance but the texture work on the gore is fantastic. The details on things when you bump the texture mesh is quite impressive despite how unnecessary it all seems. Lickers look hideous and creepy, zombies look convincing, the models on Leon, Claire and the other humans are fine (though Marvin's facial/motion capture is quite superb). Only downside is some higher textures in some areas bring down the framerate and can jaggy up the screen very slightly.

Audio: Almost perfect. Mr. X's footsteps are nail-biting tense and consistent to listen to. The binural audio really enhances the experience and having a pair of headphones makes everything feel real. Sounds coming from the game really sound easier to tell and make for tense situations. A zombie gasping and trying to grab you unexpectedly still makes me jump on my latest playthroughs. The zombies sound goofy yet at the same time intimidating. The music of the remake is the only issue, as it mostly is forgettable barring Mr. X's theme. The original score is used in very small parts of the new score but if you have the deluxe version or want to pay a bit extra, the original soundtrack is availible to play as well and is superior in all but ironically Mr. X's theme (although it's not bad at all).

Optimization/Performance: So yeah this game has a great sense of optimization. Barring that whole Denuvo nonsense, the game runs well and has a sizeable graphics option. You even have images in each option that you can tweak to what you read along with the space your PC has to run it. On the PS4 Pro, the game would run at mostly 60 fps with some slips here and there. The motion blur and other stupid things in here are visually noisy and hurts my eyes, so turning them off unlike on consoles helped alot for me. Crash wise I experienced none. 

Gameplay: a standard 3rd-person shooter that uses a classic blueprint borrowed from all the games Leon Kennedy was in for RE (2,4 and 6). The police station and exploring it of course is RE2, the dark and comedic tone of RE4 and the gameplay mechanics of 6 but streamlined significantly to avoid confusion and keep the original version intact spirit-wise. Strategy in older RE games are classics because they force you to be smart with the resources you have. It makes the fear now of Mr. X and even zombies to break down doors more plausible and no longer safe when running into a load screen door. The tension of Mr. X walking around the station is fantastic and is entirely unpredictable sans a few key plot moments. Some inclusions like gunpowder found in RE3 comes to RE2 and its a great way to push players into make decisions like making acid rounds, shotgun shells or handgun bullets something that prohibits another. Very classic survival stuff. It's a shame the side character missions are not that long or really compelling so it felt like a slight missed opportunity. Not bad per se but nothing special. Stunning a zombie is a thing now and makes headshots not always the best course for dealing with them. The initial shotgun sounds and feels weak, which could be intentional but I doubt it because it only works very close to a zombie's headshot.

AI: The only slight issue I have is the AI is fine if at times off. Zombies move so erratically at points it's hard to say where they move to you at any given time. Or how shooting them down doesn't necessarily kill and they play dead to sneak attack you. Some attacks from bosses are a little cheap on hitboxes and can feel almost like a test of your herbs and how many you have rather than skill. That said Mr. X, while a little easy to exploit, can track your commotion often and his occasional surprises make him a joy and dread to deal with on top of regular enemies. 

Difficulty: Great challenge on Hardcore. Plays like classic Re2 normal. It's easier to control and move around compared to the original though and the speed of which you can beat the game is quite fast. There is alot of factors and strategies that can make speedruns and items earned by specific clearings rather a joy to do. If you skip story cutscenes (no unskippable ones) and you know what you are doing, you easily beat it even on hardcore in a hour and half. Taking your time and being relatively new to the game and doing all the playthroughs (first and second) both ways is an easy 20-25 hr venture. 

Content: To me this game has great replay value in the main experience but the side content is ok. Hunk returns in 4th Survivor similar to the original where you guide Hunk (and eventual pieces of tofu) through a gauntlet meant to push you into extremes of really choosing your openings and making everything count. For Hunk its fun and enjoyable but for the Tofu its the only big issue I have for how unfair most of them are in a situation. Once again the AI isnt the best in this and can lead to some bs moments that you really have to exploit to make it through. Ghost Survivors is a similar gauntlet run but instead has you get items from little coin shops using keys. Killing enemies might drop items and there is a sort of backstory to them  based on characters in the game that never get their proper dues. I'm not really impressed with these either as they feel no different than the tofu challenges. That said it is easier to deal with then those challenges and can be amusing for a bit. DLC like free costumes are fanservice done hilariously well. DLC for other skins and guns are not necessary but cool additions. It's a strong piece of cake with some decent icing on it. Even at regular price this game is worth it.

Story: It's an RE game so expect campy and dumb stuff to happen. They haven't been great in story writing ever but I enjoy RE for its gameplay so much I can just roll along with it. I will say that the story and scenarios are not as compelling as the original because there is hardly anything in this that changes from first to second run. It's a hugely missed opportunity that I felt could have been given enough time in development or had no way to really change it up with racking up dev costs. Regardless its silly RE classic nonsense that has some darker scenes and moments. Echoing a bit of 4 with camp and horror mixing together.

Conclusion: RER2 is a excellent game in it's overall design and while some parts around the game are not really a big swing, the core of it's main focus is great in execution and I cannot wait how 3 is translated with all the groundwork that has laid here. From this, DMC5 and Monster Hunter World's expansion Iceborne released all last year and mostly solid titles in the past few years, Capcom have dominated gaming headlines and fans with a Re-imagining of their classic franchises, showing games can still be fun and have that arcade like joy that they have always been known for.

Gonna keep it directly to the issue at hand. The game itself isn't bad, it's a beautiful crafted remake of the old RE2 we know but to be honest, I prefer the original one over this. Why so? Let's get into it:

+ You can notice Capcom reused quite some stuff (from objects assets to the menu itself) from their previous released RE7, I'm not against that, but they could had put some effort into, I don't know, respect the original classic menu?

+ Graphics are beautiful, really astonishing when pushed to the max, but something was amiss, even if the game looked that shiny. Oh yea, the music! Where are the scores? Game is dead silent most of the time, and you would only get one short theme when getting into a safe zone and a continuous one when the Tyrant (Mr X) is chasing you. But yea, don't cry about it, Capcom is willing to sell you as a dlc the original scores of RE2, alongside the classic sfx as well, for a special fee. Instead of being in the game, they cutted it out and selling it apart. Isn't that wonderful?

+ I did talked with people that had the game before the release of the unlock-all key dlc, and they told me they noticed a difficulty increase in the game itself. And I did felt that as well. In the original RE2, a shotgun was a meanie gun, hell, even the pistol could do fine to hold normal zombies and dogs, you would blast most tough enemies with 1-2 shotty rounds and 3-4 pistol rounds. In this game, both the shotgun and the pistol felt like underpowered, 3 shotty rounds at less than half a meter against a licker and it did somehow stayed alive and killed me or 2 rounds on a zombie aiming at his head, it's stupid. Even the pistol, almost 8-10 rounds to a zombie leg to force him on the ground. Like if the game have some sort of RNG to determine if you need just 2, 3, or 10 rounds to take just one limb from a zombie. Retarded at best. 
I ended up being forced to buy that key dlc since I wasn't having any fun at all being lacking ammunition and yes, that the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ knives have a durability bar? Really? I don't remember that ♥♥♥♥ in the original game. Anyways, getting those infinite guns at least allowed me to continue the story instead of dealing with even more lame situations.

+ Mr X. When I first saw him, I really got nervous, loved that entrance and how persistant he is to get your sorry ass all around the police station. But after being moving around from quite some time, just realized that I wasn't even paying attention on the rooms I was walking into. Instead of searching each room calmly for secret items or pieces of lore to read, I was rushing all along due to being chased but that big old bastard 24/7. That actually started to get boring for me. 
The original game had specific parts when that bastard would chase you but after getting to a determined point, he would leave you alone so you could explore a bit more relaxed and dealing with the rest of the T-Virus menace. Hell, if you managed to beat his ass with enough damage, you would get some cool stuff. 
But not on this game. 
Here, this special fellow have unlimited life and he would get incapacitated for half a minute or less and then he will get up and search for your ass again. And yes, he do know where you are and he will get you through any door. That kind of perpetual harassment or pressure is annoying, since that, in the original game, after you managed to beat an important battle or dangerous situation, the game will let you have some breath. But not on this one at all. (Just imagine if this guy is annoying as hell with this new AI set, how would Nemesis act on the upcoming remake of RE3? The same AI + guns? Jesus Christ).
Just love the futility of fighting something that can't be temporary beaten even and will breathe on your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ neck and bothering you everywhere.

+ They did actually changed some parts of the original story as well to accomodate this remake or even trying to create some sort of surprise element on the people that played the original one. I did not apreciated that tbh at times.

Not gonna lie, I'm kinda disappointed. I expected a remake that would respect the old original but instead found quite some stuff that just made the experience a big no for me. If they only changed the graphics but keeping the rest as it was before, it would have being a blast. All of the previous points mentioned made me reconsider about getting the RE3 remake, I'm just gonna wait to the release date and watch people's reactions and see how the game performs, specially about Nemesis. 3/10.

Resident Evil 2 is the first horror game i ever purchased after my first playthrough what i can definetly say is: Capcom has remade Resident Evil 2 into something exciting, new, and nostalgic.
It is something that makes me want to know more about the Resident Evil Universe and play more of the games in the Resident Evil Series.

Atmosphere:

Resident Evil 2 takes place at a police station in Raccoon City: A place which should be stockpiled with weapons, ammunation and survival gear 
to survive a zombie apocalypse, instead Clarie and Leon both realized that Supplies have been expended, the halls run slick with blood. Corpses: it’s unclear if they’re truly dead or reanimated  
lay piled around every corner.  The walking dead stalk me during my first playthrough as Claire breaking windows, getting back up after shooting them in the face.  
Rooms I think are clear of threats are somehow inhabited by new zombies when I return to search for something I missed or a item i need to complete my objective. 

The police station is beautifully, gruesomely realized. Some rooms are dark as night, lit only by the blaze of Claire’s or Leon’s flashlight. Emergency lighting reflects off the water in flooded 
hallways. There is trash and rot in the attics, piled-up office furniture blocking pathways, and it’s all very realistic-looking

The game is a good teaching point for me who has never played a resident evil game before: Conserve ammo. Run away when I can. conserve healing. And shoot the zombie that is attacking
me in the head till i can confirm that it is truly dead.

Story:

Rookie cop Leon Kennedy and college student Claire Redfield trek to the town of Raccoon City in search of answers. The two are united by a chance encounter but quickly separated by a terrible
accident. What follows is a fight for survival as both Claire and Leon try to escape the city alive, then find themselves caught up in something much bigger.

Gameplay:

The game’s bizarre puzzles makes me sprint from room to room in search of a diamond-shaped key for a diamond-shaped lock. I develop rolls of film that reveal a single picture of a padlock 
combination. A half-eaten police officer dies with a notebook in his hand. The book contains the solution to an elaborate, station-spanning puzzle that requires 
three medallions culled from three marble statues — and, ludicrously, it’s my only hope of getting out of this place. 

How does Resident Evil 2 justify all this? Raccoon City’s police department is actually a renovated art museum, a certified genius as devised this series of convoluted puzzles that stand 
between me and survival.
