Let me start by saying I've never played a mainline Resident Evil game before. I sort of missed the boat when I was younger, and my one foray into the series was RE 7--a game that I hated with a fiery passion.

A friend of mine has been trying to talk me into playing this RE2 remake for months, but I assumed it just wasn't for me. Boy, was I wrong. 

The game is a technical marvel in terms of graphics, sound, and performance (I am running a 2070 Super, 8700K @ 4.7, and 16 GB RAM). It ran flawlessly for me at 120+ FPS in 1440p with no noticeable dips on near max settings (I disable stuff like depth of field automatically). 

More importantly, it's absolutely brilliant from a gameplay perspective. It took a few hours for the gameplay loop to set its hooks in me, but once it did... game over. The level design is intricate and satisfying, the weapons are a blast to use and upgrade, and even the puzzles (which I usually hate) are immersive and fun. It all felt so good that I beat the game as both Leon and Claire over a single long weekend, which is something I haven't done for at least 10 years. Then I bought the ENTIRE rest of the Resident Evil series so I can run through them before the RE3 remake comes out next month. 

Obviously, I loved the game. But I do have a handful of complaints:

-The inventory management, while necessary to keep tension high and force strategic thinking, can be a chore.

-Some weapons felt underwhelming and potentially unnecessary.

-Several of the areas require more backtracking than I'd usually like, although this problem is somewhat mitigated by the strength of the level design and availability of shortcuts.

-Some checkpoints seem a bit far apart given the relative infrequency of save rooms.

-The Tyrant (you'll know him when you see him) can get a bit irritating after he's been around for a while. He stops being scary and becomes a nuisance pretty quickly.

 -On my second run as Claire, I noticed some mismatches between her and Leon's stories that somewhat broke the game's otherwise flawless immersion. This was especially noticeable when it came to repeating puzzles that one would have expected to have been completed by the other character (didn't Leon already come through here and put out that fire?), but it also extended to a few NPC-related cutscenes that left me scratching my head.

But given the amount of content on offer, the better-than-expected narrative and voice acting, and the generally spectacular quality of the game itself, I can forgive these small faults. It's not perfect, but it's damn close. All told, this is one of the best single-player games I've played in years. And I bet you'll feel the same.

This is only a slight recommendation.  There are many irritating things about this game, from the absurdly out of place puzzles, to the inventory management (particularly early on), to the slightly confused core gun play, to finally, the boss fights.  The very worst parts of this game are its (thankfully few) boss fights.  They all follow the same script:

1. Angry-Claw, who sprouts new elbows at a geometric rate, knocks you to the ground.

2. You roll around like a dumb clod of mud.

3. Angry-Claw crowds the camera but otherwise stands there like a moron instead of finishing you off.

4. You finally get up and shoot all the eyeballs that have spewed out of his nipples and shoulders and back and butt.

5. Angry-Claw summons an elevator shaft and falls into it.

Fortunately, the rest of the game is fairly enjoyable.  The exploration, especially of the police station, is where the game shines.  The map provides a particularly nice effect here, highlighting things you've found but (surprise) didn't have inventory space for, and turning entire rooms blue once you've picked them clean.  Seeing entire floors of the station as solid blue was deeply satisfying to my easily manipulated mind grapes.

I mentioned the core gun play as a source of irritation, but that's only because the game can't decide what it wants to be.  I *do* like the gimmick of using weapons to stun the zombies.  It reminded me a bit of Alien Isolation.  But the core gun play doesn't really support that - at least not nearly as well as in AI, where stealth is a much larger component.  Instead of avoiding detection or killing things outright, you're taught how to trivially avoid the awkward zombie shambles as they try and give you little "G" kisses.  With the amount of ammo, gunpowder, and healing items the game provided, it always felt like it was straddling this cumbersome line between shooter and survival horror.

Speaking of horror, the game didn't really provide many scary moments.  It didn't try and rely on jump scares, which was nice.  But most of the tension felt like it came from timing more than scary enemies or environments.  Trying to search a room before the zombie gets back up or before the roid-rager in the trench coat kicks down the right door.  And again, as you learn more about the extent of their movements, this tension fades pretty quickly.  Though there is a section in the library where the trench coat guy can absolutely go to hell...I'd say the strongest horror elements the game offers are in the sewers section, which is unfortunately brief.  There's one enemy type in particular that comes at you while you're trudging through "water" and its very well done.

When I beat the game as Claire, I didn't have a compelling desire to go through Leon's campaign.  Or to try out any of the extra survivor modes.  Or run through the new game plus mode, which the game describes as "different".  Though, whether that difference is a gimmicky few throwaway scenes or something more weighty, who knows.  I'd have honestly preferred they just expanded the Claire and Leon base stories accordingly and left it at that.

Ultimately, it was a fun diversion, but I wouldn't want to live in the Umbrella dimension.  And not on account of the zombies or Angry-Claw.  The real horror stories are told by the blue collar workers of Raccoon City.  The sanitation crews that are constantly losing their fuse box chess sets.  The construction crews finding their wives have, once again, filled all their pill bottles with gunpowder.  The electricians who pull out their trusty Sine-Wave-Sing-and-Say to turn the power back on.  To them, Angry-Claw's rampage was a blessed release...

Resident Evil 2 is a remake of the classic horror game from 1998. I never played the original, so I can't compare this one to it. To start, the game is a horror game, so it's very scary. I'm not much into horror games, but I enjoyed the game. I felt like it didn't throw too many jumpscares at you. There are especially many jumpscares in the beginning of the game, which suits the vibe of you being new in town. In some parts of the game, you'll be constantly followed by the terrifying Tyrant, an unstoppable enemy. This forces you to move quick and these parts are very intense.

The game is about 8 hours long, but never feels dragged out. The game has two main protagonists, Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield. Leon is on his first day as a cop when the game takes place, meanwhile, Claire is coming to the city to look for her brother. Before starting the game you'll get to pick who to play as. I would recommend playing through the game at least two times to experience both the protagonist's stories, even though much of it is the same.

The gameplay primarily consists of exploration, puzzles, and survival. The ammunition is very scarce, so you'll have to make your bullets count. The zombies take a lot of bullets to kill, so you'll have to only use your guns when necessary. The puzzles are very diverse and fun to solve, which is great considering that they take up a large sum of the game.

The final thing I want to talk about is the graphics. The lighting is simply phenomenal, and the amount of detail on faces is impressive. This makes the game very immersive to play, and therefore also scarier.

Where to begin, not only is this the best re imagining of a game it might be the best game ever made PERIOD.

The atmosphere, sound, voice acting, graphics and over all detail are amazing. Its crazy to think modern day capcom could release a product of such high quality.

While the game is very impressive from a visual standpoint, with extremely detailed lighting, textures, anti-aliasing and bloom as well as more unique almost experimental graphic options, such as subsurface scattering and volumetric lighting. The game also sets out to improve upon the fundamentals of the Resident Evil franchise, that being the tank controls, inventory system, puzzles and exploration. 

With the most notable changes being the lack of fixed camera angles and seamless transitions from room to room. Which is a giant leap forward in terms of accessibility and making the game have more consistency and fluidity in gameplay, this combined with the revamped third-person or over the shoulder perspective. Makes aiming and shooting easier than ever before and compliments the tweaked and more reasonable inventory system when compared to The original Resident Evil and Resident Evil 2. 

There's only improvements in the Remaster or Re-imagining with no obvious mistakes or downgrades in any way and with the changes made purely to enhance the gameplay experience and to entice the gamer into playing, I cannot recommend this game highly enough for those who are interested in over the shoulder shooters or are fans of the Resi Franchise and Survival Horror Genre as a whole. 

Most important of all the game manages to retain the feeling of dread, the real struggle of confronting the undead and having to manage ammunition, inventory space and items that can be used in combat. Whilst either trying to avoid or confront the infected allowing you to proceed or progress with the game. The Police Station is interesting enough of a setting with it's own discrete secrets to make every puzzle solved or item obtained feel like a milestone.

[b]Resident Evil 2 Remake – A Terrifying, Immersive, and Masterfully Crafted Survival Horror Revival[/b]

[i]Resident Evil 2 Remake[/i] is a definitive reimagining of one of the most iconic survival horror games in history, blending intense suspense, strategic gameplay, and cinematic storytelling into a modern masterpiece. It preserves the essence of the original while updating visuals, mechanics, and pacing to create an experience that is both nostalgic and thrillingly fresh.

You step into the shoes of Leon S. Kennedy, a rookie cop on his first day in Raccoon City, and Claire Redfield, a determined survivor searching for her brother. Both characters bring unique perspectives and challenges, and their stories intertwine to reveal the city’s descent into chaos. Characterization is strong, with detailed models, expressive animations, and believable reactions that heighten immersion and emotional investment.

The environments are breathtakingly detailed and atmospheric. From the foreboding streets of Raccoon City to the claustrophobic police station, shadowy sewers, and secret laboratories, each location is meticulously designed with realistic lighting, textures, and environmental storytelling. Every bloodstain, abandoned object, and flickering light contributes to the sense of dread and impending danger, making exploration both rewarding and tense.

Combat is intense, strategic, and satisfying. Weapons feel powerful, encounters are challenging, and ammo scarcity forces careful resource management. Zombies and mutated creatures are relentless, intelligent, and terrifying — their unpredictable behavior ensures that no two encounters feel the same. Boss fights are cinematic, memorable, and demanding, testing both reflexes and tactical thinking. The game balances action and horror expertly, keeping tension high throughout.

The remake also refines puzzles, inventory management, and progression systems. The intuitive inventory interface, well-designed puzzles, and key-based exploration encourage players to think, observe, and plan. Every corner of the environment may hold clues, resources, or dangers, making every step forward feel meaningful and suspenseful.

Audio design is exceptional. From distant groans and sudden crashes to atmospheric music and ambient sounds, every cue heightens fear and immersion. The sound of a zombie shuffling behind a locked door or the growl of a Licker stalking its prey creates genuine tension, making players constantly aware of their surroundings. The voice acting is top-notch, adding emotional weight and realism to character interactions.

[i]Resident Evil 2 Remake[/i] is more than a revival; it is a masterclass in survival horror. It combines immersive world-building, cinematic presentation, strategic gameplay, and relentless tension into an experience that is terrifying, rewarding, and unforgettable. It respects the legacy of the original while pushing the series forward in every way.

A must-play for fans of survival horror, atmospheric storytelling, and cinematic action — [i]Resident Evil 2 Remake[/i] is a flawless, gripping, and horrifying adventure that continues to set the standard for modern horror games.

Horror movies don't scare me. Honestly, they haven't in a long time. It's probably due to me watching movies like Final Destination 2 when I was 7, or maybe it's just that I'm weird. But when it comes to video games, I couldn't be any more of a ♥♥♥♥♥. The problem with scary games hinges on the balance between horror and playability. Too often, I would try playing a horror game, find myself being too defenseless and scared, and then I'd put the game down. Outlast, Amnesia, Slender, these are all games that make you defenseless because they can't be scary otherwise. Resident Evil on the other hand took a different approach to making the players feel helpless. Tank controls work in some ways, but just aren't fun for me and many others. It's a damn shame too, as I see now what I've been missing. With Resident Evil 2's remake, I see the perfect balance between horror and playability. The game doesn't leave you defenseless, but they only give you so much ammo. Only so many herbs. The anxiety behind inventory management helps compound the achievement of progressing through the game. Each enemy isn't terrifying because you can't kill them, they're terrifying because you as a player have to ask yourself if you should kill them. The original RE2 was released in 1998, to critical acclaim and over 5 million copies sold across all the platforms it came out for. Now, the survival horror classic has been remade with a new engine, crisper graphics and a change of camera perspective, for a new generation of gamers. How has the result been?

To clarify, i have never played the original RE2. I only knew about the major story arcs and details thanks to Youtube videos and wikis.

Pros:
*Story is overall faithful to the original game, but with some new twists and changes to keep things fresh. The game is more of a "re-imagining" than a shot-for-shot remake.
*Gameplay has been updated while still remaining reminiscent to the original, the most obvious being the changed camera perspective, from fixed angels over pre-rendered backgrounds to a 3rd-person perspective in a true 3D world.
*The scare-factor is high, all from regular Zombies, dark corners and ambient noises work together to achieve a great atmosphere that keeps you tense. Even veterans of the original game will be suprised and caught off guard a few times.
*[spoiler]Mr. X[/spoiler], the tyrant who before was relegated to scripted encounters is now able to track you in several sections of the game. This makes him a much bigger threat than before.
*All the extra modes from the original (except the Extreme Battle mode) make a return in addition to some new ones.
*The game sticks to survival horror and doesn't get too action-oriented.

Cons:
*The 2nd run, replacement for the B scenarios in the original, is very underwhelming. The story is 99% the same as in the respective character's A scenario, just with minor plot sections removed. It also creates some questionable plot holes (such as [spoiler]Mr. X[/spoiler] being killed by [spoiler]Birkin[/spoiler] in Claire's scenario, yet showing up again as the [spoiler]final boss[/spoiler] in Leon's run, no worse for wear). Compare this to the original, where the stories ran parallell with each other and decisions you made in A could affect the B run.
*Some of the bosses end up being tedious, not that hard or difficult to figure out. Not completely uncommon in the series to be fair.
*Replay value isn't as high compared to the original.
*Certain plot changes feel less impactful or satisfying compared to the original

Overall though, the RE2 remake is a great game and a worthy purchase, especially on a first playthrough if you're craving some survival horror. Repeat playthroughs do get a bit more tedious, compared to the earlier games.

Final score: 8/10.

I'll admit that I never played any of the Resident Evil(s) over the years though I was a giant fan of the first movie that came out back in 2002 (Mila Jovovich FTW!). The first time I got my hands on an RE game was RE7: Biohazard and boy the scares in that game could result in spontaneous defecation to the faint of heart.

RE2 is (apparently) a remake of an old classic but since I have no point of reference (and hence nostalgia) associated with this game I think I can give an uncoloured opinion of this game. Angry Joe is right - this is the game of the year (2019), there is so much care and design that has gone in this work of grotesque art and everything else about it has been carefully aligned to make a near perfect experience.

You start off by playing as Leon Kennedy, a Racoon City police officer whose day on the job takes a horrifying turn when he begins investigating a seemingly abandon gas station. First thing you will notice is the par-excellent character and environmental design. The graphics are off the chain and clearly Capcom has pulled out all stops in ensuring that the rendition of a classic franchise is given the respect it deserves. This will of course greatly help in bringing both classic and new players into the RE lore. The sounds complement the visual aspects of RE2 perfectly, both in terms of music and SFX. As a matter of fact, the sense of perennial tension is instilled majorly by the sound design and music score of the game and MUST be applauded for what it achieves.

The story itself is basically a 7/10 to be honest and some aspects of relationship dynamics between some prominent characters, I feel, needed to be much more fleshed out; but the story gives enough incentive, that along with the gameplay, this is an un-put-down-able experience. Navigating and backtracking is actually fun AF in RE2 and so many other franchises need to learn from this game on how to get that right. The game is also dotted with smartly designed puzzles that are challenging but never feel unfair, hence the sense of accomplishment is high when you do finally solve them on your own.

Not since the original Dead Space have I felt this terror and for many a nights my ears will jump up at the sound of thumping footsteps and wonder, is Mr X coming to get me? Which reminds me to make a special mention on the model, sound and (zombie) AI - I always felt under constant threat (thanks Capcom). Inventory management too also doses you with further tension and adds to the survival element of RE2; so many times I have had to discard items after gruelling internal disputes over what items to keep and throw away.

This game is worth the hard work you put in your money and should be lauded for it's design choices. I reckon even the veteran players of the RE franchise would be mighty happy with this beautifully crafted action/survival horror gem.

Edit: I came back to give this game a full score a full year after completing it.

A great re-imagining of the game that defined the survival horror genre.

Pros:

Gameplay - is modernised and still feels tanky in a sense that your movement isn't instantanous to maneuver VS Resident Evil 6 - instead making it much more slower and realistic, forcing you to tread carefully. Which works in cohersion with the enemy animations and the pacing of the game.

Visual & Sound Design - is fantastic & intense, leaving you on the edge of your seat while playing alone. The Atmosphere of the RPD and NEST is impressive. Great visuals, sound and animations due to the work of CAPCOM team & the RE Engine.

Cons:
Story - The Game in comparison towards the original - lacks the unique different pathways - in the remake the only difference is the cutscenes and modified puzzle solutions and a few unique locations for each character/run for a decent period of time. Which makes the story cohersion broken (by solving the same puzzles that the other would have done).
I think it was intended to save on development constraints. It's why it feels weird when Leon and Claire acts like friends when they only just met.

To see the full story, you would be required to play the game twice (Run A/B) to reveal the full story. I feel like the unique sections for each characters themselves are a brilliant on building on to the story decently but it also created a paradox effect with the story, due to the game's lack of unique pathways and battling the same boss' (due to the cutscenes & excluding the unique locations).

Despite the story's paradoxical effect, I definitely wholeheartedly recommend Resident Evil 2 for any die-hard fans of the series and for anyone who would love to play a modern take on the classic Resident Evil game & importantly play a true survival horror, whereas Resident Evil 4 hinges more towards action orientated.

Welcome back to Raccoon City, survivors! "Resident Evil 2" (2019) is not just a remake; it’s a masterful reimagining of a classic that blends nostalgia with fresh, heart-pounding horror. Capcom has outdone itself, creating a game that is as exhilarating as it is terrifying.

From the moment you step into the dark, rain-soaked streets of Raccoon City, the atmosphere grips you. The RE Engine delivers stunningly grotesque visuals, with every shadow and flicker of light meticulously crafted to keep you on edge. The eerie silence is often broken by distant groans and shattering windows, making every corner a potential deathtrap. This isn’t just a game; it’s an immersive horror experience that will make your heart race.

Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield are back, looking better than ever. Leon’s rookie cop charm and Claire’s relentless search for her brother are more engaging with updated voice acting and facial animations that add layers of emotion and realism. Their interactions with other characters, like the enigmatic Ada Wong and the tragic Sherry Birkin, are fleshed out in ways that make their struggles feel palpable and their survival, deeply personal.

Survival horror at its finest, "Resident Evil 2" makes every bullet count. Every herb is a lifeline, and those precious ink ribbons in hardcore mode feel like gold. The over-the-shoulder camera brings you closer to the action, and the puzzles and exploration keep your brain as engaged as your trigger finger. And let’s not forget Mr. X—the relentless Tyrant who will stop at nothing to turn you into a Leon- or Claire-shaped pancake. His heavy footsteps are the soundtrack to your nightmares, adding a constant sense of dread.

The sound design deserves a standing ovation. The creak of a floorboard, the distant wail of a Licker, and the ominous footsteps of Mr. X combine to create an auditory experience that’s as terrifying as the visuals. Playing with headphones? Good luck. Every sound is designed to keep you on edge, reminding you that in Raccoon City, safety is an illusion.

With multiple scenarios, unlockable content, and the ever-enticing challenge of achieving the best rank, Resident Evil 2 (2019) offers plenty of reasons to dive back into the horror. The "2nd Run" mode changes item locations and puzzles, providing a fresh experience even on subsequent playthroughs. Free DLCs like The Ghost Survivors offer new challenges, ensuring the nightmare never truly ends.

Resident Evil 2 (2019) is more than a remake; it’s a masterclass in survival horror. Whether you’re a seasoned fan or a newcomer, this game delivers on every front. So grab your controller, turn off the lights, and prepare to lose yourself in the horror that is Raccoon City. Just remember: in this game, your real enemies are your nerves and the shadows lurking just out of sight.

Let me start with the gameplay. The guns are incredibly well designed, making each and every one feel like its own unique and different weapon. Some feel like they have much more power than others, and the damage output tends to agree with that feeling. The progression/map design is off the carts, too. The way the game perfectly paces itself at you if you're new, but also lets you jump ahead with experience, is really cool. The way the game can challenge you with a boss, or a swarm of enemies at an unexpected point keeps you on the edge of your seat. But, not in a "oh god i'm scared" way, more of a "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ this is awesome, what's next" way. While it can, at times, be unforgiving and ruthless, overall it is an incredibly well put together sequence of events.

The graphics are, also, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ incredible. This game feels like it got so much heart and soul put into it, from the Tyrant's control chip to the inside of the barrels having a spiral texture on them (yeah, i'm serious). The physics can be a little wacky when the corpses ragdoll, but that is kind of to be expected and adds to the tension of never knowing when a zombie is going to pop up on you.

My ONE complaint, out of the entire game, is the dialogue between Leon and Claire. I know. This big of a game and the worst thing is the talking? Awesome. The only reason I say this is because, while this does take place in 1998, the way they speak to each other after only knowing one another for like 2 hours is a bit... odd. If you found yourself in the midst of a zombie infested city, would you take the time to flirt while being swarmed with walking corpses? Probably not.

So anyway, I'm gonna get back to kicking ass and taking names in this game. It's just so well made and I can't wait for the RE3 remake coming later this year.

I'm always suspicious of remakes or remasters of old games. I tend toward nostalgia, enjoying the old games for what they were and what they stood for and how they represent the period of time in which they were released.

Resident Evil, however, managed to surpass all expectation back in the day it came out on the GameCube. Seeing how well Capcom managed to pull off THAT remake, I dared hope they might pull off something similar with Resident Evil 2.

And they did!

The cinematic camera is replaced by an over-the-shoulder view, the target practice zombies are far more threatening to deal with and the atmosphere, visuals and audio have all received such extensive overhauls that the game feels truly new and exciting once more!

The first thing anyone will notice, especially if they have played the original game, is the gorgeous visuals. Models, textures and animations, as well as the environments and effects such as weather and light are incredibly well done. The Raccoon City police station, in all of its odd quirky designs explained away by the buildings past life as a museum, is rendered in rich detail all around, from the cluttered desks and makeshift barricades to the light bleeding through bullet holes punched through doors. The visuals serve well to bring the games oppressive atmosphere to life.

As for audio, the game also manages some great little twists, especially when it comes to certain enemies. Hearing the zombies clawing and banging on windows, moaning around corners, or hearing the thumping footsteps of the more dangerous enemies moving around you, slamming doors and pausing to listen to the players own sounds, all come together to keep the small hairs on the back of the players neck standing up.

As this is still a game effectively from 1998, I won't dwell much on the story in this review, as that has not been changed notably. Umbrella Corporation is up to its usual shenanigans, through incompetence releasing monsters and viruses and horrors onto the streets of poor old Raccoon City. Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield, each with their own draw to the local police station, end up trying to survive the horror and uncover a way to get out of the city in the end.

The clever part of how the game is designed is its dual story. The player can freely choose which protagonist to play as on their first playthrough, and upon completion of that first playthrough, they will unlock an option to play again as the other character, with a slightly expanded experience that takes into account the fact that the player has already beaten the game once before. Little changes in how the map opens up, how puzzles are designed and how the story unfolds, make both playthroughs easily worth the time and effort. 

Resident Evil 2 also provides options for playing the game either in a more modern fashion, or with the retro ink-ribbon based save system or even with hardcore options for item storage, forcing the player to roam around the station, facing its dangers, more.

Lastly, and this paragraph may well count as a SPOILER, so skip to the next one if you're deeply concerned by those: 
[spoiler]hot-damn this game has done a good job of creating a memorable and terrifying antagonist in the form of a big hulking Mr X: a trenchcoat-wearing mutant crashing through doors and walls alike, turning nearly all of the game into a nerve-wracking game of cat and mouse as the player tries to slip through to their objectives while trying not to come face-to-face with this unkillable monstrocity. [/spoiler]

-End of major spoilers-

All in all, I find it surprisingly easy to recommend Resident Evil 2 to both old and new players alike. Capcom has really shown us all, once again, how to build a great remake of an old game, and I have high hopes that they will be able to keep this up with the upcoming Resident Evil 3 remake, as well as potential future releases. Finally we have a proper example, standing up tall among the other "remakes", showing us all exactly how it's supposed to be done!

But seriously, screw that mini-puzzle in the library! And screw that one big guy for constantly getting in my way while I try to move these shelv- AAARGH!

When starting the game you get to choose either Claire or Leon for the first run. This is not a common feature in any game, and when implemented it is often done only as a skin swap. In this game you will not see the complete story unless you play twice with each. At least once with each is a minimum. That gives the game some replayability even for people like me that usually do not replay games.
I played Leon first and the Claire, which by many is said to be the "wrong" way. The game director has said in an interview that not any combination is the true way. All 4 paths must be played to see the hole story. Even though I have not done this, I am certain I have not missed out on anything huge. And if I have, then I am blissfully unaware :)

Claire is here in search of her brother, Chris Redfield (from RE1), whom she has not heard from in a while.
Leon is a rookie cop, starting his first day at Racoon City Police Department (RCPD).

So the first scene is you getting to a gas station, close to Racoon City. Everything is dark and quiet. You get in and the atmosphere tells you something is up. You search around, see a guy and he points to the storage room. You get in and a zombie is eating...
I am hooked I tell you :D Go game...
After this opening, you meet up with your other character (Claire or Leon), zombies breething down your neck, and you drive off to the city.

Now Racoon City is a total mess, zombies all over the place. You have to find a way to the Police Department through all these fires, road blocks and zombies.
When you finally get there, there is still no salvation as the zombies are also in here, and you also have no way out.
You objective is to somehow find a way out of this mess. The Police Department is in shambles, and you need to figure out how to traverse this place by finding useful items, solving puzzles and managing your inventory. All the while also not get eaten by zombies. You can either run from them or shoot them. If you shoot them, then make sure to hit because ammo is sparse.

This game is tense. The atmosphere from the lighting and sounds is absolutely amazing. I never played the original, so I am not biased that way. 
The game mechanics are also very nicely done. Everything works. It does not make you feel like the mechanics are part of the problem like the controls in RE1. And it also does not take away the tension.

This game is pretty much perfect.  I actually left a negative review of the HD remake of the original Resident Evil, but this game has fixed everything I didn't like about the first one and far exceeded my expectations.  I didn't grow up with the resident evil franchise, and while I always knew it was highly regarded, I had only ever played RE4 on the Wii (which I liked).  The original RE was obviously a groundbreaking game in it's time, but was hard to enjoy as a modern gamer.  I couldn't get used to the switching camera angles, the limited options for saving (the fact that you had to use dispensable ink reels), the lack of inventory slots and a map that didn't label landmarks (like which key was supposed to go in a given door) made that game kind of a chore.

This game, however, fixes every one of those issues.  When you find a locked door, the map labels it.  If you find an item but can't pick it up, it shows up on your map so you can get back to it later.  You don't waste time running around checking every door cause you can't remember where that one thing was supposed to go.  To be clear, it still does use some of the same mechanics as the original RE, e.g. you can only save at in-game typewriters and you'll easily find yourself filling your item slots if you're not careful.  However, this game feels much more balanced, so it uses those mechanics really well.  It makes them fun.  When you get to a typewriter you feel a sense of relief, not anxiety. No more "Should I save here? Is it worth wasting an ink?" It's not quite as hard to save your game (and you're not limited in how many saves you create unless you play in hard mode)/ Inventory management is much less of a chore.  There's also an autosave feature which can bail you out if it's been a while since you saved.  There's a great sense of progression through this game as it goes on, the story is good, the suspense is REALLY suspenseful.  The graphics are as good as any modern game.

Before you buy this game, if you're not familiar with the Resident Evil or Resident Evil 2, know that the focus on these games is suspense/horror before the zombie shooting.  This is not meant to be a zombie shoot-em-up where you kill everything you see.  You need to ration your supplies and proceed with extreme caution.  Which is all part of the fun.

As a kid, I played Resident Evil 2 on the Nintendo 64. When I first saw what this was going to be like, I was hesitant, but as I played through the game I was surprised by just how solid this entry to the series is. Moving around is easy enough, and getting used to the camera takes virtually no time. What's harder to come to grips with is how to deal with the undead hoard: Headshots don't guarantee death, and can even cause waste. This goes against the usual zombie lore somewhat, but it adds to the tension of the early game. The introduction of more resilient enemies as you play though keep the pressure on you, even as you learn how to manage your ammunition more efficiently and upgrade your weaponry. Resident Evil 2, as it exists now, is always a tense, oppressive experience and I can't recommend it highly enough. 

I did buy and play through a couple of story scenarios using the DLC key: It's still possible to be caught out by fast enemies and killed if you're not able to aim accurately with the unlimited weapons, though they do trivialize the challenge once you're more familiar with the game. I bought this game on sale, and even with the DLC key, I only payed about $25 for this game in total. This is one of those rare times when I would have been satisfied if I had bought the game on day one.

***I first downloaded the free demo of this game which had the darkness bug. I decided to try purchasing the full game, and it works fine, so take that fwiw.

After starting a new game, I played for about 3 hours before I felt like I had to stop so I could have a chance at sleeping... the game can be pretty intense and as has been stated by others, very immersive in making you feel that death - agonizing, horrific and painful death - potentially lurks around every corner or on the other side of any door... Truly a "survival" game that looks as beautiful as it plays. Gun/combat system works very well and those 1 pop head shots - although rare - bring with them a welcome sigh of relief as you attempt to conserve every - last - round...

This game is very good.  I enjoy that the levels of difficulty cover a wide spectrum of playstyles.  If you want to have a good time with the game with some difficulty but light item management, that's standard difficulty.  If you want real survival horror, that's hardcore.  If you just want to get a hang of the game or enjoy the story, you have easy.  If I was still back in school with less responsibilities, I'd love the hardcore mode where you have to make hard choices as to which zombies you are going to run past and which you're going to spend your limited resources to kill.  In standard, it's much more action-oriented where you can just waste the majority of enemies without worrying about your ammo or hp for the most part.

I'm surprised by how different the weapons feel.  They're all just guns and in most games, all that changes is rate of fire and damage but here, you have sliders like efficiency vs killing speed, magazine size vs critical chance, portability, etc.  The best example of this is claire's two pistols - both use the same ammo but the 5 shot revolver has a high critical chance when the reticle focuses while the other has what feels like an unlimited mag capacity but zero critical chance and a dot sight.  It's a choice of ease of use or a random killshot along with another perk later.

Certain parts of the game are also legitimately terrifying, especially one part in Claire's first run where you control another character.  That feeling of powerlessness in that scenario is super immersive.  I really connected with that character and could relate to Claire at those times.

I think the main characters voice acting is overly blasé (except when Claire fights dogs for some reason) though I'm not sure if Leon's voice actor is just bad.  The supporting cast seems to do alright. Claire's facial expressions of happiness are way over the top and goofy.  I liked the Sarah Michelle Gellar look to her, really taking me back to the 90s and the alternate outfits could have been done a little better.

The game stays true to the old Playstation title as far as I can remember.  It all feels very familiar but fresh at the same time.  I think that makes it a classic, or at least a successful reimagining of a classic.

Resident Evil 2 is [i]amazing[/i]. I knew it was my favorite game of 2019 long before I even played it. In terms of technical stuff, it has nearly photorealistic graphics, solid sound design, and great performance. The horror atmosphere is effective and still manages to scare me occasionally, even though I'm on my 8th playthrough and already know where the surprises are. In terms of difficulty and accessibility, it has an amazing breadth. Assisted mode should make the game accessible for just about anyone, but personally I started on hardcore and after a couple playthroughs the challenge starts to shift from struggling with the moment-to-moment combat and how to continue opening up the puzzle-box that is the RPD to figuring out how to optimize your run so you can finish quickly and use fewer resources. It has really pushed me to learn the game better and improve. I was thinking about trying to 100% it, but that is no small task. I'm just starting to worry that I've plateaued before getting an S+ run. 

The only problem I have with the game is how the story is written. I know that has never been the strength of the series, and I never played the original release, but from what I've seen from it, in a lot of ways it seems like they managed to write it worse this time. The actors give great performances, but the some of the side characters lack some nuances they used to have. Leon and Claire seem to interact with each other less than they did in the original too. The biggest issue to me though is that the A and B scenarios conflict a [i]lot[/i]. There's no way to figure out the actual order of events, it's just kind of a mess. It seems like the only reason they even kept the A and B format is for the difficulty curve. None of this ruins the game or anything, I just think there's some missed potential. 

Overall, I highly recommend it. As I said in the beginning, I knew it would be my favorite game of 2019 before I even played it and I have not been disappointed.

Since RE2 was always a game meant for speed-running, that does decrease replay variance a bit.

Eighteen years ago it was Capcom who created what is perhaps the greatest video game remake of all time with the unforgetable RE1 Remake and after a long history of successes, downfalls and rising back again to restore the RE in its former glory with RE7,  it is Capcom again that delivers another near perfect remake of a legendary game and deiver a game of unparalleled quality beyond the highest expectations. It was an extremely tough task, but they did it.
Yes it's THAT good.

RE2 Remake, brings Racoon City's doomed police department to life in way that was not possible before, graphics that truly immerse you with their dark dilapidated corridors and offices, eerily empty parking lots, streets and sewers filled with the smell of death, and all that accompanied by some extraordinary sound that enhances the atmosphere of dread beyond belief. Perhaps the sound design is the true star of this action horror adventure that raises the stakes as you dive deeper into the cospiracy that led to the zombie apocalypse.
The story is more streamilined compared to the original, perfectly suited for newcomers to the series but also offering new twists and takes for old fans already familliar with the source material, in a similar way the previous RE1 Remake played with players' expectations by tweaking and adding new things into the mix. While RE2 is not as daring in the introduction of new elements as its predecessor was, it makes up with the amazing quality of its presentation, leaps and bounds beyond its competition (seriously the cutscenes alone make this one of the most beautiful games so far, with great voice talent, superb acting and intensity that puts the likes of David Cage's "emotional scenes" in shame!) - something you would never expect from a franchise that once upon a time gave us the "Jill sandwich"!
Capcom has surpassed themselves and the evolution of the RE Engine is even more impressive than the expressions and motion capturing we saw in RE7.

Gameplay wise, while it uses the over-the-shoulder angle that the franchise revolutionized with RE4, the game is a pure survival horror action adventure, with all the trappings, limited inventory space, ammo & health management, backtracking, and solving puzzles (albeit not as intricate as RE1), while trying to stay alive as you face hideous monstrosities and tough boss battles. One thing that is a welcome return compared to the more repetitive enemies of RE7 is the wide variety of foes, from the classic zombies, to the disgusting lickers and of course the main highlight, the unstoppable "Terminator" Mr.X who now stalks the entire station, randomly searching for you and attracted to the sound of your gunfire, requiring a more tactical approach, as opposed to the few scripted events of the PS1 version. 
As with its old incarnation, once you finish the campaign with one hero, you unlock a 2nd run to play with the second character, featuring an alternative storyline in order to unlock the true ending.
The game also offers three different difficulty modes so people of all types of skill can enjoy the game, with ASSISTED (weaker enemies, aimassist, more resources and partial health regeneration), STANDARD (the normal mode) and for fansof frustrating survival horror of the good ol'days HARDCORE (far stronger enemies, less resources and the return of the famous ink ribbons in order to save).
And that's not all. Once you complete the main game, you can try your luck (and patience) with its small array of bonus missions, mostly aimed at speedrunners, with tough challenging action-arcade gameplay, as you control various supporting characters throughout a variety of locations. While not the greatest content, these are FREE unlockable modes so it is always welcomed.
And as you complete various tasks during either the main campaign or the bonus content, you slowly unlock the game's gallery where you can not only see some wonderful concept art but also the 3d models of the entire cast of heroes and villains and their animations, plus completing the main game rewards you with the original PS1 outfits for the main cast updated for the curent incarnation,or if you want a stronger nostalgia shot you can download the FREE '98 versions of the two main heroes in all their polygonal glory - the extra content you can unlock and enjoy is an oasis in the current half-baked dlc-driven environment in the industry.

Speaking of DLC , yes there are some minor stuff here as well, although nothing too essential, mostly cosmetic but cool-looking costumes (with a fun one being the Noir versions of the characters where you also play the game entirely in black & white!!!) or nods to the cancelled 1.5 version with Elza Walker costume for Claire,  and perhaps the only really important DLC being that of the original soundtrack/sound effects of the PS1 game which you can enable in game to complete your trip in memory lane. However I must admit that the new soundtrack for this remake is absolutely amazing!

Capcom has once again made a great port for the PC, with many different graphical options to tweak. The game is very well optimized and even in an average and somewhat weak machine as mine, it would run quite well. I didn't encounter any bug or problem whatsoever. 

Capcom and the resident Evil franchise are now standing in a very crucial moment, with the upcoming release of RE3 remake one wonders if they will be able to repeat the success once again and deliver another high quality title. However, the opportunities for remakes are becoming less and less viable as time goes by and at one point the question will again arise: When is RE8? And what path will it follow, since the franchise has delivered stellar experiences in both 1st and 3rd person?

Until that time comes, we can relive our memories of the S.T.A.R.S. unit and Leon & Claire, their friends and foes, once more and remind ourselves why we loved them in the first place.

Characters, Leon and Claire, play for the most part, well, the same and I don't mean just gameplay wise. What I expected was different take on the areas, to see parts of the game I couldn't explore with Leon and vice versa. Why did I expected that ? Well because ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game made it look that way. If you pick one character you will meet the other one throughout the game, making it look like your stories are in parallel and I was looking forward to it, only to find out that when you pick other character, game simply [b] for 75% of the game[/b]  replaces model of character you just played with. There is small part where each character has an area you get to explore only with them and their companion. This parts, however, are really short compared to the rest of the game, like an hour if you don't rush too much. I take this as a big con because whole time through out my first playthrough Leon's and Claires stories are happening at the same time and you will get completely different experience with each one, but that's not the case. 

Finally the worst thing about this game is RNG in fu**ing shooting. Yes, that's right, mechanic from original game which should have stayed in original game. What this means is that you can get a headshot or shoot of a limb with one shot from your starting weapon, pistol, or it can take 10+ shots. This is terrible and makes no sense. Of course you have more powerful weapons like shotgun or high caliber pistols to use. Well, I experienced several times when headshot with shotgun occured after 5 shots or 3 shot with high caliber pistol. This is bad, simply stupid design to create this irrational mechanic which is there simply to make it harder I guess ? I get it in old games, but now ? When you are used from every single ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ zombie game to one shot some basic zombie with headshot from shotgun from pointblank distance, and yet, you it's random ? Why ???? This is not annoyance anymore, this is simply lazy design to keep in the game. 

Even with these issues, game is really enjoyable, atmosphere of your first playthrough will be something special, game has this horror movie ahmosphere, you are truly emerged into the situation of being alone in an area, looking for answers and way out. Story is bland and predictable with no thought, like with every RE game. Overall lore is interesting but execution of it in games is laughable, but I knew that before hand. Don't expect much from the story. 

Overall, game is fun, there are some annoying or frustrating parts, but still fun. Of course your playthrough with second character will be much shorter because codes and secrets are the same and most of the game is the same so you will probably rush through it. I got game in sale for 20 bucks and I think value of this game is around 30-40 bucks. For the full price I would feel slightly ripped of because there isn't that much content after finishing first character for non-fan of the franchise.

[h1][b]RESIDENT EVIL 2[/b][/h1]

[u]First Anniversary Review[/u]

[i]The absolute best, Survival Horror perfected.[/i]
[i]Re-enter the nightmare of Raccoon city police department in 1998.[/i]

Resident Evil 2 2019 is a remake that fully respects the original’s soul, and pays homage to the authentic Resident Evil experience by delivering you an exquisite metroidvania level design style, the good old backtracking, puzzles, inventory management, and a sense of fear and tension from the beginning all the way to the end.

[b]LEVEL DESIGN[/b]

Resident Evil 2 consists of 3 main areas: RPD (Police Station and parking), Sewers, and Nest(Umbrella lab). The RPD and the Sewers are interconnected except the lab which is a separated area once you arrive there.

- [u]The RPD[/u] layout is similar compared to the original RPD but with a few important changes. The main difference is a change in its tone, which is now much darker and violent with an oppressive atmosphere. 
The building is a complex labyrinth of rooms, much more imposing and bigger than before. It has been remodeled in certain areas emphasizing the buildings past history as a Museum that was converted into what we now know as the police station. This is the reason you see the iconic statue in the main hall, the clock tower located at 4F west side, vast halls, big walls covered with beautiful decorations, paintings, and antique items.
Comparing the rooms we can see some good examples, like the original emergency ladder having been transformed into 2 stair wings that give you access right away to the 2F. The 2F and 3F have become much larger, there are more rooms, a few of them having been redesigned like the parking zone, which gives you access to the street sections and new areas. Some paths are completely different, items have different use cases and keys are in different locations, as one would expect from a remake. 
This new version of RPD along with the Spencer Mansion in REmake 1 are some of the most well crafted, complex, and magnificent buildings in the entire history of gaming. Hard to match.

-[u]The Sewers[/u] are a special case in this version. After the announcement of the remake I was afraid of what Capcom was going to do with this area because the original sewers were just a transition towards the lab. Capcom did the unthinkable: The sewers have been greatly expanded and improved in every single way, keeping the overall pace intact. There are more tunnels, many more rooms, access to new weapons and upgrades, and more puzzles. 
This time the chess pieces are needed to exit the sewers, the G-Mutant is no longer a boss and has been turned into a regular and strong enemy. The factory has been integrated into this area as well. Lastly, there is now an optional secret passage that can backtrack all the way to the RPD.

-[u]The Nest[/u] has also been expanded and is a lot more elaborate compared to the original. To clarify: There is a lot more stuff you have to do in order to progress. There are more situations, more puzzles, and way more backtracking. The tone of the lab too has changed to look a lot more like a highly advanced tech lab, whereas the original looked more “industrial” with a darker tone.

[b]STORY AND CHARACTERS (Spoiler free)[/b]

One of the remake’s most defining features is how both sides of the story and the legendary characters are combined and integrated into this version. It no longer is a spread between 4 scenarios. The story is way more serious than before, the presentation is better, the dialogue has improved by miles, and each character has a lot of depth.
[list]
Leon Scott Kennedy is presented in the same way as the original: A rookie cop on his first day at the RPD. He has a strong sense of justice yet at the same time has a charming naivity (no malice on his mind), though it doesn’t cloud his duty and determination to help people. Ben Bertolucci and Ada Wong are a part of his story and she remains as mysterious as ever.
[/list]
The other side of the story is Claire Redfield.
[list]
Claire is established as a smart, brave and kind university student, arriving in Raccoon City in hopes of finding her brother Chris (REmake 1). At a certain point in her story, her mindset shifts when she finds the little girl Sherry and becomes her angle protector. Sherry and Brian Irons are part of her story. Irons is a maniac much like in the original, but in this version he has more screen time than ever before.
[/list]
The evil part remains the same. William Birking and Annete Birking, both have been actively working with Umbrella creating a new type of virus…

[b]GAMEPLAY[/b]

The gameplay has been changed dramatically while still feeling similar to the original’s.

1.The new perspective- No more fixed camera angles. You now have a 3rd person camera that gives you more control and accurate movement. The camera can be moved freely regardless of the direction of your character. The element of surprise the original was known for is still there, but as a result of this new perspective that is achieved through the sense of uncertainty, limited ammo, and the unpredictable nature of the enemies.

2.Inventory- Both Leon and Claire start with 8 inventory slots available to them, which can be further upgraded with new hip pouches. Each hip pouch grants you 2 additional slots. It’s also worth mentioning that this time there are less item boxes around, so you will have to change your mindset: Learn to take what you really need, leave what you don’t, and take more risk by saving less often. Survival at its best.

3.Ink ribbons (Hardcore)- The iconic item needed to save your progress at the typewriters. There is a limited amount of these items so choose wisely when to save. Expect to have some unforgettable moments with this saving mechanic.

4.Puzzles- There are more puzzles and they’re more elaborate and interesting compared to the original. There is a good variety of them such as medallions, portable safes, electronic pieces, lockers, chess pieces, signal modulator, the herbicide… Not to mention the main levels that work as huge puzzle themselves.

5.Combat- Much more challenging than before, the gunplay has been modernized yet remains reminiscent of the original. A good example of this is how you’re recommended to stand still if you want to shoot accurately due to the reticle system. The guns found in this remake are pistols (amongst which iconic pieces like the colt 45 and m1911), the shotgun, spark gun, grenade launcher with two types of ammunition, the flamethrower, the desert eagle, the gatling, and the rocket launcher, alongside with their part upgrades (there is no bow gun like in the original).

There is no dedicated dodging mechanic, so in essence you’re still playing with the old tank controls. One great addition to the combat is that there are self defence items such as the knife (like in REmake 1), grenades, and flash grenades.

[b]GRAPHICS AND AUDIO[/b]

The graphical tech and the level of detail must be seen to be believed.
The audio design is outstanding. You can clearly identify every source of sound produced by the enemies, the footsteps and the global environment sound incredibly detailed.
The soundtrack in this version has less presence in every room, except at the end of the game. This is a clear design decision to fit with the current tone and atmosphere of the remake.

REmake 2 is extremely well optimized on pc and runs like a dream. Performance is impeccable. RE engine does wonders.

Short Version: I thought Resident Evil 1 Remake was excellent, but Capcom set the new standard for remakes with RE2. It’s a pretty faithful remake with all the elements of the original amplified and twisted into a modern masterpiece. Solid gameplay, excellent presentation/visuals, and a decent reimagining of the settings/storyline/characters. This remake exceeded almost all my expectations (although both Claire and Ada redesigns are still not quite right to me, but that’s minor).

Long Version: In terms of gameplay, the controls are solid and the game does a great job with its survival-horror elements. The first 1/4 of the game was rough with limited resources and getting used to the mechanics of the game. This game really forces you to route things out in your head (decide which zombies to kill and which to not to kill) and how to approach each situation/room. You really do need to play smart and allocate your resources properly, especially when playing on hardcore. However, pass the 1/4 mark, I’ve horded enough resources to never really felt like I was short on supplies. But that’s not saying the game get easier, the difficulty does increase the further you get in the game.

There are a few flaws in the game that comes to mind. Enemies are bullet sponges, which can be frustrating, and without a knife to check if they’re actually dead-dead it can be a pain. Also, no free head-stomp on leg grab? C’mon Capcom! Lickers are insanely overpowered, they practically teleport at you and are impossible to kill with most weapons. But smart and efficient gameplay easily overcome those flaws, like never waste ammo on lickers when they can easily be walked pass.

The only real complaint I have about the game is that both scenarios are just too similar to each other. I really wished both scenarios had a more completely different path. It was the same in the original so it’s not a big deal.

Summed up: If you liked RE4 and/or RE7, or would like to play a semi action-oriented horror game with puzzle elements, you won't regret buying this game.

The short review:
As the Steam reviews suggest, Resident Evil 2 (2019) is incredibly good. It's my favorite game of 2019, and my third favorite in the series. While not as good as RE1's remake, it's still an amazing game that every Resident Evil fan needs to experience. 

If you like numerical ratings, I'd give it a 9.25/10
Pros:
Beautiful graphics and performance (I get ~100 FPS at 1440p with most settings cranked on my 1070 TI)
Wonderful audio (use headphones, IMO)
Ada is smokin' hot.

Cons: 
Didn't come out 10-15 years ago.
Not much weapon variety (though it's the same as the original except with a few additional sub-weapons)
Needed more Ada. Ada 24/7!

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1651311499

The long version: 
After almost 90 hours played, and maybe close to 15 completed runs, I'm of the opinion that while this is an amazing remake, it is not as good as the RE1 remake. It just didn't quite do what many of us were expecting or hoping for. It changed and removed a bit too much from the original, and I think that's where it falls short of Resident Evil 1's remake.  

The RE1 remake retained virtually everything from the original and improved upon it all, while also adding a lot of curve-balls to keep the game different enough to surprise even the most die-hard fans who knew the original inside and out. It is basically the ultimate game remake (I'd love to hear of one better if anyone can think of one).
 
The remake of RE2 is different in a lot of ways, and that works well at times, but also seems to have lead to cutting some content from the original, which has left me wanting. 

For instance, no longer do you fight and flee through the streets for a decent amount of time at the beginning of the game. The streets are teeming with zombies and car wrecks, which is an awesome and intense environment. The problem is that it's over far too soon - maybe 2 minutes at most are spent outside. There is no Kendo's Gun Shop, nor Kendo to deliver cheesy lines ("Who are ya?! What are ya doin' here!?" "Oh, sorry about that babe!" etc.). Though Kendo's does appear later on, it's not the same and doesn't really have the same impact. In the original, you get a (false) sense of security upon entering Kendo's Gun Shop, which is ruined moments later by a zombie attack, which greatly increased feelings of anxiety and dread when I played it first - "Nowhere is safe!". 

I understand that in [year before current year] they couldn't make a similar remake that RE1 got - which just makes me sad that it didn't get this treatment 10-15 years ago when it would have been suitable. But, that doesn't answer why some content was switched around, altered or removed.

For instance..
Where are the giant ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ spiders?! How about the roach swarms that, while often harmless and easy to avoid, are also incredibly dangerous stun-locking death traps! Why were those removed?! The roaches ARE in game, in the police morgue, but you only see them once and they are nothing but a one-time jump scare. Bring back the insta-death roaches! 

These ones in the video link below (not my channel, apologies for using without permission):
https://youtu.be/PMwZGCRr2_c?t=9  

Opposite of cutting some content, there are some interesting additions to the game and story, such as getting to learn a little about the truck driver who causes the accident that separates Leon and Claire - you even get to hear about his poor opinion of his wife who he thinks looks like a zombie.

Ada and Sherry have much larger roles in the new game which is a welcome addition. Ada's segment is a wonderful but brief change of pace to Leon's game. In Claire's, you get to play as Sherry, which I don't feel is as strong (read: good) as Ada's segment, but it's still a very powerful moment when you have to run and hide from a sex pervert (Hello RedLetterMedia fans!).

Let's also not forget Mr. X, the sexual Tyrant-a-saurus. Well, what can I say - he's awesome. I suggest you not look up how he works (how he's programmed to search for you), or you'll find yourself exploiting his behavior to make the game easier. The Ada/Sherry moments and Mr. X are the only moments that I would say are significantly improved over the original, and I simply wish there was MORE of that.

I've probably missed quite a lot to talk about, such as the 1st and 2nd games, Hunk and Tofu and other unlockables, but I've written half a novel here already, so let me finish it up.

The Resident Evil 2 Remake I had been dying for.

In the last decade(s) the Resident Evil experiences have strayed far from what made them great for me. The Zombie Survival horror that made the original trilogy my favorite was slowly being phased out. Granted, the newer games have had their pros, and have still provided a great experience overall.

Luckily the R.E.2 Remake has recaptured, revamped, and re-established the original feeling of dread and horror that I was missing in the more recent installments.

The overall experience I had, playing on Hardcore from the get go, with the R.E.2 remake was one of pure exhilaration. Especially during my first play-through, I could feel dread when moving around each corner, or creeping past another corpse, ever aware that it could pop up and cost me my limited ammunition, vital healing items, or at worst end it all. I found myself constantly planning my next moves carefully, taking every boss encounter one shot at a time, and discovering every new area with a certain degree of caution. It was tense, it was scary, it was FUN!!!

The only aspect of the game that did at times cost frustration was the pure randomness of basic zombie death rates. At times you could run through a segment, downing zombies with only a few shots, and out right killing them with anywhere from 1 to 3 well placed shots. The next run, you could make 15 or more direct head shots, and it still wouldn't be enough. Unfortunately death is almost guaranteed in Hardcore, and if you were (un)fortunate enough to be attempting the S+ rating on hardcore, death could mean redoing a LARGE section of the game, including difficult boss fights, and with such varying ammunition uses and death rates for the basic zombies, it could become frustrating.

Despite that, I definitely enjoyed the game to the fullest. In the end, completing both stories (sides A and B) on hardcore was totally worth it, and the feeling is indescribable. More so when you manage to get that coveted S+ rating, earning you some awesome weapons for your next play-through (I won't spoil the rewards).

Great remake of an already great game - the graphics are fantastic and the RE Engine looks so good here. The whole thing comes to life with a new sense of realism and fresh energy, and the tension of combat feels just *chef kiss*. If you like horror adventure games, this was one of the best to do it back in the day, and now it's even better. The modern updates here are tastefully executed; nothing has been tinkered with without good reason, and the game is faithful to the original in all the right ways while making things more convenient for modern players. 

A couple of small complaints. First, it's a bit short. For some, that'll be a plus...there's no bloat, the game is very lean and tight. Short and lean games aren't necessarily a bad thing. The game is, however, $80 CAD at full price, which is a little steep for what you're getting. I'd say pick it up on sale and you won't be disappointed. Secondly, the boss battles are pretty bad - they are probably the only lackluster gameplay element here. They feel "video game-y" in a way that runs counter to the mood and tension of the rest of the game's combat scenarios. Not a deal breaker, and these are the same bosses from the original game after all, so Capcom is just being consistent...but maybe they should have taken the chance to improve on this aspect of the old game instead of just reproducing it. If you want a spooky survival horror game, there is a 0% chance you'll be disappointed. This game is so well rounded, I can't imagine anyone thinking it's less than remarkably enjoyable on the whole.

Story is gripping and motivates you to progress and push forward. Sound production is otherworldly. Graphics are so good you'll stop and just stare at objects and scenery dozens of times throughout the game. Gameplay is intuitive, makes you think and rewards you ever so satisfyingly for smart plays, daring exploration, and puzzle solving. Super worthwhile replay-ability with collectables, hardcore mode, and the chase for S+ rankings. Cutscenes are hardly ever boring / are skippable. Tons of in-game unlockables such as item and character models, special infinite ammo weapons, dev art, and alternate costumes. Can't remember if it was preorder only or deluxe edition, but it even has classic sounds mode that replaces lots of music and menu sounds to the original nostalgic RE2 SFX & BGM. Settings have tons of graphics, sound, and display options, all of which are changeable mid-session without crashing the game. Seamless gamepad support. (I played with an Xbox One controller 90% of the time.) Scary enough to have me jump and yell periodically even after 100+ hours of playing the campaigns over and over. 

Some cons: Remodeled Claire Redfield has a sort of uncanny face and doesn't resemble the personality of the original game. The sewer portion of the game seems noticeably lower in level design quality than the rest of the areas. Bosses are kind of below average mechanics and design-wise. Sherry's stealth mission has a lame, unforgiving segment. The (free) Ghost Survivors DLC sprints are not even worth playing in my opinion; especially "No Way Out". There are some gripes to be had, but for every con there are a dozen pros. 

I am jaded and cynical about the state of the gaming industry and this game went so far above and beyond. Worth it at release for $70 (Deluxe Edition). I feel like Capcom could squeeze RE remakes out of this formula for a long time without it becoming boring and uninteresting.

After playing this game to absolute death I have to for the most part give Capcom absolute praise for bringing Re2 back for a more modern feel in 2019 compared to the original on the ps1 of 1998. It is literally one of the best re-imaginings of a game that many gamers love and remember.

It's a game that will scare the ♥♥♥♥ out of you and have you on the edge of your pc chair no matter how many times you play it because honestly, I thought after doing so many runs of this, that I would get used to the jump scares. NOPE! They still get me everytime and it's sooo satisfying because when it happens, all logic and reasoning goes out the window and you panic. You either shoot what scared the living ♥♥♥♥ out of you or you run screaming and then feel weary of what's around the corner.

Visually it's amazing to look at, sound and tone of the game are pretty indepth but also keeps you alert. The Voice acting is top notch and the story is more or less the same as the original, just some parts were changed about slightly. Other then that, it's an amazing game.

Negatives:
To get police station in the original was survival horror at it's finest, it took a lot of tries and getting used to the game as it throws horde after horde of zombie infested goodness at you. Hell if you got to the police station without picking up any items and surviving by your wits alone, a super zombie, brad vickers would be accessible to kill for a special key that gave you alternative clothing and weapons for characters.

In this version of the game, they have removed doing that completely and you can get to the police station in 2 minutes or less, no hassle, no alternative clothing or weapons and especially NO zombie brad who was killed by nemesis in RE3 and was something that linked RE2 AND RE3 together and they replace it with a very dissapointing poster of Brad Vickers on the 2nd run. So in throwing all that lore out the window, they instead make getting stuff via paid DLC. This to me was the biggest dissapointment of the remake.

My 2nd dissapointment was that in either 1st or 2nd run, Claire and Leon barely have any real interaction with each other, there was so much more in the original. Also they both more or less fight the same bosses in 1st or 2nd run, so it's still the same and nothings really changed.

With the original RE2 you could play LEON A scenario and see what you missed on the CLAIRE B run that tied both of them together, or doing the opposite would also yield different scenarios but more importantly, more diversity, different storylines and dialogue being played out. It's what made the original far more satisfying because it wasn't always the same. Doing both characters A/B runs gave it far more replayability and told are far more interesting story, gave it even greater depth.

The remake sadly doesn't do that and as much as I love this remake, part of me feels like it was a half arsed rush job just to get this game made and so much content was removed that if they kept it to how it was originally this game would be a 10/10 for me hands down, but it's not.

If you played the original 4 different times, you got more storyline and different changes that affected either scenario and you'd be happy to replay the game to see what changed and would have you invested and on the edge of your seat because things WOULD be different.

If you play the remake 4 different times, it's the same the 1st 2 times. If you did 1st run with Leon and then the 2nd run with claire and after completing do the alternative, there's zero differences. Storylines the same, bosses are the same, it's not even worth it trying to do all 4 alternative times because there's effectively only 2.

Is this a great game? Hands down it is. Visually and how it sounds, it's better then the original but in terms of storyline and greater depth, the original RE2 was and still is better then the remake and honestly the PS1 version of RE2 gives you more content, more storyline and more monsters.

It's very rare that I play through a game more than once. This game, though, I have played through ~12 times from start to finish. 4 were my first playthroughs for Leon A/B and Claire A/B, then 8 were to get S+ on both standard and hardcore mode for each storyline. I like this game so much I played through it that many times.

The sound design is partly what makes this game so great. You can hear things coming from certain directions SO WELL. The graphics are amazing (Most of the time) and the gameplay is also amazing. Then there's the story and characters which are all fantastic as well. Just about everything in this game is top tier AAA quality. Just about everything.

The problems with this game are sorta nitpicky, but still kinda bugged me. The graphics are, like I said, amazing, but sometimes there are some rogue textures that are so incredibly low quality I have to wonder how the ♥♥♥♥ that got through QA. Some blood splatters on walls and cloth textures on tables are so distractingly low res that it really pulls you out of the immersive atmosphere the game sets up.

Another issue is the A/B runs. While I love the idea, it wasn't executed too well. You do the exact same things in the B runs as you do in the A runs but with different puzzle solutions and lock codes. For example, let's say you go through Leon A first like I did. You complete the whole game and then go for Claire B. Claire starts a little bit into her A story in the B variant (Kinda confusing, I know, but if you've played the game you know what I mean) and you should pretty much be right on Leon's heels the entire game as you do the exact same things he just did. Open the same passageways and kill the same bosses (Mostly). It doesn't make any sense as you know Leon already did these things so why do they need to be repeated. It could have been done WAY better, but what we got was kinda disappointing.

The last issue is with the extra modes. The ghost survivors and the 4th/[spoiler]tofu[/spoiler] survivor. They're just incredibly difficult short runs though the game, some giving alternate storylines to what happened in the game. They're so horribly difficult and cheap though that it's more frustrating than fun to play them. They're designed to be beaten within 10 mins each, but the amount of attempts you'll need to get to the end will add up to a few hours of frustration. Not really worth playing that much.

Even with those 3 very nitpicky issues, this game is a masterpiece and I cannot wait for RE3 Remake.
