Really nice remake. Best release this year.
Not an entirely "horror" game though, more like "zombie suspenful survival" (Silent Hill 2 would be what I consider "horror").

1st Run Estimated Length: 8-9 hours.
2nd Run Estimated Length: 4-5 hours.
Extra Modes Estimated Length: 2-3 hours.

(Took me about 35-40 hours to 100%, achievements and all. YMMV)

(And 2 more mirror runs available with the other character if you want, which doubles it's length).

Some key things you should know:
- "Standard" difficulty has adaptive difficulty (the more shots you score and zombies killed, + difficulty; the more shots you miss and times you die, - difficulty).
- Zombies have a set amount of HP, so they can get back up when you put them down if they still got some HP left. They do an "Oh no..." animation raising their arm from the ground when they're gone for good. That, or you blow their head off.
- Knife damage is linked to framerate. More FPS, more damage. Console plebs cry.
- 1st Boss is a bullet sponge and dull (just repeating the same pattern for minutes). Just change your resolution to 640x480 and knife him.
- There's an extra mode with "what if" stories (5x10 min each), made for speedrunning.
- Getting an S+ Rank in Hardcore gives you a bazooka/minigun with unlimited ammo, which, if you want, makes all posterior runs a walk in the park so you can 100% everything.
- Claire 1st, Leon 2nd is Canon.

Positive points (IMO):
- Some weapons (shotgun, magnum) are powerful with scarce ammo, which makes them a delight to use.
- Graphics, music and ambientation are top notch and stick to the original theme.
- Tyrant.
- Final boss, weapons and middle section of game is different for each one of the two characters. So you will do 2 runs.

Negative points (IMO):
- No plot connection or enough differences between 1st Run and 2nd Run. This could have duplicated the replayability and made the plot much more interesting.
- Can't melee (except for knife, if that counts). You're telling me I have a shotgun in my hands and yet when a zombie gets close I can't smack him with the butt of the gun, so I have to stand there stupidly while it lunges at me? This design decision detracts from inmersion and realism.

All in all: nice work, Capcom. Eagerly waiting RE:3.

To me, one of the trickiest balances in game design is the split between fun and challenge. It’s fun to be challenged, but too much challenge can take a serious bite out of the fun. Stressful games like Dark Souls and Darkest Dungeon have found success by finding players that will accept them on their own unique terms, but that’s not the only way to bridge the gap. I know that now because of Resident Evil 2, a game that can be stressful, terrifying, and incredibly fun all at once. Honestly I didn’t even think it was possible to thread that needle so effectively, but RE2 has the magic touch that can push you to your breaking point and make you love every second of it.

Something has gone terribly, terribly wrong in Raccoon City. A vicious, unstoppable virus has torn through the town, leaving the residents either dead or undying. It’s a hell of a first day on the force for rookie cop Leon Kennedy, and a huge complication in Claire Redfield’s search for her brother. Their paths will cross several times in this chaos, as they search for both answers and escape. The architects of this disaster are still at large, and may be closer than either Leon or Claire would think, along with some shadowy figures who have their own interests here. But there’s a ruined city, a litany of puzzling obstacles, and countless zombies between them and their goal, and it’s going to take a little luck and whole lot of nerve to get through.

For the record, I never played the original Resident Evil 2, and I haven’t even played any versions of the first game in the series. I’m jumping into this with only some basic cultural literacy here, but RE2 is perfectly accommodating to newcomers. The plot is perfectly simple at its core: zombies everywhere, don’t die. I understand there are plenty of references to other games in the details, but you definitely don’t need to study the wiki to shoot zombies and collect crests. Indeed, the quality of the game’s cutscenes and voice acting is so incredibly high that you’ll surely find yourself engrossed in the unfolding drama regardless of your background knowledge. The presentation here does a ton to sell the experience of a zombie apocalypse, and heighten the tension or humanize situations when most effective.

The real star of the show, though, is the action. Following an intense intro that wastes exactly no time getting to the good stuff, you’ll find yourself in a vast police station that’s all kinds of falling apart. Zombies are breaking in the windows, crawling out of the vents, and laying in wait for their next meal. As Leon or Claire, you’ve only got what you can find to deal with them, which includes a very modest amount of weapons, ammunition, tools, and medicine. Your foes in this game are not the mindless hordes you might be accustomed to from other zombie titles, as they can take bullet after bullet to the head without breaking their pace. Every single undead is an existential threat to you, with the potential to take your health from full to zero if you don’t take them seriously. You won’t have the resources to dispatch every single zombie, either, so resource management is absolutely essential.

And this all goes double for the more exotic foes you’ll face as you descend deeper into the mystery! The result is a game that’s intensely stressful every single time you depart from a safe room, that can terrify you simply by putting a common enemy in an uncommon place and letting them do what they do. Your life is threatened here in a way most horror games don’t have the gumption to do, because not only can the monsters kill you, defeating the monsters badly can kill you. Being far away from your save point or stash of items with no bullets or no healing items is terrifying unlike any jump scare or chase scene, and perfectly evokes the true horror of zombie media, that of inevitable doom. That feeling only gets stronger when the game reveals more of its threats, one of which has become iconic in how it heralds your absolute downfall.

Resident Evil 2 is chock full of sequences you don’t want to go through. You’ll see things through windows or on your map that you know will be total nightmares to endure. And you’ll do it, because the experience is so rewarding. The tight over-the-shoulder controls and aiming give you all the tools you need to use every bullet effectively and dodge past foes. Weapon impacts are forceful and meaty, and if you’re any sort of gorehound then you’ll be treated to some top-tier blood and viscera as the bullets fly. Seriously, I have never seen a game that modeled bullet impacts on heads so effectively, and if it wasn’t happening to zombies I’m not sure I could handle it. But getting that lucky shot that splits an undead’s head like a watermelon is all the more gratifying for the absurd explosion of flesh that announces it.

Really, this is about as close as you can get to the perfect zombie survival game, if slow zombies, thin resources, and risky combat are what you’re looking for. And there’s tons of it to experience, too, with the A and B routes for both characters that reveal different bits of the story and offer different challenges. There are additional modes as well, and a fair number of unexpected twists and secrets along the way, all of which should last you dozens of hours to uncover. The only reason you’d punch out early from this one is to give yourself a breather, though, because it’s an absolute master class in turning stress and challenge into pure fun.

A phenomenal achievement: It does not merely invoke the spirit of the original game, it improves upon it in every aspect. 

The original Resident Evil 2 has been ported to a number of systems without any real alteration, but this is a full-fledged remake and every effort has been made to adapt the original's excellent story, puzzle and action elements to a more modern survival horror game. This is how almost every remake should be done: what worked the best is mostly the same, what could've worked better is now far better.

Even the technical aspects amaze me; some games are lazy ports of console versions, with few graphics settings, making them hard to run. This game's graphics options allow you to go as low 320x240 and even offers interlaced rendering, a feature I've never seen in graphics settings. This game runs extremely well on my laptop, could probably run well on a ten-year-old system and on a more modern gaming PC, it's one of the most gorgeous games released this year.

Resident Evil 2 Remastered is easily the best game I've ever purchased. It became my favorite game immediately. There's so much content and so much to do, you wont regret your purchase, I promise.

Although the Resident Evil franchise was an integral part of my teenage years, I just couldnt get myself to play the original RE:2 due to how poorly it aged throughout the years (understandably so), and as years went along I helplessly watched one of my favorite franchises take a nosedive in terms of quality with the introduction of more action oriented RE:5 and 6. The radical shift from horror survival to emphasis on third person action/shooting just didnt quite appeal to me ( and to many others ) and just as I was  about to give up on the franchise, RE:7 re-ignited my passion towards it. I was stoked to hear CAPCOM was going to remake re:2 because it meant I was finally going to be able to experience it for the first time.

Having never played the original RE:2, I dove headfirst into the remake. I knew the main beats of the story and how it concluded, but as they say, its not about the destination, its about the journey.

[olist]
[*] First of all, this game is breath-takingly beautiful to look at; from lighting to zombies being dismembered, everything is amazingly detailed. On my first playthrough, half the time I was just looking at how detailed the environment was. I tried reading every single poster or magazine scattered around the police station. Sound design is used phenomenally, you can rely on your hearing to figure out what's going on in other rooms and when you are being chased by a certain individual. The option to switch back and forth between the original soundtrack is a nice touch and greatly appreciated.

[*] After dealing with the same molded type for hours in RE:7, I was really looking forward to be reunited with the OG enemy of the franchise; the zombies. They really steal the show in the remake, and in certain difficulties they can really mess up with your progression depending on how you approach to dealing with them. New dismemberment options give players more freedom; you can cripple them by shooting at their legs and effectively limit their movements or you can roll the dice and try to get a lucky critical headshot on them, and so on. Regardless of how you choose to deal with them, its amazing to see how responsive zombies are to player movements.

[*] Change from fixed camera angles to over-the-shoulder third person view really adds up to the atmospheric value of the game. I like the concept of fixed camera angles, especially not knowing what waits the player around corners and the added scare elements it provides, but the third person view is executed so well in this game that I think even the most hardcore resident evil players who grew up playing the originals can appreciate the modern take on the game.

[*] You'll hear from some players and critics that the remake divides from the original when it comes to the way how B scenarios are handled in the remake, and it holds some truth in the grand scheme of things, but that's the only negative thing I can think of about the remake. Even with that, the way the story is retold in scenario A of Leon and Claire are so well done that I can overlook this one problem. In some aspects the game combines the previous A and B scenarios of the original RE:2 and that's okay because it adds to the overall clarity of the storyline. B scenarios differ very slightly from A scenarios in a narrative sense, but gameplay wise there are a lot of surprises that players will run across as the item and enemy placements are different from the A scenario. But other than that, the story portion of both scenarios for both characters are pretty much identical, and if I were to be picky I could find ways to whine about it.
[/olist]

Overall its safe to say that I absolutely loved this game and finished it multiple times on different platforms. It's no doubtedly my game of the year and I wish everyone will give this game and the upcoming remake of RE:3 a shot; it holds a great potential to people who havent played any survival horror games to be introduced to a whole new genre, which would be amazing for the overall diversity of the gaming industry to escape from the monolithic openworld or battle-royale mentality and could encourage studios to invest in this amazing genre.

Resident Evil 2 is a remake of Resident Evil 2. You play as Leon Scott Kennedy, a very special boy who still tries to arrest people as the city around him is turning into dust.
Or you play as Claire Redfield, the sister of boulder punching giga hunk Chris Redfield. She's looking for her brother because its 1998 and cell phones haven't been invented by John Henry Cellphone yet. 
Both stories follow Leon and Claire as they attempt to escape Raccoon City while also uncovering the secrets that Umbrella has hidden. 
Like larger blister monsters. Or unstoppable super weapons that think its okay to wear a fedora. 

Resident Evil 2 retells the story of Resident Evil 2 while stepping away from some story beats of Resident Evil 2. Leon and Clair don't even really look like how they looked in Resident Evil 2, since technology has come a long way since 1280 AD and now we have things like motion capture and actors. 

With the liberties Resident Evil 2 takes with Resident Evil 2's story, I started looking at it like a movie based on the events instead of a complete retelling of Resident Evil 2. 

Okay, I'll stop now. 

Biohazard 2 is one of those games that I loaded up, started my first playthrough, and then didn't close it until I finished my first playthrough. Something about the gameflow just kept me glued to the game from start to finish. It wasn't the story, since I'm old and already know how it ends. But it has more to do that the game is just kind of made for me.

You see from over your character's shoulder, and not from the view of a bug in the corner of the room like the original RE2. I actually liked tank controls from the original, but I also like pulling hair out of my nose, so take that as you will.

Exploring a destroyed police department made by the greatest madman known to humanity, while poking your flashlight over dark corners and committing police brutality on the undead is just kind of tickled me in the naughty bits. There's a flow to the gameplay that I can get behind, where you just kind of know where to go. I didn't even notice the location markers on my map until I was almost done my first play through. 

Enemies this time around are much tougher than they were in previous games, with the zambos being able to sometimes take entire magazines to the noggin with only having stern words to say to you later.
The stern words are biting. 

You come across other enemies in the game, lickers make a return, as well as Conrad: The Hungry Alligator. There are also some enemies missing, like the giant spider. I was told that people were having panic attacks and running out of the room during play testing. I don't know how true that is, but I'm going to believe it.
Because its funny. 

Urban Terror 2 also brings back T-00, an enemy that only shows up in some runs of the original game. Only instead of showing up as a boss encounter of sorts, now he follows you around and gives me the same mental experience as being chased by teenagers or my drunken father. 

He's not as annoying as I thought he would be, since you can avoid him completely if you know what you're doing. 

What else do I like? 

I like how the guns feel, it's nice to shoot things in this game. Please don't tell my parole officer I said that. 

Everything has a nice, meaty crunch to it when you shoot them, zombie limbs and brain domes fall apart under gun fire, and sometimes their heads just kind of rupture after one hit. It feels nice to shoot things. Which says more about me than it does about the game.

You should play Resident Evil: The Second. I'm glad I got to play it before the year is out, since I had my eyes on it since its release and I never actually got around to [strike]stealing[/strike] buying the game. 
You get a few run throughs of the game, with two stories per character. You also get some extra content with the game, letting you play as two other characters as well as the return of everyone's main man: HUNK. 
I love him.

When the original RE2 came out years ago, I was very young and didn't really get to fully experience the game/ understand it. It was too difficult for me to finish it at the time. Now that I got this new version of the game I get to appreciate all the things that it got right all those years ago while many new zombie games cant even remotely get close to it. 

[h2]Pros[/h2]

- The graphics are awesome and really enjoyable to watch. Everything has details and all the different locations that you visit feel alive and real. There are so many tiny detailed things in this game that makes everything look so real. 

- The game is actually [b]scary[/b] specially when it comes to the sound and look of the zombies. They are really creepy. And also hard to kill. most of the times you get to either blast their head with a shotgun or try to put them downs few times over with your pistol. Since they take few bullets to go down, you can easily get overwhelmed with 4 or more zombies. The bullets are generally "scarce" which makes everything a bit worse. But the overall toughness of the zombies with the creepy realistic atmosphere of the game makes the whole experience really fun.

- Another really fun thing that I enjoyed about this game in comparison with most other zombie games is that the each (or at least most zombies/creatures) are pretty unique to their location. For the most part, each zombie remains in the location and in the same state that you kill it which makes them somehow more believable and realistic as oppose to random zombie spawn and corpse disappearance that you see in other games.

- There are lots of big and small puzzles that you have to solve essentially to progress in the game that are fun when you get them down. It's actually not as annoying and repetitive as other stuffs you usually find in games. They make you feel smart :) 

[h2]cons[/h2]

- The game is rather a bit short. You can complete a walkthrough in about 5~7 hours on your first try. Probably faster on the other tries once you solved the puzzles once before. 

- There are not many (or at least many variations) in bosses. And those bosses may get repetitive. since you just have to basically shoot some obvious critical spots to take them down. If they made a couple of new and different bosses it would have been better. It could also make the game a bit longer too. 


- The very high level - general story of umbrella and G-Virus is cool and all. But the character dialogues and small inter-relationships is just a bit too much and too dramatic. We can do better if we want to. On one hand it stays true to the OG RE2 and the wired over the top characters but I guess in these years for a more global audience they really needed to rewrite few things.

This was my favorite of the series back in the day.  20 years later, it feels new and nostalgic all at once, just as their website promises.  I will say that the game feels oddly stiff and linear compared to similar contemporary titles.  I haven't owned a console since the Playstation 2 - I've been exclusively a PC gamer since then - and the console-y-ness of this game was a little jarring. I'm accustomed to a more open-world experience these days.  In this game, all of the beautifully rendered location artwork is strictly for show, more akin to a well-designed ride line at a major theme park than an actual environment you can interact with.  You're pretty much staying between invisible rails.  Each room you enter has 2 or three points you can interact with, and the rest is just scenery. Shoot at a book for instance, and nowadays we expect to see the PhysX engine kick in and send it flying artfully across the room, pages fluttering in the simulated breeze.  Here, your bullet will simply ping off of the solid lead book without effect.  

That being said, there's a frightful amount of action taking place in between those rails, and they've managed to make the game far more intense than the original PS1 version.  The voice acting and character animations really tell a believable story, and it's easy to get caught up in it. I don't think it's right to call this an action game nowadays.  Call it a well-done visual horror-novel/puzzle game with a strong action element, and you're closer to the mark, in my opinion.

If you enjoyed the original, as I did, by all means pick it up for nostalgia's sake.  If you're looking for actual zombie survival horror, i'd recommend 7 days to die for a voxel-based minecraft/zombie apocalypse mashup.  

If you're looking for innovation, you won't find it here.  This game is strictly looking backwards. But it's doing so very, very well.

This comes from someone who hasn't played the original Resident Evil 2, but IMO this stands on its own as a pretty solid product.

[list]
[*]Short campaign, but this is generally to be expected from a horror game where the same tactics over and over again can drag. Not only is the quality bar high enough to justify it however, but there are numerous bonus modes and challenge runs that have plenty of content. Certainly more unique content than Resident Evil 7 which I already thought was fine. The alternate Claire/Leon campaigns mean that there are a total of four unique playthroughs to be had.

[*]One of the more controversial aspects of this remake is Mr X/Tyrant, who did exist in the original RE2 but whose role has been significantly expanded here. There's nothing that screams "fear" quite like an absolute unit of a man in a trenchcoat, who is completely immortal (damage can take him out for a few minutes, but he'll get back up) and whose stomps are loud enough to be heard through several walls. Some do complain about him but I personally think he adds a constant pressure to vital segments of the game, and it seriously changes the way you look at the map. Plus, he isn't actually present in the majority of the story.

[*]Weapons and ammo balance is up to, if not above, the usual excellent Resident Evil standard. I felt constantly in need of more ammo, herbs, grenades, ecetera. To be honest, this aspect of the game felt even better than some previous Resi games. Every weapon felt useful (looking at you, Burner), and every pickup was a welcome reprieve.

[*]All methods of dealing damage (including melee, melee durability is a thing) are limited and enemies are extremely hardy. Common zombies will, more often than not, simply get up if you don't destroy their heads/burn their bodies, and it's mostly a matter of time as to when. As a result, unlike something like Resi 4 or 7 where I could easily clear out areas, in this game my greatest victories were when I could avoid engagements, not win them.

[*]Puzzle solving was also great, there wasn't a single one I didn't like. None are ridiculously complicated or anything, but as far as Resident Evil puzzles go, everything works out fairly logically and the process of arriving at the right solution is generally fair and fun. One particularly notable aspect is that you can Examine items in your inventory related to puzzles for clues for solving them, if you need some help figuring out what to do.
[/list]

Initially, I had a negative review of this game. Why, you may ask, while there is so much to love? I'm going through a thought process and mark each point accordingly as +/-

+ Phenomenal graphics both technically and artwise
+ High adrenaline horror survival gameplay
+ Smart gameplay with free route planning and having to actually pay attention, investigate item uses etc. there is no objective marker to follow like a zombie like in every game these days, and it makes a difference you wouldn't imagine possible if you are used to those.
+ Extremely good optimization for PC, plus deep settings

- And there I was, enjoying all of it, until the game put an unkillable monster on my back. And it literally killed the game for me - I couldn't deal with the frustration and stress. I uninstalled and reinstalled it almost a dozen times, terrified of the Tyrant every time it showed up it was frustrating because I had to run to places I did not want to go to, and it was even worse when he wasn't around, because I knew I can't use my guns - there is no melee combat, mind you, you just "consume your knife" when something gets to you - I just knew he heard it, I knew he was coming, so even if well equipped with granades, flashbangs, ammo for every weapon, several health packs, I knew I have nothing because I can't use these against an immortal enemy, and I can't use these on anything else because said immortal enemy would show up. It was unbearably frustrating and gave me anxiety I could physically feel, to the point I had to hit alt F4, and then repeat this with about 8 uninstall / reinstalls. It's not that I'm afraid to fight something, it's knowing he is made immortal until the story writer decides to give you a rocket launcher and oneshot cut him into pieces. But until then? Granade launchers, granades, flamethrower, nothing can hurt this son of a b.... you know when you understand a system designed to f.... you and you see how it works but can't do anything against it? This is it. And it ruined an otherwise top notch game for me. Sadly, I had to make him a joke. I had to look up every single guide about how to exploit his behaviour, what rooms he is secretly scipted to never look into, how his animations work and when he is avoidable and exploitable. He was no longer the terrifying Tyrant, he was an annoyance, and I'm sad I had to do this just to be able to continue playing. 

+ The reason I change this review from negative to positive is because I got past that point, and it turns out, Tyrant is merely present for about 2 hours. Once you get that key that opens the garage gate, you can say goodbye to him until the very end of the game and a few minutes in between. This second half of the game is far more linear and action packed, you are overpacked with ammo and new weapons. So the game is half horror survival puzzle thingy, and half not so scary anymore action game. I think that's a good thing, I throughly enjoyed the latter half aswell, I'm just saying this because if you expect a horror game from start to end, it's not that. 

- By the end of it, however, I was left with a bittersweet taste in my mouth. Turns out, all the questions you ask yourself are mostly left unanswered and even more pile up. You meet a new character? Well, say goodbye to Claire until the end where she awkwardly shows up without any explanation what happened to her, how she got into "spoiler location" or why, or who is that little girl with her. You are supposed to start over the game as Claire to get to know what happened to her, which is again, can be really good because it's more value for money with different routes and a whole new campaign (with much reused locations so it doesn't even make sense as a parallel story), but if you want a whole story with a decent ending and expected answers from one playthrough you are not getting it. And you'll be left googling what should you do now, after you finished it - there is Leon A playthrough, but you just unlocked Leon B playthrough that starts over and "plays a little different" whatever it means. Then there is Claire A and B playthrough unlocked answell and nothing tells me which one I'm supposed to play. Hell even forums give me incoherent answers, the whole thing is a f.... mess.

+ But a damn good one at that.

If you want to enjoy the old school survival horror Re Series with an awesome graphic, this is absolutely the game for you.
Nothing more to add about the story: if you enjoyed the game years ago, this remake simply follows the same exact steps story wise so just enjoy the breakdown in Raccoon City and how Leon transformed from rookie to the legend we know today.
10/10 for the graphic engine: not only it has an incredible crisp and awesome graphic, but I've also noticed that everything is optimised so well that it will run smoothly in old machines too.

The only downside I've found is about the combat system: is mostly random, sometimes zombies will die after 3 headshots (1 if you manage to crit like the old games) but sometimes they will die after 5 or 6 shots (and there's a chance that they will get up again if their head is not popped). Also zombies will knockdown in random situations (I had a situation where I shot an acid round towards a zombie + another 3 shots to his head, he continued to charge me like I wasn't shooting at him at all). Same goes for when a zombie grabs you: the front grabs are 100% dodgable (if you have a secondary item equipped, ofc) but the grabs from the back and from below (i.e. from crawling zombies) are simply impossible to dodge and is guaranteed that you will take damage from that attacks. The aiming system will not help you in these situations because (as a survival horror I guess) is imprecise even if your'e just backing up a little while aiming.

Overall I totally suggest this game and personally I can't wait for the RE3 remake, even if this title has a lot of frustrating combat system problems, the rest of the positive things, in my opinion, are enough to give a high personal score overall.

I haven't played the original game, so I can only look at it as a game on its own. I do know a lot about the original game; seen speed runs, read wikipedias, etc, so I know a general idea of the game. There are some differences; the sewer part is different, the parts where you split up as secondary characters are very different as well. But overall, the game is fantastic. For the first run, it will be scary, or a little nerve wrecking, given that enemies do take a lot of bullets, and there is limited sources for ammo. (Though, once you play through the game, you do realize there is more than plenty. At least in Standard Mode). 

At this point it's going to be well known, but you are chased by an invincible enemy at one point around the Raccoon Police Department. It does add a bit more tension as you can hear the footsteps of the character walking around. One major disappointment, especially for fans of the original game, is that there are not really too many differences between Route A and B. The beginning portion of the game is a little different; mainly, one room that was a safe room for the first part of the game no longer is, and you do get a couple of key items much earlier in the run, so you unlock a few rooms much earlier. The only other major difference is that there is a different type of ammunition that replaces the locations of where the 9mm bullets are at, which means you will be using a different type of handgun in Route B as compared to Route A. (For the most part). From what I understand in the original game, stuff you did in Route A did have some consequences for Route B, and one of the key villains only arrived in Route B in the original game, where in the remake the villain is in both routes. It's a shame Capcom didn't do the same thing in the remake. It would have made it much better. 

In case it wasn't obvious from the screenshots, the game is in third person. Your character is very vulnerable to damage by zombies. One neat aspect, which I know was in earlier RE games, is that you do have items you can counter with. If a zombie bites you, and you have a knife, or grenade of some sort, you can counter to avoid damage. This is especially important in hardcore as one bit can pretty much bring you down to extremely low health. It's a game play mechanic that really adds to the survivor horror element. Also, for fans  of the ink ribbon, while you can save as much as you would like on Standard difficulty, Hardcore mode does require the use of an ink ribbon. 

Overall, while I wish Route A and B scenarios were done better in the terms of cause and effect, this is just a fun game to play through. Also, it's a great looking game as well. It's long enough to feel satisfied with your first play through, yet short enough to just replay it again if you want to. And, personally, I do have a lot of fun replaying this game. Completely recommend buying.

TL;DR: Perfect survival horror. 
Originally played on PS4, and never played the PS1 classic.
Story Modes (Scariest) (Great Narrative)
Resident Evil 2 starts slow and campy with good tension and visual horror. You play as Claire Redfield, trying to find your brother Chris who was supposed to be at the STARS office, or as Leon Kennedy, a rookie cop just trying to do his job. It is recommended you play as Claire first, then as Leon in the "second run" mode because each hero(ine) encounters different challenges and this is the "canon" set of events.

The Fourth Survivor (Most Fun) (Action-oriented)
After completing both story modes, "The Fourth Survivor" Extra mode is unlocked. You play as Hunk, an Umbrella Security Services operative that has to fight his way past crowds of infected. With only the supplies on your person, you have to make a mad dash for the front gate of RPD. Tofu is your reward.

Similar to Hunk's mode, but with poison cloud zombies. Mad dash from the gun shop to the sewer breach. A few loot zombies along the way to keep you supplied.

Similar to Hunk's mode, but there are armored zombies, loot zombies, and resupply stations. Set in NEST and gives you many choices on how to fight/ flee the infected.

I remember playing Resident Evil 2 on the original Sony Playstation over 20 years ago. That was a time when developers were just beginning to scratch the surface of what 3D video games could be. The original had great level design that oozed atmosphere in every room . It knew when to add a puzzle to slow things down, and when to add a jumpscare to get the player back on their toes. The game didn't need a 15 minutes cut scene to explain the desperation of the situation Leon and Claire were in, it instead [i]showed[/i] you with gameplay.

The remake of the game is all of the things that made the original great, but with a revamped control system, modern graphics, and with the addition of a few minor quality of life changes.

Yes, most developers (and movie directors) will spend the next 10 years remaking the classic titles of our generation to gain a quick buck off nostalgia alone. But, when a developer takes a slow and steady approach to understand why the original game was so great, we get a title like Resident Evil 2 Remake. 

Everyone should play this game.

As someone trying to play the game as an action shooter, I had a hard time getting into it at first. The appeal wasn't fully apparent to me until about the second hour in. I'm glad I stuck with it though, because that's when the horror elements really kick in and there's a true sense of dread.
The game stays true to the original in all the best ways; never really holding your hand, but adding modern conveniences that make the game feel less tedious and confusing. It never really loses focus of the theme either, only ramping up near the last hour in true RE fashion.
Graphics are stunning, especially on the highest settings, and that holds true from the moment you start the game to the very end. Optimization is another sweet spot for me, as I never had a frame rate dip throughout my time.
Every aspect of the game is lovingly crafted and detailed, and for a game whose gun play is supposed to take a backseat to the horror, shooting zombies is incredibly satisfying. Chunks of the zombie's faces and limbs fall off with a well placed shot.
While I wouldn't fully recommend it to someone looking for a fast-paced zombie shooter, if you're willing to let yourself get engrossed in this experience, I fully recommend RE2 Remake

Fun Fun Fun!!   ( and scary, scary scary!!! )

CAPCOM has successfully recreated a dark, brooding, living, fully-breathing (or just barely breathing) Raccoon City in despair with its infamous Police Dept. for the 21st century for seasoned veterans and new players alike.


PROS:      Horror survival returns, zombies are frightening again, graphics are breathtaking (as always), audio, atmosphere, tension, Mr. X, Lickers, item management, pacing (mostly), 2 playthroughs for an alternate perspective (a Pro for me!), story, enough action, and yeah... a whole lot of FUN! (You will want to play this again if you are a fan or not.)

CONS:      A lack of variable enemies, the sewers area lacks intriguing enemies, the new G-Adult enemies aren't "fun" and drag the game experience down, perhaps too many cut-scenes for my liking, and maybe Mr. X is (at the very least) slightly annoying and overpowering


This REmake must have had diligent developers working on this 24/7 to achieve that perfect and harmonious "balance" of horror survival , tension, pacing, story/character progression; which serves to give the player a reason, a drive really, to move forward and find out why everything is happening and why someone should play the game which is a REmake of the original 1998 version, of course. That must have been the most challenging part, for this "balance" is what Resident Evil has ALWAYS been in my mind, and what Capcom should ALWAYS implement in their RE franchise to achieve success as this game had right at its release!

Again, the tension, and pacing is phenomenal in most of the game! The sewers part could have been handled quite a bit better with a "more enjoyable" enemy other than the new G-adult monsters that were not in the original. I dread seeing the G-adults when I have no useful ammo, but not a "oh that enemy is so cool and fun that I can't wait to run into them next time" sort of feeling. G-adults are freaky to look at, and maneuver around, but I feel it was Capcom's tactic to insert these new enemies all over the dang place in order to lengthen the game play in a cheap way. Yet, I see why they added those blasted enemies since they are in fact different than anything in the RE universe, from my experience at least. This is the sewers!! The underground of hell on earth! There MUST be a better enemy than the G-Adults that Capcom were working on but ran out of time. I would have gladly waited an extra 6 months or even year for them to fix the sewers arc. It really kills the momentum for me. There could have been special zombie types here and/or variations of the freakishly-fast Hunter from previous installments. This is Capcom! They should have created a far more interesting, fun enemy to complement the unsanitary sewers!! That is really my biggest gripe.  

Maybe also, I sort of...sort of don't enjoy the movement of the character as they feel too flimsy and vulnerable as they walk around even in full health. I understand it's RE and it is horror survival, but yeah. Vulnerability is key to making great horror games, but I need to feel like I am in control of the characters without feeling overly powerful all at the same time. It's a fine line. It's tough. It's nit-picking too. I hope Capcom works on that with RE: 3 remake!

I feel as though I nitpicked WAY TOO MUCH! Yet, that is how much I love the RE franchise!!!
This game has WAY more Pros than Cons overall. The Pros I didn't bring up are because there are too many honestly!!! I truthfully don't have the time to sift through them all. Best atmosphere of any game I have played!!!

This is now (probably) my favorite RE game and that is saying something as I have played all of main RE's and most spin-offs except RE 6 + 7 since I didn't have the time.

I wanted a RE:2 Remake game that I would look forward to starting and completing all the way through 10+ times eventually.
This is that kind of game!!!! Perhaps beyond RE:4 type of territory with Shinji Mikami at the helm. Perhaps... they truly are different beasts. This is the sort of game I envision Capcom making that can revolutionize the industry as they had in the 1990s. This game only proves that Capcom can do just about anything to add lore to a long-storied franchises' greatness.

Kudos, Capcom. Take your sweet time making these games as entertaining as possible, and the industry and gamers will BUY IT UP!

This remake is my GOTY 2019. I very rarely get sucked into games and rarely play longer than an hour at a time. I played RE2 Remake for 4 hours straight the first night, and then completed the last bit of Leon's story and all of Claire's "2nd run" the second night. [b]Playthrough 1 took 6 hours, and "2nd Run" took 4.5 hours. I played on Normal difficulty.[/b] I plan on replaying on the highest difficulty soon.

It's not super duper scary, but the tension is palpable. For me the highlight of the game was the [b]inventory management[/b], and [b]backtracking with key items[/b]. It was a lot of fun to figure out where you needed to bring a certain item, and create a mental map in your head of where you had to go next. The limited inventory was also a really fun brain teaser, forcing you to choose between key items, ammo, and meds.

The biggest negative in my opinion is something fairly consistent across all RE games: I HATE wasting ammo on an enemy only to find out that he's invincible/can only be killed with an environmental hazard. For a couple boss fights I ended up reloading the checkpoint because I was annoyed that I pumped 20 shells into the boss before I realized I was just supposed to run/stall/interact with the environment.

Overall, I would [b]highly recommend[/b] the game [b]IF[/b] you can handle playing under stressful conditions, because there are some segments of the game where you don't really get a chance to catch your breath. It's very stressful and exhausting at times when you just can't stop moving or you die.

I was a huge fan of the Resident Evil series in my younger days on the Playstation and N64, but had long thought the series had passed me by in the direction it went starting with RE4. Playing this remake of one of my all-time favourite games made me realize what I really liked about those older games and gave me a deeper insight into what was missing for me in the newer games. It wasn't the clunky controls or fixed camera angles that made those old games great in their day. What made them great was the feeling of fear you would experience collecting ammo and key items and having to carefully plan your next move to your next objective. Do I have the right items? Is this the optimal path to the next objective? Should I carry an extra healing item, more ammo, or leave space for a new key item? Every time you ventured out of a safe/save room, you were unsure if you were going to make it. Every new area came with the fear that a new monster could surprise you and get you. Even retracing your steps was scary, because there was always a chance a new enemy would jump from that suspiciously placed window you walked by safely several times earlier. There is a constant feeling of dread and paranoia. And just when you start to feel at-ease with an area, you move on to something new.  Every decision felt like it could be your last. This is made all the more exciting when the world you explore is meticulously laid out to allow for the player to come up with strategies for avoiding enemies and optimizing your limited resources.  Sometimes a plan works and you get a huge feeling of satisfaction, while other times you're left defeated as you watch your character meet a gruesome end. The design of the police station and mansion weren't very realistic, but that wasn't the point, it was about exploring a large interconnected labyrinth and making the player feel small and helpless while also giving little injections of satisfaction when you'd find a clever way to just barely make it to that new safe room.

The RE2 remake shows you can include engaging gunplay/action and modern controls, while still preserving the horror and magic of the classic games.

The RE:2 Remake is a very good return to the classics of Resident Evil, the survivor horror aspect of the series is well represented in this game. There isn't a single moment where you know you are completely safe, filled with hard to beat enemies from the simple zombie to the bosses, jump scares, menacing environment, the constant sense of imminent danger, scarce resources, it is all there. 

Ammo, healing items, inventory management are crucial parts of the gameplay. Killing everything in sight isn't a viable survival strategy, conserving your resources is crucial to defeat bosses and flight or fight is a common decision every player has to make, specially in the hardest difficulties. 

The suspence and sense of dread are constant in the main area of the game, courtesy of our well known stalker and head crusher Mr-X, making it a recurrent enemy that pursues you rentlessly across the game is one of the biggest pros in the RE:2 Remake, it can make you go from a feeling of relative safety to complete fright as you listen the foots steps getting closer and closer and the musical tone of dread. 

The game mechanics are well explained by the tutorials and it isn't that hard to solve all the puzzles, aiming is a lot easier compared to the fixed camera of the old classics, due to the default third person view and crosshairs you can actually pick where you are aiming and you will need it.

Decent remake/reimagination of a beloved classic. From the gameplay mechanics standpoint, it owes pretty much everything to RE Remake (2002), and RE7, so the game is ostensibly fun. However, it's not as fresh and definitive as some tout it to be.

[b]Positives:[/b]
+ Unadulterated survival horror: The tension never lets up with chilling atmosphere, excellent sound design, and challenging enemies. (The guns sound like a$$ though!)
+ Stellar gameplay: Over-the-shoulder perspective, updated controls, zombie physics, as well as limb dismemberment tech work wonders here.
+ Superb visuals - chiefly the impeccable lighting, and the impressive general level of detail.
+ Story tweaks flesh out few characters, and offer some different takes than the Original.
+ Bonus modes from the Original return. Some new ones included also, which albeit short, are replayable. Wish there was a bit more to them, but no complaints.

[b]The not-so-positives:[/b]
- Barring the conveniently cut content in the name of "reimagination", the total effort around scenario B aka 2nd run feels rather half-baked. The absence of "Zapping system" like the Original results in story inconsistencies/gameplay continuity errors from the 1st run, very little unique events/encounters, and extremely limited interaction between Leon and Claire.
- If you didn't get the Deluxe version, there are several DLCs you can purchase. The one that hurts the most, is that the Original's (98) soundtrack is locked behind a paywall. Capcom, with the goodwill earned for your quality games and good practices recently, why do you find ways to be cheap?
- The newer team focused more on realism, sadly with little respect to the original. This resulted in cut content not limited to enemies, character moments et al, because they wouldn't fit with their "realistic" vision...eeww. In other words, the story is a massive downgrade as opposed to the OG, which I wasn't able to analyze side-by-side, until recently. Yup, classic Capcom cheapening out, as the incorrigible gamers gobble everything up unconditionally...because "OOOH, REALISTIC GRAPHICS!! PRETTY!!!"

[b]Annoyance(s):[/b]
= Ah, the start of the notoriously shameless asset reuse phenomenon with the RE engine. From untouched assets to the complete design plus behavior of the boss fights, this owes a ton to RE7. (It still doesn't go overboard like the later remakes.)
= All guns sound like a$$. The impact of the firearms could be better also, but hey, at least the hit reactions are neat.

Note: I played this game before, just not on Steam, so my hours here do not represent the total play time I spent on this.

Note 2: While I disagree that this is a perfect remake, it is still a good game so I changed the review from negative to positive because RE3 Remake is much worse.

[h1]TLDR[/h1]
This game has already enough positive reviews, I will keep this short.
This is not a bad game in general, not a bad survival horror game and not a bad Resident Evil game, it's just a bad remake in general.

[h1] Pros [/h1]
[list]
[*] Good graphics
[*] Good gameplay
[*] Great cinematics
[*] Great arsenal of weapons and items
[*] Good redesigns, not very drastic and yet faithful and realistic
[/list]

[h1] Cons [/h1]
[list]
[*] Loses identity of the original game by changing and removing a lot of things
[*] No scenario A/B like the original with overlapping and changing plots/fates of specific characters and consistent plot
[*] The current plot as it is is inconsistent, as far as the devs are concerned, the original is still canon and this doesn't replace it (According to them) as a result of this, a lot of people are thinking that there are two Tyrants because 6 were dropped into the city, except they are wrong and only one was dropped in the RPD and follows the characters for the remainder of the story, this is according to the devs themselves which they said in an interview, so no, its not another Tyrant, he just dies in Claire's story, and survives longer in Leon's story, didn't regenerate or anything, standalone stories
[*] No Zapping (or scenario zapping as I call it) which synced items you took and didn't take and actions you did in specific places across both scenarios in the original game
[*] No Giant Spiders, Moths, Enemy Crows or Evolved Lickers or even classic Ivy (it has been made into a giant plant with zombie plant minions wtf)
[*] Hate how devs use the "realism" term for removing above enemies and everything else they did when this is a zombie game which is unrealistic in itself, realism? for a game with Zombies and a Tyrant with a hat and zombie ivy creatures? the ♥♥♥♥!
[*] Claire and Leon only meet at the start and end of the game, unlike the original, where they're always in touch.
[/list]

[h2]Other complaints / issues / missing features / inconsistencies[/h2]
[list]
[*] No Extreme Battle
[*] Not enough/non-existent RE3 references, which I assume will be added in a future update like Jill's letter, or certain elements being explained in R3make.
[*] Sponge Zombies
[*] Couldn't even get Claire's classic outfit right
[*] Missing files/documents that were important to the lore
[*] Music is awful, almost non-existent, during boss fights you just hear generic music tracks, save room theme only plays once, same with the main hall of the RPD.... the rest is just boring/nothing.
[*] Ada's theme doesn't exist in this version (not even in the classic soundtrack), which was her motif since 1998 and they even used a sample of it in RE6 before Ada departs Leon once again, referencing RE2. 
[/list]

[h3]Continuity break galore[/h3]
[list]
[*] This also retcons RE0 since we visit a portion of the factory/lab from RE2 in RE0; since it is no longer the same, RE0 is retconned, might as well remake and screw up RE0 and REmake then.
[*] "It's up to us to take down umbrella" the very line added by Hideki Kamiya (director of the original) and not Noboru Sugimura (writer of the original) has been removed, this line was so important in the development history of Resident Evil that it forced writer Noboru Sugimura to replace Jill Valentine with Claire Redfield in CODE: Veronica, and as a result we got RE3 Nemesis that has Jill as the main lead.
[*] The Tyrant drop scene is gone, not in the game. In the original, this identified him as the only and only canon name "T-00" his batch number among six other Tyrants seen near the end of RE3 (who fought with the US Army).

[h3]Retcons Resident Evil Outbreak[/h3]
[*] The RPD here is completely different from the one in Outbreak's Desperate Times scenario
[*] Further more, despite Rita Philips (who get her surname here for the first time) her story doesn't match up, Marvin says that Elliot "thought" there's a secret passage under the statue, not mentioning Rita "discovering it" and pretending this is the first time it happens, even though canonically it happened in Desperate Times.
[*] The secret passage under the statue was so small in Outbreak that only Rita was able to fit through, what happened to this now? well it is replaced with a door big enough for anyone to fit it, and it's not implied that anyone else went in through it before.
[*] You visit a portion of the labs in Outbreak which has been altered here and is no longer the same
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
When you play the 2nd run (which doesn't come close to anything like the B scenarios from the original game) you start noticing the flaws right away, the only good things are gameplay variations and few scenes that hint at a consistent storyline, the inconsistency becomes wild and obvious when you reach the main hall by any of the two characters, repetitive boss fights, puzzles, etc... it doesn't even try hard.

Hell even the Rebecca easter egg seems like a last minute addition, its just an unproportional lame edit of the RE0 HD render of that costume.

As a result of some stupid "realistic" decisions taken on this game (which people were generally fine with), RE3 remake will be much more unfaithful and drastic which hurts my soul as it's my favorite game.

The only reason this game is getting too much credit is because of hype and the fact people were desperate for a survival horror RE game, or just survival horror in general. Sure I love that this is back too but this should've been a decent remake as well, it's not just the survival horror essence - it needed to be a good, faithful remake that doesn't remove and replace, but adds and improves.

Half way through my second play through at the time of writing. What an amazing remaster. Firstly, it looks stunning. The re-mastered graphics, lighting, particle effects, gore, character models are so well done that it makes it so much more immersive, while all lending a big hand in making this title even more horrorfying. From a content perspective, you could play through this game at least 4 times to see all content. If not at least play through twice for both characters perspectives. Aside from that they offered, free DLC, in the form of additional missions, aka Ghost survivors. Whats not to love about free content?

What made this game great in the first place was also its emphasis on the survival aspect. That remains true in this remaster. Ammo and health is limited, vision is limited as dark corners in rooms hide potential threats, and movement is standard as you are not blessed with any particular parkour skills. It doesn't take much to kill you either, a few good hits from a Licker and you are as good as dead. This all makes things rather daunting when you know you have to face another unknown area with limited supplies or you need to get back somewhere, and a tight corridor filled with zombies while being chased by an indestructible being in order to reach the next save point is whats waiting for you. Overcoming the initial stress and actually doing that is what makes this game so rewarding. You get to stock up on more precious bullets, or find some healing items when you push through (not always!). The game also rewards you for sticking your neck out that extra mile, trying to solve side puzzles which are spread across a map. Accomplish these tasks, and you get rewarded with something that may really help you in the long run, i.e. flame thrower, or a sub-machine gun. These weapons help a lot and due to the scarcity of everything else it makes it that moment that much more rewarding. But the new additions don't break the game either, being held back by limited ammo and such. 

I also appreciated the level design. Backtracking to other areas, didn't feel tedious as new horrors usually lurked. Also, you usually find short cuts to take you back upon finding a particular item. A key to a side door perhaps that cuts travel time between two places (Hey Dark Souls). Alot of the tasks are fetch tasks, but this game does a good job of masking that (half the time because I was too focused on not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ my pants while running screaming through Raccoon city police station as Mr. X chased me and a licker dropped unsuspectingly from the ceiling. 

What a job well done. Cant wait for RE3.

I'm not a big fan of horror games but this one was a big hit this year so I picked it up on sale. Boy, did it not disappoint! It hooked me so much I'm on my 3rd playthrough. Replay value is very high though so I think most people play through it atleast twice.

Actually I didn't find a good explanation online in what order to play the campaigns, so I try to explain the variations. There are two characters you can play, Claire and Leon. It's not just a cosmetic difference, they have different stories, altthough playing out on the same locations.  You explore the same three big areas, but you enter from different directions, traverse in a different order, the bosses are different, and even the puzzles slightly difffer. Most importantly, you meet different side characters and get the other half of the story. So I would say it's definitely worth replaying with the other character to get the full story.

Then there is also a 2nd playthrough option for each character. As far as I can tell, here the exploration and puzzle order is also slightly different than the first time, but the bosses and story is the same. It feels more like a speed run if you want more of the gameplay.

And why wouldn't you? Ever since HL2 I didn't get hooked on a gameplay loop this much! The exploration is amazing, the combat is slow paced and strategic, the inventory management and puzzles are super fun. Being a survival horror game, it's about outsmarting your enemies and conserving ammo, so don't expect high octane action. The scares are there and they work, and they are not cheap like in most games.

BTW I didn't play the original so I don't know how it compares, but this version definitely works in 2019.

All in all, highly recommended even for non horror fans.

This is a real shame, and a bizarre mis-step in an otherwise fantastic game.

Regardless of that though I'd definitely recommend giving it a try. Fair warning mind - X gonna get ya!

Exhilarating. This is my first ever Resident Evil experience and I couldn't have loved it more.

The graphics are mesmerising; I played on medium settings and it looked phenomenal. The gameplay, while slightly more focused on puzzles than epic combat sequences, is thrilling when it wants to be and very engaging for the entire playthrough. The story is easily the worst aspect, but I give it a free pass in this regard because I know next to nothing about Resident Evil and I doubt many people invest in the horror genre in the hopes of discovering a miracle in storytelling.

The horror aspect is done brilliantly; jump-scares are used sparingly enough that they have a significant impact when they do throw one in and the whole atmosphere just hammers home that you are not the dominating force here. Killing every enemy is probably impossible with the few resources the game offers. This creates dread even when you do kill an enemy - shouldn't I have saved those few bullets for a more pressing situation?

The main complaints about the game are silly, in my opinion. I saw a few complaints that the game isn't long enough, but it took me almost 8 hours to finish my playthrough with Leon, another possible 8 awaits with the Claire playthrough and I'm looking forward to doing more runs to find all the secrets.

The following are some of my initial thoughts about the game after having played through both A and B scenarios. It is worth mentioning that I am a massive Resident Evil fan and have played them since the original release of RE1. Also, this was copied from a comment thread in which I wrote on a YouTube video review of the game. There are a few sections included that were responses to other people's comments. I also hit the character limit way before I could include the whole review. In shortest terms, I'm conflicted about it:

    There are some severely disappointing moments and design choices at work here; not least of which is the heavy recycling of animations, entire levels, items, bosses, etc.

    @___ It's late and I'm tired, but I'll list everything I can remember. (Note: I agree with every criticism ___ mentioned, so I won't be mentioning any of those here.)

The fact that neither Claire's nor Leon's campaigns feature more than a few exclusive segments—I get it; it's 2019. Video games cost millions to make now; but I can't help but place the blame on Capcom for this one. If the studio weren't under any time or budget constraints, I would like to believe that there would have been true A and B scenarios instead of what we got. It is more jarring in this game because of the dedication to photorealism. Repeating segments are more forgivable in the older console generations due to file size. And yet the original had 4 separate campaigns. If you look at the install size of the remake, it's only pushing 25 gigs. Other games that came out only a few years ago have install sizes that have to be seen to be believed—GTAV, for example, takes up one-hundred and something gigabytes and it also took much longer to make. If they really wanted to, they could have designed two entirely separate campaigns (see Cyberpunk 2077 for a more "when it's ready" quality business model).

The line that Ada says about Umbrella only selling viruses and not their engineered monsters—it goes against everything Umbrella does in every original game. What she's saying is that Umbrella only creates their monsters or B.O.W.s for their own personal use and that they create the viruses solely to mass produce for selling, which makes absolutely no sense. (I can elaborate on that further if needed; it's mostly self-explanatory.)

The line that Claire says when she reads the letter left behind by Chris—or someone pretending to be him—"This doesn't sound like Chris." I am halfway convinced that they are going to skip Nemesis and do a Code Veronica remake next because of how out of the blue the line is; for several reasons, but story-wise, it suggests that something has happened to Chris and that he is being impersonated to keep anyone who would go looking for him from becoming suspicious and doing so. And just as soon as she says the line, the story thread is never mentioned again—not once. It's so jarring and so canonically incorrect that it has to either be chalked up as a continuity error or an Easter egg. It's just too damn bizarre and lacking all explanation to be an error or a throwaway line.

The destruction of continuity via the almost absolute remodel of the police station. The original layout was used in Nemesis, Outbreak, Darkside Chronicles, and even Operation Raccoon City; now all of those are ostensibly no longer canon—which is bizarre to even consider.

Claire's new "look" is almost exactly like the Tomb Raider reboot's Lara Croft (see Claire without her jacket on; compare to Lara Croft in the first game in that trilogy—all she's missing is a bow and a red climbing hook).

The re-use of G Birkin for Claire's penultimate boss battle in the second run—why design a new Birkin transformation instead of including the fully transformed Mr. X? It's actually offensive how generic that is and how big of a missed opportunity that is. Leaving out that entire segment of the original and replacing it with an awful, generic: one-step-away from a turret section (they give her a minigun) boss fight was a very poor choice.

The jankiness of the rooms that enemies can't enter—understandable from the perspective of fairness/difficulty, but it is a total immersion "ruiner."

My own personal distaste for the entire sewer level—it's ugly and not in an ironic or contrarian sort of way. The easiest thing to compare it to would be the lake house or "Marguerite" section from RE7 or any Silent Hill game pre-"Homecoming." Those are disturbing and gross; claustrophobic, haunting, and frightening, but they are beautiful in their own—masochistic—way.

The almost "boss rush" section of the sewer level with all of the "adult Gs" that you have to fight back to back to get to the next area with the King and Queen plugs in it—probably the low point of the entire remake.

And lastly, the total redesign of the final laboratory level—the game struggles with its own vision of realism. There are some things that just don't fit together. While the lab is a tense and beautifully realized/designed level, moving away from the rusty, "grimey," industrial look of the original is really hard to fully condone.

Some cutscenes are skippable, but none of the item-related unlocking/opening/"examine" cutscenes are. Unskippable cutscenes are in the top five "game design dos and don'ts."

The second Birkin boss fight on the tiny platform with the crane—unless it goes your way, it's frustrating and somehow manages to feel like a glaring example of outdated game design. They could have done one of a thousand different things with that boss fight.

That's as much as I can think of right now. Oh, one more small gripe: why in the hell are there so many blue herbs in the first run? Those things just sit in my storage bin and do nothing but multiply.

    @___ Canon or not, the redesign removes the continuity of the design of the police station.

Also, I can see what you're saying about Chris' letter being in code.

The point is, Claire nor anyone else ever resolves that story thread. Retroactively, we know that Chris went to Europe to continue his fight against Umbrella.

It is never made explicitly clear that Chris was talking in code or that he feared his messages being intercepted by Umbrella.

It is fine to include a slight variation in how Chris' letter goes and leave it up to longtime fans to decipher; but within the context of the remake itself, it is a totally unresolved plot thread.

Claire's entire reason for being in Raccoon City is to find her brother. Clearly, Jill or someone read the letter and put it into the locked room. Why leave it laying out for all to see if secrecy was an issue?

Another thing: if Chris had to get a message to the remaining S.T.A.R.S. members and the only way he could do it was to mail a coded letter to them, why not use an alias to further throw off any trail?

You also assume that Chris and/or the remaining S.T.A.R.S. members are being spied on despite being outside of the city or AWOL.

While that's plausible and an easy leap to make, in the remake, it is only ever stated that they are to be undermined, not followed or that their mail be checked and possibly confiscated for fear of some leak.

Also, in the original, it was stated by Marvin Branagh that the S.T.A.R.S. members were openly accusing Umbrella of everything they knew them to be guilty of; so again, why would Chris write a coded message to anyone at that point? Why not find a camera or a journalist (BEN) or take it to a national level?

    That letter and the line from Ada with Leon on the elevator I mentioned (directly after the alligator scene) lead me to believe that the story was handled by people who aren't as well versed in the lore and history of RE as they should have been. It was a very poor oversight to include such convoluted plot holes and canonical errors.

The game is plenty replayable, and rewards good gameplay with infinite weapons and more game to play- the perfect rewards for people that prove interest and mastery over a game.

The Resident Evil franchise has blasted itself clean into pop culture knowledge, so there’s little need to recite the background here. To summarise, a bad company makes zombie-virus bioweapons, and they’ve just had a major outbreak. Resident Evil 2 follows two characters unknowingly driving into a city in the midst of the first major zombie outbreak, taking shelter in a police station that is more than it seems, and stumbling into the corporate conspiracy behind it all. There are effectively two ways to review this game. The first is as a remake of a classic of the genre that defined much of what Survival Horror would mean, and the second is as someone new to the pre-RE5 franchise.

If you are familiar with the franchise, this is the kind of remake that moves the bar for everyone else working on a remake of the game. It’s not a glorified remaster – the entire game has been redesigned from the ground up, with the impressive visual power of the Re engine, and the decades of new lessons learned in game design since it first came out. Every aspect of the game has been hugely upgraded. The tank controls and fixed camera that were the game’s weakest point even at launch are gone, replaced with a third-person camera and controls that genuinely feel good to play. The game is no less intimidating for it – being able to aim allows for damage modelling on enemies, especially basic zombies, to introduce entirely new strategic decisions about whether you kill, cripple, or ignore the persistent enemies. Weapons all feel good and relevant, and the subweapons work better here than in any other RE game. 

Even the narrative has been upgraded, including much better scene flow and removing the most stupid elements of the original. What remains is a tightly-interconnected structure with elaborate and complex item puzzles, made far more enjoyable by the use of a map system that flags items left behind, places finished and unfinished, and even ticks off key items you have used up.

This isn’t a remake of the game to a modern engine, or even a remake of the game as it would have been made were it designed today. This remake is like playing the nostalgic memories of how you vaguely remember it being, except it [i]actually exists[/i]. 

If this is your first older RE game, you’ve picked the best way to start. Resident Evil 2 is a survival horror game that swings between tense combat encounters and item or logic puzzles; effectively, you want to get past the zombies to collect items, which are either basic supplies, upgrades to your equipment, or essential items needed to progress in the game. An essential component of the game is that you don’t earn any rewards for killing enemies, and there is mathematically not enough ammunition in the game to kill every single enemy you encounter. But the game world consists of highly-interconnected spaces, the enemies are persistent and extremely resilient, and the item puzzles require extensive backtracking. Effectively, you have to decide whether you invest the ammo to kill an enemy, invest much less to cripple it and gamble on bypassing it, or simply run past it and gamble on not needing to return to the space. Given that the basic zombies in the game can take three to five shots to blow a leg off and anywhere up to twelve headshots to kill for good, that’s a genuine decision. Spending twenty bullets to clear out a room to find five bullets and an optional clue might not be worth it.

In classic survival horror style you explore the game world, using items you find to open up new areas and unlock shortcuts to old ones, finding supplies scattered about to keep going. You might find a weapon locker with a shotgun needing a specific item to unlock, or a safe whose code is written on a paper somewhere in the station, or a door that you need an item to open and continue. At any given time you’ll be juggling two to four key items, and with severely limited inventory space you can go light and run short of resources, or go heavy and regularly have to leave items behind. Some key items are used once and gone, but many are used repeatedly; luckily, the game will indicate that an item won’t be used again and can be discarded. The game also helpfully marks areas you have completely cleared, partially cleared, and not reached yet, as well as key items or doors you have yet to unlock.

Occasionally the game will mix things up with a new enemy, requiring you to play cautious until you adapt your tactics, or a bossfight, requiring substantial use of ammo and resources to proceed. Sometimes an unkillable enemy will pursue you throughout the entire level until you get past a certain point in the story, effectively testing your ability to navigate safely and punishing players who have been too thrifty with their ammo. This enemy can be frustrating to players who don’t often play survival horror, so two notes – firstly, it does play fair and actually walks manually around the level; secondly, it detects sound so walking instead of running and avoiding shooting make you much harder to detect.

The story may seem a little contrived at times if you are new to the RE franchise, but it’s no different from most horror movies, where sometimes things just happen because they need to for the story to exist. This has tighter narrative plotting and less hammy voicework or animation than any other RE title, so if you can enjoy horror movies you’ll be fine here. If you do like horror with a touch of melodrama and ham, this is made for you.

There are two campaigns to be played, one for each of the cover characters, each 4-6 hours long depending on your completionism. These are somewhat interconnected and you’ll often end up in the same places or fighting similar bosses, but you come from different angles with access to different rooms, and with some entirely unrelated areas. Narratively, the campaigns are happening at the same time and place, so you get the complete story only by playing both. The combined campaigns offer pretty good value for money in the genre. The campaigns also offer ‘B Sides’, which involves shuffling the enemy and boss locations around, and changing a bit of item placement, for generally a more challenging experience. There are also difficulty settings and unlockable weapons to boot, though naturally the overpowered weapons are hidden behind the extremely difficult challenges. Some DLC is available in the form of expanded stories, which are of reasonable quality though not to the level of the main events. Some connect directly to the narrative and fill out missing spaces, some are just fun asides with a different gameplay experience, and some are a comedic turn on the game. As of writing, this comes free with the main game, and so adds a good few extra hours of play one you’ve used the game up. In terms of quality hours to dollars paid, this is the best value for current survival horror games on the market.

If you enjoy modern survival horror games, RE2 is a great way to experience the principles of classic survival horror with the strength of modern game design. If you played these ‘back in the day’, this is a best-in-class entry from the era, updated with two decades of lessons learned. If you’ve never really played survival horror before, if RE2 doesn’t change your mind and get you playing, it’s safe to assume that it’s just not your genre.

pros:

review:
This game is a great step forward for the series. With more mechanics, you can actually feel the creatures stepping behind you as you sneak past. It was nice to feel like horror didn't have to be a constant game of hide and seek while also not being thrown headfirst into neverending firefights full of gore. It's got several game modes that change how some puzzles work and add extra challenge to the main story. The plot was fairly well handled with some nice voiceacting talent. Unfortunately, my fun was dulled by the zombies taking half of my ammo with constant headshots and then getting back up fairly quickly. This frustrated me more than anything else. Either make less ammo or more enemies, not sponges. That being said, the fights are still mostly pleasurable. It wasn't easy to stay alive, but I wasn't always on the verge of death. The main antagonists were well made and fairly good and making the player feel very much in danger. Some things carried over from the original game could have been improved. If you want to see the true end, you have to play both sides. This is fine and dandy until Claire and Leon start contradicting each other. At multiple points they both need the same items for the same puzzles, but since they both go through the same areas and get the items in the same way it makes the other person's journey impossible in retrospect. This was an issue in the original that could have been fixed in this version to improve the plot. Aside from the main story, there are 4 bonus missions that are all based around a limited item speedrun through past levels. Only one of these has any real connection to the main plot. Unfortunately, they made these modes as difficult as possible with new enemies and onslaughts of the hardest creatures they could find. Many times, the route you must take is highly unfair with worst possible thing you can think of around every corner with no time to stop and think. This was not fun, and often times it was highly frustrating. I would say that, even if you aren't into survival horror, this game is worth a shot if you like shooters, stealth, and puzzles. The horror mostly boils down to jump scares here and there, so no one should be all that terriffied. More like mildly startled.
