Alright, so I've played this game on higher difficulties (I am a masochist, what can I say) for about 4 hours, give or take. I feel like that's enough for me to give you an informed take on this title. I'm going to sum it up quickly: the experience is expensive, but VERY high quality and is everything a remake of a beloved game should be. There are a few cons, but they did not interfere with my immersion or enjoyment whatsoever during my various playthroughs. 

Pros:
-The graphics are blindingly shiny
-Zombie design and world building are true-to-form, and definitely add to the intense dread 
-Actually caused me extreme anxiety and tension, and I typically have little to no reaction to horror games or movies whatsoever (especially zombies)
-Faithful to the original while adding new mechanics that don't simply rely on frustrating you into being scared like the original, for example; keeps the IP integrity minty fresh
-The atmosphere and AI were insane amounts of fun in tandem, and I was fully and completely immersed in the Raccoon City police department
-The cutscenes were truly a treat, and had my nostalgic 90s kid self squealing against my will. I began to feel the way about Leon, Claire and Ava that weebs do about their 2d waifus. That part scared me the most, really. The fact that this game gave me a straight up dark night of the soul is enough for me to encourage everyone to try it. I may be slightly exaggerating...but maybe not. I haven't decided yet. Ask me again when I get my Leon Kennedy love doll in the mail. Also, I need money to buy a love doll. Venmo me like 8k so my review has more weight to it. 
-The animations when you get chomped on are great
-Voice acting gave new life to familiar faces
-Not too much or too little ammo on the A story on normal mode, but I highly suggest it for noobs to the series: on higher difficulties, you will need to utilize my strategy of simply blowing off the limbs of all the zombies instead of gambling on head shot crits and dumping ammo into it. For one, it is highly efficient. Two, it is f*cking hilarious. I see a lot of people are not familiar with that randomized mechanic and are upset their 360 no scope headshot didn't instantly kill everything in sight. There is literally nothing scary about zombie games for that exact reason, so I am mystified by this ire. It's not as though it isn't directly related to the story or anything. Why am I even being sarcastic right now? Who am I even talking to? I'm sorry for yelling.

Cons:
-Cutscenes are too infrequent, and without giving any spoilers - rather abrupt and lackluster at the end. Perhaps there were alternate endings I hadn't got as I had intentionally meandered as slowly as I could through each part of the game. If so, do let me know! I would love to take this outta my list of complaints. 
-There is some mild repetition with the zombie models that probably could have been avoided, but it's not *too* noticeable like in games such as Dying Light. It's so very minimal, which is why I wondered why it happened at all, really. Not a big deal, though.
-The Mr. X sequence is more of an annoying nuisance, instead of garnering suspense. It was the only part of the game where I remembered I was, in fact, actively playing a video game. For those too young to remember the original or have not played it, the Mr. X (or Tyrant, as I believe he is called in this incarnation) chase sequence was part of the "B Story" mode. I didn't enjoy it being part of the main story, and found it tedious and distracting. 

Even with my headphones and 3d sound, unless his footfalls are VERY close, the sound kind of seemed arbitrary. I did not really understand his spawning pattern, and it just caused me to do a lot of standing and waiting for him to p*ss off when I was low on healing items. Meh. It's a huge waste of ammo to shoot him, so sometimes I'd just let him punch me in the face to get on with it when he'd occasionally find/trap me. It's not *hard* or anything, it's just not that fun (in my opinion).
-No side quests or new areas (aside from the orphanage segment*)
-Not enough notes and whatnot lying around for you to pick up and read - one of my favorite parts of these games minimized a bit too much - we still appreciate story & atmospheric items, devs! <3
-Kinda half-a**ed "B-Story" compared to the original, which basically giving you a whole new game to play around with
-Not enough secrets for my liking, and believe me - I LOOKED. It's technically a mini-open world as you can wander about as you please, but it still is forcibly linear progression with little deviation. So long as you are aware of that, you're going to have a fantastic time inside of the story. It doesn't have any crazy RPG decision trees or anything, which I'm fine with either way.
-Story about the virus and the former survivors was actually pretty sparse given how wide this universe is after all these years, but I am nitpicking quite a bit. It was a safer option to go with what worked with the original, for sure. I'm glad a new generation gets to be terrified by this excellent game. :3

So, there you have it. While there are a few things here or there that I certainly took note of, I could not recommend this title enough. I definitely got my money's worth, and so will you. This game is really great. It's not really 'scary' (if you want more horror stuff play Resident Evil 7) but it gets you paranoid in other ways.

The atmosphere of the game is fantastic, one of the best I've experienced. The color palette, the lighting, the level design is carefully thought out and as a result I felt really immersed while playing. Of course, visuals and sound design is top notch as expected from a game of this caliber and the game should run pretty well on most gaming PCs. Also, the animations are really well done and the game feels very 'fluid' and cinematic (as does RE7).

When it comes to the story, it's quite interesting. It doesn't feel stretched out and it's easy to follow, however if you are a fan of the series or if you've played the original game (I've not) you probably know what you are getting into.

Beware, however, this game is pretty difficult and requires wise resource management and some planning before doing a few things. The zombies and especially the more 'advanced' creatures (e.g. lickers) usually require A LOT of ammo to take down, and you might want to avoid them if you're low on resources. Last but not least you will often have to make sacrifices when it comes to items, especially in the beginning of the game when your inventory space is limited you will have to decide to permanently discard items in order to get others, that are required in order to progress through the story.

My only semi-gripe with this game is the fact you have to play it twice to unlock the 'true' ending, but it's not necessary (you can just watch the cutscene on YouTube) and the game isn't particularly long (took me less than 7 hours on my first run with Leon).

Overall, it's definitely  worth playing.

This Steam Summer Sale I opted to do something I rarely do. Instead of buying several cheap titles at 90% off, I got Resident Evil 2 Remake for 15% off at $67.49. I've never played a Resident Evil game before and this was a fantastic ride. If you like horror themes that are scary but not overwhelmingly so, with the ability to fight back against the monsters and grow and improve and develop your character, this is a tremendous game.

[h1]GAMEPLAY[/h1]

Whether you start with Leon Kennedy first or Claire Redfield, you begin in slightly different areas but with a similar story. Your goal is to find out what's going on with this zombie outbreak while defending yourself against zombies... and worse. At first you'll only have simple weapons like hand guns and knives and not very much ammo. But as you explore you will find more useful items, which are needed for the enemies.

The movement, gunplay, and interactions with the environment is very enjoyable. It is a bit frustrating how easily the zombies can grab you if you're not careful but you do have to learn how to time your movements to avoid it. To improve, you can try playing the "Ghost Survivors" mode, which is basically a simulator of going through very difficult monsters you'd encounter throughout the game.

Added to all of the gameplay elements, you get tons of unlockables, upgrades and other benefits which carry through on your character and allow you to try and get the Steam achievements, some of which seem mighty tricky. This really makes the game replayable. Which is good, because you're meant to replay it at least once with the other actor.

[h1]GRAPHICS[/h1]

The graphics are gorgeous and the models are very impressive. There a number of mods which already exist that allow you to tweak your character to your liking as well and more are added every day. The contrast between dark and light is just perfect for the mood, and the fact you often have to use a flashlight in areas you know are very dangerous just adds to the overall horror mood that fills the air at all times.

[h1]PLOT[/h1]

The plot is pretty great. Whether you're playing Leon or Claire, you're trying to figure out what's behind the zombie outbreak (T-Virus). You wind up stumbling upon an even more dangerous virus with dire ramifications. Despite not having played any other Resident Evil games, I feel like I was able to piece together what's happened and how it relates to other titles. It would probably help lots if you had some inkling of the other games though.

[h1]STABILITY[/h1]

Perfect on GTX 970 for PC/Windows 10

[h1]VERDICT[/h1]

This is one of the best games in years, if not the best of 2019. Even as a remake, Capcom has done everything right in what a remake is supposed to be. It's an excellent game and doesn't pretend to be anything it isn't. There's no feature creep, no ridiculous gameplay elements. It's great. Perhaps the DLC is a bit of a ripoff, but otherwise solid for the money.

9.5/10

[h1] Dear Capcom, this is the RE we want	[/h1]

First thing first: this remake of Resident Evil 2 is a masterpiece. I'll go into details below, but in my opinion this episode gathers the two best elements of the saga:

1) the atmosphere. It's neither the pure action of RE4/5/6 (although I love RE4) nor the permanent terror of RE7. It is this thrilling anxiety, that plays with the perfect light and sound effects, this stress of not knowing what's gonna be behind this wall corner... Unlike RE7, jump scares are scarce, but this leaves room for this more subtle anxiety accompanying the player at every step.

2) the "over-the-shoulder" view. Yes, I also kinda like the good old fixed angles sometimes but mostly because of nostalgia. This episode brillantly proves that you can have a flexible third person view and yet keep the core aspects of the game, i.e. the atmosphere and the survival.

[h1] Game Design: perfect	[/h1]

When I first saw the game, I thought to myself: "Has it become a third-person shooter ?" I couldn't be more wrong. All aspects of the design are thought as a survival: apart from the classical limited inventory and reduced ammo compared to the number of mobs, the new elements of the gameplay greatly contribute. You'll discover it is sometimes surprisingly hard to hit a zombie, because the aim has an important spread unless you stand still for a few seconds, but also because zombie moves are erratic. Props to Capcom for managing to design zombies moves that both make them feel like real zombies, and serve the gameplay by making them hard to hit.

The other mobs appearing later in the game also contribute to the great game design. Lickers, especially, are a crucial point of the gameplay, as they practically force you to walk (instead of running) in some areas. When you enter a corridor with a licker, zombies, and Mr.X running after you, the adrenaline rises... and you understand how well the game is designed.

[h1] Level Design: awesome	[/h1]

Speaking of design, this is a trait of the RE series: the level design of the police station (I'll talk later about the other places) is awesome. The map is huge, the layout of the keys, locked doors and other objects is thought to keep the player both tense and curious to progress at every single point of the game. You have to visit multiple times some areas (but usually it's because you got a new key, and your perspective on this area changes), and you can ignore some others that contain only "bonuses". But what is great is that the level design is so well thought that visiting these bonus areas is not just a matter of being a completist or not. Reaching them sometimes means having to overcome zombies, lickers or worse, and the risk and the ammo consumption this represents must be put in the balance together with the potential gains, making your choices highly strategical.

And if you think the level desing is only "good", wait for when Mr. X comes into play. You will realise that the position of the doors leading from one wing of the police station to the other, the size of the corridors, the position of the lickers... everything is thought also to make the hunt with Mr. X one of the tensest moments the game.

[h1] Mr. X	[/h1]

He deserves his own paragraph. The cat-and-mouse game with Mr. X is to me the climax of the game. I don't want to spoil too much, but his AI is really good, his walking pace is very well calibrated to reinforce the fear he inspires, and the noise of his steps are both a source of stress and a key element to play the game around him. I just have one regret: there are a couple of rooms where he is programmed not to go. I know the game design was already complex enough not to have to think of how he could interfere with the player when dealing with a puzzle, but knowing there is a room nearby where he never goes kinda releases the anxiety of having him around sometimes.

Yet, I repeat: this was for me the best moment of the game, the core of what is survival-horror.

[h1] Excellent graphics and sounds	[/h1]

All these excellent points are of course enhanced by excellent graphics and light effects. With my (kinda old already) GTX 970, the game rules graphically speaking, only suffering occasional framerate drops. The light effects are particularly impressive, allowing to change quickly from the calm atmosphere of the hall to the dark atmosphere of the corridors. It is to be noted that, except when you load a save, there is hardly ever a loading time, which is VERY impressive for a game one would imagine to be very demanding resources-wise.

[h1] A few cons...	[/h1]

Yes, RE2: remake is not perfect. During the first 5 to 10 hours I was thinking to myself "these journalists rating the game 17/20 or 7/10 are a little picky, it is perfect !". Yet, after finishing Leon's campaign, I have to agree with them that a couple things could have been better:

1) Just like RE0, and I would dare to say a bit like RE1 as well: the quality of the level design decreases as the game goes further. Of course, it is difficult to rival the level design of the police station, but the levels of the sewers and the NEST are far more linear and predictable in my opinion. No more room with 10 doors with 3 different key symbols, but mostly long linear corridors and the end of which you know in advance which key you will find. The level design there is not bad [i] per se [/i]: it is just a little underwhelming after spending a few hours in the police station.

2) Again, just like the other episodes of Resident Evil, the scenario is full of promises in the first hours of the game, but as you progress through the game, you realise that not much more than the few core, predictable elements are revealed, with no big twist, no little detail hidden here and there to look after in the next episodes... a little disappointing.

[h1] Summary: game of the year contender	[/h1]

This remake of Resident Evil 2 was arguably one of the most anticipated games in the last years, which made the work of Capcom difficult: how to revisit this cult game, with a brand new look, a modern gameplay that keeps the core of the survival intact, and loyalty to the original scenario and universe ? Yet, the result is breathtaking... like our friend Keanu Reeves would say. RE2: remake is a masterpiece, and I would personally love all the episodes of Resident Evil to be like this one. Capcom, do this with RE3 and I buy it in Deluxe Edition for 80 € on day one.

This, right here, is how you remake one of the greatest survival horror games ever made.

I was a little disappointed when I learned RE2 wouldn't have fixed 3rd-person camera angles like the original. However, I now completely get why Capcom changed their mind during development, and I think it's all the better for it. This remake takes my two all-time favorite Resident Evil games, 2 and 4, melts them together like two kinds of decadent chocolate, with the new RE Engine acting as the base, and the result is what might be my new favorite of the entire franchise.

You still got it, Capcom. Can't wait for the Nemesis remake!

Resident Evil 2 (2019) is a remake to... well, Resident Evil 2 (1998). They're both games about getting out of a zombie-infested city. I played the original for the first time early this year, and I was interested to see what the remake had changed in 21 years of Resident Evil and general game design.

The first thing one can notice is, obviously, a huge leap in graphics quality. The remake looks insanely good, especially the amount of gore that is going to be on screen with you being able to cut off zombie limbs and make their heads explode. If I had to complain about something, I'd say that reflections seem to be bugged since they seem to move around in weird ways as you move, and the image quality isn't the greatest, as the game is a shimmering mess without temporal AA, and that implies a dynamic sharpen which doesn't quite seem to work properly (it's a roulette between blurry and oversharpened most of the time). That's mostly nitpicking though. Of course, the original has the charm that prerendered backgrounds provide; having constant camera angles makes for a sort of "directed experience", since the angles picked are visually interesting and may draw your eye to certain spots, and 2D doesn't age as badly.

Obviously, the game is a third-person shooter now instead of fixed-camera, and this change makes for much better gameplay. You have much more control over aiming, so you can try to take off limbs, or just headshot a zombie once to make him stagger while you get past. Zombies take up to maybe 10 headshots to actually stop rising up, and you're not gonna have that kind of ammo, so using a knife to stop them while they're on the ground or just running around them is the optimal way to go here. Overall, the game is much harder than the original: I played 98 RE2 in normal with Leon and then Claire and I had hundreds of pistol bullets by the final section, and that definitely didn't happen while playing on Hardcore in the remake. The removal of loading screens between rooms also makes it so zombies can chase you into other rooms, which is great. The remake takes the basic structure of running around trying to find keys and items to escape, and adds more interesting choices to make with its improved gameplay, not to mention a special enemy later on that constantly throws a wrench in your plans to get around the initial police station. I definitely recommend playing on Hardcore, as it removes autosaves and limits the amount of saves you can do in one playthrough. This enhances the tension you get while exploring, and in my case, it made me try being a bit cocky and say to myself "yeah I don't need to save yet, let me just explore a little more" (which sometimes doesn't end up well, but it makes for a more fun experience IMO). The limited saves are more than enough for a save every 20-30 minutes, and if you can't play a game for 20 minutes straight then... you've got bigger problems than limited saves.

Parts that weren't translated as well were the A/B campaign. You pick between two characters to play as, and in both games, when you finish one of them you get to play as the other, seeing another side of the events that unfolded. This is called the B campaign in the original, and 2nd run in the remake. The problem here is that the "2nd run" is exactly that, a second run with an alternate version of events, as opposed to just a different point of view. While in the original, some of the bosses included different forms of a creature in each campaign, in the remake you fight the exact same boss fight in both runs several times, with the cutscenes changing slightly depending on the character, which is pretty disappointing

I also have to mention the music. I bought the Original Soundtrack DLC, and I really feel that they should have either made that free or just not have composed a new soundtrack. The remake's soundtrack is mostly silent, and when you try the original version while playing the remake, it fits really well and gives the game a much stronger atmosphere. Entering rooms and listening to the iconic piano stings of the original soundtrack is much better than listening to... almost nothing. It also changes the sound effects from using menus to the original's, which begs the question, why did they change that as well? The original sound effects make the game feel a bit more 90s (it's still set in 98), as opposed to the remake's SFX that make it feel like... nothing, matching the very minimalistic UI. It's a small thing, but these small things add up to make the experience different.

Overall, RE2 remake is a very good game, like the original. It's far from a perfect remake that surpasses the original in every way, but it keeps the awesome police station exploration and adds some fun third-person shooting that doesn't lose the tension and results in a few more interesting choices to make throughout. Just get the original soundtrack DLC.

RESIDENT EVIL 2 captures the essence of the classic title and cranks it up to eleven on all fronts. 

[h1][b]Fine Status[/b][/h1]
Resident Evil is survival horror once again: [list]
[*] enemies are slow, but still menacing and dangerous up close;
[*] ammo is scarce, but weapons have weight and satisfying feedback;
[*] there isn't much background music, but 3D sound and ambiance is used to build up the atmosphere;
[*] features a fairly short story, but adds extra replayability value with unlocks;
[*] it's faithful to the source material, but expands and improves upon it thanks to the concepts and ideas that didn't make it to the original; 
[*] the environment looks and feels like there's been an actual outbreak, the police department interior is a great example.[/list]

The gunplay has a solid feel to it, despite enemies being major bullet sponges. It's not nearly as over the top as in the original, but still provides satisfying audiovisual feedback. Upon impact zombies flinch and have visible wounds, letting the player know that their attacks are connecting. Gunshots don't sound powerful, but instead weapons have moderate recoil, bright muzzle flash, while characters have smooth combat animations, making the gunplay experience feel better than in Resident Evil 7. 

Popping heads is a welcome surprise, destruction of limbs enables a more tactical approach to combat, allowing the player to decide on the best course of action: shooting a weak spot for complete elimination, stunning the target and running past by them to save up on some precious ammo and time, shooting legs to slow an enemy down and make them less dangerous, shooting arms to prevent the infected from using doors. The choice is there, the rest depends on the player's preferences.

Enemy attack animations have appropriate weight to them. Claw swings actually produce visible distortion in the air just to highlight how deadly they are, if a claw hits a hard surface then it produces sparks and decals. Grabs play a big role of startling the player, so the camera goes for a dramatic zoom, while you get a nice look at the attacking enemy. Occasionally, the grabs are supposed to disorient the player, as the character can turn around while responding to the threat.

Self-defense item (sub-weapon) mechanic is reintroduced and it's your best friend: [list]
[*] Screwed up and got grabbed? Defense item!
[*] Thinking ahead and trying to weaken or surprise the enemy? Defense item!
[*] Not sure if the zombie is finished off or is just pretending to be down? Knife (Defense item)!
[*] Got caught in a one hit KO attack? Defense item (does not apply to non-grabby OHKO attacks)! [/list]
You can't craft these (at least in the main game) and there aren't many available throughout the game, so it's a valuable and even powerful resource if you know when and how to use it. On a side note, self-defense items do not work if you're standing on stairs.

RE Engine's capabilities of rendering dense urban environments with impressive visual fidelity were a pleasant surprise. Before the first trailer hit the public, there was some concern about how the engine would hold up when going from first person in a rural area to third person in a city. In the end we got much better looking characters, new graphical features, no pre-cache stutter and a reasonable frame rate.

User experience when using the menus is great: everything is snappy and clean, every option has a simple explanation and everything is grouped properly. The interface experience is good even during gameplay, as one can do quick and precise inventory manipulations even without much practice. Another case of attention to detail is the fact that cutscenes do not contribute to in-game timer, so there's no need to skip them. As an example, RE6 chapter ranking system includes cutscene time along with gameplay time, penalizing players that enjoy slower-paced gameplay.

[h1][b]Caution Status[/b][/h1]
The experience of survival horror is enhanced by subtle sound effects and clever ambiance tracks. There's power even in “silence”, something that is predominant in Resident Evil 7 and inherited in RE2. Dynamic soundtrack is in place, changing from silence to tension, depending on enemy proximity and awareness. On the flip side, there aren't enough memorable tracks that stand out and leave the whole soundtrack being forgettable. That's something that can be remedied with Soundtrack Swap DLC, but it doesn't always blend in well enough due to soundtrack fades and timing, ending up feeling like a community mod. Ironically, the extra content has more memorable and catchy tracks than the whole main game. There are entries in the series that can pull off rich soundtrack, while retaining atmospheric ambiance and horror (see RE Revelations).

Having four scenarios ends up feeling like a late development decision. The differences between same character scenarios are fairly minimal: slightly different dialogue, guns and items. It adds a lot more replayability, but can end up being a little stale after a while. The fact that it was added to begin with was a major surprise to some, but the end result makes you wish that there was a bit more to it. Perhaps, Resident Evil 3 might fill that void?

[h1][b]Danger Status[/b][/h1]
The lack of Extreme Battle minigame, a predecessor of The Mercenaries is a missed opportunity. Extreme Battle offered a versatile approach of having multiple loadouts, difficulties and complete exploration of the game's areas with added randomization of items and enemies. Ghost Survivors follow similar footsteps of The 4th Survivor (a minigame which makes the player run past most enemies), while adding item and weapon pick-ups to the mix. Unfortunately, not everyone can enjoy this type of playstyle these minigames offer. On the other hand, the soundtrack featured in these modes stands out and Ghost Survivors has one scenario that is an exception to the rule, a scenario where you don't need to run away. In the end, since it's “free”, then we “can't complain”.

There are a bunch of reused assets scattered around the game: assets from Resident Evil 7, which can stand out a lot for players that went through RE7 a couple of times; repeating objects that end up being eyebrow raising if you notice their appearances throughout the game (and I don't mean zombies). It's a small nitpick, a common practice and, fortunately, the items in question blend in with the scenery well enough.

One negative thing about the game on a technical level is that the enemy animation frame rate is reduced if you're not within a particular distance. You can easily spot this behavior if you look at the enemies that are standing across a hall. This breaks the immersion and in-game options menu does not have anything that would disable this resource-saving trick.  

[h1][b]PC Specifics[/b][/h1]
PC release is a surprisingly well-made in-house version. The visual fidelity is higher than on consoles, options allow in-depth tweaking with useful descriptions and visual references. All visual settings are separated, so undesired effects can be toned down or turned off. As of now, RE2 has the most advanced tweaking available in a Resident Evil game, setting Capcom's quality bar for PC releases even higher. As an oddity, DX12 has a performance regression in comparison to DX11, so it's best to use the latter.

[h1][b]Conclusion[/b][/h1]
People are right: this game is not like the original Resident Evil 2, it is in its own league: a reimagined, modern take on Resident Evil 2, a completely different experience that stands on its own. With that in mind it's still worth playing both the 1998 original and the 2019 remake. If Resident Evil 3: Nemesis gets treated same way RE2 did, then it's going to be another exciting release.

First of all, I'd like to state that I have never played the original Resident Evil 2, and my knowledge of the series is rather limited; having really only played through 4, and a small, SMALL portion of Zero, I apologize in advance to the more experienced Resident Evil fans for both my lack of playing the games and lack of knowledge of the overall story of the series.

That said, this game is incredible, and I was thoroughly engaged throughout the majority of my playthrough(s) of it.

In terms of horror, this game does a phenomenal job. Yes, there are jump "scares", but they're rather few and far between and done to great effect. What this game does in the horror department that most other horror games fail to do, however, is nailing the atmosphere. The dark rooms and hallways of the police station and the parking garage and just about every other locale in the game, in conjunction with the haunting, looming soundtrack and ambient noises really bring it all together; there were a few hallways even I was hesitant of walking through (so I ran through instead, lol).

In terms of graphics, the game is beautiful. It ran really well in 4K with near-max settings (i7-7700k and a 1080 Ti), though there were a few areas where frames dipped (the 1F East Side of the Station and the Kitchen in the NEST underground are two places that come to mind), but aside from these areas and some cutscenes the game ran pretty smooth. While I was playing this game, the thought "I wish RE4 was remastered with these graphics" was quite common in my mind. I'd also like to add that this game has some of the realest gore I've seen in a game, which may be a good thing or a bad thing in your opinion (in mine it only added to the experience, so I have no complaints. It's all fake, at any rate).

In terms of gameplay, everything felt right. I found managing the inventory to be enjoyable, and being limited on space at a few moments in the game really added to the experience of tension. I like a game that makes you think, and there were a lot of times when I would be in a safe room and just open the map and plan out my routes before heading out to to whatever task needed to be done. The combat was enjoyable, and really forces you to be patient and smart with your shots and ammo consumption. I loved the fact that Leon's and Claire's 2nd acts (New Game+, basically) are slightly different from their first acts.

In terms of bugs or glitches, there were very few. Just some of the common visual bugs, like jiggling enemies after you killed them (but this only happened when they fell against a wall or other solid object in a weird way) and some vibrating bits on the characters, like Leon's jacket. But these were so minor and so uncommon that they didn't detract from my experience.

The only thing that really bugged me about this game, however, was the dialogue. It isn't too bad in Claire's story (which I found to be the more serious of the duos stories), but man I really rolled my eyes at some of the ♥♥♥♥ that was coming out of Leon's mouth throughout this game. It may just be me, but I would expect that a viral outbreak would be a pretty bad time to throw out awful "one liners" or 90's action quotes ("take that, ya overgrown ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥" really made me sigh audibly). And yeah, he doesn't do it all of the time, but man I just hate that ♥♥♥♥ in movies and games, personally.

All in all, after beating both Leon's and Claire's 1st and 2nd runs, I can say that this is the best game I've played so far in 2019, and that I enjoyed almost every minute of it. It's not perfect, but it's pretty close. And, as everyone else is saying, I wouldn't mind seeing older Resident Evil games remade in this style (like Resident Evil 3, but I'd like to go a step further and suggest that Resident Evil 1 and Zero should also be remade like this, and that Resident Evil 4 should be remastered with this engine).

Perhaps there is no such thing as a perfect game but perhaps there is such a thing as a perfect remake. 

First let me say that while understandable for reasons of design, I have an issue with the movement speed of the player. Doesn't matter if you have a biohazardous nightmare eager for your giblets, you will adopt a light jog. While it's needed to keep the zombies a threat, if you could sprint they'd be a non-issue, it does pull at your immersion when you need to haul ass to stay alive and Leon/Claire assumes power walk stance.

Now that's out of the way, the game is pure gold besides. 
+ The atmosphere is bang on, Raccoon City has seen some shiz and it shows.The REngine manages to do more than justice to the pre-rendered art heritage of the environments from the original RE2.
+ The monster design is similarly stellar. I'll admit that there are a limited number of zombie designs that you will see throughout your playthrough but they are so well done you won't hold it against the game. Lickers are made appealingly disgusting. Plant zombies are more than just reskins but you'll find that out :) You'll encounter more but the bosses are the standouts, for good reason. They are the spectacle and boy what spectacles.
+ Sound design is great, from the moans of the zambos to the clacking of Licker claws they sound descriptive of what they are and listening out for sound will help you survive a little easier. 
+ Music is on point, areas have thematic tracks that audio-strate (is that a thing? it should be a thing) an aesthetic of that area. I will admit however that because the nostalgia is strong I do frequently play with original RE2 music turned on. The fact that's an option is phenomenal for me. Oh yeah, if you turn on that audio option the classic menu noises are used too.

While I enjoyed RE7 and wouldn't mind seeing another first person entry in the series (or done by the same team under a new IP), I honestly can't wait to hear the almost inevitable news that an R3make is in the works to be eventually followed by a Veronica remake too. I'd wish for a redone RE1 and 0 in this mode too but that's not gonna happen. It doesn't matter though, RE2 remake is a glorious example of a remake done right and even if they stop at 3 I'd wager they'll have another blinder on their hands.

I have played almost all the Resident Evil games over their lifespan, and mine for that matter. I was 6 when the first one released and my dad and I played it till 2 in the morning and I had the most amazing nightmares and still consider it one of the best survival horror games of all time right under RE2 and it's followed by Code Veronica X. I never really played the spin-off's besides RE3 and after RE6 which I couldn't even complete I had lost all faith in the franchise and Capcom as a whole. When RE7 released I was stunned and fell in love with the franchise all over again. When this game was announced I was so excited I probably wet myself. I quickly pulled out the emulator on my phone and played the original Resident Evil 2 so I would be prepared for the similarities and differences this game would have. Which is where I will start with this review.

I've read reviews, watched reviews and while there is a lot of praise, there is also a lot of negativity surrounding the game as well. Most of it revolving around this game not being enough like the original. I take issue with this because after playing the original and this one in the same day they are almost exactly the same in most respects. The map layout is only slightly different and some of the puzzles have been reinvented as well as small story changes that honestly make more sense and are a good change in my eyes. There is a little less reference to the first game in the remake, but there was only one or two references to begin with in the original. A lot of the documents are very similar and most of the unique game play elements are similar although more streamlined and honestly improved. In my personal opinion as a fan of the games from their inception, and playing the original and remake practically side by side; I feel I can safely say that this remake is true and faithful to the original. So lets move on.

The other big changes are the controls and gameplay. They feel great in this game but they are different. There aren't any fixed camera angles, as they switched to the over the shoulder camera and aim controls similar to RE4 though vastly improved and much smoother. They have also introduced the counter moves from the remake of RE1 with items like grenades, flash grenades and knives. These are fun, helpful and lifesaving in intense moments during the game. The tyrant section feels almost exactly the same, the Ada sections have been altered and make her feel more like a spy, and the Sherry sections have been vastly improved from the original which I absolutely love. I hated the kid in the original. The gun play is smooth when you need to shoot, the trick is just learning when to run and when to fight. It's a survival horror game. Ammo is limited, and you're not meant to kill everything; You're just supposed to survive. In terms of input controls, keyboard and mouse as well as controllers both feel really good.

The graphics and sound design are superb. In my opinion this is one of the best looking titles I have seen in recent memory. The textures are visually stunning and the color palette sets a dark threatening atmosphere. The lighting, and graphical effects like particles and rain look stunning. The character models are some of the best the series has had and compared to other games, they really shine. The animations are smooth and the facial animations look realistic and I haven't had any sync issues. When you combine all this; You walk out onto the rain swept patio where a plane crashed, the dim lights and violent fire glimmer and reflect off the water while the tyrant lifts you off the ground. Staring you dead in the face with vacant, menacing intent. The water flows off your cloths and face as he tosses you into a wall. The game has so much atmosphere and intimidating visuals. The ambient music is rich and eerie, the combat music is pretty decent without being overwhelming and the boss and tyrant music definitely make the situation more menacing. All the voice overs sound clean, some are sort of throw back over the top. The zombies sound gutteral and visceral. Lickers sound classic. Weapons have good though somewhat muted sounds. Over all a great audio visual experience that I will compare all new games to.

This was a great retelling of the classic experience that was true to its source material. This is definitely Resident Evil 2 remade and it did a fantastic job at it. To me it is worth the full asking price as a fan. There is a lot of content and the dlc extras were fantastic and a welcome addition to expand some story elements hinted at in the original. If it's your first RE experience I don't think it will disappoint. If you think it's to expensive for the amount of time you'll get out of it or find the content lacking compared to other games, then wait for a sale. **Resident Evil 2 Remake Review – A Masterclass in Survival Horror and Replayability**

With over 150 hours sunk into *Resident Evil 2 Remake*, in a game I can now complete in just 2 hours, it’s safe to say I’m a huge fan. This remake doesn’t just modernize the 1998 classic; it surpasses it in nearly every way, creating an experience that stands the test of time while embracing modern advancements.

### First Playthrough – An 8-Hour Thrill Ride
For newcomers, the first playthrough will likely take around 8 hours, and those 8 hours are packed with tension, atmosphere, and memorable moments. The remake masterfully reimagines the original game, with stunning graphics, incredible sound design, and a suffocatingly eerie atmosphere that makes every hallway feel like a potential deathtrap. This is survival horror at its finest.

### Infinite Ammo and Speedrunning Fun
But the real fun begins once that first playthrough is done. Unlocking infinite ammo and diving into speedrunning turns the game into a completely different experience. While I don’t speedrun professionally, the thrill of racing against the clock adds a fresh layer of excitement. The game rewards players for mastering its mechanics, and completing it in under 2 hours is a satisfying achievement that keeps me coming back time and time again.

### Modding – A Gateway to Endless Fun
If there’s one thing that cemented my love for the *Resident Evil 2 Remake*, it’s the modding scene. Modding this game is incredibly easy and opens up endless possibilities for customization. Whether you’re looking for gameplay tweaks, visual overhauls, or just some fun new skins for the characters, modding keeps the experience fresh long after the main game is done.

### An Expertly Done Remake
Remakes rarely outshine their originals, but *Resident Evil 2 Remake* does so confidently and expertly. Capcom has created a near-perfect reimagining of the classic, with all the nostalgia of the original combined with cutting-edge technology. The atmosphere, graphics, and reworked gameplay have elevated it to a new level, and for many (myself included), it’s the definitive version of *Resident Evil 2*.

### Final Thoughts
*Resident Evil 2 Remake* is a benchmark for how remakes should be done. With over 150 hours logged and still having a blast with speedruns and mods, it’s a game that never gets old. Whether you’re a fan of the original or a newcomer to the series, this is a must-play that beautifully blends survival horror with modern gaming.

RE2 is an enjoyable experience, but not a flawless masterpiece. In the category of classic survival horror franchises, Silent Hill 2, Fatal Frame II, and Resident Evil 2 are usually cited as the best of the best. (This era squeezed out some great number twos.) And of those three, my vote goes to Fatal Frame. The Fatal Frame series understood something that Resident Evil has always aimed for, but never quite hit: survival horror is at its best when it emphasizes horror over survival. 
     That's not to say survival is unimportant. In fact, the RE2 remake nails its resource management elements. The player is fed the thinnest possible mixture of ammunition and herbs necessary to stay alive. Teetering on the edge of helplessness is a great way to convey the enormity of an apocalyptic zombie outbreak. But this connects to my main problem with RE2. The only way to make it out alive is to run. Unfortunately, there's nothing scary about running from zombies. They're slow, stupid, and only dangerous in confined spaces. That's where RE2 fails - and it's a significant failure. The zombie threat really isn't that menacing.
     It doesn't take long to learn the "golden rule" of the game: never shoot an enemy unless it's blocking your path. In other words, the real villains of RE2 aren't zombies, but hallways. Take, for instance, the library: a room filled to the bursting point with zombies. Never once did I fire a shot in the library, and never once was I killed there. Which raises the question, if every zombie in that room can easily be eluded, why put any there at all? 

It sheds light on a mechanic that's always baffled me in horror games. Why create experiences that are meant to be avoided?

     RE2 crowds its rooms with zombies that serve as nothing more than ticking clocks. If the designers filled the game with poison gas canisters set on a timer, it would produce the same effect. In every instance, the player's goal is to get in, collect as many resources as possible, and hurry out.
     The game’s other flaws are less significant, but still irksome. Puzzles are cryptic, even with a walkthrough, and they only get worse on the second play through. Speaking of which, the second play through needs to go lie down. All but two of the save spots get removed from the police station, which means constant backtracking. I have to blaze through the game so quickly, I can't tell if I'm enjoying it. 
     If I sound overly negative, it's because I haven’t gotten to the game's finer traits. The controls are sublime, and the game was properly designed around them. (Unlike RE6, which made the player overly powerful.) Leon and Ada have some nice moments that flesh them out as real characters, instead of the soulless action heroes polluting the series. The protagonists are even capable of actual weakness, which you would expect in a horror game, but which Resident Evil rarely delivers. The non-zombie enemies are legitimately challenging, and there are some good boss fights to enjoy. Once you leave the police station, the game starts to take off; and it’s here that you understand why fans have been gushing about it since the ‘90s. RE2 possesses a layer of polish rarely matched. Its levels are so well designed, with resources so perfectly spaced out, it becomes a thrill to race from point A to point B. This isn’t an open-world collect-a-thon with tired mechanics we’ve seen a thousand times. RE2 knows its strengths, and it plays to them without resorting to filler and side quests. Once the game abandons the police station and all the backtracking it demands, it becomes a joy to play through. I can’t emphasize enough how much fun I had with the second half of the game. My complains are numerous, but the fact that I enjoyed myself in spite of those complaints speaks volumes about just how good the RE2 remake really is. Perfect? No, but very, very worth your time.

[b]DISCLAIMER[/b] 
I have never played a Resident Evil game in my life (prior to this one of course). This includes the original version of Resident Evil 2. This review will [u]not[/u] focus on the improvements made on the original version of the game nor will I compare the story or game play to a different resident evil game. I will only talk about my experiences in this game.

[h1]THE REVIEW[/h1]

Resident Evil was a series I had always heard about, but never had the opportunity to try. I had always liked the horror genre, and games are not an exception. I had dabbled in some popular ones such as Amnesia and the like, but none of them really struck a cord with me, until I played this game. This game is the epitome of horror done right. It's graphics are beautiful, it's puzzles are intuitive and immensely satisfying,the environment is beautifully designed, and, the replay-ability is quite high.

I'll get this out of the way now, the story of this game isn't anything special. It's the standard zombie apocalypse scenario. You are thrown into a world filled with zombies and have to find a way to stop it, and find out how it happened. Not a story for the ages, but the game play and characters more than make up for it.

Prior to starting a new save, you have the option of choosing between 2 stories. First one is Leon S Kennedy, a fresh out of the academy cop hired at the  Raccoon City Police Department. On the drive to his first day, he noticed zombies walking around, and when he arrived to the Police Department, he found that it was infested by said zombies. The other option is to play as Claire Redfield. She travelled to Raccoon City in search of her brother, Chris, who went missing after the zombie outbreak. Each story shows a different perspective on the same incident, with occasional meet-ups between the 2 characters, tying the story together. Throughout the game the characters are quite emotive when it comes to them getting hurt or reacting to a stressful scenario, which gives the game even more life. The game can also have different outcomes based on the character you play first. I'm not going to tell you what order is the best, because honestly, I don't know. Pick whoever you like more I suppose.

This game's horror isn't the typical horror I had seen in other horror games. Most horror games scare the player through cheap jump scares or have the enemies as the source of the player's fear, in this game however, this isn't the case[spoiler](except Mr.X)[/spoiler]. The true horror stems from the resource management in the game. Ammo is SCARCE and I mean SCARCE. Zombies take multiple bullets to take down, and with the rarity of ammo in this game, it is easy to tell why it can be terrifying. I had found myself frantically running in the opposite direction when I ran out of ammo hoping I could get out in one piece. This combined with the tight hallways and claustrophobic rooms, the adrenaline rush I got from the fear was truly amazing. 

The puzzles are also fantastic, they are (as I aforementioned) immensely satisfying to solve and very fun as well. Many of them force you to explore the area and pick up on clues with documents that were left around. Granted, there is a lot of running around to solve a puzzle (for one puzzle I had to run from one side of the police station to another), but for the first time in a game, I didn't mind it. The atmosphere exudes a very eerie vibe (as it should) even when I knew I had cleared out all the zombies in that area. The fear of the unknown in this game was constantly in the back of my head, so I never truly felt safe. This is why I didn't mind the running, it had my mind preoccupied with survival and not just getting to point B from point A.

The graphics of this game are truly a sight to behold. They are VERY nice to look at. I spent about a minute admiring how detailed a zombie looked after I blasted it's head clean off. That being said, a stronger computer is needed to enjoy this game to it's fullest, but it is definitely worth it.

In conclusion, this game is a master piece. The characters are interesting and emotive, the puzzles and environments are brilliantly designed, and the graphics quite amazing as well. I can confidently say that this game is worth every single penny it is priced at. A must have for any steam library, and any horror fan.

As someone who has been a diehard fan of the series since the original RE2, I feel that this is the best the series has ever been. It's clear right from the start that the team that developed this game is very passionate; even the smallest detail seems to have had an extraordinary amount of care taken. 

 For example, this game has the most interesting and dynamic zombies I've ever seen in gaming. Playing this and, for contrast, RE6 back to back shows a world of difference in how they are treated. In RE6, they are basic cannon fodder that barely pay attention to the player and almost instantly fall apart as they run straight into your fire and recoil with barely any resistance. You can literally punch their heads off with ease or suplex them and not even spend a bullet on them; they feel like they're made of wet tissue and just about as intimidating.

Here, they actually react directly to sight and sound. If you are a careful player, you can quietly step around them and try to sneak past, but the smallest error can be deadly, because these zombies are absolutely tenacious and aggressive and will NOT leave you alone, going as far as to break through doors or fall off balconies to drop on top of you, breaking limbs clean off in the process. Even when reduced to a legless torso, they are still somehow fast and strong enough to catch you off guard and drag you into a crowd of the undead. They move erratically, so that the modern third person shooter mechanics don't spell an easy win with headshots. Even a shotgun blast point blank to the face isn't always enough, and you can see every gruesome detail of the muscle and decaying, slimy tissue under their skin as you cut, shoot, incinerate and even melt them down. Capcom doesn't shy away from the macabre, and every bite your character takes is enough to keep you seriously on edge, especially when on the hardest difficulty where even a single chomp is enough to end you.

This level of attention is given to nearly every enemy in the game. The Cerberus in the original could easily be fooled due to their predictable AI pattern and simple attacks. All you need is to run in a zigzag pattern and they would never catch you. Here, they work in packs, distracting you with a decoy while the rest gang up on you from behind. They even follow you by sneaking through vents and cutting off your exit while you are desperately fleeing from the crowd, creating panic inducing scenarios. The Lickers depend on sound more than ever, and can now attack from virtually any direction. The developers also show a sadistic streak here, as they like to group them together around the Cerberus packs and zombies, creating truly intense situations.

The star of the show here is the Tyrant, nicknamed by fans as Mr.X, who is even more relentless than the zombies and is always present somewhere in the halls of the RPD, waiting for you to make noise and sprint to your location. His role is greatly expanded from the original, no longer briefly appearing at scripted moments and leaving you be as soon as you leave the room. Here, he's a constant threat, and will force you into making difficult choices on the fly. Will you try to hold out and rush to solve a puzzle and risk getting cornered? Do you try to evade him while quietly, slowly walking by a Licker, painstakingly avoiding every bit of glass on the floor as Mr.X quickly gains ground on you? He keeps the game fresh on every new run, and this new, much creepier version of him is a welcome successor to Nemesis, Lisa Trevor and the Baker family of stalkers.

The game mechanics themselves feel spectacular. It's a very well-thought combination of classic and modern ideas, taking elements from nearly every title in the series and refining them into a coherent new system. The over the shoulder view doesn't diminish the cinematic qualities of the game, but greatly enhance it, making you feel claustrophobic and allowing you to soak every gloriously rendered detail in the reimagination of the iconic RPD, practically a character in itself. This building alone is full of wonderful environmental storytelling, interesting lighting and masterful layout design that really feels like a (formerly) lived in locale full of alternate routes, shortcuts, and secrets waiting to be uncovered. Between this title and RE7, Resident Evil has finally returned to it's roots in the sense that the environments are actually interesting and just begged to have you pour over every corner and explore intimately.

Some cues are taken from REmake and RE0 here; you can discard items (unfortunately, you can't just pick them back up like in 0), and you have defense items making a return from REmake along with enemies following you through rooms. RE3's gunpowder mixing returns, and even elements from Revelations 1 come into play (with a scanner device that you use briefly at certain moments.) The knife is mapped to a separate button now like in the modern RE4 style titles, but is balanced out by a risk-reward setup by doubling as a defense item with a durability aspect that allows the knife to break. Inventory management is meaningful again, having to create a careful balance between carrying what you need to progress vs. surviving with enough weapons and supplies to push through the hordes of monsters in your way.

The pacing of the game feels great, and lends itself well to speedruns like the classics, but still bursting with content if you choose to take your time and explore with plenty of secrets to find. It never gets dull, and plays with veteran fans' expectations with familiar events in interesting ways. That's not even taking into account the additional gameplay modes, mini-campaigns, and unlockable awards tied to certain actions, which is a brilliant throwback to games from the late 90's and early 2000's where this used to be commonplace.

The performances of the cast are the best the series has ever seen, with Leon clearly sounding nervous and Claire showing a great range of emotion, coupled with amazing mo-cap performances and spectacularly detailed character models having actual dynamic facial expressions and getting caked in dirt, blood, grime and rain. The script itself still retains that classic B-movie charm, but general direction of the game itself gives it a much harder edge and goes further with certain elements that I won't spoil here.

The newly composed soundtrack is stunning. I had chills when the new version of the iconic hallway theme plays out as a haunting, eerie orchestral remix, and save room theme makes a quick appearance as well (this could have stayed in the game longer; it is a beautiful composition and it just oozes atmosphere into an already stylish and immersive game.) There are intense new tracks for exciting moments that sound truly epic with operatic wails, sprinting violins, and pounding, anixety inducing bass beats. The weapons sound spot on, with the shotgun and magnum really packing a punch, the zombies screeches tearing at your eardrums, and spooky creaks and echos greet you as you cautiously tiptoe around the halls of the dead. 

 This is a game I could honestly go on for hours praising. It does have a few issues, with a couple particularly grating sequences that hamper replays and cause frustration, but not enough to take away from the brilliance on display throughout. 

Overall, if you are even a passing fan of adventure games, horror, or Resident Evil, I can't recommend this game enough! 7 months into 2019, this is by far my favourite game of the year, and possibly this console generation. Resident Evil has gone in an amazing new direction, and I can't wait to see where it goes next.

My third favorite RE game but not without its issues.

The animations are amazing on the cut scenes, the voice acting is really good (wired hearing Leon's voice changed since RE4 which I didn't think I would get used to, but I did) this is enough to keep the story that many already know interesting.

Gameplay:

Gameplay is pretty much what you would expect from a RE game, but your aiming over the shoulder, a feature which helped make RE4 more intense and also at the same time offering better controls.

The game can give quite a few scares indeed, zombies leaping out unexpectedly at times and huge boss battles.

There is a lot of replay value with two different story modes for both Leon and Clare ( Calre's 2nd run story is the best ) and different modes to unlock.

Some annoying things about the gameplay is the length of time it takes to recover/move after being hit especially in the boss battles, the Quick draw army gun takes forever to reload.
Having to place an item into a slot and reconfigure a shortcut  slot for your weapon then skip a cutscene/ run down a long corridor and have to skip a cutscene each time you get killed 
can be very tedious and seems cheap to extend the game at certain points, the game has massive amounts of backtracking already, this one of the main reasons I prefer resident evil 4 as it has a lot less back tracking and doesn't cheaply make you take many steps to get to where you were before you got killed.

Graphics:

The game has loads of atmosphere thanks to the volmetric lighting and art style, it can be a very pretty game at times.

At other times it can be an ugly mess, thanks to the horrific implementation of screen space reflections and non existent SAA (SAA is there but it does absolutely nothing) so your left with the blurry FXAA and it's bigger sibling TXAA which leaves the game looking worse than 720p even if you run it at 4K!!! the only other option I had (GTX 1080 TI) was to use DSR within the Nividia    settings (I use a 1080p TV) run the game in 4K turn the DSR smoothness to 0 and back in the game drop the volmetric lighting down to medium along with dropping HBAO+ to SSAO the game still had jaggies but a lot less. (Worth noting, setting the AA within the Nividia control panel makes no difference at all). And for screen space reflections? the worst I have seen, I have seen better floor reflections in Perfect Dark on the N64 and other games, where you look and say wow that looks really cool and my characters body doesn't make them disappear, flicker or look like fuzzed mixing pixels like RE2 does.

Also the zombies detail and modeling looks like a step down from the rest of the game, I noticed this from the demos, but I though they would improve them before the final game, but they did not. 

So many graphical settings that make little no difference at all, especially high detailed models using max VRAM, the zombies still look low detailed and everything else looks the same at max VRAM model details as it does when your using high (2GB-4GB VRAM on model details) it would have been nice if they spent the time getting better reflections and SAA to work along with getting character and shadow animations at a distance to run at 60fps 
instead of 30fps.

Final verdict:

Resident Evil 2 is really good I would highly recommend it, but its not the best Resident Evil game in the series and certainly not the worst, but its up there with the best of time.

Resident Evil 4 is the better game, so much more variation in the levels, bigger game, better story, better reflections (even on the Nintendo Gamecube), less back tracking, you could collect and sell items, upgrade your weapons, it had shooting ranges and reward system, and it was ahead of it's time for graphics back in the day (they squeezed so much out of aging hardware that at first glance you thought "it's not running on Gamecube" and if it was Gamecube needed an graphical expansion to be able to run it) plus you get the Merchant guy "WEEEELLLLL COMEEEEEEEE", Resident Evil 2 remake comes 2nd and then Resident Evil  remake comes 3rd.

All that aside, there's still loads of fun and scares to be had with RE2 and I recommend it for those reasons, just don't expect a game as good as RE4 is and don't expect a game as graphical ground breaking as RE4 was and you won't be disappointed.

TL; DR, This game is a masterpiece. This is a quality over quantity game. 9/10

[b] How does it play? [/b]
Its a Third-person shooter with horror and puzzles.
[b] Gameplay loop/routine? [/b]
Go into a room to get pass zombies and look for items (keys, puzzle pieces, or resources) to get you out of the "frying pan". Then "into a fire" when you fight a boss.
[b] Other stuff. [/b]
- Inventory management is key. You are given a limited amount of slots that can be upgraded, BUT only ammo and herbs are stackable, everything else takes up one or more slots.
- Zombies are tanky AF, and resources/ammo are fairly limited. You'll have this question in your head, "Is it worth it to re-kill this zombie?"
- You're not a expert zombie killer, you play as a rookie cop or a college student with some firearms training. If you get caught by a zombie, You need a knife or a grenade in order push it away without taking damage.
- Saves are done at typewriters located in certain areas throughout the levels. On Normal and "hold my hand mode" you can save unlimited amount of times + there is autosave. BUT in hardcore, you have to use an item to save, but there are plently of them.
- Puzzles aren't too difficult, plus you can look at the internet for help. But I recommend that you don't for the 1st playthrough, unless you're really stuck of course.

[b] Story [/b]
- The entire game is suppose to only take place in one night, from dusk till dawn. So its pretty short. But has some replayability. FYI: Its still set in 1998.
- There are two main playable characters Leon and Claire. They play the same, but their weapons and some story parts are different. I personally prefer Claire, because of her grenade launcher and for some reason backtracking is more fun with her. I don't know why, my FOV is turned all the way up though.
- Each character has a "main run" and a "2nd run", with the latter being played after beating the main run with the other character. The 2nd run is a slight remix of the main run, puzzles, order of events, and item placements are different.
- For me a Claire "main run" and  a Leon "2nd run" make the most sense story-wise. Claire really has to be ahead of Leon for the story events to make sense.

[b] Cons [/b]
- Apparently in the original, what you did in one character's playthrough affected the other in the next. This is not the case here.
- Replayability could be better, although it doesn't need a NG+ like most games now a days. They could have added a mercenaries mode like previous RE games, but not as grindy. The extra modes are nice, but a mercenaries mode would have been better IMO.

[b] Graphics and Performance [/b]
- Its pretty close to real-life, but it is corridor-scale and not ARMA III scale. So they can really beef up those graphics.
- Runs silky smooth on 1060 (laptop version).

I have never had fits of rage, or been one to break down and cry, but I was in a low spot that just really buried me from being able to see the light on the other side.

I decided that it had to be worth a shot... I must admit, I didn't beat the game, or play nearly as long as some of you. In fact, I may have only played this game a day or two.. [h1] Resident Evil 2 / Biohazard RE:2, a.k.a RE:2 Remake. Is it worth the price?	[/h1]

Resident Evil 2 is a Third-Person Shooter made by Capcom and first released in 1998. In 2019, they have remade the game and began selling under the title "Resident Evil 2 / Biohazard RE:2". But, is it worth it?

[u] Pros	[/u]
[list]
    [*]Impressively great graphics.
    [*]Can set the difficulties to make the game a casual weekend game to a Post-Apocalyptic Zombie Survival game.
    [*]The mixture of action and horror delivers the players a both beautiful and grotesque game.
    [*]A game long enough to take a long time to beat "completely".
    [*]Optimized game and almost no loading screens.
    [*]Considering that in this segment, high-end GPUs are not expensive as before and the game is more pushy to the GPU, most of the current generation computers can run this game smoothly.
[/list]

[u] Contra	[/u]
[list]
    [*]The game can be very hard sometimes, Capcom has forgot to explain the players what to do unless the player dies a lot.
    [*]The game must be finished twice in order to be completely beaten, giving the people who hates replaying a pain.
[/list]

[b] Is it worthy or not?	[/b]
I've bought this game in the summer sales for 30ish Euros and I can say that it is worth it. Not only that it gives the players a long and detailed story, the game can be challenging and demonstrate the greatness of RE Engine. Weapons are great, graphics are great, story is great, mechanics are great and this list would keep going on. For 30 bucks it is worth it, but I don't think if I could pay the full price, since this game is not really as replayable as RPG games or games such as D:BH.
This game is a GPU killer, though. My old and overclocked FX6300 didn't had any trouble, but my GPU was struggling to load the graphics. But after a point, somehow both the GPU and CPU usage was reduced. I guess at first it needs high usage, idk.

Long story short, buy this game during the sales and you won't regret it

Resident Evil 2 is one of the best games of this year so far and is probably the best horror/puzzle/strategic story based game that will be at the top of the list for a while.

RE2 is a remake of the 1998 classic however unlike most remakes, this game has completely changed the way it plays by getting rid of the fixed camera angles, changing the gun play, adding horror to both the unstoppable Mr.X and the seemingly immortal zombies, just to name a few changes, there is also small details added in by Capcom such as Lickers can only hear and not see, which is something added in later games but incorporated into this remake which wasn't in the original game for example. The game has the 2 main stories and 2 alternate stories, you can play as Leon as the 1st or 2nd run and Claire as the other one which you didn't chose for Leon, making the stories feel connected because of the way they run with each other (Leon 1st and Claire 2nd makes more sense from a reality point of view), after completing the story there is a bonus mode (Hunk the 4th Survivor) which is action filled like RE6 for example, which acts as a speedrun for players who like rush and adrenaline and after completing this, there is another 4 game modes which act similar to the 4th survivor but are more challenging and add more replayability to the game because of how different they are to the main game and each other. There is also free DLC which adds 4 new game modes similar to the previous mentioned game modes but have some different game mechanics such as vending machines where you gamble with what to take for the rest of the run and special zombie types, however the only down side to this game mode which isn't too big of a deal, is that they are 'What if?' situations, meaning they are not cannon to the story line but that doesn't change a lot to be honest.

I could go on for about 8 other paragraphs talking about how you can replay the game on an extremely hard difficulty and unlock weapons with infinite ammo for quicker runs afterwards to get easy achievements (like I did), in-game rewards and unlockables to help you out and how they can change the game, the fact that you don't need to fully explore the map and get everything to complete the game however that may make things harder for newer players, the concept art, the models and everything else that adds to the fun of this game.

If you are a major fan of the game then I would recommend getting it at any point but if you are a newcomer, you may find the game hard and different to most other games so I would advise waiting for a sale in case you don't like it, therefore you haven't wasted too much money.

Resident Evil 2 is a survival horror game that takes place 2 months after the original Resident Evil. You play as either Claire Redfield, the little sister of S.T.A.R.S Alpha member Chris Redfield, or Leon S. Kennedy, a rookie cop who was originally told to stay away from his new workplace, Raccoon City Police Department. With both characters, your goal is to find a way out of the doomed city, save as many people as you can, and uncover the truth of what happened to this city.

Right off the bat, I want to say that Resident Evil 2, both original and remake, are my favorite games in the franchise. There are so many things about this game that I love:

- Everyone's character designs, especially Leon's
- Leon in his entirety
- Claire
- The Mr. X Tyrant. While he is slow and easy to avoid, he can cause some really tense situations, such as being forced to walk through a licker hall with him right behind you
- The Raccoon City Police Station. This precinct is my favorite location in any horror game. So much so that I actually spent a summer building the Police Station in Minecraft
- The gameplay. I love the mix of third person and survival horror. The weapons are so satisfying to use in this game
- The presentation is on point here with the dark, gritty atmosphere. You never know what's around the corner
- The gore and monsters. The zombies, Lickers, the Ivy, the G-Adults, all the monsters in this game look grotesque and haunting. The noises they make sell them for me
- I really like Sherry and Ada's sections. It's a lot different from just pushing boxes like in the original
- The changes made to some of the minor characters were a really nice touch, Marvin having a more prominent role and Chief Irons being more of an unpredictable psychopath
- The extra costumes you can get. Whilst they are DLC, I still like how they look, especially Claire's Elza Walker skin
- The option to have the original RE2 music in the game was a really nice touch, especially since you can barely hear the remake's music in this game
- Sherry is a cinnamon roll
- The updated sewers. They're a lot better in this game than in the original
- Saudade
- The puzzles, despite having over a hundred hours in this game, are still fun to do
- William Birkin is horrifying as he should be. His cries for Sherry in his first form were hauntingly beautiful
- Kendo in this game was a nice change from his original counterpart
- The classic skins you get for completing the game. They are near perfect


I could go on for hours as to why I love this game. And as much as I can praise this game, there are some things I noticed that I think needed to be fixed:

- The plot holes near the end, such as:
[spoiler] The Mr. X tyrant dying to Birkin but still being present in Leon's run
Annette dying by Leon, Claire and Sherry, and then dying again after shooting Ada,
Ada's fall which she somehow survives [/spoiler]
- The music in this game, as beautiful as it is, was way too quiet. Thankfully, you can swap it out for the original RE2's soundtrack
- Some of the changes near the end as well, I found to be odd, like how [spoiler] Sherry gets over her mom's death, or Leon's reaction to Sherry being "ok" when in the original, he actively helped Claire and Sherry near the end [/spoiler]
- We really needed more interactions between Leon and Claire in this game. They have so much chemistry but they only talk a handful of times compared to the original
- I would've loved to see the Marshalling Yard again, but that's personal preference

And I think that's one of the issues. When you compare the story to the original, that's when the flaws come out more. Writing this, however, I understand that RE1 and RE2's stories have plotholes in both, where you have to work the canon out yourself.

For example: You never see Barry in Chris' side, especially when you escape, nor do you see Rebecca on Jill's side, but these two characters survive the mansion incident with Chris and Jill. However, RE2's story in the original, for the most part, intertwined with both scenarios. So for the remake's story to fall under the category of RE1's style of storytelling, it can be a letdown. Personally, I feel like if they incorporated Claire A Leon B more, [spoiler] make Ada's "death" the one in Leon's original B scenario, and make some changes to Birkin "killing" the Mr. X Tyrant,[/spoiler] this game would have been a masterpiece of a remake.

And despite these issues, I still love this game. This is still my favorite Resident Evil game. I love this remake for its gameplay, and I love the original for its storytelling. The two go hand in hand and I've never had so many issues trying to pick which game I liked more between an original and a remake. I don't want the flaws I listed to scare anyone off, because on its own, despite its issues, Resident Evil 2 Remake is still an amazing game and a perfect starting point for anyone new to this franchise. This was my first Resident Evil game I played and I'm so glad it was. Resident Evil 2 will always be one of my favorite games.

Enemies: 9/10

Zombies are absolutely terrifying and the gore mechanics and visuals really make them seem almost too real.  Mr. X is by far the biggest troll he manages to make you think he is in one place but yet he is in another showing up at the worst times when you might be facing a horde of zombies or when facing down a group of lickers, he is fast, unpredictable, and keeps the game very engaging during the R.P.D. my personal favorite part of the game.
