[B]Introduction:[/B]

Resident Evil 2 is my favorite Survival Horror game on the PSone, a game which I have done several playthroughs of over the years because I just plain enjoy the game so much that no matter how many times I play it I always end up coming back for more. It's one of the few games that I have been so thoroughly impressed and captivated by that no matter how much time passes, I can still enjoy it just as much today as I did when I first played it. The only facet of the game that I feel has aged poorly enough to subtract from my enjoyment of it is the graphics, everything else from the goofy voice acting to the clunky controls are just part of the experience for me. Obviously, when the announcement was made that the game was going to be remade I became very excited. The remake of the first Resident Evil on the Nintendo GameCube was excellent, improving on the original in every way and expanding on the content within, so that was the basis of my expectations for a remake of Resident Evil 2. The question is, did the remake of Resident Evil 2 live up to my expectations? Well, the answer isn't as simple as a yes or no, it's a little of both, so let's go over everything piece by piece so that I can tell you how I really feel about the game.

[B]Graphical Presentation:[/B]

The graphics of the original Resident Evil 2 have aged very poorly, which is to be expected from a game which was developed for the Sony PlayStation in the early days of CGI and 3D Models. As a result, I would have honestly been satisfied if Capcom had merely remade Resident Evil 2 on the Resident Evil HD Remaster's Engine, reused assets and all. Instead Capcom developed RE2R on Resident Evil 7's Engine, and the results are fantastic. Capcom absolutely nailed the graphical presentation of this game. Everything looks fantastic, and the attention to detail is amazing. The chilling atmosphere of Raccoon City and its many locales come to life (or should I say come back to life?) in Resident Evil 2, regardless of what you're playing it on, but if you can run this game in 4K UHD, then you will be absolutely amazed at just how great this game looks. My only complaint is in regards to the lighting, which is much too dark by default, so be prepared to adjust the in-game brightness above the default/suggested settings, and you may end up having to disable HDR (High Dynamic Range) altogether to be able to see in some of the darker areas of the game. Issues with the lighting are also compounded by the fact that the game gives the player absolutely no control over the Flashlight, which just turns on/off automatically in certain areas, and unfortunately it doesn't always come on as soon as you enter a dark area, so at times you'll have to walk a fair distance in the dark before the Flashlight turns on.

[B]Audio Presentation:[/B]

The sound effects in RE2R are great. I don't have a high quality sound system hooked up, nor am I by any means an audiophile, but from the bangs of firearms to the growls of monsters, RE2R sounds perfect to me. When it comes to the soundtrack however, I was somewhat disappointed. As a fan of the original game, I wanted to hear remastered tracks of all the original music, but Capcom chose to go with a more ambient, atmospheric soundtrack in RE2R. Unfortunately, I'm too biased here to give a fair review of the new soundtrack because I loved the original too much and honestly don't care for the modern trend of ambient sounds played over top of scant music as opposed to orchestrated music, so let's just say that I didn't care for it and leave it at that. Fortunately, Capcom provided the option for those who buy the Deluxe Edition of the game (I of thethink it's also sold separately as DLC) to select the original soundtrack, so those who dislike the new soundtrack and prefer the original are covered.

[B]Gameplay:[/B]

Unsurprisingly, Capcom has done away with the original method of control (often aptly referred to as "tank controls") and fixed camera angles in favor of the more modern 3rd Person Shooter controls and camera which has become the standard since RE4. Love it or hate it, you have to admit that it was the reasonable thing for Capcom to do. Personally, as much as I love the original RE2, the tank controls never felt natural nor intuitive to me, they were merely something that I had grown accustomed to over time, so I don't miss them. However, one thing that I do find disappointing about the gameplay is that a few of the enemies from the original game were omitted from RE2R, including a Mini Boss. (Crows, Webspinners, and the Giant Moth.) Granted that these enemies were mostly an annoyance/obstacle in the original game, so if anything it was a better choice to remove them than keep them as they were, but I would have preferred to have seen them reworked than outright omitted.

[B]Story:[/B]

Despite being billed as a "Remake" initially, RE2R is actually more of a "Reimagining" of RE2 in terms of story. The plot is still more or less the same, but little tweaks and additions have been made to the story, and unfortunately this is where my biggest disappointment with the game comes into play. For the most part, I like the additions which have been made to the story, but I dislike some of the changes which have been made to the original story. Namely, I dislike how Scenario B has been omitted from the game along with the way it affected the story. Capcom has replaced Scenario B with what is now referred to as Second Run, which merely shows the other side of the story from the other playable characters' perspective. Unfortunately, as a result the game now has significantly less replay value because there is no longer a sort of "what-if" scenario when you replay the game in the opposite order. In addition, instead of merely consolidating the canon events of Claire Scenario A with Leon Scenario B from the original by having the major plot elements of Leon Scenario B occur within Leon's portion of the story regardless of whether he is chosen for the First or Second Run, Capcom chose to completely omit the events from Leon Scenario B in favor of his much less interesting/impactful Leon Scenario A playthrough. As a result, Leon's portion of the story feels much weaker and less impactful than it could have, especially in terms of his relationship with Ada Wong. The events of Leon Scenario B made the romance feel much more genuine due to certain scenes between the two which don't occur in Leon Scenario A, not to mention that Ada receives more character development in Leon Scenario B which makes her character more genuine as well. Why Capcom would choose to omit the expanded story of Leon Scenario B despite the fact that it is the canon version of Leon's story is beyond me and the results of said decision reduce what could have been a perfect remake to a mere reimagining with a weaker story and less replay value. Oh, and no, it's not a retcon, Leon's canon story is still that of Leon Scenario B in the original game. In fact, Capcom themselves have taken to calling this game a "reimagining" themselves on social media since the game's release. So in terms of story, RE2R falls short of the original RE2.

[B]Final Verdict:[/B]

RE2R is nearly a perfect remake of Resident Evil 2, but the few things they removed from the game and its story prevent it from being so. As long as this game was in development and as eager as I was to play it, I would have been willing to wait as long as it took for them to develop the game with all of its original enemies, features, and story intact. The game is still great, totally worth playing, and my current top contender for GotY 2019, but it could have been even better if more time had been taken to maintain the content of the original.

The new gold standard for remakes. Resident Evil 2 Remake has updated the classic playstation 1 game for the modern era, and the quality is fantastic. The RE Engine graphics hold up amazingly well, especially considering this game is under 25GB in size. Zombies are once again a legitimate threat for the unprepared. All the classic creatures that have been reintroduced from the Lickers to Birkin have been given a fresh coat of paint and will keep you on your toes. 

Mr X is one of the main highlights of the game, once he's introduced he will hunt you throughout sections of the game much like the Xenomorph in Alien Isolation. Fortunately you should have an easier time with Mr X than the Alien. Once he looses track of you, he'll begin hunting the area searching for you and can explore almost the entirety of his surroundings with some exceptions such as save rooms. At first he can slow you down and make life difficult, but players will eventually learn tactics to handle him.

The gameplay is well executed, with the game adopting a over the shoulder third person shooter style, akin to previous games in the series. Capcom though were very aware that this could make the game easier, so changes were made to aiming and enemy strengths were adjusted to compensate. This has made the game a tough challenging, but fair game. Try not to play this game like RE5/6 otherwise you may find yourself short on resources further down the line. Like old school RE games, ammo conservation is key here. If you can get by an enemy with little risk do so. 

There could have been a bit more diversity in the first run & second rum modes, though this is only a minor issue. 

Overall probably one of my favourite games in the franchise so far, with only a couple of things I felt could have been improved upon. I can wholeheartedly recommend this game for old school fans, newcomers and players looking for a high quality horror game. Fans of RE5 & RE6 might not enjoy this style of Resident Evil however.

[h1]A Masterful Remake That Captures the Essence of Classic Survival Horror[/h1]

[b]Introduction:[/b]

As someone who hadn't played the original Resident Evil games due to their unappealing elements like tank controls, I was pleasantly surprised by the Resident Evil 2 remake. It not only surpasses its predecessors but stands out as one of the best games I've ever played. With modern technology, Capcom has revitalized RE2, improving upon it in every way while maintaining a nostalgic single-player experience that's rare to find in today's gaming landscape.

[b]Pros:[/b]

[b]Immersive Graphics:[/b] The overall graphics in RE2 remake are stunning, creating a captivating and visually diverse world.

[b]Engaging Atmosphere:[/b] The game's atmosphere is top-notch, successfully building tension and delivering an intense experience through intriguing level design.

[b]Mr. X:[/b] The inclusion of Mr. X adds an extra layer of tension to the game. While he can be avoided if you're skilled and know where you're going, his sporadic appearances keep you on your toes.

[b]Puzzles:[/b] Despite not being a fan of puzzles, I found the ones in RE2 remake manageable and not overly challenging. If you do get stuck, there are plenty of online guides available to assist you.

[b]Gruesome Gore:[/b] The game doesn't shy away from blood and gore, and it's both visually impressive and appropriately unsettling.

[b]Dynamic Combat:[/b] Combat in the game is fun and satisfying, with enemies reacting realistically to your shots. Shooting a zombie's limbs can cause them to break off, yet they may still crawl towards you, creating intense encounters.

[b]Authentic Zombie Behaviour:[/b] The zombies in RE2 remake are convincingly designed and behave as you'd expect. Their occasional "playing dead" tactic keeps you alert and adds to the overall creepiness.

[b]Stealth Mechanics:[/b] The inclusion of minor stealth elements, such as sneaking past blind Lickers or avoiding Mr. X, adds another layer of tension and strategy to the gameplay.

[b]Survival Focus:[/b] The limited availability of ammo and supplies encourages thorough exploration of each room, heightening the survival aspect of the game.

[b]Replayability:[/b] The ranking system and unlockable items, coupled with different playable characters and altered campaign scenarios, incentivize replaying the game. The second run mode, in particular, offers a fresh and challenging experience.

[b]Secrets and Exploration:[/b] RE2 remake rewards players for thorough exploration, with numerous secrets hidden throughout the game.

[b]Well-Executed Boss Fights:[/b] Although not the most complex, the boss fights are well-designed and provide memorable encounters.

[b]Intense Extra Mode:[/b] The 4th Survivor mode stands out as a fantastic addition. As a canon extension of the story, it offers an intense and frantic experience, complementing the base game perfectly.

[b]Memorable Soundtrack:[/b] The game features a compelling soundtrack that enhances the atmosphere and complements the gameplay experience.

[b]Cons:[/b]

[b]Challenging Ranking System:[/b] The way the ranking system is handled in the game can feel arbitrary and restrictive. A time constraint and save game limit can hinder players from achieving the desired rank, especially for unlocking certain rewards like infinite ammo weapons.

[b]Conclusion:[/b]

Resident Evil 2 remake is a masterfully executed game that successfully captures the essence of classic survival horror while delivering a modern and immersive experience. With its impressive graphics, intense atmosphere, engaging gameplay mechanics, and a perfect blend of nostalgia and innovation, this game is a must-play for both fans of the original series and newcomers alike. I sunk almost 80 hours into this masterpiece, completed everything except the hardcore S+ rank so far because my time became eaten by other things. I do plan to go back to them though because I love this game. I'm not fortunate enough to have played the original RE2 (seeing as it was released the year I was born), but I played RE/RE 0 HD and loved them both. So when this was announced and wasn't going to be a classic RE game with fixed cameras and such I'll admit I was skeptical. But once the 30 minute demo came out and i tried i knew it was going to be good, 

The atmosphere this game creates is incredible, I love the graphics (despite some janky light reflections at times), the sound design is exceptional, at later parts of them game when a certain enemy is patrolling its amazing to hear what room he's in so clearly, wearing headphones during these parts can make avoiding him much easier but regardless the sounds design as a whole left me pleased and really added to the horror of this title. 

As far as game play goes I must also praise that aspect, movement and shooting are responsive without feeling like an action game like any RE game between 4-6, you have to place your shots to conserve ammo and hope for crits. Exploration is satisfying and can lead to many rewards to help you take down more enemies to make backtracking easier. Which leads me to just that; backtracking. Some may hate it and call it lazy, and if it's done wrong I would agree, but I think they did it perfectly, you'll find puzzles (though usually not very hard) that you need to go find something for before you can solve it, which leads to deciding what route to take; the long one with fewer enemies? Or the direct path with a Licker? To me it was great to play it safe on my initial playthough and then learn the enemies and how to best dodge/kill them to speed up my run times. The bosses are fun as well, each is fun and unique in its own way, despite most of them being against the same boss in different forms. I also love the ramp up in pace, at the start you feel powerless and have to tread carefully, but as the game goes on you gain better weapons and skills, so naturally the pace pics up with difficulty and by the end you feel like a capable survivor (much like RE7), some may not love this but to me a game that never stops trying to smother you in powerlessness and dread becomes suffocating, and ultimately draining, making the endgame drag on and on, RE2 doesn't outstay it's welcome. Id rather play a great 6 hours than a begrudging 20 hour story that has so much filler. The game new what it wanted to be and focused on doing that well, while still adding on top of the original, rather than trying to go for quantity as a selling point. 

The only complaint I can honestly make is that between the four campaigns (Leon A/B & Claire A/B), its mostly the same bosses, puzzles and routes with only a handful of weapon variations, one unique segment and a different end boss each. While I personally am fine with this I can easily understand why it may be a downside for some. Each initial A campaign will run you ~6-8 hours blind and the B scenario will be ~4-5. So if you play all four its for sure worth the cost on sale, if not full price. I personally paid for the deluxe at launch for the costumes and original soundtrack swap, and was more than happy to pay that much for the end result!

Ultimately I love and highly recommend this game, to date I hadn't played a 3rd person RE game that I loved (yes, 4 is good but not my favorite). To me the best were REHD and RE7, they played very differently but both managed to have the tension I want in a horror game with good replayability for speed/challenge runs. Now RE2 takes that top spot for me, after seeing 3 styles of RE games I love: I can safely say that RE8 could be any of the 3 styles and I'd be happy if it was made with the same care as those games. As a final note this game made me excited for the RE3 Remake but rumors of it being outsourced to another developer is worrying (hopefully this is false), let's just hope that the team who made this game get to work on more horror projects because their product is exceptional in my eyes, and easily contends for my 2019 game of the year!

RE2 Remake is an excellently crafted survival horror game with superb atmosphere. It is absolutely worth playing if you are into survival horror and are in the mood for an incredibly tense experience.

From the deafening silence that permeates every area of the game to the sudden thrashing of a zombie as they bash a door open to pursue you, the sound design does a spectacular job of immersing you in the environment, especially if you're using headphones with the proper settings enabled (Headphones mode + Binaural Audio). I seriously doubt that the game would've been as tense as it was if the sound design wasn't this well-done.

There are some parts of the game that could be improved further in future installments, namely the 2nd Run portion of the game that I found to be somewhat disappointing in terms of potential. Another nitpick would be that the boss battles can feel bullet spongy and a little tedious at times, which I guess is to be expected by playing on Hardcore.

Other than that however, this game excels in pretty much every area you'd expect a survival horror game to excel in. Note that since I haven't played the original, I can't really speak for how this remake compares. Despite that, I can definitely say that on its own, it's probably up there with the best that the modern survival horror genre can offer.

I would recommend playing on the Hardcore difficulty for a blind first playthrough, especially if you know you are capable of handling the changes it introduces. It's an experience that just can't be matched by a second playthrough on Hardcore, because like with Soulsborne games which rely on player knowledge for some of its difficulty, the first playthrough will almost always be where the most fun is had.

One of the best remakes ever. 

The presentation is absolutely brilliant, and that's not the only thing that was modernized. The new gameplay system manages to stay true to the original despite the new perspective and more up-to-date mechanics. The tension is near constant, the difficulty is just right and the game is immensely satisfying

TL;DR - This game is a nightmare. In all the best ways. It doesn't shove jump-scares down your throat, it relies heavily on tension and action, while still being a good way to terrify yourself. The game loved itself in 1998, and it loves itself now, remaining very faithful to the original.

Story: The game takes place way back in 1998, following the events of Resident Evil 1 (And Remake, which acts as a sort of soft reboot), tasking the player with stepping into the shoes of both Leon S. Kennedy, a rookie cop arriving in Raccoon City looking to figure out what happened seemingly overnight. And Claire Redfield, the sister to Chris from the first game, who aims to locate her missing brother, and former STARS member. Both of them work together to try to escape the nightmare as it unfolds, hoping not to succumb to the same fate as the rest of the city.

Gameplay: Resident Evil 2 is very similar to more recent titles, like 5 and 6, using an over the shoulder camera unlike the old-school fixed camera angles from the Playstation 1 era. Despite this, enemies remain terrifying and bulky enough to withstand enough damage that being swarmed feels like a death sentence. Much like Remake, you have defensive options that allow to escape grab attacks, but with the added benefit of being able to finish off weakened enemies. Ammo is somewhat scarce unlike the original RE2, allowing the player the option of using gunpowder to make ammunition relevant to both characters.

Audio: The music isn't often present, which in my opinion is kind of a downer, because the music that IS in play is wonderfully orchestrated and very fitting for the atmosphere. On the other hand, weapons sound meaty and powerful, giving the impression that you're not just dealing surface damage. The voice acting is on point this time around, sounding much more natural if a bit dramatic. Characters actually express emotions and have a lot more depth than most entries in the series. General sound effects are lovely to listen to, giving life to the world around you. From rain to soda cans rolling on the floor, it all sounds daunting, giving way to a fitting atmosphere. The addition of the Soundtrack Swap DLC brings a very nostalgic feel, bringing back old music and sound effects for some elements.

Graphics: This game is pretty, that's the shortest way to put it. But with tons of options and sliders, the game can run on older computers with relative ease, or you can see multitudes of small details on higher end rigs. Textures are smooth and have quite a bit of depth. Cloth looks like cloth, windows shine and reflect, lights glow and flicker, and even the enemies look grotesque and mutated. They did not skimp on the gore either. You'll find plenty of body parts, giblets, and dismemberment here, leaving one to either gag at the sight, or revel in the carnage one can inflict.

Difficulty: 3 difficulty modes allow players to try their hand at surviving the night. Assisted gives players access to aim assist and weaker enemies and more plentiful ammunition, whereas Hardcore will force players to deal with limited saves, reduced ammunition and items, and enemies that seem to be made of steel. And they can hurt you like it, too. The latter is the truest Resident Evil experience, also allowing the player to unlock a few powerful secrets if they can earn a high grade. There are also a few unlockables, and not one DLC is remotely required to enjoy the game or it's difficulty options, resulting in a nice balanced mix for all comers.

Overall, the game is worth your money if you're into shooters, horror, and corny storylines. Despite the high notes of the story and dialogue, this is still a Resident Evil game. Plenty of camp, plenty of cheese, and plenty of gore.

There isn't much that hasn't already been said about the remake of RE2. It's gorgeous, runs as smooth as Mr.X's head, has plenty of interesting details and mechanics fleshed into it. Definitely a must-have for any RE fan, more so if you played the original however I do wish they retained the same zapping system. So instead of a proper review, I'll provide three spoiler-free tips I wish I knew when I started this game blind.

1.) Don't try to kill everything. 
RE2 isn't an action shooter, but more of a strategic survival horror where most of the time you're evading enemies as opposed to blasting everything away. Ammo is scarce and zombies are damage sponges. Even the good old combat knife from the original game is now breakable. So be picky about which zombies to kill and spend more time avoiding them.

2.) There's no Dodge button.
Fresh from playing RE: Revelations 2, I got so used to having the dodge button to avoid enemies. There isn't one for this game. Instead, shoot them to stun them then run past them when they're stunned. Which brings me to my last point...

3.) Forget FPS rules.
Conditioning from playing FPS and other third person shooter games led me to believe that shooting for the head is always the best option but for RE2, it's not always the case. On normal zombies, shooting the head does the same amount of damage as it does if you shot it in the toe. The only difference is that a head shot has a small chance to put it down for good when you get a critical hit. For stunning, go for the knees instead or just shoot a leg completely off.

That's it. Hopefully your own blind playthrough will have a less painful start than mine.

REmake 2 captures the essence of the twenty plus year old classic Playstation release and re-imagines it with modern gameplay and visuals. This game isn't quite perfect however, combat can be a little frustrating since zombies can be bullet sponges. Headshots do have a chance to deliver one hit kills but it's so inconsistent that it becomes difficult to determine whether to engage or not as, in typical classic RE fashion, resources are limited. The calculus around engagement is really frustrating when you don't know if a zombie will take seven bullets to down or three. Smart and persistent players will overcome this however. Ultimately fans of classic RE have a lot to be excited about since Capcom have delivered a product that pays perfect homage to one of the Playstation's landmark titles and what is arguably the greatest survival horror game of all time.

I should start by saying that I did not play original Resident Evil 2 so I can't compare its remake to it.

Getting that out of the way, re2 remake is how a remake should be done and Capcom did fantastic job. The game is beautiful, scary, has great music and truly feels like survival horror. Characters were done well, visually as well as story and even gameplay wise.

As for the story, the game offers A and B scenario for each character so if you choose to play Leon A you will unlock Claire B while B scenario has a "true" ending. To be quite honest they don't really feel like A and B because what you do in A has basically no impact on B except for couple moments where character from A meets with character from B. The only differences are the weapons that are character, not scenario locked and keys which are also restricted to the character and not scenario. So no matter which scenario you play, you will always end up with same keys, same weapons and even same items, all that is different is their placement. The game in my opinion also doesn't offer any sense of progress, yes you change places, get weapons, fight bosses but in the end, it is still you running around, collecting needed items and shooting at zombies while doing so. It feels like same thing just in different environment. So because of this, the game doesn't really offer that much of replayability unless you are going for every achievement and even that can be done in 4 runs. As for the "true" ending of B scenario I mentioned before, well the ending is good but it feels really "eh". I think it could've been done different and get the same or better reaction/feeling from ending. Don't get me wrong, it's not bad or disappointing ending but to be honest, it's just you fighting the guy you already fought before and you get one or two more cutscenes. Doesn't really feel like "true" ending, now does it.

Characters in this game are great. We get to see Leon on his first day as a rookie cop who somehow got into zombie apocalypse and managed to survive despite the odds. And then there is Claire, a college student who is looking for her brother but meets Leon on her way to Raccoon City and they both make their way out of the city. On his way Leon gets to meet Ada for the first time and he tries to help her get the G virus. Claire on the other hand meets Sherry, a child who got into this whole mess because of her parents so Claire decides to help save her. Mr. X is absolutely terrifying enemy who stalks you throughout the whole game. It may not sound like a big deal at first since you can either run or shoot him in head to stun him but hearing his footsteps getting louder and louder is really scary.

Gameplay is really solid, overall amount of weapons available is really nice. The game feels good even with keyboard and mouse. You don't really have to worry about not having enough inventory space since you can just store everything you don't need at the moment in item box

Besides main story, the game also offers extra modes which are The 4th Survivor and The Tofu Survivor. Both of these modes feature same route, only playable characters change. The 4th Survivor is the badass grim reaper Hunk and The Tofu survivor, well, it's literally block of tofu, in fact 5 different kinds of tofu. I don't know who at Capcom came up with that but it's great. After some time Capcom also released free DLC The Ghost Survivors, which are stories of 4 different characters we got to meet throughout main story, all of them have different routes, weapons and even feature new mechanics. 
Personally I wish there was Mercenaries mode like most of re games offer, though one of the DLC stories is fairly similar to it, it just doesn't feel the same.

So...is this game worth 60€? Not really, not to me at least. If you have enough money and feel like you won't miss 60€ then sure you can support developers by buying it at full price. With everything this game offers I'd say it's worth anywhere between 25-40€, if you manage to buy it for this price, you will definitely enjoy the game without feeling like you spent too much on it. Do I recommend this game? Yes I do, despite it's small flaws with story, it's really good game and a remake done well.

Oh boy. This game is fantastic. A must play for anyone having an itch for survival horror. First and foremost, I was playing this game at 2560x1080 resolution with an unlocked framerate. Nvidia 1080Ti, Intel 6700K @4.2Ghz,  2x8gb 3200Mhz RAM, on an SSD. I experienced absolutely no performance issues. There are however, graphical issues. Screen Space reflections seems to be broken. There are a lot of jarring artifacts. When it's working as intended, it works great. But when it isn't then it sticks out like a sore thumb. I applaud the developers for doing an excellent job. I had the internal resolution set to 150% as i found the TAA to be very blurry. Disabling TAA resulted in the game having too many jaggies. So TAA on, game rendered at 150% resolution of my screen and I also used Reshade to sharpen up the blur making the game look perfect. I also used a mod that removed the vignette in the game since the tunnel vision type effect I did not like at all.

Performance aside, this game plays out wonderfully. The story is good. The gameplay is tight, frustrating and most of the time, will keep you on edge. You will come across jump scares - but it's all fun. My first entry to Resident Evil was RE4 on the PS2. Loved the game so much I had to get RE5 on the PS3. And now I'm here on PC playing this. This game is completely different from the two I mentioned. You can't melee enemies. I do prefer the 'shoot them in the head to stun them, then go up and melee them' approach more than 'shoot in the head/leg and run away or keep shooting'. If you play like me and wish to eliminate all hostiles, you'll be disappointed as in this game your ammo is very scarce. Some enemies will die in 1 shot to the head, sometimes the same type of enemy will take a full clip or even 2 clips. It is insanely varied and ridiculous but I feel that this lack of consistency is what keeps the game engaging and truly a horrific experience.

From beginning to end I thoroughly enjoyed it. I think anyone who played the original back on the playstation 1 will def enjoy it as well. I did have 1 major issue with regards to the story. There is a second run, where you play through the game from the eyes of the other character. This sounds incredible to be honest. But I think it was VERY poorly executed. Simply because there are inconsistencies. For example, if Civillian A is killed by a boss in playthrough 1, then the second run should have the same scene but it doesn't. The way the second run starts is perfect. Claire and Leon are separated and enter the police station from different areas. But after that the game is more or less the same. Puzzles are moved around and areas you visit are one to one with just changes to when you visit them. This I found to be disappointing. I feel games like Gears of War 1 did it better. When you separated, you two went to different paths at the same time and they weren't the same. Yes later on you'd converge. This lack of consistency in RE2R further disappointed me when gamers on YouTube emphasized that it made a lot of sense on the original game. In fact, items you took in playthrough 1 wouldn't be available for the other character in playthrough 2. Which makes total sense. I do wish that little detail was in this game but oh well. The Resident Evil franchise secured it's place as one of the most successful and necessary in the horror genre. After the incredible fourth entry the series took a dip in quality as it prioritized action rather than horror. The seventh entry titled Biohazard saw a return to form for the series, though some people felt, as scary as it was, that it still drifted from what made the original games so good. 

And that brings us to the Resident Evil 2 remake. Though characters and locations are the same, the game is pretty much rebuilt from the ground up. And most importantly it took everything good from the original, and expanded on it greatly, creating what is essentially a masterpiece of horror. 

The game is split in between two stories, each following characters Leon and Claire. Each story is mostly similar, though it does have a few distinguishing  qualities. Each story is well done, the characters well written, and the gameplay scary as hell and action packed. 

The graphics are absolutely incredible as well, compared to the original obviously, but even as far as modern games it's one of the best right now. The incredible graphics make the various environments all the more scary, and while we're on that topic, I loved the different areas of the game, from the police station to the sewers, from the streets of Racoon city to the hidden laboratory. The ability to connect these maps so you can backtrack and get new items and weapons is something I appreciated from these last two Resident Evil games. 

Similar to previous Resident Evil games it has it's fair share of challenges, be it difficult puzzles, backtracking to previous locations, combat, and stealth (especially with the dreaded Mr. X.) The game requires you to be strategical, sparing bullets, sneaking, or running. 

And above all, this game is pretty scary at times. Once you've dealt with enough zombies you know what to expect, as well as how to get past these enemies. Don't worry though, Mr. X isn't the only surprising challenge throughout the game. 

All in all, I have little to no complaints on Resident Evil 2. Quite possibly a perfect game and a perfect remake.

I got this game for around $42 when it was on sale, and I feel like I stole it from Capcom for that much. The game is an absolutely amazing port and amazing game by itself, setting the standard for what a PC port is supposed to be like: 

[list]
    [*]Controls adapted for proper mouse and keyboard usage, so no laziness by simply remapping console buttons to a keyboard one-to-one and calling it a day; what I mean by this is that menus on the game are made so you can control them both by simply using hotkeys akin to what you would do on a controller, or, much more intuitively, by making use of actions with the mouse, from doing things like drag-and-drop to reorganize your inventory and chest box, to examining items, to just clicking around the menus.
    [*]Very well optimized so that it runs at 60 FPS even on my computer with relatively outdated hardware (FX-8350 with a GTX 1060 6GB and 8GB DDR3 RAM, so my CPU normally bottlenecks me and my RAM isn't anything impressive these days)
    [*]A lot of customization with regards to graphics, which is what allows the previous point to hold true if you simply tweak your settings around and are willing to sacrifice some graphical fidelity if your computer can't handle the top settings. You also get a real-time preview of how the game will look and change as you change a setting. In other words, the settings aren't just there to make the game run good - they are there so you fine-tune the game to look exactly how you'd prefer it to look. Finally, it includes an estimate of how much VRAM (that is, your graphic card's memory) the game will use with your current settings, reflecting the amount used in real-time as well.
[/list]

Outside of that, the game has a bunch of content that is bound to give you many, many hours of gameplay. I am writing this review just as I finished my Claire 1st / Leon 2nd run on Hardcore difficulty (Claire A / Leon B), yet I still know I have some more left to experience: the opposite scenarios, the Ghost Survivors scenarios, and [spoiler]for those who just feel like challenging themselves and giving a new run an interesting twist, you have the Weekly Challenges, unlocked after completing a 2nd run with either character.[/spoiler]

Gameplay is superb. I was, at first, severely turned off from even trying the game after hearing the news that it was going to give the player much more freedom of aim, foregoing the style of the classic REs and the first remake with its fixed cameras and minimal player input when shooting an enemy, for a more action-oriented approach, complete with what appeared to be autosaving by default (for comparison, I have played the first three RE games and the first REmake). I dismissed the game for a while due to it. At some point, though, I heard that a demo was available to try, so I decided I should see how the game fares for the 30 minutes of gameplay you get. Having liked the game enough (though still with some doubts about it, which I'll get to in a bit), I decided to buy it when on sale. For clarity now, I will list the things I was concerned the remake may have screwed up - these will be in italics, and will be followed by whether they held once I actually experienced it, in regular font:

[list]
    [*] [i]The lack of fixed cameras no longer allows the devs to create interesting angles to show what they want you to see at any given moment (one of my favorite examples being this small but effective one in the first remake at the 2:04:27 mark): https://youtu.be/4_i9QfjhN_s?t=7467 and may make the developers resort to cheap jumpscares to make up for it[/i]: 

Being able to craft interesting angles is obviously lost with the changes to the perspective that were made. I, however, think it makes up for it by giving you the agency to look around for yourself and see them if you happen to look. This makes for a completely different experience where things that may scare you or startle you will be noticed because you willingly looked that way in the first place.

    [*] [i]Having much more free-form aiming will make encounters with enemies much more trivial than in the classic-style REs, making the game far easier[/i]: 

The demo addresses this somewhat by showing you that zombies can still take a fair amount of bullets before going down. However, I needed to play this game on Hardcore on the full game (a difficulty that I'm quite sure the demo does not allow you to play on at all) in order to realize that enemy encounters were made much less trivial in general. Zombies can get you from Fine status (full health) to Danger status (one hit away from death) in one attack on this difficulty, which is why having the ability to aim and not miss any of your shots to critical areas is paramount to the experience. Zombies are no longer easy to dodge in tight areas, so you are forced to shoot their legs in order to incapacitate them and make them far slower, or shoot their heads in order to stun them and give you a long enough window to get past, because they will otherwise sprint at you the instant you pass too close to them and will make you take a hard hit to your health. Why the demo doesn't allow you to have this difficulty is beyond me. I understand that a demo is there to appeal to as large a public as possible, but the choice could have still been there. I personally would have bought this game instantly after trying the demo had I had access to that difficulty in it, instead of it being something I heard about later by chance (which is what finally prompted me to buy the full game). In the full game, Standard difficulty is there for those who don't want to be punished as hard, making it appealing to a wider audience, which is always a welcome feature.

    [*] [i]Autosaving, and being back on the same area you died in after choosing to continue the game, also makes this game a far less challenging experience[/i]: 

The lack of Ink Ribbons from the classic REs (for those not in the know, Ink Ribbons are a resource you find occasionally in the game which gives you a limited amount of saves that you need to carefully manage, much like your limited ammo) only applies to Standard difficulty - so, again, something that is remedied by being given the choice for Hardcore difficulty. I always liked the balance you had to strike in RE games between saving too often and running out of Ink Ribbons, and taking risks by saving less often but potentially dying and having to redo whatever you did since your last save. In other words, Hardcore gives you that experience I always enjoyed about the classic REs.

    [*] [i]The game lacks a proper soundtrack like that of the game it's based on[/i]: 

Strictly true. I bought the Original Soundtrack DLC precisely because the demo showed me most areas in the game had no music whatsoever. It's a damn shame this is something you pay for in the first place. I think it should have been an option included in the game by default, even if it had been an unlockable and not something available from the start. Having said that, the new soundtrack still kicks in in important parts like boss fights, and it is damn good when it does, so it's not like I can say they got lazy with it. It is, all in all, a matter of taste. It's just that I like having some of the background music from the original in some areas, like the police station.
[/list]

So, overall, the only qualm I have with the game is the lack of a soundtrack like that of the original, and the need to buy it separately if you want it back. While it is true that I said at first that the game felt like a steal for the amount I paid, I still think it's a bit greedy to have it a separate, paid-for thing, and most people may not feel the same way about the price of the game and said DLC as I do. 

Overall, I fully recommend this game. Whether you are familiar with the Resident Evil series or not, I believe you will find a truly amazing experience with this game.

The game is great by itself and the remake is very well done. It now features a third person point of view of the camera instead of the classic fixed cameras and the engine used is the same one from Resident Evil 7, so the graphics look really good.

Regarding the zombies, they feel really good in this game, although they are harder to deal with. They take a lot of shots to be killed and most of the time you don't even know if they are really death. Sometimes you think you have already killed them and they rise again to attack you. A feature that I like is the ability to shoot the limbs out of the zombies instead of just going for their head or their body. It makes it so you can shoot their legs to prevent them from walking or their arms to prevent them from grabing you. This way the shooting mechanic feels better and more realistic, and it helps you deal with zombies in an easier way. 

The only downside of this game is that it's a little bit short (it took me around 8 hours to finish Leon's campaign), but the fact that you can play the story from Leon or Claire's perspective makes it so there's some replayability. Also, a free dlc has been released with three mini stories of racoon city survivors that expand the game story with alternative scenarios.

A near perfect remaster of one of the greatest survival horror games of all time.

At first when fixed camera angles were not shown and a third person over the shoulder style was announced instead I was genuinely disappointed. Being the REmake of my all time favorite game though I was automatically compelled to give it a shot. So to finally see what Capcom was delivering in terms of a REmake 2 was definitely something I was begrudgingly willing to accept. I've been a fan of this series and this game particularly for a very long time. I remember the days of old when just DAYS after the original RE 1 REmake people were already discussing what RE2 REmake would be like. And now, here it is, it's real and you can buy it today. And you should. 

Because it's FREAKING INCREDIBLE. Does Capcom manage to pull off what would normally feel like a typical third person action shooter and instead create a really immersive, horrifying tension filled atmosphere with game play and controls that mimic the originals brutally unforgiving system? Yes. Do they add a few new twists and quality of life improvements made to better reflect the game's contemporary audience? You better believe it. It's a survival horror game through and through. Completing the campaigns each time to get all 4 S+ ranks was both a difficult and immensely rewarding experience that I couldn't get enough of. There is a refinement in the gameplay as years of iteration and tweaking of the formula Capcom helped to establish can be felt in every aspect of the game. It's very satisfying to say the least and above all else the RE 2 REmake FEELS like a true RE title.

Capcom is here to stay and has definitely made an impression on a fan who up until RE 7 was just about done with the series in the modern age and would find myself almost exclusively playing the older titles. However, I think I'll be playing this version for many more hours to come. Buy it. Worth every penny especially if it's on sale.

My first dive in to the Resident Evil franchise and I'm very happy with it.
This game firmly stands as one of my favourite games of all time and is definitely one of the best heavy hitters of the year. Undoubtedly.

Simply put. Great in every way.
A heavy emphasis on inventory management, picking your fights and balancing ammo make the game scary, not the things you fight, when you mess up you are punished for it either with spending unnecessary ammo, using healing items you would have needed later, or simply...death. 
Saving frequently is advised for first timers.

This game features solid backtracking that doesn't feel like filler/ time wasting playtime extenders, brilliant visual and sound design for Leon/ Claire/ Ada etc, Weapons, Zombies/ Mutants and Environments.
Suspense building off of Mr X and distant zombie groans or eerie silence are done with great effect and not over done, the never ending rain battering the windows of the RPD. It's hell in motion.
The RPD, originally a museum, has been faithfully and accurately remade from the original in great detail but altered and expanded upon for more coherent design and gameplay flow. It's works well, plays great and looks fantastic. 
The later sections of the game are also beautifully realised with brilliant lighting and texture work, animations are top notch and voice acting is to a high standard, but it's Resident Evil so it's still cheesy and campy (the good, self aware kind).

Plenty of upgrades, secrets and challenges to find and unlock with additional modes (Ghost Survivors & Tofu) and plenty of speed run goodness for the masochists out there. Infinite Ammo weaponry for S+ Hardcore runs is well worth it and makes the game far more fun for non serious playthroughs.
I highly suggest attempting to achieve every achievement for the main campaigns, reference guides if needed but it is rewarding and well rewarded to do so.

When you are experienced you could easily pass a campaign on hardcore with an S+ in under 2:30 hours.
The infinite knife is objectively OP with the damage frames exploit, look it up seriously, but it is a challenge to get and doesn't disable S+ runs so it's worth chasing to save inventory space on future playthroughs. Every other infinite weapon will disable S+, the highest you can achieve is an S using infinite bullet/ missile weaponry.

4 Campaigns with differing details and item placements.
I suggest to play this game on normal initially and enjoy the atmosphere of the game and then go hardcore and thoroughly punish yourself with map knowledge routes and inventory management.

I would recommend the original soundtrack, however, the outfits and samurai edge DLCs are purely preference and the edges are objectively not worth it.

A truly deserved 10/10 for Capcom, a big win for Resident Evil.

I was going to ramble about about how I don't do nostalgia here, but it was dragging on a bit, so I'll just say that if I like a game when I was younger, I will not forever claim that I love it and that future games can't compare unless I believe it does something to merit that. For example, Vampire The Masquerade Bloodlines' graphics and combat are getting pretty darn outdated (2004 release), but its voice acting, music, dialog writing, characters, art direction, and the overall mood that all of those things create while working together create something that has yet to be replicated. Will Bloodlines 2 dethrone it for me? No clue. 

Even if I like it more, that's just one game that could fill the void for me, whereas something like Super Mario Bros...well, SMB3, Super Mario World, etc., etc. do the same thing but better, so I won't cling to the original. Similarly with RE2, enough games came along that provided suspense/horror, inventory management, a variety of guns, multiple characters to play as, and the RE "setting," so I was fine letting RE2 drift off into nothingness for me.

Why do I go on so long about this? Well, some folks froth at the mouth at mention of the original RE2 and a lot of the reviews (the super short ones, especially) either declare it as being godly just because it's a remake of RE2, and a lot of others similar to those folks declare it to be disappointing because it's a remake of RE2 and it's not exactly what they wanted of that. To the people complaining about the soundtrack being DLC you have to buy, though, I do sympathise with you. That's some BS and I don't even remember the soundtrack, but if someone swapped out Bloodlines songs for what's in the remake, I'd be peeved since the remake's music is...well, I digress, let's (finally) get right into it!

[h1]Music/Sound[/h1]

So this is going to sound bad, but honestly, I can't recall a single song in the game...the original OR the remake. I'll say now that I do often forget a game's music almost immediately, though some soundtracks leave me impressed (Transistor, Chrono Trigger/Cross, Bastion, Undertale, some of the Final Fantasy games, etc.). I really think they should've included the old soundtrack as an option, but in any case, the game's soundtrack works most of the time. However, I think there were times it was too quiet...not quiet due to suspense, but just feeling like the music was missing.

Guns sound fine and the voice acting was nice in my opinion. All good here.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]

Yeah this looks pretty great. The characters don't look life-like or anything, but this looks amazing compared to the original. It looks pretty darn good compared to most stuff out these days and even though my PC doesn't [i]quite[/i] hit the recommended specs, I was able to run it around top settings as far as I could tell, and there were very few problems. Facial expressions on characters made emotional moments better in my opinion.

[h1]Story/Writing[/h1]

The story seems to be the same from what I recall, though the dialog (as far as I can tell) is much improved. The writing isn't amazing for dialog, but it's no "Jill Sandwich," either...though to be fair, that could have been enjoyably terrible, too. The Leon/Ada and Claire/Sherri interactions/relationships made me care more about them and what was going on with them. Also, Annette Birkin seemed better-written as a character than what I recall from the original, and I actually felt bad for her in both scenarios.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]

This is one of my favorite things about the remake of RE2: it controls pretty darn smooth and has RE 4-style camera controls. I was never into the RE 1, 2, 3, CVX, 0, etc. camera angles. They were artistically gorgeous, but the camera angles got me killed so many times trying to show me how artsy they could be. Save that for cutscenes, please.

Zombies can take significant chunks of your health off and grab you easily, so you'll want to take them out or practice dodging a few. Limited ammo is a thing, but only to a point. There's enough ammo that you can kill almost every zombie in the game on Normal once you've entered the police station's interior, as best I can tell. I'm pretty sure I killed at least 90% of them as Leon on a first run. However, bosses can be tricky...except I found that mostly knifing the first boss is the easiest way I've found to defeat it. Weird. 

I did that on my second run as Claire, which was very new to me since i never got to play a second run until the remake. Basically, you play through the other character's story, except you start the game a little ways in and items are in different spots that make the game a little bit shorter. However, you also have another type of gun which (for me) made the game more challenging since ammo was split between my starting pistol and the new gun in the second run. Getting a "foothold" in the police station was rough on the second run, but the further in you get...well, I didn't even have to try in the final three boss battles and obliterated everything with ease.

And by "with ease," I mean 75 saves on my first run, and 61 saves on my second run. C ranks, baby. C is for "Cool," not "Crappy." Remember that, y'all.

[h1]Minor Gripes[/h1]

1) 1) if you die a bunch of times in a row, the game keeps trying to make you accept an difficulty reduction every few deaths which you can't undo, supposedly. That got annoying. 

2) Mr. X is a large monster/Tyrant who clunks around the police station chasing you. He's not difficult to avoid and stops being scary after 15 minutes or so. I found waiting for him to walk by to be boring and there's no incentive to killing him (you can't). So no fun with shooting him, and no fun avoiding him. Not challenging, either. Meh.

3) Due to the player camera angle and player aiming, headshots are very easy to pull off, unlike in the original RE2. The problem then becomes that if a headshot kills a zombie, the game would be too easy. So instead, the zombies can take an average of about six or more 9mm bullets to the head, each. Occasionally one will die in a couple of shots as a critical, but it's much rarer. It "works," gameplay-wise, but I can't deny that it feels really weird shooting zombies in the head half a dozen times given the RE universe's zombie science. In RE4, sentient parasite pseudo-science kept them moving even without heads, so it didn't feel so "wrong." In any case, like I said, it works in RE2 given the aiming and camera angle, but man it feels very, very weird given the lore.

4) Once grabbed, you have to watch the entire animation that ensues of either getting bitten or using a defensive item to free yourself. You can't just pause and load your last save. You have to get done with the animations, and if you suck very badly at the game, that's a lot of unnecessary time wasted having to sit through being bitten or even completely killed and waiting for the death screen before I can load my save again.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

This is, in my opinion, a faithful reimagining of RE2 with a superior camera angle which feels like an old RE game updated to play much better without taking away the creepy tone, story, and cool locations...but making them better. Good stuff.

There's not much to say. This is literally tied with Resident 4 for best game in the entire damn franchise. 

It took what Resident Evil 7 started shifting the tone and gameplay progression back towards true survival horror and gave back that little bit what was missing by switching to the third-person, over-the-shoulder camera that truly feels like Resident Evil. This entire game was the like the perfect balance because old-school survival horror design philosophy and modernized gameplay with contemporary anti-frustration features. To list bullet points.

*It retains a form of the third-person shooter game-play from Resident Evil but makes things more tense by removing the crazy melee moves and QTEs. No more running up and landing round-house kicks to a zombies face as amusing as that was. Makes feel like a good balance of the new style and the limited tank controls of ye olden days. Just moving, shooting, throwing grenades, and the good old combat knife. 

*It actually uses the sub-weapon system from the RE1 remake in a sense where the only way you can only get out of grapple attacks like being bitten by countering with a knife (which is limited durability and most be retrieved after killing the enemy) or a grenade. This makes you think twice and about getting to close to enemies because dodging most attacks that aren't basic melee swipes you can run from consumes resources.

*Tons of puzzles and item hunting in what basically amounts to an open world just like classic survival horror instead of being broken up into stages. One optional puzzle towards the end literally has you running from the sewers clear back to the police station with no loading screens in sight.

*No more blasting your way through (at least until you earn an infinite ammo bonus weapon). Ammo is precious and enemies are extremely dangerous bullet sponges so you have to run when you can and make every round count to save up for those boss fights. Just like classic-era Resident Evil. 

*Environments that are actually creepy and extremely well designed. You feel real dread navigating the station at points in the story where Mr X is present and hearing his footsteps in the distance

*Item management with key items taking up space is a thing again with the modern convenience of an upgrade-able inventory via finding pouches. It also has a nice feature of marking key items as used and enabling the discard function for them once they've fully served their purpose to aid in managing inventory slots and free them as soon in possible.  

*The graphics are damn beautiful and a nice peak at what the REngine can actually do and the PC version give some insight into what it will be pushing on next-gen titles as the PS5 quickly approaches. The attention to detail on the animations and models is just insane.

I literally had nostalgic feels that made me flash back to playing PS2 era Resident Evil or Silent Hill because it captured the feeling and design philosophy so well. Capcom has finally found the perfect balance of action and horror to move forward and I hope that continue to carry this approach going forward.

[h1]FULL DISCLOSURE[/h1] This review comes from the viewpoint of a player that has not played the original game. I am judging it primarily based on the experience herein, not comparing / contrasting the remake with the original.

While I have only played the Resident Evil 1 remake in anticipation for this (also not on PS1) I can agree that Capcom did an excellent job respecting the foundation laid by the original title.  They managed to give it a gorgeous art-pass that in my opinion improves upon the original, keeps a great level of parity of what the original game sought out to accomplish, and adds many modern features to it which I believe will give the game great longevity for years to come.  Resident Evil 2 remake (RE2) in particular not only manages to maintain this design philosophy but in many ways manages to improve upon what made it's respective original title so great.  

[h1]GENERAL NOTES[/h1] After starting the game up, tweaking the options to my liking, and starting Leon's story I was enamored by the graphic fidelity.  While I will admit that not playing AAA titles very often will elicit more of a reaction it's still incredible to see what the RE Engine can produce.  Starting off, the game does a great job building up zombies and in ways manages to set itself apart from a trope that is overdone to death by going all-in with their grotesqueness and fear.  Much like the first game RE2 is all about strategy and resource management, sometimes the best option is to maneuver your way around enemies instead of outright killing them.  Relying on your map to pick the best path is essential and you're rewarded for knowing what threats are where by being able to avoid them and save up on your precious resources while stocking up on various supplies and key items found throughout.  It's also satisfying to use the various throw-able equipment in the situation that best fits each.

[h1]A TYRANT[/h1] One of my favorite aspects of RE2 in general was in how it handles the Tyrant which I feel is the shining star of this remake.  He's persistent but realistically tracks the player making him fair to avoid, and ups the ante while traversing through zombie infested corridors in order to escape him.  His quaking footsteps coupled with the stress inducing music drives the tension incredibly well.  At times when he was close to me I would take my chances hiding in a small room, remaining motionless so he wouldn't hear me.  Even when I wasn't near him I even became conscious of what times I needed to shoot believing that he would be alerted to the position he heard the gunshots at.  Once I even felt the rush of having him find me hiding in a small room and dodged his attack being able to escape, it was a huge adrenaline rush and felt incredibly rewarding!  This seemingly un-killable enemy compliments the game's strategic nature so well and I loved this character as much as I feared him.

[h1]EXTRA GOODIES[/h1]On to the topic of bonus content like the Ghost Survivors It's similar to the main campaigns but with remixed starting points from various places in the game and rules.  They offer much more action and reward strategy more than a player's technical prowess. The New Game + campaigns are similar in that they remix the content a bit to make it both familiar and quite worthwhile to replay the game (the ending cutscene begs for you to play the game again to experience it).

[h1]ISSUES...?[/h1] Resources in particular felt much stricter here than in RE1 despite searching every single area for supplies.  I understand and respect that this is more of a design decision than anything but I preferred how the RE1 remake handled this a little better.  Claire's campaign felt a lot more forgiving in terms of ammo and weapon effectiveness (also similar to RE1) even on hardcore but I'm unsure if this was because of the more powerful armaments or was due in part of me getting more apt at the game.  In two sections while playing after interacting with a chest the game stopped reading my inputs completely.  Thankfully I have a controller handy so I was able to save the game and reboot with it.  Had I not been so lucky I could have lost considerable progress which would definitely have been annoying.  I must give this game credit however in that the problems that I had were more inconsequential and nitpicky than anything.


Alright that's enough rambling, what you're getting is a fantastic bang-for-your-buck classic zombies experience brilliantly remade for modern audiences.  Hope you have as much of a blast as I did!

A really good remaster of a classic survival horror. The visuals are great (gore is VERY detailed and that burger the poor truck driver eats in the intro looks delicious), the story's been revamped to avoid a lot of the awkwardness from the first version's translation/script, the switch from fixed camera angles to over-the-shoulder doesn't diminish the horror in the slightest and all the classic enemies have been given a revamp that makes them more deadly to match the changes. Seriously, I still get the chills whenever I hear Mr X's theme outside of the game.

Despite this, there are some points where the game doesn't perform like you'd expect. The A and B scenarios are still there from the first game, but the only changes in the B scenario are your starting point, an upgrade from your piddly 9mm sidearm to an awesome .45 pistol, Mr X starts stalking you a lot sooner than he does in A, the puzzles are slightly different and you get to fight the Final Boss. No segment where you take the long route through Raccoon's streets to get to the RPD, none of your actions in path A affect which items are available in path B. Plus, the plot is a cut-and-paste of what happened in path A, creating plotholes big enough to fly three Jumbo Jets through with the wing tips touching (like two characters dying TWICE at different points of the story).

Also, if you're tempted to buy any of the DLC Samurai Edge guns, Wesker's is the only one worth getting. A straight damage boost is much better than a quicker draw or focus time, which makes it great if you're trying to S Rank the game.

All in all, it's definitely worth the purchase. I would've liked Capcom to take more time to flesh out path B's story so it isn't such a mess, but it doesn't matter too much. I'll take this. The game difficulty system is broken.  Normal was very difficult for me. That is what the option of 'hard' is for.  So we turn it down to easy to get a better feel for the game mechanics and...seriously?  Is THIS even the same game?  The only challenge I can seem to find here is the team in charge of developing the difficulty settings' ability to understand the balance that goes between said difficulties. [spoiler]It's especially irritating how he continues to reappear the entire game on Leon's campaign.[/spoiler]  As long as they were making changes to the original storyline for the sake of improving the game they should have either removed him entirely or given you some feasible opportunity to get away from him for more than just a minute or two

Lastly: headshots.  Ever heard of 'em?  In the original, more powerful guns seemed to have a pretty good shot at getting that sweet critical we all loved so much (no pun intended).  At just 2 or 3 paces aimed at the head the shotgun would ALWAYS get rid of a zombies headache.  In fact the rare treat used to be that a blast from the shotty would blow their legs off and leave them crawling slowly in agony.  Now an entire magazine into the head and nothing...the zombies clearly took more shots to kill than the original which is fine...but if you're going to do that then give the player some balance.

All in all I give it a 6/10

As an old fan of Resident evil series especially RE2 and RE3, I was so hyped for this remake, so much that I pre-ordered the game directly on Steam 6 or 7 months before release, I even pre-ordered the deluxe edition just to support Capcom, I don't really care about the cosmetic dlcs.. and oh boy, I wasn't disappointed.
This is a fantastic and almost perfect remake of the classic original RE2, even though the story is re-imagined, the general idea and key events are the same.
For a fan of the original like me, I don't know how to describe this. The game feels new, yet it feels familiar.. it's.. well, they really nailed it. It's like you are playing a brand new game, yet you feel you have played it before.

The graphics are awesome, lighting is excellent, lip syncing is perfect, facial expressions are well done, models and textures are detailed, animations are fluid and natural.
Controls are fluid and responsive, much better than the old tank controls, of course. The game can be played with a keyboard and mouse or a controller. No need for 3rd party software.

The game offers the same content as the original game + new extra mode (ghost survivors). You need 4 play throughs to see everything of the main game. Basically, there are 2 scenarios; A and B. Each can be played with the 2 main characters, Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield. If you play scenario A alone, you won't see the true ending. To see it, you need to play scenario B, which is well worth the effort, as you need to play the game with both characters to experience the full story. In other words, you need to see the events each character witnesses.
It doesn't end at that point, though, as the game offers post game content that will make you want to play again to play or unlock, such as infinite weapons. There are many achievements and in-game "records" (challenges) which are interesting. You will end up with a lot you want to do.

Just like the original, there are extra modes: the 4th survivor (Hunk) and the Tofu survivor. They are interesting, but as usual, not easy.

The new extra mode (Ghost survivors) is a welcome addition. You play short "what if" stories with some characters which originally have died in the main game. They are very challenging, but that's what makes them appealing.
[u]Spoilers:[/u] Ghost survivors offers 3 character stories. Once you clear them all, you unlock a 4th character story, which, as if the 3 others were not hard enough, is not a walk in the park.

Regarding optimization, the game is very well optimized. It is running at 120 fps on my computer with max settings (without supersampling), with v-sync on because my monitor's refresh rate is 120 Hz. I could easily get more frames per second if I turn off v-sync.. So far I have played about 112 hours without a single frame drop.
I'm running a core i7 8700K, GTX 1080 (8 GB VRAM), 16 GB DDR4 RAM.

So, do I recommend this game ?
Absolutely.. and at full price. You need to experience this game even if you are not into horror games. It's one of the best games out there.

[h1]I love Resident Evil 2 Remake![/h1]

[b][i]TL;DR:[/i] If you like the action horror genre, zombies (or zombie-like monsters), a key-and-lock puzzle gameplay loop, and/or just a well-rounded, polished video game--I 100% recommend you buy Resident Evil 2.[/b]

Somehow Capcom delicately danced the fine line between legacy and modernization. RE2 keeps the same narrative, location, and the other usual suspects. (It is a remastering, after all.) It even goes further with direct references to quotes and even to a few awkwardly-long sexual tension-based pauses that were in the original. However--at the same time--RE2 also updates its core mechanics. Now it features a full free-flow camera (fixed camera angles are ingrained with OG RE2's identity), beautiful cutscenes, and a top-tier level of polish.

Personally, the most engaging aspect of RE2 is it's key-and-lock gameplay loop. Think classic 2D Zelda dungeon design: "Oh shoot, I cannot get past this door. Looks like I need a key." *explores" "Oh look, a key; I remember where I can use it." BOOM, it is this gameplay loop that will keep you engaged and make you feel clever as you recall the exact location of where it may be used. I actually love the design so much I created a Boss Keys Dependency Chart on Reddit: https://www.reddit.com/r/residentevil/comments/bj8uhj/resident_evil_2_remake_leon_a_mark_brown_boss/

But the praise does not end there (however, my review does). There's sooo many other great aspects of RE2's design that will make you want to replay each campaign time and time again (I know I have... at least 6 time): the meta game that is inventory management ("Killed by inventory management"), the constant battle of choosing the tradeoffs between killing or dismemberment a zombie, an atmosphere of tension and fear of the unknown, an engaging narrative, a healthy variety of setting locations, and much, much more. [b]Just buy it--you won't regret it![/b]

Resident Evil 2 / Biohazard 2  (Remake 2019) 

Release Date: January 25, 2019 

Strengths: 
-Survival Horror (Yes, many instances when fear and adrenaline rush will be experienced) 
-Superb graphics (State of the art special effects and rendering) 
-Great story and direction (Movie like story progression, good acting by voice artists) 
-Realism (Realistic Ballistics, Characters, Models, Environment) 
-Clearly one of the most improved RE games till date in terms of graphics, gameplay and composition.


Limitations:
-No dodging ability in characters to dodge attacks (which is a big let down)
-High violence (Blood, Gore, Intense Violence. Not suitable for all players)
-Acceptable but not long enough playtime (10-20 hours of main campaign at average play speed)
-Limited enemy types and guns (enemies in main campaign are zombies, lickers, tyrant, sewer monsters,  plant-zombies, zombie-dogs and that's it!)
-Non-Destructible Environment (Even the lamps don't go off if you shoot them! Destructible environment like in Rainbow 6 Seige should have been added that would make the game perfect.)
-No Multiplayer Mode


Conclusion:

Capcom's remake of its 1998 hit Resident Evil-2 is back in 2019 with latest graphics and recreation of one of the legendary survival horror games of all time. Capcom has taken a right turn in trying to improve what made resident evil games popular in the first place rather than becoming something entirely new. Resident Evil-7 was a fairly successful experiment but what comes with Resident Evil-2 Remake is exactly what most of the fans of the series want and the reason it is an immediate hit. I am glad to say that they have done the best possible job in remaking the original title and preserving the scenes, environment and also adding new dimensions so that the player has something new to experience too. The game is built on the new RE game engine which is superbly realistic and combat is awesome. The game has inherited all great and unique features from other RE games like defensive items like knives, grenades from RE-1 Remake, gunpowder combinations from RE-3 to create different type of ammo, with some new options like bolting the windows shut with wooden boards (like in Rainbow 6 Siege) etc. and removed the unnecessary and obsolete features like ink ribbon to save the game (well in hardcore mode it is still there but for players who want an easier game mode to play, the saves are infinite and don't require ink ribbon items). The only let down is that the game doesn't include the attack dodging ability of the characters as present in many new RE games. Including this feature would've made the game almost perfect. Anyway the gameplay is very good to say the least. The main story is same to the original and you can play as Leon or Claire as in the original game. However, there are a few side stories as well, additional game content that increases the overall play time and make the original story, a bit more detailed and content rich. It's not as long as RE-4 but has a decent play time of 10-20 hours on average and even more if you intend to play it slow or choose the challenging hardcore mode. The best part of the gameplay that I found is the chasing down by the Tyrant. Tyrant (for newbies) is an unstoppable juggernaut of the Umbrella Corporation that is unleashed at the Police Station Site to hunt down any survivors (including the protagonists). He can't be killed but can be slowed down by firing. He will continue to chase you and since the ammo is limited (in normal game modes) you have to make a run for it in order to survive. He reminds me of 'Nemesis' from RE-3 although Nemesis is more deadlier and faster. Maybe we'll see him in RE-3 remake which is likely to be developed by Capcom. The game has good replayability due to new unlockable costumes and items, alternate endings, different game modes etc.  So, overall, RE-2 Remake is a genuine RE experience and probably one of the best RE games till date in terms of action, gameplay, survival horror and story. Although strictly speaking, I feel, it is overpriced if weighted with the amount of game content and play time given, but it's definitely a good game in all aspects that are included.
