TL;DR
Brilliantly modernised classic Resident Evil experience with incredible visuals, gameplay and a decent, well presented story. The game is ever so slightly let down by the lazy execution to the differences between the 4 campaign scenarios but otherwise it's fantastic.


I've played all the mainline games except the 2 Revelations ones, RE6 and RE7 of which Resident Evil 2 and 4 are my favourite entries. I would say that this feels like the classic RE gameplay structure overall but with RE4's awesomely satisfying shooting mechanics. I believe the actual gameplay is probably closer to RE7's except in 3rd person but either way it really feels distinctively like a classic Resident Evil modernised beautifully.

Something that's new (at least among the RE games I've played) is that you can now move slowly while aiming your weapon but it reduces your shot accuracy. This turns encounters with enemies into a highly dynamic dance where you're constantly juggling between standing still for precision shots, moving while "hip-firing" or just frantically running past them. Mentioning running past, it's not only a viable tactic but a subtly encouraged way to tackle the various undead monsters.

The visuals obviously speak for themselves but a special mention should go to the absolutely jaw-dropping (quite literally in some cases) viscera that fantastically gives each shot some meaty feedback. On the down side though I find the screen-space reflections and anti-aliasing options to be quite noisy, streaky and/or blurry. I've found the only way to truly get a nice crisp image is to have the resolution scale set to 200% which of course requires a beefy rig for any resolution considered high definition. For reference at 1600x900 my Radeon 270 bottlenecks at a near permanent 60 FPS above 120% scale or so but this is also with most other settings being on high or max.

Lastly the story is pretty faithful to the original and is mostly very well delivered but the differences between A and B scenarios actually just alternative universes instead of being similar to the brilliantly intertwined scenarios of the original. I found this is quite disappointing because all four scenarios (A and B for each character) just feel like remixes of each other. I will mention that the differences between the characters' campaigns are quite meaningful and interesting than the near lack of changes between the A and B campaigns.

All in all REmake 2 is an amazing game and definitely worth your time and money. This is especially true if you like the idea of replaying a shortish campaign for a better ranking by finding quicker ways through it.

Edit: About half of the bosses could've been a lot better. They are mostly OK but the one that is essentially a quick time event just plain sucks.

   Hot on the heels of the return-to-survival-horror excellence that was Resident Evil 7, this long-rumoured remake of RE2 retains not only the same engine as RE7, but the same hard-as-nails atmosphere. Gory, grimy, gritty, and all those other great things that RE7 delivered in spades...with just enough cheese to still make it a Capcom game, of course.

   For the old fans: it's all here. Everything you would want in the year of our Lord 2019; unless you're the type who thought the best thing about the original RE2 was the cringy dialogue and delirious over-acting. (Not I!) And for the new fans: no need to fret over all that talk of "tank controls", awkward inventory systems, etc...those are long gone. This plays much the same as RE7, only in third person. It's a very, very modern game in most conceivable ways...minus all those tiresome contemporary "open world" and "multiplayer" antics that have conspired to ruin the horror genre in recent years. Heck, they've even managed to remove some of the original game's less logical architectural flourishes, e.g. no more statue-pushing puzzles in common areas, that could be accidentally budged by clueless members of the general public!

   I have only one remotely notable criticism to make, and looking at forums and other reviews, I'm far from alone in feeling this. Simply put, the "regular" zombies are insanely unpredictable in terms of how many head shots it can take to kill them. I realise this is a bit of a carry-over from the old games, where you [i]couldn't[/i] actually aim for the head; so the idea was that your character was usually hitting the body a bunch of times before finally nailing that critical head shot. Now that we can aim, a la RE4 and beyond...it does feel a little absurd to be shooting zombies in the skull [i]that[/i] many times before they stop getting back up. But you get used to it, and the only ways they could've countered this would be to give us MORE ZOMBIES or LESS AMMO: either of which would've been equally controversial. I suspect Capcom would've endured complaints about this conundrum no matter [i]how[/i] they chose to "solve" it, so it's an acceptable enough decision all 'round.

   I'm not gonna say a great deal beyond that. I have a gazillion reviews before this analysing what I believe does and doesn't work in horror games. Short version: this one does virtually everything right, and I can't see it displeasing anyone bar the whiniest of whiney-bottoms. You want a bona fide horror video game? You got one. And yes: it is [i]well worth[/i] the $60 asking price (not least of all because of the extremely high replay value, courtesy of a wide range of differing scenarios and protagonists).

   Stop procrastinating and just buy it already, ya great big scaredy-pants. The chances of us getting a better horror game this year are slim to say the least (especially since no Outlasts or Evil Withins are presently scheduled)!

   Verdict: 10/10.

Inventory management and back tracking for key items are prominent mechanics that you will have to contend with and they force you to make agonizing decisions like leaving a box of precious handgun ammo for a key that you need. 
The zombies themselves are a constant threat and often take several shots to the head to kill and can even get back up after a period of time. There's also a timing mechanic added in later on in the form of the Tyrant, Mr. X. Mr. X is an unstoppable killing machine that stalks you throughout the game and forces you to carefully plan out the routes to your objective, lest you run into him. All of these mechanics put together provide you with a sense of constant dread and panic as you frantically try to solve a puzzle while you hear his giant footsteps get louder and louder.
My one complaint about the game would have to be the boss battles. While they're never boring, they can sometimes feel unfair. Oftentimes you'll be trapped in very enclosed spaces and forced to fight a boss with wide arching attack patterns. This is only made worse by how slowly your character moves. This can be an extremely frustrating experience if you haven't managed your ammo well. Other than that though the game is great.

It's been a long wait for all of the Resident Evil fans to finally experience a modern take on the classic that is RE2. And boy did Capcom surpass every single expectation there was. 

The game is a masterclass AAA-title, where they fusioned elements of the original game into modern presentation, and took liberties when adding/removing/altering certain elements. That combination works flawlessly and brought us one of the best, if not the best, game of 2019. Every single detail is carefully balanced to make the game addictive, challenging and fresh. RE Engine is definitely one of the best game engines out there right now, game is graphically beautiful, well detailed and has amazing amount of little details, especially when it comes to the enemy animations and effects. Sound department has also outdone themselves, game is filled with fantastic sound effects, that lift up the atmosphere and suspense into very intense levels. Sound mix is also professional work, as is the score. Score itself is pretty radical departure compared to the original's memorable tunes, but the new score definitely has some amazing pieces of compositions, and is by no means bad score, it fits the game perfectly and is modern. Legendary R.P.D has given a modern overhaul and Capcom took liberties in redesigning certain elements to suit the modern presentation better and to make the station feel a bit more realistic. I felt that after the R.P.D, the maps were not that incredible, especially the labs felt pretty bland in comparison, hardly any rooms to explore despite lab being huge.

Game story wise isn't nothing special compared to other RE-titles, it has that B-movie charm to it, yet, doesn't go into cheesy-section too much. Overall tone of the game's setting is much more serious compared to the original. Capcom also went all out with the gore, providing one of the most detailed gore effects in games.

When it comes to the enemies, zombies in this game are truly scary, they haven't been scary in many games for years and it's notable how well Capcom managed to design the gameplay and zombies so that you are really scared of them and they are dangerous enemies always. When it comes to the other enemies, I feel that dogs are rather disappointing enemies, not providing hardy any threat to player. Lickers on the other hand, are dangerous, if you don't know how to approach them. Bosses themselves are pretty straightforward stuff, I never felt that they are truly dangerous and beating them wasn't anything difficult after all, all of the boss battles basically had pretty obvious hints of how to take them out. Redesigned Ivy-creatures on the other hand are probably one of the best and scariest monster designs in the whole franchise, frightening and very dangerous, Capcom really delivered with those. 

Then, we come to the enemy that has stirred the fans and players alike, of how Capcom designed the gameplay with him: 

Mr.X

Unlike in the original, where he only appeared on scripted moments and rewarded you with some goodies after you downed him, here he is like the Terminator of Raccoon City. He seeks you all over the R.P.D, never giving up on the search/hunt. Capcom made a ballsy move when they decided to make him invincible, only having the option to down him for a while. X's design approach clearly was that once you've searched all over the R.P.D and killed most of the enemies, you would have too easy time over there and it would be also pretty boring to run around in a empty police station. So having this one invincible enemy running after you stirs up the gameplay suspense into second phase. Clever, but also somewhat predictable design choise, Capcom didn't want players to feel too comfortable in the game. However, X is only seeking you when you're in the R.P.D, after that he only appears on couple scripted moments.

Still, Mr.X is definitely one of the most memorable game enemies of this current generation, and will stay in our memories for sure. 




Final verdict: Masterclass example of how to remake old classic to suit modern times, without losing the original's touch.

January 21, 1998 a horror classic was unleashed to the world. 
When I say Resident Evil 2 revolutionized the horror genre it would be an understatement, the music, atmosphere, gameplay and graphics at the time were out of this world. Imagen my reaction when I found out that there was a remake in the making, all sort of ideas popped into my head,
 Is it going to be a faithful recreation of the original game, are they going to add something new, is it first person and what about the music??....................That was in 2016.
Fast-forward 2 years ………………. the game was released.

                                                       The Review

•	Gameplay

The game takes the resident evil 4 camera approach “a behind the shoulder camera “and that made the game horrifying and intense. The movement speed of the characters is slower than what I would have liked but it won’t ruin the experience for anyone in fact, it’s the opposites, every time you encounter an enemy it can add to the overall feeling of dread.
All in all, gameplay for me is a solid 9/10.

•	Graphics 

 The Re engine gave this game a new life in this day and age. The realistic graphics that this engine provides adds to the sense of dread and fear surrounding you in every corner whether it’s the lighting, the details of every enemy monster, the character models………………………
This is too good to be true 10/10.   

•	Music

 The Resident evil series was always known for its amazing soundtrack especially RE2 and 4 but, strangely enough the remake doesn’t seem to have any music at all except for the boss battles and the lovely safe room, they all have their own themes.
Capcom choose to focus on the ambient sound and that resulted in the game having an atmosphere that is petrifying ,you can’t just go and open any door or stroll without thinking about the screams you hear…….yeah and one last thing I almost sh** my pants because of the f****** footsteps.  
The overall sound design gets a 9/10.
Side note try the original soundtrack.

•	Performance 

I ran the game using a GTX 1070 on max preset 1440p.Performance wise, the game is optimized and runs like a dream. There is all kind of settings if you want to tweak the game to your liking. 
Performance gets 10/10.  

•	Final Verdict

  Capcom succeeded in recreating a horror classic that was remembered for its terrifying atmosphere, monsters, music and replayability. It seems that capcom is trying its best to please its fans and reclaim the reputation that it once had by making the game that the fans always dreamed of.
In the end, I would have given the game a 9/10 if I weren’t a fan of the series ………………………………. it’s a solid 10/10 this is how you remake a game.

[i][b]TL:DR[/b]: PC GOTY 2019 EZPZ. Full-price purchase all DLCs with 0 regret.[/i]

[b]PROS[/b]:
[list]
    [*] [b]Well made, well polished[/b]. Nary any bugs or glitches, be it minor or game breaking. Everything is smooth, especially performance
    [*] A plethora of [b]options for those who like to challenge themselves[/b], also some great options for those new to the series, for those seeking a casual, story-focused experience. Plenty of options to beat an area too. You don't have to shoot everything dead. You can run right past many areas, and maybe have to spend a couple of shots on the way to open up a window to run through past the zombies
    [*] [b]Lifelike and fluid animations[/b]. Zombies stagger drunkenly and react to every shot you put into them very realistically. Not even kidding. No exaggerated ragdolling. You actually have to wait and observe if a zombie is going to drop after the shot, or if it's still going to continue shuffling towards you.
    [*] [b]Satisfying and rewarding gunplay[/b]. Every shot sounds and feels powerful, especially if you land a tiny 9mm right between the eyes and their heads split open (this is the only way to one-shot a zombie). This also means that your character did not turn into a super-special-tacticool operator with super tight shot grouping inside 30 minutes after SHTF. Every shot has to be aimed carefully, or the recoil will punish you.
    [*] [b]Plenty of gameplay mileage[/b] and worth a good number of re-runs
    [*] [b]Excellent balance between horror atmosphere and progressibility[/b]. This is one of the few horror titles I actually played through to the end, and even restarted in the alternate storylines. Many other titles are too overwhelming and dense in their horror volume, it leaves players like me too mentally exhausted to continue playing. In this game, the variable pacing and density of the horror elements are right on point, and it helps me continue playing for much longer.
   [*] Almost [b]no jumpscares[/b]. Only time I got jumped is when I was too greedy and impatient, and I dropped my guard
   [*] [b]MODS!!!!![/b]
[/list]

[b]CONS[/b] (the description of these are very lengthy and detailed, but I swear this is just a nitpick and the cons are really very, very minor):
[list]
    [*] Cinematic visuals (film grain, desaturation, color tints) really boosts the horror atmosphere, but it might leave some graphic purists like me turned off. It is very suiting to the mood of the game however, which is why I didn't install any graphics mods
    [*] Resolution of some of the textures in the game are skimped on (especially on parts of the monster models where it is designed to stretch and expand based on the animation), most likely to improve performance. Not a big deal if you rarely come too close to a monster (like getting grabbed)
    [*] While the game supports ultrawide resolutions (21:9) natively, the real-time rendered cutscenes are artificially restricted to 16:9. The game should actually be able to render the cutscenes in 21:9 because when the cutscene comes on, the letterbox actually pop up a tad slower to cover the rest of the scene outside the 16:9 box. Maybe if I'm good at hex editing I can figure that out
[/list]

Another bit I dislike is the characters themselves or rather how they're portrayed in the remake, especially with Claire. For some reason they decided that to try and make the story seem as serious and mature as they could, they decided to have characters swear at almost everything, which I normally don't have an issue with swearing, but it's ridiculous how often it happens, and as I mentioned earlier, this is especially true with Claire. I could go on about more, but this has gotten long enough for me, so despite my personal gripes I still think this is a great game that any fan of Resident Evil should pick up.

[h1]Gimme Gimmicks [/h1]

I was pretty sure I was going to love it. 

First I'm a huge fan of the original, it was the very first game that I played.
It was the first game that I thoroughly finished, searching through every nooks and crannies to get all the lore and goodies.
I quite liked RE7, I loved the visceral ambience, the engine and the writing.
Finally I tried the 20 minutes demo they released a few month prior to launch, I must say it looked good and the controls felt smooth.

Considering all these good experiences I was confident this was a game I was going to enjoy. So I did something I rarely do I didn't wait for an interesting sale to come around, I paid the full 60 bucks.

Now that I have played and finished it, I must say I'm a bit disapointed. I barely hyped myself as I try not to do reading almost no articles about the game, just catching a glimpse of the good press it seems to have.

Individualy many elements are functioning well : good engine, good graphics, aiming and shooting mechanics feel good.

It's only when you take a global look at the overhaul of the game that it shows it's weaknesses.


[h1] There's no ambience [/h1]

Never in the game I ever felt stressed with the vibe it gave, no latent pressure, no anguish while opening a door, no well timed unpredictible zombie entries. In it's stead  I was just annoyed of another soaking bullet ennemies, and when I couldn't bother anymore, just another route planing to avoid those graby hands. Never have I met a situation where the game encouraged  me to think out of the box or be creative or challenged me to make bold actions. 

I have the strange feeling that these short comings were  partly known during developpement, that would explain the addition of this stupid tyrant ( one of the most blatant short comings of the game ).
I believe he was meant  to insert that feeling of anxiety, that ennemy that you're powerless against.
 Truth is you might get that feeling when you first meet him until you realised it's becomes just an annoying gimmick very quickly, just as zombies times 10. Run the opposite direction until you loose him until your next encounter, at that point it's just rince and repeat : he randomly pops in the room you're in, you flee, you resume the exploration of the room you were in. The only times it managed to hit me were the times he stood just in front of the door I was exiting, bitchslapped me and there goes the pointless chase ( I couldn't help but here the benny hill chase theme in my head during those chases). 
It appears you can mod him out of the game. I would personally recommend that,  still it wouldn't make the game better for me.

[h1]The writing is lazy[/h1]

The characters are poorly written, they have no chemistry.
Not once I told myself [i] ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ feels good to play Leon/Claire again[/i].
Not once I felt that sense of dread while walking through the streets of Racoon City.
Not once I felt invested with and overarching goal that The protagonists had to reach, and it shows in the objectives. It's just as the quest log is, you just work your way through the next puzzle over and over.

Ada took a big blow, if like me you remember a mysterious femme fatal with a hidden agenda you will be disapointed. 
Leon a rookie police officer must be a huge nerd cause he barely flinches at the site of zombies and takes it like just another day at work ( well none of his dialogues shows that he is taken aback).
Same thing goes for Claire and her interactions.
Basicaly those characters had apparently such involvement in the story that I would find that them just turning tail and quitting Racoon much more believable.

It's almost has if you were supposed to be involved with the characters taking into account all of the previous entries in they took part of. For a reboot it makes absolutly no sense.

[h1]Somewhat of a conclusion[/h1]


 
They are many aspects I haven't mentioned ( for exemple boss fights are stale ), either I just forgot them either they are just not strikingly good or bad.
Still after I finished the game I was a tad disapointed.

I wouldn't say it is a bad game or that it has to be avoided.

I would just caution RE2 fans that you may not get a good nostalgic feeling out of this game. 
To everyone else, it may serve as a pass time with a pretty significant price reduction, still I'm pretty sure you can find a better game to play. This entry in the RE saga is unecessary.

This game has the best zombies I have ever seen in a video game and that's not just because they look good. They're so tough it takes a lot of bullets to take down even a single one and that makes them feel dangerous because you have to carefully manage your resources throughout the game, being careful not to waste too much on seemingly insignificant enemies. This makes the unlocks you get for completing the game with a high enough rank all the more fun to play around with because now you get to enjoy the excellent gore while also plowing through tough enemies like they're nothing at all anymore.

A level design based on shortcuts that loops in on itself and makes the most of its verticality will always receive praise from me because I find it far more interesting than linear levels of rooms and corridors. The whole gameworld is interconnected without any loading screens and until you reach the Umbrella lab you can go all the way back to the beginning of the game if you want to. This makes the levels more interesting to traverse, thinking about how the area you are currently in connects to the one you were in previously and then having it all makes sense when you finally open the shortcut.

Strategic use of save points combined with inventory management is something I love in games because it means you're the one responsible for balancing the risks and rewards of bringing a small or large amount of resources with you after using an item box. The punishment for not bringing enough with you can be death due to not having enough ammo and bringing too much can result in you not having enough space left for vital items you'll need later down the line, costing you more time and resources going back to get them afterwards. Choosing whether or not to save your game can either save or cost you time and resources depending on when you use your ink ribbons, keeping the stakes intensely high all the way through for fear of having to redo a previous section of the game.

Playing this on the hardest difficulty my first time through was everything I have ever wanted out of a 'Resident Evil' game. The tension I felt when I was moving through a level while low on health and not having saved in an hour because I was out of ink ribbons was the most intense feeling I've felt playing a video game in a very long time. In most cases the greatest joy I get from video games is not a great story or big budget spectacle but the feeling of pride and accomplishment I get from overcoming a great challenge. This game was perfect for that, especially the boss fights where if I died I felt it was my strategy and misuse of resources that was the cause of my failure, not inferior game mechanics.

I do not consider myself to be a Resident Evil fan. As a matter of fact, I've been a series detractor for years. The only game I liked before this came out was RE7 (no, I do not like RE4). So imagine my surprise when I played this only to find out that this was one of the most beautiful, well-crafted, atmospheric, engaging, and  downright enjoyable horror experiences I've had since the original Dead Space.

Graphics: Nearly perfect. The only problems I've noticed have to do with the game's rather poor implementation of Screen-Space Reflections and Temporal Anti-Aliasing. There are some really weird artifacts going on with SSR, and the TAA implementation leaves the game looking too "soft." The aliasing is horrible without it (even using higher resolution scaling), so you're damned if you do and damned if you don't. 9.5/10

Sound: Zombies, Mr. X, and most sound effects are great. Guns sound a bit weak, though. They're missing that low-end punch that makes them sound like...well...guns. Also the new soundtrack isn't very memorable. Buy the original OST DLC pack and use it, instead. 8/10

Controls: Not much to complain about. Characters do what you say when you say it. Just wish they moved faster. 9.5/10

Gameplay/Entertainment: This is the first time I haven't been bothered by backtracking in a video game. It's fun to learn how to speedrun your way through the police station to get from point A to B while trying to avoid the various "denizens" of said staion. The game has solid replay value, and it actually requires multiple playthroughs to get the final ending. The game earns its price tag, IMHO. 10/10

Beautifully done with a crazy amount of graphical options to really let you push the limit on your machine to make something amazing on screen. The game itself is crazy hard to put down, even though it's pretty unforgiving at times. (Like a good horror should be! It helps the game stay scary because you don't want to lose your progress.) By the end of the game, it lets you feel like you have a handle on the mechanics and tactics to defeat the last couple of bosses. I don't want to spoil the game, so I'll only say a little bit more;

Pro's:
 - I'm pretty picky about what makes a good horror game and I thoroughly enjoyed this game.
 - Wasn't too repetitive with mechanics.
 - Although arguably a 'Con,' it makes great usage of a generally small map to tell the whole story. (I originally didn't like this at first, but by the end I actually felt like it was pretty fulfilling to get everything done.) (I don't want to explain that more for fear of spoiling the game.)
 - Very fun to come back to and keep playing.

Con's:
 - It's been a while since I played a Resident Evil game, so I died quite a few times near the end, and the game kept spamming me about wanting me to change to an easier setting to help me get past that part in the game. (Such as bosses and difficult enemy areas.) It's totally fine to ask this a couple of times, but maybe you should change it so that it doesn't ask after a couple of times. Just put something in the loading screen that says "If you're having too hard of a time, don't forget that you can change the difficulty in the menu. Be aware that this will affect your rewards at the end of the game if you do." Gosh, that would be so much better than hurtfully reminding me that I suck. (Clearly this isn't a 'Con' for those who are in love with and often play Resident Evil games.)
 - It wouldn't hurt to make the extra mode campaigns a bit more creative. (Unless they were in the original game, then ignore this 'Con.')

Overall impressions;
   I would highly recommend this game if you enjoy a good horror game that doesn't feel like it's only boring puzzles with a couple of jump scares. This game has good tension scares, rather than just tactical and jump scares. (Tactical being scared of how to handle a hard situation with certain amounts of enemies.) I'm going to start with my score: 9/10

I will then tell you my one major issue with this game; there is not enough variety between A and B scenario.  What I mean is that, if you fight a boss in scenario 1, you should not fight the exact same boss in scenario 2, at least not in the exact same way.  Or if a puzzle is completed in scenario 1, there should be a different puzzle to complete in scenario 2 that leads to the same result.  This normally wouldn't be such a major issue, but considering how well the game does everything else, there is no excuse for how much contradiction there is within the game when it comes to certain events.

Now, finally, I will tell you everything the game does right, which is everything else.

The graphics are absolutely gorgeous and gruesome, which leads to a strange dichotomy when you want to see everything, but then having to cringe as the entrails from a zombie spill out onto the floor in a sickly fashion.  You could tell that there was so much love and creativity put into nearly every aspect of the game that even the most empty of rooms feels important and tirelessly crafted. 

A feeling of joy clashes with the never ending sense of dread one has when traversing through the updated police station, which takes many cues from the original game, covered in death and viscera.  The enemies are all tough as nails, but every single one of them are fair, and once you get used to their patterns, you can skip much of the game without expending much of your ammo.

The controls are incredibly responsive, the soundtrack, though minimal, feels appropriate when used, and the story is, for the most part, well written and acted out wonderfully by the VAs.

Even the biggest division amongst players, Mr. X, is crafted in such a way as to give players a chance to strategically relearn the game in the second half, forcing you to take actions that you normally wouldn't or explore routes that you previously didn't use to avoid his lumbering and imposing figure.  But he is not unfair, nor is he a game breaker.

The Free DLC Updated, the Ghost survivors, as well as the extra game modes only further adds content to a game that had a fair amount already, and with rumored talks of another set coming, we can look forward to Capcom building up an already fantastic game into something that will be as legendary as it was the first time around.

If you're into the zombies of Romero/Fulci axis, here's a game you might want to play. Doesn't RE2 just have the best looking zombies in a while? Of course the idea of not being able to mow down undead hordes by the hundreds might seem offputting at first especially after Dead Island and Dying Light, but this was survival horror after all, built from the ground up into a new game based on 1998's original Resident Evil 2, which was fun. The game has a heavy emphasis on atmosphere, where an all devouring darkness invites you in everywhere you go. This game makes you appreciate a well lit room.

To be precise, while RE2 has been taken into the third person, it's still a puzzle adventure, not a shooter. Bullets must be used sparingly and figuring out which items to carry with you and which ones to store becomes a metagame in itself early on. RE2 is full of obviously Japanese ways of doing things, like the knife and grenades that are merely life insurances. Or what if I had ran out of ammo when running out of ammo wasn't an option? It was close, but somehow the game balances itself out and while you are made to feel like an eternal underdog, a way out is always before you. I think.

Graphics are chock full of details, gore is proper and sometimes the grotesque body horrors are nearly lovecraftian. Still, it is a game meant to be experienced a certain way and so you don't get to stray from the path much. The recurring idea is to have the player work his way out of an enclosed area and open ways into new places. Shooting zombies is practically secondary. Someone make a shooter with this kind of claustrophobic mood and we should be set. Not you Bethesda. Leave it to the Japanese.

I'm giving this a thumb down not because it is a bad game, but because it disappoints, doesn't live up to its own setup or hype, and the gameplay lacks the imagination the graphics and environment instill.

The great part is they nailed the locations and feeling of the settings.  That was the best part, and almost worth it, but not quite. 

But it really isn't that scary, and the actual play doesn't match the move cut scenes.  Repeatedly, they will have an incredibly exiting movie scene.  An example is when the helicopter crashed into the station, and a movies shows you meeting with the other character (the one you chose not to play) at a gate and fence, and hordes of zombies about to break the fence and attack.  Then when it returns to gameplay, all  the zeds are gone but three.  Same with an exciting gas tanker exploding into a firebomb in the movie, then return to gameplay where all you do is dodge a few zombies in between smoldering cars until you reach the police station.  Or at the gas station...or....again and again.  It was like being shown a race car, then told the puny go-cart you are given is the same thing.

There is also issue of Mr. X.  Some love, some hate, but I can tell you he doesn't add anything other than keep you moving.  He has so much potential, again set up in clips, that don't play out in the game.  When he first appears in a movie clip, he punches through an exterior prison wall and grabs a man, sight unseen, and crushes his head.  He then appears lifting an entire helicopter and moving it aside.  But in gameplay, he can't break walls or know where you are hiding unseen, instead prefers to gently push through doors, and isn't good at spotting you.  For some reason, he can't get into saferooms, even though a saferoom is just a room with a door, thus making the game mechanics obvious.  Mr X feels like a ripoff of "alien" in alien:isolation, where he paces the area you are while you avoid him.  Except the developers don't do anything creative like in alien where you can hide in lockers, under desks, in vents, or distract the alien with noises.  RE2, you can't duck or hide, or trick Mr. X, you just run far enough away he loses you or duck in a safe room.  It would be so much scarier if you hid from Mr. X and was afraid he would find you, than slowly jog away until clear.

This last difference from Alien:isolation to RE2 is the key where this game fails.  Aliens creates a constant tension because you decide where to hide, when to move, and how to distract, making your choices the reasons for success or failure.   RE2 doesn't require much imagination or tactics:  avoid Mr. X, kill zeds when necessary, have enough ammo for bosses.   You are never submerged in a horde of zombies like the clip movies keep setting up. You can't jump, duck, or hide like a good horror/suspense game would have.  Playing the game on harder settings only makes the zeds more bullet sponges, that's it.  So other than collecting items, solving puzzles with solutions they give you (literally), slow jogging, and hitting zeds/bosses in their sweet spots, there isn't much gameplay.

They had a chance to set up something special with the duel characters, which had me excited to play again.  When you play once, you are a character, but the other character is in the game in other places.  When you are inside the gas station, they are outside, when you are in the police station, they are outside.  So I was hoping that when I switched characters, they were going to do something cool and original like have me play the other story side.  I'd get to show up at the gas station and save the character, or this time I am trapped outside the police station trying to stay alive until the other character gets out.  But no.  When you switch characters, you play the same story and the other character is on the outside.  In the year 2019 for a $60 game, I thought they would be creative enough to give me two sides to the story, but no.

Ultimately, this is a lamer version of Alien:isolation.  The zombies in this are robots in AI, Mr. X in this is the Alien in AI. It even has the same weapon issue where a knife can kill a zombie as easy as multiple headshots,  like the wrench could kill a robot as easy as multiple headshots.  Except AI had more creative gameplay and tactical options, where here you just run or hide in saferooms.  This game tries to cover what it lacks in amazing graphics and exciting movie cut scenes, and it works for  a while, until you start wishing you were playing the game in the clips and not the one you are walking around in.

It's like a big budget hollywood movie.  Beautiful to look at, keeps moving, but doesn't engage or challenge on a deeper level.  If this game had a fair balance of poor reviews, I might give it a thumbs up, but as overhyped as it is, it deserves a thumbs down for consumers to know it isn't amazing.  It's just a good game with great graphics and mediocre gameplay.  If you want to try this game, wait until it goes on sale.

This game is stellar. I remember my siblings playing the original on Playstation a lot and now I see why. The remake does a wonderful job of retelling a classic survival horror title while being faithful to the original and introducing new things.

 I thought the graphics were beyond beautiful and the music set the mood (personally I used the original music more). The gameplay is fun as well as scary, Mr. X (Tyrant) is a fond memory of this game as he definitely helps add tension early in the game. Also, regardless of the price, you will more than likely get your money's worth since there is a lot of replay value with two different runs for each character (4 runs in total) then the achievements if you want those, and the bonus runs. I have beaten the game 9 times and done all of the bonus content and feel like I got more than what I payed for (full price) which is surprising considering this is Capcom. 

Well, this is the part where I tell you what I didn't like, which isn't much. This has probably been stated a lot, but it is that obvious if you have played the original. The two different scenarios of Leon and Claire's don't add up. Some of the puzzles are in both runs and for example you complete the Goddess puzzle, why wouldn't it be done for the other character? This is the same for other puzzles and a few other major plot points, I did enjoy the game nevertheless but it was funny to think about how a main character somehow dies twice in two different place if these events are happening in tandem for both characters. Besides the plot having some holes, I hated how the Ghost Stories DLC was literally just right. If you didn't do it just right, your run was basically over. This is because you are given limited ammo (except for HUNK) and face a ton of enemies which I get because survival horror is not about killing everything. However, the combination of enemies along with the space you typically have to work with, you will die a lot.

In conclusion, this is a wonderful remake of a great game of the past and I am glad it has been reintroduced to a new audience as well as an old one. I definitely recommend this game to horror fans, fans of the series or someone that wants a game that will be worth their time and money. Now to wait for the remake of Resident Evil 3.

A highly anticipated release for the beginning of 2019, and a definite fan favourite to existing RE players and new players to the franchise. The re-imagined version of RE2 has many changes from the original; some would say its for the better, some would say its for the worse. It all boils down to personal opinion, because this game has everything that a true survival horror, RE game, should have. Be sure to enter this game with a fresh state of mind.

This game was not designed to be a zombie horde shooter like many of the zombie games out there. The zombies in this game are bullet sponges. They take multiple shots to down, and its all randomized; sometimes one shot to the head, sometimes a full magazine and then some. It leaves you wondering if you have enough ammo to kill that zombie, or simple juke by it. 

Full of puzzles with clues that are scattered throughout to help you accomplish them. The map design and quests are entertaining. There is a lot of backtracking in this game, to promote a healthy understanding of the map for future quests. Map and route knowledge is very important. If you dont know where youre going, you can put yourself between a rock and a hard place very easily. 

The gameplay is smooth. There is no dodge button, so you’ll have to get good at dodging zombie attacks, quickly. Inventory is limited as with any RE game, so item management is key. 

Everything in this game looks great. The textures are very modern, and theres a great update to the character design. The dialog is sub-par, but the voice acting is not all that bad. The DLC has some cool skins as well. There is a community of modders out there that have done some custom work, so be sure to check those out. There is also a lot of swearing in the game, which may not appeal to parents with younger players. 

The length of the game can vary for players. Many say that this game has catered to speed runners, and that is partially true, and may even be involuntarily (or purposely) implemented into the game, as completion times, on the highest difficulty, are imperitive to unlocking the “fun” infinite ammo weapons and some achievements. You can definitely take your time playing each play through, as those infinite weapons are nothing more than an optional goal for yourself in future completions, or if you want to take your results to RE.net. 

Being one of the more expensive games on the market, this one is very worth it if youre into multiple playthroughs, and replaying within the same (or similar) environment. There is a total of 4 separate playthroughs that share some of the same puzzles, and the stories are not in canon with each other. This may be a negative to many players, but the initial key factors that make up the original RE2 are still there. There is also extra modes called Ghost survivors and 4th Survivor, that features returning characters like Hunk and Kendo. 

I’d definitely recommend this to anyone interested in a good survival horror, inventory management, game. Your first initial play-through will be between 5-10 hours, if you take your time. Keep in mind that speed runners can finish the game in under 2 hours, and in about 3 hours if everything is collected. If youre looking for a zombie shooter, like Killing Floor or Left 4 Dead, or looking for a verbatim story from the 1998 version, you will be disappointed.

I'll start off by saying I did not play the original Resident Evil 2. This is also the first Resident Evil game I have ever played from start to finish. I have never been a fan of survival horror games for two reasons: 1. i'm a massive wimp and 2. they require you to play a slower paced style that i'm not used to playing. I've always been a guns blazing type of player but this game definitely took me out of my comfort zone. Despite all that I really did enjoy the game enough to finish it. I will definitely come back to this to finish the other scenarios.

The game offers a decent amount of graphical options but lacks a good anti-aliasing method. FXAA, TAA, FXAA+TAA, & SMAA are your only options for anti-aliasing. FXAA & TAA both blur the image and SMAA introduces shimmering. For optimal image quality I would recommend you disable the game's sharpening filter, set anti-aliasing to TAA and add a bit of LumaSharpen via ReShade and of course if you have graphical power to spare, play at a higher resolution. Also don't pay attention to VRAM usage. I was able to play the entire game just fine and I went over my VRAM usage by about 6 GB.

The gameplay is fluid and fun but it won't be for everyone. One of the main complaints I have seen is that the zombies take a lot of bullets to kill. While that's true it's not as bad as some people make it out to be. I originally did disliked it towards the start of the game but I got used to it and didn't mind it later on. The game has a nice way of keeping track of your progress as well as collected notes. Items that have served their purpose will have a check mark so you can safely discard them. Rooms you have fully cleared will show up as a blue color on your map. Also fulfilling certain conditions in-game will reward you with models and concept art for your viewing. A cool addition for completionists. I now see why people prefer the old Resident Evils compared to the newer more shooter based ones.

If you're a wimp like me when it comes to horror games here's a couple of tips: 
• Pick Claire for your first playthrough, her derpiness somehow made me feel safer.
• Play the game during daylight or in a well lit room.
• Play the game on low volume, with your own music, or fully mute it with subtitles on.
• Play the game on speakers as opposed to headphones.
• Put yourself in the shoes of the character and try to make the best out of it by joking around, talking to yourself and keeping yourself busy.
• Turn up the brightness. (I don't recommend this, unless you don't mind the washed out look)
• Remove the strong vignette filter.

At the end of the day the game really isn't all that scary. And after a while you'll hopefully get used to it and enjoy the ride.

In the other hand. there are no auto save points in hardcore mode. So you'll have to use ink and the typewriters to make a save. So why adding the time, if you reload on death? If you die and hit the "continue" button, the game will load NOT the last saved point, instead it loads the very first beginning of the game. This gets very annoing because it counts the time you played, till you died and adds it to the time, when you start all over when pressing "continue". This also would'nt be that much of a problem if it would reset the whole time. There is also a "Load Game" button if you die.. but for the S+ rank you'll have to actually quit the game and reload your save from the main menu in order to NOT add the playtime when you died.

In short terms: you play like 30min, make a save before the boss, die at the boss battle and press "Load game" afterwards, your playtime is not 30min, instead its 30min + the time you spend on dieing on the boss battle. If you die on the first boss battle once and didn't quit the game and reload from the main menu, you'll probably lose 10-20 minutes that will cost you the S+ rank (on Hardcore difficulty)

The original Resident Evil 2 is one of my favorite games of all time. I assumed that this game was going to be a straight graphical remaster just like they had done with RE1 and RE0. I also assumed that this game would have a lot of the same puzzles and would be a straight up "shot for shot" remake of the old game so I wasn't expecting anything new. I was wrong. 

The original RE games have not aged as well in my mind. The tank controls and the fixed perspective can be frustrating for modern players. The series made major improvements with the shift to an over-the-shoulder perspective in RE4, but the games that followed after that were more action focused; a lot of the survival aspect of "survival-horror" was missing. RE7 marked a shift back to this trend. 

This game shares some aesthetic similarities to RE7 which is a huge positive. The acting is mostly good and the cutscenes are great. All of the classic settings have been remade and a lot of the little details I remember are in there. Mr. X, who was originally only seen in "scenario b" of the old games is in both scenarios and the way that they deal with him in this game adds a lot of tension. Much like the original RE2, there's a ton of replay value because of the 4 scenario system - they've also added several bonus arcade scenarios that build upon the lore. 

The game rewards you for avoiding unnecessary combat and it doesn't completely punish you during boss fights - in the older games, there were limited supplies during boss fights so often times you'd be screwed if you had nothing going into them. That doesn't mean the game gives you everything you need to win these fights, you still need to conserve supplies, but it doesn't punish you as much. This game also uses the gunpowder system to assist in filling supply shortages which I believe was introduced in RE3. A new addition I like are the subweapons: you can use a knife, flash grenade, or hand grenade. . These let you avoid getting hurt if a zombie grabs you by enabling you to counterattack them with these weapons.

There are a few things I don't like The only thing I don't like is the lack of a permanent weapon and I also don't like how they removed zombie head smashing from the older games. Unless you are being completely careless with ammunition, you'll be fine. A common complaint is the lack of inventory storage - veteran players acknowledge that this is part of the game as it makes you have to prioritize items, however, I think they should have allowed you to drop items in certain locations so you could pick them up for later.  

I'm glad Capcom recognized the failure of RE6 and brought the series back to it's roots with RE7 and RE2. I'm hoping that they make a RE3 remake next.

As a fan of the original, I can say without any doubt in my mind that this remake does the original justice. While the story has been condensed and there is less variation in the enemy types, the gameplay has been exponentially improved. Good graphics, music, atmosphere, and voice acting too. It's difficult enough to be fun but not so hard that it becomes frustrating or tedious. It's also scary as ♥♥♥♥. One of the most terrifying games I've ever played. If you're a Resident Evil fan or just like the horror genre in general then this game is a must play.

This is a great, yet compromised re-imagining of Resident Evil 2 -- it is undoubtedly a shining example of what players should at least expect when a developer remake's a beloved title. A must buy for any survival-horror enthusiast.

I rate it 83.212 / 100.

[h1]PROS:[/h1]

Zombies: They're scary again. They're unrelenting, they can follow you through doors, and they eat bullets for breakfast. Basically suped-up RE1 Remake zombies; except they don't turn into Crimson Heads. Remember in what rooms you left them, because forgetting can result in a very harsh surprise later on.

Lickers: The embodiment of terror on legs. They do not screw around. Mistakes will be punished severely.

Mr. X: He's gon' give it to ya. No, seriously: the meme works here. Watch out!

Areas/puzzles: Considerably re-worked, yet largely faithful to the source material -- new areas abound. Puzzles aren't really difficult, but they're serviceable enough and give you something to do.

Gameplay: Solid controls. Nothing much to complain about here. Defense items from RE1 Remake make a return. And the game does actually have some decent difficulty on standard.

Graphics: Exceptional. It's like watching a CGI movie at times, but it's in real-time. Very well optimized. I definitely see a good future for the RE engine.

Replayability: For me, there's definitely loads of fun to be had going back in and replaying over and over. Hardcore mode will strain you and the unlockable infinite weapons make mowing down zombies a blast! Unlockable 4th Survivor/Tofu Survivor when you complete any character's B-scenario. I've beaten the game 26 times as of this review. residentevil.net challenges can be fun to pursue, though you don't unlock anything for completing them.

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
 
A/B Scenarios cannot work canonically with each other. The original game had its issues with the scenarios, but this game takes the cake in sheer laziness. It's better to think of the B scenarios as more of an Arrange Mode of either character's [i]respective[/i] A-scenario. Nothing plays out differently other than puzzle solutions, item and enemy placements, harder difficulty, and an exclusive B-scenario final boss fight. That, and the immediate starting point of the game -- in which you don't even get to tour their respective part of the city. It's still worthwhile to do, however, as either character's story does have exclusive areas and story content. Again: Just think of it as an Arrange Mode of their A scenario. It'll help out against the mental gymnastics you might try to pull. Believe me.

Missing Enemies: Seriously, what happened to the spiders? I can sort of understand the argument for nixing the crows (aim issues: though I'd rather just have them left in), but the spiders? There are plenty of things Capcom could have done to make Spiders a terrifying new prospect, but nope: they don't exist in this game. No giant moth either. -_- I like the new Ivy monsters, but honestly I wish they could have been a NEW enemy in addition to the originals. Alternate varieties of base enemies have been nixed entirely. No alternate Lickers and most importantly: no naked zombies... why Capcom? Those zombies were the test subjects of Umbrella, yet they're nowhere to be found in the NEST. DAMN IT!

Speaking of the NEST: where's the rest of it? We got some concept art for some really cool areas... but they aren't in the game. Many areas from the original game are missing, as well as a fair bit of puzzles. The NEST is pretty damn barebones compared to the original, and why the hell does the wrist bracelet take up an inventory slot!? The greenhouse is cool though.

The musical score is almost non-existent. While, I'm a bit divided on this one, there are a few areas that ABSOLUTELY should have had a revamped theme playing. The NEST (again with the NEST) should have had a new version of the deeply unsettliing Underground Laboratory theme. That theme, by itself, was all you needed to convey the horrors that had been conducted in the NEST and single-handedly filled you with a sense of dread even when there is absolutely no monsters in sight. I'd go so far as to say that theme IS the NEST. And it's gone (though, to be frank, this new NEST is a bit too watered-down in content to be graced by that piece). The save room theme only barely plays the first time you visit and then never again, same goes with the RPD main hall. Re-done soundtracks for the rest of the game could have only been subtle ambiance that intensified the longer you lingered within an area. That would have been neat, but I'm not too terribly put-off by that. Still though. I really wish I could select which soundtracks to swap with DLC classic track. The old track clashes ridiculously hard with the new Mr. X -- damn near ruins the experience for me. The early section of the RPD where the zombies break in is hurt tremendously by the old soundtrack (the droning, oh dear god THE DRONING). The ending credits and boss fights should have also been left with the new tracks. It's really too bad I have to disable the old track because I can't choose. Oh well.

The free DLC is incredibly misleading. It was pitched as a what if scenario for three characters in the main game. I was expecting some new story dialogue with unique areas and gameplay, but it turned out to basically just be new versions of the 4th survivor with arcade elements. That PISSED me off for a good while. I'll admit there is still fun to be had. But that initial pitch is what hyped me up! Shame on you, Capcom.

I'm going to call it now and just say that Capcom probably ran out of money when developing this game. While I nonetheless love this new Resident Evil experience, I believe waiting at least another year before release could have brought this game to damn-near perfection. I refuse to believe this is the best Capcom could have done given Remake 2's glaring flaws.

[h1]Addendum[/h1]

I expect great things from Remake 3 and Resident Evil 8. Great things. Great things. Great things...

This is a perfect example of how you can make a Remake of a game mixed with old gaming philosophies with new ones, if you liked the original definitely give it a try. Before I'd go over a few things that makes the game great in general let me elaborate on a few of these:

1. The game encourages you to replay the story on multiple difficulties and reward you for it too: Costumes, infinite weapons, concept art and such.
2. There is a bloody demo of the thing so you can try before you buy.
3. The overall areas you visit are not huge so it is easy to memorise where you want to go and where to pick up extras
4. The garden variety zombies can be as much of a threat as a licker.

Now, at this point I'd like to put it out there, the story is not long and has many overlaps, with a few small differences for each character and different weapons. I'd say if you go with a 1st playthrough and jump into a B playthrough it will take roughly 10-14 hours (my first completionist run took me around 7-8 hours, second around 3-4 hours) to complete.

So at that point if you are not interested replaying the story you might want to skip the game as the content after that solely consist of doing: Challenges, Speedruns, collectibles. This is where the game rewards you, finishing the game on S+ rank on A scenario rewards (which is around 3 hours 30 minutes on standard with 3 saves max) infinite "fun" weapons you can use after.

The gameplay is over the shoulder so more reminiscent of RE4, but the way gun handling is done gives a bit of pressure, especially cause Zombies most often than not refuse to die from one headshot and you may find yourself needing to avoid them if you don't want to waste the ammo. It is not only the zombies who you will have to deal with but each have their own tactic to be dealt with (Even Mr X has huge limitations on where he can go). Often this can result in tense situations if you are caught unaware by it.
I think the game is graphically beautiful with interesting areas to explore.

I'd wholeheartedly recommend the game, there is a very good reason for the 95% positive reviews and if it caught your interest give the demo a try.

Many years ago, 10 year old me experienced the horror that was Resident Evil 2. I'd pop the game into my playstation at 12 at night while my mother was asleep to experience Zombie-filled halls, rather limited ammo supplies, and really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ controls. I think it's safe to assume that Romero’s Night of the Living Dead (1968), the movie that introduced the shambling reanimated corpses that paved the way for the Hollywood zombie genre, influenced Capcom director Shinji Mikami to create Resident Evil in 1996. They were both eerily quiet and dreadful experiences with sudden shocks behind the next door. After a decade long action-oriented “diversion”, we’re back to the roots – finally. The remake of Resident Evil 2 is a complete, modernized, overhaul, while still being true to the vision of the original.

Resident Evil 2 takes place in Raccoon City, two months after the first game. Most citizen are transformed into zombies by the T-virus, and things are looking grim. Two survivors; rookie police officer Leon S. Kennedy and college student Claire Redfield accidentally meets at a gas station infested with zombies. They barely manage to escape, and shortly agrees to meet up at the Raccoon police station, due to being separated in the midst of the chaos.

The story is told in a subtle, but intriguing, manner through traditional cutscenes, documents/clues found and directly through the level design itself. Immersion is a key-word here. Capcom is successful at using the videogame medium to its fullest to expose the plot, while also complementing the atmosphere and a sense of self-investigation. They are not omitting cutscenes entirely, but rather using them occasionally, to serve as rewards and breaks from the suspense. Now in order to get the full picture, you must play through the entire game two times; from both Claire’s and Leon’s perspective.

One of the most obvious changes from the original, is that fixed-camera angles have been replaced by an over-the-shoulder 3rd person perspective. Pre-rendered backgrounds are abandoned in favor of 3D surroundings. In other words; the game was built from the ground up, and not a single asset was brought over from the original. Even the concept art was redone. So, in many ways it’s a completely new game, more so than what the RE1 remake/remaster was.

With major changes such as precise 3rd person aiming, one could argue if you’d still get that same decisive sense of vulnerability as was the case with the original one. I can assure you that you definitely do. Not due to sluggish controllers though, but rather more natural design choices, such as not having any sort of assisted aiming. Zombies are animated in such a beautifully organic and unpredictable manner, that they can be hard to hit simply because of that. Your character is not overly acrobatic or inhumanly quick, like in most action games. They feel more like everyday people. Your character will be limping around and breathing heavily upon being at low health, they will get filthy clothes, bite marks and scratches after being attacked, and impressive facial animations will expose their struggles in a truly believable manner. These are not just there as show-off for trailers, but to provide palpable feedback on your status while also complementing the notion of vulnerability.

One of the benefits of having real-time rendered 3D environments is lighting. And in this game the lighting is ingenious. Be it the dynamic shadows cast out in the rooms by your flashlight, or how each scene is carefully composed to enhance the unsettling atmosphere and/or purposely limiting your vision. There are times when objects are deliberately arranged so that their shadows will trick you into believing that you are not alone. And when a certain room is “safe”, you often appropriately find the light switch to support that feeling as well. Everything is organic and logical to the situation, and never feels like they are artificially arranged for a mere game design purpose.

I was very impressed by how smooth the game dynamically shifts between ambient sound, tense music and complete silence based on the situation you’re in. It is done in such a way that it might be hard to notice, while still greatly emphasizing the intended atmosphere. The music is subtle, though perfect for this kind of game. Both the voice acting, and writing is very good as well.

In terms of gameplay, RE2 is the classical survival horror experience. It’s a slow-paced action adventure where your goal is to get through in one piece with what little you have. Ammo is sparse, and at times you might be better off fleeing instead of engaging. Inventory management is also a thing, because you may only carry so much with you at a time. Choosing whether to bring a healing herb, or a certain key item can be a tough decision, but also part of the fun upon planning your route. Fortunately, you can find hip pouches to increase your inventory slots. All items you’re not carrying with you can be stored in an item box for later, often found nearby save-spots.

RE2 is also essentially a metroidvania game. You’re investigating by searching through areas to find clues, keys and tools that will help in unlocking new parts of the map. As with most games of this genre; backtracking is going to be thing, though it’s really well executed here. The level architecture and the gameplay itself will often naturally guide you in the right direction. You may also unveil shortcuts by opening doors only unlockable from the other side, and so on. Though the game is not holding your hand all the time either, and there will be times when you’re feeling a bit lost. If this happens, carefully studying your notes, items and map should be enough to give you some idea. The map is particularly helpful, due to marking doors with key-symbols, discovered points of interest and color-coding rooms if there is more to be found there. Figuring out where to go, without turning to a guide, is genuinely satisfying. I strongly recommend against using walkthroughs if you opt to get the most out of your experience, especially on your first playthrough.

In classical RE-fashion, you will also come across a multitude of puzzles throughout the game. They are ranging from deciphering notes to unveil codes for unlocking a safe, to correctly putting together symbols in a toy box. They are all logical and never too cryptic, while also providing a healthy and delightful challenge.

The enemies in RE2 are exquisitely well-designed. The amount of work put into every single zombie is impressive, whereas each is presented with a completely unique visual design, beautiful and unpredictable animations and ghoulish sound effects. What it takes to kill them differs from one zombie to the next, and they are rarely dead when you think they are. Even though they are slow in movement, they’re genuinely both scary and dangerous. If you didn’t really “get” the whole zombie-craze before, you definitely will after this game. And when you’re starting to feel just a bit more comfortable with the zombies, the game throws even worse foes as you, and it keeps doing that until the very end, making sure you’re on your toes the entire game.

Resident Evil 2 is a fairly short game, for a standard playthrough. According to HowLongtoBeat.com, its main story takes approximately 8 hours. I prefer taking my time ransacking rooms, studying the map, and doing most of the optional puzzles. I therefore clocked in at 17 hours on my first playthrough, and 10 hours on my second. I spent only 4-5 hours on my third, though that one was clearly rushed. In order to get the “true ending”, you must play through it with both Leon and Claire, which I strongly recommend you do.

Just by the way all the different elements are complementing each other to achieve the perfect atmosphere, to how stellar the metroidvania-esque gameplay is in fact executed. Resident Evil 2 (2019) is a demonstration of what videogames are all about. Just buy it!

[i]Resident Evil 2[/i], the remake of the original 1998 survival horror classic of the same name, is a reimagining that lives up to the legacy of its precursor, updating experimenting with many of the hallmarks of the [i]Resident Evil[/i] series as well as with survival horror on the whole. It has some major shortcoming for those willing to nitpick, but make no mistake, the game is absolutely worth it for long time fans of the genre or the series.

Taking place in Raccoon City, the game tracks the daring misadventures of two unlikely heroes, rookie cop Leon Kennedy and action heroine Claire Redfield, as the two attempt to survive a zombie outbreak created by, spoiler, the Umbrella Corporation. The remake here hits all the same beats as the original: rescuing a little girl named Sherry, rendezvousing with the mysterious Ada Wong, and so on. However, new life has been breathed into all of these characters. Ada Wong's motivations are less murky and offer her character more depth, for example. (Personally, I found the expansion of Chief Irons to be positively chilling.) There is [i]one[/i] unfortunate quirk about the writing in [i]RE:RE2[/i], but I'll return to that in a bit.

Meanwhile, one can't talk about updates to the game without talking about the updated gameplay. No longer played from fixed camera angles, [i]RE:RE2[/i] features an over-the-shoulder camera with greater precision in aiming weapons and an emphasis on crowd management and dismembering zombies (an especially useful tactic, since actually [i]killing[/i] zombies proves unexpectedly difficult). While some of the clever subtext and deliberate staging of the original game is lost, the overall effect is wonderful, creating a much more believable version of the police station and secret labs. The gritty realism on display does wonders to drive home the body horror and grotesqueries of Raccoon City. Plus, I would be remiss if I didn't at least mention the inclusion of the ever menacing Mr. X, a hulking behemoth that actively stalks you through the station; many people have pointed out just how intimidating a presence he offers to the game, and his more active role in the remake really breathes life into the experience.

But with these changes and permutations come two major problems, and by the end of my playtime, they were enough to put a real damper on my experience. The first is the use of adaptive difficulty. I won't lie; I'm not very good at video games. Having said that, while I [i]understand[/i] the rationale behind increasing the difficulty to keep tension high, the way it's implemented makes the game feel as if it's arbitrarily punishing for cautious play. A fixed difficulty option would be nice, but that's far from my main complaint about [i]RE:RE2[/i].

No, oddly, my biggest problem with the game is also one of its major assets: the writing. While the game is a marked improvement over the original title in terms of nuance and performance, it feels a tad emotionally hollow, as if going through the motions of a dramatic story without any real interest in things outside of looking scary and/or cool. I found myself thinking back to another game that I think is [i]spiritually[/i] remaking the original [i]Resident Evil 2[/i], Tango Gameworks's [i]The Evil Within 2[/i]. While [i]TEW2[/i] goes out of its way to explore the inner demons and fears of its main characters, both sympathizing with and being critical of its cast, the characters of [i]RE:RE2[/i] seem...flat, with no real insight or reflection on who these characters are past simply their more self-evident quirks. That's not inherently a bad thing, but it does mean that after hours of play, it can be hard to find oneself very invested in the plot of a game that's telling a story we heard 20 years ago.

And that's really the crux of the problem here. [i]RE:RE2[/i] is a game that looks backwards while stepping forwards with the most impressive technology and polish that AAA development can buy. However, these might well be problems that many a player can look over; after all, not everyone is as bad at games as I am, and I tend to be more picky when it comes a game's writing. At the end of the day, it's good, (I'd even go as far as to suggest that this is [i]the[/i] definitive version of the [i]Resident Evil 2[/i] story.) and I absolutely recommend it to both fans of survival horror and fans of [i]Resident Evil[/i]. It isn't without its problems, but it is, nevertheless, a game experience presented with incredible care and attention to detail.

My friends and I dug the original RE2 as kids and this is a masterclass remake that respects the source material while never being shy in doing its own thing. 

Pros:

*Excellent visuals from both a technical and artistic standpoint, particularly the lighting
*Extremely well optimized as is typical of the RE Engine. Will run well on a variety of hardware
*Both Leon and Claire's campaigns are well-designed and worth playing
*Does a great job of always making you feel like there is danger around the corner
*Accommodates a variety of playstyles, from slow and methodical to outright speedrunning
*Controls well with either a pad or keyboard/mouse set up
*Free DLC that, while not ground breaking, is at least fun and replayable
*Enemies, including basic zombies, do not mess around

Cons:

*Enemies, including basic zombies, do not mess around
*Might be too short for people used to 50+ hour excursions
*"2nd Run" modes are kind of disappointing, as they are more akin to an "arranged" campaign than the B scenarios from the original

Overall, If you loved the original, you'll love this. If the idea of challenging, tense survival horror sounds good to you, this is definitely worth buying.

While I heartily recommend this game, I feel the need to start off by echoing the sentiments of several other reviewers: This is a terrible remake of Resident Evil 2, but still a good game in its own right.

The Good: My goodness this game is gorgeous, expertly presented, the theme and mood are so on point. It feels scary without oversaturating you. The soundtrack is beautifully done, and often keyed to specific enemies, raising tension and making you feel terror and dread. Good array of weapons and mechanics, lots of updated features like item stack splitting and ammo crafting, and the damage you you inflict on zombies is amazing. Blow off a foot, they hobble with a pegleg. Blow off their arms and they can't break open doors anymore. Also the game is so much faster now if you know what you're doing. You can actually make it down to the basement/parking garage in under twenty minutes if you know where to go and what to do.

The Bad: Why doesn't a headshot kill a zombie? If two to five 9mm rounds are enough to de-limb why do I am using 10-15 rounds in headshots? Either decrease the ammunition available or increase the number of zombies and make them easier to kill with headshots. Also breakable knives. Come on, a staple of the series is knocking them down and stabbing until they stop moving. I get that it's a resource that you have to manage, but slashing a downed zombie only to have your knife break because it hit the zombie AND the wall? That sucks.

The Ugly: Boss fights. You know what this game isn't? An action game with dodge mechanics and characters that run quickly. So why am I fighting bosses with wide sweeping attacks in narrow and confined spaces? Also the hit detection/hit boxes are terrible. I've been hit by a licker swinging their right arm while I was behind it and to its left. Finally, the A&B scenarios don't match up anymore. That really grinds my gears.

All in all, I still really recommend this game. It is amazing in its own right, and a step in the right direction for Capcom. #ResidentEvil3Remake #WeDoIt

There's shouldn't be much to say about this game that hasn't already been said. I never played RE2 before this remake, so I don't have a hot take on how this is more of a reimagining than a remaster. What I can talk about however, is how this triple A game feels compared to modern day triple A games. 
RE2 is in a unique position where it is a new product but still has so much of the original game's DNA. It makes me wonder how this game would play if it was made today without RE2 as the inspiration. There are almost no set pieces, no crafting, only a handful of weapons, shooting is sometimes rewarded but is not encouraged and resources are scarce. It's obviously not fair to outright compare this game to action games, which do not try to achieve an oppressive atmosphere or a slower more methodical experience. 
But that's the point I'm trying to make, I don't believe this game would've been made the same today. Obviously, it's not unique, games like Alien: Isolation, RE7 and SOMA exist. But they are far and few between in terms of releases. To further my point, Alien has crafting and massive set pieces in it. I can't speak for the latter two, but RE7 is next on my to play list.
What I am trying to say badly, is that RE2 is time capsule game. A modern day, 90s, triple A survival horror, with very little crafting and set pieces, it's like the other games I mentioned but its design philosophy is very much old school. Back-tracking, an attention to puzzles that aren't immediately solvable, no autosave (on highest difficulty) and a police station that has keys with different shapes on them. And that's what makes this game worth your time to play. Just to get a glimpse of what the industry was like a few decades ago, with a nice face lift to boot.

Ps. This didn't fit in my review, but damn the voice acting, and dialogue are so hit and miss. It's probably the one big con in this game. Claire's uncanny valley smile when she reunites with Leon at the chain fence won't leave my mind soon nor will the very crummy dialogue of that scene.
