[h1] More than I hoped for [/h1]
When capcom made the announcement video some 3 years ago that they are working on an RE2 remake I didn't think much of it, the series have been on a steady decline in the eyes of the fans... Even tho the games sold quite well, but that's besides the point. And as many I have forgotten all about it untill all the E3 demo footage, it looked quite good and it's even better than it looked like.

[h1] The return to survival horror [/h1]
Many would have said that the "Survival Horror" genre Capcom popularized some two decades ago is dead, that it just doesn't fit the modern era. This game is a proof that actually no, the genre can still stand on its own feet in the modern days. The limited resources make you question which enemy to kill and which to leave alive. Searching all over the place for some healing items and other spare consumables while having zombies behind your back. It's quite a unique experience. If you're sick of being "defensless" in modern horror games aka. the style Amnesia is most known for and can't quite find an enjoyement in "horror games" that are really more action oriented where weapons are plentiful like Dying Light or Dead Rising this strikes the perfect middle ground where you may have a lot of guns at your disposal but you never seem to have enough ammo to deal with what the game is throwing at you, it's quite beautiful and terrifying. And one can't forget the other essentials of survival horror games. Backtracking and puzzles, it's all here, you'll be walking through the police station back and forth trying to find your way to the next objective with puzzles blocking your way. Tho I have to say the puzzles were not exactly challanging, you will not get stuck on them and you can even solve some by brute force. The combination locks might take you 5 minutes with brute force to get through but that may be faster than finding a film and making the photo with the combination on it in the dark room in the first place, it's not a big deal and maybe it's for the best that people will not get stuck on puzzles but maybe a bit more challange would be nice.

[h1] Graphics and presentation [/h1]
Man does this game look ugly, in the best possible way. The RE Engine keeps on giving, this is the best looking zombie game, period. Zombies may have stopped scaring you 10 years ago, they are kind of overused by now, it feels like every other game uses zombies but this game somehow managed to make them scary again. The detail of the walking corpses is amazing, not to mention the very detailed body damage you can cause with weapons. It's quite "nice" seeing the whole face peeled off with a shotgun headshot. If you remember being amazed by the car destructions in Burnout 3, prepare to be just as amazed by the "body destruction" in RE2. It may be smarter to preserve ammo and just... shoot a leg of the zombies in some room, much easier to dodge them when you'll be making your way through it again later down the line. Everything is quite detailed in the game, never did I think that I would like a sewer area. There was not a single texture that felt low-res and the lighting is really breathtaking in some areas. The game really is a... weird joy to look at. 

[h1] Music [/h1]
Music is very important for me in a game, I can really appreciate a good soundtrack, it sometimes makes or breaks the game. The music in this game kind of falls flat, I much prefer the original OST with much more memorable tracks. I can only recall one track from the new soundtrack, the mr. X one, it makes him that much more terryfing in my opinion. Now there is an option to switch to the original OST, but you're going to have to buy the Deluxe Edition for it which sucks, I really believe this should have been a free option from the get go or maybe an unlockable but what are you going to do. Overall the music is not going to be something you think back on after playing this game, it's really not that great, it's by no means bad just eh...
On the other hand the sound quallity is amazing, Capcom really put their new studio to good use and everything in the game sounds great, from the zombies growling to the ominous mr. X footsteps through the halls, it's an experience and I highly recommend you play with headphones to get the full enjoyement out of this.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
Already slighly touched on this. The gameplay is pure survival horror at its best, you will be thinking about each shot you make, each healing item you will have to use will hurt, the game will keep you on your toes at all times. You will confidently learn the layout of the RPD station in no time, no need for a map anymore, thst's great! You will start feeling less tense about traversing the location and then the game throws the most hated enemy in this game in your face. Mr. X, he will not stop going after you, unlike the original PS game where he appeared only in scripted situations, the Mr. X in this game is very unpredictable. Some find him to be an annoyance at best but I think he's the best addition to the game by far. Lickers are a type of enemy you have to slowly walk by, since they are blind they only go after you if they hear you, easy. But with Mr. X behind you, it's not quite possible to slow down and walk, this makes for some of the most tense moments you have experienced in quite a while. The game is different in all aspects from the original counterpart, if you've been speedrunning the original RE2, it doesn't mean you will not get surprised in this game anymore, everything is familiar but also mixed. Layouts of each maps are different, enemies appear elsewhere from where you remember them and items are not in the locations you remember them being at. Everything is new but stays true to its original counterpart. This is not a lazy remake, it's a true remake and I wish more games did this.
Bosses are kind of on the easy side, I never felt too challanged by any of them and they sure as hell don't match the horrors you will experience with Mr. X chasing you down a hallway full of lickers. They are not bad but definitely not the highlight of the game by any means.

[h1] Story [/h1]
Any RE vetaran knows that RE canon is a joke and quite frankly, who's here for the story anyway, the game will not blow you away by the plot, that never was the focus of RE games. You can play as Either Leon or Clair, Leon being the rookie cop on his first day in the force and Clair being the girl just trying to find his brother, both arriving into Racoon City at the worst possible time. Right from the begining you may start questioning the logic in the game, the city is in a pretty bad zombie outbreak yet they don't seem to have any trouble getting in suggesting the city is not quarantined and blocked off from the outside world. You already encounter zombies outside the city in the opening scene for crying out loud. The few interactions Clair and Leon have between eachother after the intro scene are not very good either. Second run games where you play as the other one do not really match up either, not as good as in the original. The original had a mechanic in place where if you took some gun in the first run and then played the second run, the gun would not be there for the other character for example, that's not present here making the two playthroughs feel kinda disconnected when they shoud, in theory, be happening simultaneously. Not that it takes away from the overall enjoyement but it's just something the remake could have done much better. But again, this is not very important to the game in general so it's easy to just look past these missteps and move on.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
If you're wondering if this is worth the full pricetag, it very much is. The game is phenomenal and I did not expect it to be this good by any means. I never hoped for an RE game this good, I was expecting a mediocore experience. I don't regred my purchase at all.

I think I'm not the only one when I say that my favourite part of the classic series is [i]Resident Evil 2[/i]. The main reason is probably the fact that it took place in an urban environment for a change instead of the usual creepy manor, although we only get to spend a minor portion of the game outdoors, since the police station is basically the redesigned version of the mansion from the first part (unfortunately I've never played the 3rd part which also takes place in Raccoon City and has much more city landscape in it). So when Capcom announced the remake of [i]Resident Evil 2[/i] after the release of [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/atisz2/recommended/339340/]Resident Evil 0[/url], I was obviously excited.

On his first day of duty, a police officer, Leon S. Kennedy finds Raccoon City overrun by living dead. After meeting Claire Redfield (we can also play as her), sister of one of the protagonists of the first game, he finds the local police station deserted and almost all police officers dead. Joining forces with a mysterious female agent he makes his way to the underground laboratories of the pharmaceutical company Umbrella, where he discovers the source of the problems.

Fortunately Capcom realized that [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] was a mistake, so the only thing the game retained from it, was its engine.
Despite the improvements the game is still the same old survival-horror with slight adventure elements we remember of: provided with scarce amounts of ammunition we must get past enemies, combine and use items to solve puzzles and engage powerful bosses (these fights cannot be avoided) who tend to return in a more powerful form from time to time.
The atmosphere is even better than it was, fighting zombies in the dark corridors of the police station is scarier than ever, thanks to the great lighting effects and the shadows. The original was quite gruesome already, but this time - mainly due to the detailed visuals - it's often utterly disgusting. Zombies take damage to their certain bodyparts and lose limbs accordingly (strangely enough it applies to zombies only, so shooting a licker in the leg will not immobilize it) in the bloodiest way imaginable. They chase us through doors and the only secure place from them are the 'safe rooms' with the typewriters (used for saving our progress).
One of the new things is bringing back the use of defensive items from [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/atisz2/recommended/304240/]Resident Evil HD REMASTER[/url]. Once we are grabbed by a foe, the only way to escape is to use one of these special items, such as knives, flash- and hand grenades. What's worse, knives can no longer be used infinitely anymore to take out downed zombies, they'll break eventually. It's important to note, that these defensive items can be used actively with greater efficiency, so if we use a flash grenade to escape the clutches of a zombie it will stun that single one and no one else, while throwing it actively it'll daze an entire room of enemies.
Weapons can be upgraded (although some of them doesn't seem to do much) and we can also mix gunpowder (?) to create bullets/shells, similar to the well-known different coloured herbs.

To my surprise instead of the old fixed camera perspective the game uses 3rd person over the shoulder view, which makes the game much more playable and immersive. Finally, unlike in the 4th and 5th installment we are now able to move AND fire at the same time. Even with this 'feature' we are going to feel overwhelmed against our opponents: even the slowest zombies are basically faster than us and our basic pistols are weaker than ever. Shooting enemies in the head is no easy task: it bobbles and they love to charge at us in zig-zags, not to mention that critical hits are very rare (Wesker's pistol seems to have a higher chance). Aiming at the legs seems to be the solution once again, since now we can even dismember zombies (just like in [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Space_(video_game)]Dead Space[/url]).

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1635539525

The characters are great and so are the dialogues, there's no trace of the terrible and awkward conversations present in the original. Leon is probably the easiest for anyone to identify themselves with in the Resident Evil universe: he is not a super agent (yet, haha), just a simple cop on his first day. Regardless of this, the story is still at the level of an average B movie, but that's just how Resident Evil is. 
Leon and Claire have slightly different campaigns and I must say I was disappointed with the number of differences: 95% of the gameplay is the same, there are only about 2 rooms and areas which are only available for one of them and vice versa, the same applies to the bosses. The solution of the puzzles are slightly modified and the weapons they find are completely different (as usual, the female protagonist, Claire gets to use the more powerful weaponry - a grenade launcher and a submachinegun).
Another difference is between the 2 subscenarios, in Leon's case we control Ada, while with Claire we play as Sherry, a little girl. Both of these are about 10-10 minutes long so it doesn't provide much variety either. Because of this, playing the game through the second time with a different character feels a bit boring. There are some additional scenarios after we beat the game, but these are more like timed runs with supporting characters that add nothing to the plot.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1657966504

While the graphics seem amazing, some elements, especially the textures on some objects show signs of fluctuating quality: the cars in the garage under the police station look very bad, no matter how high we set the graphics detail. The hair of the characters looks nowhere near as good as it does in [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/203160/Tomb_Raider/]Tomb Raider[/url]. I must emphasize that the game has excellent visuals, but the contrast between a few things is noticeable. Also, if we don't set the shadow quality to high, there'll be observable stripes on the walls. In my opinion the graphics in [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] were better, except for facial animations.
The sound design is amazing, for me it was one of the best parts of the game. I like the new music, but I must admit the old one is the real deal (even if it's too loud at times even on low volume), which we can purchase as a DLC (it's included in the deluxe edition).

I was surprised that the game offers no co-op gameplay mode. For some reason I thought Capcom wouldn't release it without some form of multiplayer. This game just begs for a co-op mode. 
Storywise some parts were changed, for example the role of the police chief and for the worse unfortunately. We can only meet the mayor's daughter in an expansion scenario.
I also had some problems with the flashlight which Leon/Claire turns on/off automatically, sometimes even when being in pitch black areas. Inventory management is terrible, yet still better than in any of the classic games and this time it's at least expandable.

Capcom has made an amazing remake of an already great game that every Resident Evil - horror fan should play. It's a shame for some missed opportunities and flaws. The game provides plenty of fun, if we decide to play through all 4 (although quite similar) alternative paths and the timed runs. For me this game is right there along with [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/atisz2/recommended/254700/]Resident Evil 4[/url] as the best ones in the franchise.

PROS
+ the excellent atmosphere of the original
+ over the shoulder view
+ even scarier than the classic RE games
+ great visuals
+ superb audio
+ additional subscenarios

CONS
- very similar paths with some illogical elements
- some parts of the story are not as detailed as they were in the original
- some minor technical problems
- (absence of co-op mode)

RATING
8/10

What a great way to return to Raccoon City. This game not only stands perfectly well on it's own, but for returning fans of the original Resident Evil 2, there are plenty of subversions to your expectations to keep things fresh and frightening on your first playthrough of both A and B scenarios. Not only that, but there is a lot of homage paid to small things you might remember from the '98 classic.This game is gorgeous (or as gorgeous as the subject matter could be), and runs really well, even on mid-grade hardware. This is an excellent example of developing an engine to suit a particular type of game-- are you listening Bethesda/EA? So kudos to Capcom for putting in the appropriate time/financial investment to lay a great foundation for multiple entries.

Voice acting is pretty solid this time around, and character models look good. Some people have expressed a distaste for Claire's face model, but I have a feeling that a lot of folks will warm up to it like I eventually did. She's a more believable character, and you grow to respect her for not only her tenacity, but also her genuine personality. Leon is as young looking and naive as you would expect of a rookie cop, but never in an annoying fashion. This makes for a fun contrast to the later games that really drives home how far he's come later on down the RE time line. Even [spoiler] his interactions with Ada feel as though they are set up better, with less of a hopeless puppy aesthetic, and a little bit more development, thanks in large part to Ada's portrayal showing more humanity. I don't know if that's really a spoiler, but better safe than sorry I guess! [/spoiler] 

I have more to add about a particular point of contention, though it contains spoilers for sure, so fair warning: If you want to be totally surprised, don't click this: [spoiler] While some have expressed disdain for particular portions of the game, such as the more persistent presence of our old friend Mr. X (Tyrant) I don't  share the sentiment. Yes, he's very stressful the first time you meet and have to deal with him-- that's the point, you are playing a [i]horror[/i] game. Furthermore, others have said that once the fear wears off, he's just annoying and they'd rather he wasn't there. I find this to be a strange reaction as well, as if you take the time to experiment and understand how his mechanics work, he becomes a puzzle onto himself. I think it's genius, really. He isn't random like the Alien from Alien: Isolation felt. What he does is throw your pacing and confidence off [i]just[/i] as you begin to get familiar and comfortable with the RPD and the game's mechanics... Once you figure out his triggers, how to avoid him, and how to lose him, he transitions from puzzle to game mechanic in which to be interacted with purpose. Seriously, all of the issues I've seen people post with him are completely solved if you approach him like a puzzle, figure out how he works, and adjust your gameplay to match. In subsequent play-throughs, I can confidently limit my interaction with him to a minute or two total. For anyone who just hates the idea of solving this mechanic and wishes to simply trivialize it, look up a guide on Youtube and watch how it's done, you'll never view him the same again once you understand how to counterplay. That said, Resident Evil has always been about the slow progression from helpless to borderline badass from start to finish. Part of the fun is overcoming these things on your own and embodying this fantasy. Honestly, now that I've mastered dealing with him, I miss the fun/fear/stress and eventual satisfaction of figuring it out on the fly![/spoiler]

Anyway, to continue-- the new soundtrack is well done, but I have thoroughly enjoyed swapping over to the classic soundtrack from the original for additional playthroughs. Which leads me to another point, I LOATHE microtransactions... and sure, the "deluxe" edition isn't for everyone (a lot of admitedly well-done costumes), but the soundtrack is totally worth the price of entry ($2.99 as of this review) on it's own. While I don't like supporting MTX, I picked up the deluxe edition once reviews came out praising the game. My logic was that I wanted to reward Capcom for putting a little love into a game that, for many, was a childhood favorite, releasing free added modes that didn't exist in the original, and making an EXCELLENT PC GAME first. It's clear to me that they developed this on PC, and then made CLEAN ports to the consoles... not the other way around.

If anyone at Capcom reads this, thank you for putting in the effort. While there are small nitpicks I could toss out here and there, like missed opportunities to improve things like the "meh-ish" mid-game environments, or further expand on the adjacent connecting areas, I think my biggest request would be for the A/B scenarios to work a bit more like they did in '98-- Zapping system was cool, why opt out? I'd love more Claire/Leon interaction to build more character investment, and making the stories work together so that they not only make more sense as separate experiences, but present more substantial replay value would be at the top of my critique/wish list. Maybe in a future campaign DLC? Please consider reviving this approach in future Resident Evil endeavors, it was ahead of it's time, but would be a massive upgrade to an otherwise shining example of how to faithfully re-imagine such a classic game!

Finally, should you pick this up? Well, if you actually enjoy being scared, this one shouldn't disappoint on your first couple playthroughs. After that, there is plenty to do if you enjoy planning and executing runs on higher difficulty levels. I've also had a lot of fun going for achievements and unlockables, squeezing 40+ hours out of it with plenty more to push for, even after my first S+ playthrough. If the only resident Evil you have enjoyed was RE4, be prepared to feel much more vulnerable. You are no longer an elite government agent roundhouse kicking and suplexing your way through waves of enemies, you're a much more relatable human being trapped in a more claustrophobic environment with limited resources. Fret not, however! If you find standard mode too difficult at first, there is NO SHAME in utilizing the new "assisted aim" mode to come to grips with things, focusing more on atmosphere and less on landing shots. After that, pursue a higher difficulty if you get the inclination!

I had never played the original Resident Evil 2, so my expectations going into the remake were low but hopeful. With multiple modernized touch ups and quality of life enhancements, a 1:1 transition from original to remastered this ain’t, but what’s been lost from the old school has been gained with an excellent take on a well-established entry in the Resident Evil series. A welcome surprise was how Resident Evil 2 (mostly) avoids the folly of other horror games within the last few years: Leave all the scares to loud noises alone and make it a poorly disguised action game. Make no mistake that the game does have its segments of action, but it does so without losing sight of its original objective in being tense, exciting and worthy of repeated playthroughs.

The first major change that’ll be noticed is the lack of the traditional overhead, locked camera angles and the inclusion of over the shoulder perspective/controls; essentially the norm with the series since Resident Evil 4. While this makes the player far more effective in combat, it does mean that in snug rooms and hallways that things become more claustrophobic, doubly so when enemies are within grabbing distance. Meandering through Raccoon City’s fallen police station is deliciously tense, with lighting and sound design going a long way to ensure the place is creepy - Not in the typical sense as skin-crawling, but in the sense of having you wonder if you’re in fact alone in a room - Or if you’ll still be alone on the next pass. Zombies are gross and unsettling to look at, but it’s not their appearance that’ll get to many players, it’s the zombies you CAN’T see but can hear that’ll get to you. Hearing sluggish steps and grumbling growls but not seeing the source of those noises ran my blood cold more often than I’d care to count. The game makes zombies a frightening concept again despite being lumbering cannon fodder.

This being a survival horror jaunt, it’s par for the course that ammunition and healing supplies will be tight across your playthrough, and even with the sharper combat, Leon and Claire aren’t experienced gunslingers. For most weapons, one must pause while aiming for the reticle to shrink in order to land a precise shot, otherwise it can land anywhere within the aimed zone. With that said, you can and you will miss those valuable headshots, even on the shamblers. The slight bob and weave they do will be just enough to throw you off, nevermind when there’s other dangers approaching. This leads immediately to my first issue in that zombies seemingly take a random amount of damage before they’re downed for good, plus the randomness for landing a critical headshot (head bursting). Other enemy types make it pretty clear when they’re down and out, but run of the mill zombies don’t have the same clarity unless their head has popped. While I agree that not knowing if a zombie isn’t done for good raises tension, to walk by and suddenly find that your characters’ leg is being munched is irksome more than anything else. There’ll be plenty of jumpy moments to fill the quota of scares, but Resident Evil 2 is more intimidating with its scares than being a in-your-face annoyance; a shrieking licker is enough to rattle anyone, but it's their flighty speed barreling towards you at full tilt that’s more frightening. A sub-boss marching its massive self towards you down a hallway while zombies are ready to get grabby has a knack for raising the heart rate.

Coming off the tails of Resident Evil 7, 2 also looks fantastic across the presentation board (even if Claire resembles little of her old incarnation). The only real grating thing about the game’s presentation is the voice-acting for the cast, those including the protagonists Leon and Claire. While the characters are fine, many of the actors come off as they were directed to read their lines dramatically but not within the context/emotion of the scene. I hesitate to use the word ‘camp’, but if anything, hearing the protagonists utter curses and complaints when aiming at a zombie is at best humorous and at worst silly. My heaviest issue comes with Chief Irons’ depiction of being a creepy, violent abuser who has nothing in terms of redeeming qualities as a villain - A character designed to be a bad guy but not the kind that’s fun to boo. On the opposite end of that spectrum, seeing Ada back in action during Leon’s campaign as a super cool secret agent was a delight, especially in the brief time you get to play her… But having to go through a dull, out of place stealth section in Claire’s campaign on the other hand was something I could’ve gone without.

The map mechanic of marking passed items for later retrieval goes to show that, along with the other modern touch ups controls, that this isn’t a simple repainting of an original for the turn of a quick buck. It looks great, sounds great (sans voice acting) and plays great. With optional puzzles leading to inventory expansions and much-needed supplies, there’s a regular sense of progression even if you’ll spend a good bit of time getting Racoon City’s station layout learned. The initial scare factor does wane with future playthroughs, but I’ve already begun my third romp through the game and it’s still plenty enjoyable, especially as my skills sharpen. There’s also an assisted difficulty setting for those who need it (more of that please, devs!), alleviating a good chunk of the challenge since, near the end game, things can get rather rough. For those who enjoy horror games or shooters at a slower pace, this rendition of Resident Evil 2 gets my definite recommendation.

But not just that, RE2 has a history with me. I watched my granddad play RE2 back in the day. I'm not that old, and neither is he for the sentence I just said, but it was a bonding experience. He'd replay it over and over again, trying to go faster or save less, and I'd just be sitting there either watching him or playing Game Boy nearby.

This isn't strictly true of *just* RE2, we also did a lot of RE1 and 3, but the topic at hand is RE2.

So I'm playing the remake, and I'm feeling all the feels. The game was made by people who played the original, and they gave a ♥♥♥♥ about it. I'm going through halls that feel - if not look - exactly like the original did. And that's an important distinction there - paying respect to the *feeling* of the original rather than being constrained by it. For instance, a lot of people remember there being a staircase in the main lobby of the police station. There wasn't one! There were stairs up to a slightly higher elevation of that same floor, and there was a higher area you could only get to after dropping a ladder down later in the game. Here they just gave you stairs, because most people remember it being like that anyway, and it makes a lot more sense for a museum/police station to have a staircase up to the upper floor than just an emergency utility ladder that's always stowed away.

♥♥♥♥ like that. It's a play experience that, generally, feels really good. I really enjoyed my time with the game.

Now I'm gonna ♥♥♥♥ on it a little. Just a little.

I should mention, a core concept of all of the base-numbered RE games involve inventory management. Your ability to manage a finite carrying space between storage compartments (which all carry the same inventory you've inserted into them no matter if you've used this particular one or not) is basically half the game. Thus much of my complaint could relate to this, so I'm just letting you know this is the context for that when I'm talking about using ammo. If you run out of ammo, you're basically ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and have to start over. It almost never comes to that if you're smart, but if you haven't played the games before you might not realize what a big part of the game this is.

They implemented a variable-difficulty system. You can choose at the beginning of the game between three difficulties, but those mostly just increase or decrease maximum and minimum parameters the game uses to decide how ♥♥♥♥♥♥ you're going to be for the next little while. You can choose "standard" difficulty, but if you do well enough and play smart enough, your difficulty "score" will go up into what you'd only expect to have from having chosen the "hardcore" difficulty. The game will be harder because you've been doing better. How will it be harder?

Well, zombies are a thing, and they've changed them. You can shoot off limbs, you can cause stun animations, you can knock them down and then knife them to death. All great things! Before, all you could do was shoot them. You couldn't even really aim, it did most of that for you, and then when they fell down after a few shots they either did or didn't have a pool of blood under them indicating their actual, final death. In this game, there is no pool of blood indicating death. You can only be 98% sure that a zombie's dead. And because of the way damage is calculated and tied to the monsters' animations, you can put ten bullets in a zombie's head but not all of them "count" as damage, because some were during an animation that, regardless of how much damage he's taken, has to be played out. And there's a *lot* of these animations, and most paths of destroying a zombie's body involves watching at least one or two of these animations. I don't mean they're cutscenes, I mean the zombie model falls down and then reacts to falling down and then does a little lurch and reach forward with its hand and then it ragdolls. That's just one of the animations that, if you shoot a zombie during it, you're pretty much wasting bullets. Unless you activate a critical headshot (by luck), nothing you do during that animation matters in terms of ensuring that zombie stays down.

Zombies, in general, used to be mathematical concepts you can just add up - there's three zombies in this hallway, I'll need such-and-such amount of ammo to take them down along the way. You could make a *very* educated guess on how much ammo you'd need to succeed in any given situation regarding zombies, or any enemy for that matter. That really lent itself well to speedrunning, as you could calculate how much ammo you'd need before even getting to the situation, because you've been there before.

Now, based on your difficulty score, zombies could eat literally ten or more shots to the face and still keep coming, because the game has just decided that you haven't taken enough damage or lost enough bullets. So what "experienced" players of the game do is they don't even bother trying to *kill* most of the zombies, they just render them legless - a factor which isn't as variable, but is still somewhat variable in regard to how many bullets/knife swipes it takes - and run around them. You can still game the system, you just have to try a little harder and know some complicated under-the-hood mathematics at play to understand it. Still, a gripe is a gripe, and I can't help but gripe at the fact that I should have *♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ LIQUIFIED* this zombie's entire head, but he's still got a mouth and he's still coming at me. It's frustrating.

Also, because of euclidean and non-euclidean physics being not-necessarily-separate-things in computer worlds, the zombies can sometimes appear to *teleport* into a biting animation onto you from a distance that you would've sworn was impossible, like up some stairs, or when their back is turned to you and they instantly spin into you in a weirdly comical way. So that's not great.

I should mention, nonzombie enemies don't have most of these problems. Most of them (including bosses, I think?) have a set amount of life, and you can calculate how much ammo it would cost to inflict damage equal to that life. For instance, acid rounds are mostly useless! Which is a gripe in itself, but also there's an exception, where you only need two of them to kill a Licker. Also, you will never *find* acid rounds, you can only *make* them, so you can make literally as many as you need to kill all the Lickers in the game, store that amount, and then take two per Licker as needed. It's neat!

Then there's my other complaint about the game: Mr. X/Tyrant.

In this game he appears as a somewhat imposing trenchcoated figure that begins following you at specific intervals of the game. In the originals I'm pretty sure you could kill him permanently - here, no. Not at all. You can shoot him until he takes a knee for about half a minute and then continues chasing you. If you're stealthy and you don't run anywhere, you can confuse him into going somewhere else and losing you, but generally speaking everything you do attracts this guy and he'll always be on your ass. It's a little frustrating. It definitely works as intended, he's very scary and most players lose their ♥♥♥♥ hiding in fear for most of the game to avoid him. That said, after a while he loses his edge, and all his exaggerated punching animations and slow movement and noisy footsteps just become bothersome. He becomes just another obstacle you learn how to avoid. Which might also be intended, but at this point the player has no respect for him either, he doesn't feel fun. He's an obvious game mechanic rather than a monster to be feared. I would've preferred if you could just spend an amount of powerful ammo into his head and get it over with.

Considering they both exit out into the same end of the same hallway. If Mr.X could pursue you in these two rooms. What this game does right:
- The atmosphere is absolutely haunting, beautiful, threatening, and tense as I've ever seen in a game before. In my first two playthroughs, I almost never wanted to hit the run button (except when I felt like running for my life in reality!). I really took my time in my first playthroughs to soak in everything. It has been literal decades since I've been afraid of a video game before (and I pretty much only play zombie/horror games...), but this game really had me. I found myself sweating in nervous tension, and not being able to sleep from the horror. This obviously faded as time went on, as the more you get used to the game, the less fearful it is. But those first few playthroughs will stick with me for quite some time. And it wasn't just me, you really feel the fear in Leon and Claire as well. They talk to themselves in this game, which I think is both realistic and an amazing touch. "... you got this," Leon whispers to himself as he heads down a darkhallway, while Claire tries to reassure herself by saying, "Focus, Claire... focus!" When you miss a shot or need to reload, or when that zombie will just not go down, the characters will make a comment, including expletives galore. It's an amazing touch. 
- Make Zombies Great Again! When was the last time you felt threatened by a singular zombie in a video game? Probably one of the original Resident Evils. This remake forgoes the popular thought nowadays that every zombie can be killed by a single blow to the head. Heck, even a screwdriver can kill a zombie in one hit in today's zombie medium! Not in this game. This game features the best zombies I have ever seen, anywhere. Everything about these zombies are perfect. While yes, you can learn to dodge them, it's not nearly as easy as it has been in past Resident Evil games, and it's near impossible in tight hallways or where packs of zombies roam. You will have to shoot out their legs or hope for a lucky 1 shot headshot to get by. The zombie shrieks against the quiet soundtrack are petrifying. The zombies really are the star of the show in this game, and that's an insanely great thing. 
- The boss fights were impressive. This is something you probably don't hear often in a Resident Evil game, since the strategy is normally pretty simple... run around and aim your most powerful weapon at the boss without doing much thinking at all. In this game, the majority of boss fights rely on precision shooting with your handgun rather than pumping them with shotgun shells or grenade rounds. They all had pretty different mechanics that made them each more memorable than any boss fight in previous games. 

Where this game falters:
- The lack of death animations was a little strange. In the original, even though they were obviously in "bad" graphics, the death scenes were pretty grotesque; if it wasn't a licker chopping your head clean off, Birkin was tossing you around like a rag doll or impaling you, etc. While the zombie death animations in the remake are absolutely horrifying, if you die by a boss or a licker, the animations are really underwhelming (in 97% of cases). You kind of just get smacked and you fall on the floor and groan... and that's it. No decapitations, no maulings. Just... you died. I was pretty disappointed by this, because the death animations were so memorable in the original. It really would've been great in an updated graphics perspective. 
- [Major plot spoilers in this section] The biggest problem with this game, is the scenarios... or lack thereof. While your first two playthroughs feel pretty different, once you get toward the end of the second playthrough (and especially once you play the third and the fourth), you start raising some eyebrows and wondering what went wrong. The original featured 4 completely different scenarios, which had varying gameplay elements as well as cutscenes in each, and each pair of scenarios reasonably could have happened in the same universe. In this game? While there are 4 different playthroughs, only 2 of them play different from each other, and it's virtually impossible for any of these scenarios to happen at the same time. In every playthrough, the first 3 out of 4 bosses are exactly the same, in the exact same locations, at the same exact time. This would be okay, but again, when you compare to the original where each character faced different bosses... you are disappointed. That, coupled with the fact that certain things happen in an A scenario that would make things physically impossible to happen in a B scenario (example: Birkin cuts Mr X/the Tyrant in half in Claire's scenario, even though that same Tyrant is still chasing Leon and will become his final boss, and Claire unlocks the sample station with Sherry's locket, though it would be impossible for Leon to get there since Birkin destroys that platform moments later, etc). Gameplay wise, yes, the game is still great, and if you want achievements, you are forced to play through all 4 scenarios... but story wise, there is absolutely no point. The only difference between scenarios, is where you start the game, who speaks with Marvin, the obvious character specific points (like playing as Ada with Leon vs Sherry with Claire, etc), and who the final boss is. That's it. The original featured way more variety in the 4 scenarios, and it's absolutely disappointing that was omitted here. This scenario variety is exactly what made Resident Evil 2 so unique, so it's pretty crazy they left that out in this game. And if they really wanted to do things this way, they should have just followed the Claire A/Leon B story/events from the original, instead of lazily making the playthroughs pretty much exactly the same, except a few key moments. 

DLCs or extra content: 
- The game comes with an extra mode that is a replica from the original. You play as Hunk or Tofu (and his 5 variations) and escape the RPD. This mode is a pretty fun extra. It's nice that it's free, but it's not my favorite thing about the game. 
- On February 15th, the Ghost Survivors mode was released for free, which features 4 "alternate reality" stories of 4 characters that die in the game anyway. This mode also introduces 3 different zombie variations that aren't in the main game. 3 of the modes are pretty similar to the extra mode with Hunk/Tofu, but the 4th mode is a pretty fun experience; you holdout the gas station and kill 100 zombies (including the 3 new variations to mix things up) before Leon arrives and it ends. The modes were all pretty fun, but I would've much preferred them to been canon stories that just ended up with them dying like they did in the game, since it's not like these characters were really expanded on in the main story anyway. I hope they don't bother adding new ghost stories, and instead focus on canon scenarios. 

Future wishlist: 
- While I'd much rather them focus on Resident Evil 8 or the remake of 3 at this point, I think they should really release something like a "True Scenario" mode, that attempts to right the wrongs of the current scenario mess. I would pay for this in a heart beat. Something like a scenario where you switch between Leon and Claire, and playthrough the game in a way that makes sense and forms a canon story. I also wouldn't mind seeing an Extreme Battle mode like in the original, or a mode involving Ada and how she survives that fall, since in the original canon story she doesn't fall. 

Final words and ranking: 
- Despite the scenario issues, this is truly a great game, and probably the best single player zombie game since Resident Evil 1 remake. I hope that this game shows that the survival horror genre can still survive in the present day game climate, and that we see more of them in the future. Definitely recommend this game to any zombie fan. 90/100

It's important to note that I already don't like remakes of good games, good games don't need to be remade, and RE 2 Remake simply didn't change my opinion. 
Companies should focus on making a great game using and improving the same resources and mechanics of previous titles to deliver a new and better product, instead of hanging on the old and simply repackaging that.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is not simply a remake, that wouldn't be fair, the game does try to keep things fresh, but all of the additions made to make the game scarier and fit modern times simply never work. Monsters are far too spongy without adding additional difficulty over the original, this especially goes for the boss fights, making the already stupidly gimmicky boss fights even worse, and shooting zombies a tedious and annoying ordeal.
Zombies can barely be avoided, and while I understand that zombies were too easy to avoid in the original games, simply having to kil almost all the zombies that cross your path feels more like an action third person shooter rather than a survival horror title.
People praise this game for giving you little ammo, but I always felt like I was given more than enough to kill every single enemy in the game twice over, but that is generally just a personal thing.

It doesn't help that the Leo and Claire runs are practically the exact same with little alterations, making a second run feel like an even bigger slog to get through than it already was.
There's also little to no interaction between Leon and Claire either, so a second run is not necessary in the slightest.

The characters look terrible, their designs are atrocious, not only that but many of the more memorable characters are reduced to generic self-inserts, generic villains, and a source of film references. Nanette, which is the worst contender in this list, is completely turned into a generic bad wife and mother but great scientist trope, and on top of that her final redemption is stupid and undeserved, nor did it actually redeem her character in any way.

The new soundtrack is also terrible, generic banging drums and typical action sequence violins. The original soundtrack is available but only for those willing to pay an absurd amount of money for something that not only should entirely be in the game already, but should have been remastered and implemented if you're going to do a remake of the original anyway. It's not just the soundtrack, all of the alternative costumes are also sold to players through the store, instead of being free unlocks within the game like the original, which greatly lengthened that game's duration the right way.

I'm sorry but I didn't feel this one, but I'm glad many fans and newcomers did, don't get me wrong. There's definitely some changes I was on board with, but for the most part this did not manage to win me over. It's a good direction for Capcom to take the series, but it's also a worrisome one when Capcom puts so little focus on the future of Resident Evil, and so much on the past, especially when the past isn't being done justice. Capcom should stop milking the Racoon City era and the other initial outbreaks dry, and instead try and manage to tell a compelling story set after the foundations of the series, something they haven't managed since Code Veronica. I'm both worried and excited for the future of the franchise as a fan since the release of the second one in 1998, and I'm glad the series has moved away from things like co-op, ridiculous and grand storytelling, action sequences and arena fights, but I'm also worried that the franchise is now going to grow comfortable where they are and bring us more of that. Let's just hope they'll eventually manage to actually make something that I would want to play.

After playing through all four scenarios and extra modes we have so far, I think it's time for me to give this game a proper review. But first, let me make it clear that I've played all mainline Resident Evil games from 0 to 7, and I've platinumed the original RE2 back in the day when I was younger.

Going to just TLDR this review in bulletpoints

Pros

*Graphics are great. Optimization is excellent for PC too. The RE Engine is a masterpiece.
*Zombies look terrifying and are very tough to kill, which make them very dangerous and how a resident evil game's zombies are supposed to be handled
*Game controls like a dream
*Classic survival horror is back, and puzzles are better than the original
*Gameplay-wise, this game is better than the original
*Lickers are much more terrifying than you remember them to be
* Difficulty has been properly readjusted. The original was fun but a very easy game. This game's difficulty is just right.
* Great job done by the voice actors

Cons
*Lack of proper A/B Scenario. Issues with continuity such as Annette dying twice and Mr X still showing up for Leon when he was already ripped in half by William in Claire's campaign. Some vets might end up getting bothered by this.
*There are certain areas where capcom was either a little on the lazy side or taken out completely. The memorable run to the police station in the beginning of the game has been shortened drastically. The sewers also feel pretty empty. As for the factory, people complain about it being removed but it was really like two or three screens. I don't see it as much of a big deal. 
*Lack of alternate boss battles for each character aside from the final boss. 
*Lack of interactions with Leon and Claire by radio, though this might be nitpicking to some. Some people will miss it. Others probably won't really care too much. I wasn't bothered much by it personally but I thought it was worth mentioning.
*Some characters in the game lack sense/refinement compared to their original counterparts, such as Chief Irons already going bad on you when you meet him whereas in the original, he was pretending to be good the first time you met him. Then along the way, you read memos which flesh out his character more before you encounter him again. There are memos which also talk about Chief Irons in the remake, but the way I think they handled his character here was less interesting. There's also Annette not caring much about her child in the remake when she got infected whereas in the original, once she hears that Sherry is in danger, she drops everything and panics, which is how a mother should react. Claire also acts too much like a badass when she's just a 19 year old college student in this remake. In the original, even when she encountered the final boss, she didn't have a choice. However, in this game, she did have a choice and ended up going Rambo on William at the end.
* Certain enemies are missing, which are bats, crows, spiders and the huge ass moth you encounter in the computer room near the end of the game. Some people may be bothered by this, others wont.
* Certain scenes of the game feel a bit cheapened, such as Marvin just standing in the hallway as a zombie after awhile and the gator chase turning into a crash bandicoot segment.
* May be a pro to some, but in my opinion Mr X follows you way too frequently to where it's annoying. Some people may like it, others won't.
* Soundtrack sounds mediocre compared to the original, though this may be subjective. 
* There are no unlockable costumes in this game aside from their original 1998 costumes. Everything else, you have to pay out of your pocket. 
* The ghost survivor dlcs are really just HUNK levels reskinned, and a lot of it is trial and error. 

Now I've probably written out a decent about of cons here, but the points I've made for the pros are so good that it does outweigh a good amount of the bad. I still prefer the original personally, but I think that regardless, this game is still something many people should play. And if you're an RE fan, you probably have this game already.

My final score: 8.5/10

Let me preface this review by saying that I am a massive fan of Resident Evil. Ever since I first played Resident Evil 4 I have had a really huge love for the series, including anything from the classics, to the spin offs like Resident Evil: Outbreak, to the insanity that was Resident Evil 6. 

Resident Evil 2 is the pinnacle of the series, both in terms of expanding the original game's lore and further showing what the series was capable of. (Not to mention the amazing character Leon)

This remake had massive boots to fill, and this game feels like a 40 year old putting on baby shoes.

This remake ditches the traditional fixed camera angles of survival horror, something I feel held the original's remake back a little bit. The entirely new perspective also means that they had to flesh out the maps a lot, and they've absolutely done it. Every little detail, from the textures to the similar level motifs feels completely refreshed, and even changed around significantly from the original's design. 

The hands-down best changes they made was essentially turning every zombie into a crimson head. You can down the same zombie multiple times only for it to grab your ankle and bite into you, meaning that the player never fully feels safe when looping back through environments. It feels very similar to the crimson head mechanic in the original remake, however it can feel redundant when you've killed the same zombie up to 5 times. Another fair point to make, however, is that you should just shoot out the zombie's knees and run around them. The gore in this game is also absolutely fantastic, showing every torn muscle and broken bone in depth. 

One of my personal favorite changes they made was to the Tyrant. The Tyrant was a mechanic that appeared only a few times in the original game, and inspired the American Resident Evil 3: Nemesis. The importance of the new Tyrant, however, is that it closer ties this game to the play style of newer games like Resident Evil 7 and even lays the groundwork for a complete remake of Nemesis. 

I genuinely, highly, HIGHLY, recommend this game, however it isn't without it's flaws. The game's optimization can feel very iffy at times, and I know that I've definitely had my fair share of FPS drops, and even my friends with newer cards like the 1080 and 2080 have said that this game just generally varies in it's framerates, at least on the lower VRAM cards. Another HUGE point to make about this though is that the main menu's options are extremely in depth, meaning that the game is absolutely easy to self-optimize. 

Ultimately this game brings my trust back to Capcom. After the atrocity of RE6 and the relative differences of RE7 I was unsure of whether or not they would be able to reel it back into a classic feel for RE. This game fully re-instills my trust in them, and this remake genuinely has me excited to see a frantic chase through Raccoon City with the Nemesis, a harrowing adventure saving Chris Redfield in Europe, and possibly even a gritty remake of Resident Evil 4.

Resident Evil 2 Remake is a highly polished masterpiece of an action-adventure survival-horror game, based on the original playstation game from over 20 years ago (now I really feel old). 

Practically everything is executed perfectly in this game. The graphics and sound are mind-blowingly incredible. The visuals almost look true-to-life on a high performance system. Although there's not much music to boast about, the surround sound and thumping  background track are highly effective. Things go bump in the night around you, and you'll just about jump out of your skin as the menacing and indestructible Tyrant stomps down some distant hallway eerily hell bent on finding you. The voice acting in the cut-scenes is uncannily well done. The map is wonderfully creepy and full of small details. The game design is as tight as you could hope for in any inventory management, key-opens-door, and puzzle-solving adventure game - without being too frustrating. You are never really stuck on any of the puzzles wondering what object you found does what. Most of all, the jump scares and horror elements in this game are incredibly effective - ensuring that even the most hardened horror fan will have mini-heart attacks, and possibly nightmares.

The end result is that it is immensely fun to play, while not being too easy or difficult, or too frustrating.... and yet there's a lot here for the hardcore fan to really sink their teeth into as well. There are plenty of challenges to complete for that well-executed speed run attempt on hardcore difficulty (which is how I played it) to beat the game with as few saves as possible under 5 hours to get an S+ rating. To top it off, there are bonus scenarios once you've completed both Leon and Claire's different playthroughs including the challenging "second run" unlock. There is a lot of content and the game map gets a lot of remixing and reuse - just to trip you up when you think you've learned everything.

As for downsides: One of them is the game's extremely high asking price at the moment. Capcom has a bona-fide classic here and they know it's worth the money. If it's too much for you, and it ever appears on sale, then by all means - you should jump at the chance to add this to your library!

The other possible downside is that the game is perhaps a little too graphic with the gore and a bit too effective with the jump scares. I consider this a plus, but if you can't handle horror, or are too young for it, then leave this game well alone!

This is one well executed, and directed game. The original was already a classic, but this is so much better than that. It's a masterpiece. This is the closest the gaming medium has come to making you feel like you are an actor in a horror movie - it's *that* good.

This game sets a new standard for remakes.  It captures what makes the original great while updating things in a way that makes it feel like a game for modern audiences.  Instead of tank controls and fixed cameras to make things difficult we have modern controls but with tight areas and zombies that are agile and persistent.  Zombies are scary again!  It might be annoying how much it takes to put them down but there is a definite tension as you try to stop a zombie shambling towards you.  You can't simply mow them down as you would in other games.  One element of tension that remains from previous RE games is the lack of resources.  Part of what makes zombies hard is you can't afford to miss a shot and until you manage your resources wisely you will struggle to have what you need.  

The presentation and sound design really add a lot to the game.  I have never seen such realistic gore effects in a game before when shooting apart a zombie.  Especially with a survival horror game the realistic look and feel helps with immersion and makes things more terrifying.  There are multiple characters to play as and alternative pathways through the game.  I found these worth replaying, although there isn't a huge amount of variety between the variations.  There's been some free time trial DLC added and I'm excited to see what else might be added later.  This is definitely going down as one of my favorite games of 2019 and I'm hopeful that Capcom will give RE: Nemesis the same treatment.

I remember playing the original Resident Evil 2, and how nervous it made me. To be fair, most RE games did that, but none really did it better, in my opinion. From zombies to lickers to Mr. X to William Birkin's monster forms and the other G-virus monsters. Now, all of those nightmarish crearures are back with a vengenance! And I never though I could be so happy and excited about such a thing.

Resident Evil 2 was probably the best and most respected of the first three titles (and arguably of  all the RE games). That is, despite the voice acting, which was still ten times better than the first Resident Evil. The gameplay was fun and challenging, the story and environments were emersive, and ... the monsters!

The change to Mr. X has to be one of the best and, conversely, worst (okay, not really worst) of the challenges added to the game. The premise in the original RE2 was that Mr. X was constantly stalking you, though you could either run away or put him down temporarily, and you just would run into him later. But, now, he is an imminent threat that is actually patrolling for you! I'll admit, it usually has me running back to a safe area to hide out, paying close attention to the sound of his stomping, and peering through the crack of the door too see which way he's going. And it seems his routes are not always so predictable. He might walk through one room just to turn around and walk back. (I can almost swear that he stops and waits in a nearby room just to fool me into leaving my safe area, and stomps my way once he hears my footsteps. I'M ON TO YOU MR. X!) Hiding from Mr. X is easily the biggest time waster in the game, and in some respects, unavoidable. (E.g. when you run into an area with multiple enimies and find yourself overwhelmed.) Otherwise, options are running the other way and dogding his punches. 

The lickers are also much more formidible! A shot from a handgun used to stop them in their tracks if only for a second, and you could easily take one down with quickly repeated shots without even having the chance to attack. Now, you need to have some real fire power, and enough rounds in the case one doesn't do it. (Fire rounds and grenades are generally the best.) A plan helps, too. Like sticking close to the door when you attack. If you're really good, you can just walk around them. But, I've been in only a couple situations where that even seemed feesible. They don't tend to hesitate like they used to, and it's hard to take any risks with multiple lickers.

And, then there's the good ol' zombies. They have more-or-less the same characteristics as they used to. Hard to kill, but even more so. (Certain ones I've shot in the face/head so many times and they just... won't... die!) Still, they're generally slow, but now with surprising bursts of speed that can catch you off-guard. And ... those bastards will friggin' CLIMB UP YOU just to take a nice chunk from your neck! Don't get me wrong, I absolutely love what they did with the zombies in this game. But, be prepared and if you have to put them down, you friggin' make sure they stay down!

Oh! And the plant zombies! What a nice touch! Like regular zombies, they're hard to kill, and boy are they freaky! Fire is the best weapon for them. The flame thrower definitely, but the grenade launcher does the job, too.

They did so much that improves on the original. I certainly love when Claire and Leon react to the fact that the monsters don't go down like expected. The voice acting is also great. And Claire... she curses a lot! I'm not saying that as a positive per se, but... yeah, I'd say it's appropriate dialog.

[b]  A relic from past generation, remade to perfection... well almost. [/b]

[h1]Story:[/h1]
You play as either Steve Burnside or Elza Walker, each with their own agenda to enter the zombie infested city. They go to the police station to get help only to end up trying to escape the said police station and get out of the city...
Both characters have their own set of weapons and will encounter NPC's unique to their run. Despite each of them having to go through the same areas, their paths never really intertwine, puzzles overlap, and you go face the same bosses excluding 2, which really hurts the immersion.

[h1]Gameplay:[/h1]
Survival horror at its finest. They've done away with the tank controls and it won't be missed. You can now freely move while aiming and shooting at the cost of accuracy. Melee attacks triggered by stuns that debuted in [b]RE4[/b] is absent though. And the trusty combat knife breaks now in favor of the counterattack mechanics.

[b]+[/b] Jump scares makes a glorious return, and is as effective as the one's found on the original.

[b]-[/b] Key items take up inventory slots again which require micro management and backtracking. An odd decision given that they can be discarded, and the contents of item boxes are shared.

[b]+[/b] The main attraction of the game - the Zombies are not your average undead. These are capable of fancy crossover moves and drunken style maneuvers to avoid your aim and close the distance. These are also very talented actors at playing dead.

[b]-[/b] On hardcore difficulty though, the balance is thrown out of the window. Zombies soak up more bullets before their heads pop and shrugs off shots like they were fired from a toy gun. 

[b]-[/b] At some point you will come across the [b]Tyrant[/b] who will methodically chase you until you enter certain rooms or trigger a key event. It's akin to encountering an overpowered griefer/hacker in an online game who'll stop at nothing to ruin your day. While it serves to [strike]waste your supplies and increase your playtime[/strike] heighten the  tension, it has a major drawback of causing more needless backtracking and ultimately breaks your pace.

[b]-[/b] The [b]Ghost Survivors[/b] is a welcome addition, but it would have been a lot more fun to play if they were canon and not just another linear time attack mode.

[h1]Graphics:[/h1]
Bloody, gory and beautiful through and through. It's hard to make the game look ugly even on performance settings.

[b]+[/b] The new character models are gorgeous.

[b]+[/b] Bouncy but firm butt animations.

[b]-[/b] Claire's facial animation looks a bit weird.

[b]-[/b] It's hard to unsee Wayne Li's face since he is all over the city.

[h1]Sounds:[/h1]
The remake soundtrack is not really bad, but it just doesn't quite nail it like the 1998 one which is unfortunately a paid DLC. Lead actors are naturals when it comes to swearing, and the sound effects overall is on point.

[h1]Final Thoughts:[/h1]
Shooting zombies in the head has never felt this good (on standard difficulty at least) since [b]The House of the Dead[/b]. A huge letdown for me personally though is the Tyrant's free roaming design. It would have been less annoying if the encouters were fixed or if it can be incapacitated for good. If you know how to do a [b]Pepsiman[/b] though, then you'll be right at home evading it. Regardless, this installment is a return to form for the series (discounting 7 which looks like a completely different game), and the offerings of Raccoon City will surely appeal to those revisiting it after 21 years and modern audiences alike.

This game is fantastic. I am amazed at the level of hard work the developers have put into it. I never even touched a Resident Evil game before this one, it is my first experience with the franchise, but I can tell it has renewed many peoples interest in the series. Obviously, it is still very similar to the original RE2 of 1998 in regards to the narrative and locations; however, the game's transition to a third person shooter over the original tank controls offers a whole new experience. Some even argue that the remake is scarier compared to the original's release because enemies can now chase you between rooms.

Now about the actual gameplay, and for those unaware, this is essentially a big puzzle game, wrapped within a plot concerning secretive bio-weapons, taking place within a police station full of claustrophobic rooms and hallways. Oh and did I mention the rooms are littered with zombies? Well no worry, they are the least of your concerns; there are worst enemies that you should be afraid of. Like those lickers! "Make like your grand-ma and sneak past them."

The gameplay variety between fighting enemies and navigating the locations to solve puzzles is a lot of fun. I was actually surprised by how much I enjoyed it. So much so that I am now on my third play-through: first Leon, then Claire B, then Claire A. The station has varying paths to different building sections that you must unlock as you progress in the game. You will also explore other locations throughout the game, some places exclusive to the character you are playing as. The game offers two separate stories, one from the perspective of Leon and the other from Claire. Completing either of their stories will unlock the alternate/second (B) play-through of the other character. This system is great because you can complete Leon's first play-through, then immediately play Claire's second play-through with some plot consistency to the previous run. Or Claire first then Leon; you choose.

Yes, it is expensive, but definitely of high quality and offers a lot of replayability. The game works great, plays great, looks stunning, and has a fairly interesting narrative. [h1]Pros:[/h1]

+ A stunning remake of a classic horror game. HD "Remastering" titles, and "remakes" in general tend to be low effort cash grabs, but this does not describe the care and attention RE2 Remake goes into. It's basically a brand new game, with its own surprises and memorable moments.

+ Graphically the game is fantastic, very similar in aesthetics to RE7's engine but without the washed out appearence. The detail in gore is pretty sickening at times, and the enemies have been faithfully realized. The main cast also looks better than ever, with Leon and Claire having some fantastic interactions that sadly do not happen enough.

+ Gameplay is tense, engaging, and difficult. There are so many nuances to the way you move and interact with enemies -- you can walk around Lickers and not disturb them, you can avoid zombies by carefully shooting them before passing. Headshots aren't king in RE2, and the effect on the gameplay is terrifying to behold. Nothing ever feels "safe" even when you KNOW you killed that zombie. 

+ Story is a huge step-above the storytelling in the original RE2, with interactions being entirely rewritten to be more believable. Leon's naive personality can be a bit too on the nose at times, but overall his optimistic and driven personality are far more apparent. Ada and Claire have a lot more depth as well, with both characters feeling much more faithful to their later game personalities.

+ The playtime of the game is up there. I'm currently at 27 hours after doing pretty much everything outside of challenging achievements. Admittedly the individual first runs aren't too long depending on how fast you are, but there is value to playing both Leon and Claire's stories, which each have significant differences. Beyond that, there is a "2nd Run" that attempts to tell the story of the other character from your main choice (with an additional ending to unlock), as well as several bonus modes to enjoy that focus on speedrunning with limited supplies. The game also has rewarding unlockables for doing specific challenges, as well as bonuses to unlock such as game models to inspect. With more free and paid content on the way, there is a lot of value to be had in the purchase.



[h1]Cons:[/h1]

- There sadly is a disappointing amount of differences in 2nd Run. There are some changed item positions and enemy locations, and some difficulty changes, but ultimately the story is the exact same as a regular run. You fight the same bosses as any other playthrough and see the same story (except for experiencing the true ending at the end, the main point of doing this content). While this wasn't a requirement and the 2nd run had enough changes to keep me interested, there is something sad about the content not being different. I'd of been fine with not fighting any of the bosses and just having Leon/Claire encounter the aftermath of the 1st Run, with less supplies and more normal enemies in odd places.

- Some enemies are far too aggressive. The G-Virus Specimens you encounter in the sewer are, in particular, extremely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to deal with if you don't want to fight them. They seem to occupy spaces only just big enough to fit them and it's very difficult to get past them without either wasting resources or taking a grab or two willingly. This was particularly annoying in Leon's playthrough, since he had less resources to deal with them unless you wanted to waste your shotgun ammo.

- One of the boss battles is extremely weak -- the second one. I don't want to get into too much detail but you're hitting the boss with something and you have to time it right. The problem is, the recovery timing window feels very off and frustrating. Your character will often say something as an indicator that you were victorious but the enemy's recovery still happens too quickly. It feels extremely bland and unrewarding as an encounter, and it pales in comparison to the other boss fights in the game.



[h1]Overall:[/h1]

Capcom is killing it with the Resident Evil series lately. RE7 was one of my favorite releases a few years ago, and RE2 is shaping up to follow it. It's not a perfect game, and I think RE7 beats it in a few ways, but it's still one of my favorite gameplay experiences of the year so far. The success of this title is great to see, as well, as Capcom seems open to remaking other titles in the series, starting with RE3.  I cannot wait to see what they do with them (and, hopefully, an Outbreak remake?? That'd be really neat).

I'd recommend this game to anyone with a love for survival horror or the Resident Evil series.

Reviewing Resident Evil 2 is difficult and just goes to show how flawed the review system is on steam. Despite my marking this game as 'no' for recommended, I want to preface this review with this: this game is by no means a bad game. It's good, it can be fun to play. My complaints stem from so many small details and complaints that, piled up, makes the game a chore for me to personally trek through.

First off, game mechanics. I understand the need to make zombies more impervious to attacks to build the suspense and horror but in a game where you're supposed to avoid them, it is very annoying to be running and a zombie take up 15 bullets (sometimes more) in one go. Headshots being RNG isn't great and though you can take out their limbs and have a better time to maneuver around them after doing so, it's still extremely frustrating. I should be able to clear a room and not have to worry about those same zombies getting right back up. 

I had a case where even though I boarded up the hallway, I walked into a room. Two lickers. Mr. X behind me. And then a zombie in the middle of the hallway. I was screwed no matter what I did. Walking meant the lickers wouldn't hear me but Mr. X walks faster than I do. Running, I will get murdered by the lickers yet get out of Mr. X's range. I opted for the second and though I managed to just narrowly avoid a licker's sweep, the zombie around the corner got me, licker followed up, and then Mr. X finished me off. 

That's honestly all I have to complain about where gameplay mechanics are concerned so I would say that's a good thing and goes to show how polished the game is.

Scenery, though, is something else I need to talk about. I'm a long time fan of the RE series so when I heard about this game, I was thoroughly excited (though that lessened and became worry after RE7 and how it was handled). When entering the game, I had hoped to feel nostalgia. I didn't. No space except maybe the save room just under the stairs and that one room you open up with the knife where you see the licker walk across the window really gave me any sense of nostalgia. I didn't feel like I was playing RE2 at all. 

And something strange about this game. I didn't feel like the "stages" were separated enough. In the original game, the RPD, the sewer, and the lab all felt like different "levels". Here, I felt like everything bled together and I feel it's mostly because of the color pallets and lighting choices in the game. It gave me eye fatigue and made me tired after only one hour playing and that's not something any other game's given me before.

Finally, my biggest gripe in this game. Story.

Claire's scenario was undoubtedly the best. Annette's changes were for the better, I feel, and Claire - a character I have never really cared for story-wise in the past games - is strongly written. It's great. Leon's scenario, however, was an utter disappointment. Though I appreciate the changes made to side characters like Kendo, Ben, it's the other characters i have a problem with. Leon's scenario was always my favorite to play in the original for a very specific reason: Ada Wong. I don't mind her story change. The FBI front makes sense and works. It's her manner of speech and approach to things. This isn't Ada Wong but some cheap imitation. 

And then the Leon and Ada relationship. It's poorly written and even the classic game managed to make it seem more natural than this. How are we supposed to believe that Ada is that "woman he can't let go" from later installments when they spent even less time together than in the original and 85% of it was her berating him verbally? It's ridiculous.

All in all, it isn't a terrible game. Can be fun. But other things, small things, make me want to just uninstall and revisit this maybe once every 10 years. It was not worth the wait, personally.
