This review comes from someone who has only played Resident Evil 4, 5, and 6.

I'm honestly not a big fan of jumpscares. Horror is fine, especially if used to craft expertly well-done environments heavy with tension and fear, but when that experience is marred by an over-indulgence of jumpscares, that's when I start to get turned off. In that retrospect, RE2 manages to craft a well-done horror experience filled with tension on your first playthrough, then somehow loses almost all of that fear from the second playthrough onward due to predictability. There are admittedly quite a few jumpscares, though many are minor and predictable upon reflection, so they haven't really stood out to me as much. The horror instead comes from the incredibly durable enemies who deal extremely high damage and the limited resources scattered in the world with which to fight said enemies - aspects that surprisingly make the game still fun to play upon the fifth or sixth playthrough.

More on the gameplay: inventory space is limited, encouraging backtracking and smart management.. Shooting encourages the player to pause and aim rather than firing blindly. Enemy variety is unfortunately lacking, and you might end up wishing that there would be more different types of enemies to find on your second playthrough. Boss fights aren't well implemented- they just don't seem to fit the style of gameplay present in RE2. 

The biggest weakness for me in Resident Evil 2 is the story. For what little cutscenes and story beats are there, the character interactions are disappointingly limited - either rushed or not developed further enough to clearly convey to the player the relationships between the characters. While both Leon and Claire are great protagonists, the side characters leave a lot to be desired in the game. The bigger issue with the story, however, is that there is no correlation between the A and B routes despite being marketed as happening at the same time. The protagonists end up fighting the same bosses, solving many of the same puzzles, and exploring lots of common areas. This ultimately makes the story of RE2 feel like a disjointed mess, which is such a shame when paired with the comparatively stellar gameplay provided.

Regarding bonus content like 4th Survivor or Tofu, they're honestly not that fun unless you're itching for a challenge in speedrunning a gauntlet of enemies within a very familiar environment, though you do get infinite weapons in speedrunning the main campaigns, which is nice. The paid DLC so far seem to be lackluster thus far, not offering much more than the base game. The original soundtrack swap is almost necessary - it's difficult to swap back to the remake soundtrack after noticing the large swathes of silence present in that version. The Samurai Edge DLC are nearly useless in the game, I wouldn't advise getting those. DLC costumes are purely cosmetic, though at they moment, they're necessary if you want to install a costume mod for a character.

The game is well optimized, much like Metal Gear Solid V. Even when running on a comparatively potato computer, you can still get decent frame rates coupled with good-looking graphics. A scant few enemy cues incorporate audio, which might not be effective for deaf gamers, but it doesn't hamper the gameplay much when playing without sound.

At a time where the market is full to the brim with online shooters and massive open world games, RE2 actually comes off as very refreshing. It's incredibly small and compact, which has helped immensely in my multiple replays of the game - something I struggle to do with larger singleplayer games. 

Would I say this is my favorite Resident Evil game? No, that title personally still belongs to RE4. However, RE2 is still a very good survival horror game, with more emphasis on the survival than the horror, and I would encourage everyone, even if they're not a fan of horror, to try it out.

[h1] A Decent Remake But a Great Game [/h1] 

Comparing REmake 2 to its immediate predecessor, Resident Evil 7, will make this a hard sell; it's not an original story, not by the standards of the series or zombie media in general, it makes some poor design choices compared to its original iteration, and it doesn't try enough new things to make it a stellar remake. (could've used more creativity on par with Sherry's stealth section and less predictable AAA nonsense like Ada's hacking "puzzles")

Putting all that aside and if you don't think of it as a follow up to any Resident Evil title and consider it how the original game might be if it were developed now instead of then, you're getting damn good value for your purchase and a more enjoyable survival horror and action adventure title than any of the competition.

You get two campaigns with two different characters with their own story beats, environments, and weapon sets, as well as an alternate run once you've completed one; two bonus campaigns with their own characters and challenges, a soldier with all the best gear but with the goal of beating a time trial of getting from the Umbrella Labs to the Police Station without dying, and a block of tofu with only a knife to its name; you're also getting, as of the most recent update from this writing, an extra three challenge modes where you play as Robert Kendo surviving after the loss of his daughter, a runaway from the Raccoon City orphanage, and a different member of the Umbrella cleanup crew. All that content aside, you also get bonus outfits based on the original games' costumes bundled in.

 Now for the complaints, speaking of bonus content, I understand Campcom promised and delivered on free content with the Ghost Survivors update mentioned previously, but they're still pulling some anti-consumer ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you ought to know about. My main issue is with their decision to lock the original game's soundtrack behind a paywall when compared to the soundscape ambience in the vanilla game, it should have been an unlockable for completing the game for the first time so the second run can feel fresh. The game included the original costumes and now has the original character models as costumes for free, so why put a price tag on the soundtrack?

Also, aside from the remake and original costumes, alongside the polygon costumes they released, those are all the costumes you get for the price of the Standard Edition. The original game included more bonus costumes and had unique weapons attributed to them, now said unique weapons are included for a second run, but the costumes aren't unless you're willing to pay up. I would be fine with Capcom charging for extra costumes if they included enough unique ones in the base game to justify it, but there just isn't enough there. So if you've read this far and are considering giving this game a shot, I'd recommend the Deluxe Edition or not at all.

Now I know it may seem like I spent a good portion of this review ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ all over it, but aside from the questionable ethics of costumes and soundtracks, the core game that you get is still excellent; an engrossing atmosphere, highly-optimized graphical performance, lots of options to tweak, punchy shooting, great gore and damage modelling, level design that makes running around the same segments of the world not feel dull. Top that all off with a skin-of-your-teeth challenge that leaves you with just enough to get by.

I highly recommend it, but with that cautionary sticking point not to have your expectations set too high considering the legacy it has behind it.

Deep and ambitious game design ideas that captivated classic gamers in the old days have been brought back and mixed with modern ideas to remake RE:2 into this gorgeous version that we have today. The player must plan their route and strategy for getting by different enemies and achieving their survival goals in a police station that's full of loot, puzzles, and monsters. The monsters are all hard to kill but can be taken down in various ways that are up to the player to utilize and discover (Some more efficient than others) Enemies overall have more gimmicks like only dying to certain weapons, being impaired in certain ways, or behavior that's like the enemies from soma and amnesia where you have to progress through the game while they share the same agency as you in where they travel and stalk you down. The combat has been changed to 3rd person which as allowed for much deeper execution in how you decide to kill or takedown each individual monster. The ability to hit weak points, dismember enemies, and switch weapons quickly make for a much funner and dynamic experience.

There is so much quality and depth in this design but the content is very contained only allowing you to experience certain situations that the game has to offer for very small periods of time. When you feel like you need your whole arsenal of weapons to get by a varied set of enemies on a dangerous path. Once you complete that part you never really feel challenged in that way again. You figure out better ways to do things and the game never brings up a similar but more challenge version of that situation again. The map and goals are very easy to remember even if it's up to the player where to decide to go first. In code veronica x the map was huge and you kind of had to take notes to keep track of what you want to do next. I wish the game had more content and complexity basically but it does have depth. On the bright side there is more content coming out and extra modes to play along with the main game. Replaying the main game with different characters does diversify the experience too.

To give a spoilerful example (You can skip this paragraph): There is a room near the end where there are lickers and normal zombies, and before and after that room there are plant zombies. As claire I geared up with my grenade launcher and machine gun. I burned the plant zombies, burned the lickers, but shot the zombies down with the machine gun. It felt like I was on an extermination team playing like that but after that part I was pretty much up to the final boss and the game ended. Another example is Ada Wong, she uses a gadget to open doors by hacking their wiring so you have to follow the wires and dodge zombies to get from place to place. Only time Ada encounters zombies where she has to do that is in one specific room. Maybe Ada's gameplay isn't the most important thing in the world but it's an on going theme with the game to give a quality experience but then cut it off and never make it happen in a more complex way again.

I would have really appreciated more complex/contentful exploration and gameplay experiences but as the game is it's really rich learning how to master it with the different characters and potential gameplay styles. It has been a very valuable survival horror experience and I can't wait to play it more.

As my first real experience of a Resident Evil game I have to say I found this an absolute joy to play. My only other attempts at one of the titles was the HD remaster of the first game and one of the revelations, I think it was 2. Unfortunately I never completed them because they weren't necessarily the 'horror' games I was expecting at the time and I got kinda bored. I followed the series for a while, seeing how it turned from horror, into action and then back to horror again by the demand of its fans. I'm sure most of you are familiar with the boulder punching meme, so I won't say much on that but you get the idea. If not? Google 'Chris Redfield boulder punch' and you'll see how ridiculous and off the rails this series got at one point.

Back to the point at hand however, the actual game as it stands is pretty short, clocking at an average of 3 to 6 hours give or take and depending on whether its your first time and if your bothered with picking up lore pieces and painting your entire map blue for picking every item up in the game. For me it took just under 9 hours for my first playthrough as Leon. I walked everywhere, took my time, took in the surroundings, learning as I went and eventually finished...but that wasn't the end! Oh no, as then you get to play the game from Claires perspective. New weapons and some changes to the direction and areas you get to explore. After that you can run the game from 'Point B' which is the scenario where, everything is generally the same but with more slight changes such as starting position and item placements. If you're a completionist you'll find yourself at the very least completing this game 4 times in a row for the full Leon and Claire experience. by my final run I decided i'll try at least get under 4 hours, which I did on Standard because I'm a very chilled back, casual gamer. I'm no speedrunner,  I don't know pixel perfect strats and I have a tendency to just always pick everything up and run back and forth to the item box, constantly checking my map and shifting items around in my inventory so I was happy I could at least get an A...ranks and time really don't bother me though, it was just fun to experience. 

Graphically the game is beautiful and runs perfectly at maximum graphics settings, only hickup I had was when I tried to look at the Stage-2 G model and the game crashed. Sound, soundtrack, atmosphere were all amazing, with plenty of times the game made me jump. The Tyrant chasing me around the police station wasn't all as tense as I thought it would be...easy enough to escape or get around but it was a nice addition to keep you on your toes while exploring. I got lucky with critical headshots quite often so I knew which halls were clear.

Usually when it comes to the challenge modes in game, I skip them and move on. I'm really not interested in scores or ranks or any of that, I play a game for its story and then when I've seen it i play something else. I suppose the best example are people who play dark souls over and over again for hundreds and thousands of hours...that's not me. At the time I didn't know the extra game mode was just a nails hard time trial. It had some story but essentially it was just a glorified escape challenge, which I managed to do on my 5th attempt, just barely! I tried the Tofu Challenge and died at the fire escape on my first try, was happy with that. And then the latest DLC arrived just today...and honestly i'm somewhat disappointed that it was just more glorified challenge modes. Was really expecting some actual story based stuff with save points and all that business, but I guess if this is what Resident Evil games have always been I can't argue with it. They just felt slapped together for a bit of extra content for contents sake, albeit free as it is I think ill make a hard pass on them. I completed No Time To Mourn within an inch of my life and realised the other 2 challenges are just the same. No voice acting, no new maps, just straight up get from point A to point B, with the added challenge of unique enemies for each survivor and if you're bothered or have the skill, do it as fast as possible. The idea of 'What if' scenarios initially sounded appealing, I was just expecting something else unfortunately.

All in all however, fantastic game and if its your first entry, where better to start honestly.

This game took everything that RE7 did right and made almost all of it better. The dark days of post-RE3 seem to be finally over. No more [i]QTE-saturated linear bing bing wahoo.[/i] Someone finally figured out why people liked the originals and tried to update the formula for modern technology. And yes, the camera angles and tank controls of the original were never a deliberate design decision, they were a technical compromise mandated by how inept the Playstation was, and only replicated in REmake due to rabid fanboy outrage. RE2 Remake has its problems, like the insufficient difference between scenarios and the retconning of the dynamic between some of the characters but none of that ruins it. It plays great, looks great and sounds great.

[h1]♥Great:[/h1]
♥Aiming works well but is not overly precise so you can't just breeze through combat like it's an FPS. It can be hard to hit things sometimes and that is good in a game where you need to conserve your ammo.
♥Headshots are not powerful, they only have a slight chance of decapitation, ie. the same as in classic RE games.
♥None of the bodies of enemies you've killed will disappear. So you'll be always wondering if those zombies are really dead. Also the bodies are physics objects that can trip zombies that walk over them.
♥Zombie body part specific damage can be utilized in a variety of ways. Armless zombies have a hard time grabbing you and zombies without feet can't walk. In fact without feet they will drown if they crawl into water.
♥Enemies and bosses change appearance based on damage taken and the appearance is different depending what type of damage they've received.
♥In general, enemies are extremely tough so you are made to constantly feel like you're wasting ammo, so you'll be afraid of running out at critical times.
♥Mr. X is unpredictable and you need to constantly adapt to his random movement throughout the level. There are scripted scenes such as him breaking down a wall to get you, but even that sometimes doesn't happen just to make you question everything on consequent playthroughs.
♥All puzzles have been improved and made more sensible. The police station is no longer a place where it's impossible to work without hunting down weird artifacts so you could move around. That aspect is not gone, it has just been reduced.
♥The worst designed boss fight of the original was changed into a normal enemy that is tough and dangerous and there are several of them. It replaces the most pointless enemy of the original, the spider.
♥Even locations are resources now. The player is given resources to block windows so that zombies can't get in. The player needs to choose which areas to secure.
♥Item interfaces have some improvements like the ability to combine items directly in the storage menu.
♥Video options have a brightness calibration system that goes to extreme lengths to ensure that all players get the optimal brightness settings with any display.
♥Some video options I've never seen before, such as letting you choose the output color space.

[h1]♦As should be:[/h1]
♦No QTEs. I can't believe we still need to be explicitly stating that.
♦Player can remove weapon parts that have subjective benefits based on their preference.
♦Player can't cheat by reloading weapons in the inventory menu like in the original.
♦All enemies have sufficiently realistic senses. Zombies need to actually hear you move or see you with their eyes to be alerted. You can avoid plenty of engagements by being careful.
♦Zombies can follow you through most doors unlike the monsters in RE7.
♦Discarding items is now done manually, no more annoying text box asking you to do it. Also there are items you think you won't need anymore but actually serve a purpose so that's why the system isn't entirely automated.
♦No universal crafting items like in RE7 where you could decide whether you needed ammo or health. You need gunpowder for ammo and herbs for health.
♦Every boss battle has been improved from the original (Not exactly hard to accomplish). They have proper arenas, strategies and multiple stages.

[h1]♠Bad:[/h1]
♠The primary factor that determines the score of your playthrough is time, like it's a speedrun or something. Actually being a careful survivalist who takes no risks and receives no damage is irrelevant. Basically you need to rush through so you have the smallest chances of actually surviving without saving the game, ie. the opposite of smart.
♠Using items and keys pauses the game. No more tense door unlocking moments like in RE7.
♠Lickers have no hitstun no matter how powerful your attack is and will do immediate high-damage counterattacks.
♠There is no flashlight button. The character uses it automatically.
♠Main character will continue to repeat the same exasperated exclamations about the behavior of zombies even after having faced off with dozens of them for hours on end.
♠Readables will condescendingly highlight important information for you regardless of difficulty setting.
♠Some of the different sound environments fade in and out too quickly when moving between areas instead of there being proper simulation of ambient sound volume.
♠Aiming is over the shoulder, so the camera is offset on the right, therefore any obstacle on your right side obscures your character's aim. At least this is not a game where enemies can shoot so they can't attack you without you being able to return fire.
♠Impossible to use defense items on stairs due to animation incompatibility. The player must take the damage if they are attacked on stairs.
♠Textures often fail to load the maximum resolution mipmaps for some reason. (Could be a driver issue though)
♠Special visual effects such as volumetric lighting render in extremely low resolutions unless your settings are in maximum.

You can learn the game inside and out and beat it in 1.5hrs without breaking a sweat and STILL have a ton of fun every time you do it. 

The controls are tight, the gunplay is super satisfying and responsive, enemies react to your firepower appropriately on standard difficulty, and the game really feels like it helps mold you into an efficient machine without you noticing it much, which is about the highest praise you can give a game. 

RE2:R is an absolute must for just about any gamer, and especially for those who enjoy strong narrative driven games with an emphasis on exploration, or just plain old horror fans. Capcom showed up on a level most people did not expect with this title and I can't wait for what the future of the franchise holds from here on out.

This RE2 remake is the proof that remakes/reboots can be amazing when done right. This shows that Capcom, despite still messing up here and there throughout the years, is still listening to their fans and willing to fix their past mistakes by creating content that people actually want.

RE2 feels as welcoming to new players as it also feels refreshing to fans from the original games.

Rather than continue to go down the path of games like RE6, this game goes back to the origins of the Resident Evil games: gruesome, disturbing horror. There are no cover mechanics, no dodge abilities and no melee combat other than attacking with a knife. You rely entirely on aiming and running, except this time using a third person view instead of the classic "tank controls", which not only allows the player to get a closer look at the disturbing enemies coming their way but also to aim where they want to aim (rather than a fixed up/center/down aim from the original game).

The game looks and feels amazing - a whole new look at the classic scenarios like the police station, the sewers and the laboratory, with nothing held back in terms of gore and violence. The game still feels like the classic game as it maintains many of the original items and even the layout for some of the places, but also making some very necessary changes by either adding things that were needed or removing things that weren't. The layout of the police station is slightly different, but a lot of it is still like the original. As an example, Claire's crossbow was removed since it was an awful weapon to use in the original game, being replaced with the SMG (which is no longer a special weapon) and the grenade launcher now only uses incendiary and acid rounds, with no "normal rounds" anymore. Weapon upgrades can be found for almost every weapon in the game, instead of only for Leon's arsenal. Puzzles were reworked to feel less annoying and troublesome while still offering some challenge and the inventory, while still quite limited, can now be upgraded by finding hip pouches.

One interesting detail the game adds is that there are no more "safe doors", as enemies will chase the character through doors. Mr. X also shows up in both scenarios, further increase how tense the game feels as he'll be relentlessly chasing the character until they manage to run away or temporarily stun him with headshots. He remains present through a good portion of the game and can be heard patrolling around, requiring caution in order to avoid the areas he's patrolling.

Difficulty levels are quite balanced: Normal offers a decent challenge without feeling overwhelming, Easy has enemies somewhat weakened and offers aim assist and Hardcore is pretty much a harder version of the original game: the game can only be saved by using ink ribbons, plus enemies are harder. In addition, there are also less hip pouches to be found and some of the health/ammo items are replaced with ink ribbons.

There is also a good number of unlockables. 4th Survivor is unlocked by beating both scenarios, while Tofu Survivor is unlocked by beating 4th Survivor. There are also 5 infinite weapons that can be unlocked by achieving certain rankings in certain difficulties as well. S rank now only requires the game to be beaten under a certain time limit (according to difficulty and scenario), while S+ rank requires that plus a maximum number of 3 saves and no use of infinite weapons.

My only problem with the game is that scenarios A and B don't really feel that different. While in the classic game it felt like they were both two stories happening at the same time with different puzzles and bosses involved, this time it feels like the only difference is the first part of the game (navigating through the police station). After that, everything feels pretty much the same. Both scenarios will have the same encounters and the same bosses. If we're considering that scenario A and scenario B are two stories that are happening at the same time as Leon and Claire go their own ways, it makes no sense to consider that they're going through (mostly) the same events and fighting the same bosses.

Still, however, this is very much an incredible remake that I easily recommend, even at full price. Plus, there is also free DLC coming up in the future as well.

The original [b]Resident Evil 2[/b] was released in late 1998, and was instantly considered the best horror game ever created. The concept of what’s “best” is relevant, but one truth remains, as the old classic is always among the favorite by fans. That title, however, will never change, because changing nostalgia is impossible and with time, we adorn it, with even more elements of grandiosity. It’s a human thing to do, to celebrate our memories with further sentiments of pleasure. Another thing humans do, it’s to improve themselves, at each generation, and so, we’re welcomed with [b]Resident Evil 2 Remake[/b].

Just one month has passed since the dreadful events at Spencer Mansion, and the isolated incident seems to be behind everyone’s mind now, but another terror arises, slowly, under the innocent minds of Racoon City’s population.

Claire Redfield travels to Racoon City, on her special Harley Davidson and her lucky jacket made in heaven, hoping to find her dear brother, Chris Redfield.
Leon Kennedy just graduated from the police academy, and Raccoon City was his first place of choice, considering the strange deaths occurring just one month ago. While driving to his destination, he finds a corpse on the road. Not any corpse though, this one was quite different…

Their paths will come together, as they have to fight for survival, each in its own way, and at the same time, uncover the deepest secrets underneath Racoon City.

[i]Capcom[/i] is slowly trying to replace some original facts that have previously been settled, such as the events leading Leon to Raccoon City, where originally he had woken up later from being drunk, now he was apparently just quietly sitting at home waiting to get on duty. Probably to appease a more softcore audience, these changes weren’t the only ones. Some of those changes consist in the alternative routes both protagonists take, but that was to be expected with a remake. Their emotional side, however, shines with the modern technology. 

The game direction choice is on the spot, and the narrative very pleasant, restraining the action to the necessary basis, and not on the ridiculous cheesy stunt-level of trying to surpass Holywood. Cutscenes are worth of a movie with real actors behind each movement, and atmospherically perfect with amazing angles that pushes each scene into waves of vibrant passionate moments.

Visually, [b]Resident Evil 2[/b] stays far away as possible from cheap horror components that have been haunting games for a while now. Low-cost jump scares, complete darkness and the low-tier environments, we’ve all seen in those claimed horror experiences are nothing compared to what we can experience at Raccoon City. Instead, players feel the emptiness progressively interrupted by deadly agents, either the Mr.X or a cleverly placed zombie just slowly walking towards you.

This remake may very well have, some of the most beautiful graphics I’ve seen. Detailed not only at the large scale, but also in small everyday objects. Reflexes on the floors are outstanding, the rain effect on the concrete shines naturally, the contrast of the light against the rain over the broken windows is something stunning to look at. Not even mentioning the condensation effect present in the Greenhouse glass windows! The graphical quality [i]Capcom[/i] achieved is without a doubt a step above the Triple-A experience we’ve got used to, even with other major titles on the market.

Cloths for both Claire and Leon look very realistic, and with time, they become dirty, wet or just increasingly weary. The same treatment was used for zombies, has each zombie is visually detailed, with extreme facial expressions of rage, and pure terror. Blood is now very real, almost distinguished, from fresh to coagulated, when splattered on walls or floors. Gore went back to its fundamental horror-themed principle, of a primordial frightening human complex, in a marvelous way. Zombies are gruesome, but so it’s the ruin of the flesh in its decomposing way, and [i]Capcom[/i] expressed perfectly well the idea of simple zombies being scary, other than just rambling living dead! These are, however, very repetitive, as there’s a few of them that change in cloths but their faces and sizes remain. Other creatures such as Lickers were remade to the core, based on the originals, and are looking better than ever.

Resident Evil came along away, from fixed camera angles, to pretty much redefining third person shooters. This remake though, shows us some of the most flawless third person action we came across, with some cons and pros. Some of the changes might not please every fan, due to the game’s natural adaptive difficulty. This method defines pretty much every action, including the damage inflicted on zombies. Although it’s still a surviving horror, there are damage-critics and damage attributes, that sometimes depend 100% on the game, and not on the player skill, making it a dice roll of chances when trying to accomplish that amazing headshot that splatters a zombie head in two. The difficulty, as well as the critical attributes will define the result. It’s clearly a long way since the original, and we can’t stomp laying zombies either.

This makes [b]Resident Evil 2[/b] an incredible ambiguous game, leaving players debating external possibilities, such as knife damage being affected by the frame rate, or bullets fired under a perfectly fixed crosshair inflicting more damage than firing a gun without proper forming the full reticle first. Automatically, headshots are no longer certain to kill a zombie, unless it’s a shotgun, but regardless, it’s a mechanic that might not please everyone, even though I personally understand the necessity of [i]Capcom[/i] having a constant intensity within the game.
 
This remake is the perfect combination of a third person shooter, with a fluidity of action I’ve personally never seen in before. Hitboxes are extremely well polished, with accurate precisions, especially for playable characters. Field of View can extend the field vision for a wider perspective, without compromising the experience, or spawning bugs. PC version delivers a unique and customized experience, which is fantastic, and almost makes all the console ports we’ve been getting over the years forgettable.

If there’s one thing PC Gamers appreciate is the quality and efforts put into technical settings, and Capcom surely surprised us in the best possible way. With a very Ubisoft-look, the panel for graphical and visual details look fantastic, providing an automatic and in-time perspective over the changes each setting does while being On or Off. Textures, Volumetric Lightning, Anti-Aliasing, all the crucial options are extremely accessible while in the menu, as well as other visual effects such as Chromatic Aberration, that thankfully can just be toggled Off.

Soundtrack unfortunately is not as memorable as the original, but there is still a good effort into sound effects, who mostly serve to follow the game’s intensity, with generic orchestrated events. There is, however, a DLC to expand the experience with the original soundtrack, which should have been included from the very start! The whole sensation of terror, is back, with the genuine feeling that plagues your mind with the unknown at the end of a hallway. The game uses most of the player’s senses, including hearing sounds, to help spot where the danger truly lies in. Soundworks regarding in-game effects is outstanding!

[b]Resident Evil 2 Remake[/b] rolls back the irreplaceable feeling of atmospheric horror, desolation and still resembling extremely well with the original. Alongside the classics, this remake is without a doubt one of the best in the series, and highly recommended for both classic and new fans alike.

So... my first run through was fun, a bit annoying I couldn't actually kill enemies for the most part, but hey, some nice tense RE goodness.

Then I went to go again with Claire and I realised just how messed up everything was...

For starters, before I even got to the police station I saw how I was retreading my same steps as Leon when I expected what was written on the tin in the title menu: "Play Claire's Story", not "Play The Story As Claire".

Previous games in the franchise and the presentation gave me expectations that the game crushed. I haven't finished Claire's "story", from what I understand the only difference is about 25% of the game at the end.

You have a mode for a 2nd play through which supposedly changes some events through the story but... *shrug* once bitten, twice shy as the saying goes.

The next big issue I noticed after I got to the station was that the understanding of how the game works was ruining the fun.

In a traditional RE game you carefully progress and enjoy crafted encounters with enemies as you battle the camera, then you have modern RE games that are third-person, and that's taken away some of the tension as its easier to aim, and I don't feel this has taken away from 'what was' so to speak, but thickened the layer of action that was always there.

That said, in this you're discouraged from fighting zombies. Full stop, no buts, there is literally no reason to fight something unless its in your way or you know it will be soon, because all your basic zombies are bullet sponges.

Allow me to put enemy balance into perspective:
[list]
[*]Dogs - a few head shots.
[*]Licker - a few shot gun shells.
[*]Humble Zombie - Random.
[/list]
I have shot our humble zombies once and they have died permanently and I've shot them 5 times (which is about the max head shots I ever seem to need) only for them to go down and instantly get back up, then go back into a temporary down state until I leave the area and return before it finally dies permanently, as indicated by its head completely exploding, because you see kids, the regular "death" for a zombie is... TEMPORARY! WOOT!

For a bit more detail, shooting zombies in a particular section of the head means nothing, I've hit the same point and had wildly different results, giving them practically random health pools, but you cant afford to be wasting ammo on them or you're going to be stuffed when the next G virus fight comes along.

So hows this actually ruin the game you ask. I found myself just trying to avoid fights because I knew it would be better to have enough ammo later to be able to let loose a little and not have to worry too much about the enemy bosses (and everyone else's) very heavy animations that swing them around, making it difficult to hit, and that takes out a huge portion of the game that, as I explained, was always core to the experience.

I thought "Claire's Story" would be completely different, meaning I wouldn't know where enemies are and where to go or what I'm doing, but that not being the case, you cant help but avoid what you know is just 'in your way', rather than a challenge to dominate.

The last big issue is co op: There is no reason for this... if "Leon's Story" and "Claire's Story" were just that then I would understand that the additional work of adding in a co-op experience for both of the stories might have been no better than playing as a nameless, voiceless, faceless mook like Ada's story in RE6, but that's not what happened, we didn't get a mook partner for a story that was crafted to be SP, we got a co op story that was split apart into two SP stories with not even a mook tag along.

There is NO reason RE2 couldn't have been a co op story like RE5 with that last 25% or so brought together into a single cohesive plot, and short of something sensible like that there's no reason not to make the story a basic co op experience, satisfying many fans expectations, as we saw worked fine in Ada's RE6 story which was otherwise crafted to be SP.

That all said, the first run through was fun for the 8 hours it lasted and if the game didn't pretend there was more value to be had than that initial 8 hours I would praise it but this isn't a traditional RE game, its a sub par modern RE game that cant justify its price tag.

RE2 doesn't bring RE back to its roots, and it detracts from what makes modern RE games enjoyable. RE2 is a casualty of trying to recapture nostalgia.

TL:DR - 8.5/10. An excellent but imperfect recreation of an excellent but imperfect game. 

-Intro-
RE2 was one of my favourite games back in the glory days of the PS1. I must have finished it a dozen times if not more.  
Finally got around to playing the remake.

-Graphics-
Absolutely gorgeous looking, with some of the most transparent and customizable settings in any game to date. Everything from the damage modelling on enemies to the scenery around you looks amazing. If I had one criticism, it would be that the fire effects are a little meh.

-Gameplay-
This is a mash up of RE2, RE4 and RE7 with some of the best aspects of all 3. It's very much in the spirit of the original games, in that you don't have quite enough ammo to kill a lot of things, especially early on - meaning that this is in many ways more of a puzzle game. Insert bullet A into Zom B and run past. Only kill stuff if it's in a place you will be solving puzzles in, is blocking your way or if you have an excess of ammo. 

The core gameplay loop is, like earlier RE games, very much a matter of 'save, explore, reload, explore, die, reload, explore, expend too much ammo, reload, finally get to the next save point, repeat'. Whether this sounds great or annoying will pretty much determine your experience here. This is not (and doesn't have to be) a game for everyone.

Monsters are incredible, with some of the best realised AI to date. Each has it's on behaviour and will sometimes do unexpected things, like open a door or hang out where you don't expect. Much urine was produced in the playing of this game.

However, some design decisions are just baffling. What happened to the giant spiders, crows, moth boss, snakes, bugs etc?  The enemy types there are ...are fairly limited even compared to the previous remake of RE1. 

Certain zones also feel lesser, in particular the lab (remember the tower sized giant plant?). 

The difficulty is going to be the most divisive part of this game - this is a very challenging title, and probably works well that way - being able to blast your way through would have lessened the experience. That said, certain things like Mr. X and the difference where certain monsters spawn (lickers...) can often result in save scumming rather than trying to play better. Mostly due to ammunition.

Ammo is perhaps too limited and I found myself with an abundance of healing items pretty early, meaning that I was less scared of taking damage than of spending ammo. This is bizarre. Zombies are perhaps too tanky (8-10 head shots...what?) especially early on. Perhaps 30% less healing items and 30% more ammo, especially for Leon's Shotgun would have felt better.

-Audio-
This may be the best sounding game ever made. Music is subdued but perfect. Enemies all incorporate sound into how they respond, leading to stealth and action blending together in a lovely, stressful mix. The sounds enemies make, especially Mr X. are also insanely useful strategically. Very cool...although I feel sorry for anyone that can't play this at a reasonable volume.

-Style-
Aside from the missing monsters and somewhat weak lab section, this game feels amazing. After playing, I found myself walking down the passage at night and instinctively tensing up when I heard my own footprints and jumping out of my skin when my wife closed a door. That is a sign of true brilliance. 

Mr X. is occasionally a little irritating in that bad luck can force reloads if he catches you, say, trying to sneak past a licker. But this in turn makes him absolutely terrifying.

-Value-
With 4 modes (2 main stories, 2 B scenarios) as well as plenty of challenges, unlockable modes and similar, there is a lot of game here. I just wish that the lab had been fleshed out more and that the original monsters had been included. Also - this is Capcom and the nickle-and-diming DLC is already a thing.

-Overall-
RE2 is how you should do a remake. I hope that it does well enough that we get RE3 or ...dare I hope, Code Veronica in my lifetime. That said, there is no good reason to exclude about a third of the enemy types from the original game and the difficulty, while pretty fine for me personally, is occasionally frustrating and sometimes rises to the level of irritation. The ammo/healing items balance feels a little out of whack.

Summary:
+ Fantastic game overall
+ Great and highly customizable graphics. 
+ Phenomenal AI 
+ Brilliant audio design
+ Solid boss fights

- Mr X. can feel a little *too* persistent at times
- Gameplay loop may not appeal to everyone
- Poor enemy variety compared to original
- Some zones feel rushed, especially towards the end.

This is a solid game, but those of you calling GOTY already...should probably calm down.

Well, that's not all...I'm writing more of a recommendation on the technical aspects.
There is no in-game benchmark, but a graphics preview, which is useful. The VRAM-USAGE indicator not so much.
The big "issue" or choice is edges/ aliasing vs a very soft image. 
I've tried a lot and I want you to save time on tuning and play the game instead. Believe me, you need a ROCK-SOLID 60 fps on this title. Which at this point is impossible due to the volumetric lighting in some areas, but the game provides a lot of options. Don't use Direct X12 for now! Direct X11 is 20% faster! No visual difference, in my opinion.
Resolution and interlaced image allow to run at 60 fps even on older hardware, so here's my advice:

- Turn on TAA+FXAA
- Turn on ALL of the post-effects, yes, motion blur too
- If you struggle to geta a ROCK-SOLID 60 fps, use the resolution scaling or the interlaced image feature

A lower resolution makes the image less sharp, but the TAA+FXAA makes a 1080p image so soft, it really does not matter as much. Also, chromatic aberation and lens-distortion seem like a bad choice, but I liked the movie-like look. Well implemented effects.
Hope this helped. ENJOY!

I am a stubborn fan of tank controls and fixed camera angles, and have argued (and will continue to argue) for their merits in traditional survival horror.  I'm also a devoted fan of the Resident Evil 1 remaster, and consider it not only the best RE game but one of the most perfect games ever made, period.  So I had, let's say, particular standards going into Resident Evil 2.  I expected I'd probably dislike it, and even if I DID enjoy what i assumed would be RE2 through the lens of RE4, there was no possible way it would be half as good as REmake.

I was wrong.

RE2make is the best RE game in at least a decade.  It doesn't quite surpass the original remaster but it's comfortably within spitting distance.  Almost everything that makes a good survival horror game is here.  You have to be conscious of your resources.  You have to be conscious of your movement.  You have to be conscious of your environment and the routes and shortcuts that snake through it.  It modernizes things that might put new players off, but does so in ways that preserves almost all of the original design.  And not only that, it sprinkles in modern innovations to enhance that design, with Mr. X now serving as a dynamic navigational concern as well as a jumpscare machine, and zombies more free to wander around areas and even follow the player through doors.

It's not quite perfect (the visuals are fairly bland and some effects like screen space reflections are incredibly ugly, and most of the boss battles end up being exercises in frustration, and for some reason zombies remain completely unaffected by being hit in the fact with doors leading to a few cheap grabs).  But it's very very very good.  VERY very very good.  And should be considered required purchasing for anyone who likes the pre-RE4 brand of survival horror, or anyone who wants to get that experience without any tank-control-scented barriers to entry.

-Waiting room safe combo can be found in the observation room (on 1st floor but only way to get to room is stairs on 2nd floor)

Resident Evil 2 is not only one of (if the the) best remakes of a classic that I've ever played, it's one of the best playing games I've dug into in a long time. I was thrilled to come to the RE2 remake after playing so much of the original on PS1. I will say that it's not a shot-for-shot re-release of the original, but I think everything that has changed has been great.

I hadn't played an RE game since possibly RE4 or so, but this game feels like everything I was looking for in a new survival horror game. Every single gameplay element has been thoughtfully designed with a lot of strategy in mind, but also immersive gameplay. The amount of cinematic experiences you get from not having ammo in a certain part and have to make a big risk to get somewhere make for some great stories to share with friends.

I think one of the biggest changes, with a certain villain chasing you around more frequently than expected, make for a more interesting gameplay experience. Hiding in a room and hearing a THUMP THUMP THUMP down the hall pressures you into trying to figure out the best paths to take and best ways to avoid danger. I don't think that change really gets in the way of major puzzle solving and shows up just enough to scare the daylights out of you to great effect.

The graphics and performance are phenomenal. There's so many options for tuning that the game should run on just about any system and it looks amazing. I haven't played a game in a long time that cut seamlessly to a cutscene and everything looked like a pre-rendered movie. It was jaw dropping a lot of the time.

If you're a die hard fan of the original, you're going to absolutely love this game. The great thing about this RE2, though, is that you can enjoy it just as much even if you've never touched a game in the series previously.

Really can't recommend this one enough!

RE2 is one of my favorite games of all time and in my top 10 games of the PS1 era. I played though both scenarios all 4 ways possible, then went for the goal of unlocking all the weapons, costumes and scenarios. Learning when to shot and when to move become an almost meditative experience as you learned which enemies you needed to dodge and which to confront. There was a sort of satisfaction learning when was the best time to use each weapon, I remember the first time I learned the right time to best use the bolt gun for instance, it was a game changer.  On top of that each boss presented a unique the pattern to learn and there was something special about figuring out how to take them down with the least amount of ammo and health lost. If that wasn't enough there was the rich lore and extra items hidden in the background littering every new area, adding depth and breadth to every corner of not just the game but the RE universe. Lets not forget a highly memorable score with tunes that would time and again find themselves in later RE games in one form or another.

	The vast majority of that did not make it into RE2:”Remake.” Although the graphics recreate some areas of RE2 with stunning accuracy, such as the first rooms of the Police station, the rest of feels very “foreign,” I'll explain what I mean by that in a few lines. The score is gone replaced by ambient bumps and groans, which are atmospheric, but not RE2. The use of weapons has been gimped to the point of them almost being useless, the scaling difficulty making it pointless to engage in any combat, which in turn makes combat for a vet RE2 player like me a boring chore. I thought at first “I must be stupid, I must be doing something wrong, but no, I checked online and many other were having the same experience as me, many also frustrated with the way the game is designed to punish the player for doing anything more then running. The surprising part was how many people seemed to be loving the game, a concept I must say is completely lost on me. Even running proves impossible when the Zombies seem to be able to latch onto you from an obscene distance, sometimes in pairs or more. 

I am crest fallen over this, years ago there was a remake of the Classic RE, the original and it was truly something. The people who worked on RE1 remake took what I might liken to someone humming a tune and turned it into a full fledged song with lyrics. RE1 remake was completely faithful to the original in game-play style while building on it to add new mechanics and challenges for old players returning...like coming home and finding some angry red mean people moved in, but I loved every min of it. Not to mention the beautiful interface and remixes of old music. This was my expectation going into RE2 remake and I went on media blackout to avoid spoilers, so I ended up blindsided by RE2 remake.

Most confusing about all the love this game is getting is how people are ok with how much has been pealed off and made into DLC. The memorable soundtrack I mentioned earlier? DLC, not even a remix of the original or an orchestrated version, the original soundtrack for the game is behind an additional pay wall: Come. The ♥♥♥♥. ON.  If this were a Dragon Age remake people would flay EA alive for something like that.

After a few hours and a restart, I just gave up. Like I said above the game feels “forgien” by that I mean it feels less like an RE game and more like Outlast, Amnesia or Slenderman, only could you imagine one of those games with no hiding spots? Harder difficulty doesn't always make for better play as the makers of SOMA found out when people said they enjoyed the game more without the insta-kill monsters, they even released a patch later that allowed players to simply play the game without constantly being harassed and it was a good choice, IMO. 

That was all Capcom had to do here, was offer a choice of “classic” or “remake/reboot” mode.

Now I hear they are considering remaking my favorite of the old RE's, that being Nemesis and if it turns out like this...well not only will it miss the point of the game it will be a crying shame for old fans like me.

Obviously I don't recommend it unless such a mode is patched in but I don't see it happening since the majority seem to be enamored with the game. I'm also not turning comments on for this review because much like BOTW and FO4 we wont be able to have a civil or constructive discourse about this game till the hype dies down in about 6 months to a year.

Would still play the original over this reimagined "RE2" if I had to choose one so, for me, this game failed.

-The balance between new and familiar is what makes a great remake, and the first RE Remake that came out in 2002 perfectly achieved that: they added new rooms and maps, new puzzles, relocated items and enemies, tweaked certain areas, etc. but the overall map layout was still familiar. That didn't happen here. Beyond the amazing recreation of the RPD, the remaining areas of the game have nothing to do with what they were in the original. They didn't expand those areas, they didn't improve them, they outright destroyed the original map layouts and rebuilt them in a totally different way. This game gives a crap about all the areas but the RPD, they are just unrecognizable. Birkin's lab? Nope, that's not here, it's just a whole different place called "NEST" which also happens to be a lab.

-The Zapping System, a key aspect of the original RE2, has been removed. Now this has a "2nd Run" option which is supposed to emulate the B scenarios, but on paper, 1st and 2nd runs in this game aren't even consistent with each other so it's pointless, you still have Claire and Leon fighting exactly the same bosses in exactly the same magically restored places (except for two bosses that are Claire/Leon exclusive respectively) and you have a certain character showing up alive in the 2nd run after seeing that same character clearly die in your 1st run. So the original handled this much better.

-This reimagining also has less enemies than the original game. Infected spiders and crows have been removed. And the Ivies/Poison Ivies have been replaced with lame zombies with a grass re-skin, apparently because devs wanted this game about viruses that turn people into monsters to be "realistic", lmao. And whoever tries to defend this decision by arguing that crows and spiders, or the giant moth, "weren't interesting enemies", well, go play the RE1 Remake and see if that game removed crows, spiders, bees or Neptunes. They didn't. If an enemy "wasn't interesting in the original" then "reimagine" it and make it more interesting. Rearranging and changing things is fine and welcomed, but outright removing enemies that were in the original is total BS.

-And where the F- is the "soundtrack" in this game?... other than bosses, Mr. X, and Hunk/Tofu themes there is no music for pretty much the entire game, so essentially the only way to enjoy the music is by buying the 1998 Soundtrack DLC and playing with that.

Capcom makes a comeback with  one of its greatest survival horror games. I never played the original Resident Evil 2 on the PS1 but I read online that it was one of the most famous video games of all time. Playing the remake, history has definitely repeated itself this time around.

The game is intense and difficult making confrontation with enemies tense and nerve wracking. Items and resources are scarce and the player has to decide on whether to engage them or run from them making it a strategic fight or flight experience. The police department which forms 60% of the main game is a labyrinth to explore but thanks to the engaging map design it makes for an easy exploration. There are puzzle which require key items to solve which are scattered throughout the game map which make for a lot of backtracking to areas already visited which makes you plan your approach with caution due to the presence of zombies everywhere. The game creates a perfect balance between exploration and rewards making the player getting unique items which help them in combat. Hence, the game is not meant to be rushed through but played at its own pace slowly uncovering its secrets. Exploration rewards the players with powerful weapons, powerful ammo types and necessary upgrades to improve your existing weapons. The encounters with zombies are intense and some of the boss fights can be pretty challenging if you have not managed your resource items well. It hits the all the right tones of survival horror making you feel vulnerable and alone and keeps the players on his/her toes the whole time.

One minor gripe which people may have with this game is lack of coherence between the scenarios of the two playable characters in the game, Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield. You can play the game as any one of them and the story of the 2nd character is supposed to run parallel to the one you are playing. This is not the case however, when you finish the game with the 1st character and start another playthrough with the second one, the plot does not intersect and its basically the same story with a different weapon loadout and different items scattered throughout. However, there are some unique areas and also 2 additional boss fights in the 2nd scenario and also you get to unlock the "true ending" of the game. Personally, i didn't find it much of a problem but many people can be ticked off by it. The ideal playthrough according to me would be to start the new game with one character and then do a second run with the other character.

The game is greatly optimized and ran at a constant 60 Fps for me with zero issues. The visuals are great and the lighting and shadows truly create a claustrophobic environment. The character models are done well and the enemy designs are superb and scary. The sound quality is top notch, make sure to turn on the "Binaural" option in the in game sound settings and play with headphones for an intense experience.

A bold and welcome step by Capcom to bring back the survival horror to its full glory back to the gaming community. Fans of the original game, horror fans as well as Resident Evil fans, Capcom has everything for everyone of them this time around and we hope to see a remake of Resident Evil 3 soon. We need these types of games in an oversaturated market where most horror games make you feel invincible like Rambo killing your enemies.

This is the first RE game for me and seriously, what a treat! The best remake of a classic game hands down.

Grapically the game is gorgeous. Somber tight corridors of the police department, night outside with a constant downpour of rain, grime and dirty sewers and the technological facilities of Umbrella: everything looks crisp and atmospheric. Sound adds to that atmosphere splendidly, if sometimes falling off a bit in the voice acting department.

But what keeps the player moving and pushing forward is the gameplay, which consists of action and puzzles complimenting each other in one of the best ways I've seen in gaming. The puzzles are quite simple, but they rely on exploration, so the exploration itself is a puzzle of a bigger scale. While going through the twists and turns of the Raccoon city police department you meet the scares of this game: zombies. The enemies are slow, but twitchy and so is your aim most of the time. And let me tell you, missing is not an option, as zombies can take a lot of lead before actually dying. The clunkiness and slow speed of the encounters make up for great tense moments and after the new enemy types are introduced, your playstyle has to adapt accordingly. The pace, at which new problems are tossed at you is almost perfect as well.

The story itself is pretty basic, but you don't need an intricate story to support such a solid game. Now when you finish one character, do yourself a favor and play the other one to really see, how much faster you flow through the levels. And if you're up for a challenge after that, complete the Hunk gameplay mode, where you have to escape the RPD as quickly as possible.

All in all there's quite a lot of content and some interesting characters to explore. If you can, I recommend playing on hardcore. The only issue I had with the game were the later bosses, which were quite hard to dodge and aim at, but in the end I managed and it felt great.

tl;dr: a love letter to the Resident Evil fans and newcomers alike, try it!

Big fan of the original. Waited for this re-imagining/remake for years. It's a good game; a return to classic survival horror, but with RE4's camera, and RE7's visuals. Seems to run well on higher graphical settings, even with older cards.

WARNING: Years later, Capcom decided to retroactively increase minimal requirements and force everyone to use DX12, which is more unstable and buggy. People who bought the game and can't afford PC upgrades will no longer be able to play. They reversed this later, but still.

Also still stutters when loading assets/maps. RTX3070.

=== CURRENT BUG OR HARDWARE-RELATED ISSUES (as of v1.03) ===

- Stuttering issue seems to have been somewhat fixed. It's not as bad as before, but still happens. Shame I already finished almost everything in the game. They should have fixed it before release.

- Dunno if it's Denuvo related, but my CPU usage is always high when running this game. My PC is outdated but still relatively powerful. The only other game I play that devours my CPU is Monster Hunter World.

- There is a rare bug where the next area can fail to load, and you get stuck in limbo. Loading a save causes permanent black screen, requiring a restart. I've only had this happen once, but I know there are people who get it constantly and can't solve it. No idea if it's fixed with v1.03, but I haven't had it occur since that one time.

- Spark shot effect no longer kills the frame rate. Fixed in v1.03.

- New bug with v1.02: Spark shot can freeze the PC for 5-10 minutes. Also had it freeze once when approaching a blue herb in the lab. No idea what causes it, or if it's been fixed with v1.03.

- Recording this game with OBS has the same skip frames every 2 seconds problem that Monster Hunter World has. Possibly Denuvo related. To fix the problem for both MHW and RE2, I used Streamlabs OBS.


Below is my personal opinion on various aspects of the game. Note that I'm the type that focuses more on negatives. If something doesn't have negatives, then it's probably perfect.


=== PROS ===

- Looks pretty great, if you get the brightness setting correct and set color to Rec. 709 (makes it look a little more vibrant).

- Multiple difficulty levels. Very easy on Assisted, difficult on Standard, and very difficult on Hardcore.

- Good feeling of survival. The game keeps you on your toes, or on the edge of your seat.

- I normally don't 100% games, but the challenge in this game is what kept me motivated.

- Watching others play and react to this game is pretty fun.

- I like that zombies are much tougher than usual.

- Pretty faithful to the original (more than other remakes usually are). As in, they didn't totally ruin it.

- Unlockable option to play as the "original costumes" (although they are a little different), including for Sherry (but not for Ada or any of the other NPCs).

- Includes the extra survivor modes, with some new extras. Even more extras will be coming via free DLC, and presumably paid DLC.


=== CONS ===

- The character commentary is the worst thing by far. They often say extremely obvious or unnecessary things (eg. you approach front door, they exclaim "that must be the front door!"), or their reactions feel strange or over the top. I don't need to hear characters constantly shrieking cusswords or "WHAT TH--?!" from doing mundane stuff like shooting at nearly every zombie. Yelling out aloud when you're trying to sneak around is also terrible. There should really be an option to silence them.

- It's pretty obvious that the B scenario was rushed. It's not much different from A, and there aren't many differences between Leon and Claire's playthroughs. Better than nothing, though. It was interesting enough for me to keep playing.

- Soundtrack in general is nowhere near as good as the original. Thankfully, there's the original soundtrack DLC option, but some of the tracks are in strange places, or some tracks aren't replaced at all. You also cannot select original BGM only, you must also use the original UI SFX, which does not seem to be advertised as such anywhere. So be warned.

- Story and character dialogue, backstories, motivations, personalities and even some character/enemy designs are worse than the original. Many great quotes are completely gone. There are lots of new plotholes and inconsistencies that didn't exist before. It's probably okay if you don't think too hard about it, but it's difficult to ignore because the original was fine.

- On first playthrough, some map layouts, puzzles and events are confusing or vague. Moreso than I recall any in the original being. A few events lead to instant death on failure, but the game is forgiving and autosaves on the first two difficulties.

- There are a few situations where the character being on the left covers the camera and makes it difficult to aim. Particularly in the extra modes.

- Bowgun is gone. Weapons in general feel "weaker", either by strength or by sound effects. It also feels like the weapon upgrades aren't significant enough for how much trouble they are to get, and use up extra slots.

- Edit: Forgot to mention, there are some inconsistencies with the time period. USB sticks (a few years too early), flat screen monitors, a post 2000 car in the parking lot. Stuff like that.

- No Mercenaries mode. There will be more stuff added later, but I expect the good stuff will be paid DLC.

- Torn on whether this should be a pro or con, but aiming for zombie legs is ridiculously effective, and makes the game feel more like Dead Space.

- There are various places where random luck can really screw you over, and you can't do much about it. Only really a problem on Hardcore (you can get by on the other difficulties) and the extra survivor modes. For example, at the start of B scenario on Hardcore, zombies sometimes group together to block the pathway. Sometimes they spread out and are easy to run past. Dogs in particular are near impossible to reliably avoid. Similarly, bosses can sometimes chain deadly attacks (eg. grabs) in a row.

- There's one place in particular where the stalker enemy can really screw over players. It's almost always guaranteed that it will show up in that specific place, which can prevent people from progressing. There are ways around it (eg. stun him) that I'm not sure are immediately obvious to new players.

- The extra costumes aren't great (in my opinion). Costumes in the other Resident Evil games are far superior. I think I probably should have just bought the soundtrack, instead of the deluxe edition.

- Lack of disable vignette option. Needed to use an external program to remove it. Looks a lot better without, to be honest.


=== CONCLUSION ===

There are people who are saying this game isn't worth the money because speedrunners are beating it in 1 hour. I'd like those people to find someone who beat this game in less than an hour on first try. Because that's very unlikely, even on easiest difficulty.

My first clear was 8 hours, and then I still had to play through the other character and scenarios (3-5 hours each). Then there are the extra modes, which take around 10 minutes per clear, and several attempts to succeed. That's plenty of gameplay time. If you rush through a game and don't take time to enjoy it, that's not really the game's fault.

Maybe I'm the minority, but I'd rather play a short game that's intensely good from start to finish, than a 60 hour game with lots of pointless time-wasting and moving from point A to B. In fact, it seems this game took me around 60 hours to complete all the achievements. I usually don't bother with achievements.

Anyway, as I said, I think it's a good game, despite the negatives. I do recommend it, and would really like to see more "classic survival horror" type games like this one. If Capcom is reading this: a Dino Crisis remake would be nice.

[h1][b]Review of Resident Evil 2 PC Edition[/b][/h1]


   [b]tl;dr[/b]:  Resident Evil 2 Remake is a beautifully done game in its own right, adding gameplay features from across the franchise to create an amazing and immersive experience that will have you backtracking to look at the main hall again and again.  9/10 Highly recommended whether you love Resident Evil or this is your first Capcom game.  If you’re listening Capcom please please please do this for Dino Crisis, I’ll buy many copies of it!


[h1]Gameplay -[/h1]

   For those of you who haven’t followed this release closely, this remake of Resident Evil 2 is a reimagining of the original Resident Evil 2 from 1998.  I use the word “reimagining” strongly because the RE2 veterans will find that some areas of the game have been redesigned, or just added to lengthen the play time of the story.  Some enemies and areas were also removed to help players with particularly frustrating or nonsensical sections, and keep players moving through the game.

   With that said however, much of the game was left faithfully accurate to the original with a slight change from the Resident Evil 1 remake released a few years ago.  While Resident Evil 1 changed next to nothing from the original game, Resident Evil 2 uses the over the shoulder camera made famous by Resident Evil 4.  While some long time Resident Evil fans will find this irritating or unfaithful as a remake, I believe it allows players the ability to explore the infamous RPD from a whole new perspective, taking in the amazing visuals attainable on next generation hardware.

   Players familiar with the over the shoulder perspective used in the 4th and 5th Resident Evil installments will feel comfortable with the camera in Resident Evil 2, as it functions much the same.  Enemies in this remake are a large highlight of this release, with Capcom’s new zombie degradation system on full display.  Now, shotgun shells can cut zombies clean in half, and handgun rounds can be used to slowly chip away at a zombie, removing legs, arms, and other parts to disable enemies in the best way you see fit.


[h1]Sound -[/h1]

   The sound quality in this remake is bar setting for games to come.  While I might not be able to explain how it works, Resident Evil 2 uses a real-time Binaural System, which creates some of the best and gripping sound quality I have experienced to date in a horror game.  The looming sounds of Mr. X will quickly create dread at every corner and hearing a licker long before you see it can put ice in your veins.  If possible, I highly recommend playing with a quality pair of headphones.


[h1]Characters / Story -[/h1]

   For players returning to Resident Evil 2 versus players starting the story for the first time, much of the story will feel familiar.  Experiencing all the events of the original game in stunning modern age visuals is easily worth it.  If you are new to the story of Resident Evil 2, you will have a great time uncovering the mysteries for the first time, from Leon and Claire’s perspective, each with their own unique situations that arise during the game.  Regardless if you are new or returning, I highly recommended purchasing this game to experience the love that Capcom has put into this remake.


[h1]Replay Value -[/h1]

   Resident Evil 2 encourages its players to go back and experience the story line multiple times from multiple perspectives and encouraging the player to do so with tangible awards.  Unlike many games today that set improbable goals with achievements to encourage players to go back and play the game for a second or third time to unlock these achievements, Resident Evil 2 brings back the much more rewarding method of older games by allowing you to unlock many different in game items that are usable in your subsequent playthroughs.  

   After finishing the game for the first time, you will unlock the 2nd playthrough mode, which gives you the complete story from the other characters perspective.  Once you have beaten these modes, you can play through and try to achieve the S rank to unlock multiple different unlimited ammo weapons to use freely after they have been unlocked.  In my opinion, this is what more game developers should do these days, giving players a strong motivation to complete the game again for wacky or overpowered unlockable items.


[h1]UI Usability -[/h1]

   The User Interface will feel extremely familiar to players of Resident Evil 7.  Resident Evil 2 is built on the Resident Evil engine, which was created for Resident Evil 7, and not much was changed about the UI layout.  While this isn’t necessarily a bad thing, there is very little that has changed with inventory space, combining and examining items, or key items.  The UI functions very smoothly, with no lag or hang ups and generally performs optimally.  While the interface was not changed much at all, I think it lends itself to this latest Resident Evil well.


[h1]Final Thoughts -[/h1]

   This reimagining of Resident Evil 2 captures the magic of the original with all of Capcom’s love and creativeness in every corner of this game.  The gameplay will easily hook you and have you on your third and fourth playthrough before you know it.  The final score that I will give Resident Evil 2 is a 9/10 and only because some of the animations of enemies grabbing you can become troublesome at points, but overall can be overcome by better planning and execution.  I highly recommend purchasing this for yourself, your friends, and your family so everyone you know can experience this great remake.

[b]Resident Evil 2 Remake manages to combine both old school resident evil and the new school that started with RE4 into a perfect mish-mash of the two, managing to do what very few long running franchises pull off which is getting both old school and new fans happy with a new installment.[/b]

Just like old Resi games, you gotta plan out your routs, pick which areas to clear out and which not, make sure not to spend to much ammo, dodge enemies as much as you can, solve puzzles that make you question the sanity of the person that designed this place that supposedly people worked and lived in and of course unload all your ammo that you stocked up into the final boss at the end.

The new school elements to the game is just the camera,controls and gun play, it's not exactly like any of the Resis from RE4 to 6, as you can actually aim and move around which was not possible in 4 and 5 but you cannot do those silly dive moves and roll around on the ground like in that terrible 6th installment, so it's a good actual middle ground balance that still works well in a slower paced survival horror game.

Since there's no more door loading scenes and everything is loaded in from the get go, zombies and other enemies can now travel through rooms, so just because you left that room that was filled to the brim with zombies, doesn't mean you're safe, they can knock that door open and still get you in the other room. However, an old school element to the game is that the safe rooms where you can manually save do still function as safe havens , enemies cannot enter them at all just like in the older Resi games, so they're great places to calm down, plan ahead and have a lil' cry in the corner as you hear Mr.X stomping around in the hallways near you.

The zapping system from RE2 also returns, so there's once again Leon A,B and Claire A,B scenarios, however sadly it's not as impressive as in the original. Scenario A and B are fairly different but when you go play them again with switched characters you'll notice it doesn't change much of the key story elements depending on the character on the scenario, [a lil spoiler here for the original RE2]  in the original RE2 if you played Leon A, Ada would for an example get shot and fall off a bridge [Cannon] while in Leon B she would instead get her rear kicked by Mr.X during a big fight and die in Leon's hands instead, this doesn't happen in the Remake, so instead of having 4 campaigns to do like the original, you technically only have two this time with an additional two that just changes up some of the cut scenes and dialog flavor a bit but not the actual story events all that much. It's honestly the only kinda disappointing aspect of the remake as the rest of the game is near perfect really.

Visually the game looks outstanding but not perfect, currently the screen space reflections in the game are poorly implemented and have a lot of visual noise and artifacting, Capcom hasn't commented about this issue at all yet so it seems they simply did a bit of a poor job implementing screen space reflections. Optimization is god like, iv'e seen reports of low end PCs running the game without much any trouble and still getting pretty nice visuals, my mid range Ryzen 1600 OCed @ 3.8 Ghz and AMD RX 580 8GB runs the game on Max in 1080 res [apart from shadows, those are High] and i have an average of 90 to 100 fps, feels really damn smooth to play it, no stutters, no bad frame pacing, smooth as frekin' butter.

[h1]Bottom line : [/h1]
Game is freaking outstanding, a treat for both old school survival horror fans and newcomers alike. Worth every cent i payed for, even full priced. I cannot wait for the RE3 Remake next.
