As for puzzles they are not hard, but can be a pain in the ass to complete at times depending on how well you manage your ammo, and of course yourself. Boss Fights can be considered in the same sense really.

That is honestly why I recommend this game, really I think this is one game to at least try. Even if you have never played the first one you can get away with a lot since not much is needed to go off of to understand the story.

If you do get this game I HGIHLY suggest playing on hardcore, sure it is a pain in the ass. Hardcore says what it means in a way. Yeah the zombies take more to go down but not by much and normally you'll be trying to save ammo for the big guys anyway. As for no autosaving really it is not an issue at all you get Ink Ribbions from all over they may only come with one or two each pick up but it is not that bad. Typewritters are common before most encounters and generally have a safe box next to them so saving is not a problem in any way. Hardcore feels right and it goes along with what I was saying above you be using most things quite often and running a lot. Hardcore really only gets hard depending on how you play, you will get enough ammo to fight just about everything you would need to, but when it comes to those boss fights having certain ammo and a good amount of it could prove useful, sub weapons can save you life, and a herb mixture of G+R+B has far more value than any other healing item in the game. Your peformance impacts how well you do in this mode, and to me that is what truely makes this game a great survival horror game.

Before I end this please understand I have not touched the easier difficulties, nor do I intend to. This is ignorant in my part, but I truly do recommand this game. Even if you play on the easier difficulties, you may have the same things happen as I had happen on hardcore. Just I would not know.

Resident Evil 2 is one of the best examples on how to properly remake a 20 year old classic bestselling game, by embracing what worked back in the day, see what could be improved and also adding a lot, and I mean really a lot, of new stuff so it still feels interesting and fresh, but also leaving the player with a feeling of familiarity, especially if one has played the original game.

The RE Engine has proven to be very well performing on its previous game, RE 7, and this time around in RE 2 it really shines. We have a very nice Physically Based Rendered assortment of materials and shaders, with a lot of wet surfaces that look amazing, and performance is really, really good on a wide array of PC configurations, with a decent level of scalability, especially on the GPU side of things. The engine seems to make decent usage of 4-6 core CPUs, but it’s usually GPU limited, which normally is the ideal situation when it comes to good looking PC games.

The amount of customizable settings we have in this PC version of the game is also immense, from FOV adjustments to nice mouse sensitivity sliders for camera and aim modes (although there is a slight amount of negative acceleration, very little), and keybinds are mostly fully customizable with the exception of a couple of hardcoded keys like ENTER or DEL; I am left handed, so I use the right side of the keyboard a lot, around the arrow keys (used for movement), so I was able to play with no issues with my usual left handed binds, minus DEL and ENTER but the game doesn’t really need so many keys, so I managed. Gamepad works fine in the game, you can walk slower with it than with the keyboard, in case you need a little more immersion, but it’s not mandatory. There’s this bug I guess that makes it impossible to open doors when in aiming mode, walking with the keyboard, while you can when using the gamepad, but it’s not game breaking and you can still walk normally without aiming, open it a little, then switch to aim mode and It’ll get pushed slowly if you want, so no big deal there either.

An important thing to note about settings is Brightness calibration, you must abolutely do the steps to calibrate this, if you want the game to look as the developers intended, otherwise it'll have this grey'ish haze all over the screen, and dark zones won't look good enough. If you cannot complete the third step on the calibration menu (make the left typewriter disappear), that means you either didn't select the proper MIn/Max levels earlier, or your screen needs some serious tuning and adjusting of brightness and gamma, so better get on that then too.

And then we have the new gameplay mechanics, like knives and other sub-weapons, the new puzzles and the revamp of old classic ones, which will certainly make you smile, and of course the new way of doing the classic A/B runs, in this case called “2nd run”, which like the original game, it will tell us the story from the other character’s perspective, around the same time the other character did his/her stuff, more or less, with some clever variations added so the gameplay feels balanced but still challenging enough. In summary, to fully complete the story, we still need to do both scenarios, whether Leon first / Claire second, or vice versa…that’s your choice. Completionists will want to do all four of them, and the game records all these different combinations so yeah, it’s nice that the feature is still there, albeit a bit different.

Of course, the main change from the original, is the camera and I have to say it really fits this new imagining of the game, it simply works well, really well actually and in a fully rendered 3D world with lots of cool materials and very detailed enemies to mutilate and shoot, it would've been bad if the old fixed camera was used, or the tank controls too, which usually work well together but not so much when separated like it was the case in RE 4.


Overall this game feels like a very solid GOTY candidate so early in the year, which is amazing. This game has become one of my favorite RE games of all time, because it demonstrates that the survival horror genre, which the original games were paragon of, can still be brought to modern platforms, with improved techniques, amazing sound design (and boy, is the sound design great here, it even has Dolby Atmos and Binaural…really great), and new ways of solving old puzzles or see them reimagined.

This game is really, really good, it’s not too long if you know what you’re doing, but if you take your time on your first runs it can vary between 6 and 10 hours. Much like the original, it can also be done in a speed run fashion, more or less, or you can take your time and enjoy the amazing graphics and impressive animation and voice acting, on all the languages I checked (English, Spanish and Japanese) the voices are superb, and the facial expressions and animations of the characters are really well synched and done, you can actually feel the emotions on their faces, from the grim situation they’re all living in this game. Amazing job from Capcom there, truly.

I am ready for more Resident Games like this, Capcom, thank you for the great job on this game, made for the fans of survival horror, and for the gamers in general. Capcom, you did it, this is how you remake a game, period.

Do you know that feeling you get when you replay a game that you thought was amazing and cutting edge 20 years ago but compared to modern standards the controls are clunky, the graphics and cutscenes cringy, and the gameplay dated?  Yeah you won't be getting that feeling here.  Not by a long shot.

I just finished Re2 for the first time and wow, what a game! There's so much praise I could heap on this game, and I will start with Leon who I played with. This makes him very likeable, as he comes across as the underdog, instead of the Rambo-esque character he was in previous games that made cocky remarks in the face of incredible danger.

This cocky personality made sense in previous games because Leon had faced so much danger and succeeded, but this game does a great job of showing you fear stemming from the inexperience that Leon has.

He actually expressed fear and shock in the game which I loved. It made it seem like he really was seeing this crazy stuff for the first time. Leon is very down to earth in this game. At one point towards the end, the Tyrant comes back after you have just fought another giant monster and Leons reaction is basically "wtf". This caused me to laugh and relate to how he is feeling because it's the same reaction I had.

I am low health, just fought plenty of big scaries and then this guy shows up again. WTF.

The game also looks beautiful and even the nasty bits are greatly detailed. It's fun to shoot zombies and see their grotesquely detailed faces get further distorted with every bullet you shoot into it.

And zombies are scary again! No longer do single headshots take them out like we've seen in previous RE canon, but they can take multiple shots to the dome and they will just keep chasing you. So being conservative with your ammo is a must, especially if you're playing on the harder difficulty.

I could say a lot more but I'll end it there. I highly recommend this game to any survival horror fans. 9/10

Let me start by saying that I am a huge fan of the Resident Evil series. I've been playing these games as long as I can remember. I've played through all the old resident evil games (except the revalations games) many many times (and yes, that includes the Outbreak games as well as Dead Aim). 

So, with that in mind, it's safe to say that I know Resident Evil. I came into this one with high hopes. Like many of you, I loved the original release of RE2, and when I heard they were actually remaking this game, I did something very out of character for myself; I preordered the damn thing without a second thought. I realize that at the time of writing this review, the game has been out for less than two days, but I cannot stress this enough. BUY THIS GAME. If you like tense atmospheric horror, this is certainly the game for you. This is survival horror done right. My first playthrough, I struggled with having enough ammo for my guns, and it was great. They pretty much took the feel that RE7 had, and married it just right with the setting of RE2. 

Graphically, it's stunning. My rig runs a GTX 1060 3GB GPU, and while I can't push it with all dials cranked up to 11, it still looks great, save for one cutscene where Leon and Claire meet with a chain-link fence between them (the fence's textures were really low quality, while everything else looked extra detailed. It was a bit jarring). Other than that, I don't have too many other complaints about the graphics. 

Another nitpick that I have was that some of the facial animations outside of cutscenes (specifically when Claire was talking) the faces looked a bit unnatural or their lips weren't synced to the dialogue. I know RE7 had some of these similar issues as well. 

Finally, performace-wise, with the settings I have the game run on, I'm able to get a steady 60 fps, with some occasional framerate drops during certain animations. For example, when zombies get up off the ground in the distance, they seem more jerky than if I were up closer (this has more to do with my hardware than the game itself. If any of you run a more powerful gpu and still experience this small issue, please feel free to comment on it).

All in all, like I said at the beginning. BUY THIS GAME. It's well worth the asking price of $60. If you're still on the fence about it, at least wait until it goes on sale. This is a game you do not want to miss.

I come from Resident Evil 4, one of my favorite games and probably the singleplayer game I've ever enjoyed the most, that and Dead Space 2. I haven't played much of the games prior to RE4 but I did play a fair bit of Resident Evil 5/6. 

With that knowledge going in, here's my review:

My thoughts: One of the things this remake does well is catch that essence of the initial Resident Evil games, that claustrophobic, horror, resource scarcity feeling, whereas the later RE's kind of focused on action, killing zombies, and moreso being aggressive and thriving as opposed to surviving. "Survivor/Horror" is a great way to describe this game, because thats what it is, I'm playing on the normal difficulty and I'm feeling this game not pulling punches in the resource scarcity department, I'm not playing most optimally in my play-through, and if I had, I probably would have a few more bullets left, but I've had it more than once where I've had literally NOTHING to fight the enemy, making those choices on whether to fight, run, or sneak by have a good impact on the game and your future choices, which I love. 

Story: Leon Scott Kennedy(in my eyes) is a badass, from the previous RE games to the RE animated movies, this guy is what male protagonists are made for, these ultimate heroes who are unstoppable and show no fear in the face of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ anything, in RE2 though, this is his beginning, he's just becoming that motif, he's new to his job and he has no idea what's going on, some brownie points for the devs because Leon sometimes when you're fighting mouths off some motivation for himself ie "You got this" or "I can do this". Its really cool to see his beginning and watching him develop into a strong character, he meets some new characters along the way as well as seeing some easter eggs for other parts of the RE universe. The story isn't mind blowing, but it definitely makes me feel like im inside the RE universe, I'd give the story a 6/10.

Graphics: ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ tight af, the facials of the game are great and there's a bunch of detail into the level design, do recommend. Give'em a 9/10.

Gameplay: ♥♥♥♥ your ammo and ♥♥♥♥ your health bar, 3 hits and you die. Shooting/Melee is smooth and fun to use, though it gets a bit grindy because the zombies pretty much never ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ die, to quote a character in the game: "Nothing down here ever stays dead". Camera is nice and smooth. Unlike RE5 and earlier, you can actually move while aiming your gun! Yay! Your choices matter, so make them wisely. Plan out where you're going and how you're going to do it if you want to conserve resources for the inevitable future ♥♥♥♥-up you'll do. 8/10.

I recommend the ♥♥♥♥ out of this game, its so nice to continue to see single-player story driven games come out that are pleasing to the eye and mind. I'm almost done my playthrough of Leons story and I have around 5-6 hours of game time, there's also a playthrough for Claire, which I cannot wait to sink my teeth into.

This 2019 remake of the 1998 original reimagines the story and gameplay quite well. After the disaster that was Resident Evil 6, Capcom created Resident Evil 7: Biohazard with the new RE engine. RE7 was the biggest step in the right direction for Capcom with the Resident Evil series. They brought back the RE engine to remake RE2 (2019), giving it the realism that it deserves.

A lot of people out there are upset that CAPCOM did not implement fixed camera angles like they did with the original Resident Evil back in 2002. I completely understand why CAPCOM did this. You cannot implement fixed camera angles for a AAA title in 2019. Instead, RE2 (2019) uses a 3D, over the shoulder camera style similar to RE6 and RE: Revelations 2. 

If I listed PROs to this game, I would be here all day. I do have to say that I love how RE2 (2019) has several "easter eggs" and callbacks to the original RE2 (1998), such as certain places of business (Arukas), certain grafitti, little jabs here and there, and a certain photo that you discover in the STARS Captain's office.

If I had to list CONS:
I noticed a lot of the police cars are missing decals on them. They are just black and white with a lightbar on top. Also, the sherrif's car, badge, and uniform simply says SHERIFF county. Couldn't they specify a perticular county? Arklay County? Raccoon County? These couple things are nitpicky of me and do not dent the game the least bit.

Are you on the fence about this remake ruining your childhood nostalgia? Yes? Then this review is for you!

You know how all remakes, squels, or prequels in any kind of content have to tiptoe that line of new vs old?
The only kind of stigma that can be overcome by people who have a genuine passion for what it is they're doing.
What do we keep? What do we add? Does all of this flow with the groundwork that has already been laid?
Having completed the hardcore difficulty, I can say with absolute confidence that Capcom not only understands the franchise and their fan base, but also what it means to make good games.

Have you always wondered EXACTLY what the 50 different options for optimizing graphics settings do and how they affect the overall visual fidelity of the game? Have you ever wondered just how demanding these options are on your GPU? Never fear; Capcom has you covered. By integrating images that reflect your graphics settings in real time, you can actually make a confident decision to balance how good you want your game to look vs performance.
When the settings menus impress you, you know that you're in for a treat.

The HUD screams of easy readability & simplicity in all aspects.
They want you to remember that the menu is still a safe place (momentarily), but they also don't want you to forget your environment; even if it means that you're still staring at the zombie that's about to bite your face off.

You can tell that they spent MAJOR time refinining the control scheme for PC.
I recall some games in recent memory with less than refined control schemes (AHEM... RE6).
I was in disbelief by how bad AAA games could feel on a PC.
At no point in my game play did I ever question my actions or movements.
When you don't have to think about how the game actually plays, then you know the controls are on point.

As for the graphical fidelity... well... let's just say that when we played this game back in 98, the horrors we experienced and the nightmares we had... even if we were blowing up polygon brains, this remake is exactly what they looked like in our imaginations. The new RE engine allowed the team to create what is likely the most photorealistic video game to date. If the original team had this game engine back in 98, this is the game they would have made.

As for the game itself (while remaining as ambiguous & spoiler free as possible):
You're going to find yourself saying ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ more than you'd like to admit.
You're going to find yourself saying I REMEMBER THAT more times than you expected.
You're going to find yourself in a constant state of awe and total immersion.

You want it easy? They got you covered.
You want a real challenge? They also got you covered.
From beginning to end you will be on edge.
Resources are scarce. The 2 shots are real.

If there was a way to get it right, Capcom did just that.
Whether they remake the rest of the classics, or move on to 8, I have absolute confidence that Capcom now remembers what this franchise stands for.

This game is a dream made reality. We made enough noise and it finally happened. It REALLY happened.
Let's keep the momentum going team. I know our community can make dreams come true.

The 1998 version has scenarios A & B which are different but correlated to the plot.  In the remake, the scenarios are not significantly different and a lot of things make no sense.  For example, when William G-Type 2 kills Mr. X in Claire's scenario A, he still comes as a Boss as a transformed Tyrant in Leon's scenario B;  in 1998's Leon's scenario B, Ada gets thrown by Mr. X and sustains a fatal injury on her waist that's a part of the real canon as shown in the epilogue of Resident Evil 3 where Ada looks at her scar on her waist caused from being thrown by Mr. X.  But in this remake, whether scenario A or B, she falls to her "so called" death instead.  I feel this remake could've been a whole lot better if they still kept a lot of the original elements while adding and enhancing the gameplay like they did with Resident Evil 1 remake.  What made RE1 remake such a big success was they stayed true to the originality of the PS1 version while adding more elements to the remake version like Lisa Trevor, highly enhanced graphics, the mansion structure still being original while adding additional rooms and puzzles, etc.  In this RE2 Remake, the plot line is messed up, it has no correlation to the original canon; some parts of the gameplay is unrealistic (for example, a zombie is outside the window trying to break in, but you can't shoot it through the window before it can break in; or a zombie is behind a door with a glass window and you can't shoot through the glass before it breaks in; etc).  Overall, the environment and character designs are well done and highly detailed.  Gameplay is overall great, just a few flaws as mentioned earlier.  However, I hope Capcom remakes RE3: Nemesis nonetheless since the majority of the audience still have a general positive outlook with RE2 Remake.  Don't mind me in my harsh critique :P

Capcom's efforts in bringing back the horror elements many longtimers of the series have yearned for, are present in this game. The narrative this time around is a lot better with the dialogue being more convincing than the original. The zombies aren't exactly pushovers either, as they don't just come back once, but multiple times. The visuals are incredibly photorealistic too if your a graphic nut. While the layouts have changed a little here and there, most of the game stays consistent to it's original design, as well as some of the puzzles we remember back in the day.

To sum this up simply, I'll put it this way:

RE:7 + RE:2 (1998) = RE:2 (2019)

Even to those who've never played any of the series, it's really worth checking out. There's a demo too, so if you still find yourself sitting on the fence on it, no money's spent and don't have to rustle feathers to get it back.

The Resident Evil franchise isn’t short on beloved entries (or maligned ones, to be fair) but Resident Evil 2 in particular has stuck in gamers’ consciousness as a series highlight.

That’s why it’s no real surprise that Capcom decided to give it the remake treatment, rebuilding the game from the ground up in Resident Evil 7’s engine. I've spent the weekend screaming from my chair at the Resident Evil 2 remake, playing through by Claire and Leon's campaigns to find out what's new, what's old, and why the hell the Tyrant won't just leave me alone.

The Resident Evil 2 remake comes with the usual choice between a standard edition and a deluxe version, which includes a few alternative costumes and the brilliant option to play with the original soundtrack.

Including fan service options like the original soundtrack might suggest that this is a slavish reproduction of the 1998 original, but this isn't quite so faithful. Sure, like the original game this features separate campaigns for the game’s two protagonists, Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield, as they fight through the overrun Raccoon City, but each of those stories has been tweaked and improved, to both keep things fresh for returning players and improve the appeal for newer victims.

Take the Kendo Gun Shop for example. Anyone with fond memories of the original may be disappointed to run through the early game without setting foot in the store. But without giving anything away, the store (and its owner) pop up later in the story, and that new context is used to tweak the tone and content of the scene to better suit the new story.

Those kinds of changes have been made throughout the game, in ways both big and small. From the order you meet certain characters, to the way boss fights play out, even down to the nature of the story's MacGuffins, it's clear that every detail of the game - mechanics, music, story and more - has been questioned and considered.


None of which is to say that it's all new, and in fact you might be surprised by some of what's been left behind. You'll still heal with herbs, save at typewriters, and spend at least half of your playtime battling with the nostalgically clunky inventory system.

Those typewriters are now backed up by frequent autosaves though, and you'll now be able to focus on fighting the undead without clashing with the controls: yup, the much maligned tank controls are gone in favour of the over-the-shoulder camera and responsive controls of Resident Evil 4.

I have a soft spot for the old Resi system, which made up in tension and claustrophobia what it lost in accessibility. The fixed camera angles always held the possibility of something or other lurking just out of sight, and the fear was heightened thanks to the knowledge that just trying to turn around and run away would probably take you about half a minute.

Still, there's a balance here, and this remake feels just as grounded in horror as 2017's Resident Evil 7, rather than a return to the action games of the series' nadir. Claire and Leon are still slow - agonisingly so when you're trying to sprint down a corridor to the percussive rhythm of the Tyrant's footsteps behind you - ammo is tight, and zombies are plentiful. Not in a 'kill them all!' way, but in the proper 'panic and run and hope' because there are way too many of them to manage kind of way.

Shiny new graphics add realism to the horror, but as always it's the enhanced audio that really matters: you begin to obsess about every creak and footstep, the pounds and shrieks of the soundtrack blurring together with the creatures that stalk the police station, sewers and streets of the city.

The graphics do come into their own too though. Aside from adding a lush sheen to the whole game, they bring entirely new life to the characters with facial animations that are another step up from Resident Evil 7. It's let down a bit by the voice acting - Capcom has drawn recent criticism for the decision to save money with non-union actors, rather than reuniting the original cast - but hammy vocals are as much a staple of Resident Evil as confusingly themed keys, so it's easy to forgive in the end.

Much was made ahead of release of the developers' suggestion that the remake would no longer feature four different versions of the campaign, but it looks like that was either a case of mistranslation or something changed. Once again you have the choice to play through once as Leon or Claire - with the same basic puzzles, but different weapon options and cut scenes - and completing the game once then unlocks the 'Second Run' option, a remixed campaign that lets you experience the events of the original playthrough from the other character's perspective.

That means you'll at least want to play through the game twice - doing the second run with the other character offers you new weapons, puzzles, story sequences, and more - while the hardcore could play through four times or more, so the game's not short of replayability. Extra game modes - where you play as fan-favourites Hunk and, uh, Tofu - also appear, so there's plenty to do.


Verdict
If there's one thing that's clear about Resident Evil 2, it's that it's a labour of love. Not the kind of obsessive love that results in remakes unchanged apart from graphics, but instead a love that wants to see this classic reborn at its absolute best - with whatever changes it takes to achieve that.

No doubt some tweaks will be divisive. There are already fans lamenting the loss of tank controls; the plot changes will ignite a whole new wave of arguments about the canon; and expect a lot of people asking why they couldn't just improve the bloody inventory.

But broadly, this is a remake done right. It's been modernised without feeling modern - you will remain acutely aware that this was a game first designed in the late '90s - built primarily for the fans, while welcoming new players so long as they're willing to meet it in the middle.
A true horror experience for the modern age. 10/10

This game alone makes up for all of controversies and sh*t that 2018 threw in our faces. 

Gaming is still alive. 

Big studios are still capable of producing a high-quality single-player experiences with zero controversies, no significant content being held hostage as day-1 DLC (we're not so cheap to b*tch about a couple of skins in premium edition, right?), with butter-smooth launch (just completed my first run with 0 bugs) and a great, polished PC port.

*SPOILER FREE*

As for game itself... It's a Third-person Action game with a stron emphasis on solving puzzles. 

Graphics, animations, sound design - everything is of very high quality, which can easily be looked up in any video (including those on Steam Store). Not much sense in wasting time describing those.
I'd only like to mention cool procedual gore mechanics - apart from obvious ability to blow off zombie's limbs (you can literally reduce them to an immobile, but still "alive" nugget), there is also dynamic wound depth mechanic - repeatedly shooting Zeds in the same spot will eventually expose yellowish bones (including jaws when shooting faces). Very cool!

The challenge - I completed my first run on Normal and I don't regret it. The game gives you just enough resourses to survive and reach your next target destination. Even at times when you are carrying a formidable arsenal with some spare ammo and feel pretty safe and confident, game finds a way to reduce you to a cowering survivor with half of a pistol clip and shaky hands - the only resource I was able to stockpile was medicine (ended my game with like 5 GRB mixes and 2 sprays in my locker).

At some parts of your story you will have to move fast - and while there is no arbitrary unexplained timer (apart from one part of a game when it's logical), sometimes you will be forced to advance or borrow some time for slower playstile by expending your resources. 
I realise that paragraph above is written somewhat choppy, but it's done specifically to avoid spoilers. Point is - if you are ABSOLUTELY ALLERGIC to any kind of haste and timeframes, some parts of the story will stress you out or even completely botch your playthrough - if during these sections you move REALLY slow and expend too much resources pushing against unspoiled threat.
I personally enjoyed the change of pace - even when it almost costed me a rollback to 1-hour ago save due to aforementioned mismanagement of resources.

The story - well, if you're familiar with RE universe, you won't be surprised too much. It's well-written, well-narrated and plays organically with no obvious holes in the plot that will make you scratch your head. 
No knowledge from RE1 is needed to enjoy this story. Knowing the lore of RE1 will open up small little references here and there, but it's nothing crucial.

The puzzles are just complex enough to cause little trouble for an adult (or elder teen) player. And while there is some backtracking with all the keys and puzzle pieces, I didn't mind it at all - all locations are well-crafted and beautiful, and still hold the aftermath of battles you had in them. And modern UI and map design will help you keep track of everything, eliminating the need to memorize a lot of stuff and constantly having a notebook and a pencil at ready.

All in all - a great mix of action, puzzles and resource\inventory management with sprinkles of undead and monster spices, served on a plate of really good narrative. When I was done with my Leon playthrough I had an urge to instantly start a second playthrough as a girl - but decided to drop a review. 

Which leads me to my last point - replayability. At least one more playthrough is mandatory to experience the full story from both characters. But if you enjoyed the game so much you don't want to stop - there are always a higher difficulty, score system and a handful of really well-crafted challenges for you to gring through (no your average and boring "kill 100 zombies with grenades")

All in all - a solid 10\10 for me. I really can't think of a single drawback that wouldn't be too subjective for my own taste (like somewhat too bullet-spongy zombies and extremely brittle combat knives). 
It's a strong GOTY contender and I urge everyone to vote with your wallets, grab this beauty at full price and send a message to EA, Activision and (sadly) Bethesda that THIS IS HOW YOU DO A GAME IN 2019.

♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, where to start? This is the remaster to end all other remasters. Capcom is back at it again to show these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ how to run a triple AAA title. Personally speaking, I do not care for AAA titles, especially horror. They always seem to be bogged down by needless mechanics and endless jumpscares. Resident Evil 2, however, does not give a ♥♥♥♥ about my opinion and instead decides to blow every other game developer out of the water.

PROS:
-Visually speaking, it's a masterpiece. On par with RDR2, this game graphically feels like the next step for video games.
-Has an incredible soundtrack, with the option of the retro soundtrack for those who purchase the Deluxe Edition. [spoiler] The music that plays when being chased by Mr. X is terrifying in particular. [/spoiler] 
-It's very scary, simply put. It has a job to make you on edge and petrified, and it fully succeeds.
-RE2 controls incredibly, save for the inventory feeling a little clunky at times. When you miss a shot, it is 100% your fault.
-The multiple campaigns with key differences sprinked in adds to a ridiculous amount of replayability.
-The voice acting is surprisingly very good, along with the facial animations. This is a strange point, I know, but it's something that few studios do correctly nowadays.

CONS: 
-There's a distinct lack of enemy and boss variety. [spoiler] Truth be told, there's a lack of bosses. There are a total of 6 bosses in the game, with only one of them feeling enjoyable. 5 of them are just various forms of William Birkin. [/spoiler]
-The way that enemies interact with doorways and rooms feels incredibly game-y and artifical. Most enemies will remain locked in their spawnroom, causing them to sit directly in the doorway when chasing you. This leads to you either getting instantly grappled and losing a sub-weapon or health, or having to do an awkward shootout in a doorway by spamming the button to open the door.
-The differences between Claire and Leon's campaigns can be laughable at times, making the player wonder why there are even seperate campaigns. In a personal opinion, they could've structured the game in a chapter-style, having the player switch between Leon and Claire every now and then.
-[spoiler] The entire Ada segment is just awful and annoying. You're given a total of 3 pistol clips, and you have to deal with roughly 7 enemies that you aren't given enough room to kite or dodge. You're also given zero healing and one sub-weapon. Also the hacking was really stupid. [/spoiler]
-[spoiler] They absolutely wrecked Hunk's chapter. Every room has 6 zombies that chain grapple you, and you have to progress from the Sewers to the RPD's front door. There are 0 drops, and you are given barely any ammo or healing. The parking garage in particular is dumb, with about 10 zombies and a few dogs. [/spoiler]

SUMMARY:
Overall, the game is incredible. There are a few minor hiccups, but they are very easily forgotten. The game is a must-buy for anyone, and it's well worth the full price. Within the first two days of its release, I've already played 21 hours. 9.5/10

[h1] Resident Evil 2 is a gorgeous remake we all deserve. A survival horror game that makes an epic comeback for the fans of the series and a perfect way to introduce to the masterpiece game for the newcomers. [/h1] 

[b] Pros: [/b]

+ Gorgeous graphics 
+ An amazing remake that manages to save the atmosphere and the idea of the classic game and brings us a brand new visuals 
+ Astonishing creepy horrifying atmosphere
+ A strong feeling of the survival horror at its finest
+ Rich and captivating story, that makes you want to know what will happen next
+ Numerous collectibles to find, perfect for the achievement hunters
+ Logical puzzles that never feel out of place
+ Two story modes with different characters with alternative versions of the story 
+ Challenging bonus modes after completing the main game to entertain yourself 
+ Brilliant sound design 
+ Convincing design of the monsters and creatures

[b] Cons: [/b]

- Can be frustrating sometimes with its pacing, where the player has no idea where to go next
- Some of the enemies require to spend way too much ammo to get rid of them, so sometimes the best option is to let them be

For the last few years, we were lucky enough to get a proper remake for a few games from our childhood. My personal opinion that this is an absolutely amazing way to please the fans of the classic old games and also a good thing to let the younger players, who are afraid to launch these old games with outdated graphics, to introduce to some great titles.   

And now we have Resident Evil 2 - the game that looked so scary to me when I was a kid. It looked completely unbearable for my age and I never understood how to play it properly. So it was my chance to finish what I started back in the days.

[h1] Story [/h1]

Resident Evil 2 tells us a story of a recruit of the Raccoon City police named Leon who arrives on his service on his first day and finds out that the deadly virus affected the whole city. Now, he has to partner up with a beautiful girl called Claire - probably, the only person he can trust in this madness - and figure out what happened to the citizens and do whatever it takes to stop the contagion from spreading.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]

The game starts by showing us the start of the adventure of Leon and Claire and how they meet each other. At the very beginning of the game, they get separated and continue their own journeys. This is a very important note because after you finish the game once, you will get the opportunity to play it for the second time with another character to see the alternative version of the story from their perspective. Make sure to choose the right option from the menu, it should be marked with an orange dot and called “second run”. I thought it would be a good idea to clarify it because it seems that a lot of players get confused about that fact, and think that after they finish the game once with one character, the game is over.

In Resident Evil 2 you should always remember that this is a classical survival horror, where every single bullet should be counted and you have to play it safe, especially on the higher difficulties. The player always has to explore as much as possible to find every note, clue, and notebook to find codes for the safes and locks, because this is where you can find valuable upgrades for your guns and inventory. 

I really enjoyed how they managed to keep the exploration thing and it’s still one of the most important mechanics of the game. Resident Evil 2 requires you to do a lot of backtracking and check your map quite often to remind yourself where is your next destination. That makes the whole gameplay thing very intense because you have to think about your ammo, remember about the location of the rooms where you need to get in and always be careful with the enemies around you. Also, it has a fair amount of puzzles, that add some value to the exploration and they never feel like they are out of place.   

The game really changed and evolved a lot in terms of combat and gunplay: it looks completely gorgeous and very effective every time you shoot in your enemies’ heads. However, most of the enemies are a bit hard to take down and you will need a lot of bullets to do this. You should be careful because in this case, you risk to stay low on ammo when it comes to boss fights and trust me, you don’t want to be empty during these battles. I understood for myself that it’s not necessary to kill every single enemy in the game and sometimes it’s a good idea to avoid wasting your ammo on another random enemy when you can just run away.

Another important thing worth mentioning is, of course, the remastered version of Mr. X - the annoying, slow and enormous giant that follows you all the time, appearing out of nowhere and giving you hard times at the most inconvenient moments. This guy is probably one of the most memorable bosses in the game, especially during Leon’s playthrough. His terrifying footsteps around you will definitely give you goosebumps for the whole game and this is very atmospheric. 

My biggest complaint regarding Resident Evil 2 is that it was kinda short - it only has a few locations and I was able to complete the game in 5 hours and 30 minutes for the first playthrough and it only took me a little bit more than two hours to complete Claire’s story, simply because most of the things that you have to do are completely similar, so I knew exactly what to do next most of the time. 

After finishing their stories, the game will introduce you extra modes called 4th survivor and a Tofu Survivor. Both of the modes are fun challenges, that merge few locations from the original game and require you to get to the extraction point. These modes are completely opposite to the main game and they were made to relax and have fun, especially in Tofu survivor, where you have to escape with a giant Tofu guy using knives only.

[h1] Graphics [/h1]

Resident Evil 2 Remake isn’t just a slight touch with a renewed HD textures pack, it’s a sterling recreation of the classic original game. Every single character, model and location look absolutely amazing and you can really feel how dedicated the developers are. They managed to create a completely new game and save every single important detail of the original product. And this is simply brilliant.

[h1] Sound [/h1]

The sound is something that has been fully changed in this remake as well and it’s absolutely outstanding. I was playing this game using my headphones to fully dive into the atmosphere of this horror and it was unbelievable. I heard absolutely everything - from the Mr. X footsteps on the second floor to the enemies’ cries outside the police station, mixed with dramatic sounds on the background at the most intense moments.       

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

This game is a perfect example of what the proper remake should look like. Resident Evil 2 is a masterpiece survival horror that feels a bit short, but it’s absolutely worth it. Let’s hope that this game will start a series of successful remakes for some other classic titles because this is something that we really need.   

Enjoy!

An ambitious remake that ends up being disappointing, tedious and frustrating.
As a long-time fan of the series, I had high hopes for this, but was sorely let down.

****SPOILERS AHEAD****

[PROS]
1: Graphically stunning, the finest film-quality animation & detailed environments / characters I've ever seen. Unfortunately they're not very well optimized (as was the Street Fighter V problem), and I can't appreciate them, as my laptop (MSI GE63 Raider) starts heating up unless I keep the fans on high and turn the graphics down so far that I may as well be playing the original Resident Evil 2. For those of you with a space-age computer that can run this on max, I cannot sing this game's graphical praises enough.

2: One scene where you play as Sherry, where I had more survival horror fun in 10-15 minutes than the rest of the entire game combined.

3: Ties in some story aspects that were retconned in later games, explaining SOME of the lore a bit better than the original did. For example, Irons' death was handled much better in this remake.

4: Very good writing in that entire orphanage section; I actually got a little emotional reading some of the diaries & notes.

5: I definitely approve of the new unlockables, and how they were done. Such as the S.T.A.R.S armoury, safe deposit room etc., these are a nice little side objective to break up the overall monotony.

6: Puzzles etc. are done nicely, not as hard as RE1 but not as easy as RE0. I felt a reasonable challenge, although I would've liked more things that rely on Examining & Combining.

[CONS]
1: Physics & lighting bugs, such as Claire's ponytail frequently spazzing out for no reason, or resetting its position after every single cutaway. There are also problems with shadows freaking out if you walk up to walls holding a flashlight, and several instances of zombies & corpses flailing or getting stuck in walls / doors.

2: Several story elements you could examine in the original have been removed, such as the desks in the S.T.A.R.S office. This didn't need to be removed, and little details like this were nice in the original, letting us learn a little more about the characters.

3: Gameplay is obnoxiously tedious & frustrating.
You cannot get around zombies unless they're already looking away and you don't need to get by them; there's no way to sneak or dodge their attacks.
The point of classic Resident Evil, and survival horror in general, is saving your resources such as bullets unless you absolutely need to fight. In this game, you can't reasonably do that, as zombies will lunge several feet and grab you almost every single time.
Unless you happen to have a knife or grenade handy, zombies become less of a reasonable obstacle, and more of a toll booth where you have to pay some of your health to continue. And on normal, there is no reason it should take up to 10 headshots to bring down some zombies, wasting ammo.
In many cases, any attempt to avoid zombies becomes a game of musical chairs, luring them in circles to have any hope of continuing with your current task.
Mr. X is much faster than his original incarnation, too, and due to the game not having "closed environments" anymore, he can follow you anywhere, apart from a select few safe locations. Luring him away from your destination barely helps, as the moment he loses sight of you, he starts homing in on the area you need to get to next, patrolling there.
And if you beat him there? And didn't waste ammo killing zombies prior? Good luck, because as soon as you run, shoot or get attacked, Mr. X will hear you and come running, meaning you have to start the process over again.
All these issues could be resolved with a simple Dodge button, even if it has to rely on timing. Or possibly stealth takedowns, such as slitting zombies' throats from behind.
Frankly I find it weird that despite copy-pasting Claire's outfit from Revelations 2, Capcom took zero lessons from what made that game the perfect balance of the classic & modern games.
And forget that battle with William and the crane; 9 times out of 10 he WILL hit you, no matter what you do.
You cannot expect to create a survival horror experience that requires you to constantly waste resources and tank damage.
Also Lickers - it's a nice idea to be able to sneak around them as they're blind, however it quickly falls apart when you realize they're homing in on you anyway, which in tight spaces means there's not really much difference other than you having the chance to attack first, which - again - you HAVE to.

4: The entire sewer section and how they went overboard with... certain details. That was just disgusting, and completely uncalled for.

5: No indication of exactly what the differences in handguns are, apart from clip size. You have to experiment to work out what does what, and unless you save scum, this means wasting even MORE precious ammo.

6: The obvious: Unnecessary redesigns. It's fine if you want to make new character outfits, but don't make them the default and change what was already fine, especially when the DLC outfits just look stupid.
With Sherry's uniform, I agree the new one is better, but her hair did not need changing.
And don't think I didn't notice Annette now having the "dead mom" hairstyle, a common anime trope.

7: Also a bug where the full-screen will exit if you get a Steam achievement. A minor concern but still quite irritating, so I have to play in windowed instead.

====

Overall, I went through the whole game just feeling annoyed, like I was only continuing to justify the money I spent on the preorder. At no time was I scared, immersed or having fun, apart from that one scene in the orphanage.
A shame, too, because with just a few minor tweaks & additions, and removing some of the unnecessary ones, this could've been a great game.
Personally I'll return to having fun with RE6 & Operation Raccoon City; I cannot recommend this remake for anything other than curiosity, or as an example of how NOT to redo a classic.

Maybe when some mods come out that let you play with the classic outfits from the start (and they've been fixed) or there's actually a way to dodge zombies and conserve ammo, I could consider recommending this, but as it stands, it's just annoying.

By the time of writing this review I've finished the first run scenario with Claire. Got to the game through AMDs reward program.

I hardly remember the original Resident Evil 2. I've played it a little and watched other people play it, but it was years ago and I was too little to properly understand what was going on. However, I've got to say that this is hands down the best RE game I've ever played, and I've played every other main title. In fact, I was so hyped for this game that I played every other resident evil just to know how everything would be connected. And I don't regret it.

The graphics and details are incredibly good. I was worried that it'd make the same mistake as Resident Evil 6, with pitch black areas that had no way to be fixed and you just had to go around based on the map. The RE engine does incredibly well, and I believe that even capcom is aware of that considering that they're using the same engine for all their games now. It looks very polished, the facial animations are very beautifully done and the models are really good. The zombies look realistic and terrifying and you can see the effect every bullet you shoot at them has. It also runs very well, giving me almost twice the frames I expected it to, which shows the good optimisation of the game. There are a few issues here and there, but they're minimal and only if you're being nitpicky as I am, trying to look at every single detail for hours.

The gameplay is just as good. There are many, many puzzles in the game, and they're all very satisfying and sometimes challenging to solve. There are times when you suddenly realise that the item you have is for the thing you found hours ago, and it feels good to do detective work. Speaking of which, there is quite a lot of backtracking if you want to get everything with your limited inventory, but it wasn't an issue for me. The best part of the game in my opinion was however the mini side quest with Sherry, which was incredibly dark and scary and sort of felt more like an Outlast game. The enemies have a lot of variety, and your arsenal against them also has a lot of variety to ensure you use them all. There's a chance that you'll miss some things throughout the game, but the map shows you when there's something to be done in a room which is helpful for finding everything. Not to mention that it shows all the items. I generally don't use maps that much, but I used it every other minute in this game. The chase scenes were the best part of the game to me, along with times when you're overwhelmed. They give you a massive feeling of hopelessness and it's satisfying to escape, even if you know that you will be found sooner or later. The normal zombies and especially for me, the dogs and in the open areas such as the beginning of the game can get stuck sometimes which is a shame but it's not the biggest complaint.

The story was also very good. I didn't expect too much, but honestly, I was very immersed and hooked. I liked reading every bit of lore and while it wasn't the most insanely complex, I still had an emotional attachment to the characters. It was satisfying and it was truly scary and anxiety-inducing at times.

The music is as good as you'd expect. There are the original tracks to use if you're interested in them, but I loved the remastered audio and found it to be as terrifying as it should be, and sometimes quite heroic and epic. It was just right, based on the scenes and if I can find a place to get it I will gladly do so.

TL;DR, if you like resident evil, you'll love this. If you don't, there's a high chance you'll still love this.

EDIT: I've played and finished scenario B for Leon and I've got to say that there are many story differences and conflicts which may be confusing at first. However, I found the story to be much more mature, darker and perhaps more "action and mystery focused", although that doesn't mean much considering the game's overall atmosphere and gameplay mechanics. I found Leon's side to be very interesting despite my expectations and while I preferred Claire's scenario A ending, it was a good twist and certainly added a ton of replayability, considering that now I want to play the game twice more just to experience absolutely everything, and that doesn't even include the fantastic 4th Survivor and the hilarious Tofu mode.

More about pros and cons below.
------------
[b]PROS[/b]
------------

[b]+ Great graphics[/b]
The same engine from RE7 it looks like. It holds up well, and zombie design is great with chunks of flesh visible after shooting them few times. I think it could've been a little more gory, but it's fine as it is.

[b]+ Oppressive atmosphere[/b]
When zombies start banging on the nearby window, you rush to block it with boards only to notice there's more of them around the corner. It's tense as hell and with limited ammo you have to pick your battles.

[b]+ Rewards exploration[/b]
There are some goodies that's not easy to find unless you explore and keep in mind what you already have uncovered. Some secrets are simple, like finding a note with a safe combination, but there are some things that ain't that trivial to find.

------------
[b]CONS[/b]
------------

[b]- Bullet sponge enemies[/b]
Even regular zombies can take 10 or more headshots to put down. Also they seem to activly try to dodge your shots when you aim at them, like they know you want to line up a headshot. it's dumb and makes combat unsatisfying.
[b]<UPDATE>[/b]
It is now my belief that the amount of ammo required for killing zombies dynamically changes based on the "adaptive difficulty" the game employs. More about this issue down below.

[b]- KNIFE IS ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ BREAKING, FFS!!![/b]
Knife now has life bar. If you hit something with it - durability goes down. When it's out - it breaks and disappears. It assume it's because it can now be used as in RE1 HD Remake from Dreamcast - where you could save yourself from a zombie grab with a knife. But there knives wouldn't take your inventory slot and were 1 use only. I hate the new knives in RE2 Remake - they make conserving ammo more difficult than it should be.

[b]- HORRIBLE boss fights[/b]
Bosses also take too much ammo to bring down. 1st boss took 31 handgun bullets, 7 shotgun blasts and 2 grenades. I missed his weak point only a couple of times, hitting him in the body instead, but no shots were missed per-se. This is far too much for a boss fight. I'm not even gonna talk about the train-wreck that is the second boss fight, where you can waste entire magazines of magnum and he won't go down.
I also have to talk about Mr.X. I haven't played RE2 in a while, but I am almost 100% sure he spawned at certain points in the game to chase you for a while and then he would just ♥♥♥♥ right off and let you continue playing the game. Here he chases you all across the map. This is a bad design for this game as it makes you waste your time trying to dodge him. There's also puzzles you have to do while you are chased. I never understood the appeal of this style of "gameplay" and hated it in RE7, Evil Within and all the other games that use this mechanic. If I am to run away from something I want it to be my decision for conserving resources, not because game puts a freaking unkillable tank-man in front of me.

[b]- Remix of ideas from other RE games[/b]
This is a minor gripe. We have gunpowder mixing from RE3:Nemesis, defensive items from RE HD, and Mr.X. chasing you like the hillbillies from RE7. I liked upgrades to weapons and I don't remember if using boards to block windows was in any other RE but it feels like there are nothing really original here, and what is there could have been better.

[b]<UPDATE>[/b]
[b]- Rubber band AI ("adaptive difficulty")[/b]
This is probably the most annoying thing in the game. This game will adjust the amount of ammo you get and difficulty of the enemies depending on how well you are doing. So if you have a lot of ammunition, lots of HP and healing items, the game will craft less ammo from powder, spawn more enemies, said enemies will move more aggressively and bob their heads more in order to dodge your fire.
And most of all - they will have far more HP than normal.
At first, most zombies will be put down by 4-6 shots to the head, which is still a lot and in my opinion - too ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ much. Granted, I played on Hardcore, but bullet sponges is a horrible way of increasing difficulty. What happens after about 30 minutes of careful headshots and not getting hit? You will encounter a normal-looking zombie, but this time it will go down after 10 shots in the face. Oh, and he will get back up and take another 4-6 shots. Maybe even more after that. It's bad. And what if you die a couple of times due to bad positioning or lack of ammunition? Next time the game might make the next 3 zombies's heads explode after a single pistol shot. It's hard to judge when the adaptive difficulty takes effect and when you are just lucky with your crits multiple shots in a row
The result? You don't feel like you are getting better at the game, conserving ammunition, learning movement patterns for accurate shooting and avoiding damage. You feel like the game is controlling the pace through behind-the-scenes number manipulation.
The game's rules should be set in stone. If a zombie takes 5 shots to kill, another, same-looking zombie should take just as many. If you want an enemy take more shots - make him wear a head protection or have him be larger to communicate "hey, this guy is tougher".
This new-way-of-thinking rubber-band AI for game difficulty is bad for gaming as it takes control away from the player and puts it in the hands of an algorithm that doesn't want you to have fun - it wants to control how long you play.

The second instalment in Capcom’s long running Resident evil series arrived back on the 25th January, 2019 reimagined from the ground up; surprisingly it manages to return the series to the classic survival horror elements present in the previous entries which made the series so memorable starting all the way back in 1996 with the release of Resident Evil 1 on the original PlayStation.

So, Why was Resident Evil 2 even made to begin with?. What cascade of events lead to it being deemed necessary to create it?
 
Since Resident Evil 4 leading up to the catastrophe which was Resident Evil 6.  I am in no way saying that Resident Evil 4 is a bad game. In fact, it is considered to be one of the best and innovative games of all time; it had the perfect blend of suspenseful horror and tense action. I am merely stating that although RE4 was a good game, it set the action trend which grew to be excessive in later entries that forego the horror elements in favour for more action .The series had slowly shifted its focus on a more action-orientated approach; a stark contrast to the fundamental elements of survival horror.
 
This trend led to Resident Evil 6 which didn’t even try and conceal the fact that it was no longer a survival horror. Upon release the game was met with mediocre appraisal from fans however stole significantly well. However Capcom were not happy about losing the appeal of their fanbase and so froze all development on future games for a thorough rethink.
 
And in 2017 release Resident Evil 7 which refocused the series back onto horror with a change to a first person perspective and significantly less action. In a way the Resident Evil 2 remake was Capcom's way of apologising to its fanbase for past mistakes; fans had been asking for a remake since the first Resident Evil remake in 2002 with an improved story, less rigid dialogue, a complete graphical, overhaul smoother gameplay and added features such as the Crimson Head enemies. If there was to be a RE2 remake many would’ve hoped that it would have followed in the same vein as the RE1 remake...only it wasn;t quite exactly like it 
 
Gameplay - A rejuvenated floppy disk
Unlike the RE1 remake, RE2 features an Over The Shoulder (OTS) camera perspective, although this is attributed to the action oriented games, RE2 uses clever ways to subtly make the player play in the way of the classic fix camera angle era:
Although you can move while aiming/shooting, your crosshair significantly increases so your shots are less accurate similarly when standing still your crosshair focuses into a point making your shots more accurate and increases your chances of a critical hit. This is used to emulate the classic tank controls of the original in a modern way. Additionally, RE2 subverts the typical zombie trope of “always aim[ing] for the head”. Zombies typically take 9-12 shots to the head or can even take a whole clip! it is much more efficient to cripple them in the legs or lower body and run around them. 
 
RE2 again uses the classic survival horror elements: backtracking through claustrophobic hallways; central hubs; elaborate keys needed to unlock areas;puzzle solving; limited inventory and limiting and discouraged combat are amongst many things that make the game survival horror. Additionally, an extra sense is utilized: sound, used by the Lickers. These are mutated creatures which can only identify you by sound. So, in order to get away scot free it is necessary to walk as slowly as you can to avoid detection. 
 
Moreover, there are many boss fights in the game, something that gives the whole story ( from a gameplay perspective) structure, everytime you beat a boss it reflects a significant hurdle being overcome, like a new stage of the game is being progressed into.

There is also a sense of intimacy added to the game, this is created by both by the environment’s ambience and atmosphere and how it reacts to you. For example, if i shoot a particular zombie in a particular spot causing a wound in that spot, the game will always remember which particular zombie has the particular wound so upon returning that particular zombie is identifiable and link directly to past actions, this instills in the player that the actions made in the present will directly affect the future. 
 
Story (Beware 20 year old spoiler)
RE2 follows the story of Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield. The former is a rookie cop on his first day on the job.(What a first day) and the latter is the sister of the male protagonist in the first game (Chris Redfield) who comes to Racoon City to try and find out what happened to her brother. You do not need prior knowledge of the RE universe at all as it's only loosely connected to the previous entries.
 
These two get trapped in the city and must find a way out, along the way Leon meets Ada Wong, who in this iteration of the story is an FBI agent (although not really: she lied :( ) and is secretly a freelance agent looking for the antidote to the genetically engineered T-Virus, the virus which has caused the population to turn into zombies. And Claire meets Sherry who is the daughter of Dr Willam Burkin creator of the G virus, a new strain of the T-Virus which causes overactive mutation turning those infected into abominations. Of course at the end both Leon and Claire stumble across the Umbrella Corporations (the company behind the viruses )Lab and blow it up.
I think the reason why the re2 story holds up is that you're uncovering a mystery and has great motivation for characters.
RE2 is good because there’s an ongoing element of discovery and mystery: What is happening; why did this event happen; who's behind it and the result of it. Well the result of it is always coming after you but there is also all these third parties; such as mr x and the lickers, it’s very good because it's simple but compelling, you are discovering what the heck is happening in racoon city and you’re experiencing it along the way along with the characters, and getting introduced to new information. That, to this day, makes it a simple, effective and compelling story.
 
Atmosphere - Spooky
RE2 again uses the brilliant photorealistic RE engine that debuted in RE7, unfortunately words will not do it justice, These visuals are incredible. These things are better to be shown.
Furthermore, RE2 uses great sound design and ambience to give a really unsettling feeling to the player. This is also coupled with the zombie groans and moans, especially when you are walking down a long cold hallway, and you hear the reverbated groan of a zombie far in the distance, given you a sense and dread. This is only possible thanks to the brilliant RE engine.
 
Mr X -  Tyrannical
Mr X aka T-003, is a genetically modified terminator. He is able to follow you around, open doors or even climb up stairs and is literally invincible, though it is possible to stun him temporarily though at considerable cost to ammunition. He can also be alerted when you fire a shot anywhere on the map. And will immediately start to head towards you, we are even able to hear his paranoia inducing footsteps as the draw closer and closer.
 
Conclusion - New Classic
Spooky, Gothic starting area - check; Limited ammo - check; Unforgiving enemies - check. This game has by far the darkest story of all Resident Evil titles.

Having been a die-hard fan of the original (By far my most played in the series, not to mention on the PSX AND the N64...), I hoped in my heart of hearts that this REmake would deliver, possibly even being as good as the original.

I was wrong. It's better.

There are sacrifices made in order to adapt to the engine, and at times I was frustrated with how things -weren't as how I remembered them-, but in the whole these sacrifices are worth it when you finally breathe out after your first playthrough.

In most Resident Evil games, the initial hour or two is where you're the most terrified and, gradually, you'll become more adapted to the pacing, you'll feel that you can fight back, and you'll know when to run and when to fight. For me, not so much in this game. I was consistently low on ammunition, and every time I found an ammo dump, moments later I'd get too cocky, or have a fight where most of this new ammo was sacrificed. Excellent enemy placement, good usage of the new camera system and the lighting is just... Mwah! If there's anything the old game lacked, it was darkness (hard to pull off with the tech level of the time).

Graphics are stunning, audio (especially the use of audio cues) amazing, and the music is there -only when it's needed-. I've seen complaints that the old VAs aren't back, but honestly this series has gone through so many of them, I'm not surprised or disappointed. New ones do a good job and, at times, outshine the old ones.

If I have anything I'm not happy with, it is that I feel like fooling the zombies is a lot harder than it used to be. They seem to lock in on you a little too easy to grab a snack, but maybe I'm just rusty.

What a fitting homage to a standout classic from my childhood. Capcom got it right, again. This is a masterpiece. Period. Full stop. Capcom proved they could do remake's right when they released the RE1 remake, and eventually the HD remaster. And they've done it again with this, though they took it one step further this time and gave us a total reimagining of the game while staying true to it's roots in a faithful way. If I had total control of remaking this game, this is likely how I personally would've done it and that says a lot. The classic Resident Evil games are some of my favorite games of all time, RE2 included obviously. I grew up with them in the late 90's, I've played them all countless times at this point. I really am impressed, I can't say it enough.

Starting off, this game runs incredibly well even on modest rigs. You don't need a super rig to play this game at high framerates. It seems optimized rather well and absolutely is one of the better PC Ports I've ever played. It has a thoroughly adequate options menu, with plenty of graphical settings to tailor to your PC's specs. Gameplay is smooth, and I haven't noticed many hiccups or stuttering to speak of. The audio and lighting design is some of the best I've ever seen in any game, let alone survival horror. Speaking of audio, it's my opinion that it's a MUST to purchase/download the classic soundtrack for this remake in the extra DLC content section. Even with the modern look of the game, the classic soundtrack still pairs up with it exceptionally well and if you're a fan of the original, hearing the classic RPD main hall music start up when you walk into the police station will put a smile on your face from ear to ear, like it did me. The classic menu beeps, the classic save room music, and much more, it's all there. 

Graphically, this is one of the best looking games of this generation, easily. The facial animations in particular are incredibly life-like and the character models themselves are really well-done. Capcom really paid attention to the small details here and it shows. The lighting design is some of the best out there too, which is good because atmosphere in a game like this is everything. As far as controls go, it's smooth and intuitive in most cases. It can be a little clunky at times in specific situations however it wouldn't be a Resident Evil game if there wasn't some clunkyness. It's easy to get past and most people will be able to pick this game up and figure it out fairly quickly even if you never played Resident Evil 7, which the RE2 remake borrows a lot from in terms of control scheme, user interface, etc. 

I do have a couple of negatives I want to point out though. I am a little disappointed that Capcom has decided to move away from the "zapping" system of the original game. Fans of the original wil know what it is, it's basically how each character's scenario effected the other's, as well as there being two different scenarios for both Leon and Claire. In this game however, we have something called "2nd run" which unlocks the true ending which I won't spoil however for the most part, it feels like each character's scenario is a copy & paste of the other. Both characters visit most of the same places, at the same times and it actually negatively impacts the canon & time-line as we know it, in my view anyway. I think Capcom could've done more here, but I'm not going to hold it against them. Each character's playthroughs are different in just enough ways to make them feel fresh...but I still think the original RE2 did a much better job in this regard.

Finally, if I had to put a rating on this game, it would be a 9.2/10. It really is a masterpiece and a must buy if you're a fan of franchise, or horror games in general. I waited 20 years for this, and it was worth the wait. There's only a couple things holding it back from being a 10/10. If Capcom recreated the zapping system of the original game, and if they had included an unlockable CLASSIC fixed camera option mode, the game absolutely would've earned a 10/10 from me. As it is, it's a fantastic game that I will likely play dozens of times and never tire of, just like the original. Buy it. Now.

The amount of hate Mr.X receive got me thinking why people hate him, but not Jack or Alien.

1. Transition feedback (Mr.X is mute)
When Jack or Alien found you, there's clear indication. Jack will yell 'found you' and Alien will scream and switch from patrol to chase behavior. While Mr.X never do any of this. There's no clear indication whether he found the player or just in patrol mode when he enter the room. This mean player doesn't know what's the best action to take in the situation. RUN or HIDE.
And this bring me to 2nd problem.

2. Lack of danger/tension (Mr.X is too slow in chasing)
Mr.X don't really change his walk speed in either 'chase' or 'patrol' mode (yes, it change a bit, but both speed are still outrun-able by player so it didn't really matter), being found by Mr.X didn't translate into 'danger', it just translate into 'time wasting.' Since player can outrun Mr.X unless they are in dead-end (which Mr.X is scripted to not enter), this mean being found is 'fine...., now I have to spend 2 min losing him before getting back to where I am.' Mr.X is only a threat when player have to doing something that force them to stay in one place for some time. (cough, library, cough, cough).

3. Lack of proper stealth (Leon/Claire are too prideful to lower their head)
I think this is the most important problem with RE2 & Mr.X.
In RE7 & Alien, player can getdown behind cover for the 'high risk, high reward' of not having to go around jack or alien, but doing so also put player in their range. RE2 don't have that, so there's less way player can deal with Mr.X.

4. Map design (Police Station need new furniture)
The police station isn't optimized for 'immortal chasing enemy'. Most room are corridor-style room which doesn't provide 'table' or other object that player can use to circle around Mr.X. There's also a lot of dead end. So when opening into Mr.X player has only 1 option, get back from where they came. This also mean there's no 'high risk, high reward' of lurking mr.X to circle around the 'table' so you can get pass him without running back to previous room. 

5. He didn't kill you, the zombie and licker did (Mr.X act like timer referee when you fight)
Here's also another reason why people may hate Mr.X. He didn't catch you up and kill you, some random zombie grab you or licker make you walk, then Mr.X catch up and finish you. Mr.X act like a timer in these situation, timer that a lot of people hate. When Mr.X show up in the room where player played smart (ignore zombie to save bullet), it means player cannot make slow smart manuvour to manipulate zombie or licker out of the way, and force player to kill those zombie / licker ASAP or Mr.X will kill them.
This punish player who try to play the game as survivor (saving ammo, avoiding/evading enemy, leaving enemy alone) and reward gun-blasting player (who has happy time running around since all enemy are dead already).

Allow me to preface this review by mentioning that, at time of writing, I have completed the game once, following Leon's path on medium difficulty. This review will be as spoiler-free as possible.

I played a hell of a lot of RE2 back on the Playstation and absolutely loved it. I used to believe that RE4 was the ideal blend of tension, scares and modern gameplay and controls. The remade Resident Evil 2 has set the bar that little bit higher, in my estimation. In the interests of avoiding writing a tangled mess, I will try to break things down by categories.


Difficulty: As mentioned, I played on the medium difficulty and performed reasonably well most of the time, with reliable accuracy and decent conservation of resources. I found that the game, for me, tread a solid balance between giving me enough supplies and ammo to keep going without allowing me to stockpile massive reserves of most things (herbs being the only real exception) if I were of a mind to. I'd say that it offered an excellent middle ground and I have high expectations for Hardcore difficulty.

Graphics/Performance: I have a pretty solid PC, running the game with everything set to High or Max. Asides from some hitches I noticed during my first play session, the game generally runs nice and smooth. The game looks beautiful and I have to particularly commend the quality of expressiveness in the facial animations, both among the living and undead. The areas are well-detailed and convincing in their layout, which really adds to the atmosphere of the game.

Sound: Exceptional all round, as far as I have noticed. The ambient sounds in the various areas of the game do a solid job of keeping tension high, especially during a first playthrough. Enemy sounds seem very realistic in a lot of instances, adding to the horror of each zombie or other nasty you encounter. The guns have a really nice meat to them when they fire, at least amongst the ones available to me during my playthrough. I would comment on the solid voice acting, but surpassing classic Resident Evil games in that regard is a fairly low bar.

Puzzles: Overall, the puzzles in the game are not especially trying, though they will exercise your brain just enough to be satisfying in most cases. It's generally not too hard to keep track of what you need and where, though I was pleasantly surprised in a few instances where little secondary puzzles were available off the path towards completing the story, some of which I only realised the answers to after I had passed them by. It definitely feels like the game can hold up to multiple playthroughs.

Horror/Gore: This game does not shy away from the blood and viscera at any point. Damage to enemies that you fire upon is suitably unpleasant to look at, selling both the lethality of your weaponry and the disturbing endurance of many of the creatures you will cross paths with. That said, the game does not seem terribly interested in gore for its own sake in most instances. The overall atmosphere of the game remains unsettling throughout, rather than often feeling like (as much of) a zombie-killing romp the further you get into it, as I felt the original did.

Originality: Overall, I would say that the developers have made RE2 their own. The game retains a definite sense of familiarity while still making the story feel new (or at least freshened up nicely) in a lot of places. Puzzles, layouts and enemy/resource layouts will need to be relearned in a lot of cases, so having experience with the original will not trivialise the experience of the remake.


All in all, a solid recommendation regardless of whether you have tried the original.
