[h1]Childhood Memories w/ HD textures[/h1]

Ahh...Resident Evil 2. One of the first games I ever played at a friend's house, at the ripe old age of nine. I still get nervous playing the classic game, because it left such an impression on me. Even when I stepped foot into the first area of Raccoon Police Department I can still hear the beautiful, yet unsettling "Front Hall" theme. The fact that the game was on two discs, because it was so big at the time was borderline impressive. We'd wait for my friend's brother to come home and turn the game on, because we didn't know how to solve some of the puzzles and we really struggled to get far. No one really had any guides back then, outside of a crappy monthly released paper-based cheat and hint book that rarely had any solutions for the games that you played. Took us many weeks or even months to "get good" at the game, learn how to run through certain enemies, how to conserve ammo and unlock various secrets, like the unlimited ammo weapons or cool outfits. 

And now, after 21 years we get a remake. An actual remake, not just an updated version with better textures, but a new 3rd person camera perspective, a brand new engine that  was used to restart the whole franchise with Resident Evil 7.

[b]GRAPHICS[/b]

One of the best things about the game is that it has such a modular approach to graphics. You can tweak pretty much any aspect of the visuals to your own preference/system capabilities. Also a welcome function, which I wish more developers would add, is that all the options explain what something does with a VISUAL explanation. Since many people sometimes are not too familiar with the technobabble that those settings entail. Zombies look fantastic, with locational damage to their limbs, altering their animations and action patterns. Gore is also sublime, and purposefully designed to be part of the game, rather than just be gore for the sake of gore. Personally, the game is running very well for me (i7 8700k+GTX 1070TI) and I cannot complain. Streaming the game on my Samsung 4K TV via SteamLink I always get 60fps on a 1440p resolution. Pretty sure if I tinkered with the settings enough, I could get it to run at 4K@60fps, since as I mentioned previously, the amount of options that you tweak is more than enough to find a balance of what you want and can use. On my regular desktop monitor, the game runs at a steady 144fps without any problems. Oh and don't worry about the listed memory usage, it doesn't come near what's shown, when you actually use tools to record memory usage.

[b]AUDIO[/b]

Playing with a 5.1 surround setup, the game feels appropriately tense in audio as well. You can hear various "little" sounds behind you, and the fact that now zombies can enter through doors and follow you just adds to the tension when you hear random sounds behind you. Music is outstanding. Game knows when to accelerate game audio accordingly to what's happening on the screen and it helps to increase the urgency, when you get attacked by formidable enemies that require more effort than regular zombies. Zombie groans and screeches feel unnerving, and sometimes feel outright feral, to a point where you doubt if it's even a zombie, and might be a new unseen enemy. 

[b]GAMEPLAY[/b]

No more tank controls, more freedom and improved control design for various items in your inventory. Ammo is scarce and zombies are difficult to put down, unless you smash their head in completely. Even if you remove multiple limbs off a zombie, they can still pose a threat. "Aim for the head" was never more true, and since this is basically a motto for any type of zombie media - at least it feels genuine here. Zombies are a lot more deadlier and their lunges are harder to avoid. You are always given a choice to kill or leave them, but leaving them also has a chance of encoutering more than one of them in the same sport later on. No more blood puddles to tell you when a zombie is dead. Locations are similar to the original, including the map layout. However the key items are different, so even if you are a master speed-runner of the original game, you'll still need to learn a lot of new stuff here. Knife is actually quite useful in combat now, since it has more utility. It requires some skill and timing, but the reward is that you can effectively run away from a zombie, without wasting ammunitition This will definitely add a layer of strategy to harder difficulty runs. I've still yet to get all the weapons in the game, but all of them feel unique and fill a specific damage role for different enemy types, which is always welcome in a supposed survival-horror game. 

[b]STORY[/b]

Well, it's essentially the same story from the original game, albeit with updated voice acting, animation work and a lot more emphasis on cinematic presentation. I never really cared too much on story in Resident Evil games, but RE2 had a solid and well-paced story with interesting characters, not to mention that you also had 2 different perspectives and some little choices that affected the other character in their respective save file. Resident Evil games rely more on fanservice, rather than a "good" story.

[b]TL;DR[/b]

[b]PROS[/b]

- Multiple graphics options to choose from with visual reference and well optimized.
- Less action focused, more reliant on atmosphere and a solid pacing.
- Managed to bring back the classic feel of RE2 to an updated format in a 3rd person perspective.
- Zombies are more varied, in terms of behavior. Act according to their limb damage (to a certain degree).
- Similar layout of the locations, but the key items and puzzles are different and new.
- Controls are fluid, responsive and aiming even with a controller feels great. 
- Character animations are top-notch.
- Gunpowder crafting from Resident Evil 3 is back.
- Being chased by Mr. X - appropriate levels of anxiety.
- Replay value and multiple playthroughs.
- Hardcore difficulty requires tactical thinking and planning.

[b]CONS[/b]

- Wesker's Handgun that you get with the Deluxe Edition (or buy separately). When wielding it gives you damage protection, which allows you to take an extra hit in Hardcore mode. That's huge considering that you die in 2 hits most of the time. Items like these need to be unlockable - not a bonus if you pay for it.
- Handgun sounds are all identical, even if there are 7-8 different pistols in the game. Even the .45 ACP caliber weapons sound the same that you get in B scenarios. 
- The classic soundtrack from the original Resident Evil 2 is a DLC, and if you want to use it in-game, you'll need to buy it or instead get the Deluxe Edition. Not a fan of these type of practices. Why not let us unlock the soundtrack after beating the game?

[b] [h1] TL;DR: This game is amazing. Graphics are amazing, gameplay is modernised but feels familiar to the original, soundtrack is great. The game's story has always been one of the best in the series. Worth a buy? I'd say yes.	[/h1]	[/b]

Amazing game so far. Capcom put in the effort this time, this game is not simply just a remaster - the very same game with newer graphics - this game is a REMAKE, rebuilt from the ground up with the original game in mind.

As a result, the game has switched to a more modern over-the-shoulder 3rd person perspective, much like RE4, 5 and 6, however the new aiming system has been purposefully tuned to be less accurate and less fast-paced than in those games. This is to resimulate the horror of the original. 

I get the same horror feeling I remember from the old days where my shots whizz past and miss a zombie standing 2 feet in front of me due to my inaccuracy, before a chunk of my neck gets knawed off.

The game looks absolutely beautiful, the new RE engine the game was built on was certainly worth all the effort. You thought you were scared of zombies back in 1998? Well welcome to 2019, you're going to have some fun kid. 

There is a new soundtrack to the game, that does its job of giving the game the right horror atmosphere. The sound design is well done, with little creaks and clunks you can hear throughout the various corridors in the game, making you afraid to turn the corner.

The game follows the same general plot, allowing you to choose at the beginning to play as either Leon (a rookie cop trying to figure out what is going on in Raccoon City) or Claire (a little sister, trying to find out what happened to her brother, another policeman stationed at Raccoon City). 

The remake has redesigned their looks and given them new outfits, but for fans of the original costumes: good news! They're unlockable in the game, you just have to beat the story with each character to unlock their respective costume. There are also a few other different variations on their outfit that can be unlocked by completing various challenges/objectives (such as beating the game in 4 hours, or only walking a certain number of steps) during the game which is sure to give people a lot of replayability.

Despite all the new improvements, there are a lot of familiar elements the game brings back from the original such as:

- The old 8-slot inventory system, which can be upgraded later by hip-pouches that you find throughout the game

- The RCPD Police Station is just as much of a maze as last time, you'll find yourself consulting the map which closely resembles the classic design

- Items and plot mcguffins are scattered in the many rooms and corners of the Police Station, making the game a dangerous treasure hunt, in a maze, with zombies and other nightmarish creatures thrown in

- There is the return of the "fine", "caution" and "danger" health system which you can see in the inventory screen

- Get to [strike]smoke[/strike] apply some sweet "herbs"... for medicinal purposes *wink**wink*

And there's probably more I could bring up but you'll find out if you play the game. Speaking of, I need to get back and save Sherry. Toodaloo.

[b][h1]Review: Resident Evil 2 (Remake) – A Masterclass in Survival Horror[/h1]
Resident Evil 2 is a phenomenal return to form for the franchise. Having followed the series since the days of RE Outbreak and the original RE2 and RE3, I can confidently say the atmosphere here is unmatched. It is a relentlessly intense experience that keeps the player on edge from start to finish.

[h1]Atmosphere & Gameplay[/h1]
Even on Standard difficulty, the game manages to be genuinely nerve-wracking. The sound design is a particular standout—the heavy, echoing footsteps of Mr. X are enough to induce panic. I found myself paralyzed in "Safe Rooms" for extended periods, simply bracing for the next encounter. It is a rare game that can maintain this level of tension throughout multiple playthroughs.

[h1]Visuals & Character Design[/h1]
The character models and creature designs are top-tier. The evolution of the antagonists—specifically William Birkin’s second transformation—is visually stunning and mechanically challenging. From a technical standpoint, the game runs quite well, with only very minor, occasional framerate fluctuations that do not detract from the overall experience.

[h1]Narrative & Content[/h1]
Playing as Leon S. Kennedy during his first day as a rookie cop feels authentic. Unlike the "action hero" persona he adopts in later entries, this version of Leon feels human, vulnerable, and visibly shaken by the horror surrounding him.

The game offers incredible value through its "A" and "B" scenarios for both Leon and Claire. Beyond the main story, the inclusion of the 4th Survivor mode provides a brutal, high-stakes challenge for veteran players. The looming presence of multiple Tyrants makes every run a desperate struggle for survival.

[h1]Final Verdict[/h1]
With additional content like the Tofu Survivor and upcoming free DLC, there is plenty of replayability here. Despite any external concerns regarding DRM (Denuvo), the quality of the game itself is undeniable.

Score: 10/10 Recommendation: An absolute must-buy for survival horror fans and long-time followers of the series.[/b]

A fantastic Remake to an already fantastic game. 

Graphics 9/10-Only real bad thing about them is pretty subpar HDR, but the lighting, textures, and models are all fantastic, animations are pretty good too. 

Gameplay 10/10-It's good ol' survival horror, while the game does give you alot of ammo at the start, don't think they keep giving you that amount for the rest of the game, and when enemies are so tough to put down you'll burn through it quick if you want to clear areas.

Story 7.5/10-Story has never been Resident Evil's strong suit, especially the original ones. But the Remake adds things that give characters more depth, one character in the Original that really was just an exposition dump that you talked to for less then two minutes has much more lines and sticks around longer. The Voice Acting is pretty good for the most part. Is it still a bunch of Cliches? Yeah but the story that's there keeps your attention so it's not too bad.

Optimization 10/10- Specs-Ryzen 1400-RX 580 4GB-16GB RAM- got 75fps at 1080p for a large majority of the time with the settings at high levels. The times it slipped up were at the low 60s, and when there were a lot of particle effects such as smoke or fire on screen. Also you get literally dozens of graphics options too.

Overall 9/10- If you like Survival Horror you owe it to yourself to buy this. We rarely get a AAA survival horror game nowadays, especially one this good.

Fantastic for fans of the classic RE1,2,3,CV games, and a very compelling survival-horror for newcomers too.

[u]Gameplay:[/u]
Classic Resident Evil is back in full force. Cranks, inventory management, wacky keys, gunpower, ammo combinations, herbs - it's all here and better than ever. Every item pickup needs to be given some thought so that you don't run out of inventory space, leading to some tactical thinking as you route yourself through the maze-like environments. It will feel instantly familiar to fans of the original trilogy.

The new third-person perspective feels intuitive and fluid, and retains all of the horror, thanks to clever lighting, audio and environment design. Aiming and blowing enemies into chunks is now far more satisfying than it ever was in previous games.

Ammo management can be important; you often need to think about shooting or avoiding certain enemies, especially if you need to travel through certain areas more than once. The game also has dynamic difficulty adjustment that will subtly help you or provide extra challenge, depending on how you play. (on the Standard mode) If it detects you are being hurt a lot or running low on ammo, it will make enemies less aggressive and weaken them a bit. Hardcore mode on the other hand feels challenging and requires you to really learn the environments and enemy behaviours, as well as adding limited saves (ink ribbons) which feels much more similar to the classic RE2.

Enemies are numerous and tough - you can very quickly become surrounded and overpowered by a group of zombies in a claustrophobic corridor. They did a great job of making each zombie feel like a significant threat if you're unprepared, instead of waves of fodder. Lickers are terrifying and powerfull too.

That brings us to the gore; oh my. Sometimes you'll land a lucky critical hit, causing a zombies' head to explode. Zombies have full dynamic dismemberment which also allows you to use it to your advantage. Blow off arms and legs to slow down zombies and make them less of a threat. Characters and cutscenes are also gruesomly detailed.

Enemy variety was a big criticism for RE7, and while some of the classic enemies have been cut from RE2, there are still more than enough to keep you busy. Zombies, Lickers, Dogs, Mr. X, Ivies, G-Mutants and an assortment of bosses are used to great effect. Mr. X (Tyrant) is now more aggressive than ever and will stalk you through the police station for a while. Hearing him stomping around is terrifying, but can become annoying at times while trying to solve puzzles in confined spaces.

[u]Graphics:[/u]
RE Engine yet again flexes its' muscles and shows off very photorealistic environments, and highly detailed and dynamic characters. It does all this while running at very high frame rates too. It's very easy to max out the game and still hit 60-144fps with somewhat modern hardware.

[u]Sound:[/u]
Stellar, with full surround sound and detailed binaural support. Ambient and environmental sounds constantly keep you on edge, and enemies often signpost their whereabouts with terrifying cries and accurate positional audio. The environments and enemies are very atmospheric and creepy.

[u]Controls:[/u]
Capcom absolutely nailed the M+KB controls. I usually play third-person games with controllers, but the mouse and keyboard controls here are perfect, and feel [i]far[/i] better than the sluggish analog-stick aiming on controller. The game also features a ton of inventory management and puzzle solving, so being able to quickly drag and drop items with the mouse and navigate with the keyboard makes everything feel very snappy and nice. Headshots and overall accuracy are also made much easier and more satisfying with a mouse, and the fully rebindable keyboard makes it accessible for anyone.

[u]Story:[/u] (no spoilers)
The story is 90% the same as the original RE2, complete with some cheesy dialogue. Things are expanded, switched up and re-ordered just enough to make it feel fresh and exciting for veterans of the game. Existing characters like Marvin, Kendo and Annette are more fleshed out and memorable.

If you're a fan of the classic games, or survival horror games in general, you cannot afford to miss this.

**Addendum**


After streaming the game from my HTPC server, which runs a desktop-class Radeon RX, I was able to play through the game at 720p (max streaming speed I could coax out of my wifi).  What I discovered was a nostalgic, polished take on the original Resident Evil 2.  Viciously charming, eerily beautiful, copiously atmospheric and tense, there's *a lot* to like about RE 2.  The characters are fluidly modeled, the environmental progression is spot on and the music is oppressively frightening.
 
However, frustrating remnants of the original remain.  Absurd medallion hunting for secret rooms.  Magnum components locked away with a USB-enabled badge key.  Cringey voice lines from the protagonists.  Characters that still occasionally move/handle like shopping carts.  And let's not even talk about little Sherry Birken who cheerily asks to be adopted 10 minutes after escaping an evil corporate base stalked by mutants, undead cannibals and her biologically tainted father.  RE 2 can be a bit absurd.

So a masterpiece it ain't.  Especially when you take into account that the "B Side" campaigns are often nigh-identical to their "A side precursors".  In fact, Claire's campaign doesn't vary that much from Leon's at all (not that it did in the original either).  The Ghost survivor tales are melancholy but ultimately cheap, broken filler designed to lure masochistic players.

RE 2 was still a treat.  It allowed me to relive memories of the original.  It was polished and it looked exactly what I imagined a remake of RE 2 could be.  However, technical issues, lack of content and plot limitations keep this game from being anything but a nice diversion.

I still can't heartily recommend it after catastrophic issues I originally experienced. I'm still going to ding the score a hair.

Recommended. 

8/10.

I can't say I have been a fan since Resident Evil games first started to come out, but the first one I got into was Resident Evil 4 back when it came out for the PS2. I have been playing these remastered editions as they release, and it is nice to see Capcom putting in the work to revitalize these amazing pieces of work.  

Right away, this remake immerses you. The game is dark (not nearly as dark as some are complaining about in the negative reviews) and puts you right on edge. 

When it comes to playability, the game handles smooth, the controls are simple and easy to learn, and there is a balanced graphics system established so only use what your PC can handle. A major issue brought up in many of the negative reviews is the overall brightness settings for the game. When first booting up, you're prompted with three screens instructing you on how to adjust your overall screen size and brightness (as many horror games do). Follow the prompts and you should not have any issues. 

When it comes to gameplay, as referemced above, the controls are simple and easy to learn. Capcom brought back its mini upgrade system like from the Revalations series where you find attachments/upgrades and simply combine them to the appropriate weapon. As always with a Resident Evil game, there are puzzles, many of which match the original RE2. You are offered to start off as rather Claire or Leon, both of which take different yet similar paths, similar to Separate Ways from RE4. The voice acting is great and doesn't take away from the game at all. It is actually nice for once to hear the protagonist respond to what's going on in the world in front of him. So far, I immediately jumped to play as Leon, and he will let little, What the ♥♥♥♥'s, ♥♥♥♥♥'s, what the ♥♥♥♥ was that's, and other similar comments go while fighting off zombies. 

The game itself is beautiful offering new and smooth animations such as for reloading, using your knife, (un)holstering weapons, and getting attacked. The soundtrack and overall effect sounds make the game eerie and frightening. 

So far the game is great, the only thing is I would advise just buying the standard game. The little extra content items like the Samari Edge M9's are nice and the same goes for the different costumes, but they really don't add much to game. Especially if you have stupid pet peeves like myself. I would love to use the Sheriff's Office costume but I hate those massive patrol/trooper hats. Now if Capcom made another version without the hat, that'd be great. Back on topic if you don't mind spending the extra couple bucks then go for it, otherwise they won't improve your experience whatsoever. 

The only other thing to say is, Capcom I hope you make remakes of RE4 and RE5 as well to match the gameplay styles intoduced in RE6 and the Revalations series (quicker and more frightening).

Resident Evil 2 was one of the best games of the series, the original game in 1998 was a great success, which was also seen in 2019 when the Remake of this game was released, which was also a great success and the developers took a step in the right direction. But the same cannot be said about Resident Evil 3 Remake. This installment will give you the choice to play as Claire Redfield or Leon S. Kennedy. Both of these characters have practically the same passage through the game, only some characters change and also some places where they can go, but basically the goal is the same. Let's take Claire for example, she has a different story and arsenal of weapons, while Leon has a Shotgun, Claire has a grenade launcher, which is very effective. Claire is tasked with finding her brother Chris, who she discovers is somewhere in Europe and not near Racoon City. On his way, he meets the true nature of the virus that has escaped and is now infecting the entire city. She meets William Birkin, who used his G-Virus to avoid death and became a monster with not very nice features (If you don't know, people infected with the G-Virus try to find a family member and mate with them to spread the pathogen further). And everyone who stands in his way will be killed, it's cruel, but, it's a virus. Claire finds Birkin's daughter, whom she cares for and keeps Birkin away from her because she sees him as a death threat and not a virus spreader. You'll walk through beautiful locations from the Raccon Police Department to Umbrella's secret underground lab. I must admit that even after 20 years, the developers still stick to their Surival Horror theme, which works great and is actually the image of all Survival horror games we know now. On Hardcore difficulty you have back your favorite Ink Ribbons which are used as a Save, when you play on Normal or Assisted you have Autosave and you can save the game as many times as you want, but on Hardcore you have to find this thing to be able to save your progress. As for the actual environment in which you are, you can sometimes see continuity with older games, or even allusions to the original. I haven't played the original RE2 by myself but I've seen a whole game, so I know how the Remake is different and I have to say yes the changes are there but they are practically minor and a lot of things from the original are carried over to the Remake which is really cool (Not like RE3). I will not even comment optimization of the RE Engine itself, as the game is on the same Engine that already had Resident Evil 7 and it works great (Although I noticed FPS drops on the Next Gen version and so I switched it with an older version, it may not be the case for everyone) . If I take it all the way around, Resident Evil 2 still carries its name and the original game and gives players a unique gaming experience that is like Keanu Reeves said "Breathtaking" if you are new to the Resident Evil series I can warmly recommend this game. Although you should play Resident Evil 1 first ... you can easily skip Resident Evil 0, it's a pretty terrible installment. But for those of you who were familiar with the world of Resident Evil, you will definitely agree that this game is truly unique.

[h1]Resident Evil 2: A New Nightmare[/h1]

Resident Evil 2 is a fantastic re-imagining of the PS1 original that's sure to please the fans of the original titles as it stays faithful to 90% of the gameplay of the original and frighten new players looking to enter the world of survival horror for the first time.

The pros are many. This is one of the best looking, best sounding games around. With a good pair of headphones on and playing at night, this should at least unnerve most players and likely be too much for some to handle. Both of those strengths alone would make it worth a recommendation; and the excellent sound design actually helps with situational awareness. Resident Evil backs it up with old school Resident Evil mechanics like puzzle solving, key items, inventory boxes, threat management (and avoidance), limited carrying space, etc. The game is designed exactly with the same principles of the original games in mind and after you learn the set puzzle solutions, speed-running encourages multiple playthroughs. This game is perfectly paced and free of contents sake for contents sake. 

I don't have too many cons with game mechanically, and most of them only arise with direct comparison with the original title and the games narrative at points. The biggest one being the lack of variance between the two campaigns. Ignoring the 2nd run scenario, both Leon and Claire's campaign are structured nearly the same and you'll encounter a majority of the same bosses at the same points in the story (With some variation in the cast of characters you'll meat and a few unique locations that are special to each character). Second run does little to shake or deviate from this set structure of the game (You'll still be fighting the same bosses at the same points) but is enjoyable as a faster, more challenging arranged mode with different item placements and a unique side arm for each character to use.

So pretty much fun awesome game that you should play whether or not you're a fan of the series or even the original game. If you liked RE7 / The Original Games  / survival horror games you should have a blast playing the new Resident Evil 2. And if you liked this game, maybe try and check out the original game sometime as these games really do compliment each other rather than either serving as a replacement for the other.

[h1]This is a launch day, first impressions review[/h1]

[b][Optimization][/b] The game runs very smoothly on appropriate hardware, without frame locks. The controls are simple enough and not clunky. Full assortment of settings to tweak the game properly.

[b][Gameplay][/b] Inventory is limited as it should be and gives you multiple options on individual items. Adjacent to the Inventory are the Map and Notes. The Map keeps track of areas you have visited or have yet to visit, same with items. Notes are pretty standard, and are used for reference. When encountering enemies, you may flee or attack them with resources in mind. The melee can be used on offense or as a counter. The gunplay doesn't seem to have unnecessary bloom, and will reward your accuracy. Almost all interactions are done with "M1" by default.

[b][Graphics][/b] The character models are high-detail, and the zombies have an intricate damage model that responds to types of ammo. The remade environment looks to be without major flaws with smooth textures.

[b][Audio][/b] An audio feature that is worth mentioning is that there are no fixed sound tunnels like in the old game. The ambient noise is well-suited to the environment and creates the right amount of tensions. No music soundtrack has been heard yet.

A fully immersive, true horror title that places you in the iconic Raccoon City. This is a chance for both veteran RE fans and new-to-the-franchise fans to enjoy this polished remake. Hardcore mode is a joy simply because of the challenge of a proper horror title it creates.

A great survival horror game. After RE5/6, there are reasons to doubt the franchise, but with 7&2, Capcom has cleaned their act up, and returned to true survival horror, not just action / horror.

It's tense, exciting, fun, great exploration, somewhat simple puzzles, and good quality of life improvements over previous entries.

Extremely well made. It honestly feels more like a complete redo of RE2, instead of simply a graphical upgrade. 

Certain mechanics and gameplay features integral to RE2's design, like the tank controls and fixed camera angles, have been removed. While this might seem sacrelidge to hardcore fans, they replaced these key features with whole new ones. It isn't just a retread of RE2, it is a reimagining for a new generation.

 Now, we aren't hampered by bad controls and worse voice acting. The combat is fluid, well done, and responsive, WITHOUT being the best option or encouraged. Enemies are definitely very spongey, burt you get the feeling quick that guns are less meant to kill, and more meant to stun. The game encourages a careful dance and avoiding enemies to conserve precious resources. Simply put, expect a zombie to continuously get back up unless their head is completely destroyed. 

The graphics and gore are top notch, with one of the most impressive dynamic gore systems of the modern generation. 

This is simply the perfection of the zombie genre, and I hope to see new iterations and modes upon the existing game soon. Maybe add an "action mode" aside from Hunk that allows immediate dismembermant and headexplosions to really show off the gore capabilities.

You also have to use ink ribbons to save, making it a bit more challenging to manage inventory, as well as forcing you to think twice about making risky decisions. For fans of the old games, I recommend playing it on hardcore mode.

The sound effects are superb. From Leon/Claire moaning and groaning in pain when they get hurt, to the monsters' growls and Mr. X's menacing stomping footsteps, they really did a great job trying to scare you with sounds alone.

The story is really good, they made it more cinematic and serious. I liked that they added a playable prologue to the game to show what happened to Leon and Claire before they reached the police station. The voice acting is amazing and it's a huge contrast to the cheesy 90's voice acting from the original.

What I find lacking about the remake is the soundtrack. One of the things that makes the RE series stand out is the OST. Each moment had a special tune associated with it, such as the safe room theme, or when a licker first appeared. It made the game memorable and special. In the remake, however, the soundtrack is extremely subtle to the point where there are several places you hear no music at all. I get what they were trying to go for, but I prefer having music add to the atmosphere of the game rather than rely on pure sound effects to get you scared.

Resident Evil 2 is worthy of being one of the best horror games to date. I had a great time playing it and it makes me feel like a spooked child all over again.



It makes me feel like Leon...

Capcom have finally discovered the ingredients required to bring one of the most historically divided fanbases together under one banner again. There's a subtle embrace and acknowledgement of all their previous titles here, taking bits and pieces from RE7, RE5, RE4, RE2, etc. to concoct a new era of survival horror with slight action and comical undertones.

In conclusion, it's definitely worth full asking price and you should certainly pick it up

I remember debating for the longest time with my best friend about why Resident Evil 2 would be the best remake we all needed. We fantasized about it for years and years and eventually gave up hope, more so because other legendary games failed us enormously (Metal Gear Solid V Phantom Pain I'm looking at you).

If you played the original you're in for a treat of goosebumps and shivers down your spine. Yes you will remember every single little thing and will smile at the nods to the trademark horror of two decades ago, but make no mistake this game will surprise you in ways you can't imagine.
If you're new to the series or at least the old school masters of horror you will experience an adventure of titanic proportions and I'm willing to bet my backside that you will find it refreshing and needed in today's game industry.

Camera, characters motion, enemies motion, setting, plot, sound design, gunplay, inventory management, visual design, you name it this game gets it right and astonishingly optimized to the point I believe it's the most fluid game I have played so far (my pc is quite capable to handle every game in ultra settings, what I mean is the devs managed to make the game experience and the game engine so fluid that it stands out from the crowd).

I'm mostly amazed that the devs managed to accomplish all of this in such a small package (game is about 22gb of space) while keeping the texture quality extremely high. Also the sound part of the game is above par, the wood cracks, footsteps, water drops and even distant rain are so polished I'm quite sure you will sometimes wonder if what you heard was in game or outside.

As for the extras included in the deluxe edition I haven't had the time to look into yet except for the original soundtrack swap which I think should be kept on always. Thing with the "new" soundtrack is that you don't get enough of it really, just about 30 seconds when you enter a room and that's it, whereas with the original swap you get a more dynamic flow between action and slow paced moments.

Right now my only question to Capcom is: now that you see how succesful this is, how long will it take for a Nemesis remake?

Primarily 2 characters: Leon/Claire.
[h1]Playtime[/h1] [b]Varies, depending on difficulty and skill[/b]
Playtime can vary based off of difficulty, but playing on Hard for the first time took about 15 hours with Leon ONLY. There's a rank that you get after completing the game, depending on if you met the requirements. The S+Rank for example, requires the game to be beaten on Hard in under 2hours, using only 3 saves, and only non-deluxe weapons (aka, not equipping the DLC Samurai Edge). So technically, if the game is played right, it can be done in 2 hours. If you die, you can still respawn from your last save. It'll only count the exact time from the last save point. So if you started at 1hr 30mins and you died at 2hours, restarting back at the last point will put you at 1hr 30 minutes of play time. Pausing the game stops the timer.

[h1]Replayability[/h1]
Replayability relies on replaying the same maps from a different perspective for each character, as well as having different supporting characters of their own. They also have access to different weapons and areas of the maps.

Replayability also stems from speed-running the game to achieve S+ rating, which unlocks rewards such as infinite ammo on certain guns as well as 2 additional scenarios. There will be 3 Free DLC's in February with 3 additional perspectives.

[h1]Graphics[/h1] = Eye candy
40-70fps when using 4k/HDR with max settings, depending on the scene,
60+ @ 1080p max settings 
GPU: MSI RTX 2080 Duke edition
CPU: i7-8700K @ 5.0Ghz
Windows 10 1809

[h1]Optimization[/h1]  Good enough

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
The game is challenging and teaches you to think ahead about resources, and choosing when to engage or to run away. An impressive remake, but not at full-price. Wait for a sale.

[b]Side Note:[/b]
Don't bother with the Samurai Edge DLC's. The default pistol, when upgraded, outperforms it and is the preferred choice. You also can't use the gun if you want a S+ rating.

I've noticed a few things right off the bat that are missing from the original. I suppose that's to be expected as the remake was intended to stand out on it's own, but I will miss the creepy gun clerk's shotgun/crossbow drop and running through a city infested with ghouls of all sorts. The introduction feels a little rushed as reaching the police station felt like a breeze. Once I made it inside however, my world was turned upside down. Essentially, this game is designed to strain you, your given a fixed inventory with limited resources which is a great throwback to the original. The enemies are extremely tough and the avenues of escape have been substantially deminished. I decided to play on the hardcore setting as I wanted a limited number of ink ribbons just like in the original. Unfortunately, as zombies are now extremely hard to kill and seemingly deadly from one bite, running seems to be the best course of action if possible. I currently find myself dreading my encouter with the infamous licker as I imagine it will simply leap into the air and render my body headless but I suppose I'll have to muster some courage and find out. [h1] Resident Evil 2 Remake - this is how you do a remake RIGHT! [/h1]

By the time of this review, the Ghost Survivors DLC has just been released. This review, therefore, does not take into account any patches or changes Capcom may apply to it.

First of all, let's get one thing clear: This game is good no matter if you're a returning veteran or a complete newcomer to the entire RE series. You DO NOT have to have played the first or even be familiar with its plot to be able to enjoy this one.

Any potential spoilers in my review will be overlined in black, so don't be afraid of its contents ruining your experience.

With that out of the way, let's get going!

[h1] THE PLOT [/h1]
Generally, the plot stays true to the original RE2, with very little changes, such as [spoiler]Kendo not dying[/spoiler] and the way certain minor characters die.
As I mentioned, I won't spoil the story, so for what it's worth, I have played all RE games, except Revelations 2, RE6, and Op:RC, and always considered RE2 to have the best plot of all titles in the series.
In the main scenarios, you assume the role of either Leon S. Kennedy, a would-be rookie cop on his first day in the force, or Claire Redfield, the sister of RE mainstay Chris Redfield. A major change over from the first is that the plot takes time and effort to really [u] build and develop[/u] both the two main protagonists and the side characters, making you, as a player, feel that much more attached to them. This makes the game feel less arcade-like, and more like a genuine horror experience, featuring characters with real emotions - a welcome concept, imo.

[h1] THE AESTHETIC [/h1]
The game makes very good use of different light levels to take you on a psychological Tour de France, where at one point you may feel safe in your large, open, well-lit room, then crawl under a half-open shutter, only to find yourself in a murky, narrow corridor where your vision is at the mercy of your flashlight. Additionally, the game makes excellent use of different contrasting color pallets (such as [url=https://vignette.wikia.nocookie.net/residentevil/images/e/e1/RE2_remake_CONCEPT_ART_-_Raccoon_City_A.jpg/revision/latest?cb=20190129045452]a murky dark-green area, contrasted by a single bright-red pilot light, with rotting corpses scattered everywhere[/url]). The overall visual design is excellent, and without spoiling anything, I can assure you that the quality carries on throughout the entire game - not just the first few areas.

[h1] THE GAMEPLAY [/h1]
First of all, there are multiple game modes (scenarios) which you can select at your preference, and more can be unlocked along the way. You can generally pick between 3 difficulty levels; ASSISTED, STANDARD, and HARDCORE. The latter feels the most true to the classic RE experience, and I strongly recommend both newcomers and returning veterans to pick it.
The camera is no longer fixed at one position, like in the classic RE titles, but is now over-the-shoulder 3rd person (think RE4), increasing the level of immersion felt as you play through the horror.
True to the classic RE2, the remake features A LOT of backtracking. Many key items and the general routing at the game's different segment are quite similar to that of the original, with little changes here and there, to keep even seasoned players on their toes.
The gunplay is astounding; regardless of the type of gun you're firing, you really feel the kick of it in your fingers as you pull the trigger.
One complaint I have is the concept of ADAPTIVE DIFFICULTY. I don't have the space to detail it in this review, so you can read about it [url=https://www.gamerevolution.com/guides/491409-resident-evil-2-adaptive-difficulty-zombies-ammo#/slide/1]here[/url]. It's nothing game-breaking, though.
For returning players: There have been rumors that certain unlockable weapons and game modes have been scrapped in the remake - THIS IS NOT TRUE! It's [u] all there[/u], right from [spoiler] the INFINITE MINIGUN [/spoiler] to [spoiler]HUNK's and Tofu's scenarios.[/spoiler]

[h1] THE SOUNDTRACK [/h1]
Let's face it; Capcom has been in beast mode the last couple years, producing amazing games left, right, and center, so it was no surprise for me that RE2R turned out amazing overall - but the INSANE quality of the OST took me completely by surprise. There is one particular track that ended up being my favorite in the entire series - check it out for yourself [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z3CA_HTvULc] here [/url] (just beware that this contains spoilers to the last boss fight in Leon's scenario).

[h1] THE PERFORMANCE [/h1]
Capcom has presented us with a large array of graphical options to suit our preferences, which is always nice for a perfectionist like myself. However, getting RE2R to run optimal on your system takes a good bit of tweaking, and it's not immediately obvious which options are the most taxing for your system. Therefore, I highly recommend checking [url=https://www.game-debate.com/news/26392/resident-evil-2-remake-pc-performance-breakdown-and-most-important-graphics-options] this guide [/url] before trying it yourself.
Overall, RE2R runs really well on my PC (NVIDIA GTX 970 & Intel Core i5-4670K). However, because there are no longer any "loading screens" between each room (returning players may remember the iconic black background with the door-opening animation), it means that the game has to load the entire room more or less instantly when you transition between doors. This sometimes causes choppiness for 1-2 seconds, but only for particularly large rooms. However, I personally would have loved it if they had kept the loading screens, just for that nostalgic feeling.
In terms of crashing, I have experienced literally no cases. The game overall runs very well and reliably.

[h1] OVERALL RATING [/h1]
I rate this game a solid 9.5/10, with the final 0.5 subtracted because of the frustrating adaptive difficulty.
By the time of this review, the FREE Ghost Survivor's DLC just came out - I played through most of it already, and can honestly not believe that Capcom gave us this for free. What a great team of developers. I won't detail it in this review, mainly because it's free, so hey, whatever, but it's actually really good.
But I digress - GET THE GAME ASAP, it is unbelievably good. Thank you again, Capcom, for this amazing remake.

[h1]This is a review in progress. I will update it after I played more. I play the game on Hardcore difficulty.[/h1]

[h1]Gameplay (9/10)[/h1]

While RE2 is in third person, in terms of gameplay and feel it's much closer to the originals than to Resident Evil 4, for example. It's a Metroidvania style survival horror game in which you get more and more familiar with your environment and as you progress further, you slowly unlock previously inaccesible areas. The focus is on exploration, on solving puzzles and on resource management rather than on combat encounters.

By being said that, combat is still present here, but because of the extremely limited resources and the toughness of the zombies, these feel way more meaningful and tense. Most of the time it's simply better to play smarter and try to avoid enemies and/or save ammo when possible. This means luring zombies to a specific spot so you can then pass them safely and maybe grab some items, or taking advantage of the decapacitation system and shooting off a leg of a zombie to make him slower and less dangerous.

The good thing is that all of the core gameplay elements I mentioned above work very well together because of the excellent, interconnected level design and because of the general pacing of the gameplay. However, RE2 is not a game without its faults either.

I heard that the bosses are frustrating and basically, the overall low points of the the game because they are being designed for a type of gameplay / movement set that RE2 simply does not have. Based on my first boss encounter, I can agree with this statement. I don't want to go into too much details, but you can check Skill Up's review on YouTube if you want to learn more about this.

My other problem is a small one, but considering how old the series is, it's a mystery why this feature hasn't been implemented yet - or more specifically, why it has been implemented halfly. Here's the thing: when the inventory is full, you can pick up a Yellow Gunpowder to combine it together with the Gunpowder in your inventory. However, in the same situation, you can't reload the empty Shotgun in your inventory by picking up Shotgun Shells from somewhere. This just makes the inventory management system a little bit inconsistent.

Overall, I'm really impressed with RE2 in terms of gameplay and if you are into these types of games, you should definitely try this out.

[h1]Narrative and world building (9/10)[/h1]

Although I don't have enough experience yet with the narrative to be perfectly sure about the score I'm going to give to it, I can share some of my early thoughts about it's individual elements (characters, character interactions, dialogues, story, lore, directing, pacing).

Leon and Claire, the two main characters are instantly likeable and the chemistry works perfectly between them. It feels real and beleivable. Their voice actors definitely did a good job, but I have to say that the dialogues help a lot as well. They are straight to the point but then again, beleiavable and well written.

I liked the portrayal of the secondary characters as well. While the truck driver's appearance was brief (he is only in the intro), I really liked how he reacted to the radio show and when he hit the girl zombie with his truck. Also, I loved Ada. She is mysterious, tough and sassy, but all in a good way.

I also like how the story is going as well - it's simple too, but to quote someone, 'it just works'. My only problem is that things happen a little bit too fast. While I get why the creators decided to go on this route, I think because of this rushed pacing, sometimes the scenes don't have the level of emotional impact that they should have. I feel that if some scenes (mainly between Claire and Leon) would have been extended a little bit more with additional dialogues, they would feel even more impactful and beleivable.

Still, aside from this, my impression with the narrative is extremely positive and it's being supported by a strong technical background as well. The facial animations are simply some of the best I've seen in gaming and these help to bring scenes to life, while the camerawork and directing are also generally excellent.

One more thing: there are many things to read in this game too if you want to dive yourself into the lore. I find these readings quite interesting, especially because some of them not just help to flesh out the world of RE2 more, but they can also help you learn useful informations that you can take advantage of in the game. For example, there's a paper at the end of the hallway where you first see a Licker on the other side of the window and from that paper you can learn that it's actually possible to stealthly go past these creatures, so you don't have to fight against them. I can really appreciate smart details like this.

[h1]Graphics and optimization (9/10)[/h1]

RE2 is easily one of the best made PC games I played in recent memory from a technical standpoint. It's very well optimized to the point that it can run fairly well on even very low end PCs, while it can impress PC enthusiasts with its amazing graphics if they have a decent rig. I play this game at 3440x1440 with maximum FOV using the highest settings at a constant 60FPS with a GTX 1080Ti.

Yes, there is native 21:9 support - although cutscenes are pillarboxed -  and there is a good FOV slider. The option menu is great, there are many individual graphical settings to choose from, while you can see in a preview window what each of them does. It's also great that you can change every setting (except DirectX version) on the fly, meaning you won't have to restart the game.

From a gameplay standpoint, it's a huge plus that there are absolutely no loading screens, while from a future-proofing standpoint, it's a good thing that all cutscenes are being rendered in-game (except the intro video with the RE logo).

I don't want to talk too much more about the technical aspects of the game, but I still want to mention three more things: compared to Resident Evil 7, the texturework improved dramatically (it was one of the two technical weaknesses of that title), and textures are crisp and sharp instead of being blurry. The other two are the decapacitation system and the facial animations. They are extremely well done and the first helps to make the gameplay deeper, while the second helps in telling the story in a more effective way.

There are some problems, though. The anti-aliasing methods are still not the best here. FXAA can produce artifacts, while the game's TAA is too aggressive and it makes the image way too blurry below 1440p resolutions. There is an option to choose SMAA but sadly it's not SMAA 2TX or SMAA 2 Filmic, it's just normal SMAA that fails to smooth out edges and on the top of that, it makes the hair of the characters very weird looking.

The other two problems are just nitpicks, but the screen-space reflections are a little bit buggy and badly implemented, while the in-game VRAM counter is buggy as well because in reality, the game uses roughly half of the VRAM that it displays in the graphics settings and it can give wrong informations to players who want to properly set up their game.

[h1]Audio and art-design (?/10)[/h1]

There is an option to choose binaural audio in RE2 that makes the game more immersive and I can definitely tell the difference. I feel like I'm in the game's world. As for the art-design though, I can definitely tell that the game is fantastic. Every single room of the police station feels completely different and unique - and this has a positive impact on gameplay as well, because it makes it easier to memorize the map and navigate through it - while each of them is densely packed with small details that make the world come alive.

I might re-evaluate later. Restarting with a lower difficulty now (cannot just change without starting all over). It seems the adaptivity is not adaptive enough.

Update: After having finished Leon's campaign now,  I am not that much negative anymore, rather neutral. The game can be enjoyed, as long as you comply into the ruleset and demands that could be seen as outdated given todays general gaming expectations:
- Not being able to change difficulty while the campaign is in progress
- Essential graphic options missing
- Restricted progress save options (however, some might enjoy this or deem this as an essential part of the gaming experience)
- Instead of being outright clear about the rules and game mechanics (for example, telling the player what he is supposed to do), it feels like in the 80ies where figuring out what to do and where have been part of the game (sometime because of developers' laziness and to make the game take longer to finish, sometimes as design element or part of the game), and can be overcome only by either lots of experimenting (and dying while doing that) or looking up how each enemy / boss is best dealt with in which part of the game. While some might enjoy this aspect, I don't like to play "guess what the developer wants you to do"
- The progress in the game relies heavily on memorization: What to do where and when. Most prominent part of your grade that you receive at the end is based on the time you needed. Most weapon unlocks rely on speed running, therefore requiring you to having memorized the routes.
- The emphasis on memorization goes even so far that you have to memorize a code given in unkown symbols you see in one spot of the game and apply at another spot. I mean, screenshot or draw the thing yourself and done. Or memorize. Applying the code is easy as long as you remember it (by whatever way), but why make easy things so complicated? I expected a horror survival shooter and not a memory game.
- Following from the emphasis on memory is that shooter skills are pretty much not needed here: Fast reactions and fast pinpoint accuray in aiming are not required. Overall, I would categorize the game as an adventure with limited item inventory and action elements.
So, if you don't mind the aformentioned rules of the game and game mechanics, it is worth the full price. If you expected something else, either by having enjoyed RE 5,6,7 and Relevations 1&2, or playing the demo of this here, rather wait for a price drop or spend your money somewhere else.

Like the remake of Resi 1 for Gamecube this game isn't just a straight copy, they take the original and add to it so it's nostalgic enough for previous players but also has enough new additions that also keep players of the original uneasy. 
I'd recommend this for both veterans of the series and newcomers, as there's a lot to like for both, including an easier and harder difficulty setting for people who find it too hard/easy.

The rest is about the technical side. 

The port/PC version is pretty damn fantastic and includes features like:
- Unlocked frame rate
- Big graphics menu with visualised changes
- 21:9 support
- Key rebindings
- Good mouse and keyboard support

As for performance I'm on a i5 8400 and RTX 2080TI, I play on mostly max with volumetric on high, stuff like depth of field and film grain off (personal preference), and at 3440x1440 I'm sitting at around 130-160fps and at 4K I was around 80fps which is some fantastic numbers. 

Important note is that the game has a DX11 and DX12 option, DX12 is just worse, i went from 85fps at 4K down to 60. Hopefully they fix this as DX12 could alloy for ray tracing in the future. 

My only gripe is that the game darkens the edges of the screen, i think to give a more claustrophobic feel, but you can't toggle it off and is a little distracting when a well lit area goes dark just because its at a screen edge.

I laughed menacingly when I shot a zombie's knee off from his kneecap, I laughed even more so when I used my knife to repeatedly slice a zombie who fell through a window until her limbs had come apart, and her face was no more.

The original series will always deliver that nostalgia factor, one which I don't think these remakes can, but that doesn't mean the remakes aren't good, nor does it mean they're not flashbacks to the past and childhood. This was very well worth the £52.99 preorder for the deluxe edition.
